### Series title page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION WHICH HAVE EXISTED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, MOST CAREFULLY CORRECTED BY COLLATION WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS ISSUED IN THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; FURNISHED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY DISTRIBUTED THROUGHOUT THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH HEADINGS AT THE TOP MARGIN OF EVERY PAGE MARKING ITS SUBJECT-MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH NEVERTHELESS POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDICES: ONE OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY LEARN WHICH FATHERS COMMENTED ON EACH TEXT OF EACH BOOK OF SCRIPTURE, AND IN WHAT PLACES IN THEIR WORKS.**

**A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the thoroughness of the correction, both the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the whole course of the work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and small works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time assembled in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, CONTAINING THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III; EDITED BY J.-P. MIGNE, PUBLISHER OF THE UNIVERSAL CLERICAL LIBRARY, OR COMPLETE COURSES IN EACH BRANCH OF ECCLESIASTICAL LEARNING.**

# THE BIRTH, DEEDS, AND WRITINGS OF SAINT HILDEGARD

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, September, vol. V, 17 September, p. 629.)

## § I. Previously published Acts of St. Hildegard and their authors; certain other material to be published from manuscripts; the Life to be supplemented in this Commentary chiefly from the Saint’s writings.

[Col. 0009A]

1. Among the saints who flourished in the twelfth century, St. Hildegard, virgin, holds no ordinary place: most renowned for virtues, miracles, prophetic writings, and the remarkable celebrity of her name. I now undertake to elucidate her deeds. Her Life was printed for this day by Surius, and had already been published at Cologne in 1566. Modern writers everywhere call Theodoric, a Benedictine abbot, the author of the Life, but do not say of which monastery he was abbot. Surius observes the following concerning Theodoric: “He flourished in the year 1200 and is distinct from Theodoric, abbot of St. Trudo.” This distinction is certain, since Theodoric, abbot of St. Trudo, flourished in the year 1100. Trithemius, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, p. 138, speaks with insufficient precision about Theodoric and his age:

> “Theodoric,” he says, “abbot of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly the most chaste admirer of Blessed Hildegard, a man practised and learned both in Holy Scripture and secular literature, ready in intellect and scholastic in speech, wrote for the edification of many a Life of the same Hildegard, bride of Christ, in four books; also various letters to different persons, and certain other works unknown to us. He flourished in the time of Henry VI [who died in 1198], in the year of the Lord 1200.”

Trithemius, through a lapse of memory—or, as I think more likely, through an error of copyists or printers—appears to divide the Life into four books, whereas there are only three, as is clear and certain from the preface to each and the conclusion of the third book. More below concerning the age of the writers.

2. Trithemius is perhaps the first to have called Theodoric, the biographer, an abbot; and I greatly doubt whether he was truly an abbot. Indeed, I rather believe that he was a monk, not an abbot. Certainly, he was only a monk when he wrote the Life. Moreover, Theodoric did not alone write the celebrated Life of Hildegard. Before him, Godfrey the monk had begun to write it; the first book is his. Theodoric composed the second and third books at the command of Abbots Louis and Godfrey. All this is clearly derived from the prefaces, all of which Theodoric composed. For he begins his preface to the entire Life as follows:

> “To the venerable lords Louis and Godfrey, abbots: Theodoric, humble servant of the servants of God, greetings with devout prayers. I have received the command of your authority that, after Godfrey, a man renowned for intellect, I should put in order the Life of the holy and God-beloved virgin Hildegard—which he had begun in an honourable style but had not completed—and, weaving garlands as it were from fragrant flowers, should bring her visions, inserted among her deeds, under a division into books, into the form of a single body.”

Then, after several excuses, he explains what he has done:

> “Therefore I obeyed in such a way that the book of the aforesaid man, holding the place of the first portion, should suffer no loss of its arrangement; then, that the second book should contain the most beautiful and admirable text of the visions; and the third, the account of miracles … which we have arranged, divided, and ordered.”

Thus, the first book is Godfrey’s, apart from the preface. It contains most of the Saint’s deeds, though not her death; certain visions and miracles are also related in this book. But the second book, concerning the visions, and the third, concerning Hildegard’s miracles and death, are Theodoric’s alone.

3. Now I have proof, from the manuscript Acts composed for the canonization of St. Hildegard and to be published by us, that both these writers were monks rather than abbots. There, no. 7 reads:

> “Bruno, keeper of St. Peter’s at Strasbourg and sworn priest, says concerning the life of Blessed Hildegard … that he read in the little book concerning her life, written immediately after her death by two religious men, namely Godfrey and Theodoric, who lived with the blessed virgin; and he believes that it contains, in every respect, the truth, etc.”

From this we learn, first, that the authors lived with the Saint and were not merely contemporaries but, in many matters, eyewitnesses. For this reason Theodoric, although in his prefaces he employs many customary excuses, never pleads ignorance of the deeds, visions, or miracles of St. Hildegard as an excuse; nor does he even suggest, except rarely, that he needed others’ instruction or used others’ reports to write the Saint’s deeds. Therefore we cannot doubt that Godfrey and Theodoric were among the monks who performed divine worship in Blessed Hildegard’s monastery, and for that reason could have had every matter very clearly before them. Godfrey was probably older, and he alone would have written the Life had death not intervened. For it is clear from the preface to the second book that Godfrey had died when Theodoric wrote, since he is called “Godfrey of blessed memory.”

Secondly, we learn that the Life was written immediately after the Saint’s death. Thirdly, we learn that Baillet erred in his critical table, not only because, with Trithemius, he makes Theodoric an abbot and the sole writer of the Life, but even more because he said that Theodoric had lived “twenty or thirty years” after St. Hildegard’s death, as if he were not an altogether contemporary writer. I shall reprint this Life first from Surius, but collated with the Bodek manuscript, from which we have received variant readings.

4. We also possess another Life of St. Hildegard in our manuscript codex marked P. ms. 17; and the same Life, somewhat interpolated, has been transmitted to us from the Utrecht codex of St. Saviour. [Col. 0011B] I compared both manuscripts. At the beginning I found almost no difference, but toward the end I found certain annotations inserted into the Life in the codex of St. Saviour which are absent from our codex, itself formerly also from Utrecht. The author of this Life is unknown, but probably did not live at Mainz or in its territory, since he speaks thus of the Saint’s writings:

> “Indeed, if anyone wishes to read her visionary words, let him acquire her writings, which are now widely circulated and scattered throughout the region of Mainz.”

Furthermore, I do not think the author of that Life was strictly a contemporary of the Saint. For this reason I judge that it should not be published, especially as it teaches very little not found in the earlier Life and is almost entirely woven from the Saint’s writings, with little discrimination. Therefore, in this Commentary I shall give from that brief Life whatever I think useful for informing the reader, omitting long passages which can be read in the Saint’s own writings and have no bearing whatever on her deeds or character.

5. In 1641 Father John Gamans, frequently cited in this work, sent Bollandus another writing concerning St. Hildegard. Gamans recorded the source in these words:

> “From the distinguished parchment manuscript Passionary of the month of September, fol. 247, of the Bodek monastery of Canons Regular of St. Augustine, diocese of Paderborn, where the following is appended after the mutilated Life of St. Hildegard.”

The title of the writing is: *On the Testimony of the Miracles of Saint Hildegard, Which the Lord Worked Through Her Merits, Both During Her Life and After Her Death.* It is an abridgment of the Acts which were composed in 1233 by those who investigated the virtues and miracles of St. Hildegard and sent the Acts of their inquiry to the Apostolic See. The date and the Acts’ dispatch to the Supreme Pontiff are clear from the end of this abridgment.

But the compiler of this abridgment cut away so completely everything concerning the mere form of the Acts that I cannot discern from it whether those investigators were delegated by the authority of the archbishop of Mainz, who was then Siegfried III, or by that of the Supreme Pontiff Gregory IX. Yet from Gregory IX’s letter, to be quoted at nos. 208 and 209, we learn that those Acts were composed at Gregory’s command; to establish that investigation he delegated the provost, dean, and scholastic of Mainz. In the same letter, however, the pope complains that certain defects had been found in the Acts because not everything had been sufficiently clearly set out. Yet those defects do not destroy the historical credibility of the Acts. I shall therefore give these Acts of the inquiry after the Life, illustrated with appropriate annotations.

6. Besides these ancient documents concerning St. Hildegard, we have many of her own works, partly printed and partly still in manuscript. Among them, the letters will provide more material than the rest for enlarging this commentary. We have a great number printed at Cologne in 1566 together with several small works and the Saint’s Life, and reprinted in vol. XXXIII of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*. Martène supplied another considerable portion in vol. II of the *Amplissima Collectio*. I have found some published elsewhere, and possess some in manuscript; nor do I doubt that more still lie hidden in archives or libraries in various places. Nevertheless, I believe that all the principal letters, which had been collected into one volume in the Saint’s convent, have been published.

The Saint’s other works, which I shall review more extensively in their place, will likewise furnish some assistance for illustrating her deeds and virtues. Certain slightly later writers—such as Vincent of Beauvais, Richer of Sens, Alberic the monk in his *Chronicle*, who flourished in the thirteenth century, and several others—are not to be wholly neglected for the deeds of St. Hildegard. But we shall cite these and the others in their proper places, and shall follow or refute them as reason seems to require. There is, moreover, no need to enumerate all the Lives written in later centuries and in different languages. I have an Italian, a Spanish, a German, a French, and a Dutch one; but none adds anything to the ancient documents except errors. Baillet indeed professes criticism, and severe criticism at that; but he often corrupts more than he corrects, and rarely produces documents unknown to others. Nevertheless, we sometimes correct him, because at least he acquired a reputation for critical severity.

## § II. Birth, childhood, and monastic life on Mount St. Disibod; she is enlightened by visions from childhood and is at last compelled to write them down; how she wrote her works.

[Col. 0012D]

7. Concerning the date of St. Hildegard’s birth, the manuscript Life—both in our codex and in that of St. Saviour at Utrecht—has this:

> “In the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation, which was the forty-fifth year of the illustrious Henry, fourth king of that name and third emperor, there was in the regions of Citerior (Nearer) Gaul a virgin noble both in lineage and in the nobility of holiness, in the territory of the city of Mainz.”

Immediately afterward, St. Hildegard’s words are cited in support of the stated year:

> “After the Lord’s Incarnation in the year eleven hundred,” she says, “when the teaching of the apostles and the ardent righteousness which the Holy Spirit had established among the Christian people began to slacken, I was born, and my parents, with sighs, dedicated me to God.”

These words indeed make Hildegard born in 1100 and are cited as the Saint’s own words for that opinion. But from the Life to be published, book II, chapter 1, in which this very passage of St. Hildegard is cited more correctly, we understand that the date of 1100 is given only to indicate the time when righteousness began to slacken, and that the Saint says only that she was born in those times. The words “in those times” must be understood with some latitude, as if she had said “about those times,” since St. Hildegard assigns the year of her birth otherwise and more certainly in the preface to her principal work, which she called *Scivias*.

Certainly, in that preface she states that she was commanded to write her visions in 1141, and that she was then “forty-two years and seven months old.” According to these words, the Saint was born in 1098 or in the earlier months of 1099. But the year of her death, which must be fixed as no other than 1179, prevents us from believing that her birth can be deferred to 1099: in that year she was in her eighty-second year. Therefore she was born in 1098, indeed before 17 September, the day on which she died; otherwise she would not have begun her eighty-second year.

8. John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, in the *Hirsau Chronicle* under the year 1150, speaks thus concerning St. Hildegard’s parents and native place:

> “This most holy virgin … was born in the county of Sponheim, from the village called Bickelheim, of Hildebert, a knight, as father, and Mechtilde as mother; she came into the world in the time of Emperor Henry IV, namely in the seventh year of Gebhard, abbot of Hirsau. Her father served in the household of the counts of Sponheim with other nobles, a righteous man and devoted to God.”

The county of Sponheim lies in the Palatinate, between the rivers Moselle and Nahe, and in spiritual jurisdiction belongs to the diocese of Mainz. Trithemius connects the seventh year of Abbot Gebhard, in which he places Hildegard’s birth, with the year 1098; we too establish that as the Saint’s birth-year.

St. Hildegard herself explains in the Life, book II, no. 16, what happened to her in the third year of her life. The manuscript Life agrees, citing from Hildegard’s writings:

> “And in the third year of my life I saw so great a heavenly light that my soul trembled within me; but, because of the limitations of infancy, I could say nothing about these things.”

Also remarkable is what is related in the testimony concerning miracles to be published below, no. 7; she is said to have declared it “when she was five years old.” But in the preface already cited, she writes of these matters:

> “From my girlhood, that is, from the time when I was five years old, until the present time, I had felt in myself in a wonderful way the power of mysteries, of secret and marvellous visions, as I still do; yet I revealed it to no human being except a few religious persons who lived in the same religious observance in which I lived.”

Thus, in the third year of her life she saw a wonderful light without sufficient understanding; at five years old she began to understand the visions.

9. Certain modern writers, through a lapse of memory, place Hildegard in monastic life under Jutta’s instruction when she was five years old. But the Life, no. 2, testifies that she was about eight years old when she was entrusted to Jutta, sister of the count of Sponheim, to be trained in religious disciplines. The testimony concerning miracles, no. 7, agrees as to her eighth year, and testifies that from that age her parents offered her under the Rule of Blessed Benedict on Mount St. Disibod.

The manuscript Life cites these words of the Saint herself concerning these matters:

> “In my eighth year I was offered to the holy way of spiritual life; and until my fifteenth year I saw many things and spoke many things simply, so that those who heard them wondered from whom they came and whence they came. Then I too marvelled within myself that, while I saw these things inwardly in my soul, I also retained external sight, and that I had heard this from no human being. Therefore I was seized with great fear and no longer dared reveal my inward light to anyone. Yet, by speaking many things and often foretelling future matters, I brought much forth. And when I was wholly filled with the vision of this light, I spoke many things that seemed strange to those who heard them.”

The same matters are more fully quoted in the Life to be published, book II, chapter 1. There she also declares that, as she grew older, she became increasingly silent about her visions while she was under the instruction of her teacher, Blessed Jutta, and for several years after Jutta’s death, until God compelled her to reveal what she had seen and at last to write it down. Hence, in the preface to the book *Scivias*, she again says of these visions:

> “Meanwhile, until the time when God in His grace wished it to be made manifest, I restrained them under quiet silence.”

Concerning the manner in which she experienced these visions, she adds there:

> “The visions which I saw I did not perceive in dreams, nor sleeping, nor in frenzy, nor with bodily eyes, nor with the ears of the outward person, nor in hidden places; but, awake and looking about in a pure mind, with the eyes and ears of the inward person, I received them in open places according to God’s will. How this occurs is difficult for a carnal person to investigate.”

For the present, these things suffice concerning the Saint’s visions; more shall be given below.

10. While St. Hildegard was concealing her visions with such diligence, Jutta, her teacher, to whom she was accustomed humbly to obey, departed this life, and Hildegard herself began to preside over others. Dodechinus, abbot of St. Disibod toward the end of the same century, writes as follows in the appendix to the *Chronicle* of Marianus Scotus, under the year 1136:

> “Lady Jutta, of holy memory, died: she had been enclosed for twenty-four years on Mount St. Disibod, sister of Count Meginhard of Sponheim. This holy woman was enclosed on the Kalends of November [1 November], and three others with her, namely Hildegard and two women named Sumet [Mabillon reads *suimet*, that is, ‘of Jutta herself’], whom she too strove, as long as she lived, to imbue with holy virtues.”

This chronology does not altogether agree with the assertions concerning St. Hildegard’s monastic life beginning when she was about eight years old. For if Jutta was enclosed for twenty-four years and died in 1136, she first entered enclosure in 1112, or certainly about 1112 if those years were perhaps not complete or if some months must be added. But St. Hildegard was eight years old in 1106; accordingly, she appears to have led monastic life with Blessed Jutta for six years before Dodechinus’s date. It therefore seems necessary to say either that an error crept into Dodechinus’s numbers or that Hildegard first lived elsewhere under the instruction of the same Jutta.

Certainly, all ancient records, with unanimous agreement, make Hildegard a nun on Mount St. Disibod from her eighth year. The place was in the county of Sponheim, and there was a Benedictine monastery there, discussed at length under 8 July in the preliminary Commentary on the Life of its founder, St. Disibod. Fulchard, the abbot of the monastery, died in the same year as Jutta, and had as successor Conon or Cuno, consecrated toward the end of 1136. St. Hildegard was therefore under his obedience when, in that same year, she began to preside over a few persons.

11. After the death of Blessed Jutta, of whom we shall speak on 20 December, St. Hildegard—as she herself states in the Life, no. 17—continued as before to have visions and to keep them silent, until at length stirred by divine promptings, she consulted her monk-teacher about them. In the preface to *Scivias* she writes:

> “But after the boundary of girlhood had passed, when I had reached the aforesaid age of perfect strength, I heard a voice from heaven saying: ‘I am the living and dark light, illuminating the human being whom I have willed, and whom I have wonderfully shaken as pleased me; amid great wonders I have placed him beyond the measure of ancient human beings, who saw many mysteries in me.’”

All these things are said of St. Hildegard, whom God wished to advance to an exalted degree of visions. What follows also concerns her and teaches how greatly God humbled her, lest she should be lifted up into pride by the excellence of her visions. I give the words:

> “But I cast him to the ground, lest he should raise himself up in any exaltation of his mind. The world also had in him neither joy nor delight nor activity in those things which belong to itself, because I drew him away from obstinate boldness, making him fearful and trembling amid his labours.”

These words are certainly obscure, but their meaning is that the world possessed, in relation to St. Hildegard, nothing in which it might rejoice, take delight, or exercise itself, because she was full of the fear of God.

12. These matters are in some measure explained by the following words:

> “For he suffered in the marrow and veins of his flesh, having a constrained mind and understanding, and enduring much bodily suffering; so that no security dwelt in him, but in all his concerns he considered himself blameworthy. For I enclosed the ruins of his heart, lest his mind should raise itself through pride or vainglory, but rather should feel in all these things fear and pain than joy or wantonness. Hence, in love for me, he searched in his mind where he might find one who ran in the way of salvation. And he found a certain person [namely, a monk who was his director] and loved him, recognizing that he was a faithful man and like himself in some part of that labour which tends toward me. Holding him, and together with him striving in all these matters by heavenly zeal, he worked that my hidden miracles might be revealed. And that same man did not exalt himself above himself; but with many sighs he bowed himself toward the person whom he had found, in an ascent of humility and an intention of good will. Therefore, O human being, who receive these things not in the disturbance of deception but in the purity of simplicity, directed toward the manifestation of hidden things, write what you see and hear.”

All these things, though somewhat obscure, were directed by God toward encouraging Hildegard to write her visions, according to the advice of the monk whom she had then begun to consult.

13. She adds what she did after such a vision:

> “But although I saw and heard these things, because of doubt and an evil opinion, and because of the diversity of human words, I refused to write for a long time—not in obstinacy, but in the service of humility—until, struck down by the scourge of God, I fell onto a bed of sickness; so that at last, compelled by many infirmities, with the testimony of a certain girl of noble birth and good character, and of that man whom, as has been said, I had secretly sought and found, I set my hand to writing.”

Then, concerning the vision by which she was especially encouraged and aided to write, she recalls at the very beginning of her preface:

> “Behold, in the forty-third year of my temporal course, while I clung to a heavenly vision in trembling attention and great fear, I saw a most great splendour. In it a voice came from heaven, saying to me: ‘O frail human being, ash of ash and rottenness of rottenness, speak and write what you see and hear. But because you are timid in speaking, simple in explaining, and untaught in writing what you see, speak and write these things not according to the mouth of a human being, nor according to the understanding of human invention, nor according to the will of human composition; but according to what you see and hear from above in heavenly places, in the wonders of God. You shall utter them by setting them forth as a hearer who receives the words of a teacher and proclaims them according to the tenor of that teacher’s speech, as the teacher himself wills, shows, and commands. Thus also you, O human being, speak what you see and hear, and write it not according to yourself or any other human being, but according to the will of Him who knows, sees, and orders all things in the hidden places of His mysteries.’”

14. “And again I heard a voice from heaven saying to me:

> “Therefore speak these wonders, and write them in the manner in which you have been instructed; and say: ‘It came to pass in the year 1141 of the Incarnation of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, when I was forty-two years and seven months old, that a fiery light of utmost flashing brightness came from an open heaven and poured through my whole brain. It set my whole heart and breast ablaze, like a flame—not burning, but warming, as the sun warms an object upon which it casts its rays. And suddenly I tasted the meaning of the exposition of the books: namely, of the Psalter, the Gospels, and the other Catholic volumes of both the Old and New Testaments. Yet I did not possess the interpretation of the words of their text, nor the division of syllables, nor knowledge of cases or tenses.’”

Thus far the Saint herself; her latter words are inserted in the Life, no. 2. Now several matters require observation.

First, from the cited passages it is clear that, in humble and modest fear, the Saint for a long time did not wish to write about her visions and in some measure resisted divine inspirations inviting her to write, until, seized by a grave and extraordinary illness, she disclosed the matter to the monk and, through him, to Abbot Conon. So the Life states in no. 4, adding that she was freed from the illness as soon as she turned her mind toward writing. Stirred by this miraculous cure no less than by the equally miraculous preceding illness, the abbot, after some time, brought the Saint’s earlier writings to Mainz and shared them with Archbishop Henry and the leading ecclesiastical men there, as the Life records in no. 4 and again in no. 17, where the following words of the Saint herself are cited:

> “When these things had been brought to the attention of the Church of Mainz and examined, all declared them to be from God and from the prophecy by which the prophets of old had prophesied.”

15. Secondly, the passages cited establish that St. Hildegard’s knowledge was not acquired by study but infused by God. Thus, in the Life, no. 17, she herself says that she began writing “when I scarcely had knowledge of letters, as an unlearned woman had taught me.” Certainly, she did not know Latin, because she had never learned it. Yet enlightened by heavenly light, she understood Latin writings, so far as appears, in the sense that she knew what those writings contained, not what each individual word meant.

Concerning that wonderful manner in which she understood mysteries and was at last compelled to write them, various of her writings—some not published—have been gathered in the manuscript Life. Since they are not all contained in the Life to be printed, I shall transfer them here:

> “From my infancy, therefore,” she says, “until the present time, now that I am more than seventy years old, I have always seen this light in my soul. I do not perceive it with outward eyes, nor by thoughts of the heart, nor by any combining of the five outward senses, although my outward eyes remain open and my other bodily senses retain their power. For the light which I see is not local, but far brighter than a cloud carrying the sun; and I cannot observe in it height, length, or breadth. It is called to me ‘the shadow of the living light.’ And as the sun, moon, and stars appear in water, so writings and words, virtues, and certain human deeds take form and shine for me within it. Whatever I see or learn in this vision, I retain in memory for a long time; and I see, hear, and know at once, and, as it were in a moment, I learn what I know. But whatever I do not see, that I do not know, because I am like an unlettered woman; and from what I write from that light I set down no words other than those which I hear, and I use unpolished Latin words [an uncertain OCR addition appears to mean: ‘add: I use,’ or something similar]. Nor do I hear words as those which sound from a human mouth, but as flashing flame and as a cloud moved in clear air. I can in no way know the form of this light, just as I cannot perfectly gaze upon the sphere of the sun.”

16. “Yet I sometimes behold in this same light another light, which is called to me ‘the living light’; but I do not see it often, and I am even less able to determine its form than that of the earlier light. While I gaze upon that light, every sadness and every pain is removed from my memory, so that I then have the manners of a simple girl and not of an old woman. But my soul is at no hour without the first light, called the shadow of the living light; and I see it as though I were looking upon the firmament in a bright cloud without stars. In it I see those things which I speak from the brilliance of the living light.

“From my infancy until my fortieth year, I continued always to see the things aforesaid, and often to speak something from them, but to write absolutely nothing. Then, in the same vision, I felt my veins and marrow fully restored to strength, from which I had been weakened by many illnesses since my youth. Then, compelled by the Spirit, I disclosed these things to a certain monk whom I had chosen as my teacher. Greatly astonished at them, he instructed me to write secretly what I saw and had seen, so that, when he had seen the beginning and end of the writings, he might judge—or at least form an opinion—about what the matter was.”

17. Moreover, where the Saint testifies that illness at last [Col. 0018D] compelled her to write, in the words already quoted from the prologue to the *Scivias*, she adds:

> “While I was doing this, sensing, as I said before, the profound depth of the exposition of the books, and rising from my illness with my strength restored, I scarcely brought this work to its completion after ten years. These visions and words came to pass in the days of Henry, Archbishop of Mainz, Conrad, King of the Romans, and Cuno, abbot on the mountain of the blessed pontiff Disibod, under Pope Eugenius. And I spoke and wrote these things not according to an invention of my own heart or of any other person, but as I saw, heard, and perceived them in heavenly places through God’s secret mysteries. And again I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: Therefore cry out, and write thus.”

The date given presents no difficulty, except concerning Pope Eugenius and Archbishop Henry [Col. 0019A]. Conrad had long been king and Cuno abbot before the Saint began to write, that is, before 1141. But Eugenius was created pope only in 1145, while the beginning of Henry’s tenure as Archbishop of Mainz is placed in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 471, in 1142. I reply that these facts do not prevent us from believing that the Saint began in 1141. She seems to have named Eugenius because the greater part of that work was written under his pontificate, and because he saw and approved a part of it, although she had begun to write some things under the two predecessors of Eugenius. The same was the reason for naming Henry of Mainz, who had seen part of the work already before Eugenius. Yet from this we gather that the Saint’s writings were not conveyed [Col. 0019B] to the Archbishop of Mainz immediately when she began to write, but later, when a substantial part had been completed. Alberic, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1141, entirely agrees with us, writing thus:

> “In this year St. Hildegard, being forty-two years and seven months old, began the book *Scivias*, visited by the Holy Spirit, and completed it in ten years, etc.”

18. It remains to inquire whether St. Hildegard wrote her books with her own hand, and wholly in the language and manner in which we have them written. Trithemius, in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1147, speaks of the Saint’s writings as though he believed that she had used no one else’s assistance in writing; and he speaks similarly elsewhere. But he seems to have examined the matter more carefully [Col. 0019C] in the *Chronicle of Sponheim* under the year 1179, where he writes thus concerning works composed by St. Hildegard:

> “This holy virgin deserved from her youth to be visited by divine revelations, from which she wrote many things at the divine command for the benefit of posterity. But since she was ignorant of the Latin language, and had learned nothing from any human being beyond simple psalmody, being taught by the inward instruction of the Holy Spirit, she perfectly understood all Scripture, the arrangement, or construction, of speech. She uttered her revelations and heavenly visions partly in Latin and partly in German; these Godfrey, monk of St. Disibod, her chaplain and confessor, made Latin and suitable, reducing them [Col. 0019D] to the order and form in which they are read today. Among her other volumes there is in the same place a large volume containing her letters to various persons, homilies, lives of saints, and other things which, divinely taught, she published. The nuns of that place falsely maintain that she wrote it with her own hand, since she was ignorant of Latin and wholly unfit for writing because of her frequent illnesses and her moist head. For none of the things shown there today should be believed to have been written in her own hand, since she did not know how to write; rather, the aforesaid monk either wrote everything himself or procured its writing.”

Thus far Trithemius, whose opinion accords with the ancient documents. This monk Godfrey, or Godefrid, whose services the Saint used in writing [Col. 0020A], is perhaps the same man who composed the first book of her *Life*.

19. That all St. Hildegard’s writings were composed in the manner explained by Trithemius is inferred from her *Life* itself. There, at no. 2, Godefrid asserts that she was so ignorant of letters that “she knew neither the interpretation of words nor the division of syllables, nor had she knowledge of the cases or tenses of Latin words.” Then Theodoric, in the preface to the second book, indicates her manner of writing as follows:

> “This too is great and worthy of admiration: that what she heard or saw in the Spirit, she wrote with her own hand and uttered with her mouth, in the same sense and the same words, with a watchful and pure mind, content with a single faithful man as [Col. 0020B] a fellow initiate (*symmysta*), who, for the clarity required by grammatical art—which she herself did not know—would indeed arrange cases, tenses, and genders, but would not presume to add or remove anything at all from their sense or meaning.”

The author adds, from Hildegard’s own letter to Pope Adrian, that she had been warned by God that, when she had not “expressed in Latin speech, in a manner suitable for human beings, the things shown from above, he who possesses the file should not neglect to bring them to a sound suitable for human beings.” Therefore she employed an assistant in writing, by God’s own command, because she did not know how to express her thoughts in Latin. She herself says, in the words cited at no. 14:

> “Whatever I do not see, that I do not know, because I am as one unlearned. And concerning those things which I write from that light, I set down no words other than those which I hear [Col. 0020C], and in unpolished Latin words.”

The expression is incomplete. But I judge that the Saint means this: “I write the Latin words heard, and I add no other Latin words to complete the expression or explain what is attached to it.”

20. Therefore, so far as I can understand, St. Hildegard had the following roles in her writings. She expressed her visions in the vernacular; but the Latin words which she heard in them she wrote down herself as she had heard them. Then, under her direction, Godefrid rendered everything into Latin and suitably joined it all together. Hence the aforementioned Trithemius says: “She uttered her heavenly visions partly in Latin”—namely, the words heard—“and partly in German,” namely, the persons [Col. 0020D] and other things seen. She began to write in this way on the mountain of St. Disibod, where she had begun the monastic life, as Theodoric testifies in the *Life*, no. 14. But she completed her first work much later in the new monastery, of whose foundation we must now speak.

## § III. As the number of nuns increased, St. Hildegard founds a monastery on Mount St. Rupert; she did not see St. Bernard there, nor did she embrace the Cistercian Rule. The Saint’s writings are approved by Eugenius III; the work *Scivias* is completed.

21. After St. Hildegard had begun to commit her revelations to writing, the small community of virgins over which she had presided since the death of Blessed Jutta began greatly to increase. Since, therefore, the place where they lived became too cramped, plans were made for the construction of [Col. 0021A] a new monastery, as the *Life*, no. 6, relates; it adds that the place was revealed to the Saint. Yet illness must have intervened so that Cono or Cuno, abbot of St. Disibod, would consent to the virgin’s departure. But I add no more concerning matters sufficiently explained in the *Life*.

Trithemius, in the *Chronicle of Sponheim* under the year 1148, writes as follows concerning that new foundation:

> “In 1148 . . . the holy virgin Hildegard, appointed, as we have said, teacher of Christ’s brides on Mount St. Disibod after the death of Blessed Jutta, divinely admonished, moved to Bingen with eighteen holy virgins and built a monastery upon the mountain beyond the River Nahe, beside the tomb of St. Rupert, duke and confessor. She brought that place itself, with all its goods and possessions [Col. 0021B], into the right of ownership partly by purchase from the hand of the Count of Hildesheim, who lived in the diocese of Trier, partly by exchange, and partly by gifts from the Count of Sponheim and other faithful persons; and she commended it, for perpetual times, to the protection of the Church of Mainz, apostolic privilege intervening.”

Then, after some remarks on the Saint’s birth and writings, he again writes these things about the reason for the new foundation:

> “But since many nobles in the surrounding region entrusted their daughters to her instruction, and the place in which they were to live was too confined, with permission both from the supreme pontiff and from her own abbot, she moved, as we have said, to Mount St. Rupert with eighteen sacred nuns. Among them was Hiltrude, daughter of Count Meginhard, a virgin of most holy manner of life [Col. 0021C] and very intimate with Blessed Hildegard; for her sake the count, her father, bestowed many benefits upon that place.”

Thus far Trithemius, who places the foundation in 1148.

22. In the latest edition of *Gallia Christiana*, V, col. 653, the monastery is called: “St. Rupert of Bingen, or Mount St. Rupert or Robert near Bingen.” It is there observed that there is another monastery of Cistercian nuns, also called Mount St. Robert, in the diocese of Liège. Concerning the time and place of the foundation, the cited *Gallia Christiana* states:

> “This convent of girls of the Order of St. Benedict was founded in 1147 by St. Hildegard, its first abbess, near the town of Bingen, on [Col. 0021D] the other side of the River Nahe, where it flows into the Rhine, four German miles from Mainz.”

I believe this sufficiently accurate. Bingen is a town within the territory of the Elector of Mainz and lies on the bank of the Rhine; in Latin it was formerly more often called *Pinguia*, but is now commonly called *Bingium*. The reader further sees that the foundation is here dated one year earlier than in Trithemius—and rightly so, since it is certain that it had at least been begun in 1147. For when Pope Eugenius III wrote to St. Hildegard in 1148, as we shall see, he addressed his letter: “To the beloved daughter in the Lord, Hildegard, prioress on Mount Blessed Robert.” The foundation had therefore already been made, and begun in the preceding year, especially since the letter was issued not at the end of the year but near its beginning, in January or February [Col. 0022A].

Yet the conclusion of the same letter suggests that the foundation was recent. For Eugenius writes to her thus:

> “As for what you have communicated to us concerning that place which you foresaw in the Spirit, let this be done with our permission and blessing and that of your bishop, so that there you may live regularly with your sisters according to the Rule of St. Benedict, under the enclosure of that same place.”

To this the Saint replied:

> “But I, O Father, remain with my sisters, in the place shown to me from heaven, according to the words of your blessing, according to the Rule of St. Benedict, under the enclosure of that same place; and I desire that this always be observed, both while I live and after my death.”

23. Trithemius, in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1147, relates that St. Bernard came to Mount [Col. 0022B] St. Rupert, or to the town of Bingen, and conversed there with St. Hildegard, while he was preaching in Germany in the regions around the Rhine and exhorting the faithful to take up the cross for an expedition to the Holy Land. The event would have to be dated in 1146, if it seemed sufficiently certain. But Manrique, in the *Cistercian Annals*, and after him our Pinius, under 20 August in the entry on St. Bernard, p. 193, rightly doubted it. Mabillon too, in the *Benedictine Annals*, vol. VI, p. 410—or perhaps Martène, who completed that volume after Mabillon had long been dead and published it in 1739—adds his voice. For he candidly declares: “What Trithemius relates concerning Bernard’s conversation with her [St. Hildegard] is highly suspect.” He also adds reasons which I shall explain somewhat more fully. But first let us hear Trithemius [Col. 0022C], whose account will at least show how varied were people’s judgments concerning the Saint’s writings, and what St. Bernard thought of them:

> “Thence—from Frankfurt, where St. Bernard had preached—he went down by boat and arrived at Bingen, where Hildegard, a nun, a most devout virgin of Christ . . . built a monastery on Mount St. Rupert. With her he is said to have exchanged sweet conversations concerning future blessedness. For the holy servant of Christ was known to the saintly Bernard by her writings, and was commended to him in the Lord by the reports of many. When he arrived to visit her, after the customary prayers and offices of greeting, he ordered the volumes which she had written under divine inspiration to be brought to him.

24. “Having carefully examined a portion of them [Col. 0022D], marvelling beyond what can be expressed, he is said to have declared to his companions: ‘These writings are not human inventions, nor can a mortal person understand them unless he has been inwardly and in his soul re-formed after the likeness of God through love.’

> “To this the superior of the virgins, a devout and holy monk named Heribert, replied to the man of God: ‘Reverend Father, what you have said is indeed true. But many persons—learned and unlearned, religious and worldly—torment the soul of Christ’s handmaid with daily slanders, saying that she prattles the fantasies of her brain, or things deceitfully sent into an unlearned woman by demons.’

> “The man of God said to him: ‘We do not wonder, dearest brother, if those asleep in sins think divine revelations to be dreams, since we know that the holy [Col. 0023A] Apostle spoke truly: “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually examined” [1 Cor. 2:14]. For while all who lie in the sins of pride, lust, avarice, or other vices are, as it were, asleep, divine admonitions are accustomed to appear to them as dreams; because, if they were awake in the fear of the Lord, they would recognize the signs of divine activity as true. Those, however, who judge that these things are sent by demons show that they have absolutely no knowledge of divine contemplation. They must be judged like those who said that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ cast out demons by the power of Beelzebub.’

> “And to holy Hildegard also, through an interpreter, he said: ‘And you, [Col. 0023B] daughter, do not fear people’s words, since you have God as your protector; for their words will perish like stubble, but the word of the Lord remains for ever.’ After this the man of God went down by boat to Boppard, etc.”

Thus far Trithemius, upon whose account we shall make a few brief observations.

25. First, the words attributed to St. Bernard are entirely consonant both with his admirable holiness and wisdom and with his judgment concerning the writings and merits of St. Hildegard, expressed in the letter to be given below. For that reason I can readily believe that Bernard said similar things about the Saint’s writings when he saw them brought to Trier and was able to examine them. Secondly, that visit of St. Bernard and examination of St. Hildegard’s writings in the monastery itself appear wholly fabricated [Col. 0023C], or at least to have arisen solely from error. For all ancient writers are silent about St. Bernard’s coming to St. Hildegard, both those who wrote about Bernard and those who wrote about Hildegard, although our biographer mentions St. Bernard as a most devoted admirer of the Saint and of her writings. Moreover, St. Bernard wrote to St. Hildegard probably in 1148, and she replied, as we shall see. But the letters are written in such a way that they seem never to have seen one another.

Finally, St. Bernard does not appear to have travelled down the Rhine by boat on the journey discussed by Trithemius, since in the book of his *Miracles*, vol. IV for August, p. 338, a journey by land is described. Thus he not only did not come to Bingen [Col. 0023D], but did not even pass it by boat or come near it. Hildegard herself also was probably not yet at Bingen when St. Bernard is said to have come there to her. Therefore that visit of St. Bernard is wholly improbable; nor ought we to be detained by the fact that Baillet accepted it, though elsewhere he is not infrequently more severe than is fair in exercising criticism. For we too often find that this writer did not investigate facts concerning saints transmitted only by later authors with the diligence he ought to have employed in writing lives of saints purged of popular errors.

26. Indeed, the same Baillet with equal facility adopted another, equally improbable opinion of certain [Col. 0024A] Cistercian writers. Chrysostom Henriquez, whom he cites, in the *Cistercian Menology*, p. 316, assigns Hildegard to the Cistercian Order, though he acknowledges that she was initially Benedictine. He says that she changed her habit “at the urging of St. Bernard.” In support of his view he cites Barnabas of Montalbo, who asserts that the change was made by St. Hildegard “because of the devotion which she bore toward Lord Bernard.” He then adduces the *Annals of the Order*, in which the same claims are made. I pass over other writers who assert the same thing in error.

Our Papebroch had already observed this error under 18 June in the entry on St. Elizabeth of Schönau [Note: [Col. 0023D] See *Patrologia*, vol. CXCV.], whom some assigned to the Cistercians just as they did Hildegard, although [Col. 0024B] both were Benedictines. This seems to have occurred through confusion of several monasteries bearing the same name. For at no. 22 I observed that in the diocese of Liège there is a monastery of Cistercian nuns called Mount St. Robert, just like that inhabited by St. Hildegard near Bingen. But it is certain that the latter belonged to the Benedictine institute. The aforementioned Papebroch, p. 606, no. 11, presents himself as an eyewitness in these words:

> “We had long known concerning Hildegard, having been at Bingen in 1660 and having seen there her sacred things, bones, and writings, as well as her cowl—not white in color, like that of Cistercians, but reddish-black, like that of Benedictine nuns.”

I add no more, because the matter is entirely beyond doubt.

[Col. 0024C] 27. In 1148 occurred the events which the biographer narrates at no. 5 concerning the examination of the Saint’s writings at Trier by command of Pope Eugenius III and in the presence of St. Bernard. The biographer says that they occurred at Trier after the Council of Reims. But Pagi, under the year 1148—in which the Council of Reims, begun in March, is commonly believed to have been held—shows by several arguments that Eugenius was at Trier and held a council there before the Council of Reims. Certainly, from the *Acts of the Invention of St. Matthias the Apostle*, published by us in vol. III for February, ch. 4, p. 453, we know that Eugenius III was at Trier on 13 January 1148, since on that day he dedicated the church of St. Matthias. Since he is said to have stayed there for three months, it follows that [Col. 0024D] we must say that he was already at Trier in December 1147. Brouwer, therefore, in the *Annals of Trier* under the year 1147, writes consistently with these facts when he says that Eugenius III entered Trier on the Saturday before the first Sunday of Advent.

The pope consequently spent almost the whole of December, January, and February at Trier. Thus the events related by the writer of the *Life* concerning the examination there of the Saint’s writings in council must be dated in January or February. But, as is clear from what has been said, he erred in that minor chronological detail when he places the examination after the Council of Reims; nor is it unbelievable that [Col. 0025A] a contemporary writer could have fallen into that error, since the event had taken place more than thirty years earlier when he wrote it. St. Hildegard herself, however, did not fall into the same error: for, in asserting in the *Life*, no. 17, that her writings had been examined by Eugenius, she assigns no time other than that when the pope was at Trier.

28. Trithemius, in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1150, narrates the events at Trier somewhat more fully than they are read in the *Life*, writing as follows:

> “In the year mentioned above—indeed, in 1147—Pope Eugenius III came to Trier with eighteen cardinals and many bishops and abbots, invited by Albero, Archbishop of Trier. While they stayed there for three months, he provided most abundantly for them in food and [Col. 0025B] drink. Pope Eugenius, having summoned bishops, abbots, and many clerics from all Germany and part of Gaul, held a synod and decreed many things for the honor and benefit of God’s Church. . . . At the aforesaid council held at Trier, the miracles, visions, and writings which almighty God was working through his handmaid Hildegard at Bingen came to the ears of the supreme pontiff Eugenius through the report of very many persons. On hearing these things, the pope, wishing to investigate a new and difficult matter more carefully, sent to the virgin of Christ Adelbert—rather, Albero—Bishop of Verdun, together with certain other learned and God-fearing men, commanding them to investigate the truth of all the matters mentioned.

> “When they [Col. 0025C] reached the handmaid of God and reverently carried out the commission received from the supreme pontiff, they most diligently inquired from her not only into the sequence and reputation of the revelations, but also into their manner and causes. She answered everything simply and revealed with the greatest humility what Divinity had worked concerning her. Having received sufficient information, the papal envoys, at her request taking with them the books of the virgin’s visions, returned to the pope at Trier and reported that they had found true and sound everything that was said concerning Christ’s handmaid. Then they reverently delivered to Pope Eugenius the volumes which she, divinely illuminated, had written, together with the letter which she had given.”

[Col. 0025D] 29. The reader should here be warned that there is some exaggeration in what is said about the Saint’s “volumes.” At that time the Saint had not written many volumes, but had only begun the first work of her revelations; thus by “volumes” we should understand leaves or folios. What is added about a letter is, at the least, uncertain and not very probable. Yet she did request from Eugenius, probably through the envoys mentioned, permission to live on Mount St. Rupert. But let us proceed with Trithemius:

> “The pope caused the virgin’s writings to be publicly read before many persons; sometimes himself performing the office of reader, he read aloud a considerable part. All who heard the word of the reading, carried into admiration, praised the mercy of the Almighty [Col. 0026A], who worked such things in the frail sex. Lord Abbot Bernard was present; Louis, abbot of St. Matthias at Trier and friend of the holy virgin, was also present. Through their intervention the clouds of every doubt were driven from the minds of the hearers. Therefore, as all who were present alike entreated and urged the Roman pontiff not to permit so eminent a lamp, kindled by divine illumination, to be extinguished by the schemes of wicked persons, he gladly consented and sent to the virgin Hildegard a letter of the following tenor.”

30. I here reproduce Eugenius’s letter from the collection in vol. XXIII of the Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 537:

> “Eugenius, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in the Lord Hildegard, prioress on Mount [Col. 0026B] Blessed Robert: greeting and apostolic blessing. We are amazed, O daughter, etc.”

See below among the letters of St. Hildegard, letter 1. The Saint replied to Eugenius with a very lengthy letter, composed from a vision and written with her customary freedom. We ought not to wonder at this, since she did not follow her own mind but uttered what she received in vision, while the directing monk assisted and arranged everything. The letter begins:

> “O gentle Father, I, a poor little woman, have written these things to you—this letter—in a true vision, in a mystical breathing, as God wished to teach me, etc.”

She then gives Eugenius many admonitions in prophetic style, which may be consulted. At the end she says that she remains in the place shown to her from heaven; hence it is certain that she was already living on Mount St. Rupert when she wrote back to Eugenius.

31. She also seems already to have been living in that place when Eugenius wrote to her. His letter was sent in 1148, probably in January or February, since the pontiff departed from Trier near the end of February or the beginning of March in order to commence the Council of Reims in March. Certainly the address of the letter, “Prioress on Mount Blessed Robert,” suggests that Hildegard was then living there. Yet it does not appear equally certain that she was in that place when she herself was examined by the apostolic envoys. For the *Life*, no. 5, says that they were sent “to the monastery under which the same virgin had lived enclosed for so many years,” that is, to the monastery on Mount St. Disibod; it makes no mention [Col. 0026D] of Hildegard’s residence on Mount St. Rupert, whose foundation the author narrates after everything we have said about the examination of her writings.

We might indeed conjecture that the author wished first to relate everything concerning the writings and then the new foundation. But the envoys’ arrival at Mount St. Disibod will always create a suspicion that Hildegard was then living there, unless she was summoned thither from her new dwelling so that the examination might be held before the abbot of St. Disibod. But this summons is uncertain and asserted by no one. Thus perhaps St. Hildegard was still living on Mount St. Disibod when she was examined; and when the examination was completed, she obtained permission from the abbot and the envoys to depart for the new monastery. But whatever may be thought of those uncertain conjectures, it is certainly established [Col. 0027A] that the Saint began to inhabit the new monastery about the time when her writings were examined at Trier, that is, at the beginning of 1148 or in the preceding year.

32. Moreover, when St. Hildegard replied to Pope Eugenius, a “part of the writing” about her revelations had been completed. The Saint is speaking of her first work, which she divided into three books and named *Scivias*, a compound of two words: *Scivias*, that is, “Know the ways of the Lord.” Probably the first book of that work had been completed when she wrote to Eugenius that a part was finished. All three books were completed around 1151, for she assigns ten years to the composition of the aforesaid work, which, as we saw at no. [Col. 0027B] 17, began in 1141.

From this we clearly understand that only part of the work was seen at the Council of Trier, not the entire work, still less all the works of St. Hildegard, which were gradually written much later. The approval of the Saint’s writings at the Council of Trier consisted in this: Pope Eugenius, with the Fathers of the council, judged that what the Saint wrote was drawn not from a delusion of the devil nor from the fantasies of the brain, as some slandered, but from divine revelations. Therefore he permitted the Saint to continue writing her visions “prudently.” Yet he carefully warned her to preserve herself in humility; St. Bernard gave the same warning in the letter to be given below. They did so rightly and wisely, since Christian humility is the safest guardian and preserver of God’s gifts and virtues. But St. Hildegard herself was not [Col. 0027C] ignorant of this, taught by God and most richly endowed with heavenly gifts, among which humility holds no small place, as may be understood from her own writings.

33. Furthermore, the work *Scivias* was printed at Paris in 1513, by the press of Henri Estienne. It was then reprinted at Cologne in 1628 together with the Revelations of St. Bridget and St. Elizabeth of Schönau. I have these editions before me; I leave the investigation of further editions to others. The first book contains six visions, expounded at length; the second, much longer, seven further visions; the third, longest of all, thirteen visions. I have endeavored to read the whole work attentively and found in it many excellent teachings; but [Col. 0027D] not a few passages are too obscure to be easily understood by everyone.

The Saint rarely speaks of herself. When she does, however, she speaks with remarkable humility. Receive a few examples, reader. She begins the second book thus:

> “And I, a person unskilled in letters after the manner of strong lions, nor taught by their infusion, but remaining in the softness of a frail rib [that is, a woman], imbued with mystical breathing, saw, etc.”

This is the beginning of the third book:

> “And I, a person taken from other persons, who am not worthy to be called a person because of the transgression of God’s law—for I ought to be righteous and am unrighteous, except that I am God’s creature by his grace, which will also save me—saw, etc.”

A little later in that vision she says:

> “And again I heard him saying to me: ‘O how beautiful are [Col. 0028A] your eyes in divine narration, when dawn rises there by divine counsel.’”

And again I replied from the inward knowledge of that vision itself:

> “I appear to myself in the bosom of my soul like ashes of ashen decay, and like the dust of instability; therefore I sit trembling in the shadow like a feather. But do not erase me from the land of the living as a stranger, for I labor in great sweat in this vision, and because of the lowliness of my foolish understanding—which is mine in the flesh—I frequently reckon myself to be in the lowest and most contemptible place, so that I am not worthy to be called a person. For I fear greatly and do not dare to recount your mysteries. O good and gentle Father, teach me what your will is, what I ought to bring forth. O awesome Father, O most sweet one, O one full of every grace, do not abandon me, but preserve me [Col. 0028B] in your mercy.”

And again I heard him saying to me:

> “Now say how you have been taught. I wish you to speak, though you are ashes.”

More may be seen in the work itself.

## § IV. The Saint’s reputation shines forth greatly; St. Bernard, Conrad King of the Romans, and many bishops write to her, and she responds to them with complete freedom.

34. Baronius, in the *Annals* under the year 1148, after relating the examination of St. Hildegard’s writings, adds at no. 33 the following observation:

> “This visitation and examination made concerning Hildegard gained for her greater esteem. John of Salisbury has the following in Book I of the Letters of St. Thomas, Letter 171, at the end: ‘The visions and oracles of that blessed and most renowned Hildegard which are in your possession [that is, send them].’ [Col. 0028C] She has been commended to me and made venerable on this account: that Lord Eugenius embraced her more familiarly with a special affection of charity. Inquire also and write back whether anything concerning the end of this schism has been revealed to her. For in the days of Pope Eugenius she foretold that he would have neither peace nor favor in the City except in his final days.’”

Alberic the monk, a thirteenth-century writer, recounts in his *Chronicle* under the year 1141 much concerning St. Hildegard’s revelations, which I have already given from her own words, and he entirely agrees with what has been said concerning the written work *Scivias*. Concerning the authority of the Saint herself he observes as follows:

> “Who that Hildegard was, and how great her authority, is indicated by the letters sent to her by the great persons of the earth: by the popes Eugenius [Col. 0028D], Anastasius, and Adrian; by the emperors Conrad and Frederick; by the Patriarch of Jerusalem; and by archbishops, abbots, and provosts; as well as by one special letter of Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.”

He adds much there which I omit because it has already been supplied from elsewhere.

35. The same Alberic writes the following concerning St. Hildegard under the year 1153:

> “In the same year, a certain virgin of Christ, Hildegard of Germany, being of great renown and intoxicated with the Holy Spirit, was asked and entreated through the chapter and elders of the Cistercians, who had sent their letters to her, to write back to them, according to what God revealed to her, whether there was anything in the order displeasing to God. She wrote back the following letter in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ to the Cistercian [Col. 0029A] general chapter: ‘I, the living fountain, say to those who, clothed in my tunic for my name’s sake, are strangers in the hunting-ground of the world, etc.’ This Hildegard, though she had learned neither letters nor Latin, produced an excellent book of Letters, in which many things concerning the last times are contained; another book, entitled *Scivias*, that is, ‘Knowing’; and a third, entitled *Exposition of Divine Works*.”

Thus far Alberic.

36. But that we may understand more clearly how great was the reputation of St. Hildegard among the men whom the Church then regarded as most eminent, let us examine the letters sent to the Saint and those written back by her. Among the earliest certainly—if not the very first—is the letter of St. Bernard [Col. 0029B], which I conjecture was given in 1148, at the time of the Council of Trier:

> “To Hildegard, beloved daughter in Christ: Brother Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, [sends] whatever the prayer of a sinner can accomplish. Concerning our lowliness, etc.”

See letter 29 in the book of St. Hildegard’s letters.

37–38. If the letter of St. Bernard contributes to St. Hildegard’s glory, as indeed it contributes very greatly, the letter of St. Hildegard is no less honorable to St. Bernard—especially since she is accustomed throughout her letters to exhort, admonish, and sometimes even sharply rebuke everyone, while she praises very rarely and sparingly. Thus I find none among her letters so full of praise and at the same time free of every rebuke [Col. 0029C] and admonition. (See below among the letters of St. Hildegard.) In the published editions, Hildegard’s letter follows St. Bernard’s; nevertheless, I think that she wrote first and that Bernard replied. I also suspect, in any event, that Hildegard wrote before she and her writings were examined by command of Eugenius III, and that the said examination was instituted on the occasion of these letters.

39–40. Among the earlier princes who wrote to St. Hildegard was Henry, Archbishop and Elector of Mainz, deprived of his dignity in 1153 and dead a year and a half later, as Pagius states under the year 1153, no. 1. Writing to Hildegard, he begins his letter with these words (ep. 5): “Since we hear many good things and wonderful miracles concerning you, [Col. 0029D] it must be ascribed to our sloth that we do not visit you as often as we could, etc.” He then asks—indeed, commands—that she allow a certain nun, elected abbess, to depart with those who had come to take her away to the aforesaid office. The letter is civil, except for the rather forceful order to surrender the nun. The reader may perhaps be amazed at St. Hildegard’s reply; yet he will thereby see all the more clearly that she did not compose her letters from her own talent, but wrote what had been revealed by God. For if there was anyone whom she should otherwise have respected and loved, it was this archbishop and her protector, who, so far as we certainly know, had always shown himself kind toward her. Yet she replies in a prophetic manner and, by no obscure allusion to Nebuchadnezzar, foretells that Henry will be deprived of his dignity [Col. 0030A] and will not live very long—as in fact came to pass. Many nevertheless maintained that Henry had not been so very blameworthy and afterward died piously.

I consider that nun, elected abbess, whose election the Saint so gravely disapproved, to have been the sister of Hartwig, Archbishop of Bremen, whose death will be discussed at no. 46, and of whom the Saint probably speaks in the *Acts*, no. 23. Besides, I do not doubt that in this letter also St. Hildegard could truly have said what she wrote to Arnold, Henry’s successor: “I do not utter mystical words from myself, but only according to what I see in the living light; thus things which my mind does not desire, and which even my will does not seek, are often shown to me, yet I see them many times under compulsion.” [Col. 0030B] More will be given below concerning the writings addressed to Arnold.

41. Conrad III, King of Germany (ep. 26), commonly called emperor although he was never crowned, must likewise be numbered among those who first sent letters to St. Hildegard; for he died in 1152, and thus his letter must be dated between 1148 and 1152. It begins: “Because we are hindered by the royal eminence,” etc. He pledges her his favor and commends his son to the Saint’s prayers.

42. The Saint replied to this letter, partly admonishing Conrad gently and partly foretelling worse times, such as occurred under Frederick I, Conrad’s successor. She plainly predicts the schisms and other evils of the Church which arose under [Col. 0030C] Frederick I, to whom she afterward also wrote a letter much stronger than this. In the same prophetic spirit she adds much concerning the various periods and vicissitudes of the Church; and these matters could not be difficult to explain, if one wished to examine more closely the times then future.

43. Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne, wrote a most courteous letter to Hildegard at about the same time (ep. 11), asking for her book. St. Hildegard’s reply to Arnold is for the most part mystical and in some respect obscure. She adds a clearer statement about her book in these words: “But now, O shepherd of your people, I have sent you, as you asked, these writings of true visions—containing nothing of human [Col. 0030D] ingenuity or of my own will, but what the unfailing Light wished to reveal through its composition and through these very words, as pleased it; since even what I now write to you has been composed not by my own ingenuity nor by any human decision, but by heavenly manifestation.”

44. To approximately the same period belongs the letter of Hillin, Archbishop of Trier (ep. 13), to which St. Hildegard replied with a letter partly mystical and enigmatic, partly prophetic and exhortatory; its conclusion is as follows: “The form of the dove instructs you, and the word of God is not lacking in knowledge within you. Therefore now keep watch, and bind fast with an iron rod: teach, anoint the wounds of those entrusted to you, and you shall live for eternity.”

[Col. 0031A] 45. At about this time Gunther, Bishop of Speyer, also wrote to St. Hildegard (ep. 15), addressing her among other things thus: “That you are a good fragrance to those far away as well as those near, and, through the Holy Spirit, a consolation to all who seek you—we give thanks for this to divine mercy.” In reply, the Saint exhorts Gunther at length to amend his life. She begins thus: “The light of highest inspiration, O man, says to you: Do not cut away from yourself, through the evil habit of your deeds, the admonition of the Holy Spirit which rises within you,” etc. The whole letter exhorts him to repentance.

Much the same is St. Hildegard’s reply to the Bishop of Constance, whose name is not given (ep. 17), and whose letter is therefore of more [Col. 0031B] uncertain date. He asks for the Saint’s prayers and letters. St. Hildegard replies with no flattery, but especially rebukes the vain glory in him. She concludes her letter thus: “Rise, therefore, without delay, and walk in straight paths, before the sun sets for you and before your days fail.”

46. Also of uncertain date is the letter of Hartwig, Archbishop of Bremen (ep. 10), who is here called Hertwig. He was bishop for more than twenty years and is said to have died about 1168. He reports the death of his sister, Abbess Richardis, who had been a nun under St. Hildegard’s discipline and had been drawn away to the aforementioned dignity by her brother. Thus she may be the woman whom Henry, Archbishop of Mainz, requested, [Col. 0031C] as stated in no. 40. Hartwig further testifies that she died most piously and “desired with all her heart and tearfully” to have remained in St. Hildegard’s cloister, from which she had been torn unwillingly. He therefore asks pardon for that departure.

The Saint replied in a rather long letter, full of excellent counsels. She also praises Hartwig and his sister Richardis, of whom she says: “My soul was filled with love for her, because the living Light, in a most powerful vision, taught me to love her.” After many praises of Richardis, she commends her soul to her brother.

47. The abbot of Eberbach, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Mainz, situated approximately between Mainz and Bingen but beyond the Rhine and nearer Mainz, seems to have been among the earlier abbots who wrote to St. Hildegard (ep. 31). His name is given by the letter E, but, I think, incorrectly, since he can scarcely have been anyone other than Ruthard, the first abbot of that monastery, and the letter E does not fit the following evidence either. The aforementioned abbot requests the Saint’s prayers and offers her his services. To this letter St. Hildegard returned excellent counsels, and at its end foretold the best things for the abbot.

## § V. Anastasius IV and Adrian IV, Roman pontiffs; Emperor Frederick; bishops, abbots, and many others write to the Saint, and she replies.

48. Although it is difficult to arrange St. Hildegard’s letters [Col. 0032A] in order, since they bear no chronological indications, I have nevertheless wished, from the periods in which the persons flourished, to introduce at least some sort of order. Thus, up to this point, I have given almost only letters written between 1148 and 1153. Continuing now, I begin with the letter of Anastasius IV, sent in 1153 or 1154 (ep. 2), since he was made pope in the former year and died in the latter. Anastasius’s letter reads: “Anastasius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hildegard, beloved daughter in Christ: greeting and apostolic blessing. We rejoice in the Lord,” etc. See below among the letters of St. Hildegard.

49. St. Hildegard’s answer is lengthy. In God’s name she exhorts Anastasius to root out evils courageously. [Col. 0032B] She then makes various prophetic predictions and adds certain matters concerning her visions. Finally, she again exhorts Anastasius to correct those subject to him. She begins thus: “O person, you who are the pre-eminent armor and the mountain of instruction of the most richly adorned city [that is, the Church], established in Christ’s betrothal: hear him who did not begin to live and does not grow weary in failing,” etc.

After much else, she concludes this admonition and passes to prediction in this fashion: “… And therefore the whole earth is disturbed by the great changeableness of errors, because what God has destroyed, man loves. And you, O Rome, lying as it were at the extremities, shall be troubled,” etc. Rome was indeed greatly troubled by the schism that arose five or six years after this prediction; and the Church had already begun to be disturbed under Adrian IV by Emperor Frederick.

50. The Saint then adds words about herself, partly quoted in the *Life*, no. 14, where they are nevertheless said to have been written to Adrian IV. Thus either an error has crept into the *Life* or into the collection of letters; but the former is more likely. She finally closes the letter with this admonition: “But you, O man, appointed as a shepherd in appearance, arise and hasten to justice, lest before the great Physician you be accused of having neither cleansed his sheepfold from filth nor anointed it with oil,” etc.

51–52. Adrian IV, who succeeded Anastasius near the end of 1154, writes to St. Hildegard (ep. 3): [Col. 0032D] “We rejoice, daughter, and exult in the Lord, that the report of your uprightness is being spread so widely and so far,” etc. He adds, however, a fine exhortation to perseverance and concludes: “Furthermore, we desire to hear words of admonition from you, because you are said to be imbued with the spirit of God’s miracles,” etc. St. Hildegard replied briefly; predicting much for Adrian and serious conflicts, she exhorts him to courage, not without praise of him, so that she seems also to foretell eternal salvation for him rather clearly.

53. Probably not many years after Adrian, Emperor Frederick I, surnamed Redbeard or Barbarossa, wrote to St. Hildegard. Since he was crowned emperor in 1155, the letter must be dated [Col. 0033A] between 1155 and 1159, the year in which Adrian IV died and the schism against Alexander III arose, Frederick favoring the antipope. For the letter was sent by Frederick when he was emperor and, so far as appears, before the schism—though perhaps not before dissensions had arisen between Frederick and Adrian. Frederick writes to the Saint as follows (ep. 27): “We make known to your holiness that we already hold in our hands those things which you foretold to us when, while we were staying at Ingelheim, we asked you to come into our presence,” etc.

From this we learn, first, that St. Hildegard had an interview with Frederick at Ingelheim, between Mainz and Bingen; second, that the Saint then foretold certain things to Frederick which were fulfilled. [Col. 0033B] This interview probably occurred while Frederick was king and had not yet been crowned emperor—that is, between 1152 and 1155—though the precise year is unknown, as are the matters predicted, unless perhaps the Saint foretold to Frederick the disputes which he would have with Adrian IV. Third, we learn that St. Hildegard had some dispute to be judged at Frederick’s court; but its nature is equally unknown.

54–55. From St. Hildegard’s response it is abundantly clear that she by no means approved Frederick’s various designs—or rather, that they were openly disapproved by the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the otherwise unlearned Saint. [Col. 0033C] For she begins to address the emperor thus: “From the highest Judge these words are directed to you: It is greatly wondrous that a man possesses this necessary person—namely, the person that you, O king, are.” She then gives a less clear parable by which his rule seems to be censured, and immediately adds a clearer warning, writing: “Now, O king, provide carefully, because all regions are overshadowed by the deceitful multitude of those who, in the blackness of sins, erase justice,” etc. Whoever considers the words of this letter attentively will see that Frederick is foretold a rather long reign, but a turbulent one, as indeed it was, above all because of his conflicts with the Roman pontiffs—conflicts which he nevertheless brought to an end before his death.

[Col. 0033D] 56. The letter of Arnold, Archbishop of Mainz (ep. 6), was sent no later than 1160, and probably not before the schism that arose in 1159—to which Arnold adhered with Emperor Frederick—or at least not long before it.
