Arnold asks the Saint’s prayers. St. Hildegard replies, strongly rebuking Arnold and foretelling his destruction, as many have already observed. Baronius, under the year 1160, no. 32, relates from Conrad that Arnold was killed by the people of Mainz in 1160, on the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, and observes that in that same year, at the assembly at Pavia, he was the first to subscribe the sentence pronounced against Alexander III, the legitimate pontiff.

57. At the same time flourished St. Eberhard, Archbishop [Col. 0034A] of Juvavum, or Salzburg. Defending Pope Alexander’s cause and greatly troubled by fear of Emperor Frederick, he wrote to St. Hildegard about 1160 (ep. 12): “I, a sinner placed in the valley of tears, battered by many whirlwinds and storms of this world, suffering fears within and struggles without,” etc. He then requests the Saint’s letters, but sealed with her seal.

58. The Saint uses an entirely different style with this holy bishop than she used in the preceding letter: she repeatedly praises Eberhard and finely teaches that external labors, undertaken from charity and obedience, do not at all harm a man who loves God. The life of this St. Eberhard, whose name is not stated in the letter but is known from his see and time, is given among us under 22 June. He died in 1164.

59. The letter of Conrad I, Bishop of Worms, perhaps belongs to approximately the same time. In volume V of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 674, he is said to have died in 1163. Yet I am more inclined to think the letter was written before the Church’s schism. Whatever the case, Conrad, like the others, has recourse to St. Hildegard as to an oracle and writes (ep. 16): “We give thanks to God, who has set you as a most brilliant lamp upon a golden candlestick,” etc. He adds that his messenger will say more concerning his affairs and requests an answer. The Saint replied partly by exhorting, partly by praising.

60. Adelbert, Bishop of Verdun, who in 1148, while he was primicerius, had been sent by Eugenius III to examine St. Hildegard, was advanced to the episcopate in 1156, according to some accounts. He later exchanged it for monastic life. At about the same time, probably before the schism, he wrote to St. Hildegard (ep. 18), beginning: [Col. 0034C] “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place, who from your tender years made you his handmaid.” He then exhorts her to humility and requests prayers and letters. In reply, the Saint exhorts him to pastoral care, beginning thus: “The living Light, which displays miracles, says: You who are a father in your person and a shepherd in the tending of souls, stretch forth your arm, lest the enemy-man sow weeds over your field,” etc.

[Col. 0034D] 61. The date of the letter of the Patriarch of Jerusalem is more uncertain. From the East he wrote to St. Hildegard, commending himself to the prayers of her and her sisters. The patriarch’s name is indicated only by the letter I, and incorrectly, I think, because Amalric was Latin Patriarch throughout the time when St. Hildegard’s fame had become so illustrious. There can therefore be no doubt that it is Amalric’s letter, in which he addresses Hildegard thus (ep. 22): “From many who, over long stretches of land, come to our regions and bend their knees at the Lord’s tomb, we have often learned that divine power works in you and through you; and therefore we humbly offer it unceasing thanks, as best we can.” [Col. 0035A] He then says that he had long desired an opportunity to write, and, now that one has been offered, he makes use of it; he launches into praise of the Saint and asks for her prayers. St. Hildegard replied in a letter initially full of rather obscure allegories. She then consoles the patriarch with these words: “The struggle which you suffer inwardly and outwardly, that is, in both the inner and outer person, God will in your times so lighten around you that you may endure it. Therefore put your trust in him and do not despair of his mercy. And by doing this you shall live unto life in the grace of God.”

62. Following this comes the letter of Henry, Bishop of Bevez (ep. 23); I find no city of that name, and thus suspect the name is corrupt. Whatever the case, he too has recourse to [Col. 0035B] St. Hildegard from distant regions, writing: “The manifest favor of God toward you is a great consolation to me, a sinner weighed down by the whirlwinds of the world,” etc. In reply, St. Hildegard uses a fine parable, exhorting him to true wisdom and charity.

## § VI. The Saint is consulted by many persons concerning hidden and secret matters which she could not know without divine revelation.

63. So numerous are the letters which St. Hildegard received and answered that it is altogether impossible to assign each to its proper year, owing to the lack of chronological marks—especially as quite a few are from persons either less well known or long active in the same office. For this reason I shall arrange the Saint’s letters according to a certain order of subject matter, and shall now enumerate those in which she was consulted concerning hidden and secret matters. Their number is so great that it is manifestly clear that people held an almost universal conviction that many concealed and secret things had been revealed to St. Hildegard.

[Col. 0035C] I begin with Cuno or Cono, Abbot of St. Disibod, under whose authority the Saint had been before founding the monastery on Mount St. Rupert. He therefore knew her very well and writes to her (ep. 38): “Because Your Holiness, in him who neither deceives nor is deceived, beholds many secrets by the Spirit, I ask that, if God has revealed to you anything concerning our patron, Blessed Disibod, you make it known to me, so that with my brethren I may not delay to render him most devout [Col. 0035D] praises on this account.” He earnestly commends himself to her prayers.

64. The Saint answered the questions concerning St. Disibod, of whom she writes certain general matters there, as may be seen in the letter itself; we shall treat below of the written Life of that Saint. But the Saint did not do this alone: she also freely reproves Cuno for excessive severity toward his subjects and foretells his imminent death.

65. Adam, Abbot of Ebra, or Ebrach, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Würzburg, a man greatly praised indeed by Manrique in the *Cistercian Annals*, writes the following to St. Hildegard (ep. 30): “As soon as I first received knowledge of your name, I rejoiced with great joy,” etc. He soon requests [Col. 0036A] prayers and the Saint’s answer to his doubt, which appears to have concerned whether he ought to retain or lay down the office of abbot, as is gathered from St. Hildegard’s reply.

Meanwhile, I observe that the Saint at some time traveled toward the region of Würzburg, as we shall see that she was also in other provinces. As to the Saint’s affairs commended to the emperor by Abbot Adam, we do not know what they were. But we scarcely doubt that they were the same matters of which Emperor Frederick speaks in the letter to St. Hildegard mentioned in no. 53. Now a few words concerning the Saint’s reply. The letter is very long, almost wholly woven from not overly obscure parables, interspersed with praises of Abbot Adam and excellent counsels. In warning him not to resign his office, she introduces various virtues, especially charity and humility. I shall give only the conclusion: “And you, Father, hear: as the morning star precedes the dawn in its light, so offer help to all from the kiss of love which God has given you; and he will give you the life which he beheld on the first day.” [Col. 0036B]

66. The abbot of St. Anastasius in Rome was likewise of the Cistercian Order. Besides her general fame, he may have been moved to write to St. Hildegard not only by St. Bernard’s authority but also by that of Eugenius III, who had been elected pontiff from the abbacy of that same monastery. After first praising the Saint wonderfully, he states what he requests from her in these words (ep. 32): “… I ask that the Spirit which reveals the hidden and secret things of [Col. 0036C] his wisdom indicate to you what is expedient for me in bearing the burden of Christ’s obedience: namely, whether I should persevere or rest, so that I may devote myself to his contemplation.” St. Hildegard replies to the question proposed: “Therefore complete the support of your sheepfold and give it commands, furnishing the master’s rod and afterward applying the physician’s ointment; for it is more useful to you to keep watch in this labor, while others serve in subjection through your teaching, than to exercise yourself in your own will.”

67. Conrad, Abbot of Kaisheim—though the title reads “of Ketsheim,” and perhaps it should be read “of Reisheim,” as Trithemius has it—puts a similar doubt to St. Hildegard [Col. 0036D] (ep. 33). The Saint replies without concealing the crimes of his subjects, but intimating them in grave words. Nor does she appear to excuse Conrad himself, but exhorts him to repentance. Then she addresses him thus: “… Therefore do not abandon pastoral care …” She nevertheless adds a qualification in obscure words, indicating that he should leave office where he could accomplish no good among his own people.

68. Manegold, Abbot of the once most famous monastery of Hirsau in the Black Forest and diocese of Speyer, had asked something similar, as appears from St. Hildegard’s reply, although he does not declare this in his letter. Instead, he merely shows the great esteem in which he held Hildegard by this request (ep. 34): “I ask you, my mother and lady, remember me in your most holy prayers; love most humbly one who loves you; acknowledge in Christ one who reveres you; and write back to me, having been asked in God.” The Saint replies, predicting various matters.

I think that her words about the storm must be referred wholly to the future, although Trithemius, in his *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1161, quoting this letter, believed it was written when dissension had arisen between the monks—who wrote to St. Hildegard for that reason—and this Abbot Manegold. Trithemius indeed acknowledges that the disturbances of Hirsau monastery were predicted by the Saint, but in spoken words, not in a written letter. I shall deal with the entire matter in the following section and shall there give the monks’ letter with the Saint’s reply.

[Col. 0037B] 69. The Abbot of St. Mary’s—according to Trithemius, St. Mary of the Martyrs near Trier—put a similar question to St. Hildegard (ep. 37): namely, whether, in this office of honor and burden, preeminence and danger, she foresaw that he would merit the salvation of his soul, or whether she judged it useful for him to be released from it. St. Hildegard did not answer all the questions. Yet she intimated that the abbot was too anxious, and that he should think rather of correcting himself and his subjects than of resigning his office, concluding thus: “But I saw that the matter you ask about is unprofitable for you. Therefore restrain yourself together with your office, having taken hold of the plow. May God assist you in all your necessities and not permit you to labor uselessly.” [Col. 0037C]

70. The Abbot of Kempten in Swabia likewise has recourse to St. Hildegard, desiring to understand hidden things (ep. 40). St. Hildegard gave a rather long response, exhorting him diligently to cut down evils that are always sprouting afresh. At the end she adds an excellent consolation, having observed that sins are blotted out “through repentance and confession,” writing: “Do this, then, beloved son of God, for you shall live forever; and because you shall be a stone in the heavenly Jerusalem, you must also struggle sharply.”

71–72. With great anxiety, the Abbot of St. Martin’s at Cologne—whose name is given as A and whom I consider to be Alard, since he was contemporary with the Saint [Col. 0037D] and died before 1160—has recourse to St. Hildegard as an interpreter of God. He begins his letter thus (ep. 41): “Lady, lady, truly believed to be beloved and blessed by God: I know indeed that all which divine power works through you is true and holy.” He says that he had wished, if possible, to come to her so that she might explain everything orally. St. Hildegard’s response contains both fine instruction and great consolation together with perpetual exhortation.

73. The Abbess of St. Glodesindis at Metz was likewise anxious and uncertain. She writes to St. Hildegard (ep. 42): “Because we presume greatly upon your grace and goodwill, we do not wish you to be unaware that we are placed in great danger, while we are compelled to govern many [Col. 0038A] souls though we are not sufficient for ourselves,” etc. The Saint returned a rather long letter, in which she gives various counsels for right governance and makes it fairly clear that the office should not be laid down.

74. Thus far I have examined the relevant letters first printed at Cologne and reprinted in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Martène added very many to them in volume II of the *Collectio Amplissima*, from which I shall likewise extract some bearing on my purpose. But since many place-names there seem corrupted, I shall attempt to restore some of them from Trithemius’s *Chronicle of Hirsau*, under the year 1150, where he lists those who wrote to St. Hildegard.

Albert, Abbot of Elchingen in Swabia—where there is now a provostry of canons—writes to St. Hildegard (ep. 62), asking her to consult the divine oracle concerning his enemies and write back what he should expect from God’s mercy. In reply, the Saint partly exhorts him to greater steadfastness, partly consoles him in his affliction, and predicts that the time of divine vengeance has not yet come. [Col. 0038B]

75. Berthold, Abbot of Zwinield—Zwiefalten in Swabia according to Trithemius—complains “of the injuries and tribulations which cruel persecutors inflicted upon him,” and asks her, “seeking the will of God, to send back some consolation in writing,” suited to his intellectual capacity (ep. 65). The Saint replies briefly: “The living Light says: I saw a certain [Col. 0038C] man whom I left as though weak and lame in the eminence of teaching. How so? Those who, in the weakness of their flesh, were rebellious like naked shipwrecked men—he fled from these because of fear of conflict. But now I see him as humble, weeping, a stranger. Therefore I regard him as a son of inheritance, beaten with the rod because of the restlessness of the dispositions of his mind,” etc.

76. The Abbot of Raitenhaslach, having also been elected Abbot of Salem in Swabia, of the Cistercian Order, doubted what he should do and communicated the matter to St. Hildegard (ep. 66), “as with the bride and handmaid of Christ and one aware of God’s secrets.” He asked her “simply to disclose the will [Col. 0038D] of the Holy Spirit in this matter.” The Saint replied: “Whoever has undertaken a field or a sheepfold on account of the trust of stewardship ought not to leave it, but should govern it as the householder does. For whoever leaves his own sheepfold and receives another is called a transgressor of God’s commandments.” She adds devout counsels for governance.

The Abbot of Zwettl, of the Cistercian Order in Austria, greatly burdened by the care of his flock, asks the Saint whether he ought to lay aside the dignity of abbot, requesting (ep. 70) that she write whatever “may please the Holy Spirit.” But the Saint partly exhorts him to continue pastoral care diligently and gently, giving him salutary counsels at the end. She rejects this intention of the abbot from the outset, beginning thus: “In your mind you magnify the thought that [Col. 0039A] you wish to rest or desist from every labor,” etc.

77. Richard, abbot at Springiersbach—Sprengerbach in German according to Trithemius; formerly, in a more Belgic idiom, *Springersbach*, as I find the name recorded in a charter in Hontheim’s *Diplomatic History of the Archbishopric of Trier*, though the name varies there also; it is a house of Regular Canons in the diocese of Trier—believed himself deprived of strength “both of mind and body.” He had long wished to visit St. Hildegard when he finally approached her by letter (ep. 74). The Saint replied, exhorting him to bear the burden and consoling him as a man beloved by God.

The prelate at Hegennehe—according to [Col. 0039B] Trithemius, the provost of Regular Canons at Heyna—complains of many weaknesses and deficiencies of body and mind, as also of the yoke of his enemies; and he desires to be delivered from all these evils through St. Hildegard’s prayers. St. Hildegard replies briefly: “Avoid preeminence, if they do not listen to you,” she says. Yet she advises him more strongly to retain it and remain vigilant.

78. The Abbot of Vessra, of the Premonstratensian Order in the county of Henneberg, presents this question to St. Hildegard with the greatest anxiety (ep. 78), seeking “consolation as well as counsel,” because he considered himself useless. The Saint seems altogether to advise him to lay down pastoral care because of his lack of strength. For after several remarks intimating that deficiency, [Col. 0039C] she adds: “Therefore let him make himself like a sheep and not a shepherd. You are a man like one tossing in the waters, scarcely delivered from being drowned: so that you discern prudence everywhere, yet fail in strength, though not in will. Therefore the grace of God shines upon you also.”

79. The Provost of the Valley of God, in the diocese of Mainz in the Rheingau, where there are now nuns of the Augustinian Order, asks St. Hildegard (ep. 85) to fulfill what she had promised. From her answer, however, it is clear that he had sought counsel about laying down the provostship. The Saint strongly dissuades him from this.

80. The abbot at Rappenberg—according to Trithemius, the provost at Coppenberg, and perhaps it should be read Cappenberg, [Col. 0039D] a Premonstratensian house in Westphalia—puts an altogether different question to St. Hildegard (ep. 86). He wished to come to the Saint, but says: “Hindered amid such a tempest of storms and squalls, by which the whole Church is now shaken and disturbed, fearing for my possessions and my body, I have been unable to come.” These words seem to indicate the Church’s schism, fostered by Emperor Frederick against Alexander III. Thus the prelate, expelled from his church, probably consulted the Saint concerning it through the brother whom he sent on his behalf, of whom he writes: “For the purpose of consulting the Spirit of God who dwells in you concerning the present condition of our Church, I have sent him to you.”

To this St. Hildegard gives the prelate a fine consolation, teaching that God sends adversities upon a human being to correct him. She concludes with this exhortation: “Therefore do not fear your sufferings, because I do not see your place in dispersal; rather, God so wills the bond of your burden—that is, your office of governance—and gather the sheep that wish to run to you. Those who do not wish you, bear with compassion until they call for you; and live forever.” [Col. 0040A]

81. The following letters of three provosts (epp. 87, 88, 89) also show how great was the estimation held by many of St. Hildegard’s knowledge of every kind of hidden matter. The first is from the provost of St. Victor’s at Mainz, who confesses himself stained by many sins: “These, lady,” he says, “you know better through the Holy Spirit’s revelation; make known to me whether I have hope of salvation, whether I am predestined [Col. 0040B] to life or foreknown unto death,” etc.

St. Hildegard, however, does not answer the final question, as elsewhere she often does not, although she sometimes seems clearly to foretell eternal life for holy men. She therefore exhorts him to turn from evil and do good, and instills hope in these words: “Therefore choose straight paths for yourself, and you shall live forever.” She also inspires fear, concluding: “Therefore, O son of God, rise quickly before the sun sets for you.”

The Provost of Koblenz addresses the Saint thus: “Because in all my tribulations you have always refreshed me by your consolations [the text reads *mercasti*, perhaps *recreasti*], and all that you foretold to me has now been fulfilled, I ask that you now also entreat the Lord of mercy to console me in all things which oppress me outwardly and inwardly,” [Col. 0040C] etc. In reply, the Saint exhorts him to correct “the changeableness of his habits,” warns that God’s judgments are hidden, and adds: “But God does not command me to explain his judgments concerning you, but to pray for you.”

The Provost of St. Andrew’s at Cologne complains that he is assailed by many temptations, and consults the Saint: “I am prepared,” he says, “to do whatever you command me, whether by divine revelation or by the wisdom of your counsel. Do not be afraid, nor conceal anything,” etc. St. Hildegard responds in such a way as at once to teach the provost what his moral character is, instruct him, and admonish him to become better.

82. A certain abbot, greatly troubled by the schism against Alexander III, supported by Emperor Frederick, and on whose account many prelates were suffering persecution, sought St Hildegard’s counsel, writing as follows (Letter 95):

> “Since the Church is limping in respect of its apostolic dignity and name, and truly does not know to which head it should look, [lacuna] having taken good counsel, I flee to you and at the same time urgently beg that you will be willing to write back to me whatever, instructed by the Holy Spirit, you judge concerning this matter or concerning myself; for I am prepared to obey your counsels in all things.”

St Hildegard did not give an unqualified answer to this question, because, as she implies, such an answer would not have been beneficial. For she begins thus:

> “I saw and heard these words spoken to you: Your mind is like a plough, which overturns and divides things hard, rough, and soft. For you attend to knowing, overturning, and dividing those things which are of such hardness that you cannot break through them; and those which are of such roughness that they would wound you if you touched them; and those which are of such softness that you would crush them if you wished to touch them harshly and severely. For the hardness which has limped away from the Sun of righteousness now surrounds the Church, and you are not able to pierce it. Therefore say in your heart to God: ‘Lord, who knowest all things, I desire to obey thee in my teachers, so long as they do not compel me to resist the Catholic faith.’”

These words may be explained as follows. The hardness was in the schism itself, the roughness in secular rulers, and the softness in bishops; as though she said: The schism is too hard for you to be able to remove it; and “the princes of the world are in such roughness that they would not heed you, if you told them what you hold to be just according to your understanding,” as follows [Col. 0041B]; while bishops “now pursue such softness” that you would not know what to do with them. Yet the Saint advises the abbot to hold fast to his disciples after Christ’s example, and to leave the rest to God.

83. As many abbots consulted St Hildegard, so did no few abbesses. The abbess at Altuvich—Altwick according to Trithemius, in the diocese of Utrecht—writes to the Saint as follows (Letter 100):

> “Our Lord [lacuna] inspired my heart, I think, to abandon the burden of governance which I bear heavily, and to shut myself up in the solitude of some cell [lacuna].”

A little later St Hildegard answers:

> “O daughter, it is not beneficial before God that you should cast off your burden and abandon God’s sheepfold, when you possess that light by which you shine upon it” etc. [Col. 0041C]

The abbess at Kizingun—perhaps Kitzingen in Franconia on the Main, where the Ursulines are now established—after many praises addresses the Saint in these words (Letter 101):

> “Let your voice sound in my ears; and tell me, as I ask, by divine disclosure, which is more salutary: whether I should abandon the burden I bear, or carry it longer.”

St Hildegard answers by praising the abbess and encouraging confidence in God. The abbess at Widergoldesdorf asks the same thing again in this way (Letter 108):

> “Therefore, sweetest one, I earnestly entreat you to deign to inquire of God for yourself whether it be His will that I bear this burden or cast it off; for I have continued in it more because of the constraint of obedience than through love of God.”

St Hildegard urges her to continue steadfastly to bear the martyrdom by which, she acknowledges, the abbess is afflicted in her office [Col. 0041D], consoling her thus:

> “Yet in this matter very many saints come to God as martyrs. And therefore you too trust in God, for He will not forsake you, and the Holy Spirit will lessen your pain.”

84. The abbess of Crouchdal, called Crutendal in the *Life*, who had seen St Hildegard at her own house, begins her letter as follows (Letter 109):

> “After, through God’s help, I had deserved to be relieved of faintheartedness of spirit and of the preceding storm by your long-desired presence and gracious conversation, I rested for a little while; and because I do not doubt that your words proceed not from human ingenuity but from the true Light [lacuna], I have still deferred carrying out what I had proposed to do, in accordance with your counsel.”

It is clear from the reply that she too had been considering resigning her office. [Col. 0042A] St Hildegard answers briefly:

> “Where you see mud, wash it away; and cause that which is dry to have savour.”

She then warns her not to judge others rashly. She instructs her about the solitary life as follows:

> “For in the solitary life, which the sound of your words seeks, you would not be able to rest because of the changing dispositions of different people; for then your latter condition would become much worse than the former, and indeed as grievous as the loss of a stone.”

85. The abbess of the upper monastery at Regensburg, writing to St Hildegard (Letter 112), asks for an answer “about two inquiries”: “whether,” she says, “in the matter on account of which my heart is now especially distressed, some danger is to be feared, or whether one ought to presume upon God’s mercy.” This had been explained in another letter [Col. 0042B]. The other inquiry concerned resigning the office of abbess. To this St Hildegard replies:

> “But now, sweetest daughter, attend to the care entrusted to you with such truthfulness that you do not abandon it because of weariness or labour.”

She immediately urges zeal in good works. But she rebukes the first question—perhaps concerning predestination—in stern words.

86. A certain priest, wishing to embrace monastic life and grieved that this intention of his was being delayed, had recourse to the Saint (Letter 119). In reply St Hildegard exhorts him to constancy in his purpose; nevertheless, she does not specify the place or order to which he should attach himself. The only reason for her silence, I think, was that God had revealed nothing to her about those matters. Thus I frequently observe that the Saint does not answer questions put to her, or answers only in part, because more was requested than God wished to disclose through her. [Col. 0042C]

87. No less secret was the matter sought by a certain master of Utrecht (Letter 123), a matter about which the Saint very rarely answered when asked, although she did disclose it when questioned by certain pious persons. He complains that because of his sins he is afflicted in many ways. The Saint writes him instruction, and then adds:

> “But now, O servant of God, in the better way little windows appear in you in splendid light, so that by longing you desire the good. But on the other way [Col. 0042D] you are occupied in a black whirlwind. Yet you, O soldier, arise with clear soldiery and overcome this whirlwind, for God’s grace touches and admonishes you,” etc.

88. A certain anonymous man of Weision urgently entreats the Saint not only to offer prayers for him, but also to inquire of God concerning secrets proposed in these words (Letter 133):

> “What is the reason that He deigns not to rescue me, though I so often cry to Him, from the depths of wickedness and from the mire of filth; whether I should hope any longer for pardon; whether He will grant me a troubled and contrite spirit—my lady, inquire by earnest prayer,” etc.

But instead of answering a question of this kind, which she plainly disapproves, St Hildegard writes a useful admonition that he should remain steadfast in the good.

A certain canon of Utrecht writes thus to St Hildegard [Col. 0043A] (Letter 134):

> “Therefore in humility I entreat [lacuna] that you may set before me, through the ministry of your manifestation, the secrets of divine revelation concerning my condition, especially according to the inward person, for the instruction and lamp of my spirit. Indeed, you owe this by your promise; for when I was travelling toward Rome, I obtained this from your charity.”

But in reply St Hildegard warns him to rise more quickly and flee from the devil.

## § VII. The Saint consulted by many communities concerning matters that could be corrected, or other secrets; and invited to commit admonitions to writing

89. Thus far I have shown that St Hildegard was consulted by many abbots and abbesses, and also by other persons [Col. 0043B], concerning hidden matters which she could not know without divine revelation. I shall now bring forward entire communities of clerics or monks who wrote to the Saint for a similar reason and with equal confidence.

Let the clergy of the metropolitan church of Cologne lead the procession. They had seen St Hildegard in their city and, in astonishment, heard her give salutary admonitions. Hence Philip the dean, together with all the clergy, writes to her as follows (Letter 48):

> “Because we love your motherly compassion, we make known to you that, after you departed from us—when by divine command you had come to us and revealed to us the words of life as God inspired you—we were led into the greatest amazement because [Col. 0043C] God works such marvellous secrets of His own in so frail a vessel, in so frail a sex of humankind,” etc.

90–92. The Saint sent back a very long writing, in which, in most serious language and in God’s name, she rebukes the negligence of clerics in the care of souls and their other vices; she gives many admonitions and also intermingles many predictions. About the middle of the letter, she begins to foretell many evils by which God would chastise the Church, because churchmen were neither in conduct nor in doctrine what they ought to have been. She predicts future heretics so clearly that no doubt seems to remain on that subject. Yet she mixes in certain good things, and sufficiently declares that the heretics would not prevail altogether.

[Col. 0043D] St Hildegard seems here to have foretold Luther’s times; but this will be perceived more clearly by anyone willing carefully to weigh all that was predicted, not only to the people of Cologne, but also to those of Trier and to Werner of Kircheim. No small danger then threatened Cologne, which saw its archbishop corrupted by heretics; but it happily raised its head and expelled the heretics, as the Saint seems to warn them.

93–96. St Hildegard had likewise been at Trier, probably on the same journey on which she visited Cologne. Accordingly the provost of St Peter’s, with all the clergy of Trier, writes to her (Letter 49); St Hildegard answers him at length, admonishing and rebuking many things. After severely reproving the negligence of pastors and prelates [Col. 0044A], she proceeds to predictions of future good and evil; and I do not hesitate to observe that I find nothing in all these things which has not been fulfilled. Anyone with even a slight acquaintance with ecclesiastical history will readily see this, provided that he considers how much loss the Church suffered in the sixteenth century, and how much, even in that period, Catholics began to surpass their forebears in doctrine and morals—forebears who had lived many centuries before St Hildegard and some centuries after her. Trier suffered greatly from heretics, as the Saint had predicted; but it prevailed and reformed its former morals, as she clearly announced would happen.

97. We have already seen, at no. 47, the letter of the abbot of Eberbach to the Saint. Meffridus, prior of that Cistercian monastery, also wrote to her together with the whole community [Col. 0044B], asking for prayers and for the Saint’s letter which, they say, “we have heard that you wrote by the Holy Spirit concerning secular persons and unlearned people converted to the spiritual life, whom we call *conversi*.” Without doubt the Saint sent the letter addressed “To the Grey Monks,” that is, to the Cistercians, which is quite long (Reply to Letter 51). The letter indeed contains much praise for that order; but the Saint reproves those “whom they themselves call *conversi*, of whom very many do not turn themselves to God in their conduct.” The prudent reader will find other instructions in the same letter.

98. Werner of Kirchem—a town in Swabia [Col. 0044C], in the duchy of Württemberg, where the Saint had also been—with “the other brethren of his community,” not only earnestly requested St Hildegard’s prayers and adorned her with a remarkable eulogy, but also wished, like the people of Cologne and Trier, to have her words committed to writing (Letter 52).

99–100. The Saint begins her reply thus:

> “While I lay long in the bed of illness, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1170, I saw, awake in body and mind, a most beautiful image,” etc.

There follow the most serious complaints of that image, which, as is explained below, represented the Church, against the grave vices and sins of priests. Then follow predictions entirely fulfilled in the sixteenth century:

> “For rulers [Col. 0044D] and a rash people will rush upon you, O priests, who have hitherto neglected me; they will cast you down and drive you away, and take your riches from you, because you did not heed the time of your priestly office,” etc.

101. Surely anyone who does not see that all these things were fulfilled knows nothing of what happened in the sixteenth century in a great part of Germany and in other kingdoms, indeed in Swabia itself where these words were spoken. For greater clarity concerning the prediction, however, I observe that the consolation added in the writings to Cologne and Trier is not added here: namely, that those cities would afterwards flourish more in the faith. This in fact did not happen at Kircheim. On the contrary, another prediction is added, expressed in these words:

> “And again I, a poor little womanly form, saw a drawn sword hanging in the air, one edge of which was turned toward heaven and the other toward earth. And this sword was stretched out over the spiritual people [lacuna]. And I saw that this sword cut off certain persons from the place of spiritual men, just as Jerusalem was cut off after the Lord’s Passion.” [Col. 0045A]

This too happened most clearly in Luther’s time. Finally, a certain, rather qualified consolation is added:

> “Yet I saw that in this adversity God will preserve for Himself many God-fearing, pure, and simple priests,” etc.

102. For another reason the community of brothers at Hagenhe wrote to St Hildegard (Letter 53). They were divided by discord, which had become known to the Saint and for which she had already begun to provide a remedy. St Hildegard replied by a long letter [Col. 0045B] containing instruction concerning many vices and virtues, with admonition and exhortation to cultivate virtues.

103. The priests at Rutdelingun—perhaps Reutlingen, commonly so called, in Swabia—write to St Hildegard as follows (Letter 124):

> “We rejoiced and were delighted in the things said to us, namely that a consoling embassy would come to us. And we waited and waited, yet you have not attended to us.”

A little later they indicate that they had undertaken something new and urgently request the Saint’s prayers. I suspect that they were a community of priests who had embraced religious life and wished to follow St Hildegard’s counsels. Certainly the Saint answers as though writing [Col. 0045C] to priests who had renounced worldly concerns, saying:

> “O what sort are those who seek life in pilgrimage, and who in exile are strangers to that portion which they have left for God’s sake.”

Moreover, she praises their purpose and exhorts them to fortitude in God’s service.

104. The superintendent of a certain hospital house, called “master of the poor at Lutherum,” consults St Hildegard with his companions (Letter 136) in these words:

> “Therefore we desire to hear from you the salutary instructions of your holiness, and carefully to understand from you the state of our life,” etc.

In reply St Hildegard elegantly expounds the parable of the man who fell among robbers and was raised up and treated by the Samaritan. She warns them that, just as Christ healed Adam’s wounds [Col. 0045D] through Himself and His own, so they should imitate that true Samaritan by caring for the bodies and souls of the poor.

105. The Benedictine monks of Siegburg, across the Rhine in the diocese of Cologne, write to St Hildegard as follows (Letter 137):

> “With what special affection of charity we have chosen you as our spiritual mother and received you into the fellowship of our prayers, He who knows all secrets knows,” etc.

At length St Hildegard replied with an admonition that praises the monastery of Siegburg, though she implies that not all there were equally fervent.

106–107. The monks of Hirsau, whose abbot we saw writing to St Hildegard at no. 68, have recourse to her for another reason (Letter 138). In that monastery [Col. 0046A], formerly most flourishing, discord had arisen between the abbot and the prior, to whom the greater part of the monks adhered. For this reason they seek the Saint’s judgment. The Saint replied with a letter containing much consolation, which restored peace. She says that the disobedience of inferiors toward superiors had arisen from the latter’s lack of mercy, and all are invited to show mercy to one another.

Trithemius, who narrates this discord in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1161, after quoting St Hildegard’s letter, adds:

> “After the brethren had received these letters from Blessed Hildegard, they rejoiced not a little in the Lord; and, pierced in heart, they began unanimously to discuss peace among themselves. Abbot Manegold also—whose letter to the Saint and her reply were discussed at no. 68—following the virgin’s admonitions, expelled every bitterness from his heart and promised that henceforth he would show himself in all things, to the extent of his ability, a most wise father to his sons according to the Rule. Therefore the brethren, touched by the sweetness of his words, promised that in all things they would show themselves humble and obedient subjects to their father. Thus through the mercy of almighty God and the prayers of St Hildegard, peace was restored among those in disagreement, and the desired end was put to the disturbance.” [Col. 0046B]

Moreover, under the year 1160 the praised Trithemius writes that St Hildegard was then at Hirsau and had foretold to the monks that discord would arise unless they amended themselves. But the cited letter makes no mention of that journey to Hirsau or of St Hildegard’s prediction. Therefore, even if the Saint truly was at Hirsau at some time, as we shall see in § 12, I am wholly persuaded that the Saint’s journey there must be dated later. As regards the prediction of the reported discord, I think it was no other than that found in the letter to Abbot Manegold at no. 68. [Col. 0046C]

108. The monks of Eberbach, whose abbot had previously written to St Hildegard, as we saw at no. 47, and likewise their prior at no. 97, unanimously conveyed to the Saint this request (Letter 139):

> “And we pray with humble petition that you do not conceal from us what is in us to be corrected; but that, as shall please the Lord, who reveals many secrets to you, you endeavour to indicate it to us.” [Col. 0046D]

The Saint did what was requested and warned them to beware discord and contention.

109. The prior and monks of Zwifalten have recourse to the Saint for their reform (Letter 140). The Saint replies in a long and vigorous admonition, sharply censuring their negligence and various vices and urging them to repentance and amendment. The nuns of Zwifalten write similarly to St Hildegard (Letter 141):

> “We also ask your compassion,” they say, “that, while you attend to the divine vision, you direct admonitory words to us and do not neglect to show us how we ought to return from the way of negligence to the way of correction.”

To them the Saint sent a most vigorous admonition, reproving and rebuking them, and exhorting them to [Col. 0047A] a more regular life. Moreover, I shall show at no. 179 that Swabian monks and nuns of Zwifalten are meant here.

110. The prior and monks of Mount St Disibod, to whom St Hildegard could not have been unknown, seek her admonitions partly by prayers and partly by complaints (Letter 142). St Hildegard replied with a lengthy exhortation, into which she seems to intermingle predictions of future events, and in which she urges those monks to return to their first fervour.

111. The monks of St Eucharius at Trier write to St Hildegard as to a mother (Letter 143), praising God, who, they say, “has hitherto hidden these things from the wise and prudent, but marvellously reveals them in our days to your humility.” [Col. 0047B] The Saint replied at length, praising some things in these monks and reproving others, and teaching obedience, humility, charity, and other virtues.

There follows the letter of “the prior and monks of Cistellum” to the Saint (Letter 144), whom they say they venerate “as superior and as a most beloved mother.” If we consult the reply to this letter, we shall see that its opening is the same as the beginning of St Hildegard’s letter reported in Alberic’s *Chronicle* under the year 1153, where that letter of the Saint is said to have been written in 1153 “to the general Cistercian chapter.” Alberic is right, I think, because the Cistercian monastery is sometimes also called Cistellum, as Valesius states in his *Notitia Galliarum*, p. 146; and in fact the name *Cistella* agrees better with the French *Cîteaux* than does the common name *Cistercium*. [Col. 0047C]

Among other things, these Cistellensians address St Hildegard thus:

> “We ask your clemency that you do not hesitate to write to us, according as God shall show you, what in us and in our order—that is, the monastic order—displeases you, or rather displeases the divine eyes.”

St Hildegard did what was asked. She wrote a fairly long letter in which she vigorously complains that “the sweetest charity” has been torn apart by them. Martène printed only the earlier part of the letter because three leaves had been torn from the manuscript.

112. Finally, the last of the letters to St Hildegard printed by Martène is that of “Henry [rather, [Col. 0047D] Helinger] abbot and the convent of Mount St Disibod” (Letter 145); Martène did not print the Saint’s answer to it. Now, on the occasion of the alteration of the name Helinger into Henry—an error as certain as it is remarkable—I think the reader should be warned that a number of proper names of people and places have undoubtedly been corrupted in Martène. I have attempted to restore quite a few from Trithemius or elsewhere, though I have not been able to correct all with certainty. For although I sometimes clearly see that German names have been distorted from their natural sound by a French editor, it is not equally easy to substitute the true forms. I therefore preferred to leave uncorrected those which could not be restored by an almost certain conjecture. Helinger’s letter shows the fruit borne by the Saint’s presence at Mount St Disibod. [Col. 0048A] The request itself shows that the monks were eager to gather still greater fruit from her admonitions.

113. Their second request is appended as follows:

> “Further, with unanimous consent, opportunely and importunately we knock at the door of your charity for an account of the deeds and virtues, and likewise the life, of our patron and yours, the most blessed Disibod, in whose house you were nurtured from your very cradle,” etc.

The Saint satisfied this request as far as she wished. For we possess a *Life of St Disibod*, published by us under 8 July. The same work exists in our manuscript marked O Ms. 12. What St Hildegard truly answered to the earlier request, and whether she answered it at all, I wholly do not know. [Col. 0048B] Martène indeed says: “The response to this letter of Helenger exists among the published letters of St Hildegard”; but he is mistaken, for there exists only the answer to another letter of Helenger (Letter 39), to be mentioned at no. 123.

## § VIII. The Saint also consulted on theological and scriptural questions, and others relating to faith or morals

114. Although we cannot but marvel that the Saint was consulted about hidden and secret matters by so many men distinguished in rank and learning, I am nevertheless compelled to wonder still more when I observe that most subtle theological questions and most difficult questions from sacred Scripture were referred to an unlearned woman, wholly without acquired scholarly study; and that she did not hesitate to give theological and scriptural answers, although she sometimes gave no full answer to questions that were more curious than useful.

Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, who had earlier visited the Saint, proposed to her a highly subtle question, writing as follows (Letter 14):

> “When we were passing through the imperial court by way of you, because you are imbued with the Holy Spirit, we entrusted it to your charity for explanation. In the Father abides eternity; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the connection of eternity and equality. We now desire to see this explained according to what God has revealed to you.” [Col. 0048C]

The Saint begins with a brief exhortation encouraging Eberhard to feed his flock diligently. Then she explains the eternity of the Father, the equality of the Son, and the connection of the Holy Spirit in a sufficiently long and subtle discourse, such that a most learned theologian would sweat greatly, and perhaps in vain, to produce such an exposition. She finally concludes the letter thus:

> “Now, O shepherd and father of peoples, may God grant you to come to the light, where you may receive the knowledge of true blessedness.” [Col. 0048D]

115. A certain priest, whose name is indicated only by C, earnestly commends himself to St Hildegard’s prayers (Letter 43), “that,” he says, “being brought to the Lord by your prayers, I may deserve to be enlightened and healed from the blindness of my heart.” And shortly afterward: “Teach me also concerning the body and blood of Christ, in which is the whole hope of the faithful,” etc.

The Saint begins her reply [Col. 0049A] as follows:

> “In a true vision, with wakeful eyes, I heard and saw these words concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body: God remained what He was, and assumed what He was not.”

She adds the Incarnation of the Son of God; having narrated this, she continues:

> “Therefore the same power of the Most High which wrought flesh in the Virgin’s womb changes upon the altar, at the words of the priest, the offering of bread and wine into the sacrament of flesh and blood, sustaining it by its power.”

She adds many other things, which I omit for brevity’s sake; they should be seen in the same place.

116. Wibert or Guibert, a monk of Gembloux of the Order of St Benedict in Brabant, transmitted to St Hildegard thirty-eight most difficult questions, collected from the Old and New Testaments and ecclesiastical history [Col. 0049B]. The monks of Villers—also a very celebrated abbey in Brabant—had entrusted these questions to him when he was travelling to the Saint; and he asked her by letter to undertake their solution. In his letter, now among the shorter works, he explains why he did not carry them himself. The Saint undertook the arduous task proposed to her and answered every question. Yet this answer is such that it does not resolve every doubt. She added to her response an elegant letter in which she exhorts Wibert to virtues appropriate and necessary to the monastic profession, especially to [*enaritatem*, an uncertain reading] and humility.

117. The community of the monastery of Hunnen sought from St Hildegard teaching more useful for rightly ordering life: namely, an exposition of the Rule of St Benedict. They say that they flee to her “at a critical moment of need, as to the most secure refuge of an impregnable stronghold,” and, after magnificent praises, add:

> “Prostrate at the feet of your holiness, all together we ask the gracious kindness of your compassion that you leave us some memorial word on the Rule of our blessed father Benedict, greatly necessary to us [lacuna].” [Col. 0049C]

The Saint did what was requested and wrote commentaries on the Rule of St Benedict, printed after her letters.

118. A certain priest of Trier, who had the care of souls, both requests St Hildegard’s prayers and “words of consolation” (Letter 125), then adds:

> “And kindly show me how I may preside over those [Col. 0049D] whom I must govern under the rule of the priesthood.”

The Saint replies briefly but beautifully with several instructions. First, she warns that the sinner is one whom “the physician should frequently anoint with mercy, and should not permit the foul bruise to remain in him; for leprosy is cleansed away by the supreme Physician when a person shows himself to the priest.” Second, she observes that some come without due preparation and without a purpose of amendment. Third, she adds:

> “But a person who always abandons his wicked deeds with sorrow, so that he does not wish repeatedly to be plunged into filthy sins, is not to be bound in the manner aforesaid, but is to be anointed in his sorrows, wherever he may be. For the great Physician raises up those who are watchful, rebukes those who sleep, and kills those who persist in their evils.” [Col. 0050A]

119. A certain Parisian master of theology shows (Letter 127) that St Hildegard’s fame was great even in Paris. After various praises, he proposes to her a difficult and subtle question, writing:

> “But although we are far distant from you, having confidence in you, we ask certain things of you; namely, because very many contend that Paternity and Divinity are not God, do not delay to explain and send us what you think concerning this in heavenly matters.”

This was the error of Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, who retracted it in 1148 at the Council of Reims, chiefly through the action of St Bernard. St Hildegard answers the question proposed with remarkable humility [Col. 0050B], comparing herself to a little feather which God lifts from the earth and commands to fly.

120. A certain brother (Letter 128) complains greatly about the schism by which the Church was then divided; but St Hildegard made no answer concerning it at that time. At the end, however, he proposes another question in these words:

> “For I am often assaulted, both secretly and openly, by malicious spirits, who greatly weary me and wish to deceive me; and I ask that you make known to me by your writings what you think of these.”

The Saint gives a fairly lengthy answer, dividing aerial spirits into four groups and asserting that human beings are tempted by them in different ways. To the first group she assigns temptations “through lust [lacuna], in every kind of vice.” She says that the second group rules “in every [Col. 0050C] instability, and sends a person into mad anger.” Of the third she says that it produces errors “as if in manifestations of angels and prophecy,” and greatly harms through “vainglory, boasting, and obstinacy.” Finally, she says that the fourth group deals more familiarly with people “in manifold diversity,” yet abhors the cross and Passion of the Lord; it permits “certain good things in people,” but “takes moderation away from them in those same good things.”

## § IX. Many write to the Saint to obtain prayers, consolation, admonitions, and similar things; she replies to them

121. We have seen that St Hildegard was consulted by many concerning secret matters or difficult questions. [Col. 0050D] We shall now see her approached by the letters of very many people for various reasons, as though she were the common refuge of almost all.

I first place here St Elisabeth of Schönau, who flourished at the same time in the diocese of Trier and became famous for many revelations. St Elisabeth died earlier, namely in 1165, as has been shown by us in the account of her acts given under 18 June (*Patrologia*, vol. CXCV), where is also printed the rather long letter which she writes to St Hildegard to obtain consolation (Letter 45).

122. St Hildegard replies in her usual manner, first stating that she speaks not from her own intellect “but from the serene Light.” She then discusses the human being and God’s inspiration, by which He deigns to enlighten some people above others. Finally she turns to St Elisabeth thus:

> “Hear, O anxious daughter, for the ambitious suggestion of the ancient serpent somewhat harasses those people whom God’s inspiration has thus imbued [lacuna].” [Col. 0051A]

From the *Chronicle* of Alberic the monk, under the year 1155, it may be inferred that St Hildegard was also visited at some time by St Elisabeth.

123. Helenger, abbot of St Disibod and successor to Cono in 1155, who had known St Hildegard for a long time, writes to her as follows (Letter 39):

> “Although the whole world proclaims with true testimony that you are enriched by the jubilation of the Holy Spirit, I, who ought to have been the first to do so and to invite others to your blessedness, have until now hidden myself in idle weariness; but at last, rebuked by fear and shame [Col. 0051B], I have thought it necessary to greet you with these words.”

He soon begins to accuse himself and complain that regular discipline has been poorly observed in his monastery. At the end he says:

> “Therefore direct writings of your consolation to my lowliness,” etc.

The Saint replied with many exhortations to amendment of life. Finally, near the end, she adds:

> “But I, a poor little woman, see in you a blackest fire kindled against us; but forget it in sound understanding, lest its grace and blessing depart from you during the time of your office.”

St Hildegard did in fact have difficulties with the abbot of St Disibod concerning the free election of her directors, as we shall later see.

[Col. 0051C] 124. The abbot of St Emmeram at Regensburg—who calls himself *provisor* in the heading, though both letters sufficiently indicate that he was the superior or abbot of the monastery—implores St Hildegard’s aid for another person (Letter 35). Whether he was a monk or another person sent to the Saint is not clearly evident; nor do I find with what success St Hildegard laboured for him. Yet from her response I suspect that he was a monk troubled by severe pangs of conscience and perhaps scruples. Whoever he was, the Saint exhorts the abbot in stern language to care for his flock.

125. The abbot of Neuburg likewise writes to St. Hildegard with great feeling (Letter 36), saying that fear of war had prevented him from coming to her. He then earnestly requests her prayers. St. Hildegard replied, exhorting him to courage in pastoral care, aptly observing that in time of war a soldier must not cast aside his weapons because difficulties have arisen. The abbess at Elostat makes similar requests by letter (Letter 44), weaving a distinguished eulogy of the Saint. St. Hildegard replies briefly but very warmly, encouraging her to continue her labor for those entrusted to her. Yet, she rightly observes, prudence is necessary in God’s service. Likewise G., provost of Frankfurt, writes a friendly letter (Letter 46), to which she replies with a serious exhortation to reform his conduct.

126. I have thus far reviewed the letters formerly published which concern this subject. Many others must be added, recently brought out by Martène in vol. II of the *Collectio Amplissima*. Here the abbot of Maulbronn writes (Letter 63; elsewhere Mulbronn, in the diocese of Speyer and the duchy of Württemberg), requesting letters “by which his body and soul may be instructed, strengthened, and consoled.” Believing himself near death, the abbot of St. Michael’s at Bamberg urgently asks for St. Hildegard’s prayers (Letter 64), and for “writings of consolation.” To both the Saint replied so as to exhort them to virtue and provide useful instruction. The abbot of St. Eucharius at Trier writes to the Saint (Letter 67), requesting prayers and “words of admonition.” In another letter (Letter 68) he again demands “the promised letters,” adding at the end: “But also write back to me whatever seems good to you concerning the matter entrusted to you.” To the former letter St. Hildegard appropriately replied with admonitions concerning the feeding of the flock, and likewise to the latter.

127. The abbot of Bousonville in Lorraine, having fallen into ill repute together with his monks because of disturbances that had arisen in his monastery, writes to St. Hildegard (Letter 69), asking for “some word of consolation” on this matter, and for prayers by which they might be reconciled “to God and men.” In reply, St. Hildegard describes the condition of that monastery and exhorts them to amendment. Nicholas, abbot of Halesbrunn—Heilsbronn in Trithemius—indicating (Letter 71) that he had been accustomed to visit St. Hildegard from time to time, asks for letters by which he may be forewarned, and for prayers by which he may be delivered from evil. The Saint replies, praising his intention and exhorting him to labor. She adds certain further, rather obscure matters.

[Col. 0052C] This is followed by a letter (Letter 72) from five abbots together, of the Cistercian Order and the diocese of Besançon: namely, of Bella-vallis, Cari-locus, Clari-fons, Charitas, and Bethania. After first adorning the Saint with a splendid eulogy, they make two distinct requests. The first they state thus: “We most humbly beseech you to take care to communicate to us whatever may be divinely revealed to you concerning our condition.” The second is as follows:

“But this bearer of the present letter is a noblewoman and the wife of a man who loves her dearly. With great devotion she comes to you humble and on foot, although she could come on horseback and with a large retinue. This is the reason for her coming. For a long time she has remained barren, although she first bore children; but after they died, since she bears no others, both she and her husband are afflicted with intense grief. Therefore she flees to you, handmaid and intimate servant of Christ, trusting that by your merits and prayers you may obtain from God that she may yet become fruitful and offer to Christ the blessed fruit of her womb in the begetting of offspring,” etc.

To the first request St. Hildegard answered with excellent admonitions and instructions, while praising the abbots. To the second she replied:

“But as to your request that the matron be made fruitful with God’s help, this lies within God’s will and power; for He knows where He grants offspring and where He takes offspring away . . . Since you have asked me, I shall pray to God for her; but may He Himself do in this matter what He has mercifully and lovingly ordained.”

128. The abbot of Eberburda, situated outside Germany—perhaps the abbot of Averbode in Brabant, since the Dutch and French name of that abbey bears some resemblance to *Eberbude*—in a rather lengthy letter full of praise (Letter 73), asks for St. Hildegard’s prayers. She instead exhorts him to feed his flock diligently and also to turn his eyes upon himself. Another abbot (Letter 75), who had often spoken personally with St. Hildegard and compares her with the ancient prophets, requests “words of consolation” by which she may “raise him up as he tosses in storms.” Through various figures, she exhorts him to keep vigilant bravely, “before,” she says, “the shadow of your death draws near.”

The provost [Col. 0053B] of Flonheim—“then of the Regulars,” says Trithemius—in the diocese of Mainz, presents his prayer to St. Hildegard thus (Letter 76): “Meanwhile, I pray, let my devotion be acceptable to you; and, as I formerly asked you verbally, pray to the Lord for me, that He may reveal to you those things which concern me,” etc. The Saint admonishes him to keep watch vigorously and to correct his sheepfold, adding at the end:

“O good soldier, arise now, for the grace of God runs toward you, and you shall live forever, so that you may be a living stone in the heavenly Jerusalem.”

The superior of monks at Eberstadt complains (Letter 79) that he had received no answer to his letters and requests St. Hildegard’s prayers. In replying, she seems to disapprove some scruple in him and exhorts him to offer sacrifice, saying: “You have confidence when you think of the Son of God; yet you hesitate to break that food which you yourself wish to eat in the prompting of your mind,” etc.

129. The superior at Selbold, formerly in the diocese of Mainz, after celebrating St. Hildegard in lofty praise, not only earnestly requests her prayers (Letter 80), but also adds:

“Nor do I doubt that, through these present letters and by His revelation, you know my whole condition and everything that occurs around me—past, present, and future. Therefore, if the lowliness of my littleness may presume in any way to ask this, I beseech you, wholly submitted in soul and body at the feet of your holiness, not to disdain to gladden my soul by your writings concerning that same condition of mine: whether by admonishing me about the past and present, or by warning me and making me cautious about the future and the end of my life, if this be not disagreeable to you.”

St. Hildegard answered what he asked, though not all of it. She indicates, however, that humility is especially necessary for him, giving this reason: “For God does not dwell in that dwelling which wishes to stand in itself, but loves the house which does not know itself, and gives it the finest ointment.”

The provost at Herde writes to the Saint (Letter 81):

“What thanksgivings, most holy Lady and Mother, can we worthily render to your kindness? For in visiting our monastery you were willing neither to heed the excessive weakness of your body nor, because of the exceeding sweetness of your heart, to shrink from the difficulty of the journey; and again, by a repeated visit, you endeavored to gladden us.”

He then asks for prayers and “a reply.” St. Hildegard, answering, exhorts him to remain in his place, as though he had asked advice about changing it—which perhaps he had done in person.

130. The provost of the Augustinians at Hameln in the duchy of Brunswick, who had once visited St. Hildegard, being worn down by a long bodily illness, asks for the Saint’s prayers and writings (Letter 82). He adds: “Most holy Lady, I beg you to send word, if it is permitted, concerning the end of my sufferings.” The Saint replied with instruction and exhortation to endure bodily infirmities more courageously and steadily; but she makes no mention of the end of his sufferings.

The abbot at Wadego—called by Trithemius Wadegos, of Wadegote or Vadegote, a Premonstratensian house in the diocese of Trier—ardently desired to see the Saint and requests her visit (Letter 83), at least “by writing and prayers, if not by bodily presence.” She sent him a written letter exhorting him to caution and repentance. Likewise the provost at Underestlorf—Elversdorff in Trithemius—asks St. Hildegard in a short letter (Letter 84) for “the help of consolation.” Her reply admonishes him to fear God, to show strength in feeding the sheep, and to maintain purity in speech.

The provost of Erfurt in Thuringia commends to her a member of his household (Letter 90) who is setting out for St. Hildegard “for the love of God,” and also requests her prayers. St. Hildegard replies with salutary admonitions, saying among other things:

“Cease from your sins, for God has not sold you into destruction, but seeks you in the lost sheep that has been called back to life.”

Hartmann, provost of the metropolitan church of Mainz, asks to be taught (Letter 91) what in him displeases God and how he may amend it. The Saint replies with an admonition to flee duplicity and certain other vices, ending thus: “Now pray and trust that God will not abandon you, and dawn will soon come forth to you in deliverance.”

131. Helderic, provost of St. Simeon’s at Trier, requests St. Hildegard’s prayers (Letter 92) and celebrates her with an outstanding eulogy. The Saint replies with a serious exhortation “to wipe away the rust of sins before the shadow of death comes upon you.” [Col. 0054D] The provost at Knechtsteden, of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Cologne, placing great confidence in the Saint (Letter 93), seeks “a remedy of consolation” and wishes to be taught “in what manner he may more fully appease the offense against the divine majesty.” In reply, the Saint exhorts him to great trust in God’s help:

“You also,” she says, “trust in Him, so that you need not be ashamed to place all your works before Him; and say, as a son says to his father when he is rebuked for wrongdoing, that he should not forget his offspring in him.”

The provost of Bonn (Letter 94) declares a remarkable affection for the Saint because, as he says, he had personally found true all that he had previously heard of her by report. St. Hildegard replies by sending an excellent instruction, especially exhorting him to contempt for the world.

[Col. 0055A] 132. A number of abbesses also had recourse to St. Hildegard, in order to obtain from her prayers, consolation, salutary counsels, and similar things. First among these appears Hadelheidis, abbess of Gandersheim (Letter 96), in the duchy of Brunswick, formerly a disciple of the Saint. She declares her affection, asks prayers for herself and her flock, and promises that she will come to the Saint “when circumstances permit,” “so that,” she says, “we may speak mouth to mouth and work hand to hand what is good; and thus may the old fellowship be strengthened, which may the charity of God confirm in us.” In reply St. Hildegard exhorts her to serve the one God steadfastly.

Another abbess, whose location is not named, likewise asks for prayers and “letters of consolation” (Letter 97). In reply, the Saint exhorts her [Col. 0055B] to constancy and trust in God. The abbess at Wechterswinkel—Wekerswinkel in Trithemius, correctly read Wechterswinkel; it was Cistercian and in the diocese of Würzburg—wishes to be received among the daughters of St. Hildegard (Letter 98), and requests her prayers and “admonitory letters, which,” she says, “for the love of God I shall always observe with a willing heart.” To her the Saint replies:

“The Living Light says: Dry sand is useless, and earth which is excessively broken by the plough will not yield proper fruit . . . And dry, stony ground produces thorns and other useless weeds. Thus unsuitable abstinence, which has no just measure and right order, lays low a person’s flesh, because it is not given the freshness of proper nourishment; whence the person also dries up,” etc.

The whole letter continues to treat the same subject beautifully. The abbess of Altena (Letter 99) complains that she has long received no letters and requests them. The Saint responds through various parables, by which she exhorts her to serve God bravely.

133. The abbess of St. Mary’s at Regensburg (Letter 102) greatly rejoices over her acquaintance with St. Hildegard, declaring it to have been salutary to her; indeed, she intimates that by Hildegard’s merits she was preserved when “falling into the crisis of death.” The Saint exhorts her to patience and warns her to guard against anger.

The abbess at Kaufungen—Kessungen in Trithemius—writes to St. Hildegard (Letter 103):

“That flying scroll which was given to the prophet as food has become celebrated on every tongue, and in your mouth also [lacuna] rests [lacuna]. Run therefore, hasten, awaken the Church—indeed the princes of the Church [lacuna]. For we both rejoice and tremble that you have seen the rod from the North keeping watch over iniquity; therefore we desire to receive your consoling letters,” etc.

St. Hildegard does not answer these matters, but seriously warns the abbess to amend her life before death, which she predicts is not far away. “In the spirit,” she says, “I tell you truly: guard your soul [lacuna]. Do this before the day of death [lacuna].”

The abbess at Gerbstedt—Gerbestethde in Trithemius—asks for St. Hildegard’s prayers (Letter 104). “Moreover,” she says, “I ask that you send me something from your books, to which I may always devote myself with all devotion.” The Saint replies by discussing [Col. 0056A] Adam’s fall and Christ’s Incarnation, by which He restored fallen humanity.

134. The abbess of Mount St. Cyriacus near Erfurt (Letter 105) earnestly requests St. Hildegard’s prayers for herself and those under her care. The Saint greatly praises the charity of the aforesaid abbess, but requires in her a mind more at peace. “I shall fulfill,” she says, “all that you ask for your soul. Now cease from an anxious mind, and take rest for yourself.” She also warns her not to crush her body by excessive abstinence. Finally she gives this consolation: “I see your soul very radiant in the pure man.”

The abbess at Lubboldsberg—Lubbelsberg in Trithemius—seeks consolation in affliction (Letter 106), and obtains it abundantly. For St. Hildegard, praising her for abstaining from sins, adds:

“Therefore I see you like the radiant splendor of the sun through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and not at all as the exile of destruction; rather, through repentance, which is the sweetest mother, looking toward the sun as an eagle does; and therefore God loves you greatly.”

Another abbess, whose location is not specified (Letter 106), complains that she is greatly afflicted and endangered by “the temptations of evil spirits.” The Saint replies with an excellent admonition.

135. The abbess of Bamberg (Letter 110) wishes to be received by St. Hildegard “into the fellowship of fraternity” and strengthened by “admonitory letters.” In reply the Saint exhorts her to labor among the people and to keep her daughters under discipline. The abbess of the Old Monastery at Mainz [Col. 0056C] (Letter 111) addresses St. Hildegard thus:

“If, my Lady, you have recovered somewhat from your illness, I rejoice; but if not, I grieve from my heart.”

She also requests prayers and letters. The Saint replies: “God’s will had laid me low as if beneath the sign of death, as though my soul were sighing to depart this world; but God’s grace has now raised me somewhat in a new gift.” She adds that the feeling of compassion is pleasing to God, and exhorts her to constancy in God’s service.

The abbess of Nuss—Nusia in Trithemius—greatly anxious, writes (Letter 113) that she entrusts “the cause of her soul” to St. Hildegard and asks for a reply. The Saint exhorts her to repentance and to performing good works before she dies. [Col. 0056D] The abbess of Cologne (Letter 114), wishing to have St. Hildegard as a mother, writes to her as a daughter in order to obtain consolation. The Saint sends a brief instruction that she should remain steadfast in good things. The abbess of Didenkirchen—Didenkirkim in Trithemius—near Bonn, whom the Saint had previously visited, earnestly asks (Letter 115) for “admonitory words.” St. Hildegard replies with a fairly lengthy instruction on ruling rightly and reforming her conduct.

136. The abbess of Andernach—“near Andernach” in Trithemius—asks various questions (Letter 116) concerning the customs of St. Hildegard’s monastery. Because they seemed novel, the abbess reverently asks their rationale, even raising several passages of Scripture in objection. [Col. 0057A] St. Hildegard replies with a lengthy letter in which she explains the reasons for the adornment of her nuns and for her practice of receiving only noblewomen, as may be seen there.

The abbess of Crouchdal [Crudendal]—probably different from the woman whose letter I mentioned in no. 84, since one letter gives the name H. and the other A.—earnestly requests (Letter 117) that St. Hildegard indicate how she may appease God “for her transgressions.” The Saint replies with a long instruction in which she commends many virtues, especially charity, obedience, and humility.

137. A certain nun, indicating her name by the letter G. (Letter 118), formerly a disciple of St. Hildegard but long absent and far from her—probably because she had been promoted to some office—declares her love for the Saint in these words: “What shall I write or what shall I say to a Mother so singular and so most dearly beloved in Christ?” etc. She adds her hope of seeing her again and earnestly requests prayers. Hildegard replies with great praise and consolation for the virgin, addressing her near the end thus: “Now I rejoice concerning you, because in you have been fulfilled the things I heard and desired concerning you; and rejoice with me . . .” She concludes: “Rejoice therefore and be glad in your God, because you shall live forever.”

An anonymous person (Letter 120) makes many excuses and asks pardon because he had not visited the Saint for a long time, not even by letters; at the same time he expresses her remarkable graciousness. [Col. 0057C] The Saint sends a brief instruction exhorting him to contempt for the world. A Benedictine monk (Letter 121) asks for prayers and “letters of correction.” St. Hildegard, replying, praises his good desires and instructs him that they must be purer and that he himself must be strong.

138. Another anonymous person requests St. Hildegard’s prayers in these words (Letter 122): “I acknowledge that I have sinned; pray for me. I seek no earthly gain, no passing thing, but the grace of my God and the salvation of my soul. Help me,” etc. The Saint responds by exhorting him to repentance, of which she sets out five stages.

A certain brother (Letter 126) complains that he is weighed down by sins and surrounded by “a spirit of blasphemy.” St. Hildegard sends him an instruction in which [Col. 0057D] she says: “Thus a person who, through the knowledge of good and evil, remembers that he has sinned greatly, when he sighs to God, is born anew in God through repentance.”

The dean of St. Martin’s at Mainz, wishing to see St. Hildegard again, affectionately asks for her letters (Letter 129), by which he might obtain consolation. But she, accustomed to write what was useful rather than what was flattering, seriously exhorts him to repentance. Another superior of a congregation (Letter 130) earnestly commends himself and his congregation to St. Hildegard’s prayers. In reply she teaches, through various comparisons, the things from which he should guard against in governing his people.

A monk of Maulbronn [alternatively Mulbronn] (Letter 131) asks St. Hildegard to send him “something of heavenly admonition.” The Saint indeed sent him an elegant instruction, in which she excellently teaches that those who repent of former sins and strive to amend themselves are graciously received by the heavenly Father of the household; but not those tiresome persons who prefer to murmur against their superiors rather than reform themselves.

139. A monk of Ebrach, of the Cistercian Order, in a most humble letter (Letter 132) asks St. Hildegard for prayers and words of consolation. He receives a reply beginning:

“I see that God has not hidden His face from you, but binds you with His scourges as pleases Him. Likewise, I see that a great light of God’s consolation will come into your soul and into the joy of your body, when He Himself wills it.”

[Col. 0058B] She adds similar things, but warns him to avoid certain useless matters. A certain monk and priest (Letter 135) greatly rejoices that he had been kindly received by St. Hildegard and requests the following: “Concerning the other matters which I discussed with you more privately, when the time is fitting, take care to give me assurance in writing.” The Saint replies with a beautiful parable about three women, which the reader will find in that letter.

## § X. Certain letters of St. Hildegard to Philip, Abbot of Park, and a letter of his to her from a manuscript; her dealings with St. Gerlach; other later letters to the Saint, with her replies

140–145. John Masius, abbot of Park, of the Premonstratensian Order near Leuven, sent Bolland three letters of St. Hildegard to Philip, abbot of Park, and one of Philip to Hildegard in 1641; Philip had at one time visited her. Since, however, two abbots of Park were contemporaries of St. Hildegard, both named Philip, I should rightly have doubted whether the Philip who exchanged letters with the Saint was the first or the second, had not this note been appended to the letters:

“This Philip was the second abbot of Park, from the year of Christ 1142 until 1165, a man not only exceedingly devout but also learned. Accordingly, in his time he took care that very many books should be copied on parchment, and these still exist.”

[Col. 0058D] Among them are numbered the *Visions of St. Hildegard*. He was the first Philip, but second among the abbots; after another’s brief administration Philip II succeeded him. Thus this Philip, no less than the first, might have received letters from St. Hildegard. Moreover, Masius himself gives this testimony concerning the letters sent here:

“Copies of the above-mentioned letters of the Reverend Lord Philip, abbot of Park, to St. Hildegard, and of St. Hildegard to the same Reverend Lord Philip, have been extracted and transcribed from the most ancient codex of our library at Park, and agree word for word with the originals. I attest this on 10 October 1641. JOHN MASIUS, abbot of Park.”

(The aforementioned letters now appear in the book of St. Hildegard’s letters as nos. 56, 57, 58, and 59.)

[Col. 0059A] 146. Since we are now in Belgium, I am pleased here to relate the intercourse St. Hildegard had with St. Gerlach the hermit, who in her time lived a very austere life in the duchy of Limburg, about two Belgian miles from the city of Maastricht, in what is now the diocese of Roermond, where there is now a convent of Premonstratensian nuns called St. Gerlach. The author of the *Life of St. Gerlach*, given under 5 January, chapter 8, writes the following for our purpose:

“At that time, in the region of Mainz, there was a most holy virgin named Hildegard, that renowned prophetess of the New Testament, with whom God spoke familiarly and to whom He showed heavenly secrets.
