Consecrated to the Lord with the sacred veil by the hand of the lord Henry, archbishop of Mainz, of holy memory, although she had no learning save only the Psalms of David, she was taught by the Holy Spirit and produced great volumes concerning the divine oracles and mysteries revealed to her . . . Throughout many courses of time, this woman illuminated the holy Church with the lamp of saving teaching, strengthened it by letters sent to various persons, and made it illustrious by splendid miracles.”

147. “Therefore, while this bride of Christ, according to her custom, saw in a true vision the King and Lord of lords sitting upon His throne, and moved about examining the distinct ranks and choirs of saints standing by Him, among the most splendid choir of confessors [Col. 0059C] she saw a most radiant seat, surrounded by inestimable beauty and wonderfully adorned. Seeing it, she was greatly amazed; and, taught by a divine oracle, she learned that this glory and honor had been prepared for holy Gerlach, who regularly visited St. Servatius at Maastricht in daily pilgrimage. Assured by this revelation of the merits of Blessed Gerlach, the virgin of the Lord burned with ardor, wholly inflamed by sacred love for him; and, as a sign of the everlasting fellowship and blessedness which she was one day to receive with him, she sent him the crown with which the bishop had crowned her on the day of her consecration. This crown, as a witness to the event, is devoutly preserved in our church even now.”

This is the testimony of an anonymous author, but one who was contemporary with St. Gerlach and still more with Hildegard, since in chapter 16 he relates that [Col. 0059D] he had spoken with an old man who had known St. Gerlach in life.

148. There remain certain letters of illustrious men not yet mentioned. I have reserved them for this place because they were written in St. Hildegard’s later years, so that the scholarly reader may perceive that the remarkable renown for holiness and heavenly wisdom by which the Saint began to shine about the year 1148 continued until her death.

Rudolf, otherwise Rodulf, bishop of Liège from 1168 until 1191, writes to St. Hildegard (Letter 19), “placed in the greatest agitation of mind and body,” because, as he confesses and other writers agree, he had offended God by “innumerable evils.” He asks for the Saint’s prayers and replies “to rouse the sleepiness” in which he was, [Col. 0060A] and “that he might obtain at least the last dwelling-place of eternal rest.” St. Hildegard replies by exhorting him to a good life and to care for souls, ending her letter in these words: “May God protect you and free your soul from eternal punishment.”

149. Godfrey, bishop of Utrecht (Letter 20), declares his affection for St. Hildegard in these words: “Dearest sister, from the time when I first began to love you in the charity of Christ, your memory—sweeter than honey and the honeycomb—has never been able to depart from my mind,” etc. St. Hildegard responds with a serious and sufficiently clear exhortation.

150. The bishop of Prague, whose name is indicated by the letter H., also writes to the Saint (Letter 21). Perhaps he was Henry, who certainly did not acquire the bishopric of Prague until near the end of St. Hildegard’s life; for no other bishop of Prague with that initial lived at the same time. Whoever he was, he writes to the Saint asking her help through her prayers and requesting “good counsel.” St. Hildegard sends a serious admonition, exhorting him to greater constancy in virtue, both in prosperity and adversity.

151. Arnold I, archbishop of Trier from about 1170, graciously declares in a letter (Letter 24) his affection for St. Hildegard, and testifies that he was raised to the episcopate against his will. He therefore consults the Saint about this matter. He also asks about the possessed woman freed at Mount St. Rupert, of whom I shall speak later. Let us now hear what the Saint replied to the other matters. She begins thus:

“You are a tree established by God, as Paul says: ‘All authority is from God’ (Rom. 13:1), because according to the supreme Master every authority is named through the invocation of His name.”

She then begins to give salutary counsels, seriously warning him to guard against pride, greed for riches, injustice, and vanity, and to embrace the virtues appropriate to his station.

152. Philip, archbishop of Cologne (Letter 25), praises St. Hildegard in a letter as “imbued with the gift of divine charisma” and as “dwelling in heaven,” and asks her to inquire “from God’s hidden counsel” and send him “admonitory words, insofar as God . . . has granted.” St. Hildegard complied and sent a sufficiently clear exhortation.

153. Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders, writes to St. Hildegard:

“May your Holiness know that I am ready to do whatever I might know would please you . . . although I would much more willingly have come to you and spoken with you . . . but . . . I was unable to make time for this. For the time is now at hand when I must undertake the journey to Jerusalem . . . condescend to make known to me your counsel concerning this through your letters.”

He also requests St. Hildegard’s prayers and advice as to whether he should rather remain in the Holy Land or return to his people after undertaking the expedition. The Saint replies to the count with an instruction chiefly exhorting him to justice.

## § XI. The Saint frees her monastery from every burden; a possessed woman is freed there; the Saint’s church is placed under interdict because of the burial of a person formerly excommunicated

154. The *Acts*, nos. 9 and 10, testify that, at God’s command, St. Hildegard brought it about that her monastery on Mount St. Rupert should be free of every burden, and that the abbey of St. Disibod should hold no right over it in temporal matters; but that, for direction according to the Rule of St. Benedict, it should be subject to that abbey only in this respect: the religious virgins were to choose their own directors and provosts freely from that abbey. St. Hildegard speaks of these matters in a little work addressed to her congregation of sisters, printed after the letters:

“O daughters, who have followed Christ’s footsteps in the love of chastity, and who chose me, a poor little woman, to be your mother in the humility of subjection because of the heavenly exaltation—not from myself, but through a divine showing do I speak to you through maternal bowels: I discovered this place, namely, the resting-place of the relics of blessed Robert the confessor, to whose protection you have fled, in manifest miracles by God’s will as a sacrifice of praise; and, with the permission of my masters, I came to it and, with divine assistance, freely obtained it for myself and for all who would follow me.”

[Col. 0061C] These things were done at the beginning of the foundation, with the approval and confirmation of Henry, archbishop of Mainz. For the *Life*, no. 10, testifies that the foundation was confirmed by him.

155–156. As for the biographer’s additional statement that everything was also confirmed by Archbishop Arnold, who succeeded Henry in 1153, I think this occurred after the abbot of St. Disibod had wished to claim some right over the possessions of St. Rupert’s monastery. For then St. Hildegard, commanded and compelled by God through illness, did what she continues to narrate in the passage cited above: “Afterwards, however, by God’s admonition I proceeded to the Mount of Blessed Disibod, from which I had withdrawn by permission,” etc.

These things were done, as I have already said, during the time of Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, who presided from [Col. 0061D] 1153 until 1160. Moreover, it appears that when St. Hildegard wrote these things, she foresaw in the spirit dissensions that would arise in her monastery. For she plainly intimates that after her death it would not flourish in the same way, and anxiously warns her daughters to beware of discord. I append the Saint’s words:

“But oh, what great lamentation these daughters of mine will have after the death of their Mother, because they shall no longer suck the words of that same Mother; and thus, in groaning and mourning, for very many periods of time, they will say with tears: ‘Alas, alas!’” etc.

157–158. I find no subsequent difficulty raised for St. Hildegard concerning the free possession of temporal goods. But the abbot of St. Disibod—whether this was Helinger or Helinger’s successor, I cannot say—raised a difficulty against the free election of the provost or director. St. Hildegard wrote on this matter to Pope Alexander III (Letter 4), while the schism was still continuing; therefore the dispute must certainly be dated between 1159, when Alexander III was elected and the schism began, and 1177, when Emperor Frederick, with his adherents, submitted to Alexander and ended the schism.

I think, however, that the matter occurred either after 1170 or not long before that year, both because St. Hildegard says in her letter that the Church had long suffered under schism, and because in the writing just mentioned, which she composed when she was seventy years old—that is, around 1168—she makes no mention of this dispute. Having briefly noted these points concerning the time, let us hear the dispute itself from St. Hildegard’s letter to Alexander III, whom she addresses thus:

“Now, O most gentle Father . . . we are in great sorrow because the abbot of Mount St. Disibod and his brethren oppose our privileges and our election, which we have always possessed . . . Therefore, my lord, for the Lord’s sake help us, so that we may either retain our election or freely seek and accept others, wherever we can find them, who may provide for us according to God and our welfare,” etc.

The Saint obtained what she desired. Alexander, however, did not reply to her directly, but to Wezelin, provost of St. Andrew’s at Cologne (reply to Letter 4). It is probable that the abbot of St. Disibod preferred to consent to the election already made rather than permit a provost to be chosen from another monastery.

159. Moreover, on the occasion of St. Hildegard’s letter to Alexander, I observe that during the schism the Saint adhered to Alexander, the legitimate pope, even though the archbishopric of Mainz was then occupied by Christian, who adhered to the antipope and Emperor Frederick, but later submitted to Alexander. The Saint declares her judgment concerning Alexander’s legitimate pontificate in these words at the very beginning of her letter: “O supreme and glorious person, who were first established through the Word of God.” She then exhorts him to show himself ready to grant pardon to schismatics if they repent.

This letter, I think, gave Trithemius occasion for an error when, in his *Hirsau Chronicle*, under the year 1150, he includes Alexander III among those who wrote to St. Hildegard—unless Alexander in fact wrote to her and the letter has not been published.

160. Book III, chapter II, of the *Life* relates at length the story of a certain noblewoman who had been possessed by a demon for many years. She was taken to various places of saints renowned for their patronage, yet was not freed from that affliction until she came to St. Hildegard’s monastery, where at last the demon left her. This deliverance occurred about the year 1170, as I infer from the letter of Arnold, Archbishop of Trier (Letter 24), mentioned in no. 151. For Arnold wrote to the Saint when he had not long been elected archbishop—some date Arnold’s election in 1169, others in [Col. 0063A] 1170; there is no need to investigate this more exactly—and asked her about the liberation of that possessed woman as a recent event, in these words:

> “And we know that God, by mercifully freeing a possessed woman, has worked salvation in His holy place among you and visited His people. Therefore we most earnestly ask you to write back to us concerning the manner of the possessed woman’s deliverance. . . .”

To this St. Hildegard replied:

> “In the case of her who was possessed, we saw many wonders which we cannot now set forth in writing. But we learned that the diabolical breath gradually diminished day by day until its departure; and that same woman was freed from the devil’s torment. Yet she was then seized by an illness which she had not previously known in herself. But now she has recovered complete health and strength both of body and soul.” [Col. 0063B]

161. That woman seems to have been from Cologne and to have been named Sigewize. At any rate, the dean of the Church of the Holy Apostles at Cologne knew her very well and regarded her as a daughter, as we learn from his letter to St. Hildegard (Letter 50), in which he writes:

> “From the day on which it became known to us that you had received into the fellowship of your Blessedness our sister—or rather our special daughter—Lady Sigewize, not only we, but the whole city of Cologne, have been inflamed by God’s prompting with love of piety. Hence it is now openly proclaimed by everyone throughout all the borders of our land: ‘Behold, the fragrance of the ladies of St. Robert is like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed.’ May you therefore be blessed by the Lord,”

etc.

[Col. 0063C]

162. The Saint replied most humbly, attributing the expulsion of the demon to the good works of many people together, and beginning thus:

> “God performed His work, but He did not establish it in one manner alone.”

She then teaches that God directs the diverse good works of diverse persons toward one end. These were indeed joyful matters; but I shall now relate other things which could not but cause the Saint the deepest grief.

163. During the schism, two men were contending for the archbishopric of Mainz. One, namely Conrad, was legitimate and adhered to Pope Alexander III. The other was Christian, intruded by Emperor Frederick. Christian nevertheless afterward retained the archbishopric, for in 1177, when peace was made [Col. 0063D] between Alexander and Frederick, Conrad yielded and Christian was confirmed by Pope Alexander. From that time he was the legitimate Archbishop of Mainz and most closely united with Alexander III.

Christian remained in Italy for several years after the peace was concluded and attended the Lateran council, which began on 2 March 1179. Before that council, probably in 1178, a young man who had formerly been excommunicated but had long since been absolved was buried in St. Hildegard’s cemetery. For this reason the Mainz prelates, who administered that church in the absent archbishop’s stead, sent St. Hildegard an order that she should have the body exhumed or refrain from celebrating the divine offices in her church.

How the Saint received [Col. 0064A] that order she explains in a writing published among the letters (Letter 47), bearing this title:

> “To the Mainz prelates concerning the divine services interdicted by them.”

The work begins as follows:

> “In the vision implanted by God the Maker in my soul before I came forth into birth, I have been compelled to write these things concerning the bond by which we have been bound by our masters because of a certain dead man, buried among us without objection, under the ministry of his priest.

164. “A few days after his burial, when those same masters of ours ordered us to cast him out of our cemetery, I was seized with no small terror. As usual, I looked toward the true Light, and with wakeful eyes I saw in my soul that, if the body of that dead man were removed according to [Col. 0064B] their command, that expulsion would threaten our place with immense danger in the form of a great blackness, and would surround us in the likeness of a dark cloud such as usually appears before storms and thunder. Therefore, since that deceased man had confessed, been anointed, received communion, and been buried without objection, we neither dare to remove his body nor have we acquiesced in the counsel or command of those advising or ordering this—not because we utterly despise the counsel of upright men or of our prelates, but lest we seem, through womanly harshness, to inflict an injury upon Christ’s sacraments, by which he had still been fortified while alive.”

In the examination concerning miracles, to be given below, no. 6, that man is said to have been unjustly excommunicated. This gives rise to the suspicion that he was excommunicated [Col. 0064C] during the schism, perhaps because he upheld the cause of Alexander III, the legitimate pontiff. The same source adds concerning St. Hildegard, when that buried man was to be expelled:

> “She then marked his tomb with the sign of the cross by her staff, and thus his grave could no longer be found.”

165. I return to St. Hildegard’s writing, which continues thus:

> “But lest we should appear wholly disobedient, we have hitherto, according to their interdict, ceased from the songs of divine praise and have abstained from participation in the Lord’s Body—although by custom we had received it almost every month. While both I and all my sisters were afflicted by great bitterness concerning this and held in overwhelming sorrow, at last, oppressed by a great burden, I heard these words in a vision: ‘It is not expedient for you to abandon, because of human words, the sacraments of the garment [that is, the body] of My Word, which is your salvation and which was born in virginal nature from the Virgin Mary. Rather, permission for this must be sought by you from your prelates, who have bound you.’”

The reason for this command is then added. The Saint continues:

> “In the same vision I also heard that I would be blameworthy in this: that I had not come in all humility and devotion into the presence of my masters to seek from them permission to communicate—especially since we were not guilty in receiving that dead man, who, fortified in every Christian observance by his own priest, was buried without anyone’s objection, with the entire procession of Pingen [Pingensis]. [Col. 0065A] And thus I have been divinely charged to announce these things to you, lords and prelates. I also saw something concerning the fact that, obeying you, we have hitherto ceased from singing the divine office and celebrate it only by reading it in a subdued manner; and I heard a voice proceeding from the living Light concerning the different kinds of praises, of which David says in the Psalms: ‘Praise him with the sound of the trumpet,’”

etc. She proceeds here to say much about sacred singing, which she declares hateful to the devil.

166. She then addresses this admonition to the Mainz prelates:

> “Therefore you and all prelates must labor with the utmost vigilance; and before you close by sentence the mouth of any church singing praises to God [Col. 0065B], or suspend it from administering or receiving the sacraments, you must first most diligently examine and weigh the causes for which this ought to be done. You must strive to be led to this by zeal for God’s justice, not by indignation, an unjust impulse of mind, or a desire for vengeance. And you must always beware lest Satan deceive you in your judgments—he who drew humankind away from heavenly harmony and from the delights of paradise. Consider, therefore, that as the body of Jesus Christ was born through the Holy Spirit from the intact Virgin Mary, so also the song of praise, according to heavenly harmony, has been rooted in the Church through the Holy Spirit. The body is the garment of the soul, which has a living voice; therefore it is fitting that the body, together with the soul, should sing God’s praises through the voice. . . . Those, therefore, who without the weight of certain reason impose silence on the Church in the songs of God’s praise will lack fellowship in the angelic praises of heaven, because [perhaps: since] they have unjustly deprived God on earth of the beauty of His praise—unless they amend this by true repentance and humble satisfaction. Therefore those who hold the keys of heaven must strictly beware lest they open what should be closed and close what should be opened, because most severe judgment will be given in the case of those who preside, unless, as the Apostle says, they preside with diligence,”

etc.

I add no more from that writing, which has been drawn out to very great length, because it has almost nothing further relevant to this controversy. Indeed, since everything afterward is moral instruction, I suspect that it is not [Col. 0065D] a single little work of the Saint, but that many pieces written to the Mainz authorities on different occasions were appended to it at the end.

167–168. This writing of St. Hildegard is such that the administrators of the Church of Mainz do not seem able to have denied what she sought without remarkable harshness. For she not only came to Mainz to present the writing just quoted, but also wished to prove that the man buried in her cemetery had been absolved long before his death. Even so, she was able to obtain what she desired only temporarily and through the intervention of the Archbishop of Cologne’s authority; afterward she was reduced to the same straits.

We have all this from St. Hildegard’s letter to Archbishop Christian, who was residing in Italy, written in 1179 (Letter 8). Before that controversy she had received from him a most courteous letter (Letter 7), which Christian concluded thus:

> “Be assured that we shall assist you in all your needs and be of service to you in all things, insofar as God grants.”

In the same letter he had earlier addressed the Saint in this way:

> “And because we know that you are inspired by the divine Spirit, we desire your exhortatory words,”

etc. St. Hildegard had also answered this with an excellent exhortation concerning pastoral care, teaching that it is the bishop’s duty to feed his flock.

169–171. Yet, whether the Mainz administrators had become excessively embittered against St. Hildegard because during the schism she had plainly enough declared herself for Alexander III, or whether they took too ill her failure immediately to obey the command to exhume [Col. 0066B] the excommunicated man, Archbishop Christian renewed the interdict, doubtless at the instigation of the Mainz vicars. For St. Hildegard says in the letter already praised:

> “But when, sweetest lord, we had the greatest confidence in your mercy, after their return from Rome and the synod we received through these same prelates of ours your letters interdicting the divine services—letters which, as I trust in your fatherly piety, you would never have sent had you known the truth of this affair.”

etc.

In this same letter St. Hildegard begins by giving thanks for the gracious letters which she had previously received from Christian; from them, she says, arose her confidence to set the matter before him. Whoever considers this letter of St. Hildegard properly will find it no less courageous [Col. 0066C] than humble and supplicatory.

I cannot help wondering that the Saint was treated so harshly, especially after the absolution of the excommunicated man seems to have been abundantly proved through the care of the Archbishop of Cologne. But that the attentive reader may marvel still more, he must turn to the reply of Archbishop Christian (Letter 9).

Archbishop Christian, a man endowed with many natural gifts, was more soldier than bishop. During the schism, in 1165, he seized the Archbishopric of Mainz after expelling Conrad, its legitimate archbishop. From that time he was always occupied either with military or political affairs, repeatedly discharging the office not only of commander but also of soldier. When peace was made in 1177 [Col. 0066D] between Pope Alexander and Emperor Frederick, Christian nevertheless remained in Italy, generally occupied with military matters, despite St. Hildegard’s vain exhortation that he should come to his church. In the very year in which he wrote the letter addressed to Hildegard, he was captured after the defeat of his men, held in prison for two years, and finally died in camp in 1183. These matters may be seen more fully recounted in Serarius’s *Acts of Mainz*, printed at Frankfurt in 1722, vol. I, p. 569. If that soldier-bishop thought so highly of the “ordinances of the holy Fathers, which must not be evaded,” he could with all the more justice have sung them to himself, since, as he admitted, he was so clearly able to recognize the Saint’s innocence.

## § XII. Various journeys of St. Hildegard, and places where she publicly appeared. She founds the convent of Eibingen.

[Col. 0067A]

172. St. Hildegard strove to instruct Christ’s faithful, especially religious and clerics, in piety not only by written letters but also by teaching those who came to her in person. That their number was immense is attested by the *Life*, no. 19, where its author says that “swarms of people of both sexes flocked to her from every part of the threefold Gaul and from Germany.” In recounting the letters, various examples have presented themselves of notable people who made their way to the Saint from distant regions of Germany, Gaul, and Belgium. We have further seen that St. Hildegard was in various places and everywhere gave salutary admonitions.

Concerning these things the *Life*, no. 44, says:

> “Among these matters, this too is noteworthy concerning her: coming to Cologne, Trier, Metz, Würzburg, Bamberg—moved not merely but compelled by the divine Spirit—she announced to clergy and people what God willed. And on Mount St. Disibod, at Siberg, Eberbach, Hirsau, Swifelden, Maulbronn, Rodenkirchen, Kitzingen, Crutendal, Herde, Werde, Andernach, on Mount St. Mary, in Elsim, and in Winkelo, she made known, according to what God had revealed to her, the things pertaining to the benefit of souls.”

The places named here, together with others to be added from elsewhere, show that the Saint made journeys of considerable length into various regions of Germany, so that undoubtedly much time was spent on those travels.

[Col. 0067C]

173. Yet it may be doubted whether St. Hildegard visited so many cities and other places successively at one time, or at different times, sometimes setting out in one direction and sometimes in another. The latter seems more probable to me; indeed, it is fairly certain that some of St. Hildegard’s expeditions cannot be joined to the journey to Cologne and Trier.

For from the letter of Emperor Frederick mentioned in no. 53 (Letter 27), we know that before 1159, and probably before 1155, the Saint was at Ingelheim with Frederick and there foretold to him certain things which had been fulfilled before 1159. Perhaps at the same time when she was at Ingelheim the Saint set out for Franconia. For she had been there before the Abbot of Ebrach wrote to her, concerning whose letter I spoke in no. 65. Manrique, however, in the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1155, no. 4, thinks that the letter of Adam, Abbot of Ebrach, was written around that year; this is very plausible and may not be far from the truth, since Adam’s death is dated to 1161.

Therefore the Saint seems to have been in Franconia between 1150 and 1160; and consequently it is credible that at that time she was at Würzburg and reached Bamberg, called Babenberg by its ancient name in the *Life*. On the same journey she may have visited the Benedictine convent of nuns at Kitzingen, situated on the Main a few miles above Würzburg, but afterward destroyed by heretics, as Ignatius Gropp teaches in his *Collection of Würzburg Matters*, dissertation 6, no. 8, where he adds that the monastery is now inhabited by Ursulines. I discussed the letter of the Abbess of Kitzingen to the Saint (Letter 101) in no. 83.

174. On another journey St. Hildegard probably traveled into Lower Germany and reached Cologne. She was at Cologne when Philip, who became archbishop in 1167 or 1268 [probably 1168], was dean of that church. The journey therefore seems to be dated between 1160 and 1167. No. 92 also suggests that the Church had already for some time been divided—by the schism, I think, which arose in 1159—before she foretold to the people of Cologne the things which may be seen in no. 90 and following.

On the same journey she undoubtedly visited the Benedictine monastery of Sigeberg, situated beyond the Rhine in the Diocese of Cologne on the river Sieg, not far from the town of Bonn. The *Life* indeed writes *Siberg*, but that slight alteration of the name should cause no difficulty, especially since it is elsewhere often called Sigberg and even Siberg. The monks of Sigeberg cherished St. Hildegard with special affection as a mother, as is clear from their letter (Letter 137), which I discussed in no. 105.

Werde also lies in the Diocese of Cologne: a Benedictine abbey called in Latin *Werthina*, *Werdena*, or *Werda*, which St. Hildegard is recorded to have visited. She therefore traveled much farther, for Werthina lies on the borders of the County of Mark and on the River Ruhr. Yet there was another monastery in the Diocese of Cologne called Werda, situated on the Rhine two or three miles below Düsseldorf, where there is now a town commonly called Kaiserswerth, or Caesar’s Werda. The Saint certainly visited one or the other.

At the entirely opposite edge of the Diocese of Cologne, and almost on the boundary with Trier, lies Andernach on the Rhine, formerly called Antenacum; St. Hildegard was also there on that journey. Near Antenacum was a convent of women whose abbess wrote to the Saint, as we saw in no. 136. Such a convent was also at Didenkirchen near Bonn, for the abbess at Didenkirchen wrote to St. Hildegard (Letter 116), as was said in no. 135. How welcome the Saint’s presence there had been is clear [Col. 0068D] from the letter quoted. For, requesting admonitions, the abbess gives this reason:

> “For you promised, while you were present, to strengthen me from these things at a fitting time.”

From this letter, moreover, as from several others, we know with certainty that the Saint visited more monasteries than are named in the *Life*. Whether more of the places mentioned in the *Life* also belonged to the Diocese of Cologne or to this journey of St. Hildegard, I cannot say, since I cannot ascertain the situation of some of them with sufficient certainty.

175. We know from the letter of the clergy of Trier to the Saint (Letter 49), cited in no. 93, that St. Hildegard was at Trier during the days of Pentecost. But I find nothing certain concerning the year in which she was there. Brower, indeed, in the *Annals of Trier*, and others following him, think that St. Hildegard came to Trier in 1160; but he assigns neither reason nor conjecture for that date. Therefore I regard the year as uncertain, and equally uncertain whether the Saint came to Trier before or after her journey to Cologne.

Nevertheless, since at the end of her letter to the people of Cologne the Saint says:

> “For two years I have been greatly wearied, in order that I might proclaim these things by the living voice before masters, doctors, and other wise persons in certain greater places where their residence is,”

and since by these words she suggests journeys of about two years, I suspect that within that two-year period the Saint came both to Cologne and Trier, and to other places, so that during two years she was frequently traveling, although she may at times have returned to her monastery.

But whatever the date, this is certain: St. Hildegard foretold many things, both evil and good, to the people of Trier as well as to those of Cologne. Brower’s belief that these were fulfilled in the schism in which the Church of Trier was divided for seven years from the year 118 is by no means to be accepted—unless he means the evils said to be near at hand, which she had declared would be only moderate. For she herself indicates clearly enough that the principal evils and blessings which she foretold would come much later. Moreover, St. Hildegard could have proceeded from Trier to Metz. The *Life* certainly attests that she was at Metz; but I do not find what she did there in particular.

[Col. 0069C]

176. Among the greater cities to which St. Hildegard traveled, Trithemius in the *Hirsau Chronicle*, under the year 1160, also places Mainz, which the *Life* does not mention. I do not doubt that she was at Mainz at some point, since she could have passed through it while traveling. Yet whether she also made known there the things which she did in other cities is less certain because of the biographer’s silence.

It is more certain that she was in various monasteries of the Diocese of Mainz and there disclosed various things revealed to her by God. For this reason she was at Mount St. Disibod, where she had been educated. How much fruit of reform her admonitions produced there has already been stated from the abbot’s letter in no. 112 (Letter 145).

In the same diocese is Everbach, as it is written in the *Life*, elsewhere Eberbach: the often-mentioned Cistercian abbey in the Rheingau. The Saint could easily visit it, since it was not far away, and could profitably proclaim her message there, since the monks of Eberbach highly valued her admonitions, as is clear from their letter cited in no. 108 (Letter 139).

A third monastery of the Diocese of Mainz which St. Hildegard is said to have visited is called in the *Life* Rudenkyrchen, elsewhere Rodenkirchen, as it were “Red Church.” It was a Premonstratensian abbey and belonged to the Diocese of Mainz, as is clear from several papal letters in Martène, vol. IV of the *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 468 and following. They are addressed to the Bishops of Worms and Speyer, “and to the beloved son, the abbot of the monastery at Rodenkirchen, of the Premonstratensian Order, Diocese of Mainz.” This had already been observed in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 600, but the more exact location of that monastery is not there added.

St. Hildegard is also said to have been at Winkelo, a name which I think denotes a monastery of the Diocese of Mainz. Certainly, on the bank of the Rhine in the Rheingau, between Bingen and Mainz, is the village of Winkel, sometimes called in Latin *Vinicella*. Nearby was an abbey called Mount St. John, on which see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 582. Whether another monastery was also at Winkel I do not know.

177. On the same side of the Rhine, only one mile from her own monastery, St. Hildegard founded another monastery, and there can be no doubt that she often visited it. In the acts of the inquiry concerning miracles, no. 8, this second foundation is briefly described as follows:

> “Moreover, across the River Rhine, at a distance of one league, she founded another monastery, where she established thirty prebends,”

that is, a revenue sufficient for thirty nuns.

The place is named Hibingen in no. 3, where St. Hildegard is said to have gone “to the village of Hibingen, where she had also founded a monastery.” While crossing the Rhine she gave sight to a girl born blind, washing her eyes with Rhine water. I find nowhere an explicit date for that foundation.

In *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 654, mention is made of the monastery of Eibingen in a list of the abbesses of Mount St. Rupert, who withdrew with their nuns to Eibingen when, in the seventeenth century, the convent of St. Rupert was reduced to ashes by the Swedes. This is said to have occurred in 1632. Accordingly, the abbesses of both monasteries assumed the title, namely, of Mount St. Rupert and Eibingen. Its site and foundation are described there as follows:

> “This monastery of Eibingen, consecrated to the memory of St. Giselbert, is situated in the Rheingau, close to Rüdesheim, toward the hills. It was raised by Blessed Hildegard herself and always remained, under the title of a priory, subject and united to the nunnery of St. Rupert.”

Our predecessors Henschenius and Papebrochius were at Eibingen in 1660 and were received most courteously by the abbess, who was then living there with the nuns, as Papebrochius himself noted in his manuscript *Roman Journey*.

[Col. 0070D]

178. St. Hildegard also traveled into Swabia. For among the monasteries she visited are certainly found two in Swabia: Maulbronn, situated in the Duchy of Württemberg and the Diocese of Speyer, commonly called Maulbron; and Hirsau, belonging to the same diocese but situated somewhat farther away in the Black Forest.

Trithemius, under the year 1160, discusses St. Hildegard’s arrival at Hirsau monastery and says that before her departure she spoke these words to the people of Hirsau:

> “The divine Light greatly hates and detests the negligences of its children, because no one serves God rightly who does not utterly drive from his heart the spirit of sloth and negligence. Therefore that Light which can do all things says to you: ‘Consider your paths and do not turn aside from the straight way, because Satan has demanded you in order to test you; and unless you walk cautiously in the fear of the Lord, he will quickly and swiftly stir up a grave disturbance among you.’”

I do not deny that the Saint gave such admonitions to the people of Hirsau; but I do not think that she foretold to them the discord of which I spoke in nos. 106 and 107, because I am persuaded that this expedition of the Saint was undertaken later.

I am more inclined to believe what Trithemius adds concerning St. Hildegard’s further journey:

> “Departing from Hirsau, the most devout bride of Christ, Hildegard, made her way to the monastery of Zwiefalten, of our order, and faithfully announced the word committed to her by the Lord both to the monks and to the virgins of Christ then dwelling there.”

[Col. 0071B]

179. I think these things true, although she probably did not complete so lengthy a journey in one uninterrupted course and perhaps visited certain intermediate places. In the *Life*, indeed, that monastery is called Swifelden, not Swifaltem, as it is now commonly called; but after careful investigation I think that the same place is denoted by both names.

The monastery of Zwiefalten, commonly Swifaltem, lies in the Diocese of Constance, in the mountains of Swabia, beside a stream formed by two converging branches and, a little farther downstream, joining the Danube several miles above Ulm. I discussed the letter of the Abbot of Zwiefalten, who is called Zwinieldensis in Martène (Letter 65), in no. 75. I discussed in no. 109 the letter of the prior and monks, who are there called men of Zwiefelden, and the letters of the nuns of Swifelden (Letter 140).

From those three letters, and especially from those to which St. Hildegard answered each party separately, it is plainly inferred that discipline in that double monastery of men and women had greatly relaxed at that time, and that the monks and nuns themselves were seeking a means of reform. It can therefore scarcely be doubted that St. Hildegard undertook so long a journey in order to restore fallen discipline in that monastery.

I think that the Swinieldenses, Swifeldenses, or Swifildenses are none other than the Swifaltenses under discussion, for the following reasons. First, Trithemius, who saw all St. Hildegard’s letters, lists among the abbots who wrote to her the Abbot of Zwiefalten, and no other of a similar name. Second, he teaches that the Saint was there, although the *Life* says that she was at Swifelden. Third, the monastery of Zwiefalten was double, for men and women alike; the place called Swifelden was likewise such, since both monks and nuns wrote to the Saint. Fourth, I searched diligently to discover whether any Swifelden abbey existed in Germany besides Zwiefalten, but could find no other. Fifth and finally, in the *Ecclesiastical Miscellany of Germany*, part III, p. 864 and following, certain decrees concerning the monastery of Zwiefalten are appended. From them I see that the name of that abbey was variously written in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries: at different times it is called Swifalda or Swifeltum, but more often Swifalten.

180. On the same journey St. Hildegard seems to have come [Col. 0072A] to the town of Kircheim, in Swabia in the Duchy of Württemberg, now commonly called Kirchen. For that the Saint was there too, and foretold many grave things concerning future times at Kircheim, is clear from what was related in no. 98 and following.

Moreover, from the beginning of the vision which the Saint dates “in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation one thousand one hundred and seventy,” it seems sufficiently established that her whole journey into Swabia occurred either in that very year 1170, in which she had the vision there, spoken aloud and afterward written, or at least not long afterward.

Besides, if the inhabitants of the Duchy of Württemberg wish attentively to consider what St. Hildegard foretold at Kircheim concerning priests to be expelled, sacred places to be cut off, and the wealth of churches to be taken away, they will see fulfilled what she declared in the twelfth century would occur. Whether the Saint visited more monasteries on that journey I do not know. There certainly remain other places which the *Life* states that she visited; but up to now I have not been able to discover where they were situated, apart from the last one shortly to be mentioned in the Diocese of Mainz.

181. The first of these is called Crutendal in the *Life*, Crouchdal in the letters. It was a convent of women, and in Germany, as its German name suggests. I listed in no. 84 the letter of the abbess at Crouchdal, in which she says that she saw St. Hildegard present, and in no. 136 another letter as well, perhaps from another abbess of that monastery.

The second of these monasteries is Herde. Bucelinus, in *Germania Sacra*, part II, p. 44, says that Herde is a Premonstratensian provostship. Hugh says the same in the *Premonstratensian Annals*, vol. I, col. 816, citing Trithemius’s *Hirsau Chronicle* under the year 1150, where the Frankfurt edition has “Premonstratensian provostship.” But in the later 1690 edition, more accurately printed at St. Gall, it is called a provostship of regular canons, and the place is written Herad; thus the matter is very uncertain.

Yet it is certain that St. Hildegard was at Herde twice and, by “a repeated visitation” of that monastery, brought joy to its religious, as is understood from the provost’s letter to her (Letter 80), which I discussed in no. 129.

The last three monasteries, concerning which I find nothing in the letters, are named thus in the *Life*:

> “On Mount St. Mary, in Elsim, and in Winkelo.”

I spoke of Winkelo in no. 176; concerning the others I have nothing to say.

182. Besides the journeys of St. Hildegard just mentioned from the acts and letters, there was another, fairly distant journey into Gaul. This is wholly passed over in the *Life*. But the acts of the inquiry into the virtues and miracles of St. Hildegard, nos. 9 and 10, testify that she made a pilgrimage to the tomb of St. Martin, that is, to the city of Tours. On that journey she came to Paris, where she gave her writings to be examined; and when she returned from Tours to Paris, she received them back after examination, as will be read below.

She undertook this journey in winter, or at least in autumn, since she was in Paris during the octave of St. Martin—that is, about the middle of November—and returned there in January. The year of this pilgrimage is not known. Yet it is certain that the Saint undertook it near the end of her life, since in 1233 two witnesses were still living who had been studying sacred theology in Paris when the Saint was there. Therefore, since there are sixty years between 1173 and 1233, it is more probable that the Saint was there after 1173 than before it, lest it be necessary to say that those witnesses were more than eighty years old.

## § XIII. St. Hildegard’s writings celebrated by the praises of many; enumeration of her writings; certain works falsely attributed to her.

183. How great was the fame of St. Hildegard’s divine wisdom during her lifetime, and how great the esteem for her prophetic knowledge—that is, her knowledge of every kind of hidden thing—has been abundantly shown by the letters written to her. For I have listed more than one hundred and thirty letters addressed to the Saint, and most of them are from persons far from ordinary. Indeed, I have found all of them so remarkable in their praises of her that scarcely one fails to bear testimony, or at least to suggest the conviction, that St. Hildegard knew hidden things beyond the ordinary reach of human knowledge.

The writers of her *Life* likewise give very clear testimony concerning the Saint’s visions and her knowledge of hidden things. To these must be added the acts drawn up in 1233 to investigate St. Hildegard’s virtues and miracles; for in them many witnesses again confirm that common opinion by their testimonies. At about the same time lived the writer of the *Life of St. Gerlach*, whose praise of St. Hildegard I gave in no. 146. He calls her “the most renowned prophetess of the New Testament, with whom God spoke familiarly.” He declares that “instructed by the Holy Spirit, she produced great volumes concerning divine oracles and sacraments revealed to her, and illuminated the holy Church with the lamp of saving doctrine,” etc. From the chronicle of the monk Alberic, who likewise flourished in the thirteenth century, I have already previously quoted some things concerning the holiness and prophetic writings of St. Hildegard.

184. In the same century Vincent of Beauvais also flourished. In the *Speculum historiale*, book XXVII, [Col. 0073D] chapter 83, he writes as follows concerning St. Hildegard:

> “At the same time, in the regions of Germany, there was a certain remarkable virgin of advanced age, upon whom divine power had bestowed so great a grace that, although she was a laywoman and unlearned, she nevertheless, being wondrously carried away, would frequently learn in dreams not only what she would pour forth in words, but also what she would dictate in Latin for writing, so that by dictation she composed books of Catholic doctrine.”

He derived this from another author, whom he does not name; it must be corrected in the point that she is said to have learned her material in dreams, since she herself repeatedly testifies that she was awake and with her eyes open when she had visions. Vincent then adds:

> “This was, I think, St. Hildegard, who is reported to have foretold many future things; Blessed Bernard of Clairvaux too is said to have written to her.”

[Col. 0074A] Richer, a monk of Sens and a writer of the same thirteenth century, celebrates St. Hildegard in his *Chronicle of Sens*, book IV, chapter 15, with this encomium:

> “About thirty years ago—indeed, nearly eighty—there was in the lower parts of Germany a certain enclosed religious woman of most holy conduct and life, named Hildegard, upon whom God had also bestowed, among other gifts, the grace of prophecy. And, wonderful to relate, although she had never learned it before, she spoke and wrote Latin. For she prophesied concerning the condition of kingdoms and future events, and therefore wrote books with her own hand. She also wrote a medical book concerning various illnesses, which I saw at Strasbourg.”

185. “She indeed wrote about the order of the future [Col. 0074B] Preachers and Friars Minor, which first began to exist in our times. For she openly said that certain brothers would come, shaven high on the head, in a religious but unusual habit; that at the beginning of their order they would be received by the people as though they were God; and she foretold that they would possess nothing of their own, but would live solely upon the alms of the faithful, reserving none of those alms for the next day. Content with such poverty, they would travel through cities, towns, and regions preaching; thus, in their beginnings, they would be dear to God and men; but, falling away from their purpose, they would be held more contemptible. Hildegard is reported to have foretold these things concerning the Preachers and Friars Minor, and later their conduct proved it true.”

Thus far Richer. Yet he deserves little [Col. 0074C] credence in what he says concerning the orders of Preachers and Minors: both because throughout his *Chronicle* he shows himself angry with and hostile to the Preachers, and because he makes various errors in recounting the founding of both orders. It is therefore probable that he knew little of either order beyond the malicious rumors of the populace, which he seems eagerly to have seized upon. Certainly he declaims against the Preachers in so implausible a fashion in various places that he harmed himself more in the estimation of sensible people than he harmed the order he had praised.

Whether St. Hildegard foretold anything concerning the origin of the orders of Preachers and Minors is entirely unknown to me; indeed, it is less likely, since I have not found this sufficiently established in any other author. [Col. 0074D] I scarcely doubt, nevertheless, that Richer had seen that spurious prophecy of which we shall speak more below.

186. I pass over the encomia of writers in subsequent centuries who celebrated the prophetic writings of St. Hildegard, because no one can reasonably doubt the Saint’s renown. Yet I select two from all of them because they testify that they themselves had read Hildegard’s books.

The first is Vincent, prior of the Carthusians of Aggsbach in Austria. Sending back copied books of St. Hildegard, he wrote thus concerning them in Bernard Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. VI, p. 356:

> “My most beloved Father, a few days ago I finished the sayings of St. Hildegard, which I could have finished earlier had not the Fathers of Tegernsee—an abbey in Bavaria—advised [Col. 0075A] me not to burden myself with copying. Because of the haste of writing, I paid little attention to these sayings of Hildegard while I copied them. Therefore I shall have to read them anew. Yet some things have clung to my memory through copying, namely concerning the threefold age: the feminine, the sharp, and the declining. The first of these, whose end I hope is at hand, has greatly—more than can be believed—weakened the Church. The second, namely the sharp or keen age [elsewhere called ‘manly’ by St. Hildegard], will wonderfully strengthen her, purging her of sinful humors through many labors and sweats. In one thing I marvel and grieve: namely, that from hearing Hildegard’s prophecies or reading them I find no one who strikes his breast or rends [Col. 0075B] his garments, as King Josiah is read to have done upon finding the book of the Law. But almost all neither approve nor disapprove her. . . .

> Written by Brother Vincent at Aggsbach, on the vigil of St. Martin, in the year 1460.”

187. Trithemius, who writes of St. Hildegard in various places and in different little works, says in the *Hirsau Chronicle*:

> “We have not only read all her writings in the books of the virgin preserved in her monastery at Bingen, but also caused them to be copied for ourselves while we still presided over the monastery of St. Martin at Sponheim.”

A little earlier in the same work he speaks thus of the Saint’s writings:

> “And truly, so far as we are able to judge, her writings were not produced by human feeling or understanding, [Col. 0075C] but were rather wondrously infused by the divine Spirit; and therefore they are not commonly understood by all, but can in some measure be understood only by those whose pure mind has merited through love to be united with God.”

The same writer praises St. Hildegard, as distinguished for prophecies, written works, and miracles, in the *Sponheim Chronicle* under the year 1180; in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men of Germany*, p. 138; and finally in *Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, book II, chapter 119, and book III, chapter 334. From this last passage I transfer some words here:

> “St. Hildegard, the servant of Christ, was refined for many years in the furnace of poverty and illness; the more she was afflicted in body, the more she advanced in mind. For frequent angelic revelations [Col. 0075D] consoled the sickness of her flesh. Under her direction the greatest discipline of regular life flourished in the aforesaid monastery,”

etc. He adds many things already sufficiently stated above, and also some matters less accurate, both here and elsewhere; these can be corrected from what has previously been discussed.

188. Trithemius also enumerates St. Hildegard’s works in various places, according as he had seen them in manuscript and had had them copied for himself. In the *Hirsau Chronicle*, under the year 1147, he begins to enumerate them in this way:

> “Of her wonderful works we have seen and read the following: ‘A brief Explanation of the Rule of our holy Father Benedict,’ one book.”

This *Explanation* was printed with the letters of St. Hildegard in the Cologne edition of 1566, p. 231, [Col. 0076A] under the title *The Rule of St. Benedict Explained according to St. Hildegard*. It was later reprinted in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*.

> “‘A Book of Responses to Wigbert, monk of Gembloux, upon thirty questions,’ one book.”

This book too was printed in the same places with the letters.

> “‘The Life of St. Rupert, duke of Bingen,’ one book. ‘On the Life of St. Disibod, Irish bishop,’ one book.”

We have both Lives in a manuscript codex together with the explanation of the Rule of St. Benedict. Both were also printed by Surius and in our own work: the former under 15 May, the latter under 8 July.

> “‘Fifty-eight homilies on the Sunday Gospels throughout the yearly cycle,’ one book.”

I have not seen this work, nor do I know that it has been published. [Col. 0076B] Trithemius nevertheless lists this work of homilies elsewhere as well; in the cited *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, p. 138, he says of these homilies:

> “She composed fifty-eight very obscure homilies upon the Sunday Gospels, intelligible only to devout and learned persons.”

Perhaps they have not been published because of their obscurity. I return to Trithemius’s enumeration.

> “‘On the Sacrament of the Altar against certain heretics,’ one book.”

In *Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, book II, chapter 119, he says that this book was written against the Cathars, as the heretics of that period were called in Germany, and in France the Albigensians; they had not a few things in common with the Calvinists who later arose. This book too has not been published, unless it is that very lengthy letter [Col. 0076C] which we have among the letters under the title “To the People of Mainz.”

189. “Also a large volume, which she entitled *Scivias*, in which she discusses with great subtlety the way of the Lord and of His saints.” This work has been published since 1513 and subsequently reprinted various times. Trithemius does not mention its division into three books, but calls it a “large volume.” It is nevertheless divided into three books, and each book into several visions. Trithemius adds:

> “Also another volume, which she entitled *The Merits of Life*, and divided into three books.”

I believe this remains unpublished to this day.

> “A volume of simple medicine, a natural work and very remarkable, one book. Another book of compound medicine, one book.”

Concerning these two books Trithemius adds in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, p. 138:

> “In these two she refers the marvels and secrets of nature, by subtle exposition, to a mystical meaning, so that a woman could by no means know such things unless by the Holy Spirit.”

John Albert Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 260, writes thus of them:

> “A book of simple medicine and another of compound medicine are attributed to the same Hildegard by Trithemius; and there survive in print, under her name, four books of physics, of which the first treats remedies drawn from waters, earths, salts, and metals; the second and third, remedies from plants; and the fourth, remedies from animals. They appeared at Strasbourg, published by Johann Scotus, in 1533,”

etc. I would not venture confidently to assert [Col. 0077A] that those printed books are St. Hildegard’s; but since I have seen neither printed nor manuscript copies under her name, I prefer to leave judgment on the matter to those able to compare both.

Matthew of Westminster, under the year 1292, likewise lists certain writings of St. Hildegard and says:

> “And the book of simple medicine according to creation, comprising eight books; and the book of compound medicine concerning the causes, signs, and cures of illnesses—all of which were received and canonized by Pope Eugenius at the Council of Trier,”

etc. This final assertion, certainly—made carelessly by various persons concerning all St. Hildegard’s writings—is plainly false, because those books had not yet even been begun when, in 1148, Pope Eugenius approved the Saint’s first writings, or a portion of the book called *Scivias*.

190. After the words quoted, Trithemius adds: “A large volume,” entitled *Of Divine Works*. I believe this unpublished; but Trithemius included it in his catalogue of St. Hildegard’s works in four different places, as he did the book *The Merits of Life*. Matthew of Westminster also lists both in the passage just cited. Yet the Fabricius just mentioned thinks that these two works are not distinct from the three books of St. Hildegard’s visions printed under the title *Scivias*. Fabricius’s reason is that Trithemius, listing the beginnings of various works in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 281, assigns almost [Col. 0077C] the same opening to the book *Scivias* and to the book *Of Divine Works*. But the beginnings reported by Trithemius are not exactly the same, and we shall shortly see that these works are certainly distinct and were composed at very different times.

Meanwhile let us continue with Trithemius, who adds: “She composed a large volume of letters to various persons.” In the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, p. 138, he adds some other matters, writing:

> “To the clergy of the city of Trier [she wrote] one book concerning the future calamities of the Church; likewise, to the people of Cologne, one book on the same subject. In these she predicts marvelous things, though without fixing a time.”

These are printed among the letters, and I discussed them in § 7.

> “At the request of certain priests she also wrote one book, *An Exhortation to Secular Persons*; and for her sisters, one book of exhortation.”

The latter was printed with the letters in the place last mentioned and contains an exposition of the so-called Creed of St. Athanasius. But *An Exhortation to Secular Persons* does not appear to have been published.

> “To the Grey Monks, one book.”

This book was published among the letters, as were the other works mentioned by Trithemius, except the poems. Of these he adds: “Various poems, composed with sweet melody.” And in book II of *Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, chapter 119:

> “She composed several poems and songs, with sweet and marvelous melody, concerning vices and virtues in the form of a dialogue.”

We shall shortly see more concerning these works, hitherto unpublished.

191. The more certain writings of St. Hildegard are also listed in the Acts of the inquiry into her miracles, drawn up in 1233 and to be published below; there it is added in what order and over what span of time each was [Col. 0078A] written. There, no. 9, concerning the first work, we read:

> “She completed her book *Scivias* in ten years.”

That is, she began it in 1141 and finished it about 1151, or in that very year, as I have already observed in no. 32, where I treated that work more fully. Other works, composed during the following eight years, are set out as follows:

> “She wrote the book of simple medicine, the book of exposition of the Gospels, the song of celestial harmony, and the unknown language with its letters; all these she completed in eight years. This is gathered more fully from the introduction, or preface, to the book *The Merits of Life*.”

Here three works are listed as composed within eight years, namely from about 1151 to 1159; they are also mentioned in the *Life*, no. 14. Yet I suspect that the book of Compound Medicine was likewise [Col. 0078B] composed at that time, and that its mention has perhaps fallen out here through the carelessness of copyists. Certainly it is listed below, in no. 11 of the same Acts, among the Saint’s other works, so that there can be no doubt that the Saint wrote this work too, just as she wrote the book of Simple Medicine.

We have already sufficiently discussed above the exposition of the Gospels, which has never been published. Concerning the *Song of Celestial Harmony*, I observe that words unknown—or belonging to the unknown language—were added to the chant, as *Life*, no. 14, also says. Whether the poems which Trithemius above says were composed “concerning vices and virtues in the form of a dialogue” are different from this *Song*, and whether these can certainly be ascribed to St. Hildegard, I leave for judgment to those who can consult the manuscript codices themselves. But I do not at all [Col. 0078C] believe that the poems concerning the sect of Flagellant heretics, published by Ignatius Gropp in the *Collection of Würzburg Writers*, p. 122, in Michael de Leone’s *Chronicles*, are St. Hildegard’s.

192. After the words just quoted, the Acts continue:

> “Then, during the following five years”—that is, from about 1159 to 1164—“she wrote the book *The Merits of Life*. Finally, she wrote the book *Of Divine Works* over seven years, as is more fully clear from that book’s introduction.”

Thus this book seems to have been begun about 1164 and finished about 1171. Yet this reckoning of years does not yield so certain a date that the final work could not have been completed two or three years later. For, having finished one work, she might then have waited many months before beginning another, especially since during those same periods she wrote many letters—sometimes long ones—and several shorter works later inserted into the codex of letters and therefore counted among the letters.

These writings listed from the Acts, together with the codex of letters mentioned in no. 11, were acknowledged by “the convent” in the examination whose Acts we cite to be St. Hildegard’s. Moreover, when in the later years of her life St. Hildegard passed through Paris on her way to visit the tomb of St. Martin in the city of Tours, she gave her three principal works to the Parisian doctors for examination: [Col. 0079A] “namely, the book *Scivias*, the book *The Merits of Life*, and the book *Of Divine Works*,” as no. 9 says. They are said to have remained in the hands of the Parisian doctors “from the octave of Martinmas to the octave of Epiphany,” that is, for almost two months. The examined books are then said to have been returned through Master William of Auxerre, who told St. Hildegard “that it was the masters’ judgment that the words in them were not human, but divine.” Besides the testimony of the nuns, four sworn witnesses are cited concerning this examination of the books; two of them had studied at Paris at the same time.

193. To these most certain works of St. Hildegard must be added the volume of letters, containing at least the following works enumerated above from Trithemius: the *Exposition of the Rule of St. Benedict*; the response to Wibert of Gembloux concerning thirty—or rather thirty-eight—questions; the work addressed to the clergy of Trier concerning the future calamities of the Church; that addressed to the people of Cologne on the same subject; the exhortation to her sisters; and that addressed to the Grey Monks.

The work *On the Sacrament of the Altar* also seems to have been published among the letters under another title, namely epistle 47, where it is entitled: *To the Prelates of Mainz on account of the divine services prohibited by them*. For it begins, “In the vision which [was given] to my soul,” the same opening which Trithemius assigns to the work *On the Sacrament of the Altar* in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Certainly, in that work addressed to the people of Mainz, the Saint discusses the sacrament of the altar in several places. [Col. 0079C]

Apart from the letter to St. Bernard, which he places among the books, the Trithemius just cited lists a codex of “one hundred and thirty-five letters to various persons,” as he does also in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*. But in *Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*, book II, chapter 119, he lists among St. Hildegard’s writings “many letters to various persons, one hundred and thirty-six in number,” evidently then counting with the rest the letter to St. Bernard.

From this enumeration I infer that all St. Hildegard’s letters contained in that codex have now been published, except perhaps the final letter to the abbot of St. Disibod. For in the Cologne edition, besides the appended works, I find fifty-three printed letters, reprinted in the [Col. 0079D] *Library of the Fathers*. Martène, however, published another eighty-three of Hildegard’s letters and omitted the final letter to the abbot of St. Disibod, if it was written. Thus one hundred and thirty-six letters from that codex have been published. If, however, any letter is omitted there, the very lengthy one to the people of Mainz may be counted among the separate works.

194. Moreover, there can be no doubt that the Saint wrote more letters than the 136 inserted in the codex: another is inserted in the *Life*, and I have given three others addressed solely to the abbot of Park. Furthermore, Mabillon, in vol. II of the *Vetera Analecta*, p. 548, when listing the manuscript works of Guibert or Wibert of Gembloux—to whom St. Hildegard wrote the Response concerning thirty-eight questions mentioned in no. 116 and again from Trithemius in no. 188—[Col. 0080A] says that he saw several letters of Guibert to St. Hildegard and of the Saint to Guibert. These certainly have not been published, apart from one appended to the said questions.

Mabillon likewise says there that he saw a letter of Guibert to Philip, archbishop of Cologne, “in which he says that he is complying with the archbishop’s command to write the Life of St. Hildegard.” This may give rise to the suspicion that the aforementioned Guibert of Gembloux also wrote a *Life of St. Hildegard*. Nevertheless, I do not think he actually completed it, both because Mabillon does not say that he saw such a work by Guibert, though he found Guibert’s letters, and because no one has ever mentioned a *Life of St. Hildegard* written by Guibert. He may therefore have contemplated such a work, but probably omitted it because he understood that the Saint’s *Life* had already been written by Godfrey and Theodoric, and perhaps for another reason as well.

Whatever the reason, the unpublished letters of Guibert and Hildegard make it abundantly clear that not all St. Hildegard’s letters were inserted in the codex and subsequently published. This may again be demonstrated from Trithemius’s enumeration, on which I shall make an observation in the notes to the Miracles, letter z [below, note 83]. Probably some were not preserved because they did not seem worth keeping, and others were perhaps neglected for other reasons.

195. I find some other things cited under St. Hildegard’s name [Col. 0080C] which are not hers. Thus Matthew of Westminster, under 1292, cites among St. Hildegard’s works a certain *Mirror of Future Times*, or *Pentacronum* [read *Pentachronon*] . . . under the heading “On New Religious Orders”; from it he produces a rather long passage, which he foolishly twists against the Friars Minor.

But that work is not properly St. Hildegard’s; it was compiled from her works by Gebeno, prior of Eberbach, who flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century and was nearly contemporary with St. Hildegard. Bernard Pez, in the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, part III, supplies documents illustrating the history of the Benedictine monastery of Benediktbeuern in Bavaria. Listing manuscript codices, on p. 629, no. 14, he gives:

> “The *Mirror of Future [Col. 0080D] Times*, or *Pentachronon*, of the holy virgin Hildegard, by Gebeno, prior at Eberbach. The codex was written by a fourteenth-century hand. The work begins: ‘To the honorable men, always to be loved in Christ, Master Raymond, scholasticus, and Master Reinher, canons of St. Stephen at Mainz: Brother Seleno [read Gebeno], called prior at Elerbach [Eberbach], whatever a sinner’s prayer may avail. The holy virgin Hildegard, foundress and mistress of the monastery of St. Rupert,’ etc.”

Fabricius, in the work already cited, p. 79, treats of Gebeno, says that he flourished about 1220, and attributes to him the *Mirror of Future Times* quoted from Pez. Had he paid a little attention, he would not afterward have attributed the same work to St. Hildegard.

196. Hermann Corner, a writer of the Order of Preachers [Col. 0081A] who flourished at the beginning of the fifteenth century, knew Gebeno’s work well and excellently confirms what we have said. In his *Chronicle*, published by Georg Eccard in vol. II of the *Corpus historicum medii aevi*, under the year 1140, he writes the following about St. Hildegard after recounting her birth inaccurately:

> “She foretold many wonderful things. But how great was this holy woman’s sanctity is shown in Gebeno’s letter in the *Pentachronon of St. Hildegard*, where it is said: ‘The holy virgin Hildegard [add: foundress] and mistress of the monastery of St. Rupert, situated at Bingen, I do not think your charity can be unaware how great her sanctity and merit were before God and men. But if perhaps you do not know, read the little book of her Life; read the various letters [Col. 0081B] sent to her by the great persons of the land, and especially those of the three Apostolic Lords—namely Eugenius, Anastasius, and Adrian—as also of King Conrad and Emperor Frederick, the patriarch of Jerusalem, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and provosts; and now you may say truly: “God magnified her in the sight of kings, and the faces of princes admired her” (Ecclus. 45). This holy virgin, at God’s command—indeed, under compulsion—wrote certain books in which she prophesied certain matters very useful and necessary to our times, concerning the present state of the Church, future events down to Antichrist, and Antichrist himself.

197. “‘But because few can possess all her books or read what she prophesied concerning future times and [Col. 0081C] Antichrist in her three books—namely, *Scivias*, so named because it teaches one to know the ways; the book *Of Divine Works*; and the book of her Letters—I have for the most part gathered these things into this single little book and, as best I could, arranged them into five periods. Whoever wishes to read these five periods carefully and distinguish them attentively will behold, as in a mirror, the present state of the Church, all future times, the dangers, and the coming of Antichrist. Therefore, if it pleases you, let the book itself be called *The Mirror of Future Times*, or *The Pentachronon of St. Hildegard*, that is, concerning the five periods of which she prophesies in it. For *pente* means five, and *chronos* means time in Greek,’”

[Col. 0081D] etc.

Thus far Corner from Gebeno’s letter. He adds much concerning St. Hildegard, but it is less necessary to our purpose. These words, however, sufficiently teach whose work is cited by Matthew of Westminster. The sayings and prophecies of St. Hildegard which Matthew of Westminster brought forward are nevertheless for the most part corrupted, as the diligent reader can see by comparing St. Hildegard’s letter to the people of Cologne, cited by us in nos. 90 and following; to it are also appended some extracts from the letter to the people of Trier.

198. In the letter to the people of Cologne I find absolutely nothing that can refer to the Order of St. Francis except these words:

> “Nor will the deceivers—the heretics who are foretold—be able to move certain congregations of saints whose manner of life is holy.”

Just as the Order of St. Francis may rightly be regarded as one of those holy congregations over which, according to St. Hildegard’s prophecy, the heretics would not prevail, so it also seems to have produced some of those men whom St. Hildegard foretold would arise in those times in her letter to the people of Trier, in these words:

> “And then strong men will arise and prophesy; they will gather together all things old and new of the Scriptures and every saying poured forth through the Holy Spirit, and will adorn their meaning like a necklace with precious stones. Through these and through other wise persons, very many secular people will become good and will live holy lives. This pursuit of holiness will not quickly wither, but will endure for a long time,”

etc.

These words, I say, fit the illustrious [Col. 0082B] Order of Minors more aptly than the passages introduced indiscriminately and without discernment by Matthew of Westminster. Yet the Franciscans themselves, I think, will not be so fond of their own order as to deny that the same words may suit certain other religious orders.

199. Catholic authors who published libraries of writers have everywhere celebrated St. Hildegard with deserved praise. William Cave himself, although heterodox, praises the Saint in his *Historia litteraria*, under the year 1170, in these words:

> “Endowed with rare gifts of mind, and distinguished by remarkable piety toward God and zeal for religion, she began to be renowned for divinely granted visions and prophecies.”

He adds more, but without any detraction. Casimir Oudin, however, in his *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, [Col. 0082C] col. 1572, after quoting Cave’s words, continues as follows:

> “Accordingly, she was distinguished, as they would have it, by many revelations, which are highly esteemed among lovers of mystical visions and devout simple people; but among serious men, removed from feminine simplicity, they are of very slight weight, wholly without merit, nocturnal illusions of a perfectly empty brain. The same men hold, wholly and rightly, the same opinion of all such visions of women, especially as they affect the female sex, which is weaker.”

You see, reader, that Oudin makes nothing of St. Hildegard’s visions and prophecies, although by them she drew to admiration and affection for herself Roman pontiffs, emperors, other secular and ecclesiastical princes, [Col. 0082D] very many bishops and abbots, doctors eminent in learning, several communities of clerics and monks, and finally almost all Germany and a great part of France and Italy.

200. But let us hear the man again, wiser in his own judgment than all those persons. After listing several of the Saint’s works, he speaks thus:

> “Among Hildegard’s prophecies, the most outstanding is that which I have not yet seen printed: namely, *The Revelation of Hildegard concerning the Brothers of the Four Mendicant Orders*.”

And shortly afterward:

> “I was amazed at how clearly this prophecy, once given to me by a certain Cistercian and transcribed from a manuscript codex, depicts the four Mendicant orders along with the Jesuits, who succeeded them even much later in time.”

But he could not have written such things unless blinded by his own malice and hatred for religious men, whom he attacks so foolishly. Oudin either wished to write only what he believed true or set himself to slander without concern for truth. If the former, how could he have thought that “the four Mendicant orders along with the Jesuits, who succeeded them even much later in time,” could be depicted so clearly by the illusions of a perfectly empty brain, which he calls St. Hildegard’s visions? [Col. 0083A] How, I ask, could he believe that men to come long afterward, and their morals, could have been clearly foreseen by illusions of the brain, unless he himself had suffered foolish illusions of the brain? But if Oudin was intent only on slander, why did he not at least take care to proceed cautiously and not combine mutually conflicting statements in a brief encomium? Yet I seek these things in vain in Oudin. He wished both to diminish the authority of Hildegard’s revelations and, again, to use her authority—even against her will—to disgrace religious orders; and he could not do both without contradicting himself.

201. Let us now briefly examine Oudin’s two assertions separately. As to the first, concerning the slight credit to be given to any revelations and visions, especially women’s, I would be less inclined to oppose him in this matter if he had not exceeded proper bounds; if he had not wished to strip them of all credence too completely; and if he had distinguished between visions and predictions approved by no judgment and the visions of the most renowned [Col. 0083C] St. Hildegard and several other holy women.

For we know well enough that all women’s visions—sometimes merely fantastic imaginings—are not to be accepted as true and divine revelations. But it is no less certain that the spirit of prophecy has not been extinguished in the Church, and that genuinely divine revelations are sometimes granted to both men and women. Thus not only one who indiscriminately gives credence to every vision but also one who regards them all as illusions of an empty brain inclines too far toward an extreme.

Now, if not all visions are to be accepted indiscriminately, nor all rejected, it must necessarily be said that a distinction must be made among persons who claim to have visions. And if there is any person of the Middle Ages of whom, in the judgment of many and from other indications, it is certain that she enjoyed divine revelations, that person is St. Hildegard. For St. Bernard judged her to have been endowed by God with prophetic grace; so judged Pope Eugenius III together with the Council of Trier, and the supreme pontiffs Anastasius IV and Adrian IV. They rendered that judgment after mature examination of her person and of her writings down to that time. [Col. 0083D] For the thirty years during which the Saint afterward lived, countless persons concurred with them, including many doctors, bishops, and princes; many also who had known the Saint from childhood, and many who had often dealt intimately with her. Since Oudin wishes to set his own judgment above that of them all, he surely deserves that we should laugh rather at the man’s arrogance and pride than attend to his assertions—especially since he must be judged to have uttered them with the same levity with which, as an apostate, he abandoned his religion and faith.

202. The *Revelation of Hildegard concerning the Brothers of the Four Mendicant Orders*, as Oudin calls it—the work which he pretends to admire so greatly and generously adapts also to the Jesuits, as though there were no difference between the Jesuits’ institute or manner of life and those of the Mendicant orders, and as though the four Mendicant orders differed in nothing from one another—is an absurd declamation. Its style suits St. Hildegard so little that scarcely any other writing could be produced more foreign to her style.

The factual statements in that writing, [Col. 0084B] or the manners of men there set forth, by no means agree with the manners of the Mendicant orders or the Jesuits.
