For my part, I know not merely none of the said orders, but not even one man in any of the orders mentioned whose conduct is such as is portrayed in that writing. Indeed, Oudin’s slander is so plain—he who lived so long among Catholics—that I should be more than womanishly simple if I could believe that he thought the Mendicant orders and the Jesuits to be such as the persons described in that tasteless patchwork.

Oudin may have been perverse and utterly wicked, and for that reason may readily have formed bad judgments of others; yet I shall not easily allow myself to be persuaded that he was so foolish that he could have written without lying that the conduct of the Mendicant orders and the Jesuits is correctly represented in that writing, or that those orders were foretold in it. In any event, our predecessors have already observed, in vol. I for March, p. 667, in the notes to the *Life of St. Thomas Aquinas*, that this prophecy was probably fabricated around the middle of the thirteenth century against the Dominicans and Franciscans, when William of Saint-Amour began with others to attack the Mendicant orders; that it was afterward somewhat altered; and that it was not found in the monastery at Bingen, where St. Hildegard’s other writings are preserved.

§ XIV. The Saint’s death to be dated to 1179: burial; relics transferred to Eibingen after the destruction of the monastery of St. Rupert; miracles; attempted but uncompleted canonization; her name entered in martyrologies and her cult.

[Col. 0084D]

203. Writers do not agree concerning the year in which St. Hildegard passed to a better life. Trithemius, in his Hirsau Chronicle, under the year 1180, writes as follows:

> “In the year of Conrad, the fourth abbot, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, on the feast of St. Lambert—that is, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October—died Hildegard, the most holy handmaid of Christ, prioress and mistress of the nuns on Mount St. Rupert near the town of Bingen, which lies four miles from Mainz downstream along the river Rhine, in the eighty-second year of her life. Her body was buried with great reverence of the people before the high altar in that same church which she herself had long before built from the foundations.”

Trithemius agrees with this account of St. Hildegard’s age, year of death, and burial elsewhere also, namely in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and in the Spanheim Chronicle. Various writers followed Trithemius’s dating, which certain others suggest is not far from the truth, without further examination. But Pagi saw that Trithemius’s chronology did not accord correctly with the Life of St. Hildegard and therefore wished to correct it to the year 1178, writing as follows in no. 8:

> “This year St. Hildegard, an abbess—elsewhere called prioress or mistress of nuns—passed to God on Mount St. Rupert near Bingen, in the diocese of Cologne (rather, Mainz). For Abbot Theodoric—more properly, a monk—who flourished in the year 1200 (he would more correctly have said, who lived alongside St. Hildegard), says in the final chapter of her Life that she passed to her heavenly Bridegroom in the eighty-second year of her life, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October. He adds that this occurred at the first twilight of the night following the Lord’s day. Therefore, since the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, or 17 September, fell on a Sunday in this year, it is evident that Trithemius, in the Hirsau Chronicle, whom others commonly follow, wrongly postponed this death until 1180.”

Thus far Pagi.

204. He rightly proves, indeed, that the Saint did not live until 1180, since on that year 17 September fell on a Wednesday, or fourth feria; but he does not equally establish that she did not die in 1179, when 17 September coincided with Monday. For she is said to have died “at the first twilight of the night of the Lord’s day”: that is, at the first dawning, toward the end of the night which follows Sunday, or on Monday, as dawn was rising, as I shall demonstrate more fully in the Notes on the Life. This interpretation is not forced, but wholly necessary for other reasons. For it is clear from what was said in § 11 that the Saint survived for some time after the Lateran Council held in March 1179. Moreover, it is also necessary on other grounds, because another argument can prove that St. Hildegard certainly did not die before 1179. I shall set out the matter briefly.

From the preface to St. Hildegard’s book *Scivias*, she began to write in 1141, when she was “forty-two years and seven months” old. But if in 1141, even on the first day of that year, she was only forty-two years and seven months old, she could not in 1178 have been living her eighty-second year, in which she died; for in that case she completed her eighty-first year on 1 June 1179, or later. It is therefore certain that the Saint survived into 1179; and it is further clear from what has been said that her eighty-second year had only begun, or that she certainly lived only to eighty-one years and, at most, three or nearly four months.

205. According to Trithemius, the body of St. Hildegard was buried in the choir before the high altar. The Acts of the inquiry, no. 5, testify that a great multitude of people gathered at her tomb on the anniversary day of the Saint; nor is this surprising, since various miracles were performed both before and after her burial, as asserted in those same Acts or in the Life, no. 57. I find, however, no solemn elevation of her body. It was probably never performed, because canonization was indeed attempted repeatedly, but, as we shall see, has not been brought to completion.

Concerning a less solemn inspection of the relics, Serarius writes in his work on Mainz, book II, chapter 38:

> “While I was staying there, on Mount St. Rupert, and was looking through the volume in which the Saint’s writings are collected, mentioned a little earlier, I found the following recorded: ‘On 17 November 1489, by commission of the most reverend and most gracious lord, Lord Berthold, Archbishop of Mainz, the reverend and noble Lord Wolfgang von Bicken, canon of the Church of Mainz and vicar in spiritual matters, and the honourable Lord John Bertram of Numburg, doctor of arts and sacred Scripture, opened the relics of St. Hildegard, but without documentary evidence of her canonization. This was done in the presence of the noble and devout Lady Alheidis of Reiffenberg, abbess, and of the nuns, and of the noble and venerable Lord Peter Nothaff, canon of Mainz,’” etc.

The aforementioned Serarius, whose work was printed in 1604, had shortly before said: “In her monastery on Mount Rupert her relics are still preserved, together with a large parchment volume of her writings; likewise, her letters are preserved in the monastery of Eberbach in the Rheingau.”

[Col. 0086C]

206. But after the monastery of St. Rupert was burned by the Swedes in 1632, as stated in no. 177, the relics of St. Hildegard, St. Rupert, and others were carried elsewhere—namely, to the monastery of Eibingen, whose foundation by St. Hildegard and whose situation in the Rheingau I discussed in no. 177. For our Papebroch, in his manuscript *Roman Journey*, p. 23, recounts that in 1660 he and Henschenius made an excursion from Mainz “to Eibingen.” He then adds concerning the relics seen there:

> “There, with the abbess showing us, we saw most illustrious relics: the body of St. Rupert; the entire body of St. Hildegard, who had founded at Bingen, on Mount St. Rupert, a monastery for noble virgins. When it had been destroyed during the Swedish wars, the virgins, with their abbess, transferred themselves to this dependent house at Eibingen; the entire treasury of relics having been remarkably discovered and preserved by the Swedes themselves, who had been prompted by nocturnal lights seen around the place to permit Catholics to seek out and carry away the relics. There too was her garment, and her head covered with locks of hair turning grey from reddish colour; also a knife, as if half-sized, fitted with a hyacinth-coloured handle, given, as is reported, to the holy woman by St. Bernard together with a sheath made from buffalo hide. Among the books was a huge two-column parchment manuscript volume containing all the Works of St. Hildegard; but nowhere was there that fabulous revelation about men who were to precede Antichrist, first fabricated against the Dominicans and Franciscans and in these times interpreted as referring to members of the Society [of Jesus], which circulates through the hands of our slanderers to the applause of an ignorant populace.”

Thus far Papebroch. Furthermore, I do not find that St. Hildegard’s bones were divided or bestowed elsewhere. Yet the Acts of the Miracles, no. 5, testify that the Saint’s hair was held in veneration at Trier. Gelenius also, in his *Cologne*, when listing the sacred treasury of the church of Saints John and Cordula, includes on p. 445 something “from the hair of St. Hildegard.”

207. The Life and the Acts of the Miracles record that the Saint shone forth through many miracles both in life and after death. Yet no. 10 of the latter adds that the miracles thereafter ceased, at the command of the Archbishop of Mainz, “that she should cease from signs,” lest the divine office and the religious observance of the nuns should suffer harm through the excessive disturbance caused by the people flocking to the Saint’s tomb. The above-mentioned Serarius writes in agreement with this:

> “Moreover,” he says, “a German booklet of the Life relates that divine power was accustomed to perform so many miracles at those relics of hers that the peace of the virgins and the piety and religious observance in the church were greatly impeded by the huge gatherings of people. Accordingly, the Archbishop of Mainz came and commanded the Blessed woman herself to put an end to miracles of this kind; and she, in order to teach that superiors must be obeyed even in death, complied. Yet there were not a few either eyewitnesses or diligent and reliable investigators of these events, who, on 16 December 1233, sent accounts authenticated by their seals to Rome and petitioned the Apostolic See that this Blessed woman be entered in the catalogue of saints, male and female.”

The Acts drawn up for this purpose concerning the Saint’s virtues and miracles, which we have frequently cited already and shall publish after the Life, fully confirm all the foregoing.

208. We learn from the *Ecclesiastical Annals* of Odoric Raynaldus, under the year 1237, no. 50, that this investigation was instituted and those Acts drawn up by command of Pope Gregory IX. For in other letters there Gregory IX speaks thus of these matters:

> “When formerly the abbess and sisters of the monastery of St. Rupert of Bingen in the diocese of Mainz, our beloved daughters in Christ, petitioned us to take care to enroll in the catalogue of saints Hildegard, abbess of the same monastery, of blessed memory, who is said to have shone with many miracles both in life and after death, we caused her books—which she is believed to have composed through revelation of the Holy Spirit, although she had learned no letters save the Psalter—to be brought to us. We entrusted by our letters to the provost of the greater church, W . . ., the dean, and A., scholasticus of St. Peter’s at Mainz, the task of diligently investigating the truth, through trustworthy witnesses, concerning her life, conduct, reputation, merits, and miracles, and generally concerning every circumstance; and of faithfully sending us under their seals what they discovered, together with the aforesaid books.”

This is the Pope’s account of his command, by virtue of which the aforementioned Acts were drawn up.

[Col. 0088A]

209. But since this order had not been executed with the degree of accuracy which Gregory required in a matter of such importance, in the letters just cited he commands that another inquiry be undertaken. For in these letters, given in 1237, he continues as follows:

> “When their inquiry was sent to us, we found certain defects in it. For although it is stated in the depositions of the witnesses sent to our presence that she cured many possessed persons and sick people, neither persons, places, nor times are specified. Nor is it found therein what the mistress said, or which mistress said it, although it is there stated that the greater part of the community said the same as the mistress. Further, although the mistress herself, when first questioned, testified that she had performed many signs, the said depositions show that she said only [perhaps: merely] the same as the other witnesses and the community. Therefore we command that, proceeding diligently and prudently in the aforesaid inquiry according to the form given to them, you shall set forth distinctly and judiciously under your seals what you discover, and faithfully preserve it until our pleasure shall be known. Given at Viterbo, 6 May, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.”

I nowhere find whether this command of Gregory IX was carried out more exactly. Perhaps the earlier investigators of the miracles had in part died or been promoted to other offices. Not a few witnesses also may have been unavailable in the meantime, since four years had passed after the first inquiry and several of the witnesses were of advanced age. Whatever the reason, I find nothing concerning that repeated inquiry.

[Col. 0088C]

210. Innocent IV, Gregory’s successor, gave other letters in 1243 to the dean, scholasticus, and another canon of Mainz, repeating the deficiencies of the former inquiry, as Raynaldus testifies in the same place, no. 39, and adding the following:

> “We command that, if you have proceeded in such an inquiry by receiving trustworthy witnesses individually concerning the foregoing matters and having their statements written down as each one separately, simply, and in sequence gave testimony, you shall take care to send us the proceeding itself under your seals. Otherwise, diligently investigate the truth through trustworthy persons concerning all the aforesaid matters and any new miracles which she is said to have performed, as well as her life; and have the statements written down attentively of those witnesses whom you shall take care to examine individually, exactly as each of them, separately before you, shall have testified plainly, simply, distinctly, and in due order concerning all that he knows of the foregoing matters; and faithfully send them to us under the same seals. Given at the Lateran, 24 November.”

I do not know what effect this order had; but certainly the cause of St. Hildegard was not brought to completion under Innocent IV or under his successors throughout the thirteenth century, and thus the matter became ever more difficult.

211. Nevertheless, the canonization of St. Hildegard was attempted again in the fourteenth century, as Trithemius reports in the Hirsau Chronicle under the year 1317, writing thus:

> “Pope John XXII, at the request of Peter, Archbishop of Mainz, commanded Abbot Willichin of Spanheim and certain canons of the Church of Mainz, by apostolic letters, to go to Mount St. Rupert near the town of Bingen, where the Nahe flows into the Rhine, and make a diligent inquiry concerning the life, morals, signs, and miracles of the holy Hildegard, first foundress and abbess of the said monastery . . . . When the examination of the inquiry had been completed, the aforementioned commissioners found the religious and most holy life of the aforesaid nun sufficiently demonstrated, together with many miracles, both before and after her death. Judging her worthy of canonization, they sent to the aforesaid Roman Pontiff what was necessary to accomplish the matter. The Pope, having diligently read the testimonies sent to him, was not reluctant to canonize the virgin, as I have learned from an apostolic document, although he did not bring the undertaking desired by many to its intended result. His predecessor also, Pope Clement V, had earlier appointed commissioners in the same matter.”

This is Trithemius’s account of the attempted fourteenth-century canonization. But it was becoming ever more difficult, because the miracles had ceased at the command of the Archbishop of Mainz and no witnesses could have survived to prove miracles wrought in the earlier years after her death. Thus the solemn canonization, which could readily have been carried out had the first delegates proceeded more carefully in examining the cause, was never completed.

212. Yet from at least the fifteenth century martyrologists began to commemorate St. Hildegard, so that it is probable that her cult was permitted, even though canonization was not solemnly celebrated. The Haguenau codex, which presents a somewhat enlarged Martyrology of Usuard and was written in 1412, has the following entry on this day in our Sollerius’s supplements to Usuard:

> “In the monastery of St. Rupert at Bingen, in the diocese of Mainz, St. Hildegard, nun and prophetess.”

In the same place the register of the Charterhouse of Utrecht mentions “Hildegard the virgin.” Greven composed a longer eulogy in this form:

> “At Bingen, in the diocese of Mainz, the deposition of Hildegard, virgin of holy memory, who in the time of St. Bernard the abbot spread far and wide the fragrance of her holiness, so that very many Roman pontiffs, writing to her, commended themselves and the Roman Church to her prayers. Although she was ignorant of the Latin language, under the teaching of the Holy Spirit she dictated in Latin to scribes everything that she wrote.”

Molanus commemorates her in the following words:

> “At Bingen, St. Hildegard the virgin, who in the time of St. Bernard the abbot spread far and wide the fragrance of her holiness.”

Baronius adds in the Roman Martyrology:

> “At Bingen, in the diocese of Mainz, St. Hildegard the virgin.”

All who issue the Roman Martyrology in various languages have followed Baronius.

213. In the manuscript *Florarium Sanctorum*, composed in the fifteenth century, the following is found concerning St. Hildegard on 17 September:

> “At Bruges [read: Bingen], the deposition of St. Hildegard the virgin, in the eighty-second year of her life, in the year of salvation 1181,”

or rather, 1179. Peter de Natalibus, Bishop of Equilio, who flourished in the fourteenth century, gives a much longer eulogy of Hildegard the virgin; I find nothing in it requiring correction except the wrongly assigned day of death, 22 June. I nevertheless omit that eulogy, because everything stated there has already been explained sufficiently. Menard, in the Benedictine Martyrology, gives the following entry for this day:

> “At Bingen, in the diocese of Mainz, St. Hildegard, virgin and abbess.”

Wion, on the same day:

> “At Bingen, the deposition of St. Hildegard, virgin and abbess, who in the time of St. Bernard the abbot spread far and wide the fragrance of her holiness.”

These, along with many others, give St. Hildegard the title of abbess because she presided over the monastery she had founded. Yet she herself seems never to have used the title abbess, nor have I found that anyone called her abbess during her lifetime; she is frequently called mistress of the nuns, sometimes prioress, sometimes prior. Those, however, who presided over her monastery on Mount Rupert after the Saint were called abbesses. Bucelinus, in the Benedictine Menology, provides a summary of most of her deeds, which can be corrected in a few places from the matters discussed in this Commentary. Concerning St. Hildegard’s cult, Trithemius writes briefly in *On Illustrious Men*, book III, chapter 334: “Her feast is celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of October”; but probably this should read “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October,” that is, 17 September. I suspect that this cult began in the fourteenth or fifteenth century, because Hildegard’s name was then inserted in the martyrologies.

[Col. 0091]

# THE LIFE OF ST. HILDEGARD, BY THE MONKS GODEFRIDUS AND THEODORICUS

(*Acta Sanctorum Bollandiana*, September, vol. V, 17 September; from the Cologne edition and that of Surius, collated with the Bodec manuscript.)

## THEODORICUS’S PREFACE TO THE WHOLE LIFE

[Col. 0091A]

1. [Note: The preface is absent from the Bodec codex. I leave it to others to conjecture who the two abbots, Ludovicus and Godefridus, were.]

To the venerable Lords, Abbots LUDOVICUS and GODEFRIDUS, THEODORICUS, humble servant of the servants of God, greetings with devout prayers.

I have received the command of your authority that, after Godefridus, a man distinguished in talent, I should put in order the Life of the holy and God-beloved virgin Hildegard—which he began in an elegant style but did not complete—and, as it were weaving garlands from fragrant flowers, should combine her visions, interwoven with her deeds, under divisions into books and reduce them to the form of one body. This task seemed far too arduous for my strength, indeed even presumptuous: that I should, as it were, sit as an arbiter and pronounce judgment upon another’s work. Yet this thought entered my doubtful and anxious mind: charity supplies the strength which inexperience denies; and it is better to endure with shame the ridicule of men than to incur the danger of disobedience.

Accordingly, I obeyed in such a manner that the book of the aforesaid man, holding the place of the first composition, should suffer no loss of its arrangement; then the second book should contain the most beautiful and wonderful texture of the visions; and the third, an account compiled, divided, and arranged by us of the miracles which the wondrous God deigned to work through her. Thus the glory of the earlier writer will not be diminished, and the recollection of heavenly vision, true wisdom, and divine power will stir readers onward. For what good person would not be stirred with great longing to aspire to everlasting life by living holily, devoutly, and justly, when he sees a precious gem shining so remarkably with so many ornaments of virtues—virginity, patience, and teaching alike?

For this reason we have taken care that Christ’s lamp, once lit, should not be placed in concealment or beneath a bushel as though it ought to be hidden, but, set upon a lampstand, should shine before all who are in God’s house, to be imitated through its radiant examples of life, speech, and conduct. But if the untaught boldness of one who obeys has erred in any point in this matter, may the gracious charity of the lords who commanded pardon it, and attribute the whole fault to its own zeal, which was pleased to burden us weak persons with the undertaking of so weighty a work.

[Note: Thus far Theodoricus has spoken; then throughout the whole first book the narration of Godefridus follows. I could give here the chapter titles of the earlier division, supplied in the Cologne edition but omitted by Surius; but because the chapters are too numerous and minute, adding nothing to the titles of the narrative, I do not wish to enlarge the Life.]

# BOOK ONE: THE SAINT’S DEEDS

## CHAPTER ONE. The Saint’s birth and childhood, illumined by visions; monastic life under her mistress Jutta

[Col. 0091C]

2. In the Roman Empire, during the reign of Henry, [Note: The time of the virgin’s birth is explained more closely in the Commentary, no. 7, and the place in no. 8. It is called Gaul on this side with respect to Germany. The Bodec manuscript begins thus at [Col. 0092C]: “Henry, the fourth Augustus of this name,” etc.] there was in the regions of Gaul on this side [with respect to Germany] a virgin distinguished alike by nobility of birth and holiness of character, named Hildegard, born to her father Hidebert [Note: In the Bodec manuscript: “Her father Hildebert, her mother Mathilda,” etc.] and her mother Mechtilde. Although they were involved in worldly cares and conspicuous for wealth, they were not ungrateful for the Creator’s gifts, and they devoted their aforesaid daughter to God’s service, because the precocious purity of her earliest years already seemed very far removed from every inclination of the flesh.

For as soon as she could attempt her first speech, she indicated, by words and gestures alike, to those around her the forms of secret visions [Note: For the Saint’s visions from infancy, see Commentary § 2, where no. 9 also treats of the time when she was entrusted to monastic life under the discipline of Blessed Jutta.], which she beheld in a wholly unfamiliar contemplation beyond the ordinary sight of others. When she was almost eight years old, she was enclosed on Mount St. Disibod, to be buried with Christ and rise with him to the glory of immortality, together with the pious and God-devoted woman Jutta [manuscript: Juttha], who carefully trained her under the garment of humility and innocence; and instructing her only in Davidic songs, showed her how to rejoice upon the ten-stringed psaltery.

Apart from a simple knowledge of the Psalms, she received from no human being instruction in literary or musical art, although not a few writings of hers survive, including some volumes of no small size. But this can more readily be shown from her own words. For she says thus in her book entitled *Scivias*:

> “When I was forty-two years and seven months old, a fiery light of the greatest brilliance came from the opened heaven and flooded my whole brain. It inflamed my whole heart and breast like a flame—not burning, but warming—as the sun warms an object upon which it casts its rays. And suddenly I understood the meaning of the exposition of the books, namely the Psalter, the Gospel, and the other Catholic volumes of both the Old and New Testaments; but I did not possess an interpretation of the words of their text [Note: How wonderfully she was illumined by God, and by how many promptings she was urged to write, I have shown at length in the Commentary, no. 11 and following. Then in no. 19 I proved that she used the assistance of a monk in composing her Works.], nor the division of syllables, nor knowledge of cases or tenses.”

3. But to return to my subject: the virgin advanced in Christ by the vow of monastic profession and by the blessing of the sacred veil [manuscript: *perfecta*, “perfected”], grew, and went from strength to strength. The aforesaid venerable mother, striving on her behalf and rejoicing in her progress, saw with admiration that her disciple was now becoming a mistress and a guide along excellent paths. For loving-kindness burned in her breast, excluding no one from its breadth. The tower of virginity was also guarded by the wall of humility; on one side it was sustained by moderation in food and drink and by the plainness of her clothing; on the other, tranquillity of heart was shown in modest silence [manuscript: “the modestness of silence”] and sparing speech. All these necklaces of holy virtues, fashioned by the hand of the supreme Artificer, patience, their guardian, preserved for the adornment of Christ’s bride.

[Col. 0094A]

But since the furnace tests a potter’s vessels and virtue is perfected in weakness, she was not without frequent and almost continual pains of illness from nearly her infancy onward, so that she made use of the movement of her feet very rarely; and, while all the substance of her flesh was wasting away, her life was a kind of image of a precious death. Yet by as much as the strength of the outward person failed, so much knowledge and fortitude accrued to the inward person through the spirit; and while her body decayed, the fervour of her spirit seethed in a marvellous fashion.

4. As she grew for many years in her holy purpose, striving to please God alone, and as the time now approached when her life and teaching were to be made manifest for the advancement of many, she was divinely admonished by a voice addressed to her not to delay in writing down henceforth what she saw and heard. But she, fearful because of feminine modesty, the idle talk of the crowd, and men’s rash judgments, while she was pressed with an ever stronger compulsion not to hesitate to disclose the heavenly secrets shown to her, at length lay exhausted by a long illness. She then revealed, in fear and humility, the cause of this affliction first to a certain monk whom she had chosen as her master, and through him to her abbot.

The latter, considering in his mind the unusual novelty of the matter, although he knew that nothing was impossible to God, summoned the more prudent members of the community and judged that what he heard ought to be tested. He asked her certain questions concerning the Scriptures and her visions, and urged her to explain what God gave her. As soon as she undertook the work of writing, which she had not learned, her customary bodily capacity returned [manuscript: “power”] and she rose from her bed of illness. The abbot, having thus received certainty of an unprecedented miracle, was not content with his own judgment but judged [manuscript: “saw”] that the matter should be brought to public notice. Going to the mother church at Mainz [manuscript: “to Mainz”], he set forth what he had learned before the venerable Archbishop Henry and the chief men of the Church. He also displayed the writings which the blessed Virgin had recently produced.

5. At the same time the pontiff of the holy Roman See, Eugenius of blessed memory, having held a general council at Reims [Note: Eugenius III was at Trier toward the end of 1147 and in 1148 before the Council of Reims, as I showed in the Commentary, no. 27, where all these matters are explained.], was staying at Trier, having been summoned [manuscript: “called”] by Adalbero, Archbishop of Trier. It seemed fitting to the pontiff and to the leading clergy of the city of Mainz that the Apostolic See should be consulted concerning these matters, so that it might be known by his authority what should be accepted or rejected from the discoveries.

But the Pope, of supreme discernment, astonished at hearing such a novelty, knew that all things were possible to God and, wishing to investigate the matter more diligently, sent the venerable bishop of Verdun [Note: His name was Albero, and he freely resigned the episcopate in 1156. He is then said to have died in 1158. He is honoured with the title “Blessed” in the *Gallia Christiana* of the Sammarthani, among the bishops of Verdun. Castellanus, moreover, commemorates Albero as venerable on 2 November, where we shall investigate his cult.], together with Adelbert the primicerius [Note: This man succeeded Albero in the episcopate in 1156 and wrote to St. Hildegard, as stated in the Commentary, no. 60.], and other suitable persons, to the monastery in which the same virgin had lived enclosed for so many years [manuscript: “had been sheltered”], that they might inquire quietly, without commotion or prying curiosity, from her herself what the truth [manuscript: “what was true”] was.

When they had inquired humbly and she had simply disclosed what concerned herself, they returned to the Apostolic See and, amid the great expectation of Hildegard herself and of all those present, reported what they had heard. When the Pope had examined these reports, he ordered the writings of Blessed Hildegard, which had been brought to him from the aforesaid monastery, to be presented. Holding them in his own hands and himself serving as reader, he read them publicly before the archbishop, the cardinals, and all the clergy who were present. Proclaiming the responses of the men whom he had sent to investigate these things, he moved all minds and voices to praise of the Creator and rejoicing.

St. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, was also present there. Through his intercession and the efforts of the others, the Supreme Pontiff was urged not to allow so remarkable a lamp to be covered by silence, but to confirm by his authority the grace which the Lord had willed to make manifest in his time. In response the reverend Father of fathers, both graciously and wisely consenting, visited the blessed virgin by letters of greeting. Having granted her, in the name of Christ and St. Peter, permission to utter publicly whatever she had learned through the Holy Spirit, he encouraged her to write. He also honoured the place in which she was nurtured by sending congratulatory letters in his own name to the abbot [Note: Namely, Abbot Conon of St. Disibod. These letters, however, do not appear ever to have been published.] and brothers of the monastery.

## CHAPTER II. She founds a monastery on Mount St. Rupert near Bingen and inhabits it with her sisters; she continues to be illumined by unceasing visions

6. Thus Blessed Hildegard, with most humble confidence, disclosed and spread abroad the words which she had received neither from a human being nor through a human being, and the sweet fragrance of so holy a reputation diffused itself far and wide. Then many daughters of nobles flocked [manuscript: “flowed around”] to her, to be trained in the regular paths under the habit of religious life. Since a single enclosed dwelling could scarcely contain them all, and plans were already being considered for transferring and enlarging their quarters, a place was shown to her by the Spirit [manuscript: “the Holy Spirit”] where the river Nahe [Note: In Latin it is called *Nava* or *Navus*, commonly *Naw*. It is a small river in the Lower Palatinate, flowing into the Rhine near Bingen, beside which the monastery was founded. The place is described in the Commentary, no. 22.] joins the Rhine: namely, the hill named from ancient days after St. Rupert the confessor [Note: St. Rupert, duke of Bingen, and his Blessed mother Bertha have been treated by us under 15 May.]. He had formerly possessed it by hereditary right and there, together with his blessed mother, named Bertha, and St. Wibert the confessor, had happily completed his life in God’s work and service; and the place had acquired its name from his burial and relics.

When, therefore, the virgin of God identified to her abbot and the brethren the place to which she was to move, which she had known not through bodily eyes but through inward vision, they hesitated because they grieved over her departure. Lest the command of God should be hindered from being carried out, she fell, as before [manuscript: “previously”], into a bed of protracted illness, from which she did not rise until the abbot and the others saw that they were being compelled by divine prompting to consent, not to obstruct her, but to exert themselves to the best of their ability.

Among them was Arnold, a monk who had formerly been a layman. By his stubborn resistance he seemed to encourage the others to oppose the plan. While he was on an estate of the church in the village of Wilara, he was suddenly struck with such a severe bodily affliction that he despaired even of life and could not keep his enormously swollen tongue within his mouth.

7. By such gestures as he could make, he requested to be carried to the church of St. Robert. As soon as he vowed there that he would no longer oppose the undertaking but would assist to the best of his ability, he immediately recovered his health and began to help those preparing the dwellings. With his own hands he began to clear away the vineyards where the buildings suitable for the nuns’ habitation were to be erected.

But she for whose removal these dwellings were being prepared lay, because of the delays in carrying out the divine vision, wholly deprived of the use of her limbs. Like a rocky cliff, she could in no way be moved from the bed into which she had fallen. The abbot, not sufficiently believing those who reported it, came in to see. Though he strove with all his strength either to raise her by the head or turn her from side to side, he achieved absolutely nothing despite his efforts. Astonished by so unusual a miracle, he recognized that what was happening was not a human illness but divine correction, and that he himself must no longer oppose the heavenly command, lest he suffer something worse.

Since the aforesaid place belonged partly to the canons of the Church of Mainz, while the land together with the oratory of St. Robert was the possession of Count Bernard of Hildesheim, an embassy was sent through the intervention of faithful persons; and the virgin of God, foreknowing the outcome, obtained permission for herself and her sisters to dwell there.

[Col. 0096D] **8.** Therefore, after a long incapacity for walking, when it had now been decided on both sides that she should be sent away with her fellow-sisters [ms. adds *her own*] to the place which she had foreseen in the spirit, the abbot came in to the woman lying ill and afflicted and told her, in the Lord’s name, to rise and go to the dwelling divinely destined for her. Then she rose more quickly than speech, as though she had felt no weakness during so [Col. 0097A] prolonged a time; and amazement and wonder seized all who were present. Nor without reason: for the things which had been seen to occur [ms. *be done*] around the bedridden woman were no less astonishing. For from the time when she received a heavenly command to change her residence, as often as the affair seemed to be moving toward completion, so often did she feel relief from her affliction in her body; but, conversely, whenever she saw the undertaking being frustrated by the opposition of those resisting it, so often did she, though absent, suffer under a more intense burden.

Sometimes, suddenly rising from her bed and walking through every corner and dwelling-place of the enclosure, she could not speak at all; then, returning to her bed, when her power of walking failed, she spoke as before. She suffered from this kind of infirmity not only then, but whenever [Col. 0097B] feminine timidity made her delay or hesitate to carry out the business of the divine will, she received in herself this proof of certainty.

**9.** At last, therefore, when the handmaid of God departed from the place of her former dwelling with eighteen maidens consecrated to God [ms. *sacred*], she left behind as much grief and mourning among those whom she abandoned as she brought joy and exultation to the region which she approached. For from the town of Bingen [ms. *Binguensis*] and the neighboring villages there were many persons of rank, and no small multitude from the common people, who received her with great rejoicing and divine praises.

But she herself, entering with her little flock—indeed, Christ’s flock—the place prepared for her, magnified with devout gladness of heart the divine Wisdom [Col. 0097C] that disposes all things. With maternal affection she cherished the consecrated virgins committed to her care, and did not cease prudently to instruct them in the observances of the rule. And lest she should seem to have invaded or occupied a possession belonging to another’s right, from gifts brought by the faithful whom the fame of her name had drawn, she obtained the site of her dwelling from the aforesaid proprietors—partly by payment, partly by exchange.

Since she received it free, she ordained that it should remain free forever: thus subject only to the protection of the Church of Mainz, it was to have no defender other than the archbishop of that see itself. For if it took a lay advocate, it might seem to introduce a wolf into the sheepfold—a nearly universal disease by which very many churches throughout the world are harassed and laid waste. Toward the prelates [Col. 0097D] of the monastery from which she had migrated, she retained for herself and her daughters only this degree of subjection: that whatever was to be sought concerning spiritual matters—that is, the observance of the order and the profession of monastic life—they should receive from those prelates rather than elsewhere; and that, as circumstance and time required, they should receive priests from that monastery, whom they had expressly requested by their own free election, to support them both in the care of souls and the performance of the divine [Col. 0098A] offices, and in the management of temporal affairs.

> [Note: [Col. 0097D] On one occasion, in defense of freedom of election, the Saint appealed to Pope Alexander, as stated in the Commentary, no. 157, *Therefore*. Since Alexander was created pope in 1159, the Saint labored not merely one or two years, but for more than a whole decade, in order that everything might be properly arranged.]

**10.** All these things were decreed and confirmed not only with the permission but also on the advice of the venerable Henry and Arnold, archbishops of the metropolitan church of Mainz, and by their written instruments with the consent of the abbots. By the authority of privileges—or rather, to speak more exactly, by the prohibition of the supreme Deity—the church of Saint Disibod was forbidden to arrogate to itself any authority over the estates of Saint Rupert.

> [Note: [Col. 0097D] Henry and Arnold, archbishops, are discussed in various places in the Commentary.]

For this virgin herself, when she learned by an inward revelation that for this matter she must go to that same monastery, and was held back by a certain trembling like that of the prophet Jonah, was struck by the scourge of divine correction and nearly languished unto death. Warned by this blow, [Col. 0098B] she had herself carried into the oratory and there vowed that she would go where God commanded if the correction ceased. Then she asked to be placed upon a horse and led while supported by hands; and as soon as she had been taken a little way along the road, her strength returned and she proceeded joyfully.

When she came to the Mount of the aforesaid confessor, she explained why [ms. *how*] she had been compelled to come; and she released from those [ms. *them*] brothers of the monastery the site of her dwelling, together with the allodial lands belonging to it. She left them a very large portion of the properties which had been handed over to her together with the sisters she had received, and, moreover, a considerable sum of money, so that no ground for a just complaint might remain anywhere.

**11.** But I shall return to what the sequence of the narrative requires. [Col. 0098C] Blessed Hildegard, although she endured in herself the frequent labor-pains of fertile Leah, nevertheless nourished the beautiful Rachel’s eyes with the clear light of inward contemplation; and whatever she had seen inwardly she disclosed by speech and writing, as she knew expedient.

> [Note: [Col. 0098D] The author refers to Leah’s frequent births, not to the difficulty, which was greater in Rachel’s case.]

The matter calls for some remarks [ms. *that something be said*] about this manner of contemplation or vision, which was exceedingly rare and is known to have remained unknown, even to many outstanding saints, in this shadow of mortality; chiefly so that it may be known from her own words, insofar as she herself could disclose it. For she thus says in the letter in which she replied to the monk Wibert of Gembloux, who had inquired about matters concerning her that he had heard reported by public fame:

> [Note: [Col. 0098D] We possess Saint Hildegard’s reply to the many questions of Guibert, monk of Gembloux, as stated in the Commentary, no. 116. But I have not yet seen the letter cited here published; and I observed in no. 194 that several unpublished letters to Guibert exist.]

> “God,” she says, [Col. 0098D] “works where He wills for the glory of His name, and not for that of an earthly human being. I indeed [ms. adds *always*] have trembling fear, because I know no security of any capability in myself. But I stretch out my hands to God, that I may be sustained by Him like a feather, which lacks every weight of strength and flies upon the wind. Nor can I perfectly know the things which I see while I am in bodily [Col. 0099A] service and invisible in soul [ms. *invisible*], because in these two respects human beings are deficient.

> “From my childhood, when my bones, sinews, and veins were not yet strengthened, down to the present time—I am now more than seventy years old—I have always seen this vision in my soul. And my soul, as God wills, rises in this vision up to the height of the firmament and into the changing conditions of the different air; and it spreads itself among diverse peoples, although they are remote from me in distant regions and places. And because I see these things in this manner in my soul, I also behold them according to the changing conditions of clouds and other creatures.

> “But I see these things neither with outward eyes nor hear them with outward ears; nor do I perceive them by thoughts of my heart or by any comparison of my five senses, but only in my soul, with my outward eyes open. Thus I have never suffered in them a failure of ecstasy, but, awake by day and night, I see these things.”

**12.** Thus, as we gather from the foregoing words, this holy virgin truly possessed a wonderful and exceedingly rare manner of contemplation [ms. *very rare*]. For, in the likeness of the holy living creatures which Ezekiel saw, she went as a winged living creature straight forward and did not turn back; and again she went and turned back [Col. 0100A] (Ezekiel 1). For from the active life which she had undertaken she did not return to any low pursuits; while from the contemplative life—which, clothed in flesh, she could not constantly maintain—she returned to the active life.

> [Note: [Col. 0099] The passage in the manuscript is expressed thus: “Which Ezekiel’s prophecy touches, certainly like a winged animal,” etc.]

It was as though God said to her concerning the mode of the active life: “I will not leave thee, nor forsake thee” (Hebrews 13); He did not permit her to turn back from her good purpose. And again, as though He said to her concerning the mode of the contemplative life: “Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have made me fly away” (Song of Songs 6), He permitted her to return from contemplation of His incomprehensible majesty to the labor of active life. “Turn away,” He says, “your eyes from my contemplation, because they make me fly away, since in [Col. 0100B] this life they are not sufficient perfectly to comprehend me.”

Therefore the Psalmist also says: “Man approaches unto the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Psalm 63): because the more highly He is sought with a pure heart, the more sublimely it is understood that He is incomprehensible. In this manner the blessed virgin, while still placed in the flesh, labored in the active life and, through the contemplative life, thirsted with all her desires for the very light of divinity.

But here, bringing the first book to an end, let us bless the Lord, who looked upon His handmaid, chosen from the beginning of her birth, and advanced His beloved even to the brightness of His vision.

# SECOND BOOK ON THE VISIONS OF THE SAINT

[Col. 0099]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0099C]

**13.** Small talents cannot bear great material; but charity and obedience, by which I profess that I always owe my whole self to you, most excellent abbots Louis and Godfrey, raise my mind even from impossible things to attainable capacity. Therefore, though relying on no talent, I have nevertheless obeyed your commands in the charity of Christ and, with God’s favor, have taken care to arrange and complete the second little book on the Life of the blessed virgin Hildegard—strewn, as it were, with pleasant flowers of secret and hidden visions—from the point at which Godfrey of blessed memory ended the preceding book.

> [Note: [Col. 0099D] This Godfrey wrote the first book, except for the prologue. Everything else is by Theodoric, who writes these words.]

In it, from the words of the virgin beloved by God herself, such brightness of prophecy shines forth that she seems to have received a grace in no way inferior to that of the ancient Fathers. For just as it is read of Moses that he was continually in the tabernacle, so she too remained in the shelter of heavenly visions: that is, just as he did, so she remained with God, either in order to learn something or to teach something to her hearers. Did she not remain in the heavenly tabernacle and transcend the cloud of all carnality when the Spirit of truth taught her the text and words of John’s Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. (John 1)?

That same Holy Spirit, who flowed into John’s heart when he drew this most profound revelation from Jesus’ breast, willed through the divine grace of His condescension that she should learn what he had been worthy to declare. But let us defer speaking again of these matters, and, with that same Spirit breathing upon us, let us discuss what we have proposed. Nor should the reader be disturbed because some things that have been set down in the preceding book of her Life are nevertheless also described in the following work on her visions. For we judged it fitting that both the proper sequence [Col. 0100D] be preserved in the recital of her history and the authority and integrity of the words uttered by the Holy Spirit should not be mutilated at all in the description of her visions.

> [Note: [Col. 0099D] The principal reason for the repetition is the difference [Col. 0100D] between the writers. Theodoric did not wish to mutilate the first book by removing what had been brought forward concerning the visions, nor did he wish to omit those matters here. That prologue had been omitted in the Bodec manuscript.]

# CHAPTER I. Although ignorant of Latin, the Saint nevertheless writes books in Latin; she enjoys visions from childhood; she is compelled to write them down; she assists many with counsel and admonitions, and rightly directs her own community.

[Col. 0101A]

**14.** Therefore, in the place to which she had migrated by divine vision, the blessed virgin completed the book of her visions which she had begun at the Mount of Saint Disibod.

> [Note: [Col. 0101D] The author speaks of the first work called *Scivias*, which she began in 1141 on the Mount of Saint Disibod and completed around 1151 on the Mount of Saint Rupert.]

She also disclosed by the prophetic spirit certain matters concerning the nature of human beings and of the elements and various creatures, and how human beings should be aided by these, along with many other secrets. It is also evident how elegantly she answered letters directed to her from different provinces, if anyone wishes to consider more deeply the tenor of her words uttered through divine revelation.

> [Note: [Col. 0101D] Concerning the letters, which, like her other works, were written in the prophetic spirit from divine visions, we have set forth much in §4 and following sections.]

Both her own letters and those that had been sent [ms. *come*] to her have nevertheless been compiled into one volume. And who would not marvel that she produced, by a wondrous harmony, song of sweetest melody, and uttered, in a language previously unheard, characters not previously seen?

> [Note: [Col. 0101D] For the musical work composed by the Saint, consult the Commentary, no. 191, where I also listed her other works.]

Besides these things, she expounded certain Gospels and composed other typological expositions. Since the key of David opened these things to her, her soul could rightly rejoice and sing that the King had brought her into His wine-cellars, so that she might be intoxicated by the abundance of His house and given drink from the torrent of His delights. Accordingly, as it is written, conceiving from the fear of the Lord, she might bring forth spirit and work salvations [Col. 0101C] upon the earth.

> [Note: [Col. 0101D] The final words in the manuscript read thus: “Conceiving, she might bring forth, and make the spirit of salvation upon the earth.”]

It is also a great and admirable thing that what she heard or [Col. 0101C] saw in the spirit she wrote with her own hand and uttered orally, in the same sense and in the same words, with a circumspect and pure mind. She was content with one faithful male associate, who, for the sake of grammatical correctness—which she herself did not know—ventured to arrange cases, tenses, and genders, but presumed to add or remove absolutely nothing concerning their meaning or understanding.

> [Note: [Col. 0102D] She wrote in Latin what she heard; what she saw, I suppose, she either wrote in German or explained orally to her assistant for translation into Latin. See the statements in the Commentary, nos. 19 and 20.]

She also wrote about this to Pope Adrian:

> [Note: [Col. 0102D] The letter cited was sent to Pope Anastasius, as I observed in the Commentary, no. 50. The Saint did, however, also write to Adrian IV; hence I suppose that the author, from letters joined together in a codex, named one in place of the other.]

> “I heard this said to me in a heavenly vision: ‘Since you have not set forth in the Latin tongue what has been shown to you from above, according to the form of ordinary human usage, because this usage has not been granted you, let him who has the file [ms. *had learning*] not neglect to bring it to the fitting sound of human speech.’”

[Col. 0101D] **15.** It seems fitting, moreover, that we insert here some of her visionary writings and see from them how appropriately the saying from the Song of Songs, “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch” (Song of Songs 5), may be applied to her. These writings run as follows:

[Col. 0102A]

> “In mystical vision,” she says, “and in the light of charity [ms. *brightness*], I heard and saw these words concerning Wisdom, which shall never fail: Five tones of justice sent by God resound for the human race, and in them consists the salvation and redemption of believers. These five tones are more excellent than all human works, because all human works are nourished by them. They are not those which proceed in sounds, but those by which all human works are accomplished in the five senses of the body.

> “The first tone was fulfilled in deed through the faithful sacrifice that Abel offered to God. The second, when Noah built the ark at God’s command. The third, through Moses, when the law was given to him, which was the point [perhaps *covenant*] of Abraham’s circumcision. But in the fourth tone the Word of the supreme Father descended into the Virgin’s womb and put on flesh, because that same Word had coagulated mud with water and thus formed the human being. Therefore every creature cried through the human being to Him who made it, and thus God bore all things in Himself for the sake of the human being. For at one time He created the human being, and at another He bore him, in order to draw to Himself all whom the serpent’s counsel had destroyed.

> “But the fifth tone will be fulfilled when every error and mockery comes to an end; and then people will see and know that no one can do anything apart from the Lord [ms. *against God*]. In these five tones sent by God, the Old and New Testament will be fulfilled, and the wondrous number of human beings completed. After these five tones, a certain luminous time will be given to the Son of God, so that He shall be openly known by all flesh. Afterwards divinity will work in itself as long as it wills.”

**16.** Wisdom also teaches in the light of charity and commands me to say how I have been established in this vision. And I do not say these words about myself; rather, true Wisdom says them about me, and speaks to me thus:

> “Listen, O human being, to these words, and say them not according to yourself but according to me; and, instructed by me, say this about yourself: At my first formation, when God awakened me in my mother’s womb by the breath of life, He implanted this vision in my soul. For after [Col. 0102D] the Incarnation of Christ, in the year eleven hundred, the teaching of the apostles and the burning justice which He had established among Christians and spiritual persons began to slow down and turn into hesitation.

> “I was born in those times, and my parents vowed me to God with sighing [ms. [Col. 0103A] *with sighs*]. In the third year of my life I saw such a light that my soul trembled; but because I was an infant, I could say nothing about these things. In the eighth year of my life I was offered to God for the spiritual life; and until my fifteenth year I saw many things and spoke many things simply, so that those who heard them wondered where they came from and from whom they were.

> “Then I too wondered within myself, because when I saw inwardly [perhaps *within*] in my soul, I also had outward sight; and because I had heard this from no human being. I concealed as much as I could the vision which I saw in my soul. And I was ignorant of many outward things because of the frequent illness which I have suffered from my mother’s milk until now; it wasted my flesh, and from it my strength [Col. 0103B] failed.

> “Greatly wearied by these things, I asked one of my nurses whether she saw anything besides outward things; she answered me nothing about this, because she saw nothing [ms. *nothing of these things*]. Then, seized by great fear, I did not dare reveal these things to anyone; yet in speaking and dictating I was accustomed to tell many things concerning the future. And when I was fully inundated by this vision, I spoke many things that seemed strange to my hearers. But when the power of the vision somewhat withdrew, I behaved more in accordance with the ways of a child than with my years; I was greatly ashamed, often wept, and many times would gladly have kept silent if I had been allowed. But because of the fear I had of people, I dared tell no one how I saw.

> “Yet a certain noblewoman, to whose discipline I was subject, noticed these things and disclosed them to a monk known to her.”

> [Note: [Col. 0103D] The manuscript reads: “She disclosed it to a monk known to her.” This reading seems truer, for the woman to whom the Saint revealed the matter was Blessed Jutta, her teacher, and Jutta likely disclosed it to her own spiritual director.]

**17.** To that same woman God by His grace poured in, as it were, a little stream from many waters, so that she allowed her body no rest through good works, until she ended the present life with a good end; and God also displayed her merits through certain beautiful signs.

> [Note: [Col. 0103D] These statements concern Blessed Jutta, of whom we shall speak again on 22 December. They are more correctly given in the manuscript thus: “So that she allowed her body no rest in vigils, fasts, and other good works.”]

After her death I remained thus, seeing visions, until my fortieth year. Then, under a great pressure in that same vision, I was compelled publicly to disclose the things I had seen and heard. But I was very much afraid and ashamed to utter what I had kept silent so long. Yet the veins and marrow [ms. *and marrow*] of my body were then full of strength, whereas from childhood and youth I had been deficient in them.

[Col. 0103D] I disclosed these things to a certain monk who was my teacher, a man of good conduct and diligent attention, and, as it were, a stranger to the inquisitiveness of many people’s affairs. Therefore he willingly heard the same marvels. In wonder, he commanded me to write them down secretly [ms. *secretly*], until he saw what they were [ms. *what they might be*] and whence they came. But when he understood that they were from [Col. 0104A] God, he informed his abbot and thereafter worked with me in these matters with great desire.

In that same vision I understood the writings of the prophets, the Gospels, and certain other holy philosophers without any human instruction; and I explained some things from them, though I scarcely knew letters, as an unlearned woman had taught me. I also produced and sang, without the instruction of any human being, song with melody in praise of God and the saints, although I had never learned either a neume or any chant.

> [Note: [Col. 0104D] In the manuscript, *neuma*, a term used for musical modulation.]

When these things were brought to the attention of the church of Mainz and examined, all declared that they were from God and from the prophecy by which the prophets of old had prophesied. Then my writings were brought to Pope Eugenius while he was at Trier. He gladly had them read before very many people, read them himself, and, trusting greatly in God’s grace, sent me his blessing with letters and commanded me to commit more diligently to writing the things I saw or heard in vision.

> [Note: [Col. 0104D] On the examination of the writings held at Trier, see the Commentary, nos. 27 and 28. The remaining matters concerning her visions are explained in §2.]

**18.** Thus from the blessed virgin’s most beautiful vision, from her account of the fear she experienced at the coming of the Holy Spirit, from the Apostolic blessing, and from the permission to write which she received from him, we plainly gather that her beloved, the heavenly Bridegroom Jesus Christ, truly put His hand—that is, the operation and inspiration of the Holy Spirit—through the opening, that is, through His hidden grace; and that her inward part, namely [Col. 0104C] her mind, trembled at His touch, that is, at the infusion of His grace, because of the unusual strength and weight of the spirit which she felt inwardly.

What could be more apt? What more fitting? Certainly, just as the frequent visitation of the Lord in Elijah was signified by that sound of a gentle breeze, so her mind tasted the sweetness of the divine Spirit as often as it was raised to the heights of contemplation.

> [Note: [Col. 0104D] “The sound of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19:12) signified the Lord’s visitation of Elijah.]

And what did she do? “I rose,” she says, “to open to my beloved” (Song of Songs 5). O truly blessed virgin! Because, as it is written, she loved purity of heart, by reason of the grace of her lips she has the King—Christ—as her friend, from whom she received such a gift. According to the measure which the Holy Spirit willed to give her—for as He breathes where He wills, so He distributes to each one as He wills—she could not refuse to rise and open to her beloved. Now by voice, now by writing, opening the bolt of her door to the beloved, she performed outwardly what she had heard inwardly. What had she heard inwardly? “Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad, and divide thy waters in the streets” (Proverbs 5).

**19.** Therefore, while she was watered in this way by streams flowing abundantly with good works, like the rivers of Paradise, crowds of people of both sexes flocked to her from every direction—not only from the whole neighborhood, but from all threefold Gaul and Germany. Through God’s grace she bestowed upon them in abundance exhortations suited to both lives, the active and the contemplative. For the salvation of their souls, she proposed and resolved for them questions from the Holy Scriptures.

> [Note: [Col. 0105D] How many and how varied questions concerning sacred Scripture, theological matters, secrets, and hidden things were proposed to Saint Hildegard may be seen from the discussions in Commentary §§6, 7, and 8.]

Very many received from her counsel concerning the bodily necessities which they suffered; some also were relieved of illnesses through her blessings. Because she knew by the prophetic spirit people’s thoughts and intentions, she rebuked some who approached her with perverse and frivolous minds, as though to test her. Since they could not resist the Spirit that spoke, they were reproved and corrected, and compelled to abandon their wicked undertaking.

When Jews came to her with questions, she convicted them from their own law and exhorted them by words of pious admonition to faith in Christ. For, in accordance with the Apostle, she became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9); and to strangers who came to her, even blameworthy ones, she spoke gently and mildly, as she saw was suitable to them.

**20.** But the maidens living with her she corrected with much affection of love and maternal tenderness whenever resentment from any dispute, grief from worldly sorrow, sloth, or negligence arose among them. Indeed, she saw their wills, intentions, and thoughts so clearly that even in the divine offices she responded to them with her own blessings according to the state of their hearts [ms. *blessed without them*]. For in the spirit she foresaw people’s lives and conduct, as well as the end of the present life for some; and, according to the nature of their conduct and merits, the glory and punishments of their souls.

Yet such great mysteries she disclosed to no one except that one man to whom, as said above, she revealed all her secrets. Finally, just as she knew the time for silence, so she knew what, where, to whom, why, how, and when it was time to speak. In all these things she preserved humility, the sum of all virtues. Knowing that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Peter 5), she always praised the almighty kindness [Col. 0105D] of divine grace.

# CHAPTER II. In a vision the Saint learns the place where she is to found a monastery; on that account she suffers much, yet has God as her helper and comforter in all things.

[Col. 0106A]

**21.** Although the heavenly Bridegroom frequently visited His beloved bride, adorned with such great and such splendid dowries of grace, yet, as it is written, “the greater thou art, humble thyself in all things,” He allowed her often to be harassed by various afflictions of illness. To make this clearer, let the text of her visions be brought forward, so that virtue perfected in weakness may not remain hidden and the reader’s weariness, while he delights in alternation, may also be relieved.

Do you wish to know what she endured because she had not disclosed the heavenly vision shown her concerning her migration with her maidens from the place where she then was to another? Hear her writing thus:

> “At a certain time,” she says, “because of a darkness in my eyes, I saw no light, and I was weighed down by such a burden of body that, unable to rise, I lay overwhelmed by the greatest pains. I suffered this because I had not disclosed the vision shown to me: that [Col. 0106B] I ought to move with my maidens from the place where I had been offered to God to another. I endured this for so long until I named the place where I now am; and immediately, when my sight returned, I was indeed better, though I was not yet entirely free from illness.

> “But when my abbot, the brothers, and the people of that province learned of this move, they wondered what it meant that we wished to leave the richness of fields and vineyards and the pleasantness of that place for a waterless place where there were no conveniences. In order to prevent this and oppose us, they conspired together. They also said that I had been deceived by some delusion. When I heard this, my heart was crushed, and my flesh and veins dried up; and for many [Col. 0106C] days, as I lay in bed, I heard a great voice forbidding me to speak or write anything further in that place concerning this vision.”

**22.** “Then a certain noble marchioness known to us went to the archbishop of Mainz and disclosed all these matters to him and to other wise persons. They said that no place is sanctified except through good works; therefore it seemed fitting [ms. *seemed*] that this should come to pass.

“Then the ancient deceiver sifted me through many mockeries, so that many said: ‘What is this, that so many mysteries are revealed to this foolish and unlearned woman, when there are many strong and wise men? Therefore it will be scattered.’ For many wondered about the revelation—whether it was from God or from the waterlessness of aerial spirits, who deceive many.

> [Note: [Col. 0105D] She speaks of the place shown to her, namely the Mount of Saint Rupert, though the word *I remained* seems [Col. 0106D] to imply the contrary; but here *I remained* means the same as ‘I began to dwell.’ Yet when the Saint says ‘with twenty maidens,’ she seems to contradict the biographer in no. 9, where he says that she departed from the Mount of Saint Disibod ‘with eighteen maidens.’ Both may be true if two joined her upon arrival at the Mount of Saint Rupert.]

“And so, in this place, I remained with twenty noble maidens, born of wealthy parents, finding no [ms. *and no*] dwelling or inhabitant here except a certain old man, his wife, and their children. Such adversity of tribulations and oppressive labors fell upon me that, just as a storm-cloud [Col. 0107A] hides the sun, I said, sighing deeply and shedding tears: ‘O, O, God confounds no one who trusts in Him.’

“But again God showed me His grace, just as the sun appears when clouds withdraw, and as a mother gives milk to a weeping infant, who afterward rejoices. Then in a true vision I saw that these tribulations had come upon me in the example of Moses. For when he led the children of Israel out of Egypt, across the Red Sea, into the wilderness, they murmured against God and severely afflicted Moses, although God had enlightened them by wondrous signs.

“So God allowed me to be afflicted in some measure by the common people, by my relatives, and by some who remained with me, when they lacked necessities, except insofar as [Col. 0107B] they were given us by God’s grace in alms. For just as the children of Israel afflicted Moses, so these too shook their heads over me and said: ‘What benefit is there in noble and wealthy maidens having come from a place where they lacked nothing into such want?’ But we expected the grace of God to come to our aid, since He had shown us this place [ms. adds *alone*].

**23.** “After the pressure of this suffering, God rained His grace upon us. For many who had first despised us and called the place a useless waterless place came to us from every side, helping us and filling us with blessings. Many wealthy persons also buried their dead honorably among us. And very many, recognizing this vision in faith, came to us with great desire, as it was said through the Prophet: ‘Those who slandered thee shall come unto thee’ (Psalm 37).

“Then my spirit revived; and whereas I had formerly wept in pain, now I wept for joy because God had not consigned me to oblivion, when He established this place by exalting it and increasing it with many useful [the word *useful* is absent from the manuscript] things and buildings. Yet God willed that I should persevere steadfastly in complete security, as He had done from my childhood in all my affairs, since He left me no secure enjoyment of this life through which my mind might be lifted up.

“For when I was writing the book *Scivias*, I had in complete [Col. 0107D] charity a certain noble maiden, the daughter of the aforesaid marchioness, as Paul had Timothy. In devoted friendship she joined herself to me in all things and shared my suffering [*mihi* is absent from the manuscript] until I completed that book. But afterward, because of the distinction of her birth, she inclined herself toward the dignity of a greater [ms. *greater*] title, so as to be called mother of a certain eminent church. Yet she sought this not according to God but according to the honor of this world. After withdrawing from me, she quickly lost her present life in another region far removed from us, together with the title of dignity.

> [Note: [Col. 0107D] This abbess, whose departure grieved the Saint, seems to be the sister of Hartwig, archbishop of Bremen, who reported her death to Saint Hildegard, as stated in Commentary [Col. 0108D] no. 46.]

“Certain other noble maidens likewise separated themselves from me. Some of them afterward lived so negligently that many said their works showed that they had sinned against the Holy Spirit and against the human being who spoke from the Holy Spirit. But I and those who loved me wondered why such great persecution came upon me and why God gave me no comfort, when I did not wish to persist in sins but desired, with God’s help, to accomplish good works. Amid these things I completed the book *Scivias*, as God willed.”

24. From the preceding description of the vision and of the blessed virgin’s affliction, it is clear that the place which had been shown to her beforehand, and for which the Lord Himself punished an obstructer with blindness, was chosen and selected beforehand by the Lord as His inheritance, so that His holy name might be more earnestly glorified there—both because of the merits of Saint Rupert and of those resting there with him in Christ, and because of the advancement of the holy virgin and of those coming there with her. Meanwhile the recollection of an old history comes to mind, and a beautiful comparison presents itself to us between the prophetess Deborah [Note: [Col. 0108D] On Deborah, see the Book of Judges, chapter IV.], and the place in which she sat, on the one hand, and our prophetess and our place, on the other. For Origen says:

> “It affords no small consolation to the female sex, and urges women not to despair because of the weakness of their sex that they too can become capable of the grace of prophecy; but let them understand and believe that purity of mind, not difference of sex, merits this grace.”

For Deborah, whose name is interpreted “bees,” occupies the role of prophecy. For it is certain that every prophecy composes sweet honeycombs of heavenly teaching and the sweet honey of divine utterance, as David says: “How sweet are your sayings to my palate, more than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. 118 [119].) She is said to sit between Ramah and Bethel; and Ramah is interpreted “heights,” Bethel “house of God.” For nothing lowly, nothing abject, is found in relation to the seat of prophecy. Thus also, in Solomon, the seat of wisdom either stands at the gates of cities, or dwells on the walls of their ramparts, or acts freely in towers.

In this manner prophecy is said to have dwelt in blessed Hildegard between the house of God and the heights; and this may now plainly be seen also in a local sense, [Col. 0108D] though it can also be understood spiritually. For it teaches you, O holy soul, whoever you are that dwell there, to reject the things that are upon earth and to seek those things that are in the heights of heaven, where Christ sits at God’s right hand. There her prophecy exhorts you to ascend; there it strives to place its hearers. Blessed, therefore, be the grace of God [MS: “the glory of the Lord”] from His place, concerning whose liberation, foreseen by the blessed virgin in the spirit, she says thus in her writing:

25. “I saw in a vision, and I was taught and compelled to reveal to my prelates that our place, with [Col. 0109A] its appurtenances, ought to be released from the place in which I had been offered to God, except that we should owe submission and obedience to those serving God there, so long as we found good faith toward us [Note: [Col. 0109D] The manuscript reads: ‘so long as we found their good disposition toward us.’]. I made this known to my abbot [Note: [Col. 0109D] This abbot of St. Disibod was probably Cono or Cuno, who died in 1155, when Helinger succeeded him.], but, seized by illness, he made no arrangement concerning it, since [MS: “because also”] he ended his life a few days later. But when these matters came before the succeeding abbot, the Archbishop of Mainz, and the leading men of the church, they received them in faith and charity and confirmed that it should be done by a sealed document.

“Meanwhile I endured many assaults from certain persons, like Joshua, whom the enemy tried, above all others, to lead away into confusion as a victor; but as God helped him, so He delivered me and my daughters. But just as Joseph’s brothers [Col. 0109B] envied him because he was loved by his father more than the others, and, after selling him, brought his torn garment to their father, saying that a wild beast had devoured him, so certain malicious persons wished to tear in us the garment of the Lord’s grace and praise. But God came to our aid, just as He restored Joseph to honor. Although we had much oppression, nevertheless by God’s grace we increased, like the children of Israel, who grew ever more numerous the more they were oppressed. Therefore I looked to God in joy of heart; and because He had stood by me in tribulations, I wished to be secure.”

26. Here we may fittingly consider that, although the blessed virgin was weighed down in body by the wasting of infirmity and also by the vexation [Col. 0109C] of diabolical and human assaults, she nevertheless always deserved to be strengthened and confirmed by divine consolation. For the Holy Spirit, wishing to preserve in His chosen vessel a grace beneficial to many, diligently sought to remove from her every rust of dross by the file of correction, so that, advancing through chastisement, she might carefully seek out the Lord’s will and, in accordance with the Apostle, render rational service to God, ordering the entire course of her life according to His judgment—and deservedly so.

For, illuminating her by His free gift with the good of both nature and grace, He prepared for her grace in great abundance and glory: grace on earth, glory in heaven; grace of exalted merits, glory of ineffable rewards. Hence [Col. 0109D] she was chastised by earthly afflictions, as it is written: “God scourges every son whom He receives” (Heb. 12), so that merit might be increased in her through such trials, as is also declared in the following vision, which she describes thus:

27. “At one time God laid me upon a bed of illness and filled my whole body with the punishments of the air, so that my veins with their blood, my flesh with its moisture, my marrow [MS: “marrows”] with my bones dried up within me, as though my soul were to be taken from my body. I remained in this tumult for thirty days, so that my belly burned with the heat of aerial fire. Hence [Col. 0110A] some reckoned this illness to be a punishment. The strength of my spirit too, fixed in my flesh, failed; I was neither removed from this life nor wholly in it. My altered body was also laid out upon the ground on sackcloth; yet I did not see my end, although my prelates, daughters, and neighbors came with great weeping and saw my death.

“But in true vision during these days I sometimes saw a great host of angels, innumerable to human understanding, who belonged to that army which fought with Michael against the dragon; and they waited to see what God would command to be done with me. But one mighty one among them cried out to me, saying: ‘Alas, alas, eagle, why do you sleep in knowledge? Rise from doubt. You shall be recognized, O jewel in splendor; all eagles [Col. 0110B] shall see you, but the world shall mourn, while eternal life shall rejoice. Therefore, dawn, rise toward the sun. Rise, rise; eat and drink.’

“Immediately the whole host cried with a resounding voice: ‘A voice of joy: the messengers have fallen silent; the time for passing over has not yet come. Therefore, maiden, arise.’ At once my body and my senses were restored to present life. When my daughters, who had earlier wept, saw this, they lifted me from the ground and placed me again in bed, and thus I recovered my former strength.

“But the penal infirmity did not wholly leave me; only my spirit was strengthened within me from day to day more than before.
