For the most wicked aerial spirits, to whom the punitive torments of human beings are assigned, supplied this punishment which they inflicted upon me by God’s permission, just as torturers [Col. 0110C] did who applied coals to blessed Lawrence and other martyrs. Hastening toward me, they shouted loudly: ‘Let us seduce this woman, so that she may doubt God and blaspheme Him for involving her in such great punishments.’

“For just as, by God’s permission, Satan struck Job’s body so that it swarmed with worms, so the aerial fire entering within consumed my flesh. This also befell Jeremiah, who mourned his pain bitterly. Yet the devil could not persuade him to blaspheme God. I, however, weak in flesh and timid in mind, was greatly terrified by these punishments. But God strengthened me so that I bore them patiently, and in my spirit I said: ‘O, O Lord God, I know that all the things by which You touch me are good, because all [Col. 0110D] Your works are good and holy, since I have merited these things from my childhood. Yet I trust that You will not permit my soul to be tortured thus in the life to come.’”

## CHAPTER III. The Saint’s remarkable illnesses; her instruction of nuns; the conversion of a philosopher who had been suspicious of her; various visions.

28. “While I was still suffering these pains, I was admonished in a true vision to go to the place in which I had been offered to God and to proclaim the words which God had shown me. This I did, and in the same [Col. 0111A] pain I returned to my daughters. I also set out for other places of religious communities and expounded the words which God commanded. In all these things the vessel of my body was as though baked in a furnace, just as God tested many whom He commanded to utter His words; therefore praise be to Him.

“He also gave me great help in two of my daughters and in others, who tirelessly shared my sufferings. Sighing, I therefore gave thanks to God because people were not wearied by me. For if I had endured in my flesh so great a burden of pains not from God, I could not have lived so long. Although I was tormented by these things, nevertheless in heavenly vision I dictated, sang, and wrote what the Holy Spirit wished to utter through me [Note: [Col. 0111D] The manuscript has only: ‘what I wished to utter.’].

“When three years had passed in these illnesses, [Col. 0111B] I saw that a cherub in flaming fire—in which is the mirror of God’s mysteries—was pursuing with something like a fiery sword the aerial spirits that tortured me, so that they fled from me, crying: ‘Ah, ah! Woe, woe! Will this woman, this woman, thus depart, so that we shall not seize her?’ Immediately my spirit fully revived within me, and my body was restored in veins and marrow; thus I recovered completely.”

29. Behold how the holy virgin, now tormented in a twofold way by the pains of illness, now harassed by the terrors of demons [Note: [Col. 0111D] After the word “harassed,” the manuscript adds: “not only was she not overcome; indeed, [Col. 0112D] she was also glorified by manifold victory under angelic protection.”], was glorified under angelic protection. On the one hand, while she suffered from bodily weakness, this woman of wondrous innocence fortified herself with the virtue of patience; and, as though the divine discourse soothed the trouble [Col. 0111C] of her affliction, saying, “My grace is sufficient for you, for strength shall be perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12), she gladly gloried in infirmities, that Christ’s power might dwell in her. She presumed herself loved precisely in that for which she deserved rebuke.

On the other hand, when she was provoked by demonic cunning, this distinguished warrior again armed herself with the safeguard of apostolic teaching. What teaching? “Take,” it says, “the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6). And again: “Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of these darknesses” (ibid.). Thus, with this great art of combat and these weapons, she fought as an unconquered defender; still enclosed in flesh and set upon earth, [Col. 0111D] she battled against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

Therefore the princes of darkness themselves were terrified when they saw a woman so expertly equipped and protected by the full armor of the strong advancing against them. Terrified, I say, they fled in confusion, crying out their “Woe,” because fear and trembling came upon them when they saw the terrible cherub, like an army drawn up in battle array, protecting God’s handmaid and pursuing them with a flaming sword lest they trouble her. Thus they were amazed, thrown into confusion, shaken; trembling seized them, so that they said: “These are [Col. 0112A] the camps of God; let us flee Israel” (Exod. 14). And immediately they fled.

Thus the athlete of God’s spirit wrestled between the heavenly and infernal spirits, and, having driven back her adversaries, always gloried in joyful victory. Nor should this be passed over: when on one occasion she suffered from fevers, she saw certain saints saying, “Avenge, Lord, the blood of Your saints.” Others said to her: “You ought to bear willingly the pain which you suffer.” And behold, other saints conversed among themselves: “Will she go with us, or not?” Others replied: “Her past, present, and future do not yet permit it; but when she has completed her work, we shall take her with us.” Then all together cried: “O happy and most steadfast soul, rise, rise like an eagle, because the sun has brought you forth, and [Col. 0112B] you did not know it.” And immediately she recovered.

30. Not only when she encountered the distress of illnesses or the cruelty of demons, but also when she suffered human persecution, the Lord stood by her and turned the hearts of her opponents to what was better. She herself describes this in the conversion of a philosopher formerly opposed to her—indeed, opposed to God—in whom there truly afterward occurred “a change of the right hand of the Most High.” She also describes how she removed, by exhortations from Holy Scripture, the vanities which arose in the hearts of her daughters through Satan’s deception:

“A certain philosopher, honored on account of his wealth, long doubted concerning the things which I had seen; but at last he came to us and richly adorned our place with buildings, allodial estates, and other necessities. Therefore my soul rejoiced, because God had not consigned [Col. 0112C] us to oblivion. For with keen yet wise inquiry he investigated what these writings of this vision were and whence they came, until by divine inspiration he believed fully. He who had formerly despised us with malicious words, after God had stifled injustice in his heart, turned toward us with greater blessings; just as God drowned Pharaoh in the Red Sea when he sought to capture the children of Israel.

“Many marveled at his change and believed more firmly; and through this wise man God poured His blessing upon us like the ointment which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron (Ps. 132 [133]). Therefore we all called him father. This man, who was such a great prince in his own name, asked to be buried among us, and so it was done. Then my mind was strengthened, and I took care of my daughters in the necessities both of body and soul, as had been established for me by my teachers.

“Therefore, with great concern I looked to the true vision to see how aerial spirits fought against us; and I saw that those spirits had entangled certain of my noble daughters in a net, as it were, through diverse vanities. But by God’s showing I made this known to them [MS: “I marked this in them”], and surrounded and fortified them with the words of Holy Scripture, regular discipline, and good conduct. Yet some of them, looking at me with grim eyes, [Col. 0113A] secretly tore me apart with words, saying that they could not bear the unbearable burden of regular discipline by which I wished to restrain them.

“But God gave me consolation in other good and wise sisters, who stood by me in all my sufferings, just as happened in the case of Susanna, whom God delivered from false testimony. Although I was frequently wearied by tribulations of this kind, nevertheless through God’s grace I brought to completion the Book of the Merits of Life [Note: [Col. 0113D] See the discussion of this work in the Commentary, no. 192.], revealed to me by God.”

31. Thus the virgin devoted to God conducted herself amid adversities and prosperities: she was neither exalted by prosperity nor cast down by adversity; but maintaining one and the same strength in both, she was neither shaken by blame [Col. 0113B] nor seduced by praise. For she kept her mind, stretched tight like a bow, fixed upon every discipline; and, since it did not grow slack, she governed herself and her community by authority now gentle, now severe. For in her there was a gravity tempered by kindness, and from her tongue flowed a sweetness of speech sweeter than honey.

She possessed sound teaching in all matters, as she writes concerning human nature, the conflict of flesh and spirit, and the examples of the holy Fathers—matters which she received through divine revelation:

> “In true vision I saw the figure of a human being, who, although consisting of the two natures [Note: [Col. 0113D] That is, two parts. This manner of speaking, by which she calls soul and body two natures, occurs quite frequently in the Saint’s writings. Yet by that form of speech she should be understood to mean nothing but two parts, as is clear from the following words, where she says that the human being is ‘one building.’] of soul and body, is nevertheless one building: just as when a human being constructs a house of stones, covers it also with ashy material, and strengthens it lest it collapse and be ruined.

> “For the human being is God’s work and exists with every creature, and every creature exists with him. But the work of a human being, which is without life, is not like God’s work, which is life, just as a potter’s vessel is not like a builder’s structures. The nature of the soul looks toward unending life; but the body embraces a perishing life. And they are not of one mind, because, although they are together in the human being, they are nevertheless divided into two.

> “By this likeness, when God sends His Spirit [MS erroneously: “His Son”] into a human being through prophecy and wisdom or through miracles, He often inflicts pains on that person’s flesh, so that the Holy Spirit may be able to dwell there. But if He does not bind it with pains, it easily mingles with worldly habits, as happened in [Col. 0113D] Samson, Solomon, and others, who failed in the sighings of the spirit by inclining themselves toward the pleasure of the flesh, because prophecy, wisdom, and miracles are pleasant in joy.

> “But when a person sometimes cultivates the pleasure of the flesh through the devil’s suggestion, that person often says: ‘Ah! I stink with the foul stench of filth. Why does the spirit afflict the flesh?’ Because the spirit itself, by its nature, hates the taste of sin. But when the flesh breaks the soul’s desires because of the frequent pleasure in which it entangles itself through the stench of sin, so that the spirit cannot sigh because of this same trouble, [Col. 0114A] then the flesh afflicts the spirit, and this affliction is divided into two parts by God’s grace.”

32. “This conflict, which has been spoken of in relation to the figure that is the human being, began in Abel, whom his brother hated; and in Noah, who endured injury from his sons [rather: from his son]; and in Abraham, who bore reproaches from friends; and in Jacob, who was an exile because of his brother; and in Moses, who was afflicted by friends because they agreed with his enemies. This affliction was also among Christ’s disciples, because through the hardness of unbelief the flesh of one man [Judas] suffocated the spirit. But the others, together with the spirit, were in affliction against the flesh.

“Zacchaeus of the Gospel also was with the spirit in affliction against the flesh. [Col. 0114B] But the young man who spoke with Christ in the Gospel was not, with the spirit, in affliction against the flesh; therefore he fled from the Son of God. Saul too at first restrained the spirit in his unbelief; but God dispersed this evil in him, just as He cast Satan down from heaven into the abyss, and made Paul out of Saul.

“But Abel, who offered sacrifice in the overflowing desire of his soul, was sanctified; Cain, however, was rejected because through hatred the flesh suffocated his spirit. Noah too was justified because he sacrificed to God. But his son answered his father by mocking him in the foulness of the flesh; therefore he lost freedom, was unworthy of the name of son, and was called a slave.

“Abraham also was multiplied because, obedient to God, he diligently afflicted his own flesh against the laws of the flesh. He was turned toward a foreign nation. [Col. 0114C] But from his sons and friends the freedom of those who resisted him vanished; for those who had been free were expelled by the children of Israel. Jacob too was loved by God because in the desire of his soul he always drank righteousness and persevered in God’s blessings. But his brother Esau was stripped of blessing because of the hatred he bore toward him.

“Moses, servant and friend of God, suppressed within himself the response of the flesh through what he possessed and kept in mysteries and miracles. Hence those who hated him perished and did not reach the promised land. The Apostles oppressed their flesh. But Judas was wholly blind in the desire of his soul: he followed Christ more in order to be honored by the people than to believe in Him. [Col. 0114D] So also the disciples who did not fully possess the soul’s desire gladly heard Christ’s teaching; but because they were weary in spirit and could not bear the perfection of His righteousness, they fled from Him.

33. “Zacchaeus, amid the pleasure of the flesh, suffered the spirit’s affliction against the flesh, so that his own deeds displeased him. Therefore, when he heard that the Son of God was righteous, he immediately ran to Him and believed in Him, because he had first mourned his sins through the spirit. But the young man in the Gospel, burdened with riches and gladly hearing reports of worldly goods, [Col. 0115A] came to the Son of God asking what he should do. But when he received a perfect answer, he fell into sorrow; and because the flesh suffocated the spirit, he withdrew from Christ.

“Saul too, troublesome and hard of heart, raised the horns of pride against faith in Christ; but God struck him down, killed the will of the flesh within him, and converted him to good. But I, a poor little figure, especially loved and invoked those who afflicted their flesh in the spirit; and I turned away from those who hardened themselves against the spirit and suffocated it. Nor did I ever rest, but I was wearied by very many tribulations, until He rained the dew of His grace upon me, as He said to His familiar friend: ‘I shall be an enemy to your enemies, and I shall afflict those who afflict you, and [Col. 0115B] My angel shall go before you’ (Exod. 23). And again: ‘I bestowed great honor upon My servant and humbled all his enemies’ (1 Chron. 17).

“Yet God so constrained me in very many injuries that I did not dare to consider how great the kindness of His grace toward me was, although I saw great oppositions befalling those who resisted God’s truth. And through the tribulations and punishments which I suffered from aerial heat, my body was so trampled down as muddy earth when it is clotted with water.”

It would indeed be very useful to investigate the obscurity of sayings of such sublimity, if we had not been charged rather to set down in writing the text of the holy virgin’s visions and to explain the history of her life in a few words. For it exercises [MS: “would exercise”] our understanding, so that it may be enlarged by exertion, and what it could not grasp when idle, it may grasp when exercised. But now, since we hasten to other matters, let us set down her visions selectively with attentive pen. For she says:

34. “I beheld three towers in a vision, through which a certain hidden Wisdom made things known to me. The first had three dwelling-places. In the first were noble girls with certain others, who heard from my mouth the words of God in burning charity and always had, as it were, a hunger for this. But in the second were certain others, steadfast and wise, who embraced God’s truth in their hearts, saying: ‘O, how long will this woman remain with us?’ Yet they were not wearied by this.

“In the third dwelling-place were strong men armed from the common people. Coming vigorously toward us, they were led into wonder by the aforesaid miracles, loved them with great desire, and did this often, just as the common populace seeks protection in the firm and strong tower of some prince, that it may be defended from enemies.

“But the second tower had three dwelling-places, two of which were dry in drought, and that dryness appeared like a dense cloud. Those who were in these two dwelling-places, agreeing together, said: ‘What are these things, and whence do they come, which this woman speaks as though from God? [Col. 0116A] It is hard for us to live otherwise than those who have gone before us or who are still living. Therefore we shall turn to those who know us, because we cannot persevere in other ways.’ Thus they turned to the aforesaid common people [Note: [Col. 0115D] The wording, which is incomplete here, is complete in the manuscript as follows: ‘Thus they turned themselves toward the aforesaid common people,’ etc.], and they were of no benefit either in that group or in the aforesaid tower.

“And in true vision I heard a voice saying to them: ‘Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house’ (Luke 11). But in the third dwelling-place of that same tower were common people, who loved with manifold affection the words of God which I uttered from true vision and stood by me in tribulations, just as the tax collectors clung to Christ.

“But the third tower had three battlements: the first was wooden, the second adorned with shining stones, [Col. 0116B] the third made of a hedge. Another building, however, was hidden from me in the vision, so that I say no words about it now. But in the true light I heard that the future writing which will be composed concerning it shall be stronger and more excellent than the preceding ones.”

35. “Then, at a later time, I saw a mystical and wondrous vision, so that all my inward parts were shaken and the sensory faculty of my body was extinguished, because my knowledge was changed into another mode, as though I did not know myself. And, by God’s inspiration, drops of sweet rain were sprinkled upon the knowledge [MS: “into the knowledge”] of my soul. So too the Holy Spirit imbued John the Evangelist when he drew the most profound revelation from Jesus’ breast, where his understanding was so touched by holy divinity [Col. 0116C] that he revealed hidden mysteries and works, saying: ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ etc. (John 1).

“For the Word, which was before creatures without beginning and which afterward shall be without end, commanded all creatures to come forth and produced His work in that likeness, just as a craftsman causes his work to flash forth; for what was before time in His predestination now appeared visibly. Therefore the human being is God’s work together with every creature. But the human being is also said to be a worker of divinity, a shadowing forth of God’s mysteries, and one who reveals the Holy Trinity in all things—he whom God made in His image and likeness.

“For as Lucifer in his malice could not scatter God, so he will not be able to destroy the human condition, [Col. 0116D] though he attempted this in the first human being. Therefore the aforesaid vision taught me every utterance and word of this Gospel, which concerns the beginning of God’s work, and made me expound it. And I saw that this same exposition ought to be the beginning of another Scripture, not yet made manifest, in which many investigations of creatures would have to seek the divine mystery [Note: [Col. 0116D] Thus far extends the Bodecensis manuscript, from which I have given variant readings. But the following chapter and the entire third book are absent from it.].”

36. See how, as far as we have progressed in writing, so much has the store of the holy virgin’s notable visions, deeds, and sayings increased for us. In them the teaching and truth of highest grace so abound [Col. 0117A] that it is enormous rashness of an obstinate mind not to embrace her with the utmost zeal and revere her with every effort. For who but the divine Spirit, the best giver of graces, gave her drink from so overflowing a fountain of saving wisdom, that the abundance of spiritual teaching flowed so lavishly from her heart like a river of living water?

For the wing of inward contemplation flew within her to the hidden places of the heavenly vision, where she learned the Gospel of John. And what wise person can doubt that this holy seat was the seat of eternal Wisdom, to whom God revealed so great a treasure of inward knowledge? Certainly the integrity of moral discipline, familiar to her, so ordered the natural movements of her soul that, by a rational progress in love of divine contemplation, she might be carried upward, where in the joyful exultation of her heart she delighted to cry out to Christ her bridegroom: “Draw me after You; we shall run in the fragrance of Your ointments” (Song 1:3). There, among those possessing three lyres, she would sing the song of Moses, servant of God, and the song of the Lamb—that is, of the Law and the Gospel.

And so, having fixed the end of the second book here, let us also sing a song of praise to the Lord while we sail across so vast a sea of the holy virgin’s visions. Meanwhile let us take breath and, with the Holy Spirit’s favor, refit the sails of our ship for describing the little book of her miracles.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE MIRACLES AND DEATH OF THE BLESSED WOMAN

[Col. 0117]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0117B]

37. Now that the two preceding books on the life and visions of the blessed virgin Hildegard have been completed, it is not burdensome for me to write further concerning her miracles and virtues, but it is necessary for you, most renowned abbots Louis and Godfrey. Therefore I undertake to arrange this third book, not with confidence in my ability, but in reliance upon the obedience I have undertaken.

But why is it necessary for you? Certainly because holy love is a powerful cause: just as you loved her in life, so in death you resolved, with pious affection, not to be separated from her. Thus, for you who are moved by this holy love, it was necessary that, through me as your representative, her deeds should come to the knowledge of future generations, so that on their account [Col. 0117C] they might glorify the Lord, who is wonderful in His saints and who worked wonderfully in her, so that she might be unchanging in every good thing.

For whatever can be said of her is altogether pleasant and lovable, altogether beautiful, useful, and honorable. For she was and is distinguished not only by every holiness of character and by inward contemplation of God’s mysteries, but also by the remarkable working of notable miracles. So great is their abundance, surpassing all number, that even brilliant talents can scarcely extol her in words. Yet, if the Lord, at your prayers, deigns to grant us, as we put out into the deep, the favorable breeze of His Spirit, we hope by this second course of speech to enter the harbor of salvation, while recounting a few things out of many. Farewell.

# CHAPTER I. By her patronage the Saint heals various sick persons, including some who are absent; she expounds divinely produced letters; she visits many places for the people’s salvation.

[Col. 0117D]

38. Such powerful grace of healing shone forth in the blessed Virgin that scarcely any sick person came to her without immediately receiving health. This [Col. 0118B] will be sufficiently evident from the examples set down below.

A certain noble girl, one of Hildegard’s, had left her parents, home, and the world, and had devoted herself according to her vow to the instruction of holy Hildegard, her pious mother. At one time she was afflicted with tertian fever and could be cured by no remedy. She adopted one sole plan: to implore the holy virgin’s assistance. In accordance with the Lord’s word, “They shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall be well” (Mark 16:18), the saint laid her hand upon her with blessing and prayers, drove away the fevers, and healed her.

At a later time a certain brother Roricus, who lived religiously in a cell under monastic habit and profession, was similarly tortured severely by tertian fever. Hearing of the miracle performed in the aforementioned [Col. 0118C] sister, he devoutly and humbly sought and obtained the seal of her blessing; and immediately the fever was driven away and the sick man cured.

In the same monastery, a servant named Bertha diligently attended upon the sisters. A swelling of the neck and breast tormented her severely; indeed, the pain had progressed so far that she could neither take food or drink nor swallow saliva. Brought to God’s handmaid, she sought remedies for an illness now near to death by signs rather than words. The saint, moved by compassion, and also because of Bertha’s assiduity in good service, touched the painful places with the sign of the holy cross and restored her desired health.

[Col. 0118D] 39. A Swabian from the village of Dalevingun became swollen throughout his body. Having heard her reputation, he travelled a great distance to come to her and was not disappointed in his hope. For she kept him with her charitably for several days and, touching and blessing the sick man with her own hands, restored him by God’s grace to his former health.

[Col. 0119A] A child named Simon from Rüdesheim [Note: [Col. 0119D] Rüdesheim is a town on the opposite bank of the Rhine near Bingen.], seven weeks old, was shaken by a pitiable convulsion of all his limbs. Brought by his nurse, he was healed at her prayers, God consenting.

Moreover, she helped not only those nearby but also those far away. A certain Arnold of Wackernheim, formerly known to her, suffered such pain in his throat that he could scarcely draw breath. Since he could do nothing on his own, he devoutly sought the aid of her prayers. Trusting in God’s mercy, she blessed water and sent it to her friend; when he tasted it, the pain left him by God’s gift.

The daughter of a woman named Hazecha was ill at Bingen and, after three days, could say nothing. When [Col. 0119B] the mother ran to seek the holy virgin’s help for her daughter, she received nothing from her but blessed water. When the girl tasted it, she immediately recovered both voice and strength.

In the same town, a young man was held by so grave an illness that he was thought already to be at the point of death. The aforementioned woman, whose daughter had recovered, gave him to drink the water which she still had left and washed his face with it; immediately, his strength restored, he recovered.

40. In the diocese of Trier, a noble girl named Lutgard was wasting away in vehement love for a certain physically handsome young man. Because, on account of her guardianship, she was unable to have an opportunity to satisfy her desire, when her parents learned the cause [Col. 0119C] of this condition, they faithfully sought the holy virgin’s counsel and help through a messenger. They deserved to be effectively heard in accordance with their heart’s desire. For she first prayed to God and blessed, with copious tears, bread from her own table. When the bread was sent and given to the girl to eat, the fire of that passion was immediately and completely cooled within her.

A certain matron, Sibylla, from the city of Lausanne beyond the Alps [Note: [Col. 0119D] Lausanne is a city of Switzerland, formerly an episcopal see, but now held by heretics. It lies beyond the Alps not properly with the Germans, but rather with the Italians.], sought her assistance through a messenger. Hildegard freed her from a discharge of blood by sending her the following words in a letter: “You shall place these words upon your breast and navel, in the name of him who orders all things rightly: in Adam’s blood death arose; in Christ’s blood death was extinguished. In that same blood of Christ I command you, O blood, to restrain your flow.” And so, as the witness related, the aforementioned matron was freed in this way.

41. Nor should this be passed over: whenever small pieces of her hair or garments were applied to any sick persons, they were restored to their former health. Finally, when the wife of the Schultheiß [Note: [Col. 0120D] That is, the magistrate.] of Bingen was long in labour and was already despaired of as to her life, people hurried quickly to the monastery of the virgin of God, asking whether there might be anything to help one suffering so severely. The girls offered them a rope made of her hair, which they had preserved at some time, and instructed them to gird the woman’s bare body with it. When this was done, she gave birth safely and was delivered from death.

Likewise, two other matrons were freed through the same rope from a similar travail of childbirth.

It was no less helpful to two women of Sudernesheim. When their parents had taken them around to holy places because of their mental derangement, but had made no progress, they finally sent for the girls; and when the women had been girded with that same rope, they immediately recovered health of mind and body.

42. What of the fact that this same virgin also wished, by visions, to forewarn in their necessities those whom she held commended in her prayers? A young man named Rudolph, from Ederich, was lodging by night in a small village. When he went to bed at the time of rest, he prayed for the aid of the holy virgin. A wondrous thing! In the same appearance and clothing in which she had been in bodily life, she appeared to him in a vision and disclosed that he would fall into mortal danger from enemies lying in wait for him if he did not leave more quickly. As soon as he departed with certain companions, a band of enemies attacked at dawn some who had remained there; they recognized that they had acted foolishly because they had not withdrawn promptly in response to her vision.

Although miraculous, it is nevertheless not incredible that, while the holy virgin was still living in the flesh, she could bestow benefits upon people in the spirit. For, to declare her merit, Christ deigned to reveal to her through the Spirit the desires both of the absent and of those present. Thus a certain knight, lying at the point of death near Andernach [Note: [Col. 0120D] Called Antenacum by Baudrand; it is a town on the Rhine belonging to the Elector of Cologne, situated on the border of the Elector of Trier’s territory, some miles below Koblenz.], was visited by his friends, who discussed his affairs. By chance the hour came when, upon hearing the signal, they hastened to church, leaving only one woman to attend him. Having obtained silence, he invoked God with his whole heart and deep sighs, and humbly begged that through the merits of this holy virgin God would grant him health.

[Col. 0120D] Without delay, when his prayer was ended, he deserved to be refreshed by such a vision. It seemed to him that the venerable virgin entered to him and gently asked whether he wished to become well. When he replied that he desired it most earnestly, she laid her hand upon his head and added: “In the name of him who said, ‘They shall lay their hands upon the sick, and they shall be well’ [Mark XVII], may this illness depart from you, and be well.” At these words the vision vanished; and the sick man rose from his bed and, to the amazement of all who knew him, recovered.

43. It also seems fitting to relate what happened to a certain priest, since it constitutes in him some share of the holy virgin’s powers; and the event, rightly committed to memory as an example worthy of miracle, may, by God’s will, correct anyone who lives negligently. The matter occurred thus in the Swabian village of Rudesheim. One time, when day had already ended and night was approaching, that priest entered the church to provide light for the saints, when behold, he saw two burning candles shining upon the altar. A young student accompanied him, his regular and familiar helper in divine service. When he asked the young man why he had neglected to extinguish the candles, the latter replied that he had extinguished them.

The priest went up to put them out and found the altar cloth spread out, as it is unfolded for celebrating the divine sacrament. As he stood astonished, the young man fell to the ground, cried out, and, himself thrown into ecstasy, exclaimed: “The sword of the Lord has killed us.” Thinking him struck, the priest hurried to raise him from the ground. But, having no injury, he uttered these words: “If we see the letters that are upon the altar cloth, we shall not die.” Believing that fear had made him cry this out unknowingly, he again approached the altar. In the place where the sacred elements are consecrated, he found five letters written on the cloth [Note: [Col. 0121D] Throughout this account, *palla* means the linen upon which the sacred host is placed during Mass, now otherwise called the corporal.] without human agency, arranged in the form of a cross—namely, on the crossbar: A. P. H.; on the upright: K. P. D. [Note: [Col. 0121D] There are only five letters, even though three are read twice together, because the central P is read twice; and they are set out thus: A II. [Col. 0122D]] On seeing and carefully observing these, the young man recovered his strength and rose.

The priest folded up the cloth, extinguished the candles, and returned home bewildered. The letters remained for seven days; on the eighth day and thereafter they did not appear. Wondering about this to himself, he made the event known to religious and learned persons. Yet he could learn from no one what it portended, until at last, after sixteen years, when the fame of blessed Hildegard, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, had spread throughout the world. Coming to her, he was granted to learn—as she herself had learned through the Holy Spirit—what so great an oracle signified. For just as Daniel once interpreted letters seen upon a wall, so she interpreted the letters inscribed upon the cloth as follows: K, *Kyrium* [“Lord”]; P, *presbyter* [“priest”]; D, *derisit* [“mocked”]; A, *ascendat* [“let him ascend”]; P, *poenitens* [“penitent”]; H, *homo* [“man”].

Hearing this, he was seized with fear and accused his sinful conscience. Reformed, and having become a monk, he undertook through penance to amend the negligences of his former life; and, as the holy virgin had interpreted the letters, ascending to a higher and stricter life, he showed himself in holy conduct to be a perfect servant of God.

[Col. 0122A]

44. Among these matters, this too is notable concerning her: coming to Cologne [Note: [Col. 0122D] I have treated of these places and others in which the Saint stayed in §12.], Trier, Metz, Würzburg, and Bamberg—not merely led but compelled by the divine Spirit—she announced to clergy and people what God willed. On Mount Saint Disibod, at Siberg, Everbach, Hirsau, Zwiefalten, Maulbronn, Rudenkirchen, Kitzingen, Crutendal, Herde, Werde, Andernach, Mount Saint Mary, Elsim, and Winkel, she made known whatever concerned the profit of souls, according to what God had revealed to her.

Meanwhile, as she was travelling by boat along the waters of the Rhine near the village of Rudesheim and was hastening to a neighbouring monastery of nuns, a certain woman approached the boat carrying a blind little boy in her arms [Col. 0122B] and tearfully cried out to her to lay her holy hands upon him. Remembering with pious feeling him who said, “Go to the pool of Siloam and wash” [John IX], she drew river water with her left hand and blessed it with her right. When she applied it to the boy’s eyes, by divine favouring grace he recovered his sight.

At another time, a man suffering severely from epilepsy anxiously entreated the venerable virgin to help him. She signed him with a saving blessing in such a way that from that day forward the same illness troubled him no more. When he reported at home the miracle worked upon him, his household rejoiced and gave thanks to God.

## CHAPTER II. The prolonged illness of St Hildegard; a noblewoman possessed by a demon and unsuccessfully taken to various places is freed in her monastery.

[Col. 0122C]

45. Among the other marks of her powers, the Lord granted the holy virgin the grace to cast demons out of possessed bodies, as the venerable mother herself describes in the case of a certain noblewoman still of tender age. For she says:

“After the vision had taught me the dictation and words of the Gospel of John, I fell into a bed of illness, from whose weight I could by no means raise myself. This was breathed into me by a blast of the south wind; consequently my body was crushed with pains so great that my soul could scarcely endure them. After half a year, that same blast pierced my body so that I was in such agony as though my soul were about to pass from this life. Then another windy blast of waters mingled itself with this heat; as a result, my flesh was cooled in some measure, lest it be wholly burned up. Thus I was afflicted for a whole year; yet in true vision I saw that my life was not yet to end in its temporal course, but was still to be prolonged a little.

“Meanwhile it was reported to me that, in the lower regions of the Rhine, remote from us, a certain noblewoman was possessed by the devil. Messengers concerning her also came to me often. But in true vision I saw that, by God’s permission, she was possessed and overshadowed by a certain blackness and smoke of diabolical massing together. This oppressed the whole faculty of sensation of her rational soul and did not allow her, with understanding raised up, to sigh—just as a shadow cast before a person or some other object, or smoke, covers and envelops it. Hence she lost proper perceptions and actions, and often cried out and did unsuitable things. But when, by God’s command, this evil was diminished in her, its burden became lighter.

“As I pondered and wished to know how the diabolical form enters a human being, I saw and heard the answer that the devil does not enter a person in his form as he is [Note: [Col. 0123D] These statements do not agree with the opinion of theologians. See therefore Benedict XIV, in the often-cited work, book IV, part I, chapter 29, no. 2.], but overshadows and envelops that person with the shadow and smoke of his blackness. For if his form entered a person, the limbs would sooner be dissolved than straw scattered by the wind. Therefore God does not permit him to enter a human being in his own form. But by suffusing a person with the things mentioned above, he overturns that person into madness and improprieties; through that person, as though through a window, he cries aloud and moves the limbs outwardly, although he is not inwardly present in them in his own form, while the soul is, meanwhile, as it were asleep and unaware of what the body’s flesh is doing.”

46. “Then I saw the host of malignant spirits of the aforesaid artifice and perversity, who go through the whole world seeking persons through whom they may cause schisms and differences of conduct. At the beginning, when they were created, they despised God before the most righteous angels, saying: ‘Who is this, who has such power over us?’ Saying this in envy, hatred, and mockery, they still persist in these things and do everything in accordance with them, because they began the error of mockery at the first.

“Since, however, God wishes to cleanse the people through them, by his permission and command they stir up disturbances in the air; through the foam of the air they bring forth pestilence; they cause floods and dangers in the waters; they incite wars and produce adversities and evils. God permits these things to happen when people, through arrogance, become entangled in crimes and murders. But when God has thus cleansed his people, he leads those same spirits into confusion, as happened in the aforementioned woman. For when the wicked spirit, by God’s permission, was throwing many into confusion through her, on account of the depraved habits and sins which it had persuaded them to commit, some were terrified and thus brought to repentance, and that same malignant spirit was confounded.

“For God permits his friends to be afflicted by adversities and illnesses so that they may be cleansed of evils. Thus enemies are confounded, when the elect, through cleansing, are made into brighter stones before God. And when that woman had been brought to very many places to holy persons, the spirit that oppressed her, overcome by the merits of the saints and the prayers of the people, cried out that in the upper regions of the Rhine there was a certain old woman by whose counsel it would have to be expelled. When her friends heard this, in the eighth year of her affliction they brought her to us, as the Lord willed.”

47. It is worthwhile at this point, before pursuing further the words of the virgin of Christ, to insert the letters which the abbot of Brauweiler [Note: [Col. 0123D] It is a monastery of the Benedictine order, one hour’s journey from Cologne; I find it called Brunvillarium, Brunwillarium, or Bruwiler. According to the catalogue of abbots supplied by Dionysius Sammarthanus, *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, cols. 759 ff., the abbot praised here must have been Geldolphus, whose death is placed in 1177.] wished to send to her, and she in return to him, concerning this demoniac. From them the devil’s malice may be more clearly understood, and God’s judgments—hidden indeed, but always just—may be praised more fervently.

For after seven years that same woman was brought to Brauweiler, in order that she might be freed there by the merits of Saint Nicholas. The wicked spirit, being adjured, said that it would not leave its vessel except through the counsel and aid of a certain old woman in the upper Rhine regions—as she herself had said above—distorting her name and mockingly calling her “Scrumpilgardis.” They therefore took counsel and sent her a petitionary letter in this form:

“To Lady Hildegard, venerable mother, bride of Christ to be embraced with all one’s heart, and daughter of the most high King: G., unworthy overseer of the monastery of Brauweiler, with his brothers sitting in the valley of tears, offers, as they are able, the devoted service of complete love in their prayers. Although, most beloved Lady,” etc.

It is extant in the collection of St Hildegard’s letters, no. 60.

48. When blessed Hildegard received and carefully examined this letter, compassionately sharing the petitioners’ grief, she urged all the sisters humbly to persist in public and private prayers for the aforesaid need. After praying, she herself raised the eyes of her mind to the Lord. She wrote back as follows, according to what she saw and heard in true vision, dictated not by another but by inexhaustible Wisdom:

“To G., abbot of the church of Brauweiler: H. Since I am bound by God’s scourges in a long and severe illness,” etc.

See there, reply to Letter 60.

When the holy virgin, through the Holy Spirit’s revelation, had completed this letter, she sent it, by the hands of the man who had secretly sought it, as she says in the book *Scivias*, to the monastery where the woman was kept, so that it might humbly be read over her. When the reader came to the passage written at the end, “And I, an unlearned and poor womanly form, O spirit of blasphemy and mockery, say to you in that truth in which I, a poor and unlearned form, saw and heard these things from the light of Wisdom; and by that same Wisdom command you to depart from this human being in true steadfastness and not in the whirlwind of your instability,” the same wicked spirit roared wholly and emitted such howls, wailing with horrible cries, that it struck great terror into those present. After raging in this way for nearly half an hour, it finally left the vessel it had long possessed, as it pleased God. When the woman felt herself freed, she stretched out her hands to those standing by to raise her, for she had no strength.

49. Then she prostrated herself before the principal altar of Saint Nicholas and gave thanks to God for her deliverance. The people saw this and, as the crowd is wont to do, made a great noise; thanks and praises to God also rang out with the sounding of bells, while the brothers sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise you, God.” Alas, as is miserably said, the same ancient enemy returned by a hidden judgment of God and reclaimed the vessel it had left.

The woman, trembling all over and rising with shrieking and shouting, began to rage more than before. When those present were terrified and filled with sorrow, the wicked spirit was asked why it had dared reclaim God’s creature after leaving her. It replied: “I fled the sign of the Crucified One outwardly. But when I did not know where to go, I reclaimed my vessel, empty and unsealed.” When it was compelled by the holy virgin’s aforementioned letter and adjurations to depart, it cried out through gnashing teeth that it would leave only in the presence of that same old woman.

Then those of sounder judgment persuaded the woman’s friends and guardians to bring her to the blessed virgin. Having received the abbot’s and brothers’ blessing, together with letters of recommendation, they set out thither. The letter was in this form:

“To H., venerable lady, worthy of every act of thanksgiving: G., unworthy abbot of the men of Brauweiler, with his brothers, wishes that you may live, prosper, have the world beneath your feet, and possess whatever more excellent thing can be desired for a handmaid of Christ. That the Lord has looked upon you,” etc.

See Letter 61.

50. With these letters set before us, it seems appropriate to return the narrative to that from which it has strayed a little, and to see how God, for the glorification of his virgin, delayed this woman’s deliverance so long. The Almighty could easily have granted through other saints, to whom she had been taken about for so many years, what was sought for the possessed woman. But, transferring the glory of this miracle to the holy virgin, he wished clearly to make known to all in his own time the quality of her merits. How this happened may better be learned from her own words:

“We were greatly alarmed at the coming of the aforementioned woman, wondering how we could see or hear one about whom a very great multitude of people had been stirred for so long. But God rained upon us the dew of his sweetness, and without horror or trembling we placed her in the sisters’ dwellings without the help of men. Thereafter we yielded to her in no way: neither because of horror, nor because of the confusion with which the demon confounded those who came to her on account of sins; nor because of mocking or shameful words by which it wished to overcome us; nor because of its foulest breath.

“And I saw that it endured three torments in that woman: first, when she was taken from one place of holy persons to another; second, when the common people gave alms for her; third, when through the prayers of spiritual persons it was compelled by God’s grace to depart. Therefore, from the Purification of Saint Mary until Holy Saturday, we and our fellow provincials of both sexes laboured on her behalf through fasts, prayers, almsgiving, and mortifications of the body.

“Meanwhile, compelled by God’s power, the unclean spirit uttered many things before the people—although unwillingly—about the saving power of baptism, the sacrament of Christ’s body, the danger of the excommunicated, the damnation of the Cathars [Note: [Col. 0125D] The Novatian heretics, who arose in the third century, called themselves by the Greek name *Cathari*, or ‘Pure Ones.’ But these Cathars, who existed in various provinces of Europe in the twelfth century, are very different. To avoid repeating what has been said, see Henschenius’s observations on the Cathars of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries in vol. III of April, p. 679.], and similar matters—to its own confusion and Christ’s glory. Hence many became stronger in faith and many readier to reform their sins. But whenever I saw it utter falsehood in true vision, I immediately rebuked it. Thus it quickly fell silent and gnashed its teeth at me. Yet I did not forbid it to speak for the people’s sake when it uttered truth.”

51. “Finally, on Holy Saturday, when the baptismal font was consecrated, through the priest’s breath which he breathes into the font, together with the words which the Holy Spirit infused into human reason and the teachers of the Church—because in the first creation the Spirit of the Lord moved the waters, as it is written, ‘The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters’—that woman was present. Seized with great fear, she trembled so violently that she dug into the earth with her feet and frequently emitted blasts from the horrible spirit which oppressed her.

“Immediately, in true vision, I saw and heard that the power of the Most High, which had overshadowed holy baptism and always overshadows it, said to the diabolical massing together by which that woman was afflicted: ‘Go, Satan, from the tabernacle of this woman’s body, and make room in it for the Holy Spirit.’ Then the unclean spirit departed horribly through the woman’s shameful parts with an evacuation, and she was freed. Thereafter she remained sound in the faculties of soul and body as long as she lived in the present world.

“When this was reported among the people, all said with songs of praise and words of prayer: ‘Glory to you, Lord.’ Thus, as God permitted Satan to cover Job’s whole body with the horror and stench of worms, and as Satan thought that through his deception, by which he had denied God’s honour, he could overcome Job also—yet, with God guarding Job’s soul, he could not touch it, because Job did not abandon God in faith, and so Satan departed from him confounded, because God overcame Satan through Job, so that Satan might know that no one could prevail against God—so also, when this woman was handed over to the malignant spirit to be tormented, God did not permit her soul to fail in the good faith. Thus the enemy was confounded in her, because he could not turn her away from the justice of God.”

With these and similar words the virgin of God gently, sweetly, modestly, and humbly related the works of divine mercy performed on her account and through her, attributing nothing to herself, because she regarded flight from boasting in powers as itself a virtue.

## CHAPTER III. The Saint’s grave illness, in which she is healed in a vision; benefits bestowed upon various persons; death and burial honoured by miracles.

[Col. 0127B]

52. Therefore, after this very humble account of her power, in which she presumed absolutely nothing of herself, she immediately adds the weakening of her whole body which followed it, as though she were saying with the Apostle: “Lest the greatness of revelations exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me” [Note: [Col. 0127D] The “thorn in the flesh” and “angel of Satan” of which the Apostle speaks, II Corinthians XII.7, are interpreted in various ways. This author, with many others, understands them as a bodily illness by which St Paul was afflicted, lest he should be lifted up into pride by the excellence of his revelations. In this sense the words are aptly applied to St Hildegard.]:

“After these things”—that is, after the liberation of that woman—“a great illness again invaded me, so that my veins with their blood, my bones with their marrow, withered away; my entrails were torn apart within me; and my entire body languished as grasses lose their greenness in winter. And I saw that wicked spirits mocked at this, laughing and saying: ‘Ha! She will die, and her friends, with whom she has confounded us, will weep.’ But I did not see that the departure of my soul was at hand. I suffered this illness for more than forty days and nights.

“Meanwhile, in true vision it was shown me that I should visit certain communities of spiritual persons, men and women, and make known to them the words which God showed me. When I at last attempted this, though I had no bodily strength, my illness was somewhat eased. Obeying God’s command [Note: [Col. 0127D] I have set out the Saint’s various journeys in the Commentary, §12.], I calmed dissensions which some persons had among themselves. When I neglected these journeys commanded me by God because of fear of the people, my bodily pains increased and did not cease until I obeyed—just as happened to Jonah, who was severely afflicted until he submitted himself to obedience.”

53. After this, the bride of Christ deserved a heavenly visitation, from which she received such consolation that in its delight she said she had been filled with an exultation of inestimable joy:

“In the vision of truth there appeared to me a most beautiful and most loving man, who gave such consolation that all my inward parts were suffused, as it were, by the fragrance of balm from the sight of him. Then I exulted with great and inestimable joy and always desired to behold him. He commanded those who afflicted me to depart from me, saying: ‘Depart, for I do not wish you to torment her further in this manner.’ Departing with great howling, they cried: ‘Ah, why did we come here, since we depart confounded?’

“Immediately the illness that had troubled me left me at the man’s words, as waters stirred into flood by stormy winds; and I recovered strength, just as a traveller returning to his homeland gathers back his possessions. My veins with their blood and my bones with their marrow were restored, as though I had been raised from death. But I was silent in patience, silent in gentleness, and, like a woman in childbirth after labour, I spoke after pain.”

54. “After this I was compelled by the most humble entreaty and devotion of my abbot and brothers to write, as God willed, the life of Saint Disibod [Note: [Col. 0128D] The written Life of St Disibod has been discussed in the Commentary, no. 188, and no. 113, where I also quoted part of the abbot’s letter requesting it.], to whom I had earlier been offered, because they possessed no certain account of him. Having first prayed and invoked the Holy Spirit, I looked towards true Wisdom, instructed in true vision, and, according to what Wisdom taught me, wrote the life and merits of that saint.

“Then I wrote the book *On Divine Works* [Note: [Col. 0128D] The book *On Divine Works* that she wrote has been discussed in no. 192.], in which, as almighty God infused it into me, I saw the height, depth, and breadth of the firmament, and how the sun, moon, stars, and other things are set within it.”

The holy virgin produced many other written works and notable testimonies of prophecy and grace, as we have said above. In them we discern proofs that her soul was instructed by the Holy Spirit and devoted to divine things. Those who cherish love of learning and knowledge can find very great profit in them, since these things were ordained by God and proclaimed through her to humankind. In that teaching, God’s Wisdom sat, as it were, upon a throne of power with sublime authority, and, working wonders through her, rendered judgments concerning things.

55. Having arranged these matters as our little capacity allowed, let us turn the pen to the words of her holy daughters and faithfully and eagerly append to this work, with the Lord’s help, what they wrote as worthy of remembrance concerning her—especially what they saw, heard, and handled with their own hands concerning her blessed passing.

They say: A certain woman cruelly afflicted by a mute demon, over whom the brothers of Laach [Note: [Col. 0128D] The monastery of Laach, or “of the Lake,” of the Order of St Benedict, is placed by Bucelinus in *Germania sacra*, part II, p. 51, “in the territory of Trier, not far from Andernach.”] had laboured greatly, was carried to her on a bed with much exertion by men. The pious mother confidently resisted the demon’s audacity and presumption with words uttered by the Holy Spirit, and did not cease prayers and blessings until, through God’s grace, she freed the woman from the evil enemy.

Likewise, another woman, bound in dreadful chains because of raging madness, was brought to her. Hildegard ordered her to be unbound, and immediately, to the astonishment of all present, having recovered health of mind and body, she returned home with thanksgiving.

56. Likewise, the devil urged a certain sister from the convent of Schefenburch to holy works, prayers, vigils, fasts, and reception of the sacraments, pretending to be an angel of light. He also tried to confuse her by means of confession of crimes to which she had never been subject. Among other things he so afflicted her that she so intensely abhorred the names and appearance of certain people and animals that, on seeing or hearing them, she would make a horrible outcry for a long hour. Sent by her prioress and convent with letters to the holy virgin, she was strengthened by her and freed from the devil’s deception.

By the same power she freed two other women possessed by demons. One of them, being poor and blind, was received by her as alms and happily completed her life in a religious habit.

57. Since we are now hastening to the end of this work, let us also consider, from the account written by the aforesaid sisters, the end of the holy virgin’s life, made illustrious by the things God revealed. They say:

“When the blessed mother had devotedly served the Lord through many contests of labour, she grew weary of the present life and daily desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ. God heard her desire and revealed to her by the spirit of prophecy the end which she herself had desired; for some time she also foretold it to the sisters. Accordingly, while suffering from illness, in the eighty-second year of her age, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September], she passed in a blessed departure to her heavenly Bridegroom [Note: [Col. 0129C] In the year 1179, as I have shown in the Commentary, no. 204.].

“Her daughters, for whom she herself was all joy and consolation, stood by the funeral of their beloved mother, weeping most bitterly. Though they did not doubt the rewards and assistance to be granted them through her, they were nevertheless afflicted with the greatest sorrow of heart because of the departure of her by whom they had always been comforted. But God clearly revealed, at her passing, what her merit with him was.”

58. For above the dwelling in which the holy virgin, at the first twilight of the night of the Lord’s Day, rendered up her blessed soul to God, two most brilliant rainbows of different colours appeared in the sky. They widened to the breadth of a great open square, extending toward the four quarters of the earth: one ran from north to south, the other from east to west. At their summit, where the two rainbows joined, a bright light of the size of the lunar disc rose up; spreading widely, it seemed to drive the darkness of night away from the dwelling.

[Note: By the twilight of “the night of the Lord’s Day” is meant the dawn of the following Monday, as I observed in the Commentary, no. 204; not the dawn of Sunday itself, as the passage might be understood if nothing opposed it. Thus the Saint died on Monday, 17 September, about the fourth hour after midnight. There is both evening and morning twilight; but that morning twilight is intended here is inferred from what follows, where it is said: “A bright light . . . seemed to drive away the darkness of night.” At the first evening twilight darkness is only beginning to arise; at the first morning twilight darkness is present and is only beginning to be dispersed by a little light. Now it must necessarily be said that the Saint died not on Sunday, as Pagius believed, but at first light on Monday, while the night of Sunday was still continuing, because it is certain that she did not die before the year 1179, in which 17 September fell on a Monday. For, in the letter to Christian, Archbishop of Mainz, cited in the Commentary, no. 169, St Hildegard mentions the prelates of Mainz who had returned “from Rome and from the synod”—namely, the Lateran synod held in March 1179. She was therefore alive in 1179; and she could not have begun her eighty-second year before that year, or before June, as I showed in the Commentary, no. 204. Therefore, since these arguments make it certain that she did not die in 1178, when 17 September was a Sunday, the passage absolutely requires the explanation given above. The biographer must be said deliberately to have distinguished the twilight of the night of the Lord’s Day from the twilight of the Lord’s Day itself; he did not say that the Saint died on Sunday, but near the end of the following night.]

Within this light a glowing cross was seen, at first small, but afterwards growing immensely large. Around it appeared innumerable circles of varied colours; in each individual circle a single glowing little cross arose with its own circle, though these were seen to be smaller than the preceding one. When they had spread out in the sky, their breadth reached farther eastward; and, seeming to bend earthward toward the house in which the holy virgin had passed away, they illumined the entire mountain. It is to be believed that by this sign God showed how great was the splendour with which He had glorified His beloved in heaven.

Nor were miracles lacking before she was buried, attesting the merit of her holiness. Two persons who ventured, in good hope, to touch her holy body recovered from grave sickness. When, therefore, the funeral rites had been reverently celebrated by venerable men, she was buried in a place of veneration, where, through her merits, many benefits are granted to all who seek with devout hearts. Also, a fragrance of wondrous sweetness issuing from her tomb bathes the nostrils and breasts of certain persons in its sweet perfume. We therefore hope and firmly believe that she has an immortal remembrance with God, who in this life bestowed upon her a special pre-eminence among His gifts: to Him be praise and honour for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0131]

# PROCEEDINGS OF THE INQUIRY INTO THE VIRTUES AND MIRACLES OF ST HILDEGARD

*(Acta SS. Bolland., as cited above, p. 697, from a manuscript of the Böddeken monastery of Canons Regular of St Augustine, diocese of Paderborn.)*

1. We therefore, acting under the authority of this mandate, personally came to the monastery of St Rupert and received trustworthy witnesses, in the following manner, concerning the life, conduct, reputation, merits, signs, and other circumstances of blessed Hildegard. We rejected an excessive number of witnesses, since time rather than an abundance of witnesses could not be obtained.

[Note: I discussed these Proceedings in the Commentary, no. 5, where I observed that they were composed by command of Pope Gregory IX, who delegated the provost, dean, and scholasticus of the church of Mainz to conduct an examination into the virtues and miracles of St Hildegard. But the compiler of the Proceedings cut out all those matters.]

Elsa by name, mistress of St Rupert’s at Bingen, swore concerning the miracles of blessed Hildegard that she saw Mechthild, possessed by a demon, delivered at the tomb of blessed Hildegard. She saw Regniss and Segniss, noblewomen, delivered from demons in the same place; afterwards they served in that same monastery for the rest of their lives. She also saw very many epileptics delivered there. Likewise, sufferers from tertian and quartan fevers were delivered at her tomb upon invocation of her name.

[Note: That is, persons suffering from tertian and quartan fever.]

The prioress Agnes, sister of the mistress, swore to the same. Beatrix the sacristan, Odilia the cellarer, and the lay sister Hedwig likewise say, with one mind, that they saw these things there.

[Note: The sacristan is the officer in charge of the sacristy.]

[Note: There appears to be some error here; perhaps *una mente* (“with one mind”) was written.]

Sophia the chantress says the same. The priest Roricus, under oath, says the same, but added that when he came to adjure the possessed woman, and before he had said anything to her, she called him by both names, saying, “Henry Roricus,” although this had previously been unknown in those parts.

[Note: More probably, “to adjure.”]

He also saw four ravens then sitting in the windows below the church. Asking the possessed woman who those ravens were, he received the reply that they were her companions and were awaiting her departure. When this was said, she opened her mouth wide and breathed out the blackest smoke; thus the possessed woman was delivered, and immediately they were no longer seen. The sounder part [of the witnesses] attests this. He also added that he saw eighteen possessed persons delivered at her tomb through invocation of the same virgin. The priest Daniel, under oath, says the same. The bishop of the same place, under oath, says the same.

[Note: I do not understand who this bishop is, and I doubt whether the word is not corrupt, unless perhaps it is a chorepiscopus, who is called “bishop of the place” according to the Greek etymology of the word.]

2. When the mistress Jutta was questioned, she said concerning her that all these things had happened within thirty years.

[Note: The place of which this Jutta was mistress is not stated. Elza was mistress of the monastery of St Rupert, so Jutta was not her superior. Jutta perhaps presided over the monastery at Eibingen, of which no. 3 will speak; or she may also be called mistress because she had formerly presided over the monastery of St Rupert and had resigned the office through old age or for another reason.]

Beatrix of Koblenz, the sacristan, under oath, stated that when she was twelve years old she was offered to that monastery and lived for some time with blessed Hildegard. She saw and heard that holy Hildegard publicly foretold the day of her death in chapter. After Hildegard’s death she saw the blind Mechthild enlightened through invocation of the same virgin.

[Note: If all has been correctly explained, this Mechthild is different from the one who will testify in no. 3 that the sight of a little girl was restored to her.]

She also saw a madman restored to health. She saw the maid Metz, who had carried away earth from Hildegard’s tomb and put it in a less honourable place, rebuked and struck by blessed Hildegard. Thus compelled, after replacing the earth and being frightened by this [perhaps “contrite”], she was immediately freed. She saw Sister Clement, who is now [present], flogged because of the hair of blessed Hildegard which she had given to her brother, until the hair was most devoutly [perhaps “properly/devoutly”] restored by him.

[Note: She was probably called Clementia.]

She also saw a laywoman whose leg had developed an excessive growth of bone, so that she could not walk. When that bone was anointed with the hair of blessed Hildegard, the growth immediately disappeared and she was healed. On these particulars concerning the hair, the greater and sounder part of the chapter, together with Regina, agrees under oath.

[Note: The word *regina* is superfluous, or perhaps *cum Regina* (“together with Regina”) was written.]

She also saw the man who, in anger, pushed blessed Hildegard with his foot, deprived of his foot by the scourge of God. The sworn cellarer says the same, having lived with the blessed virgin for six years and more. She added that a woman suffering from tertian fever, imploring her aid, received water sent by Hildegard in her own cup; having tasted it, she was healed.

[Note: That is, a person suffering from tertian fever. The wording is incomplete, but it will be completed if, instead of *implorans* (“imploring”), one reads *implorante* (“while she was imploring”).]

She also added that, when two girls were serving in blessed Hildegard’s refectory, she said to them: “Take good care of yourselves for fourteen days, and do penance.” When those days had ended, they died. She added the same concerning a certain cleric, namely that the same thing happened to him. The cellarer Hedwig, a sworn lay sister, agrees.

[Note: I suspect that the cellarer’s name is missing here—she is called Odilia in no. 1—and that it should read, as there: “Odilia the cellarer, Hedwig the lay sister,” etc.]

3. Mechthild, under oath, says that she heard from her mother that she herself was born blind. When blessed Hildegard was going to visit the village of Hibingen, where she had also founded a monastery, her mother met her, carrying her and imploring blessed Hildegard’s grace. While the blessed virgin was still in the boat, she anointed the blind girl’s eyes with water from the Rhine and restored her sight.

[Note: The village is now called Eibingen; it lies across the Rhine in the Rheingau. The monastery at Eibingen founded there will be discussed again in no. 8; I treated that foundation more fully in the Commentary, no. 177.]

Irmingard, questioned and under oath, said that she had seen this same event. She further added that blessed Hildegard, though she had not previously seen her, addressed by name a certain girl who had disguised herself as a male student, namely Berrudis, and said to her: “Turn to a better state, for I know your years will go no further”—as though she meant, “You will die this year.” But when she saw blessed Hildegard, she was contrite and confessed that she was a woman; thus converted, she died in the same year. The aforesaid sworn women agree with this. The same girl, because of her beauty and so that she might not be loved by many, darkened herself with a gloomy colour; and the entire neighbourhood proclaims the same thing.

She added also that when a certain married woman was suspected of causing her husband’s death and was ordered to undergo the ordeal of hot iron, she ran to blessed Hildegard and disclosed the matter to her. Blessed Hildegard blessed the glowing iron; and when the woman carried the hot iron, she remained unharmed. Public report in the city of Bingen agrees concerning this event. She also said that, when she herself was twice near death, she was delivered after invoking the help of the same blessed virgin. She says too that she saw, both after Hildegard’s death and during her lifetime, possessed persons and epileptics delivered through invocation of her name.

4. The sworn Hedwig of Alzey says the same, adding that blessed Hildegard was always divinely illuminated while in her bed of sickness.

[Note: She testifies, I think, that Hildegard’s face or head shone with a divinely bestowed radiance.]

And, while walking through the cloister by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, she sang the sequence beginning: “O BRANCH AND DIADEM.” The sworn sacristan and cellarer agree. She also says that she saw a lighted candle upon Hildegard’s tomb while the Mass for the dead was sung. When it was extinguished, at the beginning of the Gospel it lit itself again—not once, but repeatedly.

She also saw a man who was insane, bound, and possessed by a demon, violently brought by some people to Hildegard’s tomb. At last he freed himself from their hands and threw himself into the river Nahe, which lies at the foot of the mountain. Though many bystanders believed him dead, he was drawn out alive through the favour of the same virgin. He confessed that he had been freed from the demon and protected from the water by the sleeve of the blessed virgin. Public report and the greater part of the sworn convent agree concerning this event.

Rapodo, Hilde, and Humbert, citizens of Bingen, say that they saw blessed Hildegard over many days; that she drove demons out of all who came from her province and elsewhere, cured epileptics, and performed many other signs which they themselves saw; and that there can be no doubt of her holiness.

[Note: In the margin of the copy it is noted: perhaps *hominibus* (“persons”). Yet I do not see that this correction is necessary if the manuscript clearly read *omnibus* (“all”). It is not incredible that all possessed persons who were brought to her while she lived were delivered from their affliction.]

The sworn Hartrad agrees with the foregoing and added that he saw four possessed persons and epileptics delivered through the merits of the same virgin. Henry, a sworn canon of Bingen, says that he applied the blessed virgin’s hair to two sick women, and they were immediately healed. Concerning possessed persons and epileptics he agrees with those already named—Rapodo, Hilde, and Humbert, citizens, and Hartrad, canon of Bingen. Conrad of Bingen, however, agrees from personal observation with the foregoing concerning possessed persons.

5. Likewise, the sworn mistress learned by certain report, from highly trustworthy persons, and from the lady of Dorabecq herself, that on the anniversary of St Hildegard a certain light, no longer than a hand’s breadth and scarcely capable of lasting through the celebration of Mass, had been lit in honour of the aforesaid lady. It endured from evening until the hour of Mass on the following day. On Hildegard’s anniversary the whole neighbourhood also gathers and has gathered at her tomb.

[Note: Whether this is Elza, the mistress mentioned in no. 1, or Jutta in no. 2, is not stated.]

She also learned from the elders of the monastery about a boy born blind, whose sight Hildegard restored by anointing his eyes with water from the Rhine, while between Rüdesheim—

[Note: Mechthild, born blind, testified in no. 3 that she was healed as an infant by Rhine water, citing her mother’s testimony. Here a boy born blind is said to have received sight. Nevertheless, one may suspect that the same miracle is being reported again, since the German word corresponding to the Latin *infans* equally signifies a boy or a girl.]

[Note: Some words are omitted here. It was probably written: “between Rüdesheim and Eibingen was [the place],” which was called Hibingen in no. 3, where she founded a monastery. For no. 8 says this place was one league from the Saint’s tomb. Rüdesheim lies between the two places and is nearer.]

—which is one mile distant from her tomb; and she herself, trembling before us, confessed that this was so. She also learned [perhaps “also”] from the elders that when William, archdeacon of Trier, had been given the hair of blessed Hildegard as relics, had put it in a silk reliquary-case, placed that case inside a wooden one, and set it on the altar of the church at Dalvanii, then, when the things upon the altar were burned, the silk case remained unharmed although the wooden case was completely consumed.

She also learned that a certain noblewoman of Trier had lost her mind through the spell of a young man, so that she was wholly deranged. Her grieving relatives fled to blessed Hildegard, seeking her grace. Hildegard blessed bread at her table and sent it to the sick woman; after she tasted it, she was immediately healed. The sworn cellarer Odilia and the lay sister Hedwig saw this miracle, for they were then with her at table.

[Note: That is, they saw her blessing the bread sent to the mentally afflicted girl; they must have learned of her healing from others, unless the woman had been brought to the monastery, which is not asserted.]

She also learned from the elders of the monastery that whenever any sister of the monastery entertained vain thoughts during the divine office, blessed Hildegard immediately rebuked her; and when they read the lessons, she gave them blessings according to their thoughts, expressing their intentions word for word. She saw some of these women later confess the same thing when they were in the habit of the Cistercian Order.

6. Likewise, when a man unjustly excommunicated had been buried in his monastery and, on that account, the church of Mainz suspended divine worship there and he ought to have been removed, she marked his tomb with the sign of the cross using her staff; and thus his grave could not thereafter be found.

[Note: These matters have been discussed at length in the Commentary, §11.]

Likewise, when a man had bound himself to the devil by homage, so that each year he should sacrifice some animal to him, he first offered animals, then his children, and beyond these his wife. When she became aware of this, she fled to blessed Hildegard, imploring help and setting out the affair to her in order. Hildegard gave her a portion of her own hair, and she fastened it into her own hair according to Hildegard’s instruction. Perceiving this, the demon said to the husband: “You have deceived me. I have no right over her because of Hildegard’s incantations.” The husband stripped her and placed her in a bath, in order finally to accomplish what he desired. When the devil could not possess her, he broke the husband’s neck.

Likewise, when a certain Archbishop of Mainz named Christian was being received at Bingen with the ringing of bells, she understood the bells themselves to sound, one the words, “Shepherd, mourn”; the other, “For your safety, flee quickly.” These words seemed directed to the bishop. As if speaking in the bishop’s person: “I depart; I leave the land in confusion.” She spoke these words in the Spirit before the sisters present.

[Note: Some remarks on Archbishop Christian have been given there in nos. 163 and 171, where his death is related. What is reported here cannot have occurred except during the schism, for Christian was never in the diocese of Mainz after peace was restored to the Church in 1177.]

The prioress Agnes [perhaps Beatrix is omitted], the sacristan Odilia, Sophia, and very many other sworn women agree. Mechthild also states under oath that she herself had long been tormented by a demon, that she was delivered through invocation of blessed Hildegard, and that the convent—which is still there today—saw her thus tormented and delivered.

7. She also says that she saw other possessed persons, and sufferers from quartan and tertian fevers, delivered there. Jutta agrees, adding that a certain epileptic boy for whom she prayed at blessed Hildegard’s tomb was delivered; and that the carpenter of the castle, when he had lost his mind, was delivered by Hildegard’s aid after blessed Hildegard had been invoked by his mother [perhaps “mother’s”]. Public report in the same place agrees with her.

Mechthild, under oath, says that she saw blessed Hildegard and remained continually with her; she also agrees with Mechthild, born blind. Deta too, who recovered her sight after blessed Hildegard’s death, agrees with the mistress in other matters.
