Bruno, keeper of St Peter’s at Strasbourg and a sworn priest, speaks concerning the life of blessed Hildegard—namely, as he had heard it by public report and as he had read it in the little book written immediately after her death about her life by two religious men, Gottfried and Theoderic, who had lived with the blessed virgin. He believes this book to contain truth in every respect: namely, that she sprang from noble parents.

When she was five years old, she saw a cow and said to her nurse: “Look, nurse, how beautiful is the calf in that cow: white, and marked with various spots upon its forehead, feet, and back.” The nurse marvelled and immediately reported this to her mother. The owner of the cow ordered that, after it calved, the offspring should be brought to her. When this was done, she learned that everything blessed Hildegard had foretold as a girl was true. Her parents marvelled, and, seeing that she had a character unlike that of other people, resolved to place her in a monastery. In her eighth year, entrusting her to a recluse named Jutta, sister of the Count of Spanheim, they offered her to serve the Lord under the Rule of blessed Benedict on Mount St Disibod.

8. Concerning her manner of life he says that, as the fame of her holiness spread widely, very many noble girls came to her. But because the dwelling of the enclosure could not contain them all, she was then warned—indeed compelled—by the Lord to move to St Rupert as her guide. When she had communicated this through her confessor to the abbot, and he took it ill, the miracles by which she obtained permission, her removal to the place divinely shown, the manner in which she built a new monastery in an unknown place, and established there eighteen noble girls to serve the Lord, are more fully found in the little book of her Life.

In that monastery she established fifty prebends for ladies and two for priests; further, seven for poor married women, in honour of the Holy Spirit and of blessed Mary. Beyond the river Rhine, one league away, she founded another monastery, where she established thirty prebends.

[Note: These events are set out more fully in the *Life*. The first monastery she founded, and where she is said to have founded fifty prebends—that is, incomes for fifty noble nuns—was Mount St Rupert, where she herself lived. The other was the monastery at Eibingen, which was initially subordinate; see the discussion in the Commentary, no. 177. The letters too are extensively discussed in §4 and following.]

Concerning her reputation he says that three popes, having heard of her fame, wrote to her—Eugenius, Adrian, and Anastasius—and she wrote to them. The archbishops of Mainz, Cologne, Trier, and Magdeburg; the Patriarch of Jerusalem; bishops in large number; the holy Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux; other abbots and provosts; and other prelates of churches wrote to her, and she replied to them. All this is gathered from the books of her letters.

[Note: Among the published letters of St Hildegard no letter of an Archbishop of Magdeburg occurs. Yet, among those who wrote to the Saint, an Archbishop of Magdeburg is also listed by Trithemius in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1150; there is added there “the Archbishop of Ravenna,” whose letter likewise has not been published, and “many from Italy,” though we possess only a few published letters sent to the Saint from Italy. It must therefore be said that some letters were not inserted in the collection of letters when that codex was compiled, and were not published afterwards either, as I showed in the Commentary, no. 195.]

9. Concerning her merits he says: King Conrad and Emperor Frederick, enquiring about their outcomes, heard future things, and she thereby brought them back to a better course. This is found more fully in the already mentioned Book of Letters. Each year on the day of her anniversary a great people, both neighbours and those from distant places, flock to her tomb, seeking from her health of soul and body.

Further, though she did not possess great natural understanding, in the forty-second year of her life she began, through revelation of the Holy Spirit, to write no small number of books, as is more fully contained in the prologue to her book *Scivias*.

[Note: This word is probably written corruptly, or is plainly barbarous. Yet I suspect that it denotes understanding, and that this is the meaning: although the Saint by no means excelled in natural intelligence, she nevertheless wrote many books by God’s revelation.]

[Note: The Saint had completed forty-two years and seven months when she began to write, as is clearly stated in the preface to the book *Scivias* cited here, and as was said in the Commentary, nos. 13 and 14.]

She completed her *Scivias* in ten years. She completed in eight years her book of simple medicine, her book of exposition of the Gospels, the song of celestial harmony, and the unknown language with its letters; this is more fully gathered from the prologue to the book *The Book of Life’s Merits*. Afterwards, in the five following years, she wrote *The Book of Life’s Merits*. Finally, she wrote *The Book of Divine Works* in seven years, as appears more fully from the prologue to that book.

[Note: According to the Commentary cited, no. 17, she began writing this in 1141. I assigned the dates of this and the remaining books in nos. 191 and 192.]

Concerning signs he says there that he believes in every way that the signs which the Lord performed through her during her life, and which are written in the little book of her Life, are true; and that the Lord performed through her more miracles, both in her life and after her death, than human memory can retain.

Concerning circumstances he says that, having copied her books—namely *Scivias*, *The Book of Life’s Merits*, and *The Book of Divine Works*—from exemplars belonging to her monastery, and having intended to go on pilgrimage to blessed Martin at Tours, she took the already named books with her to Paris. So that she might study them there more safely, she obtained, from the bishop then governing that place, after much labour and great tribulations, the convocation of all the masters then lecturing in theology. To each of them he gave three quires of the books for examination, from the Octave of Martinmas to the Octave of Epiphany. After examining them, they returned them to the bishop, who assigned them to Master William of Auxerre, the master in office at that time. He returned them to her—that is, Hildegard—affirming that it was the judgment of the masters that they contained not human but divine words.

[Note: The tomb and body of St Martin in the city of Tours are very well known to have been most celebrated for many centuries and honoured by a great concourse of pilgrims. We shall treat these matters under St Martin, 11 November. I showed in the Commentary, no. 182, that this pilgrimage of St Hildegard is to be placed in the later years of her life.]

[Note: Paris naturally lay on the route; by this period it had a most celebrated university. The form *Parisius* is frequently used unchanged in the Middle Ages.]

[Note: The Bishop of Paris was Maurice, who administered that see for a long time and is praised by several writers in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 70 ff.]

10. He also says concerning her reputation that his mother, living in the village called Lorche, two miles from the monastery which Hildegard had built, brought him across with her, together with very many other married women. Having learned the fame of blessed Hildegard’s holiness, she earnestly begged Hildegard to lay the hand of blessing upon her, and this Hildegard did.

[Note: I find the village of Lorich marked on various maps on the opposite bank of the Rhine, about two German miles below Bingen.]

Master Arnold, scholasticus of St Peter’s, says the same as Bruno concerning the examination of the books, since he was then studying theology in Paris. A great part of the convent agrees with Bruno, apart from Bruno’s visit to blessed Hildegard. Master John, canon of Mainz and now provost of Bingen, also agrees with the foregoing concerning the examination of the books, since he was studying theology in Paris at the same time. He says that few now living know the truth about St Hildegard better than he does.

When we asked the convent why blessed Hildegard no longer performed signs, they replied that, because after her death the Lord showed so many miracles and such a concourse of people came to her tomb, religion and the divine office were disturbed by the crowd’s tumult to such an extent that they reported it to the Lord Archbishop of Mainz. He therefore came personally to the place and commanded her to cease from signs.

11. The priest Roricus, numbered above among the first witnesses, also says that in the limbs of that possessed woman whom he adjured, the demon appeared in the shape of a great [perhaps “large”] mouse. When the hair of blessed Hildegard was applied, it fled visibly from one limb to another, blackening it like charcoal. At last, after being long wearied, it departed in the form of foulest smoke and was no longer seen with the ravens.

[Note: On this possessed woman and Roricus’s testimony, see more at no. 1.]

We send, under our seals and through the same faithful and reputable man, Bruno the priest, keeper of St Peter’s at Strasbourg and procurator of the aforesaid monastery, her writings which the convent has thus acknowledged as hers: namely, *Scivias*, *The Book of Life’s Merits*, and *The Book of Divine Works*, examined at Paris by masters of theology; the book of exposition of certain Gospels; the Book of Letters; the book of simple medicine; the book of composite medicine; and her song, together with the unknown language; as well as the little book written and preserved concerning her life. Falling upon our knees, we beseech the fatherhood of your Holiness that you may be willing to place upon the candlestick this most outstanding lamp, hitherto hidden as it were beneath a bushel, so that it may shine upon all who are in God’s house: namely, by inserting her name in the catalogue of saints and commissioning suitable men to pursue, by your authority, so pious a work to its due completion, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure.

[Note: Here the examiners—who had been commanded by Gregory IX also to transmit St Hildegard’s written works, as is clear from Gregory’s words given in the Commentary, no. 208—turn to the pontiff; after enumerating the books they were sending, they request canonisation.]

These proceedings were conducted at St Rupert’s. Given in the year of the Lord 1233, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0139]

# NOTICE CONCERNING THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF ST HILDEGARD

By Dr F. A. Reuss, Professor at Würzburg.

Saint Hildegard was born in the castle of Beckelheim, situated on the left bank of the River Nahe, at the beginning of the year 1099, to parents of noble birth and knightly rank: her father was Hildebert, a vassal of Count Meginhart of Spanheim, a just man devoted to God; her mother, Matilda. [Note: [Col. 0139B] Acta SS. Bolland., Sept. V, 629. Mabillon, Annals of the Order of St Benedict, VI, 353. Surius, in the Life, 17 September. Oudin, Supplement on Ecclesiastical Writers, p. 452. Du Pin, New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors, IX, 185. P. Leyser, History of Poets, p. 437. Saxius, Onomasticon, II, 241. Heckel, The Noblest Women of German Antiquity, II, 51. Harless, Women’s Contributions to Natural Science and Medicine, 138. Braun, The Rhine Voyage, II, 194. Bodmann, Antiquities of the Rheingau, I, 420. Vogt, Rhenish Histories and Legends, I, 364; III, 112.]

When she was eight years old, she was entrusted to the care of Jutta, abbess on Mount Saint Disibod and sister of Count Meginhart; there she began to learn examples from Holy Scripture and to recite the Psalms. These studies, as well as reading the lives of the martyrs of that region, Bertha and Rupert, so affected the girl—who was endowed with remarkable gifts of intellect—that she sought above all the peaceful tranquillity of monastic life. [Note: [Col. 0139B] Trithemius, Annals of Hirsau, I, 416. Theodoric the monk, *Life of Saint Hildegard*, above, I, 1: “As soon as she could attempt her first speech, she indicated, both in words and gestures, to those about her the forms of secret visions which, beyond the ordinary sight of others, she beheld by a wholly unfamiliar contemplation. When she was nearly eight years old, she was enclosed on Mount Saint Disibod with the devout lady Jutta, who instructed her in the songs of David and showed her beforehand how to rejoice upon the ten-stringed psaltery. Apart from a simple knowledge of the Psalms, however, she received no instruction in letters or in the musical art.”]

Accordingly, consecrated to Christ by a solemn vow, together with Hiltrud, daughter of Meginhart, and other girls of her own age, she embraced the Rule of Saint Benedict. Soon becoming among the virgins of her convent a conspicuous example of pure piety and subtle learning, she was unanimously elected abbess by the nuns after Jutta’s death in 1136. [Note: [Col. 0140B] Dodechin, Appendix to Marianus Scotus’s Chronicle, under the year 1136. Alberic’s Chronicle, under the year 1141. Magdeburg Centuries, XII, 10.]

From her earliest childhood she had weak and frail health and was troubled by frequent illnesses. Yet, despising and loathing every earthly pleasure, she was illumined by a singular and extraordinary divine favor—with heavenly light and an unusual knowledge of things—and was able to expound the doctrines of the Church and to speak intelligently in Latin, though her teacher had never instructed her in it. [Note: [Col. 0140B] Theodoric, *Life of Saint Hildegard*, I, 1: “When I was forty-two years and seven months old, a fiery light of immense brilliance came from an open heaven and flooded my whole brain; it set my whole heart and breast ablaze like a flame—not burning, but warming, as the sun warms an object. And suddenly I understood the interpretation of the books of the Gospel and of other writings.”]

Indeed, with prophetic understanding she interpreted to the astonished rulers of her age the destinies and manners of times to come, [Note: [Col. 0140B] Hence she was called the Rhenish Sibyl. Vincent of Beauvais, *Mirror of History*, XXVII, 83. Philip of Bergamo, Supplement to the Chronicle, XII, under the year 1158. Pez, *Treasury*, II, 519. Serarius, *History of Mainz Affairs*, ch. 37. Johann, *History of Mainz Affairs*, 195. Gudenus, *Diplomatic Codex*, I, 229, 247.] and with a healing hand cured every kind of disease and bodily defect.

In the year 1148, instructed by an oracle of the divine voice, she left the convent of Saint Disibod and, with eighteen virgins, moved to a mountain near Bingen, where Henry, Archbishop of Mainz, and the counts of Spanheim and Hildenheim had founded for her a new and larger monastery at the tomb of Saints Bertha and Rupert. At that time Saint Bernard, [Note: [Col. 0141] Neander, *Life of Saint Bernard*, 210, 300.] received as a guest by Hildegard on his journey, praised her revelations in his honeyed speech at the Synod of Trier before Pope Eugene III. [Note: [Col. 0141] Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, XII, under the year 1148.] The Pope ordered them to be read publicly and wrote honorably to Hildegard (Letter 1 below); she immediately replied with her customary freedom, in a letter composed in vision.

Thereupon Hildegard acquired great renown and received letters from the most celebrated men of that age, either seeking her counsel on matters pertaining to religion or asking for her prayers to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0141] Theodoric, *Life*, II, 4: “Not only the whole surrounding region, but all three divisions of Gaul and Germany flocked to her. For in the spirit she foresaw the lives of men and the glory and punishments of souls. Her gravity was tempered with kindness, and from her tongue flowed a sweetness of speech sweeter than honey.”] Roman pontiffs Anastasius IV and Adrian IV wrote to her, as did Emperors Conrad III and Frederick Barbarossa, and many other bishops, prelates, and counts.

In 1150, stirred by the Spirit of the Lord to teach the nations heavenly truth, she undertook journeys into various regions of Germany and Gaul. In 1165 she founded the convent of Eibingen; [Note: [Col. 0141] Caspar Lerch von Dirmstein, *On the Origin of the Very Ancient Monastery of Rupertsberg*, 4.] in 1173 she went to Paris. In 1174, after returning to her convent and completing various books of revelations, she was at last worn out by age and burning with desire for the life above. In the eighty-second year of her life, on 17 September 1180 (1179)—the end of life which she herself had long foretold—she died in a blessed passage, illustrious through miracles. [Note: [Col. 0141] Theodoric, *Life*, III, 32: “God plainly declared at her passing what merit she possessed before him. Above the dwelling in which the holy virgin surrendered her blessed soul to God at the first twilight of the night of the Lord’s Day, two exceedingly bright rainbows of different colours appeared in the sky. They spread out to the breadth of a great square, extending toward the four quarters of the earth. People who presumed to touch her holy body in good hope recovered from serious illness. A fragrance of marvellous sweetness also issued from her tomb.”]

Her relics were transferred from her burial place in the choir of the buildings of Saint Rupert, burnt in the Swedish war, to the church at Eibingen, [Note: [Col. 0141] Papebroch, in *Roman Itinerary*, p. 23, relates [Col. 0142] that he saw Saint Hildegard’s relics at Eibingen in 1660. The comb used by Saint Hildegard is described in *Garments of the Christian Middle Ages*, I, 38.] where they are now devoutly venerated. Three canonical investigations were undertaken—first by Gregory IX (1237), then by Innocent IV (1243), and again by John XXII (1317)—but remained incomplete because miracles had ceased and witnesses were lacking. [Note: [Col. 0142] For the acts of the investigation into the virtues and miracles of Saint Hildegard, see below, col. 131.] Nevertheless, from the beginning of the fifteenth century martyrologies began to commemorate Saint Hildegard on 17 September.

She certainly holds a distinguished place among the prophetically gifted virgins of the Middle Ages: Elizabeth of Schönau, Gertrude, Bridget, and others renowned in subsequent centuries for their exceptional gift of prophecy. In both the character of her visions and her age, Hildegard is closest to Elizabeth, Abbess of Schönau (1129–1165). [Note: [Col. 0142] Meiners, in the *New Göttingen Magazine*, 1794, III, 4.] Yet Saint Hildegard differs even from her in this respect: as she herself reports in the preface to Book I of *Scivias*, she received her revelations neither in dreams, nor while asleep, nor through bodily eyes or the ears of the outward person, nor in hidden places; but while awake, looking about with a pure mind, through the eyes and ears of the inward person, in open places, according to God’s will. [Note: [Col. 0142] Theodoric, *Life*, I, 8: “I see these things neither with outward eyes nor hear them with outward ears, nor perceive them by thoughts of my heart or through any cooperation of the five senses; but only in my soul, while my exterior eyes are open. Thus I have never suffered a failure of ecstasy in them, but see them wakefully by day and night.” Cf. G. Arnold, *Theological History of Mysticism*, p. 280. Schmid, *Mysticism of the Middle Ages*, p. 83. Sailer, *Letters from Every Century*, IV, 3. Roess and Weiss, *Lives of the Fathers and Martyrs*, XIII, 111. Tersteegen, *Lives of Holy Souls*, III, 475. Aschbach, *General Church Lexicon*, III, 275.]

Under the name of Saint Hildegard there survive:

I. WORKS PRINTED IN TYPE.

The three Books of Visions entitled *SCIVIAS*, the principal work of the holy virgin, completed over ten years, begin: “Behold, in the forty-third year of my temporal course, as I clung with great fear and trembling attention to a heavenly vision, I saw a very great brightness,” etc. They were published:

a.) At Paris in 1513, folio, by Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples, under the title: *Book of Three Men and Three Spiritual Virgins: One Book of Hermas, One Book of Uguetinus, Two Books of Brother Robert, Three Books of Hildegard’s Scivias, Six Books of the Virgin Elizabeth, Five Books of the Virgin Mechthild. A Study for the Devout.*

b.) At Cologne in 1628, folio, under the title: *Revelations of the Holy Virgins Hildegard and Elizabeth of Schönau, of the Order of Saint Benedict.*

The book of Letters, [Note: [Col. 0142] A collection of the Letters is also found in Martène, *Very Ample Collection of Ancient Writers*, II. The letter of the Abbess of Kitzingen and Saint Hildegard’s reply are extant in the *Archive of the Historical Society at Würzburg*, V, 3, 109.] published from the archetype of the monastery of Saint Rupert by Justus Blanckwalt, priest of Mainz, Cologne, 1566, quarto, by the heirs of J. Quentel and Gervinus. Added on p. 275 is the *Life of Saint Hildegard* composed by the monk Theodoric. We owe a German translation of this Life—already mentioned by Dahl in his study, *Saint Hildegard, a Historical Treatise*, Mainz, 1832, octavo, p. 51—to Ludwig Clarus, *Letters and Life of Saint Hildegard, Translated into German for the First Time*, Regensburg, 1854, octavo, 2 volumes.

[Col. 0143]

*Life of Saint Robert or Rupert the Confessor, Duke of Bingen*, who flourished in the ninth century, published by Johann Busaeus at Mainz in 1602, quarto; in Surius under 15 May; and with notes by Henschenius in *Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. III, p. 504.

*Life of Saint Disibod, Bishop and Confessor*, who died in 674, written in 1170; in the same Surius under 8 July and in *Acta Sanctorum*, July, vol. II, p. 588.

*Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict*, addressed to the congregation of the convent of Hunnen.

Thirty-eight Questions, with answers, addressed to Wibert, monk of Gembloux.

*Explanation of the Athanasian Creed*, published by Blanckwalt with Saint Hildegard’s letters and with the two preceding writings.

*Book of Divine Works of a Simple Person*, edited by Giovanni Domenico Mansi in the additions to Baluze’s *Miscellanies*, vol. II of the Lucca edition prepared by him, p. 335. [Note: [Col. 0143] “The book *Scivias*,” says the most learned editor in the additions to Fabricius’s *Library*, vol. III, p. 263, “and the *Book of Divine Works* are two volumes wholly distinct from one another, both said to have been written by the holy virgin. The books of *Scivias* are well known; she produced them in the forty-third year of her life. I possess a noteworthy parchment codex of the *Book of Divine Works*, in folio, adorned with vermilion and images shining with gold. Since it is little known, I undertake to describe it here somewhat more fully. It is divided into three parts. The first ends with the fourth vision and contains one hundred chapters. The second begins with the fifth vision and continues to the sixth; it contains forty-nine chapters. The sixth vision and the third part begin together; they conclude with the tenth vision and chapter 38. She began to write this work, as is read there, in the sixty-fifth year of her life, and in the year 1163 of the Lord’s Incarnation, while the disturbance of the Apostolic See had not yet subsided—when Frederick was harassing the Roman pontificate—under Frederick, Emperor of the Roman dignity. She mentions her earlier visions and does not pass over her preceding writings: ‘As I have stated in my earlier visions’; and below: ‘Since all that I had written from the beginning of my visions.’ At the beginning of the [Col. 0144] second vision she also speaks of the egg which she had seen in vision, just as she had described it in the third vision of the book *SCIVIAS* twenty-eight years earlier. The title of the entire work is: *Book of Divine Works of a Simple Person*. It contains many curious matters: on the system of the whole world, the external and internal physical constitution of man, changes in the air, human diseases, and other matters of this sort.”]

Four books of *Physics*. They appeared at Strasbourg, through Johann Schott, in 1533. We publish them much enlarged from a Paris manuscript codex.

Individual selected prophecies have been published, some of which must certainly be considered spurious:

No place or year (: 1500:), quarto: *Two Notable Revelations. One Is Said by Abbot Joachim; the Other by the Holy Lady Hildegardis (sic), Revealed to Them by God, Very Nearly Prophecies.*

1527. Nuremberg, quarto. *Saint Hildegard’s Prophecy concerning the Papists and the Named Clergy, whose Fulfilment Has Begun in Our Times and Is to Be Completed. A Preface by Andreas Osiander, preacher at Nuremberg.*

1529. Haguenau, octavo, by Hieronymus Gebwiler, director of the literary youth of Haguenau. *A Little Book on the Present Tribulation of the Clergy and the Event of Times to Come, from the Prophecies of the Divine Hildegard.*

1620. No place, quarto. *Prophecy or Revelation of Hildegard, about 450 years ago, concerning these our last times, so clear and manifestly expressed; by Georg Bellamer of Ubi[o].*

An unknown vision of the holy virgin from a Vienna manuscript codex appears in Mone’s *Anzeiger für Kunde des deutschen Mittelalters*, VII, 613. [Note: [Col. 0144] Other visions seem to lie hidden in manuscript codices at Basle, Saint Gall, and Middlehill, according to Haenel, *Catalogue of Manuscript Books*.] B. M. Chladenius wrote a theological-critical examination of the visions: Wittenberg, 1716, quarto. [Note: [Col. 0144] Theophilus Spizelius, *The Holy Library Uncovered*, p. 19.]

II. WORKS FROM MANUSCRIPT CODICES NOT YET PUBLISHED.

*Book of the Merits of Life.* Various poems. *Heavenly Harmony.* *Unknown Language*, with a Latin translation. [Note: [Col. 0144] J. Grimm undertook to explain it in Haupt, *Journal for German Antiquity*, VI, 321.] Treatise on the sacrament of the altar. Fifty-eight homilies on the Gospels. Books of simple and compound medicine.

The prophecies concerning the destinies of the Seraphic Order and the Society of Jesus, and likewise the work entitled *Pentachronon*, must be judged spurious and unworthy of the holy virgin. [Note: [Col. 0144] Engelhardt, programme on Saint Hildegard’s prophecies concerning the Friars Minor, Erlangen, 1833. *Jesuitical Elixir Enlarged with the Prophecies of Saint Hildegard*, 1645. On German words occurring in Saint Hildegard, compare Hoffmann, *Old High German Glosses*, I, 31; the same author’s *Storehouses*, I, 318, and *Summaries*, 6; Pez, *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, I, I, 414; Mone, *Anzeiger*, 1834, 110; 1835, 239; Haupt, *Journal*, IX, 388; Grimm, *German Mythology*, II, edition, 1121, 1155.]

The Reverend Ludwig Schneider, parish priest at Eibingen, a man deeply versed in matters concerning Saint Hildegard and guardian of her relics, has promised shortly to publish the unpublished works of the holy virgin from very ancient codices preserved at Wiesbaden.

[Col. 0145]

BOOK OF LETTERS OF SAINT HILDEGARD THE ABBESS, CONTAINING

Various letters of supreme pontiffs, emperors, patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, dukes, princes, and very many other magnates of both secular and ecclesiastical rank, addressed to Saint Hildegard, together with the holy replies of Hildegard herself to them.

(*Library of the Fathers of Lyons*, vol. XXIII, p. 537.)

FIRST LETTER.

[Col. 0145A]

EUGENE THE PONTIFF TO HILDEGARD. By apostolic authority he grants her permission to utter and write whatever she has learned through the Holy Spirit, and encourages her to set down without fear what has been revealed to her. (G)*

EUGENE, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in the Lord HILDEGARD, provost on Mount Blessed Robert, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We marvel, daughter, and marvel beyond what can be believed, because God has now in our own times displayed new miracles, pouring his Spirit into you so abundantly that you are said to see, understand, and utter many mysteries. We have learned from truthful persons that this is so, for they declare that you have both seen and heard. But what can we say concerning these things—we who possess the key of knowledge, so that we can shut and open, and yet through folly neglect to do this wisely? Therefore we rejoice in the grace of God; we rejoice also in your belovedness. We warn you that you should know that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4). Preserve and guard the grace that is in you, so that you may wisely utter what you perceive must be uttered in the Spirit, and may hear the saying: “Open your mouth, and I shall fill it” (Psalm 70).

As for the place which you have indicated to us, and which you foresaw for yourself in the Spirit, let this be done with our permission and blessing and that of your bishop, so that you may live there with your sisters under enclosure, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

HILDEGARD’S REPLY. She admonishes the pontiff concerning the secrets which he held in his heart and declares the divine will and good pleasure concerning them.

[Col. 0145C]

O gentle Father, I, a poor little woman, wrote these things to you in a true vision, in a mystical breath, as God wished to teach me. O radiant Father, in your name you came into our land, as God predestined, and you saw writings of true visions, as the Living Light taught me, and heard it with the embraces of your heart. Now a part of this writing has been completed. Yet that same Light has not left me, but burns in my soul as I have possessed it from my childhood. Therefore I now send you this letter in God’s true admonition.

My soul desires that light from Light may shine in you, pour pure eyes into you, and rouse your spirit for the work of this writing, so that your soul may thereby be crowned with that which pleases God. For many prudent men, drawing from earthly entrails, scatter these things so as to change their own minds because of the poor form built from a rib, who is unlearned among philosophers.

Therefore, you Father of pilgrims, [Col. 0146B] hear him who is the mighty King, who sat in his palace and had before him great pillars girded with golden belts and richly adorned with many pearls and precious stones. Yet this King was pleased to touch a little feather, so that it might fly in miracles; and a strong wind upheld it lest it fail.

Now he who is Living Light in the heights, shining in the abyss and hidden in the secret place of receptive hearts, says once more to you: “Prepare this writing for the hearing of those who receive me. Make it green with the sap of sweet taste, the root of branches, and a flying leaf against the devil; and you shall live forever. Take care not to despise these mysteries of God, for they are necessary in that necessity which lies hidden and has not yet openly appeared. Let an exceedingly sweet fragrance be in you, and do not grow weary on the straight road.”

But he who speaks and does not keep silent says these things because of the weakness of those who are blind to see, deaf to hear, and mute to speak amid the nocturnal snares of the deadly trap of thieving ways. What does he say? “The sword flashes and circles, killing those who are of perverse mind.”

O you who in your person are a shining breastplate and the first root in Christ’s new nuptials, divided into two parts: first, in that your soul has been renewed in the mystical flower of virginity; second, in that you are a root of the Church—hear him who is sharp in name and flows in a torrent, speaking to you: “Do not cast away eye from eye, nor cut light off from light; but stand upon the level path, lest you be accused in your soul on account of those entrusted to your bosom, and do not permit them to be plunged into the pit of perdition by the power of banqueting prelates.

“A gem lies in the road. A bear comes, sees it to be very beautiful, stretches out its paw, and wishes to lift it and put it in its bosom. But suddenly an eagle comes, snatches up the gem, wraps it in the covering of its wings, and carries it into the enclosure [Col. 0147B] of the King’s palace. Before the King’s face the gem gives great brilliance, and is greatly loved by the King. Because of his love for this gem, the King gives the eagle golden shoes and greatly praises it for its worth.”

Now you who sit in Christ’s place in the care of the ecclesiastical see, choose for yourself the better part: be an eagle overcoming the bear, and adorn with the enclosures of the Church the souls committed to you, so that, coming upward in golden shoes, you may rescue yourself from another’s control. For the Living Eye sees and says—it has wisdom, discerns every creature, raises them all up, and keeps watch: “The valleys lament over the mountains, and the mountains fall upon the valleys.” How so? Subjects, stripped of the discipline of the fear of God, are driven by rage to climb the mountain peaks and accuse their prelates; and their recklessness does not accuse its own wicked deeds. But they say: “I am useful, that I may be a prelate for usefulness.” And they regard all the works of prelates as unworthy, because they resent that the latter are superior to them.

For subjects are now black clouds; they are not girded at their loins, but scatter all the ordinances of the field, calling them contemptible. They do this because they are poisoned by envy. A poor man displays great folly when his garments are torn and he continually looks at another, considering what colour that person’s garment may be, while he does not wash his own from filth. But the mountains leap over the key of the way of truth, and their paths are not prepared [Col. 0147D] to fly to the mountain of myrrh (Song of Songs 4). Therefore the stars are darkened by a diverse cloud. The moon stands still; the stars cry out that the moon is falling. The sun presses upon them, because none of them shines, but they are entangled in a whirlwind.

Therefore, O great shepherd, named after Christ, give light to the mountains and a rod to the valleys. Give precepts to the masters and discipline to the subjects: justice sprinkled with oil to the mountains, and the bond of obedience mixed with a good fragrance to the valleys. Make their paths straight, so that they do not appear contemptible to the Sun of righteousness. Make them pure, so that you may have eyes everywhere. Let your mind be watered from a pure spring, that you may shine with the sun and imitate the Lamb.

The poor little form trembles as she speaks in the sound of words to so great a teacher. But, O gentle Father, the Ancient One and mighty warrior says these things; therefore hear:

“It shall be directed to you from the supreme Judge that you root out and expel heavy and ungodly tyrants, lest they stand in great mockery in your fellowship. But be merciful in public and private afflictions, because God does not despise the wounded, nor the pains of those who tremble before him. Therefore, O shepherd of sheep, hear these things concerning those who toil in the weariness of many burdens. The Light says: ‘God’s judgments upon each person are mystical, according to that person’s merit. Yet many people wish to carry out an investigation by their own zeal and through ignorance of their own conduct, but they do not know my judgment. Hence, beyond measure they lie in their own estimation, like wolves snatching prey. Therefore, although someone deserves to be judged for crimes, it does not please me that a person should seek judgment for himself according to his own decision. This I do not will. Rather, discern every case according to the motherly bowels of God’s mercy, who does not separate from himself the beggar and needy person, for he desires mercy more than sacrifice’” (Hosea 6; Matthew 9, 12).

“Now the black men seek to wash away blackness through their own foulness, but they themselves are polluted and deaf, lying in a pit. Raise them up and help the little ones. For you who are shepherd of peoples, hear, that you may live eternally.”

The Living Light says: “Tell the audacious people, who invent terrors for themselves on the path of wandering ways: A certain lord possessed a city of marble. Hunters came and looked upon that city, wishing to scatter its right ordinances, which appeared in that flower discovered by a virginal mind.

“And behold, a great and lofty mountain, very beautiful and made of polished stones, appeared toward the east. On it stood, facing east, a certain building made of wood and stones of ordinary construction. Then many streams, as though from the midst of the east, flowed into this building. In the same building there was a very strong fragrance of good wine, yet mixed with water. And a great crowd rushed into that building, walking there with bent bodies. Others stood in a valley before the aforesaid mountain and watched those who went bent within that building.

“And behold, above the same mountain there also stood another marble building, of the whitest and soundest stone, like a great tower facing north. In a most radiant flask, full of the finest balsam, something hung like a burning fire, while much oil flowed over its floor. Yet a wind sometimes coming from the north stirred that balsam and oil. Then many of the people entered that building: they were sprinkled with that oil and marked with that balsam upon their foreheads. A voice came from heaven saying: ‘These are marked.’ Those marked in this way could not wash away the mark, but remained marked, just as those reborn in Christ ought to preserve their baptism.

“Those who were marked did not go over to those who had not been marked, nor accept their fellowship; for if they had done so, they would be called foolish and useless. But those who had not been marked went over to those who were marked and accepted their fellowship, and from this chose the best part for themselves, as a star multiplies its brightness in a cloud and as a female form is crowned in virginity.

“And a great man girded with a golden belt stood above these buildings, placing his right arm over the marble building and his left over the other. This understanding refers to the two instruments of ecclesiastical dignity. For the omnipotent Father established a noble part, separated from secular affairs and burning strongly before God in its hidden places. Certain plotters, despising it, wish to destroy its rectitude, which appeared manifestly in the Son of God.

“Yet the mountain of justice, polished by many justifications, rises at the dawning of truth. On it rises a useful institution directed toward God and nevertheless assisting men, giving humanity the light of usefulness, so that much teaching and the fragrance of right writings flow to it from the strength of truth; but some repeatedly pour these things out in various directions without reason. Hence many walk crookedly in it through perversity, and some who hanker after earthly things imitate their foulness.

“But on the same mountain of justice, that aforesaid part—burning before God in its hidden places—rises in its integrity in order to resist the devil. It has the best part in God and shows mercy in its example. Yet many temptations sent by the devil trouble both the best part and mercy itself. Many people, however, pass over to that part and attain true mercy when they choose the best part for themselves. Therefore they are called marked before God. Those who receive the mark of this part remain firmly in it, as in their baptism. Hence they do not descend in fellowship to their own people who lack that same mark, lest they become empty like fools. Those who lack the mark of that part, however, ascend in fellowship to the same order and thereby increase in very many goods.

“This is also shown by the one girded with a golden belt” (Revelation 1): “he declares himself to be both God and man, ruling both groups—the one and the other—with the arm of his strength. He protects these, so that they may burn strongly in him, casting aside secular things; and he covers those with the arm of his gentleness, so that they may be useful under divine protection as they profitably offer the light of truth to their neighbours.”

Now you who are Father of peoples, discern clearly these words sent to you from the supreme Judge because of the need of those who wander. For pride wishes to oppress humility, which ought not to be, just as it would be unfitting if the moon wished to fight with the sun, desiring to make its brightness equal to the sun’s brightness.

Therefore, because of this foolish matching, the spring of waters cries out to you, its imitator: “By me, the Living and Sharp One, restrain and correct the black plotters and stealthy spies who are turned into lead by their crooked sins, who are sprinkled from the north with the devil’s wickedness, and who stretch themselves out in opposition to the head of their prelates through excess of iniquity. Therefore drive them from pastoral care, which bears the punishment due to dogs. And although some prelates are darkened by the changeableness of their conduct, nevertheless it is not fitting that some should be cast aside on account of certain subjects.

“Therefore examine these things with a most pure eye, so that your honour may not fail—an honour which, because of its name, touches him who was and is upright and just, preparing his paths in all his instruments and foreseeing them before the ordinances of ancient days. May he make your eyes pure, he who does not despise the orphan and the poor” (Psalm 9), “because you are the mountain of myrrh and incense” (Song of Songs 4) “above the valleys, the pits of filth.

“Therefore hear him who always keeps watch with living eyes and is not wearied by storms, which are the portion of the cup of those who resemble idols, as though made hard by their prosperity. But you, who wish to possess the authority of great honour in the King’s palace, extend the justice of the Most High to his honour. This befits you, for your sake, for the sake of your illustrious name.

“Now look upon the fiery giver who pours good understanding into human beings. But what person can sound forth against that voice? Can this voice make a little feather fly so that no sword can move against that feather? It can.

“Now you, O imitator of the exalted Person, the Living Spring cries this to you: it does not befit your person to have the eyes of the blind, the tracks of viperish manners, and stealthy plunder, stripping God’s altar bare. Why should you do this? But whoever does this cannot loosen the strap of the Lord’s bodily sandal. Therefore, O all of you, correct yourselves.”

But I, O Father, remain, both while I live and after I die, with my sisters in the place shown to me from heaven, according to the words of your blessing, under the enclosure of that place and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; and I desire that this always be observed.

SECOND LETTER.

ANASTASIUS, POPE, TO HILDEGARD. He approves her writings and asks that she offer prayers to God for him. (G)*

[Col. 0150D]

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HILDEGARD, beloved daughter in Christ, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice in the Lord and are glad that the name of Christ is glorified in you day by day, so that in admiration we say: “Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like you—magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, performing wonders?” (Exodus 15). For we have heard and seen many things concerning you. We also know that our predecessor of pious memory, to whom we succeeded by divine grace in nourishing Christ’s bride, loved, embraced, and heard you with great affection.

Following in his footsteps, we have taken care to write to you and desire to see your replies, seeking those things which God works in you. Yet we limp in good works, in which we sigh because of the weariness of both body and mind, since through our negligence we do not lift ourselves upward to heavenly things as we ought by right. But he who knows hidden things knows both our will and our ability.

Therefore we exhort, request, and earnestly charge you to pour out prayers to the Lord together with your sisters, that through his power we may be able to raise ourselves to righteousness, so as thereby to obtain eternal rewards, without ceasing in this present life to strive toward them. Peace be with you and with all who are yours.

HILDEGARD’S REPLY. In God’s name she exhorts the pontiff courageously to root out evils. She then prophetically foretells various things and adds certain matters concerning her visions. Again she exhorts Anastasius to correct his subjects.

[Col. 0151B]

O person, you who are a pre-eminent armour and the mountain of instruction of a richly adorned city, who have been established in the betrothal of Christ, hear him who did not begin to live and does not grow weary in failing strength. O man, weary in the eye of your knowledge when it comes to restraining the boastful speech of pride among the people placed in your charge, why do you not call back the shipwrecked, who cannot rise from their great falls except with help? And why do you not cut off the root of evil, which chokes the good and useful herbs, possessing a sweet taste and pleasant fragrance? You neglect the king’s daughter—namely justice—who is in the embraces of heaven and who [Col. 0151C] had been entrusted to you. For you allow this king’s daughter to be cast down upon the earth, because the diadem and adornment of her garment are torn by the uncouth conduct of those various people who bark like dogs and, like hens which sometimes attempt to crow at night, send forth a foolish raising of their voices. These are hypocrites: in their voices they display a feigned peace, but among themselves grind their teeth in their hearts, like a dog that wags its tail at companions it knows but bites with its teeth a worthy soldier useful in the king’s house. Why do you tolerate depraved habits in people who dwell in the darkness of folly, gathering every harmful thing to themselves, [Col. 0151D] like a hen that cries at night and terrifies itself? Those who act thus are not rooted in what is beneficial.

Therefore hear, O man, him who greatly loves keen discernment, which he established as the chief instrument of rectitude, to fight against evil. You do not do this when you fail to root out the evil that wishes to choke the good. Instead, you permit evil proudly to raise itself up; and you do this from fear of those who are the worst plotters in nocturnal ambushes, loving the money of death more than the beautiful king’s daughter, namely justice. Yet all the works God has made are most luminous. Hear, O man. For before the world’s rising, the heavenly Father thundered in his hidden place: “O my Son.” And the globe [Col. 0152A] of the world arose, receiving what the Father had thundered, while the different kinds of creatures still lay hidden in obscurity. But in that which is written, “And God said, ‘Let there be’” (Gen. 1), the various kinds of creatures came forth. Thus through the Word and because of the Father’s Word, all creatures were made in the Father’s will. God sees all things and foreknew all things. But evil, neither in rising nor in falling, can of itself do, create, or effect anything, because it is nothing; it is reckoned only as a deceitful choice and a contrary opinion, so that a human being works evil when doing what is contrary. God sent his Son into the world so that the devil, who came to know evil by embracing it and suggested it to humankind, might be overcome by him, and so that [Col. 0152B] humankind, which had perished through evil, might be redeemed. Therefore God despises perverse deeds—namely fornications, murders, robberies, seditions, tyrannies, and the dissimulations of wicked people—because he crushed them through his Son, who utterly scattered the spoils of the Tartarean tyrant.

Therefore you, O man, who sit in the Lord’s chief seat, show contempt when you embrace evil: you do not reject it but kiss it, because you tolerate it in wicked people by silence. Thus the whole earth is disturbed by a great succession of errors, because what God destroyed, man loves. And you, O Rome, lying as though at the point of death, will be troubled so that the strength of the feet on which you have stood until now will weaken, because [Col. 0152C] you love the King’s daughter, namely justice, not with burning love but as if in the numbness of sleep; thus you drive her away from you. Accordingly, she herself wishes to flee from you unless you call her back. Yet great mountains will still offer you the jaw of assistance, lifting you up and supporting you with the great timber of great trees, so that you will not be wholly destroyed in your honour—that is, in the splendour of Christ’s betrothal—but will retain some wings of your adornment, until the snow of diverse mockeries comes, emitting much madness. Beware, therefore, lest you wish to mingle yourself with the rites of pagans, lest you fall.

Now hear him who lives and shall not be destroyed. The world is now in wantonness; afterward it will be in sorrow, then in terror, so that people will not care if they are killed. In all these things there are at times seasons of insolence, at times seasons of contrition, and at times seasons of the lightning and thunder of various iniquities. For the eye rages, the nose snatches, the mouth kills. But the breast will save, where dawn will appear like the brightness of the first rising. What follows in a new desire and a new endeavour must not be spoken. But he who is great without failing has now touched a small dwelling-place, so that it might see that miracle, form unknown letters, utter an unknown language, and sound a melody of many kinds yet harmonious within itself. And it was said to it: “What you have uttered in the language shown to you from above, not according to the form of human custom, since that custom has not been given you, let him who has the file not neglect to polish into a sound suitable for people.” But you, O man, appointed as a shepherd appearing before others, arise and run swiftly toward justice, so that before the great physician you may not be accused of having neither cleansed his sheepfold from filth nor anointed it with oil. But where the will knows no crimes, and where a person has not seized desire [Note: [Col. 0153D] That is, has not consented.], there a person does not wholly fall into the deep judgment. Yet the fault of this ignorance is wiped away by scourges. Therefore, O man, stand in the straight path, and God will save you, so that he will lead you back into the stable of blessing and election, and you shall live for ever.

## LETTER III

### POPE ADRIAN TO HILDEGARD

He exhorts her to perseverance. (G)*

[Col. 0153B]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hildegard, beloved daughter in Christ, prioress of Saint Robert’s, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice, daughter, and exult in the Lord because the report of your integrity has spread so widely and far that you become to many “a fragrance from life unto life” (2 Cor. 2), and the crowd of faithful peoples cries out in praise of you: “Who is this that ascends through the wilderness like a little column of smoke?” (Song 3). Since we judge your soul to be so kindled by the fire of divine love that it requires no exhortation to do good works, we thought it superfluous [Col. 0153C] to multiply words of exhortation to you or support your spirit, sufficiently sustained by divine power, by any reinforcement of words.

Nevertheless, because a fire becomes greater when the breeze blows, and a swift horse is urged to its course by spurs, we thought it fitting to set this before your religious devotion: do not let it escape your memory that the palm and glory are owed not to the one who begins, but to the one who finishes. The Lord says: “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2). Consider, therefore, daughter, that the serpent who cast the first human being out of paradise desires to destroy great persons, such as Job; and, having devoured Judas, he seeks authority to sift the apostles (Luke 22). Since you know that many are called but few are chosen (Matt. 20), gather yourself within the number of the few; persist in holy conduct to the end; instruct the sisters entrusted to your governance in works of salvation, so that, through the Lord’s gift, you may be able with them to attain that joy which “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). Moreover, we desire to hear admonitory words from you, because you are said to be filled with the spirit of God’s miracles. We greatly rejoice in this and give glory to divine grace.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She foretells grave conflicts for the pontiff and exhorts him to courage.

[Col. 0154A]

He who gives life to the living says: O man, you shall endure by suffering the fierce hardness of lionesses and the strength of leopards, and you shall experience shipwreck amid the seizure of plunder, because you have been given to toil for all those who run to you. For you possess an intelligent understanding against the most savage ways of men, and amid their raging you will restrain the manes of galloping horses that do not cease to run along the paths of plunder. Yet, disputing against yourself, you sometimes incline as if toward the virtue of certain people, where you conceal the purses of some who are dead in battle on open roads. Therefore you shall suffer [Col. 0154B] the battle of Shimei’s conflicts; but you shall destroy the movable goods left by those who go to the pit through their harshness. Yet you possess a vein of very strong nails, which does not willingly go to unleavened bread in the form of sardius.

Therefore seek in your breast the salvation of waters, lest you enter the whirlwind. Rather, rest in gentleness despite the languor and bruising of those mixed with the wasting of diverse wounds, thereby imitating your Saviour who redeemed you. But this heavy burden of authority that you bear is not under God’s indignation, even though the ways of bears and panthers, and sometimes the venom of asps, will confront you and those who follow you. But God’s sword will kill them, while a good leader rises among them. Now [Col. 0154C] I warn you to put a bridle upon your subjects and not allow them to speak evil against you.

Thus the true light says to you: “Why do you not strike the most wicked servants who secretly lie in wait for you, like stinging spiders?” Therefore keep vigorous watch, as the condition of the people’s conduct at this time requires. O most gentle Father, remember that you are a human being on earth, and do not fear that God will abandon you, for you shall see his light.

## LETTER IV

### HILDEGARD TO POPE ALEXANDER

That the abbot of Saint Disibod’s opposes the privileges of the convent on Mount Saint Rupert.

O highest and glorious person, first established [Col. 0154D] through the Word of God, through whom every rational and irrational creature was made according to its kind: to you that same Word, by the clothing of his humanity, granted in a special manner the keys of the kingdom of heaven—that is, the power of binding and loosing (Matt. 16). You also, most excellent Father, are the material source of all spiritual persons who sound the trumpet of God’s justice in the Church, which shines clothed about with various ornaments, while some provide others with good examples by imitating the lives of the saints. Although they do anything rightly, they attribute it to God, not to themselves; and they rejoice in their good imitators, following the earlier holy ones, who tamed their flesh and strengthened themselves [Col. 0155A], fighting against the devil’s vices with manifest victory in the heavenly warfare, and who with good will looked to God like angels.

So you also, gentle Father, imitate the kind father who received with joy his penitent son returning to him, killing the fatted calf for his sake (Luke 15) [Note: [Col. 0155D] Something appears to be missing here.]; and who washed in wine the wounds of the man wounded by robbers (Luke 10): the confusion of darkness signifies both the severity of correction and the compassion of mercy. Be also in the Church the morning star that ran before the sun of day—the Church which, long confused by the darkness of schism, lacks the light of God’s justice. Therefore, according to God’s zeal, correct; and anoint the penitent with the oil of mercy, because God desires mercy more than sacrifice (Hos. 6).

[Col. 0155B] Now, O most gentle Father, my sisters and I bend our knees before your fatherly compassion, praying that you may deign to look upon the poverty of a poor little form, for we are now in great sorrow because the abbot of Mount Saint Disibod and his brethren oppose the privileges and election which we have always possessed. We must always make careful provision that this not be taken from us, since, if they did not allow us to have devout and religious men such as we seek, spiritual religious life among us would be altogether destroyed. Therefore, my lord, help us for the Lord’s sake, either that we may retain our election or that we may freely seek and obtain elsewhere persons who can provide for us according to God and our needs.

Again we pray you, most merciful Father, not to despise our petition or these messengers, who, instructed by our faithful friend, turned aside to us while seeking you; grant what they seek to obtain from you, so that after the end of this life, now already declining toward evening, you may attain the unfailing light and hear the sweet voice of the Lord: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I shall set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25). Incline, therefore, the ears of your compassion to our supplications, and let a bright day come to us and to them, so that through the pardon of your generosity we may together give thanks to the Lord, and that you too may always rejoice in eternal blessedness.

### REPLY OF POPE ALEXANDER TO PROVOST WEZELIN

Concerning appointing a provost for the convent on Mount Saint Rupert, notwithstanding the opposition of the abbot of Saint Disibod’s.

[Col. 0155D]

Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the provost of Saint Andrew’s in Cologne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You should know that it has come to our hearing, on behalf of our beloved daughter in Christ Hildegard, prioress of Mount Saint Robert at Bingen, and the sisters of that place, that although they had, as was customary, elected a master and provost for themselves from the monastery of Saint Disibod, the abbot of that place was unwilling to grant what had been done concerning a member of his monastery and still refuses to assign that person to them. Since it is fitting that careful provision be made for the said sisters in matters concerning the salvation of souls, we command your discretion by apostolic letters: when you have been asked concerning this matter, summon both parties before you; having diligently heard the arguments on both sides concerning the election of the provost, decide the case through justice. If the said sisters cannot have a provost from that monastery, arrange at least that they have a suitable one from another.

## LETTER V

### HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, TO HILDEGARD

That she should allow a certain nun, elected abbess, to depart with those who had come to take her away.

[Col. 0156B]

Henry, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Mainz, to Hildegard, beloved mistress of Mount Saint Robert the Confessor, his grace with paternal affection.

Since we hear many good and wonderful miracles about you, we must attribute it to our sloth that we do not visit you as often as we could. But impeded by very many affairs, we can scarcely, and only tardily, lift our soul to eternal things. To come, however, to our purpose, we make known to you that messengers of a certain religious and noble church known to us have come to us, earnestly requesting that the sister whom they seek, who lives with you in a religious habit, be granted to them as abbess according to their election. We also command you this by the authority of our prelacy and fatherhood, and in commanding impose it upon you: present her now to those seeking and desiring her for their governance. If you do this, you will henceforth experience our favour more fully than you have thus far; but if not, we shall command you again more forcibly and shall not cease until you fulfil our commands in this matter.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

By the example of Nebuchadnezzar, she foretells that Henry will be deprived of his rank and will not live very long, as indeed happened.

[Col. 0156D]

The clear spring, which is not deceptive but just, says: These grounds advanced concerning authority over this girl are worthless before God, because I, the high, the deep, and all-encompassing one, who am piercing light, neither established nor chose them; rather, they arose from the presumptuous boldness of ignorant hearts living together. Let all believers hear these things with the receptive ears of the heart, not with ears that hear outwardly like livestock, which catches sound but not a word.

The Spirit of God says in zeal: O shepherds, weep and lament at this time, because you do not know what you are doing when you scatter offices established in God among the resources of money and the folly [Col. 0157A] of wicked people who have no fear of God, where your malicious and threatening words of curse ought not to be heard. Your rods, now proudly raised, are not extended in God but in the penalties of the presumptuousness of your criminal will. And he who is, O man, says to you: “Hear how in many services you neglect me. Heaven is opened for the Lord’s vengeance” (Exod. 3), and now the cords have been loosened among enemies. But arise, for your days are short (Job 14), and remember that Nebuchadnezzar fell and his crown perished (Dan. 4). Many others also fell, who rashly exalted themselves into heaven (Gen. 3). Ah, you ash, why are you not ashamed to scatter yourself on high, when you ought to be in rottenness? Let the raging now be ashamed. But you, arise and abandon the curse by fleeing it.

[Col. 0157B]

## LETTER VI

### ARNOLD, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, TO HILDEGARD

He requests the prayers of the saint.

Arnold, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Mainz, to Hildegard, virgin dedicated to God and mistress established on Mount Saint Robert, his grace with fatherly affection.

We know that the Spirit inspires where he wills and how he wills (John 3), distributing his gifts to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12). We say this without any hesitation concerning you. For what wonder is it if he teaches you by his inspiration, who formerly made farmers and [Col. 0157C] gatherers of sycamore fruit prophets (Amos 7), and made a she-ass utter human words (Num. 22)? Therefore we neither ought nor are able to reject God’s gifts. We ask your love to help us by your prayers to the Lord, so that our days may at least be spent in fear and love of our Creator, and that, perfected in good things, we may deserve to possess life in the length of days of perpetual blessedness.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She strongly rebukes Arnold and foretells his death.

O Father, the living light gave me these words for you: Why do you hide your face from God, as though in the agitation of your angry mind? For I do not utter mystical words from myself; rather, I see them in the living [Col. 0157D] light, so that things my mind does not desire and even things my will does not seek are shown to me; yet I often see them under compulsion. Still, I ask God that his help may not be to you like exile, and that your soul may be devout in pure knowledge, looking into the mirror of salvation, so that you may live for ever. May the splendid light of God’s grace never be cut off from you. Rather, may God’s mercy protect you so that the ancient plotter may not deceive you. Now let your eye live in God, and let the greenness of your soul not wither.

The living light says to you: Why are you not strong in your fear? You have zeal, as if you were sifting wheat, so that by overcoming you cast down what is contrary to you. But I do not wish this. Wipe the restless mind from the eye of your heart, [Col. 0158A] and cut injustice away from yourself and from your people, because a time of wars in human conduct is now at hand, so that people are neither under discipline nor under the strictness of the fear of the Lord. Do not fear to restrain them for good. If for this reason you endure tribulation and distress, do not be afraid, for the Son of God endured the same. Therefore arise toward the Lord, because your time will come swiftly.

## LETTER VII

### CHRISTIAN, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, TO HILDEGARD

He commends himself to her prayers.

Christian, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Mainz, to Hildegard, beloved mistress of the sisters of Saint Robert at Bingen, the devotion of his favour [Col. 0158B] with both paternal and filial affection.

Hindered by very many affairs, we write briefly to you although with such an enlarged heart we long with all the effort of our mind for your holy love. And because we know that you are inspired by the divine Spirit, we desire your words of exhortation; for, while we endeavour to serve the earthly kingdom outwardly, we often neglect the heavenly King inwardly. Therefore we commend ourselves to your prayers and to those of the sisters with you, so that, helped by them, we may by God’s aid be mercifully delivered from the whirlwinds and storms of this age in which we labour greatly. Know for certain that we shall be present to you in all your needs and assist you in everything, as God grants.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She excellently exhorts him to pastoral care.

[Col. 0158C]

The mystical vision says to you: O person in authority, you have been appointed by Christ himself in Christ’s stead, just as “all authority is from God” (Rom. 13). No one has been found like God. He is the Father of all, because all things proceed from him, and therefore he governs them. The priest holds priestly office because, through the pure sacrifice that became human, he set humanity free. For that priest is established by oath, as it is written: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). God had indeed predestined in himself that he would become human without any stain of sin, without any need of corrective repentance, and without any mixture or division such as exist in human beings with sins, in order thus to conquer evil, as was prefigured in Melchizedek.

But you, O man, who are now in daylight, before night comes, when you can work no more, strive to teach your people God’s commands in true authority and govern them in right justice as God governs them; through great diligence hold them in mercy, because God liberated them through himself. In this manner, indeed, magistracy, lordship, and authority are from God. Also make friends for yourself through mercy from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings (Luke 16). Now, O Father [Col. 0159A] and teacher, after Christ listen to this poor little form writing to you from the true light, so that you may extend aid to all of us who are in need and flee to you. Thus, because of the joy you bestow upon them, you may be received into the joy of the eternal dwellings and live for ever in the eternal blessedness for which God created you.

## LETTER VIII

### HILDEGARD TO CHRISTIAN, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

She states that, after a certain young man, once excommunicated but long since absolved, had been buried in the cemetery on Mount Saint Rupert, she received an order from the prelates of Mainz that she must order his body exhumed or refrain from celebrating the divine offices in her church; she implores the pontiff’s help. [Note: [Col. 0159] See the commentary cited above, § XI, no. 167.]

[Col. 0159B] O most gentle Father and lord, who in the stead of Jesus Christ have been appointed shepherd over the sheep of the Church: we humbly give thanks to the highest God and to your fatherly compassion because you mercifully received the letters of our poverty; because, in your mercy, you deigned to send letters on behalf of us who were troubled and distressed to our prelates at Mainz; and also because of the sweet words of your customary clemency, through which the lord Herman, dean of the church of the Holy Apostles at Cologne, so consoled and gladdened us that, in all our tribulation and distress, we confidently flee to you as daughters to a beloved father.

Therefore, good lord, we your servants, seated in the sorrow of tribulation [Col. 0159C] and distress, prostrate at your feet in a spirit of humility, tearfully reveal to you in pure truth the cause of our unbearable suffering. We do so in confidence that the fiery love which is God (John 4) may inspire you mercifully, with fatherly compassion, to hear the lamentable cry that we, afflicted in our tribulation, raise to you.

O gentle Father: when our prelates at Mainz ordered us either to cast out from our cemetery a dead young man buried among us—who long before his death had been absolved for a year and fortified with all the sacraments of the Christian faith, as I had already indicated to you in letters—or to cease from the divine offices, I looked, as is my custom, to the true light. In it God commanded me never to let him be cast out with my voluntary consent, since he himself had received him from the bosom of the Church to be appointed to the glory of salvation. For the darkness of great danger would arise for us from this, since it would be contrary to the will of that truth. If this fear of almighty God had not stood in my way, I would humbly have obeyed them and, should they order any dead person carried out in your name—you who are our Lord and advocate—I would willingly have consented, provided that he was not excommunicated, in order to preserve the right of the Church.

After we had ceased for some time, not without great grief and sorrow, I came to our prelates at Mainz, compelled by the burden of a most grievous illness, at the command of the highest judge in a true vision of my soul (whose command I did not dare [Col. 0160A] to resist). I presented in writing the words I had seen in the true light, as he commanded me, so that they might learn from them what God’s will was in this case. Asking their pardon before those then present, I sought mercy from them with bitter tears, mournfully and supplicantly. But since their eyes had become so darkened that they could not look upon me with any regard for mercy, I left them full of tears.

Yet when very many people were moved to compassion for us, although they could not help us as they wished, my faithful friend—the archbishop of Cologne—came to them at Mainz. A certain knight, a free man, stood by, who wished to prove with sufficient witnesses that he and the aforesaid deceased man, while the latter was still living in the body, had together been involved in the same offence; that they had also together been absolved, a year ago, in the same place and at the same hour, by the same priest; and that the priest who absolved them was himself present. Once the truth of this matter had been established for them, that prelate, relying on you, obtained permission that the divine offices might be celebrated securely and peacefully until your return. But through those same prelates, after their return from Rome, from the synod, we received your letters forbidding the divine offices—letters which, I trust in your fatherly compassion, you would never have sent if you had known the truth of this case. And thus, most gentle Father, by your own command we were placed under the former bond [Col. 0160C] with far greater grief and sorrow.

Therefore, in the vision of my soul, in which you have never troubled me by any word, I was commanded to say with heart and mouth: “It is better for me to fall into human hands than to abandon the command of my God” (Dan. 13). Therefore, most gentle Father, I beseech you in the love of the Holy Spirit: for the compassion of the eternal Father, who for human salvation sent his Word in sweet greenness into the womb of the Virgin, do not despise the tears of your grieving and weeping daughters, who, through fear of God, endure the tribulations and distresses of this unjust bond. May the Holy Spirit fill you so that you may be moved with such mercy toward us that you too may obtain mercy for this after the end of your life.

## LETTER IX

[Col. 0160D]

### CHRISTIAN, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, TO HILDEGARD

He sympathizes with her affliction and directs that he has informed the Church of Mainz: “if the absolution of the aforesaid deceased person is demonstrated to it by the truthful testimony of good men, the divine offices are to be celebrated for the sisters of Mount Saint Rupert.”

Christian, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Mainz, to the reverend and beloved lady in Christ Hildegard, and to all Christ’s brides serving God with her: may they ascend from strength to strength and see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83).

[Col. 0161A] Although in the admirable and praiseworthy power of God and the mercy of our Saviour we are quite insufficient, indeed utterly unworthy, nevertheless, dearest lady in Christ, trusting diligently in your aid that we may be made worthy, we give thanks to him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends, namely the Father of lights (Jas. 1). He was pleased worthily to dwell in your soul and illumined it with his true and inestimable light. By grace going before and following after, your holy devotion has been granted to sit with Mary at the Lord’s feet (Luke 10) and to attend to visions of the heavenly Jerusalem.

These manifest signs of your holy conduct and wondrous testimonies of truth bind our soul [Col. 0161B] to your commands—indeed, I would say, your prayers—so firmly, dearest lady in Christ, that whenever we know anything may contribute to your holy desires, we ought rightly to incline our heart’s purpose to it. We hope, and, after God, place our highest confidence in your holiness, that through the most holy fragrance of your prayers we may receive God’s grace going before and following after, and that, through the intercession of your holiness, this sinful soul of ours may at last find its Creator’s mercy favourable to it.

For this reason, we grieve with you all the more deeply over the tribulation and affliction that the sacred community endures together with you through the suspension of the divine offices, because we are able more clearly to perceive your innocence in this matter. But because it was established that the deceased buried at your church [Col. 0161C] had incurred a sentence of excommunication during his life, and because that same church was still uncertain of his absolution, it was altogether too dangerous for you in the meantime, on account of the statutes of the holy Fathers, not to be avoided, to disregard the outcry of the clergy and the scandal of the Church, until it should be proved by the suitable testimony of good men, before the Church, that he had been absolved. Therefore, sympathizing from the depths of our heart with your affliction, as is fitting, we wrote back to the Church of Mainz in this manner: if the absolution of the aforesaid deceased person is shown to it by the truthful testimony of good men, we command that the divine offices be celebrated for you. We ask and earnestly entreat your holiness [Col. 0161D] that, if through our fault or ignorance we have troubled you in this matter, you do not withhold mercy from one asking pardon. Deign to pray to the Father of mercies that he may restore us safe and sound to your holy presence and to the Church of Mainz, for the honour of God and of your church, and for the salvation of our soul. May the Lord preserve your health and holiness.

## LETTER X

### HERTUVIG, ARCHBISHOP OF BREMEN, TO HILDEGARD

He announces the death of his sister, Abbess Richardis.

Hertuvig, archbishop of Bremen and brother of Abbess Richardis, to Hildegard, mistress of Saint Robert’s in Christ: in the place of a sister, and more than a sister, obedience.

[Col. 0162A] I inform you that our sister—that sister of mine, indeed yours; mine in body, yours in soul—has entered upon the way of all flesh. She thought little of the honour I had bestowed on her, inasmuch as she obeyed the heavenly King, her Lord, rather than the earthly king; she made a holy and devout confession; after confession she was anointed with holy oil and received the fullness of Christian rites. She tearfully desired your cloister with all her heart; commending herself to the Lord through her mother and John, she signed herself three times with the sign of the cross, confessing Trinity and Unity in perfect faith, hope, and charity. We are certain that she died on the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

I therefore ask you, if I am worthy, insofar as I can: love her as much as she loved you. If she seems to have failed in anything, it did not arise from her but from me. At least take account of her tears, shed over leaving this cloister, of which there are many witnesses. Had death not prevented her, she would scarcely have come to you once permission had been obtained; and since death has detained her, know that I shall come in her place, if it pleases God. But may God, the rewarder of all good things, reward you here and hereafter according to your every wish for the good you showed her—alone among all and above all her relatives and friends—good for which she rejoiced before God and me. Offer your sisters thanks for all their good deeds.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She praises Hertuvig and Richardis. She offers outstanding admonitions.

He who saw you on the first day, and gave you eyes to see, [Col. 0162C] together with the flying wings of every creature; and who made the human being a mirror in the fullness of all his wonders, so that the knowledge of God might shine clearly in him, as it is written: “For you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81)—may he look upon you and direct you according to his will. A human being touches God, who has neither beginning nor end, where rationality in the human being imitates God, and the knowledge of good and evil displays God. Thus is the wheel of eternity.

May God himself also make you flee that evil which began on the first day, lacks good will, and always opposes God. May he also make in you windows that shine in the heavenly Jerusalem—beautiful structures in the virtues—and make you fly [Col. 0162D] in the embraces of God’s love, as he said whom God had suffused: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60). And again: “I, a poor little form, saw in you the light of salvation.” Now fulfill the commandments of God, which his grace gives you and which the Holy Spirit teaches you.
