And in the Spirit’s mystical gift I say to you: You are a praiseworthy person, necessary to humanity, possessing succession in the most high God—that is, the pontifical office. Therefore let your eye see God, let your understanding perceive his justice, and let your heart burn intensely in the love of God, so that your soul may not fail, but may be most earnestly devoted to building the tower of the heavenly Jerusalem. And may God give you a helper—namely, the sweetest mother, mercy. Be also [Col. 0163A] a bright star, shining in the darkness of wicked people’s nights; and a swift stag running to the spring of living water.

Consider: at this time many shepherds are blind, lame, and plunderers of the money of death, choking the justice of God. But God, who knows all things, knows where pastoral care is useful. Therefore a faithful man should not go about seeking prelacy. But if he seeks it, desiring power in his restless mind more for pleasure than by considering the will of God, he is a ravening wolf in his own person; and his soul never seeks spiritual things, but there is simony.

Therefore I say to you also in the Spirit: O what a great wonder there is in the salvation of the souls of those people who hold prelacy without simony, upon whom God so looks that his glory [Col. 0163B] is not overshadowed in them. Rather, he acts in them like a strong warrior who strives not to be overcome by anyone, so that his victory may stand firm.

Now hear: Thus it happened concerning my daughter Richardis, whom I call my daughter because my soul was filled with love for her, since the living light in a most powerful vision taught me to love her. Hear: God held her in such zeal that worldly pleasure could not embrace her; rather, it fought against her, although she herself appeared, like a flower, in the beauty and splendor of this world’s harmony.

But while she was still living in the body, I heard it said of her in a true vision: “O virginity, you stand in the royal bridal chamber.” For she has fellowship, in the virginal branch, in the holiest order; therefore the daughters of Zion rejoice. Yet the ancient [Col. 0163C] serpent wished to draw her away from blessed honor through the lofty nobility of human lineage. But the supreme Judge drew this daughter of mine to himself, cutting away from her all human glory. Therefore my soul has great confidence concerning her, although the world loved her beautiful form and prudence while she lived in the body. But God loved her more. Therefore God was unwilling to give his beloved friend to a hostile lover—that is, to the world.

Now you, dear one, sitting in Christ’s place, fulfill the will of your sister’s soul, because the necessity of obedience demands it. And as she was always solicitous for you, so now be solicitous for her soul, and do good works in accordance with her zeal. Therefore I cast away from my heart [Col. 0163D] the grief which you caused me in this daughter of mine. May God grant you, through the intercessions of the saints, the dew of his grace and blessed recompense in the age to come.

## EPISTLE XI

### ARNOLD, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE, TO HILDEGARD

He requests her book.

Arnold, by the grace of God Archbishop of Cologne, to Hildegard, a burning lamp in the house of the Lord, of the Mount of St. Robert, abiding under the protection of the God of heaven:—

If you are well, and all things around you are directed by the Lord, we rejoice with you. May we also prosper through your merits. Since, as we have long intended, we are entirely unable to come to you, we commend ourselves to you as far as we can at present; [Col. 0164A] we place our hands in yours, join faith to faith, and commend our whole selves to you.

Moreover, do not hesitate, setting aside every obstacle, to send us by the bearer of this letter the book which you yourself, inspired by the divine Spirit, have written; for we neither wish nor are able to be without it, whether it is finished or unfinished. In this we do not wish to tempt God, but desire to behold his wonders.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She speaks mystically and somewhat obscurely; nevertheless she adds clearer words concerning her book.

In a true vision I saw these things; therefore hear. I see a certain man standing in the valley of a great mountain, who possesses choice in the taste of his soul. This same man sends the thought he has [Col. 0164B] into the height of the same mountain. The mountain’s air receives it, so that it takes on a fiery color from there, like oil kindled by fire. But clean birds, separated from unclean ones, come and receive that air into their wings; and from it they become swift in flight.

When the most noble Father sees this, he says: “Where do you come from?” They answer: “A certain stranger standing in the mountain’s valley sent up to us into its height a most sweet wind, and from it we have become swift in flying to you.” And the same master of the household says to them: “Although this man stands far from me, nevertheless, because of the course by which he sent you to me, I wish to love him.”

Let him who wishes to watch well understand this meaning. God often makes lambs from wolves because of the prayers of saints, just as he makes righteous persons from sinners. Therefore he who knows all things says: “Take care lest you love God in dens of robbers, and lest you name him amid vanities—so that you invoke God only in words and not in works. To him who speaks in word I shall respond; but from him who speaks in word I am estranged. For I wipe out obstinacy, and I crush by myself the contradiction of those who despise me. Woe, woe to the evil of the wicked who scorn me. Hear this, O human being, if you wish to live; otherwise my sword will strike you.”

But now, O shepherd of your people, I have sent you, as you requested, these poor writings of true visions, containing nothing of human ingenuity or my own will, but what the unfailing [Col. 0164D] light wished to reveal in its composition and in these very words, as it pleased it—just as what I now write to you is composed not by my own ingenuity or by any human decision, but by heavenly revelation.

## EPISTLE XII

### EBERHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG, TO HILDEGARD

He commends himself to the holy woman’s prayers and requests her letter.

The minister and archbishop, though unworthy, of the Church of Salzburg, by God’s grace, to Hildegard, sister and teacher of St. Robert in Bingen: whatever the prayer of a sinner may avail; and, after victory over this flesh, entrance with the prudent virgins into the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom (Matt. 25).

I, a sinner placed in the valley of tears, worn down by many whirlwinds and storms of the world, suffering fears within and conflicts without (2 Cor. 7), earnestly entreat your love to deign to pour out prayers for me, so that divine mercy may open over me the depths of its compassion and mercifully rescue me from all tribulations. For the emperor is attempting to use force against us because of the schism now present in the Church.

For your charity, virgin worthy of God, ought to remember that, when I was at Mainz in that emperor’s carriage, I particularly commended myself to your holy prayers, so that through your intercession the condition of my life might have advancement in the Lord and a blessed consummation. You also promised my lowliness that, once you had received my letter, you would not be troubled to write back to me according to what the Lord should deign to reveal to you. My lowliness claims from your holiness the debt of that promise. Farewell, virgin of God, and remember me. Whatever you write in reply, place it under seal.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She praises Eberhard at length. She beautifully teaches that outward labors undertaken from charity and obedience do not at all harm one who loves God.

O person who stands in the place of the living Son of God: I now see your condition as though two walls joined by an angular stone. One appears like a white cloud; the other somewhat shadowed. Yet the brightness does not mingle with this shadow, nor does the shadow mingle with that brightness. These walls [Col. 0165C] are your labors, joined to your soul: on one side, your intention and sighs pant in brightness along the narrow way toward God; on the other, the circuit of your labor belongs somewhat shadowily to the people subject to you.

Yet you hold the brightness of your intention as something belonging to your household, while you regard the shadowiness of worldly labors as something foreign to you; you do not allow these to mingle, and therefore you often have weariness in your soul. For you do not regard your intention toward God and your labor for the people as one thing. Yet when you pant toward heavenly things with good intention, and care for the people in God, they can be united in one reward; just as Christ clung to heavenly things and yet bent down to the people, as it is written: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81; John 10): gods, namely, in heavenly things, and sons of the Most High in the care of the people.

Therefore, O Father, moisten your labors with the fountain of wisdom, from which two daughters have drawn, clad in royal garments—namely charity and obedience. For Wisdom has ordered all things with charity, sending forth many streams, as she says: “I alone encompassed the circuit of heaven” (Ecclus. 24). And because God gave humanity a command through obedience: the garment of charity is that which beholds the face of God in the angelic order, but the garment of obedience is the wrapping of the Lord’s humanity.

These maidens knock at your door. Charity says to you: “I desire to remain with you, and I want you [Col. 0166A] to place me in the bed of your couch and hold me in loving friendship. For when you touch and wipe wounds with mercy, I lie in your bed; and when you keep the simple and those who live well in God with benevolence, I am in your loving friendship.”

But obedience says to you: “I remain with you because of the bond of God’s law and commandments. Therefore hold me vigorously and with strong force, not as a steward but as a most illustrious friend. For at the beginning of baptism you received me, and in a certain stage of your advancement you retained me—namely, in the discipline of subjection and in prelacy, where you obeyed God’s commandments. For charity is my material, and I arose from it.”

O Father, Wisdom tells you truly: Be like the master of a household who reluctantly listens to the folly of his children and yet does not abandon his own prudence, just as I too join heavenly and earthly things together for the people’s benefit. Therefore touch and anoint wounds, and touch the simple and those who live well; rejoice in both offices, with God’s help.

Now, O Father, I, a poor little form, see that your will desires the gate of virtues that will come to you, so that in these virtues you will bring the mill of your bodily end to completion. May he who is, and who searches all things, keep your soul and body in his salvation.

## EPISTLE XIII

### HILLIN, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER, TO HILDEGARD

He asks her to deign “to let some drops from the king’s wine-cellar fall upon him in writing.”

Hillin, by the grace of God humble minister [Col. 0166C] and servant of Trier, and likewise its archbishop, though unworthy, to Hildegard, most illustrious sister: to follow the Lamb and the Bridegroom wherever he goes (Rev. 14).

Since the wisdom of God, which chooses the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong (1 Cor. 1), has been pleased to choose in your virginity a delightful dwelling for itself, it has more abundantly poured out upon you the grace of its light in a spirit of counsel and ampler knowledge. By this outpouring of light, I believe, it has willed that the minds of others also might be stirred to better and more salutary pursuits (Heb. 6) and enlightened through you, venerable mother, to be embraced with most sincere charity.

It remains, therefore, most beloved virgin of Christ, to extend more widely into this stormy sea the branches of the true vine (John 15), beneath whose shadow you rest and whose fruit is sweet and delightful to your throat (Song 2); to pour out more freely in every direction, for the gain of souls, the most sweet flavor of the heavenly cup with which you are intoxicated (Song 5); and to give freely what you have freely received (Matt. 10), lest perhaps you be accused of wishing to hide under a bushel the lamp kindled for your neighbors’ benefit (Matt. 5; Luke 8, 11).

Therefore, holy mother, together with the others who flee to the harbor of your consolation, relying upon the overflowing abundance of my hope and longing, I ask—and I beseech your maternal compassion through holy charity—that from that wine-cellar of the king (Song 2), by whose abundant delight you are wonderfully intoxicated even in this life, you would deign to let some drops fall upon me, a sinner, in writing through the bearer [Col. 0167A] of this letter: both for the sake of him who granted you the power to do so, and so that experience of the truth may prove what rumor hesitantly conveys to certain ears concerning the grace poured into you from heaven. May he who began a good work in you bring it to completion in the land of the living (Phil. 1).

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She writes prophetically and exhortatively.

Wisdom speaks, saying: “Now is a squalid time for womanly form. Alas, alas! Adam was the New Testament of all justice and the root of all human seed. Afterwards, in his race a masculine spirit arose, which went out among the troops like a tree spreading itself into three branches. The first troop [Col. 0167B] was such that Adam’s sons chose whatever their capacity possessed. The second was that men rose up in the recklessness of murder. The third was that they did whatever they wished in idols and similar errors.

“Now this tree is dry, and the world has been overthrown amid many dangers. For this time looks back to that time when the first woman made a gesture of assent to the first man in deception (Gen. 3). Yet a man possesses more powers than a woman can accomplish. But woman is a fountain of wisdom and a fountain of complete joy, whose parts a man brings to perfection. Ah, ah! This time is neither cold nor hot, but squalid.

“After this there will come a time which, amid great dangers, will bring forth masculine powers in fear, justice, and men’s fierceness. Then the error of wandering errors will blow like four winds, which pour out their renown amid great dangers.

“But now, O shepherd, hear: the grace of God has not appointed you in vain; therefore preserve his justice. When you do good works, you quickly grow weary; but when you are called to harmony, so that you stand for prayer, you immediately grow dry. Ah, ah! You who stand in Christ’s place, hear again.

“A certain king held a certain city in great honor and entrusted it to three men from among his people, so that they might have charge of guarding it. He entrusted the tower to the first, the city’s plain to the second, and its wall with its battlements to the third. You have been placed in the tower; your people are in the city’s plain; but your clergy stand upon [Col. 0167D] its wall with the battlements. Therefore, if the city wall is attacked and its plain plundered, guard its tower, and be such that the entire city may not be destroyed; then it shall not be scattered. The form of the dove teaches you, and the word of God is not lacking in knowledge within you. Therefore watch (Rev. 3), bind fast with an iron rod (Ps. 2), teach, anoint the wounds of those committed to you, and you shall live for ever.”

## EPISTLE XIV

### EBERHARD, BISHOP OF BAMBERG, TO HILDEGARD

He proposes a very subtle question: “In the Father eternity remains; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the bond of eternity and equality.”

Eberhard, by the grace of God Bishop of the Church of Bamberg, though unworthy, to Hildegard, venerable [Col. 0168A] sister and teacher of St. Robert: the service of devout devotion and the merit of eternal blessedness.

By the favor of heavenly grace, the renown of your holiness sweetly resounds everywhere in the ears of peoples, so that we can truly say: “We are Christ’s good fragrance to God” (2 Cor. 2). And since the Lord has looked down from heaven upon the children of humanity, to see whether anyone understands, or perhaps to seek him who dwells in you (Ps. 13), having smelled the fragrance of your good repute, we come with all our heart to the Lord who is venerated and consulted in you.

What you have bestowed upon many, you will not deny to me alone. For when we were passing through the emperor’s court by way of you, because you are filled with the Holy Spirit, we entrusted this matter to be set before your charity: “In the Father eternity remains; in [Col. 0168B] the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the bond of eternity and equality.” We now desire to see this expounded according to what God has revealed to you. May the Lord be with you, and may we be aided by your prayers.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

After a brief exhortation urging Eberhard carefully to feed his flock, she proceeds to the question.

He who is (Exod. 3), and from whom nothing is hidden, says: “O shepherd, do not grow dry in the sweet flowing of balsam’s fragrance—that is, *viriditas*, greening vigor—which must be offered to foolish minds that do not possess the breasts of maternal mercy from which to suck. Those who do not have these fail. Therefore offer your people the king’s lamp, lest they be scattered through harshness; and rise, living in light.”

Now, O Father, I, a poor little form, looked toward the true light; and according to what I there saw and heard in true vision, I send you the exposition you asked for—not in my words, but in those of the true light, which never suffers any failure—in this manner:

“In the Father eternity remains”: that is, nothing can be cut away from or added to the Father’s eternity, because eternity remains in the likeness of a wheel which neither begins nor has an end. Thus eternity is in the Father before every creature, because eternity always was and always is. And what is eternity? God. Yet eternity is not eternity except in perfect life. Therefore God is now in eternity. But life does not proceed from mortality; life is in life.

For a tree does not flower except from greenness; nor is a stone without moisture; nor is any creature without its own power. Thus living eternity itself is not without flourishing. The Father’s Word brought forth every creature into its appointed office, and thus the Father is not idle in his most powerful force. Hence God is called Father, because all things are born from him. Thus eternity remains in the Father also because he was Father before the beginning, and eternal before the commencement of the shining works, all of which appeared in the foreknowledge of eternity.

But what remains in the Father is not like a cause in a human being, which is sometimes doubtful, sometimes past, sometimes future, sometimes new, sometimes old; rather, what is in the Father is always stable. The Father is brightness, and that brightness has radiance, and that radiance has fire; and they are one. Whoever does not hold this in faith does not see God, because such a person wishes to divide from him what he is; for God is not divisible.

Even the works God created do not retain the full propriety of their names when a human being divides them. Brightness is fatherhood, from which all things are born and which surrounds all things, because they are from its power. For that same power made the human being and breathed into him the breath of life (Gen. 2). And a human being has in this same power an effective effect within himself. How? Flesh from flesh, and good from what is good, is issued in good repute and is increased in another person by good example. These things are in a human being both bodily and spiritually, because one thing proceeds from another.

[Col. 0169B] A human being greatly loves useful works because they come into action from his knowledge. So too God wills that his power show itself through all its kinds, because they are his work. And radiance gives eyes; and that radiance is the Son, who gave eyes when he said: “Let there be” (Gen. 1). Then all things appeared bodily in the living eye. Fire, which is God, penetrates these two names; for it would be impossible for brightness to lack radiance. And if that fire were absent, brightness would not shine nor radiance gleam. For flame and light lie hidden in fire; otherwise it would not be fire.

“In the Son, equality.” How? All creatures were in the Father before time, as he ordered them in himself; afterward the Son completed them in work. How? Just as a human being possesses in himself the knowledge of a great work, which he afterward brings forth in his speech, so that it proceeds into good report. The Father orders, but the Son works. For the Father ordered all things in himself, and the Son completed them in work.

And there is light from light before time in eternity, which was in the beginning; and this is the Son, who shines from the Father and through whom all creatures were made. Moreover, the Son put on a garment from the human being whom he had formed from mud—a garment that had not previously appeared bodily. Thus God saw all his works before himself as light; and when he said, “Let there be,” each thing put on a garment according to its kind. Then God bent himself down to his work, and thus in this respect equality also remains in the Son of God in relation [Col. 0169D] to humanity, because he put on humanity, just as God’s works put on their bodies.

For God foreknew all the works he accomplished. Hence he bent himself down to humanity in humility toward humanity; for divinity is so perfect that it would spare nothing in humanity which fights against the good, unless it had put on humanity, because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

For all visible, tangible, and tasteable things were made through him; and he foresaw all these for some human need: some for the embrace of charity, some for fear, some for discipline, some for caution in every matter. “And without him nothing was made”: this nothing is pride. For it is an opinion that looks to itself and trusts in no one. It wills what God does not will, always reckons upon what it itself establishes, and is dark because it despised the light of truth and began what it could not complete. Therefore it is nothing, because it was neither made nor created by God.

It began in the first angel, when he looked upon his own splendor and conceived an opinion, not seeing from whom he had that splendor. Instead he said within himself: “I wish to be Lord and want no other.” Thus his glory vanished from him; he lost it and became prince of Gehenna (Isa. 14). Then God gave that glory to another of his sons, made with such mighty power that all creatures attend him, and set in such strong power that he would not lose that glory in anything.

In the curse by which the devil refused God, folly in the human being desired to be like God in honor—namely, to be as God is. Yet humanity did not lose the love by which it knew God to be God. Therefore the devil’s substance is altogether dark, because he did not will to be God’s brightness. Adam wished to be God’s brightness but desired to be in his fellowship. Therefore he is perfect in his substance, having something bright, though nevertheless full of many miseries.

“In the Holy Spirit, the bond of eternity and equality.” The Holy Spirit is fiery and an inextinguishable fire, which sometimes appears through burning and sometimes is extinguished. For the Holy Spirit floods and joins eternity and equality, so that they are one, as a man binds together a bundle; for if the bundle were not bound together, it would not be a bundle but would be scattered. And it is like a smith joining two forces of bronze together with fire. Hence it is like a flashing sword, brandished on every side.

The Holy Spirit shows eternity and kindles equality, so that they are one. The Holy Spirit is fire and life in this eternity and equality, because God lives. The sun is white, its light burns brightly, and fire burns in it; it illuminates the whole world and appears as one whole. But every thing in which there is no power is dead, just as wood cut off from a tree is dry because it has no greenness. The Holy Spirit is the foundation and the giving of life.

For eternity would not be eternity without the Holy Spirit, nor would equality be equality without the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is in both, and the one God is one in the Godhead. Rationality also has three powers: sound, word, and breath. In the Father is the Son, as the word is in the sound; the Holy Spirit is in both, as breath is in sound and word. And these three persons, as stated above, are one God.

Eternity is in the Father because no one precedes him and eternity did not begin, as God’s works have a beginning. But equality is in the Son, because the Son never departed from the Father, nor did the Father lack the Son. But in the Holy Spirit is union, because the Son always remained in the Father and the Father with the Son; for the Holy Spirit is fiery life in them, and they are one.

[Col. 0171A] And it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 1). That is, all creatures, seen and unseen, including those unknown to humanity, do not lack spiritual life. For flowers come from greenness, and the fruit of trees from flowers. Clouds too have their course. The moon and star likewise burn with fire. Trees bring forth flowers through greenness; water has fineness and wind, cleansing and sending forth streams. Earth too has moisture with sweat. For all creatures have what is seen and what is unseen. What is seen is weak; what is unseen is strong and vital. The human intellect seeks this, so that it may know what it does not see. These are the powers of the works of the Holy Spirit.

“And that which contains all things.” What is this? “The human being contains all things” (ibid.). How? By ruling, using, and commanding. God gave this to humanity according to himself. Humanity possesses knowledge of voice. This is rationality, which sounds with the voice. Voice is body, rationality soul, the heat of air fire; and they are one. Therefore, when rationality is heard speaking and creating through the voice, all its works are accomplished, and it has the power to create; for as it commands, so it will be.

Therefore none of God’s works are empty. If someone possessed a vessel full of money, he would take great joy from it; but if there were nothing in the vessel, he would value it very little. Emptiness is in wicked works, and they flee the fire of the Holy Spirit. Then delight in sin is present to them, through the devil’s suggestion.

But when a person counts his wicked deeds as nothing, recognizes them as such, and yet turns back from them, he resembles the prodigal son who, after his hunger, remembered his father’s bread and said: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15): against heaven, because in rationality I am heavenly; and before you, because I know you to be God. Then he rejects the devil and chooses his Lord anew.

Thereupon all the devil’s vices are confounded and all heavenly harmonies marvel, because what they previously reckoned as mud in uselessness, they afterward see as a pillar of cloud in principal usefulness. For those whom they saw as vile they afterward choose as more beautiful, because they count all the devil’s vices as nothing—for there is no usefulness in those wicked works—and produce usefulness in good works. These are the works of the Holy Spirit.

Now, O shepherd and father of peoples, may God grant you to attain the light, where you may receive knowledge of true blessedness.

## EPISTLE XV

### THE BISHOP OF SPEYER TO HILDEGARD

Gunter, by the grace of God minister and bishop of the Church of Speyer, to Hildegard, teacher of the Mount of St. Robert in Bingen: eternal salvation in Christ.

We give thanks to divine mercy because you are a good fragrance to those far away as well as nearby, and a consolation from the Holy Spirit to all who seek you. Therefore let your love know with certainty that we gladly regard the honor and benefit of your church; and by every means through which we can bring your will concerning the advancement of that church to effect, we shall gladly do so.

But we earnestly ask your holiness to intercede with God for us out of love for us, make him favorable to us by your prayers, and know, with all doubt removed, that if God grants us life, you shall not lack honorable recompense. For it is just that you should bestow upon us the help of your prayers, just as we concern ourselves with your need. We also desire your reply.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She strongly exhorts Gunter to amend his life.

The light of highest inspiration says to you, O man: [Col. 0172B] “Do not cut off from yourself, through the evil habit of your deeds, the admonition of the Holy Spirit that rises within you; for God seeks in you what he once sought when he attended to bringing back the lost sheep, when he wiped away human crimes. And the ancient deceiver was confounded when the mightiest warrior overcame him.

“God looks upon you through windows, because he is pious and merciful. Let no one mock this through any conceit of his own will. Hear: do not cut off from yourself this cause of admonition, lest God strike you with his scourges. For in his zeal he wishes to cast down this hostile cause: that his companions mock him in his manifestation through their associates. Therefore he brandishes the bow of his admonition, showing that none can resist him.

“Therefore you, O man, enveloped in much blackness, rise swiftly toward ruin and build in heavenly things, so that the black and filthy may blush at your exultation when you rise from your blackness; for your soul scarcely lives because of your deeds. Yet you behold your own condition, as if through a figure, in relation to another life; this intention shines within you like the dawn of light. Your mind sifts and shakes itself amid great torments, where a gross nature afflicts you in twisted desires. Escape this moisture.

“Hear, O man: A certain man possessed land that showed great power when the plough overturned it, so that it brought forth in abundant growth every fruit sown in it. Then that man was pleased to make in that land a garden of spices, in which spices would grow with sweetest fragrance for the healing of wounds and scars. And that land became better than it had been before.

“Now you, O man, choose which of these two conditions is more useful to you. For the foundation of the heavenly Jerusalem was first laid from stones wounded by great falls and defiled with the scars of vices, but which afterward suppress their crimes in penitence. The Maker of the world first laid this foundation from rough and unpolished stones, and these stones support the entire city of God. Therefore flee the wantonness of this world in the shipwreck of impurity; be like sardius and like topaz, and swift like a stag to draw from the most pure spring with your tongue, and you shall live for ever.”

## EPISTLE XVI

### THE BISHOP OF WORMS TO HILDEGARD

He adorns the holy woman with praises and asks for an answer.

Conrad, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Worms—though unworthy—to Hildegard, beloved sister of the Mount of St. Robert: with, alas, a small offering of prayers, sweet devotion in every service.

We give thanks to God, who has placed you, a most bright lamp, upon a golden lampstand and has caused the brightness of his light to shine far and wide through you in his house. Therefore, most beloved sister and daughter, we earnestly pray that, through the rays by which we confidently believe the Sun of Justice illuminates you, the clouds of our mind—which oppress us through the unfitting storm of tribulations and flood of diverse thoughts—may be driven away.

[Col. 0173B] We should indeed need to communicate very many things to your holiness, if the length of words did not prevent us from explaining them to you. Yet through the present bearer we speak with you in person by living voice, and with our whole heart we beg for the reply of your admonition.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She praises and exhorts him.

You are a person set upon the chair of Christ, and you have an iron rod in your hand for ruling your sheep. Look to the Sun of righteousness, and to the many stars, which are the kinds of virtues, so that you may not fail in the food of life; for he is a good shepherd who always flourishes in good works and feeds his sheep in upright greenness. May he grant this to you who sounded forth on the first day (Gen. 1), and by whose word every creature came forth, [Col. 0173C] and who on the last day will sound the trumpet, so that he will raise up all the children of humankind (1 Cor. 15).

For certain people who live righteously are the dwelling-place of God, because God dwells in them. For a human being is God’s building, in which he has his abode (John 14), since he sent into that person a fiery soul, which, together with rationality, flies in expansion, just as a wall encompasses the breadth of a house. But the person who has been made righteous through God’s commandments in his works, in which he has not neglected God’s law, builds the heavenly Jerusalem. Yet the one who acts according to the flesh and not according to the spirit will fall away from the holy building. But the one who cuts away from himself the possession of his own will adorns the heavenly building with pearls, precious stones, [Col. 0173D] and the finest gold. Therefore make yourself such that you become a precious stone and are an ornament in the highest Jerusalem.

## LETTER XVII

### THE BISHOP OF CONSTANCE TO HILDEGARD

He requests the holy woman’s prayers and letters.

The bishop of the Church of Constance, by the grace of God, though useless and unworthy, to HILDEGARD, bride of Christ, of the monastery of St Robert at Pingis: an increase of deepest charity and the most blessed course in both lives.

The fame of your wisdom, spread far and wide and reported to me by several truthful persons, has moved me to desire to seek from distant regions your consolation and support, and to commend myself to your prayers. For it is hard that one who does not know how to govern [Col. 0174A] the direction of his own life should become a judge of another’s life. Therefore I earnestly beseech your love, with sincere devotion, that by your prayers you may assist me before the Lord and strengthen me by your reply; for both my own will and earthly care draw me away from God’s service in almost every way.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She rebukes his empty glory.

The Most Just Light says: O man, rebuke your mind, which pierces the counsel of the ancient prelates, whom the windy mind of vanities did not touch. What is your estimation of yourself, you who are not ashamed to walk in darkness through the relish of your own work? For the revelation of him from whom nothing is hidden shows, through the living eye, that the bow of God’s zeal threatens human rashness. [Col. 0174B] Why do you not see where the mammon of iniquity is (Luke 16), by which you excuse yourself?

Many laborers come in their causes and seek the narrow and constricted way; but you move your lips through the boastful swelling of your heart’s dispositions and bring them back to indignation. Therefore direct yourself from darkness into straight paths, and enlighten your heart’s understanding, lest the Father of all say to you: “Why do you climb in folly a column that you did not make?” For the day grows dark for one who does not walk in the paths of the straight journey. Guard against this; rise quickly, therefore, and walk straight paths before the sun sets for you and before your days fail.

## LETTER XVIII

### THE BISHOP OF VERDUN TO HILDEGARD

He exhorts the holy woman to humility and requests her prayers and letters.

[Col. 0174C]

ADELBERT, by the grace of God minister and bishop of the Church of Verdun, though unworthy, to HILDEGARD, his most illustrious mother, of Mount St Robert: delight in the present and eternal visions of God.

“Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place” (Ezek. 3), who from your tender years has made you his handmaid. But I, as though a blind person wished to show the way to one who sees, suggest to your charity that you acknowledge this grace with humility, considering the ancient prophecy of Balaam (Num. 23). Although he directed his latter end in the contrary direction, it is nevertheless memorable in his vision, when he said: “He falls, and thus his eyes are opened” (Num. 24), clearly signifying humility [Col. 0174D] in vision. The Teacher of the Gentiles also said: “Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me” (2 Cor. 12), etc.

Let these things, then, be said to you more from the confidence of my affection than from presumption in teaching. Moreover, know that I cannot at present come to you, although I am near you. Yet in my adversities I seek you as a faithful patroness in your prayers, and ask to be helped by the intercessions of the sisters of your community, handmaids of God. It has been a long time since I was granted a writing from you; I pray that I may at least now deserve one.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She exhorts him to pastoral care.

The Living Light, which shows miracles, says: You who are a father in your person and a shepherd in the care [Col. 0175A] of souls, stretch out your arm, lest the enemy man sow tares over your field (Matt. 13). Therefore attend to that garden which the divine gift planted; and take care that its spices are not dry. Cut away corruption from them and cast it out, that corruption which chokes their usefulness. Thus make them green.

For the sun hides its rays, and the world too withdraws its joy. And I say: Do not darken your garden in the weariness of silence, but in true light, with discernment, correct those things that are to be corrected. Enlighten also your temple through benevolence, and kindle fire in your censer, placing myrrh upon it, so that its smoke may rise to the palace of the living God; and you shall live forever.

## LETTER XIX

### THE BISHOP OF LIÈGE TO HILDEGARD

He says that he is “placed amid the greatest turmoil of mind and body,” because, as he confesses, he had offended God by innumerable evils. He requests the prayers and replies of holy Hildegard.

[Col. 0175B]

RUDOLPH, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Liège, to HILDEGARD, handmaid of Christ, of St Robert at Pingis: unceasing service to the King of kings, and attainment of the prize of eternal blessedness.

Placed amid the greatest turmoil of mind and body, I have resolved to write to you, because I stand greatly in need of God’s mercy; and I do not deny that I have offended and provoked him by innumerable evils. Therefore, dearest sister, since I truly know that God is with you, I entreat and beg your holiness through his mercy that [Col. 0175C] you may altogether extend a hand to me as I am tossed about and flee to you for refuge.

Let it be your care to watch in devoted prayers for the removal of my negligence; and whatever has been shown you from the unfailing and living Light to awaken my drowsiness, write back to me. May the most merciful God grant that through your writings I may receive from you the surest consolation, and that through the protection of your intercession I may obtain even the final dwelling-place of eternal rest.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She exhorts him to a good life and to care of souls.

O, the Living Light says: The ways of the Scriptures lead straight to a high mountain, where flowers and most precious spices grow, where a most sweet wind blows and makes them give forth a strong fragrance, and where roses and lilies show splendid faces. Long ago that same mountain was not visible because of the shadows of blind, living air, since the Son of the Most High had not yet illuminated the world. Then the Sun came from the dawn, illuminating this world, and all peoples saw its spices. The day was greatly adorned, and a sweet report arose.

O shepherds, now it is fitting to weep and mourn that, in our time, the mountain is covered by these blackest clouds, so that no good fragrance comes from it. But you, be a good shepherd, noble in conduct. And as the eagle looks upon the sun, so remember and consider where you may call the sluggish and the wanderers back to their homeland, and bring some light to this world, so that your soul [Col. 0176A] may live and you may hear that most loving voice from the supreme Judge: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matt. 25); and so that your soul may flash in this portion, as a soldier shines in battle when his companions rejoice with him because he has been victorious.

Therefore, O leader of the people, fight in a good victory; thus correct those who stray, wash beautiful pearls free from corruption, and prepare them for the supreme King. Let your mind, in good zeal, pant to recall these pearls to this mountain, as God’s gift established them. May God protect you and free your soul from eternal punishment.

## LETTER XX

### THE BISHOP OF UTRECHT TO HILDEGARD

He declares his affection for the holy woman.

GODEFRID, by divine favoring grace bishop of the people of Utrecht, to his only, special, singular HILDEGARD, teacher of the sisters of St Robert: greeting from him who commands salvation in Jacob (Ps. 43).

Dearest sister, from the time when I first began to love you in Christ’s charity, your memory—sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 18)—has never been able to depart from my mind. For the power of God compels me to love you: the power that dwells in you, works through you, and makes you more familiar than others to that Bridegroom who eternally saves all who hope in him (Ps. 16). And because charity has been poured out in your heart (Rom. 5), I ask you, by the charity in which you abound toward all, to strive with every diligence and every effort to pray to God for me, so that in this age I may deserve to be relieved of the burdens of my sins.

May the Lord [Col. 0176C] bring you there where blessed eternity is, eternal happiness, joyful tranquillity, and gladness without end. As one thirsting for a fountain, so I long for your writings.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She exhorts him to perseverance in good.

O you, a person taken and called by God, so that you may act according to him by imitating him: for God builds, governs, and anoints all things. Almighty God created the world through his Word; he also governs it and sanctifies all things in water, washing away human sins. For God created all creatures, governed them, and imbued humanity among them, just as an artisan makes his vessels beautiful through fire.

But afterward the most lofty day bent down into dark [Col. 0176D] night through disobedience in Adam’s fall; and for this reason people lived in sins and forgetfulness, as though God did not exist. Then God flooded the whole earth with the waters of the deluge because of people’s criminal sins (Gen. 7), and thus the saints, the Law, and the prophets arose. Finally the Son of God came, for it was not fitting that he should be present in an empty time in which he would find no justice, just as humanity was not created before every creature showed him forth. Yet the Son of God came to redeem the whole world through obedience, through the chrism of baptism, and through repentance.

Now you, prudent shepherd, do not belong to the childish time that does not know the Lord; rather, be in the time of the righteous and holy, and in the manifestation of the prophets, laying hold of justice in your works. Just as God foresaw all things before he worked them, so govern your people according to him. You too, in Christ’s place, offer help to the people, lest you be like a trumpet that sounds but does not act. Rather, be the good fragrance of virtues, so that you may live forever.

And say: “I will exalt you, O God, my King, and bless your name for ever and ever” (Ps. 144). For when you understand that you are seated in the episcopal chair, praise God in all your ways; exalt him in good works; repeatedly chew over his commandments without weariness; kiss him through faith and embrace him in good works. In good conduct show God himself, your God; in his judgments magnify him as a just king, so that you govern your people rightly and anoint with mercy, [Col. 0177B] and do not drag behind you a harmful crime—namely, that you receive a gift in return for justice. Thus invoke his name, having fear toward him in all these matters, because he is king. Do this on every day of your life, as long as you live in this age, so that afterward you may live forever in the boundless age.

## LETTER XXI

### THE BISHOP OF PRAGUE TO HILDEGARD

He asks her to assist him by her prayers and offer good counsel.

H., by the grace of God useless minister and bishop of the people of Prague, though unworthy, to HILDEGARD, bride of Christ and teacher of St Robert at Pingis: whatever small gift of his prayers he can offer, with all devotion.

[Col. 0177C]

We glorify our Lord God by magnifying him. Illuminated by his Spirit, you assist the tribulations of many by consoling and relieving them, and, with that same Spirit cooperating, multiply the fruit of good work in the minds of many, as we have also heard reported concerning you throughout many regions of the earth. Therefore let your holiness know that we have a great desire to see you and enjoy conversation with you in Christ; but the great difficulty of distance prevents this.

Since we have learned that your charity has assisted the needs of many, encouraged by this confidence, we implore your love that you may assist us, shaken by worldly tribulations, with your prayers and offer good counsel. [Col. 0177D] For since we heard your name and the grace bestowed on you by God, we have always held your memory in our hearts, and we desire that the same grace which is from the true Light may always remain with you.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She exhorts him to greater constancy in virtue, both in prosperity and adversity.

The Voice of Life and Salvation says: What is this—that a person eats and does not wish to know what the grape is which, after the destruction of the people, sweated from the earth in another manner, when God wiped and sifted the earth into another condition than when the first human mocked it? This means that a person is fickle through the changes of his dispositions and through times of light and darkness.

[Col. 0178A] For sometimes a person raises himself somewhat into prosperity, and sometimes falls into dangers. In neither of these states does he look upon the embrace of the king’s daughter, namely justice and truth; rather, he cuts the crown from her head when a shepherd flees and does not defend Christ’s Church, because he does not hold his weapons firmly, but plays in his conduct like a wanton child who has no concern.

The person who does this desires to eat and live according to his own will, just as human nature demands food; and he does not see with sharp eyes where discernment is—the discernment that has sweated forth from wisdom, which is understood in this grape. For when Adam, at the world’s beginning, mocked obedience, the ages of ages perished until the outpouring of the waters, when God cleansed the earth of horrible iniquity and gave it another power.

There Noah brought forth in vineyards the most noble shoot of obedience (Gen. 9), which Adam, like a wanton child through the simplicity of his dispositions, had fled. But in Noah the earth brought forth the strength of the grape, and after him wisdom too rose up in salvation. Now, O you person, who go about in your dispositions through the streets of your changes and do not look ardently, considering your own remedy and that of another: rise, looking to the sun in right moderation, and do not flee the light, casting it away through the harshness of iniquity, so that you may not be ashamed when the supreme King examines the works in your sack, and you shall live forever.

## LETTER XXII

### THE BISHOP OF JERUSALEM TO HILDEGARD

He commends himself to her and her sisters’ prayers. He launches into praise of the holy woman.

[Col. 0178C]

I., by God’s grace and appointment servant and bishop of the people of Jerusalem, to HILDEGARD, beloved daughter and teacher of Mount St Robert at Pingis, that is, in the diocese of Mainz: the humblest prayer and greeting in Christ.

From many persons coming into our regions across long stretches of land and bending their knees at the Lord’s tomb, we have repeatedly learned that divine power works in you and through you; for this we humbly offer him unceasing thanks insofar as we are able. We have long had a message for you, dearest daughter, but because a messenger was lacking until now, [Col. 0178D] our desire came wholly to nothing. But now, since after a long course of time an opportunity has presented itself, we have judged it fitting to address by this letter both you and all your sisters, who, I hear, are subject to you in Christ.

If, amid the excessive hardships by which we are continually oppressed—attacked on one side by the sword of pagans, on the other by the snares of evil spirits—we had any sweet words at hand, we would think it worthy to exalt you as Christ’s bride, always intent upon Christ’s mysteries. But she whom divine grace has allowed to be joined to angelic praises has no need to be exalted by human praises. We call those women happy who deserve day by day to attend and be satisfied by your sweetest discourses.

For we may quite properly call happy [Col. 0179A] those who, relying upon the mirror of divine whitening, strive daily to receive from the Lord the prize of their course through their merits. Happy, he says, and exceedingly happy are those for whom, in return for heavenly rewards, all earthly things have become worthless, and by whom everything in this life that seems sweet, delightful, and excellent to other mortals is despised, trampled underfoot, and counted of no value. Behold the true daughters of Jerusalem, in whom no blemish is found (Song 4), in whom the world has nothing to love, who also follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14).

Now, O daughter, referring ourselves to the consolation shown to you from heaven, we humbly ask and commend ourselves to your prayers and to those of all your sisters, that you may mercifully intercede for us before him, while we are tossed in the storms of worldly cares, and you desire to enter his bridal chamber after the end of this life. May the Lord grant, O beloved one, that you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life (Ps. 127).

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She consoles the patriarch.

The Living Light says this in its miracles: The first root appeared in the day and flowered in all its branches, and established two ways. One way was full of buildings in which eagles and other birds dwelt. The other was full of great choice, in which giants ran together and fought against these eagles and other birds, but could not prevail over them. Then the sun came forth and had golden shields upon its farthest arm, and fought against those giants.

For the fall of the first angel had fallen away from life, and afterward Adam’s fall lacked the light of paradise; and Adam himself walked, at the devil’s suggestion, with all his children (Gen. 3). But the sun shone forth in topaz and sapphire—that is, in mercy and charity, which brought forth the incarnate Word of God. The sun shone equally, just as it had come forth in the beginning, and remained so that absolutely no shadow of change fell upon it, as had happened in the first angel, in Adam, and in the devil’s suggestion. Therefore it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

[Col. 0179D] For mercy is to be understood in the topaz and charity in the sapphire—virtues which this priest put on as a priestly testimony for humankind. Now you, O Father, who stand in the place of this priest: let your soul flow like the water that flowed from the rock at Moses’ rod, so that your words may give unbelieving hearts the drink of salvation, and so that the day shining in your soul may grow in a multitude of virtues.

You see yourself anxious in your soul upon the way that tends toward God. But when your mind enters a whirlwind through the changing fortunes of your labors and others’ labors, the dove will pour herself over you and make you a simple tower before God’s sight. And the battle that you suffer inwardly and outwardly, namely in both persons, God will lighten around you in your times in such a way [Col. 0180A] that you can endure it. Therefore put your trust in him, and do not despair of his mercy. Doing this in God’s grace, you shall live unto life.

## LETTER XXIII

### THE BISHOP OF BEVEZ TO HILDEGARD

He requests her prayers and letters.

HENRY, by God’s grace called bishop of Bevez in name only, to HILDEGARD, beloved teacher of the sisters at Mount St Robert of Pingis: whatever a sinner’s prayer is worth in a contrite spirit and humility.

Blessed be God, who has blessed you in every spiritual blessing (Eph. 1), so that, through the fragrance of the ointment with which God has anointed you with the anointing of his mercy, the devotion of many is drawn through you even in distant parts of the world. For God’s manifest favor toward you is a great consolation to me, a sinner weighed down by the whirlwinds of this age, although I am very far from you in body, but not in mind.

For we confidently trust, without doubt, that through your merits and prayers Christ’s mercy lies open to all who faithfully seek the help of your prayers. Therefore, having no confidence of attaining salvation through our actions because of distrust in our own conscience, we beseech you through the charity of the Holy Spirit, though in distant regions, to entreat the Lord by your prayers for forgiveness of our sins. Moreover, may your love not be reluctant to write to us whatever consolation or admonition, however small, [Col. 0180C] is necessary for our salvation. May he who can do all things, and from whom no thought is hidden, deign, according to his good pleasure, to fulfill by prayer the desire of our heart.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She employs a beautiful parable to exhort him to true wisdom and charity.

The Living Light showed me these things and said: Say to that man: I saw something like a beautiful form of virtue, which was pure knowledge. Its face was very bright, its eyes like hyacinth, and its garments like a silken cloak. It also had upon [Col. 0180D] its shoulders an episcopal pallium like a sardius. And it called the King’s most beautiful friend, namely charity, saying: “Come with me.” And when both had come, they knocked at the door of your heart, saying: “We wish to dwell with you.”

Therefore take care not to resist us; rather, be strong in resisting vices, worldly affairs, and the changes of those winds which rise in whirlwinds like evil smoke and fly like waters in a storm. These are the disturbances of human minds in anger and similar things. Do not keep silence in weariness, but let your voice be like a trumpet resounding in the Church’s ceremonies; and let your eyes be pure in knowledge, so that you are not too sluggish to cleanse yourself of the unworthy dust of your burden. For you are full of the drops of night (Song 5).

[Col. 0181A] And the persuasion of pride has thus spoken to you: “Do not wash yourself.” But we do not wish this. Rather, we wish you to wipe away every dark thing from yourself and not to be afraid of the many terrors of your enemies, who speak neither rightly nor well concerning you. O soldier, give us a dwelling in your heart, and we will bring you with us to the King’s palace.

## LETTER XXIV

### THE BISHOP OF TRIER TO HILDEGARD

He graciously declares his affection for holy Hildegard and testifies that he was promoted to the episcopate against his will. Accordingly, he consults the holy woman, writing: “But because we do not know by whose calling we have been promoted, this most greatly causes us anxiety.”

[Col. 0181B]

ARNOLD, by God’s grace humble elect of the Church of Trier, to his beloved kinswoman in Christ, HILDEGARD of St Robert: greeting and love from him who is salvation and love.

Friendship is of heavenly kinship, because old age does not harm it but benefits it; and it is true, for it does not know how to stand still but grows and advances daily in some respect. Since from early youth we have embraced one another in the arms of true love, we wonder why you love a flatterer more than a true friend, when the prophet says: “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. 103). We count our brother, the provost of St Andrew, as this flatterer of yours; but we wish ourselves to be understood as the true friend.

Since we know that our advancement is material for your sword, we have thought it fitting to inform your love that, by God’s grace, we have returned safely. But because nothing is blessed to anyone which he himself regards as punishment, we say before God and before you that the dignity to which we have been called, against our will—God being witness—has never, as usually happens, loved us or caressed us. This is because our ignorance and frailty lament their own insufficiency and bewail their own unworthiness.

But because we do not know by whose calling [Col. 0181C] we have been promoted to such a ministry, this most greatly causes us anxiety. If we knew it to be from God, we would believe that he who had begun a good work in us would also bring it to completion (Phil. 1), although we propose to be advanced to the priesthood more by necessity than by virtue.

And we know that God, in his holy place (Ps. 67), has wrought salvation among you (Ps. 73), mercifully freeing a possessed woman, and has visited his people (Luke 7). Therefore we most earnestly ask that you write back to us the manner of the possessed woman’s liberation; that, by looking more often into the true Light, you may more often impart to us some saving grace through your letters; and that you may raise your hands, in Moses’ example, by interceding for us to the rock of refuge (Exod. 17), while we fight against Amalek in the valley of worldly misery.

When these words were being written in the presence of our faithful and beloved abbot of St Eucharius, he sweetened our words with his assistance. Therefore we wish you to send your reply to us through him.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

After salutary instruction, she seriously warns him to beware of pride, greed for riches, injustice, and vanity, and to embrace virtues befitting his station.

[Col. 0182A]

You are a tree established by God, as Paul says: “All authority is from God” (Rom. 13), because every authority is named according to the supreme Master through the invocation of his name; hence in it, the tree has the greenness of the honor of its name. Let that which is without God, and that which the left hand works, not be present in you, lest in the falling sickness of pride you fall with the first angel (Isa. 14), namely Satan, who wished secretly to snatch honor against God. Many seize this according to their own will, taking no care in whatever way it may be conferred upon them.

This is nothing before God, because without him nothing was made (John 1), and thus God kills whatever does not touch him. Therefore be watchful, so that through God’s commandments, multiplied like the leaves of a tree, you may bear witness to the people as much as you can through his grace. For the many tribulations of your burden, such as poverty, constrain you, because riches and great sums of money do not love heavenly things. Therefore poverty takes self-will away from a man of God, so that he may sigh for the heavenly homeland.

Therefore it is fitting that the poor person love the poor, and the rich acknowledge the rich, because wisdom gives the poor a ring and denies the rich an earring. This is present to you because of [Col. 0182C] your priestly office. “I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have loved your truth and your salvation” (Ps. 11). What is being said? God’s justice does not hide itself, but extends its paths and is not ashamed to run upon them. Nor does it conceal wounds by preferring evil to good, as though it said that in justice there are life and hell and that one must run in both directions.

In this deception justice does not waste itself away, nor does it kiss injustice with many words; rather, it tramples it utterly down. Truth also does not praise works performed without God, but prepares itself like a valiant soldier for battle, to oppose them. Let God’s justice be your shield, and clothe yourself with his truth as with a breastplate, so that you may appear before God well armed and not a fugitive in the company of vanity; and learn to suck the breasts of justice.

Learn also to heal the wounds of sins through repentance in mercy, as the supreme physician left you a saving example for saving the people. You, indeed, who are placed in the greenness of the blessed man through the instruction of his name, who does not attend to the impious devil—so called impious because he loved no good—see that you do not glory in treasures of money (Ecclus. 31), which is malicious in the end, because after the thirtieth year it fails, as though after one year.

But exult on Mount Zion, where the aid of the Most High is eternal in eternity, and every spirit praises the Lord (Ps. 150). Be yourself an ivory mountain, from which windowed darts fly against your adversaries in the upright judgment of God’s justice. [Col. 0183A] Run also into the height of God’s law and justice like a mountain-goat, lest you fall unarmed through instability and your children rise from the side of the Church and ask you for the food of justice. Therefore learn good teaching, so that through you they may be fed.

But I, as you commanded, looked into the true Light and could scarcely see the beginning of good works. Do you indeed perform good works more diligently, so that afterward, by God’s grace, I may write more. Be a faithful friend to your soul, so that you may live in eternity.

As for the possessed woman concerning whom you inquire: we saw many marvels which we cannot now set forth in writing. But we learned that the devilish blast diminished day by day until its departure; the same woman was freed from the devil’s harassing, and then was afflicted also by an infirmity which she had not previously known in herself. But now she has recovered the full health of both body and soul.

## LETTER XXV

### THE BISHOP OF COLOGNE TO HILDEGARD

He praises the holy woman and asks her to inquire “from God’s hidden counsel,” and to send him “admonitory words, as God shall grant.”

PHILIP, by God’s grace archbishop of the people of Cologne, to HILDEGARD, beloved sister, wonderfully infused with divine inspiration: may you gloriously see in heaven him to whose embrace you continually long to cling.

Although diversity of places deprives those whom Christ’s charity has united of the mutual sight and desirable grace of conversation, the nearness of their souls will nevertheless always hold them together. Thus it is most desirable to me that in this year, when the opportunity of travel and the long-desired grace of seeing you occurs. But the sickness and frailty of your body have troubled and struck my heart, and the hearts of many in our land who embrace you in Christ, always longing for the preservation of your life and the eternity of true salvation.

Therefore we have been pleased, and have judged it fitting, to inquire and be made certain about your condition, and especially to tell and make known to you that we are daily so disturbed by the whirlwinds and storms of worldly matters that we sometimes even attempt to lift the eyes of our mind toward heavenly things. But since the zeal of many knows that you have been filled with the gift of divine charism, in which the assembly of the faithful Church rejoices, [Col. 0183D] and we too rejoice according to the measure of our discernment, recognizing in you one who lives beneath the covering of flesh and yet, according to the Apostle’s word, has her conversation in heaven (Phil. 3):

Endowed with such a gift, therefore, like a finder of the good pearl (Matt. 13), inquire from God’s hidden counsel what we ask, and send us admonitory words as God grants you; for, according to the Truthful One, there is no usefulness in wisdom and a hidden treasure (Ecclus. 20). Farewell.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She relates what she heard and saw in a vision, and adds a distinguished exhortation.

In the mystical breathing of true vision, I saw and heard these words: Fiery Love, which is God (1 John 4), says to you:

A star that shines beneath the sun may have a name in accordance with its part: it is called bright, because it is illuminated by the sun more than the other stars. But how would it be fitting for that same star to hide its light so that it shone less than smaller stars? For if it did this, it would not retain its glorious name, but would be called by a blind name; since, although it were called bright, its light would nevertheless not be seen.

Likewise, a soldier who comes to battle without armor will most certainly be trampled by his enemies, because he has not enclosed his body in a breastplate, put a helmet upon his head, or covered himself with a shield; and so he will be taken in great shame.

But you, who are called a bright star by reason of the episcopal office, and who shine with the name of the high priest, do not hide your light—which is the words of justice—from those subject to you. For you often say in your heart: “If I frightened those subject to me with words, they would regard me as troublesome, because I cannot overcome them. If only, by keeping silent, I could retain their friendship.” It is therefore not profitable for you to speak and act in this way.

But what then? Do not terrify them with dreadful words because of your episcopal title and the nobility of your body, like a ravening hawk; nor strike them with perilous words as with a club. Rather, mingle words of justice with mercy, and anoint them with the fear of God, setting before them how dangerous injustice is to their souls and their blessedness. Most certainly, most certainly, most certainly, in this way they will heed you.

Do not associate yourself with them in their foul and unstable habits, nor observe what pleases or displeases each person; for if you do this, you will appear lesser than the rest before God and men. Such things do not befit your person. Consider also that clean animals which chew the cud would be made lean if the food of swine, by which the swine themselves grow fat, were mixed with their fodder. So too, if you joined yourself to foul habits and to the fellowship of sinners, you would be defiled; by this the wicked would rejoice, while perfect men would be disturbed, saying: “Ah, ah! Woe, woe! What kind of bishop is ours? He shines upon us by the straight paths of justice!”

Correct and turn your people away from hostile unbelief, so that you may not be naked of the breastplate of faith. Show them from the Holy Scriptures the way of justice; put the helmet of hope upon your head and the shield of true defense upon your neck [Col. 0184D] (Eph. 6), so that in all the miseries and dangers of the Church you may be, as far as you are able, its defender.

Hold the light of truth in such a way that you may appear a worthy soldier in my service—for I am true Love—and that in a shipwrecked world and in the harsh wars of wickedness you may be vigorous and strong, so that you may shine as a bright star in eternal blessedness.

Now, O Father, you who bear a pastoral title, do not disdain the poverty of the person writing this. For I have neither composed nor uttered these things according to myself or according to the lofty human being; but I have written them as I saw and heard them in true vision, while awake in mind and body, because you commanded me to write something to you.

## LETTER XXVI

[Col. 0185A]

### CONRAD THE EMPEROR  
[Note: [Col. 0185D] The third of this name.]  
TO HILDEGARD

He pledges his favor and commends his son to the prayers of the Saint.

CONRAD, by the favoring grace of God king of the Romans, to HILDEGARD, virgin consecrated to God and mistress of the sisters of Saint Robert at Bingen, greeting and his favor.

Because we are impeded by the royal height and shaken by diverse storms and tempests, we cannot visit you as we wish; nevertheless, we do not omit to approach you by our letters. For, as we have heard, the confession of highest praise truly abounds in you through the holiness of your innocent life and through the magnificence of the Spirit wonderfully coming upon you from above.

Therefore, although we lead a worldly life [Col. 0185B], we hasten to you, take refuge with you, and humbly seek the aid of your prayers and exhortations, because we live very differently from the way we ought. Know certainly that, in every matter and every need of yours, we shall hasten to help and support you wherever we can. And so I commend my son, whom I desire to survive, most earnestly to your prayers, as I commend myself.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She not obscurely foretells schisms and other evils of the Church that arose under Frederick I, Conrad’s successor. She adds many things in the same prophetic spirit concerning the various periods and vicissitudes of the Church.

[Col. 0185C]

He who gives life to all says:

Blessed are those who worthily stand beneath the candlestick of the highest King, and whom God has cared for in great providence, so that He does not cut them off from His bosom. Remain in Him, O King, and cast filthiness from your mind, for God preserves everyone who devoutly and purely seeks Him.

Hold your kingdom in such a way, and provide justice for each of your subjects, that you may not become estranged from the heavenly kingdom. Hear: in one respect you turn away from God; and the times in which you live are frivolous, as though in a womanly person, and incline even toward a contrary injustice that attempts to destroy justice in the Lord’s vineyard.

Afterward worse times will come, in which true Israelites will be scourged and the Catholic throne will be shaken in error; and therefore their final deeds will be blasphemies, like a corpse in death. Thus this sorrow smokes in the Lord’s vineyard.

After these, times stronger than the former will arise, in which God’s justice will be raised a little and the injustice of the spiritual people will be marked for expulsion. Yet they will not dare to be sharply provoked and exasperated into contrition. Then other times will press upon them, in which the riches of the Church will be scattered, so that even the spiritual people will be torn as though by wolves and driven from their places and their native land. Therefore the foremost among them will pass into solitude, thereafter living a poor life in great contrition of heart and humbly serving God [Col. 0186A].

For these first times are foul in relation to God’s justice, but those that follow are wearisome. Those that then come upon them will raise themselves a little toward justice; but those that later rise will divide all things like a bear and heap up riches for themselves through evil. Yet those that follow them will display the sign of manly strength, so that all dealers in spices will run toward the first dawn of justice with fear, modesty, and wisdom; and the princes will unanimously maintain concord, raising it like a warrior as a banner against the wandering times of the greatest errors. God will destroy and exterminate these errors according to His own knowledge and good pleasure.

And again He who knows all things says to you, O King: “As a human being hearing these things, restrain yourself from your own will and correct yourself, so that you may come purified to those times in which you will no longer be ashamed of your deeds.”

## LETTER XXVII

### FREDERICK THE EMPEROR TO HILDEGARD

He reports that certain things foretold by the Saint in conversation at Ingelheim have been fulfilled. He asks for her prayers. In a dispute between certain persons and Saint Hildegard, to be settled in his court, he promises to judge with regard only to equity.

FREDERICK, by God’s grace Emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, to Lady HILDEGARD of Bingen, his favor and every good.

We make known to your holiness that those things which you foretold to us, when we were staying at Ingelheim and asked you to come into our presence [Col. 0186C], we now have in our hands. Yet in every undertaking we shall not cease to labor for the honor of the realm.

Accordingly, we most earnestly exhort your charity that, with the sisters committed to you, you pour out prayers for us to almighty God, that, while we labor in earthly affairs, He may so turn Himself that we may be able to obtain His grace. You must also know for certain that in every matter of yours brought to us by you, we shall consider neither anyone’s friendship nor anyone’s hatred, but purpose to judge equitably with regard only to justice.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She censures Frederick’s various schemes. She foretells that his reign will be quite long but turbulent.

[Col. 0186D]

These words are directed to you from the highest Judge.

It is very remarkable that a human being has this necessary role, namely, the role that you, O king, possess. Hear:

A certain king stood upon a lofty mountain and looked into all the valleys, seeing what everyone did in them. He held a rod in his hand, by which he rightly apportioned everything: what was dry, so that it might become green; and what slept, so that it might awaken. This rod also removed the punishment of stupor from those who were engaged in great effort.

But when that man did not open his eye, a black mist came and touched those valleys. Ravens also came, and other birds, which scattered whatever lay around them [Col. 0187A].

Now, O king, provide carefully, for every region is overshadowed by the deceitful crowd of those who, in the blackness of sins, erase justice. Plunderers and wanderers destroy the Lord’s way. O king, govern idle, alien, and most savage dispositions with the scepter of mercy. For you have a glorious name: you are king in Israel. Your name is very glorious!

See therefore, when the highest King considers you, that you may not be accused of having failed to judge your office rightly, and then be ashamed. May this be far from you! It is plain that it is just for a ruler to imitate his predecessors in good, since the ways of those prelates are most black who run after wantonness and corruption. Flee this, O king.

But be an armed soldier, firmly resisting the devil, lest God scatter you and the earthly kingdom be ashamed on this account. May God free you from eternal perdition; may your times not be barren; and may God protect you, that you may live forever.

Cast away avarice; choose abstinence, which the highest King greatly loves. For it is very necessary that you be prudent in your affairs. For in mystical vision I see you living, before living eyes, amid very many storms and adversities; yet you have a period of rule in earthly matters. Beware, therefore, lest the highest King cast you down because of the blindness of your eyes, which do not rightly see how you should hold in your hand the rod of right government. See also that you are such a person that God’s grace does not fail in you.

## LETTER XXVIII

[Col. 0187C]

### PHILIP, COUNT OF FLANDERS, TO HILDEGARD

He seeks Saint Hildegard’s prayers and her advice whether he ought rather to remain in the Holy Land or, after undertaking the expedition, return to his own people.

PHILIP, Count of Flanders and Vermandois, to Lady HILDEGARD, servant of Christ, greeting and abundant affection.

May your holiness know that I am prepared to do whatever I know would please you, because your holy manner of life and most honorable life have very often sounded in my ears, sweeter than every fame. Although I am a sinner and unworthy, I nevertheless love Christ’s servants and friends with my whole heart and gladly honor them with every reverence, mindful of that Scripture: “The persistent prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5).

Therefore I send to the favor of your compassion the bearer of this letter, my most faithful servant, that he may speak with you on behalf of me, a wretched sinner. I would much more gladly have come to you and spoken to you of what I desired; but my affairs, so many and so great, arise every day, and I could not attend to this.

The time is also now at hand when I must undertake the journey to Jerusalem, for which I require great preparation. Deign to make your counsel known to me concerning it through your letters. I believe that the report of my name and deeds has often reached you, and that I stand in need of much of God’s mercy.

Therefore, with the greatest insistence in prayer, I humbly entreat you [Col. 0188A] to be willing to intercede with the Lord for me, a most wretched and utterly unworthy sinner. I ask also humbly that, insofar as divine mercy grants you, you inquire of God what is expedient for me, and report your counsel to me by your letters through the bearer of this letter: what I should do and how I should do it, so that in my time the name of Christianity may be exalted and the dreadful savagery of the Saracens brought low; and whether it will be beneficial for me to remain in that land or to return, according to what you may perhaps have heard, have known by divine revelation, or will come to know concerning my condition.

Farewell in Christ, beloved sister. Know that I greatly desire to hear your counsel and that I have the greatest confidence in your prayers.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She sends instruction in which she especially exhorts him to justice.

[Col. 0188B]

O son of God, because He formed you in the first human being, hear the words which, awake in body and mind, I saw and heard in my soul when, on account of your earnest inquiry, I looked toward the true Light.

God gave Adam a commandment in Paradise, and after Adam’s transgression of that commandment expelled him—who had consented to the serpent’s counsel—from Paradise by just judgment (Gen. 3). By a just judgment He also drowned in the flood those human beings who had wholly consigned Him to forgetfulness, so that they neither desired nor sought Him (Gen. 6), while through the ark He saved from the flood those who loved and sought Him (Gen. 7).

But the most gentle Lamb, namely the Son of God, by His blood, which He poured out while hanging on the cross, saves all crimes and sins that a human being acknowledges through true repentance [Col. 0188C].

Now attend, O son of God, so that with the pure eye of justice you may look to God as an eagle looks to the sun, and so that, without the self-interest of your own will, your judgments may be just. Otherwise the highest Judge—who gave the commandment to man and who also calls him to Himself in mercy through repentance—may say to you: “Why did you kill your neighbor without my justice?”
