Bind men liable to judgment according to the Scriptures of the saints, who were pillars of the Church, with law and with fear of death; yet in all things consider the curse of that man who committed murder in his anger [Col. 0188D].

For all your negligences, sins, and unjust judgments, flee with the sign of the cross to the living God, who is the way and the truth (John 14), and who also says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 18).

And if the time comes when unbelievers endeavor to destroy the fountain of faith, then resist them insofar as you can through the help of God’s grace. For I see in my soul that the concern you have over the distress of your soul is like the dawn that rises in the morning. Therefore may the Holy Spirit make you a burning sun in pure and true repentance, so that you may seek Him and serve Him alone, and thus live forever in highest blessedness.

## LETTER XXIX

[Col. 0189A]

### BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, TO HILDEGARD

He extols her merits and holiness.

To HILDEGARD, beloved daughter in Christ: Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux—whatever the prayer of a sinner may avail.

That some appear to think of our lowliness very differently from what our conscience knows it to be must be attributed not to our merits but to human foolishness. Yet I hastened to write to the sweetness of your devout love, though the multitude of my affairs compels me to do so much more briefly than I would wish.

We rejoice over the grace of God which is in you, and we admonish you to receive it as grace and endeavor to respond to it with every affection of humility and devotion, knowing that “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4). As far as lies in us, we exhort and beseech you (1 Pet. 5).

But where there is inward instruction and an anointing that teaches concerning all things, what can we teach or admonish? For it is said that you search out heavenly secrets and, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, discern matters above human beings. Therefore we ask, indeed humbly entreat, that you remember us before God, together with those who are joined to us in spiritual fellowship. For when the Spirit is united to God, we trust that you can greatly help and support us. “For the persistent prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5).

We too continually pray for you, that you may be strengthened for good, instructed in inward things, and directed toward things enduring [Col. 0189C], so that those who have placed their hope in God may not falter in despair because of you, but may be well strengthened in the progress of the blessing which you are known to have received from God, and may advance better and better.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She adorns him with great praises.

In the spirit of mysteries I say to you, O venerable Father: in the great honors of God’s power you are wonderfully and greatly to be feared by the unlawful folly of this world. Under the banner of the holy cross, with lofty zeal and burning love for the Son of God, you seize men for battles to be fought in Christian warfare against the savagery of tyrants. This is what I, greatly constrained in a vision that appears to me in the Spirit of mystery—not seen by the outward eyes of flesh—declare.

I, wretched and more than wretched in a woman’s name, have seen great wonders from my childhood, which my tongue cannot utter except as the Spirit of God teaches me how to speak them. Most certainly and gentle Father, hear me, your unworthy servant, in your goodness. Since my childhood I have never lived securely; and understand in your soul, through your mercy and wisdom, according to what you have been taught in the Holy Spirit, that what has been said to you concerning me is so.

For I know, within the text, the inward meaning of the exposition of the Psalter, the Gospel, and other books, which are shown to me in this vision. It touches my breast and, burning my soul as a flame [Col. 0190A], teaches me these depths of exposition. Yet it does not teach me the letters of the German language, which I do not know. I know only how to read simply, not by the analytic division of a text; for I am an unlearned person, without any instruction in outward material matters. But inwardly, in my soul, I am taught.

Therefore I speak to you, not doubting concerning you, but seeking consolation in your wisdom and compassion, because, as I hear people say, there are many schisms among men. For I first spoke these things to a certain monk, whom I had examined as one of more approved manner of life, and I showed him all my secrets; and he consoled me, saying that these things were great and fearful.

Father, I wish you to remember me in your prayers for the love of God. Two years ago I saw you in this vision, as one who looks at the sun and does not fear, but is very bold; and I wept because I blush so greatly and am timid.

Good and gentle Father, I place myself in your soul. Pray for me, for I endure great labors in this vision, that I may speak what I see and hear. Sometimes, because of this vision, I am laid prostrate upon my bed in great infirmities because I keep silent, so that I cannot rise.

Therefore I lament before you in sorrow, because I am changeable, like a tree shaken by motion in a winepress in my nature, sprung from the root rising in Adam, who through the devil’s suggestion was made an exile into the alien world. But now, rising, I run to you.

I say to you: You are changeable, yet you are always raising up the tree, and you are victorious in your soul—not only raising yourself, but raising other human beings also to salvation. You are an eagle looking upon the sun.

I beseech you by the serenity of the Father; by His marvelous Word; by the sweet moisture of compunction, namely the Spirit of truth; by the holy sound through which every creature resounds; by that same Word through whom the world arose; and by the height of the Father, who sent the Word in sweet greenness into the Virgin’s womb, from which that hymn drew nourishment as honey is enclosed around a honeycomb: do not languish idly in response to my words. Put them into your heart, so that you do not cease, but pass through the form of your soul, looking to God on my behalf, for He wills you.

Farewell, farewell in your soul, and be strong in the contest in God. Amen.

## LETTER XXX

### ADAM, ABBOT OF EBRA, TO HILDEGARD

He commends himself to the Saint’s prayers and seeks her written reply to his doubt, which appears from Saint Hildegard’s response to have concerned retaining or laying down the office of abbot.

To his most beloved lady and mother HILDEGARD, mistress of the sisters of Saint Robert at Bingen: Brother ADAM, though unworthy, Abbot of Ebra—his small portion, such as it is.

When I first received knowledge of your name, I rejoiced with great joy (Matt. 2). God increased my joy when, by a gracious and marvelous nod, He directed that your face should be seen and your voice heard in our land, and granted me the mutual conversation which I scarcely dared hope for.

Concerning the matters in which I told you I was anxious, I trust you have not forgotten me. Because different people think differently—some one thing, others another—if this is good and salvation before the Lord, blessed be God; if it is danger, pray to God that He may grant me good and salvation of soul, and exclude every danger.

Now I send a letter and our messenger to the lord emperor on your behalf, and I hope that through God’s grace we shall be heard. Wherever you need our service, we shall be ready to serve you. We also entreat you to deign to pray for us, because we are truly in a storm through concern for our brothers, that the grace of the Holy Spirit, which works many wonders in you through the prophetic Spirit [Col. 0191B], may look also upon us and strengthen us. We ask also that you deign to comfort and forewarn us by your writings.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

In advising him not to lay down his office, she introduces various virtues, especially charity and humility.

In true vision, the Spirit awake in the body, I heard these words:

He Who Is (Exod. 3) says: “The sun shines and sends forth rays. A certain man, friend of the sun, had a garden in which he desired with great zeal to plant many spices and many flowers. The sun, in the fire of its rays, sent warmth over the spices and flowers, while dew and rain gave them the moisture of greenness.

“Then from the north came forth a twisted figure with black hair and a horrible face; and from the east came a most beautiful youth, with white hair and a full and friendly countenance. They came to that garden.

“The twisted figure said to the youth: ‘Where do you come from?’

“He answered: ‘I come from the east to the garden of this wise man, because I had a great desire to come to it.’

“The twisted figure said: ‘Listen to me: a dangerous wind, hail, fire, and pestilence will come upon that garden and dry it up.’

“But the youth answered: ‘It will not be so, it will not be so, because I do not wish it. Rather, I shall bring forth a most pure fountain and water that garden.’

“The twisted figure replied: ‘Ha, ha! This is as possible as if a locust could bore through a hard stone.’

“And thus that figure, in its deceit, brought winter over that garden and sought to dry up its spices and flowers. But the aforesaid youth, occupied with his service upon his harps, did not see it. When he afterward saw it, he called loudly upon the sun to come in the sign of Taurus and bring again the greenness of summer upon that garden. Taking a horn of ivory and a horn taken from a stag, he cast that twisted figure down to the ground by them.

“Then he said to the man whose garden it was: ‘Henceforth do not trust carelessly in yourself, but so surround your garden with great defense that the blackest birds may not dry it up in storms.’”

Now, O Father, you who through the highest calling stand in Christ’s place, understand that these words are spoken to you.

Hear, then: God’s grace shines like the sun and sometimes sends forth its gifts in this way: in one mode, in wisdom; in another, in greenness; in a third, in moisture. Wisdom falls into a rich nature; greenness undergoes great labors; and moisture enters into hard bitterness.

But you, the man who is a friend of God’s grace, possess the garden of a people, in which, standing in Christ’s place, you ought zealously to plant many good desires and good works. God’s grace, in the power of its gifts, sends the efficacy of good will upon those desires and works, and makes them flourish through the dew and rain of the fountain of living water.

But from the devil come vices: unrest in vain glory and tumult because of one who resists just discipline for my sake. From God, however, virtues proceed in contempt of worldly things, with the full benevolence of submission in charity; they come to this people. The vices ask the virtues why they have come. The virtues answer that they have come from God to the people of God’s friend, because they have a great desire to build up within it a sacrifice of praise.

The vices say, so that these words may be heard: “Great ruin, wrath, and division with much unrest will rush upon this people, so that it will become weary in God’s service.” The virtues answer: “It will not be so, because we shall not cease from good things; rather, the living fountain will flow out and defend this people by its mercy.”

But the vices say with laughter that this is as possible as for frailty fixed in flesh to be able to endure without a wrinkle. Then in their deceits the vices bring a cold mist of ignorance upon this people, so that its good desires and good works are already failing when it trusts in itself.

But the virtues, rendering God their service in praises, permit this by God’s just judgment, so that men may understand what they are. When they return to themselves in the humility of virtues, those same virtues, with great diligence of watchfulness, hold fast to God’s grace, so as to place Christ’s Passion upon their minds and thus bring that people back to the first praise of God. And, considering the divinity and humanity of the Son of God, they cast down those vices in contrition.

They also say to him under whom this people stands: “Warned by this, do not trust in your own strength; but see to it that you flee to God’s grace, so that you may strengthen and admonish your people in every way, lest the devil’s snares overthrow them through negligence by diverse vices.”

I also saw what seemed to be a most beautiful maiden, shining with so great a radiance of splendid countenance that I could not look upon her perfectly. She wore a mantle whiter than snow and brighter than stars. She was shod as though with purest gold. In her right hand she held the sun and moon, and gently embraced them. Upon her breast was an ivory tablet, on which appeared the figure of a man of sapphire color; and every creature called this maiden “lady.”

She herself said to the figure which appeared upon her breast: “With you is dominion in the day of your power, amid the splendors of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109 [110]).

And I heard a voice saying to me: “This maiden whom you see is Charity, who has her dwelling in eternity. When God wished to create the world, He inclined Himself in most sweet love and foreordained all things necessary, just as a father prepares an inheritance for his son; and so, in great ardor, He disposed all His works.

“Then creation recognized its Creator in these appearances and forms, because charity was thus at the beginning the material principle of that creation, when God said: ‘Let it be,’ and it was made (Gen. 1); for every creature was formed through her, as it were in the twinkling of an eye.

“She shines in such radiance of splendid countenance that you cannot look upon her perfectly, because she manifests the fear of the Lord in such pure knowledge that mortal man cannot bring it to its end. She has a mantle whiter than snow and brighter than stars because, without pretense, she embraces all things in shining innocence through most splendid holy works.

“She is shod as though with purest gold because she has paths which are in the best part of God’s election. She holds the sun and moon in her right hand and gently embraces them, because the right hand of God embraces all creatures and is also extended among nations, kingdoms, and every good. Therefore it is written: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand’ (Ps. 109 [110]).

“On her breast is an ivory tablet, because in God’s knowledge integrity always flourished in the Virgin Mary; and upon it appears the figure of a man of sapphire color, because the Son of God shone forth in charity from the Ancient of Days.

“Every creature calls this maiden ‘lady,’ because it proceeded from her; and she was the primal one, creating all things, as the figure upon her breast shows, because God put on humanity for humankind’s sake. For all creation was fulfilled in God’s command, as He Himself said: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ (Gen. 1).

“The heat of the true sun descended like dew into the Virgin’s womb and made from her flesh a human being, just as He had also formed Adam’s flesh and blood from the mud of the earth. And the Virgin bore Him in integrity.

“But it was not fitting for Charity to lack wings. For when creation made its first circuit, so that in its distress it wished to fly and fell, the wings of charity raised it. This was holy Humility. For when the dreadful awareness cast Adam down, the Godhead looked sharply lest he should wholly perish in his fall, but so that He might redeem him in holy humanity.

“And were these not wings of great power: that Humility raised in the Savior’s humanity the human being who had been lost? For Charity created the human being, but Humility redeemed him.

“Hope is like the eye of Charity, heavenly love like her heart, and abstinence her joining-bond. Faith is like the eye of Humility, obedience like her heart, and contempt for evil her joining-bond.

“Charity was in eternity, and in the beginning all holiness brought forth all creatures without an admixture of evil and produced Adam and Eve from the pure creation of earth. As these two generated all the children of men, so these two virtues produce all the remaining virtues.

“These virtues knock at your door, O man to whom I speak, and say: ‘O dwelling-place of this man who abides with us in the morning, he is now weary.’

“And Charity says to you: ‘O friend of faith, we do not wish you to withdraw from your official bond. For when God wished to scatter all creatures throughout the circuit of heaven, we held all His works in our embrace and labored with Him. But man fell, and we wept with him; nor did we leave him, though he struck us on the cheek.’

“And Humility says to you especially: ‘Alas, alas! With what great pains I have sustained humankind! Yet you say: “I want to flee.” But you have a burden to carry into the vineyard, and you stand still; you do not wish to walk, but become entangled in weariness and look toward another road. Certainly our companion will not do this.

“‘When the people love you, labor with them. But when the roaring of the wind issues forth with the unrest of warfare and changing dispositions, look to me, and I will help you with the whole power of my wings.

“‘Samson, strongest of men, lost his strength through a woman’s foolishness (Judg. 16). Beware, therefore, lest the same happen to you if you give your answer by yielding to weariness. Solomon’s glory also was emptied through women’s foolishness (2 Kings [1 Kings] 11).

“‘See also carefully lest, through the changing character of these your perceptions, the greenness that you have from God may increase; but preserve the ornaments of gold and precious stone which Charity and Humility possess in you.

“‘You also, because of the bracelets which wisdom has given you and for which the people run to you, give glory to God and labor with the people; and so you will remain with the sun.’”

And you, Father, hear: As the morning star goes before the dawn in its light, so offer help to all from the kiss of love which God has given you; and He will give you the life which He beheld on the first day.

## LETTER XXXI

### THE ABBOT OF EBERBACH TO HILDEGARD

He earnestly seeks the Saint’s prayers and offers her his services.

[Col. 0194D]

To the venerable lady and mistress HILDEGARD at Bingen, beloved by God and men: Brother E., [Note: [Col. 0193D] See the Bollandist commentary, no. 47.] though unworthy, Abbot of Eberbach—his small portion, such as it is.

We magnify and glorify on your account Christ our Savior, who looks upon those who fear him, powerfully exalts the humble, and has done great things for you, because he is mighty (Luke 1). As we ourselves have heard and seen, he has chosen the sanctuary of your breast as a dwelling for himself, and has made known to you the divine knowledge, the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom (Psalm 50), introducing you into his chamber among the flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys, into the flowering fields of the everlasting mountains. His left hand is under your head, and his right embraces you [Col. 0195A] (Song 2), so that you may truly say: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” In all these things your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens have loved you, and we run after the fragrance of your ointments (Song 1). We also ask the Lord that he may deign to preserve for you both the gifts of nature and the gifts of his grace: for his glory, for your crown, for our joy, and as an example to many. We pray also, and humbly entreat, that you may deign to remember us as well, and at the coming of your Bridegroom commend our littleness to him; so that, as we rejoice and are glad at the report of your holiness, so through your intercession we may deserve to receive joy and exultation. If you deign to receive anything of our service, we gladly undertake it [Col. 0195B]; indeed, as we do now, we shall act and are ready to serve every holy wish of yours.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She returns excellent admonitions and, at the end, foretells the best things for the abbot.

“He Who Is” (Exodus 3) says: “Serene light sees the fold and the appointed meal of every community that has an office in its ministry, distributing the food of refreshment in right moderation, lest the faithful who cleave to it lack joy of soul. The pastoral steward ought, with most steadfast character, to display arrows in his quiver and to bestow the spices [Col. 0195C] of medicines with ample kindness. But the black tyrants bear scourges of slaughter; the worthy soldier fights without weariness at mockery; and a sweet disposition seeks sufficiency through labor for the common good. Festive dispositions, uprightly girded, are equipped with every virtue, so that they hunger to accomplish justice.

“But those who are most savage and strangers to the noble mother Mercy slaughter the simple sheep that are in the courts of the King’s house. Alas, alas for those who thus rage in slaughter! Unless they repent, they are strangers to the King’s house, because they scatter the Lord’s sheep. But you, O shepherd, show a cheerful face amid the misery of the poor, who are faint-hearted and unable to take hold of the plough of discipline. Let those who are good and benevolent be to you a harmony of the Holy Spirit. Take care [Col. 0195D] also that you do not grow sluggish in the light. Let your understanding keep watch and not be double in its sound, so that you do not dictate one thing inwardly and utter another outwardly. Those who do this darken their faces in darkness. But if afterwards they fear in trembling because in their heart they do not receive what they display upon their face, they are delivered from unbelief, shut up in repentance.

“But for you, O man, there shall be refreshment in the girding of your loins, where you hold true desire in your hands, when you do not neglect the treasure of true wealth. The earth sleeps for you, because the shipwreck of the world does not harm you. At the end of your time God will raise you up. He will establish you in great honor. O good servant, you will praise him, and he will save you forever.”

## EPISTLE XXXII

[Col. 0196A]

### THE ABBOT OF ST. ANASTASIUS TO HILDEGARD

Whether he ought to retain or lay down the office of abbot in order to devote himself to contemplation.

To his beloved in the Lord and most devoted sister HILDEGARD, by God’s grace mistress in the monastery of St. Robert, Brother E., called abbot of St. Anastasius, greetings and prayer.

Glory to God, for you are the good fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2), both among your own people and among ours. Through you Christ’s good name is blessed and praised, he who is sanctified in you. For you glorify and bear Christ in your body (1 Corinthians 6), worthily according to the worthy calling by which you were called (1 Corinthians 7), making yourself, by cooperating with the grace given you, a vessel of honor in the Lord’s house, presenting yourself to all. And since you are a familiar [Col. 0196B] instrument of Christ and a receptacle of his Spirit, we humbly ask you to pray in spirit and truth for me and those entrusted to our care: that he may accomplish in us both the willing and the doing according to his good will (Philippians 1), so that we too may finish the course of the good contest in Christ (2 Timothy 4) and rejoice together in his praise (Psalm 105).

Moreover, I ask that the Spirit who reveals the mysteries and hidden things of his wisdom may show you what is expedient for me in bearing the burden of Christ’s obedience—namely, whether I should persevere or rest, in order to be free for his contemplation. Whatever may be revealed to you concerning this, do not hide it from me; for “my heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Psalm 107), to do your will [Col. 0196C] (Hebrews 10). We need your counsel, assistance, and good will in having copied for us the book which you wrote. For we earnestly desire to possess it and to behold in it the wonders of God. Furthermore, I earnestly ask that we may be visited by a written reply from you and consoled in labor and patience for Christ through the breasts of consolation that are in you. Farewell; greet your sisters and pray for us.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

That he should adhere to his office.

“He Who Is” (Exodus 3) says to you, O man: “Your mind rises eagerly through the reputation of good works, and you lift yourself on high, desiring more than you perform. [Col. 0196D] But at times your very mind deceives you, sifting your motives and saying: ‘These things are excellent,’ though you do not at present perform them. Therefore, if you shake off from yourself the very purpose that you entertain in your intention, then carry out the support of your sheepfold and give it commands: that is, first offer the master’s rod, and then administer the physician’s ointment. For it is more useful for you to watch in this labor, while others serve in subjection through your teaching, than to exercise yourself according to your own will. For if you subjected yourself, weariness would surround you, so that your mind would wither.

“Therefore keep watch over your flock, giving it the good examples which your soul desires, lest your mind be reduced to mockery. For he who stands on a height and cries into the valley sometimes does not know in either place whither [Col. 0197A] he will go. Therefore stand in humility, so that, with God’s help, you may practice the good works you have begun; remain in Christ’s footsteps; do not deceive yourself; and you shall live forever.”

## EPISTLE XXXIII

### THE ABBOT OF KEISHEYM TO HILDEGARD

He proposes to the holy woman a similar doubt.

CONRAD, abbot of Keisheim, though unworthy, to the most holy Lady HILDEGARD, superior of the cloister of St. Robert at Bingen, devout prayers with humble service.

From the first time that I was able to hear of the marks of your virtues, most holy mother, and of the special gift bestowed upon you by God, although I was unknown to you in bodily presence, [Col. 0197B] I nevertheless loved you with all the affection of my mind. I rejoice with you in your glory, because you have deserved to find the Beloved whom my soul sought, and you need not wander after the flock of companions; for he who feeds among the lilies has rested in your tabernacle, filling your garden with an abundance of diverse delights (Song 1).

Yet, dearest lady, I wonder why, since you are a little stream flowing from the very fountain of goodness, pouring out your kindness upon all who desire to know and hear through you the mighty works of God, you shut up the bowels of compassion against me, who am laboring in great anxiety of heart, and so slowly send the small favor which I seek out of charity rather than presumption. Therefore I beseech you with all devotion to intercede for me with the Bridegroom himself, who rests in the chamber [Col. 0197C] of your heart and willingly inclines the ear of his mercy to your petitions; and ask him to reveal to you whether it is more useful for me to lay down the burden of pastoral care or to bear it longer, since I am grievously oppressed by it and consign myself to forgetfulness. But in this I shall know that you have been heard: if I receive your answer from him. Farewell, beloved of God.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She does not conceal the crimes of his subjects, nor does she seem to excuse Conrad himself, but exhorts him to repentance. Yet she adds a qualification in obscure words, intimating that he ought to leave the office if he could accomplish no good among his people.

Keen light sees and says: “O man, you are pale through the uncertainty of your mind, as though you could not stand. And why is this? I see your works; indeed, they touch me. But you know the recognition of rebels. Why then are you ashamed before my altar to look toward my sanctuary, so as to adorn it like a temple that has living eyes?

“O burden, where the good shepherd lifted his lambs upon his shoulders! For where sheep do not walk in straight paths, the gentle shepherd ought to raise them through the concern of his mind, correct and anoint them, and teach them in good works. And as a hand works through an arm, and as an arm in turn moves at the shoulder, so let the shepherd offer his sheep examples in the hand of good works, medicine in the arm of assistance, and the remedy for diverse vices through the bond of the Cross, as though in the shoulder of authority. For truly repentant persons must have their sins [Col. 0198A] forgiven.

“For the devil vomits forth the force of his heart, the taste of his throat, and the burning flame of his viperous mouth. O man, hear the lament of grief over the pouring out of crime which lies in the contagion of the flesh, in the beautiful form of man. Weep, O virginity, for the integrity of your first origin. For the hand of the supreme Craftsman formed you and placed you in the garden of delight. But the burning mind of man deceived him through the vain choosing of his own will, by the pride of the criminal deceiver’s counsel. Thus he was cast out through the taste of disobedience. And so his belly transgressed, although earlier his side had been pierced by the most holy gift. But now his thigh is polluted by sweating venom. Thus man touched the taste of the serpent’s throat when he burned in his venomous [Col. 0198B] veins. Hence afterwards he fornicated in viperous desire, which is a burning flame from the devil’s mouth.

“Now she has prepared food in obedience. And because God made woman from the rib (Genesis 2), the devil thereafter suggested homicide, so that he might lead all his works by another path into the disclosure of sins boiling over through the force of his heart. O man, how great are the crimes that you commit in the likeness of the ancient traitor! How so? For that most evil accuser was cast down backward and cut off from all blessedness. And because he was cast backward, he devised in the malice of his heart to lead man backward into a contrary sin. Thus man abandoned the form of the rib; accordingly the formation of man perishes there in this outpoured seed.

“Therefore let the earth mourn and [Col. 0198C] the heavens tremble because of these crimes. For when man sins through the taste of his deed without abandoning the formation of the rib, he still perceives something of what is God’s handiwork. But these crimes, falling backward, belong to no creation, because the man who commits them does not see himself to be a human being. O man, why do you cast away what you are made to be? Ah, ah, O man: God formed you with great care, but you entangle yourself in many crimes. Yet God will again bring you back to himself through his Son. Therefore rise through repentance and run quickly to me.

“Now you, O soldier, be strong and armed upon level paths; make greenness where greenness is; care for the girding of the loins of those who are with you; and restrain yourself in good works, so that your heart may be illumined [Col. 0198D] in the sun and you may not grow weary on the straight road, fighting against yourself. Therefore do not abandon pastoral care, because the perfumer who possesses a watered and fragrant garden should see that his garden yields the usefulness of fruits and does not fail. For when your eye sees and your knowledge keeps watch, why do you sleep like one weary in the girding of your eye’s right foresight? Go about diligently with good foresight, lest you unhappily hide your talent (Matthew 25); for it does not profit you to cast off the bond by which you are bound while you have under your custody two living eyes, or one, or any part capable of life. But if you have no living eye among your own, but only continual lameness, then flee and refrain from your stewardship.”

## EPISTLE XXXIV

[Col. 0199A]

### THE ABBOT OF HIRSAUGIA TO HILDEGARD

He adorns the holy woman with great praises.

To his most holy lady and mother HILDEGARD, M., the unworthy abbot of Hirsau, prayer with service.

I have heard indeed that at Cyrene a certain vein of waters flows with wine; and that you, good mother, among the Alemanni, appear as a spring of waters entering and leaving, and as the smoke of sweet spices, like myrrh and incense. For, my lady, you draw in and pour forth, and you proceed in particular forms and practical matters from power and motion into contemplation. Therefore I have long had, and still have, an impulse to love you, honor you, admire you, serve you and those belonging to you, and in [Col. 0199B] all things, by word or deed, to be at the service and in the prayers of you and your women, insofar as it is permitted me. I ask you, my mother and lady: remember me in your most holy prayers; love one who loves you most humbly; recognize in Christ one who reveres you; and write back to me, asked in God.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She foretells various things.

“O sweetest Father and brother in Christ’s love: I see a pot surrounded by so great a charity that I can scarcely see whether it is a pot. Yet there I also see some bitterness of taste, opposed indeed with great struggle, and afterwards a whirlwind, which nevertheless is predestined for God’s reward. Therefore keep watch vigorously, for the condition of the people in their conduct requires such things at this time.

“O gentlest Father, I, a poor little form, do not see in the true light that you should depart entirely from your office. Remember, however, that you are a man on earth, and do not fear excessively, since God does not require diverse things from you. For you are in God’s presence like the smoke of myrrh and incense; therefore Mount Zion asks that you be food in the house of Jacob. But if anyone cuts down the pillar that supports the whole house, he brings down the house. Therefore look forth through the seven windows, considering where the hawk may come, and beware lest it deceive you. Feed your sheep, then, with the gentleness of correction, because the day of salvation does not flee and you are not yet ashes. Be also a mirror of life in the eyes of life.”

## EPISTLE XXXV

### THE STEWARD OF ST. EMMERAM TO HILDEGARD

On behalf of a certain man despairing of his salvation.

[Col. 0199D]

To the most religious servant of Christ HILDEGARD, A., unworthy steward of the monastery of St. Emmeram at Regensburg: perseverance in every good thing bestowed by the Father of lights.

We give thanks to our God, who has wondrously adorned his Church by giving you to it. For through you all the righteous gloriously rejoice, and those who have hitherto despaired are blessedly made glad, because they hope that through you they can be reconciled to Christ. Therefore the bearer of this letter, as he declares, despairing of his salvation, recently lamented his miseries to me and begged me to send him, with commendatory letters, to the presence of your blessedness. Hence, O handmaid of Christ, I humbly entreat your mercy and compassion, urging him upon you, that for the love of almighty God [Col. 0200A] you may labor with all your strength, together with all who obey you, for his salvation. Moreover, O beloved of God, I implore your graciousness to deign to commend me and all entrusted to me to Christ in your continual prayers—he who is both rewarder and reward of the labors of his saints. Amen. Farewell.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She exhorts the abbot in grave words to the care of his flock.

“He Who Is” (Exodus 3) says: “O man, you must look about everywhere in order to drive away the plotters against your sheep. See also that you examine the scars of their wounds, for many mists surround the spiritual people [Col. 0200B], and these mists are full of vices. When the devil sees them, he swiftly sends his persuasion against that person in mockery and moves him about everywhere with flying darts in diverse ways.

“These mists are distresses and unbeliefs in various forms which carry punishments rather than feasts. For where these are, there is sadness, rare victory, and dry veins in those same people when they seek out their sins in the disquiet of their mind, always looking toward misfortune as though they could not be saved. They even contradict God’s glory, though not as if God did not exist. Rather, a certain mist envelops their knowledge, suggesting this to them with deceptive words. Yet they resist and know that things are not so; but they perceive them in their awareness in the way that a person’s hearing takes in most shameful words, though it knows them to be evil.

“These punishments often make martyrs, when a person does not carry their vices into deeds. Now, O man, set as a watchman over your sheep, examine with the eye of your knowledge where these mists are in your fold; and anoint with mercy and consolation the persons who labor under these punishments. But correct feasting crimes with the rod of discipline, lest they go into the pit. For in your conscience the light of a sword shines, yet in your conduct there are whirlwinds. But look to the true light, and you shall live.”

## EPISTLE XXXVI

### THE ABBOT OF THE NUENBURGENSIANS TO HILDEGARD

He says that fear of war prevented him from coming to her. He earnestly requests her prayers.

[Col. 0200D]

To HILDEGARD, most blessed religious woman, E., abbot of the brothers of Nuenburg in name alone, wishes whatever the affection of the inner and outer person can desire.

Since the fame of your holiness has sprinkled the ears of all with its sweet report, it has most ardently stirred my mind to see your face. Therefore, last summer, as I was about to take up the expenses for my traveling provisions, I hastened toward you. But I was frightened by the storms of wars. Yet I sent you a messenger with a letter, through whom I received no reply other than this. Lest this should have occurred through the messenger’s negligence, I shall repeat again what it contained.

First, I give heartfelt thanks for fellowship in fraternity received from you; next, I ask to be aided before God by your prayers [Col. 0201A] both in pressing circumstances and in dangers. For, being placed in government, I am driven about by worldly whirlwinds; therefore I flee to the harbor of your holiness and prayer, so that in these things, in every way and above all things, I may not . . . . . . sin. And although I ask these things earnestly, above all I beseech through your prayers that, when my life’s course is complete, I may deserve to be saved by the Lord in body and spirit.

Among these pressures, one more important than the others threatens, concerning which I ask you to entreat the Lord more urgently. Send through the bearer of this letter some pledge of salvation by which I may prosper and remember you. I shall not lack the desire to come to you until, if life accompanies me, I fulfill it in deed. Farewell.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She exhorts him to courage in pastoral care: a soldier must not cast aside his arms in time of war because difficulties have arisen.

[Col. 0201B]

“Your mind is like something that has the fastening of lights and distributes them here and there; but it is often disturbed by the cloud of whirlwind and blackness, of fires and waters, until the sun pierces all things through its fiery sphere. You have weariness through doubting, and because of the various wars arising from human conduct you do not wish to labor. For the new soldier rejoices when he bears arms, because a soldier is named amid the strongest force when his enemies fight against him. But if he says, ‘I cannot overcome my enemies,’ and casts away his arms, he is called a fool because of people’s mockery; for his arms do not [Col. 0201C] flash in the vigor of battle.

“For you, master, calling yourself naked, lie like a serpent in holes, since by armor you do not strive to overcome the diversity of human storms. But it shall not be so. For in the first age the Lord established stewards and procurators over every possession, that they might render account to him. When a steward has received gifts, let him gather arms and arrows to himself: with the arms, instructing the raging by the Scriptures; and with the arrows, instructing the impious, deceitful, and thievish by the parables of the other Scriptures.

“But when meanwhile a great storm comes, with blackness of fire and water, wrath, forgetfulness, and transgression of God’s commandments, let him yield until that storm lessens. Let him apply medicine with the sun of the Scriptures, as it is written: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ (Hosea 6; Matthew 9). Mercy calls for a prayer which God may love and which the Holy Spirit may make fiery between us and you, so that it may lead us into the heavenly Jerusalem. Amen.”

## EPISTLE XXXVII

### THE ABBOT OF ST. MARY’S TO HILDEGARD

After setting forth much in praise of the holy woman, he asks whether he should retain or resign his office.

To his lady HILDEGARD, resplendent in the honor of holy religion, H., uselessly called abbot of St. Mary’s, whatever service of prayers and petitions he can offer, and the affection of due service.

We would rather speak to your presence than write to your absence [Col. 0202A], if either time were available to us or the length of the journey did not obstruct our wish. Indeed, we have on occasion obtained an audience, though a very brief one, with your holiness, and therefore we should often wish to hear you, because then whatever we hear is pleasing. But we have now taken confidence to write to you on this occasion: the bearer of this letter, beloved in Christ by us both, commended your blessedness to the prayers of our poor community while he stayed with us, as he has done in many monasteries; and he reported that you requested this of us through him as intermediary.

Therefore, though we are nothing, we make and shall make remembrance of you, and humbly beg with bowed heart and body that we, together with all ours, may deserve your intercessions. Through him to whom you live devotedly, from whom you have received the pledge of the Spirit, we ask this singular and secret favor of you: strive to obtain from the Lord the familiarity of asking, so that among the other charisms of revelations he may deign to disclose to you the condition of our lowliness—namely, whether he foresees that I may deserve salvation of soul in this office of honor and burden, prelation and danger, or foresees that it would be useful for me to be released from it. And if you receive any revelation concerning this matter, may your charity not disdain to comfort our sadness, in writing conveyed through this same bearer of the letter. For we thirst for your salvation, as we have said; and we pray that the Lord may furnish you [Col. 0202C] with an increase of necessary humility amid the greatness of your revelations, so that you may preserve for humankind with such a light the lamp which you received kindled from heaven that, with unfailing oil, you may be able to meet Christ whom you await when he comes in glory (Matthew 25).

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

He is too anxious; he ought rather to consider himself and the correction of his subjects than resignation from office.

“In the mirror of true vision I saw you very troubled, like a mingled cloud when dangerous air is stirred in an entangled wind of a great downpour. Such are your thoughts, through your restless mind, concerning this matter which you have embraced in the midst of your heart. And I heard a voice saying concerning you: ‘A man labors with plough and oxen upon dry ground, saying to himself: “I cannot endure this great work, because it is hard for me.” Then he goes to waterless places where soft flowers nevertheless grow without human labor, though they are choked by useless weeds, and says: “I shall leave the plough and remove these useless herbs. What usefulness is there in this?”’

“Now, man, see whether he is the better person: the one laboring usefully with the plough in the earth, or the one rooting out useless herbs among flowers. But I have seen that the matter which you seek is useless for you. Therefore restrain yourself, together with your office, having taken hold of the plough. May God help you in all your necessities and not permit you to labor uselessly.”

## EPISTLE XXXVIII

[Col. 0203A]

### THE ABBOT OF ST. DISIBOD TO HILDEGARD

He asks her to disclose to him whatever God may reveal to the holy woman concerning St. Disibod. He earnestly commends himself to her prayers.

CUNO, abbot of the mount of St. Disibod, though unworthy, to HILDEGARD, his most beloved lady and mother of the Mount of St. Robert: by God’s grace, the little that he is.

Because, hindered on every side by various occupations, I have for some time delayed visiting, greeting, and speaking with you, now that an opportunity has presented itself I commit myself all the more earnestly to your prayers, because—alas!—I recognize that I am growing old rather in an increase of sin than in any progress in righteousness. But because your holiness, in him who neither deceives nor is deceived, sees very many secrets by the Spirit, I ask you to disclose to me whatever God may reveal to you about our patron, blessed Disibod, so that with my brothers I may not delay to offer him most devout praises for it. But because by no power available to me can I shake off from myself the negligence that is in me, I seek with devout heart the aid both of you and of the other daughters of God living with you. I commend to the prayers of you all not merely my own insignificant person but also the brothers entrusted to me and our place, just as, when I am with you, I am accustomed often to do by word of mouth.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

After some general remarks about St. Disibod, she freely rebukes Cuno for excessive severity toward his subjects and foretells his imminent death.

[Col. 0203C]

“O how great is the folly in that man who does not correct himself, but seeks what is in another’s bosom and does not conceal the crimes he finds there, according to the manner of rushing waters! Let him who does this hear this answer from God: ‘O man, why do you sleep amid the sound of taste, which sounds before God like a harmony? And why do you not deny the wantonness of sensuality through searching the house of your heart? Yet you strike me on my cheeks when you reject my members in their wounds, where you do not look to me, the one bringing back the straying sheep to the flock (Luke 15). Therefore you will answer me out of the house of your heart [Col. 0203D] and out of the city which I made and washed in the blood of the Lamb. Why are you not afraid to break a human being whom you did not create? For you do not anoint him so as either to govern or cultivate him; rather, you correct him excessively. Now the time of your failing is at hand. But God, who created you, does not wish to destroy you. Therefore understand these things.’

“But, O Father, you asked me to write to you if I saw and understood anything concerning blessed Disibod, under whose patronage you stand. This is what I heard, saw, and understood concerning him in the vision of the Spirit, in this manner:

‘O wondrous marvel: the hidden form excels in lofty and honorable stature, where living height brings forth mysteries. Therefore, O Disibod, you shall rise at the end, aided by the flower of all the branches of the world, as you first rose. And, O greenness of God’s finger, in which God established a plantation shining forth on high like a set-up pillar, you are glorious in God’s preparation. And, O height of the mountain, you shall never be scattered in God’s discernment. Yet you stand far away as an exile; but it is not in the power of the armed man to snatch you away.

“‘And O bishop of the true city, who in the temple of the cornerstone, ascending into heaven, were cast down upon earth for God’s sake: a stranger to the seed of the world, you desired to become an exile for Christ’s love. O mountain of the enclosed mind, you continually opened your beautiful face in the mirror of the dove. You lay hidden in secret, intoxicated by the fragrance of flowers, shining out to God through the lattices of the saints. Your eye was upon the keys of heaven, because by your clear-sighted life you sold the world. You always possessed this contest in the Lord, gracious confessor.

“‘For in your mind the living fountain drew forth most pure streams in brightest light along the path of salvation. You are a great tower before the altar of the most high God, and you overshadowed the worship of this tower with the smoke of spices. O Disibod, in your light, through examples of pure sound, you built the members of wondrous praise in two parts through the Son of Man. You stand on high, unashamed before the living God, and protect with green dew those who praise God with this voice: “O sweet life, O blessed perseverance, which in this blessed Disibod has always built up glorious light in the heavenly Jerusalem.” Now let there be praise to God, working manfully in the form of beautiful tonsure; and let the heavenly citizens rejoice over those who imitate them in this manner.’”

But you, O Father, who asked these things of me, a poor little form, make yourself such in God’s sight that, when your time in this world fails, your time may be happily prolonged in eternity, so that you may appear in the salvation of the righteous.

## EPISTLE XXXIX

### HELENGER, ABBOT OF ST. DISIBOD, TO HILDEGARD

He accuses himself and complains that regular discipline is poorly observed in his monastery.

To HILDEGARD, his beloved mother, to be embraced above every precious thing, H., her son and steward of the fold of blessed Disibod—alas, not in deed but in name only—wishes whatever is better than temporal good.

Although the whole world cries out in true proclamation that you have been enriched with the Holy Spirit’s jubilation, I, who ought to have been the first to invite others to your blessedness [Col. 0204D], have until now remained hidden in sluggish weariness. But now, at last struck by fear and shame, I have judged it necessary to greet you in words. For over those whom I ought to benefit, I strive rather to rule, seeking my own interests rather than those of others. Yet I have borne the burden and heat of the day in the Lord’s vineyard until now, though lukewarmly, and, with God’s help, I have resolved to persevere until at some time I receive the denarius (Matthew 20).

But now, my mother, at the Lord’s wedding-feast the spiritual wine has wholly failed, because the fervor of monastic religion has almost perished. For the mother of Jesus is not there, nor is Jesus himself, nor are his disciples invited; and thus every adversity rages against us. Therefore there is no need to prolong matters with much wordiness, [Col. 0205A] especially since I am unskilled in speech and knowledge. I know, my mother, I know that from the sole of my foot to the crown of my head there is no goodness in me. Therefore send writings of your consolation to my humility, so that the book of eternal life may have your name in Zion. Farewell.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She exhorts him to amend his life.

In the spiritual vision which is from God, I heard these words: “It is exceedingly necessary for the person who wishes to find his soul in its desires to destroy evil works and to possess blessed knowledge of how to live; and likewise that his soul may be mistress and his flesh handmaid, as the Psalmist says: ‘Blessed is the man whom thou dost instruct, O Lord, and dost teach from thy law’ [Col. 0205B] (Psalm 93).

“And who is this man? Namely, he who has his body as a handmaid and his soul as a most beloved mistress. For even if he is fierce in impiety like a bear, yet rejects that fierceness and pants after the Sun of righteousness, who is pious and merciful, he is pleasing to God; so that God sets him over his commandments, giving him an iron rod in his hand to instruct his sheep toward the mountain of myrrh (Psalm 2).

“Now hear and learn, so that you may blush in the taste of your soul over these things: for at times you have the ways of a bear, which murmurs secretly within itself; at other times also the ways of an ass, because you are not prudent in your affairs but wearisome, and in certain other matters useless. Therefore you do not always carry the bear’s wickedness into effect in impiety. At times you also have the ways of certain birds which are neither among the things above nor among the things below, yet overcome the things above, while the things below cannot harm them.

“To such conduct the noble Father replies: ‘Hey, hey! I did not will this changeableness of your conduct, that your mind should murmur against my righteousness and therefore not seek a right answer concerning it. Yet you conceal within yourself a certain murmuring, according to the murmuring of a bear. And when you possess good understanding, you care little for it and again lapse into weariness, and you do not complete your prayer. But you gladly do the way that pleases your body and do not entirely cut it off from yourself. Moreover, your desires sometimes ascend to me in a certain part that is not wholly holy in deed, but lies only as though in a profession of faith. Yet I have sometimes chosen such persons on account of their changeableness of conduct, that I might hear the sound of their understanding—what they thought of themselves—though they were found useless and fell.

“‘But now let your mind not mock the work that God has made, because you do not know when he may strike you with his sword. I, a poor little form, see in you a blackest fire kindled against us; but forget it in good understanding, lest God’s grace and blessing depart from you during the time of your office. Therefore love God’s righteousness, that you may be loved by God; and faithfully believe his wonders, that you may receive eternal rewards.’”

## EPISTLE XL

[Col. 0206A]

### THE ABBOT OF KEMPTEN TO HILDEGARD

He commends himself to her prayers.

To HILDEGARD, bride of Christ, yet a handmaid acceptable to God and humankind, H., abbot of the Church of Kempten in name alone: devoted service together with continual prayer.

Blessed is God, whose Spirit “breathes where it wills” (John 3), and who is accustomed so to fill and enrich the inner recesses of your heart with the sweetness of heavenly harmony that he has made you exceedingly wonderful and venerable to men and women alike. For now—now, I say—the report of your holiness, spread far and wide, readily shows that he who is mighty has done great things for you (Luke 1); and there is no doubt that he has looked upon you, his humble handmaid, while taking care to instil into you things unheard of by all of us. That heavenly King has now taken you to himself as bride—indeed, as daughter—holding your hand; and, leading you according to his will, has brought you into the chamber where, leaning upon your beloved (Song 3), you have deserved to hear his secrets and diligently proclaim them to mortals. These things befit your holiness, who, as we have learned by report, from the very cradle of infancy heard: “Hear, O daughter, and see” (Ps. 44), etc. And we: “How great are the things that we have heard and known” (Ps. 77). And this: “As we have heard, so have we seen” (Ps. 47). Therefore, that he who began may accomplish in you the efficacy of his own power in these matters, we pray with all our vows; and we humbly beseech that you likewise take care to pray for our sins and disclose to us something concerning our own condition and that of our Church which has been divinely revealed to you.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY. She sends a notable exhortation.

O human being, “turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 16); for a human being has within himself that which continually wanders in the mind and sets before itself a thousandfold number which it by no means accomplishes—just as Adam did not consider what he was doing when he desired to be like God. Yet he did not possess that evil of envying God for having honour and power. O Son of God, cut off every power through faith. For Adam thought that he would rejoice together with God in power and honour, which was great vanity; yet he knew that God was God. Thus it is also present to every human being to know that he has God, whom he believes to be his Creator and deliverer. Therefore flee to God, because in faith you know him to be God, as it is written: “All the nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord, and shall glorify thy name” (Ps. 85).

That is: the human being, who was made together with the creatures, knows that he has God. Therefore let him abide in sound faith, seek and worship God earnestly, and glorify his name. For it belongs to every human being to turn away from that evil of doubting that God exists—the God who created him—but to love him who created and delivered him; and in him to love his neighbour who does him good; and not to imitate the devil, who hated his Creator, though that Creator had bestowed many good things upon him. [Col. 0207A] The devil did not know God by loving him, and therefore does not seek deliverance from him, though he knows him to be above himself. Yet Adam did not reject God in this hateful respect, but in great vanity sought his likeness. The devil did not find in Adam the hatred with which he hates God, but deceived him by his counsel. Thus he ranges about with his thousand arts, seeking the person who doubts in faith.

For by a thousand arts he prevents a human being from doing good. When a person longs to do good works, he sends his darts against him; when he desires to embrace God with all his heart in love, the devil flies over him with harmful disturbance, lest this should be upright before God. And when he seeks the flourishing growth of virtues, the devil says to him in his suggestion that he does not know what he is doing, and teaches him to establish for himself, according to his own peculiarity, a law which he himself knows well. Against these things there is battle, as it is written: “A thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty” (Song 4). This means: the first shield is confession of sins, which the old Law did not possess and was therefore blind. Repentance after confession of sins, as the good shepherd commands, is the garment covering the nakedness of the old Law. Thus the tower of David—her exalted neck—is in the humanity of the Saviour, from which hangs all the armour of the mighty: those who live well in marriage according to the commandment of the Law, the continent, and the virgins, who hang from this tower. All these things the old Law foreshadowed; Christ manifested them in his Incarnation through himself, and after his Ascension he will fulfil them through his disciples and through all who follow them until the last day. These are the thousand shields hanging from it, with which battle is made against the ancient serpent—who seduced the rest in the first human being (Gen. 3)—so that, when a human being stands amid his enemies, he may defend himself with them and fight everywhere, lest he be slain by his enemies.

As the bridegroom speaks to the bride in the Song: “My head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the night” (Song 5). What is said? To Christ Jesus, who is the head of all, human beings are joined as it were like hairs; they are full of offences through the sweetness of the flesh and sinful transgressions. The Church regenerates them anew and purifies them, through repentance and confession, from the foul stench of the dust of sins, just as hairs are shaken and loosened by dew and drops; as wool too is shaken free of dust and cleansed. Thus do you, beloved Son of God, for you shall live eternally; and because you shall be a stone in the heavenly Jerusalem, you must strive zealously.

## EPISTLE XLI

### THE ABBOT OF SAINT MARTIN IN COLOGNE TO HILDEGARD. He commends himself to her prayers.

To HILDEGARD, beloved of God, his lady, A., an unworthy minister of Saint Martin at Cologne, wishes, after the course of this present life, the possession of Paradise in its eternal loveliness.

Lady, lady, truly believed to be beloved [Col. 0208A] and blessed by God: I know assuredly that all which divine power works through you is true and holy. Nor do I doubt that you can obtain whatever you ask from God (John 14), as faithful persons affirm who have proved this in truth. Therefore, as confidently as I dare, I ask your holiness to implore God’s mercy for me, a sinner, that he may deign to grant some consolation to me, who am exceedingly tossed about and labouring in miseries. For my spirit has been unexpectedly distressed within me, and my heart troubled within me (Ps. 142), because of what—alas! through my sins deserving it—I have suffered for many years and suffer now especially; and no one except God can know it, before whose eyes all things are naked and open (Heb. 4).

Because the things I experience concerning myself are known to God alone and could surely not be believed by any mortal if recounted—for he would hear things untried and beyond belief—I beseech you, through the grace of our cooperating and protecting Holy Spirit, that whatever may become known to you through his revelation, or whatever he may deign to show you concerning hope for me, be reported in writing, in every respect as the matter stands, through this most reverend lord abbot, as he himself has promised. Venerable lady in Christ, would that I had been able to come into the presence of your holiness, which I should have desired above all things, and speak with you face to face. Without doubt I would believe that I should explain to you, point by point, what I have hitherto hidden from everyone’s knowledge.

What then? I know, Scripture teaching and Christian faith maintaining it, that no one living in the flesh ought to despair of God’s mercy. Led by this hope, and especially knowing that God is manifestly with you, I have dared to set before you in this letter the causes of my miseries, not doubting that I may in some manner be consoled through you—a thing for which I pray most earnestly, if it is possible. May Christ, your bridegroom, hold you steadfastly in his embraces.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY. She offers a beautiful instruction and great, enduring consolation, with exhortation.

I heard these words from the Living Light: You are like a craftsman who casts many vessels but does not make them shining through fire. Learn from this that your works must not lack the brightness [Col. 0208D] of charity. But surround them with discernment, so that each of your works may be rational. Let these also be done in abstinence, prayer, and the good practice of the saints, who flowed forth like streams from the living fountain and gave people food which they could swallow with joy.

For if thistles are given instead of bread, they cannot be eaten. So too, if teachers speak harsh, grating words to disciples, they do not build them up but lead them into error. A teacher ought to sift the words of his instruction through maternal sweetness, so that disciples may joyfully open their mouths and swallow them. A mill indeed grinds grain and divides it into many kinds. Thus too the planters of the Church took legal precepts from the Old and New Law. The old Law showed, through prophecy, that Christ the Lord would be born; but Christ himself sent forth his word by preaching it throughout the whole earth.

The mill is the old Law, which brought forth in Christ every grain of truth. The pure flour, sifted from all chaff, is virginity, which is the material of every spiritual life in the Church and gives birth to the offspring of obedience. Therefore obedient children are the kiss of Christ’s mouth. A teacher should hold obedient disciples in the embrace of charity, not in the offence of anger, because they are God’s kiss and should be fed with the bread of pure flour. But disobedient children must be given hard flour—that is, harsh correction. To those, however, who entirely abandon obedience, bran must be offered, which those animals that lack understanding eat.

But be prudent, and keep the memory of those who ate manna (John 6); drink from the streams of living water; be peaceful and God-fearing, so that you may flower in his garden amid the flourishing of other good spices. Flee the folly of those who abandon the sun they see and seek another which they neither see nor can find. But flee the new compounders of spices, who want to lay down the law according to their own peculiar will and cannot prevail. Therefore now begin in him who is, so that you may end in him who was and who is to come.

You have been placed by God on two ways: thus he calls you by sound knowledge and protects you from evil knowledge. On these ways are shining works and many sufferings of troubles and afflictions, when you lift yourself by the two wings of the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore three powers must also be added, which God placed in the human being: understanding, sensation, and bodily movement; all of which are known to him according to his capacity. In these three powers and in these two aforesaid ways God holds you. For through the spirit you see God with understanding; through the body you experience evils with sensation. You know good and evil, and you are both spiritual and bodily.

God’s grace calls you through admonition, and the Holy Spirit kindles you with his fire, so that you may love God and ascend to God with good works. [Col. 0209D] But the devil’s suggestion sometimes draws you away from God’s admonition and prevents you from loving God; by his own burning it shows you to be human and consequently declares that it is impossible for you sometimes to do invisible things. The devil’s suggestion blows a certain black and evil changeableness into the human being when it denies God. For when the devil denies that God exists, he knows that he is a deceiver; because when he knows that he himself exists, he knows that God exists.

He has a certain share in the sin of human beings born into the world, through which he tears many in the flesh. Whoever says in his heart that God does not exist (Ps. 52) denies the existence of heaven and earth, of all living things that are in God and with God, and of himself. It is great folly that a human being who sees and knows himself should say doubtfully, “I am not,” for even a little particle of dust does not exist without God. But when a human being overcomes his body in this doubt, he also slays the devil in spiritual wickedness; therefore he shall receive reward and a crown before God, his angels, and all the heavenly host.

The devil’s blast also brings many illicit things before a human being, things which sound knowledge is ashamed to name. His counsel is that vainglory should come upon a human being, as he did where he built a great ruin by which he caused the wheel of human birth to whirl in a torrent (James 3). His burning is that he provokes to very many illicit things the human being whom he knows to have been made in God’s image; and therefore he shows him many impossibilities among created things. Yet he himself has no power in them. Thus he sends his persuasions into a human being, so that the person may accomplish his evil in thought; and so he brings the path of God’s law into derision, so that each person may establish a law for himself, as though he were God, according to the peculiarity of his own will. This greatly pleases the devil, since he wishes neither himself nor anyone else to be subject to God.

But you, O Son of God: God, who created you, desires you through the victory of his warfare, so that you may appear in the eye of his knowledge; for he will not abandon you. Therefore look upon the sun through faith, that you may be a faithful servant; and in the night attend to the moon when vices seek to oppress you. Thus may the fear of the Lord pass through everything in you, and you shall not be harmed, but shall live eternally.

## EPISTLE XLII

### THE ABBESS OF SAINT GLODESINDIS TO HILDEGARD. She sets forth her anxieties and doubts, “because she is compelled to govern many souls.”

To her most beloved sister in Christ, Lady HILDEGARD, A., though unworthy abbess of Saint Glodesindis at Metz, greetings in the true Saviour.

Because we place great confidence in your grace and goodwill, we do not wish you to be unaware that we are set in great danger, since we are compelled to govern many souls though we are not equal to the task. Therefore we earnestly ask your holiness and beseech you in the Lord Jesus to strengthen and exhort our ignorance by your letter: whether we should remain in the obedience imposed upon us, or withdraw so that another may succeed us and do better—if the Lord Jesus should deign to reveal anything concerning this to you. Farewell; and, for God’s sake, pray to God for me, and write back your good pleasure quickly.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY. She gives various counsels for proper governance and makes it sufficiently clear that the office should not be resigned.

Mount Zion is high, and its shadow stretches into the valleys, thereby displaying its height. There are also other mountains in this earthly pilgrimage, by which it is supported and which are beautiful for peoples to behold. In the height of Zion and of the other mountains are signified prelates and teachers, who are the support of the Church; and female disciples are called daughters of Zion. But if this mountain were to fall, or if others were to destroy it, it would be a great wrong. Therefore everyone who holds a teaching office should carefully consider how he may lay down his office and how he may be deposed by others.

For just as mountains provide protection to many of their inferiors, so those who stand in the teaching office are, through doctrine and the obedience rendered to them in God, a defence of many against the snares of their enemies. Therefore, as long as any teacher can utter words of instruction, he should not cast away the rod of correction which he received from God’s hand. For mud is often cast out by mud, just as teacher and disciples are cleansed through one another. For fear of his disciples, the teacher will afflict himself and be punished by the torments caused by unruly disciples, so that he may imitate the supreme Teacher who thus went before him. And he shall say: “I showed them thy commandments” (Exod. 18), etc. He shall also say: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13).

Learn from these things not to flee because of the cloud of your disciples’ instability, nor because of weariness from labour. For many flee more because of the weariness of labour than because of that necessity—that they cannot overcome their disciples. A clear day, not darkened by a storm, possesses joy in fullness. Adam possessed it before the Fall. But the first deceitful deceiver darkened that day by his suggestion; and within it are seven wounds which wound the soul.

The first wound is vainglory, which gathers to itself what it neither harvested nor sowed and claims for itself what was not given it by God. The first deceiver taught this, because he himself had done it; and therefore vainglory does not seek God. The second is that a human being realizes that he can sin and then stores up for himself pleasure of the flesh, embracing and kissing that pleasure through taste. The third builds ruin, with great pains, amid squalid habits, so that a person lives as if dead to God and scarcely even hopes that God knows him.

The fourth is deception, by which a person excuses and defends himself concerning the aforementioned sins, claiming that they are not dangerous enough to be shown to him; and thus he becomes so hateful toward people that he trusts no one. The fifth is pride, which says that a person cannot abstain from sins because of the flesh of his humanity and that it would therefore be unsuitable to depart from fleshly desires. Pride rashly lays down this law for itself and therefore has no regard for God. The sixth wound is that a human being seeks his salvation from a creature and asks it to show him everything; thus he holds his Creator in derision and asks nothing of him, as though he could not help him. The seventh wound is the bondage of idolatry, which worships the devil and despises God.

These seven vices have, as an army subject to them in their affairs, more than the number of branches on a tree, because all these things lay hidden in the transgression of eating—that which Adam ate. Therefore God said to him: “In the hour in which you eat, you shall die by death” (Gen. 3). God gave him this commandment lest he do anything like the devil—that is, exist without a commandment, as the devil wished to exist. Therefore no human being can be secure in this life because of the first suggestion of the devil that Adam accepted.

Therefore, O daughter of God, gird yourself with the most powerful armour of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which you may subdue these seven vices, lest you be wounded while mourning over them. Rise as a good soldier, overcoming them in the strongest battles, so that you may live eternally. May God see you, O daughter, in the mirror of salvation.

## EPISTLE XLIII

### A CERTAIN PRIEST TO HILDEGARD. He asks to be instructed about Christ’s body and blood.

To HILDEGARD, the chaste dove hiding in the clefts of the rock (Song 2), C., the least priest among Christ’s servants, offers the devotion of his deepest prayer and whatever pertains to eternal salvation.

Because by God’s grace your light shines beneficially before men (Matt. 5), I glorify your Father, who has set you forth as a burning lamp for the illumination of the Church. Though frail and sinful, I nevertheless rejoice from my heart in your holiness, since by a singular privilege you cleave to the embraces of the heavenly bridegroom. I also wish your charity not to be unaware that day and night I desire to see you face to face; making constant remembrance of you in my prayers, I sometimes embrace you in mind, though absent in body, as though present.

Therefore I most humbly beseech your perfection to commend me to your bridegroom, under whose shadow you rest, as one begging beside the way (Mark 10), lest the passing crowd silence my cry; but that, brought to the Lord by your prayers, I may deserve to be enlightened and healed of the blindness of my heart. Teach me also concerning Christ’s body and blood, in which lies the whole hope of the faithful. Make known to me in the Lord how you see, in the spirit, a priest who approaches the same sacrament while uncorrected or corrected. May the Lord, who is in all things and above all things, pour into you those things which befit the glory of his holy Church. Farewell.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY. Concerning Christ’s body and blood.

[Col. 0212D]

**[AUGUSTINE.]** In a true vision, with wakeful eyes, I heard and saw these words concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body: God remained what he was, and assumed what he was not. That is: the Godhead remained eternally as it was before time, as though it were not divided at all. But the Incarnation of the Son, which had not yet appeared as flesh and blood, lay hidden before time, predestined in the Father’s heart.

At the time when it was predestined, the Son put on flesh and girded himself with the strength of his power, as it is written: “The Lord is clothed with strength; he has girded himself” (Ps. 92). The angel announced these garments of the holy Incarnation to the simplicity of the Virgin (Luke 1), in whom he found the foundation of humility, as God had established it, because she called herself the handmaid of the Lord. There the same angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (ibid.).

For the Holy Spirit visited her more excellently than all human knowledge, pouring himself into her in a manner unlike that in which he would ever be poured into any woman in giving birth; and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, since in its warmth it so soothed her as entirely to wipe away from her every heat of sin by its sweetest overshadowing, just as a person seeks shade because of the sun’s heat. Thus the same power of the Most High which fashioned flesh in the Virgin’s womb converts, upon the altar and at the priest’s words, the offering of bread and wine into the sacrament of flesh and blood, nourishing it by its power.

Therefore the birth, Passion, burial, Resurrection, and Ascension of the Son of the heavenly Father appear in this same sacrament, just as the circle of a coin displays its lord. This occurs so that the wounds of human beings—who are entangled in sins through Adam’s transgression and continually sinning in their sins—may be healed, wiped clean, and anointed in Christ’s wounds and blood; and thus they may become his members. This will continue until the last day.

And again I saw this: even if a priest lacks the dignity of holiness because of the many corrupt scars of his sins, nevertheless, if he is not bound by the bond of a superior master, the power of the Most High performs its miracles in that same offering. All who receive the same sacrament faithfully from his hand are illuminated as by a ray of sunlight. But if he is righteous in faith and works, his soul is illumined above the radiant brightness of the sun.

But all who, by the counsel of the ancient serpent, perpetrate delusions and schisms in this most holy offering are like the lost angels, who denied that God is one in his honour when they wished to be like him. Thus these people wish to accomplish the peculiarity of their own will through these sacraments, and consequently perish with those angels unless they run to God through confession of sins, repentance for them, and a tearful cry, saying: “Ah, ah, for we have sinned” (Lam. 3). Then God the Father receives those who wounded his Son through ignorance.

The Sadducees, who err in every way, obstinately deny this sacrament and the resurrection of life, as though someone should err by saying that flesh without spirit and spirit without flesh are a human being—which cannot possibly be. Therefore these people are worse than all other erring persons: since even the smallest creature made by God cannot be completed merely by one designation, how could a human being, who comprehends every creature, be defined by one designation? Winter dries up and summer flowers; nevertheless, winter retains its greenness for summer until summer brings forth its fruits in fullness. Such are body and soul: the body fails, but the soul remains in unfailing life, wherever it may be.

## EPISTLE XLIV

### THE ABBESS AT ELOSTAT TO HILDEGARD. She is greatly troubled in governing as abbess.

To HILDEGARD, her lady, O., unworthy governor of Christ’s handmaids at Elostat, wishes, through her who has intimately tasted the heavenly gift, to attain that perfect good.

Blessed is Jesus Christ, whose good fragrance you are to God in every place (2 Cor. 2), because no longer merely the fragrance of balsam but the very substance of sacred ointment has flowed into you. Its most sweet fragrance has so made your name pleasant to the hearts and ears of all that all alike commend the marks of your humility and graciousness and glorify in you your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).
