Therefore, blessed mother, grant pardon and bear with no small part of my folly; indeed, allow my great folly briefly to disclose before you the sorrow of my heart, and when you have heard it, I beseech you, console your handmaid. For I bear an unbearable burden, since I am commanded to correct the crookednesses of my sisters, while I can scarcely avoid even a few of the dangers which assail me everywhere (2 Cor. 11). Therefore, when you go forth to see King Solomon in his beauty, remember those things which I have asked of you with my whole heart. Farewell.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY. She kindly exhorts the abbess to continue labouring for her community, but indicates that prudence is necessary in God’s service.

O daughter of God, as long as you have ability among his daughters, labour; and, sighing to God in faint-heartedness, keep your rule, for your labour cries out and prays to God. For the human being who labours in the cavern of God’s righteousness and on the narrow way (Matt. 7), yet assents to Adam’s fall, seeks the scourges of repentance for it; and let no one doubt that after the scourges of repentance the heavenly gate receives him.

For whoever tears up the field of his body through discernment will not be harmed by the sudden onset of death, because the harmony of the Holy Spirit and joyful life will receive him. But one must beware lest through an excess of labours a person kill his own body; rather, let him restrain sins with rationality. Daughter, remember that you do not have the power to create a human being. Therefore gently pray to God that he may give you a better life; this is more acceptable to God than imploring him in excessive sorrow. May God make you a temple of life.

## EPISTLE XLV

### ELIZABETH, MISTRESS AT SCHÖNAU, TO HILDEGARD. She asks for prayers and words of consolation.

To Lady HILDEGARD, venerable mistress of Christ’s brides who are at Pingia, E., a humble nun and mistress of the sisters at Schönau, offers devoted prayers with all affection.

May the grace and consolation of the Most High fill us with joy. For I learned from the words of my comforter, whom you carefully urged to comfort me, that you had kindly shared my distress. As you said had been revealed to you concerning me, I confess that I recently conceived in my mind a certain cloud of disturbance because of the foolish talk of people who say many untrue things about me. I could easily bear the talk of the crowd, if those too who walk in religious habit did not more bitterly grieve my spirit. For they also, driven by I know not what goads, mock the grace of God in me and do not fear rashly to judge things they do not know.

I hear that some people circulate letters written from their own spirit under my name. They have spread the report that I prophesied about the day of judgment (Matt. 24), which I certainly never presumed to do, since knowledge of its coming escapes all mortals. Yet I shall reveal to you the origin of this report, so that you may say whether I have acted or spoken anything presumptuously in the matter.

As you have heard through others, the Lord “has magnified his mercy” (Luke 1) toward me beyond what I deserved or could in any way deserve, so much so that he has frequently deigned to reveal to me certain heavenly mysteries. He also frequently indicated to me through his angel what would come upon the people in these days unless they repented of their wickedness, and commanded me to announce these things publicly. But, in order to avoid arrogance and lest I appear an author of novelties, I endeavoured, so far as I could, to conceal all these things.

[Col. 0215C] Therefore, when on a certain Sunday, according to my usual custom, I was in an ecstasy of mind, the angel of the Lord stood before me and said: “Why do you hide gold in mud?” That is, why do you hide the word of God which has been sent through your mouth into the earth—not to be concealed, but to be made known for the praise and glory of our Lord and the salvation of the souls of his people? Having said this, he raised a scourge over me and, as though in great anger, struck me most bitterly five times, so that for three days my entire body was weak from that blow. After this he placed his finger upon my mouth and said: “You shall be silent until the ninth hour, when you shall make known what the Lord has done with you.” I indeed remained mute until the ninth hour.

Then I signalled to my mistress to bring me a certain little book which I had hidden in my bed, containing in part the things the Lord had done with me. When I offered it into the hands of the lord abbot who had come to visit me, my tongue was loosed into these words: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to thy name” (Ps. 113). Afterward, when I had also revealed to him certain other matters which I had not wished to be committed to writing—namely, the great vengeance of the Lord which, I had learned from the angel, would soon come upon the entire world—I earnestly asked him to keep that word hidden with himself.

But I was commanded to devote myself to prayer and ask the Lord to give me understanding whether he wished what I had said to be covered in silence or not. After I had afflicted myself for some time, persisting in prayer about this matter, during Advent, on the feast of Saint Barbara, during the first watch of the night I fell into ecstasy. The angel of the Lord stood before me and said: “Cry aloud and say: Alas, to all nations, for the whole world has been turned into darkness. And you shall say: Come forth! He who formed you from the earth calls you and says: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of God is near’” (Matt. 3).

Moved by this address, the lord abbot began to publish the word before Church authorities and religious men. Some received it with reverence; others did not, but spoke maliciously. Thus it came about that many among whom this message had been circulated afflicted themselves throughout the season of Lent in great fear through repentance and devoted themselves to alms and prayers. At that time a certain person, led by I know not what zeal, sent letters to the city of Cologne in the lord abbot’s name, without his knowledge—God knows—in which certain terrible threats were read aloud before all the people. Therefore, although foolish people mocked us, prudent persons nevertheless, as we heard, gave respectful heed to the message and did not scorn to honour God with fruits of repentance.

It happened on the Wednesday before Easter, when after great bodily labours I had entered ecstasy, that the angel of the Lord appeared to me. I said to him: “Lord, what will become of the word which you spoke to me?” He answered: “Do not grieve or be troubled if what I foretold does not occur on the day I appointed for you, because the Lord has been appeased by the satisfaction of many.” After this, on Friday about the third hour, I entered an ecstasy of mind in severe suffering, and he again stood before me and said: “The Lord has seen the affliction of his people” (Exod. 3) “and has turned away the wrath of his indignation from them” (Ps. 84).

I said to him: “What then, my Lord? Shall I not be an object of mockery to all among whom this word has been circulated?” He said: “Bear patiently and willingly everything that has happened to you on this occasion. Give careful heed to him who, though he was Creator of the whole world, endured the mockery of human beings. Now the Lord is testing your patience for the first time.”

Behold, my lady, I have explained to you the entire course of the matter, so that you may know my innocence and that of my abbot, and may be able to make it known to others. I beseech you to make me a participant in your prayers and, as the Spirit of the Lord suggests to you, to write back some words of consolation to me. The grace of Christ be with you.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY. She says that she does not speak from her own intellect but from the “Serene Light.” She discusses the human being and the inspiration of God, by which he deigns to illuminate some persons above others.

I, a poor little woman and earthen vessel, say these things not from myself but from the serene light: Man is a vessel which God built for himself and filled with his inspiration, so that he might accomplish his works in it; for God [Col. 0217A] does not work as a human being does, but at the command of his ordinance all things are perfected. Herbs, plants, and trees appeared; likewise the sun, moon, and stars came forth in their appointed service; and the waters produced fish and birds; and, I pray, beasts also arose, all of which serve humankind, as God established them (Gen. I). Man alone, however, did not acknowledge him. For when God had prepared great knowledge for man, man exalted himself in his own mind and turned away from God. The God of all had so regarded him that he might perfect all his works in him. But the ancient deceiver beguiled him and infected him with the crime of disobedience, through the delight of an unsuitable wind, while he sought more than he ought. Ah, woe! Then all the elements involved themselves in the alternation of light [Col. 0217B] and darkness, just as man did in transgressing God’s commands. Yet God watered certain human beings, lest humankind be wholly brought to derision. Abel was good, but Cain a murderer (Gen. IV). Many saw God’s mysteries in the light, but others committed very many sins, until that time came in which the Word of God shone forth, as it is said: “Fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. XLIV).

Then the Sun of righteousness came forth and illuminated people in faith and works by good works, just as the dawn first appears and the remaining hours of the day follow, until night approaches. Thus, O daughter Elisabeth, the world changes. For the world is now weary in every greenness of virtues: that is, in the dawn, the first, the third, and most strongly the sixth hour of the day. And [Col. 0217C] therefore at this time it is necessary for God to water certain people, lest his instruments remain idle. Hear, O anxious daughter: the ambitious prompting of the ancient serpent somewhat afflicts those people whom God’s inspiration has thus imbued. For when that serpent sees an elegant gem, he immediately roars, saying, “What is this?” And he afflicts it with many miseries of a burning mind that wishes to fly above the clouds, as though they were gods, as he himself does.

Now hear again: those who desire to accomplish God’s works must always attend to the fact that they are earthen vessels (II Cor. IV), since they are human beings; and they must always consider what they are and what they will be. Let them leave heavenly matters to him who is heavenly, for they are exiles, ignorant of heavenly things, but merely singing God’s mysteries—like a trumpet, which gives sounds only and does not act, but into which another breathes so that it may give forth a sound. Let them also put on the breastplate of faith, being gentle, meek, poor, and wretched, just as that Lamb was whose trumpet-sound they themselves are; and let them have the simple manners of a child. For God continually scourges those who sing upon his trumpet, foreseeing that their earthen vessel may not perish but may please him. O daughter, may God make you a mirror of life. And may he help me also, who lie in the faint-heartedness of fear, sometimes sounding a little, like the small sound of a trumpet, from the living [Col. 0218A] light, that I may remain in his service.

## LETTER XLVI

### THE PROVOST AT FRANKFURT TO HILDEGARD

He commends himself to her prayers.

To Hildegard, his lady beloved in Christ, G., provost in Frankfurt only in name: after Martha’s labor, Mary’s consolation.

I have longed greatly to behold your person. But since various affairs have hindered us, God has at least now given us the opportunity through letters to embrace and greet you. Nor do we wish you to be ignorant of our name and person; together with our greeting, we wish to embrace and honor you with every diligence, and to beseech God for you, to the extent of our power, day and night [Col. 0218B]. We therefore ask your clemency to be willing to remember me, a sinner, before the mercy of the divine majesty. Farewell, while “today” is spoken in the heavenly realm.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She urges him to amend his conduct.

In a true vision I saw and heard these words: The first light of day glows red; afterward dawn is unveiled, and sometimes it is entangled in a great shifting of clouds. Then the north wind rises and makes great sighing, because the earlier times of day were beautiful without the shifting of storm. Therefore, O man who possesses knowledge of good and evil, consider carefully what your conduct has been and what works have stood before God from your childhood, lest the zeal of the Lord strike you, and lest your soul, when it departs from your body, [Col. 0218C] say: “Alas for me! Where am I walking? Where shall I go? What kind of days await me? What deeds affect me? Those, namely, which the mill of my body has supplied to me.” Beware also lest you tremble when the heavenly citizens say to you: “See what God is like. Now you shall live forever.”

## LETTER XLVII. TO THE PRELATES OF MAINZ

Concerning the divine offices forbidden to them by these prelates.

[Note: [Col. 0217] See the Commentary on the Life and Deeds of St Hildegard, prefixed to this volume, § XI, nos. 163 and following, col. 63.]

In the vision which was impressed upon my soul by God the Maker before I came forth to be born, I was compelled to write these things concerning the bond by which we have been bound by our superiors because of a certain dead man, who was buried among us without accusation, under the care of his priest. [Col. 0218D] A few days after his burial, when those same superiors ordered us to cast him out of our cemetery, I was seized with no slight terror. As was my custom, I looked to the true light, and with wakeful eyes I saw in my soul that, if the body of that dead man were carried out according to their command, that expulsion, in the form of a great blackness, would threaten grave danger to our place and would surround us like a dark cloud that commonly appears before storms and thunder.

Therefore we have not presumed to remove the body of the deceased—who had confessed, been anointed, and received communion, and had been buried without objection—nor have we acquiesced in the counsel or command of those urging or ordering this. This was not because we wholly despised the counsel of worthy persons or of our prelates, but lest we should seem, with womanly harshness, to inflict injury upon Christ’s sacraments, with which he had been fortified while still alive. Yet, lest we should be entirely disobedient, we have hitherto ceased, according to their prohibition, from the songs of divine praise and from partaking of the Lord’s body, from which, although we had customarily communicated nearly every month, [Col. 0219A] we have abstained.

While both I and all my sisters were afflicted with great bitterness over this and held in immense sorrow, at last, oppressed by a great burden, I heard these words in a vision: “It is not expedient for you to forsake, because of human words, the sacraments of the garment of my Word, which is your salvation and which was born in virginal nature from the Virgin Mary. But you must seek permission for this from your prelates who have bound you.”

For since Adam was driven from the bright region of Paradise into the exile of this world (Gen. III), the conception of all human beings has been corrupted as a consequence of the first transgression. Therefore it was necessary, by God’s impenetrable counsel, that from human nature a human being should be born without the contagion of every injury, through whom all predestined to life might be cleansed from every defilement; and that he might remain in them, and they in him, always for their protection, being sanctified by sharing his body. But whoever, like Adam, is disobedient to God’s commands and wholly forgets him must be separated from his body, just as by disobedience that person has turned away from him, until, purified through penance, he is again permitted by his superiors to partake of the same body of the Lord. But whoever knows himself to be under such a bond neither in conscience nor in will may safely approach reception of the life-giving sacrament, to be cleansed by the blood of the immaculate Lamb, who, obedient to the Father, permitted himself to be sacrificed on the altar of the cross in order to restore salvation to all.

In the same vision I also heard that I was blameworthy in this: that I had not come with all humility and devotion into the presence of my superiors to seek from them permission to communicate—especially since we were not liable to blame for receiving that dead man, who had been fortified with every Christian rite by his priest and buried, without anyone’s objection, with the entire procession of Pingensis. [Col. 0219D] Thus these things have been divinely imposed on me to announce to you, lords and prelates.

I also saw something concerning the fact that, while obeying you and thus far abstaining from the singing of the divine office, we celebrate it only by reading, and that faintly. I heard a voice proceeding from the living light concerning the different kinds of praises of which David says in the Psalms: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psaltery and harp” (Ps. CL), and so on, up to: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (ibid.). By these words we are instructed through outward things concerning inward things: how, according to the construction and character of material instruments, we ought especially to direct and shape the offices of our inward person toward the praises of the Creator.

When we attend diligently to these things, we recall how man sought the voice of the living Spirit, which Adam lost through disobedience. Before his transgression, while still innocent, Adam had no small fellowship with the voices of angelic praise, which the angels possess by their spiritual nature, being ever called by the Spirit who is God. Adam therefore lost the likeness of the angelic voice which he had in Paradise; and in the knowledge with which he had been endowed before sin, he fell asleep in such a way as one awakened from sleep becomes unaware and uncertain of the things he had seen in dreams, when, deceived by the devil’s suggestion and resisting the will of his Creator, he was, as a consequence of his iniquity, enveloped in the darkness of inward ignorance. [Col. 0220B]

But God, who preserves the souls of the elect by the light of truth for their former blessedness, devised this by his counsel: that at times he might renew the hearts of very many by the infusion of the prophetic Spirit, so that by that inward illumination they might recover in some measure what Adam had possessed before the punishment of his transgression.

Moreover, so that they might remember that divine sweetness and praise in which Adam himself delighted in God before he fell, and might not remember it in this exile [the printed negation is problematic], and might also be stirred toward these things, the same holy prophets, instructed by the same Spirit they had received, composed not only psalms and canticles to be sung for inflaming the devotion of their hearers, but also diverse instruments of the musical art, to render them with manifold sounds. They did this so that hearers, as stated above, instructed and exercised through outward things—both through the forms and qualities of those instruments and through the meaning of the words recited with them—might be taught concerning inward things. [Col. 0220C]

Those holy prophets were imitated by zealous and learned persons, who also discovered by human skill certain kinds of instruments, so that they might sing according to the delight of the soul. They adapted what they sang to the joints of their fingers, which bend in flexion, so that, recalling Adam formed by the finger of God, which is the Holy Spirit—in whose voice there was, before Adam sinned, the sound of every harmony and the sweetness of all musical art—they might understand that, if he had remained in the state in which he was formed, the frailty of mortal humankind could by no means bear the power and resonance of that voice.

When the devil, his deceiver, heard that man had begun to sing by God’s inspiration and was thereby invited to remember the sweetness of the songs of the heavenly homeland, he saw the devices of his cunning brought to nothing. He was therefore so terrified that he was grievously tormented by it; and afterward, through manifold contrivances of his wickedness, he continually strives and seeks to devise ways not only to disturb or take away from the human heart, through evil suggestions, unclean thoughts, or diverse occupations, but also from the heart of the Church, wherever he can, through dissensions, scandals, or unjust oppressions, the confession and beauty of divine praise [Col. 0221A] and of spiritual hymns.

Therefore you and all prelates must labor with the greatest vigilance. Before you close by sentence the mouth of any church that sings praises to God, or suspend it from administering or receiving the sacraments, you must first investigate and examine with the greatest care the causes for which this should be done.

You must take care that you are drawn to this only by zeal for God’s justice, not by indignation, an unjust impulse of mind, or desire for vengeance. Always beware lest Satan deceive you in your judgments—Satan who drew humankind away from heavenly harmony and the delights of Paradise. Consider, therefore, that as the body of Jesus Christ was born from the Holy Spirit out of the intact Virgin Mary, [Col. 0221B] so too the song of praise, according to heavenly harmony, is rooted in the Church through the Holy Spirit. The body is the garment of the soul, which has a living voice; therefore it is fitting that the body, together with the soul, should sing praises to God through the voice.

Thus the prophetic Spirit, by symbolic signification, commands that God be praised with cymbals of jubilation and other musical instruments (Ps. CL), which the wise and diligent have discovered; for all arts pertaining to human use and necessity have been discovered from the breath which God sent into the human body (Gen. II). Therefore it is right that God be praised in all things. And because, on hearing a song, a person often sighs and groans, recalling the soul’s nature of heavenly harmony, the prophetic Spirit, considering and knowing this nature—for the soul is symphonic—exhorts in the psalm that we “give thanks to the Lord with the harp” and “make melody to him with the ten-stringed psaltery” (Pss. XXXII, XCI): wishing the harp, which sounds below, to refer to the discipline of the body; the psaltery, which gives forth sound from above, to the intent of the spirit; and the ten strings to contemplation of the Law.

Those, therefore, who impose silence upon the Church in songs of God’s praise without the weight of certain reason shall lack fellowship with angelic praises in heaven, since they have unjustly robbed God on earth of the beauty of his praise, unless they amend this through true repentance and humble satisfaction (Wis. XI). Therefore those who hold the keys of heaven must strictly beware [Col. 0221D] lest they open what ought to be closed and close what ought to be opened; for “the harshest judgment will be upon those who preside,” unless, as the Apostle says, they preside with diligence (Rom. XII).

And I heard a voice saying: “Who created heaven? God. Who opens heaven to his faithful? God. Who is like him? No one. Therefore, O faithful ones, let none of you resist or oppose him, lest his strength fall upon you and you be unable to have any helper to defend you in his judgment. This is a womanly time, because God’s justice is weak. But the strength of God’s justice sweats forth and stands as a warrior against injustice, so that injustice, defeated, may fall.”

O true Wisdom, who are the eternal God without any beginning or formation: what great mysteries you made in creatures subject to your work, namely humankind, when you sent forth the powers of your might in creation! [Col. 0222A] You made the beautiful roof with its most beautiful windows—the firmament with its luminaries—and in it you placed the sun, which by its light rules and illuminates all things above the earth and beneath it. The other lights also cleave to it and shine through it, just as all creatures obey you and have life in you according to their kind.

But you, the highest, touched the lowest creature and clothed yourself in humanity from it, through which you wholly overcame your enemy, who through envy seduced in Paradise the human being whom you had formed. For you, true Love, eternal God, having wisely created, ordered, and prepared all your creatures, finally formed man as one to be called, as it were, to a prepared banquet, in a very brief interval. This is called the beginning of day, when dawn rises before the sun; and at once you breathed into him the breath of life (Gen. II), just as the sun immediately after dawn sends forth its rays in shining. The breath of life is the soul, which is fire; its flame is rationality, through which the powers of the soul are known in the knowledge of good and evil, just as the sun is known through its brightness.

The interval in which the Lord placed Adam in Paradise and showed him the glorious delight of that Paradise, granting him every fruit thereof except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, was as though from the first to the third hour. The interval in which Adam named all the animals and birds of heaven, which he saw and knew in the vision of his knowledge, and in which he heard the Lord speaking to him in the splendor of his divinity, extended as though from the third to the sixth hour. For at that time God appeared to him in the eastern region; Adam saw not his face, but a certain brightness of his face. Made glad by that knowledge, God cast him into sleep. Thus, happy in spirit and desiring sleep, he fell asleep like a son before his father. [Col. 0222C]

In that sleep God raised Adam’s spirit to that height from which he had sent it into his body with knowledge of good and evil, and showed beforehand the things that were to come—namely, concerning his offspring, for filling the heavenly Jerusalem. In that same sleep he took a rib from him and built it into a woman. When she was brought and seen, Adam rejoiced greatly. He and his wife, considering what they ought first to eat or do, stood there; she, standing nearer the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, awaited her husband. But the ancient serpent, perceiving that she looked toward another, as angels look toward the Lord, undertook to deceive her. The interval in which these things occurred was as though from the sixth to the ninth hour.

The woman whom the Lord had built in Paradise from the rib of the living man (ibid.), while God had in his foreknowledge and foresaw that Life, through whom all life subsists, would one day descend into a woman, through whom man would enter the glory of the heavenly Paradise—this woman, deceived by the serpent, offered the food of death to her husband. When they had thus been stripped of their brightness, the brightness of God, which had earlier appeared to Adam, appeared to them like a flame in the southern region and said: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. III). By this he prefigured what he had in his good pleasure: that he would seek and draw him back through the garment of his humanity, to be assumed from female form. And the day of their salvation had declined. This interval was as though from the ninth hour of day until evening. Afterward, expelled from Paradise, they came into the world and found night already upon the earth. Then, too, according to human nature, they discovered all things necessary for themselves and the other animals and appropriated them for their use. [Col. 0223A]

These things are spoken by him who, breathing life and mind, is the one God. The mind of almighty God is his Son, to whom the work belongs, namely every creature; for through the Word of God, who is his Son, all things were made (John I), which were vivified by the breathing Life in the height of heaven and in the lowest region, which is earth, an obstacle to the shining things above. God granted his work the capacity to praise and to act. And because he is the standard-bearing warrior against his enemies, the dwellers in darkness, he assigns to darkness all who attribute to themselves what the grace of the Holy Spirit has worked in them. They are called apostates, because they look to themselves rather than to the Raiser of life; and, with the blindness of their knowledge, they cast behind them the paternal service which they ought to render him. They, with all the works they have stored up for themselves in darkness, which were done without him, [Col. 0223C] shall be tormented with him who wished to be like the Most High (Isa. XIV).

For such persons are the devil’s entrails, because they act by his counsel, are stripped of the brightness of divine light, and, at the instigation of that tyrant, destroy the Scripture and doctrine dictated by the Holy Spirit. As heaven cannot be rent before its time, so neither can the words of the Holy Spirit be changed.

Concerning the priestly office, which was shown in the first priest Melchizedek in the shadow of God’s miracles (Gen. XIV), and which was hidden from human beings before him because, through their softness, they could not receive it, God showed me these things: I saw a cloud glowing like dawn, [Col. 0223D] and in it a ram hanging in thorns, just as the ram offered in place of Abraham’s son hung there (Gen. XXII). Its horns were like sapphire and gave forth from themselves the radiance of topaz; its whole body appeared the color of a white cloud.

This ram signifies Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who, without admixture of any contagion, was born most white from virginal nature. Its sapphire horns signify his sweetest and coeternal brightness, through which, in true humility, he assumed humanity in order to free lost man. He came forth, God and man born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; this is expressed by the radiance of topaz shining from the sapphire horns. The cloud glowing like dawn signifies the multitude of angels who minister to the sacrament of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, accomplished through the power of the Most High. This power overshadowed Mary, as she conceived the same Son of God from the Holy Spirit, from every heat of human will; and the ram hanging in the thorns, as stated above, signifies him.

The thorns signify the nails by which his body was fastened to the cross, the lance by which his side was pierced (John XIX), and the harshness of his entire passion, which he endured most patiently as the gentlest lamb for our sins. For among animals the sheep is patient, humble, gentle, and clean. Therefore God also gave garments of skins to the first human beings, who through disobedience had been stripped of the brightness with which they were clothed: he gave them sheep-skins for clothing and set the sheep’s meanings against the cunning of the ancient serpent; he covered them with such a garment lest they depart Paradise naked (Gen. III). [Col. 0224B]

For the eternal God, who eternally possessed in his knowledge the garment—that is, the humanity—of his Son, in whose image he made man, as Moses testifies that man was created in the image and likeness of God (Gen. I), called the deceived man and clothed him in such a garment. By this he showed that his unique and coeternal Son, the Word, whom he commanded to be clothed in humanity from virginal nature in order to seek and free man, would, in the signification of a sheep, be patient, humble, gentle, and clean without any stain of contagion.

John the Baptist and the other prophets, understanding this in the Holy Spirit, very often call him by the name of Lamb and sheep (John I). For he is the immaculate Lamb, “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. XLIV), who was conceived not from male seed but through the Holy Spirit, by the power of the most high God, and came forth, God and man, born of the flesh of the Virgin Mary.

By that same power of the most high God, the offering of bread with wine and water is transubstantiated, at the priest’s words, into the flesh and blood of the Savior which he assumed from the Virgin Mary, just as wood is changed by the heat of fire into a burning coal. Through this sacrament of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, who, as he himself testifies, is the living bread (John VI), the souls of those to be saved [Col. 0224D] are nourished.

Therefore, O priests ordained to the Lord’s table, prepare yourselves to sacrifice the fatted calf (Luke XV), which lacks every leanness of sins. Clothe yourselves with the breastplate of true faith and the shield of hope in eternal life (Eph. VI), and surround your neck with the stole of observance of God’s commandments, so that you may serve him fittingly. For you are angels of the Lord of hosts (Mal. II); because just as God was incarnate from the Virgin Mary at the words of the angel Gabriel (Luke I), so that through his birth, passion, and ascension lost humanity might be freed and saved, so at your words the same body and blood of the same Son of God are made, with a representation of his birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension, for our salvation and that of all the faithful, [Col. 0225A] both living and dead.

Run therefore with longing and joyful heart to the ministry of the immaculate Lamb, from which much salvation comes to you and the other faithful. On account of its celebration sins are forgiven, souls are freed, and many dangers of soul and body are escaped. The holiness of this sacrament is invisible to us, just as we cannot see God or any incorporeal creature; yet through it our soul and body are sanctified and invisibly refreshed through forgiveness of sins. But if anything unworthy happens to the Lord’s body—for example, if it seems to decay or to be gnawed or consumed by an animal—these things occur only in the visible sacrament, or in its outward appearance alone; the power and grace of the sacrament itself remain divinely preserved whole and incorrupt.

When the priest speaks over and over God’s words, the body of the incarnate Word of God is made anew: through him all creatures came forth which had not previously appeared, and he also was incarnate from the Virgin Mary, as it were in the moment of a blink, when she humbly said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke I). The flesh of that Word of God blossoms in the priest’s words, and the transformed flesh remains. The Lord Jesus Christ had not yet suffered when he spoke these words and foretold to his disciples that he would suffer and pour out his blood for the washing away of sins—that is, a washing which could not occur through any flesh before him, but through his flesh, which is divine, without the bruise of sin, from the fire of the Father. [Col. 0225C]

In the words spoken separately by the priest over each sacrifice, by the power of the Most High, the sacrament of the body and blood of Jesus Christ is made separately, as it were in the moment of a blink. When the service of the altar has been fittingly completed, much forgiveness of sins comes to the living and the dead. But if, through negligence, wine and water are lacking, or water alone is present, the Lord’s body is made in the aforesaid words, containing blood within itself. Yet the blood which was shed in his passion is not made in the chalice, because wine and water were lacking or water alone was present. Therefore the same words and signs must be repeated anew, because the sacrifice of wine and water was omitted; and immediately from water and wine blood is made—not dry, but whole and flowing—while the body remains as it was made in the preceding words. It is, however, adorned with the blood that had previously been lacking and with the joy of the Redeemer through which man was freed. [Col. 0225D]

These things, son of God, shown to me in the true light, I have written to you so that you may become a priest of God with a joyful heart. May the Holy Spirit bring it about that you imitate the Lamb of God in true humility, patience, and gentleness; that you wash away through true repentance the daily sins which cannot be avoided; and may almighty God preserve you from the burden of grave sins, which are committed as though at a banquet, so that while you live you may serve him in purity and, after the end of this life, rejoice eternally with him in the highest blessedness.

O servant of God, who in good will gathers many things to yourself for your own benefit and that of others, yet are blameworthy in this: you do not diligently turn over the good soil in the field of your Lord. Hear: In the matter which you entrusted to me, I see clearly in this respect that through you it is prevented that the goods of that church should be squandered by a useless provost. But in this brightness I cannot at all see that through you the religious life of the spirit will be restored among them. For just as a muddy well, foul and long-standing with the rot of unclean worms, cannot easily be cleansed, so too the evil habit of sins will be difficult to prevent among them. Whoever drives off and pursues a wolf so that the sheep are not snatched away by it, and then afterward leads them to right pasture, does well. Now, however, choose, by the counsel of good and holy persons, what is better for you according to the present state of the Church: namely, that the lesser evil should be chosen. [Col. 0226B]

“While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, gave it to his disciples, and said: ‘Take and eat: this is my body’” (Matt. XXVI). He blesses the bread, namely, with that blessing by which he came forth from the Father’s heart. By saying that he broke it, he showed that his body would be pierced by the fixing of nails, tormented by the suffering of the cross, and afterward changed. For just as grain, ground by the mill, becomes bread with water and fire, so his body, crushed by much affliction of punishments and the passion of the cross, and strengthened through resurrection unto immortality, became the bread of life for the faithful.

Because that body was conceived not from a carnal father on earth but from the Holy Spirit in the Virgin, it could not and ought not be reduced to ashes or scattered; through it the soul and body of every human being are refreshed unto salvation, just as bread strengthens the human heart (Ps. CIII). Mary was the earth in which holy divinity sowed the grain, namely his Son, from whose body every believer ought to live, just as people live from bread made from grain—that is, at his supper. Yet he gave them his body, by his divine power, impassible for salvation, because the joys of eternal salvation lack the suffering of every pain. This was possible for him because, in another nature, he is man; and therefore he blessed that same bread in his divinity. [Col. 0226D]

Again, by breaking the bread he made known to them that he desired to hand over that same body of his, capable of suffering, to death for the redemption of the human race, and that no one else could inflict death upon him if he himself did not will it. “And taking the cup, he gave thanks” (Matt. XXVI), he who would redeem humankind from the stain of sins by the shedding of his blood. And he gave them the blood of the new covenant, accomplishing salvation, which certainly could not be found in the Old Covenant.

When he said that he would not drink of this fruit of the vine until he drank it new in the kingdom of his Father, this is to be understood as though he said: “Until, through the shedding of my blood, I receive them and the other holy souls joyfully into the kingdom of my Father.” Before his passion the Lord Jesus gave his disciples at supper his body, capable of suffering, that it might be food of life to them, by which both souls and bodies might be sanctified. But through the shedding of his blood, which was shed on the cross, the rational soul is renewed and gladdened from the Fall of the soul, just as wine gladdens the human heart (Ps. CIII).

Thus Christ, who at the supper was impassible by his divine power, was also moved by divine mercy toward humankind and afterward willed himself to be capable of suffering. For unless he could die as one capable of suffering, man would not have been freed; and thus God and man would have remained alone, without the fruit of redemption, as he himself says: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII). Man therefore had to be freed not by power [Col. 0227B] but by justice, having been assigned to death by a righteous judgment. Therefore the Son of God was given over to death, so that through the satisfaction of the innocent, justice might be rendered to the sinner.

Whoever suffers vomiting because of bodily weakness and desires Christ’s body with entire devotion: let the priest not presume to give that person this sacrament, out of reverence for Christ’s body, which lies hidden under the appearance of bread. Instead, let him place the Lord’s body upon that person’s head, and invoke God, who sent the soul into the body, that he may deign to sanctify that person’s soul by body and blood. Let him also place it upon that person’s heart, saying: “Almighty God, whose Son Mary received in faith, grant, we ask, [Col. 0227C] that in true faith the soul and body of this person may be sanctified through the sanctification of his body and blood.”

For the divine sacrament lies hidden under the appearance of bread, just as the human soul is invisible. Therefore the invisible soul immediately draws invisible holiness into itself, because the human spirit at once perceives him who sent it and will never depart from him who receives it in faith. But that holiness is removed from the unworthy person, as from Judas. Therefore, for caution and reverence, the Lord’s body must be withheld from one suffering vomiting. Yet faith in the same sacrament must be held most firmly: that which has been solemnly consecrated under the appearance of bread.

John, who is a mirror of holiness and virginity, because for that reason he rejected earthly marriage, [Col. 0227D] and whom the Son of God—who descended from his Father into the virginal matter of his humanity, which he adorned with every ornament of virtues—loved above the other saints in a special manner, setting him as the seal of his hidden miracles, says in a mystical vision: “I saw the holy city” (Rev. 21), etc.

This is to be understood thus: the heavenly Jerusalem, which was to be adorned before him by the supreme craftsman, namely almighty God, just as the matter of all things appeared before the creation of the world; and just as he raised up the man whom he had formed from clay by the breath of life (Gen. 2), so also the holy city Jerusalem, which awaited her husband, namely the Son of God, to whom she was to be betrothed, [Col. 0228A] through the outpouring of his blood, was made new with every ornament. For when the elements were wrapped in darkness, she descended with the victorious standard to the cross upon which the Son of God hung, and received this dowry from him who was conceived and born in virginity: namely, that she too, a virgin by spiritual generation, should bring forth children, because by the crimson blood of the Son of God the heavens were illumined and the gate of paradise, closed to humanity at Adam’s expulsion, was opened.

For God willed that Jerusalem, which is built from the holy works of human beings and appears adorned for her husband as for her bridegroom, should be made for the praise of his humanity; just as he created the angels for the praise and honour of his divinity. And he heard a voice saying as it were: “I who, by my word, when I said, [Col. 0228B] ‘Let it be,’ thundered above all creatures, say that you should know and make known these things shown to you concerning the heavenly Jerusalem, for the protection and salvation of the human being, who was made in our likeness: namely, a voice in the soul and a tabernacle in the body, just as I too am voice in the trumpet, which gives sound through its voice.”

For God showed to his beloved John the holy city built from living stones, which are human beings, and likewise from their works (Rev. 21); in it Jesus Christ, standing as the cornerstone, joins the two walls in the temple of the heavenly Jerusalem. He also dwells among human beings through the garment of his humanity, and they are his people, whom he redeemed with the dowry of his blood; and he [Col. 0228C] is their God, because in delivering them by great power he despoiled the ancient serpent. Thus he stands as the God of power, the God of mercy and loving-kindness, and the complete Good above all creatures: no darkness ever touched him, but he is the mightiest judge over it.

For through his humanity, and likewise through the adornments of the heavenly Jerusalem, God wipes away from his people every tear of ignorance and unbelief, in which they were blind to the true faith; and, by forgiving confessed sins in pure repentance, he saves them from the power and dwelling-place of the death of Gehenna. Likewise, in the sweetest and bitterest report of the humanity of the Son of God—who, when the hunger of expectation had ceased, went forth into all the earth in the great fullness of joys—the mourning of Adam and [Col. 0228D] his posterity, who could not gain entry into the heavenly kingdom, and the cry of the prophets, who amid great sighing called upon God for the redemption of the people, shall no longer exist.

Likewise, the pain and harshness of the law, in which no one could redeem the guilt of any sin through the pardon of mercy, shall no longer exist, since the noble Son of Man, who is just and merciful, mercifully washes away all human sins in true repentance. Thus, through the complete goodness of his humanity, all the aforesaid pains which existed at first have passed away. These things that John saw and heard in the holy revelation are true, because the Son of God completed his works in great splendour, as his Father willed; whence he also sits in great power upon his throne, trampling down all his enemies. [Col. 0229A]

He also makes all things new. For as all creatures, proceeding from first matter through the word of God—namely, “Let it be”—were illumined; and as the first man, formed from clay, was changed into flesh and blood by the breath of life, so too the sinful person, renewed through repentance for sins by the mercy of the Son of God who sits on his throne, is made new. For the blessed person, whom God made a tabernacle of Wisdom, endowed with the apprehension of the five senses, continually ascends by God’s grace from newness to newness until the end of life, with holy desires for good works, with hunger for righteousness, and for the sweetest virtues, of which one can never be satiated; and thus shall happily attain the glory of unchangeable life, which [Col. 0229B] endures always without weariness and without end.

For God thus makes all things new until the last day; but what he may wish to make after the last day, in his power and possibility, is known to himself alone. Then blessed people, who lived in the aforesaid newness, shall have joy of all joys without end in the sight of God, amid harps and harmonies and the sound of every praise.

O servant and son of God, because he formed you in the first human being, strive through abstinence from fleshly desires to make for yourself a tabernacle in the heavenly Jerusalem through holy desires and good works; and adorn it with most beautiful windows through hunger for righteousness and the love of God. For as a house is illumined through [Col. 0229C] windows, so all virtues are illumined and made known through love. See also that you patiently endure the tribulations which you suffer, because through them every virtue is made more elegant within you; and see that you carefully preserve in your heart the beautiful form of which I have spoken to you, so that it may shine in the heavenly Jerusalem.

In the true vision which I always see with wakeful eyes in my soul, now that I am seventy-three years old, I have been compelled by the living light to write these words: God is the living fountain, who sent forth waters when, through the word “Let it be,” he said: “Let there be lights” (Gen. 1), etc. These lights bear the firmament—namely, the sun, moon, and stars—[Col. 0229D] and are their mirror, because they cast their rays into them. He himself is shining fire and eternity before the ages; in him his image, namely the form of the human being, shone always and ever without time.

For the human being, whom he formed in his image and likeness, is his work and the garment of his divinity; and, working according to the Creator, uses the creature for personal benefit in whatever manner he wills. For the human being was created from muddy and watery earth (ibid.), which is soaked through by the moisture of the waters that it covers and is weighed down by its own weight. But the waters, together with the heat of the sun—which possesses a certain image within the circuit of its wheel and is moist through the watery air—bathe the whole earth; and thus, mingling with one another, they bring forth every kind of growth. [Col. 0230A] The waters, which are the mirror of the same sun, restrain it lest it burn the earth by excessive heat; and it constrains the waters lest they inundate the earth through immoderate rains.

God also placed within the human being the fiery rationality of the soul, which is the breath of life; through it the person is strengthened and made firm in flesh and blood, as food is through fire. The soul works through the body, and the body through the soul; the soul is the greenness, or vital freshness, of the body, and thus the complete human being exists, in whom are fire, water, and watery air, by which one draws in and emits moist breath. For as the sun, from the appointed place of the wheel of its circuit, together with the moving wind, accomplishes all its powers and virtues through the heat of its rays; so also [Col. 0230B] the rational soul in the body, with its moist breath, directs whatever it wills and accomplishes it in the creature which it knows through rationality.

Soul and body, with their individual powers and names, are one just as flesh and blood are one; and through three things—namely body, soul, and rationality—the human being is perfected and acts. For the soul pours itself into the whole body and, working there with rationality, supplies it with taste and nourishment. Thus the human being is every creature which the person knows and recognizes through rationality, and which in every respect is subject to that person by God’s command.

For God is hidden fire, which no mortal can behold. But the angels, who are fiery, continually behold the fiery countenance; and the splendour of the Father, his Son—of whose garment, which belongs to time, the prophets prophesied, and who was always without time before the ages with the Father, as John the Evangelist testifies, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” [Col. 0230C] (John 1). But the Word which was in the beginning with God, incarnate from the Virgin Mary, went forth as a living fountain, refreshing with the water of life all who believe in him, as he himself says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7).

He also extinguishes every fire of filth through the inextinguishable fire of his divinity, because he was begotten in the Father before the ages, whose will eternally possessed the garment of that same Son. The same Son of God also willed to be baptized in waters, where the paternal voice testifies that he is his beloved Son [Col. 0230D] (Matt. 3; 17), who before the ages was with him in eternity, and who through the beautiful form of his humanity shall trample down all his enemies who seek to fight against him.

For in the waters he recalled how he created them through his word, above which the Spirit of the Lord—who is the living fountain—was borne (Gen. 1), moving them and making them flow, so that they cleanse every impurity and can contain no decay. For God concealed his humanity from the devil, whom he cast down from heaven with a great multitude of demonic spirits (Isa. 14); and, without the devil’s knowing it, he completed their number with blessed human beings. Thus God, through Adam’s fall, shall repair the ruin of the devil, who is wholly lost.

The Son of Man also ate and drank, as he permitted human beings to do, through which flesh and blood grow and are nourished, lest they fail by drying out in their appointed work. [Col. 0231A] But the serpent contaminated this food when the first human beings, consenting to him, were expelled from paradise (Gen. 3); hence, by the devil’s suggestion, they conceived their children in sins and brought them forth in pain. But the Son of God wiped away this death-bearing human conception when he was conceived and born, through the Holy Spirit, from the Virgin Mary, without any sin of male nature (Luke 1–2).

The Son of God also gave his body and blood in bread and wine to his disciples (Matt. 26), because these two things especially suit and correspond to him. For just as a grain hidden in the earth rises by secretly coming to birth in its greenness, through God’s grace, by no other coagulation than [Col. 0231B] the heat of the sun and the moisture of water (John 12); and just as a cluster of grapes becomes green and grows not by pruning but through the mystical grace of God; so too the Son of God, without every coagulation and greenness of sinful fleshly nature, came forth as true man from hidden divinity.

For the fire hidden in a deep dry pit, where later thick water was found, with which sacrifices were sprinkled and which were consumed by a great kindled fire (2 Macc. 1), signifies that God is inextinguishable fire and the living fountain. For God himself, whom that fire and water signify, is so hidden in his lofty depth that he surpasses every understanding of human intelligence. Therefore he so consumed every fleshly desire in the Virgin Mary that his Son clothed himself in humanity from her without any burning of sin. For the Holy Spirit, who is the living fountain, bathed her with his sweetest moisture, as dew descends upon grain; so that by the power of the Most High she was overshadowed from every burning that comes upon people at birth through the devil’s suggestion, and from every pain of human nature and generation, as the angel said to her: “And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Col. 0231C] (Luke 1).

But the first origin of unclean coagulation, which arises without the Holy Spirit, is cleansed and purified by the Holy Spirit in the waters of baptism, as gold in fire; because the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters [Col. 0231D] (Gen. 1), and caused them to move and flow. They are moreover a spiritual element above the others, and in them animals are born and fed whose nature differs from that of other animals.

For a human being anointed through God’s grace with chrism and oil, and kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, is sanctified in baptism and born again, to the confusion of the ancient serpent who touched that first origin (John 3). Thus by God’s grace the person is powerfully rescued from him in this manner, and is regenerated to eternal salvation in the font of baptism through the living fountain, namely the Holy Spirit.

That same power [Col. 0232A] of the Most High which came upon Mary, making from her the flesh and blood of the Son of God, descends upon the offering of bread and wine, with the wounds of Jesus Christ open, so that the same offering of bread and wine is secretly transformed into flesh and blood in the sight of God and the holy angels; just as grain and wine grow through a hidden greenness which human beings cannot see. But because after the washing of baptism people very often fall into sins, the wounds of that same Son of God remain open as long as the rational human being sins, so that through repentance and confession the person may be cleansed and received in those same wounds.

But those called heretics and Sadducees deny the most holy humanity of the Son of God and the holiness of his body and [Col. 0232B] blood which is in the offering of bread and wine. Therefore the devil—whose beginning is from him who has neither beginning nor end, and who at the beginning of his honour opposed the unity of eternal divinity—through these people sprinkles the whole earth with the dust of death. For he is a liar (John 8), since he pours the blindness of unbelief into the eyes of these people, blinding them so that they cannot either hope in or believe in the true God. Thus, in the manner of a viper, he bites all holiness and honour of God through these people who follow him at his suggestion and who utterly despise the living God through unbelief.

For they do not hold in right faith the true God, who is invisible, nor the human soul and spirit, because all their intention tends toward fleshly things. Therefore, like him who deceives them, they trample all things of God underfoot, because, despising the words of truth, they glory in falsehood and their false teaching. But the lost angel knows through his rationality that the rational human being has the capacity to do what he wills; and he recognized this in the first human being, who had received a command from God. Thus, in the same way in which he deceived the woman, he seeks to destroy among these people what God commanded—namely, that they should increase and multiply—by suggesting that they should live not according to the command of the law but according to what they themselves choose for themselves at the devil’s prompting.

> [Note: [Col. 0231D] Observe the statement: “not according to the command of the law.” Anabaptists and concubinarians are indicated here, who [Col. 0232D] observe no command of the law, not being truly continent.]

He also suggests to them that they should constrain their bodies by wasting them through fasting, and afterwards fulfil every desire of their incestuous longing. Thus, at his urging, they fall away from all holiness of the legal commands of almighty God; for they are dead to all the commands which God set forth through Moses and his other prophets, and which he later revealed through his Son. Therefore through them the whole earth is polluted.

Hence you, O kings, dukes, and princes, and all other Christian people who fear the Lord, hear these words, and drive this people from the Church by depriving them of their possessions, not by killing them; for [Col. 0233A] they are the image of God. May the fiery Spirit of God, who is the living fountain, pour himself into you through his grace, so that you may do these things before the day of God’s vengeance, lest you fall short of all honour and blessedness of body and soul.

God gave the human being a command in which the entire law was hidden; but the human being transgressed it, and therefore was judged through the fall of expulsion, becoming mortal in two ways: by dying in body and by lacking the vision of the true light. Thus the person could not remain in that dwelling and lost the aforesaid vision. For the person truly knew God and recognized that God’s command had to be kept; but because the servant was obeyed and because consent was given to the woman subject to him, the just judgment of the just Judge came upon him.

And God gave this judgment concerning those who refuse to acknowledge a master in obedience and who transgress all the commandments of the law; hence their bodies were given to death, because they were dead in the light of the law. Yet masters, who stand in Christ’s place, ought to consider whether such persons have any amendment in themselves before delivering them to death. And the heart of those masters must be most pure in this matter, so that in judgment they do not take account of any injury or blasphemy inflicted on them by those persons, and thus deliver the blood of the condemned to death with judgment. But if their heart is not pure, let them withdraw from the presence of this judgment, lest their words kill their neighbours—most carefully attending to the Gospel of the Lord, [Col. 0233C] where it says: “Do not judge, lest you be judged. For with the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged” (Matt. 7).

Nor should they judge according to what they themselves determine or according to the pleasure of their own will, but according to the judgment of almighty God: so that whoever proves intolerably hostile to all the commands of the law and refuses to abstain from criminal sins should be judged according to God’s judgment, not according to human will. But if, through fear of death, that person promises to amend the fault, God’s judgment should be deferred once and twice; and if, having thus been tested, the person does not amend, he or she shall be liable to the punishment of judgment according to the word of the Son of God. In this way every person should take care regarding every judgment, that it not be done according to human will. [Col. 0233D]

One must also consider what James says concerning the rich and the poor—concerning the rich person, namely, who is well adorned with gold and clothing (Jas. 2). For the rich person desires to be honoured on account of great wealth, and is received and honoured, namely because of assistance in adversity and fear of the power by which such a person often harms others. But the poor person must be received for Christ’s love and because that person is a human brother or sister. These are not to be treated as equals, since that would be without discernment: for if one made the rich and poor sit in one seat, the rich person would scorn it and the poor person would be frightened by it.

For the poor person is to be received and cared for because of the love of God, since that person is a human brother or sister; and although God permits the rich person [Col. 0234A] to possess riches and withholds them from the poor, he nevertheless loves the form of the poor person, which is his image. For through the pride of wealth the rich command people whom they can harm and treat them as though they were not human beings in their own form. In this way the good name of the human being—that the person is the image and likeness of God—is blasphemed.

God therefore commanded: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Lev. 19; Matt. 5): that is, recognizing your own form in the neighbour, suffering with that person in all things, and grieving over all evil that person has done, because your own form is blasphemed through that person’s evils. And when a human being does this, that person performs a good work according to the Son of God, who put on flesh in order that [Col. 0234B] he might suffer with humanity.

But whoever despises the poor sins not only against that person but also against almighty God, who took on the form of a human being, through which he gave the law and by which that person will be rebuked, since these are transgressions of the law. “For whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2). For whoever keeps the other commandments of the law but lacks one commandment, not loving it because of hatred but possessing it as though it were merely a painter’s picture, does not perfectly fulfil the other commands.

So too, when a person is impaired in one limb, whether by birth or some misfortune, the other limbs suffer with it, and they will have neither perfect comfort nor aid in that impaired member. Food that is not [Col. 0234C] well cooked and is tasteless gives a person neither strength nor taste; one scarcely lives by it. So also one who does not have fiery love does not rightly cook all the commandments of the law, but possesses them as an infirm limb. And whoever neither gathers nor learns works from wisdom, but joins and performs them from the self, is compared to a person who makes from wood an image in human form that cannot live. Thus that person and those works are dead; that person is also like one mute, lacking the voice of rationality. Therefore such a person is guilty with respect to all God’s commandments and shall answer to the Lord for them at judgment, because they were performed according to personal will.

The transgression of the law’s commandments belongs to pagans, unbelievers, and their followers, [Col. 0234D] because they lack faith. But those who are faithful through baptism and faith, who act as far as they can in God’s commandments, groan with their whole heart and breathe after God, asking his help and doing penance for what they transgress—for some seek God from childhood, others from youth, others in old age, and ask all things from him—though they have sinned, are nevertheless not rejected in judgment. For in all these, O Jerusalem, a multitude of saints, righteous persons, elect persons, penitents, and tax collectors shall come to you (Isa. 60).

Divine brightness, brightness that shines amid your work: you are that root which sent forth many branches, and you are the sun with your innumerable spheres, namely [Col. 0235A] your saints and elect, whose number no one can comprehend. For in the beginning you fashioned one root and made it wakeful through the breath of life (Gen. 2), and you said to Jeremiah: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” He answered you: “I see a wakeful rod” (Jer. 1).

A certain root proceeded with its branches and was darkened by the deadly fruit which night vomited upon it; hence it multiplied its branches in darkness and wished to trample down the righteousness of heaven. But you, bright divinity, shone forth in the waters and gathered them together as into a wineskin (Ps. 32), in which all human beings, except Noah and his branches, were submerged (Gen. 7). But you instructed Noah to work your miracles; therefore he performed his work with the joy of a child, as if in a child’s understanding, [Col. 0235B] because he did not yet know or comprehend what you had said to him.

You also cast before him an airy vapour which shakes the veins and marrow of a person, so that, unhindered by human senses, the structure which you taught him might be built as if in a child’s delight. So too you do in those human beings in whom you are going to work your miracles, when through your inspiration they utter things foreign to human perception. But after Noah had made his structure on the height to which you had raised him, you raised from it the first structure of Abel, which had passed away in his outpoured blood, and so inspired Noah that he built an altar upon which he offered sacrifice to you, the most high God.

Bright divinity, who possessed innumerable spheres of life, you first formed the human being from the clay of the earth and placed that person in the place of paradise (Gen. 4), so that the person might have fellowship in angelic praise. But the serpent moved its eye in deceit and deceived that person with lying words, accusing you before him; the serpent itself had first opposed you. The devil did this so that the human being might be expelled from paradise and might not return to the place from which the devil himself had been expelled, a newly created work that the devil recognized as other than himself.

Bright and fiery divinity, in the fiery spheres that you had within yourself, through the holy image of your humanity you crushed the serpent’s head, so that it might never raise itself up before you completed your work. For it did not touch the fire which you are. Rather, it became a liar in a certain light of brightness; therefore your humanity was hidden from it, [Col. 0235D] and therefore the angels who touch your fire departed from it. Afterwards you made your work, namely the human being, with fire and brightness, so that it might never be made altogether like that lost one. You shall gather human beings in so great a number to your image that neither angels nor souls can count them.

For some people are fiery and turn toward the fire; some are in the light of brightness and fall from the light; and later they rise again to the fire and become pillars of heaven. You, bright divinity, are fire and brightness; by them you also made the earthen vessel from which you put on your garment. Thus, existing in three powers, you also established your work in three powers. You established Adam in brightness, [Col. 0236A] and preserved Noah in fire, so that from him a new world might proceed with the fire of holiness, by which the serpent’s gluttony was shut up and its power so burned and overcome that those regenerated through fire and water, persevering in the true faith, can by no means perish.

For in your fire you dried up the water, lest it flow into Noah’s vessel, in which you prefigured that the death of human perdition should end, just as human beings ended in death by water. O holiness of water, in which your Son crushed death, whom the Virgin conceived from your fire and who dried up in her every stain of watery sin, so that she should not be harmed by it, just as Noah was not harmed. For in these signs you foresaw what you accomplished in Mary, who crushed the serpent’s head (Gen. 3), by which the first woman was deceived. [Col. 0236B]

O Noah, you are a saving sign, because God secretly taught you how you might be saved through water (Gen. 9), and inspired your heart to build a table for sacrificing to him. You are like the dawn, which is a spark of the sun. In you God prefigured the new and old holiness of prophets and wise persons, and the observance of integrity, which was planted not in a man’s side but in the form of a woman, who was not under the man’s power; just as the power of the water could not harm you.

God also caused a new world to proceed from you and gave you the earth watered by waters, in which you planted vineyards, though you were ignorant of the force of wine, through which human senses are laid bare. For as the son who covered your nakedness, honouring you as a father, gloriously retained his freedom, while another was reduced to his servant, so evil knowledge is the servant of good knowledge. Nor were you as crooked in sins as your sons, just as Adam’s sons were more criminal than Adam himself.

The holy and elect are in the blessings of freedom, as are those who returned through repentance from the slavery of sins to freedom. To all of them is given a trumpet to sound, whose voice may resound before God’s throne (Rev. 5). The angels also harmonize praises to God with their voices for the works of good people still living in the body; these works are continually multiplied and ascend before God upon the golden altar that is in his sight, and from them the angels continually sing a new song to God.

For the golden altar is to be understood as the works of the saints, [Col. 0236D] which they performed while remaining in the body and which flash like a golden altar in God’s sight, and by which they imitated the Lamb, namely the Son of God.

Those saints also number their works, and the works of those blessed people who act happily, with the sounding trumpet, whose voice is like the sound of many waters (Rev. 1), mingled with the sweetest sound of the encircling firmament. By this voice of praise they seek help for those whose works and merits are touched by the holy works which ascend upward over the altar before God. Thus they pray to God for them, so that they may not be hindered from good works by the deception of Leviathan, [Col. 0237A] which will work with the elements through their examples. Their sounding trumpet signifies this: that God is praised and glorified by them, as by the angels whom he has filled with his brightness.

For the voice of the saints, by which they praise God for their own works and those of other good people, is like a sounding trumpet. Hence they sing a new song before the throne and the Lamb (Rev. 14), and the earth—that is, earthly peoples—echoes their voices, praising God through their merits and saying: “Glory to you, Lord.” O holy Divinity, you are glorified in heaven by hidden angels, who are sparks of your brightness; and you are praised on earth by the human being, whom you formed from clay for your garment.

John the Evangelist shone with God’s brightness and burned in the flame of the Holy Spirit; therefore he was heavenly in his body, as the human being had been before the Fall. Hence the weight and heaviness of his body remained upon earth while he himself was lifted to heavenly things, as if in the twinkling of an eye; just as after the last day every bodily heaviness shall be burned up while holy souls fly to heaven. John the Baptist, filled in his flesh with the strength of divinity [Col. 0237B] (Matt. 3), was wholly dead to the serpent’s foam; therefore he rebuked sinners with bitter words. God sent him before his humanity, before the fullness of time came in which God became human (Gal. 4).

Now I invoke and adore you, that you may preserve me, faint-hearted as I am, who saw and heard these words—as you alone know—in the songs of blessed souls; and gather into the bosom of grace all who diligently labour with me for the pure faith of your name, so that we may never be strangers from you. For you alone know my ignorance: I am not studded with the learning of the Scriptures which recount your miracles, just as times are discerned in the stars. Therefore I ask you to free me from every blackness of malignant spirits and preserve me from every doubt of my ignorance in body and soul.

Again I ask you, gentle Father, to love with the fire of your love those who labour with me, and to write them in the book of life, which is your knowledge, so that they may never be separated from you. O Noah, who are the beginning of holiness and of the branches that proceeded from you, we ask you not to forget us in the songs of your praises because of [Col. 0237D] our negligences, but, through love for him who chose you in his miracles, deign always to remember us before God in your praises and prayers. Amen.

Holy Divinity, who exist whole without any division, through your Word you bring forth in every creature by a pure name. The forms fashioned through your Word in their own kind have not vanished from life. One creature lives from greenness; another, clothed in flesh, from its sentient nature; another from its windy breath; another from the air of flowing water. For, prefiguring in Abraham, you inscribed the whole and undivided obedience of the garment of your Word; and you kept it pure and whole for the deliverance of those who repent of the disobedience that arose in Adam.

[Col. 0238A] You commanded Abraham to wound himself in his flesh, which through deception had been changed from the holiness of chastity into incestuous desires; this you washed away by water and baptism in hidden mysteries, by which he too was unknowingly deceived. When Abraham wounded his flesh at my command, he confounded the devil, who did not know that mystery and was confounded in that part of the human being by which he had also deceived humanity.

You also commanded him to sacrifice his beloved son to you (Gen. 22), in whom you prefigured your Son to be sacrificed for the people. But your angel forbade the drawn, quivering sword to fall upon the bound one, and showed him a ram not begotten from other sheep, but as a manifestation of your miracle.

For the human being whom you formed was deceived by the devil. Therefore all human nature has been so contaminated that every human being is wholly conceived in the sins of fleshly desire. Human nature too became so warped and twisted that no one could free a companion from the devil’s captivity. Therefore within yourself you ordained the tunic of your Son, stretched out from simple earth which had germinated from nothing else; the warmth of its blood was kindled by the heat of the Holy Spirit. And as an egg is born from flesh and, warmed by a hen, sends forth a chick, [Col. 0238B] so the Virgin, warmed by the heat of the Holy Spirit, gave birth to a son; and just as a chick could never come forth from an egg without the warmth of the hen, so the Virgin could never bring forth the Son without the warmth of the Holy Spirit.

This whole mystery was prefigured in the ram [Col. 0238C] that hung in the thorns, as the Lord said to Adam: “When you have worked the earth, it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). In the labours of his work malicious vengeance was shown to him, because he despised God’s command, which he began but did not complete, and did not abase his own glory. Therefore the bright garment, which had been without any obscurity, was taken from him and torn apart, just as thorns and thistles also tear a human being.

The Son, born without any male blood, in the brightness of God through the heat of the Holy Spirit, he alone was suspended upon the wood for Adam’s crime. Since he had no equal, he freed souls by despoiling hell. And who is this who did this? God, certainly: he who, without any beginning, defect, or change, [Col. 0238D] is that day whose brightness has never been illuminated by any light. Yet he himself is the light of all his making and creation, of whom David says: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII).

That is: God is inextinguishable light, which shall never grow old, vanish, or become wearisome; and he is the King of glory, whose glory endures without any harmful darkness and does not fail, as human times fail, which begin, wither, and are always changing. But it shall remain steadfast and unchangeable in its own greenness, like the tree planted beside flowing waters (Ps. I). For neither angel nor human being can, by any number, end or count the glory which is God himself. For he is complete [Col. 0239A] fullness; and therefore angels shall never be satiated in beholding him, because they continually see in him things unknown and new, with glorious delight.

He himself is strong and mighty, because in his strength he mightily brought forth all creatures and established each one mobile within its own kind; and thus all created things were made without blindness and without defect. He is the Lord mighty in battle, who fought against the dragon, overcame him in heaven, cast him down in hell to the punishments of his wickedness, shattered the gates of hell, and took with himself the souls of those who had acknowledged him. No other could do this unless he were mighty.

O pure, true, fiery Divinity: in your mighty power you planted the first immortal and unchangeable earth, in which the first human beings defiled themselves by transgressing against your command and [Col. 0239B] will; and you expelled them from that bright region by your strong power. Yet, after the outpouring of the waters of the clouds, you rebuilt their ruin through the new offspring which proceeded from Noah, after you showed the serpentine race what you could do in your mighty power against the dragon’s fury.
