Yet in yourselves, according to your order, exercise forethought and right understanding, lest you judge unjustly.

It would be unfitting for lion, calf, human being, and eagle to oppose one another in their meanings. Rather, each of these can, in the figure of the human being in which they are designated for the healing of human beings, render justice to the other, heal, anoint, and sanctify baptism with humble obedience. For every priest whom God has anointed and named priest can also heal the wounds of sins with judging justice, because he has this office from God; therefore let him not neglect to fulfil it.

And I, a little poor and unlearned woman, saw a certain beast. Its face and forelegs were like a bear’s; the rest of its body was like that of an ox, except that its hind legs were like an ass’s feet and it had no tail. It had three horns on its head.

[Col. 0265A] Two of these, resembling an ox’s horns, were beside its ears; the third, in the middle of its forehead, resembled a goat’s horn. The face of this beast was turned eastward, but its hind part westward. This is to be understood as follows.

This beast, whose face and forelegs are like a bear’s, signifies certain people who secretly possess beastly habits. They utter gentle words, yet in the examples set by their footsteps—where they ought to proceed forcibly toward rectitude—they show the recklessness and harshness of perversity. The rest of its body resembles an ox, except that its hind legs are like an ass’s feet and it lacks a tail. For these same people pretend, like an ox, to bear God’s yoke, yet in their subsequent examples reveal in themselves the habits of the ass that falls beneath a burden. Nor do they show themselves to have a tail, because in them fails what the Lord commands: that an offering be presented with a tail (Lev. IV). That is, they do not bring to the end of blessedness the good which they began in humility and poverty.

[Col. 0265B] Its three horns upon its head, of which two resemble an ox’s horns and are beside its ears, signify three modes of life standing in chief intercourse: two imitate the appearance of those laboring in the Lord’s field and giving heed to the word of the Lord. But the third, in the middle of its forehead, resembles a goat’s horn, because it displays these spiritual people in the strength of their self-confidence, striving in the roughness of a goat to climb a height upon which they cannot remain.

At this height they despise other peoples, as the Pharisees despise publicans and regard them as useless (Luke XVIII). They also attach themselves to certain administrative affairs of districts, so that through these they may be considered better and more eminent than the other two horns, and thus may seem to climb to the height of holiness. For they join themselves to secular concern, acquire manifold wealth, as though turning over the whole earth by their labours, and thereby take in a breadth of riches greater than they ought.

[Col. 0265D] They act like that young man to whom the Son of God said that he should sell whatever he possessed and give it to the poor; but he went away sorrowful, because he wished to possess both worldly riches and eternal life (Matt. XIX), which was difficult to accomplish. These people want to possess heaven and earth together, which is impossible. For amid the acquisition and possession of riches they cannot stand without the pride of exaltation and the property of pleasure, just as it would be impossible for a person to stand on the summit of some mountain and not fall when shaken by the storm of a mighty wind.

Nor do they possess that love and fear which a needy person has when he extends his hand for help and alms. Rather, they wrap themselves in the folly of the ass, which allows itself to be loaded with great burdens until it collapses beneath that burden. They wish to possess both the yoke of spiritual life and worldly concern, but cannot stand in them; therefore they fall like an ass.

[Col. 0266A] Hence the face of the beast is turned eastward and its hind part westward: for while they seem to attend to spiritual life, they also cling to secular life, thereby imitating the fallen angels, who, trusting in themselves, fell from heavenly glory (Isa. XIV).

The third creature, having something like a human face, signifies those secular persons who do their works with concern for body and soul, yet ascend to God with good intention, as though flying with wings. For every good desire is emitted from the heart of the just like a ray of the sun and is therefore seen as a wing. They also run to observe the commandments of the Law and of the priest; they are moved in mercy to distribute alms; they look to the earth, considering how they may increase upon it; and in the begetting of offspring they reckon themselves equal to the dust of the earth. They call themselves sinners, and thus in secular life possess more punishment than pleasure from carnal joy.

[Col. 0266B] Thus they come to their masters, namely the priests, changing the face with which they had tasted sins; and through the grace of the Holy Spirit they confess their sins in repentance and are renewed, as it is written: “You will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. CIII).

What is said? O God, in the new Spirit you will renew the will of the person who had been eager to sin; thus you will turn him from evil eagerness to good desire. For through penitents you renew the face of the earth when a person senses and knows himself so entangled in sins that he cannot keep from sinning, yet turns himself to renewal through repentance. For if a person did not sin, he would not be renewed.

Some are renewed in another way: when they flee sins because of the punishment of repentance, so that they do not seek to sin. Others are renewed in another way: when, because of love of virtues, they avoid sins which they sense in themselves and which they could commit. Thus they receive renewal through the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0266D] For as the earth in its season of greenness does not fail to bear fruit, and as in the dry season it grows pale and withers, then returns again to its greenness, so God also established the human being to be renewed within himself through his works. Scripture must be rightly divided in all a person’s works, just as many waters are divided from one water, as God also divided water over the whole world.

These secular persons also always examine and consider themselves: what they are, how they live, and how they may remove sins from themselves. Living thus in the fear of God, they are among earthly things yet do not abandon heavenly things. For they sacrifice to God within themselves when they worship him; and they flash like the moon when they sigh toward him from the depth of their heart. But when they wane in sins like the moon, they immediately rise again through repentance, just as the moon rises after its waning through the sun.

[Col. 0267A] They too “sleep between the midst of the allotments, [with] the wings of the dove covered with silver” (Ps. LXVII), because, where they sleep lest they sin, they are among masters flying in the simplicity of pure knowledge. They do this when they turn aside from sins begun and rest from them, just as a bird bends its head between its wings in order to rest: loving heavenly things and confessing their sins in earthly affairs through repentance.

Hence “blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. XIV): they are those who live in the secular state according to the Law. O what a great miracle is in them: that by living thus and abandoning sins through the bitterness of repentance, they become human beings! They will also be like the creature that has a human face, because they oppose themselves to earthly sins through repentance and become alien to them, just as the nature of animals is alien to human nature.

[Col. 0267B] Therefore they appear silvered in the knowledge of good works, because they have the simple character of a child who does not know sin, since they do not wish either to embrace or nourish sin. And when they strive to shine in this simplicity, the hind parts of their back will appear with the pallor of gold. For those hind parts, in which they were previously strong in sins when they had been accustomed to sin, are now cast behind them and show wisdom in the fear of the Lord, because they shine gilded in good deeds.

But the fourth creature, like a flying eagle, shows certain persons restraining themselves from sins, who rise from the secular people described above to continence. This occurred in Mary Magdalene: rejecting all her sins, she counted them as mud and thus chose the better part (Luke X), taking her seat in the dawn of holiness. In the Old Testament, many abandoned sins because of weariness with this world, and many also restrained themselves from sins out of love of righteousness.

[Col. 0267C] But now, in the new sun—that is, Christ Jesus—they are called continent, because they turn to the simplicity of a child who does not know sins, when they reject sins and do not know them in their will. They ascend to heavenly things in two respects: because with good intention and holy desire they love things above more than others who had not previously known the world; and because, as the eagle seeks heights beyond other flying creatures, so they fly upward, being turned so toward the brightness of eternal life that they cannot be sated by it. In the ardour of the true Sun, they trample down what they formerly did while entangled in sins.

In the most powerful force of holiness they consider how great the pains and how heavy the burdens are in sins which they themselves had formerly touched by experience. Now they kill those sins in themselves as a deadly corpse and constrain and pursue their body as a slaughtered sheep. Thus they look upon the burning sun, casting back and counting as dust all the secular things that they had known before; despising the fear of Gehenna in burning love for God; and trusting that they ought to persevere in faith and hope.

[Col. 0268A] They do this in the manner Isaiah describes: “The seraphim covered his face with two wings” (Isa. VI). These wings signify faith and hope, because in faith faithful persons see God and through hope desire eternal rewards. “With two they covered his feet”: these confound sensuality and understanding, since these same people cover the nakedness of their sins so that they do not fulfil the carnal desires of their own will. “With two they flew”: these signify love of God and neighbour, because, loving God above all things, they assist their neighbour in his needs. Thus they fly above all things in the strength of God when they transcend all earthly things and carefully consider everything concerned with sins, in order that they may afflict themselves through abstinence from sins. Thus, too, in the fullness of desire they adorn the heavenly Jerusalem with the precious stones of good works.

[Col. 0268B] On the joyful way of God’s commandments they do not sleep, but always, in the newness of their soul’s desire, sound like a singing trumpet. These are the burning sighs which those born in the nocturnal darkness of sins direct to God when they know him in fear and love, saying that he is holy who created all things; that he is holy who has never been mortal; and that he is holy who shattered hell and brought his elect forth from it.

For blessed people will never cease from doing good and praising God; and when they cease from working, they will nevertheless not desist, after the end of their life, from the praise of their Creator.

But I, a little poor woman, weak and frail from my infancy, was compelled in a mystical and true vision to this writing. Lying in bed in severe illness, I wrote it at God’s command and with his help, in order that I might present it to prelates and masters marked for God’s service, so that they might consider in it as in a mirror who and what they were, and might show and explain it to those who are subject to them in obedience.

[Col. 0268C] And I heard a voice from heaven saying: “Let no one despise these words, lest, if he despises them, God’s vengeance fall upon him.”

## LETTER LII

[Col. 0268D]

### WERNER OF KIRCHEIM, WITH THE OTHER BROTHERS OF HIS COMMUNITY, TO HILDEGARD

They earnestly request the prayers of Saint Hildegard and wish to possess her words committed to writing.

To HILDEGARD, virgin immaculate in mind and body and dedicated to God from the cradle: WERNER of Kircheim, with the other brothers of his community, though unworthy rendering service to God in their parishes—may you, after the example of Deborah, with God as guide, trample hostile troops (Judg. V).

Because the fragrance of your virtues has spread through no small extent of lands, since by the grace of the Holy Spirit your pure heart has been enlightened not only to do good but also to prophesy future things and contemplate heavenly things, we have thought it fitting, though unworthy, to entrust ourselves to your holiness under the claim of brotherhood.

[Col. 0269A] And indeed, because we believe that we are to be with you as Christ’s least members, we confidently say that you should not deny to those who ask whatever we request of you in his name, when you are able to grant it. Therefore we ask your kindness, mother and bride of the Lamb, that you remember us more earnestly in your prayers, being assured on our part that, insofar as they have power before God, we shall always make remembrance of you while praying (Phil. I).

We further presume to ask you one petition: that you do not neglect, in maternal mercy, to write down and send to us the words which, with the Holy Spirit teaching you, you disclosed before us and very many others present at Kyrcheim, concerning the negligence which priests show in the divine sacrifice. Thus they may not slip from our memory, but we may hold them more attentively before our eyes. For, since we give more attention than is necessary to earthly and secular concerns, we often carelessly send transient words into the wind. May maternal love flourish in you.

### HILDEGARD’S REPLY

She introduces the image of the Church, pouring forth most grievous complaints against the sins of priests. She foretells various things which were altogether fulfilled in the sixteenth century.

Lying for a long time upon a bed of illness, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1170, I saw, while awake in body and mind, a most beautiful image in female form. She was most excellent in sweetness and most beloved in delights, of such great beauty that the human mind could by no means comprehend her; and her stature reached from earth to heaven. [Col. 0269C] Her face also shone with the greatest brightness, and her eye looked toward heaven. She was clothed in a most white garment of white silk and wrapped in a mantle adorned with most precious stones—namely emerald, sapphire, baccae (berries), and pearls—and she had shoes of onyx about her feet.

But her face was sprinkled with dust, her garment was torn on the right side, her mantle had lost its graceful beauty, and her shoes had become black. In a great and mournful voice she cried out to the height of heaven, saying:

“Listen, O heaven: my face has been defiled. And mourn, O earth: my garment has been torn. And tremble, O abyss: my shoes have been blackened. ‘Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests’ (Matt. 8), but I have no helper or comforter, nor a staff upon which I may lean and by which I may be sustained.”

And again she said:

“I lay hidden in the heart of the Father until the Son of Man—who was conceived and born in virginity—shed his blood. With that same blood he betrothed and endowed me, so that I might regenerate, in the pure and simple rebirth of Spirit and water, those contracted and defiled by the serpent’s foam.

“But my fosterers, namely the priests, who ought to make my face blush like the dawn, [Col. 0270A] my garment flash like lightning, my mantle shine like precious stones, and my shoes gleam in whiteness, have sprinkled my face with dust, torn my garment, made my mantle shadowy, and blackened my shoes. Those who ought everywhere to adorn me have deprived me in all these things.

“They defile my face by handling and receiving, buying and selling, all manner of improper things together with the body and blood of my Bridegroom, amid the great uncleanness of their licentious conduct, the great filth of fornications and adulteries, and the most wicked rapacity of avarice. They envelop them in such pollution as though an infant were placed in mud before swine.

“For just as, when God made man from the slime of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life (Gen. 2), he immediately became flesh and blood, so too the same power of God transforms the offering of bread, wine, and water upon the altar, at the words of the priest invoking the Godhead, into the true flesh and true blood of Christ, namely my Bridegroom. Yet because of that blindness by which humanity was blinded in Adam’s fall, a human being cannot see this with bodily eyes.

“For the piercings of my Bridegroom’s wounds remain fresh and open as long as the wounds of human sins lie open. Those same wounds of Christ are defiled by priests who ought to make me white and serve me in whiteness, as they run from church to church in their excessive avarice.

“They also tear my garment because they are transgressors of the Law, the Gospel, [Col. 0270C] and their priesthood. They darken my mantle because they entirely neglect the precepts established in them. They do not fulfil them in abstinence, as in the emerald; in the giving of alms, as in the sapphire; or in other good and just works—by which God is honoured as by other kinds of gems—with good will and perfect deed.

“My shoes, moreover, are blackened above because they neither follow the straight nor the hard and rough paths of justice, nor offer good examples to their subjects; though beneath, in my shoes, as though in my secret place, I retain the whiteness of truth in certain persons.

“For false priests are deceived in themselves, because they wish to possess the honour of priestly office without its work. But this cannot be, since reward is given to no one unless the labour of the work has first been performed. Where the grace of God touches a person, there it causes that person to work so as to receive reward.

“Therefore, when God rains down in vengeance the various pains that are hostile to humankind; when mist covers the whole earth so that its greenness withers and its adornments grow dark; and when the abyss trembles, because in vengeance and suffering it will be stirred to fury together with heaven and earth—then princes and a reckless people will rush upon you, O priests, who have hitherto neglected me. They will cast you out and drive you away, and take your riches from you, because you did not attend to the time of your priestly office.

“And they will say of you: ‘Let us cast these adulterers, robbers, and persons full of every evil out of the Church.’ In doing this, they will wish to regard themselves as having rendered service to God, because they say that the Church has been defiled by you.

“Thus Scripture says: ‘Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together as one’ (Ps. 2). For, by God’s permission, very many nations will begin to rage against you in his judgments, and many peoples will devise vain things concerning you when they reckon your priestly office and consecration as nothing. The kings of the earth will join in your overthrow and will seek earthly things; and the princes who rule over you will assemble in this single counsel, namely, to expel you from their territories, because by your most wicked deeds you have driven the innocent Lamb away from yourselves.”

And I heard a voice from heaven saying: “This image represents the Church. Therefore you, O human being, who see and hear these lamenting words, proclaim them to the priests appointed and ordained to govern and teach God’s people, to whom it was said with the apostles: ‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature’ (Mark 16).

“For when God created man, he marked every creature in him, just as the time and number of the whole year are set down in a small space of parchment. Therefore God called man ‘every creature.’

“And again I, a poor little womanly form, saw an unsheathed sword hanging in the air, one edge of which was turned toward heaven and the other toward earth. This sword was extended over the spiritual people, whom [Col. 0271C] the prophet had formerly foreseen when he cried in wonder: ‘Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?’ (Isa. 16).

“For those who, raised up from the earth and separated from the common people, ought to live holy lives and to be like doves in the simplicity of their conduct and works, are now corrupt in their conduct and works. And I saw that this sword cut off certain places of spiritual persons, just as Jerusalem was cut off after the Lord’s Passion.

“Nevertheless, I saw that in this adversity God will preserve for himself many priests who are God-fearing, pure, and simple, as he answered Elijah when he said that he had left for himself in Israel seven thousand men whose knees had not bowed before Baal (3 Kings 19). Now may the unquenchable fire of the Holy Spirit be poured into you, that you may turn to the better part.”

## LETTER LIII

### The Brethren of Hagenhe to Hildegard

They pray that she will not neglect to calm and uproot the discord that has arisen among them.

To HILDEGARD, the chaste dove hiding in the clefts of the rock (Song 2:14), the brethren, alas, troubled at Hagenhe: the devotion of their prayers and whatever pertains to eternal salvation.

Because, by God’s grace, your light shines beneficially before humankind (Matt. 5:16), we glorify your Father, who has set you up as a burning lamp for the illumination of the Church. And although we are sinners, we nevertheless rejoice wholeheartedly with your holiness, which by a singular privilege clings to the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom. We do not wish your charity to be unaware that day and night we desire to see you face to face; and, continually remembering you in our prayers (Rom. 1:9), we sometimes embrace you in mind as though present, though absent in body.

Therefore we humbly entreat your perfection to commend us, beggars by the wayside, to your Bridegroom, beneath whose shadow you rest secure (Song 2:3; Luke 18:35), lest the passing crowd restrain our cries. Rather, aided by your prayers to the Lord, may we deserve to be enlightened from the blindness of our hearts.

We say this so that you may not neglect to calm and uproot the dissension which you know has arisen in our community, as you have begun to do, the Holy Spirit instructing you. And send us also letters of admonition concerning this, because unless it is quickly extinguished, we shall easily incur great danger both to souls and bodies. May the grace of the Holy Spirit, which inwardly teaches you and shows you many secrets, deign to make these matters known to us also, according as it pleases him.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She sends a distinguished instruction, admonition, and exhortation concerning many vices and virtues, urging the pursuit of virtues.

I, a poor little form, long burdened by much illness, was compelled through true Wisdom to set forth these words of Wisdom itself [Col. 0272C] to the people of this place. And I heard that the same Wisdom set before this people its work: namely, how it had established heaven and earth in right measure, so that the brethren of this people might recognize how their institution had first been established and how it has now been forsaken.

And it said:

“I have encompassed the circuit of heaven” (Ecclus. 24:5), “establishing its height and depth so that they might not exceed their proper measure; and I ordered the breadth of the whole world so that it might not disorderly pass beyond its measure. I also made the sun to shine by day and cover the darkness, and the moon to shine by night with the stars.

“For in that word, when God said, ‘Let it be,’ all these things were made and persist even now. Therefore, O peoples, consider yourselves in these things as in a mirror, so that you may remain in that which you have begun.

“For God breathed the breath of life into man (Gen. 1); and thus vivified, he became flesh and blood. Then God granted him fellowship with the angels, with praise and service, and subjected the rest of creation to him. For God had granted him the light of eternity. But, amid all this honour, he listened to the worm; and thus, by transgressing God’s commandments, he was blinded and extinguished.

“Therefore the devil rejoiced within himself and said: ‘The God whom I could not overcome in heaven, I have overcome in his work—that is, in man, who is another god.’ For the devil called man ‘god,’ just as he also wished himself to be God.

“But God, in the ancient counsel which he held in himself before the ages, devised how he might preserve his ordering in such a manner that no one could resist him in it. He hid that same ancient counsel within himself from the knowledge of all creatures. Therefore the devil neither knew nor knows it, and will remain ignorant of that counsel until the last day, when, in his greatest confusion, he will perceive and know certain things concerning it, through which he will be utterly confounded.

“For the devil thought that humankind was irrevocably lost, as he wished it to be. In great savagery and forgetfulness of God, people forgot that they were human and lived inhumanely, until that ancient counsel chose for itself a certain sanctified people.

“And God prefigured sobriety and virginity in Abel, who became a martyr for righteousness’ sake (Gen. 4) and did what his father had neglected to do. The sanctified people knew themselves to be human and lived humanely; from them Noah also arose, whom God preserved in the ark (Gen. 6).

“But God, wishing to submerge iniquity, opened the mouth of the abyss and drowned a very great multitude of creatures in water. Then he swore by himself that he would never again destroy all flesh by water (Gen. 9), remembering that humanity was to be regenerated and saved through water.

“After the Flood, however, the ancient counsel showed many miracles to the confusion of the devil, who rejoiced inwardly at Abel’s murder, saying: ‘Behold, the work of God which I drove from Paradise lies divided upon the earth.’ But sanctified Noah worked in the Holy Spirit and built an altar to God. In it the ancient counsel prefigured that altar which John saw in the Apocalypse (Rev. 8), upon which the prayers of the saints ascended. For when a person prays in repentance for sins and seeks salvation from God, that person is called holy.

“The ancient counsel also wrought many signs in Abraham, who left his country and kindred together with his own will and entered in holiness upon the hard law through which death was confounded and the serpent’s wickedness wounded with an incurable wound. This happened when he fulfilled God’s commandments—what Adam did not do when, transgressing God’s commandment, he followed his own will.

“That same counsel established the purification of the Law in Moses and prefigured through the blood [Col. 0273D] of goats and calves that the innocent Lamb would be sacrificed for humankind. For the Son of God, coming forth from the Father’s heart, was born of a virgin and fulfilled all these things in himself.

“Virginity arose in the Son of God and, with its banner raised, penetrated the heavens; for this Son of the Virgin was wholly whole and wholly holy. Through him there arose the great order of virgins, which the old law had not known.

“He himself was also priest when he sacrificed himself for humankind upon the altar of the cross. Priests too were joined to him in his priesthood because they ought to imitate the angels, who are God’s messengers. For the angels, by the obligation of their office, show God human deeds as though in writing. Priests do the same when they receive human sins through repentance and show them to God through mercy granted.

“So too did the steward (Luke 16), who was accused before his master as though he had squandered his goods, when he ordered each of his master’s debtors to write down less than was owed. This steward is also the Synagogue, which could obtain no release through the blood of goats and calves, but prefigured the sacrifice of the innocent Lamb. Through this it feared being deprived of its office; and it said within itself that it could not endure the harshness of the Law which commanded: ‘Whoever does this or that shall surely die’; nor endure the shame of being cast out, so that it might be restored by no petition for mercy.

“Yet while many were converted in the Son of God to forgiveness, it was praised for the forgiveness of deserved punishment; for when a servant gives recompense to his master through repentance and confession, he is much praised by him because he loved him greatly, as Mary Magdalene loved Christ.

“This Scripture concerns priests. Therefore it is fitting that they imitate Christ, love chastity, and flee incest. For the Son of God suffered on the cross in order to make the unjust just; and he draws them also to himself, as was said concerning the steward. But Abel was a martyr for righteousness.”

After the Passion of the Son of God, a multitude of martyrs arose, who suffered for his faith and confession. Other martyrs accompany them—namely, those who conquer themselves by fighting against sins and vices; these are the wings of the martyrs mentioned above. [Col. 0274C] Those who unjustly persecute them will incur God’s vengeance.

Those too who persecute virginity by affliction, so that they inundate it with sorrows, will not escape God’s vengeance. Thus it often happens that nobles, by God’s judgment, become ignoble, the rich become needy, and they are subjected to many other dangers and calamities.

Those who unjustly oppress and blaspheme the priestly office are guilty like Cain, who killed his brother; thus they must be restrained and punished by his punishment. For the priestly office derives its teaching authority from the Lord God.

Therefore Wisdom built a tower among the multitude of this place (Prov. 9), adorned it with berries, topaz, and sapphire, placed watchmen in it, and built a winepress beside it. Wisdom entrusted the press to certain people, who were to press wine in it, and also made a house alongside it, in which Wisdom commanded others to be, in order to manage all things pertaining to the fields.

But a strong and pestilential storm of madness arose. Those guarding the aforesaid winepress hurled darts at that same tower, while others remaining in the said house threw stones against it; and those who were in the tower cast stones back at them.

This tower signifies the height of teaching: it is adorned with pearls, that is, with those who have lived from childhood in innocence and holiness; it is made bright with topaz, that is, with those who choose the better part and renounce the world; [Col. 0275A] and it is adorned with sapphire, that is, with those who deny worldly pomp and themselves for the love of God.

Its watchmen are those who preside over their subjects in teaching. The winepress signifies the office of those who, bound through consecration, devote themselves at the altar to the ministry of Christ’s Passion and cultivate and guard the vineyard of the Lord of hosts.

But the house signifies the custody and restraint of those who, though unlearned and living in the world, leave the world and themselves for God’s sake, labour in necessary bodily matters, and nevertheless preserve the spiritual life. The storm, however, denotes rashness: those who remain in the winepress direct the sharp points of pride against their superiors; and those who stand in the house direct the hardness of disobedience against them. Therefore those same superiors, provoked to injury, show themselves harsh to their subjects in words of anger.

But Wisdom appoints to all these a truce for amendment, just as in the Gospel the cultivator of the vineyard said to his master concerning the fig tree: “Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure” (Luke 13:8). To dig around it is for a person to suppress the will of personal possession; otherwise that person will never be able to obey. But to put on manure is to submit in humility and subjection to a superior. For when a person inclines to obedience, that person reckons all carnal desires and himself as though they were mud.

Therefore I, a poor and weak little form, say to you, the aforesaid brethren of this place: May the unquenchable fire of life burn within you and so suffuse you with its light that you may be able to remain in it, as you first began. For when a fruitful time of correction and amendment has arisen among you, the stones of your tower will receive their brightness as before.

## LETTER LVI

### Hildegard to Philip, Abbot of Park

She sends him a certain penitent woman who had not confessed properly, and whose sin she had instructed her to disclose, as will appear from Philip’s reply.

[Col. 0275C]

To PHILIP, abbot, HILDEGARD.

O Father, who fears God amid all your negligence and loves him, so that you sigh to him even over every sort of useless thing: run to the fountain of living water, washing not only yourself but also the other sick persons whom you see wounded. Pour into them the wine of repentance, and do not cease to anoint them with the oil of mercy.

For in this you imitate him who is the living fountain and the complete wheel: he receives sinners fleeing to the help of his mercy, and judges by bitter judgment the impious who oppose him. No mountain can touch the circumference of this wheel, because its shadow is over all heights; nor can it be darkened by any low things, since it surpasses all things. For God lives through no one except himself; therefore he has neither beginning nor end.

Thus whoever flees to the help of his grace shall never fall away from the blessedness of eternal life; rather, through the living God, the spark of salvation is kindled anew, because he does not will the death of the sinner, [Col. 0276C] but that the sinner may begin to live through him.

Now, O gentle Father, who stand in Christ’s place, receive this woman, Ida, who has not yet perfectly disclosed her hidden wounds. Cure her most diligently, and all others who flee to you, with the medicine of repentance, so that you may live eternally in the wheel of the true Trinity.

## LETTER LVII

### Philip, Abbot of Park, to Hildegard

Reply to the preceding letter.

PHILIP, by God’s grace called abbot of the Church of Blessed Mary at Park near Louvain, to the venerable HILDEGARD, mistress of the handmaids of God at Bingen: the good of eternal salvation.

Believe, venerable mother; believe, beloved of God: since I first learned, through the renown that proclaimed your virtues by which divine kindness has wondrously glorified its handmaid, I have loved you. Speech concerning you, with praises, has very frequently occupied me without weariness [perhaps *fastidio*, “weariness,” rather than *fastigio*], and you have most often been the meditation of my heart.

The labour of the journey which I undertook testifies to this: I wished to see your venerable face—the mirror, that is, of your illumined mind—and to speak with you face to face. Thanks be to God: I attained the sweetness of your presence, which I had sought and long greatly desired, and you did not deny to my unworthy self the fellowship of conversation with you.

But I regret that I yielded to my brethren who had come with me and would permit no delay with you, as I wished. Yet I hope that I shall still enjoy you in the Lord, whether in this present life or after it, being brought into the loveliness of Paradise by your prayers.

Pray therefore, venerable Mother—pray for one who loves you and venerates God’s grace in you—and for the congregation of brothers and sisters which I must govern: that the Lord may grant us peace and concord, forgive our sins, and make us persevere in his service.

Regarding the penitent woman, Ida: I obeyed your will, which I believe to be God’s will, imposing penance [the text has *jungens*, perhaps *injungens*] for the sin which, the Lord revealing it, you disclosed to her completely. But because she is worn out by old age and has already long been weakened by the disciplines of penance, I ask you to grant her such relief as you know and foresee to be beneficial to her soul.

## LETTER LVIII

### Hildegard to Philip, Abbot of Park

She offers distinguished admonitions.

To PHILIP, abbot, HILDEGARD.

The faith which a person has toward the Lord through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and with an ardent heart is exceedingly glorious when, in the embrace of love, it embraces invisible things as though they were things whose visible presence delights.

So also it is praiseworthy in you that, for love of God, you deigned to see and hear me, a weak and unlearned womanly form. A wind blew from a high mountain and with its breath moved a little feather before splendid citizens and towers—a feather having in itself no power of flight except through the wind. Almighty God undoubtedly took care to do this in order to show that he can work through a thing which presumes nothing of itself, not even the least.

But you, who stand manfully in the office of prophets, to which the care of the apostolic order is joined, extend the aid of your prayers to me, whom you saw lying before you upon the bed of my infirmity, where I still lie. May I be able to remain in God’s grace, for retaining no security in myself, I have placed all my hope and confidence in the mercy of God alone.

Now, O Father, who stand in Christ’s place, exercise care over the sheep of your congregation with the rod of God’s commandments, by which you may rebuke and rule them, lest they be lifted up in pride. This vice is like a city not founded upon a rock and therefore destroyed in falling, because it has no firm foundation.

Anoint frequently with the oil of mercy sinners wounded by whatever crime, lest they stink in the evil habit of sins like Lazarus four days dead. Raise up in all your people the horn of salvation—that is, true humility. This virtue is compared to a sapphire-coloured cloud through which the sun shines mightily. In this imitate the true Sun, the Son of the Virgin, who descended to earth in the utmost humility and in that humility also ascended to the right hand of his Father.

Cut away from them their evil habit of sins, and strive to adorn them in this way like a necklace with precious stones, so that you with them, and they with you, may come together to eternal joy. Now may the grace of the Holy Spirit make you a lamp of true charity to Almighty God, who may also deign to grant you eternal reward for the help which you now give to soul and body.

## LETTER LIX

### The Same to the Same

Written in response to Philip’s inquiry because he feared a sign which had happened to him while celebrating the divine offices, and about which he was greatly troubled. Hildegard removes his fear.

[Col. 0278B]

To PHILIP, abbot, HILDEGARD.

O good and faithful servant of God, who fearfully investigate the cause or meaning of the sign of God recently shown: this lies within the knowledge of the Spirit of God alone, who has no beginning and to whom no creature can be likened. Hear what I answer to your question.

I see what happened to you as like a branch divided into many little branches. Therefore it was not done for you alone, but also for your subjects and many others, so that the hearts of those who hear it may be afraid, correct their negligences, and celebrate only with divine fear and reverence, lest they become subject either to God’s judgment or to the mockery of demons by God’s own permission.

For I also saw that this occurred through a certain mockery by aerial spirits, God nevertheless permitting it for the causes mentioned above. Therefore, sweet and gentle Father, do not be disturbed. Rather, give thanks to God if any who hear this are corrected because of you.

And do not for this reason delay further in exercising the priestly office; but, purified by confession and penance, strive to serve God in the celebration of Masses. Therefore, servant of God, rejoice and exult in the Lord without trembling, because God loves you and will receive your soul.

## LETTER LX

### G., Abbot, and the Brethren of Brunwiller to Hildegard

Concerning a demon-possessed woman.

> [Note: Col. 0277. See Book III, chapter 2, of the Life of Saint Hildegard written by the monks Godfrey and Theodoric, which appears at the beginning of this volume.]

[Col. 0278D]

To HILDEGARD, venerable lady and mother, Christ’s bride to be embraced with all the inward affections, and daughter of the most high King: G., whatever sort of overseer he may be of the monastery of Brunwiller, together with his brethren sitting in the valley of tears, devoted service of every love in their prayers, as they are able.

Although, most loving lady, your face is unknown to us, the fame of your virtues is exceedingly renowned among us. And though we are absent in body, we are nevertheless continually present to you in spirit; the Lord of knowledge knows the affection of our love toward you.

Thus, in our land this report has been heard and widely spread: this thing has been done concerning you by the Lord, who [perhaps *quia*, “because”] has done great things for you, who is mighty and whose name is holy. But the source of living light shines forth in you by what and how great miracles—your name, clergy, people, and the outcome of events all bear witness.

For what shines in you is not a human work but a divine one: grace going before, a surpassing gift, not dictated by human reason but proceeding from the most radiant fountain. But why delay? We are more inclined to weep than to speak.

Therefore, O most merciful lady, may the sweetness of your holiness not count it rashness that, in simplicity of heart but compelled by extreme necessity, we presume to disclose to you the cause of our need. For we do not doubt that we shall receive good counsel from you.

A certain noblewoman, possessed by a malignant spirit for several years, arrived among us, brought by the hands of friends so that, with the aid of blessed Nicholas, under whose patronage we are, she might be freed from the threatening enemy. But the cunning and malice of this most crafty and wicked enemy have led nearly thousands of people into error and doubt, to the great detriment of holy Church, as we fear.

For we, together with a multitude of people, have laboured in many ways for the liberation of this woman for three months already; yet, what we cannot say without sorrow, because our sins demand it, we have achieved nothing. Therefore all our hope after God is in you.

For this demon, once adjured on a certain day, finally disclosed to us that this possessed woman was to be liberated through the power of your contemplation and the greatness of divine revelation. Does God, then, intend something great in her liberation? Certainly.

Therefore the most abundant goodness of our Redeemer will deign through you to bring the labour of our undertaking and sorrow, but also of joy and exultation, to complete fulfilment, so that all human error and unbelief may be annihilated and the possessed handmaid of God set free. Then we may say with the Prophet: “This has been done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes” (Ps. 117:23), and: “The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. 123:7).

We urgently and humbly entreat your holiness to endeavour to indicate to us by letter what God has intimated to you concerning these matters or revealed in a vision. Farewell.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She gives counsel concerning the woman’s liberation.

To G., abbot of the Church of Brunwiller, H[ildegard].

Since I am constrained by God’s scourges in a long and severe illness, I can scarcely answer your petition even a little. I say these things not from myself but from him who is.

There are diverse kinds of malignant spirits. But this demon concerning which you inquire has arts resembling human dispositions in vices. Therefore it gladly remains with human beings, and for that reason it somewhat disregards and mocks the Lord’s cross, the relics of saints, and other things pertaining to God’s service, and does not greatly fear them. It does not indeed love these things, but pretends to flee them, as a foolish and negligent person makes light of words and threats brought against him by the wise. Therefore it is expelled with more difficulty than another demon.

For it will not be expelled except by fasts, scourges, prayers, alms, and God’s own command [the text seems to lack *non*, “not”]. Hear therefore—not the answer of a human being, but of him who lives.

Choose seven priests of good testimony, proved by the merit of their lives: six in the names and order of Abel, Noah, Abraham, Melchizedek, Jacob, and Aaron, who offered sacrifice to the living God; and the seventh in the name of Christ, who offered himself to God the Father on the cross.

After fasts, scourges, prayers, alms, and the celebration of Masses have preceded, let them approach the suffering woman in humble intention and priestly dress, wearing stoles. As they stand around her, let each hold a rod in his hand, in the figure of the rod with which Moses, at God’s command, struck Egypt, the Red Sea, and the rock. Thus, as God there showed miracles through the rod, so here, after the most wicked enemy has been driven out by rods, may he glorify himself.

The seven priests shall represent the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that the Spirit of God, who in the beginning moved over the waters and breathed the breath of life into the human face, may blow the unclean spirit out of the afflicted person.

And the first, who shall be in Abel’s name, holding a rod in his hand, shall say: “Hear, malignant and foolish spirit, whoever you are that dwell in this person: hear these words, not premeditated by a human being, but made manifest through him who is and who lives,” etc.

## LETTER LXI

### G., Abbot, and the Brethren of Brunwiller to Hildegard

The same woman is again tormented by the demon.

To the venerable H[ildegard], worthy of every thanksgiving: G., unworthy abbot of Brunwiller, together with his brethren, wishes her life, advancement, the world beneath her foot, and whatever more excellent thing may be desired for a handmaid of Christ.

The whole world already knows that the Lord has looked upon you and poured out his grace upon you. But we, who [Col. 0280D] until now have spoken to your holiness through our messengers and letters concerning the need of the woman possessed by an evil spirit, now at last send her in person to you with great hope, returning to the city of necessity; and we devoutly add prayer upon prayer, that the nearer she is to you bodily, the more gracious you may be toward her spiritually. For the demon, adjured by your letters, which you sent at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, had left the possessed vessel for a short hour; but alas! we do not know by what judgment of God he returned, and, invading again the vessel he had abandoned, now torments it more fiercely than before. When we in turn adjured him and pressed him strongly, he finally replied that he would leave the possessed vessel only in your presence. Therefore [Col. 0281A] we send her to your holiness, so that the Lord may accomplish through you what, because our sins demanded it, we did not deserve; and, the ancient enemy having been cast out, may he [Col. 0282A] who is mighty above all be glorified in you. May your motherly love prosper.

## Notice Concerning the Following Letters

(D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 1013.)

[Col. 0281]

You have about fifty letters printed in the Cologne and Lyons editions of the *Libraries of the Fathers*, besides one addressed to the abbot of Brunvillar, which occurs in the *Life of St Hildegard* composed by Theoderic, abbot of Saint-Trond, in Surius under 17 September. We found many more in a highly reliable manuscript of Himmerod Abbey, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Trier. The manuscript, written about five hundred years ago, contains various minor works of Hildegard: namely, letters addressed to her by different persons, together with her replies to their various inquiries; the *Life of St Disibod*, the *Life of Duke St Rupert*, and of St Bertha, his own mother; a short exposition of the Rule of St Benedict; and the six books of the *Book of the Merits of Life*, which she composed in the sixty-first year of her age, that is, in the year 1158, during pressure upon the Apostolic See, while Frederick was reigning as emperor of the Romans. The first book contains 124 chapters, the second 85, the third 84, the fourth 70, the fifth 85, and the sixth 45. From this you may conclude that Trithemius, who ascribes only three books of the *Merits of Life* to St Hildegard, did not see this work in its entirety. Yet he lists many other of her minor works, which it seems superfluous to recount here.

But to return to the letters: the Himmerod manuscript contains all those published in both *Libraries of the Fathers*, and in addition eighty-four which do not appear to us at all unworthy of public notice. For, besides the fact that all writings of the saints commonly breathe a piety that contributes greatly to their readers’ salvation of soul, in all the letters addressed to Hildegard one will not encounter a mere account of spiritual or moral matters: almost all are historical. Some were written on the occasion of the schism raised by Frederick between Pope Alexander III and the antipope Victor IV; in one, a doctor of the University of Paris asks what should be believed concerning the opinion of Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, condemned at the Council of Rheims; in others there is discussion of how regular discipline should be restored in decayed monasteries. In several, too, persecutions inflicted upon monasteries, and the writers’ temptations and inward dispositions, are set forth. Not a few abbots and abbesses ask her whether they ought to retain or resign their office. Hence it is clear that all these letters contribute greatly to illuminating both ecclesiastical and monastic history.

Moreover, it should not be passed over incidentally that, when consulted by the abbot of Rettenhasel, who had been called to the abbacy of Salem, whether he should relinquish both offices, Hildegard replied: “Whoever has undertaken the care of a field or a sheepfold for the sake of the faith ought not to abandon them, but should govern them as a householder. For he who leaves his own sheepfold and receives another is called a transgressor of God’s commandments.” I should like those to heed this who so easily move from see to see, contrary to the prescriptions promulgated by the canons and the holy Fathers. Finally, we owe these letters to the kindness of the most reverend and distinguished Robert, abbot of Himmerod, who not only permitted them to be copied from his manuscript, but of his own accord even sent the manuscript itself to us at Paris.

## Letter LXII

[Col. 0281B]

### From A., Abbot of Eberbach, to Hildegard

He asks her to consult the divine oracle concerning his enemies and to reply what he ought to expect from God’s mercy.

To HILDEGARD, beloved spouse of Christ, A., called abbot of Eberbach in name alone: after the vale of tears, the joys of the citizens above.

Gladly, despite so great a distance of land between us, we offer your blessedness the duty of greeting, embracing in you the mighty works of God, who has caused you to flourish in the holiness of a purer life and has granted you, beyond human expectation, by the spirit of prophecy to touch things present, review things past, and foresee things future; so that, doubly honoured by the newness of the divine gift, [Col. 0281C] you are truly wondrous and worthy of veneration to people of this age. For the Dayspring has visited us, and now, as the age collapses, has laid his hand upon us: he who in our happy time has granted one such and so great to shine amid the clouds of this wicked age. Through her intervention we rejoice to obtain forgiveness of sins, relief from labours, consolation for sorrows, and knowledge of the hidden ordering of God.

[Col. 0282B] Our conscience accuses us; guilt terrifies us; sins rebuke us. Within we are troubled; without, we are endangered. Nowhere is there security for us; on every side the enemy resounds around us. On the right a deceitful friend lays snares; on the left a savage enemy attacks. Concerning these matters, and others about which our messengers shall consult your maturity, consult the divine oracle; and, most holy mother, write back to us whatever we should expect from the mercy of God.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She consoles the afflicted man, exhorts the sluggish, and rouses him to fight manfully.

He who sees and is not changed by alteration says: You, human being, do not yet have the wings of flight that endure storms and that belong to the right tempering of the air. Rather, you are like a column standing in a street without the apparatus of a building and without the ascent of a ladder, so that you are spattered with the ladder’s mud. For you are gentle and not sharp-sighted with the eye of correction for reproving the perverse and black habits of men. Yet the grace of God beholds you, not as one enclosed in hardness of heart, but merely asleep in the numbness of self-indulgence, so that you do not heed God. Therefore [Col. 0283A] do not regard your Lord as a steward; rather, look to him, [against] wickedness, as a most valiant soldier fighting most bravely, armed with breastplate and helmet.

For these are now times as though in forgetfulness of God, weary in Christ’s contest. Yet report flies amid lies through the alternation of vanities, as though people saw God; yet they do not know him. Where then is the person who walks in the straight path? There are few. But he who is says: “No human being can, by the vomit of his chatter, precipitately draw the sword of my vengeance from its sheath before the time of my will in vengeance arrives.” Therefore, O human being, arise and make your spirit radiant in me, so that you may vigilantly seek where to find me, and you shall live.

## Letter LXIII

### From H., Abbot of Maulbronn, to Hildegard

Anxious about the governance of souls, he asks for the aid of her prayers.

[Col. 0283B]

To HILDEGARD, venerable mother and sister, H., abbot of Maulbronn in name—would that it were in merit!—perpetual salvation from the Lord.

We have heard good things of you, O servant of Christ. We have heard them, and we render thanks to the giver of all good things. Therefore I, such as I am, send writings to you, not without hope of being heard, and ask for some special assistance from your prayers. For I have been entrusted with an arduous and anxious charge, namely the governance of souls; I ask, seek, and knock that through you I may be helped by the Lord with power and a happy result. Nor should it [Col. 0283C] be burdensome or unworthy of you to send me a letter of your own, by which my body and soul may be instructed, strengthened, and consoled. Farewell.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She exhorts him to good works and to restrain in himself concerns about worldly matters.

Prudent man of true light: O human being, these words must be heard. Whoever wishes to pass to life must have the contemplative vision of the soul’s living eyes, because God keeps watch over such deeds. For when the submersion of the loins of an ashen cause comes, vomiting forth various crimes, then let the person bridle the taste of his mind and waste away in the unbearable deed of hardness, rising to the dawn of light—that is, to the mercy which has laid death low and crushed the foul entrails of Gehenna, [Col. 0283D] where that same mercy wiped away human crimes. Thus a person should have windows by which to restore himself in goodness.

But, O you who are noble in your will, observe that many rivers surge within you, quarrelling in great tumult. O strong bond, and so many breasts of the pleasures of sprouting vices! Stand also in the example of the turtledove, bending your knees when you conquer yourself. O living image, open the enclosure of your mind into a beautiful face, as is fitting for you in the sight of the highest King. Beware also lest you be vehement lead because of the hardness of your mouth, if you do not anoint the wounds of painful scars. But kiss God in your mind, and let not your desires be ashamed to carry out upright and just works in his good will. Now let there be [Col. 0284A] refreshment for you in your labour; restrain worldly concerns within yourself; and make the face of your spirit beautiful as a dove, so that the windows of heavenly Jerusalem may receive you. The Lord will not forsake you, but will give you the refreshment of salvation.

## Letter LXIV

### From B., Abbot of St Michael’s, Bamberg, to Hildegard

That she may implore divine mercy, so that it may moderate the scourge by which he is afflicted, and that he may have his soul, soon to depart this world, commended to her.

To Lady H., betrothed to the highest King and mistress of the sisters of St Rupert, B., unworthy abbot of St Michael’s in Bamberg: whatever his prayer [Col. 0284B] and devotion can accomplish.

We hear that you burn in the love of him who redeemed us by his own blood, and according to our measure we earnestly beseech him also that he may keep forever the gifts entrusted to you. We desire your presence with great longing of heart; but, impeded by the obstacles of sins, we have hitherto been unable to obtain it. Therefore, by him whom you love, we most earnestly beseech your sweetness that you may implore the mercy of the Lord for me, that he may deign so to temper the scourge of mercy by which he has touched me and touches me daily that I may deserve to find salvation here and mercy and grace in the world to come. But if divine predestination should deign soon, as I hope, to call me from these darknesses, [Col. 0284C] I wish my soul to be commended to your hands and prayers. Send us writings of your consolation through the present messenger.

### Hildegard’s Reply

That he may keep vigorous watch and honourably bear the Father’s rod, which will benefit him.

In the fiery admonition it has been predestined that this people shall hear in a living voice what is drawn from the torrent-stone amid the darkness of God’s mysteries. But I see you sometimes shining in your purpose like the dawn, yet at times undergoing labour and distress in yourself and in others, so that you are wearied by it as intensely as though you did not know what [Col. 0284D] you could do. But now hear the most noble householder admonishing you: “Keep vigorous watch and rise in the light, that you may honourably bear his rod by day. For if the outward person is sometimes wearied under God’s scourge, the inward person rises all the stronger, through the strongest power which wishes to sustain you in the revolving wheel of his grace.”

## Letter LXV

### From Berthold, Abbot of Zwiefalten, to Hildegard

Suffering persecutions, he seeks from her some aid of consolation.

To HILDEGARD, servant of God of Mount St Rupert at Bingen, BERTHOLD, abbot of Zwiefalten in name alone, dust and ashes: whatever the prayer of a sinner can accomplish.

[Col. 0285A] Long desiring conversation with you, I wished to cry aloud to you face to face concerning the injuries and tribulations that cruel persecutors inflict upon me while they strive to reduce me to nothing. For although I have often been made more cheerful by the consolations of your words, I have nevertheless been made more sorrowful by their obscurity, because they scarcely lay open to my understanding. Therefore, sending this messenger to you, I beat upon your ears with tearful and pitiable petitions, asking that, according to the capacity of my little intellect, as you seek God’s will concerning the distresses that press upon us, you may send me some consolation in writing. For I greatly fear that my mind may be scattered by the storm of unwonted tribulation and submerged in the depth of despair.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She declares that a son of inheritance has been wounded by the rod because of the restless habits of his mind.

[Col. 0285B]

The living light says: I saw a certain man whom I left, as it were weak and lame, in the eminence of teaching. How so? Those who, in the weakness of their flesh, were rebellious like naked shipwrecked men, he fled because of fear of battle. But now I see him as a humble and weeping pilgrim. Therefore I regard him as a son of inheritance, struck by the rod because of the restlessness of his mind’s habits. Yet I wish to restore him to the primitive Church as a blessed man, when the mountain in Taurus is submerged. Now live forever.

## Letter LXVI

### From G., Abbot of Salem, to Hildegard

The abbot of Rettenhasel, elected abbot of Salem, wishes to renounce both offices and asks her to investigate God’s will.

[Col. 0285C]

To his most beloved lady and mother in Christ, H., G., servant of the brothers at Salem: whatever the prayer of a sinner can accomplish.

Everyone who loves Christ also possesses the Spirit of Christ, and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12). But you, sweetest mother, have been sent, by a gift of the Holy Spirit special among the other members of Christ, to visit the end of this world. For the Holy Spirit, truly speaking through you and in you as in his instrument, is openly recognized [Col. 0285D] and revealed. Indeed, I have seen and read the very great sacraments of God’s mysteries which, through you in the book written by you, the Lord of knowledge has opened and disclosed to unworthy people. Therefore I believe and hold with complete certainty that the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from God the Father and the Son, will through you both shine forth by speaking and flash forth by shining against the spirit of falsehood, who is soon to come from his father the devil.

Therefore, with you as the bride and servant of Christ and one knowing God’s secrets, I humbly and simply seek the judgment of your will concerning the anxiety of my heart—if, nevertheless, this disposition and desire is not contrary to his will. By the common counsel of the brothers of Salem, after the abbot of that house had died, I was elected father; although previously, for a long time, I had administered the same pastoral care, albeit [Col. 0286A] uselessly, at Rettenhasel. God, who knows hidden things, himself knows that I have always had, and still have, both this administration and that entirely against my will. Therefore I ask that, as I simply seek it, you may simply make known to me the will of the Holy Spirit concerning this matter: namely, if it is safer and more salutary to lay aside this burden, deign to tell me so; but if not, may I deserve to know this also through you. Whatever you wish, however, let sealed letters sent by you to me through the bearer of this letter report it. Farewell, my lady, in the Lord.

### Hildegard’s Reply

One who has undertaken the governance of a sheepfold for the sake of faith ought not to relinquish pastoral care; but one who leaves a sheepfold in order to take another is a transgressor.

[Col. 0286B]

Whoever has undertaken the care of a field or a sheepfold for the sake of the faith ought not to abandon them, but should govern them as a householder. For he who leaves his own sheepfold and receives another is called a transgressor of God’s commandments. But you, shepherd, hold the rod of correction according to the Father’s mercy and according to a shepherd’s care. Nor should a shepherd make himself a thief. How so? A thief takes away what he wants and leaves what he does not want. So too many shepherds, according to their own will, choose what they want and reject what they do not want. They often despise perfect disciples and seek the wandering and empty. But a merciful father corrects his own son in all love and does not take away from him what is good.

In your community [Col. 0286C] I see some shining like the dawn through good works and patience; but I see the greater part, through the alternation of their habits, cloudy vanities, and their possessiveness, excusing themselves in words. Admonish and correct these as much as you can. For God chose the Old and New Testaments and left them to his children, that they might be taught through the Holy Spirit to live by a right law. God, however, wants you. See, then, that you do not depart from him.

## Letter LXVII

### From B., Abbot of St Eucharius, to Hildegard

He praises God’s gifts in her and commends himself to her prayers.

To HILDEGARD, radiant pearl, B., poor servant of Christ [Col. 0286D] and unworthy abbot of St Eucharius: may you please the bridegroom of virgins in your profession of virginity.

We have heard and know the fame of your virtue—indeed, the virtue of divine mercy working in your earthen vessel. We have heard and known it, and at once recognized in you the fulfilment of that prophetic saying: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke,” etc. (Lam. 3). Truly, you have borne much and more than much: for what we fear to undertake, you have passed through with a manly spirit and made so customary that you can say with the Apostle: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

But although, hindered by the surges of this turbulent age, we have long refrained from greeting your holiness through our messengers, it must not be thought that the fire of charity which once began to burn toward you in our hearts has cooled in any respect. [Col. 0287A] Therefore, in no respect should your blessedness forget our feebleness before him with whom you are one spirit; and continually urge the sisters entrusted to you to act likewise for us and for our house. We desire also your words of admonition, and from the depths of all our hearts we wish that you may always be well. Farewell.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She gives him pious counsels, especially that he may exercise gentleness toward those subject to him.

He who is says: O human being, you are clothed with the breastplate of faith and wrapped about with the girdle of holiness. A person sees his face in a mirror, yet does not thereby have full joy, because he sometimes doubts whether [Col. 0287B] his face is beautiful or not. For your mind is like a building seen from afar and sometimes covered by mist. You are also precipitous like a burden which a carrier bears for sale. Therefore consider whether an ox or an ass is more useful; green land or dry; a noun or a pronoun; a mountain or a valley among a person’s enemies. Yet a good master is far more useful than the rest of the crowd, just as air is useful, producing diverse fruits upon its wings. For a person’s works avail little without the master’s providence.

Now beware lest you waste away in the exercise of mastery while you still have, as it were, one eye of life; but give light to yours in motherly sweetness, and wipe their wounds without a reputation for tyranny, because a good physician anoints people’s wounds with mercy and does not delay in this. For he gave his own sheep a kiss and washed her in his blood. But you, O human being, place mercy—the king’s beautiful friend—in the chamber of your mind; clothe holiness with sweetest charity as with purple; gather the sweetest spices into your breast as a diadem of beauty, and [Col. 0287C] you shall live forever, like a mountain of myrrh and incense. Therefore keep watch, bearing your burdens with the key of recompense, so that when the sun shines above all things without the storm of diverse tempests, you may then appear there to your benefit.

## Letter LXVIII

### From L., Abbot of St Eucharius, to Hildegard

He testifies to his reverence for her and asks that she reply concerning a matter entrusted to her.

[Col. 0287D]

To the holy virgin H., consecrated to God, his beloved mother, L., abbot of St Eucharius in name alone: greeting, and such an affection of devotion that, if anyone besides me knew it, he would know either nothing or things that cannot be known.

It would seem quite ridiculous if eagles sent letters of greeting to butterflies, stags to fleas, or lions to earthworms. So too—indeed, more than this—it is astonishing, or, to speak more truly, laughable, that a sinner of little or no worth in divine or human arts presumes to write to one whom God has made marvellous, with a wondrous prerogative of chastity and such lofty and eminent excellence of intellect, that you surpass not only the acuteness of philosophers and dialecticians but even that of the ancient prophets.

Nevertheless, most pious mother, you will not deny forgiveness in your customary kindness to this rash presumption, since the cause of writing back will be the boldness of familiarity. Neither will the difficulty of the journey deter me from writing to you and often coming to you, while the usefulness of your discourses invites me—the more pleasing because acquired by greater effort. For we possess more pleasantly what we acquire by labour. Therefore, lady, let not our importunity move you, since compassionate charity will supply the strength that bodily weakness denies you. I await with great longing the letters you promised, which do not delay to send through the bearer of this letter. And write back also whatever seems right to you concerning the matter entrusted to you.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She teaches how he ought to conduct himself toward those under his care.

[Col. 0288B]

In a true vision I saw and heard this: A certain man diligently cultivated a garden, but a mist came over it and dried it out. That man left the same garden uncultivated; afterwards he overturned that same garden by digging it and placed roses, lilies, and other good fragrant plants in it. But again the flowers of these plants were shaken by an oncoming storm. Then that same man said within himself: “I shall make a field out of this garden, in which I shall sow wheat and barley.”

Now listen, you who are called Father. This garden was your beginning, which at first was somewhat clouded by varied change; but later, through the admonition [Col. 0288C] of the Holy Spirit, you turned it toward a better part and delighted in the Holy Spirit as in good herbs. Yet weariness sometimes exhausted you, just as a storm bends flowers. Now it has pleased God to make you a cultivator, so that with great solicitude you may look around on every side and set the plough straight in the ground, because it will not benefit you to grow sluggish through weariness. Do this according to the examples of the saints, and from their conduct learn the habits of a pious father. Love the good and upright; correct the empty and delinquent; and patiently endure those who are hard as stones, lest you fall upon them in hardness and in the rush of anger like an eagle. Instead, do everything with moderation, lest [Col. 0288D] you scatter Christ’s flock.

Restrain yourself also, live according to the Rule of the most learned master, and receive instruction from the most mighty man, who brought forth waters and divided them into streams; who makes the earth germinate and fruit-bearing plants blossom; who raised mountains and set them above valleys; who established the firmament with all its adornments; and who brought forth winds to blow and air to fly with fire. This same man is also blessed, because all blessedness proceeds from him; and he is called “man” because he created all things and bore manfully all things that are virtuous and strong.

Therefore imbue your understanding with the streams of the waters of Scripture, with the conduct of the saints, and with how they lived. Restrain your body, lest it make the devil’s riches sprout instead of virtues through good teaching; [Col. 0289A] attend also to the mountain of virtues. Do this through humility, and bring forth flowers among your brothers as from trees. Be also the sun through teaching, the moon through discernment, the wind through vigorous mastery, the air through gentleness, and fire through the beautiful discourse of teaching. Begin these things in the beautiful dawn and complete them in radiant light; persevere also vigorously in them, that you may live forever.

## Letter LXIX

### From W., Abbot of Bosenweiler, to Hildegard

Suffering persecutions and calumnies, he asks her for prayers and letters of consolation.

W., by God’s grace, though unworthy, abbot of Bosenweiler, to H., his most beloved virgin consecrated to God: that which is most blessed in eternal life.

[Col. 0289B] Since in the storms of tribulations God’s grace has granted you to be a harbour of salvation to all who flee to you, we too, in peril, do not hesitate to stretch out suppliant hands to you. Therefore, by this present letter, we make known to you that our church, which by God’s mercy has for many years been held in great honour, has now, because our sins demanded it, been stained by a detestable report of disgrace. For certain of our own people, instigators of evils, at the suggestion of the devil, who is always hostile to good people, do not cease to burden our house, us, and the whole community with every disturbance in their power. And, to state it all briefly, their unbridled pride has brought things about so that everyone says our sins, formerly hidden, have now [Col. 0289C] been made manifest.

Therefore, bringing this burden of oppression to you for relief, we humbly ask you to write us some word of consolation concerning it. Above all, we earnestly beg that by your prayers you may reconcile us to God and to men. Farewell.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She teaches that his monastery is sustained by God’s aid and warns him to avoid certain things.

In the vision by which my soul often sees, I behold while awake, in your place, a whirlwind—as if amid the shifting of a radiant, black, and troubled cloud—and that place greatly disturbed. But in your soul I see three colours: first, the blackness of malice and anger; second, the smoke of a taste for uselessness; [Col. 0289D] third, the likeness of a radiant dawn of goodwill and longing that pants after God. Yet I see a glorious light ascending to God in some of your community; therefore God sustains that place by his help.

But you, good shepherd, look at the field which is blessed by God in the fullness of its fruits, and over which a black mist comes that greatly harms it and makes its fruit worse than before. This is the weariness and malice in the heart of one who knows what is good and can accomplish it, but occupies his mind in both directions—namely, weariness and malice—and is thus hindered from good work. Son of God, flee these things and work in the fruitful field with the fire of the Holy Spirit before the day comes when you will no longer be able to work.

## Letter LXX

[Col. 0290A]

### From R., Abbot of Zwettl, to Hildegard

He asks for advice whether he ought to relinquish pastoral care.

To the holy and venerable mother H., R., servant of God’s servants at Zwettl: may you see the King of kings in his beauty in the land of the living.

The manifestation of the Spirit given to you for the benefit of many proves that God’s grace has been poured out upon your lips. For we believe that you have received that Spirit of wisdom and understanding which is from God, which blows where it wills (John 3), has mercy on whom it wills, and hardens whom it wills (Rom. 9). Knowing this, I have been pleased by this letter to consult your prudence—or rather, through you to invoke the Holy Spirit, the author of your prudence, to disperse the darkness of my mind.

[Col. 0290B] For I bear a heavy burden, namely the office of pastoral care. To carry it to the end is difficult and laborious for me, as something for which neither the merit of my life nor my instruction in wisdom is equal; but to lay it down is equally dangerous. I therefore beseech your holiness to console my faint-heartedness amid this uncertainty and deign to write back to me whatever pleases the Holy Spirit.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She gives him pious and salutary counsels for governing those under his care.

In your thoughts you exaggerate that you wish to rest or desist from every labour, and so you do not raise your hand to perform the work of your master; but with gnashing teeth you say within yourself: “I cannot endure all the things [Col. 0290C] that oppose and contradict me.” For this time resembles the time of the children of Israel, when their leaders laboured greatly to instruct them in God’s commandments; but they looked into the pit of their own possession, despising God. This now also happens among the children of Israel—that is, among the spiritual people who are in the contemplation of God.

But however the children of Israel sinned, God never left them without a teacher. Finally, the immaculate Master came, who in his humanity wounded all iniquity and was mightiest above all, because no one appeared equal to him. But consider what he suffered from the unjust and what an example he left to teachers. [Col. 0290D] Yet you say within yourself: “I can accomplish no good in them.” Now look into yourself and see how you may bear and endure them, so that neither they are blamed with you nor you found guilty with them. But whoever loves justice, afflicts injustice, and shares in none of it, even if he is not heard by his disciples, is righteous. For Christ gathered his beloved and chosen ones, although he was not received by all people.

Look also into yourself with the encircling band of God’s justice, as it is written: “Within, clad about with variety in golden fringes” (Ps. 44). That is: in your spirit and heart be gentle and mild. Be so also in golden fringes, so that you may do these things wisely by expanding them, and correct those subject to you with the encircling band of justice, possessing charity with that variety so as to scatter it everywhere, just as the winds are divided in their powers.

[Col. 0291A] For the north wind strikes and spares in no way; but another wind, in some respect like it, supports it. Another wind is opposed to these in gentleness; but yet another tempers them all. The north wind is firm correction, in which a certain anger lies hidden. But another wind supports it with severity and discernment, so that a person may correct justly. The wind gentler than these teaches a person to be merciful and compassionate, so that he remembers that every other person is also a human being like himself; and thus this wind is the eye of the same winds. But the burning wind tempers, apportions, and discerns all these winds with charity, namely, [Col. 0291B] lest the north wind fall with the falling sickness, as Satan fell, but may persevere in uprightness; and so that that wind, which is severe, may stand firm in the constancy of just retribution, as it is written: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Eph. 4).

That is, anger ought to be such that it does not join itself to iniquity through consent, nor wholly bind a person to a hateful accusation.
