Therefore let that gentler wind, tempered by the aforesaid burning wind, persist with measured correction, as one does who strikes his son with a rod yet loves him. Temper, apportion, and discern yourself in this manner; correct yourself in faith and fear of God; and then the jesting woman of vices and the clouding of restless habits will flee from you, and the fire of the Holy Spirit will burn within you.

## Letter LXXI

[Col. 0291C]

### From Nicholas, Abbot of Halesbrunn, to Hildegard

He asks her for letters of consolation.

To the venerable mother and lady H. of St Rupert, much beloved in Christ, Brother NICHOLAS, called abbot at Heilsbronn: whatever may be wished more happily or hoped more sublimely.

Confident that you have always delighted in providing what is more useful for all, I earnestly ask that you may also advise me with your customary affection. Why I have not visited your holiness for so long, I believe is not unknown to you, since I have desired it from my very depths. But what I cannot do in deed, I accomplish in mind. Whether this is so requires no witness other than you. Now [Col. 0291D] I humbly ask, seek, and knock, that divine consolation may be given me through you: namely, that I may be forewarned by your letters and delivered from evil by your holy prayers. For nothing is impossible to God, and we know that this will not be denied to you. Farewell.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She praises his good disposition toward God and exhorts him to labour.

The True Light speaks in the Light through the mouth of Wisdom: “The old Law left behind official signs, and it grew weary in hearing the word; it would not labor, and thus it came to an end. Then the Church arose under the King’s banner, observed that same Law with a most pure eye, did not grow weary, but labored willingly. Do likewise, O good soldier.” And again: “When a warrior leads out his army, if some worthless man allows his banner to fall, another most valiant man raises it and bears it vigorously. Therefore his lord loves him greatly and gives him a great reward. So it will be with you also, if you labor vigorously with Christ in Christ’s stead.

“But your mind gleams in a certain good intention toward God, though a whirlwind-wind of a certain uselessness wearies you; yet the Holy Spirit will cast it away from you. The streets of certain cities are muddy, the shoes of certain people are full of rottenness, justice is clouded together with iniquity, and the commandments of the Law have been violated through transgression of God’s commandments. Therefore let the shepherds howl and sprinkle themselves with ashes, because those appointed to ranks in the Church no longer wish to know what they are. For the head lacks eyes and the feet have no paths, because the crimes of men’s superfluous wickedness have not yet been wholly purged by God’s hand. Yet these evils will end before long, and a better light will shine than the former.

“Now certain people are divided into two parts in their heart: in one part, they wish, through the arrogance of their own mind, to know everything; in the other, they hate the progress of those who walk in the straight way. The most evil devilish troop, which is called the heart of evil, harasses them most sharply and harmfully. This kind of malignant spirits does not dare to oppose what God has established, but draws every matter aside, so that what they themselves desire and choose unto perdition, they call, in their own judgment, good and holy in God; and thus they lead the people in great mockery. But as to how this kind is to be escaped: it is destroyed in the humility and steadfastness of faithful people.”

## EPISTLE LXXII

**THE ABBOTS OF BELLEVAL, G. OF CHÂTEAU-LOCI, A. OF CLAIRFONTAINE, R. OF CHARITY, AND G. OF BETHANY, TO HILDEGARD.** They praise the divine gifts in her and send her a noble but barren woman, that, through Hildegard’s merits and prayers before God, she may be able to bear children.

G., called abbot of Belleval; G. of Château-Loci; A. of Clairfontaine; R. of Charity; and G. of Bethany, to H., Christ’s most choice bride [Col. 0292D]: may you flourish in grace and join in the song of praise.

With all the joy of our hearts, we render thanks to God, the giver of every spiritual anointing, who does not disdain to renew in our time the ancient miracles of His condescension. From this we readily perceive that we are by no means deprived of the promises by which He formerly comforted His own, saying: “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Although we may be found unworthy of these promises, nevertheless we recognize your heart, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, as so filled with them that, although unlearned in composing books and doing very many other wonderful things—things now astonishing to those present—the heavenly harmony breathes wondrously upon you, and things previously unknown to mortals are made manifest through you.

And what wonder is this? For now—yes, now, I say—you are the true and immaculate Bride of Christ, leaning upon your Beloved, “whose left hand is under your head, and whose right hand embraces you” (Song of Songs 1), who has brought you into His chamber and has excellently disclosed His secrets to you [Col. 0293A]. Wishing earnestly that the Lord may strengthen you in these things, we most humbly ask that you take care to have something concerning our condition divinely revealed to you and communicated to us.

But this woman, the bearer of the present letter, is noble and the wife of a certain much-beloved man. With great devotion she comes to you humbly and on foot, though she could come on horseback and with a large retinue. The reason for her coming is this. She has remained barren for a long time, although she formerly bore children; but after they died, and as she bears no others, both she and her husband are deeply afflicted with grief. Therefore she flees to you, a handmaid and intimate servant of Christ, trusting that through your merits and prayers you may obtain from God that she may yet be made fruitful and offer to Christ the blessed fruit of her womb in the begetting of offspring. Therefore, asked by her and by her husband, we ask you to stand before God for them in this petition, so that they may deserve to obtain what they desire.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** After giving them various pious admonitions, she says that it lies within God’s will whether to make the matron fruitful or not; meanwhile, she promises to pray for her.

[Col. 0293C]

O persons who, through God’s grace, are in the Lord’s calling of pastoral care: learn from Adam’s first calling, when God said to him, “Where are you?” (Gen. 3), after he had become a transgressor through disobedience. Then his name itself was as it were dark earth, and God gave him clothing, knowing that because of him He would assume the garment of humanity. In a clear voice of mercy He also called him back when the wandering son came to himself and remembered himself, saying: “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here through hunger!” (Luke 15). And his father received him with joy.

Now it is fitting for you, teachers, that with the first eye of brightness you should see that God called Adam back by an alien way: namely, by the kiss of humanity in the fatted calf, saying thus: “Man had perished through disobedience, but I will bring him back through repentance.” But also ascend the lofty mountain, make tabernacles in the valley, and remain in them a long time. For when you look upward, following God you ascend the mountain. Then look also into profound humility, because the Son of God in His humanity bore the whole human being. In all your works—in yourselves and in others—attend to humility and persevere in it for a long time.

Take care, therefore, that your mind not be like a black mountain, where metals are made in glowing coals by the arts of smiths. Such are foul habits in evil custom: at times thinking, at times desiring, at times doing things which are useless, which do not produce holiness but bring about the injury of wantonness. Flee these things, soldiers of God; behold that light which you have tasted a little, and rise swiftly toward holiness, for you do not know when you will meet your end.

For God gave rationality to man. Through the Word of God, man is rational; an irrational creature, however, is like a sound. Thus God established every creature in man; but to rationality He gave two wings, of which the right wing signifies good knowledge and the left wing evil knowledge. By means of these man is, as it were, a flying creature. Man is also like day and like night. When day overcomes night in a human being, the person is called a good soldier, because by military strength he overcomes evil [Col. 0294B].

Therefore, O sons of God, serve Christ as soldiers by day. In the stillness of mind flee the cloud which darkens the day; shun also the nocturnal snares which, through self-will, speak excess in the expansion of the heart. Be as the day touched by falling dew in the morning and afterward tempered in tranquil moderation, so that you may test everything with discernment and rightly provide what is good both for yourselves and for others.

Therefore dwell in the dove’s caves with pure simplicity, that you may have “the voice of exultation and salvation in the tabernacles of the righteous.” For God placed in rationality the living voice of the breath of life: namely, the voice of exultation, which sees and knows God in faith together with good knowledge. This same voice sounds in a well-resounding trumpet through works of benevolence. For the voice possesses the embrace of charity, so that it gathers the meek even through humility and anoints wounds through mercy. Charity also flows with the rushing water of the Holy Spirit, that is, with the peace of God’s goodness. Humility prepares a garden with every fruit-bearing thing of God’s grace, having the circle of all the verdure of God’s gifts. Mercy, moreover, exudes balm for all the needs that confront humankind.

This voice of charity likewise sounds in the harmony of all praises of salvation. Through humility it sounds on high, where it sees God and fights victoriously against pride. Through mercy it cries out with a tearful and joyful voice, because it gathers the poor and the lame to itself, and because it asks help from the Spirit so as to fulfill all these things in good works [Col. 0294D]. It sounds in the tabernacles, where the saints thunder through those edifices which they have prepared for themselves in this world. But you, O sons of God, join yourselves to the voice of the good where they have been commanded, and God will receive you, because He desires you, and you shall live forever.

As to your request that the matron be made fruitful through God’s help: this lies in God’s will and power, because He knows where to grant offspring and where to take offspring away. For He judges not according to human sight but according to inward judgment. Since you have asked, I shall pray to God for her; but may He do in this matter what He has ordained to be done piously and mercifully.

## EPISTLE LXXIII

[Col. 0295A]

**N., ABBOT OF EBERBURD, TO HILDEGARD.** He gives immeasurable thanks to God for the gifts bestowed on Hildegard and asks her support in prayer.

To H., the most glorious handmaid of Christ of Bingen, crowned with the flowers of holy virtues: N., humble and unworthy overseer of the brothers at Eberburd—may you be rewarded with the Gospel’s daily denarius for your zeal in good purpose.

I shall never cease to render immeasurable thanks to God, who has placed the eminence of your person as a burning lamp, not hidden beneath a bushel but upon a lampstand; who does not cease to guard and comfort your reverend holiness through angelic visitation and the grace of His Spirit; and who has scattered the good fame of your reputation like a sweet fragrance, not only throughout Germany but also far and wide in our region and other parts of the world. Thus you may rightly say with the Apostle: “We are Christ’s sweet fragrance unto God in every place” (2 Cor. 2).

Rejoicing with such a summit of your holiness, we are compelled to say: “How beautiful you have become in delights, daughter of a prince; we shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine” (Song of Songs 3). In these breasts we who are weak find what we may flee to; and all who are strong and robust, taking solid food according to the wisdom given you by God, may say without reproach: “Your lips, O bride beloved of God.” For you, a city set upon the mountain of virtues, cannot be hidden [Col. 0295C], because the Lord has established you as an immovable and unshaken pillar in the midst of His Church. Through you His people, redeemed by His blood, may learn amid the distressing crises of this world what they ought to seek and what to avoid; instructed by the examples of your good virtues, they may advance day by day and, rising without sluggishness from virtue to virtue, may see the God of gods in Zion.

Trusting, therefore, in the protection of your prayers, even if I am unworthy to receive the crown of labors, let it at least be granted me first to have escaped punishment. I earnestly commend myself to your prayers, for I have often offended God’s mercy by grave sins. Farewell, most beloved lady; pray to God for me, unworthy as I am, and greet me with the words given you by God.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** She exhorts him vigorously to teach his flock and to turn his eyes upon himself.

[Col. 0295D]

The darts which come in the unbelief and insulting malice of words are like a dangerous wind that suddenly enters a person’s heart. This is the tempest of the first angel, in which he himself despised God. Yet I often see, in the prosperity of a person whom God greatly loves, that these punishments are set before that person, because the enemy recognizes that person’s blessedness and wants to crush him in this tempest, that he may fall with him. But he cannot snatch him from God’s bosom. Nevertheless distress and tribulation encounter him through the elements, though within the moderation by which God preserves him.

Just as the Church received a new birth of new offspring in Christ’s blood, so it was necessary and fitting that the dowry of the Holy Spirit—that is, water—should be joined to Christ’s blood, because corruption is also in every human being’s blood. But I admonish you, O householder on Mount Zion, to be a trumpet sounding vigorously among the spiritual people of your flock, so that they may not fail in charity and obedience and may live forever. And again, keep eyes everywhere within yourself to behold justice and truth, so that your soul may always keep watch, lest you be hindered amid the tumult of this age.

## EPISTLE LXXIV

**RICHARD, ABBOT OF SPRINCHERSBAT, TO HILDEGARD.** Wearied by pastoral care, he consults Hildegard whether he should retain or lay it aside.

[Col. 0296B]

Richard, unworthy minister of God’s servants at Sprinchersbat, to H., the most holy and God-worthy steward of the community of Saint Rupert: after this world’s end, may you receive fellowship in the heavenly city.

The reason why I have for the moment ordered this letter, or indeed its bearer, to stand and speak for me before your holiness is that I myself have wished to come in my own person and on my own behalf, but have been unable to do so. I confess that until now I have spent not a few days and years vainly pondering this. For how much and how greatly I have always desired from the beginning the presence and conversation of your magnificent holiness, I now call God Himself to witness—not falsely but truly and truthfully—He to whom all things are naked and open.

Unhappy man that I am, set in the stewardship or administration of pastoral care and almost wholly bereft of the strength both of mind and body: since I see myself altogether useless, weak, and unequal to this stewardship and administration, I can only grieve and weep, and increasingly desire to be delivered from this body of death (Rom. 8:24). Therefore now, most holy one and blessed among women, I desire, according to custom, to seek the Lord through you and to consult the Lord concerning my case: whether I should now cease and withdraw from this very occupation and stewardship. If that were permitted, I should above all wish to learn and ascertain it through you. I therefore beg you, for God’s sake, to let me know the tenor of this matter as swiftly as possible by a sealed and closed letter according to custom, and to gladden my sorrowing heart in the Lord through your counsel and aid.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** She exhorts him vigorously to bear the burden imposed upon him by God.

Hear God’s mysteries. When a lord who possesses a household subject to him chooses someone from that household, giving him a place of sanctification so that he may bear the lord’s burden with him, that man nevertheless excuses himself as unworthy to bear the burden. But if his lord does not listen to him in this, because it pleases him that he bear it, let him not try to move his lord; rather, as far as he is able, let him humbly obey him. If afterward, in that same matter, some failure of usefulness should creep in because of the weakness of his understanding and knowledge, it shall not harm him, because his Lord will provide for it.

Now, Father and friend, look in Christ’s stead upon this saying and hear: for your mouth is heavenly, and your mind flourishes with a cloud. Therefore let your root ascend, worship the Lord your God, put on the breastplate, and fight against raging vices by fleeing wantonness and not embracing avarice. The God whom you invoke secretly will receive you into His love.

## EPISTLE LXXV

**A CERTAIN ABBOT TO HILDEGARD.** He gives thanks to God for the gifts bestowed upon Hildegard, of which he himself has been a witness, and asks for words of consolation amid his wavering.

One holding the office of a poor prelate, to his lady and mother H. of Saint Rupert at Bingen: the affection of deepest love and prayer.

As the multitude of the faithful proclaims, it is no wonder that God, when sought by you, is found and appears to you, because you have unfeigned faith in Him and, what is greater, by His favor and grace you consecrated to Him the integrity of your childhood, and since then have lived before Him in holiness and justice, as a vessel of election. Without doubt, He who has established you to live in this way, and above all He who makes known through you the secrets of His mysteries, also judges you worthy to be heard in whatever you ask in His name.

Certainly, the things concerning you that I have heard and partly seen, I believe without any ambiguity to be divine and holy; nor can I doubt them for any reason, since I know that nothing is impossible for God. For just as God has sometimes willed and been able to disclose the secrets of His divinity through prophesying men, so also through holy women, as Joel bears witness: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; and upon my male and female servants I will pour out my Spirit.” Moreover, Deborah, Huldah, Hannah the mother of Samuel, Elizabeth the mother of Saint John the Baptist, and other women devoted to God are recorded to have possessed the spirit of prophecy, though they were married. How much more, then, you, wholly free from carnal frailty, who from childhood have preserved chastity for God?

Lady, I render immeasurable thanks to almighty Mercy, because I have deserved to attain even so much acquaintance with your blessedness. Therefore I humbly knock at your maternal bowels, asking that you direct words of consolation to me in your writing and raise me, who am greatly tossed amid storms—as you have often done by your living voice—now also by writing, to strengthen my memory.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** Under certain figures, she exhorts him to good works.

Your mind is like a snowy cloud, which is an airy cloud through which the flashing sun passes; and it is also at times like a turbid cloud that bears a storm. For the snowy cloud is the weariness of a wandering mind; the airy cloud directs pure knowledge through patience that possesses faith; but the turbid cloud bears the turbulence of great sorrow in restless minds [Col. 0298A].

Now learn that the snowy cloud has the air of the north, which causes all verdure to wither and from which flowers fall. Flee these things; stand and remain in the pure air. Remember your Creator in that life which you do not know, and do not flee Him when, though you see Him, you do not know Him. Your spirit, which is called soul, also gave forth fragrance from that life when the soul proceeded from it. For the soul sets forth and tests works, whether they are good or bad; and in those same works the most mighty Spirit is a mill. But build the edifice of good works, so that when the circle of your soul is idle, it may find this edifice. If it does not find it, it goes to ruin. Therefore keep vigorous watch before the shadow of your death draws near. The fiery Holy Spirit will help you in this.

## EPISTLE LXXVI

**H., PROVOST OF FLANHEIM, TO HILDEGARD.** He commends himself to her prayers.

To the holy and venerable mother in Christ, Lady H. of Bingen: H., provost of Flanheim, though unworthy—much devotion of prayer and service.

God, the inspector of hearts, knows how gladly I would honor your holiness with services, if by divine ordinance I received the opportunity and means. Meanwhile, I pray, let my devotion be acceptable to you. And as I formerly asked you in speech, pray for me to the Lord [Col. 0298C], that He may reveal to you the things concerning me, so that I may deserve to give thanks to God for the good things and to make satisfaction for the evil by fruits worthy of repentance before I die. Whatever the Lord may reveal concerning me, deign to signify to me in writing, and hold me commended in your prayers. I would have written more familiarly and at greater length, had bodily sickness not prevented me.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** That he should correct his sheepfold and behold God in the most pure fountain.

The Living Light tells you to keep vigorous watch and not gather weariness into the basket of your mind as though you were a stranger—namely, so that you have no power of speech [Col. 0298D]. But God requires this of you, that you use the power you possess: correct your sheepfold. Therefore accuse yourself because in this matter you do not behold God in the most pure fountain, but only say, “God, my God, help me,” while by acting thus you do not touch Him. O good soldier, now arise, because God’s grace runs toward you; and you shall live forever, so that you may be a living stone in the heavenly Jerusalem.

## EPISTLE LXXVII

**W., ABBOT OF HEGENNEHE, TO HILDEGARD.** He discloses to her the deficiencies of his soul and the weakness of his body, and asks that her prayers may heal both.

To H., beloved of God and venerable mistress of the sisters of Saint Rupert at Bingen [Col. 0299A]: W., prelate of the brothers at Hegennehe, though unworthy—may you receive the gift of knowledge and wisdom and the reward of perpetual integrity.

As soon as I heard the fame of your holiness, I hastened to greet it by sending you my letter. But because I do not know whether it was brought into your presence or not, I add new letters to the former ones and do not cease to send them repeatedly until I learn that they have been presented to you. Now, in this letter sent to you, I, very poor and needy, flee to the help of your prayers, because apart from the outward form of a human being I do not know what gifts of the Most High I have received. My sight grows dim, my hearing dull, my tongue is bound by poverty of speech; through failure of voice and devotion of mind I fall silent in divine praises; my understanding is hindered by slowness, my memory emptied by instability; my mind swells with pride, is kindled with anger, constrained by sorrow, cast down by sloth, and continually confounded by faint-heartedness and shame.

To all these evils there has been added a grave and burdensome sickness, through which, unless I escape by God’s mercy through you, danger to my life must soon threaten me. But because God is pious and merciful and “will fulfill the will of those who fear Him,” I ask that through your prayers I may escape all these evils of body and soul, and that, after the yoke of my enemies’ dominion has been lifted from me—for their yoke has been made exceedingly heavy upon me—He may bestow upon me some portion of the multitude of His mercies [Col. 0299C]. Has He kept a blessing even for me? I beg that He may bless me also.

I ask your holiness too, if indeed I dare to ask, that you instruct me concerning the future state of my life. Presumption has made me venture to seek all these things from you because common report has spread abroad that all these things are possible for you through Christ who dwells in you. Farewell, lady; may God make me worthy both of your answer and of the help of your prayers. For, living and dead, I commit myself to your holy prayers.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** That he should flee prelacy if he is useless to his own people.

[Col. 0299D]

The Living Light says: “The first cause which you have endured in your heart has produced a river; the second has shown brightness; but the third, which concerns pastoral care, is the best—if your sheep hear your voice. But if they do not hear you, flee prelacy, provided nonetheless that you render an account of your talent. For if you cannot work among your brothers through your office of teaching, be like them in subjection.

“But I tell you: you are wearied by the tedium of the diverse changes in the course of your mind; therefore it is more fitting for you to bear hardship for your other brothers than to restrain yourself alone in subjection. Live, then, in the fiery Giver, and do not be slow in wakeful understanding.”

## EPISTLE LXXVIII

[Col. 0300A]

**THE ABBOT OF VESCERA TO HILDEGARD.** Doubting whether he ought to retain his prelacy, he seeks help and counsel about whether he should relinquish the care of souls.

To his venerable and most beloved sister in Christ, Lady H.: F., of the brothers of Vescera—may you see the Lord God in Zion.

How great, though I am a sinner, is my desire to see your blessedness may be judged from this: though far away, I behold your presence in spirit. For who would not desire to see and speak with one who, not to mention other things, being filled with God’s Spirit, frequently pours forth heavenly mysteries? For this reason I have sent you this letter, hoping to receive at once consolation and counsel regarding the cares by which I am severely burdened.

For behold, I who cannot sufficiently render an account for myself tremblingly bear the care of many others, compelled by fear of God and love of the brethren. When I considered that I held the office of prelate, which I could not fulfill by deeds, pains suddenly seized me like those of a woman in labor, especially because prolonged exhaustion has almost taken from me every understanding of knowledge. Therefore, lest the Lord’s flock be endangered through my negligence, I have thought of relinquishing the care I undertook and transferring myself to another place.

I therefore humbly beg you to strengthen my doubtful mind with your counsel and to send me word in your writing what the Lord’s will is in this matter. I know your humility: you do not shrink from conversation with us, since the Lord spoke with tax collectors. Behold, in this case I await your judgment, since whatever you suggest to me through the Lord’s inspiration, I have resolved to undertake. But you, moved by compassion for my distresses, pray to the Lord with still greater affection. A returning abyss of continual anxieties surrounds me, and the sea of pressing cares almost swallows me. Have mercy, then, mother; have mercy on a son crying to you from afar, and make haste to lift up by counsel and prayer one who is already slipping away. May you always prosper in the Lord.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** She raises him while he is wavering and assures him of God’s grace.

[Col. 0300D]

The Secret Light says: “You are frightened as though by the wind, and you slumber in the tree of your mind’s greenness. But the person who possesses the greenness of his inward heart builds upon the height of the wall. A shepherd, however, who feeds a sheepfold but has no inward help in the needs of his fold and flees when weary—pastoral care will do him no good. Therefore let that man make himself like a sheep and not like a shepherd.

“You, human being, are like one tossing in waters, scarcely saved from sinking: you look everywhere for prudence, yet fail in strength, though not in will. Therefore God’s grace shines upon you.”

## EPISTLE LXXIX

[Col. 0301A]

**N., ABBOT AT ELVESTAT, TO HILDEGARD.** He complains that she has not replied to his frequent letters and prays that she may deign to relieve him, surrounded as he is by hardships.

To his lady and teacher H.: Brother N., needy and poor, at Elvestat—may he, together with the flock entrusted to him, be admitted to the everlasting company of virgins.

I have often knocked upon you with many letters and approached you in person with many petitions, but I have never been able to obtain from you the letters you promised. Is it, God forbid that one should believe it, because the lowly stock of my race or the abjection of my person does not admit this? Or perhaps, as is more believable, because no merits intercede for me? “I am debtor,” says the Apostle, “both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. 1); and Truth Himself says: “Permit the little children to come to me” (Mark 10). Is there respect of persons with you, mother? Far be it!

But now, though I have often cried to you, hear me, poor as I am, at least once; pray our Lord for this wretch, that He may deign to relieve His little servant, who trusts in you and is surrounded by many varied tribulations and hardships.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** She seems to exhort him to celebrate more often.

The Serene Light says: “He who gives words for chewing over says: O man, you have confidence in the Son of God in your thinking; nevertheless, you hesitate to break that food which you yourself wish to eat at your mind’s prompting. How and why do you go about sifting different things and looking everywhere for where that thing may be found which belongs in the ceremony? Why do you do this? God builds in every cause worked well and justly. Therefore rise to the Light, and you shall live forever. For God has for Himself a holocaust in His instrument. Blessed is the one who always holds God in all his concerns, because the devil will never deceive him. Live, then, O man, and be victorious in the shadowy world.”

## EPISTLE LXXX

**H., ABBOT AT SELBOLTH, TO HILDEGARD.** That she may not disdain to pray to God for his calamities and miseries.

To Hildegard, venerable handmaid of almighty God: H., humble and modest overseer at Selbolth—may you abound in every grace of divine bounty, and afterward be joined in the heavenly bridal chamber to Jesus Christ, Lord of all kings [Col. 0301D].

Blessed be the mercy of almighty God, who in these times of wickedness has bestowed you upon His faithful as a shining lamp in darkness for their consolation. Having heard the fame of your blessedness for a long time, and having long since learned that the things said were true, I rejoice and take delight in your blessedness so greatly that, although my petition has no standing before God, nevertheless—what may seem folly and foolishness—always remembering you in my prayers, I ask and desire that the Lord may always preserve in you the benefits of His mercy bestowed upon you, increase them more and more in you as they are preserved, and make you a companion of His saints in eternal glory.

But since I cannot visit bodily your presence, for which I am held by great longing, I approach you by this letter, as far as I can, humbly and suppliantly. Again and again, pitiable as I am, I cast myself at the feet of your graciousness, asking that you may not disdain to pray earnestly to almighty God for my calamities and miseries. For I do not doubt that you can obtain from the Holy Spirit, the indweller of your holy breast, everything you wish. Nor do I doubt that through this letter, by His revelation, you know my entire state and all that happens around me, past, present, and future.

Therefore, if my lowliness and smallness presume in any way to ask this, prostrate in soul and body at the feet of your holiness I beseech you: for the sake of that same state of mine, whether by admonishing me about the past and present or by forewarning and making me cautious about the future and the end of my life, if this is not contrary to you, do not disdain to gladden my soul through your writing.

**HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE.** She exhorts one who wavers to humility.

God’s grace has brought you to waters for drinking, yet your mind has not been built up in the edifice in which you are. Therefore provide for the castle of your mind, discerning what and what kind of works yours are. For by day you look toward God in good intention, as though you were sound in your soul; but you are in a mingled cloud when, amid the tribulation of sighs and vexations arising from the condition of your labor, your mind is divided. At times your mind also rises on high, as though you were useful. Test yourself, therefore; keep living eyes in your work; cast yourself down upon the earth as one who does not know himself, and you shall live. For God does not dwell in the dwelling that wishes to stand in itself, but He loves the house that does not know itself and gives it the finest ointment, so that you may have a good and saving life.

## EPISTLE LXXXI

**H., PROVOST AT HERDE, TO HILDEGARD.** He gives thanks because, though infirm, she visited his monastery, and commends himself to her prayers.

To H., his most blessed lady and, if he may dare to say it, most beloved mother: H., though unworthy provost at Herde and most devoted servant of her holiness, together with all his people—submission, prayer, and most devoted service.

What thanks, most holy lady and mother, can we worthily render to your kindness? For when you came to visit our monastery, you were willing neither to heed your body’s extreme weakness nor to shrink from the difficulty of the journey because of the exceeding sweetness of your heart; and you further endeavoured to gladden us by a repeated visit. For the grace of the Holy Spirit knows nothing of sluggish delays. Therefore you, beloved and chosen bride of the supreme King, worthy by the mercy of that Bridegroom himself to hear the praises of special commendation: “Behold, you are fair, my beloved; behold, you are fair; your eyes are those of doves” (Song of Songs 1)—you, I say, crowned with many kinds of garlands of virtues, who among the daughters of Jerusalem breathe forth the good and sweet fragrance of Christ like a lily among thorns, who shine out like a heavenly luminary amid the darkness of this age by the orderliness of your life and holiness, offer us sinners the consolation of hope when you so often extend to us the favour of your motherly visitation.

Although we, companions of that evangelical Publican, are unworthy to lift our eyes to heaven, yet, since through the instrument of your mouth we are granted to hear the voice of him who dwells in you, the Lord Christ, we have become as those comforted. Therefore, humbly giving thanks and bending the knee to Christ the Lord, who deigns to console us unworthy people through you, we also beseech you, our lady and mother, with humble prayer: deign to pour out prayers for us sinners to him who has brought you into the chamber of his mysteries, so that through the intercession of your merits he may mercifully deliver us both from sins and from enemies, and may bring us with you from the shipwreck of this troubled age to the harbour of eternal blessedness and security. May the Lord go before you with blessings of sweetness, and may the Father of all consolation hear you as you pray for us. Through you we humbly greet the convent of holy women who faithfully serve our Lord Jesus Christ with you and under your direction; we earnestly commend ourselves to their prayers, and with every devotion desire your reply.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. She exhorts him to remain in his place and avoid wandering.

[Col. 0303C]

He who pours good and sweet understanding into human beings says these things: The most sweet fragrance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit is present among faithful people; therefore, wherever holiness is found, there a person can be restored to life in this shipwrecked world. Hence, O worthy soldier of Christ, seek the salvation of your soul while the living fountain fills your mind with its sweet infusion, for the doubts which you have set in your mind do not produce security in you. Therefore stand in your place, loving there the first gift which was given you from above when your soul was restored to uprightness; for it is not beneficial to your soul to seek another change of condition. Rather, flee this wandering, lest your mind be thrown into confusion by trembling. Now become such that you may become a friend of God; do not flee God’s sacred rites, and God will save you.

## EPISTLE LXXXII.

### H., PROCURATOR OF THE MONASTERY OF HAMELEN, TO HILDEGARD. Afflicted by a severe illness, he wishes to learn whether the end of his sufferings is near.

To Hildegard, jewel of the people of Bingen, true bride of Christ, likewise formed in regular discipline: H., unworthy procurator at Hamelen under the Rule of Augustine, offers not the abstinence but the devotion of prayer.

Over a long interval of spiritual charity, and now especially because of my frequent bodily illness, I have repeatedly sought your presence. For you know, daughter of Christ, that when I once presented myself to you, an exceptional sickness clung to my body, and, since it has still not ceased, I am grievously tormented day and night. Since human frailty is blind to divine punishment, I do not know whether I have fallen into illness or temptation because of the increase of my benefactors; and by God’s grace I am what I am, for I do not cease to offer almighty God the weight of my slight labour, both in vigils and in prayers for various matters. Most holy one, if it is permitted, I beg you to write back concerning the end of my sufferings. Trusting in you, the mother of your daughters, as an intermediary in seeking the Lord’s help, I entreat the aid of your compassion; I ask for your help, and beg that through your prayers my sickness may be drawn out of me. “For the continual supplication of a righteous person avails much” (James 5). But I, no small sinner, dangerously overwhelmed by infirmity of body and soul, cannot set forth much. I ask that writings be sent to me for examination, if there are any directions to be prescribed concerning the divine mysteries. Farewell, my lady, and pray to your Bridegroom for me.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. She exhorts him to have recourse to God.

He Who Is says: The king sees a ladder darkened amid the changeability of sickness. Then the sun shone forth and tore apart that darkness. This pleased the king, and he said: “This restless ladder is wearied, because at times it climbs to steep heights and at times is darkened.” Such is your mind, O man, on the day of your soul’s questioning: you ascend to me in broad joy, and then again, amid harmful sickness, you cultivate a declining disease, as though the cause of salvation need not be sought. It is impossible for ashes to remain unmoved. Look to me, and always seek the ointment of healing in daylight and in storm, and you shall live for ever. Observe the pure law, flee doubt, and God will save you.

## EPISTLE LXXXIII.

### H., ABBOT AT WADEGO, TO HILDEGARD. He asks that, if she cannot visit him in person, she should at least do so by letter.

To Lady H., venerable mistress of the brides of Christ who are at Bingen: H., prelate at Wadego, though unworthy, offers prayer together with the service of affectionate love.

Charity without affection seems like a cold fire. For just as fire without heat cannot weld iron to iron, so charity without affection can never bring it about that believers should be one heart and one soul in the Lord. True charity is itself affectionate. It makes the soul cleave to God, so that it becomes one spirit with him. Like a unifying glue, it joins together the minds of the faithful, making them of one will in God; it makes them rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. This, certainly by the Lord’s gift, makes the remembrance of your holiness sweet and delightful to me in holy love. In the celebration of the divine office, it continually whispers remembrance of you into my heart. It also makes me long for the fulfilment of my affection with frequent sighs. For a very long time I have desired to see you face to face, speak with you mouth to mouth, and attain intimacy with you, so that I might at some time receive from you edification and consolation. For I am exceedingly weak inwardly in my soul and need much healing. Therefore, because I have great confidence both in you and in the love with which I love you, I ask that you not neglect to visit me at some time. If this cannot happen through bodily presence, let it happen by writing when it pleases you; but always let it happen through the help of your prayers.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY. That he should beware of enemies and do penance.

He who is not silent but looks keenly upon all things says: When a wise man builds a city upon a high mountain in accordance with his desires, it is fitting that with great care he should guard against his enemies destroying his building amid many terrors. Hear therefore, O son: diligently guard your temple, lest your enemies be able to destroy the city of God within you. Whoever shines in his breast through fear of God, so that he mourns his sins before the face of his mind, is a worthy soldier; and from God he receives this answer: “O dear son, I find good savour in you and delight in you.” But whoever has a pale face in his mind, saying, “I do not know what I am, or what my fellow companions are,” is indeed a worthy soldier, but he leads his mind into weariness; and to him I give this answer: “O man, you do not know what you say. First mourn your sins, and afterwards wipe away, insofar as you can, those of your brothers; and have patience, for God sees all of you sinners, yet does not despise those who do penance.” Therefore live in God and walk in motherly blessedness.

## EPISTLE LXXXIV.

### N., PROVOST OF UNDERESTLORF, TO HILDEGARD. That she may grant him the help of consolation.

N., by God’s favour beloved provost at Underestlorf, wishes Sister Hildegard, mistress on Mount St Rupert, to abound in the spirit of strength.

Devotion to your pious reputation has touched the minds of many, especially religious persons, and sweetened them with a certain sweetness of holy love. Therefore we render thanks for the grace divinely bestowed upon you to the supreme giver of all good things, who has imparted manly strength to a woman’s breast—not only for avoiding shameful deeds and crimes, but also for providing needy persons with necessary counsel and aid. But because we speak to ears occupied with many concerns, we do not dare to prolong our discourse. We therefore ask your clemency graciously to grant us the aid of your consolation.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. Under a figure, she exhorts him to fear and fortitude.

He Who Is shows me these things, saying: Say to this man: “O man, I see you as a wooden tabernacle made by craftsmen’s hands. At its door two figures knock. One, full of eyes, has black hair; her name is Fear of the Lord, and she says to you: ‘I wish to perform sanctification with sacrifices within you. Yield to me, therefore, and I shall enter your chamber, and with musk and spices I shall give you good savour.’ O soldier, beware lest you be slow to run with your flock and to lead it to uprightness with the living eye.

“But the other figure, sounding like a trumpet in a white cloud, has something like a circle of cloud about her; her name is Fortitude, and she says to you: ‘Ha, ha, ha! Why do you sleep in your knowledge like a rustic in his habits, who gladly keeps silent and does not wish to fight in breastplate, helmet, sword, and spear? Sound forth, then, like a trumpet over many waters; do not be silent, and I shall help you with my companions. Stand at the wall of the temple; do not be fearful because of the unrest of the winds, but learn to be a pillar in the king’s palace. Flee also double tongues, which are wounds of the soul; rather, speak everywhere in truth according to the likeness of the sun, and we shall gladly prepare our dwelling-places within you.’”

## EPISTLE LXXXV.

### FREDERICK, PROVOST OF VALLIS DEI, TO HILDEGARD. He commends himself to her prayers.

Frederick, by God’s grace provost at Vallis Dei, though unworthy, to H., devoted servant of Christ: may you receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God your saviour.

We render most heartfelt thanks to God because you are strong in him, flourish in the beauty of virtues, and, together with the sisters entrusted to you, lean with all the affection of your hearts upon the Beloved who comes from the Beloved; for we trust in the Lord that you remember us before him. Yet I have been impeded by many affairs and have not sent a messenger as I wished. Therefore I ask that your love not be burdened, but that now, through the present bearer, you fulfil what you promised, so that thereby you may gain a reward from God. Together with all the sisters, I beg you to remember me before Christ.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. Under a figure, she warns him not to abandon his people, but rather to help them and do penance.

Now I say to you: A man who owns a vineyard or a stony field and says within himself, “It is laborious to work here,” and thus abandons them, is a weary labourer. But when the time of fruits comes, his lord will say to him: “Go to the fields and seek fruit among flowers, which sometimes bloom and sometimes wither.” Yet he finds nothing there.

Hear: the vineyard is the priestly office. But the man who holds a rod of correction over a burdensome people possesses a stony field. Wearied by these things, he says within himself, “That life is another life, and this life is better for me.” Thus what he devises at one time, at that same time he abandons, like a flower that withers. But if you did these things, it would have to be said to you what was said to the steward who was accused before his lord concerning his stewardship, and who thought within himself about his dismissal; he wrote for each person less than was owed. Therefore his lord said to him: “The children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16). The first angel, when he fell, refused to sigh in penitence, nor does he permit others to sigh. But let the priest raise himself up and hasten to help others. Consider these things now, and remain with the children of this world in the wiser part; for if you acted according to the thoughts flying about within you, you would fail on both sides, and in penitence would remember what you had done wrong. But remain with this people and do not abandon them, that you may live for ever.

## EPISTLE LXXXVI.

### N., ABBOT AT RAPPENBERH, TO HILDEGARD. He seeks her counsel concerning the present condition of the Church.

To his reverend lady, the virgin and bride of Christ H.: N., prelate of the servants of God at Rappenberh, wishes the reward and everlasting crown of holy virginity and devout life.

The fame of your religious life and conduct acceptable to God, spread everywhere throughout the Church, delights many more than the scent of balsam and other perfumes. We too, though dwelling in cells like underground caverns, have at last begun to smell that fragrance. Therefore I, least of all, desiring only to follow this scent, had resolved to come to you; but in so great a whirlwind of storms and tempests, by which the whole Church is now shaken and disturbed, I was delayed, fearing for my possessions and body, and could not come. I ask, however, through Christ who dwells in you, that you hear the present bearer of this letter, our beloved brother, as though I myself were present. For I have sent him to you to consult the Spirit of God dwelling in you concerning the present state of our Church.

> **Note:** [Col. 0307D] Here he seems to indicate the schism which the emperor Frederick stirred up in the Church when, having rejected Alexander III, the legitimate pontiff, he procured the installation of Victor IV, an antipope, in the see of Peter. [Col. 0308D]

Do not disdain to share with us what belongs to God, to charity, and to compassion, so that we, comforted through him who comforts many within you, may breathe again. We do not presume to embitter your sweetness further by uncultivated speech. Yet we earnestly implore you not to be unwilling to indicate something to the brother now present and finally to write back at least a very little at the very edge of this sheet. Farewell in Christ, with all those committed to you by Christ; and remember me, for his sake, before him.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. She exhorts him not to fear torments, but to receive sheep fleeing to him.

[Col. 0307D]

I see darkness in some part of you. How so? Because your heart is entangled by that sadness which is carried around in uncertainty like a mill, saying: “What or what sort of cause is mine?” Now it is fitting for you to look upon the day which first rises in the purest dawn, but afterwards is surrounded by changing storms. Thus is your life. For if you always had prosperity, you would be like a crab, which does not walk straight. Therefore God permits you to be wearied, because the father strikes with a rod the son whom he loves, in this manner: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Psalm 84). That is, God proves through the human being, whom he formed from the mud of the earth, every truth.

Hard and stony earth is scarcely broken by the plough; but good and soft earth is cultivated in joy. In both respects God is true: he breaks the hard and harsh person through toil, but embraces with the kiss of charity the sweet and kindly person, who willingly fulfils every good work. And the grace of God, which floods all that is hard and kindly with the sun of righteousness, knowingly hears all who cry out to him through the sighs of their hearts. For just as God established the sun to illuminate all the earth and not to endure darkness, so God’s power, through his grace, rejects this hardness, lest it fail to answer the one who calls upon him. Therefore do not fear your torments, for I do not see your place in dispersion; rather, God wills the binding of your burden thus. Gather the sheep that wish to run to you. Those that do not wish to do so, bear with compassion until they call for you, and live for ever.

## EPISTLE LXXXVII.

### G., PROVOST OF ST VICTOR’S, TO HILDEGARD. Entangled in many sins, he asks whether any hope of salvation remains for him.

To H., mirror of divine contemplation: G., castaway of the people and provost of St Victor’s at Mainz, offers whatever sighs of a contrite and humbled heart may avail.

Drawn by the fragrance of your good reputation and encouraged from profound iniquity to hope for salvation, I shall venture, in a spirit of devout presumption, to lay open and bewail my miseries before your graciousness, and to seek help and counsel therefrom. For I can scarcely express in speech how many miseries have befallen me, how much shame and confusion I have incurred, how many tears I have poured forth. Yet this is no wonder. For when soul and body were defiled with so many shameful deeds and impurities, by the most just and most kind judgment of God—if indeed it is lawful to confess it—sufferings followed that were deserved as divine correction, though not proportionate to my offences. For I have often fallen into abominable wickedness both in deeds and in thoughts, matters which you, lady, know better through the Holy Spirit’s revelation. Therefore not everything concerning my soul is rightly ordered; it is unnecessary to write these things, for the Spirit teaches you all things.

Prostrate at the feet of your holiness, since I am dust and ashes, I ask with most humble devotion that you invoke over me the Comforter and Deliverer of our souls, and make known to me whether hope of salvation remains for me—whether I am predestined to life or foreknown for death. But I beg that this presumption not be reckoned to me as folly. Moreover, may the Holy Spirit, who has a dwelling within you, grant you to answer all my petitions according to my faith and humility. Farewell.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. She encourages him to rise and exhorts him to turn away from evil and do good.

[Col. 0309A]

Light in serenity says: A certain man climbs upward and goes amid a storm. Therefore remember, son, to make straight paths in the savour of good understanding, as the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36); “seek peace and pursue it” (Psalm 33). Gather good things also to yourself, so that your soul may not fail; for God does not abandon the righteous, but in his mercy receives sinners. Therefore choose straight ways for yourself, and you shall live for ever; keep pure eyes in your mind, so that illusion may not deceive you.

For you sit amid thorns, look around on every side, and gather diverse things to yourself; goodwill remains in you, yet there is a certain defect in your works. Therefore rise now, and do not grow weary of rising from the thorns, lest they choke you; for God does not delight in work built among thorns. Therefore, O son of God, rise quickly before the sun sets for you.

## EPISTLE LXXXVIII.

### S., PROVOST AT CONFLUENTIA, TO HILDEGARD. Since all that St Hildegard had foretold about him has been fulfilled, he seeks consolation regarding the things that oppressed him outwardly and inwardly.

To H., beloved in Christ: S., though unworthy, provost of the brethren at Confluentia, offers greeting in the Lord.

Because in all my tribulations you have always *mercasti* [perhaps *levasti*, “raised”] me by your consolations, and all that you foretold to me has now been fulfilled, I ask that you also now entreat the Lord of mercy to console me in all things that press upon me outwardly and inwardly. If you see anything concerning me, especially whether I may dare to hope for any hope in the future life from the gracious Jesus, write it down, O most beloved and loving one. For the rest, know how earnestly I pray the Lord that before my death I may turn from my sins through worthy penitence. Farewell.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. God’s judgments are hidden; he even punishes the sins of parents to the fourth generation. Nevertheless, he should hope in the Lord.

O you who are the handiwork of God’s finger, correct the changeableness of your conduct, and do not stretch yourself out into the tossing of your mind, from which you cannot excuse yourself, because God has foreseen all things. Yet God does not command me to expound his judgments upon you, but to pray for you, because certain deeds of your parents, done previously, now have eyes for vengeance; for God sometimes extends his scourges even to the third and fourth generation. Nevertheless trust in the Lord, that he may deliver you from the sword-hand of your enemies.

But I speak more of the salvation of souls than of human misfortunes; and therefore I often keep silent about these matters, because the Holy Spirit has not poured out disclosure amid the confusion of the peoples’ crimes, but rather just judgment. Now may God place you in the field of life, that you may live for ever. And I say that no weight in the balances is comparable to the days, months, years, or other times ordained by God. Rather, the living God alone, King of kings, whose judgments are just, must be earnestly entreated to absolve the sins of sinners through those prayers which are sought out in the Holy Spirit; for many occasions have torn themselves apart in folly, just as idols, through the clamour of unbelief, desired what brought peoples forth into mockery.

## EPISTLE LXXXIX.

### A., PROVOST OF ST ANDREW’S AT COLOGNE, TO HILDEGARD. Tempted inwardly and outwardly, he has recourse to her to learn what he must do.

[Col. 0310B]

To Lady H., dearest lady and mother: A., unworthy provost of St Andrew’s at Cologne, wishes you always to fare well in the Lord.

Dearest lady, you know, both from the words of my presence and by divine revelation, with how many tribulations of temptation my soul is distressed within and without. Now therefore, because I fail and see no progress in myself so far as God is concerned, I have written to you, my lady, prepared to do whatever you command me either by divine revelation or by the wisdom of your counsel. I beg you: do not be afraid, do not conceal it, nor hide my iniquity, however much I fear and dread that I shall be plunged wholly into the abyss. Therefore intercede and pray for my poor soul, most dear mother, powerful in Christ. May the Lord be with you and with all your people.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. She exhorts him to perform good works.

The Light that wholly lives says: O man, hear. There was a certain valley which sometimes dried up and sometimes flowered, and was not steadfast in the grasses that yield usefulness; it was lovely for human beings to behold, but not very useful for refreshment. Such is your mind. For when you look at yourself and think that you are not strong in your good conscience, you immediately dry up as though you had no hope. Then, when your mind rises like a mountain of myrrh and incense, ascending in fear, you struggle within yourself, as though dead, with trembling powers; and then you pray, saying: “My crimes are excessive amid the wounds of my sins.”

But then you waste away in the streets—that is, in your own will—and hasten toward worldly things; you do not complete good works by exercising yourself in them. Yet your estimate is of such a kind that you say: “I wish to do good works.” But good works do not thus receive the form of brightness in you, so that you waste away in sins. Cry out, therefore, through good works, and God will receive you. Hear: see that you wither in evils and grow strong in goods. Cry out by beginning to see God in good will, and perform good works in perfection. Whoever does good sees God; but whoever merely has an opinion of the good is like a mirror in which some form shines, though that form is not in it. Therefore rise and begin good works; perform them in perfection, and God will receive you.

But you answer: “I have worldly care.” What kind of conversion is this? Yet I show you that you should have mercy, kindness, and the virtue that tramples pride; that you should stretch out your hands to those who are failing and lie in the fullness of pain; and that you should spare those who wrong you. Thus do not feed the cultivation of idols, which is avarice; do not strike the face of God—that is, the blessedness God has given another—nor kill through envy, and you shall live.

## EPISTLE XC.

### A., PROVOST OF ERFURT, TO HILDEGARD. He commends the bearer of this letter to her.

To Lady H., beloved bride of Christ: A., though unworthy, provost of Erfurt, offers the affection of devoted prayer and service.

We do not cease to raise thanksgivings to your holiness, whose renown has spread far and wide and who greets very many with so sweet a greeting of letters. For we long with longing to see you, at some time to be gladdened by the most gracious words of your consolation, and, aflame, to be made joyful through the presence of your countenance; we pray this from the depths of our heart. May divine mercy, therefore, which has divinely begun so holy and magnificent a work in you, divinely bring it to completion, and through your continual prayer make us sharers in that same goodness. We now most faithfully commend to your love the bearer of this letter, namely one of our household, who is journeying to you for the love of God and out of devotion to you, so that, having been graciously received by you, he may deserve to hear through you the words of the Holy Spirit speaking through your mouth.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. That he should keep the eye of his heart pure and turn away from sins.

God foresees you, seeking a sacrifice from your heart in simplicity, for he is true and desires no duplicity along the one way which is faith among neighbours; likewise the eye of God in simplicity beholds human blessedness. May God grant this to you and free you from every tempest of burning vices. Therefore make the eye of your heart pure. For you are as though weary and abandoned from the house of him who created you; but you shall be recalled among strangers. Therefore cease from your sins, for God has not sold you into destruction; rather, he seeks you in the lost sheep, which has been recalled to life. Why do you doubt as though you were not in salvation? Seek God, then, in the straitness and pain of your soul, and you shall live.

## EPISTLE XCI.

### H., PROVOST OF THE DOMO AT MAINZ, TO HILDEGARD. He desires to learn from her what displeases God in him and what must be corrected.

> **Note:** [Col. 0311] That is, the cathedral church, which is called a *domus* (“house”), French *dôme*; hence canons are also called *domheres* in French.

To the lady H., most worthy of every honour: H., provost of the Domo at Mainz and a filthy sinner, offers whatever a servant and son may offer to his most beloved lady and mother.

My mind burns and fears: it burns to speak, yet fears the greatness of your wisdom and eloquence. For it has been granted you, in abundant blessedness, both to perceive wisely and to utter profitably. The authority of the dripping Scriptures has found a seat in you, abides with you, and makes you its cabinet. Added to this, you are approved by the gifts of discipline, made the adornment of the Church and an example to peoples. Would that it were granted me from above to cling to you continually, always to hear you, and without interruption to be nourished by your companionship! Then at last I would not be cheated of my desire, for I have always desired to hear you.

Therefore, I beseech you to deign to declare to me in your sealed letters whatever displeases you in me, and how, God himself and our Lord granting it, I may be able to drive it from myself. May your holiness flourish for ever; may all your daughters, my most dearly beloved sisters, flourish and remain faithful.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. That by good works he should make himself worthy of God’s protection.

The mysteries of God utter these words: O man of God, through the bond of the law God knows you in the dark alternation of certain works. Yet from afar, as if only in opinion, you behold light coming forth from gleaming light. Now run, so that you may perform good works without the dishonour of the duplicity of two ways—that is, where one sound belongs to the mouth and another to the mind. Take care, moreover, that God may love you in good works, for he stretches out to you the hands of his protection; but you are weak and flee. Beware, therefore, lest you hide yourself from that protection, lest God strike you with his rod, because he seeks you.

For you did not rightly foresee those paths which you wished to seek when you ascended into heaven. But now you are shaken between two sides: God’s promise and the devil’s arts. God leaves you a loosened rope so that you may know what you are. Yet you shall not altogether fall into the pit of sadness. Now pray and trust that God will not abandon you, and dawn will soon come forth to you in deliverance.

## EPISTLE XCII.

### HELDERIC, PROVOST OF ST SIMEON’S AT TRIER, TO HILDEGARD. He praises God’s wondrous gifts in her and commends himself to her prayers.

[Col. 0312D]

Helderic, brother of St Simeon’s in the church of Trier, a provost in name alone and one among those sitting and weeping by the rivers of Babylon, to H., daughter of Zion: may you one day see in yourself the God of gods.

Drinking in the most sweet fragrance of your blessedness from the report of many and with my own ears, I rejoiced and marvelled at the things said to me. I rejoiced, I say, because in this age, truly most wicked and set in evil, that fair Bridegroom beyond the sons of men is known to have chosen for himself such a bride. But I marvelled because he seems to endow her, even in this exile, with an unusual and unheard-of gift of grace. For who has ever read or heard that an unlearned or wholly illiterate woman should breathe forth such outpourings from the deepest abyss of divine mysteries, or offer such abundance from the rivers of living water to the thirsty? Truly God is wonderful; truly blessed is the Lord God, who alone performs great wonders. But what wonder is it if he makes his rational and reasoning human being his instrument as he wills, when he also made a brute animal the teacher of a teacher? For God does as he wills, of whom it is written: “He has done whatsoever he willed” (Psalm 113).

I beg your love to endeavour to commend my humility more earnestly and frequently to your Beloved, knowing that the same exchange shall faithfully and unceasingly be returned to her by me.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. That by good works he should forestall death.

You, servant of God, take heed to turn aside, in your brief time, from the injustice of iniquitous mammon; and take great care to shake off the rust of sins before the shadow of death comes upon you, when you can work no more, lest you then say in lamentation: “Alas for me, because I was found in negligence!”

Consider also the householder who called labourers into the vineyard from the first hour until evening, and asked others why they stood idle; they answered that no one had hired them. From the first hour until evening, the Lord calls labourers and asks others why they stand idle, and they excuse themselves because no one hires them. It often happens that a person lives from his earliest age until evening—that is, old age—in forgetfulness of God, and keeps thinking for so long about correcting this within himself, until by God’s grace, struggling inwardly, he says: “Why did I not do good works? For God did not prevent evil from drawing me away.” Thus in old age, through weariness with sins, he begins to repent.

Such a person appears on the Lord’s paths like an earthen vessel not put into the fire, because he cannot work; and so, first by his merit, through God’s grace, he will receive a reward which he can no longer alter through subsequent ages. For in childhood, youth, and mature age, a person often does evil and afterwards good. This cannot occur in decrepit old age. Now open your eyes to watchfulness; consider and amend through action all the negligences of these ages, that you may live for ever.

## EPISTLE XCIII.

### H., PROVOST AT KNETHSTEHTDE, TO HILDEGARD. He asks how he may appease God for his sins.

To H., venerable servant of Christ: H., however unworthy, by God’s grace provost at Knethstehtde, wishes strengthening by the grace of the Holy Spirit and fulfilment in a good end.

If it were possible for me to be present and converse with you in turn, I would desire it by every means. For I would set out before you in fuller account the things concerning me, which the Lord alone knows; I have not wished to entrust them one by one to this present place for the sake of brevity. We have heard, most beloved one, of the grace which the Father of lights, “from whom is every good gift and every perfect gift from above” (James 1), has bestowed upon you. Trusting greatly in this grace, I have thought it fitting to approach the sweetness of your charity through these present letters, earnestly begging that you do not cease to implore divine mercy with devout prayers for my miseries. For I know that I have offended it in many ways, and I perceive that I have not done so with impunity.

Therefore, since I have had a greater hope in the grace which I have recognized in you, I judged it useful to seek the help of your prayers, which are heard, hoping to receive from you some remedy of consolation. For Christ’s sake, I ask that you not omit to provide this in your writings, adding to them in what order I may best appease the offence against the divine majesty. Farewell always in Christ.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE. That he should sigh to God and have recourse to him with confidence.

[Col. 0314C]

In a mystical vision, in response to the request contained in your words, I looked and heard a voice saying to you:

“I compare you to a tree which bears its figs in summer, whose fruit is somewhat damaged by storms and clouds, and which is renewed again by the dew of heaven and the pure air. Such is your mind: when you have confidence in some prosperity, as though producing figs, you are wearied by the changeability of your dispositions as by a storm; and you are also harmed, as by clouds, by those who are under your burden. But then sigh toward God and say: ‘To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame’ [Psalm 24].

“For within you is a breath [Col. 0314D] which God has given life without limit, and to which he has given the wings of reason. Therefore fly with them to God through faith and good desire, lifting up your soul to him; and acknowledge God himself as your God, in whose knowledge you existed and from whom you received your beginning. Ask him, therefore, that by the breath of his Spirit he may teach you his good things and deliver you from adversities. Trust also in him, so that you may not be ashamed to set all your works before him; and speak as a child speaks to his father when rebuked for wrongdoing, asking that he not forget his offspring in him.

“I, moreover, will gladly ask God mercifully to defend and deliver you, by his grace, from every excess of restless dispositions, and from other sins and dangers that may confront you.”

## LETTER XCIV

[Col. 0315A]

**H., PROVOST AT BONN, TO HILDEGARD.** Since he prays for her unceasingly, he in turn requests her prayers.

To HILDEGARD, bride of Christ and most approved teacher of the sisters of Saint Rupert at Bingen, H., unworthy provost at Bonn: service with every devotion.

If the Lord—alone powerful, alone good, alone gracious, alone merciful—deigns, as I hold by faith, to incline the ear of his majesty to the voice of any sinner, then he is invoked for you by my untiring heart and by the cry of my mouth. For I call God, knower of all secrets, to witness that from the time when I first heard, through report, of your goodness—and afterward proved it in you yourselves [Col. 0315B]—I have been wholly inclined toward love of you. If you deem it fitting, I have made you a participant in all that I have since then either said well or done well. The same, therefore, I both hope for from you and claim almost as a debt—yet more truly for God’s love and because of your goodness.

Finally, neither fire, nor iron, nor water, nor the threat of any other fear or danger, nor even death itself, will be able in any way either to threaten or to remove the integrity of your love from my soul. Farewell.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** She rebukes him for loving the world and exhorts him to purify his desires through fear of God and good works.

[Col. 0315C]

O man, you who love the world and keep it in your will: in the grasp of your dispositions you are like a storm, which is seldom clear and yet is not very dangerous. This means: you are often deprived of consolation in your affairs, and at times are oppressed in all your concerns by weariness and sadness, and at times by doubt. Therefore arise and call upon the God of Israel, saying: “Examine me, O Lord, and test me; burn my inward parts and my heart” [Psalm 25].

That is: examine me, Lord, through faith and hope, so that faith may be an eye for my seeing and hope a mirror of life. Test me in good obedience as you tested Abraham, so that I may act against my own will: that I may abandon my will [Col. 0315D] for your sake, enter into your commandments, and become your loving friend. By these things burn my inward parts, which overflow from the sins in which I was conceived, and prevent them from deceiving me. For I act against myself, so that I may always burn in the fire of the Holy Spirit, desire your righteousness day by day, and ascend from virtue to virtue.

But, O man, your mind is also like a cloud that bears neither hail nor rain, but is divided by the sun. For because of the security of your trivial words and ways, you do not have the cloud with hail—that is, anger—or rain—that is, contention. Yet through good works you limp in longing for things above. Therefore purify your desire, with the fear of God, in good work; and in this manner kiss God, saying: “Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am needy and poor” [Psalm 85; Col. 0316A].

For when, through the kiss of love for God, you touch God by performing good works, he immediately inclines his ear to your desire and prayer and fulfils it. As a word also sounds through hearing, so you proclaim that you are in great need, because you require help; and that you are also in great poverty, because you lack the power to accomplish good. But may God accomplish this in you.

## LETTER XCV

**H., ABBOT, TO HILDEGARD.** As the Church suffers from schism, he asks what he ought to do.

To Lady H., true servant of God from the monastery of Saint Rupert, H., holding the office of prelate: whatever the prayer of a poor man, though a sinner, may avail.

Since everyone wounded by deadly poison hastens, like a stag, to the true spring—that is, Christ—and casts off from himself the poison’s harmful effects, I, burdened by troubles of this kind, have recourse to the spring which God has deigned to reveal to us through his Spirit, seeking a remedy.

For I do not doubt that you know how almost all former religious observance has by now perished in haste, because hateful presumption has shamelessly occupied its place. Therefore, since the Church falters in apostolic dignity and name, and truly does not know to which head it should look, while every wanderer takes an example from this and shuns the religion of good conduct, those who are led by the Spirit [Col. 0316C] of God are greatly troubled as to what their end ought to be in the will of God. Accordingly, after taking good counsel, I flee to you and earnestly beg you to write back to me whatever, taught by the Holy Spirit, you may think concerning this matter or concerning myself. For I am ready to obey your counsels in all things.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** One must obey one’s teachers so long as they do not oppose the Catholic faith, and flee to God, who will not abandon his Church.

In the vision which, from my childhood, I have seen with the waking eye in my spirit, I looked upward by a way other than that by which I was born into this world; and I saw and heard these words spoken to you:

“Your mind is like a plough, which overturns and divides hard, rough, and soft ground. For you strive to know, overturn, and divide things which are so hard that you cannot break through them; things so rough that they would wound you if you touched them; and things so soft that you would crush them if you wished to touch them harshly and roughly.

“For hardness, which has stumbled away from the sun of righteousness, now surrounds the Church; you cannot pierce it. Therefore say in your heart to God: ‘Lord, who know all things, I wish to obey you in my teachers so long as they do not compel me to resist the Catholic faith.’ For apostolic power, now divided into two parts, refuses to bind itself to its proper character; and the princes of the world are so harsh that they would not listen if you told them what you know to be just. The pupils of teachers [Col. 0317A] now pursue such softness that you would doubt, as though you did not know what you ought to do with them.

“For a teacher ought to teach holy and just things and offer good examples, as Christ also did: many ran to him, and many fled from him. Yet he gathers his beloved and chosen ones to himself. Therefore hold with utmost zeal those who kiss you through obedience and embrace you through charity; do not abandon them, but leave the others to God, so that you may say with the Prophet: ‘I have declared your truth and your salvation’ [Psalm 39].

“Therefore direct your hope toward the one God, for he will not abandon his Church. This indeed is the Church’s hope: that she may become clear-sighted. This hope is secure, although sorrow will remain for a long time, during which many communities of spiritual persons will be shaken and many also destroyed.

“But I see in you the dawn as brightness: that is, zeal for good works in a good will is in you. I also see a storm moving about within you because of these and other vicissitudes, a storm which at times darkens your brightness. Lessen this, and have confidence that you will end in God and live eternally.”

## LETTER XCVI

**HADELHEID, ABBESS OF GANDERSHEIM, TO HILDEGARD.** Brought up by Hildegard, she requests her and her sisters’ intercession, and mutual fellowship between the sisters of the two convents.

[Col. 0317C] HADELHEID, unworthy abbess of the church of Gandersheim, to H., beloved mother of Saint Rupert, free bride of Jerusalem: kisses of the Bridegroom.

A good tree, known by its good fruit, must by no means be consigned to forgetfulness; for, bearing fruit in sweetness, it has merited the sweet love of good people. Therefore one who embraces what is sweet and good less well than he ought is rightly judged inferior to a brute animal. You, then, dove of Christ—not deceived, but great and pure of heart—do not fall from my heart, just as good does not make evil, light darkness, or sweet bitterness. Therefore you too ought often to remember me, since it is certain that I am joined to you by the closeness both of love and of inward devotion.

I do not wish the flower of our former nurture to have withered in your heart—the flower which once blossomed between you and me [Col. 0317D] when you gently brought me up. By love for it and by the charity of your beloved Bridegroom, I adjure and beg you that your prayers and entreaties may be offered to God for me, for my flock, and for the place entrusted to me by your permission. Entrust us also to the prayers of all your sisters. I ask, further, that you obtain for my sisters fellowship in your religious fraternity among those same sisters of yours—indeed, mine. Whenever anyone passes from you to us, let them bring letters and make known whatever else you may wish in Christ.

When time permits, if it pleases God, I shall not delay in coming to you, so that we may speak mouth to mouth and work hand to hand what is good. Thus may the ancient fellowship be established, and may the charity of God confirm it in us. You who dwell in the gardens, listen; and greet all your fellow-dwellers—namely, my sisters—from me most warmly, and gladden me with letters of recommendation.
