**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** She should practise good works with pure faith in the day of her prosperity, and give God what belongs to him.

O daughter of God, your mind is occupied in great anxiety by two paths. Through a certain anxiety you waste away, as though you despaired of your life. Thus, at times, when you have ascended the mountain of faith, you ascend to God and question him as though you did not know what to do in this doubt.

But walk in the day of your prosperity with pure faith, performing good works; and give God what belongs to him. For you see the sun, which is that honour that God will not yet take [Col. 0318B] away from you; and you hold the world in sighing and in fear of God’s law, as the moon is held in the night. In both respects, then, serve God, because he desires your sacrifice and requires good works from you during your life before you die.

May the light of God’s grace cover you, and may he anoint you with the unction of his mercy, by which he anointed David when David saw God through confessing his sins. May he anoint you with the unction of the Holy Spirit’s greenness, and perform good and holy works in you through that devotion by which true worshippers worship God. Keep God’s commandments now, and you shall live eternally.

## LETTER XCVII

**N., ABBESS, TO HILDEGARD.** She asks for Hildegard’s prayers for herself and her community.

[Col. 0318C]

To the most loving lady and most beloved mother in Christ, N., unworthy though abbess of the sisters of the church of . . . ., wishes to see the King of glory in his beauty and rejoice with him forever.

Blessed be God, who deigns wonderfully in our times to disclose through you mysteries of his secrets never before heard by the world; who confirms our faith through you, O most holy mother; and who ineffably illumines his holy Church with the powers of his signs, more radiant than usual, as with rays of a new sun. O who has ever heard such things? Who has seen such things? Therefore let each of us say—let us all say—“Blessed be God.”

I long most ardently to see the face of your holiness and hear divine words from your mouth [Col. 0318D]; but since, owing to the circumstances of time and place, I cannot fulfil this through bodily presence, I shall always see you in heart and mind, and I shall always love you. I also beg your holiness, O most merciful mother, to deign to intercede before God—who undoubtedly hears you—for me, a sinner, and for our community, which joins me in supplication to you.

Know also that your memory will always be held in blessing among us, and that the Lord’s name will be magnified through you. Pray for us, most merciful mother and lady. Above all this, we ask, both for God’s sake and because of maternal affection, that you not delay in shortly sending us letters of your consolation. May Christ our Lord deign to gather us with you in his kingdom.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** She should not be unstable or investigate vain matters.

[Col. 0319A]

Take care that you do not have a wandering mind of instability, in which a sapphire-coloured cloud cannot appear and which frequently also covers the sunlight. Make every effort, however, to stand firm, and do not investigate every vain and foolish inquiry; for those who do this often fall, deceived away from Christ’s charity.

Just as the sapphire cloud is obscured by the wandering mind of instability, attend to Christ’s embrace, seek every good thing from him, make your works manifest to him, and he will give you blessedness. For without him human salvation is vain: grace and salvation are obtained not through a human being but through God, where also the holy Scriptures, which flow from the divine fountain, offer breasts for people to suckle [Col. 0319B] from.

Learn, therefore, to flee this vanity which covers the light of the sun—that is, which separates a person from Christ—and you shall live eternally and be crowned by Christ.

## LETTER XCVIII

**M., ABBESS AT WETHDERSWINKEL, TO HILDEGARD.** She asks Hildegard to receive her and her sisters among her daughters and help them by her prayers.

To Lady Hildegard, most reverend mother and most worthy of every praise, M., called by God’s grace abbess at Wethderswinkel, with all her sisters: filial love and all submission.

Since we have learned that, by God’s grace, the fragrance of your holiness has spread far and wide throughout the world and has grown so greatly that the marks of your virtues are now commended with worthy reverence by all the children of the Church throughout the whole world, we too, though unworthy, desire by the privilege of special love to be enrolled under your motherhood. As far as our smallness permits, we rejoice with your great dignity.

Therefore, sweetest mother, we implore your holiness with all the affection of our hearts to deign to receive us in the place of daughters and to cherish us under the protection of your holy prayers, so that, aided by your most holy merits, we may deserve at last to reach the finish of the course we have undertaken. I, who appear to preside over the others not by merits but solely by the dignity of my name, entrust myself with special devotion to your holiness in earnest prayer [Col. 0319D], asking that through the gracious intervention of your prayers I may so discharge the care of all entrusted to me that I may become a sharer with them in your eternal life.

Know that I have always wished to receive something from you through which I may retain memory of you—namely, letters of admonition, which for God’s love I shall always observe with a willing heart and every devotion. Some of our sisters also, embracing you with special love, wholly commend themselves to your most pure prayers.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** Discretion must be preserved in abstinence.

The Living Light says: “Dry sand is useless, and earth too greatly broken by the plough will not yield fitting fruit, because it does not retain the proper measure of its compactness. Dry and stony ground produces thorns and other useless plants. So too unsuitable abstinence, which lacks due measure and proper order, casts down a person’s flesh because it is not given the greenness of proper nourishment. Hence the person also withers.

“Where this happens, certainly the winged virtues will perish: namely humility and charity, the fairest flowers. For excessive abstinence lacks the greenness of virtues; instead, there grows there the windy reputation of uselessness, and many terrors arise there as though they were holy—yet they are not holy. Those who live in this vanity have anger and not peace, and are useless in many of their dispositions.

“The person who wishes to have a royal life in spiritual habit should wither away from sumptuous feasts of unsuitable foods, from which wantonness arises; and from very strong wine, in which lust quivers, as do other stirring evils possessing no health. Chaste people, loving their souls, should flee these things. Yet they should use proper grain and the strength of a drink that does not blaze in the fire of its colour.

“I do not take away from a person what I have given for food; but I do not acknowledge horrible foods, because vanity is in them. Nevertheless, let no soul flee to me through unsuitable abstinence; rather, let a person cling to me in right measure, and I shall receive that person. And let no one strive amid the gnashing of his teeth for an unearned reward in works; for I give to each according to his recompense, according to his merits, as he loves me.”

## LETTER XCIX

[Col. 0320C]

**H., ABBESS OF ALTHENA, TO HILDEGARD.** She rejoices in God’s gifts and wishes to see her.

To Lady and Mother H., beloved and venerable in Christ, intimate object of her affection, H., unworthy abbess of Althena and penitent sinner sitting with Mary at Jesus’ feet, wishes to see her Beloved as he is.

I rejoice in your blessedness, most beloved of all women, because—as can be demonstrated by the clearest proofs—you have found, insofar as is possible for mortals, him whom your soul loves. And now, happily at leisure with him in the hidden peril of your heart [reading uncertain], you taste and see that the Lord is sweet [Col. 0320D].

Since I perceive that this is so, I must bear patiently that for a long time now you have neglected to visit me, though so devoted to you, by your letters. For I believe that, if you could turn the gaze of your mind even for a moment away from contemplation of your Beloved, and move your foot outside the dwelling-place of rest, you would certainly not fail to comfort me more often through your messenger—one who would gladden me concerning the condition of your state and report mine to you.

For even if I am not granted to see your beloved face again in this life—which I cannot say without tears—I shall nevertheless always rejoice concerning you, for I have resolved to love you as my own soul. Therefore with the eye of prayer I shall see you until we arrive there where we may deserve to see one another eternally [Col. 0321A] and to contemplate our Beloved face to face in his beauty.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** Under figures, she exhorts her to wage war for God.

O you who are a teacher in the brightness of the leaping fountain—which is in the place of Christ—hear: “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” [Revelation 5]. This means the following.

The Son is like a root, the splendour of holy divinity. For he roars like a lion when he casts into hell the first angel and those imitating him in his fall, so that there also he drives every injustice away from himself with gnashing teeth; and thus he is the root of strength. He draws to himself all who confess him in faith and touch him in good work; and for this reason he conquers all things like a lion.

Now hear me admonishing you. God established one way for all, that all might walk in it. But two men stood at the side of that way, and one said to the other: “I walk as gladly in the streets as on the road.” The other said: “So do I.” Then they looked at thorns and briars, and desired them. And the Lord said to them: “These men do not want me, nor do they wish to fight under my banner; therefore they are cut off from me.”

Then from the East came soldiers splendidly arrayed in arms, saying: “We wish to walk this way.” And the Lord gave them the wings of a certain master-builder, and the cherub looked upon them with his eyes. They were made so strong from the Light that they could not be satisfied with the contest of the good fight. But other men grew weary in a short time, and so perished because they had not been fed with the food of life.

Now, dear daughter of God, look to those militant soldiers, so that you may be with them in some measure and live eternally.

## LETTER C

**S., ABBESS AT ALTUVICH, TO HILDEGARD.** Wishing to renounce the burden of government and be enclosed in a solitary cell, she asks that God’s good pleasure be made known through Hildegard.

To H. of Saint Rupert, of blessed memory, S., abbess in name only at Altuvich in the Church of Utrecht, wishes to enter the choir illumined by the Light of lights.

Since no human being can renounce worldly desires and sigh with all intention for the heavenly homeland unless this is granted from above by Christ’s help, I wish to make known to your religious community what I have conceived in my mind under God’s prompting and through the cooperating grace of his Spirit.

Our Lord, who does not wish any of his sheep to stray, but as a good shepherd desires to call all back to the way of eternal salvation, has, I think, inspired my heart to abandon the burden of government which I bear heavily and to enclose myself in the solitude of some little cell. The desire for this purpose lies within me, but the power and fulfilment are in the authority of our Lord.

Therefore, because I know that you are of such merit before God that through revelation of the Holy Spirit you can know what it is expedient for a person to do, I humbly beg your kindness to consult the Lord for me as to whether my way of life is pleasing to him. Let me not henceforth be marked by that Gregorian sentence which says: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to fall away from it for the worse.”

For the rest, may you fare well in the Lord. May your kindness not refuse to indicate in writing through this present bearer what I have asked, and to reveal whatever God’s grace through his Holy Spirit may be pleased to disclose to you concerning these matters.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** It is not useful for her to cast off the burden of government.

In the true vision of God’s mysteries, hear these words:

[Col. 0322B] “O daughter sprung from the side of man, and figure formed in God’s building, why do you waste away, so that your mind flies amid the changing clouds, which a storm drives about, and thus is sometimes bright as light and sometimes darkened? Such is your mind because of the tumult of the dispositions of those who do not shine before God.

“But you say: ‘I wish to rest and seek a place where my heart may have a nest, so that my soul too may rest there.’ O daughter, it is not useful before God that you cast off your burden and leave God’s sheepfold, when you possess the light by which you shine for it, so that you may lead it out to pasture.

“Now restrain yourself, lest your mind blaze through this sweetness, which greatly harms you in the fluctuations of solitary life. Rather, live, because God’s grace desires you. Take care, therefore, not to draw yourself away from it in the wandering of your mind. May God help you to keep watch in pure knowledge.”

## LETTER CI

**SOPHIA, ABBESS AT KISSINGEN, TO HILDEGARD.**  
[Note: D. de Reuss of Würzburg extracted this letter, with Saint Hildegard’s reply, from the archive of Kitzingen monastery and transmitted it to us; it is found in Martène, but less complete. EDIT.]

She asks whether she ought to abandon the burden she bears.

To HILDEGARD, teacher of singular merit, adorned with sapphires of spiritual virtues, SOPHIA, called abbess at Kitzingen but making little progress: unfailing service of prayer.

Having heard of the prerogative of your holiness, I fly on swift wings to the bosom of your charity, desiring to be commended to you for the light; through the true Light, you have merited to be revealed for the enlightenment of the nations. For who does not delight in the household of Mother Sophia? Who does not willingly lend an ear to heavenly harmony? Or who would not desire to hear the instrument of the Holy Spirit, set to quivering tones of so many virtues and mystically distinguished by the raised carvings of so many miracles?

Indeed this sound has gone out into all the earth, whose harmony the Spirit proceeding from the Father has seasoned. Therefore cry aloud with strength, you who proclaim peace in breadth: all nations beyond the rivers of Ethiopia will come to you, offering gifts of praise.

For I too, though not according to the prize, yet according to hope, run with the others toward the racecourse, because according to the Apostle’s saying, “It depends not on one who wills nor on one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” [Romans 9; Col. 0323A]. Whoever obtains a share in your most holy prayer, which you freely bestow on all through the obligation of neighbourly love and love of God, has obtained it.

I bring with me a noble pair: namely, a praiseworthy nun and a most perfect, welcome sister, whom the heavenly Father has begotten for me in spirit, no less for her than for me, desiring acquaintance with you, venerable mother most worthy of every praise. Let your voice sound in my ears, and declare to me by divine revelation what is more salutary: whether I should abandon the burden I bear or carry it longer.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** The burden she bears, being acceptable to God, must not be abandoned.

O Sophia, in mystical vision I say to you: may your soul be strengthened by God, touching God in right sighing. It is good for you to bear the burden of labour which you have undertaken in God, provided that the sheep are willing to hear God’s admonition through your teaching. Even if no spark shines in them, do not leave them, lest the ravager seize them.

May your soul shine in God, and may your days burn in the fiery Giver. Trust in the Lord, and be diligent for yourself and your daughters, according to God’s command and the devotion which God has given and gives you in the embrace of his charity. Do not abandon it, because you ought to hold this world in your heart as a place of pilgrimage. May God help you become a living stone in the heavenly Jerusalem.

## LETTER CII

**R., ABBESS OF SAINT MARY AT REGENSBURG, TO HILDEGARD.** She commends herself to Hildegard’s prayers, by which she declares that she was snatched from the jaws of death.

[Col. 0323C]

By God’s grace, the humble steward of the women serving Saint Mary of the lower monastery at Regensburg, to her special friend HILDEGARD: whatever continual prayer and the devotion of worthy service accomplish.

If the means and opportunity for serving you are denied me, my affection finally employs this remedy: that through letters sent as swiftly as possible I may learn of the well-being of both your outer and inner person. Know, dearest one, that although precipitous mountains and the chasms of springs tear me away from your presence, my heart is joined to you in the benevolence of perfect faith [Col. 0323D] and love.

I attribute the longed-for knowledge of you, and its happy fulfilment for one who desired it unto salvation, not to my own merits but to God’s freely given mercy, who in his goodness works graciously with his faithful servants. Yet believe that I do not misuse your friendship, because I enjoy it most fully when, called through God’s grace to the sweetness of inward delight, I dare and am able to speak more familiarly with him concerning some matters.

Under the consolation of that same charity, I ask you to let me know by definite written signs whether, according to my request and our agreement, remembrance of me has afterward availed anything with you. In the grace and favour of your friendship, I faithfully and lovingly greet our sisters in the service owed to them: they, recovering strength of virtue in the spirit of God’s power, stood bravely for me and, if I may say so, following the lead of your good deeds, restored me safe when I was falling into the crisis of death. Farewell.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** She should correct herself from certain evil habits and look to God.

O daughter of God, approach your Father in the formation of the first human being, and look upon him so as to do his will, because he created you. For recently he admonished you by chastising you, and because of a certain cause which I see in you, he will still admonish you concerning an evil habit which it is good for you to avoid.

Look also to him, make all your ways known to him, and imitate the dove of mercy. For she bears witness to every good work and possesses the exile-like sorrow of labours. Learn from this to possess a pure mind. And when your mind wanders restlessly, embracing many things which you cannot accomplish, then stand in steadfastness and learn moderation, for the dove also is moderate and steadfast.

When violent anger wearies you, look to the pure fountain of patience: anger will immediately end, the storm will cease, and the wave of turbulent water will subside, because the dove is patient. But when you are in weariness, so that natural impulse shakes you, attend to the exile of this life and to how you sigh in expectation for another life. Do this according to the dove’s sorrow; gather every useful thing from other good people; live according to the dove’s example; and you shall live eternally.

## LETTER CIII

**N., ABBESS AT KAUFUNG, TO HILDEGARD.** She urges her to rouse the leaders of the Church.

To Lady and sister HILDEGARD, N., a sinner and abbess in name only at Kaufung: may she not hide beneath the bushel of silence the light of knowledge.

Overtaken by the messenger’s unexpected haste, I could write nothing polished to you as lady and mother; instead I utter common words to you as a beloved sister. Receive them accordingly.

That flying scroll which was given to the prophet for food has become famous in every mouth; and it is fitting that it should also rest in your mouth, wise as you are. O what a precious treasure this is! Take care, therefore, not to swallow it with a fool. Run about, hasten, rouse the Church—indeed, the princes of the Church—to whom it is said in Peter: “Simon, could you not watch with me one hour?” [Matthew 26].

For we both rejoice and tremble that you have seen the rod from the North watching over iniquity; and we desire to receive your consoling letters. Farewell in Christ, always mindful of me in invoking him, so that I may deserve to become a participant in the grace that is in you.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** She has few days left, and should forestall death by good works.

In the Spirit I tell you truly: guard your soul, lest it be defiled by iniquity. Gird your body also with God’s righteousness. Do this before the day of death, because afterward you will be able to find no remedy except insofar as you find one through God’s grace and the adornment of your works.

For your enemy, the hawk, circles about, trying to discover how he may wound your soul. Guard yourself from him through zeal for good works and abstinence from sins, because your days do not have a long span. Therefore may the Holy Spirit kindle his fire in you, so that you remember these words.

And therefore again I tell you this parable: trees wither in winter, blossom in summer, and produce their figs. Now attend to this in your soul: consider how long you have been in winter through the transgression of spiritual life; and through the change of your dispositions hasten swiftly into the greenness of the Holy Spirit, which is summer. In this way produce the flowers of virtues and gather your sheaves as quickly as you can. Meanwhile, nevertheless, guard yourself from sins, because in truth I tell you: if you seek God’s grace, it will not flee from you.

## LETTER CIV

**N., ABBESS AT GERBSTEDT, TO HILDEGARD.** She asks to be helped by Hildegard’s prayers and promises her own in return.

To the venerable Lady H., burning and shining lamp, N., by God’s grace abbess at Gerbstedt, though unworthy: may you so contend in zeal as to gain the eternal prize.

Since, as the Apostle testifies [Romans 12], each person is a member of another, all the Church’s children ought greatly to rejoice that the fame of your holiness, flying everywhere, has made known the fragrance of your virtues throughout the entire Church. This fragrance, breathing even in our regions, has stirred our hearts no little to render thanks to the author of every good.

Therefore I, least among the faithful, desiring to share in your merits, beg most earnestly that I may deserve to share in the constancy of your prayers. If you grant this request, I promise you my prayer, though most worthless, yet most ready. I further ask your graciousness, beloved lady, to send me something from your books, to be served always with every devotion. Moreover, may your memory flourish among us all the more abundantly as your goodness gladdens us by these things. Farewell.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.** Concerning the fall of the first parents and their raising up through Christ.

[Col. 0325D]

You, daughter of God, rise in the night through the four elements, which in the day bring all works to completion. For night brings forth sorrow through darkness, and day joy through light. For it is written: “Day pours forth speech to day, and night makes knowledge known to night” (Ps. 18). This means: God is that Day which is not darkened and which is never changed through the ages of ages; and he chose for himself a day—that is, bright light from light—because he made his own creature, namely humanity, whole, together with all that belongs to it. But the serpent, coming, breathed upon the woman through speech; she received it and leaned toward the serpent. [Col. 0326A] And as she had tasted this from the serpent, so she gave the same to her husband; and it remained in the man, because man fully carries out all works. God did not command this to be done; rather, the serpent deceived the woman by flattering and playful words. Thus the taste of the flesh was received from the serpent, and it is therefore slippery, light, and deceptive, according to the serpent’s counsel. For in its deceit the serpent concealed a curse from humanity, since, had it shown humanity its destruction, humanity would not have consented to its counsel. And as humanity has knowledge of good and evil, so the serpent has deceit and curse.

But afterward the swift stag and the strong lion had, in his chamber, the means of dividing this matter. For God chose for himself a virginal enclosure, in which he prepared humanity for his Word, because the Virgin [Col. 0326B] does not know the mingling of the taste of the flesh; and thus the Word of God was made a human being in an alien manner. So too Christ the man came forth from day to day, and thus deceived the serpent which had blasphemed humanity. For Christ the Day overcame all the night’s harmful things, because he washed away, through amended repentance, the taste of the flesh which the serpent had sweetly introduced into humanity; and he makes humanity other in this way, when he gathers that person, his member, to himself. The serpent also, with its deceit in which it hides wickedness, often harms many and makes them uncertain, so that they do not know God, tearing them apart without faith and without hope. Yet many fight against this, saying: “My Creator will not destroy me, unless I perish because of my sins.” This struggle is likened to the torturers of the martyrs and to the pain of Christ’s wounds. But the first woman was the aforesaid night, and she made knowledge known to night, namely to her husband. You, however, daughter of God, make yourself beautiful through the martyrdom of good work, so that your soul may shine in God.

## LETTER CV

### From N., Abbess of Mount St. Cyriacus, to Hildegard

She commends herself and those entrusted to her to Hildegard’s prayers.

To HILDEGARD, mirror of holiness, N., unworthy abbess of Christ’s handmaids dwelling on Mount St. Cyriacus at Erfurt: may you enjoy the joys of eternal brightness.

Glorious things are said of you, servant of God. Therefore I ask you to stretch out to me, weighed down by the burden of sins, the hand of your prayer, in imitation of your Beloved, who stretched out his hand to the leper. For I have learned that you have been anointed with the oil of gladness above your companions. Therefore, kneeling in prayer, I adjure you: when you have attained those heavenly and eternal things, and the Holy of Holies within, have pity on my miseries, praying your Spouse and mine for me, and reconciling my transgressions to his favor. How, beloved of Christ, could you possess charity if you refused to sympathize with the weaknesses of others? Therefore let me and the sisters entrusted to me be commended to your holiness; and pray that our foot may stand in the straight way, so that, walking perfectly, we may reach the day of joy. Intercede with him who hides us in the secret place of his countenance from the disturbance of men, that he may deign to protect us [Col. 0327A] in his tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues, and grant us both the will and the ability to do what he commands—he who keeps truth for ever. Therefore we now make known to your holiness the full number of our sisterhood, and we earnestly entreat that we may have assurance of your prayer. May the glory of your holiness flourish, bloom, and prosper.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She exhorts her not to be troubled in mind and not to exceed moderation in abstinence.

O daughter of God, you are surrounded by Christ’s charity; yet you are constrained by the bitter conflicts of your body and resist the devil by opposing him. I see that the ordering of the community in which you are is pleasing to God, and is vigorously rising toward a better state, [Col. 0327B] and is being built up more in good conduct than it was when first established. Let your soul rejoice in God and remain devoutly in him.

Yet you neither know nor can conceive how to break the bonds of those who are bound—namely, those who walk in the paths of mockery. How so? A certain person looked toward a great tower lest he be moved; yet he could not prevent this, and cried out amid restless cries: “Woe, woe!” Thus he was led into the people’s mockery, as they said: “What will it profit you always to fight against those who do not want you?” But look toward the high mountain, and toward him who answers you with loving charity: “My daughter, my daughter, what do you wish? I will fulfill all that you ask for your soul.”

Now cease from a troubled mind and take rest for yourself. For I see in the true Light that [Col. 0327C] this is beneficial for your soul. Yet take care to keep your land in solitude and not crush it, so that it cannot, when worn down by the plough of labor, put forth the green growth of the herbs and spices of virtues. I often see that when a person afflicts the body by excessive abstinence, weariness arises within; and vices entangle themselves with that weariness more than they would if the body were fed justly. But because a well-disposed soul of charity has been established in you, take care that you do not often heed that which commands the flesh to be wounded. Rather, apply to yourself duly ordered seasons of healing ointments, so that you may live for ever. I see your soul shining very brightly in the pure human being.

## LETTER CVI

### From N., Abbess at Lubboldesberge, to Hildegard

She asks her for consoling letters.

To HILDEGARD, spouse of Christ on Mount St. Rupert, N., humble governess of the sisters at Lubboldesberge: a devout prayer in Christ.

How long I have desired, and still desire, to see your face and rejoice in your conversation, God, the searcher of hearts and reins, knows; yet, with my sins preventing me, I have never been able to attain the fulfillment of my desire. Nevertheless, since I have often learned that many who cannot see your face have received consolation through your letters, I too, a sinner, hoping for the same, have dared to seek your counsel by this present little letter, if perhaps divine mercy may purpose through your goodness [Col. 0328A] to console my affliction. For manifold is the contrition of my heart, which I desire with all my inmost being to have lightened through you.

### Hildegard’s Reply

God loves her greatly.

Day makes light clear, and night darkens the shadows. If night wishes to fight against day, it cannot extinguish it; but if day wishes to overcome night, it has the power to conquer it. May the true Light be present to you, which God provided for humanity on the first day. For the Father loves the Son, although he sees him go forth; provided, however, that he does not seek a fitting time for sinning, as though God did not exist. God sees your soul in the wandering of your mind; nevertheless, your mind scorns unlawful sinning, which tears the soul apart. [Col. 0328B] Therefore I see you as the glittering radiance of the sun through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit: not at all in the exile of destruction, but looking toward the sun like an eagle through repentance, which is the sweetest mother. Therefore God loves you greatly. Now live for ever.

## LETTER CVII

### From N., Abbess, to Hildegard

Beset by temptations, she asks for Hildegard’s counsel and the aid of her prayers.

To HILDEGARD, venerable and beloved in Christ, N., a sinner and abbess of the sisters in name alone: prayer and communion in all works done, or hereafter to be done, in the praise of God.

Dearest one, we know that you have always been provident in all matters and have not yet failed in this. Therefore we ask you kindly to receive our letter and hear what it contains. For we complain to your holiness that we are often attacked by temptations of evil spirits, drawn in various directions, and, unless strengthened with God’s help, overwhelmed by their storms. Therefore, for the sake of eternal recompense, we implore your holiness again and again, and even a third time, to help us by the counsel of your goodness. Whatever you decide concerning this matter, report it not orally but by letter through the bearer of the present letter.

### Hildegard’s Reply

One must abandon one’s own will and fleshly desires in order to obey God.

[Col. 0328D]

O daughter of Adam, I have been taught thus in true vision: whoever does this—abandons the desires of his or her body—is like Abraham, who left his country, and like the wise man who builds his house upon a rock. For the person who cultivates another life in this earthly life is shown to have an angelic life, because the storm of this age does not move that person, nor is that person cast down by the terrors of diabolical deception. But as Abraham left his country and obeyed God’s commands, so such a person leaves fleshly desires and obeys God’s commands through almsgiving, prayers, and other good works. Yet one must take care to remain steadfast in these good things, lest one be seduced by the devil, who deceived the first human being [Col. 0329A] and stripped that person of glory. In all one’s good deeds, one must also obey the teaching of the heavenly judges, whose tongues are the keys of heaven. May God bring this battle’s victory to completion in you, so that the angels may praise you, the saints rejoice in you, and you too be received into eternal joys.

## LETTER CVIII

### From N., Abbess at Widergoldesdorf, to St. Hildegard

Wishing to resign her office, she asks Hildegard what she ought to do.

To her lady HILDEGARD, pious mother of Christ’s handmaids serving the Lord God at Blessed Rupert’s, N., humble minister and so-called governess of the sisters [Col. 0329B] serving God and Saint Mary at Widergoldesdorf: heartfelt love and devoted service.

Lady, I know that all your ways are mercy and truth, and rightly so, because mercy, which drew the Son of God from heaven to earth, has looked upon you, and heavenly Wisdom has prepared its seat in you. Therefore, sweetest one, I earnestly beseech you to inquire of God whether it is his will that I bear or cast off this burden, since I have continued in it more through the constraint of obedience than through love of God. Therefore, if I dared, I would gladly leave my place of authority, because it seems very hard to me to submit to all others’ dispositions and remain in their will; and for that reason [Col. 0329C] I do not hope to receive any reward. Farewell. Let a wise mind be content with a few words.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She should steadfastly bear the burden laid upon her and trust in God.

This person is very strong, and it is a great gift of God in one who is so endowed in understanding that they can support heaven. This is the meaning: no one who is able by God’s rod to sustain the congregation of the saints should flee. But, daughter, may God’s gift inspire you to bear his light diligently.

There is, however, a certain human nature which at one’s first arising rises like smoke; it bears pain and bitterness, and many thoughts, fear, and doubt become entangled with it. This [Col. 0329D] is the martyrdom which you, daughter, possess; in it you endure distress, fear, and pain in the uprightness of life. Yet in this respect very many saints come to God as martyrs. Therefore trust in God, for he will not abandon you, and the Holy Spirit will lessen your pain.

## LETTER CIX

### From H., Abbess of Crouchdal, to Hildegard

She asks Hildegard to tell her what in her is worthy of correction.

To HILDEGARD, prudent steward of the household of the supreme Householder, H., humble and unworthy abbess of Crouchdal: maternal reverence together with the charity in which we are united in Christ.

After, with God’s help, I deserved to be relieved by your long-desired presence and gracious conversation, I rested for a while from my former faintness [Col. 0330A] of spirit and storm. Since I do not doubt that your words proceed not from human ingenuity but from the true Light, which has illuminated you more than other people, I have still postponed carrying out the plan which I had intended to perform, following your counsel. I want you to know, dearest lady and sister, that as I greatly desired to see you before, so I desire it no less still; and, though I cannot do so in body, I am always joined to you in heart. Since it is certain that charity abides in you and you in charity, I beseech you by it not to delay writing to me whatever the living Light, through its Spirit, has revealed to you concerning me as deserving rebuke or correction.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She judges others in matters in which she would not wish to be judged.

[Col. 0330B]

He who sees all things says: “You have eyes for seeing and for looking around on every side. Where you see mud, wash it away; and make green what is dry. Make the spices you possess give forth fragrance as well. If you did not have eyes, you could excuse yourself. But now you have eyes: why do you not look around with them? Yet you have grand speech in your rational faculty. For you often judge others in matters in which you do not wish to be judged; though at times you wisely say what you utter.

“Therefore attend carefully to bearing your burden, and gather good work into the sack of your heart, lest you fail. For in the solitary life which the sound of your words seeks, you could not rest [Col. 0330C] because of the changing dispositions of different people; for then your latter state would become far worse than your former, and indeed as grave as the loss of a stone. But imitate the turtledove in chastity, and diligently tend the chosen vineyard, so that you may behold God with a straight and pure face.”

## LETTER CX

### From L., Abbess at Bamberg, to Hildegard

She asks for a reciprocal fellowship of sisterhood from Hildegard and her convent.

To H., beloved lady and mother, venerable in religion and dignity, L., called abbess at Bamberg though unworthy: together with all those committed to her by God, whatever a humble and devoted, frequent prayer can accomplish.

[Col. 0330D] We rejoice with your blessedness in Christ, as much as we can according to our measure, because the Lord, who foreknew you and chose you beforehand for himself, has in our times illuminated and filled you with the spirit of prophecy. Christ has especially gladdened us in this: that he not only foreknew and predestined you, a woman, for this purpose, but has also illuminated many through his grace by your teaching. Therefore we render the greatest thanks to him for you and humbly beseech that he may mercifully bring to completion what he began in you, until he leads it to eternal things. We earnestly ask you to deign to receive us into the fellowship of your sisterhood, to commend us to your holy convent, and to strengthen us by your admonitory letters. May your love prosper.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She exhorts her to labor and to hold her daughters under discipline.

[Col. 0331A]

O mother, the person who does not dig and make fruitful the field that has fullness of fruitfulness sins, because that person does not labor for the Householder’s reward. For who established ox and ass? God, of course: he created them for human service. Why, then, should a person not labor for personal benefit, when that person is wholly God’s work and God did not create that person empty? For God makes the human being like the firmament, which bears sun, moon, and stars in order that they may shine upon every creature and show forth the seasons of seasons. But if a black cloud covered all these, creation would fear its own ending.

[Col. 0331B] You, daughter of God, know that you are this field, because through your good will you have an embrace with the people, so that they can receive your words and deeds. Therefore do not shrink from laboring with them, nor sin through idle leisure, because useless weeds often grow in idleness. Set before yourself also the appearance of the firmament, lest, deceived by the devil, you hide the light of your reason under black wickedness, as though you scarcely lived. In all these things keep your daughters under discipline; for as a child fears being struck by the rod, so a teacher ought to be feared by all. Do not fear affliction in these matters; rather, through it increase your rewards in eternal life, so that the breathings of the Holy Spirit may flow in you.

## LETTER CXI

[Col. 0331C]

### From N., Abbess of the Old Monastery at Mainz, to Hildegard

She asks Hildegard to endeavor to appease God for her sins.

To her lady H., a virgin dedicated to God, N., abbess in name alone of the sisters of the Old Monastery of the Church of Mainz: after prolonged illness, the blessedness of heavenly life.

If, my lady, you have recovered somewhat from your illness, I rejoice; but if not, I sympathize from my heart. Behold, I write to you in the boldness of familiarity, asking you to regard my devotion toward you and strive to appease the Lord’s countenance for my sins. For I ask you in the bond of charity to admonish me through the bearer of this letter, [Col. 0331D] so that you may gladden me by your reply, insofar as the Holy Spirit grants you.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She should bear her burden most devoutly and persevere in God’s service.

God’s will had laid me low as though under the sign of death, as though my soul were sighing to depart from this world; but now God’s grace has raised me somewhat in a new gift. Yet God’s mysteries say—as I see in true vision—“Whoever helps anyone in pain in my name will be helped in my portion, which is the reward of praise.” Your mind burns as though sprinkled with burning oil; therefore at times you are exhausted in sorrow, as though you did not know what you could do. Now live in God and bear your burden most devoutly [Col. 0332A] to the extent that you can according to your strength; and may God grant that you persevere in his service.

## LETTER CXII

### From E., Abbess of the Upper Monastery at Regensburg, to Hildegard

She asks whether she may relinquish the care entrusted to her, and whether she ought to fear anything concerning matters about which she had already inquired.

To the reverend mother H., greatly beloved in Christ, E., by God’s grace—if she is anything at all—abbess, though unworthy, in the Upper Monastery at Regensburg: such prayers as she can offer, with the affection of sincere faith and love.

My soul greatly desires to see your face, dearest lady, and for a long time my ears have been attentive to hear the words [Col. 0332B] of your mouth. In my great longing I once greeted your holiness by letter, but received no reply. Therefore I ask, and, prostrate at your feet from afar, humbly entreat, that through the present messenger you may deign at least to answer me concerning two inquiries: namely, whether some danger is to be feared, or hope placed in God’s mercy, regarding the matter for which my heart is now so deeply troubled. I wish to know your counsel concerning the care entrusted to me: how or when I may be released from it. Again and again I urgently implore your charity, if there be in you any bowels of mercy, not to be reluctant to relieve by your writings the great distress pressing upon my heart.

### Hildegard’s Reply

One must not inquire into what God wills to remain unknown, nor abandon the charge laid upon one.

[Col. 0332C]

O daughter of Adam, God is that rationality which has neither beginning nor end and through which the human being is rational; and this same rationality is living life within the human being, which shall never fail. Now look and attend to the Scriptures rooted in the root of the Holy Spirit, and written also from the rationality that is God. For Scripture is a mirror in which we behold God through faith, because our adversary watches and does not sleep. Therefore we must fight against him with it, and must not put God to the test, but worship him devoutly.

For the devil knows and sees that [the human being] [Col. 0332D] is changeable and of varying dispositions, and for this reason does not permit that person to rest in the peaceful habits of tranquillity. Often a person, as if in an impulse, wishes to know from God what it is not permitted to know, and thereby abandons God’s service. Hence the devil greatly rejoices and sees that person fail on both sides. Such inquiry is foolish, like that which is sought from a false prophet. In all these matters God must not be tested but worshipped. For out of his most savage wickedness the devil often sends darts into the human heart, by which a person may confound God. But the blessed person neither wishes to do these things nor consents to them, but lives among them as under the passion of death.

A person naturally sins through original sin; but afterward, when one repents and leaves it for God’s honor, [Col. 0333A] one resists the devil through faith. God will never destroy the person who offers to him the greater part of sins; but he forgives that person the other, lesser part of sins. Now, sweetest daughter, prudently oversee the care entrusted to you in such truth, lest you abandon it through weariness or labor. See that you rightly consider whether your thought concerning the Church of that place is good or bad, because a great sin will be present to you if you do not consider this rightly. For a tree full of flowers is beautiful to behold; but when its fruit ripens for eating, it is much more useful. The desire to work well gladdens the human mind like flowers; but devotion to the work, namely when the fruit begins to grow, is much better. When a person has accomplished good works, [Col. 0333B] ripe fruits appear, and those good works provide that person with the food of life in eternal pastures when that person departs from this life. Therefore, good daughter of God, bring your good desires to completion in good works, so that, when your soul leaves your body, a most beautiful reward from God may shine forth for you. May God’s grace teach you this.

## LETTER CXIII

### From N., Abbess of the Monastery at Nussim, to Hildegard

She seeks the support of Hildegard’s prayers amid the unsettled condition of her monastery.

To H., her lady and most beloved mother, N., abbess, though unworthy, of the sisters at Nussim: a small measure of prayer and service with heartfelt devotion.

Since, by report now spreading abroad, we do not doubt that your blessedness has learned of our condition—how it has been changed from that which, alas, it vainly wished to be back into what it formerly was—we ask you, for God’s sake, to grant us the help of your prayers all the more generously and urgently, because we are now driven and distressed in many directions by the burden that has come upon us, with a wavering mind. For we know that God is terrible in his counsels over the children of men; and thus, fearing his hidden yet never unjust judgments of severity, we wholly entrust the cause of our soul both to you, in whom we have greater confidence than in all other mortals, and to your reverend sisters; and we desire your reply with all our heart. Farewell.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She exhorts her to repentance and to doing good works.

[Col. 0333D]

O servant of God, run in the circuit of the sun with your heart’s intention; sighing to God for your sins, pant for him; and work good works before your days decline, when afterward you cannot work. Consider also that steward who was accused before his master and reduced in writing the debts of his master’s debtors. Do likewise. For where you did not well maintain your office, help your daughters through the aid of your counsel, and be toward them in the movement of mercy, as fitting rain rises over the grass and calls forth much fruit. Through repentance and mercy you will be wiser than the children of light—that is, the fallen angels—[Col. 0334A] because they were unwilling to do this. When you have done these works, they themselves will receive you after your death into eternal dwellings.

For if you turned your plough rightly into the earth and had fitting rain, you would be a germinating earth. But the dew by which you should have germinated has failed in you, while you go about with the wheel which you call your salvation, though it is ash-covered. Therefore turn your plough, together with the knowledge of holy Scripture, into your heart; have rain through sighs of good intention; and through happy practice retain the dew of blessing by good works. Do this before the day of your death, that you may live for ever.

## LETTER CXIV

### From N., Abbess of Cologne, to Hildegard

Desiring to have Hildegard as a mother, she asks for consoling letters.

[Col. 0334B]

To her lady and mother H., dwelling in the land of Jerusalem, N., abbess in name alone in the place of the holy virgins of the Church of Cologne: most devoted prayer and due service.

How greatly I rejoice in your blessedness I cannot express in words. Although I am separated from you in bodily sight, I am nevertheless bound to you by the inward affection of charity. I desire to see you and to explain to you the sorrow which I bear in my heart without any human consolation. You, who are full of all charity, I desire to have in my mother’s place. After God, I have also placed my hope in you, [Col. 0334C] and henceforth I desire to be consoled and gladdened by you. Therefore may the tears and groans of your beloved daughter move you. Remember me, and pray to God, who became poor for us, that he may deign to free me from everlasting poverty or place me in the lowest rank of eternal blessedness. Farewell, and greet all your community on my behalf.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She should bear her burden firmly and restrain her sheep.

Bear your burden firmly on the straight path, and restrain your sheep as much as you can. This is better for you than the various wandering of the mind, because God has equal power in every place according to human works. With God’s help prevent your mind from wandering, like a day which proceeds partly in pure sunlight and partly in a storm. For at one time your mind is in such bitterness that you cannot bear it; at another, in weariness and other conditions. Now rise in the purest sun and the proper warmth, because God wants you, however you may waver, since he has set you as an eye for others; therefore do not depart from him.

## LETTER CXV

### From N., Abbess of Didenkirkim, to Hildegard

She asks for admonitory words that may build up her soul.

To H., mistress of St. Rupert’s and enlightened by the grace of divine light, N., abbess of Didenkirkim near Bonn, though unworthy [Col. 0335A]: from one so small to one so great, and from one unworthy to one worthy, the urgency of prayer and the perseverance of due service.

Trusting so greatly in your piety and humility, I have sent you this letter through its bearer, written to this effect: if it be permitted and does not offend the eyes of your compassion, most loving mother, send me in a brief writing some admonitory words which may build up my soul and give me confidence in God. For when you were present, you promised at a fitting time to strengthen me by such words. Furthermore, though I dare not ask more, I will nevertheless use the prayers of the Canaanite woman, who answered the Lord in the Gospel, saying: “Even the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table” (Matt. 15). With the same devotion of faith I ask you a second time [Col. 0335B] to place before me, who greatly desire it, a brief portion from your table—that is, from that vision in which you frequently see many marvels—concerning the matters mentioned above. Remember that I recently sent parchment for this purpose. Nevertheless, insofar as it lies in us, we ask God in supplication to bring to a persevering end, through gratuitous mercy and goodness, the good which he began in you.

### Hildegard’s Reply

She exhorts her to cultivate the land of her heart, so that she may be useful to her own community.

You have a troubled mind because of muddy places and the care of many waters which fail as they flow. For muddy places belong to those who have a succession of very bad dispositions; [Col. 0335C] and failing waters belong to those who are hard and stony and are not softened by the little streams of holy Scripture’s teaching. But you say within yourself: “Who or what am I? And how could I bear such things?”

Now hear the parable of a wise man. A certain person wished to dig out a hollow place. But, as he dug with wood and iron, fire flew out from a certain stone into which he had dug, so that the same place could not be pierced through. Yet he marked out the width of that place and, with great labor, bored some cavities in it. That person said within himself: “I have labored greatly; but whoever comes after me will labor more lightly, because he will find all these things prepared for him.” This person will indeed be praised before his lord, because his work in length and breadth [Col. 0335D] is much more useful than work in soft earth overturned by the plough. Therefore his lord counts him as a most valiant soldier, one able to sustain his army well, and sets him before other farmers who yield fruit in their seasons. For whoever labored first surpasses the labor of the one who follows. The Maker of the world first began to create, and afterward gave his ministers the task of working according to him.

O daughter of God, restrain your land within yourself, lest it dry up without the fruitful usefulness of daughters. Gather your heart into one, and do not fix it in the excess of restless dispositions, lest you drive your daughters away from you. Be like good earth, frequently watered with fitting rain, so that it may bring forth good and pleasing herbs. [Col. 0336A] How? When a person feeds the flesh moderately, that person has cheerful and gentle dispositions; but when one lives in excess of food and feasts, one makes every harmful vice sprout within oneself. But one who emaciates the body through immoderate abstinence always goes about angry. Be good earth in all these matters, so that you may console your daughters when they weep, correct them rightly when they rise in anger, and subject them to regular discipline through yourself when they are raging. Those who turn away from you in forgetfulness, call back with historical words and the words of the Gospel, in the presence of yourself and two others; and if they then do not obey you, obey the supreme Master and remember Jacob, who exchanged Joseph’s two sons with his blessings. Now [Col. 0336B] consider the beginning of your good endeavor, so that you may enjoy a confident end and receive eternal rewards from the supreme Master.

## LETTER CXVI

### From T., Abbess of Andernach, to Hildegard

She seeks certainty about certain customs of Hildegard’s monastery, especially whether it admits only noble-born virgins.

To HILDEGARD, mistress of Christ’s brides, T., called mistress of the sisters of Andernach: may you at times be joined to the highest spirits in heaven.

A widely circulating report concerning your holiness has sounded in our ears certain wonderful and astounding things, and has especially [Col. 0336C] commended to our smallness the excellence of your supreme religious life and singular vocation. For through the testimony of many, we have learned that numerous heavenly secrets, difficult and rare for mortals to understand, are divinely revealed to you, and that whatever things you ought to do are ordered not by human deliberation but by God’s teaching. Another matter concerning your custom has also reached us: namely, that on feast days your virgins wear certain white veils as an ornament, and appropriately woven crowns placed above upon their heads, with angelic images inserted on both sides and at the back, and with the figure of the Lamb fittingly impressed on the forehead; furthermore, that their fingers are adorned with certain rings. All these things, we believe, you direct toward love of the heavenly Spouse, although [Col. 0336D] it is right that women should adorn themselves with modesty, not in braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing.

Moreover—and this seems no less astonishing to us than all these things—you admit into your fellowship only women distinguished by birth and freeborn, which we also greatly wonder at. Yet we know that you do this for a reasonable cause, since you are not ignorant that the Lord himself chose fishermen, humble persons, and poor persons in the primitive Church; and that Blessed Peter, after the nations had later been converted to faith, said: “In truth I have learned that God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10). Nor are you forgetful of the Apostle’s words to the Corinthians: “Not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the ignoble and despised things of this world” (1 Cor. 1). [Col. 0337A] Following, as far as we can, all the institutions of the Fathers who went before, by which everyone—and especially spiritual persons—ought to be formed, we also know that your own institutions are wholly just and holy. Yet, venerable spouse of Christ, the novelty of your custom so incomparably exceeds the measure of our smallness that it produces in us no little wonder. Therefore we, though very small, rejoicing deeply in your progress, nevertheless wished to send our letter to your holiness in order to learn something more certain from you about this matter, humbly and most devoutly beseeching that, through its authority, such religious observance may be increased, and that your dignity may not disdain soon to write back to us. Farewell, and remember [Col. 0337B] us in your prayers.

## Hildegard’s Reply

Women ought not to seek adornment; virgins are suited to white garments; persons of noble and humble station must be distinguished, lest they come to hate one another.

The Living Fountain says: “Let a woman remain hidden within her chamber, so that she may have great modesty; for the image of dreadful wantonness breathed great dangers into the first woman. How? Woman’s form flashed and shone forth in the first root, in which that was formed wherein every creature lies hidden. How? Namely in two parts: in one part from the work of God’s finger, and in the other from heavenly beauty. O what a wondrous thing you are, who laid your foundation in the sun [Col. 0337C] and surpassed the earth!

“But Paul the apostle, who flew to the heights and was silent on earth, so that he did not disclose what was hidden, considered these matters. A woman who is subject to the male authority of her husband, joined to him in the first rib, ought to possess great modesty, so that she ought not to display or reveal the glory of her husband’s own vessel in an alien place that does not belong to her. And she should do this in accordance with that saying in which the Ruler of the earth declares: ‘What God has joined together, let no human being separate’ (Matt. 19), in defiance of the devil.

“Hear: the earth sweats forth the greenness of grass until winter overcomes it; and winter takes away the beauty of its flower, and it conceals the greenness of its blossom, then being unable to reveal itself, as though it had never withered, because winter has taken it away. [Col. 0337D] Therefore a woman ought not to exalt herself in her hair, nor adorn herself, nor seek eminence through any crown or gold or other thing, except by the will of her husband, according as may please him in proper measure.”

These things do not apply to a virgin; rather, she stands beautiful in the simplicity and wholeness of paradise, which never appears dry but always remains in the full verdure of the flower of the branch. A virgin does not have the covering of the verdure of her hair as a command, but by her own choice covers herself in deepest humility, because a person conceals the beauty of the soul lest a hawk snatch it away through pride.

Virgins are joined in the Holy Spirit to holiness and to the dawn of virginity; therefore it is fitting that they should approach the high priest as a burnt offering [Col. 0338A] dedicated to God. Accordingly, through permission and revelation in the mystical breathing of God’s finger, it is fitting that a virgin wear a white garment, in the clear signification of Christ’s betrothal, seeing that her mind is made firm in woven integrity. She should also consider who it is to whom she is joined, as it is written: “They have his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads” (Rev. 14). And again: “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (ibid.).

God also makes examinations—searchings—of every person, so that a lower order may not rise above a higher, as Satan and the first human being did, who wished to fly higher than they had been placed. And what person gathers his whole herd into one stall—oxen, asses, sheep, and goats—without scattering it? Therefore there should be discernment in this matter, lest a diverse people, gathered into one flock, be scattered by the pride of exaltation and the disgrace of difference; and especially lest moral decency be broken apart there when they tear one another in hatred, when a higher order falls upon a lower and when a lower rises above a higher. For God distinguishes people on earth just as in heaven, distinguishing angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, cherubim, and seraphim. [Col. 0338B] All these are loved by God, yet they do not have equal names.

Pride loves princes and nobles in the guise of exaltation; and then hates them when they destroy it. And it is written: “God does not cast away the mighty, since he himself is mighty” (Job 36). [Col. 0338C] Yet he does not love persons, but works that have savor in him, as the Son of God says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). Where humility is, there Christ always feasts. Therefore those people must be distinguished who seek vain honor more than humility, seeing things that are above them.

A diseased sheep too should be put away, lest the whole flock be contaminated. God pours good understanding into human beings so that their name may not be erased. For it is good that a person should not seize a mountain which he cannot move, but remain in the valley, gradually learning what he is able to grasp.

These things were spoken by the Living Light and not by a human being. Let whoever hears see and believe whence they are.

## Letter CXVII

[Col. 0338D]

### A., Abbess of Crouchdal, to Hildegard

That she may pray to God that the writer may be able to make satisfaction for transgressions committed in her office.

To her most beloved lady H., divinely illumined by the most sacred gift of divine and most true visions: A. of Crouchdal, abbess in name alone, [sends greetings] with the most overflowing gift of perfect charity.

Your utterances, my lady, flowing from that most holy soul of yours, from that height of your contemplation, as from the summit of the eternal hills into the deepest valley of other souls, like rain upon grass and drops upon herbage, water them, pour themselves into them, and cause them to put forth a shoot without thorn; they cause [Col. 0339A] them to send forth living shoots of heavenly desires, springing with wondrous fragrance up to the throne of the glory of the highest God.

Therefore I, your handmaid, desire to behold letters from your holiness and to be refreshed by the breath of your most sweet consolation, as by a gentle breeze. For, my mother and lady, all my hope, security, refuge, and protection depend, after God, upon your motherhood; therefore I flee to you alone and entrust myself, after Christ, to your counsel and aid.

I therefore ask again in supplication and entreat mercifully that you pray to God for me, and graciously instruct me what I ought to do concerning my many transgressions, through which I offend both in the burden of the title [perhaps: “office,” *muneris*] imposed upon me and in other faults, as I asked above. [Col. 0339B] For I fear, and very greatly fear, that I may incur God’s displeasure. Farewell.

## Hildegard’s Reply

She commends to her charity, obedience, and renunciation of her own will.

In a true vision I heard these words, which you sought from me with burning desire because of the admonition required by great necessity:

“Most glorious is the praise where faithful governance possesses these battle-lines: namely, that one which, stationed as guardian of the tower with shields, breastplates, and other arms, fights against those who wish to destroy its tower; and likewise that one which so fortifies its city with worthy soldiers that its walls are not seized by enemies, its gate is not opened to the treacherous spies of its foes, and its inhabitants are not slain. [Col. 0339C] Such persons are in blessedness.

“But those who do not act thus are more squalid than peasants who wisely manage their farms through themselves and their livestock so that they do not lack pasture. Of these one must not say: ‘Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a rod of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and incense and every powder of the perfumer?’ (Song 3); nor: ‘How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince!’ (Song 7).

“That is: one who, in the exile of this world, which is understood by the wilderness, opposes his own will and in all his works rises to God with sighing, as it is written, ‘The smoke of the spices rose in the sight of the Lord’; who has chosen mortification of the flesh—such a one causes every virtue to grow within himself from the smoke of spices and the mortification of flesh, and he is never sated with them. Of the heavenly angels and saints it is said of one who does this: ‘How beautiful are your steps,’ that is, your pursuit in which you walk in this mortification, ‘daughter of a prince.’

“But one who is neither cold nor hot should be rejected from the prophet’s mouth, because he labors in neither earthly nor heavenly things. [Col. 0339D] I compare him to locusts: they neither fly rightly with birds nor walk rightly upon the earth with animals, but like a whirlwind they go swiftly and come to nothing without profit.

“O daughter of the sacred name, open your ears and with an attentive heart hear the meanings set forth in this parabolic discourse: how great is the glory, in [Col. 0340A] highest praise, of the towers of this city thus established. The tower of this city is charity joined with concord. And why is it called a tower? Because from the most high God it flowed as a spring leaping forth and encompassing the whole earth; for God so disposed all creatures in full charity that no want exists in them.

“Therefore learn that holy persons in whom charity dwells do not fail in any necessity, because their hearts are surrounded by gentleness and peace as by the flowing fragrance of balsam. Hence the ancient serpent cannot tear them apart; for as a foul odor is separated from the fragrance of balsam, so the devil flees charity and hides himself from it in a cave. But wherever holy persons in whom charity does not dwell assemble in the name [Col. 0340B] of the Lord, they are like a city without a tower and handsome houses without height. Thus in this confusion the wealth of justice and rule, because they have no firm dwellings, is despoiled, and so they are frequently destroyed.

“For just as a tower adorns and supports a city, charity adorns and supports all virtues. The soldiers of charity stationed in the tower are obedience, faith, and hope. Obedience is surrounded by a shield because it is always subject; faith is clothed in a breastplate because it proves all the good things that are in God, which the eye has never seen; and hope embraces heaven and all its adornments through faith. Faith, moreover, always looks to God through obedience, doing what he has commanded it.

“For God is charity, because all his work is merciful; but through humility he descended from heaven to free his captives, who had abandoned charity when they did not know him. [Col. 0340C] He did this through his humanity and left us the same example. How? When we relinquish our own will in the offices of this world, we walk after his footsteps. But when we gather in one flock in his name, as other birds gather to the eagle, we imitate Abraham, who left his people and the land of his homeland and performed circumcision in a foreign land according to God’s command.

“But when, through a person like ourselves, we obey God’s commands, we are multiplied in blessings like the stars of heaven, as God also promised Abraham through his angel; and we seek what belongs to another according to his incarnation, reckoning ourselves as nothing and laboring in the spiritual life. When we do this, we fortify our tower on every side through humility with worthy soldiers. And we are worthy soldiers when we overcome the pleasure of this world, conquer the fury of anger, endure our poverty for Christ’s love, cast away from ourselves the hostile murders of hatred and envy, do not despise other sinners like ourselves or pronounce unjust judgments against them, and do not seek false witness against the just and innocent. [Col. 0340D]

“These are worthy soldiers who guard our city on every side, so that [Col. 0341A] the wall of our holy rule and manner of life is not pierced by enemies—that is, hateful and envious dispositions—and so that the gate of peace is not rejected through contradiction. For if this occurs, the fastening of our gate is opened, and our enemies walk securely into our city.

“Let us not be like those who are ever of wandering heart and say: ‘We do not want what human reason sets before us and chooses, because what we ourselves set before us and choose is more useful and more just than that.’ These are plotters who destroy our city through their schemes, because they reject what has been established by our ancient and holy master-physicians concerning fasting, vigils, prayer, and the other virtues, and choose their own will in place of God, who created them.

“O daughter of holiness, now hear: your tower is empty without worthy soldiers, and the guardians of your city have fallen asleep; thus they have been led into barrenness, especially because of the self-will that belongs to them. [Col. 0341B] Therefore your tower and city are so dry that they scarcely stand. Rise, then, from your sleep, for the ropes of your ship, which are the custom of holy life, have not yet broken. But, absorbed in great folly of conduct, you seek rumors that might suit you. This does not profit you.

“For just as in desert dwellings there are large, small, and blind mice that gnaw people’s garments, so by these things every holy custom is torn apart. The large mice are restless minds of impiety; the small signify folly, which is nocturnal—that is, removed from the way of truth; the blind show the vanity of this world, blind to the light of justice. Hence it is written in the Gospel: ‘Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste’ (Luke 11).

“Now see in what great fire of the Holy Spirit you have been planted. Therefore he does not wish to be without his ministry in you. Attend with diligent heart to the original rule of St Benedict and of the other masters, so that you may not perish but live eternally. [Col. 0341C]

“But all of you, O masters, take care not to be like those foolish farmers who rejoice when they see a plough moving straight on its own, but, when it turns crookedly, are wearied by setting it straight. Also beware lest the householder say to you: ‘You are useless to me [Col. 0341D], because you do not rightly carry out your stewardship.’ Rather, consider carefully what need and adversity your subjects experience, and protect them with every care.”

## Letter CXVIII

### G., a Religious Woman, to Hildegard

How grievously she bears Hildegard’s absence.

To Hildegard, her most beloved mother in Christ: G., hers and truly wholly hers, [wishes her] that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (II Cor. II).

What I should write or say to so singular a mother, beloved as though in Christ, I wholly do not know, because the very force of love has taken from me all knowledge of speech. Indeed, the wine of sorrow with which your divine absence has made me drunk has afflicted me so deeply that it has produced in me a weariness not only of writing but even of living. [Col. 0342A]

For I would think it better never to have seen you, never to have experienced you as so kind toward me and bearing such maternal affection, than now, separated from you across so great an expanse of places, to mourn you without pause as though lost. Yet I hope in my God—and therefore in mine, because I have nothing dearer—that he will not permit me to put aside the foul form of this body before he has made me joyful through your sweet sight and honeyed conversation.

But if, because my sins demand it, this should not happen, still I trust his mercy that he will not disappoint my hope of granting me to see you there [Col. 0342B] where we shall never be separated from his vision. What more? I ask you, my most beloved mother, that with him in whose embrace you continually dwell, and beneath whose shadow you rest like a young deer from the heat of temptations and vices, you may deign to pray for me: that he may show himself to be found by me, who still wander and seek him but—alas!—do not find him at all; and that he may one day make me sit beneath the shadow of him whom I desire. Farewell.

## Hildegard’s Reply

She rejoices that G. has embraced the narrow way.

O daughter of God, hear these words spoken to you in the pure knowledge of faith: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2). This refers to the Son of God, who, contrary to the laws of the flesh, was born from the inviolate earth of the Virgin Mary. The flowers of all virtues and the ornaments of every spice came forth, having in themselves the fragrance of the sweetness of virtues.

For the garden of these virtues arose in the wandering son, who, returning to himself, ran to his father—that is, to the almighty Father—confessing his sins; and the Father received him with the kiss of the humanity of his Son. [Col. 0342C] And then the voice of the turtledove is heard when, for God’s love, we leave the world together with our own will, just as the turtledove, unlike other birds, remains alone when it loses its companion.

So you too, dearest daughter, acted when you abandoned the pomp of this world. O how beautiful were your sandals, daughter of the King, when for God’s love you entered the strait and narrow way of spiritual life! Therefore, O daughter of Zion, rejoice, because the Holy Spirit dwells in the midst of your heart. Consider that your consoler has placed you like a lily among thorns, when, possessing the pomp and riches of this age—which the Son of God called thorns—you chose the spiritual life.

You also glowed like a rose in Jericho amid the sufferings of your conversion. [Col. 0342D] Now I rejoice concerning you, because what I heard and desired concerning you has been fulfilled in you; rejoice with me as well. I truly desire, in true choice, that you may become in God’s sight a wall adorned with precious stones and pearls, and in the praises of all the heavenly host. Therefore rejoice and be glad in your God, because you shall live eternally.

## Letter CXIX

[Col. 0343A]

### B., a Priest, to Hildegard

He is distressed that his intention to abandon the world is delayed; he asks her prayers and requests her book for copying.

To Hildegard, most worthy teacher of Christ’s brides: B., by God’s grace, though an unworthy priest of God and a sinner, [sends] the devoted assurance of deepest love and every service.

I am weary of my life, because I am filled with bitterness, and because I still defer the purpose of which you are aware, most holy virgin, while waiting for certain faithful friends of mine. My path, to use prophetic words, is hedged about on every side with thorns and a wall. Yet I do not wholly refuse the scourges that in every way instruct Israel; but because they do not produce deliverance along with temptation, I fear greatly lest I fall and fail to attain the end of my purpose. Not that my heart is not gladdened amid sins and hardships, since I place great confidence in your consolation, which I frequently behold. [Col. 0343B]

Therefore, virgin devoted to God, all of us who, after God, sigh toward you earnestly ask, seek, and knock: do not cease in any way from your usual prayers until merciful God deigns, for our sake, to indicate to you either a fixed place for our dwelling or, if this seems to you a trial in relation to God, at least now a well-discerning rule of religious life. We believe without doubt that God has ordered these things through you; you have experienced this in fact. For nothing happens on earth without cause.

Therefore, as you were freeing my soul in part from its distress by God’s judgment in hidden things, do not, as a sinner bound by duty, shrink from freeing all of us from the error of uncertainty through the means ordained in you by God. Henceforth I desire your letters concerning these matters and others. Moreover, I greatly desire to copy your book. [Col. 0343C]

## Hildegard’s Reply

She encourages him to pursue his purpose.

The Spirit says: “It is most praiseworthy and wonderful that a pilgrim hastens to his homeland. O how great is the grief and sorrow then among the fellow citizens and acquaintances of one who feasted and played with them! And how greatly the wanton blush because their companion abandons the vessel that he bore with them!

“See that you have been foreseen with great care in the eye of the Living One, as the gentlest Father seeks his sheep. Companions who sit idle in spaciousness enjoy mutual peace; but the strongest soldier is amid great storms. Stand in the path of uprightness and prepare your soul to fight those who are ever at war in the king’s service.

“See: if some winged creature of the hornets departed from its companions and, looking upward, began to fly toward the sun, the whole swarm of flies would rush upon it, wanting to overwhelm it. But the sun would cover it with its light so that they could no longer see it, and thus it would escape. Then that whole swarm would be scandalized, and so it would become a worthy soldier. [Col. 0344A] May God stretch out his hand to you, that you may live eternally where the sun is not darkened.”

## Letter CXX

### V. to Hildegard

He excuses himself for having visited her neither in person nor by letter.

To Lady H., most full of religion, wisdom, discipline, moral character, and finally every virtue of both the inward and outward person: V., hers in every respect, [wishes] to labor with Martha in the sixth age, to be restored in the seventh, and to rejoice with Mary in the eighth.

How I could have withheld myself so long from the sight and conversation of your sweetness, more pleasing to me than every taste of honey, or how I could meanwhile have delayed at least to visit you by a little letter, I cannot sufficiently wonder even at myself; I attribute it entirely to the sluggishness of my own insignificance.
