[Col. 0344B] I greatly fear—and deservedly—that I may, God forbid, have offended your kindness by such ineptitude on my part. For although you had previously known me neither by voice, bearing, face, nor even reputation, when I first came you most kindly received me—something most difficult to do—and at once deigned, a thing I count great, to refresh me with participation in your conversation.

But because I repent, you will forgive me. My mind was never unwilling, though the means were lacking. Therefore I promise, if I can promise anything, that, if God gives the means, I shall make amends as soon as possible. Meanwhile, for God’s sake, deign to remember me, a most wretched sinner, in your prayers.

## Hildegard’s Reply

She exhorts him to contempt of the world.

[Col. 0344C]

He who is Life showed me these words, saying: “You are like water that is stirred in a storm and then becomes still again in calm. Victory says to you: ‘Enter willingly into yourself’; but you strike me when you hide the face of your mind, so that you are doubtful and lack flying wings in security, because you are not in the embrace of contempt for the world.

“O human being, resurrection will soon come to you if you shake off the dust of ashes from yourself, saying: ‘If I cannot stand in the sun, yet I wish to withdraw myself from the mud of dust and wash my garment from the changeableness of the ways of this age.’ Then the dove will give you ointment [Col. 0344D] and cleanse your wound. Now arise and live in eternity.”

## Letter CXXI

### T., a Monk of St Benedict, to Hildegard

He wishes to enjoy her presence, or at least to be strengthened in God by her letters.

To the most serene and truly blessed Lady H., adorned with the Spirit of divine vision: T., the least of the monks of St Benedict, though an unworthy priest, [sends] the service of devoted obedience with every submission of humility.

“Those who trust in the Lord shall understand truth, and the faithful shall abide in love,” etc. (Wisdom 3). By many truthful reports I have learned and believe that these most sacred words, uttered through the mouth of heavenly Wisdom, have been fulfilled in you. [Col. 0345A] For, as I find testified in the sacred Scriptures, I hold most faithfully that with God no word is impossible.

Thus, although I have not seen your holy revelations, I did not doubt that the report which I learned through public rumor was true. I know in truth that, because you have placed your trust in the Lord, you have therefore understood his truth; and because you faithfully rest in love in him, you have received the gift of divine revelation, the Spirit of heavenly consolation, and the peace of God’s elect.

Now because the mercy of almighty God has been found more abundantly in you than in other mortals, I humbly ask—not testing you or acting proudly, but simply beseeching through you the grace of God alone—that you remember the Lord’s saying: “Do not despise one of my little ones.” [Col. 0345B] Therefore consider lest you despise the letter of my lowliness; rather, I ask you mercifully through the love of Jesus Christ to hear my prayers, intercede with God for my sins, sustain my life by your holy prayers, and deign to admonish my negligences in letters of your correction.

For correction born of your most sweet charity is most desirable to me. Thus I judge myself unworthy of the beloved gift of your letter, yet I desire to receive from you the reward of my faith. For I believe that, through the Spirit by whom you perceive all things past, present, and future, even the secrets of my heart are open to you.

Truly I have never seen a day sweeter to me than the day when I might come into your presence. I would rather walk barefoot merely to hear your words; and it would be most delightful and desirable to me if I might deserve to receive either your most excellent visions or some letters of your blessedness. [Col. 0345C] May the almighty Father, through the power of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ and through the working together of the Holy Spirit, deign to preserve you unharmed for a long time for the correction of his holy Church.

## Hildegard’s Reply

His desires are good, and he should be strong in battle.

The Living Light says: “O human being, streams flow from me toward the verdure of your mind; yet your mind is bound and also sharpened by the changing ways of a scattered wind in darkness. Your hidden thoughts sometimes deceive you within your mind, and the savor of your work sometimes touches you.

“But the countenance of your desires looks toward me through the joy of ascent, which you are not yet able to grasp in your work. The desires that build a tower in the height of the sweetness of good fragrance are very good. Therefore angels rejoice in the works made by God’s finger, works that taste God by breaking the food of sinful wickedness.

“Now you, O soldier, be strong in battle as long as you live in your body, because your enemy does not grow weary and the combat does not fail. [Col. 0345D] Such are your works that the gentlest Father rejoices over you, that his word may make your soul bright, and that the fiery Lover may pour into you the ointment of salvation and the verdure of the flower of wisdom.”

## Letter CXXII

### B. to Hildegard

Burdened by sins, he asks for her prayers.

[Col. 0346A]

To his most beloved and most desired lady and mother H.: B., a sinner, [wishes her] to rejoice forever with Christ the Lord after this fragile and passing life.

I would consider myself blessed if I deserved to be consoled by letters from your holiness. But because it belongs to a prudent physician frequently to visit a wounded person and to cut away superfluous and rotten flesh lest the corruption later become worse if it is not carefully and diligently removed, I ask you, for love of the gracious Redeemer, to inspect more often the wounds of my injuries, so that by God’s mercy [Col. 0346B] and your counsel no trace of corruption may remain in them.

O sweetest and most desired mother, for a long time I have wished to come to you leaning on my staff. O sweetest lady, I always look upon you with the eyes of my heart; in mind I speak and live in your company. I know that I have sinned against my God in his work. I acknowledge that I have sinned: pray for me. I do not seek earthly gain or a transitory thing, but the grace of my God and the salvation of my soul. Help me. How great a support to me is the continual protection of your prayers.

Therefore, lest I should be wholly disappointed of my desire, my lady, wishing to satisfy me, I have arranged to send this client to you with this letter; he embraces you as lady and mother with devoted love. May God grant you the consolation of the present life and perpetual blessedness [Col. 0346C] with the saints. Amen.

## Hildegard’s Reply

She exhorts him to repentance and recounts its various stages.

I heard this in a true vision: “God’s work in a human being has five operations. The first is that the human being was formed; the second, that he received the breath of life; the third, that he understood what he was able to do; the fourth, that he undertook a good work; the fifth, that he came to know evil.

“This likeness can concern every human being. In the first instance it means that one remembers one’s sins with sighs, recognizing that they are useless; in the second, that one turns aside a little from sins; in the third, that one reveals them by confessing them; in the fourth, that one performs penance; in the fifth, that one makes oneself a stranger to evil.

“Therefore, O human being, in these works which God performed in humanity, perform penance with fear and trembling, because you have shattered his work in some respect. For as long as you live and have the ability, in the hearing of a priest you shall offer something of praise to God in groaning and sighing.” [Col. 0346D]

## Letter CXXIII

### H., Master of Trajectum, to Hildegard

Refined in the furnace of tribulation, he wishes to be refreshed by her writings and to learn whether he belongs among the saved.

H., greetings, noble bride of Christ, destined to receive the marriage-feast of incorruptible life. Who, what kind of man, how great, how I am situated, and whence I come—namely, H., unworthy master of Trajectum—you may learn from the present bearer.

[Col. 0347A]

Christ’s good fragrance, like poured-out ointment, breathing far and wide from you into our unworthy ears, has filled them with the report that, through the visitation of heavenly grace, you are so often illumined from above by the splendor of divine light that it is sometimes granted you, through the grace of God dwelling in you, to contemplate events of various causes and outcomes of affairs predetermined by God’s hidden providence, especially when you urgently ask that this be revealed to you. [Col. 0347A]

For this reason I, humble and cast down, driven by varied pains and manifold adversities—undoubtedly provoked by my own unspeakable guilt—commend myself to your [Col. 0347B] merciful prayers from my inmost heart. I adjure you by him who redeemed you to himself at his own price, that by your righteous labors you may strive with untiring labor to reconcile me to his merciful goodness.

For I have been wholly humbled and bent down to the end, like a lost vessel cast from before his eyes, because evils without number have surrounded me and my iniquities have overtaken me; they have risen above my head like a heavy burden. Besides all these things, I sought one who might grieve with me, and there was none; one to comfort me, and I found none.

Therefore, not in empty rashness or superfluous curiosity, but as one refined in the furnace of tribulation, I humbly and eagerly await [Col. 0347C] refreshment from your desired reply. From it I desire both to learn, by discerning the predetermined judgment of the heavenly Dispenser concerning the condition or outcome of my distresses, and to receive from you counsel for healing through his inspiration.

But above all and through all things, I thirst ardently to be assured by you whether the Godhead has at last foreordained that I should be numbered among the assembly of the saved. Farewell, rejoice, live, and may your name be in the book of life.

## Hildegard’s Reply

That he should turn from evil and do good.

The mystical breath and voice of Wisdom sounds: “God is eternal, and he held this counsel within himself: that he wished to make a great work, so that all his miracles might sound within it through rationality. He delighted greatly in this ancient counsel, and his work ought to build very many edifices of good; and thus God made the human being.

“Now the human being is the image of God, into which God sent a golden breath, which possesses within itself two paths in the knowledge of good and evil: one sustains heaven; the other shows evil. The one sustains heaven, because God perfected the power of his might in the golden breath of the human being through shining works; the other touches the state of the blackness of the first beginning of evil, which wished to fight.

“In these two paths the five senses of the human being, together with wisdom, knowledge, understanding, and will, are counted worthy of great honor, just as the orders of angels are appointed to God’s praise and stand [Col. 0348A] before him.

“But now, O servant of God, little windows in shining light appear in you along the better path, so that you desire good by longing for it; yet on the other path you are occupied in a black whirlwind. But you, O soldier, arise with bright soldiery and conquer this whirlwind, for God’s grace touches and admonishes you, as you can also understand in the knowledge of your secret. Thus turn aside from evil and do good, and God will seek you out and rest in you.”

## Letter CXXIV

### C. and B., Priests at Ruthdelingun, to Hildegard

They commend themselves to her prayers.

To Hildegard, a virgin intimate with God and wondrous above the people of this age: C. and B., unworthy priests [Col. 0348B] at Ruthdelingun, [wish her] to persevere, as she has begun, in the fear and love of God, and unceasingly to illumine the darkness of the world through the Living Light which she beholds.

We rejoiced and were delighted at the things said to us, namely, that a consoling embassy would be sent to us. We waited and waited, and you have not yet given heed. Therefore we were saddened, awaiting the grace of God, who has not abandoned those who hope in him. But now, since you have instructed us to send an envoy to you, we have been comforted.

Yet, beloved of God, because we wish to remind you how, through the vicissitudes of this instrument in which we desire to conduct ourselves like untrained and delicate soldiers, we hasten onward in upright hope, we earnestly beg you, holy mother, to intercede unceasingly for us with the Helper in times of need and tribulation [Col. 0348C], that he may direct our paths, since after God we place our confidence in you. Nor do we say this as though we bitterly regretted being burdened beyond measure by this undertaking; rather, that your holiness may obtain for us weak persons from the merciful God some consolation—which our sins obstruct—lest we fail. We do not presume to communicate anything further about this to you in detail; rather, we wish to entrust the measure of our petition to the inward Judge, who knows what is expedient for each person. For he himself says: “Your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask”; he knows the remedies appropriate to each individual in their proper times, and does not cease to provide them.

Yet this alone we wish to cry out [Col. 0348D]: “Woe, woe to the earthly cause—when does it suppose that it will hide itself from the living eye?” Furthermore, we greet in the Lord your superior, your sisters, and all who dwell with you; and we devoutly ask that they remember us, their poor ones.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY  
### That they should run to God and fight bravely for his sake

The Living Light says:

“O most valiant soldiers, who contradict within yourselves the contradiction of double-tongued persons, listen. What sort of people are those who seek life in pilgrimage, and who in exile are strangers to that portion which they have left for God’s sake? For the hands of workers continually prepare riches. O how great is that holiness which tramples poison amid deadly pestilence! Hence, in the overthrow of sin a beautiful flower grows, a companion of the angels.

“But you, children of pilgrimage, run and pass over to me, and prepare for yourselves many riches; for the Living Eye sees you, which ever gazes into the mirror of the dove. Now labour, and do not grow weary because of the tedium of a deceitful and small work, for the Sun of Light has prepared eternal life for you. Run diligently to God, for his day is coming.

“And leave that man who is bound by his own uncertainty amid many changes, like water surging in many storms, as you would leave a tree that cannot bend like a rod; for his own will looks anxiously to its own care. But let him consider himself in this way: if no guilty crime boils within him [Col. 0349B], let him take care of himself.

“But you, my lovers, run to me, for I see your groaning as bright and strong gold, and I see your mind as joyful and possessing desires of goodwill. Enter, therefore, into battle as strong retainers. For those who are in exile cannot have certain victory while remaining in the body; rather, they must flee the pestilence of the shipwrecked world and strengthen the pillar of their mind with the cornerstone. Therefore, O most valiant soldiers, do not grow weary through the changing fortunes of this instrument, because God will seek out his lambs among wolves.”

## LETTER CXXV  
### From B., a priest of Trier, to Hildegard  
### That she write him words of consolation and show how he may preside over those whom he must govern under the rule of the priesthood

[Col. 0349C]

To the holy virgin of God, the venerable bride of Jesus Christ: B., by the grace of God a priest of whatever sort in the Church of Trier, though unworthy of the dignity of the priesthood, sends himself.

Although I rarely behold you with bodily eyes, that wondrous power of our soul called imagination presents to me daily the serenity of your countenance, gladdens me with the pleasant recollection of you, and stirs me to the praise of God. For in our own days he has deigned, through you, to declare by manifest revelation and evident example what Holy Scripture daily recalls: namely, how the Holy Spirit spoke wondrously as the light of chaste souls in the ancient Fathers and in holy, unlearned apostolic men of God [Col. 0349D].

For it seems to me that you can say with Peter in David’s words: “Because I have not known learning, I shall enter into the power of the Lord” (Psalm 70). Therefore, by that merciful clemency of the loving divinity which in an unprecedented manner has illumined the innermost recesses of your holy breast with its most brilliant rays, I earnestly beg you to be willing to aid me, a wretched sinner, by your prayer.

I ask also that, through divine consolation—because you frequently rest upon heavenly vision—you write back to me words of consolation and graciously indicate how I may preside over those whom I ought to govern under the rule of the priesthood. Farewell.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY  
### She teaches how he ought to conduct himself toward sinners

[Col. 0350A]

The Spirit of Truth says in his mystical gift:

“A physician should often anoint with mercy a man who has wounds in himself and sprinkles them with oil, yet cannot bear wine poured into those wounds; nor should he permit the stinking bruise to remain in him. For leprosy is cleansed away by the supreme Physician when a person shows himself to the priest.

“But many come to me with the wordiness of their minds, wishing to learn with seeing eyes what may heal their wounds, yet they are unwilling to touch me by means of their tongues sweating forth diverse words. Their inward mind does not understand me; thus they bring forth the habit that swallows them up in transgression [Col. 0350B], amid the ancient vices of their drunkenness. Yet they say: ‘We have drunk the bitterness of correction and wiped away our wickedness.’ In this way they refuse to leave their evil paths.

“Certainly, such people ought to be bound, lest they be able to move about by worldly paths, since they refuse to abandon their iniquities. But a person who continually abandons his iniquities with sorrow, so that he does not wish repeatedly to plunge into filthy sins, is not to be bound in the manner described; rather, he is to be anointed in his sorrows wherever he may be.

“For the great Physician raises those who are watchful, corrects those who sleep, and kills those who persevere in their evils. Therefore, little one, consider prudently in these two categories what necessity is required.”

## LETTER CXXVI  
### From Brother S. to Saint Hildegard  
### Burdened by sins, he commends himself to her prayers

[Col. 0350C]

To Lady H., spiritual mother: Brother S. . . . the least of the brethren of the church, yet more darkened than all by the filth of sins—may he minister spiritual food with Martha and long with Mary for the joys of heavenly life.

I rejoice greatly, O spiritual mother, that you have found grace in the sight of the Lord our God, and that the lamp of your blessed soul, for the sake of his coming, has hitherto been kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit without the wearying delay of that time. Therefore, O fellow initiate of God (*symmysta Dei*), since you flourish in the integrity of chastity with the prudent virgins and keep the eye of contemplation fixed continually upon divine brightness [Col. 0350D], the devotion of my faint-heartedness prays that you will take care, by your most righteous prayers for me, to appease the face of the Lord, whom I have grievously provoked by my hardened perversity.

For I am certain that our God, refuge and strength, will willingly deign to hear your prayer for me, so that in his mercy, after the spirit of blasphemy by which my most unhappy soul is surrounded has been driven farther away, and after I have been justified through you, he may not give me perpetual tossing to and fro. I also ask this of your abundantly generous goodness: that through the bearer of this letter you write back to my littleness a letter from your holiness.

Give your holy women, observers of the monastic religion, as many greetings and prayers from me [Col. 0351A] as there are eternal dwelling places in the house of God. Farewell.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY  
### That he should sigh toward God through repentance

Your mind circles like a bird, arranging and dividing every matter into which it enters. For your beginning was consecrated, because the grace of God so imbued you that you are able to receive virtues and many other good things.

But some people are windy; through sensuality they have an apprehension of the greenness and moisture of the earth, and of air and waters. For God, as it pleased him, said, “Let there be,” and in this every creature came forth in its own kind, as it is written: “God spoke once; these two things have I heard: that power belongs to God, and to thee, O Lord, mercy, for thou wilt render to each according to his works” (Psalm 61) [Col. 0351B].

For by his command God created all things, and did this once, when he said, “Let there be.” And in this, moreover, he made known two things: first, that it was great power that God gave the law to humankind; secondly, that mercy belongs to him who rules all things, because through his Incarnation he renders what must be rendered. For he forgives sins to everyone who sees and acknowledges them through repentance; but he casts out the person who is unwilling either to see or acknowledge them, and sends him to the just recompense of his deeds.

For God cast down into the pit of misery the first angel, who exalted himself unjustly; and he sent the first human being into the prison of this world because of the folly of vain glory. For he established none of his works as empty. The first angel possessed great knowledge and wisdom, but because of his great wickedness he refused to render honour to his Lord, and fell, and thus remained. But man fell through tasting food. Therefore the Son of God offered himself as a sacrifice for that sin.

Hence, when a person remembers through the knowledge of good and evil that he has sinned greatly, and sighs toward God, he is born anew in God through repentance. But you, son, learn by day and by night, that you may live forever.

## LETTER CXXVII  
### From V., Parisian master of theology, to Hildegard  
### He asks Saint Hildegard whether it may be said that paternity and divinity are not God

[Col. 0351D]

To Lady H., eminent virgin of Christ: V., humble and unworthy Parisian master in title and office, offers prayer and whatever is judged fitting for a person of such holiness and nobility.

Because you, lady, have made yourself a handmaid of Christ, he has raised you above yourself; and it is believed that, while you are still placed in the flesh, he has revealed to you in part the secrets of the virginal bridal chamber, so that you may be believed one of those of whom it is sung: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 2).

But because the prophetic and faithful soul says and repeats: “My secret is mine, my secret is mine” (Isaiah 24), and because King Hezekiah, who opened the chambers of spices and the treasures of the Temple to Babylonian messengers, grievously offended God in this, blessed are those who so surpass us sinners that they investigate heavenly things, yet await, in their paths, the growth of a spirit of discernment from such matters—by God’s gift—more through testing than through revelation; and who also learn from people below what they should bring forth from their visions and what they should keep silent about [Col. 0352A].

Thus, when God orders their gift by humility, they seal up certain matters and do not publish things that might disturb apostolic and ecclesiastical teaching. Consider these things, prudent woman, for “the woman who fears God shall herself be praised.”

It is said that, raised into heavenly things, you see many matters and set forth many things in writing, and compose forms of new song, although you have learned none of them [Col. 0352B]. We are not at all amazed by these things, for they do not exceed your purity and holiness, without which such things are not received by a human being. We may know that whatever is revealed there concerning the saints signifies glory; whatever is absent is done here requires a pattern of humility.  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] Perhaps read *absconditur* (“is hidden”) for *abest agitur* (“is absent, is done”).]

Although we are far from you, we have confidence in you and ask certain things of you. Since very many contend that paternity and divinity are not God, do not delay in explaining and transmitting to us what you perceive concerning this in heavenly things.  
[Note: [Col. 0351D] The principal author of this teaching was Gilbert of Poitiers [Col. 0352D], bishop of Poitiers, who retracted it at the Council of Reims under Pope Eugenius III.]

May your love prosper.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY  
### She answers that it was shown to her in vision that paternity and divinity are God

[Col. 0352C]

I, a little form amid the smoke of spices from the high mountain, say:

“The sun descends with its light and illuminates the many indignations amid the changes of places. Thus, master, in your teaching you have many little streams in the Scriptures, which you sometimes scatter among others, both great and small. But I tremble greatly because of the lowly form that is in me.

“Now listen. A king sat upon his throne and set before himself great and exceedingly elegant columns in great adornment—ornaments of upright ivory, bearing all the king’s garments in great honour. Then it pleased the King to lift a small feather from the ground and command it to fly as that same King willed. The feather, however, does not fly by itself; the air bears it.

“Thus I have not been instructed by human learning, nor by powerful strength, nor do I flourish in bodily health; but I stand in the help of God. And I tell you, as I have been taught in true vision, what paternity and divinity are, since I have understood from you that this is most necessary for many people, so that they may be strengthened truthfully in the true faith.

“For I saw and learned in the true Light, watchfully and in open vision—not by seeking within myself—that paternity and divinity are God [Col. 0352D]. For a human being does not possess the capacity to speak of God as he speaks of a person’s humanity, or of the colour of an object made by human hands.

“Therefore the Living Light says in the secret word of wisdom: ‘God is full and whole, and without beginning of times; therefore he cannot be divided by speech as a human being can be divided. For God is the whole and not another; therefore nothing may be taken away from him or added to him. For paternity and divinity too are he who is, as it is said: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3), and so forth. He who is possesses fullness. In what respect? In doing, creating, and bringing to completion.

“‘Whoever says that paternity and divinity are not God names a point without a circle, denying him who is eternal. Whoever denies that paternity and divinity are God denies God, because he wants there to be some emptiness in God. But this is not so: God is full, and that which is in God is God. For God cannot be shaken out or sifted according to human fashion [Col. 0353B], because in God there is nothing that is not God.

“‘And because the creature has a beginning, human reason discovers God through names, just as the creature itself, in its own nature, is full of names.’”

Now listen again, O man, to the little form speaking to you in the Spirit: God wishes you to make straight paths, to be subject to him, and to be a living stone in the cornerstone, and not to be erased from the book of life.

## LETTER CXXVIII  
### From Brother O. to Hildegard  
### He laments the Church’s division through schism and asks her to offer prayers for it and for himself, since he was troubled by demons

[Col. 0353C]

To Hildegard, beloved mother: Brother O. offers the service of filial love.

O beloved mother, what shall infants do when they have no one to give them milk? “Little children ask for bread, and there is none to break it for them” (Lamentations 4). The sun, too, has set a cloud before itself so that prayer may not pass through. What then shall a weak person do, seeking a remedy of salvation and finding no help of consolation?

The Church has been wounded by schism through the word of division. “Behold here, behold there”: what is to come upon the head is already spreading through the body, and there is no health where this sword has passed. What then do you say, honoured mother? Do you think that the one whom it is altogether necessary to seek can be found? I think the physician is absent as long as I smell the rottenness of the wound [Col. 0353D].

Therefore approach the Inaccessible One; enter where access is not open to everyone; say to your Beloved: “Why do you sleep, Lord? Those seeking you stand outside.” Your soul is not wounded by charity if it has been struck by the sword of dissension. May the health of your prayer come to them, that they may be one.

And when you have poured out your prayer before the eyes of the Lord, return to us and report to us what you have learned within, insofar as he grants it, whose speech is with the simple. I, too, have a foul soul, divided and wounded along many paths. I most devoutly implore your charity to be willing to pray to God for it.

For I am very often attacked by evil spirits, both secretly and openly; they weary me greatly and seek to deceive me. I ask you to report to me in your writing what you perceive concerning them.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY  
### On various kinds of demons and how he may overcome them

I see your soul in two parts: in one it seeks to rise; in the other it seeks to remain. But God gathers your mind according to his will and not according to yours, and therefore you are greatly afflicted. For what you say, that you are wearied by evil spirits, I see in adversities of this kind.

For aerial spirits are divided into four parts. The first part prepares a burning in every kind of vice and renders a person uncertain through lust. The second part flits about in every instability; as the wind is scattered here and there [Col. 0354B], it throws a person into mad anger. The third produces error as though by the appearance of angels and prophecy; it remains in no one state in any way, and injures people through empty glory, boasting, and obstinacy.

But the fourth part associates with the other parts described above; it exists in manifold diversity, and is not greatly given to cursing but is greatly scourging in terror. It gladly dwells with people, flees the Lord’s Passion and Cross, and tolerates certain good qualities in people, yet takes away their moderation in these same goods. Thus, by its suggestion, it allows them to rise in their minds to a greater height than they can achieve, and so does not allow them to rest.

For it does not fear holiness and especially not vanity, but it has great hatred for strength and stability. And as pigs eat husks because of their fatness, so it often remains with people in pleasure; and when driven out by a human being, it howls with cries as though enduring punishments. For when a person takes hold of strength, stability, and moderation, it flees from him and cries and howls, saying: “Where shall I feed? Where shall I have food?”

Therefore everyone should dread and fear, because this part of the evil spirits does not fear to dwell both with evil and with good. For when a person bears hatred within holiness, he enters into great truth and will be like a mockery to God and human beings. But how can that part of the spirits be driven out and bound?

[Col. 0354D]

When, in the first age, as at the first hour, while he is a child, a person begins holiness, he should not speak about himself, but should listen to masters and teachers; thus he binds the devil as it cries out and howls.

But in the second age, as at the third hour, when a person is young, he should long preserve holiness in silence and keep silent; and in all diligence and perfection he should seek what is good, lest he fall into pride. Thus he kills the devil.

In the third age, as at the sixth hour, a person should not remain silent for long; rather, in humility he should ask a master what must be sought, because that age is not scattered into wantonness. Thus this kind of dead thing appears dead.

But in the fourth age, as at the ninth hour, when a person is inspired by God [Col. 0355A], he should seek counsel from masters and wise people, because then he is weak in the heat of the greenness of the flesh; and he should give thanks to God.

The first age flees patience, but it is wholly holy in holiness when joined with patience. The second age thinks that it has no need of the fear of the Lord, but it must possess the fear of the Lord within holiness. The third age willingly has the fear of the Lord; indeed, let it be joyful in holiness, because uncertainty easily enters there. The fourth age extends sighs toward God, and joys must be supplied to it in all things, lest it fail.

For the first angel fell and perished through wantonness in the first age, as in childhood. In the second age, as in youth, many believers and unbelievers wished to raise themselves to heaven and spoke very many things from themselves; therefore they fell. In the third age, as in manly strength, prophets came and said with great fear of the Lord: “We are not in these things, but you, O God”; thus they persevered and filled the whole earth with joy.

In the fourth age, as in full stability, more and more virtues will arise through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in people devoted to good works; and thus the world will fail. Yet this time has not yet reached the point of bringing forth the judgment of the universe. Nevertheless, all kinds of demons diligently produce errors in people because they fear being overcome.

But you, O man, who are in youthful age, stand firm in stability, and listen to the words of philosophers, wise men, and those speaking in the Holy Spirit [Col. 0355C], that you may live forever. Say also this: “May that Power which created me as a human being free me from aerial spirits; and may fiery Love, which appointed me to unfailing life, not allow my works to be mingled with them.”

## LETTER CXXIX  
### From N., dean of Saint Martin’s at Mainz, to Hildegard  
### He desires to see her and commends himself to her prayers

To Hildegard, most reverend lady and most beloved mother: N., unworthy dean of Saint Martin’s in the Church of Mainz, offers the little that he is.

It is not necessary for me to write how great is the reverence with which my mind lies prostrate before your holiness [Col. 0355D], how sincerely I love you, or how ready I am to serve you if you deign to use whatever service I can offer. I greatly desire to be comforted more often by your writings, because the splendour of divine wisdom that illumines you inwardly reveals these things to you.

I had indeed intended to see you now and be comforted by your words; but I am hindered by bodily weakness and cannot come at present. When an opportunity is given, God willing, I shall see you; and what I cannot ask from you in writing, I shall seek by living voice.

Meanwhile, most beloved mother, I ask you to pray to our Creator and Redeemer for me, that he may so order our life according to all his will that he himself may be pleased in us. I also ask that, if you need anything from my service [Col. 0356A], you command whatever seems good to you. Yet I desire again to be comforted by your writings through the present messenger.

May God deign to preserve you and always illumine you with his Holy Spirit, most blessed mother, worthy of every office of reverence from me.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY  
### An exhortation to repentance

From excessive food and immoderate drinking of wine immoderate vices grow; and the human flesh often languishes so that it can scarcely live. Then, through the weariness of sins by which that flesh has been exhausted, it is weighed down as though by heavy sleep. But the devil rouses it again to sin and sets before it times for repentance; thus that person awakens from such torpor to sin, and in this manner the devil diligently exhorts him to sin.

Many people also, through the devil’s deception, defer repentance for their sins and are thus found in perdition. But when a person sighs over his sins, he sings in harmony with the praise of angels; and when he does good works, he flashes like the sun. Yet when he begins these adornments, the devil falls upon him with a great storm of despair—the same devil who had previously stirred him by evil counsels to sin.

But let that person consider the tax collectors and sinners: how much they sinned, how they rose through repentance, and how afterwards they became pillars of heaven. Let him see this, put on the breastplate of faith and the helmet of hope, and thus overcome his enemies.

But you, servant of God [Col. 0356C], see that in your childhood you lived luxuriously, and in your youth you lived with the sins and pleasures of the flesh. Therefore, let weariness for sins now be yours, and begin to do good works before the shadow of this life declines from you, so that you may answer with joy the voice speaking thus to you:

“You ought to have been a garden in which I might feed my eyes; but you are not, because useless grasses, thorns, and briars have grown there, and all of them have choked the useful herbs.”

Cut these away with the sharp sickle of repentance, and imitate that son mentioned in the Gospel, who returned to himself and ran to his father, who received him joyfully and kissed him in his humanity. Sow also the seed of fruitful virtue in your garden, and make yourself like the woman seeking the lost drachma [Col. 0356D], so that joy may arise in heaven over you, and that you may become a jewel in heavenly life and live forever.

## LETTER CXXX  
### From N. to Hildegard  
### He commends to her faith his soul, body, and whole congregation

To the venerable and most beloved mistress H., most fitting vessel of divine election: N., by the grace of God, offers what he is and whatever his sole service is worth, together with continual prayer.

I wish you well in spirit and mind, and for the state of all your affairs I fall day and night at the feet of God in devout prayers. Dearest one, if God’s ordering has separated us in this life, nevertheless the indissoluble bond of blessing has joined us together indissolubly [Col. 0357A].

I ask in return for that love that you remember me in your prayers and commend me to your holy community. Why say more? I commend to your faith my soul and body and our whole congregation. May your blessedness prosper forever.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY  
### That he may understand what is beneficial and what harmful

Your mind is like a valley when a mountain rises within you; and again you think that you are building a city when, with obstinacy, you condemn some matter. For the person who strikes a wound festering in corruption with blows draws out poison mingled with blood. But this does no good. Such is the mind of the person who wishes to spare in nothing.

But a good physician anoints wounds. Human negligence is like a whirlwind, and its fury like a great tempest. Therefore understand now what is beneficial and what harmful, because certain earthly creatures resemble human works.

Birds pertain to human goodwill; cattle to human understanding; wild beasts to human wisdom. Worms that the sweat of the earth casts forth correspond to people’s many thoughts; misshapen worms to their malice; poisonous ones to anger; and savage beasts to the negligence of their works [Col. 0357B].

Therefore look to the North and see how a tempest rises like smoke into the clouds. Thus human works are sometimes useless. But the person who keeps good watch by looking around in every direction draws away thunderbolts through goodwill and gentle knowledge. Such a person should not be a warrior in the throwing of a stone, nor negligent amid the wind of the whirlwind.

The sun shines; therefore let a person anoint every matter with mercy. For a builder who does not lay his foundations rightly casts down his tools. Let a person therefore foresee what downfall may come.

One who sighs is to be endured. But one who despises God is to be corrected, if correction is effective; if it is not effective, a suitable time for this should be sought, lest he die. Let a person work through himself and illumine his own soul.

But a mind that does not devise murder is not a murderer. Yet if that cause comes about in deed [Col. 0357D], let the person always grieve and pant toward God, because what God built has been destroyed.

## LETTER CXXXI  
### From H., monk of Maulbronn, to Hildegard  
### That she send him something of heavenly admonition

To Hildegard, beautiful olive tree and precious pearl: H., a monk of Maulbronn in name alone—may he go forth with a burning lamp to meet the heavenly Bridegroom.

“O how beautiful is the chaste generation with brightness; for its memory is immortal, because it is known both before God and among human beings” (Wisdom 4). It is clear from the shining marks of virtues that you, daughter of the highest King, have sprung from this beautiful and blessed generation, since in the outward appearance of your splendid work you bear the form of the inward person [Col. 0358A].

By such an adornment of virtue the likeness of your mother is portrayed: following her example, you sought wool and flax and wove a striped garment as the covering of your soul. For the striped garment is put on when every faithful soul is clothed with the virtue of charity woven with many figures.

In this royal garment shine humility and obedience, compassion and self-restraint, bodily chastity and holiness of mind—indeed, thousands upon thousands of similar things. Clothed about with this variety of virtues, you stand at the right hand of the highest King, like that prophetic queen, where you found the inestimable treasury of wisdom. Hence you have shown mortals the brightness of eternal light as though from an abyss.

Hear then, daughter, see, and incline your ear, so that, since charity consists in love of neighbour [Col. 0358B], through the help of your prayer I may experience pardon for whatever I find in myself less than perfect. For I know without doubt that you are heard more especially by him in whose contemplation you frequently have occasion to remain.

I ask also, with your favour, sister and lady, that you send me something of heavenly admonition, so that through it you may set the memory of your holiness before the eyes of my heart. Why say more? Though absent in body, I greet you as present in spirit, earnestly praying that you remember me, a sinner—you who always stretch the step of your mind forward with the Apostle. Farewell.

## HILDEGARD’S REPLY  
### Under a parable she teaches that one must labour in this world

The Shadow of God’s Mysteries says:

“The wind blows and the air moves in change; the clouds gather together, so that at times they are turbid, black, white, and pure. Thus you act, soldier of God. For at times you are in worldly sadness, as when the wind blows; in the pleasure of the devil’s many snares, as in the changing air; and in your restless dispositions, like gathering clouds. Thus your dispositions are sometimes foul in turbidity, terrified in blackness, gentle in whiteness, and useful in purity.

“Therefore listen. A certain lord stood upon a great mountain and called his servants, saying: ‘Pay what you owe.’ One of these servants stood before him, but another sat. The one who stood answered: ‘Lord, I have come from the far region of exile, where amid many crimes and sins I learned diverse changes of disposition. O woe, that I have so transgressed your commands! Therefore, through fear born of love for you, I swear that I desire to repent with my whole heart. Yet I have always loved your sun, moon, and stars in great honour.’

“His Lord answered him: ‘Good servant, as the wheel goes around me, I receive your answer thus, saying: I who live without beginning and without end wish to place you in great honours above all that you have loved, nor will my power condemn you, because through repentance you called upon me.’

“But the servant who sat answered disdainfully: ‘Your sun burned me, your moon touched me, your stars crushed me; even the hairs of my head were tainted by your dew, and your rains flooded over me. Therefore, hindered by all these things, I could not look upon you [Col. 0359A]; hence I do not even know what I can say.’

“And his lord answered him: ‘Most wicked servant, when I established the sun, moon, and stars, did I need your assistance? And why are you not ashamed that you touch me so rashly in your answers? Therefore you have deserved to be bound hand and foot and cast into darkness until you pay everything.’”

But you, soldier of Christ, attend to the parable as applying to yourself. This lord is God, who keeps watch on high, because God must be invoked by all. He addresses men in his admonition thus: “You must be judged by your works.” But some labour in divine honour, while others grow numb in the weariness of tedium. Those who honour God say: “By the devil’s suggestion, in Adam’s fall, we fell into exile [Col. 0359B], and in our works we contracted many vices; this transgression we shall mourn with sorrowful lamentation. Yet for the glory of your name we promise that we desire to abstain from our sins. Nevertheless, we have venerated in love your honour, your justice, and the Scriptures given through you.” And the Lord, who is incomprehensible, praises them and sets them over many good things, nor does he condemn them, because in repentance they called upon him.

But those who grow numb in weariness of divine things say: “Your honour has afflicted us; your justice has wounded us; the multitude of your Scriptures has choked us; the freshness of your Spirit has overthrown the pleasure of our mind; and the outpouring of your zeal has wearied us, so that we cannot look upon you in joy, nor are we able to excuse ourselves.” And the Lord calls them [Col. 0359C] most wicked servants, saying that he had no need of their help in his acts of justice, and asking why they are not ashamed to attack him in the rashness of their words. Therefore they are to be bound and sent into punishments, while they reckon all their vices within themselves.

But you, O soldier of Christ, understand these things also as applying to yourself. For the servant who stood signifies you. When you were in the world, you did few good things; but the admonition of the Holy Spirit shook you and turned you toward good. Take care, then, not to imitate the servant who sat: that is, do not say that you burn in the Rule as in the sun; do not despise teaching as though it were the moon; do not grow weary of the fellowship of your brethren as though it were the stars; do not bring the admonition of the Holy Spirit into the mockery of your mind as though it were dew [Col. 0359D]; and do not disdain correction as though it were rain. Rather, always embrace God in good will and right judgment; embrace him and hold fast to him, and you shall live.

## LETTER CXXXII

**N., a monk of Ebra of the Cistercian Order, to Hildegard. He commends himself to her prayers and asks her for words of consolation.**

To his lady and mother HILDEGARD, the most blessed olive-tree of Christ: N., sinner of Ebra, an unprofitable monk of the Cistercian Order—may he live in the Lord and die in the Lord.

May your belovedness know that I have sent you this very short letter because I could not devise anything sufficiently worthy of your holiness [Col. 0360A], and because, with a trembling mind, I scarcely presumed to write anything to so great and such a person; indeed, I did not judge myself worthy of this. Therefore, if, with your favour preserved, I dare, I tremblingly commit myself, though filthy, with bent knee, to your prayers in the bowels of Jesus Christ. And, so far as I can, with grace cooperating and according to the measure of my sloth, I shall most willingly remember you and your household in Christ. Though absent in body, I am with you in heart and affection, God being witness.

Therefore keep me now in your remembrance; commend me continually, as I trust you will, to Christ and to St Mary; and endeavour to console me with your words of consolation according to the divine revelation. May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with you.

**Hildegard’s reply. She promises him future consolations, since he is pleasing to God.**

[Col. 0360B]

I see that God does not hide his face from you, but binds you with his scourges, as pleases him. Likewise, I see that a great light of God’s consolation will come into your soul and into the joy of your body, when he wills it. God lives in your tabernacle, nor is his grace darkened in it; hence you will be praiseworthy before God in your soul, although you doubt this, because a victorious man is beloved by his Lord.

But the mystical light says: “The earth that has the richness to bring forth shoots produces many fruits. Yet tares and other useless plants very often thrust themselves among them. But at times a certain moderating force of a wind rises over this earth, whose power is such that it causes the useless plants to weaken, while not injuring the useful fruits.

“Now hear: certain people, who are capable of many things through the richness of their nature, mix useless works into this fullness of knowledge through the pleasure of the flesh. But the admonition of God’s grace sometimes warns them—through contrition of mind, through the sorrow of weakness, through bodily illness, and through similar things—to avoid evil and perform good works. Understand this as applying to yourself.” Therefore may God pour upon you dew from heaven, and you shall live for ever.

## LETTER CXXXIII

**V. of Wession to Hildegard. Oppressed by sins, he asks whether he ought still to hope for pardon from God.**

[Col. 0360D]

To HILDEGARD, holy and friend of God, bride of Christ: V. of Wession, a broken reed, a form of evil, food for the devil.

It is written: “Having no covering, they embrace the rocks” (Job 24). But, alas, in this age the stones that obstruct the way of iniquity have been removed from the road. The mountains that should fall upon sinners have given way; the hills that should cover Christ’s fugitives have withdrawn. Men’s shameful deeds, travelling unhindered in their course, stand naked before God, and, with nothing intervening, rush headlong against the stone of stumbling and the rock of offence.

Among and within these things, my lady, I—despairing, daily dashing myself against this rock—am crushed [Col. 0361A] and broken, yet still presume to hope in God’s mercy. Therefore, by that mercy of God, I adjure you: do not cast me away as I lean upon you, nor despise me through him who for our sake deigned to be despised. I beseech you by the price of the blood of Jesus Christ, your beloved Bridegroom, flowing from the cross, by whom he betrothed you to himself and took you as his bride: incline your merciful ears to what this present letter says of me. Plead with your Bridegroom and diligently inquire why he disdains to rescue me, though I so often cry to him from the depths of wickedness and the mire of filth; inquire, my lady, whether I may yet hope for pardon, whether he will grant me a troubled and contrite spirit; and commit to writing what ought to be communicated. Farewell again and again. Repeating these same requests, I adjure you through Christ [Col. 0361B] not to abandon me.

**Hildegard’s reply. He is to restore his mind to good things and hunger for justice.**

In the true vision of God’s mysteries I write by seeing, hearing, and knowing in one manner. But you, O man, are like a cloud which advances and retreats, and which is somewhat bright on either side, yet through which the sun is often obscured, so that one waits long for it to shine. And it is written: “Behold, those who remove themselves far from you shall perish” (Psalm 72).

That is: those who possess the day of good knowledge, but look toward an alien stirring-up of uselessness and toward varieties of darkness, which seek no help in reason but are vain, wither away and possess no greenness in God. For when Adam shone full of innocent holiness [Col. 0361C], he was caught in transgression, so that he perished in violating God’s commandments, when the diadem of innocence—that is, the most beautiful daughter of the king—was cut away from him.

Now restore your mind to good things, and look into the fountain of springing water. Do not seek diverse causes in an alien house, for every cause that is not useful will wither, because it was not planted by God. Let your mind be pure in God, in hunger for God’s justice, and on the straight path, and God will receive you. Therefore let the labours which you have undertaken and perform for God suffice you. But direct your mind and thoughts toward God as far as you can. I too shall always pour out my prayers to God for you.

## LETTER CXXXIV

[Col. 0361D]

**H., a canon of Trajectum, to Hildegard. That she may reveal to him the secrets of divine revelation concerning his condition.**

To H., who imitates Christ’s poverty in a frail sex: H., canon of Trajectum, desiring the riches of the rich Christ—greetings in the Lord who commands salvation for Jacob.

I desire to experience in myself the Spirit of God speaking in you and writing through you in a wonderful and inestimable manner. Far be it from me to entertain any doubt concerning you, that the Spirit of God speaks in you. Rather, admiration with those who admire, and devotion with the devout, urges and provokes me to desire a more familiar experience.

Therefore, in humility I beseech your humility [Col. 0362A] that, through the ministry of your disclosure, you may set forth for my instruction and the safeguarding of my spirit the secrets of divine revelation concerning my condition, especially according to the inner man. Indeed, you owe this by your promise, because I obtained it from your charity when I was travelling to Rome. May the Spirit of the Lord remain with you. Amen.

**Hildegard’s reply. He is to rise quickly and flee from the devil.**

God was offended at the tree because of the serpent’s malicious words. Then too, in the beautiful formation in which God had created man, good knowledge in man blushed because of the evil desire that [Col. 0362B] he had desired. Therefore God called to him as though he were on an alien road: “Adam, where are you?” (Genesis 3). And he gave him clothing, saying thus within himself: “Through the tunic of my humanity I desire to seek you.” Afterwards, in his holy humanity, he recreated man anew, so that, when he has fallen, he may rise through repentance in God’s humanity.

Therefore you, O man, rise more quickly; wrap yourself more quickly in God’s tunic; flee from the devil. And I, in the outpouring of my prayer, when my soul looks to God, shall gladly pray for you, and you shall live.

## LETTER CXXXV

**M., monk and priest, to Hildegard. He asks for her prayers and those of her sisters, promising his in return.**

[Col. 0362C]

To HILDEGARD, most beloved and singularly honourable mother and lady in Christ: M., an unworthy monk and priest, the little that he is.

If one must glory—indeed, since it is permitted to glory in the Lord—it is fitting that I too rejoice, not in myself but in the Lord, who has granted to my unworthiness such grace of familiarity with your holiness as my humility could neither deserve nor presume to hope for. Therefore, first giving thanks from my inmost heart to divine mercy and then to your graciousness, because you have treated me kindly when present and have judged me worthy of your greeting even when absent, I make known to your goodwill that you should deign to greet in my name all your fellow-sisters and my ladies [Col. 0362D], and remind them that the aid of fraternity and prayers which they promised me may never fade from their memory. For I too, in every way and insofar as the Lord grants, have done and do what I promised them, God being witness.

I also trust in the Lord that, if life remains with me, I shall not cease to pray for all of you: that God’s grace, which has so far preceded you, may continually follow you, and may crush Satan beneath your feet, so that my smallness too may obtain, through your prayers, the salvation I do not deserve. As for the other matters which I discussed with you more privately, when it is opportune, take care to inform me by writing. Farewell always in the Lord.

**Hildegard’s reply. Under a parable she exhorts him to charity, flight from the world, and love of true wisdom.**

[Col. 0363A]

Dear son, hear this parable, which I saw in a true vision.

A certain noble and beautiful lady possessed a chamber adorned with gold, and she frequently chose to have two maidens of elegant countenance dwell with her. Many crowds, seeing this lady, praised her face and wished to dwell with her. But she said to them: “I shall give you gifts that please you, because it would benefit neither me nor you for us to be together. For I do not wish to give my nobility and beauty over to foxes and dogs and to mockery.”

But [Col. 0363B] a certain wrinkled woman, with a red and black face, wished to liken herself to this noble lady and unworthily assumed her nobility and beauty. This same wrinkled woman walks upon mountains and runs through regions and every place, seeking praise and honour, but no one gives it to her. Rather, all say: “This woman is restless and undisciplined, belongs to the devil, and must be driven away by all.”

There was also a certain merchant woman who gathered to herself, from every art, everything beautiful for the eye to see, and strove to make these things unknown and marvellous to people in sight and hearing. Afterwards she set a beautiful and exceedingly pure crystal in the fire of the sun; it was so kindled by the sun that it gave light to all. Thus she kept all her arts in moderation.

Now, my son, consider the first woman and her maidens; flee the wrinkled woman with every effort; but take the merchant woman to yourself. For the first woman is charity with her maidens, namely benevolence and generosity. The wrinkled woman, with red and black face, is worldly love, through which lustful people entwine themselves with one another in shameful desire. The merchant woman is philosophy, which establishes every art and discovers the crystal—that is, faith—through which one comes to God. But I trust in God that you may have a share with these, because in the fiery crystal you have offered God the gifts of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection.

## LETTER CXXXVI

[Col. 0363D]

**N., priest and master of the poor at Lutherum, to Hildegard. He desires to hear saving instruction from her and is prepared to obey it.**

To Lady H., radiant with the splendour of divine light: N., an unworthy priest and master of the poor at Lutherum, that is, in the hospital house—may he, when the glory of the Lord appears, be joined with the elect.

Recalling often the grace and goodwill which many have experienced in you, we give thanks to almighty God, who deigned to bestow in so frail a sex—in a woman deprived of bodily strength from childhood—a manly spirit adorned with many virtues [Col. 0364A]. May the Lord increase his grace in you and in all who are with you, and grant that in a spirit of goodwill you may remember before the Lord both us and the many who have placed their hope in you.

We therefore desire to hear the saving teachings of your holiness and to have the state of our life carefully understood by you. Whatever God reveals to you concerning this, deign to write back to us, knowing that we have resolved, according to our ability, to obey your counsels and admonitions. For we have been charged to serve the poor, a duty which we cannot fulfil without the burden of a troubled mind. Therefore we desire to learn from you whether it is more useful for us to shut ourselves within a cloister or to continue amid this turmoil. May God reveal to you what [Col. 0364B] better pleases him in this matter.

**Hildegard’s reply. He is to imitate Christ’s example, who, as the true Samaritan, healed the man who fell among thieves both by himself and through the innkeepers—that is, the apostles.**

In a true vision, with wakeful eyes in my spirit, I heard these words: “O son, who are the image of God, hear this exposition. For the Son of God said to those who had said this to themselves, what they had chosen for themselves: ‘A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho’ (Luke 10).

“The Son of God said this concerning the first man. When, through the serpent’s report, which he heard through the woman, he perceived that he could sin, he chose for himself, by his own choice, that which he had heard through the report. For the mind is as a man, and choice as a woman. When a person chooses some matter for himself and draws it to himself through choice, he loves it greatly—just as Adam loved the choice which he heard through the woman, because the woman was joined to him as choice is joined to the mind.

“When Adam did this, he descended from the vision of peace and became like the moon that wanes. Yet, although he was an exile, he still knew his Creator, and in that knowledge he was like the moon that sometimes waxes. ‘And he fell among thieves’ (ibid.): this was his own self-will, which deceived him, as a thief deceives men with the hissing of deceit until he captures them. ‘They also stripped him’ (ibid.) [Col. 0364D]: that same self-will stripped him of all the glory that he had in paradise, just as thieves strip people of their property and divide it among themselves.

“Therefore every person who would be blessed should flee that which his own will chooses for him; it is as harmful to him as Adam’s listening to his woman was to Adam, and it inflicts the greatest wounds upon him. If he wishes to be healed, he must seek a physician with great sighing, because Adam’s transgression also sent him into the exile of this pilgrimage, so that he scarcely lived with knowledge of good and evil.

“Neither Abel’s sacrifice, which Noah fulfilled by building an altar, nor Abraham’s ministry of obedience, which Moses completed through the Law, could raise him; but the Samaritan raised him. This Samaritan is the Son of God, wholly incarnate in the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit—that is, in the integrity [Col. 0365A] of the Virgin—without any of Adam’s blindness which human nature has in sins. This Son of God raised Adam with his members from the pit of hell.

“He also poured oil and wine into his wounds: oil, when in his Incarnation, moved by mercy toward him, he revealed himself to him; wine, when he enjoined repentance for sins upon him, as it is written: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’ (Matthew 3).

“‘And setting him upon his own beast, he led him to an inn’ (Luke 10). His body is like a beast, because on his shoulders he bore man onto the wood of the cross. This also shows that, when he made man, he created beasts with him. Thus, when he formed man, he foresaw his Incarnation; and when he joined that same Incarnation to himself as he willed, man, beholding God himself both as God and man together with all creation, knew him. He gave the whole world to man as a tent, like an inn; and he led him into that inn when, through his Passion, he freed him and healed him through mercy and repentance.

“‘And the next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper’ (ibid.). On the next day after his Resurrection, he left man to his representatives—that is, the apostles—and the rest who followed their example [Col. 0365B], commanding them also to do as he had done. For just as God, when he made man, created beasts with him, so under the Old Law people first sacrificed to God through creatures, namely birds and cattle; but afterwards, through the victim of Christ’s Incarnation, they themselves sacrificed invisibly in the Holy Spirit.

“For we know his Incarnation through ourselves, but cannot behold his divinity; rather, we embrace it by faith. So too we know this world, but behold eternal life in faith. We see our bodies, but do not behold our souls in any way, except that we know only that we do not live without a soul. So also all works are of two kinds, some obscure and some manifest; and in this way likewise we shall have the Creator of all things in his humanity and divinity.

“In this manner God left man to his representatives in the two Testaments, so that they should treat him as he had shown them: anointing his wounds with mercy and cleansing him through repentance, and this until the last day. Then, when he returns, he will give the dwelling-place of eternal inheritance to all who have done in good will what he showed them.

“Now you, O steward of God, do thus. Take care that your mind may not be dark, without sun, moon, and stars: that is, do not, according to your own self-will, choose this and that as seems good to you, pronouncing this and that good, for your mind is now a dark cloud. But look to that true Samaritan, and as he did, so do you in the ministry to which you have been appointed by your Master. For it pleases God that mercy should be bestowed upon the needy and that sinners [Col. 0366A] should be led to repentance. Do this too, as far as you can, aiding the one who gives that same alms for his sins, so that you may live for ever.”

## LETTER CXXXVII

**The monks of Sigeberg to Hildegard. They complain that she does not write to them, and ask her to disclose something concerning the condition of the monastery of Sigeberg and send admonitory words.**

To Lady HILDEGARD, most beloved lady and mother: the brethren, united in heart, of St Michael at Sigeberch—whatever servants owe their lady, or sons their mother.

He who knows all secrets knows with what special affection of charity we have chosen you as our spiritual mother and admitted you into the fellowship of our prayers [Col. 0366B]. Your own belovedness could also have observed it from the frequent messages which we send you. Yet you, by contrast, have never shown us a mother’s affection; you have never offered us letters of admonition, which, as a mother to her children, you ought to have directed even to the unwilling, much less to those who desire them.

Nevertheless, as we have begun, we do not cease to knock at the door of your heart, so that, if you do not rise because you are our mother, you may nevertheless rise because of our importunity and give us what is necessary. We ask that, instructed in a true vision, you may disclose to us something concerning the condition of our place, and send us words containing admonition and correction. These, most beloved mother, are the matters whose investigation we chiefly desire from you, humbly requesting [Col. 0366C] that you write down both these and the other things which you know to be more necessary for us. And, as we have received you, so may you receive us into the fellowship of your prayer. Farewell.

**Hildegard’s reply. Some of them shine like stars; others grow weary in the darkness of exhaustion; and concerning the fall of the first angel through pride.**

In the vision of the Spirit, in which I often see, I saw and understood these things. I see this congregation as a cloud that appears, like that light when day departs and night approaches. Among you I see some shining like stars in good intention, but others growing weary in the darkness of exhaustion. Therefore rise, and take hold of discipline, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way.

I also saw something like a crown having two circles, one lower and the other upper, filled everywhere with angels. In the middle of this crown the archangel Michael stood like a tower, so that the two circles clung to him like two walls. Upon his breast shone the form of the Son of Man, around which was written: “The Lord shall send forth the rod of your strength from Zion: rule in the midst of your enemies” (Psalm 109). Stretching out his right arm, he held a shield in his right hand; and beside him there appeared something like a cloud, like golden smoke ascending from a censer, in which the merits of prayers and the holy works of this people shone brightly [Col. 0367A].

And I heard him saying to this people: “So long as I see in you the brightness of holiness, I desire to fight for you against the black darts which I see blazing from impious tyrants toward the dwellings of your place.” Then I understood that this rod of strength was Aaron’s rod, which flowered in branches of virtues. God had placed an angel on the first day, who through pride cast himself down from blessedness. But God looked upon the rod of inheritance on Mount Zion, which flowered as the power of greatness in man, where almighty God arose in virginity.

This flower went forth from Zion, and from it flow many waters giving forth a most sweet breeze. These are the verdant works of holiness in the minds of people, so that they know God in all things. Therefore God’s countenance shines in those who cut away from themselves the devil’s suggestion, fighting against him as it were in the midst of his power, when they have two wings: when they love God more than themselves and perform most holy works. Then they stand like a pillar of cloud in the midst of their enemies, striking them on both sides—loving God and performing most holy works—which gleams like the sun in the splendours of the saints.

But the first angel preferred to surpass God and stand in his honours rather than to love him or perform good works. Therefore man honours the divinity when he conquers himself where he could, by his own power, do evil. When virginity remains in him beneath the banner of the King, and when others, having tasted sin, return from the mill of iniquity and leave the world, all this belongs to the splendours of the saints, whom the Word of God thus brought forth in the Father’s will. Therefore it is manifestly said to this company in the Holy Spirit: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you in the splendours of the saints; may all who bless you be filled with blessings, and from those who curse you may blessing flee.”

## LETTER CXXXVIII

**The monks of Hirsau to Hildegard. They complain of their abbot, who, though not injured, did not cease to burden them with reproaches and calumnies, on the occasion of a discord that had arisen between him and the prior.**

[Col. 0367D]

To Lady HILDEGARD, divinely chosen for the edification of the Church: the poor and little flock of monks at Hirsau—may they be so adorned by divine mercy that they know how to console Christ’s humble in tribulation.

Blessed be the glory of the Lord, which from its high throne has looked down in a wonderful and unprecedented order, since it has willed so great a light of its grace to shine upon the world through you. Hence all the children of the Church rejoice; but especially we, who are filled with the light of a new spiritual exultation, since we hope, in the sorrow that we endure because of the failing of our Order, to be gladdened through you by divine consolation.

Therefore, briefly consider the things that produce our greatest anxiety and most deeply gnaw at our minds. God is witness that we disparage our lord abbot in nothing. Yet we grieve that he has, in many ways, forgotten paternal gentleness toward us; that he indulges certain of his familiars too freely; and that he exercises unrestricted authority too immoderately in all matters [Col. 0368A]. Indeed, we perceive that our reputation is torn apart over these matters by the gravest calumnies and slanders; and, especially because of the lamentable discord that arose long ago among us and has lately been stirred up between our abbot himself and the prior, we mourn that secular people hold our religious life in the greatest contempt.

Uncertain, therefore, what we should do, we most humbly implore that through your prayers the divine will may in some degree shine forth to us concerning these things. If we should be granted to learn from you, by consoling letters, what is especially necessary and what in these matters is pleasing to God [Col. 0368B], we shall always strive to repay this benefit, to the extent that alone we can and know to be most pleasing to your charity, by the return of our prayers.

**Hildegard’s reply. God does not forget them, provided only that they trample down vices and do penance.**

The serene light says: “O mourning sheepfold, adorned with the sign of the bond of obedience, be steadfast in your thoughts, and let your desires pant for the love of God. Consider, then, where prosperity or adversity lies. Hear the measure of the valleys. Valleys sometimes grow green and flower from the dew of heaven and the heat of the sun [Col. 0368C], and sometimes they wither and fail amid changing storms. Yet I do not utterly forget these valleys, which sometimes lose their beauty because of the changing weather, as though they would never again rise in their beauty.

“So too I shall not forget this place in which you stand, because wisdom shall not lack there the material of holiness, since it first advanced in uprightness. But be a shining sheepfold in victory, trampling down the vices that shake you in a restless time. Do not be ashamed to accuse yourself because of your evil works, for God anoints and wipes away every wound in repentance.

“Yet the living eye has marked a past cause in that grief by which you are disturbed at the obstinacy of your superior prelates: the sweetness of the anointing mother, namely mercy, was withheld from some of your sheep lying in guilt, who were not rightly judged in the penalty they received in their penance. For unsuitable rain makes the earth dry. So too, if a person has sinned and has no one to anoint him, he immediately flees into despair and withers, because no medicine is offered him according to what he can bear.

“Now, dear sons, hear the voice of the living light. Take hold of the mercy which did not arise from you but comes from God, and therefore do not withhold it from those upon whom it should be bestowed. Draw them back, then, to the health of their souls.”

## LETTER CXXXIX

[Col. 0369A]

**The monks of Eberbach to Hildegard. That she may not conceal what ought to be corrected in them.**

To Lady HILDEGARD, whom God chose for himself as a handmaid and made privy to many of his secrets: the poor flock of brethren at Eberbach—may they happily enter the wedding feast with the Bridegroom of faithful souls and heavenly citizens, among the number of prudent virgins, with true lantern and burning lamp.

The Spirit of the Lord never deserted those whom he chose and predestined for himself, but nourished their purpose in fatherly gentleness. Thus he chose you, blessed and happy soul, as the instrument and vessel of his election. Beloved lady, we ought to obey your maternal admonition [Col. 0369B], for the Lord’s truth speaks through you. We gladly receive your admonitions and humbly pray you not to conceal from us what must be corrected in us. Rather, as may please the Lord who opens many secrets to you, endeavour to make it known to us. May the Angel of Counsel and Strength, who is always around you, keep and guard you sound and unharmed. Amen.

**Hildegard’s reply. They are to beware lest they cast away the blessedness which seems to be in them by God’s predestination.**

The mysteries of God command me to say these things in the shadow of vision: “You have climbed a very high mountain and wished to look into the valley. Meanwhile a great storm came upon you—ah, ah!—the languor that is in your loins, as the tried servant, David, says: ‘All day long I went mourning, because my loins were filled with illusions, and there is no health in my flesh’ (Psalm 37). Therefore your eyes grow faint through want.

“Take care, then, not to cast away backward the blessedness that seems to be in you through God’s predestination, by the excess of rash conflicts. For when God had made the face of the first angel like a most elegant and flashing lamp, he entered into rashness; therefore his glory perished within him. Since he desired no good things, he planted its brightness in another vineyard.

“And because God has no fellowship with evil, beware lest God’s special grace depart from you through the work of the ancient serpent. For he rejoices in himself and says: ‘I find my will with discord among the spiritual people, and I walk among them with lifted neck.’ Therefore resist the devil, lest the light of brightness fail you, as it was taken away from him because of his pride.

“Those who sometimes fall and rise again will not lack the inheritance of God’s grace, though they are bowed down in the whirlwind of God’s vengeance. Yet afterwards God rebuilds in them the root of the first beginning of the sacrifice of God’s power. And I say to you, who are God’s planting: concerning your place, the mysteries of God say this: ‘I shall never destroy you, so long as you do not resist me in impious rashness which does not desire to be washed,’ as the rashness of devilish art likewise shows, as stated above. In Abraham’s blessing, the living light blesses you.”

## LETTER CXL

**N., prior of Zwiefalten, to Hildegard. How they may restore the discipline that has collapsed in their monastery.**

To his most beloved lady of St Rupert, HILDEGARD, most worthy of reverence through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit: N., prior of Zwiefalten, with his other brethren, whose names God knows—the offering of due prayer.

If you are well and flourish according to your desires in prosperous circumstances, we earnestly hope for this in every way. But because the abyss of despair has enclosed us in restoring the religious observance of our monastery [Col. 0370B], and the sea of its irrationality has covered our heads, we cast ourselves humbly and suppliantly before your face and ask, with all devotion, the aid of your counsel.

For we hope that through your prayers you can obtain from the Lord that you should disclose to us, by a revelation of the Holy Spirit, something useful to us in these matters, since we are often troubled by the importunity of certain of our brethren. We ask your holiness all these things: do not disdain to write back to us in return. Farewell, and pray earnestly to the Lord for us sinners.

**Hildegard’s reply. She rebukes their negligence and exhorts them to come to their senses.**

[Col. 0370C]

Serene brightness says: The most mighty light of divinity knows and understands all things perfectly. Who touches this understanding, or who comprehends it, save the one who sees in the sapphire eye that God the Father, above all things, is so immovable in his justice that he leaves no iniquity cast down unpunished, because that iniquity itself touches him?
