And God the Father so delighted in himself that through his Word he created every creature; hence his creature pleased him, and he embraced that creature which touches him by loving him. O great delight of this work! God the Father is immovable in his uprightness, yet, admonished by his Son, he spares the wicked so that they may bring forth fruit. [Col. 0370D] For he beholds his Word made flesh, and remembers that through his Word all creatures were made.

In this manner also God’s saints touch him in admonition through their clear voice, like a white cloud flying like the fleeting watery air. Hear therefore, you who break forth in your crimes. You are called the mountain of the Lord because you ought to imitate the Son of God by your manner of life. Why, then, do you neglect the maternal bowels of charity and uprightness, becoming like those who chastised their bodies at Horeb under the Law, yet again wandered on another path? So too do those watchmen who sound aloud while on guard, yet undermine the city by ambushes. Your mind is like a cloud bearing storms: now possessing anger through negligence, [Col. 0371A] now the filth of beasts through wantonness; there you neglect the peace-offering, saying: “We do not wish to resist ourselves, because we cannot gird our body in restraint, since we were born from Adam.”

For in the king’s palace you do not wish to restrain your liver—that is, your appetites—as you ought. Why then are you not ashamed that, though snatched as it were from a stable of asses and placed by the heavenly Lord in the great honor of consecrated observance, you run back to the true stable of asses? Alas! In this you have become like Balaam, who raved amid the wounds of burning scars, raging in the region of the shadow of death. Therefore do not abandon the mountain of sanctification in the emptiness of pleasure. Alas for shamefulness, which has been cast backward [Col. 0371B] into a strange place! For those who transgress holy observance perish.

Take hold of discipline, and do not go astray from the way of justice, as though you had no law, and as though the sun did not shine upon the censer of blessing; lest at some time the Lord grow angry and you perish from the right way while you lie in transgression. O fearful and venerable sacrifices, which do not possess the unbelief of idols, nor the burden of wounds inflicted by those who strike! Alas for the sorrow of misery: God will destroy within you the murmuring of the Ninevites unless you swiftly run to the olive tree of sanctification. Why are you bent over in these lies, as though you were not blind? Yet you are blind when you do not foresee that condition into which you were born through Adam’s fall, and when you hold it [Col. 0371C] in the arm of embrace, laughing and cackling as though you did not possess it. Flee, therefore, and do not sin, so that your salvation may come swiftly. See, and walk on the straight path.

## EPISTLE CXLI

**THE NUNS OF ZWIFALTEN TO HILDEGARD. That she should show how they ought to return from the way of negligence to the way of correction.**

To HILDEGARD, illumined by the special grace of divinity, the humble community of the sisters of Zwiefalten: may you be increased in the gifts received from heaven.

Divine mercy has wonderfully glorified its omnipotence in you, whom it took from fragile matter and has taken care, in a new order, to fill with the treasures of its grace. [Col. 0371D] We therefore rejoice in your brightness and humbly commend ourselves and all that is ours to your prayers. We also ask your kindness, when you attend to the divine vision, to direct words of admonition to us and not neglect to show us how we ought to return from the way of negligence to the way of correction. May your belovedness prosper in Christ.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY. That they should avoid pride, neither be dancers nor go out beyond the monastery, and should return to their first betrothal.**

He who sees all things and from whom nothing is hidden says: A certain noble man joined to himself, with the utmost [Col. 0372A] care, a bride very beautiful in face, with sapphire eyes, whose figure was proportionate and not crooked through any unevenness, but lovely in every adornment. She too was very lovable in all that belonged to her, so that every harmony of citharas and every kind of musicians befitted her. Such also was her character that she did not wish to be a concubine or a dancer in a harlot’s dress, nor did she wish to wander through various streets or speak for the mockery of young men.

O vanity and filthiness of diabolic darts! O disgrace of girls’ wantonness! Tremble at this saying. When a woman withdraws herself from union with a husband, unwilling for God’s sake to be joined to a man, O how great is her nobility then, since betrothal to the heavenly King befits her! [Col. 0372B] For she has refused a carnal husband, and so she ought to embrace God and cleave to her Lord, because she has no earthly husband. For she must remain as Eve was before God presented her to Adam, when she then looked not to Adam but to God. So should a woman act who refuses a carnal husband for the love of God: let her look to God and not to another man whom she had previously been unwilling to have.

But, because of the deceitfulness of the ancient serpent, it is very hard and bitter that the freshness of the flesh should always be dry within itself. Nevertheless, when a woman is most strongly armed—so that she places herself in the chamber of the heavenly King and embraces that King himself with sweetest charity, unwilling to cultivate the service of carnal heat in concupiscence, [Col. 0372C] but desiring to set the countenance of her mind upon God, refusing the pleasure of her flesh—then let her look as an eagle at the sun and as a dove through its windows, considering and striving to withdraw her mind from worldly riches and delights and from the company of a carnal husband.

Therefore, a woman who does not wish to enter a carnal husband’s chamber because of love for God ought to be with me in the spiritual life—I who am without beginning and without end—and must not secretly love a rustic in stolen embraces. But if she does this, she is not with me, for she has viper-like habits. Hence, a woman who burns so that she cannot leave the world ought not to enter danger or climb the high mountain, lest afterward she sink into the lake; for [Col. 0372D] she was first betrothed to me and afterward went to carnal embraces.

For the Virgin Mary was joyful in the warmth of the Holy Spirit, and her virginity blossomed. But let no female form begin what the Holy Spirit has not placed within her, lest she afterward remain empty. The woman who wishes to look to me must not be divided by a scattered heart over the ambition of this world, nor crooked through the flaming grandiloquence of pride; rather, she must be steadfast in every adornment of the virtues and in the nobility of charity and justice, which rule over every beauty belonging to the heavenly King.

Now, O company of maidens, hear what the heavenly voice sounds to you. Do not be a concubine, nor set your mind upon the lofty vanity of pride, so that [Col. 0373A] you would wish to allot the King’s honor to each person according to her rank, as though you thought it impossible for me to distinguish the sun, the moon, and the other ornaments of heaven. A harlot treats all things as alike and equal: a prince just as a peasant. Whoever does this dishonors me, making wisdom like ignorance, piety like vanity, and the other virtues like copper.

Now, O maidens, do not be dancers, after the likeness of the worst habits, following whatever pleases you, lest, if you do so, you deceive one another in every matter. For a dancer dances for each person according to that person’s will. Nor should you walk with open doors, because of the filthiness of your minds; nor make signals with wanton gestures through the unrestrainedness of your hearts, [Col. 0373B] as though in the streets you loved what you had despised in the King’s embraces, when you place a peasant in your embraces in place of royal love.

Therefore, a woman who does not wish to have the company of a carnal husband should in no way be out in public, because this does not befit her; rather, in body and mind let her remain hidden, like a dove in a cave, lest a hawk—that is, a male mind—seize her. Now you, O company, rise quickly to the first and royal betrothal with your first and principal husband. For he calls you. Therefore make amends and correct that in which you have offended him, and he will receive you into eternal salvation, and you shall live.

## EPISTLE CXLII

**A., PRIOR, AND THE CONVENT OF MOUNT ST. DISIBOD, TO HILDEGARD. They complain that, though she was raised among them, she neither writes to them nor sends admonitory words.**

To HILDEGARD, most truly filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, A., unworthy monk and prior of Mount St. Disibod, with the brethren of that place: may you ascend from virtue to virtue and see the God of gods in Zion.

Since you send the words of your admonitions into foreign regions and cause very many people to desire the way of uprightness, we, who have known you almost from the cradle and among whom you lived for many years, wonder why you withhold from us, who thirst, the words of heavenly visions. For we know how [Col. 0373D] you were raised among us, taught among us, and lived among us: you applied yourself to no work except women’s work; you were instructed by no books except a simple Psalter; and without reproach you loved a good and holy manner of life. But divine mercy, as it willed, steeped you with heavenly dew and opened to you the greatness of its secrets. And although we ought to rejoice with you in these things, God snatched you from us against our wishes and transferred you to other people. Why he did this we can neither investigate nor know; but unwilling and willing alike, we endure it in great distress.

For we hoped that the salvation of our place rested in you, but God arranged otherwise than we wished. Now, however, because we cannot resist God’s will, we yield to it and [Col. 0374A] rejoice with you, since by divine revelation you have disclosed very many things hitherto unseen and hitherto unheard, and opened what had hitherto been closed. For, full of the Spirit of God, you write many things which you have not learned from a human being and at which holy and learned men marvel. Therefore, although we are far from the holy because we are sinners, we humbly beg you, both for the Lord’s glory and for the sake of our old and just familiarity, to remember us, give us words of consolation, and assist us before God, so that God may deign through the merits of your prayers to supply in us what is lacking. Farewell.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY. That they should return to God.**

[Col. 0374B]

In a true vision I heard a voice saying the following against the injuries which both spiritual and secular persons utter against justice:

“O Justice, you are a stranger and a sojourner in the city of those who compose and choose for themselves parables from the service of their own will, and who do not thirst either for your mysteries or for your friendship—you who are the king’s purple-clad friend. Therefore you cry out because of that lot in which no justice rests, and in affliction you say: ‘I blush deeply, so that I hide my face beneath my cloak, lest those who lie in wait for me see me.’ But they say: ‘Whatever comes from us benefits everyone.’ Therefore, O Justice, you have great zeal, so that whoever resists you is guilty before judgment.

“And again, in affliction you say: ‘Whence do you come?’ ‘From the Father’s bosom, and all regions have been gathered with me; and where all the conditions of peoples and all the institutions of generations were established, there I was present; and thus pillars of cloud were raised in me. [Col. 0374C] But now I am the weariness of those who sprang up in me at the first root. Therefore, before I grieve in these things, I sigh because of the people’s ignorance; and, like flooding waters, my roar is like the sound of many waters in a loud voice, because of the excess of foolish people in the chattering of their habits and in the din of dishonesty. Ha, ha, O eagles, who passed through me by the water of restoration like a gleaming dawn and a flashing gem: now you sleep and are like foolish animals, which sometimes go forward, sometimes walk backward, and sometimes mingle with one another as they go.’

“But concerning this mountain of the sons of God I saw the following in a mystical breathing. I saw a mountain of great size, upon whose summit sat a great man. In each of his hands he held the law of God, as though written on a sheet, as is read concerning Moses. Beneath this man’s feet stood a certain company of people, surrounded by spiritual circumcision. They all received the instruments of that law with joy and sighing, saying: ‘O Lord our God, whenever we come to you, we shall gladly obey you.’ Yet at times they mingled themselves in a certain whirlwind, and at times many crimes occurred among them, [Col. 0375A] which nevertheless they washed away with many tears in the sprinkling of the blood of Christ Jesus.

“For when a human being lay in sins so great that by himself he was unable to raise himself from them in any freshness, God said: ‘I wish to raise the human being through myself, and again plant him in the bowels of mercy, so that he may sit in the mirror of confession—he who could not by himself rescue himself from the bowels of the devil.’ But I, a little poor woman, although I saw many crimes in these persons, nevertheless did not see in them the pride which, in obstinacy, despises sinners by the casting of stones.

“But beneath their feet I saw another company of people, surrounded by a white cloud, with beautiful faces and looking toward heaven. Yet they sometimes engaged in wantonness, with the stirring up of many useless things, like fat bulls; so that, even as they looked at heaven, they bent their bows and shot arrows against heaven, struck against heaven with leaden clubs, and thus set their mouths in heaven while their tongue passed over the earth. [Col. 0375B] Therefore thunder came upon them, hail fell upon them, and many clouds covered them. And they murmured as to why such foulness should so surround them.

“And the grace of God answered them thus: ‘I gathered you for great blessedness, but in your rashness you cast me away, saying: “Who can reach you? What word can overcome you? What hills, or what tongue, can strike you?” Just as the children of Israel neglected God when, through Abraham’s blessing, he raised over them the horn of blessings and lifted them into his bosom through the joy of honor. But they murmured in deceit, resisted God in rashness, and forsook holiness through the shedding of Christ’s blood. Then blessing went backward from them and vanished, because they turned themselves toward the fall of death. And from their sacrifices and burnt offerings God built another city of the Church, until all the waters of the wells are drawn out into the valley of black clouds. Then all the eagles in the encircling wheel shall be gathered into one flock, because they formerly were in blessing.’

“I also saw another company of people beneath their feet, before whose eyes a ram of golden color hung in thorns. They looked upon it amid the fragrance of myrrh and incense and with a flashing countenance; and certain streams flowed from the hands of that great man seated on the mountain’s summit to their breasts. They cried in a clear voice to the bosom of wisdom: ‘God once gathered us in many sacrifices, but we all sin under many obligations. Therefore we have been placed upon the winepress with the prophet, saying: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there is not a man with me”’ (Isa. 63).

“And truly, where the net was cast into the sea and gathered fish of every kind, as those fishermen selected good fish into vessels, so God’s grace selected for glory those who are humble in heart and devout in the fear of the Lord, not intent on plunder. [Col. 0376A] Now let the first voice which gathered you to God’s praise make you good at the root, like the first ones consecrated in the temple walls. But you, O mountain, hear God’s admonition: God established you like Mount Sinai, to sacrifice to him an offering of praise. Now turn to God and be the King’s lampstand, so that you may not be ashamed of your first root, as God’s right hand planted you.”

## EPISTLE CXLIII

**THE MONKS OF ST. EUCHARIUS AT TRIER TO HILDEGARD. They desire to be aroused by the spurs of her admonition.**

To HILDEGARD, who continually cleaves to the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom, and to all those living with her in Christ, the whole convent of the monastery of St. Eucharius at Trier: that which is better than anything else.

Those who strive to do the will of the Father who is in heaven are called the Lord’s brothers, sisters, and mothers (Matt. 13). But whoever strives, by admonishing others—as though nursing them—to draw them to better things, will especially obtain the dignity of a mother. Thus, not without reason, we venerate you above others as a mother in the Lord, being abundantly refreshed inwardly from the breasts of your consolation and instruction. We likewise magnify with you him who alone does great wonders, who has hitherto hidden from the wise and prudent what he has wonderfully revealed in our days to your humility.

Therefore, because we cannot run with enlarged heart in the way of God’s commandments, [Col. 0376C] we earnestly desire to be aroused by the spurs of your admonition, according as God has granted you. Moreover, know without doubt that we have delighted in your writings, namely the book *Scivias*, as in all riches. Finally, we humbly request to be aided before God by your holy prayers and fortified by your counsels.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY. She praises their holy way of life.**

You who have put on Christ’s tunic and wish to imitate him, hear what the Psalmist says: “Who makes the cloud your ascent, who rides upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103). What is this? In the ordering of the world, you established the cloud as the ascent of living flying creatures, which are in the height of the air. This is also so understood: God foreknew that he would establish within himself a spiritual people, as the prophet says: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60).

Spiritual minds are like clouds, which are as it were the material of the heavenly lights—namely, the sun, moon, and stars. So obedience is like the material of humility, charity, and the other virtues. In them the faithful fly like doves when, through the binding of their own will, they conceal their desires from themselves, so that through the cave of innocence they gaze upon the sun, as though they were not human beings under the will of their flesh. Thus the Creator of all walks upon the wings of the winds when the heavenly Son came forth as a beautiful flower in the humility of chastity and thus remained in gentleness. [Col. 0377A] Hence it is written: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon one who is humble and gentle and trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). These are the wings of the spiritual people; but those who lack them will fall like birds that have no wings for flight.

In these things also the multitude of the sea is converted and the strength of the nations comes. For an innumerable crowd of people runs to these wings. But certain ones among them look toward the north through the whirlwind of vainglory and pride and through the excesses of worldly habits, trusting in themselves and not following the Psalmist, who says: “It is good to hope in princes” (Ps. 117). What is this? It is much better and more profitable to look toward and fly into the cloud through Christ’s tunic than to trust in oneself, as occurred in the case of the lost angel, who in pride wished to surpass him before whom he was unable thus to stand, but fell like lead into the abyss.

In this pride Adam too fled from life and found an alien pilgrimage, in which he looked to his Father as to a stranger during his exile—though he had known him well before, when he was innocent in humility. So too the children of men trust in themselves, deceived as though placing hope in princes. But when God cried, “Adam, where are you?”, he foreknew that the work of his finger would not be wholly destroyed but would one day be redeemed, as it is written: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance, Mount Zion, in which you dwelt” [Col. 0377C] (Ps. 73). What is this? God remembered the human being when, through a woman, he crushed the serpent’s head, where the Word was made flesh and Mount Zion came to be, in which God dwells in humility and the Son in the Father’s heart.

Now, you gathered congregation, listen, so that you may be Mount Zion. For God foresaw from the beginning that he wished to make every creature. The Father’s Word rose in the Virgin as the rod, the human being; and that rod was the material of every virtue of holiness, from which you too, O spiritual peoples, have come. For Eve brought forth the whole human race, but this rod restored it anew in its greenness when the Son of God came forth from her womb. Thus you are the spiritual Mount Zion, because the Father planted you in his Word.

For the Son of the most high Father dwelt in the tabernacle of the Virgin Mary and came forth from her like a mighty lion, so that the whole world saw him. He also gathered you spiritual peoples in himself as you fly to him like clouds, not bearing your sins in a will that puts them into action. For he was without sin. And you imitate him when you walk after him, rejecting yourselves lest you sin—not becoming like dust which the wind casts from the earth’s face, nor like the poison of asps, nor like lead in violent waters. [Col. 0378A]

When you run after vainglory, you are like dust scattered here and there, which sows no fruit of justice and plants no chosen vineyard, but produces great renown and harms your souls. When you are in the malice of pride, you conceive the incurable poison of asps, which kills you. But when restlessness of minds rises among you, you are like lead falling violently into a well. For vainglory and malice are the inward parts of pride, and hatred and envy minister to those who are thus entangled together in restlessness of mind. Therefore peace and security flee from there, Christ’s charity withdraws, and those who are in these evils fall like lead into violent waters because they have no wings of uplift.

For the Lord’s zeal cries out against them in his vengeance, as it once thundered when he cast the proud enemy into the abyss, as the Psalmist says: “Lift up your hands against their pride unto the end: how greatly has the enemy acted wickedly in the sanctuary!” (Ps. [Col. 0378B] 73). For God exalted the most holy works when he divided light from darkness, because there pride, with all the inward parts of the devil, fell utterly when it looked toward the north and reduced its shield to nothing, where it wholly perished.

Yet afterward pride again built many cities among human beings without length of days, added punishments to punishments, and made ruins amid a multitude of afflictions, where people said: “We do not know God, nor do we wish to worship him.” Thus the enemy acted wickedly in the sanctuary.

Now the living light says to the children of this congregation: You are the walls of the temple, because the primitive Church planted you. Therefore flee vainglory, pride, and the whirlwind of many disturbances. [Col. 0378C] See these things now with living eyes, and hear them with inward ears that hear. Yet I do not see your place in dispersion, although it will suffer many scourges. Therefore live and keep watch in God.

For in a true vision I also saw some in this congregation gleaming like the dawn, some shining like sapphire, and some bright like the light of stars. Those who gleam like the dawn have the fear of God and gladly observe for God’s sake the precepts of the rule, although through the flesh they sometimes appear to wander, like a victim led to slaughter. Those who shine like sapphire possess the charity of God and therefore do not commit grave sins; though they sin, they gladly chastise themselves even for their transgressions, and have this as a habit. But those who shine like starlight possess goodwill and therefore do not quarrel with people; they retain the harmlessness of childlike ways, gladly abstain from grave sins, and regard them with hatred.

I saw others in the blackness of bitter smoke because of their habitual foul conduct. Some of these are bitter on account of their own self-will, love possessions, and therefore do not love spiritual observance; instead, they often afflict those who are in the three modes mentioned above. [Col. 0379A]

And I heard a voice crying from heaven: “So long as this congregation remains in these three modes, it is not abandoned by God.” But I heard that same voice say to those who were in the aforesaid blackness: “Rise, North Wind, and come, South Wind; blow through my garden, and its streams shall flow before it.” This means: Depart, evil of iniquity; come, good of justice; and water the planting of holiness with virtues, so that works which do not wither may shine within it.

For the North Wind consists of quarrelers, who wish through words of strife, the excuse of avarice, and provocations of injury to cast down the sweet and useful herbs of the virtues, just as the North Wind casts down everything. Yet those whom they afflict in this manner learn patience, and cry to God in tearful groaning for their own sins and for the sins of those others. Thus they are sometimes tiresome to sin; and therefore the smoke of spices ascends from their hearts, which angels receive, and so through the north wind greenness is given to the good.

Those also who gladly possess property throw things at those who shine in the three aforesaid modes in order to shame them; and even under necessary pretexts of their obediences, they seek ways to afflict them. Often they involve themselves in the uncleanness of the flesh, like a pig wallowing in dung, and at times wear out others with the motions of a serpent’s eye and a most grievous habitual conduct. [Col. 0379B]

But you who love injustice, remember this admonition, so that you may recognize the possessions of your own will as idolatry, separated from the angelic orders—that is, from the spiritual people—just as an idol of falsehood is separated from the true God. Leave other sins as well, and flee to the spring that leaps up so that you may be washed. Consider also the washing of that covenant by which you left the world, so that you may depart from sins; and strive that your sacrifice may become fat, so that you persevere in the good which you have begun.

For whenever a person sacrifices his own will upon the wheel of his flesh, it is a sacrifice to God. This is acceptable to God as Abraham’s sacrifice was, when he bound his son in obedience to sacrifice him to God. One tames the hands who abandons wicked deeds; one binds the feet who restrains the paths of one’s own will; one bends down in obedience as Isaac bent his head to the sword; and one tames the body who casts aside carnal desire. In these things is the victory that bears the banner, fragrant with good report and the sweet odors of the virtues. Whoever has it walks secure before all enemies.

In this way the sacrifice will become fat, like a fatted calf without any blemish, through which the soul fails from leanness, because full goodness is fat. [Col. 0379D] For Christ, worn down by injuries, did not sin and thereby sanctified the patience of the saints. Therefore you faithful, prepare your hearts for the battles of him who gave you an example; cast aside concern for those things of which you have no need; and strive to appear in Alpha and Omega. You are darkened in the sensuousness of sins; but when you rise from sins, the beautiful forms of virtues will appear within you. Therefore may God’s right hand protect you.

## EPISTLE CXLIV

[Col. 0380A]

**N., PRIOR, AND THE CISTERCIAN MONKS TO HILDEGARD. They desire to learn from her what displeases God in their order.**

To HILDEGARD, honorable lady and teacher of the sisters of St. Rupert at Bingen, to be embraced in the arms of sincere charity: N., unworthy prior, and the entire poor and humble congregation of Cistercian brothers—may they follow the Lamb among choirs of virgins wherever he goes.

Though separated by distance of place, since we cannot enjoy your desired bodily presence, we gladly greet and address you by the service of a letter. [Col. 0380B] For we venerate you in Christ as our superior and hope to have you before God as our mediatrix and most dear mother. Having heard the report of your good conduct and your faithful administration in God . . ., we render to God service for your stability and the service of prayer, for your salvation.

Therefore, O lady, we write you this letter of greeting so that you may remember us and endeavor that those subject to you do the same. For we have heard much concerning you, and greatly rejoice that you are able to search out the mysteries of God and disclose no small matters from his hidden things. Accordingly, we ask your clemency not to hesitate to write back to us, according as God shows you, concerning whatever displeases your—indeed, God’s—[Col. 0380C] eyes in us and in our order, namely the monastic order. Farewell.

**HILDEGARD’S REPLY.**

[Col. 0380D]

“I am the living fountain, whose pilgrims, clothed in my tunic for my name’s sake, are amid the vexation of the world. O it is lamentable and mournful that heaven has been torn apart and day darkened! Therefore the denarius must now be called back into the court of the voice of praise.

“O children of Israel, why do you corrupt the sweetest charity, which flows in me, lofty and gazing into the deep, with fullest power? And because it flows in me, living waters flow from it as well. It stands in the form of a rod: for just as in a virgin there are sweetest embraces because of her integrity, so charity also has the sweetest embraces of the virtues. But now it mourns, because rash people tear it apart through the chattering of their murmuring. Thus it flees from them to that height whence it came, and weeps because its children, whom it nourished from full breasts, fail, unwilling to be wiped clean from the rottenness of flying minds.

“O those wretched people! Why do they join themselves to the misery of estrangement and pilgrimage, withdrawing themselves from the womb of the royal nuptials of the new bride, who is always prepared for her Bridegroom as a virgin for her husband when she is not yet joined to him in knowledge but still remains uncorrupted in her integrity? Yet these separate themselves from that bride, and therefore they are darkened and clouded, as though they had broken heaven.

“What is this? As the firmament of heaven, with all its ornaments—the sun, moon, and stars—illuminates the world, and as a craftsman makes wooden things from wood, stone things from stones, and other instruments from other materials, so they ought to shine for the remaining people and show them the good way. But charity has been torn apart in them. Thus virginity, which ought to shine in them like the sun, widowhood like the moon, and the remaining people like stars in their light, fail, because sweet maternal bowels do not warm them. Rather, a crooked woman, full of wrinkles and blackness, full of viper-like habits and gnashing teeth, horrible in all that she does, most wickedly sends them forth after the habits of pigs, though they ought to be holy, elect, and persons who have left the world. [Col. 0381B]

“For they tear apart within themselves the garment of innocence through thorny habits and anger, and corrupt their vital parts in wrath; they blind their living eyes in despair, defile all their garments through the folly of their habits, and think themselves wiser than their teachers. Alas, alas, children of Israel: at your first origin he did not establish you in this mystical and golden fashion.”

The remainder is wanting, since three following leaves have been cut from the manuscript codex.

## EPISTLE CXLV

**HENRY [read: HELINGER], ABBOT, AND THE CONVENT OF MOUNT ST. DISIBOD, TO HILDEGARD. They desire her to write what displeases God in themselves, and ask her to commit the Life of St. Disibod to writing.**

[Col. 0381C]

HENRY, by the grace of God servant at Mount St. Disibod and overseer of the Lord’s sheepfold, with the entire congregation of his brothers, to the venerable mother Lady HILDEGARD of St. Rupert: may you, most fully illumined—as we know most truly—by the ray of divine splendor beyond the capacity of human understanding, abound in the gifts of the sevenfold Holy Spirit and, for the sake of divine recompense, minister draughts from that same fountain to those who thirst.

Because, beloved mother, through the prompting of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete of almighty God, and likewise through the command of Him who [Col. 0382A] “wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2), we have lately learned that your holiness has come among us. Therefore, as far as we can—although we are unable to do so worthily—we continually render thanks to that same Paraclete. For, to confess the truth, we have most fully felt among us and within ourselves the warmth and touch of His illumination: all the incentives to hatred and enmity, long entrenched over many years, have been cast away by unanimous agreement, and we have come together wholly into the unity of true charity, as though in one body and one soul.

Therefore we earnestly entreat the charity of your holiness: by the sight of the divine grace of the aforesaid splendour bestowed upon you—through which matters closed to your charity and hidden from other mortals are opened to the eyes of your heart—[Col. 0382B] reveal to us, as you are bound to do, whether we have truly come together in that true charity which is the beginning of all good things, or whether some root of dissension still lies hidden among us. For you departed from us with your sisters in body, indeed, but not in spirit, as we truly hope and know. We also ask that you make known to us in writing whatever else, whether greater matters—to say nothing of lesser offences—you recognize as opposed to the eyes of the divine Majesty.

Moreover, with unanimous consent we knock, opportunely and importunately, at the door of your charity concerning a written account of the deeds, virtues, and life of our patron, and yours, most blessed Disibod, in whose house you were nurtured from your very cradle [Col. 0382C]. We earnestly urge the ears of your compassion and, pouring forth unwearying prayers, beseech you that the memory of your blessedness too may thereby be held in the praises of this same our Father: namely, that you disclose to us whatever God reveals to you concerning him. May the almighty Father of eternal mercy kindle the mind of your charity with the light of His splendour, and supply draughts for the refreshment of those who earnestly desire them.

(The reply to this letter is said to be found among the published letters of St Hildegard [Note: **[Col. 0381]** This is mistaken: only a reply to another letter of Herenger, Epistle 39, survives. **Editor**]; and the Life of St Disibod composed by her is also found in Surius, 8 July.)

[Col. 0383]

# THE THREE BOOKS OF THE *SCIVIAS*, OR VISIONS AND REVELATIONS, OF SAINT HILDEGARD

[Note: **[Col. 0383]** From the first edition, entitled: *Book of Three Spiritual Men—Hermas, Uguetinus, and Brother Libertus—and Three Spiritual Virgins—Hildegard, Elisabeth, and Mechtild*, edited by Jacques Lefèvre of Étaples, printed by Stephanus the Elder, Paris, folio, 1513, as is noted at the end of the volume: “Issued at Paris from the workshop of Henri Estienne, printer, opposite the School of Decretals, in the year 1513, on the sixth day before the Nones of June [8 June]. May the devout prayers of readers benefit before God those who have laboured in any manner upon the publication of this devout and pious work. He who printed this work, partly at his own expense and partly with the assistance of his associate Jean de Brie, has enriched literary scholarship.” At the end of the index one reads: “Volgatius of Prato, reviser of the work in the printing-house, greets the readers and asks their prayers to God for himself.”]

# BOOK ONE

## PREFACE

[Col. 0383A] Behold: in the forty-third year of my temporal course, while I clung in great fear and trembling attention to a heavenly vision, I saw an exceeding great brightness. In it a voice from heaven spoke to me, saying:

“O frail human being, dust from dust of the earth and ashes from ashes, speak and write what you see and hear. But because you are timid in speaking, simple in explaining, and untaught in writing these things, speak and write them not according to the mouth of a human being, nor according to the understanding of human invention, nor according to the will of human composition; but according to what you see and hear concerning them in the heavenly places above, amid the wonders of God. Set them forth in explanation just as a hearer, receiving the words of his teacher, proclaims them according to the tenor of that teacher’s speech, when the teacher himself wills, shows, and commands it. [Col. 0383B] Thus you also, O human being, speak what you see and hear; and write it not according to yourself or any other human being, but according to the will of Him who knows, sees, and orders all things in the hidden places of His mysteries.”

And again I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: “Speak, therefore, these wonders; and, thus instructed, write and speak them in this manner.”

It came to pass in the year 1141 of the Incarnation of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, when I was forty-two years and seven months old, that a fiery light of most intense brightness came from an open heaven and poured through my whole brain. It kindled all my heart and breast as a flame does—not burning, but warming—just as the sun warms an object upon which it casts its rays. And suddenly I understood the meaning of the exposition of the books: namely, the Psalter, the Gospels, and other Catholic volumes [Col. 0384A] of both the Old and New Testaments. Yet I did not possess an interpretation of the words of their text, nor the division of syllables, nor knowledge of cases or tenses.

But from girlhood—indeed, from the time when I was five years old until the present—I had felt within myself, in a wondrous manner, the power of mysteries and of secret and marvellous visions, as I do still. Yet I disclosed this to no one, except certain few religious persons who lived in the same manner of life as I did. Until the time when God in His grace wished it to be revealed, I kept it restrained in quiet silence.

The visions which I saw [Col. 0384B] I did not receive in dreams, nor while asleep, nor in frenzy; nor did I receive them through the bodily eyes or ears of the outward person, nor in hidden places. Rather, awake and alert, in a pure mind, through the eyes and ears of the inward person, I received them in open places, according to God’s will. How this is so is difficult for a carnal person to investigate.

But after I had passed beyond the boundary of childhood and reached the aforesaid age of full strength, I heard a voice from heaven saying:

“I am the living light, illuminating darkness. The human being whom I chose, and whom I wonderfully shook, as pleased Me, in great marvels beyond the measure of people of former times who saw many secrets in Me—I have placed that person thus; but I laid that person low upon the earth, lest the mind be raised up in any exaltation. The world, moreover, had neither joy nor delight nor occupation in those things which belong to it in that person, because I withdrew that person from stubborn audacity, making that person fearful and trembling amid labours. For that person suffered in the marrow and veins of the flesh, with a constricted mind and understanding, and endured much bodily suffering. Thus no security dwelt in that person, but in every affair that person judged himself or herself guilty. [Col. 0385A] For I enclosed the ruins of that heart, lest its mind should exalt itself through pride or vain glory, but rather should feel fear and sorrow in all these things, more than joy or wantonness.

“Therefore, in love for Me, that person searched in the soul for where he might find one who was running the way of salvation. And that person found someone and loved him, recognizing that he was faithful and, in some part, like that person in the labour which tends toward Me. Holding fast to him, that person strove together with him in all these matters through heavenly zeal, that My hidden marvels might be revealed. That same man did not exalt himself above himself, but inclined himself in many sighs to the person whom he had found, in the ascent of humility and in the intention of good will.

“Therefore you, O human being, who receive these things not in the disturbance of deception but in the purity of simplicity [Col. 0386A], directed toward the revelation of hidden things, write what you see and hear.”

But although I saw and heard these things, because of doubt, poor self-estimation, and the conflicting words of people, I long refused to write—not in obstinacy, but in the service of humility—until, laid low by God’s scourge, I fell upon a bed of sickness. At last, compelled by many infirmities, I set my hand to writing, upon the testimony of a certain noble and well-conducted maiden and of that man whom, as stated above, I had secretly sought and found. While doing this, I perceived the profound depth of the exposition of the books, as I have said; and, rising from illness with strength restored, I scarcely brought this work to completion in ten years [Col. 0386B].

These visions and words occurred in the days of Henry, Archbishop of Mainz; Conrad, King of the Romans; and Cuno, abbot on the mountain of the blessed bishop Disibod, under Pope Eugenius. I spoke and wrote these things not according to any invention of my heart or that of any other person, but as I saw, heard, and perceived them in heavenly places through the secret mysteries of God. And again I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: “Cry out, therefore, and write thus.”

# FIRST VISION

[Col. 0385]

**SUMMARY.—** On the strength and stability of the eternity of God’s kingdom. On the fear of the Lord. On those who are poor in spirit. That virtues coming from God preserve those who fear God and are poor in spirit. That the purposes of human actions cannot be hidden from God’s knowledge. Solomon on the same matter.

[Col. 0385C] I saw, as it were, a great mountain, of iron colour; and upon it sat one of such great brightness that His brightness dulled my sight. From either side of Him there extended a gentle shadow, like a wing of wondrous breadth and length. Before Him, at the foot of the same mountain, stood a figure wholly full of eyes. Because of the multitude of its eyes, I could discern no human shape in it. Before this stood another figure, of childish age, clothed in a pale garment but wearing white shoes. Upon its head such great brightness descended from Him who sat upon the mountain that I could not look upon its face. From the One who sat upon that mountain there came forth many living sparks, which flew around these figures with great sweetness.

[Col. 0385D] In that mountain there also appeared, as it were, very many little windows, in which something like human heads appeared, some pale and some white. And behold, He who sat upon the mountain cried out in a most powerful and penetrating voice, saying:

“O frail human being, dust from the dust of earth and ashes from ashes, cry out and speak of the entrance into incorruptible salvation, so that those may be instructed who see the marrow of the Scriptures but will neither speak nor preach it, because they are lukewarm and dull in preserving the justice of God. Open to them the enclosure of the mysteries, which they timidly hide without fruit in a concealed field. Therefore expand yourself into the fountain of abundance and flow forth in mystical instruction, so that those who wish you to be contemptible because of Eve’s transgression may be shaken by the outpouring of your irrigation. For you do not receive the keenness of this depth from a human being, but receive it from above, from the heavenly and terrible Judge, where this serenity will shine powerfully in splendid light among the shining ones. Rise, therefore; cry out and speak what is made manifest to you by the most powerful strength of divine aid. For He who rules all His creation mightily and graciously floods with the brightness of heavenly illumination those who fear Him and serve Him with sweet love in a spirit of humility, and leads those who persevere in the way of justice to the joys [Col. 0386D] of eternal vision.”

Therefore, as you see, this great mountain of iron colour signifies the strength and stability of the eternity of God’s kingdom, which no assault of passing changeableness can destroy. And the One seated upon it, of such great brightness that His brightness dulled your sight, shows Him who, in the kingdom of blessedness, rules the whole earthly world in the splendour of unfailing serenity through His heavenly divinity, [Col. 0387A] incomprehensible to human minds.

But the gentle shadow stretching from either side of Him like a wing of wondrous breadth and length is, both in admonition and chastisement, the sweet and gentle protection of blessed defence, justly and mercifully showing ineffable justice in the perseverance of true equity.

And before Him, at the foot of the same mountain, stands a figure full of eyes on every side, because before God the fear of the Lord, gazing in humility upon the kingdom of God and encircled by the clarity of good and just intention, exercises its zeal and steadfastness among human beings. You cannot discern any human form in it because of those eyes, for it so rejects, by the keenest sharpness of its inspection, every forgetfulness of God’s justice that people often experience in [Col. 0387B] the weariness of their minds, that mortal inquiry cannot investigate its vigilance in its own weakness.

Thus before it appears another figure, of childish age, wearing a pale tunic and white shoes. For, with the fear of the Lord preceding, those who are poor in spirit follow; because the fear of the Lord, in the devotion of humility, firmly holds the blessedness of poverty of spirit. This poverty seeks neither boastfulness nor loftiness of heart, but loves simplicity and sobriety of mind; it attributes its just works not to itself but to God, as though in the paleness of subjection, clothing itself in the garment of a pale tunic, and faithfully follows the white footprints of the Son of God.

Such great brightness descends upon its head from Him seated upon the mountain [Col. 0387C] that you cannot look upon its face, because the serenity of the visitation of Him who praiseworthily rules every creature pours into it such power and strength of blessedness that you cannot comprehend its abundance through mortal and infirm consideration [Col. 0388A]. For He who possesses heavenly riches humbly subjected Himself to poverty.

But the many living sparks which come forth from Him who sits upon that mountain and sweetly fly around these same figures mean that diverse and most powerful virtues, shining in divine brightness, come from almighty God. Surrounding those who truly fear God and faithfully love poverty of spirit with their aid and protection, they ardently embrace and caress them.

And the many little windows visible in that mountain, in which there appear human heads, some pale and some white, mean that the aims of human actions cannot be concealed or hidden from the most profound and penetrating knowledge of God [Col. 0388B] in the highest height. For people very often display in themselves both lukewarmness and whiteness: at one time weary in both heart and deeds, they sleep amid dishonour; at another time awakened, they keep watch in honour. As Solomon testifies according to My will, saying: “A slack hand produces poverty, but the hand of the strong prepares riches” (Prov. 10).

This means: that person made himself weak and poor who refused to work justice, erase iniquity, or remit a debt, remaining idle where he should have performed the marvellous works of blessedness. But the person who performs the strongest works of salvation, running in the way of truth, receives the fountain of springing glory, in which that person prepares for himself or herself the most precious riches on earth and in heaven. Therefore whoever has knowledge in the Holy Spirit and wings in faith [Col. 0388C] must not transgress My admonition, but receive it by embracing it in the taste of the soul.

# SECOND VISION

[Col. 0387]

**SUMMARY.—** That the blessed angels, terrified by no onslaught of injustice, are not drawn away from the love and praise of God. That Lucifer, considering the beauty and power of his strength, grew proud and was therefore cast out of heavenly glory with those who agreed with him. That God would have been unjust had He not cast him down. The words of Job on the same matter. On hell, which in its devouring appetite holds the submersion of souls. That hell was made at the devil’s downfall. That Gehenna awaits the impenitent; other punishments are appointed for those to be purged. The words of Ezekiel on the same matter. On the devil’s fraud in deceiving the first human being through the serpent. That the devil did not know that the tree was forbidden except from Eve’s answer. What must be observed or avoided in marriage. The apostle’s words on the same matter. Why, before the Lord’s Incarnation, some had several wives. Why neither a human being nor an angel could free humankind, but only the Son of God. The words of Wisdom on the same matter. That relatives must not be joined in marriage. An example from milk. Why marriage among relatives was permitted in the Old Testament and forbidden in the New. That a man should marry only when of vigorous age, and only a marriageable woman. On avoiding unlawful and lustful defilement. Why a woman after childbirth, or after being violated by a man, should remain in seclusion and abstain from entering the temple. Those who defile themselves in intercourse with a pregnant woman are murderers. Hosea on the same matter. In praise of chastity. John on the same matter. That, after Adam’s expulsion, God fortified paradise. That because humankind proved rebellious against God, the creature formerly subject to humanity opposed humanity. On the pleasantness of paradise, which gave sap and strength to the earth as the soul does to the body. Why God made humankind such that it could sin. That a human being ought not investigate the highest things, since one cannot examine even the lowest. That humanity now shines more brightly than formerly in heaven. The comparison of a garden, sheep, and a pearl to the human being. In praise of humility and charity, which are brighter than the other virtues.

[Col. 0387D] Then I saw, as it were, an exceedingly great multitude of living lamps, possessing much brightness. Receiving a fiery radiance, they attained a most serene splendour. And behold, there appeared a lake of great breadth [Col. 0388D] and depth, having an opening like the mouth of a well and belching out fiery smoke with great stench. From it there also rose a most foul mist, reaching as far as an end almost imperceptible to sight; and, in [Col. 0389A] a bright region, it blew upon a white cloud, containing very many stars, which had come forth from a beautiful human form, and drove both it and that human form out of that region. Once this had happened, a most brilliant splendour surrounded that region, and all the elements of the world, which had previously remained in great peace, were turned into utmost disturbance and displayed dreadful terrors.

Again I heard Him who had spoken to me before, saying:

“Those who follow God with faithful devotion and burn in love for Him with worthy affection are not drawn away from the glory of heavenly blessedness by any terrifying assault of injustice. But those who attend to God falsely are not only not advanced to greater things; they are also justly cast down from those things which they falsely imagine they possess.

[Col. 0389B] “This is shown by this immense multitude of living lamps possessing much brightness: it is the countless host of heavenly spirits, shining in blessed life and existing in great beauty and adornment. For when they were created by God, they did not seize proud exaltation, but remained steadfast in divine love. Receiving fiery radiance, they attained such serene splendour because, when Lucifer with his followers attempted rebellion against the heavenly Creator, these angels, having zeal for God at the fall of Lucifer and those who consented to him, put on the vigilance of divine love, whereas the others incurred the blindness of ignorance by which they refused to know God.

[Col. 0389C] “How was this so? At the devil’s fall, the greatest praise arose in those angelic spirits that persevered with God in uprightness. For, enlightened in vision, they clearly recognized that God remains immovable in His power, without any change of changeableness, so that He can be conquered by no combatant. Burning in His love and persevering in uprightness, they despised every dwelling-place of injustice.

“But Lucifer, cast from heavenly glory because of his pride, was, at the beginning of his creation, such and so great that he felt no deficiency either in his beauty or his strength. Therefore, as he beheld his beauty and considered within himself the power of his strength, he found pride, which promised him that he could begin whatever he wished, since he could accomplish [Col. 0389D] what he had begun. Seeing the place where he imagined he could establish himself, he wished to display there his beauty and strength, and said within himself: ‘I wish to shine there, just as this One shines here.’ All his host assented, saying: ‘What you will, we also will.’

“And when, lifted up in pride, he wished to accomplish what he had conceived, the zeal of the Lord extended itself in fiery blackness and cast him down with all his company, so that they became dark in contrast to the serenity they had possessed. What does this mean? If God had not cast down their presumption, He would have been unjust, since He would have cherished those who wished to divide the integrity of divinity. But He cast them down and reduced their impiety to nothing; likewise He removes from the sight of His brightness [Col. 0390A] all who try to oppose themselves to Him. As My servant Job shows when he says: ‘The lamp of the wicked shall be extinguished, a flood shall come upon them, and He shall apportion the pains of His wrath. They shall be as chaff before the wind, and as ashes scattered by a whirlwind’” (Job 21).

This means that the glory of arrogant wickedness, issuing from false prosperity like a light of honour according to the will of the flesh of those who do not fear God—rather, who despise Him in perverse impiety, scorning to know that no one can overcome Him, and wishing in the fire of their ferocity to burn up whatever opposes them—will in the hour of God’s vengeance be trampled like earth. From the heavenly judgment there will fall upon these wicked persons the rejection of the indignation of everything under heaven, so that they will be burdensome both to God and to human beings.

[Col. 0390B] Since God does not permit them to possess what they desire, they rage among human beings on every side, worn down by pain through the fury of their madness, because they burn to possess what God does not permit them to swallow. And when they thus depart from God, they are likened only to useless things, so that they would wish to do no good either for God or for human beings, cut off from the grain of life in the foreseeing eye of God’s inspection. Therefore persons of this sort are given over to such crushing, because they are dispersed in the lukewarm taste of an evil report, receiving no approaching rain of the Holy Spirit.

But the lake of great breadth and depth which appears to you is hell, containing within itself, as you see, the breadth of vices and the depth of destructions. [Col. 0390C] It has an opening like the mouth of a well and emits fiery smoke with great stench because, holding the submersion of souls in its devouring appetite, it shows them pleasantness and sweetness, then through perverse deceit brings them to the perversion of torments. There fire burns with the suffusion of most foul smoke, and a boiling, deadly stench flows forth. For these dreadful torments are prepared for the devil and those who follow him—those who turn away from the highest good and neither take care to know nor understand it. Therefore they were cast down from every good, not because they did not know it, but because they despised it in great pride.

What does this mean? At the devil’s fall, these outer darknesses, containing every kind of punishment [Col. 0390D], were established, because those malicious spirits received the misery of diverse punishments in place of the glory prepared for them, and put on densest darkness in place of the brightness they had possessed. How was this so? When the proud angel raised himself upward like a serpent, he received the prison of hell, because no one could prevail against God. Just as it would be unsuitable for one breast to contain two hearts, so neither should there be two gods in heaven. But because this devil with his followers seized proud presumption, he found the lake of destruction prepared for him. Likewise those people who imitate them in their deeds become participants in their punishments according to their merits.

Yet certain souls, having the fullness of condemnation, [Col. 0391A] are cast away from the knowledge of God; therefore they will undergo the infernal punishments without the consolation of deliverance. But others do not exist in forgetfulness of God. Receiving, in the higher judgments, purification from the sins into which they have fallen, they finally experience release from their bonds and, delivered, come to rest.

What does this mean? Gehenna awaits those who hold God in the forgetfulness of their hearts without repentance. The other torments are for those who, although they do evil works, do not persevere in them to the end but at last look toward God amid their groans. Therefore let the faithful flee the devil and love God, casting away evil works and completing good ones with the beauty of repentance, as My servant Ezekiel, inspired by Me, exhorts when he says: [Col. 0391B] “Turn back and do penance for all your iniquities, and iniquity shall not be your ruin” (Ezek. 18).

This means: O people who until now have lain in sins, remember your Christian name. Turn yourselves toward the way of salvation and perform other works in the fountain of repentance. You who formerly committed many crimes in many vices: rise from your evil custom, and that iniquity in which you were defiled will not bring you down into the ruin of death, because you have cast it away on the day of your salvation. Thus the angels will also rejoice over you, because you have departed from the devil and run to God, knowing Him better in good deeds than you knew Him when you were in the mockery of the ancient deceiver.

[Col. 0391C] The most foul mist which rose from that lake and reached an end almost imperceptible to sight means that the devil’s fraud, emanating from the deepest destruction, secretly assailed the venomous serpent, which contained within itself the wickedness of a deceitful intention, in order to deceive humankind. How was this so? When the devil saw the human being in paradise, he cried out in great indignation: “Oh, who will attain me in the dwelling of true blessedness?” Thus he knew within himself that he had not yet brought to completion in another creature the malice which he had within himself. But, seeing Adam and Eve living in childlike innocence in the garden of delights, he rose with great cunning to deceive them through the serpent.

[Col. 0391D] Why? Because he understood that the serpent resembled him more than any other animal; he sought secretly to accomplish in its deceitfulness what he could not openly accomplish in his own form. And when he saw Adam and Eve turn themselves away in both soul and body from the tree forbidden to them, he understood within himself that they had a divine command there, and that he would most easily overthrow them in the first act which they undertook. He did not know that that tree was forbidden except insofar as he learned it through the test of his deceitful question and from their answers.

Therefore, through the most foul mist, he blew upon the white cloud in that bright region—which had gone forth from the beautiful human form and contained within itself very many stars—because in that place of delight the devil assailed Eve, whose mind was innocent, through the serpent’s seduction, to bring about her downfall. Eve had been taken from innocent Adam, bearing in her body [Col. 0392A] the entire multitude of the human race, shining in God’s predestination.

Why did he do this? Because he knew that a woman’s softness could more easily be overcome than a man’s strength; and because he saw that Adam burned so vehemently in love for Eve that, if he overcame Eve, Adam would carry out whatever she said to him. Thus the devil drove her and the human form from that region: that is, the ancient deceiver expelled Eve and Adam from the seat of blessedness by his deception and thrust them into the darkness of overthrow.

How was this so? He first deceived Eve, so that she might entice Adam to give assent to her, because she could lead Adam more swiftly than any other creature into disobedience, since she had been made from his rib. Therefore a woman more swiftly casts down a man when he does not shrink from her and readily accepts her words.

[Col. 0392B] Yet a perfect woman was given not to a boy but to a perfect man, namely Adam. So also now, when a man is fertile at a mature age, a mature woman should be joined to him, just as proper cultivation must be given to a tree when it begins to put forth flowers. For Eve was formed from Adam’s rib, with the heat and moisture implanted in it. Thus now a woman, having received seed from the man’s strength and heat, directs herself toward bringing offspring into the world. For the man is the sower, while the woman receives the seed. Hence the woman remains under the man’s authority, because, as the hardness of stone is to the softness of earth [Col. 0392C], so the strength of man is to the softness of woman.

That the first woman was formed from man means the union of a woman’s betrothal to a man. This must be understood thus: this union is not to be practiced vainly or in forgetfulness of God, because He who took woman from man established this union well and honourably, forming flesh from flesh. Therefore, just as Adam and Eve became one flesh, so now man and woman become one flesh in the union of charity, for the multiplication of the human race. Perfect charity must therefore exist in these two, as it did in those first two.

[Col. 0392D] Adam could have blamed his wife for bringing him death by her counsel; yet he did not put her away as long as he lived in this world, because he knew that she had been given to him by divine power. Therefore, because of perfect charity, let no one put away his wife, except for the reasonable cause which the faithful Church sets before him. Nor should there be any division between them at all, unless both, with one mind, wish to look toward My Son, saying in ardent love for Him: “We wish to leave the world and follow Him who suffered for us.”

But if these two disagree in one devotion concerning leaving the world, they must not separate entirely from one another. For just as blood cannot be separated from flesh while the spirit remains in it, so neither husband nor wife should divide from one another; rather, they should walk together in one will.

[Col. 0393A] But if there is transgression of the law in fornication, either in the man or in the woman, then, whether they disclose it themselves or are denounced by their priests, they shall undergo the censure of spiritual instruction according to what is just. A husband may bring complaint against his wife, and a wife against her husband, before the Church and its prelates, concerning the violation of their union, according to God’s justice. Yet not in such a way that husband or wife should seek another union. Rather, they shall either remain together in the uprightness of their union, or together abstain from such union, according to what is shown them through the discipline of ecclesiastical institution. They must not tear one another apart with serpentine laceration, but love one another with pure love; for neither man nor woman can exist unless they have been begotten by this coupling.

As My friend Paul testifies, saying: [Col. 0393B] “As woman is from man, so also man is through woman; but all things are from God” (1 Cor. 12).

This means: woman was created for the sake of man, and man was made for the sake of woman; for as she is from man, so man is from her, lest either be divided from the other in the unity of their offspring. For in one work they work as one, just as air and wind intertwine their operations. How is this so? Air is moved by wind, and wind is interwoven with air, so that all growing things are subject to them within their circuit.

What does this mean? Woman cooperates with man and man with woman in the work of children. Therefore very great crimes occur where fornication produces division in the days of the creation of children, because there man and woman cut off their own blood [Col. 0393C] from the foundation of its proper place and cast it into an alien place. The devil’s fraud and God’s wrath will remain with such persons, because they have violated the covenant which God established for them. Therefore woe to them when their sins are not forgiven.

But although man and woman cooperate with one another in their children, as has been shown, nevertheless all things—man, woman, and the other creatures—exist by divine disposition and ordering, because God made them according to His will.

Before the incarnation of my Son, certain persons among the ancient people had many wives at once according to their own will, because they had not yet heard the openly declared prohibition concerning this matter which, when he came into the world, my Son [Col. 0393D] set forth through the most proper ordering of this union between husband and wife, so long as they should live this life, according to the union proclaimed in Adam and Eve. For this union is to be practiced not according to human will but according to the fear of God; since it is better to have a lawful marriage according to the ordinance of ecclesiastical discernment than to seek fornication—although you human beings, disregarding this, exercise your lust not only with human beings but even with beasts.

Let upright faith and the pure love that acknowledges God be between husband and wife, lest, when their seed has been defiled through the devil’s art, divine vengeance strike them, as they bite and tear one another, and as they sow their seed inhumanly in the [Col. 0394A] wantonness of beasts. Therefore, when envy torments them after the manner of a viper, and when the stained excess of their seed is in them without fear of God and without human discipline, those born from them are often, by the just judgment of God and as a chastisement for this perversity, deprived of the proper formation of their limbs and cast down from the prosperity of their life—unless, accepting their repentance, I show myself merciful to them. For those who invoke me in repentance for their sins, I shall accept their repentance for love of my Son. Whoever raises a finger toward me in repentance—that is, whoever extends to me the groaning of his heart in repentance, saying, “I have sinned, Lord, before you”—my Son [Col. 0394B] shows me that repentance. He is priest of priests, because repentance offered to priests in love of my Son grants cleansing from sins to those who perform it.

Thus, by worthily performing their repentance, human beings come out from the jaws of the devil; for when he wished to swallow the hook of divine power, he grievously wounded his own jaw by it. Even now faithful souls pass through it from perdition to salvation. How? Because priests, being invokers of my name at the altar, receive the confessions of the people, where they show them the remedy of salvation. Therefore, so that they may have God merciful to them, let them not defile their seed amid diverse vices. For those who emit their seed in fornication or [Col. 0394C] adultery make their children, who are born from them in this way, more negligent. How? Does one who mixes mud or dung with pure clay make a durable vessel? So too, does one who defiles his seed through fornication or adultery beget children of strength? Yet many of these suffer from diversity in their dispositions and marrow; but many of them become prudent both for the world and for God. And with such persons the heavenly Jerusalem is filled, when, abandoning vices and loving virtues, they imitate my Son in chastity and great labours, bearing his martyrdom in their bodies according to their capacity for suffering.

But where I do not will children to be born of a man, there I take away the male powers of seed, so that it may not coagulate in the mother’s womb; just as I [Col. 0394D] deny the fruitful powers of the earth wherever I will to do this by my just judgment. Yet why do you wonder, O human being, that I permit children to be born in adulteries and in other crimes of this kind? My judgment is just. For from Adam’s fall I did not find in human seed the righteousness which ought to have been in it, when the devil drove it out through the tasting of the fruit. Therefore I sent my Son into the world, born of a virgin without any sin, so that through his blood—in which there was no defilement of flesh—he might take from the devil those spoils which he had seized in humankind.

For neither a human being conceived in sin, nor an angel without the covering of flesh, could rescue from the devil’s power a human being lying in sins and oppressed by bodily heaviness, except him who came without sin and possessed a body clean from sin [Col. 0395A] and who liberated humankind through his Passion. Therefore, although human beings are born in sins, I nevertheless gather them into the heavenly kingdom when they seek it faithfully. No perversity can take my elect away from me, as Wisdom testifies, saying: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them” (Wisdom 3:1).

This means: the souls of those who embrace the way of uprightness are, with devout affection, engaged in the works of their heavenly helper. Thus, because through good works they look toward heaven in the height of righteousness, the torment of perdition does not crush them; for the true light nourishes them in the fear and love of God.

But after Adam and Eve were expelled from the place of delight, they learned within themselves the work of conceiving and bearing children; [Col. 0395B] and so, falling from their disobedience into death, they conceived the sweetness of sin when they learned that they could sin. Yet, by turning my right ordinance in this manner into the lust of sin, when they ought to have known the stirring of their veins not in the sweetness of sin but in love of children, they gave it over, at the devil’s prompting, to lust; for, losing the innocence of their begetting, they delivered it into sin. Therefore, since this was accomplished not without diabolical persuasion, that same devil also cast forth his darts toward this work, so that it might not be completed without his prompting. For he said: “My strength lies in the conception of human beings; therefore the human being is mine.” And seeing that humankind must be a participant in his punishments because it had consented to him, he again said within himself: [Col. 0395C] “All iniquities are contrary to the most mighty God, because he is in no way unjust.”

And this same deceiver placed the greatest seal in his heart: namely, that the human being who had voluntarily consented to him could not be taken away from him. Therefore it was my secret counsel to send my Son for the redemption of humankind, so that humankind might be restored to the heavenly Jerusalem. No iniquity could resist this counsel, when my Son came into the world and gathered to himself all who wished to hear and imitate him by abandoning sins. For I am just and upright, willing no iniquity—the iniquity that you, O human being, embrace when you learn that you are able to do evil.

For Lucifer and humankind, at the [Col. 0395D] beginning of their creation, attempted to rebel against me and could not stand: they fell from good and chose evil. Lucifer embraced all evil and rejected every good; he did not taste it at all, but fell into death. Adam, however, tasted good when he accepted obedience; but he desired evil and accomplished it in his desire when he became disobedient to God. Why this happened is not to be investigated by you, O human being. Nor can mortal humankind know what was before the constitution of the world, or what will be after the last day; God alone knows these things, except insofar as he permits his elect to know them.

Moreover, that fornication which makes itself common among human beings is abominable before me, because from the beginning I established male and female [Col. 0396A] in honour, not in shame. Therefore those hypocrites who say that it is lawful for them to fornicate with whomever they wish according to the appetite of beasts are unworthy in my sight. Despising the honour and loftiness of their rational nature, they look to beasts and make themselves like them. Woe to those who, living in this way, persist in this shamefulness.

Nor do I will that kinship of blood should intermingle in marriage, where the ardour of love in consanguinity has not yet diminished, lest shameless love arise there through the recollection of kinship. Rather, let blood of another stock come together, which no longer feels any awareness of consanguinity burning within it, so that human discipline may govern its work. For milk [Col. 0396B], boiled once or twice, does not lose its flavour; but when it has been thickened and boiled for the seventh or eighth time, its powers having ebbed away, it has no pleasing taste except in necessity.

And just as awareness of consanguinity in one’s own spouse is not to be known, so also awareness of the kinship of a former spouse is to be abhorred in another union. Let no one join himself to such a union, as the Church also forbids through her teachers, who established her in much solicitude and honour. That in the Old Testament people were joined, by the command of the Law, within consanguinity of their own blood was done because of their hardness, so that they might have peace with one another and so that such firm love might be among them, lest the tribes, divided by joining themselves to the Gentiles, should break my covenant. [Col. 0396C] This remained until the time came when my Son, bringing the fullness of love, transferred the union of consanguinity in carnal coupling into another lineage, with modest shame.

Therefore, since the bride of this same Son of mine has now received in holy baptism the bond of my fear and upright justice, such a consanguineous union must now be far from her. For fornication without shame and without moderation of lust would be more inflamed toward shameful work in the embraces of a man and woman of familiar blood than in those of strangers. For I set out this work through this human being, to whom this matter in humankind is unknown, and who received this discourse not [Col. 0396D] from a human being but from the knowledge of God.

But what now? When a male is at a strong age, so that his veins are full of blood, then he is fertile in his seed. Then let him take to himself a woman in the betrothal of lawful institution, who, being likewise at a vigorous age, may receive his seed with modesty and bear him offspring in the way of uprightness. But before the years of his strength, a man must not emit his seed in the excess of lust; for this is a testing of sin at the devil’s prompting, should he attempt to sow his seed in the desire of lust before that seed can have proper coagulation in fervent heat.

And when a man is already at his strongest in the work of generation, let him not then exercise his powers insofar as he can at that time; [Col. 0397A] for if he then looks toward the devil, he performs a diabolical work and makes his own body contemptible, which is wholly unlawful. Rather, as human nature teaches him, in the strength of heat and abundance of his seed, let a man seek the right course with his wife; and let him do this with human discipline, for the sake of children.

But I do not will that this same work should be done during a woman’s separation, when she is suffering the flow of her blood, which is the opening of the hidden members of her womb, lest the flow of her blood cast out the received mature seed and thus the emitted seed perish. For then the woman sees herself placed in pain and confinement, experiencing, that is, a portion of the pain of her childbirth. Yet I do not condemn this time of pain in woman, for I gave it to Eve [Col. 0397B] when she conceived sin through tasting the fruit. Therefore a woman at this time ought to be relieved with great assistance of mercy. Yet let her keep herself within the hidden bounds of discipline—not, however, so that she bars herself from entering my temple, but rather that, by faithful permission, she enter it in the office of humility for her salvation.

But because the bride of the Son of God is always whole, a man whose open wounds have divided the integrity of his members through the touch of an injury shall not enter my temple, except with fear in a case of great necessity, lest he be seen as Abel was, whose whole members—he who was the temple of God—his brother Cain cruelly broke. Likewise, after a woman has borne offspring and the hidden members of her body have been ruptured, let her enter my temple only according to the law given her by me, [Col. 0397C] so that the holy sacraments of this my temple may remain inviolate from every defilement and pain of man and woman. For a most pure virgin bore my Son, and she was whole, without any wound of sin.

For the place consecrated in honour of my Only-Begotten must be whole from every corruption of bruise and wound, because that same Only-Begotten knows within himself the integrity of virgin birth.
