“But others tear themselves away from that image, attack it, and oppress its established ordinances. For these abandon the maternal womb and sweet nourishment of the Church, weary her with varied errors, and therefore tear apart her established laws with diverse oppressions. Some of these humbly return to her through the fruit of repentance, because, having sinned gravely, they punish themselves gravely through worthy repentance for the restoration of life. But others remain through contempt of hardening in the pride of death. Neglecting life, with hardened heart they receive the judgment of death because of their obstinate and unrepentant madness.

“As Ezekiel says in his mystical vision: ‘The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed in sorrow, and the hands of the people of the land shall be troubled. According to their way I shall deal with them, and according to their judgments I shall judge them; and they shall know that I am the Lord’ (Ezek. 7).

“What does this mean? When the soul in which royal rationality resides senses the presence of sinful delight, because it knows evil, it then takes on mournful assent. How? Because rationality, wisdom, and knowledge have been inspired in it by God; and therefore, even though it consents to the body, it nevertheless judges evil unworthy, sensing that it is not good. Hence, when it is polluted by diverse crimes through the working flesh, it draws deep sighs and pants after God.

“And when a criminal act has there been accomplished with the spirit of pride, then the body, like a dishonored prince, will be clothed in shame, exercising its dominion in uncleanness. For as a human being grieves when covered with vile garments, so too he mourns when a report of disgrace proceeds from him to his own shame. Therefore the wicked deeds of those persons who, in their evil acts, have been cast down to earth away from heavenly commandments, will be troubled, because they do not possess garments of salvation—that is, blessedness with God. For malignant disturbance will possess those who lack this happiness.

“Therefore, according to the way of iniquity in which they always stand—that is, cultivating the way of sin and setting no righteousness in the path of their heart when they are moved by the Holy Spirit—I shall deal with them thus, granting them no mercy. For because they do not understand the knowledge of good, they do not fear me; rather, with the frenzy of perversity they despise me, the Creator of all, doing whatever they will.

“Therefore I shall judge them according to their judgments, which are those deeds that they commit in their desires: rendering them no rewards of happiness, but setting penalties of perdition before them, because they offer me no honor. And in this they shall know that none can free them from it except me, who am Lord of all.

“But whoever sees with wakeful eyes and hears with attentive ears, let that person offer the kiss of embrace to these my mystical words, which flow forth from me, the Living One.”

## FIFTH VISION

[Col. 0475]

**SUMMARY.**—That the apostles and their spice-selling followers, namely the priests, surround the Church most splendidly with their teaching. An example from Abel. That ministers of the Church ought to preserve chastity. That those among them who live according to rule in the enclosure of obedience, without the care of the spice-sellers, acquire a heavenly reward. On the state of the most noble perfection of virginal joy. On the maidenly image. On the multitude wonderfully adorned which surrounds it. The words of John on the same subject. That virginity offered to God must be prudently preserved. That one who returns after violating the covenant of virginity will lack the flower of integrity; for she is received not as a mistress but as a handmaid. An example on the same subject. That there is a great difference between heavenly desire and earthly concupiscence, such that, unless humanity had been redeemed by the blood of the Son of God. On those who, imitating Christ’s Passion in the ardor of charity and being a living fragrance, take up the way of hidden regeneration. Words of the Gospel on the same subject. That the virginal order and this order which vows the way of hidden regeneration are not contained in the commandment of the law. An example from John on the same subject. That those who are a living order vowing the way of hidden regeneration should, for the necessity and benefit of the Church, undertake ecclesiastical governance, casting away the contagions of worldly matters. Gospel words concerning John. That in the clothing of these persons, unlike the clothing of other peoples, Christ’s incarnation and burial are signified. That the first light of day signifies apostolic teaching; dawn, the beginning of this manner of life; and the sun, the discerning path in Benedict, who is as it were another Moses. That those found approved in this manner of life should undertake an additional priesthood for the necessity of the Church. That no one should suddenly undertake their manner of life unless tested by inward examination. That the secular people, preserving God’s law, greatly adorn God’s Church. That neither husband should leave wife nor wife husband for this purpose unless both consent. Words of the Gospel. That the aforesaid ecclesiastical institutions strengthen the Church in her ranks and orders. That harmony must be preserved in every order, while diversity of customs, singularity, and novelty of life and clothing must be avoided. Words of John on the same subject. A comparison concerning craftsmen. That each person should humbly be content with the institution of his predecessors. Gospel words on the same subject. The Gospel concerning those who make laws for themselves according to their own hearts. Further words of the Gospel. That in these novelties God casts down some and silently tolerates others, whom nevertheless he judges in the future. That it is permitted to ascend from a lower rank to a higher, but not from a higher rank to a lower. An example concerning souls and angels. That those who are a living order vowing the way of hidden regeneration signify the grain of strong food; the spice-sellers, fruits of sweet taste; and the secular people, flesh. That these three ecclesiastical institutions proceed in two ways. That one who casts away the sign of religion received by the will of the heart will receive the judgment of strict examination. Words of David on the same subject. That those who receive the sign of feigned religion, bound not by love of God but by some worldly restraint, resemble Balaam. An example concerning Balaam. That one who foolishly receives the sign of religion and fulfills it badly goes to ruin. Words of Jeremiah on the same subject. That one who wishes to subject children to holy religious life should do this not imprudently but wisely, with their consent and without compulsion. An example concerning a field. That one who draws back those willing to follow God through the spite of malice commits sacrilege. Words of Moses. That one who voluntarily undertakes God’s service and afterward neglects it in contempt must be strictly recalled. Words of the Gospel. That those living under discipline who refuse all correction should be expelled lest they contaminate the Lord’s flock. Words of the Apostle on the same subject. That those who feign conversion are deceived, and those who convert with their whole heart are received by God. Words of David on the same subject. That God does not know one who has uttered unrepentant blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, or one who has hurled himself into death. Gospel words. Words of David on the same subject. That one upon whom the blasphemy of despair falls, if he resists torment, is more swiftly aided by God. That one falls into perdition who separates body and soul which God has joined. Words of the Gospel.

[Col. 0475B] After these things I saw that a certain brilliance, white as snow and transparent like crystal, shone around the aforesaid female image from the crown of her head to her throat. But from her throat to her navel another brilliance of red colour surrounded her. From her throat to her breasts it glowed like the dawn; but from her breasts to her navel it shone like purple mingled with hyacinth. And where it glowed like the dawn, it extended its brightness upward into the secrets of heaven, in which there appeared an exceedingly beautiful maidenly image, bareheaded, with somewhat dark hair, clothed in a red tunic flowing about [Col. 0476B] her feet.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying: “This is the flowering in the heavenly Zion, mother and flower of roses and lilies of the valleys. O flowering one, you shall be betrothed to the son of the mightiest king; and you shall bear him a most renowned offspring, when in your time you are strengthened.”

And around this same maiden I saw an immense multitude of people standing, brighter than the sun. All were wondrously adorned with gold and gems. Some among them had their heads veiled with white coverings, ornamented about with a golden band; above whose heads the likeness of the ineffable Trinity—as was shown to me above in a figurative manner—appeared, as though carved in a sphere upon those very veils. On their foreheads was the Lamb of God; on their necks, the form of a man; on the right ear, a cherub; and on the left, another angelic form. Thus from that likeness of the glory of the heavenly Trinity a kind of golden ray extended toward these forms. But among them appeared certain others who had mitres on their heads and the cloaks of episcopal office about their shoulders.

Again I heard a voice from on high saying: “These are the daughters of Zion; and with them are the lyres of lyre-players, every kind of musician, the voice of all gladness, and the joy of joys.”

But beneath that same brilliance, where it glowed like the dawn, I saw dense darkness appearing between heaven and earth, [Col. 0477B] so dreadful that human speech cannot utter it. And again I heard a voice from heaven saying: “If the Son of God had not suffered upon the cross, this darkness would in no way permit a human being to attain the heavenly brightness.”

But where the same brilliance shone like purple mingled with hyacinth, it burned, strongly binding the aforesaid female image. Yet another brilliance, like a white cloud, surrounded the same image from the navel downward, fittingly, though it had not yet extended beyond it. And these three brilliances, spreading broadly around the image, displayed in it many steps and ladders well and fittingly ordered.

But when I saw these things, I fell to the ground, my strength dissolved by the excessive trembling that had seized me, [Col. 0477C] and I could give no answer to anyone. And behold: a very great brilliance, like a hand, touched me; from this I recovered strength and voice. And again I heard a voice from it saying to me:

“These are great mysteries. Consider the sun, the moon, and the stars. I made the sun to shine by day, and the moon and stars to shine by night. The sun signifies my Son, who came forth from my heart and illuminated the world when he was born of the Virgin at the end of time, just as the sun illumines the world when it comes forth and rises near the end of night.

“But the moon signifies the Church, betrothed to that same Son of mine in a true and heavenly marriage. And as the moon continually has increase and decrease in its condition, yet does not burn of itself except insofar as it is kindled by the sun’s light, so too the Church is in a circuit of motion: her children often advance in the increase of virtues, and often fail in diversity of morals and in the scattering of adversities. Thus she is very often attacked in her mysteries by most rapacious wolves—by evil persons, Christians, Jews, and other unbelievers—and in this she is not kindled by herself unto endurance, but is enlightened in me through my Son so that she may persevere in good.

“But the stars, differing from one another in the brightness of their radiance, signify peoples of the various orders of ecclesiastical religion.”

Therefore you also see that a certain brilliance, white as snow and [Col. 0478A] transparent like crystal, shines around the foreseen female image from her crown to her throat. For apostolic teaching surrounds the Church of the faithful, the incorrupt bride of the Son of God. It proclaimed his most pure incarnation—he who descended from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, and who is the strongest and brightest mirror of all believers. Thus that teaching, shining most splendidly around the same Church, faithfully enclosed her from her beginning, when she first began to be built, until the time when she was able vigorously to swallow the food of life.

How? Apostolic teaching shone around the Church at its head when the apostles first began to build it by their preaching: namely, when, travelling through diverse places, they gathered [Col. 0478B] labourers who would strengthen it in the catholic faith, and who would themselves provide presbyters, bishops, and every ecclesiastical order, and faithfully establish the laws concerning men and women who are joined in marriage, and other such matters.

Accordingly, following this teaching are the dispensers of spices, bearing the likeness of the priests of legal testimony, who were placed under the law of circumcision to nourish peoples with inward food. Thus the apostles also chose those orders through which they adorned the Church by heavenly inspiration.

What does this mean? Their successors, bearing most healthful spices in their stead, faithfully pass through streets, villages, cities, and other places of regions and lands, proclaiming the divine law to the people. They are discerning fathers and stewards, appointed to set forth in their teaching ecclesiastical discipline for all people and to distribute to them the food of life. They must also show themselves such in their own lives, lest my sheep stumble at their works, but rather follow rightly after them. For they have the office of openly supplying the food of life to the people and discreetly ordering faithful offices for each person, while binding themselves so that they do not seek carnal union. For they ought to offer spiritual food to believers and an unblemished sacrifice to God, as was prefigured in innocent Abel, of whom it is written: “Abel also offered of the firstborn of his flock, [Col. 0478D] and of some of them” (Gen. IV).

What does this mean? At the rising of the dawning age, the sanctification of royal manifestation shone forth in him who was innocent in his life; and it powerfully touched the house of almighty God—not earth, but heaven. How? Because Abel, in his integrity, offered God both the intention of his will and the full performance of that same will: when he conceived in his heart to offer him the first produce which he possessed in his substance, and when he completed that also by perfect action. So too does the believer who honours the supreme Father and renders him due reverence.

Therefore, just as Abel was set over his flock, guarded it in order to feed it, and in simple devotion offered God the first offspring of it and the rich nourishment of those same offspring, [Col. 0479A] so too the aforesaid dispensers of spices, who have been set over the children of the Church—that is, Christ’s sheep—by his own dispensation, in order to feed them, must faithfully nourish them with the words of ecclesiastical discipline, strongly defend them from the snares of the ancient deceiver, and offer some gifts from them to the Inspector of all by sincere discernment.

How? If they cannot make them wholly perfect, let them offer God some fruit issuing from them: first, the upright intention of their good will, like the simple first shoot from the firstborn of their flock; and then the perfect work of action in that same will, like a sweet fruit from their fatness. But whence was it that Abel worshipped God so devoutly? The faithful chastity of integrity had impelled him to such devotion.

Therefore those established in consecration, who ought to offer God the most holy sacrifice, must approach his altar in the sweetness of chastity. For if they themselves are authors of corruption, how can they extend the hand of healing medicine to those wounded by corruption? Therefore, that they may confer healing remedy upon others with greater confidence, I will that they manfully imitate my Son in the love of chastity. If they fall, let them hasten to rise more quickly through repentance; fleeing, as naked, the disgrace of sin, seeking healing medicine, and faithfully following Abel, whose sacrifice was acceptable to God [Col. 0479C].

But those among them who, enclosed in subjection, restrain themselves in the love of my Son and observe in their conduct the rule against evil persons which they set forth by my inspiration—though they do not bear the pastoral care of the dispensers of spices—nevertheless, although they do not carry their burdens of anxiety, because they are subject to their superiors for the sake of eternal rewards, acquire for themselves with those same dispensers of spices a heavenly reward in the chosen city.

But that you see another brilliance of red colour surrounding the image from its throat to its navel means this: after the teaching of the apostles, when the Church was so strengthened that she could truly discern the health-giving food and transmit it to the inward parts of her strength, there arose the most noble perfection of ecclesiastical religion. It tasted heavenly sweetness with burning ardour and, binding itself most harshly, stretched itself toward the cooking of more hidden strength, [Col. 0479D] yet did not arrive at the division of carnal bitterness, because it rejected the union of human coupling.

How? The same brilliance glows like the dawn from her throat to her breasts, because this perfection spread itself from the taste of wondrous growth to the sweetest nourishment of ecclesiastical religion in virginal delight. And it shines from her breasts to her navel like purple mingled with hyacinth, because from most noble nurture they fortify themselves for the restraint of inward chastity, imitating the passion of my Son, which he faithfully bore in his heart for heavenly love.

Therefore where it glows like the dawn, it stretches its brightness upward into heaven’s secrets, because that perfection which flourishes in the honour of virginity wondrously directs its strength not downward to earthly things, but upward to those that are in heaven.

In it appears the most beautiful maidenly image, bareheaded and with somewhat dark hair. This is most serene virginity, innocent of every foulness of human lust: it has a mind naked of every bond of corruption, yet while its children are in this world it is not able wholly to leave behind the toil of darkening thoughts; nevertheless, it strongly opposes them in order to resist them. [Col. 0480B] Therefore it is clothed with a red tunic flowing about its feet, because it perseveres through the sweat of labour in virtuous works to the end of broad and blessed perfection, surrounded by a diversity of virtues and imitating him who is the fullness of holiness.

And as it is shown to you in the secret of heavenly light, it is the most noble shoot in the heavenly Jerusalem: namely, the glory and adornment of those who poured out their blood for love of virginity, and of those who, keeping their virginity for Christ in the brightness of humility, rested in the sweetness of peace. For it, being betrothed to the Son of almighty God, who is king of all, brought forth for him a most noble offspring: that is, the most excellent choir of virgins, when it was strengthened through advancement in the peace of the Church.

But that you see standing around this same maiden an immense multitude of people brighter than the sun, all wondrously adorned with gold and gems, means that the foremost choir of virgins embraces most noble virginity with most ardent embraces. They all shine before God with a brightness more fervent than the sun appears upon earth, because, trampling themselves underfoot, they have manfully conquered death. Thus they are most fittingly adorned in highest wisdom for the most brilliant works which they humbly performed for Christ.

Therefore some of them have their heads veiled with white coverings and ornamented with a golden band, because, shining in the glory of virginity, [Col. 0480D] they show that those who seek the adornment of virginity should cover their minds from every harmful heat and faithfully lay hold of the brightness of innocence, adorned with the most beautiful radiance of chastity.

Above their virtues appears the likeness of the ineffable Trinity, as was figuratively shown to you above, as if carved in a sphere upon those veils. For they show that human intentions must firmly and vigorously hold the honour of the heavenly and glorious Trinity—as was most truly prefigured for you in the vision of the mystery—in the embrace of love and the steadfastness of chastity.

And the Lamb of God on their foreheads, the form of a man on their necks, a cherub on their right ear, and another angelic form on their left [Col. 0481A] declare that in reverence for their chastity they shall imitate the gentleness of the Son of God, put away the arrogance of the proud neck, regard themselves as frail human beings, embrace true and unfailing knowledge in the favourable course of their hearing, and seek angelic protections in the adversity that meets this same hearing. Thus a golden ray stretches from the very likeness of the glory of the heavenly Trinity toward these forms, because the ineffable Trinity does not cease to work the wondrous miracles of its deep wisdom for unbelieving people who seek virtues and flee diabolic seductions.

But among them appear certain others who have mitres upon their heads and cloaks of episcopal office about their shoulders. For among those who flourish in the honour of virginity, some also stand in the heavenly city who, while vigorously bearing in the world the dignity of the ancient fathers and the glory of higher teaching, nevertheless did not lose the adornment of virginity.

Therefore, as you hear, all these who preserved their integrity with sighs for heavenly love are called daughters of Zion in the heavenly dwelling, because they imitated my Son in love of virginity. And with them are resonances of spiritual sounds, invocations of melodies of every kind, ornaments of the agility of prosperous minds, and the golden vision of shining stones and gems.

How? Because they have this from the Son of God: a sound comes forth from the throne, to which the entire choir of virgins sings together in greatest longing, sounding in harmony a new song. John, the beloved virgin, testifies to this when he says: “And it sang as it were a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders” (Rev. XIV) [Col. 0481C].

What does this mean? In those faithful people who, embracing chastity with good intention, preserve their virginity inviolate for the love of God, their good will breaks forth wondrously in praise of their Creator. How? Because in the dawn of virginity, which always clings to the Son of God, there is hidden a most mighty praise. No earthly office and no bond of law can prevent it from singing a heavenly song in a voice of exultation to the glory of God.

How? It is because, having a swift course, that song wondrously comes forth in the newness of freedom. Before the only-begotten Son of God—who is the true flower of virginity—was incarnate and, returning from the world to heaven, sat at the Father’s right hand, it had not been heard. But just as new customs, not seen before, when they are seen are received with wonder, so this new mystery, not heard before, became known in heaven as it resounded in honour of virginity before the majesty of God—for God could do this—and before the four wheels, which, running through the four parts of the world, bore like living creatures in the New Law the truth of all the righteousness and humanity of the Saviour; and before those ancients who, filled with the Holy Spirit, showed human beings in the Old Law the way of uprightness by their own course [Col. 0482A].

What does this mean? God softened, in the new grace, the severity of the ancient ordinance.

But because virginity is so glorious before God, those who have offered it to God of their own will should preserve it prudently. For this holy purpose, undertaken with the highest devotion of virginity, must be faithfully guarded. Therefore those who have entered upon this same sacrament must beware lest they go backward. For they are the dearest imitators of my Son when they offer themselves to God so that they are not bound by expectation of marriage nor burdened by worldly business, rejecting carnal union so that they may not be subjected to all the care of their flesh, but desiring to cling to the glorious innocence of the innocent Lamb.

Accordingly, the man who deliberates in his heart that he will join no rib [that is, no woman] to himself, but desires to persevere in the modesty of virginity for love of my Son, shall receive his fellowship, provided that he perseveres in the works of chastity itself. For he has offered these holy gifts to my Son in the vow of the most sacred covenant of ecclesiastical religion, for the glory of heavenly recompense.

But if afterward, abandoning this covenant, he commits adultery because of the shameful goad of his flesh, he has reduced his freedom to slavery. For he has wickedly corrupted, through the baseness of his pleasure, the honour of his neck, where he ought chastely to have imitated my Son; and because he uttered a lie, vowing to live chastely and not fulfilling it. Therefore, if he persists in the guilt of his rashness, [Col. 0482C] he shall endure the strict judgment of the most just Judge, because neither baseness nor falsehood shall appear in heavenly glory.

But if, before his end, he repents of this guilt with bitter tears, then the flood of my Son’s blood receives him, because he has abhorred his fault. Yet it does not restore him among his companions who flourish in the glory of integrity, because, abandoning their fellowship, he rejected the freedom of his covenant and reduced it to slavery to sin.

Likewise, the maiden who of her own will is offered to my Son in the most holy betrothal is most fittingly received by him, who wishes to have her thus joined to himself in his fellowship. How? That she may embrace him with chaste love, just as he loves her in his secret place; for she is always lovely to him because she seeks him rather than an earthly bridegroom. But if she afterward transgresses her covenant, she shall then be defiled before those who are in heavenly joy. Therefore, if she persists in that same rashness, she shall by just judgment lack heavenly glory. But if she repents, she is received as a handmaid and not as a lady, because she deserted the royal betrothal and loved another more than him whom she ought to have loved.

And he who violated her by seducing her, if he wishes to amend his guilt, must repent as though he had torn heaven apart, lest he fall into the destruction of death; for he rashly corrupted a heavenly betrothal.

What does this mean? If a great prince has a bride very dear to him [Col. 0483A] and a slave of his slaves corrupts her by adultery, what does that lord do? Truly, in the greatest anger he sends his executioners to destroy him, because he has dishonoured him in his own inward parts. But if that slave, then afraid, entreats all those sent men to intercede for him, and moreover casts himself weeping at his lord’s feet so that he may spare him, then that king, because of his goodness and because of their petition, allows him to live and restores to him the fellowship of his fellow slaves. Yet he does not reward him as he does the other lower-ranking servants and his familiar friends, although among other fellow slaves like him he grants him due favour.

So it shall be with the one who, by seduction, violated the bride of the eternal King. For the highest King, exercising his judgments in most upright zeal, delivers to destruction the one who, in this act, held him in his mind as though he were an object of mockery and forgetfulness. But if that wretched person, anticipating the day of this indignation, humbly entreats God’s elect to obtain pardon for him from their Lord, and furthermore looks weeping upon the humanity of his Saviour, so that by his grace he may be absolved from his sin, then the King, considering the blood poured out for the redemption of the human race and the love of the heavenly citizens, rescues him from his guilt and from diabolic power, lest he go to destruction, and places him in the salvation of blessed souls. Yet he shall not be adorned with the rejoicing of the royal betrothal in which the other friends of God rejoice with those sacred virgins consecrated to my Son by heavenly dispensation [Col. 0483C]; nor, as one who has lost the modesty of virginity, shall he be crowned with the adornment of virginity, although among his other elect he is granted joy in the heavenly city with inestimable recompense.

But that, beneath the same brilliance where it glows like the dawn, you see dense darkness appearing between heaven and earth, so dreadful that it exceeds even what human language can utter, means this: beneath virginal glory, between spiritual and carnal understanding, the fall of the first parent was openly known—most dense in the obscurity of unbelief, so that no human being could explain its terror.

How? Because in the incarnation of the Son of God, who was born of a virgin, heavenly desire ascended and earthly lust was shut out. For Adam’s transgression was wondrously restored to salvation through the blood of that same Son of God, whereas previously no one but God’s Only-Begotten, sent by the Father into the world, could dissolve it for entrance into heaven. Therefore, as you hear in the figurative manifestation, unless that same Son of God had poured out his blood for humanity’s salvation, that transgression would so oppress humanity that it could not attain the joy of the heavenly citizens.

But that, where the brilliance shines like purple mingled with hyacinth, it burns while strongly binding the aforesaid female image, signifies the perfection of those who, imitating the passion of my Son in the ardour of charity, vigorously adorn the Church in its restraint [Col. 0484A].

How? They are the lofty building of a rising treasure in divine counsel. For when the Church, now strengthened, had grown firm, a living fragrance came forth to adorn her, vowing the path of hidden renewal.

What does this mean? Then there arose a wondrous order which touched my Son in the likeness of his example. For as my Son came into the world set apart from the common people, so this company lives in the world separated from the rest of the people. As balm sweetly sweats from a tree in fragrance, so too this people first arose singly in the wilderness and in concealment, and afterward, like a tree, gradually spread its branches as it advanced in the multitude of fullness.

And I blessed and sanctified this people, for they are to me most beloved flowers of roses and lilies, which germinate in a field without human labour. Thus no law binds this people to seek that narrow way; rather, with me sweetly inspiring it, it enters upon it freely, without a command of law, accomplishing more than is commanded of it. Therefore it gains very great reward from this, as in the Gospel, where the Samaritan led the wounded man into an inn, as it is written: “On the next day he brought out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said: Take care of him; and whatever you spend beyond this, I will repay you when I return” (Luke X).

What does this mean? On the first day of salvation, namely when the Son of God, wondrously incarnate, remained bodily in the world, he accomplished many astonishing works in his humanity up to his resurrection, [Col. 0484C] by which he healthfully restored wounded humanity to true remedies. But on the next day, when after his resurrection all mysteries of truth had been openly set forth in the Church, he brought forth in figurative manifestation the New and Old Testaments, the most certain demonstration of eternal life and sweetest food for the believing people.

He gave these writings through his grace to the shepherds of the Church who guard his flock, and said to them in the words of his gentle admonition: “In ecclesiastical ordinances take care of the Christian host, redeemed in my blood and entrusted to you; let it be your concern that it not err by failing in anything pertaining to life. But whatever, beyond the things I handed down for you to observe, you add in your good will—doing more, that is, than was commanded you—I, who am your guide and saviour, now leaving the world and ascending to the Father, shall, when I return to judge the world and establish it in unfailing stability so that it may no longer weaken through passing times, repay you the reward of your labours and your good will with increased fruit.”

And I shall say: “O faithful and good servant, who serves faithfully: whoever adds more by his vow than is commanded him in the law shall receive a double reward, because I hold him glorious in my name, for he loved me greatly.”

And I say: neither the virginal order, nor this order of singular devotion, nor those who imitate them as those dwelling in the wilderness, are under a command of law. Just so, the prophets were not established by human beings under the carnal law; for these also live only by walking in my inspiration, and they add more than was commanded them. This is not done by the priestly order and the remaining institution of priestly office, because these were commanded in Abraham and Moses in the Old Testament. The apostles, taking them from that same law and rightly ordering them in the Holy Spirit according to my will, handed them down to the Church to be observed.

But apostolic teaching itself was established in the Gospel through my Son, when his disciples were sent to pour out the words of truth into the whole world. What then? When the apostles proclaimed the way of salvation to the people, the most brilliant dawn of the daughters of Zion arose in the love of my Son: those, namely, who strongly restrained their flesh and harshly mortified evil desire within themselves.

And as that chaste virginity then followed my Son in burning love, so also this order of singular devotion, greatly beloved by me, has imitated his incarnation. They are my upright temples, like the choirs of angels worshipping me; and they bear in their bodies the passion, death, and burial of my only-begotten Son. Yet they do not die by sword or other terrors by which human beings perish; rather, they imitate my Son by rejecting the will of their flesh, when they renounce all worldly things and adornments in which the world delights, as is written in the Gospel concerning John, the lamp of the world: “John himself had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt about his loins” (Matt. III) [Col. 0485C].

What does this mean? He in whom divine grace had raised up wonderful abstinence possessed through that same grace the defence of this virtue: in his mind he despised worldly honour and riches; and by the restraint which he imposed in the mortification of vices upon the pleasure of his flesh, he strongly subdued the wanton motions of his body. He instituted greater structures than his predecessors, that is, by walking hard and rough paths he trampled earthly desires underfoot.

How? By vigorously performing many works of virtue, he loved chastity ardently and also provided a path of healing for those who devoutly sought it. Therefore those who are a living fragrance, vowing the way of hidden renewal, should follow that same John, shining amid the greatest darkness of the age, through the keenest practices of blessed virtues in their lives. They should flee the foolish height and breadth of worldly things; restrain their body in the constraint of their expansive mind; reject evil desire; and, shining most serenely with instruments more excellent than those who before them simply walked in the Lord’s way and made simple dwellings, seize the sharp and narrow path, strongly trampling beneath their feet the things that belong to worldly pleasures.

How? By despising themselves and subjecting their bodies to Christ’s service in works of virtue, they turn aside from wantonness through severity of conduct, and by their good examples shine most brightly to other people. For they also faithfully imitate the angelic choir.

How? In their rejection of worldly things: for as angels neither seek nor desire earthly things, so these men wondrously follow them in this manner, despising everything transitory.

Therefore, just as my Son is the messenger of saving sacraments, the priest of priests, the prophet of prophets, and the builder of blessed towers, so also, if necessity arises, one among such people who possesses the root of fragrance with usefulness [Col. 0486B] may be messenger and priest, prophet and counsellor for ecclesiastical building. He is not to be wholly separated from them, provided only that the eye of brightness shines in him, that he does not sleep in regard to ecclesiastical use but remains watchful for its instruction, rejecting the occupation of worldly business and the contagions of worldly things.

For neither angels, priests, nor prophets conceal God’s justice; rather, at his command they set it forth in truth. This is as with John, who was not a reed shaken by the wind, and whose austerity these men follow. Concerning his likeness it is again written in the Gospel: “And all the region of Judaea and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem went out to him, and were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins” (Matt. III).

What does this mean? With sighs and groans they went out from the delight of vices to him, in whom divine grace worked: the whole devout will of simple confession and, in unanimous fashion, the whole effect of the vision of peace among those people whose hearts had been shaken by fear of death toward love of life.

How? Because John, the forerunner of truth, had made known to them both bitterness and sweetness. Therefore they sought from his uprightness the washing of repentance, so that, turning aside from evils and rising toward goods, confessing their crimes, they might deserve to attain him who would not announce to them a remedy in the shadow of antiquity, but would confer true salvation upon them in the light of newness [Col. 0486D].

But as John himself, teaching people who came to him and washing them with the river of irrigation, received their words of repentance to the honour of the coming Saviour, so now also, in the name of that same Saviour who came and brought salvation to the faithful, those who, through the inspiration—namely, of the Holy Spirit—add more to the work by the thundering testimony of sanctification must not neglect to do this. In their renunciation of worldly things they undertake a new austerity according to that likeness which, by the command of that same testimony of sanctification, they entered through renewal by Spirit and water, putting on the new human being through rejection of diabolic servitude.

But wherever the goads of pressing necessity present themselves, let them extend the hand of devout help to those who seek it—admonishing, raising up, and healing—provided that they have worthily attained that dignity through ecclesiastical promotion. In this they should faithfully imitate their predecessor, so that what he displayed as it were in shadow they may truly fulfill in the newness of light.

For they are the girdle of the Church, binding her very tightly, because they are occupied with the incarnation of my Son and also exercise the angelic order: namely, ceasing at no hour from singing with sound or praying in compunction—not with empty cries like useless dust or dry matter without the strength of compunction. They also do not refuse to work for their own need, yet do not seek worldly things with their hands, but strictly examine themselves in charity and humility.

O my most mighty and most loving people: I behold in them that affliction which my Son suffered in his flesh, because they too die according to his death when, abandoning their own will and subjecting themselves to discipline for the sake of eternal life, they walk according to the command of their superiors.

Therefore their clothing is not like the clothing of other peoples, because it too signifies the whole and incorruptible incarnation of my Son, which differs greatly from the generation of other human beings. For the legal authority of man and woman did not touch that incarnation, just as this people is not compelled to this restraint by any written law [Col. 0487C]; but whoever undertakes it by voluntarily vowing it for the love of God must persevere in it, lest, turning back, he fall as Lucifer did, who abandoned light and received darkness. Such clothing, according to the radiance of the heavenly spirits, circles about with the wings of its subtlety, and denotes the incarnation and burial of my Son; for he who offers himself to the strongest obedience has in his clothing the sign of the incarnation, and he who renounces secular affairs in works of righteousness bears in that same clothing the sign of his burial. Therefore, whoever is clothed in the same garment with pure intention is relieved by a wholesome remedy. And thus whoever receives it through the invocation of the Holy Spirit in blessings must not cast it aside; for whoever despises it by casting it off in persistent [Col. 0487D] evil shall be with him who scorned the angelic order and fell, to be buried in death.

What is this? This people has not been spurred to this restraint by a commandment of the law, but has undertaken of its own will to keep my covenant, and thus to illuminate my Church by its holy manner of life. How? As the dawn of the sun is seen after the first light of day, so this order arose after the voices of the apostles. What is this?

The first light of day denotes the faithful words of apostolic teaching; the dawn shows the beginning of this way of life, which first sprouted in solitude and caves after that blessed teaching; but the sun declares the discerning and well-ordered way in my servant [Col. 0488A] Benedict. I led him through burning fire, teaching him in the garment of his way of life to venerate the incarnation of my Son, and in the renunciation of his own will to imitate his passion. For Benedict himself is like another Moses, lying in a rocky cleft and tormenting and constraining his body with much harshness for love of life, just as the first Moses too, writing upon stone tablets a harsh and hard law by my command, gave it to the Jews. But as my Son pierced that same law through the sweetness of the Gospel, so too my servant Benedict made the purpose of this order—which before him had been a highly diverse manner of life—a discerning and level way through the sweetness of the Holy Spirit’s inspiration, and thereby gathered a very great company [Col. 0488B] into his religious order; just as my Son united the Christian people to himself through the sweetness of his fragrance.

And afterwards the Holy Spirit inspired sighs of life into the hearts of his elect, so that, as the crimes of peoples are washed away in the laver of baptism, they too might cast aside secular pomp in signification of the passion of that same Son of mine. How? For as a human being is converted from diabolic power in holy baptism, casting off the crimes of the old stain, so these people renounce earthly concerns in the sign of their garment, in which they also possess an angelic sign. How? For they have been appointed, in my will, as protectors of my people.

Therefore let those among them who are found tested in holy life be appointed pastors of my Church [Col. 0488C], because angels too, untouched by any stain of earthly concern, are guardians of my people. For as angels stand before God in a double honor, so the people of this religious order are in a double life. How? Angels serve God without interruption in heaven, and also continually protect human beings on earth from diabolic snares; so this people imitates the angelic order when, despising earthly things, it serves God daily, and when it also protects other people by its prayers from malignant spirits by day and night. Therefore, if my Church has no upright shepherd, then a company of this religious kind should aid her by crying out and weeping; and one found proven among them should, if necessary, receive the priesthood of oversight [Col. 0488D] and stoutly defend her in my zeal.

But no one should undertake the religious life of these people suddenly, as though awakening from sleep, unless he has first examined by an inward testing, in the restraint of his mind, whether he can persevere in this purpose; lest, if he has undertaken it of his own will in the covenant of blessing and afterwards, casting it aside in the perversity of his error, has mocked me without repentance, he perish miserably in the condemnation of death. Therefore, O my dearest children, who are greatly scattered in opposition, rise quickly in humility and charity, and agree manfully and with one mind to your holy purpose.

But, as you see, another radiance like a white cloud modestly surrounds the aforesaid female figure from the navel downward, though it does not yet extend beyond it [Col. 0489A]. This is the secular life, which, in the whiteness of serene intention, embraces the Church with the reverence of righteous assistance from the fullness of her burgeoning strength as far as that extremity to which she has not yet advanced in her children. How? Because around the navel is the germ of the members, from which the whole human race is generated. Thus there too in the Church is shown the secular people, through whom she is to be advanced to her full number in her orders, when kings and dukes, princes and governors with their subjects, and likewise other rich persons, poor persons, and needy persons living among the remaining people are signified there.

And through these the whole Church is greatly adorned; for when secular people faithfully keep the law of God established for them [Col. 0489B], they adorn the Church exceedingly, and embrace God with many embraces when they obey their teachers with sincere humility and devotion, and when, with almsgiving, vigils, continence, widowhood, and the other good works that belong to God, they discipline their bodies for love of God. Therefore those who keep the law established for them according to my will are very dear to me.

But if any one of them desires, in renouncing secular things, to bear the yoke of my liberty, let that person come quickly to me—unless he is joined in the bond of carnal union, which bond he must not rashly dissolve except by the will of the one whose partnership he possesses. How? Neither husband should leave wife nor wife husband for this purpose unless both will it; and then, if they have thus resolved, either both should remain [Col. 0489C] in the world or both should separate themselves from the world. For it cannot be that one foot remains in the body and the other is cut off from the body while the person remains whole. Likewise, it is not fitting that the husband cultivate the world while the wife abandons the world, or that the wife remain in the world while the husband flees the world, if they wish to find their beauty in the heavenly life; for if this is done indiscreetly and foolishly, it will be called not an offering but robbery.

Therefore those joined to one another in carnal union by legal right should live together in unanimity, and neither should foolishly tear himself or herself from the other without the other’s consent, and without the ordering or authorization of ecclesiastical authority, as it is again written in the Gospel: “Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX). What is this? In creating the human race, God took flesh from flesh and joined it into one union, establishing that this union should not be precipitately separated one from the other. How? Because in the union of man and woman, where flesh is joined to flesh and blood to blood by legal sanction, they are not to be divided from one another by their foolish precipitancy, unless this should happen for a just cause or by the reasonable devotion of both persons bound together; for God, in the secret of his wisdom, graciously ordained this union of male and female for the propagation of humankind.

And because this union was fittingly established by him, therefore foolish human desire must not make a cutting-off in these two parts, nor should either part carry the dowry [Col. 0490A] of its blood to an alien place. For just as God commanded that a human being should not kill another human being, so he also commanded that a human being should not, through the cruelty of fornication, sever his blood from its right place. Therefore a person should suppress the ardor of his desire and should not transfer his fire to an alien fire. For if this burning will should conceive the heat of another will through the fervent concupiscence of a stronger or weaker cause, then truly, by the desire of his mind and the binding embrace of that thought, they are coagulated into one. For the outward seeing eye kindles the inward heat into burning. And although that body does not commit this sin with that body, nevertheless the living will performs the work of ardor in them, so that all their inward parts are shaken because of their conscience [Col. 0490B]. Therefore let the barriers of the outward person be guarded with such careful watchfulness that the inward person may not be wounded through tasteless negligence.

And, as you see that these three radiances spread broadly around that image, this means that, in honor of the heavenly Trinity, the aforesaid three ecclesiastical institutions strengthen the blessed Church everywhere in a wondrous fashion, embracing her in the expansion of sprouting shoots and in the diffusion of blessed virtues. They also show in her many ranks and ladders, well and fittingly arranged: these are the different orders among both secular and spiritual persons, through whom the same Church, by goodness of conduct and discipline in virtues, leads her children, reared with [Col. 0490C] sweetest reverence, to heavenly things. How? When they despise earthly things and love heavenly things. What is this? Because they faithfully fulfill in divine love the legal precepts established for them.

But as there is one God in three persons, so there is one Church in these three aforesaid orders, whose founder is he who is the planter of all good things. Whatever he has not planted cannot stand. Therefore the institution which he has not established will fall into great delusions. How? Because God has not planted those who attempt to ascend to higher things on the breath of pride and refuse to be subject to their superiors. This occurs where a lesser order strives to raise itself above a greater [Col. 0490D] order established in my will by the ancient counsel of the chief masters; and where some wish to extend themselves in diverse signs of their clothing according to their own customs, as they imagine in their madness—as though the order of angels wished to raise itself above the order of archangels.

And what would this be? They would be as nothingness and emptiness, who would wish in their vanities to divide the rightly established orders of God in this way. But this ought not to be: that anyone should summon those who, in the madness of their diversity, always wish to be new in their purpose, and are untrained in the knowledge needed to express what is in their minds, abandoning the well-trodden way and the well-smoothed ark of the ancient Fathers, which the Holy Spirit inspired in them. Therefore [Col. 0491A] many of these people, in great pride, abandon the established ordinances which the Church possesses in the ancient Fathers; and they do this in very many schisms of their diverse institutions.

For they wish to be called fruitful trees in their various circuits; but they cannot even be called empty reeds, as is shown to beloved John concerning him who, withering in time, is cast away, as it is written: “I know your works: that you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Apoc. III). What is this? O fool, who withers shamefully within yourself, I, who know secrets, see with my all-knowing eye all the works of your desires. For you have not altogether escaped the works that belong to the fire of the fiery illuminator [Col. 0491B], nor have you altogether cast away works that bring the ice of cold rigor.

How? You are neither wholly cold in evil works nor wholly fervent in good actions; but, hanging in both through the instability of your mind like a lukewarm wind, you do not know which you are, because you consider neither the deserved penalties of evil nor the worthy rewards of good. How? Because you gaze into so great a depth that you cannot find its bottom, and because you climb so high a mountain that you cannot ascend its summit. O, it would be better for you to know yourself an unprofitable servant and a sinner than to be so situated in time that you scarcely look toward righteousness. For if you were separated from good actions, you would recognize yourself as a sinner; [Col. 0491C] or if you withdrew yourself from evil works, you would possess some hope of life.

But now you are like a lukewarm wind, which brings neither moisture to fruits nor imparts heat to them. You are like one beginning and not one perfecting; for you touch good in its beginning but are never nourished by it in perfection—like a wind that strikes a person’s mouth, and not like food that descends into his stomach. Which, then, is dearer: an empty sound or a perfect work? But a perfect work is more acceptable than an empty sound. Therefore work in the silence of humility and do not exalt yourself in pride, for those will be counted as nothing who reject the fellowship of sanctification of those who love me in the service of gentleness. Through foolish pride they pursue what they disdain to fulfill through sweet meekness [Col. 0491D].

But if, by beginning in rectitude, you attempt to enter into the force of my words, which provide food to the faithful, and if then, growing dull in them and showing no sweetness of righteousness touching you, you fall into worse things, then I too, because of the lukewarmness of your negligence, shall begin to cast you out, expelling you from that same force of my words. For, showing no savor of sweetness through the efficacy of your action, you do not pant after the inner things of blessed reception. Therefore, cast out in this way, you will be trampled down, just as food is thrown from a person’s mouth because of the tastelessness of its flavor before it is received into the stomach.

But what now? Winds fly, and the noises of winds resound [Col. 0492A]; but roots do not flower and do not produce shoots. For those who ought to be under my yoke are wanton and do not walk according to discipline. What is this? They leap over the straight way and make for themselves many useless tabernacles. Such people have no fervor of righteousness but grow dull in themselves. They burn neither in the law established for them nor act according to the manner of life of their preceding fathers; rather, each plants a certain singularity for himself within himself, sets himself a law according to his own will, and thus, in his own thoughts and in great instability, raises himself to flight through inflated pride. And because these persons do not adhere to the right covenant of their fathers, they always wander, new and untrained, in great instability [Col. 0492B], here and there according to their own will.

Therefore I compare them also to foolish builders. When they erect a great building on high, they do not imitate the prudence of those builders who, excellently taught in many tools and tested by diverse trials of construction, know well all things belonging to building and arrange all their implements properly. Rather, empty and foolish, they trust in themselves because they wish to seem wiser than others, and so arrange their buildings that they are unstable in storms and consequently are thrown down by winds, because they are set not upon rock but upon sand. So too do those [Col. 0492C] who, trusting in themselves in their pride, wish to appear wiser than their ancient fathers and refuse to walk according to their covenant. They establish laws for themselves according to their own will in great instability, and therefore are very frequently shaken into sins by diabolic temptations, because they rely not upon Christ but upon the instability of their own conduct.

Therefore, lest the inspiration of the Holy Spirit that worked in the ancient Fathers be emptied through proud inflation, I wish it to suffice for the faithful person, in humility, that which has been established for him by his predecessors; lest, if he vainly desires more than he ought humbly to have sought, he later withdraw, grown lukewarm, from it [Col. 0492D], and thereby receive the shame of confusion, as it is written in the Gospel: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place, lest someone more honorable than you be invited by him, and the one who invited both you and him come and say to you, ‘Give this man place,’ and then you begin with shame to occupy the lowest place” (Luke XIV).

What is this? When you have been admonished by heavenly inspiration to come through your faithful labors to that tabernacle which always abounds in nuptial life, so that it constantly rejoices in sincerity, honor, and sanctification—in the virgin branch and in the blessed mother, namely the Church—and does not grieve in corruption, confusion, and the casting down of its shoot and flower, then restrain your mind in humility and do not raise it in exaltation [Col. 0493A]. How? When, in the love of God, you have cast secular concerns from your body, then you will rise like a most beautiful flower, flowering without dryness with the Son of God in the heavenly Jerusalem, in whom all the adornments of souls appear. For the old human being brings forth all human abominations, but the new builds up all the sanctification of virtues.

Therefore, when you have come to this sanctification, blush to imitate the ancient serpent, who cast himself down from the place of blessedness through the appetite for empty glory. What is this? If you see someone more adorned than yourself, beware lest you rise above him through the desire of your mind, saying: “I wish to be above him,” or, “I wish to be as he is.” If you exalt yourself in this way, are you then a faithful servant, when you provoke the Lord to anger, setting yourself against him? But if you recognize someone as possessing a stronger gift of nature, grace, or fortune than you possess, and then disparage him through envy, you do not walk on the level way but proceed by bypaths.

Therefore strive to serve God in humility and not to revel in pride; nor exalt yourself above him through the vanity of pretense—him who, under just examination, shines with a greater desire for eternal life than you burn, being thus invited to the summit of that same blessedness by heavenly ardor, by him who graciously reveals himself to all who love truth. Lest, coming with his all-knowing eye, he who called you through the service of humility and called him through the gift of charity by the inspiration of blessed [Col. 0493C] admonition should distinguish you by his righteous judgment, saying: “You who have raised yourself through blazing pride to a place whose companion you are not, leave your empty glory, and give to this beloved one of mine, in the office of subjection, the height of honor which you have rashly seized.”

And what then will become of you? For if you are cast down in this way, you will begin to feel through the narrowness of sorrow and sadness the extremity of rejection, and you will shrink from yourself thus cast out, because the guardian of souls will take from you the alien honor which you fraudulently invaded. For, opposing yourself to him, you tried rashly to seize what you ought not to have possessed; therefore what you wished to possess will be taken from you, and what you did not wish to possess will be given to you. Thus also, when a lesser order exalts itself above a greater one, it is cast down and crushed by my just judgment [Col. 0493D], because I do not will pride to stand otherwise before my eyes than in the abasement of confusion. For if a maidservant exalted herself above her mistress, she would be so much the more despised by all who looked upon her because she attempted what she ought not to have desired.

Therefore those who make laws for themselves according to their own hearts and do not seek my will in this come more thereby to abasement than to advancement, as my Son again testifies in the Gospel, saying: “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. XV). What is this? Every shoot of knowledge in heart, mind, and conduct arising in that fertility of nature by which a human being lives—when a person sows it in himself in such a way that afterwards, burning in heat, it is joined to him according to his wish to bring it to completion—namely, when it is displaced through exaltation of mind, wantonness of flesh, excessive defilement, a pretext of excuse, or alternation of activity, proceeding imprudently upward or downward, neither discerning what kind of foundation it has nor caring to know whether it is useful or useless: truly this will be destroyed by righteous judgment. For that Father, who is the inhabitant of heaven and of all righteousness, did not plant such a planting; and therefore, cast out, it will wither, because it did not rise from the dew of heaven but came from the sap of flesh [Col. 0494A].

How? Because, in doing this work through his foolish knowledge, a human being was unwilling to look to the righteousness or will of his Creator, but looked instead to him who tirelessly agitates the wheel of his flesh. For that which sometimes seems good to people, when they refuse to fix their eye keenly upon God, through the deception of their minds—if the inspiration of the Holy Spirit does not warm it—will go to destruction, because this empty glory passes away.

For when vain people are afflicted by weariness in one matter, they are made new in another by empty glory, frequently exalting themselves in pride, stimulation, and a spirit of jealousy; and also frequently contending in annoyance, indignation, and opposition against other institutions which have flowed from me, and likewise oppressing one another in the other good things which are not directed toward the dullness of weariness but toward advancing day by day in the ardor of desire. For what has flowed from [Col. 0494C] me always gives the soul a sweet and pleasant taste in one who advances perseveringly, and does not look backward in instability.

Therefore blessed is the person who, trusting in me, places his hope and the beginning and end of his works not in himself but in me. Whoever does these things will not fall; but whoever wishes to stand without me will go to ruin. And who are those who make themselves new through empty glory and trust in themselves because of the weariness they suffer in my commandments? For I am not to be despised in my gifts as an old garment is burdensome in human thoughts, since they are always new in simplicity, and the older they are, the dearer they are.

Therefore whatever people devise in themselves without my inspiration, in vanity of conduct, will melt away through their empty pursuits; and although it may sometimes seem to stand in human sight, yet, cast away from my eyes, I regard it as nothing, as it is written in the Gospel: “Let them alone; they are blind leaders of the blind. But if a blind man gives guidance to a blind man, both fall into a pit” (ibid.). What is this? Let those who are perverse in their deeds melt away in their perversity, because they refuse to correct themselves in the uprightness of good works. And because they call themselves righteous in their own estimation while they are vain in their actions, they become blind through that very complacency, because they disdain to walk in the way of righteousness and propose the way of iniquity rather than truth to those people [Col. 0495A] who hasten to follow them in evil works.

Therefore those who in this way lack the sight of rectitude, thinking themselves righteous while they are unrighteous, fall together into the pit of despair when they show the way of false righteousness to persons ignorant of the way of true teaching; for neither these nor those know where they are going. Yet among these, in my indignation, I sometimes cast down certain things openly before human beings; other things I sometimes silently tolerate before human beings through the moderation of clear vision; nevertheless, I avenge them in the future by the weighing of my just judgment. Therefore let the faithful person strive to ascend to the height of virtues, and not descend to the depths of secular things. How?

One who is on a lower rank can ascend to a higher [Col. 0495B] one; but one who is on a higher rank ought not to decline to a lower. What is this? For praetors can attain to dukes, and dukes can rise to kings; but it is not fitting for kings to descend to dukes, nor for dukes to lower themselves to praetors. For if kings subjected themselves to dukes, or dukes submitted themselves to praetors, all the people would cry out indignantly and hold them in derision.

Thus those who are secular can enter upon the way of the aforesaid *pigmentarii* (“spice-dealers”); and those who are on the way of these same *pigmentarii* can pass to the aforesaid persons who are “a living fragrance, vowing the way of secret regeneration.” It is not fitting that those who are a living fragrance, vowing the way of secret regeneration, should pass down to the *pigmentarii*, nor that the *pigmentarii* should fall back into the secular state. But if those who are a living fragrance, vowing the way of secret [Col. 0495C] regeneration look toward the *pigmentarii*, or if the *pigmentarii* pass over to the secular: alas, alas, alas! will be spoken over them by the souls of the righteous, and they will be held before me in rejection, unless they return through worthy repentance. For if a higher rank falls upon a lower one, both will be destroyed. So it will also be with those who abandon their right path and walk backward.

For who, having put on my Son, could put on such a son? No one—and truly no one. But rejoice in your Father, because I often see greater persons among the lesser, and find lesser persons among the greater; for pride falls and humility rises.

Therefore have peace, charity, and humility among yourselves, as the souls of the righteous have with angels [Col. 0495D], and angels with archangels. For the souls of the righteous do not envy the office of angels, nor do angels disdain the glory of archangels. What is this? Archangels show greater things in greater necessity; angels announce lesser things in frequent interchange; but the faithful people humbly obey. Therefore let each person faithfully exercise his or her office. How? Those who are “a living fragrance, vowing the way of secret regeneration,” when a greater occasion of ecclesiastical necessity arises, should recall the unavoidable reasons for their assistance as archangels do. And those who exercise themselves in the work of the *pigmentarii*, with continual determination in frequent matters concerning the business of their institution, as angels do; and let people who desire [Col. 0496A] to attain the highest blessedness faithfully receive their words.

How? For those who are “a living fragrance, vowing the way of secret regeneration,” are like grain, which is dry and strong food for human beings; so too that people of mine is harsh and hard to the taste of the glitter of secular things. But the aforesaid *pigmentarii* are like apples, which offer a sweet flavor to those who taste them; so they too make themselves pleasant to people through the usefulness of their office. The common secular person, however, is reckoned as flesh, in which chaste birds are also found; for those who live in the world, living carnally, beget children, yet among them are found imitators of chastity—namely widows and continent persons—who fly toward heavenly desires through the appetite for good virtues.

But these same orders [Col. 0496B] of ecclesiastical institution move along two ways. How? Those of spiritual persons and of secular persons. How? As day and night. What is this? Day possesses the brightness of the sun and the serenity of shining air, which signifies that spiritual persons contain in themselves both the order of those who are a living fragrance, vowing the way of secret regeneration, and the order of the aforesaid *pigmentarii*. But night holds the light of the moon with the stars and the darkness of shadowy obscurity, which shows that secular persons contain in themselves both righteous people shining in their works and sinners weighed down by the darkness of offenses.

But whoever has left the night of secular persons and, for love of life, has turned to the day of spiritual persons must be steadfast in this deed, lest, if he walks backward, he be likened to the old Adam, who, transgressing the commandment [Col. 0496C] of life, was driven out into secular miseries. Therefore let no one be hasty in abandoning the world and boldly entering my covenant of his own will unless he has first been examined in a great testing; for whoever has received my Son through the tunic, I do not will him to leave him. For one who has clothed himself in his incarnation and taken his cross into his hands—would it be fitting for him to cast aside his Lord? By no means.

Therefore attend to these things. If a person has confessed in the will of his heart and vowed in the devotion of his soul to bear my yoke in the renunciation of secular things; if then, in that very ardor of his heart, through the will of his longing soul, he has received the sign of religious life in the seasoning of righteous intention [Col. 0496D], let him remain in it, lest, if he afterwards casts it aside in contempt through persistent evil, he receive the judgment of strict examination. What is this? Because he despised him whose sign he received in himself and then trampled underfoot, just as the Jews despised him when they fastened him to the cross in the madness of unbelief. For as the Jews did not fear that wickedness, so this person does not fear to cast aside the same passion in his vow.

For what a human being promises me, that he must also render, as David testifies, saying: “I shall enter into your house with burnt offerings; I shall render to you my vows, which my lips uttered” (Ps. V). What is this? Through the intention of good and righteous action I shall enter, O my God, into the establishment of your most holy gift, namely, leaving behind the bed of my pleasure in burning desire [Col. 0497A], so that nothing is sweeter to me than to pant after you, Creator of all things. And therefore I shall render to you the vows which my mouth uttered with my soul, because I wish to fulfill what I had first promised you, the just Judge, in my burning desire: namely, that I should direct my actions toward you—a thing which I foolishly transgressed. But now, desiring to return to you, I wish to avoid evil and do good, because the rationality and understanding burning within me seek, through the discernment of true discipline, rather to pant after you, the living God, than through the folly of false opposition to imitate the devil.

Therefore, O human being, when you have offered your heart to me in this way, consider how you may fulfill it prudently. For my eye sees most keenly what the will [Col. 0497B] of a human being says to me. Where what is mine is concerned, I require it most strictly. Therefore, O foolish and more than foolish persons, why do you impose upon yourselves such great burdens, thinking it so easy for you to abandon your carnal will? For by the law given you from my commandments you are not compelled to leave the world unless you have first exercised yourselves through many labors, so that you may be able to put a bridle upon the carnal desires that are within you.

But you are like a lukewarm wind: when vainglory has puffed up your mind, then out of some hardship you speak thus, saying: “I no longer wish to toil in the world, but I resolve to flee from it swiftly. And why should I wear myself out in fruitless labor?” But [Col. 0497C] when you say these things within yourselves, you think that they will end as you have planned. For many seek me with an unstable mind, so that they are marked only outwardly by the sign of religious life; they do not seek me with pure eyes, nor do they simply examine themselves in true teaching, to see how they may escape the devil who desires to devour them. just as the dove, which, looking into the purity of water, sees the hawk attempting to snatch it and escapes; but they do not thus escape the devil when they see him approaching in the Scripture of teachings; rather, in the sudden sleepfulness arising in them from the blindness of their mind, they run to me like a lukewarm wind.

For some, casting off not their own will but only their worldly condition, undertake the spiritual religious life [Col. 0497D], because, enduring many miseries and privations in the world, they cannot possess riches; and therefore they leave the world because they cannot have it as they would wish. Others are stupid and foolish in relation to the world, so that they are despised by other people and unwilling to govern themselves; and therefore they flee the world because they are mocked by it. Others, suffering bodily weakness and infirmity and laboring greatly amid these calamities, leave the world not for my sake but in order to relieve these pains more pleasantly. Others endure such straits and oppression from their carnal masters, to whom they are subject, that they withdraw from the world out of fear of them—not in order to obey my commandments, but so that their carnal lords may no longer exercise their power over them [Col. 0498A].

All these come to the spiritual religious life not because of heavenly love, but because of these earthly troubles that they endure. They do not consider whether I am salty or tasteless, sweet or bitter, a dweller in heaven or on earth. What is this? They pay heed neither to the seasoning nor to the sweetness of the Scriptures; nor do they consider how people who seek what is above dwell in their hearts. And because they are unwilling to search these matters out, they cast away fear of me and proceed according to their own desires; therefore they are strangers from both sides and are called fugitives. Hence I do not say that they have left the world and come to me; rather, they stand accused in this: they fear the servant and despise the Lord, because they follow earthly motives [Col. 0498B]. They do not revere me; and therefore they are called timid in small things and bold in great ones.

Thus they are also like Balaam, who, seeing the Israelite people beautiful in their tents, desired with a feigned mind to have his dwelling among them, saying: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last things be like theirs” (Num. 23). What is this? When a person is at some time shaken by sighings of the soul so as to begin works of righteousness, then, as desire rises up, he longs for them mournfully, saying within himself: “I, wretched as I am, hindered by many sins and obligations, earnestly desire that, by rejecting carnal lusts, my soul may abandon all the wickedness of iniquity, and that through that contrition by which the righteous despise themselves, it may remain in the dwelling-place of good works” [Col. 0498C]. How? So that my end may be found in upright actions, like those people who work God’s righteousness: so that the completion of my good works may equal the beginning of their righteous intention.

But if the person who says these things within himself, after the time of those sighings has passed, is assailed by temptations of malignant spirits and, overcome by carnal desire, returns to wickedness, he does what Balaam himself did when deceived by the evil of covetousness. How? Although Balaam was afterward touched by that schism through which he had earlier wished to curse my people—when I opposed him through my angel and his own ass—yet I brought him in my zeal to the point that he blessed that same people with the blessing of the words which I had placed in his mouth [Col. 0498D]. After that desire by which he had wished, in his death, to be made like the Israelite people, he returned to his former schism and, for the wages of death, by his counsel scattered my people through fornication, as he had promised, saying: “Yet, going to my people, I shall give counsel what your people shall do here at the end time.”

What is this? Namely: “When I return to the path of my desires that concern the adornment of the flesh, then I shall enter into those lusts which I formerly knew.” How? “For I know what is in my flesh, to which I honestly render service; and I, who am steeped in these matters that are always present to it, show you, O human being—who likewise burn in the same delightful things—a goad in the hidden place of my mind for your desires. By the suggestion of my pleasure I kindle your smoldering ardor so that, through awareness of the marketable earthly things flourishing in your heart, you extinguish that burning desire by which you formerly yearned for those works called holy [Col. 0499A], thus setting an end to them and abandoning them at a convenient time as though you had never known them.”

Therefore, O human being, just as Balaam, after that upright desire by which he formerly looked upward, bent himself downward to deceitful lusts, so also do those who seek me falsely. When they see those who have truly rejected the world walking simply and persevering praiseworthily and truly in a strict and blessed manner of life, they call them beautiful and sweet, and immediately, in a sudden impulse, take up their way of life, desiring to live according to them [Col. 0499B]. But after they have joined themselves to them, just as Balaam looked upon the Israelite people, they are often recalled to carnal desires through the various wickednesses that they previously had in their hearts while they were in the world, because those desires had formerly ruled them.

Therefore, when they are thus entangled, they pollute my chosen flock with their poison and hostility, shaking it with many storms and scattering it by the counsel of their wickedness.
