Therefore you have become nothing through your pride, by which you fell from every glory of salvation; for you have absolutely no strength, no blessedness, nor shall you be found ever again to possess any glory in the eternity of the heavenly realm, because you are confounded [Col. 0575C] in them for ever without end.

But that you saw that great radiance which had been withdrawn from them suddenly return, at their extinction, to the very one seated on the throne means that the clear and great splendour which the devil lost through his pride and obstinacy, when the seed of death entered into him and all his followers—for Lucifer was of purer light than the other angels—returned to God the Father from whom it had come forth and was preserved in his secret place. For the place of the glory of that splendour ought not to be vacant; rather, God preserved it for another created light.

For the splendour of him whom God commanded to rise naked and not covered with flesh—that is, the devil with all his company, [Col. 0575D] though bright in splendour—he preserved for the clay which he formed into a human being, covering it with the most lowly nature of earth, lest it exalt itself into the likeness of God. For he whom God created bright in much splendour but not covered with so frail and wretched a covering as the human being has could not stand in his pride, because there is only one God without beginning and without end in eternity. Therefore, among crimes, the most wicked is for anyone to represent himself as God.

Now I, the heavenly God, preserved the illustrious light which I withdrew from the devil because of his evil, carefully concealing it with myself, and gave it to the clay of earth which I formed in my image and likeness. It is as when a person’s son dies and his inheritance does not pass to his children [Col. 0576A] because he died childless: the father takes the son’s inheritance back to himself and appoints it in his mind for another son not yet born to him, intending to give it to him when he is born from him.

For the devil fell without an heir—that is, without a good work in right intention—because he never did or began anything good. Therefore another received his inheritance, who also fell but nevertheless had an heir, namely the beginning of obedience; for he received it with devotion, although he did not complete the work belonging to it. But God’s grace completed that work in the incarnation for the salvation of peoples, restoring the good inheritance. Therefore humankind received its inheritance in Christ, because it did not disdain God’s commandment in the beginning, whereas the devil altogether did not desire the service of his Creator in goodness, but honour in pride; hence he did not receive his glory, but perished in perdition.

[Col. 0576B] And as Goliath rose up despising David, so the devil raised himself in presumption, wishing to be like the Most High. And as Goliath, ignorant of David’s strength, despised him as altogether worthless, so the devil, swollen with pride, scorned the humility in the humanity of the Son of God, who, born into the world, sought in all things not his own glory but the glory of the Father. How? The devil did not desire to imitate this example, submitting himself to his Creator as the Son of God submitted himself to his Father.

Nevertheless David cut off Goliath’s head in the hidden strength of God, as it is written by [Col. 0576C] inspiration of the Holy Spirit: “David, taking the head of the Philistine, brought it to Jerusalem, but he placed his arms in the tabernacle” (1 Sam. 17). This means the following. My most mighty Son took the spoils and plunder of the devil when he cast down the head of that ancient serpent. Where? In the Virgin’s womb, which crushed this head. Through whom? Through her same Son. What is this crushing? Holy humility, appearing in mother and son, struck the first beginning of pride, which is the devil’s head.

Thus the victorious humility of my Son according to the flesh brought that head into holy Church, which is the vision of peace, showing it that through this most mighty humility the devil’s pride had been slain. But his most mighty weapons are his manifold [Col. 0576D] vices, by which he overcame the human race, which worshipped him as God, terrifying it by his vicious arts as weapons commonly terrify people. My Son shattered these weapons, placing them in his tabernacle—that is, in the passion of his body when he suffered upon the cross. Hence he also left this battle in the tabernacles, that is, in the bodies, of the elect members of his body, so that they too may divide the devil’s weapons with him. How? So that, as he conquered the devil in his passion, they too may conquer him by restraining themselves in their desires and not consenting to his vices.

And according to this likeness, as Goliath’s glory was given to David, so I gave to Adam and his race the glory that was taken from the first angel—namely, to that race which confesses me and keeps my commandments—after the devil’s pride had been slain. But whoever has ears of inward perception, keen for hearing, let that person pant after these words in the burning love [Col. 0577A] of my mirror, and write them in the conscience of his or her soul.

## SECOND VISION

[Col. 0577]

**SUMMARY.**—That faith, great in power, arose openly in Abraham’s circumcision. That faith is joined to fear of the Lord, and fear of the Lord to faith. That the faithful build good works upon faith throughout the four parts of the earth. On the four squares. That a person ought to walk humbly and wisely flee the snares of the devil. On the four corners of the building and what they signify. Again, another interpretation of the same corners. That people are given by God the Father fortification and defence for good works, and are watchful because they are flesh of ashes. On contemplative knowledge. Words of Paul. Words of Solomon. On the operation of two causes. That right institutions arose in Abraham and Moses. That contemplative knowledge began to appear in Noah, while iniquity nevertheless reigned without interruption until Abraham and Moses. Words of Paul on the same matter. That upright work was shown in Abraham and Moses; transparent righteousness in the Incarnation of the Son of God; and burning work through baptism in the Church, enduring to the end of the world. Words of David on the same matter. That Christ’s members still remain incomplete in his elect, and that the Church still lacks the future perfection which it shall possess. How the number ten, diminished through Adam, rose in the Son of God to ten, and ten to a thousand. Words of the Gospel on the same matter. That human sins are erased in Christ’s five wounds. That through the Holy Spirit inspiring the five senses, a human being discerns good and evil. That a human being should labour in soul and body to avoid evil and do good in prosperity and adversity. That the human mind ought to possess wisdom and discernment in order to know God. That a human being, composed of four elements, should worship the catholic faith with equal devotion. That the faithful person should ascend from virtue to virtue. That the Son of God was sent into the world at the time preordained by the Father, in order to accomplish the Father’s will in the redemption of humankind. That no person can investigate the pride of evil or its end in a creature at work, nor the beginning or end of heavenly righteousness and the just dispensation of God’s will.

[Col. 0577B] Then I saw, within the circumference of the circle extending from the one seated on the throne, as it were a great mountain joined to the root of that immense stone upon which the cloud, with the throne and the one seated upon it, was placed, so that the stone appeared raised in height and the mountain spread out in breadth. Upon that mountain stood, as it were, a quadrangular building formed in the likeness of a square city, with a somewhat oblique position. One of its corners faced east, another west, one north, and another south.

The building bore around its circumference one wall of two forms: one form was like radiant splendour, like daylight; the other like a construction of stones joined together, at the eastern corner [Col. 0577C] and the northern corner. Thus the bright part of the wall stretched from the eastern corner and ended at the northern corner, wholly unbroken and without any interrupted place. The other part, namely the stony part, extended from the northern corner to the western corner and to the southern corner, ending at the eastern corner; it had two interrupted places between the western and southern corners.

The building was one hundred cubits long, fifty cubits broad, and five cubits high, so that its two side walls were of one length, and its other two walls, at its front and rear, of one breadth. Moreover, the same four walls were of equal height everywhere around the building, except for its battlements, which rose somewhat above its height. The breadth between the building and the splendour extending down into the depth of the abyss from the aforesaid circle was one palm at the summit of the eastern corner. Elsewhere, that is, on the northern, western, [Col. 0578B] and southern sides, the space everywhere between the building and the splendour was so broad that I could in no way comprehend its extent.

And while I was marvelling at these things, he who sat on the throne again said to me: Faith, which appeared as though in pallor among the ancient saints, with the work of righteousness built from above through the Father’s goodness, came forth into the light in open manifestation when the Son of God was incarnate, with burning works burning brightly. For the Son of God, not desiring transitory things, taught by his example that they should be trampled underfoot and heavenly things loved. But the earlier Fathers, not fleeing the world nor separating themselves from it, worshipped God only with simple belief and humble devotion, because it had not yet been shown to them that they should abandon all things.

Therefore, that you see within [Col. 0578C] the circumference of the circle extending from the one seated upon the throne a great mountain joined to the root of that immense stone, upon which the cloud with the throne and the one seated upon it are placed, so that the stone appears raised in height and the mountain spread in breadth, means that in the mighty and strong work of the power of the heavenly Father, who works mightily, stands a mountain signifying faith. This faith is great in power, rose openly in Abraham’s circumcision, and advanced even to the Son of the heavenly God after the downfall of the ancient serpent, being inspired into human beings by the Holy Spirit; so that, faithfully working in the Father’s goodness, they believe him to be almighty God, who was able to overcome so great an enemy, and so that, raised by that same belief, they may attain that glory [Col. 0578D] from which the devil, cast down through his pride, perished.

And this same mountain is set at the base of the aforesaid stone, which bears the mystery of the fear of the Lord, because faith is joined to the steadfastness of the fear of the Lord, and the fear of the Lord likewise to the strength of faith: namely, when the Son was sent by the [Col. 0579A] Father to be born of a Virgin, and when from the Son true faith first sprang up as the foundation of good work. The fear of the Lord brings it forth with all the virtues, touching God in His height, so that God, reigning above all things in the wisdom of faithful minds, may be faithfully worshipped. How? Because the fear of the Lord keenly penetrates the secrets of heaven with the sight of circumspection; for it is itself the beginning of righteous intention, together with which blessed faith also extends before God into the breadth of perfection when it is enlarged unto holiness in good works.

But the fact that upon this mountain stands a four-sided building, fashioned in the likeness of a square city, means that, upon faith, the goodness of the Father builds good works and draws to heavenly things many of the faithful, gathering them from the four corners of the earth. Thus instructed in the steadfastness of virtues, they are graciously ordered by the heavenly Father in His bosom—that is, in His inward power and mystical counsel—with four squares in faith. How? I, who am the Most High, ordained in My work the first square of humankind, namely Adam, whose race, while he slept, weakened itself through the great division and proceeded as far as the second square, that is, Noah, under whom the Flood occurred and in whose ark I also prefigured the mysteries of My Son.

But in that square which is Noah, through My admonition I revealed that bright portion of the wall of the aforesaid building; for there, drowning sinners in the Flood, I intimated to human beings that they should flee death and seek life, thus openly laying before them the contemplative knowledge [Col. 0579C] of the recognition of two ways. What is this? A human being flourishes and is vigorous in the living life which is the soul, through which he contemplates and recognizes two paths, namely good and evil, because he is affected by either side of these. Thus, while remaining in the body, he works either good or evil with soul and body; and he begins this indeed through the activity of his mind, so fulfilling his own will in action.

Thus through My admonition the contemplative knowledge of the two ways was shown in us: namely, the most penetrating consideration by which evil is rejected and good loved. This proceeds, with the issuing forth of circumcision, in the forecourse of the will of God, as far as the third square, in which Abraham and Moses are joined in circumcision and [Col. 0579D] Law. That circumcision and Law proceeded in this manner as far as the fourth square of the Holy Trinity, in which the Old Testament was completed in the Son of God with its outward signification. Hence an inward shoot also arose through the Son of God in the Church: He, born and suffering for the salvation of human beings, rising again and returning to the Father, restored unto salvation, through human souls, that corner which had been hidden and diminished in Adam’s fall.

But the fact that the building is set somewhat obliquely means that man, who is God’s work, cannot, because of his frailty, walk firmly without sin and boldly overcome the devil without fear of the frail flesh. Rather, he must avoid him through humility and wisely flee his snares lest he sin, [Col. 0580A] faithfully joining himself to good works. Thus he stands fast in the Son of God, who, as though seated in the corner, is the corner-stone, joining by this covenant the chosen work in man.

But the fact that one corner faces east, another west, one north, and another south, means that the Son of God was born from a Virgin and suffered in the flesh, so that at the rising of righteousness man might be restored to the life to which all righteousness belongs. This is the eastern corner, from which the salvation of souls rises, so that God completed in His Son all righteousness prefigured from Abel down to Him. In Him the ordinance of the carnal observance of the Old Testament was ended, salvation now coming to faithful people through faith, which the Son of God brought when He was sent [Col. 0580B] by the Father into the world at the end of times. This is the western corner.

Against the devil, too, righteousness raised itself in Abraham and Moses, who prefigured the promised grace through which the man whom the devil had deceived was saved—having slain him like a thief in Adam’s fall. This is the northern corner. Hence also the wretched and mortal fall that occurred in the human race was afterward nobly and magnificently restored by heavenly grace with full fruit, in the burning work of God and man. This is the southern corner. The southern corner also signifies this: the first man Adam was created by God.

But the fact that the contemplative knowledge of the recognition of the two ways does not begin to shine from this corner, that is, from Adam himself, is because his race [Col. 0580C] was disordered. It did not worship God knowingly through the dutiful service of the Law, but merely fulfilled its own will in utter evil; so that it shone neither in the right knowledge of God nor in true blessedness. Rather, it lay in death; and only in the Father’s heart was hidden what He had decreed to do with man.

The eastern corner also signifies Noah, where righteousness began to show itself and where the prefigured contemplative knowledge was openly manifested, showing all the holiness that was afterward to be fulfilled in the Son of God. And because every righteousness had its beginning in the Son of God, who is the true East, this building must therefore first be called eastern in honor of holiness, which was also first truly declared in Noah.

The northern corner, moreover, is Abraham and Moses, who opposed Satan by the execution of works and enclosed the aforesaid contemplative knowledge, as though building around it with precious stones and with the gilded work above of God’s transparent righteousness, which was circumcision and the Law. For righteousness before circumcision and the Law was, as it were, naked and without work.

And the fourth, western corner also prefigures the true Trinity, openly manifested in the baptism of the Savior, who raised up the full and holy city of Jerusalem with all His work, returning to heaven in the salvation of souls.

But the fact that the building has around it one wall of two forms, one like a bright radiance [Col. 0581A] such as daylight, the other like a joining together of stones connected with one another at the eastern and northern corners, means that through the Father’s goodness one security, that is, a fortification and defense in good works, has been given to human beings on every side. Surrounded and strengthened by it, they may abandon fleshly desires and flee to the one God, who is their stronghold.

This wall has two forms because one form of the wall is like the contemplative knowledge of the two ways. Man possesses this knowledge through the most penetrating and certain investigation of his own mental contemplation, so that he may be circumspect in all his ways. The other form of the wall is like man’s ash-colored flesh, because man was created by God as one who works, a work made for working.

And this contemplative knowledge shines with the splendor of daylight, because through it human beings see and consider their deeds. It is the shining ray of the human mind cautiously surveying itself. Indeed, this illustrious knowledge appears in man like a white cloud passing through the minds of peoples swiftly, just as a cloud is quickly dispersed in the air; and it shines like daylight, because it is declared white on account of the most radiant work which God graciously works in human beings: namely, that when they avoid evil, they may accomplish the good which shines in them like daylight.

In this knowledge, moreover, every work proceeds in man. How? Man has two ways. [Col. 0581C] How? He is one who knows good and evil with perception. When he passes away from evil by working good, he imitates God, who does good within him, for God is righteous and does not will unrighteousness. But when he works evil, he is entangled in sins by the seducer, the devil, who does not wish to cease until he senses him bound in evil works, because the devil seeks iniquity and flees holiness.

But if a man withdraws from evil and works good, then he receives the highest good, because for the love of God he has overcome himself—God who gave up His Son for him to the death of the cross. Hence this knowledge is contemplative, because it is like a mirror in this manner: just as a person looks at his face in a mirror, to see whether it has beauty or blemish, [Col. 0581D] so he examines in knowledge good and evil in the deed accomplished, which he considers within himself. For this consideration lies in rational perception, which God inspired into man when He breathed into his face the breath of life in the soul.

For the life of beasts fails, because it is not rational; but the human soul never fails, because it will live eternally, since it is rational. Hence man recognizes, in the consideration of good and evil, whether he himself is a reprobate or chosen work, formed through the grace of God and inspired with rational perception at the dawn of his creation. That grace restores him again in the election of baptism and in the salvation of the soul under the New Testament, as My most beloved Paul says concerning that election of grace: “A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11).

This means: the remnant whom the snare of death did not seize, so that they might turn aside according to the devil’s example, have been saved through manifest salvation when God sent His Son to be incarnate. This is the election of grace revealed for the salvation of human beings. How? The grace of God established man, but he fell into evil works. Then the election of grace was shown in the chosen vessel, when the Son of God was born of a Virgin, in whom no fall could occur.

For if any human being makes something useful which is then taken away from him by another, he chooses for himself something else, more useful, which no one can take from him and in which he may fully abound. So did the grace of God. It formed [Col. 0582B] Adam, the first man, whom the devil withdrew from the innocence of work; but the same grace afterward brought about the fullness of good works through the Son of God in the salvation of souls.

But if the grace of God accomplished salvation, salvation was not accomplished from the merit of human beings. How? The righteousness of work failed in Adam, so that man could never return to salvation through the merits of his own works unless he were restored by that same grace in the most righteous Son of God through His works, because He became obedient to His Father; and unless man were also cleansed through baptism, which the Son of God gave to human beings together with good work—a work which the grace of God works with man, and man works with it. Therefore the grace of God is with this work, and this work arose from grace.

[Col. 0582C] But if salvation were from human merit and man’s righteous work belonged to him of himself, so that the grace of God did not kindle that work, grace would not be grace. How? Then man would be from himself and not from God; no creature would give thanks to God; and the grace of God would be nothing.

But now the grace of God establishes man, upheld by rationality, so that he may work righteousness through knowledge of good and evil; so that through this knowledge he may seek good, rejecting evil, and thus recognize life and death, choosing by this in which part he wishes to remain. As Solomon says in the understanding of wisdom: “He has set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand to whichever you wish” (Ecclus. 15).

This means: God placed in man, at the first awakening of the soul, a great and keen power—namely, awareness of evils and goods—which are water and fire. For just as water constantly overflows and conceals in itself many deadly animals and very many useless things, so man too overflows in his evil deeds, concealing them lest they be made public. And just as fire burns, enduring no impurity unburned within it, and as a craftsman by fire makes his ornaments purer after rust has been removed, so good makes man pure, tearing from him the rust of wickedness.

For water and fire oppose one another, smothering and killing each other. So too does man: in evil he kills good, and in good he kills evil; and in either case he always silently hides his desires within himself, turning them this way or that.

[Col. 0583A] And amid this stirring of desires he has the choice of the way which he desires; and he turns himself to it with the will of action, as though stretching out his hand to it: namely, accomplishing good work with God’s help through grace, or doing evil while the devil lies in wait through the suggestion of his devices. Man himself considers these things in the knowledge of his rationality. For in that knowledge he examines good and evil, and from it there arises in him the desire of choice between the two ways, namely good and evil, according to his own will.

What is this? Choice is when a man sees certain things in the desire of his mind as though in a mirror, saying within himself: “Would that I could do this or that!” He has not yet approached it in deed, but holds it in his knowledge, set as though at the head of two ways—that is, possessing knowledge of the occasions of good and evil—and thus, according to his desire, finally inclines toward that work, either upward or downward.

And the other form of the wall, which you see as a joining together of stones and which displays the human race, also signifies the right institutions that arose in the minds of human beings: in Abraham and Moses and in the others who were the preceding shoot of God’s Law, with all the appurtenances of God’s righteousness in the Law down to the final time. How? Namely, God’s work is in man and through man, so that God sent His Son for human salvation at the end of the Law, sinless and working in a human body, and laying the foundation [Col. 0583C] of faith upon Himself. In this way He bore the human race along with the first man, expelled from paradise for transgressing righteousness, accomplishing all this marvel in man through His Law, where you comprehend the Christian multitude, which is this building in the Father’s goodness, and the fact that man is to be restored in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Therefore the two forms of the wall are joined together into one in the eastern and northern region, because in contemplative knowledge and human work there is a common ending of the unrighteousness in which the human race was entangled in forgetfulness of God. That unrighteousness first raised itself from Adam in frenzied injustice before the Flood, so that it was cast down with all its people because of great iniquity in the Flood of waters. There contemplative knowledge began to appear by My inspiration when God’s admonition raised Noah with knowledge of the good.

Yet the stubbornness and desire of evil proceeded destructively northward in its remembrance, so that the iniquity of rebellion against God was not trampled down until Abraham, in whom it was choked as at the northern corner, when the most penetrating blade of God’s righteousness arose in him.

But the fact that that bright portion of the wall stretches whole and unbroken from the eastern corner and ends at the northern corner means that contemplative knowledge began to appear as a fortification of human minds from the eastern corner—that is, from Noah’s days. Before Noah, iniquity labored [Col. 0584A] to accomplish whatever it could perpetrate in provoking God; human beings followed their desires more than they loved the worship of God. For the first race of humans from Adam, when contemplative knowledge was hidden, the devil swallowed up in every exercise of his will down to Noah, in whom that knowledge was openly revealed, as has been said.

Nevertheless, the devil still trusted that he would possess the whole human race, unrighteousness proceeding thus in obedience to his command as far as the northern corner—that is, to Abraham and Moses. For before them unrighteousness, in contemplative knowledge, was as though whole in its wickedness, and not yet interrupted or broken by the established righteousness of God’s Law, because circumcision and the Law had not yet been given. In those patriarchs the devil then began to be confounded, whereas previously he had seemed to reign confidently in the world, as Paul, My bright vessel of election, declares: “Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a figure of the one to come” (Rom. 5).

This means: death reigned, with no one fighting against it and no one overcoming it in battle, from Adam until Moses. How? Because the severity and observance of the Law had not been given before Moses, except that circumcision, performed in Abraham by God’s command, had lightly prefigured it. But the vice of death went on from error to error as it pleased.

Then Moses, a strong soldier in the will of God, arose and prepared the strong weapons of righteousness, through which death was destroyed in its worship by the instruments [Col. 0584C] of the Law. For the Law conceals within itself all salvation of souls, with the prefiguration of the Son of God, because death also ruled over the innocent, who, because of the simplicity of their restraint, did not know in their deeds the work of Adam’s transgression among the nations—Adam, who is a figure of the one to come. How? Adam was created by God righteous and innocent of every conception and inception of sin; likewise the Son of God was born from the Virgin Mary, coming without any stain of sin.

But, as you see, the stony portion of the wall extends from the northern corner to the western and southern corners and ends at the eastern corner. This means that the righteous works of human beings, by which they are fortified in God, proceeded as it were from the northern corner—that is, from Abraham’s circumcision, with Moses’ Law and the appurtenances of their righteousness among human beings—as far as the western corner, where transparent righteousness arose in the incarnation of the Son of God. From there it extended further to the southern corner, where the burning work was kindled through baptism and the remaining righteousness of the chosen and new bride of that same Son of God, for the restoration of Adam unto salvation. Thence it was further extended and set its limit at the first eastern corner, thus returning to the Most High Father.

How? The Most High Father, in His mystery, was ordering every righteousness according to how the fall of the first man should return, through the salvation of souls, [Col. 0585A] to God. Because man had fallen, I therefore rose in mercy and sent My Son for the restoration of the salvation of souls, as David, My servant and psalmist, shows when he says: “But his delight is in the Law of the Lord, and on His Law he meditates day and night” (Ps. 1).

This means: in the Law of righteousness which My Only-Begotten, born from a Virgin, showed to the world—He who, being one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, rules over every age—the will of the Father was that the Son Himself, incarnate and seen as a visible man, should be Lord and exalted in the flesh above every creature for salvation.

How? Because the Son of God, begotten of the Father before the ages and afterward born in the world from a mother at the end of times, remained unincarnate and invisible in the Father, just as a will is invisible in a person before it issues into action. Thereafter He appeared visibly in the flesh for human salvation. Thus the omnipotent Father meditates with His Son upon all righteousness against Adam’s first fall. Where? In the love of the Son of God, who, abiding in the Father before times in the glory of divinity, was afterward wonderfully incarnate under the appointed time of the world. The Father sent Him from His heart into the world as the supreme priest over all righteousness.

Accordingly, the Son Himself gathered the Law of righteousness, receiving it from the Father, and made it the Law of human beings who would believe in Him. But in that Law which the Father willed to establish and found in His Son, He meditates in the day. How? Namely, in the day which He Himself is: before He created any creature, when no darkness of iniquity existed in any creature, [Col. 0585C] He meditated upon this Law of His Son.

And also in the night. How? Because, in created beings, when evil began to raise itself up—which is like the darkness of night—in angel and in man, the Father also meditates until the last day, to which His works that He ineffably performs extend, revealing and opening the Law of His Son, when in Him He perfects all the good things that must be accomplished in man.

But the fact that the stony portion of the wall has two broken places between the western and southern corners means that the work of the human race, in the fortification of its defense, is still imperfect in two respects. The members [Col. 0585D] of the incarnate Son of God remain as yet imperfect in His elect: this is the first broken place, as it were from the west, because the Son of God was sent into the world at the end of times. Then the Church also remains as yet imperfect in all her virtues, in which she ought to stand and be built in the heavenly Jerusalem: this is the other broken place, as it were toward the south, when the Church shall be perfected in heavenly things.

But the length of that building is one hundred cubits. This means that the number ten was diminished in transgressing man and recovered in My Son through the manifold hundredfold number of ten, namely the many virtues in the salvation of souls. From this ten, through the hundredfold number, the perfect thousandfold number then ascends [Col. 0586A] in all virtues, so that the thousand devices of the devil, by which he deceives the whole flock of the beloved ones of almighty God, may plainly be emptied out.

What is this? I, the Almighty, established at the beginning burning and living lights that should shine in their splendors; but some remained in My love, whereas others fell by despising their Creator. Yet it was not fitting for Me, the Creator, to leave My institution empty and ineffectual. How? The angelic creation of the proud host ascribed to itself, in deceitful glory, the good which its Creator had bestowed upon it for its own knowledge, imagining that it could be like its Creator; and so it fell into death.

Then God foresaw that what had fallen in that lost host must be restored more strongly in another. How? [Col. 0586B] He created man from the mud of the earth, living in soul and body, that he might attain the glory from which the transgressing devil with his imitators had been cast out. For man is very dear to God, since He made him in His image and likeness, that in the perfection of holiness he might work all virtues, just as God created all creatures. Man was also to fill, by working in the humblest obedience and in the work of virtues, the order among the glorious angels through the rendering of praise; that at this summit of blessedness he might adorn the praise of the heavenly spirits, who with continual devotion praise God, and in that same blessedness fulfill what the lost angel, falling in presumption, had nullified. Therefore man is the complete number ten, accomplishing all these things through God’s power.

But the number ten by its nature multiplies into a hundred for this reason: man, having fallen through diabolical seduction, is at last admonished by God through divine mercy and inspiration and begins vigorously to acknowledge God through the Law and prophecy of the Old Testament, and then more keenly through the holiness and all the adornments of the Church’s unconquered constancy. Thus man began to perform all virtues from Abel, fulfilling them down to the last righteous person. This is the hundredfold number of the length of this building, which God shows human beings in mystical figure, lest they despair after falling into their iniquities, [Col. 0586D] but, rising from them, labor most vigorously in God’s work.

For everyone who falls into sins, when he rises from them, will be stronger than he was before; just as God restores greater and stronger virtues in man by sending His Son into the world to raise up the fallen human race than the first man works. Hence man works more strongly in soul and body than if he were without bodily heaviness, because he fights within himself amid many dangers, accomplishing most strenuous battles. Victorious, he faithfully serves his Lord God and thus knows Him in his warfare, chastising his body. For the angel, lacking the heaviness of an earthly body, is merely a radiant and pure soldier of heavenly harmony, persevering in the vision of God; but man, burdened with bodily corruption, is a strong, glorious, and holy soldier with restored work, who works for God in soul and body. Thus, through the hundredfold number of present labor, he reaches the thousandfold number of future recompense: that is, on the last day, receiving his full reward, he will rejoice without end in soul and body in the heavenly dwelling.

Thus the diminished number ten was recovered through My Son, who, born of a Virgin and suffering on the cross, led man back to heavenly things, as He Himself says in the Gospel: “What woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found [Col. 0587B] the drachma which I had lost” (Luke 15).

This means: holy divinity possessed ten drachmas—that is, in the chosen angels and in man, ten orders of heavenly distinctions—but lost one drachma when man, following diabolical seduction rather than the divine command, fell into death. Therefore He lit the burning lamp, namely Christ, true God and true man, the most radiant sun of righteousness; through Him He swept the house, that is, the Jewish people, and amid the Law He diligently sought every sanctification which belonged to salvation. There He established a new sanctification and thus found His drachma, namely man, whom He had lost.

Then He called together His friends, that is, worldly righteous observances, and His neighbors, that is, spiritual virtues, saying: “Rejoice with Me in praise and be glad together; build the heavenly Jerusalem from living stones, because I have found the man who had perished through the devil’s deception.”

But the fact that the breadth of this building is fifty cubits means that the whole breadth of human vices—of those who ought to have built in God’s work but followed their own desires rather than cultivated God’s work—is mercifully wiped away and forgiven in the widespread five wounds of My Son, which He suffered on the cross. Thus the wounds of His hands erased the works of the hands in Adam and Eve’s disobedience; the wounds of His feet freed the paths of human exile; and the wound of His side, from which the Church arose, erased the guilt of Adam and Eve, [Col. 0587D] since Eve was created from Adam’s side.

Therefore My Son was fastened to the wood, that He might abolish what transgression had wrought through the wood; and He was given vinegar and gall to drink, that the taste of the deadly fruit might be washed away. And its height is five cubits: this is the excellence of divine teachings in the Scriptures, which concern God’s work in the five senses that are in man. The Holy Spirit inspired these for human benefit, because with his five senses man looks toward the height of divinity, discerning each thing, namely good and evil.

Hence its two walls, on either side of it, are of one length, because, in the building of God’s goodness, man must labor most steadfastly, as though in the two walls of soul and body, through both kinds of circumstances, prosperity and adversity. How? That he may avoid evil and work good. How? Because the profound and incomprehensible divine power established man so that with all his strength and all his understanding he might worship God with equal devotion through the length of intelligible rationality. For it is fitting that God, Creator of all things, be worshipped most worthily before all things and above all things.

Therefore its other two walls, at its front and its end, are of one breadth, because in God’s work wisdom and discernment are like two walls: wisdom, as it were, in the upper and discernment in the lower part. God breathes these into the human mind, for the magnitude of its breadth, by His equal and just gift, so that it may know [Col. 0588B] Him.

But the fact that those four walls are of equal height everywhere around the building, except for its battlements, which rise somewhat above its height, means that man, set among the four elements, will everywhere hold the Catholic faith on high through the Father’s goodness, with equal devotion and worship, worshipping the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who works all His works in them.

How? Every work which the Son of God has worked and works, He completes through the Father’s goodness in the Holy Spirit. What is this? The Son redeemed man through His incarnation according to the Father’s will, and this is great goodness. For the Father so ordained that His Son should be born of a Virgin, conceived of [Col. 0588C] the Holy Spirit, taking humanity upon Himself for love of man, in order to lead him back to the restoration of life. Thus man might have a share with God, entering through Him into salvation in the right and Catholic faith, in which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must be known as one true God.

There are also battlements of greater height there. How? When man looks toward the summit of a good mind, he builds up the height of faithful walls, ascending in the virtues of God’s work above intelligible faith: that is, knowing that God is in the power of His divinity. Upon this faith he then builds a higher structure of the virtues, the most excellent battlements. How? For he builds higher virtues, not being satisfied merely to have faith in God, but ascending to the flourishing palm—that is, from virtue to virtue—by which the most upright faith is exalted and adorned like a city with battlements.

But the fact that the breadth between the building itself and the radiance extending from the aforesaid circle into the depth of the abyss is one palm at the summit of the eastern corner means that the expanse of heavenly mysteries lies between the work of the Son of God, shown as a building—He who lived bodily in the world without sin, performing many virtues in the Father’s goodness—and the Father’s power, like radiance extending in its greatest strength downward and upward. This occurs when He sent His Son [Col. 0589A] into the world at the head of the corner facing east, that is, in the righteousness first prefigured in Noah by the admonition of the Holy Spirit, foreshadowing the perfect righteousness revealed in the incarnation of the Son of God.

Thus, in these mysteries, there was as it were the space of one span—the extended hand from the thumb to the other fingers. This is the appointed time in the Father’s bosom when He willed to send His Only-Begotten in His most powerful hand, so that He might thus move about with all the joints of the fingers, which are all His works in the Holy Spirit, and fulfill the will of His Father by suffering on the cross on account of the wretched and contemptible disobedience which the devil instilled into the first man through his suggestion. For this reason, to redeem [Col. 0589B] man, God’s mercy bent itself down to earth through the humanity of the Son of God, while the height of divinity remained incomprehensible.

But the fact that elsewhere—that is, on the northern, western, and southern sides—the breadth everywhere between the building and the radiance is so great that you cannot comprehend its extent in any way, means that no human being burdened with a mortal body can know the pride of evil in the entrails of the northern devil; nor its end in created beings acting in the setting of fallen man; nor the beginning or end of the burning south, which is heavenly righteousness. Nor can he consider how these things are extended and distinguished between the work and the power of My knowledge in all peoples, whether elect or reprobate. All are placed under the most equitable examination, so that they will be examined with the keenest and most diligent strictness according to My commandments.

Yet all of them ought carefully to trust that I feed them in all their necessities, because all these things are so hidden in My secrets that neither human sense nor understanding can in any way grasp or comprehend the breadth [Col. 0590B] of their depth, except insofar as My permission grants it. But whoever has keen ears of inward understanding in the burning love of My mirror, let him thirst for these words and write them in the conscience of his mind.

## Third Vision

[Col. 0589]

SUMMARY.—That divine virtues, budding under the Law, bear abundant fruit under the new Law. That virtues work in human beings by God’s will. On the condition of heavenly love, discipline, mercy, and victory. On their dress and what it signifies. Specifically, on heavenly love, its dress, and its meaning. Specifically, on modesty and what its dress signifies. On mercy. Specifically, on victory, its dress, and its meaning. On the condition of patience and groaning, and what it signifies. On their dress and what it signifies. Specifically, on patience, its dress, and its meaning. Specifically, on groaning, its dress, and its meaning.

[Col. 0589C] After this I saw, and behold, as it were in the middle of the length of the aforesaid bright part of the wall of the depicted building, there stood a tower of iron colour, set externally against the wall itself, four cubits broad and seven cubits high. In it I perceived five figures, standing separately, each beneath its own arch, and above them each had something like a turreted cone. The first faced east; the second the north wind; the third toward the north; the fourth toward the pillar of the Word of God, at whose base the patriarch Abraham sat; and the fifth toward the tower of the Church and toward those people who ran to and fro within that building.

They had one likeness in this: each was clothed only in what seemed to be a separate silken garment, and shod with white shoes, except the fifth, which appeared armed on every side. The second and third had bare heads, loose white hair, and lacked the covering of cloaks. But the first, third, and fourth wore white tunics.

Their difference, however, was this. The first figure wore upon its head a pontifical mitre, with loose white hair, and was clothed as it were with a white mantle, purple being woven into its two lower borders. In its right hand it bore lilies and other flowers, and in its left a palm. And it said:

“O sweet life, and O sweet embrace of eternal life, and O blessed happiness in which eternal rewards are found: you are ever in true delights. Yet I can never be filled, never sated with the inward joy that is in my God.”

The second wore a purple tunic, standing like a youth not yet fully of manly age, yet of great gravity; and it said:

“The dreadful enemy who is the devil will not frighten me; nor will a human enemy, nor this world, while I stand in the discipline of God, before whose sight I always stand.”

The third covered its face with the white sleeve of its right hand and said:

“O filth and uncleanness of this world, hide yourselves and flee from my eyes, because my Beloved was born of the pure Virgin Mary.”

The fourth had its head veiled with a white veil in womanly fashion and was wrapped in a saffron-coloured mantle. Upon its breast it bore an image of Jesus Christ, around which was written on its breast: “Through the tender mercies of our God, whereby the Dayspring from on high hath visited us” (Luke 1). And it said:

“I always stretch out my hands to strangers and needy persons, to the poor and weak, and to those who groan.”

The fifth, moreover, was armed: a helmet was placed upon its head; it wore a breastplate and greaves, and iron gauntlets. In its left hand it bore a shield hanging from its shoulders; it was girded with a sword and held a spear in its right hand. Beneath its feet there lay something like a lion with gaping mouth and tongue stretched from its mouth; and there were also certain people, some sounding trumpets, others playfully making noise with certain instruments of amusement, and others playing various games. That figure, trampling both them and the lion beneath its feet, sharply pierced them with the spear it held in its right hand. And it said:

“I conquer the strong devil, and you, hatred and envy, and you, O filth, together with those who play by deceitful deception.”

But within that building I saw two other figures standing toward this same tower. The first appeared standing upon the pavement of that building, as if in an arch of fiery splendour whose interior was painted with diverse images of evil spirits and which stood opposite the aforesaid tower. The other stood only alongside that arch on its outer side, occupying no arch. Both at times looked toward the aforesaid tower, and at times toward the people entering and leaving the building.

They too were clothed in silken garments and veiled, with a white head-covering tied in womanly fashion; they were not wrapped in mantles, but wore white shoes. The first had upon its head something like a triangular red crown, red as a red hyacinth in its colour; it also wore a snow-white tunic whose folds were everywhere marked with green. And it said:

“I conquer in the east with the most mighty Son of God, who went out from the Father, coming into the world for the redemption of humankind, and who returned again to the Father when, dying upon the cross in the greatest affliction and rising from the dead, he ascended into heaven. Therefore I do not wish to be confounded, fleeing the miseries and pains of this world.”

The other wore a white tunic, but of a somewhat pale colour. On its right arm it bore a cross with an image of Jesus Christ the Saviour, inclining its head upon it; and it said:

“This child endured many miseries in this world; and therefore I desire always to weep and to have sorrow because of the joy of eternal life, to which the good sheep are to be led through the noble Son of God.”

And I saw that all the aforesaid figures spoke their several words through God’s mystery for the admonition of humankind.

Then again he who sat upon the throne and showed me all these things said to me:

By the strength and steadfastness of God’s will, the divine virtues sprang up swiftly in the Old Testament. Yet there they did not fully offer their sweet and pleasant taste to those who cultivated them as if in ignorance, because at that time only the severity of the Law sharply rebuked sinners. But afterwards, through God’s grace, bearing very abundant fruit under the new Law, they offered strong and perfect food with the highest sweetness to those who hunger in love for heavenly things. Formerly, as has been said, they were a certain hidden manifestation and sign of things to come, as this vision also shows with its accompanying details.

For this tower which you see standing, as it were, in the middle of the length of the aforesaid bright part of the wall of the depicted building, bears the type of the forecourse of God’s will, which was manifested in circumcision in many ways and with diverse meanings. Thus God showed the Law as a sign of that circumcision, and through the Law the grace of the Gospel. For when faith was proclaimed in faithful Abraham, circumcision also arose in him as a mystery of true prefiguration. By divine power the strong virtues were equipped, beginning in Abraham as if in the middle of the length of speculative knowledge between the two paths of human choice, beneath the defence of the most steadfast goodness of the heavenly Father. They were afterwards to be revealed by God’s will, signifying beforehand in a figure what God wished to do before he openly showed it in deed.

It is iron-coloured and set externally against the wall: this is the strong and unconquerable justice of God, showing itself as if externally in that speculative knowledge through circumcision, which was outwardly formed in the flesh, and placed with the blessed virtues in the spiritual things of the spiritual wall that God established in humankind.

And the same tower is four cubits broad, because by God’s will those virtues work in the human being, who is set beneath the extension of the four elements by which he is bodily sustained in the body. It is seven cubits high because in the height of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit there is such firmness that the tower raised itself in such a way that from it the Church should come forth in the incarnation of my Son, prefigured in the circumcision of the Old Testament.

[Col. 0592C] That you perceive five figures standing separately in it, each beneath its own arch and having above it something like a turreted cone, means that from this tower—that is, from the strength of circumcision—depended five strong virtues. This does not mean that any virtue is a living form in itself, but only a radiant sphere shining from God to assist humankind. For the human being is perfected with the virtues, since they are the work of the human being working in God.

Therefore these five virtues are placed in this tower after the likeness of the five senses of humankind, because with great zeal they touched circumcision, cutting away iniquity from it; just as the five senses of the human being are circumcised in the Church through most holy baptism. Yet they do not work in human beings by themselves, because the human being works with them and they with the human being, just as the five senses of the human being do not work by themselves, but the human being works with them and they with the human being, thus mutually bearing fruit.

They stand separately, labouring with the greatest zeal in a distinct bearing of teaching that has a turreted summit: that is, an eminent and well-ordered dignity of most vigorous constancy. The first figure faces east because that virtue looked toward the Son of God with the lament of love, that he might one day come, openly speaking of the eternal life which circumcision possessed in concealment.

The second figure looks toward the north wind because it considered the eastern region and the region of the north wind: in great discipline looking toward God as toward the east, rejecting the unseemliness of undisciplined wantonness—that is, that God was not held in reverence—and despising the fact that the Law of God was not worthily maintained among that people, as in the north wind.

The third stretches toward the north because it most forcefully casts down superfluous fornication, despising it and protecting itself from it by the institution of the Law.

The fourth figure turns toward the pillar of the Word of God, at whose base the patriarch Abraham sits, because it was turned and attached to the incarnation of the Son of God, which it touched as it were in Abraham’s foundation, with the prefiguration of marvellous depth: the ram hanging in the thorns.

The fifth looks toward the tower of the Church and toward those people running to and fro in the building, because it raised itself victoriously to destroy every injustice that arose in Adam. It looks toward the strength of the catholic Church, so that it may fight victoriously and without interruption against the vices of the devil; and toward those people who move about in it amid diverse varieties of conduct, showing them, in the fear-inspiring zeal of God, that they should persist as sheep of righteousness.

That they have one likeness means that they worship God with equal devotion in human deeds. For each is clothed only in what seems to be a silken garment, because every one of these virtues has within itself a sweetness and pleasantness that neither burdens nor constrains people. But as balsam sweetly sweats from its shrub, so they gently work the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom in human minds, without the filth and hardness of injustice.

They are shod with white shoes because they rightly follow my justice in the whiteness of the heavenly kingdom, passing over the devil’s subjection and wholly trampling his tracks in humankind. But the fifth virtue appears armed in every respect because it looks toward the Church, in which the strongest battles against diabolical vices are accomplished. There it extends its victory everywhere with the most precious armour, which is the invincible strength of God, passing through and slaying every injustice in the overthrow of diabolical fraud.

That the second and third have bare heads, loose white hair, means that, for love of me, they impose upon themselves neither the penalty of toil nor the burden of riches or of desire. Rather, with bare head—that is, with their conscience open—they reveal to me all their hidden things, ever burning in my love, while they cast away from themselves every confusion and the wantonness of fleshly desire. They begin this in white hair, which is the brightness of a mind desiring good works.

And they lack the covering of mantles because they cast away from themselves pagan customs, together with the immodesty and filth of the devil and all worldly cares; for “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3). The first, third, and fourth also wear white tunics: this is the possession of innocence, prefiguring the incarnation of my Son with the sweetness of chastity. He rescued humankind from death, clothing it with life in salvation.

Their difference means that their power is variously present in the gift of the Holy Spirit: one virtue has this instrument of the soul, another has another; nevertheless, they are one endeavour in God, so that the heavenly Jerusalem may be perfectly built through them. For they are the work that human beings perform, through which they come to God.

Therefore this first figure signifies heavenly love, because it ought to dwell in people as the mind’s chief concern. It wears upon its head a pontifical mitre, with loose white hair, because it is greatly crowned in the high priest Jesus Christ, in the high priests of the Old Testament, and in those who said to the same Son of God: “Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens and come down.” It stands with its hair uncovered, appearing white and without a womanly head-covering, prefiguring in them that the priestly office was to be stripped of the marital office at the coming of my Son. He is to be imitated by his priests in chastity for salvation, because they must always cleave so to the most perfect heavenly love that they shake off the evil habits of human beings and the contagion of sin, being a clear and white part in God’s spiritual gift.

It is also clothed as it were with a white mantle, purple woven into its two lower borders. This means that the grace of God has surrounded it with the whiteness of gentleness, supported and adorned at the boundaries of its protections with the beautiful ornaments of charity. For the embracing of divine grace ought to be present at the end of every good work, consisting of two parts: namely, the virtue of love for God and for one’s neighbour.

That it bears lilies and other flowers in its right hand means that in good work it has the white rewards of the lilies of eternal life, the brightness of eternal light, and other little flowers of holiness, which are its companions joining themselves to it in heavenly love. But that it bears a palm in its left hand means that, in remembrance of death, it possesses the palm rising from the hidden place of blessed virtue. With this it overwhelms death as with torrents of stones, as it also declares in its words to the children of God, mentioned above.

The second figure represents discipline, because after the burning love of heavenly life there arises the constraining of carnal desires in the discipline of great contrition. It wears a purple tunic because it is surrounded in human beings by my Law and by mortification of the flesh. This is the example of my Son in the purple garment: my same Son was born in love from the most pure Virgin, and love worked in every way within him.

It stands like a youth not yet fully of manly age, yet of great gravity, because discipline is always in childlike fear, as a child is in restraint, fearing his teacher under instruction. Therefore I, the Almighty, am always the teacher of discipline, because toward me it is as if not manly: it does not wish to be powerful in the office of its own will, but always faithfully to fear in the great strictness of reverence, as it also most clearly shows in the aforementioned words.

The third figure signifies modesty, because after discipline arises the shame of modesty, which drives from itself the confusion of sin. Therefore it covers its face also with the white sleeve of its right hand: it protects its inward conscience, as the face of the soul, fleeing fornication and diabolical defilement and defending itself with the white garment of innocence and chastity. It has this in its right hand—that is, in the salvation of its work—because it powerfully cleaves to contempt for every filth of Satan, which it wholly casts away from itself, as it also declares in its aforementioned admonitory words.

[Col. 0595B] The fourth signifies mercy, because after modesty the virtue of mercy raises itself toward the needy. In the heart of the eternal Father too there is the true mercy of his grace, for through it he ordained in his ancient counsel what he first mercifully showed Abraham in circumcision: leading him out of his land and commanding that he and his seed be circumcised. Then he showed him great wonders in the true Trinity, through which he also foretold his Son in a figure. All this is that mercy which Abraham himself prefigured in offering Isaac.

It has its head veiled with a white head-covering in womanly fashion. This is the covering and beginning of salvation, as it were the head of one who pities, leading lost souls back from the exile of death beneath the brightness of a kindly veil. For it makes souls white and humankind radiant when one has been covered with mercy by God. For those human beings who hold God in indignation while they are still in sins, it shines upon them after heavenly mercy has been bestowed upon them, like a ray of the sun in gentle sweetness. For mercy, in a womanly person, is the most fruitful mother of souls rescued from perdition.

For as a woman covers her head, so mercy presses down the death of souls; and as a woman is gentler than a man, so mercy is gentler than the mad frenzy of crimes in the madness of the sinner before his heart is visited by God. Thus this virtue too appears in womanly form, because in virginal matter enclosed in feminine chastity there arose in the womb of Mary the most sweet mercy, which was always overshadowed in the Father until the Father made it visible through the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb.

It is wrapped in a saffron-coloured mantle because it is surrounded by the most splendid sun, the sign of my Son shining from heaven into the world as the brightness of the sun upon the earth. For my same Son is the true sun enlightening the world with the sanctification of the Church.

That it has the image of my Only-begotten upon its breast means that I inclined that same Son of mine into the breast of mercy when I sent him into the womb of the Virgin Mary. Therefore it is written around it upon the breast of this virtue: “Through the tender mercies of our God, whereby the Dayspring from on high hath visited us” (Luke 1).

What is this? That throughout my all-encompassing power, it is shown in the secret knowledge of mercy’s breast that my Son is true mercy. How? As was said above in the words of my servant Zachariah in the Gospel: “Through the tender mercies of our God, whereby the Dayspring from on high hath visited us.” This means: through the tender mercies of the Father is salvation, which was hidden in the Father’s heart as entrails remain within a human being: namely, that his Son would be incarnate at the end of time, when God visited humankind.

How? Namely, by the heavenly bread which is his Son, born in the flesh from the Virgin Mary. Coming from on high—that is, going forth from the Father’s heart—he bestowed the greatest mercy upon those who seek him, as this virtue itself also addresses the children of God in the words quoted above.

The fifth figure prefigures victory. For after the mercy that I showed in circumcision, when I willed to send my Son into the world, victory rose up in the same circumcision, thus proceeding with greater strength unto my Son and with him unto the last day. For in my Son I overcame the ancient serpent, who raised himself upon his head, seizing the human race through a thousand wickednesses by which he enclosed it as in his chain. My Only-begotten overcame those wickednesses through all the warlike arms that rose in his incarnation, he who is the flower of all virtues.

What is this? After mercy, victory rises when a person conquers himself and the vices of others. How? In the five virtues mentioned above: first is heavenly love, namely in this, that a person knows and acknowledges God, loving him above all things. Then, because of that faith, the same person is bound into the law of discipline, by which he restrains the offences of sinning through good and upright modesty.

Therefore in these three powers the person will be justified in his heart, and so he considers another matter: the distress of his neighbour, for whom he will provide in all necessities as for himself. Thus at once the person rises as a most mighty soldier with these three powers, in which he is perfected in his mind, imitating my Son, the true Samaritan, in mercy. Thus in victory he passes beyond the powers of the devil with the arms of the most victorious virtues, when he conquers himself and governs his neighbour, slaying every evil in these virtues, namely by casting away pride, which expelled Adam from paradise.

And this virtue is armed with a helmet placed upon its head, because the person should sigh with full heavenly desire toward God, who is the head of all, in order to attain eternal salvation. It also wears a breastplate, so that the person may resist the devil, restraining the unjust will of fleshly desires, subject to God in true fear and just trembling, faithfully fearing his strict judgment, as David says when admonished by me: “Thy lightnings enlightened the world: the earth trembled and shook” (Psalm 76).

This means: Your wonders and secrets, O Lord of all, shone forth and appeared marvellously. How? Like lightning, which is partly seen and partly hidden: for your mysteries are now understood and now unknown. For there is no nation spread across the breadth of the whole world, which was wonderfully created in your will, to which the name of your glory and the power of your majesty have not wonderfully come in diverse ways and by marvellous signs, even if the light of faith and truth has not yet perfectly enlightened it for its salvation.

Therefore, stirred in great sighs, the person turns away from his own will and leaves his desires, trembling before the heavenly judgment. For previously, while walking in earthly actions, he had imprudently forgotten himself; now he wisely returns to himself.

The aforementioned virtue also wears greaves so that, with the straight way set forth for it, a person may flee the paths of death through bodily chastisement. It wears iron gauntlets also, so that the person may escape the works of the devil through circumcision of the mind and through the most upright faith, believing in God and thus avoiding the snares of the most savage enemy.

It also has in its left hand a shield hanging from its shoulders, because on the left side, which is the devil’s battle against humanity, the person is surrounded by the grace of God’s strongest commandments. By these the person is surrounded and defended with such strength of faith that the devil may not corrupt him by his persuasions, nor may the person subject himself to his vices, being protected by God and encircled from the shoulders. For God’s grace cleaves to the soul’s upright strength toward God in the bond of love for God and neighbour.

It is girded with a sword, by which a person ought to restrain himself through bodily chastisement in the severity of God’s word, cutting away iniquity from himself and from others. It also holds a spear in its right hand: this means that a person should be bold with confidence in God to overcome all the devil’s cunning. He does this with the most strong peace of the Lord, which is true justice, against the most wicked conflict of devil and human being; this can scarcely be overcome without God’s help.

That beneath its feet lies something like a lion with gaping mouth means the devil, whom victory has cast down beneath the feet of the straight way of life and truth, while Satan himself, gaping in most fierce and bitter cruelty, sought to swallow the human race. The tongue stretched out from its mouth is his supposition by which, in terrible iniquity, he thought utterly to devour the whole race of humankind descended from Adam.

And that there likewise lie beneath its feet certain people means those sluggish pipes of the devil under his agility, who bend themselves toward the beginning of every evil. The virtue itself has protected them, proceeding rightly in God’s zeal and justice, because murderous perverse schemes subject themselves to that devil, serving him in diverse manners.

Some of them sound trumpets because they rave with the sound of every evil, and, puffed up, rage with burning minds, hating God’s justice—one generation after another doing this in great pride. Others make playful noise with certain instruments of amusement because they are deceitful in fantastic delusions pertaining to the devil, and because they are obstinate in the twisting wantonness of pride that envies God’s discipline. Others also play various games because they occupy themselves in the diversity and filth of vices which, devising them in themselves according to the pleasure of their own will, they fulfil through diabolical snares.

This same figure tramples all these and the lion beneath its feet, because with exceeding zeal it drives away all these vanities of arts and crushes Satan’s persuasions in God’s justice. And with the spear which it holds in its right hand it sharply pierces them, because through confidence and boldness toward God it most powerfully transfixes them, overcoming and wounding all these uncleannesses in sufferings. For they are mocked by God and accounted as nothing, as it also shows in its aforesaid admonitory words.

But that you see two other figures standing toward this same tower within the building means that, within that work which the heavenly Father performed through his Son—openly showing him in the manifest work in which he had been shown in circumcision, under shadow—two virtues arose. These are Christ’s example in the one, and following his footsteps in the other. They appear, with the greatest strength and reverence, in answer to the forecourse of God’s will, because in themselves they disclose the fruit prefigured in circumcision.

The first of them appears standing upon the pavement of that building, as if in an arch of fiery splendour painted within with diverse images of evil spirits and placed opposite the aforesaid tower. This means that the same virtue is perfected in earthly matters by trampling them down in the goodness of the Father, while it diligently passes beyond the desires of the flesh in the example of the Son of God.

How? It passes through the adversities of the world with much endurance, strongly tested and sifted in the arch—that is, in the height of worldly power—which is fiery in the terror of calumniating pride, followed by the diabolical host. This power draws the inner carnal desires of souls loving worldly things to its own will. The same arch, through earthly power, also sometimes sets itself in many ways against justice, resisting the covenant established in God. Yet the victorious virtue overcomes all these things, by God’s help in good people, although they are greatly attacked and wearied by the snares of the wicked.

The other stands only beside that arch on its outer side and is in no arch. For when the first virtue patiently conquers the swollen power which has inflicted many punishments upon it, this virtue proceeds outside that same power. It has arisen, as it were, outside it from the sufferings the first endured, escaping its rage; yet it remains beside it, which is the remembrance of the afflictions from which it took its origin. It stands without the depression of the arch because it is free from the power of this world, openly bearing Christ’s cross.

That both sometimes look toward the aforementioned tower means that they are the full work prefigured in the forecourse of God’s will in the circumcision of the Old Testament, considering the beginning of their root. Yet they are greater than that same beginning which they had in circumcision, because the shining work surpasses the commencement of doctrine. At times they also look toward the people entering and leaving that building. This is their admonition in the Holy Spirit to peoples who walk toward God in the way of the Law of justice, and to those who are in the crimes of the devil and wish to depart from the right way. They exhort them to imitate the virtues in goodness.

They too are clothed in silken garments because they have that sweetness by which a person is not burdened in the vexation of the toil of persecutions. They are veiled in a white head-covering tied in womanly fashion because it is right that a person should be subject to God as his head, continually placing him around his mind in the whiteness of love, so that he may embrace him with joy and gladness, just as a woman holds her husband in the honour of fear and love, as God established.

But they are not wrapped in mantles because they lack every worldly concern, turning themselves only toward those things which are eternal in God in the life to come. They wear white shoes because they shine in the paths of justice through the whiteness of faith in human minds, so that people too may follow the tracks of their example.

The first figure signifies patience, because it arose in Abraham’s horn—that is, at the beginning of obedience—when, by obeying God in circumcision, it signified the first sound of obedience after Adam’s fall, anticipating active obedience in the true Word, who is the Son of God, just as sound precedes word. It stands in the northern region, namely opposite the wickedness and unrest of the ancient serpent.

It has upon its head something like a triangular red crown, red as a red hyacinth in its colour, because at the beginning of the minds of faithful people it is greatly crowned through faith in the Holy Trinity. They despise their flesh for God’s love and do not hesitate to pour out their blood for love of God and true faith. For the Son of God, appearing in the flesh, overcame death with the redness of his blood, through which the Church is adorned, as it were with a noble red hyacinth in its beauty.

It also wears a white tunic whose folds are everywhere marked with green, because it has clothed itself in the garment of God’s work, adorned in the whiteness of perpetual light: namely, in its folds, which are afflictions and groans, saying, “O when shall I come to the sight of the true light?” This desire is happily possessed in the present life in a shadowed example. Through it the adversities of the faithful are adorned in the greenness of the soul, marked with many calamities, enduring all these things for God in patience, as this virtue itself also declares in its aforesaid words.

The other figure represents groaning, because after patience amid adversities there rises in my elect the groaning of the remembrance of life, arising at my admonition: for from my heart I sent my Son because of the groaning of my people. For my people in the Old and New Testaments had and have this remembrance of the mind, which groaning embraces in its mournful adornment, because it is true compunction of heart.

For this reason it too stands in the northern quarter, that it may oppose the unrestrained uncleanness of diabolical snares. It wears a white tunic, though of a somewhat pale colour, because it is surrounded by good works in the whiteness of faith; yet it displays a troubled pallor because it always has sighs and tears for eternal happiness.

That it bears upon its right arm a cross with the image of the Saviour, inclining its head upon it, means that on its right side—that is, in the right side of its strong work—it embraces the passion of my Son, panting with the whole desire of its intention and bowing itself toward him, imitating him in pains and afflictions, as it also shows in the aforementioned words of its exhortation.

Therefore you also see that all the aforesaid figures utter their several words through God’s mystery for the admonition of humankind. For in all virtues the kindness of God teaches with sweetest gentleness, exhorting the minds of peoples to leave evil and raise themselves toward good. But whoever has keen ears of inward understanding, let that person, in the burning love of my mirror, pant after these words and write them in the conscience of his or her mind.

## FOURTH VISION

[Col. 0599]

SUMMARY.—When the severity of the Law was softened in the incarnation of the Word of God, the mighty powers manifested themselves, and the justice of God was made plain. That the patriarchs signified in mystery that the Law was near. That no pride can withstand God’s strength. That God’s justice is to be feared, and that its height surpasses all creatures. That the Word of God has three sharp, cutting points: the old Law, the new grace, and the interpreters of the divine books. On the first knowledge of the divine Law, the working of the Gospel, and the refined wisdom of the principal teachers. That from the beginning of the Law God extended the times of the patriarchs and prophets to the manifestation of his Son. That the patriarchs and prophets, reverencing evangelical doctrine, marvelled at the incarnation of the Son of God. That the Word of God lay hidden through the type of prefiguration in the souls of the ancients, from the first elect person to the last. That the teaching of the Son proceeds from the Father and returns to the Father, spreading into the fruit of blessing and thus reaching the teachers of the Church. That, while Christ preached, apostles, martyrs, and other elect persons came into being. When the Gospel had been spread abroad, the wisdom of divine Scripture was extended among human beings; at first it was pursued with less zeal, and at the end it is weak as the charity of many grows cold. That at the beginning of a good work a person ought to be fearful, in the middle strong and steadfast, and at the end humble. That the mysteries of the Son of God, set forth in the deepest secret of the Father in the Old and New Testaments, have been disclosed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, when they are shown to the man of ashes only in shadow. On God’s knowledge, and what its appearance signifies. That angels are around it, and why they have wings.
