On those called “compelled sheep.” That God constrains some with a gentler scourge, others with a stronger one, and others with the greatest affliction of mind and body. An example concerning Pharaoh, Moses, and Aaron on the same matter. On the kinds of chastisements and God’s consolations, as he examines human ways. The words of Solomon’s wisdom. Why God’s knowledge looks upon people clothed in a new garment.

[Col. 0601A] Then, beyond the aforesaid tower of the forecourse of God’s will, but one cubit below the angle facing north, I saw something like a column of steel-blue colour, placed externally against the aforesaid bright part of the wall of the same building. It was very terrible to behold, and of such magnitude and height that I could in no way discern its measure. This column had three angles, sharp like a sword from bottom to top. The first faced east, the second north, and the third south; and it was joined somewhat externally to the building itself.

From the angle facing east branches proceeded from its root to its summit. Near its root I saw Abraham seated on the first branch, Moses on the second [Col. 0601B], Joshua on the third, and then the remaining patriarchs and prophets, seated in order, each upon a separate branch and rising upward, according to the time in which they had succeeded one another in this world. All of them turned toward the angle of the same column which faced north, marvelling at the things which they saw in it through the Spirit as things to come.

But between these two angles—the one inclining eastward and the other northward—the column before the faces of those patriarchs and prophets was, from bottom to top, as though turned on a lathe and rounded, and full of wrinkles, as a shoot is accustomed to spring from the bark of a tree. From the second angle, facing north, a splendour of wonderful brightness went forth, stretching and bending back toward [Col. 0601C] the angle facing south. In this splendour, spreading to so great a breadth, I saw apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and many other saints walking in great joy.

But the third angle, facing south, was broad and extended in the middle, while at the bottom and summit it was somewhat slenderer and more constricted, after the manner of a bow drawn for shooting arrows. At the summit of this column I saw such brightness of light that human speech cannot utter it. In it there appeared a dove holding in its mouth a ray of golden colour, which illuminated that column with great brilliance.

As I looked there, I heard a voice from heaven rebuking me with great terror and saying: “What you see is divine.” At this voice I trembled so greatly that I dared not look there any longer.

Then I also saw within the aforesaid building something like an image standing on the pavement of that building before this same column. At times it looked at the column itself, and at times at those people moving about in the building. That image was of such splendour and brightness that, because of the excessive radiance shining in it, I could discern neither its face nor [Col. 0602A] the garments with which it was clothed, except only that, like the other virtues, it appeared in human form.

Around it I saw a most beautiful multitude, possessing angelic form and wings, standing in such reverence that they both feared and loved it. But before its face I saw another multitude in human form, appearing in dark clothing and standing in great fearful constraint. The aforesaid image looked upon those persons who came from the world and were clothed with a new garment in the same building, saying to each: “Consider the garment which you have put on, and do not forget your Creator, who created you.”

While I marvelled at these things, he who sat upon the throne again said to me: “The Word of God, through whom all things were made, was begotten before time from the heart of the Father; but afterward, at the end of the ages, as the holy men of old foretold, he was incarnate of a virgin. Although he assumed humanity, he did not abandon divinity; but, being one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he sweetened the world by his sweetness and illuminated it with the radiance of his brightness.

“Therefore this column which you see beyond the aforesaid tower of the forecourse of God’s will signifies the ineffable mystery of the Word of God. For in the true Word, that is, in the Son of God, all the justice of the New and Old Testament was fulfilled; these things were expounded through divine inspiration for the salvation of people who believe faithfully. This occurred when the same Son of the heavenly Father deigned to be incarnate of the most sweet Virgin. For after [Col. 0602C] the mighty virtues had manifested themselves through the forecourse of God’s will at the beginning of circumcision, then too the mystery of the Word of God was declared in strict justice: namely, it was intimated through the utterance of the patriarchs and prophets, who foretold that he would be manifested with all justice and with all ministries subject to God, and with the greatest severity, which touched God’s cutting justice, leaving no injustice unharmed without cutting it off through legal precepts.

“But its standing one cubit below the angle facing north means the surpassing nearness, in the human and individual course, which came from the patriarchs speaking in their signs of the strict justice of this same Word [Col. 0602D] of God, even to the Law, as though in the northern region opposing the devil. Thus it is of steel-blue colour and is placed externally against that bright part of the wall of the building, because the strength of the Word of God is unconquered and insuperable. No one can resist it through empty rebellion or base pride. Thus also the fathers of contemplative knowledge, through the fortifications and acts of justice, were as though externally joined to it; they had not yet been fixed in the fiery and perfect work lifting itself up in the Son of God, which they only foreshadowed in the outward sound of their words.

“It is also very terrible to behold, because justice in the Word of God is fearful to human knowledge amid the wicked judgment of unjust judges, who judge only according to themselves. It is likewise of such magnitude and height that you cannot discern its measure, because the Word itself, namely the Son of God, in the greatness of his glory and the height of his divinity, surpasses all creatures in the Father’s majesty, so that no human being in corruptible flesh can perfectly contemplate this.

“That the same column has three angles, sharp like a sword from bottom to top, means that the circling and active strength of the Word of God, which the Old Testament prefigured as to be made manifest in the New through the Holy Spirit, has three cutting points: the old Law, the new grace, and the exposition of faithful teachers. In these, the human being performs what is just, from the beginning of his undertaking—as at the bottom, when he begins good—to his ascent toward perfection, as to the summit, when he brings it to completion. For everything just has been, is, and remains for ever in the most simple Godhead which penetrates all things, so that no power can persist in its wickedness when the glory of his mercy wills to overcome it.

“And the first angle faces east: it is the first dawning of the beginning, to know God in the divine [Col. 0603C] Law, before the perfect day of all justice. The second faces north, because after the beginning of good and established activity, the Gospel of my Son and the other precepts arose in me, the Father, against the northern region where every injustice arose. The third faces south and is joined somewhat externally to the building itself: it is the deep and refined wisdom of the principal teachers, whose works of justice are strengthened through the heat of the Holy Spirit. They made plain what had been obscure in the Law and the prophets, and in the Gospels displayed the shoot which they rendered fruitful for understanding—both for the nations, in the outward material of the Scriptures, through the work of the Father’s goodness, and for those who gently ruminate upon their mystical meaning.

[Col. 0603D] “That branches proceed from the angle facing east, from its root to its summit, means that in the dawning of the knowledge of God through the Law of justice, as though in an eastern angle, branches appeared: namely, in the time of the patriarchs and prophets. For that sharp column of divinity extended all these things from the beginning of the root—that is, good beginning in the minds of his elect—to its summit, which is the manifestation of the Son of Man, who is all justice.

“Thus near its root you see Abraham seated on the first branch, because this age, which first arose in Abraham when he left his native country with a tranquil mind in obedience to God, was breathed upon by the divinity pervading all things. [Col. 0604A] You see Moses on the second, because thereafter the planting arose by God’s inspiration at the beginning of the Law given through Moses himself, in prefiguration of the Son of the Most High. You see Joshua on the third because afterward he received this Spirit from God, so that he might establish more firmly the observance of God’s Law in the divine command.

“Then you see the remaining patriarchs and prophets seated in order, each upon individual branches rising upward, according to the time in which they succeeded one another in this world. For in each period of the succeeding patriarchs and prophets God inspired from above a particular shoot, reaching to the height of each of his commands, while they rested, in their own days, suitably and in order in the justice shown to them, faithfully subject to the divine majesty, as they came in their times.

“All these turn toward the angle of the column facing north, marvelling at what they see in it through the Spirit as future things. For all, admonished by the Spirit, turned through the Holy Spirit and saw the evangelical teaching of the strength of the Son of God opposing the devil. They spoke of his incarnation and marvelled that he, coming from the Father’s heart and from the Virgin’s womb, manifested himself in great wonders in his work and in the work of those who followed him. These, wonderfully imitating him in the new grace, will trample transient things underfoot and strongly pant after the joys of eternity.

“But the fact that between these two angles—one inclining eastward and the other northward—the column before the faces of these patriarchs and [Col. 0604C] prophets is, from bottom to top, as if turned on a lathe and rounded, and full of wrinkles, as a shoot is accustomed to spring from a tree’s bark, means this: between the two summits, namely between my manifest knowledge and the following teaching of my Son, the one Word who is my Son lay hidden through the type of prefiguration in the souls of the ancient fathers abiding in my laws, from the first elect person to the last saint. He was adorned with a mystical circlet, because he well composed and polished all his instruments, manifesting himself merciful to all through noble grace. Thus he was prefigured in the wrinkles of circumcision, which was a shadow of future things in its appended signs, possessing within itself, through the severity of the Law, the most upright hidden shoot of the highest and holiest incarnation.

“But the splendour of wondrous brightness which goes out from the second angle facing north, stretching and bending back toward the angle facing south, means that from the second—that is, the New Testament opposed to the devil—go forth the words of my Son, which proceed from me and return to me. For when the sun shines in flesh, which is my Son, the light of the holy Gospel gleams in his preaching, spreading from him and from his disciples into the fruit of blessing and turning back into the fountain of salvation. Thus it reaches the rulers: namely, the profound investigators of the words of the Old and New Testament, who show that wisdom has been raised up in that sun illuminating the world, which burns greatly at its side, like midday in its elect.

[Col. 0605A] “And in that same splendour, spreading to such great breadth, you see apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and many other saints walking in great joy. For in clear light, while my Son preached and spread the light of truth, apostles were made ministers of true light; martyrs became strong soldiers faithfully shedding their blood; confessors became diligent followers after my Son; virgins followed the heavenly shoot; and my other elect rejoiced in the fountain of joy and the fountain of salvation while the Holy Spirit poured himself over them, so that they might blaze and flow from virtue to virtue.

“But the third angle, facing south, is broad and extended in the middle, while at the bottom and at its summit it is somewhat slenderer and constricted, after the manner of a bow drawn for shooting arrows. This means that, when the Gospel had been spread abroad, the wisdom of the saints burned in the fervour of the Holy Spirit. They sought it in depth so that through it they might discover the typical shoot of profundity—namely, what they ought to understand in the Word of God. This wisdom was immediate, that is, broad, because through faith strengthened and fortified in the Christian people, the meaning coming from the souls of holy teachers was broad as though in the middle. These teachers, searching out the deep roughness of the Scriptures, set it forth for the knowledge of many who learned from them. Thus they extended their understanding in the expansion of the wisdom and knowledge of divine Scripture, [Col. 0605C] which at first, as at the bottom of ecclesiastical institution, was still pursued more slenderly and with less study, because the peoples had not yet embraced it with the love that they later did. At the end of the age, however, as at its summit, the studies of many will grow cold, so that divine knowledge will not be dear to them in the love of working; rather, they will hide their conscience from themselves, as though good need not be changed into action, knowing it only outwardly, as in sleep.

“Therefore this angle is broadest in its middle amid roughness, because the harsh works of God’s worship, stripped of the shadowing of the Old Testament, stretched out from their more constricted beginning toward their middle. These are the strongest virtues in loftier study, when the people were quicker, through the words which are God’s, to oppose wickedness—that is, the devil—and to cast out and trample all his vices underfoot with great severity of God’s justice. Yet it finally descends into forgetfulness of itself, becoming more constricted in the fervour of the Holy Spirit near the end of the world. It is extended as wood is drawn with a string for battle, because a person must raise himself in soul and body against vices: narrower at both ends and broader in the middle, so that in his first and final work he may be watchful in great fear and humility, and in the middle strong and steadfast, shooting the arrows of good works through the gift of the Holy Spirit against the devil’s snares.

“For at the beginning of good a person has slenderer strength; but in the continuation [Col. 0606A] of his activity, when he performs good, he has stronger strength, because the Holy Spirit has passed through him by his infusion. Yet this active strength cannot be frequent. Hence he will again be of more constricted strength, as though at the end of his work, through the frailty of his flesh. Thus the bow of one fortifying himself against diabolical vices must always be drawn.

“That at the summit of the same column you see such brightness of light that human speech cannot utter it means that the heavenly Father set forth the mysteries of his Son in his highest and deepest secret. The Son shines in that same Father with clearest radiance; in him all justice was brought forth, both in the legal declaration and in the New Testament, which is the greatest brightness of shining wisdom. No earthly person can express this in any speech while in corruptible flesh.

“And the dove appearing in the same brightness, holding in its mouth a ray of golden colour which illuminates the column with great splendour, is the fiery Holy Spirit in the flashing light of the Son of God shining in the Father’s heart. Through him the mysteries of that most high Son of God, coming from supreme height for the redemption of the people deceived by the ancient serpent, have been disclosed. Thus the same Holy Spirit inspired all legal precepts and new testimonies, giving the Law of the brightness of his mystery before the Lord’s incarnation and showing his power in that same brightness in the incarnation of the Son of God. In the deepest character of his inspiration he has a golden splendour: namely, the excellent and most surpassing illumination of his anointing, in rich and great mystical outpouring, opening the secrets of the only-begotten God to the ancient heralds, as has been said. They typologically displayed the Son of God, and marvelled greatly at him as he ineffably proceeded from the Father and wondrously arose in the dawn of the perpetual Virgin. He also powerfully kindles the text of the Old Testament and the Gospel into a spiritual shoot in which all justice is raised up.

“Therefore, because of the immeasurable power of divinity, it is not possible for you to gaze upon the divine brightness, which no mortal person can see except as I show it in shadow to whom I will. Therefore beware lest you rashly presume to direct your attention toward that which is divine, as the trembling which seized you also demonstrates.

[Col. 0606D] “But the image which you see within the aforesaid building standing before this column upon the pavement of the building means that within the work of God the Father this virtue manifests itself, declaring the mystery of the Word of God. For it has opened all justice in the city of the Almighty among the people—namely, that of the Old and New Testament—standing upon the pavement, that is, over all earthly things in the work of that same merciful Father, since all earthly things, as well as heavenly, are in his providence.

“That it sometimes looks at the column itself and sometimes at those persons moving about in the building means that the power of divinity considers both its secret which it has brought forth in the Word of God, and the people it perceives as working in the Father’s goodness—whether they touch it or do not touch it in their work—for it knows the quality of each according to his zeal.

“This image represents the knowledge of God, because it foresees all people and everything in heaven and on earth. It is of such splendour and brightness that, because of the excessive radiance which shines in it, you cannot discern either its face or the garments with which it is clothed. For it is terrible in terror, like threatening lightning, and gentle in goodness, like the splendour of the sun. Thus it is incomprehensible to human beings both in its terror and in its gentleness: through its terrible brilliance, divinity is as its face, and through the brightness it has in itself, its garments are as garments of adornment. Even the sun cannot be looked upon either in its burning face or in the beautiful clothing of its rays.

“It is present with all things and in all things, and is of such beauty in its secret that no person can know with how great sweetness it endures human beings, or how it spares them in manifest mercy, until the hardest stone can no longer be pierced in its impenetrable hardness. This stone is the hard and incorrigible person, who in no way wishes to turn aside from evil. Yet it appears in human form like the other virtues, because God, in the virtue of his goodness, made the human being most deeply adorned with rationality, knowledge, and understanding, so that, loving him with inward love and worshipping him with the greatest devotion, he might despise the creations of demons. God especially loves the person to whom alone he gave such and so great an honour.

[Col. 0607C] “But the most beautiful multitude which you see around this image, having angelic form and wings, and standing in such reverence that they both fear and love it, means that everywhere the blessed and exalted spirits in angelic ministry worship God’s knowledge with inexpressible and most pure praise—a worship which a person cannot fulfil so worthily while still in a mortal body. They embrace God in their ardour, because they are living and exalted light; not because they have wings like another flying creature, but because in their spheres they blaze through God’s strength, as though winged. Thus they reverence me, the true God, persevering in right fear and true subjection, knowing my judgments and burning in my love, because they continually behold my face, desiring and willing nothing other than what they see pleasing to my discerning eyes.

“But the other multitude which you see before its face, appearing in human form and dark clothing and standing in much fearful constraint, consists of human beings in God’s knowledge. How so? A person is in God’s sight in great honour when he foresees that person as belonging to himself, once that person is set aside who strives rather to persist in perdition than to be in God.

“But the persons whom you see in this multitude are called compelled sheep. They have human appearance because of human works, and shadowy clothing, which is doubt in the works of sinners; nevertheless, they stand in fearful constraint, fearing God’s judgment. They are called compelled sheep because I compel them in many ways to reach life, having been rescued from death through the blood of my Son. Thus the compelled sheep are those persons who, against their will, are compelled by me through many tribulations and afflictions to abandon their iniquity, which through the will of their own flesh and the flower of youth they would most gladly have practised for as long as they clung to the world. They wished to remain in the heat of lust until the fire of the flesh deserted them through the cold of old age. Yet I constrain them all in different ways, according to what I see in them, so that they may cease from their sins.

[Col. 0608B] “For some of them, in whom the world does not burn with such strong desire, I do not constrain with a stronger scourge but with a gentler one. I do not see in them the bitterness which is in others; when they feel my correction, they immediately abandon their will with haste, renounce worldly pomp, and come to me.

“But others I rebuke with a stronger lash, because through the vice of their flesh they are so burning and obstinate in sins that, unless they were strongly restrained by me, they would not be fit for my kingdom. My knowledge foresees and knows them, and constrains them according to the excess of their bodily nature.

“Again, I overcome some in the greatest and strongest affliction and misery of their minds and bodies, because they are so rebellious and so excessive in the work of carnal pleasure that, unless they were constrained by most grievous calamity, they would not cease from crimes through the wantonness of their flesh. While they were in the prosperity of their own will, they would not turn to God. For where one person entirely falls into despair through faintheartedness of mind, another makes sport through the foolishness of his pride; and by what one is wholly trampled down into despair, another is scarcely constrained in the fullness of his spirit.

“In this way I restrain those who belong to me when they oppose me in their works. Because I know them, they are at least compelled by the bodily and spiritual calamities which they suffer to come to me, so that they may be saved. Thus Pharaoh, terrified, at last compelled the Israelite people to depart from his land, as it is written: ‘And Pharaoh, summoning Moses and Aaron by night, said: Rise, go out from among my people, both you and the children of Israel. Go and sacrifice to the Lord, as you say. Take your sheep and herds, as you requested; and, departing, bless me’ (Exod. XII).

“This means: burdensome and most grievous crimes, which cling to this world amid many afflictions and miseries, weigh down exceedingly many persons, who say in their hearts: ‘Alas, alas! Where shall we flee?’ Then these same afflictions, quarrelling, drive them away from themselves, so that the people themselves hasten to withdraw from them. For within themselves they wither in their bodies from the weight of the scourge of God’s hand, unable to live joyfully in worldly pleasure, because [Col. 0609A] God seeks them. This is the calling of the righteous through diverse calamities in the dark works of the night of sinners.

“Thus Pharaoh, that is, diabolical vices, call in the cry of afflictions and miseries Moses—that is, those persons whom God constrains by the strongest spiritual or bodily pains—and Aaron, those whom he restrains by lighter adversities. Summoned in the night-time of evil works, the vices say to them in their oppression of human pleasure: ‘Rise from your carnal habit and go out from the old dwelling you had with us. Separate yourselves from the common people whom we possess when they worship us; withdraw from worldly occupations to which we gladly cling—you who were terrified in us when you were in our captivity, and with you the children of God, who see him in knowledge of him. Therefore go, leaving us by another way, and offer yourselves to God through the unconquerable causes by which, as you say, you have overcome us in your desires. Take also your gentleness, in the sheepfold of meekness, by which it is hard for you to labour with us because you wish to endure another suffering in following the Lamb. Take up, in the strength of the herds, the most victorious arms with which you overcame us and which we cannot resist, in the newness of mind which you now wish to possess. Separate yourselves from us as you long wished when you fiercely attacked us; and, going to the homeland for which you grieve in your souls, embrace the other life which leads you away from us. Bless, in the praise of God, [Col. 0609C] that battle in which you departed from worldly causes and occupations.’

“I too, almighty God, as I compel the aforesaid sheep to cross over to me, likewise strengthen my columns—that is, the stronger heirs of heaven—in the foundation of chastisement, according to the wickedness of the entanglement of sin in the assault of Adam’s transgression by which they are attacked. For they could not stand if my grace did not strengthen them.

“Some of them, whom so heavy a weight of vices does not oppress, I chastise with gentler correction, because if I constrained them with a sharper lash, their spirit would entirely fail and they would fall into despair. For they are not bound by the blast of a greater whirlwind of diabolical suggestion.

“But others, burdened by a heavier mass through a variety of most savage habits and excessive desires in the diabolical struggle, I hold in the hard constraint of most grievous pains, so that they may not depart from my covenant. They stand by it, desiring with all their longing to lay hold of me and observe my commands. For if I corrected these gently like the former, they would regard my corrections as nothing, because they are attacked by the most grievous contest of the ancient serpent.

“There are also certain exiles from the heavenly homeland whom I do not acknowledge, because they entirely abandon me, deceiving themselves through the rapacious frenzy of their own minds. They neither seek me nor wish to know me, but suffocate good desire within themselves. Thus they ask no help from me, greedily delighting only in their own affairs, as they delight in carnal desires.

[Col. 0610A] “Some of these do whatever they wish in excess and in delight of the flesh, yet without being in hatred and envy. They wallow in pleasant pleasures, possessing the delights and sweetness of their flesh. I allow them the fruits of the earth in prosperity, so that they do not fail in poverty, because they too were created by me and do not consume the people through their wickedness. Therefore it will be given them according to their desires.

“But others are of such ferocity and excessive bitterness of gall, hatred, and envy, returning evil for evil and unwilling to endure any injury inflicted upon them, that if they possessed worldly honour and riches, they would destroy heavenly virtues in people so that they might not be worshipped in them. Therefore I take fruits and riches away from them and cast them down into great miseries, so that they cannot raise themselves to so great an evil as lies in their will. For they would perpetrate diabolical works if they had the means.

“Thus I oppose the ways of human beings, both good and evil, weighing their ascents by a right measure according as my eye sees their desires. As wisdom also bears witness through Solomon, saying: ‘All human ways lie open to his eyes; the Lord is the weigher of spirits’ (Prov. XVI).

“This means: all paths breathed by the living mind of human beings, in the presence of his knowledge—namely, insofar as a person has the circuit of understanding concerning useful fruitfulness and the weakness of uselessness—are open to the sight of almighty God. Thus God sees through all things; absolutely nothing is hidden from the gaze of his divinity, because he knows all things. He looks upon everything in this way so as rightly to order each thing.

“How so? For he is the weigher of spirits, soothing them in the sweetness of consolations and tranquillities, and chastising them amid the tribulation of pains and miseries, so that they may be shaken out to the right measure. They cannot exceed this measure against him either by running or fleeing, except so far as he tests them according to their merits. Their weighing is what is shown in the testing of their recompense, whether in this age or in the age to come: namely, how they worshipped God.

“Therefore these spirits are weighed justly, so that human rationality is neither raised higher nor cast lower than God repays by his just judgment. For he so resists it that no soul has such power in the excess of anything as to be able to oppose God. He judges all things most rightly, opposing them by his justice, which they cannot resist so as to be able to do more than his ordinance permits. For as lead rightly weighs money, so God, with an equal balance, sets such an obstacle before good and evil that they can in no way escape the most equitable rule of his judgment: these receive glory and the joy of life according to their merits; those, the punishment and sorrow of death, according to what God most sharply foresees in them.

[Col. 0611A] “That the aforesaid image looks upon those people who come from the world and are clothed in a new garment in the same building means that God’s knowledge knows those who, abandoning the perfidy of their unbelief, put on the new person in baptism under the power of God’s work for eternal life. It moves them not to turn back and go to the devil; or, if they have strayed into that path, to return to God their Creator, as it says to each of them in its words of admonition, as was said above.

Whoever has keen ears of inward understanding, let that person, in the burning love of my mirror, pant after these words and write them in the conscience of his or her soul.

VISION FIVE.

[Col. 0611]

### Summary.—On the form of God’s zeal and what it accomplishes

That God carefully examines human sins, either punishing them in the human body or by the punishment of the age to come; or else the person himself will cleanse them through repentance in soul and body. Job’s words on the same matter. Those who sin with fear deserve, through God’s grace, to rise again through repentance in purification; if they do not find this fully here, they will find it in the future. How, in human rationality, good answers evil and evil answers good unto death. That a human being has within himself two calls: one calls to life and the other to death. The Psalmist’s words on the same subject. That the wonderful and astonishing judgments of God’s zeal were seen in the Old Testament so that God might be feared. That God is not moved from the rectitude of judgment by deceptive or flattering speech. That heavenly vengeance does not exceed human deeds by punishing more severely. David’s words on the same subject. That the Lord’s eyes see every injustice in order to punish it; so that, although human understanding cannot search out God’s judgment, human crimes are nevertheless not neglected without examination. That the zeal of the Lord, judging human works justly, is terrible to every creature. That the power of the Holy Trinity, in great sweetness and righteous vengeance, subjects human minds to itself according to the diversity of their intentions. That God’s zeal first conquered the devil in Christ, then drove him away in the elect, and thirdly will utterly crush him in the son of perdition, sparing those who fear and chastising rebels. That the hardened, who despise God’s justice and accept neither God’s admonition nor human exhortation, are cast into perdition. That the elements complain of the hardness of the impenitent and bring vengeance upon them. That God brings upon rash persons, who sin presumptuously and knowingly, the vengeance of Cain and Pharaoh and of those who worshipped the idol at Horeb and who were initiated into Baal-peor. Concerning God’s justice, which arose in Abel, was cultivated in the other elect, and became sweet in the Son of God: when it is transgressed, God’s zeal—then present, present now, and enduring—avenges it. Whoever, in a dog-like manner, abominates the Church, destroys the dedication of a church, or destroys things belonging to churches, is cast out by God’s zeal. That the dedication of a church was prefigured in Jacob’s deed. Wherever Christ’s body is to be offered, there ought to be a marked stone, even if, because of some impossibility, there cannot be a church there. That a church ought to have a ground for its establishment attached to it from the labor of the people. How and for what reason Jacob gave tithes of all his substance. Those who destroy churches, pollute dedications with homicidal blood or fornication, lack the marked stone in the sacrifice, or plunder tithes or the possessions of the church: O woe to them, woe to those miserable people! Those who distribute the Church’s possessions to dogs and swine—that is, wicked people—will be thrown by God’s zeal, together with their seed, from the highest rank to the lowest. How God strikes believers and unbelievers by His vengeance. Those who think themselves wise and exalt their own power through unjust judgments: how miserably God’s zeal burns them up. That in God’s zeal there is no cry of a threatening voice, but the immovable and firm power of just judgment. That knowledge in a human being is like a mirror in which the desire for either good or evil lies hidden. How fear proceeds from dread, trembling from fear, and how through these three a person ought to do what is just. On the first root, that is, human discernment, and on the aforesaid fiery grace in Christ. That no one ought to mutter against his Creator in excuse for sin.

[Col. 0611B] After this I saw, and behold: in the northern corner at the junction of the two forms of the wall of the said building there appeared, as it were, a head of wondrous form, placed immovably upon the outside of that corner at the neck. It was as high from the earth as that corner itself was high, yet it did not exceed it, but was equal to it only at its summit. That head was fiery in color, glowing like a flame of fire; it had a terrible human face and looked northward in great wrath. But from the neck downward I saw none of its form, because the rest of its body lay altogether hidden and enclosed within the aforesaid corner. The head itself I saw as, so to speak, the bare form of a human head: covered neither with hair in the manner of a male figure nor with a veil according to female custom; yet it appeared much more masculine than feminine, and exceedingly terrible to behold.

It had three white wings of marvellous breadth and length, like a bright cloud—not raised upward, but extended straight out separately from one another. Yet the head itself slightly surpassed them in height. [Col. 0611C] The first, rising from the right cheek, stretched northward; the second, which was also the middle one, ran from its throat toward the north; and the third stretched from the left cheek toward the west. At times they moved with great terror and struck in those directions; at other times they ceased from striking. I did not hear that head utter any words; but, remaining motionless in itself, it sometimes struck with its wings toward the places toward which the wings themselves stretched, as has been said.

And again I heard Him who sat on the throne saying to me:

God, who exercised His zeal severely among the ancient people, shows Himself gentle and sweet in the new people because of His love for His Son. This is not because He now carelessly overlooks or lightly esteems the sins of offenders; rather, He mercifully awaits the inward and true repentance of a pure heart, while He does not tolerate the wickedness of the hardened but punishes it by His just judgment.

Thus this head which you see appearing in the northern corner at the junction of the twofold wall of the said building signifies the zeal of the Lord: the unyielding vengeance upon iniquity that seeks no remedy. It rises openly through the mystery of the Word of God, disclosed through the figures and utterances of the patriarchs and prophets and foretold in their meanings. So too His zeal is seen in the form of a head, because it is known above every fear in the severity of its vengeance, just as a person is known by his face. It burns against the northern region because, swift and sharp in God, it slays the devil and every evil. For in Abraham and Moses also the two parts of the defense of those who act—the contemplative knowledge of the two possible courses, namely the two ways of good and evil—join the human race to God’s work; because a person must act most strongly against the devil, in the knowledge of good and evil, in every matter through the goodness of the Father. [Col. 0613A]

But the zeal of the Lord avenges the transgression which takes place through speculative knowledge in the works of people who violate God’s commandments, where there is no place for pardon. Where is this? Namely, where there is neither fear of the Lord nor fear of man in the acknowledgment of God. And such a heart, hardened and dead in the filth of iniquity, so that it neither fears God’s judgment nor respects a human face, the zeal of the Lord, in God’s law, puts to shame and crushes by its vengeance through just judgment. How?

After a commandment has been established, where there is a transgression of the law, there is zeal that removes injustice through the most upright judgment. That injustice was removed in the Old Testament with the severity of recompense in the outward person [Col. 0613B]: when the transgression of the law was avenged bodily in that person. After the grace of the Gospel, that same zeal acts through repentance; and after human death it acts through the punishments and torments of Gehenna. For I examine human iniquities—conceived, brought forth, and twisted in those who perform them—in such a way that I avenge them either bodily in the human body, or in the punishment of the future age; or else the person himself shall cleanse them through the repentance of forgiveness, while living in soul and body, with which he also committed them. As my servant Job says in my Spirit:

> “I change my countenance, and am tormented with pain.  
> I feared all my works, knowing that You would not spare the offender.  
> But if I am wicked even so, why have I labored in vain?”  
> (Job 9)

This means: “I shall change my inward aspect.” How? I shall overthrow that which I am: mutable and overflowing in the blood of my veins, having in myself at one time pleasure, at another anger, and at another crushing sorrow. I behold this in myself as though I saw a pleasing face when I would gladly accomplish that very thing. But I shall change it against my will, turning myself to the work of good action.

And when I do this, I am grievously tormented by this scourge: I restrain myself, withdrawing from my recognizable face—that is, from the work of my will in its contrary pleasure—and joining myself to contemplative reflection, seeing God in a good conscience and not in the lust of the flesh, through which I do not attend to Him. And from these two causes I fear all my works. How? When I do a good work, I fear that it is not perfect before God, because I do not perceive it clearly but dimly, as in a mirror: sometimes knowing it in spirit, and sometimes ignorant because of the burden of my body. But when I do an evil work, I am ashamed through the conscience of my spirit, because in inward understanding I know that God will not spare those who have knowledge in their sins—that is, when a person understands what in his deed is opposed to God. Rather, he must be cleansed either by vengeance in the body, or by the punishment of repentance, or by the punishment of torments in the other life. [Col. 0614A]

Therefore He does not spare the offender if he does not repent. For no authority is given to him to sin so that he may sin; rather, he must be chastised either here or there. Consequently, if I am thus wicked and so hardened that I am unwilling to be softened so as to turn away from my own affairs, which are my sins—so that I do not look upon that great contest opposing me, namely that I am in frailty, but that I always stand opposed to God in my known motives, because I was conceived in sins, always desiring to work iniquity and not fearing to be judged by the Lord—why then, if I am confined in such vain labor, do I often, with the knowledge by which I acknowledge God, oppose iniquity within myself?

Yet I am not so powerless as to be ignorant of good and evil. Hence, if I reject understanding from myself by saying, “I do not know God,” I lie, because that very knowledge convicts me as blameworthy: I am God’s debtor when I begin to commit iniquity. But I do not labor in vain when, in a good conscience, I oppose evil, because I am God’s work; therefore I turn myself to Him and thereby receive a good reward.

Therefore I, the Lord of all, testify that a person must wash away his sins with the pain of groaning, or with the contrition of repentance, or with fitting vengeance, whether in this age or in the future, as has been said. How? Those who sin in fear and in the sorrow of repentance, fearing their sins, deserve through God’s grace often to rise from their offenses in their purification. Yet, if they do not find that purification more fully in this age, they will find it in the future unto life.

But those whose hardness of heart is so great that they neither desire nor wish to know their sins in the fear and sorrow of repentance, but remain in such wickedness as though God were not to be feared by them, shall obtain no purification of sins either in this life or in the next. Instead, they shall have punishments without the consolation of purification unto life, because, from the rationality with which they were created by Me, they refused to render an account of their disobedience. How?

Understanding, within human rationality, has two paths in the knowledge of good and evil, to which two responses belong: good and evil. How? Good answers evil when it resists it in the Lord. But evil answers good when it opposes it with the devil. Yet those answer evil with good who always restrain themselves in evil, lest they delight in their own pleasures. [Col. 0615A] But those answer good with evil who do not at all withdraw themselves from wicked acts, but delight in their lusts, unwilling to answer the call of evil. How?

A human being has within himself two calls: namely, the desire of fruit and the lust of failure. How? Through the desire of fruit he is called to life; through the lust of failure he is called to death. But in the desire of fruit, when a person desires to do good, saying within himself, “Do good works,” there is a response against evil, so that he may avoid it and produce useful fruit. But in the lust of failure, when he desires to perpetrate evil and thus exhorts himself, “Do the work of your pleasure,” there is likewise a response against good, because he does not wish to resist his iniquity but delights to arrive at failure, despising Me in this response and treating Me as an object of mockery by not rendering Me the honor due to Me.

And because he turns away from good, not grieving and afflicting himself through fear of Me, he turns to mockery concerning heavenly things, as the Psalmist says through My manifestation:

> “They have set their mouth in heaven,  
> and their tongue has passed through the earth.”  
> (Psalm 73)

This means: Many people are foolish in rationality, unwilling to understand the innumerable fear of the Lord. They withdraw from themselves the good desires by which they ought to pant after Me and know the true God. They refuse to give assent to good knowledge, which always stands by the person so that he may work good deeds in God. Yet they often embrace bitterness in opposition to good, stripping themselves and taking good treasure away from themselves while storing up for themselves a treasure of diverse iniquity. [Col. 0615B]

In these things they place the wandering of their mind in heavenly matters as though their mouth were badly covered, scorning them within themselves through mocking frenzy and saying in their hearts: “We can perform these works of our will as freely as those things called heavenly, which the ancients—unknown to us—established as it pleased them.” Thus they mock the words and ordinances of the ancient Fathers, which were established in Me through a heavenly work.

And in the savor of a wicked work, as it were upon their tongue, they stir themselves and pass onward in the boldness of their own ability; so that they stubbornly fulfill their desires, unwilling to restrain their bodies against vices, but roll about without the labor of their spirit in the desires of their flesh as upon earth, which is the devil’s seduction. [Col. 0615D]

And the fact that you see the aforesaid head of wondrous form means that in the zeal of the Lord are God’s wonderful and astonishing judgments, which no person burdened with sins can know. Its being placed immovably on the outside of that corner means that My zeal against the devil, as was shown in the Old Testament through Abraham and Moses, outwardly appears in contemplative knowledge and human practice before the sight of the peoples, so that they may fear Me, sensing My terror face to face. For My justice also threatens the north—the most cruel iniquity of Satan.

It remains immovable because God cannot at all be moved or softened from the rectitude of His judgment by deceptive or flattering speech, when crimes are not corrected. It is fixed, as though by the neck of His strength, to the law established by God for human action, rendering to everyone who does not observe the commands of the law the punishments he has earned, according to his evil works in which, filthy, he has withered away. It also opposes its supreme strength—as though with the power of its neck—to the devil and his followers, setting itself against their injustice. [Col. 0616A]

It is as high from the earth as that corner is high, because God, in the supreme justice of His vengeance, surpasses all earthly things. That vengeance has this height because, in the prefiguration of Abraham and Moses, human works were indicated through the law. For divine judgment stands at the summit of contemplative knowledge and of the actions of peoples in order to cast down their ignorance when they refuse to know God.

Yet it does not exceed that corner but is equal to it only at the summit, because heavenly vengeance does not exceed human deeds by avenging evil in them more or more severely than their deserts. Rather, in the excellence of His justice, it judges everything rightly by an equal and just judgment. Thus David again knew in the Spirit when he said:

> “I have known, O Lord, that Your judgments are equity,  
> and that in Your truth You have humbled me.”  
> (Psalm 113)

This means: Through Your goodness I have known in myself, O Lord, that You have not killed me for my sins, nor taken from me in soul and body the power to act; and that neither because of Your power nor because of Your wrath do You judge those who know or those who are ignorant beyond their deserts. For I do good by struggling against myself, but I do evil through the lust of the flesh. Therefore You give reward to good and judgment to evil, yet judge only what is equitable and just.

How? If You pressed more severely than human deeds deserve in their completed action, there would be no equity of judgment. But if You neglected them weakly, so that You did not summon to repentance and there were no searching examination in the cleansing of iniquity, then You, a just God, would soothe and foster injustice. For death was once the most bitter judgment in Adam’s death; but now grace has been restored in repentance, calling the person back to life—something which could be accomplished by no one but You, God. This is Your most righteous and equitable judgment: purification unto life with grace, because Your judgments measure each work by a right measure. [Col. 0616C]

For all that You do is in truth, so that You exercise no deceptive excess beyond measure; for what is more in excess or less in deficiency than is just is false. Yet in the many mercies of Your power You spare, not killing anyone through the capacity of Your most brilliant might. You count this within Yourself: that You spare through repentance. Therefore, because of Your mercy, I have humbled myself, giving glory to Your name, though at times I have also been troubled, because of my deserved faults, by Your judgment. [Col. 0617A]

The head’s fiery color, glowing like a flame of fire, means that in the zeal of the Lord there is a fiery obstacle against evils, red in the most powerful burning of His vengeance, having a terrible human face. For the eyes of the Lord see every injustice face to face, so that the faults of diverse crimes are not left neglected before God without His terribly examining them by His just judgment. And this is because the unjust works of a person are monstrous and horrible, displaying a human face in acts of fleshly desire.

It looks northward in great wrath because God, in His vengeance, abhors every evil that arises from diabolical suggestion. Yet the fact that from the neck downward you see none of its form, because the rest of its body is entirely hidden and enclosed in the aforesaid corner, means that no human understanding can search out to its end the right judgments in God’s zeal that powerfully scatter the wicked deeds of various persons. For they are concealed and covered in the corner of contemplative knowledge and human action, so that they cannot be seen or comprehended by any investigation—except that at times they are known when the deed is displayed in the occasion of God’s vengeance, just as a human face is seen according to the desires of that person’s will. [Col. 0617B]

Thus even in that vengeance there is no pretence of any leniency, but always just judgment according to human sins. For their crimes are not neglected without examination, as has been said, because the zeal of the Lord is His examination.

The fact that you see the head itself as the bare form of a human head means that this same zeal of the Lord is subject to no mortality, remaining bare of every subjection to weakness and justly judging human works. Nor is it covered with hair in the manner of a male figure, nor with a veil according to female custom, because it has no anxious concern to overcome anyone superior to itself by any masculine strength, nor does it possess any feminine softness of a timid mind unable to overcome what opposes it. Yet it is more masculine than feminine, because God’s most powerful strength is more in masculine vigor than in the softness of feminine negligence. [Col. 0617C]

It is exceedingly terrible to behold, because zeal is terrible and fearful to every creature when that creature feels it in the occasion in which its vengeance is given. But its three white wings, of marvellous breadth and length like a bright cloud, signify the expansion of the ineffable power of the Holy Trinity, which no person can comprehend in the breadth of Its glory or in the length of Its power. It shines in the great sweetness and brightness of divinity, and by righteous vengeance subjects human minds to itself in their great diversity, as clouds moving about.

The wings are not raised upward, but are extended separately in a straight direction; although the head itself slightly surpasses them in height. This means that the Lord’s vengeance is not lifted up in any arrogance but adapts itself to every case according to its deserts, extended according to the most upright standard of His corrective just judgment. Yet the possibility of God’s power—like the head of that same vengeance—goes before, in the height of its strength, the human works which the true Trinity does not endure without examination; though It does not avenge and crush them as sharply as the capacity of Its power could do. [Col. 0618A]

The first wing, rising from the right cheek, stretches northward because God first conquered the devil and all evil through His just judgment, from the right-hand side of salvation in His Son. The second wing, which is also the middle one, runs from His throat toward the north because, after the salvation accomplished in the Son of God—when faith had already been strengthened as it were in the middle, and the sweetness of the elect had been tasted—He also drove away through them the roaring enemy, rescuing them from his jaws. The third wing stretches from the left cheek toward the west because, when Satan has been driven away from God’s elect, he will also be utterly crushed on the left-hand side of perdition in the son of perdition, when the world is already tending toward the setting of its end.

At times the wings move with great terror and strike toward those regions, because the zeal of the Lord moves to vengeance as a terrible and most fearful judgment to every creature, exercising its judgments of striking wherever it pleases the divine majesty by just judgment. For where fear, love, and honor of God are faithfully maintained in reverence, God shows Himself gentle and sweet and does not exercise His vengeance. But He terribly and justly chastises the hard and rebellious. [Col. 0618B]

Therefore the first wing of My vengeance strikes and casts into the abyss of perdition those people who are so hardened beyond the hardness of stones that with their inward eyes they always contemptuously despise My justice. Looking backward through the knowledge of their understanding, they give greater consent to fleshly desires and diabolical persuasions than they are willing to know true justice, or to return by any consent of their own, by My admonition, or by a human exhortation. In this way they torture the spirit of their knowledge through their iniquity, because they love and do the devil’s injustice more than My justice.

They pour into their hearts, as it were, molten lead—that is, the loose desires of wicked softness—casting it, as though to establish iron hardness, namely forgetfulness of God. They are hardened as though they were iron, so that neither the cause of God nor that of any human being makes them spare themselves or any iniquity. [Col. 0618D]

Over these people the elements, together with the rest of creation, cry out and complain that humanity’s so lowly nature, in its brief span, is so rebellious against God, while they themselves always fulfill the Lord’s commands in fear and reverence. Thus they cry out terribly against humankind. How? Not in the sense that the elements cry out with a voice or complain with the knowledge of a rational creature; rather, according to their own mode, they cry out in the noise of their sounds and utter complaints in the fear of terrors. For when the just judgment of God brings them, or another creature, upon human beings who are rebellious, they neither stand nor conduct themselves otherwise than divine power turns them by its command.

Why do those hardened people so cruelly imitate Satan? Because in the hardness of their iniquity they refuse to submit to God their Creator; therefore he fell from every blessedness, and they too will perish with him by following him. [Col. 0619A]

But the middle wing of My zeal strikes mad people and every presumptuous evil that they knowingly and rashly commit. This first raised itself in a human being in the blood of Abel, whom his brother hated because he was dear to God on account of the offering of his substance, which he distributed with good will. It also raised itself in Pharaoh, who was warned by My wonders; terrified by My terror, he unwillingly let My people Israel go, yet afterward in his madness wished to draw them back, on account of which My zeal swallowed him up. It likewise raised itself in that people of Mine which, knowing Me and seeing My wonders, worshipped an idol at Horeb. Therefore the crown fell from its head, so that God’s law became perishable for them in the two stone tablets—other tablets like these [being supplied] because the former had fallen from their glory and blessedness—all this being avenged by My vengeance.

Thus Moses, My servant, exercised vengeance at My will against that contrary people which so often opposed Me in this zeal of Mine, when he strongly commanded My elect that each should kill his brother, friend, and neighbor. And again, when he fervently told the judges of that people that each should kill his neighbors who had been initiated into Baal-peor: there I avenged Myself, when that iniquity fighting against Me was slain. [Col. 0619C]

But God’s justice first arose in Abel. After him many other elect were found from among all those evil and perverse generations, who gathered and cultivated My more subtle commandments, as did the children of Israel. Among them too mourning and sorrow arose, as they longed for the humanity of My Son. But once the manifestation of that same Son of Mine, whom I sent to be born of a Virgin, had been accomplished, all the justice of the law was cooked and seasoned, becoming sweet and savory food for every people believing in Me, while the apostles of truth revealed truth itself.

Therefore, in all these aforesaid generations, this zeal of Mine avenged and avenges My justice when it is knowingly transgressed. For God, who was then, is now and will remain forever; and My zeal, which was then, is now and will always stand, until tribes and peoples come to an end. God’s justice does not come to an end, but shakes off every rust of injustice. [Col. 0619D]

For this reason, in this same zeal of Mine I remove this iniquity: namely, that of the person who, in a dog-like manner, abominates the Church flourishing in Me; or who through the madness of his iniquity destroys the dedication established by Me, or other established ordinances belonging to My temple. These rose powerfully in the prefiguration of My servant Jacob, as this Scripture has it:

> “Jacob, rising in the morning, took the stone which he had placed under his head, set it up as a memorial, poured oil upon it, and called the name of the city Bethel.”  
> (Genesis 28)

This means: Jacob rose in the morning because he himself arose as an early lover of true justice in the established temple. He gave it a fitting name because from him was to arise the most upright temple—namely, the Virgin Mary, from whom the Sun of Justice shone forth.

Taking the stone which, in the figure of the altar, he had placed beneath his upper head—that is, Christ—so that it might be sanctified in His name, who is the true Rock, and be called sanctified, because every sanctification of an altar is placed beneath the power of almighty God, the head of all the faithful, he set it up as a memorial of the book of life and as an image of the chief fragrance of the heavenly Jerusalem. For as Christ is the head of His members in the heavenly Jerusalem, so every sanctified altar is the more excellent part of its church. He poured oil over it in the sanctification of chrism: this is the poured-out grace of almighty God in holy baptism. [Col. 0620A]

And he called that sanctified place the house and temple of God, according to the name of the city of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the living temple of the living God.

Therefore, by this example and signification, a stone is to be raised in a church ordained in My name; that church is marked with a stone because I am the firm Rock to whom all the justice and law of Christians pertains. For wherever there is a sanctified place in which the body of My Son is to be offered, I desire a stone marked in My name to be there, because I am the truest strength—even if, because of some impossibility, there cannot be a church there. For My servant Jacob raised the stone in his prefiguration in My name, as has been said, because My Son also took flesh from his stock.

But a church so dedicated to Me ought not to be empty of this obligation, but ought to demand a ground for its establishment which is attached to it from the labor of the people who serve it. Likewise the heavenly Jerusalem, with Christ as its head, does not wish ever to lack its justice, as it looks toward the labors of its children, whom it will receive in God. How? [Col. 0620C]

They are to withdraw themselves from diabolical slavery, restraining themselves from the voluntary desires of their flesh and afflicting themselves against themselves by cutting off their own possessions for love of heavenly things. They are not to use all these things, but to take some away from themselves and offer them to God for His honor. Thus My servant Jacob, who went before, likewise established a tithe of all his substance when he said, as is written again:

> “Of all that You shall give me, I shall offer tithes to You.”  
> (ibid.)

This means: “From all that You shall give me, I shall offer You a tenth part, because this is Your law: first, O my God, in my soul, cutting off from it my own will and offering You justice against myself; and afterward, a tenth part of all my substance which I possess upon earth.”

What is this? Every faithful person who is comprehended in the tenth order of heavenly citizens ought always to give to My temple a tenth part of his substance, because of that restoration by which he has been counted within the tenth number of those who are numbered—that is, of those who exist in the knowledge of God and belong to the true temple, namely the heavenly Jerusalem. [Col. 0621A]

But those who, forgetting My fear, destroy churches dedicated in My name through the violence of their iniquity; or remove their dedications, which arose from Jacob’s example, by polluting holy places either with homicidal blood or with the pollution of seed poured out in adultery or fornication; or who in the heavenly sacrifice neglect the dedication established by the ancient Fathers, without the marked stone which Jacob raised in his prefiguration; or who abandon the justice established by Me concerning tithes or the possessions of My temple—O woe to the miserable, woe to the miserable, woe to those miserable people who so shamefully deceive themselves and are so perverse before the eyes of My majesty! They neglect, as has been said, My institutions, all of which have been carried over from the old law. For out of the Old Testament the new law has been brought forth in My Son according to the mercy of grace; and from all the justice of the law and prophets, what was less has become greater in that same Son of Mine, who openly displayed in Himself, in all justice, every sign of the earlier Fathers which they had spoken secretly in shadow. [Col. 0621B]

And those who abandon all these things, so that they contemptuously trample underfoot like mud the food of life which has been made from both Testaments, and distribute it to dogs and swine and other beasts—that is, to wicked people—giving it more to pagan customs and vain ignorance than to Me, almighty God, and preparing it for their own use according to their own will: them and their seed I shall abandon, casting them down from the highest rank to the lowest, and from riches into poverty, in the vengeance of this zeal of Mine. [Col. 0621C]

The third wing of my vengeance strikes both believers and unbelievers in their impious and unjust works. It strikes believers who do not perform good and just works according to their own good will: they see the faith clearly, and [Col. 0621D] the justice of God is known to them, yet they sit in the darkness of evil deeds. Groaning, they are unrecognized after the darkness of iniquity, wishing to revel in perversity. Yet God does not permit them to carry this out according to their own will, but cuts it off from them by His vengeance, while they are so darkened that they have forgotten Him and would most willingly depart from Him.

But it strikes unbelievers in their unbelief, so that their iniquity too is taken away from them with the recompense of vengeance, since they are not allowed to complete that evil which they would gladly do. Hence the malicious devil, overcome by the blessedness of faithful human beings sparkling before God’s eyes, would draw them into the darkness of death according to his wickedness; but he can no longer grasp them except insofar as their deeds are such. But there is another class of people upon the earth, who possess prosperity in the form of a discerning spirit, so that they are wise in remembrance of God, kindled according to their own will with understanding. Therefore they then wish presumptuously to possess in themselves the knowledge of wisdom, doing whatever they have conceived; and they mingle justice with iniquity. Yet they are foolish in wisdom, because they reckon themselves as though they were full and perfect for possessing, comprehending, and attaining, according to their own choice, the fullness of whatever they have conceived.

And when they wish to raise their wings through their own power in provinces, cities, other places, and other affairs in which they are then occupied [Col. 0622A] with authority—wherein they do not wish, by looking to God, to have an intelligible measure of what they do—then they are poured out and cast down before God’s eyes because of their impious and unjust judgments, which they had previously rendered without knowingly possessing the fear of the Lord. Thus, through this zeal of mine, they shall become a great lamentation and a cause of weeping before every people that sees and hears the time of judgment upon their iniquity: some of them still living in this life amid many miseries and many failures of theirs; others taken away by a most wretched death amid diverse sufferings. In so varied a reversal my zeal avenges and burns away every injustice, because it is against me.

But when you do not hear the aforesaid head uttering [Col. 0622C] any words, but it remains motionless in itself, merely striking its wings from time to time in the direction toward which the wings themselves are extended: this means that in the zeal of the Lord there is no outcry of a threatening voice raising itself in pride. Rather, steadfast in the power of His strength and in His righteous judgments, He avenges by His vengeance, confounding and crushing, after the madness of their deeds, actions deservedly performed without fear of the Lord, according to the extent of the vengeance of His judgment—as has been shown to you in a most truthful manifestation.

And because God is just, every injustice must be examined by the Just One; for God Himself knows well the discriminating examination that exists in human knowledge. For knowledge in a human being [Col. 0622D] is like a mirror in which the desire of the will, whether good or evil, lies hidden. Therefore, placed between these two sides, a person inclines by his will toward the side he desires. But the person who turns himself toward good, embracing it in faithful action through God’s help, shall laudably receive the reward of blessed recompense, because he has despised evil and done good. But one who inclines himself toward evil, swallowing it through perverse action at the devil’s suggestion, shall miserably incur the penalties of just retribution, because he has neglected good and committed evil.

Therefore, submitting himself to God in great devotion and humility, a person should faithfully work out his salvation, which flows from the highest Good, so that his soul may be intoxicated with inward holiness, because in well [Col. 0623A] ordered and rightly arranged examination and fear he serves his Creator. How? For dread—that is, the beginning of distress—produces fear; and fear stirs trembling, through which a person ought to do what is just. How? What a person begins to feel as distress through dread, he has from the gift of the Holy Spirit by means of rational understanding; and therefore it can in no way happen that he does not know God. The knowledge which he has of God produces fear in him, insofar as he begins to fear according to the things that belong to God. And if, with zeal, he possesses these things while knowing God, then fiery grace in Christ shakes him again, admonishing him thereafter to begin to tremble, so that he may be terrified through compunction and faithfully work God’s justice.

[Col. 0623B] Therefore now, O human beings, understand and learn whence these things come. What is this? It is God who works in you what is good. How? He established you so that through rational understanding you may perceive Him in your works, which you do wisely with discernment. For an irrational animal performs all its works without understanding, wisdom, discernment, or modesty; nor does it know God because it is irrational, but only senses Him, since it is His creature. But the rational animal, which is the human being, has understanding and wisdom, discernment and modesty in those works which it performs rationally. This is the first root which God’s grace fixed in every human being when it stirred the soul to life.

[Col. 0623C] These things, then, mentioned above, flourish in rationality, because in all these things human beings know God, so that they may will what is just. Therefore the overflowing, perfect, and prosperous work in a human being’s good will, which that person embraces in his Savior, namely in the Son of God—through whom the Father works all works in the Holy Spirit—this fiery grace, given anew in Christ Jesus, kindles and admonishes. Therefore, in the joy of the Holy Spirit, let a person perform works of justice, not doubting in perverse unfamiliarity; that is, let him not say that anything is lacking to him in all these things, either in the first root initially implanted in humanity through God’s gift, or in the fiery grace of the Holy Spirit again touching that root in admonition. Thus, after perversely falling, let him not afterward [Col. 0623D] be distressed concerning things done through blameworthy impulse, as though his inward root had possessed anything less; namely, lest, after falling and being placed in [Col. 0624A] necessity, he murmur within himself, saying: “Alas, alas! What have I done, that I could not foresee my works in God?”

Let him also proceed without the weight of unbelief, so that he does not distrust God in his works, but may be secure, without the tearful complaint of a perverse deed. For He, existing as God and human, is not divided into two, but Christ is one—not by a transformation of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of flesh, which divinity joined to itself and so suffused with its brightness that, as a ray of the sun shines in the sun, so it shines. Yet thereby neither the substance of divinity nor the substance of flesh has been confused with the other; rather, in the true unity of person, Christ, the true Son of God, is one.

For just as no change occurs in the rational soul through a human being’s flesh, but that rational breath is from God, permeates the whole human body, and moves all the actions of the acting human being—so that soul and flesh are one human being—so also, beyond all doubt, the Son of God, born before the ages, having fully clothed Himself, as stated above, in flesh assumed from the Virgin, is God and human, one Christ, called Christ indeed through the anointing of God’s grace. In His holy humanity He was wounded by the piercing of nails and a lance because of the one wound of the first human being, which that man had inflicted upon all his race, in order that He might heal it with the bruise of His blood, suffuse it with the anointing oil of grace, and bind it through repentance when a person grieves that he has sinned.

Wounded, His spirit descended into the pit of the infernal deep, [Col. 0624C] and there drew very many to Himself: namely, He took the first human being from hell, and all those who had never touched God in the customs of human honour, and placed them in the place of delights and joys which they had lost in their first parent. But in rising on the third day from the death of His sleeping body, He signified the three persons of the Godhead; and, ascending to heaven with that same body, He went there and sits in dominion at the Father’s right hand. This is the salvation of the believing people, granting life to those whom He redeemed by His blood. And all these were foreknown before the times of all beginnings, because the Father’s Word, through whom all things were made, put on flesh in order to redeem the human being whom He had formed.

But whoever has the keen ears of inward understanding, let that person pant after these words in the burning love of my mirror, and inscribe them in the conscience of his soul.

## SIXTH VISION

[Col. 0623]

[Col. 0623] **SUMMARY.**—Words concerning abstinence. Words concerning generosity. Words concerning mercy. Words concerning truth. Words concerning peace. Words concerning blessedness. Words concerning discernment. Words concerning salvation. That none of the faithful should disdain to be subject to teaching authority, since even through the teachers of the Israelite people, the rulers of the time of grace were prefigured in the Law. What the severity of the Law concealed as though beneath a veil, the incarnation of the Son of God illuminated through the grace of the Holy Spirit. That a person who exercises the dignity of teaching acts in God’s place. That besides the special teaching office there are certain greater persons of secular power, and lesser persons among the people, who are governed by both. That the inward is understood through the outward. Why God allowed one class to excel and another to be subject. Isaac’s words to Jacob on the same matter. Here is indicated a threefold order: rulers, free persons, servants. That secular and spiritual persons are divided into four and four. That no one should usurp spiritual or secular dignity for himself either by plunder, theft, or purchase. Those who possess mature understanding and a good conscience, seeking neither flighty words nor human praises, are worthy of election to rule. Whoever obtain governing authority while disregarding whether it pleases God or not, flee from God’s face and belong to the devil’s party; they are not resisted, so that at some time they may be punished more severely. That the aforementioned distinctions among human beings have existed, do exist, and always shall exist throughout the span of human time, according to the authority of divine Providence. That within the condition of secular persons—that is, greater and lesser—there are three divisions. That spiritual teachers ought to preside over the people in unity of faith. That secular governing power and the people should mutually touch one another with purity of innocence and simple devotion. That six virtues prefigured the others in God’s work. Concerning the state of abstinence, generosity, mercy, truth, peace, blessedness, discernment, and salvation of souls, and what it signifies. Concerning their dress and what it signifies. Specifically concerning abstinence, its dress, and what it signifies. Specifically concerning generosity, its dress, and what it signifies. Specifically concerning mercy, its dress, and what it signifies. Specifically concerning truth, its dress, and what it signifies. Specifically concerning peace, its dress, and what it signifies. Specifically concerning blessedness, its dress, and what it signifies. Specifically concerning discernment, its dress, and what it signifies. Specifically concerning salvation of souls, its dress, and what it signifies.

[Col. 0625A] And after these things I saw, between the northern corner and the western corner, the wall of the aforesaid building, entirely arched on its inner side after the manner of a lattice, yet not open like a lattice, but solid, with something like a picture of human beings in each arch. On the outer side of the same wall I saw two other, smaller walls, extending the length of the space from the aforesaid northern corner to the western corner, joined to these corners on either side, in the manner of a vault. The height of these two smaller walls was three cubits. The width between the inner arched wall and the middle wall was one cubit; and between the outer wall and that same middle wall there was the width of one palm, as it were [Col. 0625B] a child’s hand.

Within that same building I also saw six figures standing upon the pavement of the building before the aforesaid arched wall: three together at the front of that wall near the corner facing north, and three likewise together at the end of the same wall beside the corner extending westward, all looking at the pictures in the arches of that wall. At the very end of the same wall I saw another figure seated within the building upon a single stone, placed on the pavement like a seat, leaning her right side against the wall and turning her face toward the column of the true Trinity. But at the same end I saw another figure standing on the wall in a higher place, likewise turned toward the aforesaid column [Col. 0625C] of the true Trinity.

In these figures I saw the following appearance. They were clothed, like the earlier figures, as though in silken garments and white shoes, except the one to the right of the middle figure among the three which I had seen at the far end of the same wall. She was of such purity and brightness throughout that, because of her excessive splendor, I could not see her form distinctly. The figure standing upon the wall, as mentioned, alone wore black shoes. Yet all lacked cloaks except the middle figure of the three standing at the first part of the wall, who was clothed in a cloak.
