That the holiness of the true Incarnation, shadowed to human minds, is known inwardly through faith and work, and is made manifest outwardly through report and speech. That to God alone is known how many and what manner of persons are yet to come, so that the body of Christ may be completed. That all the works of the incarnate Son of God and the gathering of the Church from the four parts of the world are in the Father’s will. That in Christ all virtues work fully with keen zeal and are openly manifested in him. That the seven virtues signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Words of Isaiah on the same matter. Words of Solomon on the same matter. Concerning the state and clothing of the aforesaid virtues and what they signify. Concerning humility. Concerning charity. Concerning the fear of the Lord. Concerning obedience. Concerning faith. Concerning hope. Concerning chastity. Concerning the grace of God, its state and clothing, and what they signify.

[Col. 0651C] Then, in the southern region, in the aforesaid stone wall of the building shown to me, beyond the aforementioned column of the true Trinity, I again saw what seemed to be a great shadowed column, appearing both within and outside the building. It appeared so shadowy to my sight that I could not discern either its size or its height. Between this column and the column of the true Trinity was an interrupted space three cubits long, empty and without a wall, as was shown above, with only a foundation laid there.

This shadowed column stood in this building itself, in that place where I had previously seen, above in the heavenly mysteries before God, the great square splendor of brightest whiteness, manifested to me in the deepest mystery and signifying the secret of the heavenly Creator. Within it another splendor shone, like dawn, having in itself an airy brightness of purple light on high; through it, in mystical vision, the mystery of the incarnate Son of God had been shown to me.

In this column, from its bottom to its top, was an ascent like a ladder, where I saw all God’s virtues descending and ascending, going laden with stones to their work and intent upon completing that work. And I heard the radiant one who sat upon the throne saying: “These are God’s most mighty workers.”

But among these virtues I saw seven especially, and I considered their forms and garments with the greatest care. They all had this likeness: like the other virtues mentioned above, they were clothed, as it were, in silken garments. They all went with white hair, bare heads, and without the covering of mantles—except the first, veiled on the head in womanly fashion and clothed in something like a chasuble, transparent as crystal; except the second, who had black hair; and except the third, who appeared unlike human form.

The first, fourth, and fifth were clothed in white tunics. All also had white footwear, except the third, who did not appear in human form, as has been said, and the fourth, who was shod with crystal footwear shining wondrously. This was their dissimilarity.

[Col. 0652D] The first image wore upon her head a golden crown with three branches rising higher, and adorned with a splendid ornament of most precious green and red stones and white pearls. On her breast she had a most radiant mirror, in which the image of the incarnate Son of God appeared with wondrous brightness. And she said:

“I am the column of humble minds and the slayer of proud hearts. I began in the least things and ascended to the heights of heaven. Lucifer raised himself upward above himself, and fell downward beneath himself. Whoever wishes to imitate me, desiring to be my child—if he thirsts to embrace me as mother by accomplishing my work in me—let him touch the foundation and gently ascend upward to the heights.

“What does this mean? Let him first consider the lowliness of his own flesh; then, with a sweet and gentle mind, let him advance step by step from virtue to virtue. For one who first grasps the highest branch of a tree in order to climb very often falls in a sudden fall. But one who wishes to climb and begins at the root does not fall so easily, if he walks cautiously.”

But the second seemed wholly like a hyacinth of lofty, airy color, both in her form and in her tunic. Two girdles, wondrously interwoven with gold and gems beyond estimation, were attached to that tunic, so that one girdle descended over each shoulder of the image to her feet, before and [Col. 0653B] behind. And she said:

“I was provoked to indignation in heaven when Lucifer bit himself with hatred and pride. But O, O, O humility! She would not endure this. Therefore he too was cast down in a great ruin. But when the human being was formed—O most noble grain and O sweetest shoot—the Son of God was born human for humanity at the end of time.

“And because Lucifer wished and attempted to tear my garment and integrity, therefore I appeared as brightest splendor in God and in the human being. But now the blind and dead call my namesakes brothels, prostitutes, and incestuous women. Yet as it is impossible for mud to touch heaven, so impossible is it for this filth to touch my will.

“Therefore I shall make for myself wings in the other virtues, with which I shall cast away these useless things that Lucifer scattered through the world. O virtues, where is Lucifer? He is in hell. Therefore let us all rise, draw near to the true light, and build very great and strong towers in the provinces, so that when the last day comes, we may bring forth abundant fruit both in spiritual and bodily things. And when the fullness of the nations has entered, then we too shall be made complete on earth and in heaven.

“O most shameful Lucifer, what did your sudden rashness profit you? In your first splendor, when you were created by God, you madly and frenziedly wished to trample me underfoot and cast me from heaven. But you fell into the abyss, and I remained in heaven, afterward descending to earth in the incarnate Son of God. And through me was completed the multitude of the faithful, armed with a thousand just and good arts—whom, if you could, you would long ago most gladly have plundered.

“O humility, you who raise those trampled and crushed as if from the earth to the stars! O humility, most glorious queen of virtues, how strong and invincible a protection you are everywhere for your own! No one falls who loves you with a pure heart. Likewise, I am with you a most useful and greatly desired defense for my own; for, being very slender and subtle, I seek out the tiniest openings of those who honor me, and I pass through them most sharply.”

But I saw the third image in that same form in which I had seen it in the former vision—namely, larger and taller in stature than the other virtues, unlike the human form, having very many eyes on every side [Col. 0654A], living wholly in wisdom, and clothed as though in a shadowy garment through which, nevertheless, its eyes looked forth. It trembled with great fear before the aforesaid radiant one seated upon the throne. And it said:

“O woe to miserable sinners who do not fear God, but regard Him as though He were a deceiver! Who can escape the fear of the incomprehensible God, when He Himself allows the guilty person to perish if he does not cast evil away from himself? Therefore I shall fear the Lord God exceedingly and exceedingly. Who will help me before the true God? Who will deliver me in His terrible judgment? Absolutely no one but that same just God. Therefore I shall seek Him; to Him I shall always flee.”

The fourth bore a snowy-white band about its neck, and had its hands and feet bound with a white binding [Col. 0654B]. And it said:

“I cannot run according to my own will along the worldly way, nor through the contagions of human self-will; and therefore I desire to return to God, the Father of all, whom the devil rejected and whom he was unwilling to obey.”

The fifth likewise wore a red collar about its neck, and said:

“One God in three Persons, of one essence and equal glory, is to be worshipped. Therefore I shall have faith and trust in the Lord, and I shall never erase His name from my heart.”

But the sixth was clothed in a tunic of pale colour. And before it, in the air, appeared the cross of the Passion of the crucified Son of God; toward it the figure raised its eyes and hands with great devotion, and said:

“O merciful Father, spare sinners. You did not abandon the exiles [Col. 0654C], but lifted them upon Your shoulders. Therefore we do not now perish, since we have hope in You.”

But the seventh was clothed in a tunic of brighter and purer crystal, shining in whiteness as water shines when it is suffused with sunlight. Above its head stood a dove, its wings spread as though for flight and turned toward the figure’s face. And there appeared, as it were in its womb, as in a mirror, a most white child, upon whose forehead was inscribed *innocence*. It also held a royal sceptre in its right hand, while it laid its left hand upon its breast. And it said:

“I am free and not bound. I have passed through the most pure fountain—the sweetest and most loving Son of God. I passed through Him and came forth from Him [Col. 0654D]. I tread underfoot the most proud devil, who has no power to bind me. He has been cut off from me, because I remain always in the Father on high.”

But at the summit of the aforesaid shadowed column I saw another most beautiful image, standing bareheaded, with curling, somewhat dark hair, and a masculine face of such burning brightness that I could not distinctly behold it as a human face. It wore a tunic of purple and darkish colour. Over both shoulders of this same image a single band, of reddish saffron colour, had been woven, extending in front and behind down to its feet. About its neck it wore an episcopal pallium, wondrously adorned with gold and most precious gems. A most white radiance surrounded it everywhere [Col. 0655A], so that I could behold it nowhere except in front, from its head down to its feet. But its arms, hands, and feet were shadowed from my sight. Yet the same radiance which surrounded it was full of eyes on every side, wholly alive, and streaming this way and that as a cloud is wont to spread out, now making itself wider and now narrower.

And that same image cried in a loud voice to the world, saying to humankind:

“I am the grace of God, my little children. Therefore hear and understand me, for I give the light of the soul to those who understand me in admonition; and I keep them in that same blessedness, lest they return to iniquity. And because they have not despised me, I also desire to touch them by my [Col. 0655B] admonition, so that they may begin to do good works; and I speak of myself to those who seek me in simplicity and purity of heart.

“And while I bestow pearls, admonishing and exhorting the human being to good—namely, when the human understanding is touched through me—I am for that person the beginning. That is: when the human faculty understands my admonition by hearing, so that this same faculty is led in the soul to consent to my touch, then I am in that person the beginning of the good which he ought to undertake, I assisting him in this way. Then there is also a struggle there: whether what I give is accomplished or not.

“How is this to be understood? In this way: when I admonish a person so that he begins to groan and weep over his sins, then, if his will assents to the admonition by which I have admonished him—since a person in his faculty experiences a change of mind in the same way as he raises his eyes to see, his ears to hear, his mouth to speak, his hands to touch, and his feet to walk, according to the desire which is in his soul [Col. 0655C]—if then the will receives my admonition, it immediately lifts itself up, subdues and overcomes the faculty, so that the faculty learns what is unfamiliar to it in its customary way.

“How? It changes itself, because whoever is compelled must follow the will that is above him. For it is subject to the will in service, since it is inferior to it; and it will follow it whether it wishes to or not. For I give good at the beginning, warm it in the mind, and grant the work to the will for accomplishment. This I do through admonition, exhortation, and the warmth [Col. 0655D] of the gift of inspiration from the Holy Spirit. But if the will resists these gifts, then these things which I have mentioned are reduced to nothing.

“Therefore, at the time when a person can receive, in the burning of gifts, the signs of proclamation which arise from me, let that person hasten toward it; and let the will come more swiftly to good things and accomplish this work in brightness. For a person has knowledge of good and evil in order that, in all his works, he may understand God all the better, avoiding evil and doing good. For thus he worships God with fear, embracing Him in perfect charity.

“How? Namely, if he opens the inward eyes of the spirit to good, and denies and casts away, in the outward person, the evil that he could have done. For this reason earthly creation too is subject to his power [Col. 0656A]: that he may understand and love God more fully, and carry out in it the work of his knowledge with understanding, by which he fears and loves the Almighty, who assigned to him the great honour of the service of very many creatures. Hence, for these reasons, a person brings forth what he knowingly comprehends in his understanding: discernment among creatures, so that he knows what things are lovable and hateful, useful and useless. And after this, all his works are enclosed within the faith by which he understands God, so that they please both God and His angels.

“At times I touch a person in that person’s soul and admonish him to begin to work righteousness and avoid evil. But he scorns me, thinks that whatever he chooses to do is possible for him, and appoints for himself time for repentance until the time when his body consents with him in the simplicity of cold old age, and when, because of old age, it becomes burdensome for him any longer to sin [Col. 0656B]. Then I again admonish and exhort him toward good, and that he resist in his soul.

“When he neglects me, he is often brought, through many adversities—such as those he suffers in wealth and other similar things—to the point where he must, almost against his will and contrary to himself, do good. In such an embittered state of mind he takes little pleasure in accomplishing what he had earlier proposed to perform in a time of prosperity, when it seemed to him that nothing contrary could harm him, while he had arranged within himself to do those things for as long as pleased him.

“If this person receives me uncertainly, I do not [Col. 0656C] nevertheless wish to abandon him. For although he receives me in this way, he has not wholly despised me. Therefore I have not laboured in him in vain. For I am not wearied of touching ulcerous wounds surrounded by gnawing worms in the innumerable multitude of vices, by the stench of evil reputation and disgrace, and by the infirmity of inveterate iniquity and sins; nor shall I disdain gently to touch them, at the time when I begin to draw out the devouring bruise of malice—that is, when I behold and touch those wounds with the gentle warmth of the Holy Spirit’s inspiration.

“But often, when pain of this kind becomes inveterate through its old fomentation, so that sin begins to burn fiercely in a person’s soul, and when the wounds of sins thus arise in pain [Col. 0656D], becoming a coagulated work of this uncleanness, like a rising ball or heap of the great filth of worms and of enveloping muddy fomentation—from which arise the deadly poisons of scorpions, serpents, frogs, and other similar venomous worms—and when they harden like stone into such hardness that no one thinks to break them, these are unbearable burdens of crimes in those persons oppressed by heavier burdens. What then is to be done?

“Then indeed, because of their unbelief, people cannot trust that it is possible for such a person to turn to God from his iniquity, because they see him as though he were food for the devil. Yet I do not wish to abandon that person. Rather, with intervening help and combat I desire to stand for him in the contest [Col. 0657A], where I first begin gently to touch, as it were, the hardness of that stony sin, since it is as though difficult for him to be broken amid the immense stench of horrible crimes. These are the aforesaid causes of great filth and wickedness; they are like a rotting corpse and food for the devil, which he has most certainly swallowed into his belly.

“How? Scripture has the Son of God saying: ‘My food is to do the will of my Father’ [John 4]. Conversely, the devil’s food is to cast a human being down into death; by it he breathes upon, with such poisons as have been mentioned, those who consent to him in their will and turn aside after him. This is also the devil’s desire and continual endeavour, because every evil arises from this filth.

“Yet many of these people [Col. 0657B] understand me. How? When I first touch them, that person says inwardly: ‘What is happening to me? I do not know, nor do I know how to think of anything good.’ And again, without knowing, he sighs and says: ‘Alas, I am a sinner.’ But he feels nothing more, because he is weighed down by the mass of his sins and because the darkness of iniquity has troubled him. Then I touch his wounds again. And because he had formerly been admonished through me, he then understands me better; and looking into himself, he says again: ‘Woe is me! What shall I do? I do not know, nor can I devise what will become of me because of my many sins. Ah! Where shall I turn, or to whom shall I hasten who will help me cover and wipe out in penitence the most shameful crimes within me?’

“Then he again looks into himself with that same struggle which he formerly had in his zeal for sin [Col. 0657C]; and with the same desire with which he had formerly laboured in sins, he turns himself to true repentance. And because that person has thus been awakened by my admonition from the sleep of death which he had chosen for himself as life, he no longer wishes to sin, in thought, word, or deed, in those crimes which he previously pursued ardently. Instead, with utmost zeal he raises himself to me in most powerful repentance.

“Therefore I immediately receive him wholly, and thereafter let him go as though free, so that he shall no longer suffer grievous assault in the aforesaid lusts—as do my dearest children, whom I admonish amid manifold misery by the fiery arrows of diabolical persuasions, because he then has no need of these. For [Col. 0657D] he will always grieve for his past sins, becoming so angry even with himself that he performs such severe penance as to deem himself unworthy even to be called a human being.

“But this is victory amid the stinking filth of those persons whom I do not wish to reject, because after their sins they finally sought me. For to those who do not spurn me, but receive my admonition and seek me devoutly, I am ready to do whatever they desire. But those who reject me in contempt are dead, and I do not know them.

“For there are many people who, when they sense that I am present and understand that their mind has been touched by my admonition, flee from me through the evil habit of sins they conceived, swallowing them within themselves in will, consent, and deed. Therefore [Col. 0658A] they too are reckoned before God as nothingness and emptiness, because they refuse to be conscious of what they can do when touched by me.

“But I do not wish to be in the pollution of those sinners who refuse to receive my admonition. They are unwilling to purify themselves through that exhortation, so as to turn themselves away from their sins. Nor do they desire to eat that food which is the Scripture of the Gospel, by which all believers ought to be satisfied, or to taste its flavour according to what has been given to them. Rather, they hasten to flee the grace of God, because they do not wish to see, hear, or think what they must do when they are called by the admonition of good.

“They flee good admonition as a worm enters the earth, hiding itself from all the beauty of this world. These most wicked [Col. 0658B] people do likewise, fleeing the commandments of God and defiling themselves in the dregs in which they wrap themselves unto death, when they hide themselves in their malice, unwilling to come forth from the stench of wickedness into the light. Such persons do not belong to me. For I do not wish to be divided hither and thither in the pollution of mud.

“How? I desire to be with those who understand me through pure repentance; there I also join myself to human corruptibility, because I desire to cleanse it. But those who do not wish to receive me, I reject from myself, unwilling to be with them, because I have no share with them. For they are in the portion of foolish ignorance, unwilling to understand me; and because I do not wish to be in the work belonging to the adhesion of hardened perversity, which is unto death.

“Those who spurn me in this way imitate the lost angel, who, though he could see God [Col. 0658C], was unwilling to behold Him so as humbly to acknowledge Him. Therefore he suddenly fled all heavenly glory, falling into death when he wished to make himself like God in equal honour. These people despise me because they work evil deeds, carrying out the unlawful desires of the flesh in their pleasures. And because they despise me, they do what they wickedly will. They despise God; in the same way they neglect His commandment.

“Therefore, very often in my indignation, they are allowed to carry out whatever they wish to the full measure of their mind, because the life of eternal blessedness flees them as though they were nothing. They often fail both in the prosperity of this present life and in that to come, because they are hard and immovable toward the blessedness [Col. 0658D] of good. For I abandon the stubborn sinner who perseveres in evils; I give life to the one who looks into himself and turns to me from sins in my fear, with pure repentance.

“For I am the column of firm stability, which never abandons one who seeks me. Whoever grasps me and joins himself to me inwardly and faithfully will never fall into perdition. But whoever keeps me in the forgetfulness of his mind and raises himself above me in pride—that is, whoever trusts more in himself than in me, and therefore disdains to have confidence in me because he counts the grace of God for nothing, since I am in his soul as a whirlwind—such a person holds me negligently in mockery, proudly, with exaltation, in despair: not because of the weight of sins [Col. 0659A] which he has committed, but because through pride he mocks me, saying, ‘What is the grace of God?’ Him I shall cast down and kill; and I do not wish to raise him up among my elect, because he is dead to eternal blessedness.

“Likewise, those people who have no confidence that they can rise from the more grievous faults of their sins, thus rejecting almighty God and His grace—despairing in excessive sorrow as though they could not be saved from the enormity of their crimes—fall away, cast off by me, and plunge bitterly into death, dying in the lower hell in the torment of eternal death.

“Now I shall also speak concerning my beloved children, who receive me with open understanding, willing spirit, and keen intellect; who touch me with groaning and tears [Col. 0659B], receiving me with joy and embracing me with every intention. O my flowers, who, when they sense that I am present, suddenly rejoice in me, and I in them! They are sweeter and more pleasant to me than love for the most precious stone, and than shining precious pearls in the minds of people who embrace them with ardent desire.

“They are also to me most noble squared stones, because before my sight they are always lovable to me. I continually desire to polish and cleanse them, so that they may be placed rightly and fittingly in the heavenly Jerusalem. For they continually feast with me in their minds by good will, and can never be satisfied with my righteousness. As soon as they sense my touch, they hasten to me like a stag to a fountain of water.

“But I often leave them, so that [Col. 0659C] it seems to them as though they are without help. I do this so that the outward person in them may not be puffed up through pride. Then they weep and mourn, thinking that I am offended with them; but in this way I search out their faith. Yet I hold them with a strong hand, removing from them exaltation and not allowing them to know what they are in their hidden goods, because I desire to produce manifold fruits in them, while their souls grieve and their hearts are wounded with pains.

“For I often permit diabolical persuasions to assail them with fiery arrows from the blast of the unclean, burning fire of the spirit of fornication, which wounds their bodies in the weakness of fragile nature. I permit this so that in this way they may be so strongly imbued with the inspiration of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0659D] that afterwards they become notable heralds and fervent in virtues.

“For they shall be under trial like gold in a furnace: that is, tested in mockery and indignation, so that they shall be counted as nothing, and very often be stripped of their possessions by robbers, and torn in adversities by the dissension of the people like lambs by wolves. Yet just as sheep do not die when a wolf scatters and disperses them, so these people do not die in the death of the soul, but rather live more fully, purified in adversities.

“For a good tree, that it may bear fruit, is watered, pruned, and dug around; and caterpillars are removed from it so that they may not gnaw away its fruit. What does this mean? Namely, a good person should not be hard—that is, maliciously opposed [Col. 0660A] to the righteousness of God—but gentle and pliant toward every good; cutting evil away from himself, examining himself in the scrutiny of his works, and removing from himself the assault of hostile enemies.

“Yet before a person perceives me in thought, or that person’s understanding understands me within, I am for that person the head and root of fruitfulness, and the strength and power of the firmly founded city built upon the solid rock. Therefore let every faithful person hear me saying:

‘O human being, is it fitting and proper that a rational person should be without understanding, like an irrational beast which does nothing except what its lust demands? O wretched people, who refuse to know that great glory which God gave them in His likeness! Yet it cannot be as they wish: that they may freely, and as though by hereditary right, do every evil that they desire, as if they possessed this by the nature of their bodies, unwilling to consider that they possess the honour of being able to do good works.

‘God established all things justly in His ordering. And who can resist Him? What does this mean? Namely, who can be compared by any likeness to God’s ordering, whether in wisdom or in discernment concerning His things? And why is it that they do not wish to take away from themselves the capacity given to them, namely that they can do good and evil?

‘How? For when I admonish them by my touch, those who grasp me as soon as they sense I am present can, with my help, bring the good work they will to its effect. But those who despise me fall into weakness of themselves and into evil. Yet perverse people strive to excuse themselves, claiming that they cannot do good works; and they do this so that the outward person in them may exercise its will in freedom.

‘Now, O my dearest children, who are sweeter to me in fragrance than every spice, hear me as I admonish you. While you have time to do good and evil, worship your God with sincere devotion. Again, O my sweetest children, who rise like the dawn, you who ought to burn in charity like the sun in its ray, run and hasten, my dearest ones, upon the way of truth, which is the light of the world: Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who redeemed us by His blood [Col. 0660D] at the end of the ages, so that after your passage you may come to Him with joy.’”

And again I heard Him who sat upon the throne saying to me:

“Those who desire heavenly things must believe faithfully and not investigate obstinately how the Son of God, sent into the world by the Father, was born of a virgin. For human understanding, weighed down by a fragile and mortal body and by the very heavy burden of sins, cannot discern the secrets of God beyond what the Holy Spirit reveals to whomever He wills.

“Therefore, through a mystical mystery, this column also which you see in the southern region, in the aforesaid stone wall of the building shown to you, beyond the aforesaid column of the true Trinity, signifies the humanity of the Saviour. Conceived by the Holy Spirit and born [Col. 0661A] of the sweetest Virgin, He is the Son of the Most High: a most strong column of holiness, sustaining the whole edifice of the Church.

“His humanity appears in the burning faith of the stones of faithful peoples, who work most strongly in the goodness of the heavenly Father, manifested after the declaration of the Trinity. For when the Trinity in one God had been established as certain for the believing people, they also believed in the incarnate Word of God: true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to be worshipped in the unity of divinity as one true God.

“This column is great and appears shadowed within and without the same building, because the holiness of the true Incarnation is great and beyond estimation. It is shadowed to human minds so that it cannot be considered [Col. 0661B], except insofar as it is possible to behold it by faith, to be known by inward people labouring in divine worship through faith and work, and to be made manifest by reputation and speech to outward people occupied with leisure.

“It appears so shadowy to your sight that you cannot know either its size or its height. For My Son, among human beings in the mortality of flesh, because He was to undergo death for the people, appeared as though shadowed—that is, mortal—yet without every stain of sin. Nevertheless, His true Incarnation, in the mystical greatness of God’s secrets, is incomprehensible; and in the excellence of divine power it is beyond estimation, exceeding every cognition of human understanding.

“But the fact that between this column and the column [Col. 0661C] of the true Trinity there is a broken space three cubits in length, empty and without a wall, as was shown to you above, means this: the incarnate Son of God, true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is still hidden in His members, who are the faithful people yet to be born until the end of the world. Through living works they are made members of their Head, as you have been wonderfully and figuratively taught above.

“How many they shall be and of what sort, over the length of coming times—that is, those who shall worship the same Trinity in the unity of divinity with faithful devotion in the mystery of the ineffable Trinity—their place is empty, since they are still to be born and are without the built wall of good works. Yet a foundation has been laid, because they are in the presence of God, and because the faith of their salvation, which they shall possess, already stands firmly established. Thus a person should have hope and trust in none but God, not delaying in reliance on His mercy, but trusting in Him, who is the most strong foundation of the faithful soul.

“But the fact that this shadowy column stands in this same building at the place where above, in the heavenly mysteries before God, you first saw that great, square, and most radiant brilliance of whiteness, which was revealed to you in the greatest mystery as designating the secret of the heavenly Creator, means this: the incarnate Son of God fulfilled according to the secret will of the Father all His works which He performed bodily in the world while suffering many injuries [Col. 0662A].

“What also does that brilliance signify? It is great in signifying the mysteries of God, and four-cornered, because many of those born throughout the four parts of the world shall attain to knowledge of Christ. It is of exceptional whiteness, because no darkness can obscure the most radiant divinity. There the same secret of the high and glorious majesty is figuratively disclosed in the great depth and mystery of the knowledge of the Creator of all, who created everything, so that no one came to the aid of the Creator in this matter, nor did anyone resist or oppose Him in it; but He created all things solely by the will of His goodness through His Word.

“Therefore another radiance shines within it, like the dawn, having in itself on high an airy brightness of purple light. Through this, in mystical vision [Col. 0662B], the mystery of the incarnate Son of God was shown to you. For in the secret of the highest God is declared the brightness of dawn, namely the Virgin Mary, who bore in her womb the Son of the heavenly and Most High Father, who poured forth His purple blood, shining with the most radiant light of salvation, as the Incarnation of that same Son showed you through mystical shadowing in this secret vision.

“But the fact that in the aforesaid column there is, from its bottom to its top, an ascent in the manner of a ladder, means this: in the incarnate Son of God all virtues worked in their fullness. He left in Himself the footsteps of salvation, so that both the least and the greatest among the faithful may fittingly find in Him a step upon which to set the foot for the ascent of virtues, that they may reach the best [Col. 0662C] places in which virtues must be practised.

“How? In the best places of good hearts, the virtues gather for their most holy work, so that they may bring the Son of God to completion in His members—that is, in the elect people. Therefore in Him is an example of perfection for all believers occupied with the law of God, so that they may advance from good to better, knowing the manifestation of the true Incarnation, in which the Son of God was truly shown in flesh. In Him is found the most faithful ascent to heavenly things.

“For this reason you also see here all the virtues of God descending and ascending, burdened with stones for their work: because in the Only-Begotten of God the most radiant virtues descend, as it were, through His humanity, and rise upward, as it were, through His divinity [Col. 0662D]. They descend also through Him into the hearts of faithful people, who, abandoning their own will with good heart, make themselves pliant toward upright works, just as a workman bends down to lift a stone which he is to carry to a building.

“In Him they also ascend upward when they offer heavenly works, brought to completion in people, to God with thanksgiving, so that the body of Christ may be completed as swiftly as possible in His faithful members. Therefore they also carry, as it were, stones to higher places. These are winged and radiant works, which people perform with them for their protection; for every action offers God its wings, by which it raises itself from the dregs of the human mind, and has also a shining brightness by which it shines before God [Col. 0663A]. For that which flows from the fountain of eternal life cannot be blocked or hidden.

“For just as a fountain ought not to be hidden, but made public, so that every thirsty person may come to it, draw, and drink, so the Son of God is neither blocked nor hidden from His elect, but is manifest, making Himself ready for the recompense of works, in order to reveal in just reward those works which are completed by people for His will.

“Therefore let the faithful person walk to God in faith and seek His mercy, and it shall be given. But He will not be found by one who does not seek Him: just as a fountain does not flow to people who merely know of it and are unwilling to come to it, but they must approach it if they desire to draw its water, so should a person act. Let that person approach God through the law established by Him [Col. 0663B], and he shall find Him; and the food of life and saving water shall be given to him, so that he shall endure hunger and thirst no longer.

“Therefore the aforesaid virtues have the earnest endeavour of completing this same work, because they run most zealously, like torrents of water, toward the divine work, so that the members may be joined to their Head—more radiant than the sun—in most noble completion through radiant attainments. For this reason, as you heard, they are called the strong workers of God, because they are always vigorously engaged in the good works of faithful people.”

But the fact that among these virtues you see seven especially, whose forms and garments you also contemplate insofar as it is permitted you: this signifies that among diligent works these seven most excellent virtues designate the seven most ardent gifts of the Holy Spirit, because, in the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, the most illustrious Virgin conceived the Son of God without sin, namely in the sanctification of the holy virtues. These virtues were openly manifested in that same Only-Begotten Son of God, as though illuminating the hearts of the faithful in their form and spreading themselves in the unity of faith as though in their attire, as my servant Isaiah testifies, saying: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11).

This means: The Virgin Mary came forth from the narrow confines of worldly oppression into the sweetness of honorable conduct, as someone leaves the house in which he had been shut up: he does not rise above the house itself, but walks straight ahead before himself; and as a little stream of wine is pressed from the winepress, not raising itself above the press, but flowing moderately into its own place. And why a rod? Because she was not thorny in her conduct nor knotted with earthly desires, but smooth—that is, not joined to carnal lust—having sprung from the root of Jesse, that is, from him who was, as it were, the foundation of the royal lineage from which that undefiled mother proceeded in birth.

And from the root of that rod there rose a most sweet fragrance, which was the intact purity of that same Virgin, aspiring to the highest summit, while the Holy Spirit watered her in such a way that the nourishing flower was born from her. How? As a flower grows in a field where no seed has been sown, so the heavenly bread arose in her without the root of male intercourse and without any human burden, but born solely in the sweetness of divinity, untouched by any outrage of sin, coming while the twisting serpent did not know and did not even approach him.

Thus that flower secretly deceived him, so that it rose upward and raised on high the human race conceived in sin, which that serpent had earlier deceitfully deceived and dragged down with itself into perdition. And because this flower was the Son of God, the Spirit of the Lord—that is, the spirit of eternal divinity—rested upon him. How? When humility was exalted in the ascent of that flower, there pride was cast down in derision—the pride which the first woman embraced when she wished to know more than she ought—while the second woman subjected herself to the service of God, recognizing herself to be small and confessing her God in humility. The Holy Spirit rested ardently upon him; in him lay hidden chosen love, which saved the lost people by wiping away the crimes and wicked deeds of men.

For the fullness of time was in him, because living light shone forth in him, and in it the harmful fruit, together with the evils following it, withered away. In him arose the medicine of the dead, which raised that banner which overcame and crushed death. For holiness lacked no power in him, since he was conceived without any mixture of sin, as is often found among the children of men, who are born amid a multitude of diverse crimes.

But when that flower, by acting and teaching, gave every inspiration of righteousness, it then brought forth fruit in the fullness of the Holy Spirit. For the Son of God himself, clothed in flesh, openly demonstrated in his work what the Holy Spirit had earlier moved mysteriously and, as it were, in secret by his inspiration. That the Holy Spirit is signified as resting sevenfold upon this flower is because, when God created all things through his Word in the Holy Spirit, he rested from all his work on the seventh day.

Moreover, these gifts are doubled in their signification, because body and soul, joined together, ought to work in a twofold love through the anointing of the Holy Spirit, with the fear of the Lord set alone; for this fear, as though revering love in trembling, indicates that the one God is to be worshiped above all things. Therefore the Spirit of the Lord also rules over the strongest virtues which shine forth from him, as branches proceed from a root, because there is one God from whom all good things come and through whom all good things are wisely ordered.

And because the Spirit of the Lord rested upon that flower, the spirit of wisdom also remained upon him, because great wisdom appeared when God created all things through his Word. Wisdom was thus poured out in him, because that same Word was wisdom. Yet the Word, not yet incarnate, was invisible; but incarnate it appeared visible, because the Word which was before every creature in the Father’s heart, through which all things were made and without which nothing was made, shone forth as a flower under time—that is, gleaming in humanity—and brought sound understanding to men through its testimonies.

What does this mean? Understanding is fittingly joined to wisdom, because, since man was created by God in wisdom, he ought worthily to understand his Creator. Therefore before the virginal birth God was to be understood without any doubt. But after the birth, bringing forth in flesh the aforesaid virginal flower, that same flower was to be understood as God and man, though not without wonder. And understanding, formerly invisible, was seen visibly in the flower, when that flower brought forth this intelligible ground: namely, that man wisely understands God in his works.

How? Wisdom is the origin of good works when man wisely reveres his God. Understanding adheres to it, because when man performs good through wisdom, that good is then spread to others, so that they may joyfully understand in him the good fragrance and sweet savor shining forth from it. In this virginal flower also, counsel follows understanding, because man, possessing understanding, was to be liberated by divine counsel.

Therefore the spirit of counsel and strength rested upon him, because this counsel existed timelessly with the Father: that his Word should be incarnate, accomplishing all his works in time according to the Father’s will and fulfilling obedience through himself, so that it might shine from him upon men and they might learn to imitate him in their deeds. When this appeared in the strongest power, wholly arising from divinity, strength hid itself within him, so that he might conquer the devil all the more strongly the more secretly he concealed himself from him by counsel. How?

Strength fittingly adheres to counsel, because God’s counsel, through the strength of his Son, destroyed the devil’s kingdom. Thus the same Son of God, namely the most mighty lion, crushed the death of unbelief through the most splendid light, which is faith; for it is great strength for a man, by counsel, to believe what he is unable to see with bodily sight.

What does this mean? Counsel, together with the strength joined to it, pierces the hardness of stony hearts, hardened by the habit of wicked conduct. Passing through such unsuitable hardness, it causes carnal work to be cast off and God’s work to be accomplished most fittingly. Therefore in the aforesaid flower strength is accompanied by knowledge, because through God’s strength men come to his knowledge, so that they may know him.

Hence the spirit of knowledge and piety also rested in him through heavenly sweetness, because he knowingly shared the sufferings of men. He was also the hope through which entrance is made into salvation, when in great piety he knowingly wiped away the world’s crime through his death. What does this mean? Piety is rightly joined to knowledge, because the Son of God knowingly fulfilled the will of his Father in great piety.

For this Son, born alone from a virgin, poured among the peoples the shoot of heavenly power, so that they might follow the fellowship of angels, which is chastity of purity; for this power arose in heavenly piety. Thus, when the rod came forth from Jesse, the virtues of this flower might germinate—virtues which the first woman drove away when she consented to hear the serpent’s counsel, so that the entire human race fell in her, deprived of the joy of heavenly brightness—unless the flowering of that rod knowingly raised it up through piety in the holiness of salvation.

How? The Holy Spirit inspires knowledge adhering to strength which conquers the devil, when God is known most devoutly through faithful people in ardent desires and is embraced with the most longing inward touch of the faithful soul. And in the virginal flower, piety is followed by the fear of the Lord, because when piety is present in faithful people, they acquire the fear of the Lord in order to fulfill his commandments.

Therefore the fear of the Lord filled that flower, because he had such a fullness of virtues in himself that no empty place was found in him where deadly pride, delight in honor, or transgression of the law could find a seat. Rather, he was wholly full of the fear of the Lord, seeking not alien glory as the first angel and Adam sought it, but honoring his Father in all his work and offering him worthy obedience.

Thus the fear of the Lord is the beginning of all righteousness, because it is the end and beginning of the other virtues, as the seventh day of rest shows both the completion and the origin of creatures. How? Fear shakes and stirs trembling, which is the root from which fruitful virtues germinate. Thus this flower is full of the fear of the Lord, because every shoot of good works adheres to him, for he is their substance. That flower brings forth the greenness of every virtue, being filled beyond all others with their fruit, in order to accomplish every good thing, as Scripture also says of him: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2).

This means: The Son of the Virgin, the most sweet lover of chaste love, whom the faithful soul apprehends, desiring to crown its integrity by his most sweet embrace, having abandoned a carnal husband and joined itself to Christ, loving him in a most sure covenant and beholding him in the mirror of faith—he is the most beautiful fruit of the fruitful tree. That is, the Son of the Virgin comes forth from virginal brightness like an apple from fruitful bloom, offering food of refreshment to the hungry and the juice of sweetness to the thirsty. In this way he excels the woodland trees, that is, the sons of men who are conceived in sins and spend their lives in them, not bearing such fruit as he brought forth, because he came forth from God bringing the full fruit of the sweetness of life; whereas the others have neither greenness nor fruit from themselves, but from him.

How? Through his incarnation he gave salvation to the world, appearing as God’s beloved Son among the sons of men. Through his fervor they were green and bore fruit, but were not fruitful with so great a fullness as that with which he was filled, because he was wholly holy, coming forth from God and born of a virgin. And why “beloved”? Because he tramples down that which obstructs the faithful soul hastening toward heavenly things.

Therefore the holy soul, by the most equitable judgment, calls him beloved. Through the faith of love, leaving itself behind, willingly panting toward him amid the great struggle of carnal pleasures, and rejecting itself in the ardor of tearful desire, it clings to him as a woman to the husband with whom she is united in the joy of her own will. Therefore, when at the beginning of guarding chastity it begins to sigh toward him, it says to itself: “I wish to cast down carnal pleasure and join myself to him, beneath the shadow of whose love—by which he has overshadowed me, in the ardor of his burning desire, from the opposing fire—I sit.”

How? While, having an intoxicated zeal in his love, I suppress within the consent of my soul the subjection to the fiery love of the flesh. And for this reason his most sweet fruit, which I tasted in my soul while sighing toward God, is sweeter to me in it than every sweetness of flesh which I felt in its desires.

And why is it sweet? Because he who was born of a virgin has the most sweet flavor and the strongest ointment, dripping like balsam. This is resurrection unto life, in which the dead were raised, containing the greatest medicine, which wiped away the wounds of sins through his incarnation—a condition full to overflowing with holiness and sweetness in every kind of virtue, together with virginity.

Therefore, O virginity, which consists in fiery ardor, most strong shoot, gleaming from the star of the sea, which always fights and tramples down every foulness of shame against the most savage darts of the devil: rejoice in heavenly harmony, in the hope of fellowship with angels. How? The Holy Spirit makes music in the tabernacle of virginity, because virginity continually meditates upon the Word of God, considering how it may embrace Christ with all devotion, burning in his love. It forgets what is frail in man through the lust of the flesh in the ardor of passion, cleaving to the one husband whom sin has never touched, to whom it is joined without any lust of the flesh, ever flourishing with him in the joy of royal nuptials.

But now, the fact that you see a likeness among the aforesaid virtues, so that all of them, like the other virtues shown to you above, appear clothed, as it were, in garments of silk: this signifies that in their order those lights produce devout unanimity in the minds of men, just as the remaining virtues have in God the softness of garments—that is, the gentleness of devotion—in their regard for holy souls, which lack the thorns of hardened vices.

But the fact that some walk with white hair, their heads uncovered and without the wrapping of cloaks: this signifies that, in the union of the brightness of innocence, they do not possess in the members of faithful people the binding connection of wicked conduct; and that they are not surrounded by worldly pursuits, wholly fleeing the vicissitudes of vices.

But the first, in a womanly manner, is veiled about the head and clothed in a garment, as it were, transparent like crystal, because, humbly subject to God, she bears the bond of subjection. By heavenly vigilance she casts down every diabolical exaltation; cleaving to the devout head, that is, Christ, she also urges the most humble priest—purest and without all dust of sin—to the most radiant purity of heart, because constrained, humble, and pure priests ought to be high priests.

The second has black hair, plainly showing that in Christ, her head, she wipes away the blackness of sins in men. The third appears unlike a human form, because it has this ministry: to shake man so that he may be frightened and tremble at God’s judgment. Therefore it lacks human appearance, because man often, placing God second, forgets his fear—something which this virtue wholly refuses to do.

The first, fourth, and fifth are clothed in white tunics, because they are surrounded by the garment of innocence which Adam lost when he transgressed the gracious command, but which was afterward recovered unto salvation in the brightest lily of flourishing virginity, clothed in the work of simple submission to God. Before God it shines as the brightest star burns before human eyes.

All also have white footwear, except the third, which does not appear in human form. For they are a most beautiful work in people who bring the desires of the flesh within themselves to nothing, following the example of their Savior, who is most splendid brightness. One of them does not imitate a human being because it has no regard for any audacity, ever watchful and not negligent, unlike man, who often forgets himself through obstinacy. It is the dispenser of just admonition, so that every faithful person may cautiously consider God’s judgment.

The fourth alone is shod with crystal footwear shining wonderfully, because, restraining itself in its will, it travels Christ’s most luminous path, thus even suffocating death within itself through the fiery ardor of the Holy Spirit. The fact that there is dissimilarity among these virtues signifies that, although they possess the unanimity of one devotion, they nevertheless work different works in men.

Therefore the first image represents humility, which first revealed the Son of God when God, who holds heaven and earth in his power, did not disdain to send his Son to the earth. It therefore bears upon its head a golden crown with three branches rising higher, because, surpassing and sweetly preceding the other virtues, it is crowned with a golden crown—namely, the most precious and radiant incarnation of the Savior, who adorned it, as it were, upon its head, that is, in this mystery, when he was incarnate.

The crown is triangular because the Trinity is in unity and unity in the Trinity: namely, the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one true God, surpassing all things in the height of divinity. It gleams with much ornament of most precious green and red stones and white pearls, because that same humanity of the Savior showed in itself the highest and deepest goodness of his work, which the Son of God himself accomplished in that greenness, when the virtues were green in his teaching; in the redness of his blood, when he suffered death on the cross, saving man; and in the most radiant whiteness of his resurrection and ascension. With all these the Church was illuminated and adorned, just as the object on which precious stones are set is made bright and beautiful.

The fact that it has upon its breast a most shining mirror, in which the image of the incarnate Son of God appears with wonderful brightness, signifies that in humility, which is in the heart of the consecrated temple, the Only-Begotten Son of God shone forth in most blessed and radiant knowledge, devoutly, humbly, splendidly, and most firmly, in all his works which he carried out bodily and in which he especially revealed himself to the world.

Thus humility also marks the hearts of the elect faithful in their most illustrious part, setting its tribunal in them and governing and directing all their actions, because it is the firmest foundation of all good things in men, as it also shows in its aforementioned maternal admonition.

But the second signifies love, because after that humility by which the Son of God deigned to be incarnate, the true and most ardent lamp of love was also shown, when God so loved man that, for love of him, he sent his Only-Begotten Son to be incarnate. It appears wholly of the heavenly blue color of hyacinth, both in its form and in its tunic, because the incarnate Son of God, through his humanity, illuminated faithful and heavenly persons, as an object upon which blue hyacinth is placed is illuminated. He also kindled them with love, so that they might faithfully assist every person in need.

Thus this virtue is clothed in the tunic of God’s sweetness, having the office of shining upon all people in right light through devotion, deed, and practice. Therefore two girdles, wonderfully woven with inestimable workmanship and adorned with gold and gems, are set into that tunic. These are the two commandments of love in God’s sweetness, composed by the marvelous gift of the highest Giver: good and chief intention, as it were gold, and just works, like the brightest gems.

Thus one girdle descends from each shoulder of that image to its feet, before and behind, because it bears these commandments with much diligence: one toward God, as on the right shoulder, and the other toward the neighbor, as on the left shoulder, as it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22).

This means: You ought so to love the Lord your God, who is your Lord—that is, Lord by that honor through which he rules every creature—and your God, because he has no beginning but is the Creator of all things. For love of him you must first overcome and cast down in your heart the flesh of your body, which is very difficult for you. For once the flesh has first been conquered, your spirit will afterward reign in you; and then you will understand God in your soul so as knowingly to keep his commandments and not fulfill them through lazy labor.

Then all the powers of your body and soul are subjected to God, because this first victory has occurred in your body; so that in all these proposed matters you may comprehend the most mighty God in your mind. This is like a firm fortress against the snares of your enemies, so that no enemy can overcome his strength in the aforesaid matters, because your mind must contain all these things, confirming and strengthening within itself everything that you do.

Therefore do this with all your heart, all your soul, all your strength, and all your mind, so that nothing may fail you in faith and you may not consent to anything which opposes God and divides you among alien things. Rather, gather yourself to the sweetness of his love, loving yourself also. How? If you love God, you love your salvation. And as you then love yourself in all these things, so you shall love your neighbor, because every faithful person is your neighbor, existing in the Christian name and in faith. Thus you should rejoice in that person’s upright prosperity and heavenly salvation, that he may be faithfully preserved in the faith, just as you rejoice in your own salvation.

Therefore this twofold work of love is to be in man, descending to his feet, that is, to the end of completion; before him, namely appearing in God’s law; and behind him, namely in assistance to man. Thus man should pursue love, so that, having cast away death, he may attain the perfection of life, as this same love also declares above in its words.

The third image signifies the fear of the Lord, which arose in the minds of the faithful after that love which God manifested to men when he willed that his Son should undergo death for them, so that they might understand the heavenly commandments more fully and fulfill them more perfectly than before. You now see it in the same form in which you saw it in the preceding vision, because the unchangeable God is to be held in like, not unlike, honor and reverence in every creature and work of his, as was explained to you above.

It is of greater and taller stature than the other virtues and unlike human form, because beyond the others it brings narrowness and trembling upon men, so that, continually considering with penetrating eyes the greatness of supreme majesty and the height of his divinity, they may fear. For God is to be feared by all people with great reverence, because they were created by him and not by another.

Accordingly, this virtue has no human appearance, because it rejects that opposition by which God is resisted through evil deeds—as has been said above—fixing its knowledge only in the fear of God and walking the most straight paths of his will. Therefore it has many eyes on every side, living wholly in wisdom, because through the eyes of sound understanding it looks around everywhere, contemplating God in all his wonders, so that it may have a straight path in his good works and flee, through the knowledge of God, the devil’s confusion in evils.

It shines wholly in wisdom in this manner, because it despises everything deadly and harmful to the spirit, flees death and abandons iniquity, and wisely builds itself a house in life. It is also clothed, as it were, in a shadowed garment through which those eyes look, because it is surrounded by the strongest restraint, breaking the desires of the flesh in men, and through that abstinence it looks into the light of life, in which man shines wonderfully in blessedness.

Its heart trembles before me in much fear, because it places narrowness and trembling in the hearts of fervent people, so that they may always hold in fear the turbulence and fragility of their flesh, lest they fall into sins and put their confidence in themselves or other people, rather than in him who reigns forever, as it also showed above in its lament.

The fourth declares obedience, because after that fear which is shown to me in reverence, my commandments are fittingly obeyed. Therefore it bears a snow-white bond around its neck, because it makes the minds of men most pure, men who through the submission of faithful subjection everywhere abandon the strength of the neck of their own will and cleave to the innocent Lamb, namely my Son.

Its hands and feet are bound with a white bond, because it is bound to Christ’s work and to the life of truth in the whiteness of true faith, neither acting nor going according to itself, but according to the voice of God who presides, as it also demonstrates in its aforesaid words.

The fifth signifies faith, because after obedience, by which the people obey my commandments in hearing, they also become believing in faith, faithfully fulfilling in work what they diligently received in admonition. It has a red collar around its neck, because, faithfully persevering everywhere in its strength, it is adorned by the martyrdom of blood, placing its confidence not in deceitful vanities but in God, as it also declares of itself above.

The sixth prefigures hope, which, after the completion of believing in God, rises toward life in an uninhabited land, but hidden in the heavens until the time of everlasting recompense. To this hope yearns with its whole desire, as a hired laborer toward his wages and a child toward the inheritance owed to him.

Therefore it is clothed in a tunic of pale color, because confidence in its work is surrounded, as it were, by pallor: it has not yet been rewarded in the present, but awaits with much weariness what it continually longs for with sighs. The fact that the cross of the passion of my crucified Son appears before it in the air, toward which it raises its eyes and hands with great devotion, signifies that through the martyrdom of that same Only-Begotten Son it prepares abundant confidence in the minds of the faithful through heavenly desire, so that with humble and sincere intention they may raise themselves to him in the inward sight of faith and in the brightest works of their labor, as this virtue also showed above in its prayer.

But the seventh represents chastity, because after people have fully placed their hope in God, a perfect work grows in them. Thus they begin to restrain themselves from carnal desires in chastity, which feels very sharp abstinence in the flower of the flesh, as a young heifer feels the ardor of desire but nevertheless refuses to look toward a male.

So chastity rejects every impurity amid most beautiful desires, panting toward its most sweet beloved, who is the sweetest and most loving fragrance of all good things, in the delights of every virtue, to be beheld by its lovers in the fear and beauty of the soul as the virtue of steadfastness.

Therefore it is clothed in a tunic of crystal, brighter and purer still, shining so white that it glistens as water when flooded with the sun. For it is most bright in simple intention and most pure, without any dust of the burning lust of desires, wonderfully strengthened through the Holy Spirit, and surrounded by the garment of innocence, shining in the brightest whiteness of the fountain of living water, which is the most radiant sun of eternal brightness.

But the fact that a dove stands over its head, with wings spread as though for flight and turned toward its face, signifies that chastity, in its beginning, as though in its head, is strengthened by the spreading and overshadowing of the dove’s wings—that is, by the protection of the Holy Spirit. This enables it to fly over the changing assaults of the devil, while, through the fiery love of holy inspiration, it directs itself toward the place where chastity reveals the countenance of its sweetness.

Therefore there also appears, as it were, in its womb, like an image in a mirror, a most white child, upon whose forehead is inscribed “innocence,” because in the inner being of this most pure, manifest virtue there is inviolable, most beautiful, and most certain integrity. It has a childlike form because of the integrity of simple childhood, just as its forehead—that is, its knowledge—shows not arrogance and exalted pride but simple innocence.

And the fact that it holds a royal scepter in its right hand, while placing its left hand upon its breast, signifies that in the right hand of salvation, through the Son of God, king of all, life has been manifested in chastity; while it confounds and brings to nothing the left hand of lust, through that same defender, in the hearts of those who love him.

How? Because it is unwilling to leave lust any freedom. Rather, as a bird of prey, seizing a putrid corpse, holds it fast and reduces it to nothing, so chastity casts away and utterly crushes that lust, foul-smelling before God, so that it cannot even breathe beneath it, as this virtue also declares above in its words.

But that at the summit of the aforesaid shaded column you see a tall and most beautiful figure means this: in the very highest and most excellent mercy of the Almighty, in the incarnation of the Savior itself, the most resplendent virtue—namely, the grace of God—was made manifest; and this is the strongest fullness that exists in God, urging human beings to do penance, so that through it they may be released from the wickedness they themselves have committed. She stands with head uncovered, [Col. 0673A] because her dignity and brightness are open to all who seek her. She has curly, somewhat dark hair, because the Only-Begotten of God clothed himself, in a virgin’s flesh, with humanity free from the stain of sin, among the Jewish people, twisted and entangled in the blackness of their unbelief.

And she has a manly face of such burning brightness that you cannot clearly gaze upon it as upon a human face; because, in the grace of God, in the mighty power of the Almighty, the Lord of life appeared in life, so burning in most radiant divinity that he surpasses every inward and outward sight of a human being while that person is still burdened by bodily heaviness. Nor does he appear so openly in his mysteries as to lie bare before human judgment, but hidden; because the judgments of divine grace are secret.

That she is clothed in a tunic of purple and somewhat dark color means [Col. 0673B] that the work of God’s grace, burning in charity, bends down toward the blackness of sinners, as though toward a human garment. How? In that it exhorts them to salvation, raising them by penance from the mud of sin to the sight of light. For as day drives away darkness, so grace takes away crimes, rebuilding sinners through penance unto life.

Moreover, over both shoulders of this same figure a single girdle, of reddish saffron color, is interwoven, extending before and behind down to her feet. This means that the grace of God, bending down toward faithful people, raises them to heavenly things in its strength and mercy. How? By these two paths of the girdles: namely, touching the distress of frail flesh sweating in its bloody struggle, and the strength of the soul’s vigor languishing in the body, [Col. 0673C] and drawing them, in the red and saffron splendor of the humanity and divinity of the Son of God—that is, of the most serene sun—to love of things above. Thus the faithful person, touched by wholeness of grace, resists within himself the desire for sin: before himself, indeed, toward virtues; behind himself, toward the mortification of vices; so that, with a good and true end, he may manfully complete his works, clothed in their desirable and delightful texture.

But that she has about her neck an episcopal pallium, wonderfully adorned with gold and most precious gems, means that Christ, the Son of God, being the Father’s supreme priest, possesses everywhere, in most mighty priestly power, an office which ought to be adorned through God’s grace with the gold of wisdom and the gems of virtues by his imitators in the members [Col. 0674A] of these same faithful people.

Accordingly, a most brilliant radiance so surrounds her everywhere that you can see her nowhere except from the front, from her head downward to her feet. For grace is surrounded by the most serene brightness of the Almighty’s mercy; in the mystery of divinity it lay hidden, invisible and less welcome, in times past before the Savior’s humanity, but from the incarnation of that same Savior to the last of his members, who will be near the end of the age, it is made manifest more openly in its works, insofar as human understanding can grasp this.

But her arms, hands, and feet are shaded from your sight, because the strength, work, and goal of the course of God’s grace in human beings do not appear fully to anyone burdened with a body. [Col. 0674B] That the radiance surrounding her is full of eyes on every side and wholly alive means that divine mercy, joined to God’s grace, displays many compassions—the eyes of its countless mercies—looking upon the sufferings of those who desire to follow God; and it is wholly living, preparing for them in the consolation and salvation of their souls no destruction whatever, but life.

And it spreads this way and that as a cloud is wont to spread; for it goes before the righteous, that they may take care not to fall; it follows sinners, that they may repent and rise again; it makes itself manifest by a heavenly gift to all who seek it. Thus it now makes itself broader, now narrower; because in the miseries and grieving hearts of the faithful it sometimes overflows in abundant fruitfulness, while at other times it contracts itself in the wicked and hard hearts of sinners because of their dryness. [Col. 0674C] Therefore it also goes before and follows, touches and admonishes human beings, as has been said: so that those who desire to be children of God may joyfully receive its words and, having received them, fulfill them—despising transient things and embracing those that endure—as this same virtue addresses the children of God in its preceding exhortation.

But whoever has keen ears of inward understanding, let that person pant after these words in the burning love of my mirror, and write them in the conscience of his or her soul.

## NINTH VISION

[Col. 0673]

### SUMMARY

Words of wisdom. Words of justice. Words of strength. Words of holiness, which was three-headed. Words of the right head. Words of the left head. That, upon the incarnation of the Son of God, the calling of the new people arose as a new construction, fortified by the defenses of virtues. That the Church, illumined by the light of the humanity of the Son of God, is shown to humanity’s inward and outward knowledge. That the Church renders all her adornment to her bridegroom. That the human heart cannot search out divine wisdom in the work of the Church. That concerning the Church, a proclamation still remains hidden in the knowledge of God, and by diligent industry it does not cease daily to hasten toward perfection through its teachers. That the Church is invincibly surrounded by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. How ecclesiastical teachers, flourishing in apostolic doctrine, strengthen the Church by their united work. That teachers of the Church have led the erring to the way of truth by faith and works. That the apostles and their successors, namely apostolic men, maintaining one tenor, ought with great solicitude of mercy to preside over the Bride of God. Solomon’s words on the same subject. A parable on the same subject. That those who live carnally should attend, through knowledge, to the power of God. On the manifold diversity of those entering and leaving the Church. On simoniacs and the hidden divine judgments concerning them. Words of the Apostle Peter on the same subject. That the dignity of rule is good, ordained by God for the benefit of the times, so that through it people may learn to fear God; whoever resists it resists God. On simoniacs who repent and those who do not repent. That God gave the new Bride the gifts of the Holy Spirit for defense and adornment. On Wisdom, her appearance and clothing, and what these signify. On the appearance of Justice, Strength, and Holiness. On Justice. On Strength. On Holiness.

[Col. 0675A] After this I saw, beyond the aforesaid column of the Savior’s humanity, a tower of most brilliant radiance set upon the aforementioned stone wall on the southern side of the building previously seen, in such a way that it could be seen both inside and outside that building. Its breadth, throughout the inner part of its circuit, was five cubits; but it was of such height that I could not distinguish it.

But between that tower and the column of the Savior’s humanity there had been laid only a foundation, with no wall yet built upon it; only a broken and empty space appeared, one cubit in length, as had also been shown above. And this tower had not yet been built to completion, though it was continually being constructed by many workers with great skill and speed. Around [Col. 0675B] its summit it had seven battlements, constructed with marvelous strength.

From the inner side of the aforesaid building I saw something like a ladder raised to the top of that tower. From bottom to top, upon its steps, stood a multitude of people with fiery faces, white garments, and black shoes. Among them were some of like appearance but greater in stature and splendor, gazing upon the tower itself with great diligence.

Then, on the northern side of the same building, I saw the world and human beings begotten from Adam’s seed moving about between the aforesaid luminous wall of speculative knowledge belonging to that building and the circumference of the circle extending from the One seated upon the throne. Many of them passed into and out of that same building, between the tower of the advance course [Col. 0675C] of God’s will and the column of the divinity of his Word, through the aforesaid wall of speculative knowledge, as a cloud spreads this way and that.

But those who entered that building were clothed in a most white garment. Some of them, rejoicing with great joy in the sweetness and gentleness of that garment, retained it; but others, made sorrowful as though by its weight and difficulty, wished to take it off. This virtue, whom I had earlier heard called the Knowledge of God, kindly restrained them repeatedly, saying to each one: “Consider and keep the garment with which you are clothed.”

And I saw that some of them, rebuked by those words, retained the garment with much sweat, although it seemed difficult to them; [Col. 0675D] but others mocked those words, and, madly stripping off and casting away that garment, returned to the world from which they had come. Searching out many things, they learned many useless vanities of the world. Some of these at last returned into the building and, taking up again the garment which they had cast off, put it on; but others, unwilling to return, remained shamefully naked in the world.

And I saw certain people, most filthy and utterly black, as though aroused to madness, coming from the north and rushing into that [Col. 0676A] building. Assaulting the aforesaid tower in Bacchic frenzy, they hissed at it like serpents. Some of them, ceasing from this madness, were made clean; others persisted in the same wickedness and filth.

Within that same building, facing the same tower, I also beheld seven marble columns of white color, turned into marvelous roundness, standing seven cubits high. At their summit they had, as it were, an iron and circular platform, fittingly raised somewhat upward in height. At the top of this platform I saw a most beautiful figure standing and looking toward the people in the world. Her head flashed like lightning with such brilliance that I could not look at it fully. She had reverently placed her hands upon her breast, while her feet upon that same platform were hidden from my sight. She wore on her head a circle in the manner of a crown, shining with great radiance. She was clothed in a tunic of golden color, from whose breast down to the feet descended a single girdle, adorned with most precious gems of green, white, red, and gold, with a purple gleam shining through.

And she cried out to the people in the world, saying:

“O sluggish ones, why do you not come? Would you not be helped if you were willing to come? When you begin to run upon God’s way, gnats and flies, with their buzzing, hinder you. But take the fan of the Holy Spirit’s inspiration, and quickly drive them away from yourselves. You must run, and you must also hope for help from God. Do not offer yourselves deceitfully for God’s service, and you shall be strengthened by his hand.”

[Col. 0676C] But on the floor of that building I saw three other figures. One of them leaned against the aforesaid columns, and the remaining two stood before it, beside it. All directed themselves toward the column of the Savior’s humanity and toward the aforesaid tower.

The one leaning against those columns appeared of such breadth that the width of five people standing beside one another could be measured upon it; and of such height that I could not perfectly discern its length. Indeed, it extended its gaze through the whole building. Having a great head and bright eyes, it looked most keenly toward heaven, being wholly white and translucent like a most serene cloud.

[Col. 0676D] I saw no other human form in it. And it cried through the whole building to all the other virtues, saying:

“Let us all rise bravely, for Lucifer is spreading his darkness throughout the whole world. Let us build towers and strengthen them with heavenly battlements, because the devil is the adversary and assailant of God’s elect. As he first greatly desired and attempted in his brightness, so now he greatly desires and attempts in his darkness. For, blowing and scattering abroad, he spreads his malice and wickedness, and he does not wish to cease from this. Against these things we have been appointed as heavenly soldiers, to overcome him in his malice and wickedness; otherwise people will be unable to be saved in the world because of his assault.
