The breath proceeding from the right side of the leopard’s mouth as far as the crab’s head; the breath issuing from the left side of that mouth as far as the stag’s head; the breath extending from the mouth of the stag’s head as far as the midpoint of the space between the heads of the leopard and lion; and the breath extending from the mouth of the stag’s head as far as the midpoint of the space between the heads of the leopard and bear—all were of equal length. All these heads breathed into the aforesaid wheel and toward this image of the human being.

Below the feet of the same human image, in the sign of watery air, there appeared something like a wolf’s head sending breath, as it were, from its mouth. From the right of this mouth, a breath extending somewhat lengthwise took, in the middle of the half-space between the heads of the wolf and bear, the form of a stag’s head; and from its mouth another breath, as it were, came and ended in that same midpoint. But from the left side of the mouth of this wolf’s head, the breath proceeding from the mouth extended itself and rose, in the middle of the half-space between the wolf’s and lion’s heads, into a crab’s head with two claws, as though with two feet; and another breath, as it were, issuing from its mouth, settled in that same midpoint.

By the same measure of space by which these heads were distant from one another, their breaths were extended in length and form on either side, as has also been said above concerning the others; and they sent their breaths into the wheel previously shown and toward the image of the human being standing in it.

But at the right of this image, in the sign of bright fire, I saw something like a lion’s head. A breath, as it were, issuing from its mouth extended somewhat from each side of the mouth; on the right it formed into a serpent’s head, and on the left into a lamb’s head. The serpent’s head, appearing in the middle of the half-space between the lion’s and wolf’s heads, emitted, as it were, a breath that extended to that same midpoint and joined the breath issuing from the crab’s head between the wolf and lion. The lamb’s head, appearing in the middle of the half-space between the lion’s and leopard’s heads, produced, as it were, a breath which extended to that midpoint and met in conjunction the breath from the crab’s head between the leopard and lion.

But the lengths of their breaths proceeded according to the spaces by which these heads were separated from one another, as had been shown concerning the upper heads and their breaths. They showed themselves to breathe into the aforesaid wheel and toward the aforementioned human image.

At the left of the same image, in the sign of black fire, there appeared something like a bear’s head, which gave forth breath, as it were, from its mouth. Extending somewhat lengthwise to the right and left of its mouth, it ended on the right in a lamb’s head and took on the form of a serpent’s head on the left. From the mouth of this lamb’s head another breath, as it were, extended to the midpoint of the space between the bear’s and leopard’s heads. But from the mouth of this serpent’s head another breath, as it were, proceeded by extending itself to the midpoint of the space between the bear’s and wolf’s heads.

The breath coming from the right side of the bear’s mouth as far as the lamb’s head; likewise the breath proceeding from the left side of that mouth as far as the serpent’s head; the breath issuing from the lamb’s mouth as far as the shown midpoint of the space between the bear’s and leopard’s heads; and the breath extending from the serpent’s mouth as far as the midpoint of the space between the bear’s and wolf’s heads—all were of one and equal length. All these heads also gave breath into the aforesaid wheel and toward the aforementioned human image.

Above the head of this image seven planets were marked, ascending separately from one another: three in the circle of bright fire, one in the circle of black fire beneath it, and three in the circle of pure ether beneath that. Moreover, toward the south at its side, and also beneath its feet, the sun appeared marked and distinguished in its circle in the same manner and order.

From the middle of the sign of the highest and first planet, marked above the head of the same image, certain rays, as it were, issued: one descended to the sign of the sun; one shone toward the right foot of the aforesaid crab’s head which proceeded from the leopard’s head; and one extended to the right antler of the stag’s head which likewise issued from the same leopard’s head.

From the middle of the sign of the second planet, one ray, as it were, inclined above the sign of the sun; another proceeded toward the lamb’s head that came from the sign of the lion’s head; and another was directed to the aforesaid line which extended from, as it were, the beginning of the eastern side of the wheel to, as it were, the end of its western side toward its northern region, with the lamb’s head placed above there that issued from the sign of the bear’s head.

Likewise, from its middle the sign of the third planet extended one ray to the sign of the sun, directed another to the serpent’s head proceeding from the sign of the lion’s head, and extended another to the aforesaid line toward the serpent’s head issuing from the sign of the bear’s head.

The sign of the sun also emitted certain rays from itself: one touched the sign of the leopard’s head, another the sign of the lion’s head, and another the sign of the wolf’s head, but not the sign of the bear’s head. It directed another ray above the sign of the moon, and fixed another, extending as though over the brain and down over both heels of the aforesaid image.

From the middle of the sign of the fifth planet, which is nearest below the sun, a ray, as it were, ascended to the sign of the sun; another extended to the crab’s head which issued from the sign of the wolf’s head; and another was directed to the left horn of the moon’s sign. From the middle of the sign of the sixth planet, which is nearest above the moon, one ray, as it were, extended upward to the sign of the sun, another was directed to the right horn of the moon’s sign, and another extended to the stag’s head proceeding from the sign of the wolf’s head.

From the sign of the moon a ray, as it were, shone over both eyebrows and over both ankles of the aforesaid image. And, as was stated above, the sign of the sun appeared marked in the same manner and order by its rays toward the aforesaid places above the crown of this image, likewise toward its right side, and also beneath its feet, in its own circle toward the same places.

Around the circumference of the circle in which the likeness of bright fire was seen, sixteen principal stars appeared: four between the leopard’s and lion’s heads, four between the lion’s and wolf’s heads, four between the wolf’s and bear’s heads, and four between the bear’s and leopard’s heads. Of these, the eight that lay in the middle of the stars standing on either side between these heads—namely, two between each two heads—extended their rays, as it were, into the sign of thin air opposite them. But the remaining eight, which appeared nearest to the aforesaid heads on either side of these middle stars, directed their rays only toward the black fire.

The circle of pure ether and the circle of strong, white, bright air seemed full of stars, which sent their gleams toward the clouds opposite them. Thus, from the clouds on the right side of the aforesaid image, two tongues, as it were, separated from one another issued and directed from themselves, like certain little streams, into the aforementioned [Col. 0755A] wheel and toward the same image. But from the marked clouds on its left side, likewise two tongues, somewhat separated from one another, turned into the same wheel and toward the image itself, as though flowing from themselves in certain little streams.

In this way the image was interwoven with and surrounded by these signs. I also saw that from the mouth of the aforesaid image, in whose breast the wheel appeared, there issued a light brighter than daylight, in the likeness of threads. By these threads it measured in straight and distinct proportion the signs of the circles, the signs of the other figures distinguished in that same wheel, and each sign of the limbs of the human form—namely, of that image which also appeared within the wheel—as is made manifest in its preceding and following words.

[Col. 0755B] That the Divinity, like an unbroken wheel, having neither beginning nor end and bounded neither by place nor time, embraces all things within itself.

II. And again I heard a voice from heaven saying to me:

“God, who for the glory of his name composed the world from the elements, established it by the winds, made it bright by interweaving it with stars, and filled it with the remaining creatures, surrounded and fortified within it the human being with all these things. He pervaded him everywhere with the greatest strength, so that they might assist him in all things and take part in his works; so that he might work with them, because without them the human being can neither live nor even subsist. This is made manifest to you in the present vision.

“For in the breast of the aforesaid image there appears a wheel of wondrous vision, with signs of approximately this form: like that instrument which twenty-eight years earlier you had seen symbolically in the shape of an egg, as it had been shown to you in your earlier visions. For, without forgetfulness, in the knowledge of true love—which is God—the form of the world exists, indissolubly revolving and wondrous for human nature. It is neither consumed by any age nor increased by any novelty, but as it was first created by God, so it will endure until the end of the age.

“For the Divinity is, as it were, wholly entire in its foreknowledge and its work, and in no way divided; because it has neither beginning nor end and cannot be comprehended by anyone, since it is without time. And just as a circle contains the things hidden within it, so the holy Divinity infinitely contains and surpasses all things, because no one has been able to divide it in its power, surpass it, or bring it to an end.”

Why the sphere of the world was shown or described in the book *Scivias* in the form of an egg, but in this book in the likeness of a wheel.

III. But that the aforesaid instrument was designated in your earlier visions in the form of an egg shows that the distinction of the elements alone is signified in that likeness. For, since the world is distinguished by the elements, the discriminating shape of an egg bears some resemblance to the distinction by which it is differentiated through the elements. Here, however, only the circuit and the [Col. 0756A] straight proportion of those same elements are shown in the wheel. Neither representation fully possesses the likeness of the world’s form, because a globe, being whole, round, and movable on every side, more closely imitates in every respect the form of the world, which itself is whole, round, and movable.

Concerning the two circles of bright and black fire: why one is placed beneath the other, how they cooperate with one another, and what they signify.

IV. But that at its highest part, around the circumference of its roundness, there appears a circle resembling bright fire means that the first element, fire, is first because it is light; it embraces and illumines the other elements, passes through all creatures, and supplies them with the joy of its light. It signifies the power of God, who is above all things and grants life to all.

Beneath it another circle is shown like a circle of black fire, because this fire, existing under the power of the former, is judicial and almost infernal, made for the punishment of evils. It spares nothing upon which it falls by righteous judgment, because it shows that everyone who sets himself against God will be turned into the fall of blackness and many calamities.

For in summer, when the sun rises high, this fire exercises God’s vengeance in the burning of lightning; but in winter, when the sun descends low, it displays judicial scourges in frost, hail, and cold. For every sin is examined according to its kind either by fire, or cold, or certain other punishments.

[Col. 0756C] The circle of bright fire exceeds this circle of black fire by twice its density, because this black fire has such strength and bitterness in its blackness that it would overshadow and scatter the bright fire above, unless the latter surpassed it in density. This signifies that the punishment of human sins contains so many perils of penalties that the human being could not endure them if the grace and mercy of God did not forestall them. These two circles are joined together as though one circle, because they burn with the heat of fire, and because God’s power and judgment, held together in one rectitude, are not separated from one another.

Concerning the circle of pure ether, which is third: what its constitution accomplishes, what it signifies, and why it has the same density as the two upper circles.

V. But below the same circle of black fire is another circle resembling pure ether, everywhere of the same density as the circles of the two aforesaid fires. This is because beneath the aforesaid fires, bright and black alike, pure ether surrounds the world in its roundness, proceeding from them like flashes from flaming fire when fire expands its flame. It signifies the pure repentance of sinners, which is stirred up in the human being through God’s grace as though by the bright fire, and through fear of him as though by the black.

It has the same density as the two aforementioned fires because, shining from both fires, it has in itself the density of each: it is neither gentler in the gleam of the bright fire nor harsher in the impact of the black fire than [Col. 0757A] God’s just judgment determines. For neither day nor night displays in itself anything other than what the divine will ordains.

This ether also restrains higher and lower things so that they do not exceed their boundary. It does not fall upon any creature in judicial judgment, but through its subtlety and fairness it often withstands it, just as repentance restrains the punishment of sins. That it has the density of these fires means that the penitent person should consider in the bright fire the fall of the first angel, who was bright; should consider in the density of the black fire the fall of human beings sinning in unbelief and rashness; and, contemplating God’s power and just judgment, should repent purely and worthily.

Concerning the fourth circle, which appears in the manner of watery air: how great its density is and what it signifies.

VI. But beneath that circle of pure ether is another circle, as though a circle of watery air, whose density in its roundness is as great as the density of the aforesaid circle of bright fire. This signifies that beneath the aforesaid ether, around the circuit of the firmament, are those waters known to be above the firmament; their density in their circumference is the same as that of the aforementioned bright fire.

This watery air signifies holy works in the examples of the righteous. They are like transparent water and cleanse unclean works, just as water washes away all filth; and they exist in the perfection of this capacity according as divine grace kindles them in the fire [Col. 0757C] of the Holy Spirit.

Concerning the circle of strong, white, bright air: with what usefulness it occupies the fifth place, how great its density is, what it too signifies, and why it is joined to the upper circle so as to be, as it were, one.

VII. Beneath that same circle, namely that of watery air, another circle is shown, of strong, white, and bright air, having in its rigidity the likeness of a sinew in the human body. Set against the dangers of the upper waters, it holds back their floods by its strength and tenacity, lest they overwhelm the earth in a sudden and untimely outpouring. It also signifies that discretion strengthens holy works in such moderation that a person may restrain the body so that, being not unjustly constrained, it may not fall into ruin [Col. 0757D]. It is everywhere in its circuit of the same density as the aforesaid circle of black fire appears to be; for this one is established in equal measure for the benefit of human beings, just as that one is established for the punishment of their sins.

But whenever, by God’s just judgment and for the punishment of evils, the lower waters are drawn upward in excessive quantity through the clouds, some moisture from the watery air passes through this strong, white, bright air, as a person’s drink passes into the bladder while it itself remains whole; and this causes those waters to descend in a dangerous flood. Thus discretion also distinguishes human actions everywhere by a just moderation for their salvation, when God’s judgments do not go beyond their sins in vengeance, but judge them justly; for protector and ruler hold one another in just equity [Col. 0758A]. These two circles are also joined to each other in such a way that they appear to be like one circle, because they are moistened by moisture and impart moisture to others; just as discretion contains good works in its moderation, lest they fall into ruin.

### Concerning the sixth circle, which seems to proceed from the upper regions in the likeness of thin air: what efficacy it has in its place, and what is figuratively represented through it in a mystical sense

VIII. And beneath this circle, namely that of strong, white, bright air, there is marked, as it were, another thin air, which shows itself as proceeding from the upper circles or elements like breathed-out air. Nor is it separated from those elements, just as a person’s breath proceeds from the person and yet is not separated from him [Col. 0758B]. This air also seems sometimes to bear clouds raised high and bright, sometimes low-hanging and shadowy; the aforesaid watery air ejects and gathers them again, as a smith’s bellows sends out and draws back its blast. Thus, when certain stars placed in the aforesaid element of fire rise in their revolutions, they draw these clouds upward, and they become bright. But when they descend in their revolutions, they let the clouds down, and thus they are shadowy and sow rains.

And the aforesaid thin air seems to diffuse itself, as it were, throughout the whole of the aforesaid wheel, because everything in the world is nourished and sustained by it. So also, under the protection of discretion, the upright desires of faithful people, dwelling in the subtlety of justice, show themselves to have proceeded from higher virtues and strengthenings through the Holy Spirit, since they do not turn away from them but cling to them without interruption in all devotion. They possess in those faithful persons a steadfast mind, now shining in confidence, now trembling in humility, directed toward God; this arises from holy works and the examples of the righteous and is gathered back to them, just as a laborer receives recompense from his work [Col. 0758C].

For when good knowledge, kindled by the Holy Spirit, rises in people through its justifications toward heavenly things, it draws their minds with it and makes them pure there. But when, in those same justifications, it bends down to bodily necessities, it sends their minds back to these, so that amid such cares they seem, as it were, clouded [Col. 0758D], yet bearing the rain of tears, because they deeply lament being bound at all to earthly things, although they submit themselves wholly by entrusting themselves to divine power.

### Why these six circles are joined to one another without intervals, and what is indicated by this connection

IX. All these six circles were joined together without any interval, because if divine ordering had not made them firm by this union, the firmament would be torn apart and could not stand. They show that perfect virtues, united in a faithful person, are so strengthened through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit that, fighting against the vices of the devil, they accomplish every good work with one accord.

[Col. 0759A]

### How the first circle sets the others aflame by its fire, the fourth tempers them by its light, and what this figuratively shows in us

X. The highest circle, as it were, pours its fire over the other circles, while the watery one moistens all the others with its moisture. For the upper element, which is fire, strengthens the rest by its power and brightness, while the watery one imparts greenness to the others by its moistening; just as God’s power sanctifies faithful people in the wonders of His grace, while the works of the faithful magnify the mercy of their Creator in the true humility of holiness.

### Concerning the line that appears stretched across the aforesaid wheel, as though from the first rising of the sun to its final setting, and what this signifies mystically

XI. And a line stretches in the firmament toward the northern part, as though from the beginning of the eastern side of this wheel to the end of its western side [Col. 0759B], as though distinguishing the northern region from the other regions. For from the first rising in the east—that is, where the sun first rises when the days begin to lengthen—to the final setting in the west, namely where the sun proceeds no farther, the line, that is, the path of the sun, bends away from the northern region. The sun does not immerse itself in those parts, but holds them, as it were, in neglect, where the ancient deceiver chose for himself the seat of his dwelling; and therefore God deprived them of the sun’s approach.

So too, from the beginning of good works, which are in God’s power, to their good completion, the faithful person opposes the rectitude of justice to iniquity [Col. 0759C], separating devilish arts from good and holy works. For whoever wishes faithfully to cling to God will strive to avoid those things that harm the soul, so as to hear what is written.

### A testimony from the Apocalypse, and how it should be understood as expressing the same point

XII. “To the conqueror I will give hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name, which no one knows except the one who receives it” (Rev. II).

Its meaning is as follows: Whoever flees the left-hand side has a great battle against the twisting serpent, which always seeks to draw that person with itself toward the left. And if, persevering in this struggle, that person puts Satan to flight by not consenting to his counsel, I, who am, shall give that person the living bread which came down from heaven [Col. 0759D], hidden from every abasement of human will and from every deceit of the ancient serpent. I shall also give them a share in Him who, being the cornerstone, is God and man in white brightness; and in Him is the name of the new regeneration, namely Christ, from whom Christians also take their name. No one, while living this perishable and temporal life, fully understands this, except the one who attains the life of eternal blessedness in the reward of heavenly prizes.

### How the mass of the earth, like a globe, is founded immovably beneath the aforesaid six circles, equally distant from the five upper ones and in the midst of the sixth—that is, the thin air—and what significance is gathered from this

XIII. A globe is also marked in the middle of the aforesaid region of thin air [Col. 0760A]. It is equally distant on every side in its circuit from the region of strong, white, bright air, signifying the earth, which exists in the middle of the remaining elements so that it may be tempered by them all. Thus, raised equally from them on either side and joined to them, it continually receives from them greenness and strength for its support.

The active life likewise signifies the earth. Moving, as it were, in the midst of upright desires and ranging in every direction, it restrains itself by the equal moderation of devotion within the powers of discretion, when faithful people attend in due measure now to spiritual duties and now to bodily necessities. For those who love discretion direct all their works to God’s will. And its breadth across is equal to the depth of the space from the summit of the highest circle to the extremity of the clouds, or from the extremity of the clouds to the summit of the same globe [Col. 0760B], because the earth has been rounded into this mass and strengthened by the supreme Creator, lest it be dissolved by the tumult of the upper elements, the force of the winds, or the flooding of waters.

For every faithful person, with an enlarged heart, considers the greatness of God’s power and observes the instability of the mind and the weakness of the flesh; and thus moderates all that is done, lest, exceeding the right measure in necessary matters either above or below, that person fail. As Paul also exhorts the faithful, saying:

[Col. 0760C]

### Words of Paul appropriate to the same meaning, and how they should be understood

XIV. “Do all things without murmurings and hesitations, that you may be without complaint and simple children of God without reproach, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. II).

Its meaning is as follows: A person stands as though at a crossroads: if that person seeks salvation from God in the light, it will be received; but if evil is chosen, that person will follow the devil to punishment. Therefore a person should bear human nature and all personal works without murmurings—that is, without the swellings of sins—and without disputings, possessing perfect faith. Thus one should not doubt, when loving good and hating evil, that in the future judgment one will be delivered and separated from the lost, who turn away by embracing evil instead of good [Col. 0760D].

Those who do these things, harming no one, shall be without the outcry of stubborn complaint; and, as children of God in the simplicity of good works, they shall remain blameless, without any deceitful fraud, before the judgment of those who boast that they are strong in crooked and perverse deeds. Among them they shine in the perfection of true faith as the heavenly lights, which illuminate the world in their office according to the ordering of the Creator of all things. So too, by their teaching that looks toward life, they turn very many people toward God, just as the Son of God shone without sin before all in the world.

For God placed two lights, the sun and the moon, in the firmament, which signify knowledge of good and evil in a person [Col. 0761A]. As the firmament is established by sun and moon, so a person moves this way and that through knowledge of good and evil. But as the sun completes its course without diminishing its circle, so good knowledge completes its course, not desiring evil but suppressing, rebuking, and correcting evil knowledge, because it has no usefulness. It calls it hellish when it has fulfilled its desires. And as the moon wanes and grows, so evil knowledge despises good knowledge and calls it foolish and as though nothing; yet it knows it, as the devil knew God, although he opposed Him.

### Concerning the image in human form appearing in the middle of the aforesaid wheel, with head, feet, and hands extended to touch the circle of strong, white, bright air; and what both the image and its position signify

XV. That an image of a human being appears in the middle of this wheel, whose head above and soles below reach to the aforesaid circle of strong, white, bright air, while on the right side the tips of the fingers of the right hand, and on the left the tips of the fingers of the left hand, are stretched out on either side to the same circle marked in roundness [Col. 0761B], because that image extended its arms in this way—this signifies that in the structure of the world the human being is, as it were, in its middle, since the human being is more powerful than the other creatures dwelling in it: small indeed in bodily stature, but great in the power of the soul.

The head moves upward and the feet downward toward both the higher and lower elements; likewise, through works performed by the hands on the right and left, the human being penetrates them, because in the powers of the inner person there is this capacity for action. For as the human body surpasses its heart in size, so the powers of the soul surpass the human body in their strength; and as the human heart is hidden in the body, so the human body is encompassed by the powers of the soul, since they extend throughout the whole circle of the earth [Col. 0761C].

Likewise, a faithful person, existing in the knowledge of God, tends toward God in both spiritual and worldly necessary concerns; and in prosperity and adversity alike that person pants after Him, continually extending all devotion toward Him in these matters [Col. 0761D]. For as a person sees every creature everywhere with bodily eyes, so in faith that person beholds the Lord everywhere and knows Him through creatures, understanding Him to be their Creator.

### Concerning the four heads of beasts appearing in the four parts of the same wheel, and what they signify both in the world and in the human being

XVI. Toward these same four regions there appear four heads: as it were the head of a leopard and of a wolf, and the heads, as it were, of a lion and a bear. For in the four parts of the world there are four principal winds, not indeed existing in such bodily forms, but imitating in their powers the natures of the beasts named. A person likewise, standing as it were at the fourfold crossing of worldly cares [Col. 0762A], is assailed by very many temptations: in them that person remembers, as in the leopard’s head, the fear of the Lord; as in the wolf, the infernal punishments; as in the lion, fearing also God’s judgment; and as in the bear, is shaken by very many storms of distress in bodily tribulation.

### Why the principal eastern wind appears in the form of a leopard’s head above the head of the human image in the circle of pure ether; and why its two neighboring winds are shown, one in the likeness of a crab’s head and the other like a stag’s head

XVII. Above the crown of the aforesaid image, in the region of pure ether, you see something like a leopard’s head sending forth a breath from its mouth. This signifies the principal eastern wind coming from the pure ether like a leopard [Col. 0762B]—not because this wind has the bodily form of a leopard, but because, as the leopard has the lion’s ferocity without its intelligence, and as it is milder and weaker than the lion, so this wind rises in the fierceness of terror and then quickly ceases to blow, turning to mildness. For it has fierceness from the upper black fire and mildness from the pure ether in which it is.

On the right side of the same mouth, it bends somewhat lengthwise and takes the form of a crab’s head with two claws, as though with two feet; for, extending toward those regions, this wind there assumes the nature of a crab. But on the left side of its mouth, curving somewhat lengthwise in the opposite direction, it ends in a stag’s head, because in those regions it imitates the swift stag [Col. 0762C].

From the mouth of this crab’s head another breath, as it were, proceeds as far as the middle of the space between the heads of the leopard and the aforesaid lion. For the neighboring wind, arising according to the nature of a crab, sends forth its blasts unevenly like a whirlwind, so that it ranges now here, now there in instability, like a crab that now advances and now retreats; and thus it reaches as far as the middle between east and south. But from the mouth of the stag’s head another breath, as it were, comes as far as the middle of the space between the leopard’s head and the bear’s head. For another neighboring wind proceeds in accordance with the stag’s nature, sending forth strong and swift gusts, and quickly ceasing in this, as a stag strikes powerfully and runs swiftly but does not persist long in this; and in such a manner it hastens and confines itself as far as the middle between east and north [Col. 0762D].

The breath proceeding from the right side of the leopard’s mouth to the crab’s head, and the breath issuing from its left side to the stag’s head; likewise the breath extending from the mouth of the crab’s head to the middle of the space between the leopard’s and lion’s heads, and the breath lengthening from the mouth of the stag’s head to the middle of the space between the leopard’s and bear’s heads—these are of equal length. For the principal eastern wind extends with equal length from both sides toward its neighboring winds, and those neighboring winds reach with the same length to their boundaries both toward the south and toward the north [Col. 0763A].

### Why these heads breathe toward the human image in the wheel, and a moral description of their meaning

XVIII. All these heads breathe into the aforesaid wheel and toward this human image, because these winds temper the world by their blasts and preserve the human being for salvation through their ministry. For neither the world could endure nor human beings live if they were not sustained by the blasts of these winds.

But when a person raises oneself upward in the intention of the soul, remembering evil deeds and then resolving to repent of them, then above that person’s head, with that same intention, in the region of pure ether—that is, in repentance itself—the fear of the Lord rises like a leopard [Col. 0763B]. Bringing forth contrition, as it were, from its mouth—that is, from its power—it stretches the mind of the person in prosperity until it reaches the crab’s head, namely confidence, from which, as though two claws—that is, two feet—hope and doubt extend. In adversity it extends the same contrition of that mind until it leads to the stag’s head, which is faith.

For when a person recalls the weight of sins, that person enters upon repentance and does not cease to fear God in it, even though worldly prosperity is possessed as though on the other side, until confidence is grasped, from which hope and doubt arise as from two feet. From confidence hope rises, though doubt sometimes joins itself to it: while a person trusts in God, that person hopes, as by proceeding, to attain forgiveness of sins; but when considering their multitude and gravity, that person often doubts, as by retreating, whether those sins are forgiven, although trusting in God [Col. 0763C].

But when sometimes, amid adversities as though on the other side, a person suffers bodily contrition, that person turns to the riches of faith, which, in the horns of true consolation, reduces the unbelief of doubt to nothing. Hence, as it were, from the mouth of the crab—that is, from confidence—another breath comes forth, namely steadfastness, and proceeds to the fullness of perfection, where it stands between the fear of the Lord and God’s judgment. For when anyone trusting in God is steadfast and perfect in good works, that person gathers to oneself the fear of the Lord, lest one sin more grievously, and considers also God’s judgment, lest sins be added to sins [Col. 0763D].

And from the stag’s mouth—that is, from faith—another breath, which is to be understood as holiness, comes and extends to the fullness of perfection between the fear of the Lord and bodily tribulation. For the faithful person, strong in holiness, endures in this perfection, so as truly to fear God and, for this reason, never cease to discipline the body.

Thus the breath—that is, contrition in prosperity, proceeding from the fear of the Lord toward confidence; the breath, likewise, namely the same contrition in adversity, issuing from that fear toward faith; the breath—that is, steadfastness—tending from confidence to the fullness of perfection which is between the fear of the Lord and God’s judgment; and the breath, namely holiness, extending from faith to the fullness of perfection which lies between the fear of the Lord and bodily tribulation [Col. 0764A]—as was said above, all invite the person to blessedness with one and the same mode and equal zeal in the breathing forth of their powers. Although they have diverse operations, they nevertheless tend to one blessedness. For one virtue proceeds from another in the work of uprightness.

All these heads, that is, these virtues, are in the knowledge of God and attend to God’s knowledge; they assist the person in necessary concerns both bodily and spiritual. For when the fear of the Lord inspires a person, that person begins to revere God and proceeds wisely in accomplishing good and upright works. Confidence, by which a person trusts in God, touches that person along with steadfastness, so that one may trust steadily in God and raise thoughts toward Him; for the minds of the faithful are strengthened by the virtue of steadfastness [Col. 0764B].

Faith, together with holiness, judges the things that must be judged in unbelief; rapidly spreading itself, it quickly instructs believers, when their hearing abandons every tumult of perverse thoughts and inwardly overturns slippery pleasures as well. But if a person abandons the greenness of these virtues and turns to the dryness of negligence, so as to lack the moisture and greenness of good works, the powers of that person’s soul fail and wither. If, however, the person is inundated excessively by the luxury of pleasures, as by an unsuitable flood, the mind melts away, moving on slippery ground [Col. 0764C]. But if one walks the straight path, all one’s works are directed toward prosperity, as is written in the Song of Songs:

### A testimony from the Song of Songs suitable to the same point, and how it should be understood

XIX. “The king brought me into his storehouses. We shall rejoice and be glad in you, remembering your breasts more than wine; the upright love you” (Song I).

Its meaning is as follows: Because I, the soul of the faithful person, securely follow with the step of truth the Son of God, who redeemed humankind through His humanity, He who is ruler of all has brought me into the fullness of His gifts, where I find every abundance of virtues and where I confidently ascend from virtue to virtue. Therefore all of us who have been redeemed through the blood of that same Son of God [Col. 0764D] shall exult with the whole body and rejoice with the whole soul in You, O holy Divinity, through whom we subsist, calling to mind the sweetness of heavenly rewards above all the sufferings and tribulations we have endured from the adversaries of truth. We count them as nothing while we taste the delights which You set before us in the manifestation of Your commandments.

Thus those who are upright in works of holiness love You with true and perfect love, because You grant every good thing to those who love You and because You finally give them eternal life. Wisdom also pours and sets forth in the storehouses—that is, in human minds—the justice of true faith, through which the true God is known. There that faith so represses the winter and all the moisture of vices that they can no longer grow green or increase; and there it draws and joins all virtues to itself, as wine is poured into a vessel to be given for people to drink [Col. 0765A].

Therefore the faithful, exulting and rejoicing in true confidence of eternal reward, bear the sheaves of good works which they have performed; they thirst for God’s justice and suck holiness from His breasts. Nor can they in this manner grow weary, but they delight continually in contemplating the Divinity, because holiness surpasses all human understanding. For when a person receives uprightness, that person leaves oneself behind, tastes and drinks the virtues, and is strengthened through them, as the veins of one drinking are filled with wine. Nor is such a person officious and immoderate in the vices of unbelief, as one drunk with wine is beside oneself and does not heed what one is doing [Col. 0765B]. Thus the upright love God, because there is no weariness in Him, but perseverance in blessedness.

### Why the principal western wind appears in the likeness of a wolf’s head beneath the feet of the aforesaid image in the circle of watery air; and why its two neighboring winds are shown, one in the form of a stag and the other in the form of a crab’s head

XX. That beneath the feet of this human image, in the region of watery air, there appears something like a wolf’s head emitting a breath from its mouth means this: under the power of Him who became human for the sake of human beings, the principal western wind comes breathing from watery air in the western region like a wolf [Col. 0765C]. It is in the form of a wolf, which hides in the forest and is rapacious while seeking food, signifying that this wind, emerging from its hiding place—that is, from the watery air—now brings forth the greenness of herbs and now suddenly oppresses it by drying it up.

From the right side of its mouth it also breaks forth somewhat lengthwise and, in the middle of the halfway space between the wolf’s and bear’s heads, assumes the form of a stag’s head. From this head’s mouth another breath, as it were, comes and ends at the same midpoint. For as this wind seeks those regions, in the middle of the halfway space between west and north it turns to the nature of a stag, so that there a neighboring wind comes forth and, like a stag striking hard and running swiftly, sends its blasts as far as that midpoint.

But from the left of the mouth of that wolfish head, the breath proceeding from the mouth lengthens and, likewise in the middle of the halfway space between the wolf’s and lion’s heads, rises into a crab’s head with two claws, as though two feet [Col. 0765D]. From its mouth too another breath, as it were, comes forth and remains at the same midpoint. For, exercising its offices in those regions, this wind returns, in the middle of the halfway space between west and south, to the nature of a crab that moves forward and backward; because there its neighboring wind proceeds in instability, blowing now here, now there like a crab, and diffuses itself as far as the aforesaid midpoint.

By the same measure of the spaces by which these heads are distant from one another, their forms and breaths also extend lengthwise on either side, as has been said above of the others [Col. 0766A]. For by the measure by which these winds are separated from one another, they also send forth the breathing of their blasts. One wind directs its blasts toward another, and in that meeting they do not exceed their boundary; nor does one wind, by blowing, surpass another, unless this occurs by God’s judgment. If at times it happens by the decision of divine judgment, terrors arise there and many adversities of evils break out.

### Why these also, like the foregoing heads, direct their breaths toward the human image, and their moral meaning

XXI. These too send their breaths into the wheel shown before and toward the human image standing in it, so that the same winds sustain the world, the human being, and everything in the world by their powers and offices. Therefore, when any of the faithful trample underfoot the perishable things of earthly desires, as it were beneath their feet, by doing good works according to righteous examples, then from those holy works, as from watery air, the unveiled infernal punishments come forth like a wolf [Col. 0766B]. For when they cease to sin and tend toward the way of uprightness, they show that they have feared infernal punishments which devour souls.

When these punishments bring, as it were, a breath—that is, contrition—into human hearts from their mouth, which is their devouring, because the faithful abhor them, that same contrition, although a person may proceed prosperously in deeds, extends itself according to God and, in the fullness of perfection between infernal punishments and bodily tribulation, takes the form of a stag’s head—that is, faith. From its mouth—that is, its power—another breath comes, namely holiness, and remains in that same perfection [Col. 0766C].

For when a person fears infernal punishments, that person often wears down the body for a long time by various tribulations of miseries until reaching the perfection in which one burns wholly in faith, believing that God will rescue one from infernal punishments. Thus holiness rises in that person when, rejecting worldly works, one immerses oneself wholly in spiritual things.

But when, through the left-hand adversity of the devouring of the aforesaid infernal punishments, a person is bodily chastised by very many calamities through God’s permission, contrition likewise rises in that heart. Seeing that one has no prosperity in this present life, the person extends oneself from this point and so reaches the fullness of perfection between infernal punishments and God’s judgment [Col. 0766D], rising into the crab’s head, namely confidence, which has now hope and now doubt. For a person placing works in God sometimes hopes to have obtained forgiveness of sins and sometimes doubts; but finally another breath comes forth from confidence, signifying steadfastness, and leads that person to this perfection of virtues, so that thereafter one does not doubt God’s goodness at all.

The efficacy of these operations is prolonged by the same tenor by which these assertions are distinguished from one another. For infernal punishments, though they are to be feared, nevertheless make faith together with holiness, and confidence together with steadfastness, stronger when a person afflicts oneself in contrition because of fear of them. Thus, when hell is feared, a person is judged more cautious in everything [Col. 0767A]. And all these, beholding the vision of God who comprehends all things, also impel the person by the strength of their powers to accomplish God’s will.

For infernal punishments bring it about that God is feared: when a person truly fears punishments, one ceases to sin; and when seeing good examples in other people, one often endures many indignations within oneself, so that, patiently bearing them, one displays holiness in all works. But when proceeding prosperously through the support of good works and suffering no adversity, one joins oneself through their power to the swiftness of uprightness, so that, possessing temporal prosperity and not doubting God’s grace at all, one confidently entrusts oneself to it, using perishable things as though advancing before oneself, lest one be deprived of eternal things in heaven by following behind them [Col. 0767B].

But whoever lacks the greenness of the Holy Spirit is suffocated in unbelief, consumed in perverse acts, and incurs Tartarean submersion, because that person has not striven to entrust oneself to God’s grace. Of this Isaiah, my servant, speaks, saying:

### Words of Isaiah pertaining to the same point, and how they should be understood

XXII. “I will take away its hedge, and it shall be for plundering; I will tear down its wall, and it shall be for trampling. And I will make it deserted. It shall not be pruned, nor dug, and briars and thorns shall rise upon it; and I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. V).

Its meaning is as follows: Everyone who does not trust in God and does not attend to how one was created by God, but reproaches Him as though He were guilty of that person’s sins and had not established straight paths in that person; who does not wish to look upon the rising and setting of the sun, moon, and stars, which God placed in heaven, nor upon wind with air, earth with waters, and the other creatures—all of which God created for human beings, that through all these things they might know to what great honor they were created—such a person despises Me, who am without beginning and without end, and destroys every creature, knowing neither it nor oneself perfectly [Col. 0767C].

Therefore I shall take away that person’s defense, because there is no other helper; and strangers to life shall plunder that person. I shall also tear down that person’s protection, and that person shall be crushed by demons and thus abandoned by good angels. For every entanglement of that person’s desires shall be taken away and distributed to dogs and beasts, because that person knew Me less than animals do, though they do what they were created to do. Therefore that person shall also be trampled like dung and abandoned from every blessedness.

Nor shall that person be counted among the children of God, nor overturned from sins by the hoe of faith, because that person imitated him who wished to possess God’s likeness, who proceeds from no one and is without end [Col. 0767D]. Therefore, through pride, dissensions and angers, furies, rise up within that person, utterly tearing that person away from all the glory of the heavenly inheritance. And thus, lacking the dew and grace of the Holy Spirit, that person turns to such dryness that no fruit of good works is produced.

But as a person asks God that dreadful power may be restrained and that necessary things may be granted, so one should also ask God that evil knowledge may be overcome within oneself [Col. 0768A].

### Why the principal southern wind is shown at the right side of the same image like a lion’s head in the circle of bright fire; and why its two neighboring winds are seen, one in the form of a serpent and the other in the figure of a lamb’s head
### XXIII

But at the right of the aforesaid image of the human being, in the sign of bright fire, you see something like a lion’s head. Directed from the southern quarter toward the human being’s right-hand side, it shows the lion, issuing from the aforesaid element of bright fire, as the principal southern wind. For just as the lion is strong and exercises its will in [Col. 0768B] its strength, so the south wind is strong and impetuous in fire and from fire; and, when the days stretch out in length, it is powerful, and in that power it prepares the collision and breaking-up of clouds, and dangers in the sudden discharge of rains.

From its mouth, as though a breath were issuing, something extends somewhat from each side of that mouth. This is because that wind, proceeding from the southern quarter, stretches itself in both directions—this way and that—and thus on the right it takes the form of a serpent’s head, but on the left the head of a lamb. For on the right this wind takes to itself the nature of the serpent, which entreats gently but lays snares sharply: like serpents, it sometimes [Col. 0768C] produces gentle breaths, but meanwhile also sends forth strong stings and blows. On the left, however, it is changed into a lamb, which is mild and gentle, because in those regions it shows itself pleasant and not dangerous.

And the serpent’s head, appearing at the midpoint of the space between the lion’s and wolf’s heads, emits as it were a breath extending to that same midpoint and joining the breath which comes forth from the crab’s head between the wolf’s and lion’s heads. For, according to the serpent’s nature, as was shown above, this wind, collateral to the principal south wind, rises at the midpoint of the length lying between south and west, and extends its currents of air to that same midpoint between south and west. It does not cross this boundary, [Col. 0768D] any more than the others do, except by God’s judgment; and there it receives the breath rising from the collateral wind between west and south.

For if the length of the space between south and west is divided into four parts, the boundary on the southern side of the first part—which is also the beginning of the second part—is midway between the beginning of the first part and the boundary of the second; and the boundary of the second part, which is also the beginning of the third, is the midpoint of the whole length between south and west. Likewise, on the western side, the end of the first opposing part—which is also the beginning of the second opposing part—is midway between the beginning of the first part there and the end of the second there; and the boundary there of the second part, which is also the beginning of the third, is the midpoint [Col. 0769A] of this length extending oppositely between west and south. There the collateral winds meet one another. Thus these winds, both principal and collateral, between east and south, south and west, west and north, and north and east, are connected with one another and distinguished from one another in equal fashion, as stated above.

But the lamb’s head, appearing at the midpoint of the space between the lion’s and leopard’s heads, produces as it were a breath. Extending to that midpoint, it meets in conjunction the breath coming from the crab’s head between the leopard’s and lion’s heads. For, according to the lamb’s nature, as shown above, another collateral wind rises in these regions—that is, in the middle of [Col. 0769B] the space between south and the midpoint of the length between south and east. It also directs its breath to that same midpoint; and there it meets, with its noise, the current of air from the wind imitating the crab’s nature, which rises between east and south, so that very many terrors and collisions often arise there from their encounter. The lengths of their breaths also correspond to the spaces by which these heads are separated, as was shown concerning the preceding heads and their breaths. For in accordance with the distance separating the beginnings of these winds, they send out the currents of their breaths as far as the places where they rise and where [Col. 0769C] their currents meet.

### Why these heads, like the preceding ones, emit their breaths into the wheel and toward the same image

### XXIV

They appear to blow into the aforesaid wheel and toward the stated human image because the winds, both the principal ones and those collateral to them, preserve by their strength the whole world and the human being, in whom all creatures lie hidden, lest they fall into ruin. The collateral winds are the wings of the principal winds, and continually, though gently, they do not cease to blow with the air. But the principal winds, in their strongest powers, are summoned only by God’s judgment for vengeance near the end of the world.

Thus the south and north winds, by God’s judgment, [Col. 0769D] send forth their collateral winds according to God’s will: the south with great heat and great flooding; the north with lightning, thunder, hail, and cold. The principal winds—namely, the eastern and western—more gently and slowly summon their collateral winds to perform God’s judgments. Yet when they stir them up to these things by God’s will, they do so in summer by cold or drought, or in winter by heat, rain, or similar evils hostile and harmful to the earth and humankind.

And just as the winds hold the circle of the earth by their powers, so also in their offices they make humankind know and understand what it ought to do. When these winds send out their breaths over the earth, they also scatter them beneath the earth; and there, entering [Col. 0770A] certain underground hollows in places where they have no outlet, they move the earth. But where they have an outlet, they seem to certain people to arise there, although they do not arise there, but in the higher elements; and, as stated above, they scatter themselves both beneath and above the earth.

### That the human being must carefully investigate how all these things concern the salvation of the soul and the execution of God’s judgments, which leave nothing unexamined

### XXV

Let the human being understand how all these things concern the soul’s salvation. For the appearance, in the sign of bright fire denoting divine power, of something like a lion’s head—that is, God’s fearful judgment—means that God, judging everything by just equity, leaves nothing [Col. 0770B] unexamined.

This same judgment, extending its power toward uprightness on both sides, sets before the person advancing in prosperity the serpent’s head, which signifies prudence; but it shows to the person labouring in adversity the lamb’s head, namely the form of patience. For in prosperity a person must prudently fear God’s judgment, so as to flee the deceit and craftiness of evils and not abandon the path of truth in vain security. In adversity, one must have patience under that judgment, knowing that God often bears with the crookedness in human deeds by overlooking it.

And the serpent’s head—that is, prudence in the fullness of perfection, appearing between God’s judgment and the punishments of hell—causes a breath, [Col. 0770C] namely providence, to proceed from itself. For when a person, terrified by God’s judgment, prudently fears the punishments of hell lest he suffer them deservedly, he diligently provides good works; and this providence, extending itself in this way to the perfection of uprightness, is joined to constancy, which arises from the crab’s head—that is, from the strength of confidence—and lies between the punishments of hell and God’s judgment. For the faithful person strives to be constant in making every good provision for eternal life.

But the lamb’s head, signifying patience, appears in the fullness of perfection between God’s judgment and the fear of the Lord, and produces as it were a breath, namely gentleness. Having reached upright perfection, it associates itself with the constancy arising from true confidence [Col. 0770D] between the fear of the Lord and God’s judgment. For when the blessed person is patient under reproaches and shows gentleness in them, that person must embrace constancy so as to be brought to a good end.

### That no order of virtues, distinct from itself or within itself, is to be neglected, because the effect of virtue leads everyone to justice or to the uprightness of heavenly things

### XXVI

But just as the order of these virtues is distinct from itself and within itself—so that one virtue displays these powers and another those powers—so their operations are also present in human beings. This is to be understood also of the remaining virtues: good works follow a good will, and likewise, [Col. 0771A] turning toward the knowledge of God because they are in the knowledge of God, they lead the human being equally to every justice and to the uprightness of heavenly things.

For all virtues run swiftly toward human salvation, although they do not all appear together in one person. God’s judgment terrifies and examines the human being, and no human work remains which is not tested by God’s judgment, because God’s just judgment judges all things justly. Prudence also imparts its powers to the human being together with providence, so that, prudently rejecting worldly luxury, the person may embrace chastity. Patience, moreover, touches the person together with gentleness, so that he may patiently endure the temptations of the flesh. For in both sexes, male and female alike, the burning of fleshly desire must be lulled by these virtues [Col. 0771B] without the weariness of negligence.

Therefore none of the faithful should treat these virtues negligently, lest they leave him dried up in aridity or choked by fleshly desires. Rather, let them imitate the virtues through good works, so that the virtues may preserve them in all holiness. But if a person neglects God, that person also often incurs, by God’s just judgment, bodily chastisements, as stated above: being subject to God’s scourge through the higher and lower elements and creatures, through heat and cold, dryness and moisture, and many other kinds of pressure, because, failing to consider the constancy of the virtues, the person refused to understand what ought to be done.

For when virtues instruct people in spiritual matters, they also make them prudent in bodily matters, so that, even when the virtues do not yet appear openly in them, [Col. 0771C] they often silently shake them toward the fear of the Lord. But when they reveal themselves in them, so that those persons openly cultivate the virtues through charity, then they will appear previously to have possessed the fear of the Lord in temporal matters. Now, strengthened by the power of blessed virtues, they have withdrawn from carnal things and turned to spiritual things more for the desire of heavenly things than for fear of hell’s punishments—as David testifies when he says, “in my will”:

### Testimony from Psalm CXVII [Psalm 118], agreeing with this, and how it should be understood

### XXVII

> [Col. 0771D] “The right hand of the Lord has wrought might;  
> the right hand of the Lord has exalted me;  
> the right hand of the Lord has wrought might.  
> I shall not die, but live,  
> and proclaim the works of the Lord.”

Its meaning is clear as follows. At first, through fear of God and of the punishments of Gehenna, a person turns away from the left; afterward, through love of God, the person ascends to the right, that is, to the desires of heavenly goods. Once this has begun, the person puts on the strongest armour, because good knowledge has been separated from evil knowledge.

For this reason the eye is compared to this twofold knowledge: it has a watery circle situated beneath its whiteness, just as a vessel contains a mirror within itself. Evil knowledge, understood through the left, is like the vessel of good knowledge, which is received through the right. For the right eye of good knowledge looks round everywhere and considers that fleshly desire is useless and does not behold the light of [Col. 0772A] truth; and that when it delights in incestuous deeds, it is afterward choked by sorrow as by a watery drowning. Thus the right side of good knowledge raises itself toward God, tramples evil pleasure underfoot, and removes sorrow.

Therefore the right hand of the Lord—that is, his strength—works this virtue, so that people may know him through faith and perform their works in his fear. That same right hand also exalts me through repentance, though formerly I was defiled by sins; and it works virtue even after repentance for my sins, so that I burn with such desire in God’s love that I cannot be satisfied thereby. Hence I shall not die in sins, since through repentance I rise again from them; but through the true and pure [Col. 0772B] repentance which I have toward God I shall live in eternity. Thus, delivered from death, I shall proclaim the wonders of the Lord in his fear and love, because he did not hand me over to death but rescued me from hellish destruction.

### Why the principal northern wind appears at the left of that human image as a bear’s head in the circle of black fire; and why its two collateral winds appear, one in the form of a lamb’s head and the other in the form of a serpent’s head

### XXVIII

At the left of the aforesaid image, in the sign of black fire, appears something like a bear’s head. From the northern quarter it shows the principal wind, namely the north wind, often coming forth as a bear from black fire, bringing what is contrary to humankind in the dangers of storms, because it comes from black fire. And therefore, [Col. 0772C] just as a bear growls in anger, and as it is vicious in its nature, so this wind sometimes, as if growling, produces disturbances, noises, and dangers in storms.

But the fact that it gives forth, as it were, a breath from its mouth, extending somewhat at length to the right and left of its mouth, ending on the right in a lamb’s head and taking on the left the form of a serpent’s head, signifies that this wind, issuing from the aforesaid northern quarter and proceeding at length on either side, passes on the right into the mild nature of the lamb, which is gentle and not dangerous, because in those regions the wind sometimes shows itself mild. But on the left [Col. 0772D] it imitates the serpent, which first glides gently but afterward moves headlong and, when it can prevail in no other way, fearing the person, begins to supplicate. So this wind advances there at first deceptively and without noise, but at last shows itself dangerous, treacherous, and harsh; and when people think they are already perishing, it returns again to mildness.

From the mouth of this lamb’s head another breath extends to the midpoint of the space between the bear’s and leopard’s heads. For, in the likeness of the lamb, this wind collateral to the principal wind proceeding from the northern quarter sends out its blowing powers to the midpoint of the extension between north and east, because in those regions [Col. 0773A] it presents itself as mild as a lamb, although elsewhere it rages as if in anger.

But from the mouth of this serpent’s head another breath proceeds, extending to the midpoint of the space between the bear’s and wolf’s heads. For, as the serpent’s nature is, so this wind, neighbouring the north wind at its side, reaches those regions where lies the midpoint of the length extending between the principal northern and western winds, now exercising its powers gently, now rushing headlong as if deceitfully.

The breath coming from the right side of the bear’s mouth to the lamb’s head, and the breath coming from the left side of the same mouth to the serpent’s head, are of the same form; likewise, the breath issuing from the lamb’s head to the shown midpoint of the space [Col. 0773B] between the bear’s and leopard’s heads, and the breath extending from the serpent’s head to the midpoint of the space between the bear’s and wolf’s heads, are of one and equal length. For the principal northern wind extends equally on either side toward the winds collateral to it and subject to it. These collateral winds, tending toward east and west, likewise reach their end in the same measure of length in which the principal wind that is their beginning, as stated above, comes to its end.

### Why these likewise, as the preceding heads, direct the force of their breaths into the wheel and toward the same image

[Col. 0773C]

### XXIX

All these heads also send their breaths into the aforesaid wheel and toward the stated human image, because the aforementioned winds, through the breaths of their powers, hold together the circuit of the world and urge the human being dwelling in it to consider what is useful, lest the person perish in ruin.

Accordingly, whenever any wind of all the aforesaid kinds, either naturally or by God’s ordering, has sent forth its breaths, then, if no obstacle resists, it penetrates the human body. The soul receives it and naturally conveys it inward, to whatever bodily member accords with its nature. Thus through the breaths of winds a person is either strengthened, as stated above, or weakened.

But when a person has worldly [Col. 0773D] prosperity, bodily affliction issuing from the judicial fire—that is, God’s vengeance—like a bear constrains the person. It does not permit the person to proceed according to pleasures, but, stretching from its course a breath—that is, misery—over both prosperity and adversity, it causes the person in humility to desire and possess poverty of spirit. Thus, advancing rightly in this way, the person embraces patience as in the lamb’s head and, avoiding evils, imitates prudence as in the serpent’s head. For through bodily afflictions a person often arrives at spiritual riches, and through those riches obtains the heavenly kingdoms.

From the mouth of the lamb’s head, signifying patience as stated above, another breath—that is, gentleness—reaches the perfection [Col. 0774A] lying between bodily affliction and the fear of the Lord. From the serpent’s head, signifying prudence, another breath—namely providence—proceeds to the perfection between bodily affliction and the punishments of hell. They admonish the person chastised through God’s vengeance to despise earthly things and long for heavenly things, as was also shown concerning them above.

For the beginnings and ends of the aforesaid mysteries, in their deeds and significations, serve one and the same equal purpose: the instruction of humankind, although they seem to have different works. And all that the knowledge of God shows to be suited to the soul’s salvation leads to its deliverance and, by its powers, urges the human being to cleave faithfully to the Creator in body and soul.

Therefore [Col. 0774B] let the person strengthen himself toward holiness, fleeing carnal desires and rejecting the excesses of foul vices. Let him wisely serve God, who loves continence and chastity; and let him be neither excessively dry nor excessively moist in the work of virtues. For whoever refuses either to chastise or restrain the flesh will go to the destruction of the soul. But whoever, by mastering himself, loves the virtues and retains them through love will place the soul in eternal life, when corrected and chastised by the Lord, as David, speaking through my inspiration, says:

### David’s words in the same Psalm CXVII [Psalm 118], suited to the same subject, and their explanation

### XXX

> [Col. 0774C] “The Lord has chastened me severely,  
> but he has not handed me over to death.”

Its meaning is clear as follows. A person is often capricious and undisciplined, and is not afraid unless all the veins are filled with pains. Therefore the devil deceived the first human being when that being entered into great vanity, desiring to be what it ought not to be; and so great sorrow with pain was poured into that person.

For from labour a person receives fear; from vanity, forgetfulness; and from transgression of the law, foolish confidence. But the fear of the Lord surpasses all these things, because through fear a person trembles before God and truly recognizes that there is no benefit in many other things. Fear comes first in a person, and afterward embraces charity, when the person loves God and considers [Col. 0774D] how God may be appeased, so that he may not remember that person’s iniquity.

But when a person seeks God in love, God often chastises that person through labours, so that the person may confidently say: “He who is Lord of all has severely chastened me, a sinner, with his scourges; but in that very chastisement by which he scourges me, he has not handed me over to the death of hellish punishments. For I sought him in love and confessed my sins to him; and in this I am patient and prudent, because I know his judgments upon my sins to be right. With two wings—the knowledge of good and evil—I strive to fly to him, subjecting the left wing to the right, so that I may walk in a straight and even path.”

### Concerning the seven planets, appearing at distinct intervals in different circles of the wheel of the aforesaid image

[Col. 0775A]

### XXXI

Above the head of the aforesaid image, the seven planets are marked one above another: three in one circle of bright fire; one in the circle of black fire beneath it; and three in the circle of pure ether beneath that. For each takes its beginning from the east, and, surpassing another in the height of its circuit, when it has completed its course returns again toward the east to repeat its rising and continue its course.

Three have their courses in the aforesaid bright fire, one in the circle of black fire below it, and three beneath them in pure ether. Those running in the same fire [Col. 0775B] are excited to their own fires by that fire, and the same fire is strengthened to its burning by their powers, just as wood is kindled by fire and fire is strengthened in burning by wood. They are three because, if there were more, they would make that fire burn too fiercely and would confuse it with their circuits; but if fewer, that fire, deprived of fitting assistance, would become sluggish in its burning.

The first illuminates the sun’s brightness by its brightness; the second supplies the sun’s heat by its heat; the third maintains the sun’s course in upright order by its course. The sun is surrounded, directed, and restrained by these, so that it may give right tempering, by its heat and brightness, to the firmament and the whole world.

But the three moving through the aforesaid ether—which has purity from the higher [Col. 0775C] fire and the lower water—are tested by it for the purity of their brightness, and by their purity they suffuse it. They are neither more nor fewer than three, because they neither exceed nor fall short of what is needed to strengthen its purity; rather, they attend it in fitting proportion, neither burdening it with excess nor destroying it through scantiness.

The first in that ether, above the moon, assists its increase and protects it from being excessively kindled. The second, nearest to it, preserves it in its waning so that it may not wholly dissolve. These attend and follow the moon as in a ministry, and suitably and distinctly urge it toward the tempering of the whole world.

### How these planets were set in the firmament by God, the Creator of the world, and concerning their various effects

[Col. 0775D]

### XXXII

Toward the south, at the side of the same image and also beneath its feet, the sun appears marked and distinguished in the same manner and order in its circle. For it runs toward south and west—not that it is beneath the person’s feet, but because, in the west, as it seeks the setting region of the world with the revolution of the firmament, it declines from the northern quarter, and rises again in the east with that same firmament.

From the middle of the highest sign—that of the first planet marked above the head of that image—certain rays as it were issue forth. One descends to the sign of the sun, signifying that rays of strength proceed from the power of this principal planet, first displayed in the east because there the daylight proceeds; one of these rays is directed to the sun, [Col. 0776A] helping it and tempering its course, lest it cast forth its fires excessively.

But one ray shines upon the right foot of the crab’s head proceeding from the leopard’s head. This signifies that, from the quarter opposed to this wind, that planet rises and sends a ray to strengthen the advance of that wind, which moves before and behind and proceeds from the principal [Col. 0776B] eastern wind to which it is collateral; it restrains it by its stability, lest it advance further than God permits.

Another extends to the right horn of the stag’s head, which also issues from the same leopard’s head. For another ray coming from this side of that planet resists the strength of this wind, which issues there from the principal wind, checking its impulse so that it may send out its breaths according to the upright order of fitting necessity. It is like a man holding the arms of his enemy so that he may kill neither himself nor others. Thus creation is restrained by the Creator, and each creature is supported by another.

From the middle of the sign of the second planet, a ray as it were bends down over the sign of the sun, because this planet, displaying its powers, touches the sun with its ray and soothes it into gentleness. Another issues toward the lamb’s head coming from the sign of the lion’s head, because from the strong part of its brightness a ray extends to the beginning of the collateral wind signifying gentleness, which proceeds from the greater wind of the southern quarter. It holds [Col. 0776C] this wind lest it turn its gentleness into fierceness, but enables it to remain mild without insolence.

Another is directed to the aforesaid line extending in the firmament from the beginning of the eastern side of the aforesaid wheel, as it were to the end of its western side, toward its northern quarter. Above there is placed the lamb’s head proceeding from the sign of the bear’s head. This signifies that a ray coming from the robust force of that brightness is led toward the course of the other collateral wind which issues from the aforesaid greater wind of the northern quarter. It opposes that wind by its tempering, so that it may send forth its breaths evenly.

From the middle of the sign of the third planet, one ray as it were extends to the sign of the sun, because this planet, like those above, attends the sun through the strength of its power [Col. 0776D] and the brightness of its own heat, and serves it in tempering, as a servant serves his lord when promptly prepared for every will of that lord.

But it directs another to the serpent’s head proceeding from the sign of the lion’s head, showing that from its power a ray extends to the beginning of the collateral wind which now displays cunning and now prudence, since it arises from the principal southern wind. It holds this wind back by checking its breaths, lest it rage excessively in its movements.

It extends another toward the aforesaid line, in the direction of the serpent’s head issuing from the sign of the bear’s head. This signifies that from the vigorous force of its heat, in which it is strong, brightness also extends to the beginning of the collateral wind which often exercises craftiness and sharpness in its motion, and which likewise proceeds from the principal wind of the northern quarter. It resists that wind’s force, lest it inflict greater harm and danger on humankind than the judgment of the divine examination permits, [Col. 0777A] as was shown above concerning the others.

The aforesaid planets are assistants to the sun, and without them the sun could not exist. They add heat to the sun, just as sight, hearing, and smell supply heat and strength to the brain.

As you see, the sun’s sign also sends out certain rays from itself: one touches the stated sign of the leopard’s head, another the sign of the lion’s head, another the sign of the wolf’s head, but not the sign of the bear’s head. For the sun, being the greatest of the planets, warms and strengthens the whole firmament with its fire, illuminates the circle [Col. 0777B] of the earth with its brightness, and resists by the powers of its strength the principal eastern, southern, and western winds, lest they exceed the limits established for them by God.

But it does not touch the northern wind, because that wind, existing as the sun’s enemy, rejects all brightness of light. Therefore the sun, as though scorning it, sets against it not a ray issuing from itself but only the path of its course, by which it beats back that wind’s fury; and it does not approach those regions, because there the devil, opposing God, displays his wickedness.

Another ray extends over the moon’s sign because the sun sets it aflame with its heat, just as the whole human body is covered by the person’s sensory faculty and intellect. Another, as it were, stretches over the brain and fixes itself by extending as far as both [Col. 0777C] heels of the aforesaid human image, because from the highest part down to the lowest the sun imparts strength and tempering to the entire human body, especially strengthening the brain. Thus, vigorous in understanding, the brain holds all the body’s powers; and, being the person’s upper part, it fills all the inward organs with sensory faculty, just as the sun illuminates the earth.

But when the elements beneath the sun are at times disturbed by storms, the sun’s fire is clouded, as though there were an eclipse. This signifies errors and is then shown when human hearts and minds are turned into error, so that they do not walk rightly in the law but wage many conflicts with one another.
