The aforesaid ray touches the human being’s heels because, [Col. 0777D] just as the brain governs the rest of the body, so the heel supports the whole human body. Thus the sun tempers all the human members by its powers, just as it gives life to the remaining creatures.

From the middle of the sign of the fifth planet, which is nearest below the sun, a ray as it were rises upward to the sign of the sun, because this planet, subject to the sun by the strength of its ministry, strives to soothe it so that it may not send out its fires beyond measure. Another extends to the crab’s head proceeding from the sign of the wolf’s head, indicating that from the strength of this planet a ray spreads to the beginning of the collateral wind issuing from the principal wind of the western quarter, restraining its instability, as was said above of the others.

But another is directed to the left horn of the moon’s sign, showing that from its vigour [Col. 0778A] it also sends a ray to the moon’s weaker side, whether it is waxing or waning: in its increase, helping it to recover its light all the more quickly and strongly; in its decrease, enabling it to diminish all the more gently and without danger.

From the middle of the sign of the sixth planet, nearest above the moon, one ray as it were tends upward to the sun’s sign, because from its strong power, having the moon’s neighbouring proximity, a ray rises to the sun, restraining its heat through the gentleness of subjection lest it burst forth excessively. Another is directed to the right horn of the moon’s sign, because its strength sends a ray to the moon’s stronger side, holding it back so that it may avoid the northern [Col. 0778B] quarter, approach the sun in due order in its waning, and, once kindled by the sun, depart from it distinctly.

Another extends to the stag’s head proceeding from the sign of the wolf’s head, because from the robust brightness of its radiance a ray extends to the beginning of the collateral wind issuing from the principal western wind, beating back its sudden speed so that it may not pass the limit set before it by divine ordering, but may proceed in a straight extension.

At the moon’s sign also, as you see, a ray as it were shines over both eyebrows and both ankles of the aforesaid human image. For by its natural power the moon tempers the human body, so that, just as an eyebrow preserves the eye for sight and an ankle supports a person, so through God’s ordering [Col. 0778C] the human limbs are tempered by the moon’s powers from top to bottom. This does not occur, however, with the same perfection as by the sun’s power, because the sun touches the human body more perfectly, while the moon does so more sparingly through its ministry.

The moon performs its course in heat and cold: it is warm while increasing, but cold while decreasing. The sun, however, is hot from east to south, but afterward draws coldness to itself as far as west. Before its waning, the moon receives its light from the sun, because the sun kindles the moon’s extinguished circle with a spark, as with a lamp breathed forth from itself; and then the moon is on high. But after it has been kindled, it descends to its place.

And as the sun kindles and illuminates the moon’s circle, so it also strengthens all lower things, both those [Col. 0778D] of the firmament and those beneath the firmament. The moon is its helper, illuminating lower things, just as the sun illuminates both higher and lower things. But because of watery moisture, the cloud beneath it, and the air over the earth, the moon is much colder than the sun; and the sun would burn up many things if the moon did not oppose it, because the moon tempers the sun’s heat by its cold moisture.

Accordingly, by this divine ordering the sun and moon serve humankind, bringing either health or weakness according to the condition of the air and breeze. This is shown where the sign of the sun sends out its rays, as it were, from the brain to the heel, while the sign of the moon sends its rays, as though from the eyebrow to the ankle, of the aforesaid image of a human being. [Col. 0779A] For when the moon is waxing, a person’s brain and blood likewise increase; but when the moon is waning, the brain and blood in the person diminish. If a human brain remained in one unchanging condition, the person would fall into frenzy, appearing even more ungovernable than a beast. And if the blood in a person always remained in one measure, so that it experienced neither increase nor diminution, the person would very quickly be torn apart and could not live.

When the moon is full, the human brain is also full, and then the person is sensible; but when it is empty, the human brain too is emptied, and then the person is to some extent devoid of understanding. When the moon is fiery and dry, the brain of certain people [Col. 0779B] is fiery and dry; consequently they suffer ailments in the brain and are less rational, so that then they do not have full understanding for any undertaking. But when it is moist, the brains of those same people become excessively moist; thus they suffer in the brain and are emptied of understanding. When, however, the moon is temperate, a person has health in brain and head and flourishes in understanding, because through the temperateness of the outward elements the humours within the person remain at rest; but through their agitation and disturbance a person’s humours are often unsettled. For without their moderation and service a human being could not live.

But also, as was said above, the sign of the sun appears marked in the same manner and order in which it was shown above the crown of this image, sending its rays to the aforesaid places; it appears likewise at its right side and beneath its feet, in its aforesaid circle and marked at the same places. For the sun, by the same station and revolution in which it stands in the eastern region and sends the brightness of its rays to the places previously shown, likewise shines in the southern and western regions, in the distinctions and revolutions shown above, upon these same places. It is driven by the force of the firmament’s revolution from east through south and obliquely to west, although in its courses it strives to run contrary to the motion of the firmament. For the aforesaid planets are carried round contrary to the firmament, from west to east, [Col. 0779D] in order that by their fire they may preserve its fire and renew it for burning. For if they revolved with it from east to west, its fire, hastening forward while receiving no renewal from behind, would grow torpid. Therefore they are borne gradually contrary to it, so that, while it hastens forward, they shake its fire free from torpor, as it were, upon its back. But they avoid the northern region, because there is there a place of darkness in the north; for light and darkness do not agree with one another. Thus the aforesaid planets were arranged in the firmament by the Creator of the world.

But you, O human being, who see these things, understand that they also bear upon the inward things of the soul.

[Col. 0780A]

### What it signifies that three of these planets are seen in the circle of bright fire, one in the region of black fire, and likewise three in the circuit of pure ether

XXXIII. Above the head of this image the seven planets are marked separately from one another: three in the aforesaid circle of bright fire, one also in the circle of black fire beneath it, and three in the circle of pure ether below that. They signify that, through the three ages of the world—namely, before the Law, under the Law, and in the Gospel—the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit surpass all human understanding in excellence.

The sun, moreover, set in the circle of black fire beneath it, signifies God Almighty, who alone fought against His enemies in righteous judgment and mightily overcame them. The three established in the circle of pure ether beneath it [Col. 0780B] show that the three Persons of the Godhead are truly to be worshipped by humankind in the good disposition of submission through pure repentance, where a person submits his whole self to God. Thus also, at the image’s right side and beneath its feet, the sun appears marked and distinguished in the same manner and order in its circle at the aforesaid places. For in God’s judgment, in the salvation of souls, and in the example of good works, these same gifts manifest themselves by the same operation, as was shown above, in their respective meanings; since the judgment of God, the salvation of souls, and the examples of the righteous exhort people to fear God and worship Him purely.

### To what the rays of the first three planets, seen in this vision as issuing from them, are directed; and what is signified both by the planets themselves and by their rays

XXXIV. From the middle of the sign of the highest and first planet, marked above the head of the same image, certain rays issue as it were. One descends to the sign of the sun. This means that from the desirable and pre-eminent gift of the Spirit of wisdom—whose powers surpass the whole height of human understanding—there proceeds a holy breathing-out toward the sign of the sun, that is, toward the Spirit of fortitude. It joins itself to that Spirit, so that in the faithful person the strength of holiness may proceed wisely, lest the person rashly presume to do what cannot be accomplished.

But one ray shines toward the right foot of the crab’s head [Col. 0780D] proceeding from the leopard’s head. This shows that, in the salvation of souls, the proclaimed breathing-out of the Spirit of wisdom extends itself toward the upright course of confidence which arises from the fear of the Lord, strengthening it so that it may trust in God with fear of the Lord and may not frivolously regard His mercy as worthless.

Another extends toward the right horn of the stag’s head, which likewise proceeds from the same leopard’s head. For, in chastisement, the breathing-out of uprightness manifests itself and expands toward the strength of faith—which also arises from the fear of the Lord—leading it into the straight way, so that it may turn away from the devil’s arts, while it does not cease to chastise a person because of ignorance of the truth.

Likewise, from the middle of the sign of the second planet, a ray bends down over the sign of the sun, [Col. 0781A] signifying that from the abundant fullness of the spirit of understanding an outpouring of intelligence also comes to the Spirit of fortitude. This also makes known that every faithful person should understand subtly that one must serve one’s Creator with a strong mind and renounce the devil.

Another ray goes out toward the head of the lamb, which comes from the sign of the lion’s head. For, in order that a person may proceed prosperously toward the Creator, the breathing-out from the Spirit of understanding extends toward patience, which proceeds from God’s judgment. It shows that, when a person imitates patience, prosperity and tribulation alike ought to be borne with an even mind.

And another is directed to the aforesaid line which extends in the firmament from the beginning of the eastern part of the aforesaid wheel, as it were to the end of its western part, toward its northern [Col. 0781B] region; above it is placed the head of the lamb, which proceeds from the sign of the bear’s head. This means that, in order that every faithful person may avoid what is adverse to the soul, the breathing-out again coming from the Spirit of understanding extends toward the rectitude of justice. This justice separates the devil’s snares from righteous works, from the beginning of good deeds abiding in God’s power to their end; patience, issuing from bodily tribulation, stands above it. It admonishes a person that, when God’s judgment chastises him, he should bear that chastisement patiently, lest he be struck more severely.

The sign of the third planet likewise extends one ray from its middle to the sign of the sun. This signifies that the Spirit of counsel directs a breathing-out from its power to the Spirit of fortitude. Although these gifts of the Holy Spirit have different names, they nevertheless lead humankind to blessedness by one purpose and work. Thus the Spirit of counsel tempers fortitude, so that a person may raise himself well and in an orderly manner toward God.

But it directs another toward the serpent’s head, which proceeds from the sign of the lion’s head. For in the prosperity of true salvation, the Spirit of counsel extends its breathing-out toward prudence, which proceeds from God’s judgment. It intimates that a person should chastise the body prudently, lest, if one afflicts it without discernment, one be overcome by foolish mortification and collapse beneath the burden.

But it lengthens another toward the aforesaid line, in the direction of the serpent’s head proceeding from the sign of the bear’s head. This means that, lest a person fall into adversity of soul, [Col. 0781D] the aforesaid Spirit of counsel turns its breathing-out again toward the rectitude of justice, where prudence appears above, extending from bodily tribulation. By this it teaches the person who fears God’s judgment to take care not to fear it excessively and fall into despair, but prudently to escape it through the counsel of good inspiration.

### Why the sun, placed in their midst, appears to emit more rays than the others; and what it or its rays signify

XXXV. You also see that the sign of the sun, emitting certain rays from itself as it were, touches one time the sign of the leopard’s head, another time the sign of the lion’s head, another time the sign of the wolf’s head, but not the sign of the bear’s head. This means that the Spirit of fortitude, pouring out its breathings, touches in one direction the fear of the Lord, in another God’s judgment, and in another the punishments of hell. It shows that a person should fear to sin because of the fear of the Lord, should abandon sins because of His dreadful judgment, and should cast off the habit of sins because of the most cruel punishments of hell.

But it does not touch the sign of the bear’s head, because the Spirit of fortitude withdraws itself from bodily tribulation that is not undertaken simply for God’s sake—for the bear sometimes displays human traits in itself and sometimes beastly ones. For when a person inflicts tribulation on the body without discernment, the body itself, affected by labour and weariness and often exhausted, collapses; and, when the person doubts being able to persevere in such things, he growls almost in anger, like a beast. [Col. 0782B] Hence neither the tribulation that a person inflicts upon himself without right moderation, nor that inflicted upon him by others even against his will, calls upon the Spirit of fortitude, because it lacks the equity of discernment. For being unstable, moving now upward, now downward, as if flying outside the right measure, it cannot possess strength—that is, it cannot remain in one state; for fortitude, without wavering this way or that, remains always strong.

But the person who, because of fear or love of God, afflicts the body with the moderation of discernment and uprightness rejoices inwardly in spirit as at a feast. Therefore this mortification should not be regarded as affliction, but rather as a blessing; and here the Spirit of fortitude works, so that this faithful person may remain in these works of uprightness, because they are with God.

The sun sends another ray over the sign of the moon, because the Spirit of fortitude joins itself to the fear of the Lord: namely, so that every faithful person may be strong in the fear in which one ought to fear God, lest, overcome through frivolity, one be cast down from the place of blessedness. It also fixes another ray, extending it as it were over the brain and down over both heels of the aforesaid image, because the same Spirit of fortitude inspires a person to bring the intention and beginning of a good work to its right completion; for blessed is the person who constrains himself to a good end.

[Col. 0782D]

### To what the lowest three direct their rays, and what is represented both by them and by their rays

XXXVI. Likewise, you see that from the middle of the sign of the fifth planet, which is nearest beneath the sun, a certain ray rises toward the sign of the sun. This means that from the power of the Spirit of knowledge—which through the nearness of right action ought to be present to the Spirit of fortitude—a breathing-out rises toward that same fortitude. For knowledge raises itself to fortitude in order to be strengthened by it and not turned into folly.

Another extends toward the head of the crab, which goes out from the sign of the wolf’s head. This means that from the power of the strength of knowledge a breathing-out extends toward confidence which proceeds from bodily tribulation; for when a person knowingly and simply, with the safeguard of discernment, chastises the body, one is confident that one’s sins have been punished and cleansed.

But another is directed toward the left horn of the sign of the moon, because when knowledge withdraws itself from temporal things, setting temporal things aside, it pours out its breathing toward the fear of the Lord and takes hold of it in order faithfully to instil fear into people.

From the middle of the sign of the sixth planet, which is next above the one [i.e. the moon; the printed wording is uncertain], one ray as it were rises toward the sign of the sun. [Col. 0783A] It shows that from the protection of the Spirit of piety, which in its sweetness is near to the fear of the Lord, a breathing-out rises to the Spirit of fortitude and, strengthened there, arms itself so that it may resist malice. For whoever resolves to walk piously should join fortitude to himself, in order to be able to persevere in piety.

And another is directed to the right horn of the sign of the moon, showing that, proceeding prosperously, the Spirit of piety embraces the prosperity of the fear of the Lord, making known also to people that they should possess the fear of the Lord together with piety. Another extends toward the head of the stag, which proceeds from the sign of the wolf’s head. This signifies that, rejecting adversity, the Spirit of piety brings forth its breathing toward faith which arises from the punishments of hell, so that a person fortified with piety and faith may so escape the punishments of hell as not to lose heavenly blessedness through the impulse of stubbornness.

What you see—how from the sign of the moon a ray shines as it were over both eyebrows and both ankles of the aforesaid image—shows that a saving breathing-out coming from the fear of the Lord admonishes a person [Col. 0783C] to guard the sharpness of the mind, lest one incur blindness of soul. It exhorts one to direct the strength of the inward spirit toward the way of uprightness, so that, walking in truth, one may attain eternal blessedness. For just as the eyebrow protects the eye, and as the ankle supports the human body, so the fear of the Lord forms the inward sight, lest it forget God, and preserves the inward strength through which a person is borne toward every useful and right thing.

### That every faithful person, though eminent in virtues, is nevertheless sometimes beneficially deprived of them and assailed by temptations, lest deceived by presumptuous pride one perish

XXXVII. But also, as was said above, the sign of the sun appears marked in the same manner and order in which it was shown above the crown of this image, sending its rays to the aforesaid places; it also appears at its right side and beneath its feet, marked at the same places in its circle. For the mystical gift of the aforesaid Spirit of fortitude, by the same moderation and outpouring with which it bathes a person’s purpose in its breathings, likewise inspires toward the desired holiness of a right beginning that person’s perfect works and examples, by which one builds up one’s neighbours, in the fullness of blessedness. For when virtues cause a faithful person, consenting to them by good will, to begin what is right, they also exhort that person to bring it to advancement and to set before others in them an example of justice through a good completion.

Yet, although these same virtues protect a person through diverse forms of inspiration, they nevertheless permit one often to be tempted, as it were toward that north, through the temptation of the flesh and the devil’s arts. Thus one may learn through these things how to defend oneself from them, lest, lifted up beyond the right measure by presumptuous pride, one afterward fall into worse things and perish—as those who were lifted up in presumption perished, of whom it is written in the words of the prophet Isaiah.

### A testimony drawn from the book of Isaiah to set forth these matters, and how it is to be understood

XXXVIII. “Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit; and its mighty ones, its exalted ones, and its glorious ones shall descend into it. Man shall be bowed down and the male humbled, and the eyes of the lofty shall be brought low” (Isa. 5).

Its meaning is clear as follows. A person remaining in sins is likened to the waning moon, which has a dark circle when it wholly declines and is rekindled. For when one sees oneself dark, one is often stirred by God’s grace to seek God’s grace worthily; and when one has worthily invoked God’s grace, the Holy Spirit kindles one to behold the true light, just as the moon is rekindled by the sun.

But after one has been strengthened by good works so that one cannot be satiated by them, one must take every care not to ascribe them to oneself, as though they were from oneself rather than from God; thereby making oneself, as it were, into God and reckoning that one can do whatever one wishes. So Satan too thought, who wished in his own independent possession to be as God; therefore he brought his own brightness into oblivion.

For this reason hell has enlarged its soul, that is, the punishments which it contains, and has opened its devouring appetite without ceasing, since it is without all joy. Thus it is not satiated even in the desire of its own swallowing-up; for just as unclean birds desire to devour the corpses of animals, so hell, in its wickedness, draws to itself and devours the mighty who fight against God, the exalted who raise themselves unjustly, and the glorious who seek their own glory rather than God’s glory. Thus the person who consents to the aforesaid evils will be bowed down, just as the unhappy spirits mentioned above were bowed down with their prince; and the one who ought to possess manly strength will be humbled when one turns from good to evil. The eyes—that is, the knowledge—of those who in the height of pride think themselves wise will be reduced to nothing, because they lose the reward of the glory of humility, while impenitent they seek glory from the people for good works. But if thereafter they repent, they will be received, as penitents, in the blood of the calf.

### Concerning the sixteen principal stars, set in equal arrangement in the circle of bright fire to strengthen the firmament and moderate the winds around it

XXXIX. You see also, around the circle in which the likeness of bright fire appears, sixteen principal stars. They show that in the circle of the higher fiery firmament the greatest stars have been set, as was said: four between the leopard’s and lion’s heads, four between the lion’s and wolf’s heads, four between the wolf’s and bear’s heads, and four between the bear’s and leopard’s heads; that is, four between the eastern and southern winds, four between the southern and western winds, four between the western and northern winds, and four between the northern and eastern winds. By their powers they strengthen these regions of the firmament and temper the winds themselves.

But if they abounded in excessive number, they would burden the firmament by their superfluity; or, if they were few in number, their scarcity [Col. 0785B] would not suffice to consolidate the firmament. For God has withheld from every creature both superfluous excess and unworthy deficiency. There are four between two winds because, by their equal and necessary—not excessive—number, they jointly hold in their powers the regions of the firmament in which they have been placed, as nails hold the wall in which they are driven. They do not move from their places, but revolve with the firmament and strengthen it.

Of these, the eight middle stars, positioned between the two stars standing on either side of them at these heads—namely, two between each pair of heads—extend their rays as it were toward the sign of the thin air opposite them. For these stars, which are the middle four stars between the aforesaid winds, since there are four between two winds, as has been said, extend their rays into the thin air, just as veins descend from the human head to the feet. And as those veins strengthen the whole human body, so these stars likewise consolidate the whole firmament by their powers and resist the winds near them, lest they disturb the firmament beyond its proper measure. They bring the air into right temperance and are equally near one another, so that one may support another for the strengthening of the same firmament.

The remaining eight, however, which are seen on either side of these middle stars, nearest the aforesaid heads, direct their rays as it were only toward the black fire. For these, standing in the middle, possessing wings, and placed near the winds as shown above, send rays proceeding from themselves only toward the black fire, opposing it lest it emit the fury of its heat without measure. [Col. 0785D] These stars are placed and separated from one another in equal moderation around the circuit of the firmament, so that they may sustain that firmament evenly with their powers.

### That the distinct number of other stars, placed in the two circles—of pure ether and of strong, white, bright air—warms the firmament and restrains the clouds from exceeding their bounds

XL. What you see—that the circle of pure ether and likewise the circle of strong, white, bright air are as if filled with stars, which send their gleams as it were toward the clouds opposite them—means that the upper pure ether and, below it, the strong, white, bright air are fully filled and strengthened with greater and lesser stars. Since they exist without any excess, they warm and strengthen the whole firmament with their fires, and, pouring their rays into the clouds beneath the strong, white, bright air, they pierce and hold them so that they do not exceed the boundaries established for them by God.

### What benefit belongs to the four formations, appearing like tongues on the image’s right and left because of their mobility

XLI. Therefore, on the right side of the aforesaid image, the same clouds put forth from themselves two tongues, as it were, separated from one another, and from these direct certain streams into the aforesaid wheel and toward the same image. This means that, for the salvation of humankind, two defensive barriers, separate from each other just as the two principal winds in those regions are distant from each other, go out from the clouds appearing toward the southern region. Thus certain breaths also proceed from these clouds into the common air through which diverse creatures are sustained and direct themselves toward the human being, because that person, like other creatures, cannot lack higher aid and ministry.

But on its left side, from the clouds marked there, two tongues likewise, somewhat separated from one another, turn toward the same wheel and the image itself, flowing from themselves as it were in certain streams. This means that, in order that every contrary thing may be removed from the human being, two restraining defences, separated from each other—as the principal winds of those regions too are separate from each other—proceed on both the person’s left and right from the clouds that are in the northern [Col. 0786C] region. These, as was said above of the others, preserve the things that exist in the world—namely, the human being and the remaining creatures—as God has ordained for them.

These four tongues proceed from the four principal winds, because they breathe them forth to restrain the clouds. For as the principal winds strengthen and hold the whole firmament, so these formations, which appear like tongues because of their mobility, contain the clouds beneath the firmament, lest by flowing this way or that they exceed their measure.

[Col. 0786D]

### A mystical and lucid explanation of the number, order, and position of the sixteen principal stars

XLII. In this manner, as stated above, this image is interwoven and surrounded with these signs, because the human being is so strengthened and defended by the power of the elements and the assistance of the other creatures that no assault of adversity can tear one from one’s state, while divine power preserves one.

But all these things must also be understood in another way. For the sixteen principal stars appearing around the circle in which the likeness of bright fire is seen mean that within the wholeness of divine power there are principal teachers who taught and teach that the ten commandments of the Law are fulfilled through the six ages of the world: four between the leopard’s and lion’s heads, [Col. 0787A] four between the lion’s and wolf’s heads, four between the wolf’s and bear’s heads, and four between the bear’s and leopard’s heads. For these same teachers exhort all the faithful, throughout the four regions of the world, to fear the Lord, His judgment, the punishments of hell, and bodily tribulation, so that through fear of these things they may cease from sinning, even if they have set aside the love of God.

Of these, the eight middle stars, positioned between the two stars standing on either side of them at these heads—namely, two between each pair of heads—extend their rays as it were toward the sign of thin air opposite them. They signify that the eight beatitudes, abiding in the perfection of the aforesaid virtues and proclaiming love of God and neighbour, pour their breathings with the utmost zeal into the desires of faithful people, so that, however deeply they may be devoted to the world in many ways, they may set temporal things aside and hasten toward heavenly things.

But the remaining eight, seen on either side of these middle ones nearest the aforesaid heads, direct their rays as it were only toward the black fire. They show that these same beatitudes, aiding the true perfection of the other virtues both in prosperity and adversity, send the keenness of their breathings toward the judicial fire, intimating to those who ought to serve God in spirit that no sins, however slight, are to be neglected, since they will be examined through God’s judgment and vengeance.

### Likewise, a mystical explanation of the distinct multiplicity and arrangement of the other common stars

[Col. 0787C] XLIII. What you see—that the circle of pure ether and likewise the circle of strong, white, bright air are as if filled with stars, which send their gleams as it were toward the clouds opposite them—means that the integrity of true repentance and likewise the integrity of discernment in holy works flourish in the manifold brightness of rationality. For just as the stars are varied and numerous, so repentance and discernment in holy works display within themselves very many powers of blessedness and make the minds of the faithful rational by their brightness, because they instil in them that all the works they perform may appear rational before God.

### Likewise, a mystical explanation of the usefulness of the four breaths moving like tongues at the image’s right and left

XLIV. Therefore, on the right side of the aforesaid image, the same clouds, putting forth two tongues as it were separated from one another, direct from them certain streams into the aforesaid wheel and toward the same image. This means that the minds of blessed people show that, for their prosperity, two testaments have been directed from themselves, distinct from one another: one according to the flesh, the other according to the spirit. Yet they agree in one, just as these tongues have one form. By their testimony the world is filled, and they teach the human being to look toward the Creator.

But on its left side, from the clouds marked there, two tongues likewise, somewhat separated from each other, turn toward the same wheel and the image itself, flowing as it were in certain streams from themselves. They signify that, when a person is attacked through devilish temptations, one should gather to one’s mind, as two testaments, the love of God and neighbour. These are somewhat distinct, because the love directed toward God is greater than love of neighbour. In this way one extinguishes the wheel of worldly cares and likewise the desire arising from attacks of the flesh, by the watering of righteous admonition.

### That every faithful person, devoutly following the footsteps of the Son of God, strengthened by the protection of virtues amid temptations, may attain heavenly joys; and that the words of Isaiah are fittingly expounded in confirmation of this

[Col. 0788B] XLV. In this way, as stated above, this image is interwoven and surrounded with these signs, because the faithful person who faithfully follows the footsteps of the Son of God is defended and adorned by the brightness of the blessed virtues and is thus surrounded, so that, rescued from the devil’s snares, one may happily be brought to the blessedness of heavenly joys, where one shall rejoice forever. My servant Isaiah bears witness, saying:

> “This one shall dwell on high; the fortifications of rocks shall be his height. Bread is given to him; his waters are sure. He shall see the king in his beauty; his eyes shall behold the land from afar” (Isa. 33).

Its meaning is clear as follows. The person who turns from the left side to the right, considering that God rests upon the humble and quiet in heart, overcomes the proud devil when one crushes oneself, saying: “God has enlightened me with two eyes, by which I consider how great glory light has amid darkness. There I may choose by what way I shall walk, since I shall be either seeing or blind; and I also know what guide I should call upon for day or for night.

“For by hiding myself in darkness I can do wanton works which I could not accomplish in light, because there I am observed by all who stand by. Yet in darkness I shall receive no reward, but a condemnable punishment. Therefore I shall wound the oppression of my heart, by which I delight in sins, and I shall call upon the living God, that He may lead me into the way of light and heal my wounds, lest I be ashamed of them in the light.

“When I do this, the cords of my captivity will be broken. For I shall thus hold captive my enemy, to whose suggestion I had consented in darkness, because he has been deceived in me.”

The one who so acts shall dwell in the heights of heaven, and the fortress of rocks, which is Christ, shall be one’s exaltation. There the bread of life is given, the refreshment of which one can never weary; for one continually delights in the sweet taste of true charity. Therefore one becomes a flowing stream from living water, and by the gift of the Holy Spirit all one’s works flow so in holiness that the dove-like eyes of the Holy Spirit behold them. Hence these waters are sure, because they shall neither be exhausted nor dry up, nor shall a person be satiated by them. For they flow from the east; and while one remains in the body, one will neither see their height [Col. 0789A] nor discover their depth, because the waters in which a person is reborn to life are also suffused by the Holy Spirit.

In this manner the faithful person will see the king in the beauty of blessedness and, in one’s knowledge, behold the land of the living when one separates oneself far from sins in heart and body, so that one may also consider what to choose.

### Concerning the exceedingly bright light, proceeding from the mouth of the image that bears the wheel upon its breast in the likeness of threads, by which it appears to measure the signs of that image, wheel, and the circles shown before; and concerning their mystical meaning

XLVI. You also see that from the mouth of the aforesaid image, upon whose breast the aforesaid wheel appears, a light brighter than daylight comes forth in the likeness of threads. For from the power of true charity, in whose knowledge is the circuit of the world, proceeds its most elegant ordering, shining above all things and containing and binding all things together.

With these threads it measures in a straight and distinct measure the signs of the aforesaid circles, the signs of the other figures distinguished in that same wheel, and the individual signs of the members of the human form—namely, of that same image—which likewise appear in the wheel, as stated above. This is made clear in its preceding and following words, where through it the powers of the elements and the other higher adornments belonging to the defence and ornament of the world, together with all the joints of the members of the human being who rules in that world, are fittingly distinguished and suitably adjusted to a just measure, as has often been revealed to you.

But from true charity, which is wholly divine—the good more precious than every desirable thing—there comes that which gathers and draws to itself all who seek it. By divine prompting it weighs with right judgment the merits of heavenly desires and spiritual groanings proceeding by divine prompting, as well as every human work offered for the love of God. This is evident to all who love God perfectly, as I speak through Jeremiah, my servant, saying:

### The words of the prophet Jeremiah pertaining to the same subject, and how they are to be understood
XLVII. “I the Lord search the heart and test the reins, giving to each according to his way and according to the fruit of his devices” (Jer. 17). This is understood as follows: Those who love God seek no one but him through any pretext of false excuse, nor do they wish to hold any converse with another through the whisperings of the desires of their flesh. Yet man often carries out his own wishes, just as Adam also tested what he could do. But man cannot serve God and the devil at the same time, because what God loves the devil hates, and what the devil loves God disregards. This is so in man: for the flesh delights in sins, while the soul thirsts for justice; and between these two there is a great struggle, because one part is opposed to the other.

Nevertheless, the work which a human being begins is completed in this manner through great conflict, just as a servant is compelled to serve his lord; for the flesh, with the soul subjected to it, attacks sin, while the soul, with the flesh laid beneath it, performs good work. But when a person runs according to the desires of the soul, he rejects himself for the love of God and makes himself a stranger to the desires of the flesh. This is what the righteous and holy do; Abel too did it, he who looked toward God. At the shedding of his blood the whole earth trembled, so that afterwards it was called a widow—that is, deprived of the integrity of holiness through Cain’s murder, just as a woman in widowhood is deprived of the comfort of her husband.

For I, the Lord of all, search contrite hearts which reject sins, and test the reins of those who restrain themselves from tasting desires. I repay a person according to the labor of the steps of his ways [Col. 0790C], and according to the fruit which he brings forth in the deliberation of his thoughts; for I have before me all the fruits of humankind written down. The person who abandons the wishes of his desires is righteous; but one who follows all his will in desires cannot be called righteous. Yet if he turns to good, his scars are washed in the blood of the Lamb; and then, when the heavenly host sees them healed, it is stirred to wondrous praise of God. Therefore, let every person who fears and loves God reveal the devotion of his heart in these words, and know that they are uttered for the salvation of human bodies and souls, not by a human being, but through me who am.

## THIRD VISION

[Col. 0789]

[Col. 0789D] A simple compilation of certain visions touching upon natural philosophy: concerning the winds that drive the firmament round above and below; concerning the upper circle that sends forth a wind to move the planets backward from west to east and to regulate them in their course; concerning the humors of man, which take on the qualities of air and winds rushing against one another; and concerning the veins and intestines of the entire human body—how they adhere to and cooperate with one another in their various offices, and for what causes they sometimes depart from their equilibrium or temperateness.

### I

I saw, and behold: the east wind and the south wind [Col. 0790D], with their neighboring winds, by the blasts of their strength moved the firmament, causing it to roll from east to west above the earth. There the west wind, together with the north wind and their neighboring winds, received it and, impelling it by their breaths, cast it back from west to east beneath the earth.

I also saw that, from the day on which the days begin to lengthen, the aforesaid south wind, with its neighboring winds, gradually raised this same firmament in the southern region upward toward the north, as though supporting it, until the day when the days cease to lengthen further [Col. 0791A]. And from the same day on which the days begin to shorten, the north wind, with its neighboring winds, abhorring the brightness of the sun, gradually depressed that firmament by driving it from north to south, until the south wind began again to raise it through the lengthening of the days.

I also saw that in the upper fire there appeared a circle which encompassed the whole firmament from east toward west. From it a wind compelled the planets to move from west to east, contrary to the revolution of the firmament. And this wind, unlike the other aforesaid winds, did not send its blasts into the world, but merely regulated the course of the planets, as has been stated.

Then I also saw that, through the differing quality of winds and air when they meet one another, the humors in a human being are stirred and altered and take on the quality of those winds. For in each of the upper elements there is air suited to its quality, by which that element is driven through the force of the winds into its revolution; otherwise it would not move. From each of these, through the service of sun, moon, and stars, the air which moderates the world is breathed forth [Col. 0791B].

But whenever, either through the heat of the sun’s course or through God’s judgment, any element is affected in any region of the world, that element, stirred there together with the moving air, emits from that air into the aforesaid lower air a blast called wind [Col. 0791C]. This immediately mingles with it, because it is also in some measure from it and is somewhat like it; and thus it affects the human being. Consequently, the humors within him, when they are of the same quality as that wind and air, are often altered either toward weakness or toward strength according to its quality.

And again I saw that whenever one of the winds of all the aforesaid qualities is aroused in any region of the world, whether through a different course of sun and moon or through the judgment of God, as stated above, so that, with the air there stirred and tempered to it, it sends forth its blast, that same air, breathing through the world and preserving in due order the things that are in the world, renders a person somewhat changeable in his humors according to that same blast. For when a person whose natural constitution accords with that blast draws this altered air into himself and sends it forth—because the soul receives it and conveys it into the body’s interior—the humors within him are also altered, and often bring him either sickness or health, as shown above [Col. 0791D].

For the humors sometimes rise fiercely against a person like a leopard, but afterwards become milder. Like a crab, now advancing and now retreating, they frequently show change in themselves. Like a stag, leaping and striking, they sometimes disclose diversity in themselves. They sometimes attack a person as in the rapacity of a wolf, and with it as in the quality of the stag and the crab, as stated above [Col. 0792A]. At times too, like a lion, they continually display their strength in him; and like a serpent, they produce in themselves now gentleness, now sharpness. Like a lamb, they sometimes pretend to be mild; but like a bear, they sometimes mutter as though in anger, and at other times manifest with it the quality of the lamb and serpent, as shown above. For the humors in a human being are frequently changed in this fashion.

Accordingly, often thus altered they pass to his liver, in which his knowledge is tested—a knowledge proceeding from the brain, moderated through the powers of the soul, and touching the moisture of the brain, so that the brain may be fat, strong, and sound. For on the right side of a human being are the liver and the great heat of the body; therefore the right side is swift to raise itself and to work [Col. 0792B]. On the left, however, are the heart and lung, which strengthen that side for burdens and have heat from the liver as from a furnace.

But the veins of the liver, touched by these stirred humors, shake the little channels of human hearing and sometimes confuse that person’s hearing. For through hearing health or sickness is often brought to a person: namely, when he is excessively shaken by joy over prosperous things, or excessively contracted in sorrow over adverse things.

I also saw that these humors sometimes tend toward a person’s navel, which, standing forth like the head of the internal organs, gently closes them so that they are not dispersed, and preserves their passages and heat, and that of the veins, in proper balance—although it is often disturbed by their impulses; otherwise the person could not live. But they also sometimes seek the person’s loins, which in their powers are, as it were, playful, deceitful, and dangerous, and which are restrained by nerves and the other veins. In them too rationality flourishes, so that a person knows what to do and what to avoid. Hence he has delight in those acts, which are warmed and strengthened on the right side of the body by the breath of human respiration and by his liver. Thus a person receives discernment and discipline concerning how to restrain the storms of the other humors, so as to accomplish his works with discipline [Col. 0792C].

These same humors sometimes touch the veins of the kidneys and others which extend toward the veins of the spleen, lungs, and heart. All these, together with the internal organs, are shaken on the left side when the lung warms them, while the liver heats the right side of the body. The veins of the brain, heart, lungs, and liver, and the others, bring strength to the kidneys. The veins of the kidneys descend to the calves and strengthen them; then, returning upward with the veins of those same calves and joining one another either in male potency or in the female womb, they impart to those places powers for begetting offspring, just as iron is sharpened by a stone [Col. 0792D].

For the muscles of the arms, the calves, and the swellings of the legs are full of veins and humors; for just as the belly holds the internal organs and food within itself, so the muscles of the arms and the calves of the legs retain veins and humors within themselves. By their strength they fortify and carry the person, just as the belly nourishes him [Col. 0793A].

But when a person sometimes runs hurriedly or makes a journey by walking, the nerves below the knees and the little veins in the knees, stretched excessively, affect the veins in the calves, which are many and connected together like a net. Thus, returning in weariness to the veins of the liver, they cause these to affect the veins of the brain; in this manner they cast the whole body into fatigue. The veins of the kidneys, assisting the left calf, affect it more than the right, because the right calf is strengthened by the liver’s heat.

The veins of the right calf also rise to the veins of the kidneys and those parts, and their veins affect the veins of the liver. The liver warms the kidneys as they lie in the fat which comes from humors, so that they are stretched out, quickly inducing delight, producing it, and quickly ceasing; for when the liver gives a person heat, he is playful and cheerful [Col. 0793B].

Therefore, when the humors in a person are stirred in a proper measure and sometimes affect the veins of his liver, as stated above, its moisture is diminished, and the moisture of the chest is also thinned. Hence they drive the person, thus dried out, into sickness. Phlegm in that person also becomes dry and poisonous; it rises in this manner to his brain, brings his head into pain, makes his eyes ache, and causes the marrow in his bones to wither, so that he sometimes suffers the falling sickness when the moon is in eclipse.

The moisture in his navel, driven away by the same humors, sometimes turns into dryness and hardens; hence his flesh becomes ulcerous and scaly, as if he were a leper though he does not have leprosy [Col. 0793C]. The veins of his loins, improperly affected by them, similarly disturb the others, so that proper moisture in him is dried up; and thus, moisture being left behind, eruptions arise in him.

The veins of that person’s kidneys, sometimes touched by the aforesaid improperly stirred humors, shake the other veins attached to them in the calves or elsewhere in the body, as stated above, and dry out the marrow of his bones and the veins of his flesh. Thus the person languishes for a long time, drawing out his life in this sickness.

But sometimes the aforesaid humors cleanse the chest of a person with excessive moisture and moisten his liver with this moisture. Hence very many and varied thoughts arise in that person, so that he now thinks himself exceedingly foolish. Then the same humors rise to the brain, infect it, descend to the stomach, and generate fevers there; and thus that person remains ill for a long time [Col. 0793D].

They also sometimes constrict the little channels of the ears with an excess of phlegm, and these infect the veins of the lungs with the same phlegm, so that the person coughs and can scarcely breathe. This same excess of phlegm passes from the veins of the lungs to the veins of the heart and puts it in pain; and that pain, moving to the person’s side, arouses pleurisy and shakes him as if he had the falling sickness during an eclipse of the moon [Col. 0794A].

An excessive inundation also stirs the internal organs at a person’s navel and thus rises to his brain, often making him frenzied. It shakes the veins in his loins and affects melancholy in him, so that he is disturbed in this way and becomes sad without discernment.

Sometimes the same humors, through unsuitable moistening, affect the veins of a person’s kidneys; and these, thus stirred, infect the veins of his calves and the other veins of his body with excessive inundation. If that person then also abounds in excessive food and drink, they sometimes bring upon him gross leprosy, because his flesh becomes thickened. But if the aforesaid humors, neither excessively moist nor otherwise disordered, are diffused through a person’s limbs in an even and suitable balance, he remains sound in his body and vigorous in knowledge, whether for good or for evil [Col. 0794B].

## That All Creatures Serve Human Benefit No Less in Soul Than in Body; and What Is Signified by the East and South Winds, with Their Neighboring Winds, Being Seen to Turn the Firmament from East to West

### II

And again I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: All creatures that God made both in the higher and in the lower regions he joined to the benefit of humankind. If a person overturns them by wicked deeds, they themselves bring God’s judgment upon him with vengeance. Although they assist human beings in bodily necessity, they must be understood to have regard no less for the salvation of their souls [Col. 0794C].

For, as you see that the east wind and the south wind, with their neighboring winds, move the firmament by the blasts of their strength and cause it to roll from east to west over the earth, this signifies that the breathing-forth of the fear of the Lord and the breathing-forth of God’s judgment, together with the other virtues, touch the human being’s inward spirit with the strength of their holiness. They cause him, as though in the east, to begin good things, and to live and persevere in them until their good consummation—as though at the west—which convicts carnal things. For when a person fears God, he greatly fears incurring God’s judgment for his transgressions. Therefore, when he begins good things in such a way as to persevere in them, he strives for eternal recompense [Col. 0794D].

There the west wind, together with the north wind and their neighboring winds, receives it and drives it by their breaths from west to east beneath the earth. This is because the breathing-forth of uprightness, with the breathing-forth of chastisement through bodily tribulations and other scourges, terrifies and shakes the human spirit with the punishments of hell. When that spirit, already declining as though toward the west, ceases to perform good works in the weariness of fatigue, these bring it back to the rising of justice beneath earthly calamity. They exhort it not to succumb, as though overcome by sluggish ease at the end of righteous works, but to return vigorously to the beginning of holiness; for the reward of blessedness will be given not to one who begins and is negligent, but to one who begins and brings to completion [Col. 0795A].

## What Is Signified by the South and North Winds Respectively Raising and Gradually Lowering the Firmament at Different Solstices of the Year

### III

You also see that, from the day on which the days begin to lengthen, the aforesaid south wind, with its neighboring winds, gradually raises the same firmament in the southern region upward toward the north, as though supporting it, until the day on which they cease to lengthen further. This is because, when good works are extended in the light of truth by a faithful person, the breathing-forth of uprightness coming from the fire of justice, together with the other virtues, fittingly and orderly raises that person’s inward spirit in burning justice. It raises him upward against the desire of the flesh, worn and tested by very many temptations, as far as good faith [Col. 0795B].

But from the same day on which the days begin to shorten, the north wind, with its neighboring winds, abhorring the sun’s brightness, gradually lowers that same firmament by driving it from north to south, until the south wind begins again to raise it toward the lengthening of the days. This means that, when weariness and slowness seize a person in good works and lead him into fatigue, bodily tribulation also affects his spirit inwardly with contrary thoughts. By this tribulation the same person had earlier afflicted himself in many ways while resisting diabolical persuasion, but, overcome by weariness, had neglected the brightness of those works. It instills in him the thought that he should restrain himself in these afflictions and lay aside the rigor that he had in them, because the grace of God, as though in the south, will kindly and mercifully pardon his sins. Thus it gradually deceives him, until the fire of God’s gifts, judging these things rightly, restores his spirit, amid this struggle in the flesh, to its former vigor of virtues [Col. 0795C].

## What Is Signified by the Circle Appearing in the Upper Fire, Both as Encompassing the Whole Firmament and as Sending Forth a Wind Blowing through the Upper Regions and Regulating the Planets’ Course by Moving Them Backward

### IV

You also see that in the upper fire there appears a circle encompassing the whole firmament on every side, from which a wind goes forth and compels the seven planets to move from west to east against the firmament’s revolution. This is because in divine power there is the wholeness of holiness, which protects on every side the inward spirit of the person who joins himself to God.

From it comes a breathing-forth that causes the mystical gifts of the Holy Spirit to touch that person when he begins to grow numb in weariness, so that he may shake off numbness and rise vigorously toward justice. Yet this is often burdensome to the human spirit, because it can scarcely at times lead on the body in which it remains by divine disposition, so that the body may obey it; for the spirit often consents to it as to its dwelling-place in carnal desires. Thus the breathing-forth of God’s gifts often resists a person’s will [Col. 0795D].

And this wind, like the other aforesaid winds, does not send its blasts into the world, but only regulates the course of the planets, as stated above. For the aforesaid breathing-forth, proceeding from the wholeness of holiness, does not reveal itself, as do the other virtues that turn a person devoted to the world from evil to good. When a person begins to do good through God’s gift, he is not yet made perfect in the fullness of holiness. But when he has at last truly attained their perfection, the breathing-forth of holiness holds him in the full and perfect gifts of the Holy Spirit and does not allow him to waver either this way or that.

For as the column of holiness, founded below upon Christ, is raised above toward heavenly things, so, with Christ holding him—Christ upon whom the seven good gifts of the Holy Spirit rested—he cannot fall when shaken by the storms of diverse temptations [Col. 0796A–B]. And he will say, as is written through Habakkuk at my inspiration:

## Words of the Prophet Habakkuk Added to Explain the Same Meaning, and Their Exposition

### V

“The Lord God is my strength; he will make my feet like those of deer, and will lead me victorious upon my high places, singing psalms” (Hab. 3).

This is understood as follows: God, who created me and, as Lord, has authority over me, is my strength, because without him I can do nothing good. Through him I have the living spirit by which I live and move, and by which I know all my paths. Therefore, when I truly call upon this same God and Lord, he will set my steps in the swiftness of his commandments, just as a deer hastens when it desires a spring. In this way he will lead me upon that height revealed and enjoined upon me in his commands, placing earthly desires beneath me by the victory of strength, so that, when I attain the blessedness of heavenly things, I may render him unwearied praise [Col. 0796C].

For as the sun, set in the firmament of heaven, rules earthly creation and nothing can overwhelm it, so no faithful person who fixes heart and mind in God can be torn away from him. Since he is fixed in God, he truly despises all earthly things; consequently no one takes offense in him. He is not moved by any tumult through fear of death, nor is his time known to be lamentable in any labor. Nor is he found in robbers’ caves—that is, in deceitful hatred, in which a person is often deceived—nor does he walk in the whirlwind of instability, according to the unstable habits of people who do not look upon their Creator and carry out their deeds according to the freedom of their own will. Therefore he is likened to a crab walking backward and to a whirlwind which dries up herbs [Col. 0796D].

## What Is Signified by the Humors in a Person Being Stirred and Altered According to the Diverse Quality of Winds and Air Meeting One Another

### VI

Then you see that, through the differing quality of winds and air when they meet one another, the humors in a human being are stirred and altered and take on their quality. This signifies that, through diverse modes of the breathing-forth of virtues, and through the quality of human desires when they agree with one another, a person wills the things of God. Thoughts of people that had been removed from God, once turned toward good, submit themselves to the dignity of virtues and holy desires [Col. 0797A].

For in each of the upper elements there is air suited to its quality, through which that element is driven by the power of winds into its revolution; otherwise it would not move. This signifies that, alongside every higher virtue and strengthening, there is a desire suited to the faithful person, by which he is strengthened through the breathing-forth of virtues for the overthrow of evil; otherwise he would not be turned toward good. And from each of these, through the service of sun, moon, and stars, the air which moderates the world is breathed forth. This shows that from all the higher strengthenings of virtues, from the spirit of strength, from the spirit of the fear of the Lord, and with the other illuminations of good breathings-forth, desires that pant in the hearts of the faithful for heavenly blessedness are kindled [Col. 0797B].

Whatever good a person does proceeds not from his own merit, but from the gift of God’s grace. But whenever, either through the heat of the sun’s course or through God’s judgment, any element is affected in any region of the world, that element, stirred there with the moving air, sends from that air into the aforesaid lower air a blast called wind. This is because, when powers for human salvation are stirred through the spirit of strength and through the divine ordering of the higher virtues, where the desires of faithful people rise to God and call upon him, those powers, summoned with heavenly desire, direct from God a breathing-forth toward the minds of those people, so that they may be capable of turning toward every good [Col. 0797C].

For when a person calls upon God purely and faithfully, by righteous judgment God surrounds him with protection, because, having cast off evil, he hastens toward good. This immediately mingles with it because it is in some part from it and is somewhat similar to it. This signifies that the minds of the righteous agree with the breathing-forth of virtues: because, while they love what is just, they are of the virtues; and therefore in this way they make themselves like them.

Thus the same air affects the person, so that the humors within him, when they are of the same quality as that wind and air, are often changed either toward weakness or toward strength. This is because those same minds of the blessed, turned toward justice, subdue carnal desires within themselves and fix their thoughts upon the breathing-forth of virtues and the devotion of heavenly desires, adding weakness to vices and strength to virtues [Col. 0797D]. For when a person reasonably restrains his flesh for God’s sake, he raises the inner spirit upward toward blessedness, as Wisdom attests, saying:

[Col. 0798A] Testimony from Solomon’s Proverbs Inserted to Illuminate This Meaning, and How It Is to Be Understood

### VII

“The house of the righteous has great strength, but in the fruits of the wicked there is disturbance” (Prov. 15).

This is understood as follows: Just as the sun, when it ascends high at noon, burns most intensely in its heat, so too the house—that is, the mind—of this righteous person, who performs all his works as though he stood before God’s judgment, displays very great strength in itself as it progresses from virtue to virtue. Nor is it diminished in this: just as the sun is not weakened either by its ascent or by the distribution of its heat in its course. For the more the blessed person grows warm in good, the more he is set aflame by happy zeal [Col. 0798A–B].

For his dwellings are in the places above, where he abides with all intention and desire, and he cannot be sated with their sweetness. His strength too is higher than the firmament and reaches to the depth of the abyss, because the human being is strongest together with all creation, and every creature serves him. The earth is sometimes shaken and moved by the movement of the firmament; and the firmament serves the earth by pouring rain upon it, lest its parts be separated from one another, and so that through air and dew it may laudably bring forth its fruits.

But the blessed person draws all earthly things away from himself, and neither through crushing distress nor through fear of earthly desires ceases from ascending toward the heavenly height and building good works in the joy of eternal life. But in those fruits which the wicked person produces in evil and perverse works there is disturbance, because he totters as he is inundated in the disturbance of the world. He does not walk in the day or hope in eternal light, but eats the husks of swine and finds no life in them, because he does not cast off carnal desires [Col. 0798B–C].

## That Through the Manifold Interdependence of Winds and Air, the Diverse Course of Sun and Moon, or the Supervening Judgment of God, a Person Also Undergoes Change and Sometimes Encounters Variations of Health and Sickness; and What Is Figured by This in His Spiritual Life

### VIII

Again you see that, whenever one of the winds of all the aforesaid qualities is aroused in any region of the world—whether by a diverse course of sun and moon or by God’s judgment, as stated above—so that, with the air there stirred and tempered to it, it sends forth its blast, that same air, breathing through the world and preserving in due order the things that are in the world, renders a person somewhat changeable in his humors according to that same blast.

This signifies that when the breathing-forth of virtues and very many gifts arises in a faithful person—wherever the Holy Spirit breathes them forth—through the inspiration of the spirit of strength and humility, the spirit of the fear of the Lord, a contrite spirit, and the ordering of divine contemplation, so that the person’s upright desire, corresponding to it, attends it through flowing inspiration, that same desire, investigating whatever is beneficial and inclining itself toward it with devotion, conforms itself to that inspiration [Col. 0798D].

Thus the same desire also shakes that person’s heart. For when the person whose natural quality accords with that blast draws this altered air into himself and sends it forth, because the soul receives it and conveys it into the body’s interior, the humors within him are also changed and often bring him either sickness or health, as shown above. So too, when the will of a person agrees with this good breathing-forth, he examines in rumination that desire separated from evil; and because the soul more secretly inscribes it by itself, the storms of thoughts flooding within him are also altered, so that they now promise him adversity and now prosperity [Col. 0799A].

## That the Humors in a Person Are Moved Now More Sharply, Now More Mildly, According to the Character of Certain Animals or Beasts; and That, According to the Change or Impulse of Those Humors, His Affections and Thoughts Vary Through Frequent Alternation

### IX

For the humors sometimes rise fiercely in a person like a leopard, but afterwards become milder; and, like a crab, now advancing and now retreating, they frequently show change in themselves; and, like a stag, leaping and striking, they sometimes manifest diversity in themselves. This is because, however much a person may have the fear of the Lord, thoughts nevertheless sometimes arise in him which later, affected by weariness, descend into vanity. At times, like a crab, through confidence of a good ending they urge him onward [Col. 0799B–C]; but then, pulling him backward and suggesting [perhaps *innuendo*, “insinuating”] that he cannot persevere in this way, they deceive him. At times, like a stag, they make him secure through faith, but afterwards sting him by making him waver in faith.

They also sometimes attack a person as in the rapacity of a wolf, and with it as in the quality of the stag and crab, as stated above. For at times, like a wolf, they set before a person the punishments of hell and falsely promise that he can escape them solely through the stag—that is, faith—and through the crab—that is, confidence—without other righteous works; but afterwards they often lead him into despair.

At other times, like a lion, they continually display their strength in him; and, like a serpent, they bring forth in themselves now gentleness, now sharpness. Like a lamb, they sometimes pretend to be mild when they set God’s judgment before a person; but afterwards they persuade him not to fear it, because, as a serpent proceeds prudently, they deceitfully suggest how he may escape it by gentle cunning. They also exhort him, as though he were a lamb, to fear nothing in patience, as if he were not bound by sins [Col. 0799D].

But like a bear they sometimes mutter, as though in anger; at other times they manifest with it the quality of the lamb and serpent, as shown above. For at times, like a bear, they mutter that a person bears bodily tribulation for God, through which, as though in the patience of a lamb and the prudence of a serpent, they show him to be chastened and cleansed from sins. Then once again they render him uncertain in this through many variations.

For the humors in a person are often changed in this way, because thoughts, transformed by such whirlwinds and in other fashions, lead him now into a just security, now into despair, and sometimes also raise him upward through right devotion. Accordingly, often thus altered they pass to his liver, in which his knowledge is tested—a knowledge proceeding in moderation from the brain through the powers of the soul and affecting the moisture of the brain, so that it may be fat, strong, and sound. This signifies that a person’s thoughts often direct themselves, as it were, toward his liver—that is, toward the strength of justice, in which the righteous person acts through knowledge—because the powers of the soul show knowledge of good and evil; through justice, this knowledge embraces life in believers, just as the Son of God gathered sinners and tax collectors to himself and made them strong in the abundance of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0800A–B].

## That a Person Is More Ready for Work on His Right Side Because the Liver, in Which Is the Source of Heat, Lies on the Right; but More Able to Bear Burdens on His Left Because the Heart and Lung, Situated on the Left and Possessing the Pulse of Respiration, Are There; and What These Things Spiritually Signify in Him
X. For on the right side of the human being are the liver and the great heat of the body; therefore the right side is quick to raise itself and to act. But on the left are the heart and lungs, which strengthen that side for bearing burdens; [Col. 0800C] and they receive heat from the liver as from a furnace. This signifies that on the right—that is, in the prosperity of the salvation of the good and upright person—justice works together with the Holy Spirit, so that he, raising himself prosperously toward God, may accomplish every good thing. On the left, however, so that he may avoid adversities, he desires to be strengthened by the power of justice, confessing God with an upright heart.

But when the veins of the liver are disturbed and touched by these humors, they shake the small channels of a person’s hearing and sometimes confuse that hearing. For through hearing, either health or sickness is often brought to a person: when he is shaken beyond measure with joy over prosperous things, or contracted beyond measure with sadness over adverse things. This shows that the course of justice, stirred by upright thoughts, turns a person away from evil [Col. 0800D] hearing and directs him toward good; for hearing sometimes brings into his soul both things that are holy and things that are shameful, so that a person may sometimes not know how, or may not wish to know how, to set a measure for himself either in good things or in evil things.

For good knowledge without good hearing is mute, because good hearing receives what good knowledge knows; and it takes great care to treat and dictate what is brought to it through good knowledge. After it has arranged all these things suitably, it rests by ceasing from them for a while, like a person who puts treasure into his chest: that is, when it understands good and evil, storing good in the secret place of its heart and utterly casting evil away from itself, as Isaiah exhorts when he says:

[Col. 0801A] Words of the prophet Isaiah suitable for establishing these meanings, and the sense in which they are to be understood.

XI. “Loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion, for thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and without silver you shall be redeemed” (Isa. XLII).

This is understood as follows: Break by repentance the bond of the first captivity and transgression, O human being, you who had been numbered among the daughters of heavenly peace in Paradise; for when you lost it, you were subjected to many evils. Therefore he who is Lord of all says to you who are entangled in sins willingly committed: In this manner you were sold without a price, just as God promised pain to the first woman, who, because she transgressed the divine command, was deprived of Paradise and lost the name “daughter of Zion.” But [Col. 0801B] you shall be redeemed without the silver of earthly covetousness, where our Redeemer arose in virginal nature and appointed us to be born again through Spirit and water unto life, as though he had restored us to our hereditary place.

Whoever perseveres justly in this birth shall not be moved from the height of Zion. Therefore let the faithful person raise himself toward God, casting away his sins and leaving every evil behind; and let him pant in his desire for heavenly things, seeking from God the help of good works. If he remains steadfast in this petition, as the blind man sitting beside the way did, the grace of God immediately looks upon him; and if it then sees him attending to the light and raising himself from darkness, it will be present with him in all things, inspiring in him those things [Col. 0801C] which are just and holy. For this person, turning away from evil, delights in good and holy works and tastes their sweetness, because he does not wish to depart from God but turns himself away from the serpent’s deceit.

What it signifies in a human being that the humors within him, sprinkling the navel, which is the head of the entrails, and the loins, in which wantonness is located, sometimes also touch the veins of the kidneys and of the flanks, and through these ascend even to the veins of the spleen, lungs, and heart.

XII. You see also that these humors sometimes tend toward the human navel, which, standing out like the head of the entrails, gently closes them lest they be scattered; and which preserves their courses and heat, and those of the veins, in proper balance, although it is often disturbed by its impulses. Otherwise a person could not live. For when a faithful person excludes evil hearing, he constrains, by his good thoughts, the navel of diverse desires, so that he may attain the life of true blessedness, since that navel often provokes him to the unrest of evils.

But they sometimes also attack a person’s loins, which are deceptive and dangerous in their powers, as though they were playing, and which are held in check by the nerves and other veins. Rationality likewise flourishes in them, so that a person knows what he should do and what he should avoid. Thus he has pleasure for those works; and they are warmed and strengthened on the right side of the body by the breath of human respiration and by the liver. Hence a person receives discernment and discipline concerning how to restrain the storms of the other humors, so that he may accomplish [Col. 0802A] his works with discipline. For he girds up the loins, in which luxury resides, and, strengthened in this for the salvation of his soul through the virtue of justice, he accomplishes it discreetly and honorably.

The same humors also sometimes touch the veins of the kidneys and flanks, which tend toward the veins of the spleen, lungs, and heart. All these, together with the entrails, are shaken on the left side when the lungs warm them; but the liver kindles the right side of the body. For by these same upright thoughts a person most firmly constrains the kidneys, which often touch his heart through unjust desire and shake it toward evil when the levity of the flesh touches them; and he does this by walking in the paths of justice.

That the veins of the brain, heart, and liver, by strengthening the kidneys, and the veins of the kidneys, by strengthening the calves in their descent, [Col. 0802B] and by returning upward together with their veins and joining one another at suitable places, confer on both sexes the power to beget; and that the muscles, arms, and legs are full of veins and humors, with a brief explanation of these matters.

XIII. Just as the veins of the brain, heart, lungs, and liver, and the others, bring strength to the kidneys, and the veins of the kidneys descend to the calves and strengthen them, so, returning upward with the veins of those same calves and joining one another either in male strength or in the female womb, as the stomach receives foods, they impart to those places the power to produce offspring, as iron is sharpened by a stone. For after a person, having lulled desire to sleep, has constrained those kidneys by chastity, he also cleanses them in chastity through the good knowledge that is in him, [Col. 0802C] surrounds them with the course of justice and continence, and thus, inclining himself toward continence in those matters in which he was formerly incontinent, strengthens continence itself lest it fall into frivolity.

Therefore, when he tends toward God in that same continence, fortifying himself through it in both the male and female sex, supported by diverse virtues, he brings forth offspring of holiness when he walks the straight path of discernment. For the muscles—the muscles of the arms and the calves—and also the swellings of the legs are full of veins and humors. As the belly retains within itself the entrails and food, so the muscles of the arms and the calves of the legs preserve within themselves veins and humors; by their strength they strengthen and carry the person, just as the belly [Col. 0802D] nourishes him. For abstinence is, in the human being, the grasp of the strength and sustaining of justifications, surrounded by the course of the groans of good thoughts; it also retains the inward parts of the soul in fullness, preserves them unto the perfection of salvation, and nourishes the whole person—body, that is, and soul—in holiness.
