That excessive stretching of the nerves and veins throughout the entire body causes fatigue in a running person; by what connection or impulsion of veins that momentary pleasure is aroused; and the moral and useful interpretation of these matters in the human being.

XIV. But when a person sometimes runs hastily or makes a journey by walking, the nerves beneath the knees and the small veins in the knees, excessively [Col. 0803A] stretched, touch the veins in the calves, which are numerous and connected to one another like a net. Thus, returning in fatigue to the veins of the liver, they cause the veins of the brain to be touched; and in this manner they cast the whole body into weariness.

Likewise, when a person sometimes takes up the way of uprightness indiscreetly, the immoderation of this course bends him toward all kinds of incongruous things and leads abstinence itself in him into an unjust mode of knowledge. Thus, when he abstains from lawful things without measure, he incurs weariness in other virtues; and when he thinks that he is returning to justice and possesses superabundant knowledge, he prepares for himself a snare of fatigue. For, through this unsuitable abstinence, making light of the recklessness of audacity and presumption, he doubts that he can persevere in this fashion alone, [Col. 0803B] and so falls into the snare of despair.

But the veins of the kidneys, coming to the aid of the left calf, affect it more than the right, because the right calf is strengthened by the heat of the liver. Thus the course of desire is increased more by abstinence when that abstinence is unsuitable and indiscreet than it is diminished by it, because it is neither according to God nor for God. For abstinence which works with discernment is strengthened by the virtue of justice.

Moreover, the veins of the right calf ascend to the veins of the kidneys; their veins touch the veins of the liver; and the liver warms the kidneys as they lie in the fatness that comes from humors, so that they are quickly stretched out, bringing in and leading out pleasure, and quickly ceasing. [Col. 0803C] For when the liver gives heat to a person, he plays and is cheerful. So also abstinence which is truly in God overcomes the course of desire, draws it to the judgment of justice, and examines it there, so that it may utterly perish. But justice, reducing to nothing that desire which lay in the fatness of impurities, burns it with the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that the evils within it are stretched out into contrition and bitterness, although they had first displayed in themselves a pleasure, however brief; for the justified sinner shall reap a reward in joy.

For what reasons phlegm and humors, sometimes corrupted in a person, cause him to incur either falling sickness or other illnesses in the body; and by what evils, according to their meanings, he is usually afflicted in the soul.

[Col. 0803D] XV. Therefore, when the humors that are in a person are unjustly stirred and sometimes touch the veins of his liver, as was said above, its moisture is diminished and the moisture of his chest is also thinned. Thus they drive the person, so dried out, into sickness. The phlegm too becomes dry and poisonous in that person; it rises in this manner to his brain, brings his head into pain, causes his eyes to ache, and makes the marrow in his bones wither, so that he sometimes incurs falling sickness when the moon is in eclipse.

For when a person’s thoughts take on fierceness, hardness, and tyranny within themselves and thus turn aside to every vanity, they oppress by this tyranny the justice which, drenched with the dew of the Holy Spirit, ought to germinate in him through the holiness of good works; [Col. 0804A] and they weaken and dry up his other virtues. They also lead his knowledge—its principle and intention—and the strength of just action, which formerly flourished within him, as it were into falling sickness, into despair, because the light of truth that shone for him is now diminished.

Likewise, the moisture in his navel, driven away by these humors, sometimes turns to dryness and hardens. Hence his flesh becomes ulcerous and scaly, as though he were a leper, though he does not have leprosy. The veins of his loins, unjustly affected by them, disturb the others in the same manner, so that the proper moisture within him is dried up. Thus, once the moisture has departed, eruptions arise in him. For the moisture of continence, which should, as though in his navel, [Col. 0804B] destroy desire, is driven away by these fierce, hard, and unlawful thoughts and is not drenched in him with the dew of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when it deserts him, his sins rot through evil habit, so that they become apparent to all, stinking like leprosy. His loins, not girded with chastity, are disturbed by those same thoughts, so that, with the shoot of good fruits dried up within him, perverse examples rise up in him as eruptions. This too Hosea demonstrates through the Holy Spirit, saying:

Words of the prophet Hosea appropriate to these matters, and the sense in which they are to be understood.

XVI. “In the house of Israel I saw a horrible thing: there Israel was defiled by fornication” (Hos. V).

This is understood as follows: In those hiding places, in which this person—who ought to look upon God with a pure heart—lay as though resting in sins, I, who search out every hidden transgression, saw a most abominable thing: namely, that he was entangled in the fornication [Col. 0804C] of most unclean and stinking violations, polluting himself in them as a pig wallows in mud. He ought to have sought, looked upon, and embraced purity, but instead made himself contemptible and dissolute in all things.

For uncleanness enervates a person and almost removes him from his own mind, so that he cannot attend with the perfection of honesty either to things that concern the world or to things that concern God; because the burning of the flesh, together with his own will, suggests, as if blowing upon him, pride, [Col. 0804D] vain glory, and every evil.

That the veins of a person’s kidneys, when sometimes affected by humors unjustly stirred, disturb other veins and thereby dry up even the marrow of the bones; and what inward affliction, represented by this, seizes the human being.

XVII. The veins of the kidneys of that same person, sometimes affected by the aforesaid humors unjustly stirred, shake the other veins attached to them in his calves or in the rest of his body, as has been stated. They dry up, in dryness, the marrow of his bones and the veins of his flesh; and so the person languishes for a long time, prolonging life in this languor. For when a person neglects to constrain his navel and loins, so that he even [Col. 0805A] permits his thoughts to wander through tyranny and through all kinds of useless things, he despises the course of virtues joined to abstinence, and abstinence itself, which ought to be maintained discreetly and in order for the preservation of chastity. Therefore his other works, lacking the infusion of heavenly dew, turn to dryness and cause his soul to languish until it returns to the vigor of the virtues.

What the humors, excessively abundant in a person’s chest, stirring the liver and the veins of the ears or kidneys, and ascending from the navel to the brain, signify in his spiritual condition.

XVIII. But sometimes these aforesaid humors flood a person’s chest with excessive moisture and moisten his liver with this moisture. Hence [Col. 0805B] very many and diverse thoughts arise in that same person, so that he now thinks himself excessively wise, now excessively foolish. Then these same humors ascend to the brain and infect it, descend to the stomach, and generate fevers there; and so the person is sick for a long time.

These matters likewise show that, if a person’s diverse thoughts, having put aside fierceness, spread themselves out in softness, pliability, and slippery vanity, they strive to suffocate justice within him by that softness. Thus, when they rise up in him in this way, they now raise him up as if in wisdom and now cast him down as if in folly; confusing his knowledge, they bring voracity upon him, so that his soul, entangled in these evils as in a lingering sickness, [Col. 0805C] often suffers dangerous oppression.

They also sometimes affect the small channels of the ears with an excess of phlegm; and these infect the veins of the lungs with the same phlegm, so that the person coughs and can scarcely breathe. This same excess of phlegm passes from the veins of the lungs to the veins of the heart and puts it in pain; and when this pain goes to the person’s side, it arouses pleurisy and shakes him as though he had falling sickness when the moon is in eclipse.

These things also signify that diverse thoughts sometimes cause such turmoil in the same person that they so confuse the hearing of his soul that it can neither understand good nor gather it into itself, but treats it with disgust, as though coughing it out. They likewise so agitate his heart through madness [Col. 0805D] that he can receive no rest beneficial to his soul; instead, wavering here and there in uprightness, he walks as though dying, because the light of uprightness is now darkened for him.

The excessive flooding also stirs the entrails in a person’s navel and thus ascends to his brain, often making him frenzied; it shakes the veins in his loins and affects melancholy in him, so that he is disturbed in this way and becomes sad without discernment. For through the immoderate disturbance of slippery effusion, thoughts move desire in him according to their own pleasure. They also rend his knowledge so that it is defiled in wicked acts, rendering him as if insane and incontinent in shamelessness. Sadness likewise darkens him when he cannot fulfill the pleasure [Col. 0806A] of his flesh.

Sometimes the same humors, through unsuitable moistening, affect the veins of a person’s kidneys; and when these have been stirred in this manner, they infect the veins of his calves and the other veins of his body with excessive flooding. If that same person then also abounds in excessive food and drink, they sometimes bring upon him gross leprosy, because his flesh becomes thickened. This demonstrates that impure and slippery pleasure sometimes touches a person’s thoughts and draws him toward shameful softness; it drives from him strong abstinence, which ought to tame his flesh, and softly leads him into voracity, which kindles the flames of lust. Thus it infects with the putrefaction of sins, as with leprosy, the person who does not resist the pleasure of his body. For one who does not mortify his flesh by suitable abstinence, but nourishes it together with vices and desires, heaps up for himself the fatness of sins and thus makes himself stink before God in filth.

What advance in the inward realm of thoughts is signified by the same humors when they are equally and proportionately balanced in the human body; and testimony from the Song of Songs agreeing with this, together with its exposition.

XIX. But if the aforesaid humors are neither excessively dry nor excessively moist, but are distributed through a person’s limbs in an equal and suitable balance, he remains healthy in body and vigorous in knowledge, whether for good or for evil. This likewise signifies that if a person’s thoughts are neither too hard in fierceness nor too slippery in pliability, but are well and fittingly ordered in moral integrity both according to humanity and according to God, they make him tranquil in body through gentleness and subtle in knowledge. Thus he does not turn aside, fleeing the world’s favor, either to the right or to the left; but, supported by very many virtues, he pants for heavenly joys, as it is written in the Song of Songs (ch. VII): “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince.”

This is understood as follows: You who delight in good works in your heart while panting for God, through whom you have the hope of eternal life which shines [Col. 0806D] joyfully for you as when the sun rises: you display to others most beautiful steps on the way of the Son of God when you impose upon yourself the mortification of the flesh as though it were sandals, covering, that is, the nakedness of your sins, where in good will you love God more than yourself.

Then the soul is also called the daughter of the prince—of that prince, namely, who is called the Prince of Peace, who overcame the ancient serpent, liberated his people, and washed away in his blood every enmity that existed between God and humankind. The angels announced this peace to human beings in the humanity of the Son of God, and greatly rejoiced in it, because God had so joined himself to earth that people might behold him in human form, while the angels perfectly behold him as both human being and God.

Therefore every person [Col. 0807A] who fears and loves God should disclose by these words the devotion of his heart, and know that they have been uttered both for the salvation of human bodies [Col. 0808A] and souls—not by a human being, but through me who am speaking.

## FOURTH VISION

[Col. 0807]

[Col. 0807A] Different visions briefly comprised under one chapter: concerning the firmament; how great its density is together with all that adheres to it; how the harmful effects of certain circles are repelled or moderated by the opposition of others; and concerning the milky band appearing like a bent bow.

I. And I saw that the firmament, together with everything adhering to it, had from its highest point to its lowest point above the earth as much thickness as the earth had from its highest point to its lowest point. I also saw that the upper fire of the firmament, when sometimes stirred, sent forth onto the earth certain scales like sparks, which inflicted blemishes and ulcers on human beings, animals, and the fruits of the earth.

I saw also that a certain mist descended at times from the black fire to the lands, drying up the earth’s greenness and parching the moisture of the fields. But the pure ether resisted both these scales and this mist, lest they inflict wounds beyond measure upon the aforesaid creatures.

And I saw further that from the strong, white, and bright air another mist sometimes stretched down to the lands, inflicting a great pestilence upon people and cattle; as a result, many were subject to diverse illnesses [Col. 0807C] and very many incurred death. Yet the watery air opposed this mist, moderating it so that it might not inflict injury beyond measure upon creatures.

I also saw that moisture boiling up over the earth from the thin air raised up the earth’s greenness and caused all fruits to come forth by germination. This air also bore certain clouds above, which supported all the higher things and were strengthened by all the higher things. In that same air I saw a cloud of white color, which, at both its ends, was fixed, as it were, here and there into other clouds of the firmament; its middle, remaining bent like a bow, stretched into the aforesaid air. And again I heard a voice from heaven saying to me:

[Col. 0807D] That God, the Creator of all things, strengthens lower things through higher things; through them he also purifies sinners by punishing them; and what the density of the firmament, everywhere equal to that of the earth, signifies in the human being.

II. God, who created all things, established the higher things so that through them he might also strengthen and cleanse the lower things, and might introduce into the form of the human being those things appointed also for the salvation of the soul. For you see that the firmament, with all that adheres to it, has from its highest point to its lowest point above the earth as much thickness as the earth has from its highest point to its lowest point. For, O human being, as is shown and said to you, the firmament and the earth are of equal thickness; and as much empty space of air lies above the earth up to the higher barriers, so much [Col. 0808A] empty space of air also lies beneath the earth down to the lower barriers. There is likewise as much empty space of air toward the south and toward the north, between the earth and the opposing barriers of the firmament there.

This signifies that the inward spirit of a human being manifests its powers in heavenly and earthly matters in proportion as the human body endeavors to act in those same ways through its strength. For where soul and body agree with one another in uprightness, they attain the heavenly rewards in one joy.

Concerning the firmament, suitably arranged by the Creator for every operation through fire, ether, waters, stars, and winds; whence the scales are produced that fall like sparks from the bright fire of the upper circle and injure both the earth and its inhabitants; and what inward retribution is shown by this.

III. You see also that the upper fire of the firmament, when sometimes stirred, emits onto the earth certain scales like sparks, which inflict blemishes and ulcers upon human beings, animals, and the fruits of the earth. For God strengthened the firmament with fire lest it dissolve, lightened it with ether so that it might move, drenched it with waters lest it dry up, illuminated it with stars so that it might shine, and sustains it with winds so that it may continually complete [Col. 0808C] its course.

For in the four regions—that is, east, south, west, and north—the firmament is driven in its revolving course by the winds. But when its bright fire is overcome, through the ordinance and judgment of God, by the moisture of the lower water, so that it departs from the proper measure of its burning, it sends forth scales hot with burning and moist with water for retribution, as was said above.

This shows that the power of God, holding the human spirit in its own power and provoked by just judgment, sends its retribution upon the perverse deeds of human beings, so that they may be confounded and cast down, because they display in themselves not human but beastly customs, having no fruit of good works.

[Col. 0808D] That the black fire enclosed in the second circle, when stirred either by God’s judgment or by the collision of winds, emits a mist that dries the earth’s greenness; that it is dangerous now through heat, now through inundation of the members; and what these matters signify.

IV. And a certain mist descending sometimes from the black fire to the lands dries up the earth’s greenness and parches the moisture of the fields. For when burning and cold are stirred within that fire by the will of God, the mist descends, as has been said; smoky from dangerous burning and moist from harmful cold, it serves as a punishment of sinners.

For this black fire burns when stirred by the south wind, but from the north wind it receives an excess of cold in hail; yet the east wind calms both. The west wind, however, leaping in the watery air, [Col. 0809A] when the black fire is sometimes disturbed, causes a dangerous inundation. This signifies that from judicial examination another retribution extends to carnal desires, overturns them into the dryness of contempt, and entirely consumes their fatness, because God reduces to nothing that which sets itself against him.

That the circle of pure ether, by its gentleness, moderates higher and lower things, resists the scales of the first circle and the mist of the second lest they injure the lands too greatly; and what benefit or meaning belongs to the smoke proceeding from upper waters heated by heavenly fire.

V. But the pure ether resists these scales and this mist lest they inflict wounds beyond measure upon creatures, [Col. 0809B] because the ether, existing midway between fires and waters, mitigates the higher things by its purity and gentleness and moderates the lower things. It produces no wounds from itself; for if each of the elements struck the creatures and nothing came to their aid, they could neither endure nor subsist.

By divine ordinance, moreover, the waters are sometimes compressed by fire lest they flow out in unsuitable effusion. Hence they emit a certain smoke, which is not harmful, just as a person’s breath injures no one. This same smoke, by suitable moisture, moderates the lower things lest they extend their wounds beyond what they should, just as pure repentance moderates divine retribution and vengeance and makes God favorable to his creature.

[Col. 0809C] Concerning the pestilential mist that extends to the lands from the circle of strong and white air: whence it is produced; how the density of the watery air resists it lest it be excessively harmful; that no scourges are ever brought upon human beings except by God’s judgment; and what all these matters signify.

VI. You also see that from the strong, white, and bright air another mist sometimes stretches down to the lands, inflicting great pestilence on people and cattle, so that many thereby are subject to diverse illnesses and very many incur death. For when a mist proceeds from that air from time to time, as has been said, the upper waters to which that same air clings below because of their nearness are moved beyond measure, by the will of God, by the upper fire. Through restless burning they now boil, [Col. 0809D] and through the grievous cold that is in the black fire they now grow cold; thus the mist, steeped in both, is harmful in both respects.

But these scourges do not come forth unless, provoked by the sins of human beings, they are brought upon them by God’s just judgment. They demonstrate that from the discernment of holy works retribution proceeds against actions performed without discernment, inflicting immoderate affliction upon persons who have no moderation in sin; so that it weakens in them those things that are indiscreet according to the body and entirely mortifies those things which, for the salvation of the soul, lack discernment. For discernment moderates everything useful to both body and soul.

Yet the watery air opposes this mist, moderating it so that it may not inflict injury beyond [Col. 0810A] measure upon creatures, because by its watery quality it diminishes the strength of that mist. Thus holy works, in the examples of the righteous, show this retribution which proceeds from discernment in what ways it strikes immoderate things.

Concerning the moisture that emanates from the thin air: what benefit it has; that drops of rain are changed into snow by the upper cold; and that the same thin air defends and makes the earth fruitful from above.

VII. That moisture boiling up over the earth from the thin air raises the earth’s greenness, causes all fruits to come forth by germination, and also bears above certain clouds, which support all higher things and are strengthened by all higher things, occurs because that same thin air emits snow from itself. The snow is spread upon the earth as though flying when, through the sun’s descent, cold is on the earth, because drops of water are changed into snow by the upper cold.

But in the burning of the sun’s ascent, this same air sweats out above the earth falling dew in the likeness of a honeycomb; from the sweetness of the east wind, it sometimes melts into sweet rain. This air restrains dangers from above and is like a shield defending the earth, just as a shield protects a man from many blows. From the most sweet and temperate heat of the sun it emits over the earth the dew of blessing which Jacob gave to his son.

Sometimes this air smokes from the ascent of water and from the moisture of dew. This is not harmful, however, but touches every fruitfulness of the earth, cleansing it from [Col. 0810C] the filthy stench by which it has been affected through some storm.

How clouds in that same air are modified by upper fire or cold, appearing sometimes bright and sometimes shadowy; how they release rain, as if pressed from certain breasts, not suddenly but gradually; and what they signify in us.

VIII. The same air bears and supports above itself the aforesaid clouds, sometimes bright and sometimes shadowy. They have, as it were, separate breasts through which they send rains to the earth, just as milk is drawn from breasts. They sometimes stretch themselves toward the higher regions and receive strength from each of them. For they are strengthened by fire, lightened by ether, drenched with waters, and congealed by cold, [Col. 0810D] lest the discharge of rain through the individual breasts be poured excessively thick upon the earth.

These clouds are also that brightness which people call heaven, because the fixed courses of the sun, moon, and stars are seen through them like forms through a mirror, so that people suppose they see their arrangement. Yet this is not so, because the clouds show only the operations of these constellations, as in the shadow of a mirror; and they flow like water in which all things placed before it are seen.

They signify that a thought proceeding from the right desire of a faithful person, setting good works before itself for fruitful usefulness, touches that person’s greenness so that it may produce manifold fruits of holiness and raise human minds toward heavenly things, [Col. 0811A] so that they may pant for them and be strengthened by them. For when a person tends through right desire toward the fruit of good works, he despises earthly things and so fastens himself to the things above in heaven that he shows himself entirely changed, as though he were not a human being.

Concerning the cloud called milky: how, by its extension or curvature, it strengthens the air enclosed by it; and what this signifies.

IX. In that same air you also see a cloud of white color, which, where it ends on both sides, is fixed as it were here and there into other clouds of the firmament, and whose middle, remaining bent like a bow, extends into the aforesaid air. For among the same clouds that this air supports by bearing them above, another cloud having, as it were, a milky color is stretched out. It strengthens that same air as a column supports a house. So also, in the aforesaid order of right desire, the minds of certain persons are so constituted that in both secular and spiritual affairs they await the reward that is the end of their works. For they accomplish both earthly and heavenly business so that they may please the heavenly Judge; and although the perfection of their minds sometimes feels the frailty of the flesh, as though bent, [Col. 0811B] it nevertheless perseveres in right desire, as my servant Job also shows when he says:

Words of Job agreeing with this, and the sense in which they are to be understood.

X. “And the righteous shall hold to his way, and he that is clean of hands shall add strength” (Job 17). [Col. 0811C] This too is clear in meaning: the person who loves righteousness will hold fast to the paths of uprightness by an effort of strength; and the one who is free from defilements will acquire holiness through good works, when, abstaining from evils, he turns himself toward everything pleasing to God, so that he may attain that life which has no end. For the righteous person receives wisdom; and wisdom belongs to that rational faculty which knows what is living and what is mortal, and teaches right paths. But the blindness of the heart which arises from the taste of the flesh clouds pure knowledge, when a person tries, in accordance with his own will, to make himself capable of doing whatever he wishes. Therefore he remains blinded until he feels both himself and his wounds, so that he displeases himself, reflecting how he can stand if he has departed from God.

[Col. 0811D] That a human being, strengthened in God after the likeness of a certain firmament, ought always diligently to contemplate him and his works, because God made the human being, among all creatures, especially rational for knowing and glorifying himself.

XI. In these reflections let a person contemplate almighty God as a seal, affirming all his miracles and signs, and thus strengthening his own house after the likeness of the firmament, so that no terror, whether of fear or of love, may tear him away from God. God therefore placed the firmament as the footstool of his throne, and it has an encircling circle, in likeness of the power of God, which has neither beginning nor end, just as no one can see where a revolving wheel begins or ends. [Col. 0812A] For God’s throne is his eternity, in which he alone sits; and all living beings are sparks of the ray of his splendour, proceeding from him as rays proceed from the sun. And how could God be known to be life except through living things which glorify him, since, praising his glory, they proceeded from him? Therefore he set living and burning sparks toward the brightness of his countenance; they behold that he has neither beginning nor end, and, having no weariness in looking upon him, they gaze upon him eagerly and without disgust; nor will this contemplation ever pass away. But how would it be known that he alone is eternal if he were not thus contemplated by the angels? If he had not these sparks, how would his glory appear full? And how would it become known that he is eternal, [Col. 0812B] if no brightness proceeded from him? For there is no creature which does not have some ray—namely greenness, seeds, flowers, or beauty; otherwise it would not be a creature. And if God did not possess the power to make all things, where would his power be?

That God marked the beauty of his works in the first angel; that, in order to show in what region of the world hell lies, he illuminated three regions by the presence of the sun and moon but left the fourth—that is, the northern—region empty of light; and that darkness is exposed by the brilliance of light, while light is more pleasing through the contrast of darkness.

XII. God marked all the beauty of the works of his power in the first angel, adorning him with stars, with the beauty of verdure, and with every kind of [Col. 0812C] shining precious stone, as though he were a star-studded heaven; and he named him Lucifer, “Light-bearer,” because he bore light from him who alone is eternal. For I have displayed my works in three walls—that is, in the east, south, and west—but I have left the fourth wall, in the north, empty, where neither sun nor moon shines. Therefore in that region, beyond the firmament, is hell, which has neither a roof above nor a foundation beneath. And the darkness which exists there is also a ministry of all the luminous things of my praise; for how would light be known except through darkness? And how would darkness be recognized except through the radiant brilliance of my ministers? If this were not so, my power would lack fullness, and all my miracles would not be named. But now my power is full and perfect, and there is no defect in my miracles. Since light is without darkness, it is called light. For the seeing eye is light, but blindness is darkness. By these two things all matters are known, whether good or evil: by light, indeed, the works of God; but by darkness, flight from God, which does not touch the light—in those, that is, who through their proud side refuse to confess him.

Concerning the pride or swelling of the first angel and his followers against God, their casting down into the place of darkness, and the cry of the blessed angels who detest them.

XIII. An innumerable multitude of sparks, [Col. 0813A] which attended the first angel before his ruin, shone in the splendour of all his adornments, as the world is illuminated by light. But when he perceived that in all his adornment he ought to serve God, he withdrew from love of him and stretched out toward darkness, saying within himself: “It is very glorious for me to act by myself and to make works, as I see God doing.” His whole company agreed with him, saying: “We shall set the throne of our lord in the north, against the Most High.” And they deliberated within themselves that they would always make error and schism with God’s ministers, because their lord would be of power and magnificence as great as their Most High’s. Then the eyes of the one eternity blazed forth, and eternity itself thundered with a great peal; and through the ministries of the angels it cast down the first transgressor with his entire host. [Col. 0813B] And the angels of God cried in the voice of thunder: “What wicked presumption can make itself equal to God our Creator, who is from himself? But because you, who exist by his command, have held this judgment of yourself—that you wished to be like him—you shall go into ruin.” Immediately he fell backward, with the others clinging to him, into the place of the aforesaid darkness like heavy lead, because he wished to wage war against God, whose works he did not see shining in darkness.

That God, in the hidden counsel which he had from eternity—that he himself would become man—made the human being in his image and likeness, to resist the devil, who was always unable to discover this mystery, and to take his place; and that in the human being, compacted of soul, bones, and [Col. 0813C] flesh, he recapitulated all the creatures of the greater world.

XIV. Therefore God himself made open war against him, namely in such a way that he looked upon his own garment, which he had possessed in his knowledge without beginning. Satan, who had fled from him, will never be able perfectly to behold this garment until he has completed all his warfare against him; then he will see it in the greatest pain of his confusion, when he is wholly confounded by that same just Judge at the end of the ages. And in his ancient counsel, which was always with him, God ordained how he would accomplish that work, and he formed a human being from muddy earth, just as he had ordered that person’s form before the ages; even as [Col. 0813D] the human heart contains rationality within itself and arranges all sounding words which it subsequently sends forth. So also God made through his Word when he created all things, because in the Father the Word, who is the Son, lay hidden, as the heart lies hidden in a human being. And God made the form of the human being in his image and likeness, because he wished that this form should also cover the holy divinity. Therefore he marked all creatures in the human being, just as every creature proceeded through his Word.

Thus, in the human head—that is, in the encircling wheel—is the crown of the brain, to which a ladder is set, having steps of ascent: by the eyes in seeing, by the ears in hearing, by the nostrils in smelling, and by the mouth in speaking. In these the human being sees, knows, distinguishes, divides, [Col. 0814A] and names all creatures. For God formed the human being and enlivened him with the living breath, which is the soul; he also compacted him with flesh and blood and strengthened him by building him up with bones, just as earth is strengthened by stones. For as earth cannot exist without stones, so a human being could not exist without bones. The firmament likewise does not possess sun, moon, and stars apart from the appointed places in which they perform their course, for these heavenly bodies could by no means be established without the designation of their places. Therefore all their places were fixed in proper measure, so that the wheel-like circle of the firmament might revolve rightly. All these things are likewise marked in the human form, although not in the same order or with the same perfection as they exist in the higher regions; [Col. 0814B] and they also pertain to the soul.

How the outward bearing, or form, of the human being is assigned to the soul according to its inward progress or decline.

XV. The summit of the head signifies the beginning of the soul’s work. With its encircling rationality, it disposes and orders every human work; and the soul itself, existing as the crown, discerns in the human body those things which the body seeks and desires. It performs these by ascending and descending four steps: sight, hearing, smell, and taste, through which it also understands and senses creatures. Its fleshly vessel stretches itself with it toward creatures, drawing them to itself according to its will. With [Col. 0814C] every growing creature, it flies like air through all the body’s desires, accomplishing them; and through knowledge of the names of creatures according to the body, it rises either into love or into hatred of them.

For the height and breadth of a human being, when the arms and hands are extended equally from the breast, are equal; just as the firmament has equal length and breadth. Through the measurement of human length and breadth, which are equal in a person, knowledge of good and evil is understood: it knows the good in usefulness and evil in uselessness. Through the taste of the flesh and blood of the other members, the soul is ensnared as a beast is caught by a hunter, so that the soul can scarcely sigh before [Col. 0814D] the body fulfils its desires; and afterward it often makes the body sigh with it.

That in their constitution the firmament and the human being have received much likeness from God their maker, and what this demonstrates in the human soul.

XVI. The roundness of the human head displays the roundness of the firmament; and the straight and equal measure of that head demonstrates the straight and equal measure of the firmament. For the head has a proper measure everywhere, just as the firmament is established in equal measure, so that it may have a regular circuit on every side and no part of it may exceed another part improperly. For God fashioned the human being in accordance with the firmament, [Col. 0815A] strengthened human power with the forces of the elements, and consolidated the inner parts of the human being with their powers, so that a person draws them in and sends them out by breathing, as the sun which illuminates the world extends its rays from itself and draws them back again.

Thus the roundness and equality of the human head signify that the soul acts in sins according to the will of the flesh, and again restores itself to righteousness through sighs. In this too there is equality: as it has delighted in transgressions, so, grieving for them, it afflicts itself, and does this through shame. For the soul stands in shame and does not delight in sins; yet through the taste of the flesh it acts with the flesh. When a person has lived in sins until wearied by them, the soul, often overcome through shame, calls the person back from them. Likewise the soul is overcome through the nature of the flesh. Thus, as long as body and soul live together, they have a strong conflict together: where the flesh delights in sins, there the soul grieves. [Col. 0815B] And this is a great shame to evil spirits, because they have never been able to erase repentance from the souls of the righteous; whereas they, in their fall, because of the great hatred which they have against God, never consider penitently what they have done. In these ways the soul displays roundness and equality within itself, because knowledge of good contends against knowledge of evil, and knowledge of evil resists knowledge of good. Each is tested by the other. But knowledge of good is like the full moon when it overcomes the flesh by acting well; when it is overcome, it is like the moon in waning, whose circle appears shadowed.

[Col. 0815C] That in the human head, through three equal distinctions of measurement—from the crown to the throat—the three upper circles of the firmament, with the two circles interposed to them, are represented; how the density of these circles is assigned through an equal division around the head; and how these likewise correspond by signification to the powers of the soul.

XVII. In the human head are also signified the three upper elements: from the surface of the skull to the forehead, bright fire with the black fire beneath it; from the forehead to the tip of the nose, pure ether; and from the nose to the throat, [Col. 0815D] watery air with the strong, white, bright air placed beneath it. These regions are separated from one another by equal measure, just as the density of the higher fire with the black fire, the density of pure ether, and the density of watery air with the strong, white, bright air are of equal measure.

For there are three powers in the soul: comprehension, by which it comprehends heavenly and earthly things in the power of God; understanding, by which it understands many things, even knowing that sins are evil and neglecting them through repentance; and motion, by which it moves everywhere within itself when it accomplishes holy works, with its dwelling-place, after the examples of the righteous. This comprehension and understanding unite themselves as one with the soul’s motion, so that if the soul comprehended more than it could understand [Col. 0816A] or move, it would be in an unjust measure. These same powers are harmonious in the soul in this way: no one exceeds another.

For the soul’s comprehension encompasses the whole body with all its appendages, moving everything in it in proper measure toward those things which the flesh desires through sensation and taste; just as a builder rightly measures his building for people to dwell in it. The body is moved through the soul; nor can the soul fail to move the body toward various works, because it understands what the flesh desires, since the flesh lives through it. The soul, being life, is also living fire in the body; but the body is a made work. Therefore it cannot refrain from operating in two ways: either according to the taste of the flesh or according to the soul’s desire. The soul’s good work is like a most beautiful building before God and the angels; but its evil work appears like a building made of mud and defiled by much dung. [Col. 0816B] Therefore the soul which performs good works is praised by the angels of God, while the soul which performs evil works according to the taste of the flesh is rejected from praise.

Likewise, in the straight and equal measure extending from the top of the human head forward to the eyebrows, to each ear, and backward to the beginning of the neck, the equal density of the elements with their attached constitutions is signified. In the soul, likewise, three powers are equal: exhalation, knowledge, and sensation, by which it accomplishes its works. Through exhalation it begins what it can do, and this is like the front part of the head; through knowledge it extends itself, as it were, to both ears; and through sensation it bends back, as it were, to the beginning of the neck. These powers are equal in this way: the soul does not begin by exhaling more than knowledge can comprehend or sensation can bear. Thus they act harmoniously because none exceeds another, just as the head has a proper measure.

A description of certain measures found in the lips, ears, shoulders, and throat of the human being; how, in accordance with these, the inward person ought to conduct himself in God’s work or in repentance; and that evil spirits and the impenitent are often greatly confounded because they cannot take repentance away from a human being.

[Col. 0816D] XVIII. The upper and lower lips, both of which alike expel the phlegm of the head and belly, are of one measure in the human mouth, just as the black fire, effecting purification in God’s vengeance, and the strong, white, bright air, moderating it by tempering, are of equal density. This is also shown in the measure which proceeds equally from one human ear to the other across the back and slope of the head, from the ear-openings to the shoulders, and from the shoulders to the end of the throat.

These things show that a person, casting away from himself evils of both soul and body, in the higher things—that is, heavenly matters—and in the lower—that is, earthly matters—ought with equal zeal to praise God with his mouth, because [Col. 0817A] he is the protector of souls and bodies alike. Likewise, the one measure, as stated above, extending from ear to ear, from the ears to the shoulders, and from the shoulders to the end of the throat, signifies that a person, receiving God’s commandments through the ears, faithfully placing them on the shoulders, and as it were drawing them into himself through the throat, ought to preserve an equal and discerning measure in all things, so that he may attain that equity where there is no weakness.

For as long as the body sins, the soul, given over to sins in the body, is troubled; and in proportion as the body is afflicted through abstinence in repentance, the soul rejoices in the reward of eternal glory. For as a person considers the beginning of his works, so he should diligently consider their end and their merits. The soul is sent into the human form in order that this form may be enlivened through it. And because it acknowledges that it has come from its Creator, therefore even a person situated either in some sect or in the right faith names God, since he has this implanted within him from the good powers of the soul. [Col. 0817B] Therefore, seeking God’s name, he rises toward the heights and sifts out a discipline through a certain law by which he may venerate the one whom he names.

The soul also knows that God’s judgment will fall upon transgression of the law. Therefore, because of the sins which it has stored up in sorrow, it sometimes causes its covering to bring forth tears, just as phlegm is expelled through the lips; and with this sorrow it so takes hold of the body in which it lies hidden that it makes the body blush for its unjust works. [Col. 0817C] Nevertheless, the body follows the taste of the flesh and often resists the soul, lest it rise to that height in which it senses God; and so it blinds the soul. Yet it cannot oppress it so completely that the soul does not grieve for sins, even though the person delights in them. Evil spirits never possessed such repentance; hence they are deeply ashamed because they cannot take it away from a human being.

Concerning the two powers of the soul: one is assisted in things pertaining to God; the other exercises its office in enlivening and governing its body.

XIX. The soul has two powers, by which it tempers the labour and rest of its endeavours with equal strength. By one it ascends to the height by sensing God; by the other it possesses the whole body in which it dwells, acting in it because it delights to act in the body, since that body was formed by God and the soul is swift to bring the body’s work to completion. [Col. 0817D] It rises into the brain, heart, blood, marrow, and entire body, filling it; nor does it raise the body beyond, or more than, the body’s capacity permits. For although the soul dwelling in the body strives to perform many good things, it cannot advance further than divine grace grants it.

It also often acts according to the taste of the flesh until the blood is somewhat dried in the veins through fatigue and sweat is emitted through the marrow; then it withdraws itself into rest until it warms the blood of the flesh and fills the marrow. [Col. 0818A] Thus it awakens the body to watchfulness and renews it for labour. For while it sometimes gives itself to fleshly desires, it often falls into weariness of them; but when it has renewed its powers thereby, it turns itself wholly back to God’s service. But when it acts according to its own desires, raising itself to God, it follows the words of David, who says by my inspiration:

Words of David and the meaning in which they should be understood as pertaining to the various exercises of soul and body.

XX. “Protect me under the shadow of your wings from the face of the wicked who have afflicted me” (Psalm 16). This is clear in meaning: You who are the defender of all the faithful, defend me in the repose of your most powerful powers—I who am under your authority, adoring and worshipping you and looking not toward a strange and deceitful god. Deliver me from the most wicked and shameful desires of evil spirits, which afflict me in the pleasure of the flesh.

Therefore, in the perfection of this victory, the soul says: “O flesh, and O members in which I dwell, I rejoice exceedingly because I have been sent into you; for when you consent to me, you send me toward eternal rewards.” But the soul which perceives that depraved works touch it speaks sorrowfully: “Alas, because I have been sent into such a dwelling, which draws me into the shadow of death; for its pleasure makes me run like a mill and perform works of death.”

[Col. 0818C] That, as the firmament and the various properties of its circles fulfil the offices of the earth, so the whole body is governed by the head and the senses which chiefly flourish in it; and that, correspondingly, the soul has been given a ruling principle—reason—by which it seeks heavenly things, and other powers by which it administers the body.

XXI. The whole human body is joined to its head, just as the earth, with all its appendages, cleaves to the firmament; and the whole person is governed through the sensitivity of the head, just as the various offices of the earth are fulfilled through the firmament. In the same way, experience of heavenly and earthly things belongs to the soul, and rationality—by which it senses heavenly and earthly things—is implanted in it. For as the Word of God passed through all things in creating them, so the soul passes through the whole body in acting with it.

The soul is the greenness of the flesh, because through it the human body [Col. 0818D] grows and flourishes, just as earth is fruitful through moisture. The same soul is also the body’s moisture, because it moistens it so that it does not dry up, as rain drenches the earth. If the moisture of rain descends properly, orderly, and not excessively, it makes the earth germinate; but if it flows down disorderly, it destroys the earth by suffocating it together with its seed. Certain powers proceed from the soul in enlivening the human body, just as moisture proceeds from water; and therefore the soul delights in acting with the body.

If a person acts according to the soul’s desire, all his works become good; but if according to the flesh, they will be evil. For the flesh sweats out moisture through the soul, because the soul’s breath moves the flesh as its nature requires; and from the soul’s breath a person has desire for all manner of things. [Col. 0819A] The soul ascends to heavenly things and knows through sensation how it should judge every work according to its merits. And as the whole body is ruled by bodily sensation, so the rational soul gathers to itself all the works of the human limbs, considering what they can perform according to their desires. In this way it makes the human limbs germinate as moisture makes the earth germinate, because it is diffused through the whole human body as moisture is spread throughout the whole earth. And as earth produces useful and useless things, so a human being has within himself a sigh upward and a taste for sin.

[Col. 0819B] Concerning the intervals and reciprocal cooperation of the seven planets; how the same planets are to be marked out in seven places of equal measure from the summit of the human brain to the bottom of the forehead; and how, in accordance with these, the soul, subsisting with its body in five senses, ought to exercise itself in good dispositions and works according to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

XXII. From the upper summit of the vessel of the brain to the furthest limit of the human forehead, seven places are separated from one another by equal measure. Through these, the seven planets, equally distant from one another in the firmament, are represented: the highest planet is marked at the aforesaid summit, the moon is shown at the aforesaid extremity of the forehead, and the sun is displayed in the intervening space. The remaining planets are marked on either side of this position—two above [Col. 0819C] and two below—and are equally distant both from one another and from the boundary of the sun’s place and of the other planets, because these spaces in the human head differ from one another by equal measure, just as these planets in the firmament are separated by equal measurements of space.

The highest planet is marked at the summit of the head because it has a larger circuit of revolution than the others. The moon is assigned to the forehead because, as shame is marked in the human forehead, so in the moon, which appears openly like a forehead, the times and qualities of times are distinguished. The sun is placed in the middle because it is, as it were, prince of the others, having above itself the protection of two planets, like a shield against the higher fire, and beneath itself the support of two others, sustaining both itself and the moon. But by as much space as the highest planet is distant from the sun in its higher degree, so much also is the moon distant from it in the lowest degree of its circuit; the others, as stated above, having equal spaces between themselves.

[Col. 0819D] The upper and lower part of the firmament is round like a turned bowl; and in its upper roundness the sun is placed, passing through that firmament above and below and pouring forth its brilliance as wine is poured from a bowl. These things signify that the soul in the human body, from the beginning of its works to their completion, ought to venerate with equal zeal the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: at the beginning of its action it should approach wisdom; at its end it should have fear; and in its middle it should place fortitude, fortifying itself with understanding and counsel in heavenly things and surrounding itself with knowledge and piety in earthly things. [Col. 0820A] It ought to embrace these with equal devotion as aids to itself.

Accordingly, the soul must take care first to extend itself wisely, but at the end to restrain itself fearfully and with shame. Between these it should adorn itself with fortitude and with the beauty of understanding and counsel, and should strengthen itself with knowledge and piety, as stated above. Each of these is joined to the others, completing every good work in integrity. For the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of fortitude, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord so instruct the human soul that it walks wisely in true strength and has fear in that strength, while it likewise holds itself with an even mind toward the heavenly Creator in the other five gifts of this kind. The movement of the rational soul and the work of the body with its five senses—which together constitute the whole person—have an equal measure: the soul does not move the body beyond what it can do, nor does the body act beyond what is moved by the soul; nor do the distinct senses separate themselves from one another. Rather, they hold together in lofty strength and illumine the whole person, in both higher and lower things, toward every good.

[Col. 0820C] That the human brain, divided into three cells and furnishing sensitivity to the whole body, holds the place of the sun, which illuminates three regions of the world and strengthens all things on earth by moderating or warming them; and that it also kindles the moon with its fire.

XXIII. The human brain, consisting of three cells and no more, subject to moisture and furnishing sensitivity and flourishing power to the entire body, displays the powers of the sun. The sun illuminates the eastern, southern, and western regions, but avoids the northern; it often imparts greenness to the earth through the wholesome sweetness of dew and rain, and strengthens the creatures of the whole world by tempering them with its power. Likewise the brain is held in the strength of the skull, as the sun’s powers are strengthened by the heat of the higher bright fire.

[Col. 0820D] When the sun makes its course through the length of the days, its fire is more dangerous on earth than when it declines, as though hiding its face. For when it declines [Note: [Col. 0819D] Something appears to be missing.], and when the stars meet it and sustain it with the air, it descends in this manner beneath the footstool of the Lord’s feet, remains there in its station, and governs all things which are beneath the earth, as a hen warms her chicks. Then, rising over the earth through the bright day, it strengthens all things upon it, just as a hen draws her chicks from the eggs. A human being works by day and sleeps at night, just as the sun works in the two aforesaid ways above the earth and beneath it: by day it shines above the earth, while [Col. 0821A] at night, with its descent, the earth above is darkened. And as, through the powers of the soul, human flesh revives in its weakness—for the soul sustains its flesh and blood so that it does not fail—so the moon is kindled from the fire of the sun whenever it wanes.

That likewise the soul, governing its body by its powers and worshipping God as one in the Trinity, seems by imitating that planet to make, in alternation, a kind of day or night: now strengthened by the spirit of fortitude, signified by the sun, and shining, raised high by the light of holy works; now acting while succumbing to the desires of the flesh.

XXIV. [Col. 0821B] Likewise the soul knowingly governs the human body through its powers, when the person understands and senses in goodness, perfection, and holiness, knows what pertains to God, worships the true God in the Trinity, and does not seek another god in deception. The same powers of the soul are joined together and operate as one. When the soul is touched by the spirit of fortitude in such a way that it considers everywhere the beginning of works, their perfection, and their end, it turns away from evil things and thus brings into the body in which it dwells the sweetness of heavenly gifts. Through these it brings all the body’s members to integrity, because its powers are united through the strength of God’s power.

But when that same fortitude strengthens the soul in this way, it makes the entire human body serve under its dominion, so that it often draws forth tears with groans; then it holds the person in such humility and tranquillity that he can govern himself in both worldly and spiritual matters, fittingly instructed in every good thing. [Col. 0821C] Therefore, through good endeavour, the soul rises high like one acting well in daylight. But when it is overcome by consenting to the flesh’s desire, it is depressed as in nocturnal sleep, now fortifying itself with strength, now joining itself to sloth.

Through good endeavour it is like day, considering all things; through sloth it is like night, foreseeing nothing. But as night is sometimes illumined by the moon and darkened again when the moon is withdrawn, so human works are mixed: now bright, now dark. When the soul, compelled through the body, performs evil with it, its power is darkened through lack of the light of truth. But when afterwards it feels itself burdened by sins, it raises itself upward against the will of the flesh, afflicting the flesh and reproaching it for all evil works. Thus the light of blessedness rises when the night of sins has been overcome, so that through the soul evil knowledge is overcome together with the flesh, and the flesh is subsequently chastised through repentance and correction of its depraved works. [Col. 0821D]

When the flesh is constrained in this way, the soul makes it seek heavenly things with itself, because, strengthened with it by the spirit of fortitude, it swiftly subjects it also to the fear of the Lord. For the soul helps the flesh and the flesh the soul, because every work is accomplished through soul and flesh alike; therefore the soul revives with the flesh in doing good and holy works. Yet the flesh often suffers weariness when it works with the soul. Therefore the soul then yields to the flesh and permits it to take pleasure in some work, just as a mother makes a crying infant laugh. In this way the flesh performs some good works with the soul, yet mingled with certain sins; and the soul tolerates this lest the flesh be overwhelmed. For as the flesh lives through the soul, so the soul revives by acting well with the flesh, because it has been placed in the work of the Lord’s hands.

As the sun rises, overcoming the night, until midday, so a human being advances upward by avoiding depraved works. As the sun declines after midday, so the soul consents to the flesh. And as the moon is rekindled by the sun lest it fail, so human flesh is sustained through the powers of the soul lest it perish.

[Col. 0822B] That, as all the veins of the body supply heat to the brain, which draws moisture from the inner organs, so the upper circles stand by the sun with their fires, lest it fail through heat when it at times diffuses dew and rain; and that correspondingly there are found harmonies or discords between soul and flesh.

XXV. And because the brain is moist and soft, it is cold; all the veins and all the members of the body supply it with heat. So too all the higher things that shine in fire attend upon the sun—which at times causes dew and rain to descend upon the earth—supplying it with fire, lest it fail in heat. But because it is moistened by moisture and strengthened by heat, it supports and governs the whole body, just as moisture and heat united cause the whole earth to put forth growth.

For moisture rises to the brain from the heart, the lungs, the liver, and all a person's internal organs, and fills it; and when the brain has been filled with the moisture of these organs, some of that same moisture descends to the other inner parts and hastens to fill them. Likewise, the soul's knowledge draws forth the moisture of tears when sins grow cold within it; and the tenor of uprightness, together with the other good works, brings it the heat of heavenly desires. Thus also the other virtues come to the aid of fortitude, which imparts the moisture of holiness to every faithful person. And when the soul is thus suffused with the dew and heat of the Holy Spirit, it subjects the flesh to itself and compels it to serve God along with it.

From good thoughts and upright confessions, [Col. 0822D] concerning the usefulness of justice and the fullness of inward desires, the vigor of holiness reaches toward the soul's knowledge and strengthens it so that, through that same greenness, the whole person may be fortified against every adversity by such safeguards of patience that thereafter he cannot be moved into the various paths of vices. For just as the higher stars supply fire to the sun, so all a person's inner parts bring the soul's powers to their respective functions; and while the soul, in order to accomplish justice, disregards sins, it ascends upward with rationality. But when afterward it perceives that the body is in want, it condescends to it lest it fail.

For the soul is a living breath that animates the entire human body; nevertheless, against its will it is often subject to the flesh's pleasure. Wishing to persist in good, [Col. 0823A] it is like the sun; but the flesh, abiding in its own taste, is like the moon. Thus, when the flesh fails through sinning, just as the moon suffers diminution, that same soul nevertheless often raises itself upward like the sun against the will of the flesh; and so the person rises again through its complaint, just as the moon is rekindled by the sun. Therefore through moisture the flesh takes pleasure in sins, and through heat it mourns in repentance, because moisture is from the flesh and heat from the soul. Through these two every work, namely evil and good, is accomplished, just as by them the strength of the earth brings forth everything useless and useful.

For this condition has been established in a human being: the flesh delights in sins, and the soul is afflicted by them, so that all human works are carried out by flesh and soul, [Col. 0823B] because the soul dislikes the evils that please the flesh. For the flesh is mortal, but the soul immortal; the soul lives without the flesh, whereas the flesh cannot live without the soul.

The soul, indeed, is a rational breath, and its wisdom is in the dwelling-place of the heart. By this wisdom it reckons and orders everything, as the master of a household arranges all his possessions in his house. From it, moreover, it possesses prudence, by which it rightly assigns everything useful to its vessel, just as the heart is covered by the lung; and from this too it gathers discernment to itself, distributing everything justly, as the human internal organs are themselves rightly and discreetly joined together.

For the soul is fiery; consequently it warms all the paths assigned to the heart, and cooks them together into one, holding them jointly [Col. 0823C] so that they are not separated one from another; and it fills them, so that none of them lacks anything. Thus also, together with wisdom, it prudently orders in thought all the body's functions; and, ascending to God through faith in good and holy intention, it recognizes that it was sent by him. For as moisture rises from the lower parts of the body to the brain, so the soul, by knowing God with holy desire, draws all the functions of the human body upward. And as that same moisture descends again, filling the lower parts of the body, so too the soul condescends to the body, lest its functions operate to God's offense.

That, just as the brain and intestines, when they overflow with humors, need purging, so too the air and earth in autumn seem to be cleansed in certain places—the former by long coagulated threads, the latter by foul foam—and that in the same way the flesh is proved to be dried by venereal sweating, and the soul purified by the labor of repentance. [Col. 0823D]

XXVI. The brain also, when full, foams forth rheum from itself; and the internal organs, when they are full, make evacuation. These things occur frequently in a person, just as moisture and heat descend upon the earth and make it germinate; but after its fruits have fully attained maturity, moisture and heat are drawn upward again.

Therefore, at the beginning of cold weather, when winter seems to be approaching, the air rises upward and is coagulated in some degree by the sun's heat, so that it flies, stretching itself out like threads; and then the earth too is softened by the moisture from above and spews out foul foam. Similarly, when the functions of the flesh are fulfilled, the flesh [Col. 0824A] emits sweat; and thus pleasure arises in it, and afterward the person begins to act according to the taste of pleasure.

But when the soul, in its knowledge, perceives that it has performed deeds according to the will and concupiscence of the flesh, it often inspires the flesh with the affliction of sins because it has wrought evil. Then it withdraws itself from the flesh's concupiscence, lest it know sin; and thus the body too desires to abstain from sins. Nor does the soul ever refrain from afflicting the body and bringing upon it the harshness due to sins committed. Hence a person is always in affliction: that is, the soul has a complaint against the flesh while the flesh nourishes pleasure. Therefore evil is recognized in the work of sin as in an evacuation.

For the soul often acts amid the flesh's pleasure, which afterward [Col. 0824B] it rejects, just as the earth, touched by moisture and heat, brings forth useless and useful herbs. And when the long-standing habit of sins makes sins hateful to a person, then the soul often inspires the body to seek repentance for them from God. So too moisture and heat are often drawn upward again; and thus, between these two, a person works both evil and good.

At times also, when a person's flesh attends to its own pleasure, the soul stretches itself toward the heat of rationality, although it is often impeded by its earthly dwelling. For when the body, by its strength, draws back the coagulation of its conception through sinning, the rational soul grows cold by consenting to the flesh. Yet afterward that same [Col. 0824C] soul stretches itself upward toward rationality; setting evil works before it, it also touches the human heart and makes it groan and weep. In this way it overcomes the flesh, so that the body does not carry out the effect of sin according to the strength of the soul, but, touched by the dew from above of the Holy Spirit, lays aside its former hardness and, considering its sins, reckons them as mud.

That the vessel of the brain corresponds to the higher fire which kindles the sun, and that the moisture of the watery air provides moderation for that sun and its heat, and sets a limit to its course lest it burn up the things beneath it; and how, in accordance with these things, the soul, placed under God's power and judgment and endowed with rationality, ought discreetly to govern both itself and its body in all things.

XXVII. Therefore the vessel of the brain, which stretches from the forehead toward [Col. 0824D] the eyes, signifies the higher fire beneath which the sun burns. That fire is mingled with the gentle moisture of the watery air; and this moisture is the sun's point, through which it cannot pass beyond the boundary of its place. Rising to the sun through the purity of the ether, this moisture moderates its burning, lest it consume the things upon the earth by excessive heat.

So too the soul, possessing knowledge and rationality within itself together with manifest modesty and salutary circumspection, displays the power of God, under which is that fortitude which imparts blessed sighs to the minds of faithful people. Those same sighs restrain the judgment of God's fortitude, lest it show itself in excessive severity; and by true repentance they so soothe the examination of that same fortitude that, when a person repents, it consigns his sins [Col. 0825A] to oblivion.

And as wind makes fire burn, so rationality moves and illuminates the human soul. For rationality is in the soul as wind is, and as light is in fire; and the soul is a breath sent by God into a human being, unfailing and rational. As fire would not be fire without its burning, so the soul would not be intelligible without rationality, while the rest of creation passes like wind because it is not flaming fire.

For rationality guides the soul everywhere together with knowledge, considering things in a thousand ways and knowing what a person does. Hence, when the soul itself understands good in its knowledge, it burns in joy like the sun and is heavenly. Yet the soul cannot always remain in this burning of heavenly things, because the human flesh would fail. Therefore it gives the body refreshment in some matter, just as my Son, while bodily remaining in the world, at one time prayed, at another time labored, and afterward refreshed his body. He did this without sin, because he was conceived without sin.

And as the point restrains the sun lest it pass beyond its boundary, so the soul, by consenting to the body, tempers it lest it fail. It does this in great purity, so that the human body may not be mocked by evil works, nor destroyed through excessive heavenly intention, just as moisture tempers the sun lest it be consumed. Therefore the soul loves discernment in all things; and consequently, whenever the human body eats or drinks without discernment, or does anything else of this kind indiscreetly, [Col. 0825C] the soul's powers are torn asunder. For everything must be done with discernment, since a human being cannot always be in heavenly things.

And as the earth is split by the excessive heat of the sun, and through unsuitable rain the sprout does not arise beneficially, whereas through the right union of heat and moisture the earth brings forth all useful things, so by just moderation all works, heavenly and earthly alike, are discreetly and rightly ordered and accomplished. Those whose heaven has been illumined loved and still love this discernment; but the devil was unwilling, and is unwilling, to possess it, because he tends either toward excessive height or excessive depth, and therefore, having fallen, will not rise again.

That, just as the blackness of the brain, coagulated by heat and moisture, diffuses phlegm or bruising through the human body, so the black fire in the second circle brings storms and lightning into the world; and that likewise the soul, corrupted by pride, and the flesh, corrupted by concupiscences, have varied conflicts, resisting one another in turn. [Col. 0825D]

XXVIII. The brain also has a certain blackness above, because the breath of a person, being moist, sends that moisture upward; and at its extremity, where it proceeds no farther, it makes blackness. This blackness resists burning, lest the brain burst into fever, just as the black fire restrains bright fire lest it pass beyond its boundary. The same blackness of the brain sends phlegm and bruising into the rest of the body, just as this black fire [Col. 0826A] often produces storms, thunder, and hail upon the earth.

In this way, when the soul stretches its knowledge upward in favor of pride, it as it were blackens it above; because there human sighs, extended into pride, lack the purity of true light. Thus this same disturbance opposes heavenly fortitude in such a way that that fortitude does not stir the same knowledge with the heat of heavenly desires. So too God's vengeance, which gradually examines human sins, often restrains its power lest it utterly crush the sinful person.

And the darkness of that same knowledge frequently brings concupiscence and the recklessness of sins upon a negligent person, because he does not look to heavenly judgment; just as that same judgment, in vengeance, crushes the diverse transgressions [Col. 0826B] of offenders.

Indeed, because the soul has an embrace of love for the body with which it works, it often consents to it. But when it again recognizes the blackness of this consent in fiery rationality, it causes the flesh to afflict itself by repentance, and strengthens it again lest the person fail in his senses. For the soul remains in the human body according to what it finds in that body's humors, just as a bee makes its honeycomb with honey in its vessel, now pure, now turbid.

When the soul thus ascends with fiery rationality so that the body cannot bear that ascent, it descends again and strengthens the body, because the flesh is like fragile earth. Thus soul and body have diverse conflicts between themselves, because a person performs bright and dark works with soul and flesh.

That the whole human body is strengthened by the brain as the upper and lower regions are strengthened by the sun, which is in the midst of the planets; and concerning the fact that, with three parts of the world illuminated by the sun, God left the fourth dark and cold; and the mystical meaning of these things according to the inward person. [Col. 0826C]

XXIX. And, as has been said, the whole human body is sustained by the powers of the brain, just as the upper and lower regions are strengthened by the sun. For the sun shines upon the upper and lower regions and courses through the whole firmament except the northern quarter. When God strengthened the whole earth together with its creatures, he left one place empty, so that creation might recognize [Col. 0826D] what and how great the brightness of God is; for through darkness light is honored, and the dark part serves the bright part. This is the empty place, because Lucifer chose it when he wished to make himself equal to his Lord.

The sun rises in the east and grows stronger and stronger in its heat at noon; but after midday it declines toward the west, and so completes its course until morning. And because it does not proceed into the northern region, there is coldness on earth in the morning and around evening.

But I, who am without beginning, am fire by which all lights are kindled, light that covers darkness; nor can darkness comprehend the light. Therefore light does not mingle itself with darkness, nor can darkness pass into light. For as a person was established by God in good knowledge, which is the light [Col. 0827A] of truth, and then declines toward evil in bad knowledge, which has an empty place in which there is no ordering of merits or rewards, so heaven and earth, light and darkness, are signified also in a person.

Indeed, all human works are governed through knowledge, just as the other virtues are held together through the spirit of fortitude. For this spirit is powerful both in spiritual and secular matters, and defends a person from the snares of the ancient serpent, who, empty of all blessedness, displays the brightness of God, so that what is good may be known through evil; for a servant ought to be subject to his lord.

For fortitude, being strong in the beginning and in the performance of good works, avoids evils in a person after their completion, and thus returns to its beginning and does not seek evil, because in both the beginning and the end of perversity the heat of the Holy Spirit is absent; instead there are numbness and negligence, drawing a person toward harmful things.

But he who is without beginning is this light, which kindles all shining things and drives away every adversity of darkness, because it cannot be destroyed by them. And as a faithful person is governed by God, while a perverse person is alienated from him, so all the elements in a person are orderly distinguished. The soul too appears like fire, but rationality in it is like light; and it is suffused with radiant rationality in the same way that the world is illuminated by the sun, because through rationality it foresees and knows all the works that it performs in a person.

For a person has taste [Col. 0827C] and desire within himself, and through these two the blood in his veins is moved together with the heat of his marrow. Thus that person acts as a wheel completes its course when it is impelled to run, because the body, having taste and desire, drives the soul this way and that, so that in accordance with these impulses it often directs its steps.

What the rising or setting of the sun signifies in human actions; and what it signifies when it is at one time hidden by clouds or excessive storms and does not appear, and at another, after these have been cleared away, restores its light to the earth.

XXX. The sun too, obscured by a black cloud and overwhelmed by lightning, thunder, and excessive rains, does not appear; but when all these cease, it pours out its light again. In this it signifies the human soul: when it is so oppressed by the body that it acts according to the flesh's concupiscence, the light of rationality in it is clouded, because anger is like lightning, avarice like thunder, and unlawful desires of the flesh like excessive rains.

But when afterward it has cleansed itself from these through repentance, it is again illuminated in the brightness of true light, hoping that it can be delivered and saved. Therefore the soul breathes out rationality as fire sends forth sparks, and through it discerns heavenly and earthly things. Hence, if the body is so overcome by it that it performs just and good works, it will rejoice in eternal life; but if it is thus [Col. 0828A] oppressed by the body that, neglecting good, it does what is evil, it consigns itself to the places of Tartarus.
