It also rejects the devil, who wished to be like God; and by this it is separated from the northern region: whether it performs good or evil, it does not call itself God, but through rationality knows itself to be a creature from God. The soul also often teaches its earthly vessel to perform works that are heavenly; again it consents to the flesh's concupiscences, from which, tearing itself away again, it afflicts its vessel when it rises to its duties, sifting out by repentance all evils in that same vessel, as barley is cast out from wheat.

These are the soul's works. For when it works good, it is like the sun burning at noon; but when it breathes toward evil, it is like the sun declining toward its setting. Yet when it afterward rises through repentance, it is as the sun when it turns away its brightness from storms.

Nevertheless, when a person grows through the powers of the soul, while his veins and marrow are not yet full or strengthened, he cannot yet know heavenly things because of the body's tenderness, nor can he discern infernal punishments, because his body has not yet been brought to maturity. Thus the soul is then unoccupied with its vessel, because that person then has no fear, just as people in the first age of the world lacked fear of the law.

But in the full age of a human being, the soul is strengthened together with the body and compels it to do good works. Yet the body declines from its will, exercising its powers according to the flesh's concupiscences; and it strives to do this [Col. 0828C] as long as it lives, unless it is restrained by repentance through the soul's powers.

That the forehead, situated between the brain and the eyes, gathers the illnesses arising from the brain and the stomach, just as the moon receives what descends from above and rises from below; and that the eyes, by their whites and pupils in their moisture, signify the pure ether, the stars, and vapor rising from the waters beneath; and the manifold consideration of these things in the dispositions of the soul.

XXXI. As has been said, the forehead, with pure ether signified from it down to the end of the nose, stands between the brain and the eyes and sustains the constitution of brain and eyes. It contains in itself the infirmity that arises from the brain and stomach, just as [Col. 0828D] the moon beneath the sun, surrounded by stars, often receives what descends from the upper regions and what rises from the lower.

For the eyes, which behold very many things, show the stars of the firmament, which shine everywhere. Their whiteness signifies the purity of the ether, their brightness its splendor, and the pupil the stars that are in that same ether. Their moisture shows the moisture by which that ether is moistened from the waters below, lest it be injured by the fire above.

This, therefore, is how the soul, placed in true repentance between knowledge and circumspection, impels its vessel through God's grace toward repentance. Modesty also, dwelling between knowledge and circumspection, marks their path, because it proceeds rightly when it loves chastity and, concealing all harmful things within itself, reduces them to nothing lest they break out openly. So too the fear of the Lord, enclosed by the strength of heavenly virtues, rightly regulates within itself eternal and transitory things.

For circumspection, by which a faithful person foresees whatever good things concern him, shows his burning desire for the things above. The consideration of circumspection, by which a person diligently considers the things that he sees to be beneficial to his soul, seeks the sincerity of true repentance; while the penetrating insight of this consideration loves the beauty of that repentance when a person sees himself cleansed from sins. Its intention also, which is like the pupil of the eye, makes clear the burning and shining works that are in it; but forgiveness of sins, groans, and sighs, by which repentance [Col. 0829B] is shaken with the moisture of tears lest it be struck by God's powerful judgment, adorn it.

For the soul looks about on every side as it begins and performs every work, because it is fiery and breathes with air, and accomplishes and discerns all things with knowledge and rationality. The soul, strengthened in the body, begins to act vigorously and desires to do so; but very many infirmities of the flesh meet it in the marrow, blood, and stomach. For the blood of a person grows hot from the heat of the marrow, and the blood of the stomach burns from the weight of foods. These infirmities are a certain obstacle to the soul's powers, because from the ardor of the flesh there springs up incest, which Satan has deceitfully woven; it rises to the soul from earthly things and suggests to it that a human being is flesh and ought to live [Col. 0829C] according to the flesh. Thus the soul itself is often compelled through the body, which is below, to perform evils with it.

For the works of the soul are with a movable body, just as the moon is surrounded by stars. The soul itself, skilful through knowledge, is with the rest of creation, so that the works of its skill, whether they are from the upper or lower regions, are seen and known in its vessel, just as stars shine bright or dark in the firmament. Bright knowledge appears in a person as the whiteness of the eyes; understanding shines in him as their brightness; and rationality shines in him as their pupil. Therefore a person is compelled to strive toward heavenly things with groaning and weeping, where he judges himself unworthy of the reward of eternal recompense because he knows himself burdened with many sins; and so he strives at least to escape the punishments of judgment.

For what reasons tears, gathered from the humors of the body, flow from the eyes, and rains from the lower waters drawn upward flow from clouds; and a careful exposition of these things according to the affections of the soul.

XXXII. When a person is stirred in his heart by either joy or sorrow, the small veins of his brain, chest, and lungs are shaken. Thus the small veins of the chest and lungs send humors upward to the small veins of the brain, which receive them and pour them into the eyes. So they bring the person to tears, just as, when the firmament is stirred by winds at either the beginning of the moon's waxing or waning, [Col. 0830A] it shakes the sea and the other waters of the earth with its sound; and these send forth smoke and moisture from themselves.

But the clouds, receiving this smoke and moisture, stretch them toward the moon; and the moon, drinking them as if thirsty, sends them back again to the clouds and causes them to produce suitable rain. For in this way rain descends upon the earth from the lower waters which the clouds draw upward and then send back again.

So too, when the soul in a person sometimes rejoices from confidence in his salvation, or grieves as though under the pressure of its sins, human knowledge is stirred by fear together with the conscious confession of repentance. Raised upward with these in sighing, and looking about at that person's works, it draws tears from him and makes him mourn. For when the fear of the Lord shakes a person, it compels him, thirsting, to weep amid groans.

Hence it happens that when a person sometimes weeps over the adversity of worldly affairs, he often turns his mind toward the desire for heavenly things, disregarding worldly matters. For when a person departs from God and consigns him to oblivion, his soul immediately trembles; and thus all the person's members, filled with its powers, are moved into an alien path, as though God were not to be revered and feared. But the soul sets before its vessel shame and confusion over sins and makes it sigh, so that these sighs bring forth tears. And from these sighs and tears the greenness of repentance arises.

Therefore, renewed again in good works, the person examines the burdens [Col. 0830C] of his sins with such diligence and repentance that the flesh of his members is somewhat dried up, and such bitterness grows in his heart that he often says within himself: “Why was I born for such great crimes? I have sinned with my soul against God, and with it I do repentance, sighing to God, who deigned to assume Adam's form from the Virgin. Therefore I trust that he will not despise me, but will absolve me from my sins and, through the countenance of his holy humanity, receive me, repentant, in true faith.”

Then soul and body join themselves into one and, in harmony, breathe toward God. For sins do not please the soul; it is compelled to consent to the flesh only through the stupor of carnal concupiscence. If the soul had pleasure in sin, a person would always be befouled in the mire of sins. For the soul does not delight in sins, although it works together with the body, just as the elements that sustain a person do not compel him to sin; yet by God's judgment they judge him in sins, while in good works they show sweetness and gentleness toward him.

Whenever the soul is compelled to perform evils together with the body, it fills the body with sadness, because those works displease the soul itself. But when it has performed what is good with the body, it makes that body rejoice. Therefore a person who does good is loved by others through God's grace without knowing it; and sometimes he advances so far [Col. 0831A] that he desires to perform good works without satiety, just as angels, beholding the countenance of God, cannot grow weary of contemplating him.

His soul, having the joy of good action, condescends to the body and shakes it away from sins. Through humble repentance it sends into it sighs and tears, so that it may grow green in virtues, just as clouds draw waters upward and send them down again.

That, as no visible form is without a name, so neither is it without measure; and what the equal measure of the outward eyes signifies in the inward person.

XXXIII. Now, as no visible form is without a name, so none is without measure. Therefore both human eyes have equal measure, and their seeing vessels are equal in their circumference. For God separated virtues from vices and holy works from sins, just as he distinguished from one another the creatures known to a person by their forms and names. Thus, in circumspection, by which he foresees every good thing for himself as by an eye, and in the consideration of his good intention, a person should possess sincere and equal discernment: lest, if he exceeds measure in good, he fall into the abyss, or lest, if he embraces excess in evil, he perish altogether in despair. [Col. 0831B]

That the judgment of the rational soul ought to assign reward to good and punishment to evil; and that in comparison with eternal recompense no repentance would suffice, even if it surpassed all the sand and drops of the sea.

XXXIV. The soul also shows through rationality what and how great sins are, and demonstrates the measure of sinning and repenting. For by the powers of the soul a person is instructed in repentance when, with every effort, he afflicts his sins by repentance, just as rain extinguishes fire. Yet, compared with eternal glory and ineffable recompense, he can scarcely comprehend how he may be saved.

For even if repentance in name were beyond the sand and beyond the waters of the sea, it could scarcely comprehend the salvation of its joy in comparison with the ineffable glory of eternal life. And, ah, where is the one who, turning away from sins, does not fulfill the concupiscences [Col. 0831D] of his flesh?

For the knowledge of the rational soul exists in two modes: it knows good and perceives evil, assigning reward to good and punishment to evil. These are the soul's functions, by which it often assists the body in acting according to what the body demands. Hence a person is like day in good things and like night in evil things.

That, as a person is strengthened by the eyes and other senses, and heaven is illumined by the sun, moon, and stars, which assist one another with borrowed light, so the soul is illumined by the works of true repentance and quickly washed from sins by sighs or tears.

XXXV. A person sees through the eyes, smells through the nose, and tastes through the mouth. So too, by the power of sun and moon, certain rays are sometimes sent from the highest stars, which attend upon them in service, to the other stars, so that one light is stirred by another. When the soul sees wicked and shameful works, it grieves; when it has learned of them through evil report, as through smell, it sighs; and when it has performed them with the body, as through taste, it makes the person pour forth tears and imparts repentance to him: repentance through knowledge, sighs through the report of sins, and tears through their effect.

Repentance is the illuminator of the soul, and within it are sighs and tears; it quickly washes away faults in a person. In it sighs and tears are produced, and they belong to true repentance, just as, through the spirit of fortitude and fear of the Lord, the other virtues, stirred into action, effectively illumine a faithful person. [Col. 0832B]

That, as the head and the upper regions are supported by the chin and by clouds, as bones in a person are hardened by fire and marrow is coagulated by cold, and as the earth is cultivated for fruit-bearing through summer and winter, so the minds of the faithful are strengthened for every good thing by the fire of the Holy Spirit and the dew of compunction, and weakened by the inertness of numbness and negligence.

XXXVI. Just as everything in a person's head is held together by the chin, so in the same way all the things previously mentioned are sustained in their appointed places by clouds. This signifies that the minds of the faithful should seize the stability of good works so as to reach heavenly things by persevering in good.

Heat also signifies bones, and cold marrow, in a person, because [Col. 0832C] the soul cooks the bones by fire and coagulates the marrow by the cold which it draws into its vessel. So the whole earth is tested through summer and winter, so that its fruit is coagulated beneath the ground by the cold of the firmament and dissolved by its heat.

For the sun's heat and moisture from the waters are united and mixed in the clouds in such a way that through them every fruit upon the earth is governed and strengthened. The sun's heat and the waters' moisture cultivate, make fruitful, and complete the whole earth, as a turner brings his vessels to completion. They are also joined together in the clouds with such firmness that, until the last day, they will in no way be dispersed or separated, entering and going out, or scattering themselves in one direction or another.

And in a person the soul is strengthened for all good things by the fire of the Holy Spirit, and weakened by the cold of numbness and negligence. For the fire of fortitude and compunction of the human mind, mingling together, bring forth good fruit in a person. They strengthen and adorn him in every usefulness so that he cannot be separated from God's service and love.

For when a person incurs the vexation and weariness of sins, through that same vexation sins are so constricted within him as fire is pressed down by thick smoke, lest it burn in its strength. When, through the soul's powers, the flesh's pleasure is broken apart in the human mind, immediately sighs for the heavenly homeland are woven within him, just as a bee builds honeycomb with honey [Col. 0833A] in its vessel. There that same person's new and old works, mixed together, are governed by true humility, lest they dry up, burned by the heat of pride.

Therefore fruitful virtues are accomplished in the vessel of the Holy Spirit—in which wisdom builds itself a dwelling—through the fire of the Holy Spirit and the moisture of humility, so that the same person gathers to himself virtues most serene before God and his angels, as though amid the fragrance of every aromatic spice, where they thereafter do not fail.

Further, on the usefulness of the senses in the human being and of the stars in the world; and on the fact that the devil’s deceit, by which he deceived Eve and through her poured original sin upon the whole of her posterity, is like a mist which rises from harmful air, covers the earth, damages its fruits, and obstructs sight so that the brightness of day cannot be seen.

[Col. 0833B] XXXVII. Moreover, through the sight of the eyes, hearing, smell, the rational faculty of the mouth, and touch are governed and known—so that it may be known both what they are and how they are—just as through the sun, moon, and stars the whole constitution of the firmament is governed and illuminated. For a human being sees through the eyes what he knows with wisdom, and receives the same things through hearing, smell, and taste. But what he gathers in his breast, he knows through knowledge, though he does not see it through the eyes. Thus too the serpent’s deceit was hidden; it revealed itself when it first asked Eve what she did not know and deceived her, because she herself was without deceit. This beginning arose in the first original sin through the devil’s deception; it is like a mist which rises from harmful air [Col. 0833C] and covers the whole earth, preventing the pure day from being seen, and which, as it were, eats away at the works of wisdom by marking them out. So deceit has neither delight nor joy, nor is it at rest in any respect.

These things also indicate that each of a person’s senses inclines toward that person’s intention, just as the virtues hasten to that person’s correction when he has asked this of God. For wherever a person’s intention leads him, there he also directs his senses; yet, as long as the thoughts of his heart remain hidden, they are unknown. So too, when Eve was deceived by the devil, she did not know his cunning, because he had so entirely covered himself that his deceit could not be seen by the first parent. Hence he overturned the whole world into evil, because he had nothing good in himself.

That the eyebrows, given as a defense for the eyes, signify the courses of the moon, subject to monthly increases and decreases; and that accordingly the soul must maintain constancy and security in the fear of God amid prosperity and adversity.

XXXVIII. The human eyebrows signify the courses of the moon: namely, one path by which it goes beneath the sun toward its restoration, and another by which it withdraws from the sun when set ablaze by it. The eyebrows are the eyes’ defense and protection, just as the moon is the safeguard and nourishment of the stars. For, when set ablaze by the sun, it begins to increase and receives fire both from the stars and from the sun, thereby assisting them so that they do not abound excessively in fires; but, when it is waning, [Col. 0834A] it pours its fires into the stars, not into the sun, because the latter, existing as a prince, always remains in one state.

In the same way, the soul sends constancy and security in the human being toward the fear of the Lord, as though they were its paths. For while a person fears God, prosperity sometimes meets him and adversity also sometimes meets him; in these he must walk rightly, so that he is neither lifted up by prosperity nor crushed by adversity. Hence, when he is fortified with the spirit of strength, he shows himself strong in all things. These virtues provide protection for a person’s intention, just as the fear of the Lord is the foundation and shield of the other virtues; for when it is clothed with strength, it gathers the remaining virtues to itself and shows them fortified both by strength and fear, [Col. 0834B] whereby it causes a person to cling to heavenly desires both in adversity and in prosperity.

On the nose, mouth, and ears: how much they avail in the human being; what their different effects signify in the elements of the outer world and in the soul’s inner faculties; and that in all things the examples of the saints must be followed.

XXXIX. Moreover, from the nose to the throat, with watery air and the strong, white, shining air placed beneath it set forth beforehand, the human nose signifies the air which moves the waters; the mouth, in its rationality, shows their moisture; and the ears reveal the noise and sound of those waters, which suitably overflow through the wind of watery air and the rising of clouds. For by the hearing of the ear a human being’s inward parts are shaken, just as the elements are penetrated by the sound of the upper [Col. 0834C] waters; the mouth of rationality is suffused with moisture, just as the upper regions are moistened by the humidity of these same waters, lest they be consumed by dryness; and the nostrils are filled with smell, just as these waters are stirred by air.

That the nose extends upward in length toward the higher regions means that this watery air sends its moisture into the purity of the upper ether and the heat of the upper fire, and receives from them the tempering of strength, lest it be dispersed or dissolved by flowing away. The brain and veins are likewise cleansed through the nose, because these same elements too, when stirred, are often cleansed in the upper regions by moisture and smoke. For the pure ether is suffused with the moisture of watery [Col. 0834D] air, as was said above, just as repentance is illumined by the works and examples of the righteous; and as the hearing of the ears receives words of knowledge, in which His words resound.

The breath of smell and the moisture of the rational mouth join together and possess a wet moisture. And as water flows and sounds and, by its moisture, suffuses the whole earth, so watery air moistens the upper elements. The soul’s breath also has a straight course through the nose and mouth; it neither ascends nor descends beyond its proper boundary, just as this watery air keeps the courses assigned to it. These things also indicate that the soul, made in a human being by God’s gift, when it attentively tastes with discriminating understanding and good savor the examples of the righteous—which the hearing of others had instilled in the soul with the freshness of words—stirs the heart within, so that, suffused by the grace of the Holy Spirit, it may retain the fragrance of virtues with every desire. Therefore temperance, receiving the fragrance of blessedness and considering the works of the faithful—which they accomplish both by persevering in good things and by desisting from evil through repentance—commits them to God’s power, lest they be dissolved by excess. For, through temperance, the knowledge of good savor having cleansed a person renders that person strong in good everywhere. Repentance, indeed, is often raised up by true groans, where true and holy words are uttered for the edification of the faithful. The virtue of right moderation must be present in these things, so that a person may arrange all works well and raise himself toward heavenly things with a just gaze, [Col. 0835B] without exceeding his proper measure.

And just as in watery air there is a certain blast which descends upon the earth with the moisture of dew and moderates the greenness and dryness of fruits—greenness in summer, but dryness in winter—and as through this blast the fruits of the earth receive strength, so through the human mouth the whole person is nourished. And just as the world is illumined through the sun’s brightness, so through this same blast all higher breaths are moderated and brought forth. Likewise, through the examples of the righteous compunction sometimes arises in the faithful person, bringing that person the freshness of good works and the dryness of evils: namely, when, as though in summer, he desires good things, and when, as though in winter, [Col. 0835C] he despises evil things. Thus, delighted and nourished in these fruits of righteousness, he may always direct himself toward heavenly desires.

That in the human tongue the flooding of waters is shown, and what is figured inwardly by this same outward overflowing of waves.

XL. In the tongue is shown the rising of waters by which they are lifted up for flooding; for as words are formed through the tongue, so the waters themselves are generated into waves through their rising. This signifies that the soul, desiring to abide in heavenly desires, urges its vessel to the praises of its Creator and causes it to offer continual prayers with devotion of mind. The soul is moved by moisture and sounds with fiery noise; by being fiery it knows God, and by being breath it pants after God, who is spirit. When it accomplishes what is good, it has a straight course, like pure air free from dark clouds; but when it works the rottenness of sins, it is like a flooding of waters which overturns the pure course of the air.

But when afterward it withdraws from sins—as is written in the Gospel concerning the steward who, abandoning sins and reducing debts, turned himself to mercy—and when after sins it seeks God’s grace, that grace may raise it like Lazarus four days dead, drawing deep inward sighs, weaving its correction as though it were a firm hedge, and persevering in good works so as not to approach again the habit of sins, it practices steadfast repentance as a firm foundation, lest [Col. 0836A] it again do evil by beginning to sin anew.

What virtue or strength is expressed in us through the teeth, which are not hollow and have no marrow.

XLI. In the teeth is shown the restraint of these same waters, strong and firm in accordance with the character of the teeth: namely, the strong, white, shining air which contains these waters, lest by exceeding their measure they be dissolved. This shows that the human mind, strengthened and restrained through the soul by God’s grace, is kept from flowing out too much through evil thoughts, so as voluntarily to draw them to itself through unlawful desires—thoughts which now become, through works of sin, like a storm in a person, and now, through repentance for them, like a medicine.

[Col. 0836B] For human teeth are not hollow and do not have the softness of marrow, because they are not clothed with flesh; rather, through the brain and all the structures of the human form, which are set according to the firmament, they are coagulated and hardened, and through the heat and moisture of the head rise into hardness. These things signify that the rational soul, subsisting in the infinite equality of life, receives neither increase through the body’s growth nor loss through its decline, because it is the breath of almighty God, who wonderfully created through His Word all creatures ordered in His foreknowledge. For the soul, invisibly infused into the body by the power of its Creator, visibly moves the body; and while enlivening it, remains invisible within it, [Col. 0836C] just as God, by a certain invisible power of His capacity, established from the greenness of the earth, the heat of the air, and the moisture of waters every creature which He created for human service, and provided for that same soul a garment—namely, the body—unknown and alien to its nature.

Why an infant, although it has bones, is born without teeth; why people often lose those same teeth when they decline into old age; and what is signified by this.

XLII. For while an infant is tender and does not yet possess strength of blood, it lacks teeth because it is also cold. But after its blood is strengthened and suffused with heat, its teeth arise and are strengthened. When, however, it has reached old age, [Col. 0836D] its blood diminishes and its heat is weakened; its teeth in turn, through coldness, pass into decay and disturbance. So too, when the soul is first embodied by the command of almighty God, it warms its body, created from the four elements, with its fire until it departs from it by the command of almighty God.

The soul itself greatly rejoices in a person’s infancy, because of that person’s innocence while he is still nourished at the breast on tender food; for he has not yet tasted sins, just as Adam too, before transgression, lived purely and simply. But when, with the growth of time and strengthened bones, a person has received the strength of his flesh and blood, innocence ceases, because then the taste of sins arises in the person; the soul, acting contrary to its nature, is oppressed within him and overcome through living in sins by means of the body. And just as the sun’s brightness is withdrawn from people after its setting, so after the commission of sin the soul is tormented, groaning and weeping over the loss of the joy it formerly possessed. For the taste of sins defiles body, blood, and all a person’s inward parts by the work of sins; but after sins have been committed, a person is often driven, through weariness of his sins, into grief of heart by the soul’s sighs.

How and whence teeth are formed in children, why they are meanwhile gripped with severe pain, and what these things signify in us.

[Col. 0837B] XLIII. While the infant is tender, fluid descends from its brain to the gums and, together with certain other humors, makes little hollows in them, where it remains hidden until the aforesaid maturity, as little flowers lie hidden through winter in the branches of a tree. But afterward, when strength of blood and heat have risen in it like summer, that fluid, coagulated with the other humors and the heat of blood, bursts forth into teeth, just as, when summer heat arrives, little flowers begin to appear on tree branches.

Before teeth arise in the infant, while the gums are hollowed out by the fluid of the brain and other humors, it is meanwhile afflicted by the severe pain of weakness. Later, when childhood has passed and it is established in the fullness of its blood, with the soul’s holiness already failing within it through the taste of flesh, it embraces wantonness; therefore, a person of that age must be kept under the great guard of fear. So the soul rules the body while a person, still set in uncertainty, considers what to choose or do, and what not to choose or do. Yet in the body it is immediately led and bound as a captive; and when a person, through the taste of sin coagulated by burning blood, commits evil, it too, together with its body, acts contrary to its nature, although unwillingly. And as summer heat brings the shoots of the earth and the fruits of trees to maturity, so a person, delighted by the enticements of the flesh through the heat of his blood, does not cease to accomplish whatever vices he is able.

[Col. 0837D] That the teeth, which grind and move about the foods by which a person is nourished, have the likeness of a mill; and how the soul imitates this inwardly.

XLIV. The teeth also, which grind and move about every food by whose strength a person is nourished, are set in the likeness of a mill, which is turned by the watery air and whose circular stone burns with heat. For as a person prepares the food by which he is refreshed through grinding it with his teeth, so the soul also works with burning zeal within him whatever he has chosen according to his will. The soul itself, through which a person receives perception and taste for accomplishing any work, whether good [Col. 0838A] or evil, urges him most ardently, as his mind turns like a mill through thoughts, in the manner of fire which burns more fiercely when kindled by the blast of bellows.

Thus the soul also works in the four elements from which a person was created whatever the person wills through the capacity of rationality, carrying it about through the desires of his heart, just as a mill constructed by human skill is turned most swiftly by water. And as, to preserve the speed of its rotation, it is suitably and frequently strengthened by human skill, so, while it remains in a person, the soul is aided by God’s grace in good; yet at other times evil delight and consent are introduced into it by the devil’s suggestion.

That the chin, throat, and neck, having different offices in the body, signify varied clouds in the world and manifold effects of virtues in the soul.

XLV. Through the chin, which hangs curved like a bow and raises the human face; through the throat, which receives all the strength of nourishment and sends it in due measure to the belly; and through the neck, which supports the whole head by its strength, is signified the diversity of clouds. Some, weighed down by rains, bend themselves a little downward, but in fair weather display, as it were, the cheerfulness of the upper regions. Some, touching the earth with the power of air, temper it in such a way that it brings forth an abundance of fruits for the use of the other creatures. Others, like [Col. 0838C] a column, bind together the entire revolving firmament by bearing it.

For a person, stretching through the soul a confident hope toward God, knows with the two eyes of rationality—the knowledge of good and evil—the heavenly homeland and the punishments of hell. For with his face, which is raised by the chin, he sees every visible thing and considers by understanding what it is like. As a person discerns all things through the soul, so he arranges them in order that they may be done honorably before God and people; just as the throat sends the food it receives in due measure to the belly for strengthening, so that a person, thus strengthened by true and pure faith, may worthily be able to behold the royal seat of the true Solomon, who is Christ.

[Col. 0838D] For faith scatters all thoughts arising in a person from sin, but directs toward the true King, through the soul’s sighs, those thoughts which proceed from itself in simple truth. This strong and true virtue likewise supports the other virtues as the neck supports the head; and as clouds sustain the revolution of the firmament like a column, so it preserves in people by good perseverance all good and holy works which build the heavenly Jerusalem. But unbelievers, who, setting faith aside, do all their works wrongly through unbelief, are unworthy before God and are, not without justice, assigned to the punishments of hell, just as digested food is expelled with stench.

[Col. 0839A] That through the hair, which outwardly adorns the head fittingly, are shown the drops of dew or rain by which the earth is fertilized and clothed in the beauty of grasses or fruits; and inwardly the cultivation of innocence, chastity, and humility, by which the soul shines before God.

XLVI. The hairs hanging from the head signify drops of rain, which descend separately through the clouds and, watering the whole earth, bring it through greenness to fruitfulness. Likewise, the soul, sent by God into the mortal and failing body of an infant, raises it up by enlivening it with its powers. While the infant still remains in natural simplicity, the soul is beautifully adorned as though clothed in an elegant garment of innocence, because it drives away every vice, which is like a storm, producing the fruitfulness of all [Col. 0839B] virtues after the manner of the earth, which brings forth its fruit by germinating under gentle rain.

For innocence is a queen clothed round with a golden garment, by which chastity is understood; its virtues multiply like rain, and humility is the head of that chastity. These two virtues, joined together in a person, cause heaven to resound with praises and fill the earth with examples of holy virtues.

Why, on the heads of some people, the hair retains its strength and is not rooted out, whereas on the heads of others it is weakened and falls away in baldness; and how this signifies both fertility and barrenness—of fruits outwardly in the earth and inwardly of virtues in the soul.

XLVII. That hair upon the heads of certain people retains its strength above and is not plucked out, so that it is not uprooted, occurs in those whose flesh is moist with humors; for these nourish hair, just as irrigated earth produces an abundance of grass. This shows that the soul works the fruitful virtues of good deeds through its powers in those people who, with devout minds gladly hearing the words of God, often produce through the fiery inspiration of the Holy Spirit the moisture of tears in sighs and longing for heavenly things. Their holy intention, as though in the richness of good earth, joyfully produces the fruits of fruitful works, so that the soul, with the body consenting to it in good works, may now rejoice exultantly in Christ [Col. 0839D] and, truly strengthened by the sweetness of His love, continue in blessed perseverance in such a manner that it does not wither through failing by any wandering into spiritual or fleshly vices.

But where hair is plucked from people’s heads so that they become bald, this is because their flesh is dry in heat; for heat passing to the crown gradually and one by one pulls out the hairs when they lack moisture, just as earth lacking moisture is deprived, through its dryness, of the greenness of grass. So those people who live in such hardened forgetfulness of God that they refuse to consent to the soul’s will either through the admonition of the Holy Spirit or through the teaching or counsel of faithful teachers are likened to dry earth, which lacks moisture and through its dryness bears no fruit. For they order all their works according to the will of their own desire and not according to the soul’s nature. Hence, oppressed by the manifold alternation of sins, they reach toward heavenly things with no hope of blessedness; nor do they desire to be of service to people on earth through the help of anything beneficial. Since these people are not warmed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, they lack discernment, the mother of virtues; consequently, because of the instability of their conduct, what pleased them before now displeases them. Therefore they are deprived of the stability of holy virtues, just as the head is stripped of its hair.

What the position of a person, having east before the face, west behind, south on the right, and north on the left, signifies in the soul’s various effects.

[Col. 0840B] XLVIII. Therefore a person faces east and, as though setting, looks toward east; extending his arms, just as south and north are separated from one another, he directs his right arm to the south and his left to the north. In this way the soul, working in a person with its powers and the four elements through knowledge of good and evil, flies toward the east through knowledge of good and looks toward the west through knowledge of evil. Thus a person, kindled by the knowledge of good through the fire which is God, may fly with the south in the perfection of most holy works; but in the working of evil deeds may be punished, according to what he has sinned, in the punishments of the north.

For the soul, which makes the body capable of sensation, makes a person cold or hot through its powers, so that by it he feels the heat of the south and the cold of the north. This may be tested in human breath, which a person emits hot or cold according to his will. In the creature which he discerns by sight, a person also works good or evil with the soul according as the flesh desires; and the soul, in fear and love of God, does good as though on the right side. Therefore evil knowledge is overcome in the person by good knowledge through the assistance of God’s grace, just as the left hand is pressed down by the right, which has greater strength.

The soul, which is a breath from God, remains invisibly in the body; moving it toward whatever work, it is known not by sight but by the power of rationality, just as [Col. 0840D] wind is perceived not by sight but by its sound and movement in its blowing. Yet what these things are, human knowledge can neither grasp nor understand.

That, as the shoulders and arms with their hands adhere to the neck, so the four principal winds with their collateral winds adhere to the firmament; how thought, speech, intention, and groaning in human beings correspond to those same four winds; and what it means that the right side has greater power than the left.

XLIX. As the shoulder blades and shoulders, with the arms and hands, adhere to the neck, so the four principal winds with their collateral winds are joined to the firmament. The bends of the arm, the shoulder with the shoulder blade, and the hand with the fingers give assistance, just as these principal [Col. 0841A] winds with their wings—that is, their collateral winds—support the firmament; and hand is joined to hand, as the wing of each extends toward the wing of the other.

These things signify that the soul, which is life through the Life that is God, and a breath from the Spirit of God, has no end of living as the human body does; it enlivens and sustains the body by its powers, just as the stars sustain the firmament together with its point, which is the earth, which the Word of God, establishing it in the midst of the firmament, made fixed and illumined. Indeed, the soul, sent by God, descends invisibly and secretly into the body, causing a person to know God through faith, to look toward heaven, and to do heavenly things.

And as dew falling invisibly upon grass makes it fruitful, so God mercifully waters with the hidden sweetness of His grace the person who places hope in Him, tramples underfoot the earth—that is, the desires of the flesh—and raises his whole body toward heaven to bear the fruits of good works; but He condemns contrary works to the eternal punishments of Gehenna. For a person performs all works, good or evil, with the four elements, after the manner of the four winds which exercise their powers in the upper regions of the air and yet sometimes cast their blasts down into filth and muddy impurities.

The four forces in a person—namely thought, speech, intention, and groaning—correspond to the four principal winds. As each wind has the power to send its blasts right and left, [Col. 0841C] so the soul, equipped with these four forces, may incline by natural knowledge wherever it wishes, choosing either good or evil.

The south wind has two collateral winds as though two wings. One of these, toward the east, is hot and signifies good and holy thoughts, kindled through the fire of the Holy Spirit by the zeal of devout intention. The other, toward the west, is cold; it signifies crooked and useless thoughts, not warm in the fire of the Holy Spirit, and cold, evil works. The fiery breath, which is the rational soul, feels the works of flesh and blood in which a person delights; although it naturally sighs toward heavenly things, it nevertheless supplies strength [Col. 0841D] and heat to the body even amid the foulest stench of sins, as the sun warms with its rays the fetid rot of the most filthy worms.

But the north wind is useless to all creatures; it too has two wings, one extending eastward and the other westward. These signify the knowledge of good and evil in a person, through which he considers in his mind, as in a mirror, what is useful and useless, just as the earth is governed above and below through the firmament. The wing of the east wind which tends toward the south shows the person who ascends to God through good works in the embrace of true love; but the wing which looks toward the north signifies a person defiled by the pleasures of the flesh. And as these two collateral [Col. 0842A] winds are joined to the east wind as two wings, so good and evil are joined to the soul: good in joy and gladness, through which it shines before God like the sun in its strength; evil, through which good and holy works are darkened by the blackness of sins, as the brightness of the sun is obscured by dark clouds.

For through the good intention of his soul a person greatly fears the punishments which he knows to be in the north, although the body, accustomed to sinful delights, often weighs down the soul. This intention of the soul too has two wings: one is the fear of God, kindled in a person through the admonition of the Holy Spirit; the other is the renunciation of sins, which afterward, when the fear of God has been set aside, a person very often repeats. The west wind likewise has two wings, one extending toward the south and the other toward the north. These signify that a person perceives good and through good knows evil. And the right wing shows that the soul has desire and longing for good works, whereas the left shows the person’s folly, through which he perpetrates evils contracted through the debt of original sin.

That the soul, sent into the body through God’s Spirit, suffuses it wholly with its powers, just as the blowing of winds courses through the whole world.

L. The soul also is spread through the whole body, just as the windiness of these winds runs through the whole firmament. For the soul, sent into the body through God’s Spirit, suffuses it wholly with its powers. And as the blowing of winds [Col. 0842C] runs through the firmament, so it causes a person to love God most ardently and to practice most holy virtues having a honey-sweet savor, because the sayings of the Lord become sweeter to his mouth than honey and honeycomb. Thus the soul most diligently suffuses its firmament—that is, its body—with the incomparable adornment of virtues and the most delightful beauty of holy works.

That, as a person is governed and sustained by arms and legs, so winds assist one another in strengthening the firmament; and what these things, as well as the gentle blowing or turbulent course of those winds, figure in the soul.

LI. For a person governs and sustains his whole self with his arms and legs, and is windy, just as the four principal winds with their collateral winds hold within themselves the whole firmament, and as each of them helps the others to strengthen the firmament. These things signify that the soul flies in a person with four wings: sensation, understanding, and knowledge of good and evil. Through sensation it works in the person according to the taste of the flesh; through understanding it discerns whether its works please God or people. By the two wings of the knowledge of good and evil, a person accomplishes every work in the soul; their difference makes known what he is, because through the soul he seeks salvation from God, but through the flesh honor from people. Thus sometimes through knowledge of good he ascends to heaven, and sometimes through knowledge of evil he is cast down to earth.

But when a person is at some time touched inwardly by the grace of the Holy Spirit and feels himself weighed down in soul by the burden of his sins, he repents of his wicked works and sighs toward God. And just as winds run through the firmament now in a gentle breeze and now in a great storm, so a person is always occupied either with good or with evil.

How the turns of winds are to be determined in the bends of the arms and joints of the shoulder blades or hands; and that, as right and left, firmament and earth, cooperate in certain respects, so a person accomplishes all works, though contrary, through knowledge of good and evil.

LII. In the bend of the left arm the principal east wind is signified; in the bend and [Col. 0843B] in the joint where the hand is joined to that arm, its collateral winds are shown; and in its shoulder blade and hand the blasts of those same collateral winds are made manifest. In the bend of the right arm the principal south wind is shown; in the shoulder and the joint by which the hand is joined to that arm, the collateral winds of this wind also are declared; and in the shoulder blade and hand of that arm are marked the breaths of its collateral winds.

This means that the soul, possessing the likeness of wind in the human limbs, naturally causes any of them to bend and move, while a person also works with it according to the taste of the flesh. Therefore it cannot excuse itself from sin, because a person was conceived and coagulated like milk through the burning of lust; through the soul he works good on the right side and evil on the left. And as each wind is joined to another, so the soul is joined to the body. A person tends toward God in good knowledge, but in evil knowledge—which is subject to good knowledge as a maidservant to her mistress—he inclines himself toward evil. And as a mistress is often offended through her maidservant, so good knowledge is sometimes overcome by evil knowledge. Just as hands are joined together for work, and as the firmament and earth, though far distant from one another, agree in some association, so a person accomplishes all his works through these dissimilar forms of knowledge which he possesses.

On the threefold division of the human body and the thickness of the sphere of the world; and how human life, in childhood, youth, and old age, corresponds to that division.

LIII. From the crown of a person’s head to the end of the throat, from that end of the throat to the navel, and from the navel to the place of evacuation, there is an equal measure; just as there is an equal measure from the summit of the firmament to the lower part of the clouds, from that lower part of the clouds to the summit of the earth, and from that summit of the earth to its lowest limit. For the soul works from the first day of birth to the final day of a person’s life according to the requirements of childhood, youth, and old age: in childhood, namely, through innocence; [Col. 0844A] in youth, through the taste of flesh, which criminal sins often follow; but in old age it has weariness of activity, and therefore strives quickly to set an end to its works, whatever they may be.

For as the supreme Craftsman established the firmament with its walls in equal measure, so the soul that works in the body possesses, from the beginning of its work to its end, an equal capacity for working with the knowledge of good and evil, neither of which works without the other.

That the upper part of the earth is tender, soft, and penetrable, whereas its lower part is tough, hard, and impenetrable; and what is found in the human soul accordingly.

LIV. But the middle part of the earth, that is, its upper part [Col. 0844B], is tender, soft, and penetrable; whereas its other half, namely its lower part, is tough, hard, and impenetrable, so that its hardness and strength even surpass the hardness and strength of steel. In the same way the rational soul possesses a certain greenness or vitality in its powers, by which it penetrates the softness of the flesh, the hardness of the bones, and all the veins—like weapons which, in cutting through the hardness of steel, acquire greater solidity for cutting whatever things they encounter. And as loaves are baked by the fire of an oven, so the works of the body are completed by the soul’s burning zeal. For the soul works inseparably with the body in all its acts, cleaving to it as a woman to her husband, from whom she cannot be separated, since the two are one flesh; and it sustains the body by love, as the hard part of the earth sustains its soft part.

What the measurements of the shoulders, elbows, hands, and feet, down to the end of the great toe, being in some proportion like the winds, show concerning the qualities of the inner person.

LV. Moreover, the measurement from either shoulder to the bend of each arm, and from that bend to the tip of the middle finger of each hand, is equal. The hand also, from its joint to the topmost tip of the middle finger, has the same measure as that from the ankle to the end of the great toe; just as every principal wind, together with its collateral winds and their blasts, has one measure.

For through the power of reason a person sometimes takes pleasure, with vain intention, in good and holy works. When he begins to perform them, his blood—which was conceived in sins—is wholly stirred within him by the labor of the work begun; and thus, through weariness of working, he leaves his work unfinished. He even mocks, on account of the pride of his mind, the good which he had first begun not in God but by trusting in his own strength. And as much as he had delighted in it before beginning it, so much afterward does he blush at its incompleteness; and, because he has done such a thing, he begins to grieve and mourn.

The measure from the shoulders to the bend of each arm signifies the works a person performs through pride of mind; and the measure extending from the bends of the arms to the tip of the middle finger of each hand shows that a person should erase through repentance the works which he has performed through pride of mind. Hence, while the soul remains in the body, it can never possess complete joy, because body and soul oppose one another. Unable to endure their conflict, a person fails within himself from the greatness of his sorrow; and, groaning, he humbles himself before God with a contrite heart through frequent sighs. Thus humbled by the fear of God, he turns aside from evil works and from deeds contrary to the soul, performing the good signified by the hands and running in the ways of God shown by the feet. For the movement of hands and feet signifies that the soul ought to rejoice in good works; but their cessation from movement indicates that the soul ought to grieve and mourn over evil works.

[Col. 0845B] What the measurement across the front from thigh to thigh, and the measurement lengthwise from the navel to the place of evacuation, corresponding proportionally to the breadth and thickness of the earth, show in the soul’s diverse dispositions.

LVI. The measure which lies across the front from thigh to thigh is of the same length as that from the navel to the place of evacuation, because the breadth of the earth across is as great as the thickness of its depth. For when a person sins often, if at any time he consents to the soul in a good work, he rejoices; yet in that joy he has the pain of fear, because he fears that he may perhaps be unable to complete the work he has begun. With this fear, which he keeps within himself through the powers of the soul, he performs the good work until the soul draws the person to itself through weariness of sinning.

Thus every person placed in this life now consents to the will of the soul, now to the pleasure of the flesh. Thus also all God’s holy and chosen martyrs, while they still lived in the world, bore the banner of Christ’s passion. For while the flesh sins, the soul has hunger as a fasting person does; and when the flesh hungers—that is, ceases from sins—the soul rejoices in good works, like one refreshed by food.

The measure from the navel to the place of evacuation signifies the wantonness of the flesh, to which a person sometimes consents and sometimes resists, just as the service of his servant now pleases and now displeases any master. And as the earth is sustained by its thickness, so in its length and breadth it produces things useful and useless. The thickness of the earth, which is compared to a servant, signifies the desire of the flesh; but its length and breadth show abstinence, which here is reckoned as mistress.

How the space from the end of the throat to the navel signifies the air; and how the soul, which gives life to the whole body and moves it to act, is compared with that air, which penetrates every empty space and tempers the earth in diverse ways for bearing fruit.

LVII. Moreover, in the space between the end of the throat and the navel is signified the air, which descends from the clouds to the earth and by its natural power tempers the creatures of the earth. For the soul, which consists through divine power as a living spark and rational breath [Col. 0846A], penetrates the whole body by animating it, moves about it in love, and impels it to every kind of work; and, although it has arisen amid the taste of sins, it compels the body to work with it.

Descending from the height of heaven to earthly things, the soul makes the person whom it animates understand that he was created by God. It is also likened to the air, which appears to stand between heaven and earth, because through it a person performs good in higher things and evil in lower things. For this air passes through every region of the earth, tempering it: where it is dry, making it moist; where it is rich, compacting it with heat; where it is watery, drying it; where it is hard, softening it. And it does this down to the middle of its depth; it turns the earth, as it were with a plough, toward heat and toward cold, and by a proper tempering makes it fruitful.

In the same manner, when the soul perceives that its body is dry of every greenness of virtues, it is turned to mourning and lamentation; through rational knowledge and the spirit of compunction it drives its body to sighs and tears, because it recognizes that its works are wicked. Thus it causes its dry body to grow green again through the moisture of divine grace. But if a person attempts, presumptuously trusting in his own powers, to undertake greater things than he can accomplish, the soul draws him back again to the measure of his capacity and orders his works better. And if he then lives in forgetfulness of God, as though in security, it shakes him with the fear of God and empties him of forgetfulness of God.

But when a person, seeking a strange god, is led into the hardness of unbelief and is so troubled by the soul with tribulations that he can have neither hope of salvation nor any joy, the soul, by this sorrow, draws him through its own admonition toward the better part and makes him sigh for the true God. Thus the body is recalled through the soul—which is a living spark and life from God—to hope of pardon and to discerning and pursuing every kind of work; abandoning the error of doubleness, it is led into the straight path of good works, just as water flows in a straight channel in its course. Thereafter, by living well, it becomes strong in the fear of God.

The most pleasant heat, together with gentle cold, imparts moisture to the earth and makes it fruitful in trees, herbs, and grains, so that all these grow green through that same moisture [Col. 0846D]. Likewise, in the most pleasant warmth of faith and in the strongest patience for enduring every injury, the soul strengthens a person; and it sets before him to be fled from the works which he previously did while not living well, and in which he was not permitted to excel. Thus it makes him fruitful in good works and causes him to grow green in holy virtues.

At times the same air sends snowy cold upon the earth, which covers it all and through which it is warmed for germination. Therefore the earth brings forth its own cold, until it is inwardly prepared by germinating for its fruitful office; and then it imparts greenness to the fruit of all things that germinate. For the soul tempers a person from the taste of his works [Col. 0847A], by which it compels him to turn about as in a mill, because it is that air which causes the blood—through which a person receives sense and understanding—to flow. It also makes the flesh emit sweat, through whose heat a person has sense and through whose moisture, which is cold and damp, he has understanding. Therefore every fruit of his works consists in sensation and understanding.

How birds are borne aloft by the air for flight, and certain fish likewise are nourished in waters so as to live for a time without food; and how in this manner one who follows not the flesh’s desires but those of the soul flies through contemplation and is nourished by the sweetness of the Scriptures.

LVIII. Certain birds of great strength, flying into this same air in summer [Col. 0847B], are strengthened by it; and this air, at times descending into rivers, strengthens certain large fish so that they can remain for some time without food. Similarly, when the soul has drawn the body to its consent, it flies to the height of heaven like a bird into the air; and as a bird cannot fly without air, so the body is moved not through itself but through the soul.

But when a person at times consents to the desires of the soul, he burns wholly in the love of God. Thus, flying day by day in the delight of eternal joy, he takes pleasure in contemplative faith and in the wisdom of the holy Scriptures, by whose sweetness he is invisibly nourished and strengthened—like a fish which, strengthened by the air and by the flowing of waters, sometimes lives in the waters without food.

How sea and rivers are moved by the air, and the body by veins filled with blood, and by the virtues of the soul; through these, as earth watered by streams, it may bring forth shoots of good works.

LIX. This air, together with watery air, moves the sea, from which divided rivers flow; they water and strengthen the earth. This is also shown by veins connected to one another, strengthening the whole person with blood. The soul likewise, which is airy, and through which all human works are accomplished just as all fruits of the earth are accomplished through the air, sets its works before a person through the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that by thoughts, which overflow like the sea, he may distinguish useful from useless things.

The same person often suffers shipwreck when, refusing to consent to the good thoughts of the soul, he is submerged in great confusion on account of his sins [Col. 0847D]. Thus he rows amid the grievous labor of the ship of thoughts, unless by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit he builds them upon the rock, which is Christ. For when the human mind, enlarged through various virtues, is raised to the praise of God, it builds a stable foundation upon the rock, which cannot be moved by the winds—that is, the various temptations of the devil. For just as veins together with sinews strengthen the human body so that it may not be dissolved, so the virtue of humility joins and strengthens good works lest they be scattered through pride.

Rivers send out streams which assist the earth with their greenness; all these are moved by the aforesaid air, which by its heat and moisture causes all things to germinate. Thus, when the soul overcomes the flesh’s delight and establishes the foundation of its desires in the person, soul and body complete their works in one accord. Hence, rejoicing in holy works, it flies in the sweet fragrance of virtues. And as greater rivers send forth diverse streams that make the earth germinate, so the soul, ruling the body, raises up within it charity, obedience, and humility together with other strongest virtues, through which it leads the person to the praise of God by the exercise of good works.

How, as earth dissolved into mud by summer heat and winter cold is impregnated for every kind of germination, so a person, while soul and flesh conflict with one another, now brings forth the fruits of virtues, now of vices.

[Col. 0848B] LX. For the earth is always muddy from summer heat and winter cold, and this mud impregnates it for germination. In this way the body ought to be subject to the soul as a maidservant to her mistress—though the soul is often overcome through the body, as a mistress through a maidservant—and the soul performs every good thing in a person, just as summer brings all fruits to ripeness.

But when the body, entangled in the corruption of sins, is opposed to the soul, the person says within himself: “I cannot live in such hardness as to be able entirely to deny my flesh what it desires; but what I can do is enough for me.” Yet, lying in the corruption of his sins, he sometimes remembers the former virtues which he performed; repenting of his muddy sins, he returns with joy to the righteous works and holy virtues which he previously possessed. And as muddy earth keeps all fruits within itself during winter and brings them forth in summer to the joy of human beings, so a person adorns and renders more elegant his former virtues as though with precious stones.

How the human breast contains the heart, liver, and lung, just as the air contains heat, dryness, and the moisture of the breezes; and how memory likewise contains, ordering the soul’s thoughts and its works.

LXI. The human breast shows the fullness and perfection of that same air. For as the breast [Col. 0848D] holds within itself the heart, liver, lung, and the other inward parts of the belly, so this air comprehends within itself the heat, dryness, and moisture of the breezes. In such a way, the soul in a person’s breast considers and, as it were, writes down the thoughts of every useful or useless matter, discerning them and arranging how the rational person ought to carry out that matter.

The soul also gathers every work of a person, whether soft because it pleases the flesh or hard because it is contrary to the flesh, and presents it for examination within itself. And because it is fiery, it dries up by its heat the enticements of the flesh; once these are dried up, it produces groaning accompanied by the moisture of tears, through which the soul adorns its works by performing every good thing. For the soul hates the flesh’s delight; and because it is airy, it displays to its flesh its evil works and the wounds of the storms of diabolical suggestion, summoning the person to recognize what kind of works his own are—just as the heart, with all its appendages, strengthens a person, moistening everything with its breath.

How the heart is enlivened by the liver, lung, and other intestines joined to it; and how the time of day and night, and the air of calm and storms, are varied by alternations; so human life amid fleshly and spiritual conflicts is now troubled by the whirlwind of vices, now gladdened by the brightness of virtues.

LXII. For the human heart indicates its heat, the liver its dryness, and the lung its moisture; because, as the heat of the heart, the dryness of the liver, and the moisture of the lung animate a person, so the heat, dryness, and moisture of air and breezes strengthen the things that are in the world. By the same reasoning, as the heart warms and strengthens a person together with all the vital parts joined to it, so the soul, together with the virtues bestowed upon it by God, completes human actions, granting him holy desire for good works.

But when it recognizes that this work of desire is evil, grieving over what it has done, it drives the person again through compunction to tears; and he then becomes like one who, delighted in good works, weeps for joy. The soul also directs every human work, whether good or evil, done in whatever disposition, according to the desire of the flesh. And as the aforesaid air breathes upon every creature—now germinating and flowering [Col. 0849C], now drying up and failing—so the soul changes the works of the flesh, varying them now with joys, now with tears.

And as sun and moon never complete their course without alternations of clouds, so a person cannot bring any good work he has begun to completion in the same purity in which he proposed it, without some storm frequently disturbing him. In the likeness of day and night, which sometimes shine more clearly in their light and sometimes fail in their light through changes of clouds, a person experiences the conflict of body and soul. Through the flesh’s desire he fails in goodness, but through the soul’s desire he rejoices and advances in it, because in all his works he is animated by its warmth, just as the aforesaid air moves among all creatures.

How, as the belly encloses and retains the internal organs and food crushed by the grinding of the teeth for the use of the whole body, so the soul ought to store in the secret place of memory the thoughts of its correction and chew them over with attentive discernment.

LXIII. And as food is sent through the throat into the belly after first being broken by the mill of the teeth, and as the human breast moderates through thought and knowledge everything belonging to the person, and as the belly contains and encloses the person’s internal organs, so the aforesaid air sends green powers into fruits and thereby preserves the things of the world for human salvation.

In the same way the soul chews over and entrusts to memory every human work, leaving none of them unexamined. As food is sent through the throat into the belly and is crushed by the teeth, so the soul, with its breath, writes down human works by discerning them; and it gathers this writing through thoughts, so that a person may know what sort of works his works are. He continually examines them in his thoughts, as certain forms of things in which they are shaped.

Therefore a person cannot forget his works, because they are kept enclosed in his thoughts as internal organs are enclosed in the belly. In all his works he flourishes through the soul, because it is airy. Thoughts, together with knowledge, are in the human breast like the servants of all his works, because they prepare them beforehand, just as the left hand serves the right, and winter serves summer because it preserves all that summer brings forth [Col. 0850B].

The soul too is the servant of thoughts, and thoughts are like a notebook in which the soul is written, because with them it refines all human works and, as though by writing, prepares itself for that to which it is compelled through the body. For when a person performs evil works according to the flesh’s desire, he is nevertheless sometimes pierced by compunction through the soul’s power and sheds tears, because the flesh’s evil works displease the soul, although it often serves the flesh, subject to it in consenting to them. The soul also recalls to his memory, as if by writing, with tearful sighing, the evil works which the person has committed through fleshly delights; and as winter preserves within itself the fruits of summer, so the soul diligently sets before the sinful person the sigh through which he may be saved.

How the swellings of flesh which rise upon the breast and are called breasts signify both the fertility of the outer air and the person’s inward desires clinging to the heart; and how, as woman compared with man is soft and weak, so fleshly delight has no strength in comparison with the powers of the soul.

LXIV. In the breast, in which all things a person wishes to do are gathered, certain swellings of rising flesh become breasts. These signify the fertility of the air described above, because, as breasts show a person’s strength and fullness, so they make manifest that air’s abundance for the fertility of the earth. Thus the soul knows what enables it to fly upward like air, because as mind is present in the heart, so knowledge is known to be present in the soul. Therefore all human works are completed through it.

And as the human body is clothed in diverse kinds of garments, so the soul is covered, as though by garments, with each and every work of the flesh, whatever it may be. These works continually appear upon it, visible only to souls and spirits, because whatever a person sows, that shall he also reap, carrying back at the end the sheaves of his works. For human desire clings to the heart as breasts to the breast, wherein all the breast’s strength consists. Therefore the soul is compelled to cooperate with the flesh through desire, so that through it—because it is airy, moist, and warm—all works are accomplished, just as the abundance of the whole earth is richly brought forth through the air.

In that place a man is mighty in his powers [Col. 0851A], but there a woman pours out milk for infants who cannot be refreshed by food. Thus the powers of the soul are most strong, because through them it knows and perceives God, even though it also serves the desires of the flesh. Therefore it wastes the body with sorrowful sighing when the body disdains to serve God against its own will, like a servant who departs angrily from his master.

For fleshly delight has no power over the soul’s strength, which sins displease; rather, it is driven by the movement of burning blood. Therefore, through the powers of the soul, the body is so afflicted that it can never accomplish grave sins joyfully without the pain of sighing. Compared with the powers of the soul, this delight has no strength for acting well; but it is fed by the taste of the flesh, as an infant is nourished on its mother’s milk, because it is wholly weak, as woman is if compared with man’s strength. But the soul’s desire is sharp as a flying arrow, which wounds the person into whom it is shot. Therefore fleshly delight is often subjected to the soul’s powers, whether it wishes or not.

Accordingly, the soul’s desire speaks thus in command to the person living securely amid fleshly delights: “Consider that your work is like fetid mud; therefore it is turned into confusion, because every sweet fragrance has breathed far away from you.”

How woman, on account of her weakness, looking to the man’s care, ought always to be subject to him and ready to serve; and what their outward common intercourse signifies in inward matters.

[Col. 0851C] LXV. Thus woman is weak and looks to man so that she may be cared for through him, just as the moon receives its strength from the sun; and therefore she ought always to be subject to man and ready to serve. For she covers man by the works of her skill, because she was formed from flesh and blood—which man was not, since he was first clay. Therefore, in his nakedness, he looks to woman so that he may be covered by her.

This means that the flesh’s delight looks with great trembling toward the soul’s desire, because it is often rebuked and overcome by it. Yet it cannot be overcome by the powers of the soul, because, just as woman looks to man to be cared for by him, serving him with fear, so fleshly delight always looks to the soul. But when a person has wholly failed through fleshly delight, he is stirred up again through the admonition of the soul’s desire, considering within himself that, since he has been placed by God in such great honor, why he does not desist from vices. Thus the soul frequently draws its body back to the love of good works.

For a person always has within himself this diversity of activity: the angels are with God in joy, while evil human works are judged through them in the anger of His judgment. The soul is also a breath from the Spirit of God; sent into the human body, it does nothing by itself. Rather, whatever the body asks of it, this it kindles in its own nature, with the knowledge of good by which it perceives God and with the knowledge of evil by which it fears Him. It rejoices always in good works as fire, and afflicts the body in evil ones.

For through the soul’s powers a person comes to life again, so that, understanding the works he has done according to the desire of the flesh, and by which he had stripped the soul of its powers, he is moved to tears by which the soul is clothed as with a shirt [Col. 0852A].

How whoever has wiped away sins through repentance should not afterward blush for them; and how one who afflicts himself through fasts and prayers adorns his soul as with a purple garment.

LXVI. Therefore, whoever has wiped away his sins through the tears of true repentance, like Mary Magdalene, who wept over the Lord’s feet, shall no longer blush for them. But when, after tears, he mortifies his flesh by fasts and prayers, he adorns his soul as with a purple garment, through which the scars of wounds are so covered that they never appear upon it.

The soul always seeks repentance from a person, because he has the taste of sins; and it asks that he act through repentance, just as a woman covers a man by the subtle skill of her work. But the person who has turned aside from the sins by which he was occupied through the taste of the flesh, performing good works with all zeal, adorns his soul with golden crowns and every ornament. Therefore angels rejoice over it, which had been the lost sheep, and it rejoices with them.

Vices and virtues are fruitful like a woman, because vice gives birth to vices and virtue to virtues. And the man who is strong and powerful according to God completes all his works, both good and evil, with the woman who first brought about the fall, and through whom those same evils were afterward repaired for the better.

How, as air brings the earth’s fruits to maturity through heat and moisture, so heart, liver, and lung warm the belly for preparing and digesting food; and how God consumes the perverse habits of sins with the fire of His zeal.

LXVII. But the heart also warms the belly, the liver strengthens it, and the lung moistens it, so that it retains the food it receives until evacuation; just as the air described above brings the greenness, heat, and moisture of all germinating fruits to their maturity. Thus also the soul, which is rational and fiery, possesses rationality together with wind, just as blazing fire does not emit its flame without wind. And, in the circling course of the knowledge of good and evil, it possesses discernment by which it knows what pleases God, and also understands that God, in His zeal, burns up the evil habit of sins, as it is written:

Words of David pertaining to the same matter, and how they ought to be understood.

LXVIII. “Smoke descended in His wrath, and fire blazed forth from His face; coals were kindled by Him” (Psalm XVII). This is clear to the understanding as follows: when a person through sinning is led into forgetfulness of God, the wrath of God’s vengeance rises against him, and his sins are tested before God by fire. For as extinguished coals are kindled by fire, so God prepares punishments for burning up sins.

For through the knowledge of good and evil, the person knows that he is to be punished for his evil deeds, and that good works, flying in God’s praise, ascend above the cherubim. This knowledge warms the confident hope which a person has toward God and strengthens him in the fear and love of God. Through these virtues the moisture of tears is brought forth; through them also all the good things to be completed in a person are preserved, just as the belly, through heart, liver, and lung, preserves the food it receives until evacuation.

All works, good and evil alike, are brought to human recognition through the rationality of the airy and rational soul—with the greenness of knowledge, the heat of sensation, and the moisture of wisdom—just as the aforesaid air brings the greenness, heat, and moisture of all germinating fruits to their maturity [Col. 0853B].

How the tenderness of the belly, enclosed by ribs and bones, signifies the softness of fruitful earth interspersed with stones; and what is expressed through these in the differing condition of human life, with a fitting verse from Psalm XVI offered as testimony.

LXIX. The belly, supported by ribs and other bones that lack the juice of marrow, signifies soft and fruitful earth interspersed with stones. By this example, the soul does not have the taste of sins in its own nature, although it works sins with the body and kindles the body for works which the taste of its flesh demands, in the likeness of the airy wind which moves the whole earth to germination. For the soul contains the body in all its work, as soft fruitful earth is made firm by stones interspersed within it.

And as a tender infant speaks about sins which it has not yet tasted, and as Adam before transgression knew sin but did not taste it, so the soul does not naturally taste sin in the body which sins. But the soul that performs holy and good works is glorious before God in the heavenly kingdom according to the merits of its works; whereas great punishments await the soul that perpetrates evil works through God’s judgment.
