A blessed person is praised before God and human beings for his good works, and therefore his soul rejoices. But a person entangled in slippery sins is led into great confusion before God and human beings. Therefore, fleeing people because of his sins with the sweat of shame, once he recognizes himself culpable in these matters, he laments himself as dead and stripped of every honor of blessedness, saying: “They have received me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s whelp dwelling in secret places” (Psalm XVI).

This is clear to the understanding as follows: when a person has sinned, he is stripped of all blessedness because of his sins, since through his own will all holiness is snatched from him, as a lion snatches what it wishes to devour. And because of the wretched confusion of his sins, he hides himself from people, blushing for his sins as a lion’s whelp in secret places, lest his works become known. Thus every human work will receive either reward in glory or punishment in God’s judgment [Col. 0854A]. But the soul rejoicing in holiness says to God: “O most high God, I render all my vows to You in praise, because without You I can do nothing of myself, except insofar as You kindle it within me through the grace of the Holy Spirit.”

How, as flowers are shaken off when fruit follows, hunger is driven away when satiety arrives; and how in the same way, once repentance has been accomplished, the soul that was wasting away as though in famine through sins is satisfied with God’s justice in the performance of holy works.

LXX. Hunger, which asks for food, reveals the flowers of fruits; but when the belly has been filled with fruits, hunger ceases, just as flowers fall when fruits emerge. Similarly, the soul, which is breath from God and, always seeking truth with knowledge of good and evil, is a treasury of righteousness, understands in its nature that God must be loved above all things, since it came forth from Him as a spark from fire. It also makes human works flash like sparks, because through it a person is enlightened as through a spark.

The soul makes a person sigh over his utterly worthless works, which he performs with it against God; and, hungering for God’s justice within himself, it afflicts him until, recognizing his sins, he pours out tears with repentance for them. Therefore, when a person has trampled down his sins by repenting in this manner, the soul is satisfied with God’s justice. But when afterward it has gathered to itself the flowers of virtues together with good works, filled with good works it immediately no longer hungers—the soul which before suffered hunger in grieving over evil works—because this hunger fails through the fruits of good works, as flowers fall away [Col. 0854C].

By what correspondences the stomach, the world, and the soul strengthen one another; and how God never wills a person to exist without the law of a commandment; and what the greenness of summer, the dryness of winter, and the vast capacity of the world signify within that person.

LXXI. But the stomach, whose seat is in the belly, into which foods are sent and from which they are discharged, and which is bound together with the intestines like a sack, represents the capacity of the world, which creatures fill by sprouting and growing, and which they render, as it were, empty by failing. That is to say: man, who waxes and wanes like the moon, acts through the soul, which is filled with all creatures [Col. 0854D]; and as blood is in the veins, so all human actions are in the soul. When it has been filled with good works according to its desire, it ascends to the eternal dwelling, where it is refreshed with the food of life; but when it is occupied with evil works, it descends, doomed to perish, into the stinking corruption of infernal punishments.

For God, who gave Adam the commandment, wills man to be under a commandment; in observing it, the soul joyfully gathers works of salvation, whereas it is sent weeping into the exile of perdition when man, abandoning the commandment, consents to the desires of his flesh. But as the stomach, which receives and discharges food, is bound together with the intestines, so the soul works in man with all creatures, whether in the ascent of good or the descent of evil. And as creatures flower and grow green in summer, but wither and fail in winter, so it flowers and grows green in rejoicing over good works, and withers and fails in grieving over evil works.

Nor is it beneficial for the stomach to be empty, just as it would not be useful for the capacity of the world to be emptied of its various creatures. This capacity is also the steward of the earth’s productive powers, since it leaves it neither desolate nor empty of anything necessary to the office of bearing fruit. For if the world were narrow and confined, so that it lacked spaciousness, it could not bear the fullness of creatures which it now contains. So too it would not benefit man if he possessed only one kind of knowledge, for then he would be as though empty, unable to begin or accomplish any work, or to distinguish [Col. 0855A] the light of day from the darkness of night. But now he is filled with two kinds of knowledge: through good knowledge he loves God with good works, and through evil knowledge, knowing evil works, he fears Him.

The soul dwells in the body with great care, like a householder in his house, who is always careful lest he be plundered of his goods. For it always takes care lest man, through the entanglement of sins, be stripped of the holy desires which are brought about through it. But when man, weary of his sins, has at some time consented to the soul, it rejoices at this, sets before him all his sins in bitterness, makes heavenly desires sweeter to him than honey and the honeycomb, very often makes him holy, and leads him to the heavenly [Col. 0855B] kingdoms.

For as man would perish if his stomach were always empty, so the soul could by no means exist without these two kinds of knowledge. And as the world would wither if it were empty of good and evil fruits, so the soul would be dry and empty if it lacked the works which man performs through these two kinds of knowledge. For it rightly administers with discernment all that belongs to man, directing it upon the straight path; and through the goodness of God, from whom it is divine, it trusts that by the holy works which it works with man it will have a dwelling in the land of the living. Through the knowledge of good, moreover, by which it knows evil, it judges that evil to be unjust, although it is often compelled to perform that same evil through the body. And if it did not possess this knowledge [Col. 0855C] of good and evil, it would be like a bellows with which a smith does nothing. And as the world would be without all fullness of fruits if it did not sprout in greenness, so it too would be without the honor and blessedness of good works if it did not flourish in the rational power of knowing good and evil.

That, in the likeness of the air assisting the earth to bear fruit, the soul also moves the body by its powers to carry out whatever works are required; if these are upright, adorned for eternity it perfectly beholds God, the angels, and blessed souls, but if they are perverse, it is driven away from that vision as unclean.

LXXII. The aforesaid capacity of the world contains air within itself. By imparting greenness to the earth through its powers, it makes it fruitful; and when its fruits have reached maturity, it inclines them toward dryness by windy cold. Yet although it outwardly dries the earth by this coldness, the earth is thereby inwardly enriched, so that it may sprout in summer. Therefore the Creator of all, who established the earth for work, made the soul, through which man performs all his works, after His own likeness. It is invisible to man, who is God’s own work and will work until the last day, just as the holy Divinity is invisible; but after the last day, when man has wholly become spiritual, he will perfectly behold the holy Divinity and all spirits and souls.

This same soul is a fruitful power, which makes the whole man live by moving him with itself. And as a man is clad and covered with a garment woven from threads, [Col. 0856A] so it is covered, as if putting on a garment, with all the works which it performs with man, whether good or evil, just as with the body in which it dwells. When it has departed from the body, good works appear within it like a garment shining with the brightness of the purest gold and adorned with every ornament; but evil works stink within it like a garment polluted by every uncleanness.

It also works with man in the likeness of air, which sends its powers into the earth, through which the earth is fruitful and brings its fruits to completion, and which dries the whole earth by the cold of winter. Yet it preserves within itself warmth for the earth’s fruitfulness. Thus through the powers of the soul childhood, adolescence, youth, and old age perform and bring to completion the fruits of good works; decrepit age [Col. 0856B] dries these up, as it were, through failure, yet in true faith they will be preserved after man’s end for the rewards of eternal blessedness.

That, as the earth, if it became green twice in a year and bore produce everywhere, would turn dry and become dust, so the soul would fail in its work if it served all its desires and pleasures of the flesh without restraint; and that, like the earth bearing fruit unequally, it is by reason of its mutability and the conflict of the flesh now in advancement and now in decline, and cannot in this life perfectly attain either the faith commended in the Gospel or the vision of God lost in paradise.

LXXIII. If the earth became green twice in a year and bore produce everywhere, it would turn to dryness and become like dust. By this is signified that, if the soul likewise consented to the desires and will of its flesh, it could accomplish no work. For it is a living breath, which passes through and gives life to the whole body by a noble touch, just as the breath of the aforesaid air makes the whole earth fruitful. That same air is, as it were, the soul of the earth; touching its moisture with its breath, it makes the earth grow green. And as this air—whose greenness signifies blood and whose moisture signifies sweat in man—is invisible and impalpable in the earth, so the soul, impalpable in the body, warms the blood and works visibly in it through rationality.

For man understands through the soul that he has God; and therefore he always establishes a law for himself, whether by himself or through another. This is natural to him, because the first [Col. 0856C] man received the law in the commandment which, at the serpent’s counsel, he rejected. Expelled into this exile after transgressing God’s commandment, he could not inhabit paradise, although he longed for it with many sighs. Likewise, when the soul has been overcome through the body, it draws many sighs in sorrow; but when it has subjected the body to the desires of its own nature, it rejoices with great joy.

And as the earth does not bring forth its fruits equally in cold and heat, so the soul, acting badly and well, has unequal works. From this nature, in which the soul is often overcome through the body and the body through the soul, man can by no means possess that pure faith through which he could lift a mountain and cast it into the sea, as the Lord said to His disciples concerning the mustard seed; nor can he possess the faith which Adam had when he saw the invisible brightness of God with his outward eyes, and in which he did not doubt that he could do whatever he wished. But after the transgression neither Adam nor any human being could have this vision. Therefore the faithful man looks toward God with the inward sight of his soul in the mirror of faith, and trusts that he will be saved by Him who can do all things. In this faith many, mortifying the desires of their flesh, performed many signs [Col. 0857A].

That, as the veins of the heart, liver, and lungs assist the stomach in receiving and discharging food, and continual, excessive fullness or emptiness would harm that stomach, so the soul is present with the body in all its works, but would be weary if it allowed the body always to follow the desires of the flesh.

LXXIV. From the heart, liver, and lungs certain veins extend like pipes, and assist the stomach in receiving and discharging food. In this manner the soul, which with great power awakens the body when it finds it asleep, perceives God in its many courses. And as the veins attend the stomach when it is filled and emptied, so it is present with man in every good and evil, so that through it man exercises thoughts, the hardness of malice, and the softness of fleshly desire, both beginning and completing them. And as streams of blood run to the stomach, so it passes through the whole body by its powers.

Moreover, as it would not benefit the stomach [Col. 0857B] to be always full or always empty, so it would harm the soul if the body always lived amid the delights of fleshly desires; for it would fail, having in its powers a hunger for the desires of its own nature—as feeling and body also often fail in the person who sins incessantly amid the fatness of his flesh.

That, as human flesh is injured if it receives either excessive nourishment or less food than is necessary, so the soul is injured if it adheres to severity or relaxation more or less than is just; and that the stomach, receiving clean foods but rejecting foul ones, signifies the man who delights in sins but is afterward purified through repentance.

LXXV. Therefore, if foods are received excessively, a man’s flesh becomes sick through an unhealthy discoloration; or if they are taken in less quantity than necessary, the flesh is weakened by deficiency. Thus the stomach is a proper steward of the reception and discharge of food.

Likewise, when the soul has overcome a man by its fiery power, so that he mortifies himself by abstaining from fleshly desires and from his own will, then, puffed up with pride at the devil’s suggestion, he often says while despising others: “I am holy, and I deserve to be praised and honored by all.” Thus, with the eyes of his soul blinded by pride, he cannot possess joy and heavenly desire because of excessive sorrow; and troubled within that man he says: “Alas, alas! Blinded by foul pride, I have been stripped of heavenly desires, in which I saw and understood God.”

Therefore let the man who performs good works not through flesh and blood, but through the powers of the soul by which he knows and perceives God, guard himself most diligently against pride [Col. 0857C] in good works, lest through it he lose the rewards of eternal blessedness. For as a man’s flesh becomes sick if he receives food either excessively or less than is necessary, so the soul fails through the arrogance of pride and through excessive abstinence without discernment.

But the soul which gives life to the body, and understands God in the Trinity of unity, is a humble spirit, and displays its humility in a man’s childhood, when he has not yet acquired pride or hatred in the taste of sins. It rejoices in him until that same man is stirred through fleshly desires to sins, for which it always laments in sorrow. For it can never work fully according to the desire of its nature in the earthen vessel of the body, since the flesh seeks exile and even life; but it afflicts the body, by whose sin it is often afflicted, by setting before it unclean and stinking sins with grief, and makes it recognize those sins in sadness.

For the stomach, which receives foods and again discharges them in foulness, signifies the man who delights in sins and afterward is turned through repentance to distress over sins [Col. 0857D].

That, as the navel is the strength of all the inward parts attached to it, and the circumference of the earth is the receptacle of other creatures, so everything done through body and soul, whether good or evil, refers to the soul itself; and that there is a great difference between those who sin through pride and those who sin through negligence.

LXXVI. All the inward parts of the belly are attached to the navel, just as the remaining creatures look to the circumference of the earth. For the navel is the strength of the belly, just as the circumference of the earth is the receptacle of the other creatures. This signifies that the soul, which mediates all human works, rejoices in holy and good works by confessing not in itself but in God; and it grieves shamefully over sins in which it knows its vessel to be entangled. Through this grief it afflicts that vessel—that is, the body—as with a goad, and man, constrained within himself, says: “Why does my soul grieve me so greatly over the sins in which I was born and from which I cannot restrain myself, when I trust that I shall amend them before my end?”

Thus man comforts himself in sins and rejoices in them as though amid the sound of feasters. Therefore the soul, from whose nature this consolation does not proceed, is filled with sadness, since it is life proceeding from divine rationality, which moves man, who is every creature. For God, who wove for Himself the garment of His humanity from the virginal flesh of the Virgin Mary, out of the lowliest nature of man, greatly loves humility, through which He overcame the pride and malice of the devil.

But the soul supports man in good and evil as a column supports a house. For when a man flees in God through the pride of holiness, through the soul he understands himself to be hateful to God and men; and it does not permit him to possess joy while afflicting him in this manner. Many indeed perish through the pride of holiness [Col. 0858A], and very many lose the rewards of their labors, so that at their end they can scarcely be saved, sighing toward God.

But those who have sinned through negligence of holiness and fleshly desires, without pride, God forgives many sins when they sigh over them in repentance; and many of these afterward become holy and a pillar of heavenly Jerusalem. For as the navel is the strength of all inward parts attached to it, so all works, whether good or evil, look to the soul, because it is the strength of them all.

That the navel is also compared with the earth’s muddy and watery uncleannesses discharged in marshes, because heat, cold, and moisture press food and drink, digested beneath it, downward to be expelled; and that likewise the soul, overcome by the pleasures of the flesh and entangled in filthy works, must be cast down into lower places of punishment unless it is cleansed by the sighs of repentance.

LXXVII. The navel, together with the bodily channels of the heart, liver, lungs, and all the inward parts, rises to assist in man’s nourishment; and the breath of the soul moves all these, as the air strengthens all the earth’s powers by blowing through them. The same navel extends to the end of the loins, like the earth which always discharges certain muddy and watery uncleannesses in marshes. And because the heat, cold, and moisture by which man is governed lie hidden in the navel, food and drink, by which man is sustained in flesh and blood, flow downward there and are cast out like mud [Col. 0858B].

For the man who works through the powers of the soul with every creature according to God is, according to the nature of the earth—of which one part is soft and another hard—both hard and soft. In his softness the soul grieves through the taste of the flesh when that man, overcome by these things, does not consent to it. For as air strengthens all creatures to grow, and as the navel together with bodily channels rises to assist food, so the soul passes through, contains, and brings to completion all human works by its powers.

It is also covered by the works of the body, as a worm is covered by its dwelling which it makes from mud. And as mud is moved by worms which are sometimes unseen, so man is moved to filthy works by the invisible soul. And although it draws all a man’s works to itself as a hook draws a fish, yet it is so overcome by the body that it can in no way resist it. It knows, moreover, that it must be punished and brought to judicial torments for the sins it is compelled to perform through the body, because all things are seen as if written within it. Therefore, as long as it remains in the body, it sends forth sighs of pain; for as the navel extends to the loins, so sins extend into it. And when it is sent into punishments, this is as food from man is discharged into mud and as the earth discharges muddy uncleannesses [Col. 0858C].

That, as the earth and man—the former in summer, the latter in youth—grow green and flower, and likewise the former in winter and the latter in old age dry up and fade, so the soul, remaining in the body and compelling it to serve itself, grows green in good works and in the examples of the Son of God by ascending from virtue to virtue; and afterward, drawn out of the body, adorned as though with precious stones, it rests before God while eagerly awaiting the reception of the body in which it had labored.

LXXVIII. Man is brought to flourishing completion in childhood and youth, and afterward inclines to dryness through old age, just as the earth is adorned by flourishing greenness in summer and afterward is turned pale by cold in winter. For when the soul has so overcome its body that it consents to it with a simple heart in good will and delights in good works as in the sweetest food, that man says in heavenly desire: “How sweet to my throat are the utterances of your righteousness, even much sweeter than honey to my mouth!” Thus he lives with childlike simplicity, in innocence, without the taste of the flesh.

But the soul imbues this man with its desires until, ascending from virtue to virtue, he grows strong and flourishes in the good works and examples which the Son of God left to humankind. For it rejoices and is adorned in him, unstained by the corruption of sins. And as in winter’s cold the greenness, flowering, and ripeness of all fruits fail, so man fails in all good and evil works through death. But the soul of the man who has happily completed good works in childhood, youth, and old age ascends before God bright with these same works and adorned as though with precious stones [Col. 0858D], and can scarcely await the body through which it worked, so that they may dwell together in a joyful abode.

What the strength or wantonness of the kidneys, and the richness of the earth—which, when moderate, produces abundant fruit, but when immoderate, produces fruit that is empty though it may appear plentiful—signify among the soul’s various dispositions.

LXXIX. In the kidneys, in which both strength and slippery wantonness are diffused, is signified the richness of the earth. For as sometimes a man’s powers, and sometimes unsuitable things, arise in them, so also the earth’s moderate richness produces an abundance of fruits, while its immoderate richness sometimes produces empty fruits, though they appear very numerous.

For man accomplishes through the powers of the soul, in wisdom, knowledge, and discernment, everything he does beneath the course of sun and moon in the seasons of the months. Through it also, because it is fiery and airy, he does good and evil in accordance with the moon which waxes and wanes. Through the powers of the same soul, which possesses understanding of heavenly good, man thinks and does all things; and he distinguishes through rational discernment the times of times and the elements with which he does good and evil, and names everything he knows. And as strength of integrity and weakness, prosperity and uselessness, lie hidden in the kidneys, and as the earth through the sun, moon, and air brings forth all things useful and useless by which man lives, so this strength is in the soul, so that by its powers man may do good and evil, useful and useless things [Col. 0861A].

That the earth is established in the middle of the air and fortified against storms by mountains and hills, some hot or cold, and some tempered by heat and frost, like a city secured with towers and ramparts; and that in this way the soul, in its manifold conflict against the desires of the flesh, is adorned and defended by the protection of holy works.

LXXX. The earth is in the middle of the air as a honeycomb is in the middle of honey, raised with varied hills, so that in one region it has hills uninhabitable through excessive heat, in another through excessive cold, and in another hills tempered by heat and cold. For it is strengthened by hills as a city is by towers and ramparts. The hills cover the valleys, and mountains defend the earth against varied storms; therefore it too is surrounded and strengthened by mountains and hills as though by a wall.

This signifies that the soul, wholly implanted in the body by God’s command, knows that in it it will perform, with every creature, works both heavenly and earthly. It understands also that God, who judges all evil works in man’s good works, is praised by all His angels and saints, because He is king and ruler of all in heaven, and deliverer in the lower regions, having delivered man by assuming mortal flesh. It knows that this wondrous God performs many miracles in His saints.

For when man sins according to the taste of his flesh, he is often recalled through the soul in repentance. But if he overcomes the soul by never ceasing from sins, the soul laments within him with a tearful voice, because the hunger of its nature is never refreshed while it can scarcely have any hope of salvation in God. But when the grace of God at last makes that man recognize his sins in bitter repentance and strengthens him to abandon the world, the soul greatly rejoices. Thus human works are likened to the earth, which the air holds on every side, above and below; and the soul with the body is as air with earth, and as the honeycomb in the midst of honey [Col. 0861B].

For as the earth has hills suitable for habitation because tempered by heat and cold, and others untempered and uninhabitable, so man performs good works through which he is led to the heavenly homeland, and evil works through which he is led to places of punishment. But when the soul has become victorious by overcoming the will of the flesh, it delights, because it is spirit, in good works according to its own nature, and serves God in the love of faith just as the angels who behold His face do. It also compels the body, to which fleshly desires are opposed, toward good and holy works. And when it has conquered it through the strongest battles of good works, it is adorned and strengthened by those good works like a city with towers and ramparts.

For it is humble; and through the lowly nature of flesh by which it is oppressed, it gives forth a lamentable voice, by which it never permits the man who raises his neck in pride to possess full joy. From the nature of the same soul, he cannot even rejoice in repentance for the distress of his sins; and so in a true ascent of humility the soul restrains man, lest he wander along the vain paths of pride. For the soul, which climbs by the ladder of humility to the high mountain that is the dwelling-place of heavenly Jerusalem, always warns man to depart from pride and bend himself to humility, lest he be submerged through the deceit of the ancient serpent. For as valleys are defended from unsuitable rain by hills, so men are defended from evils by humility. And as the earth is defended from varied storms by mountains and hills, by which it is defended and strengthened as though by a wall, so the soul will reach the heavenly homeland through holy works fortified by humility as though by a wall, escaping the devil’s confusion [Col. 0861C].

That, as the earth is so placed that it is tempered everywhere by the sun, so the soul, subject to God, should be filled with the light of wisdom through the power of discernment.

LXXXI. The earth is so situated in relation to the sun’s course that it is tempered by it in every part. So too the soul, when tempered with wisdom, moistens man with drops from the spring that leaps up, which is God, so that, knowing God, he may walk in the broad places of discernment and holy desire and, for love of Him, abandon the taste of his sins. But the man who acts according to the desires of the soul is illumined through it with holy works, just as the earth is illumined by the sun in all its functions.

That man, made in the likeness of the earth, has bones without marrow in the place of stones and bones with marrow in the place of trees; and that, according to the quality of his morals, he receives by signification either the hardness of stones or the pleasantness of a flowering garden or fruitful orchard.

LXXXII. The earth is strengthened by stones and trees, and man was made according to it, because his flesh is as earth; his bones without marrow’s juice are as stones; while bones with marrow are like trees. Hence man constructs his building, according to himself, from earth, stones, and wood.

The soul, to which the desires of the flesh are opposed and which is the support of the whole body, pours its powers into it and performs and completes every work with man. And man becomes a flowering garden in which the Lord delights His eyes, when he acts according to the soul’s desire; but when he acts according to the will of the flesh, he does not shine before God’s eyes, like the sun suffering eclipse.

For the man who has done good works is likened to an orchard full of every good fruit, like earth strengthened and adorned with stones and trees; but when he perpetrates evil works through the hardness of sins, he is fruitless before God, like hard earth without fruit. Man’s flesh signifies good knowledge, which possesses fruitful softness; his bones signify evil knowledge, which hardens itself against God; and the bones in him which lack marrow signify his evil works.

But the soul works in man according to God; for as God established heaven in full joy for heavenly beings and gave earth to human beings to inhabit, so the soul performs good works, which are heavenly, in joy with man, and evil works, which are earthly, in sorrowful complaint. Therefore the knowledge of good and evil is the soul’s inward parts, through which it teaches man humility, the material of all virtues, and by which it so constrains man in his powers amid sins that he can never accomplish them in joy. And as a man foresees all the structures of the house which he wishes to build according to his will, so the soul arranges all works in man according to its ability [Col. 0861D].

Likewise, that as the air sustains and contains the earth, equally placed on every side in its midst, so body and soul, joined by God, although widely different in nature, ought patiently to support and instruct each other in jointly fulfilling their Creator’s commandments.

LXXXIII. The earth is placed in the midst of the air, so that air is present in equal measure above the earth, below the earth, and on either side of the earth. The soul also, a living breath sent by God into the body, instructs man to obey God’s commandments with patience in this laborious life. It dwells and remains in him amid a separation as great as that between heaven and earth, so that he who cannot fully comprehend by his knowledge what he himself is may look toward his Creator by striving in labor with patience and obedience.

For as the air is about the earth’s middle, sustaining and containing it, so the soul dwells in the middle of the body, sustaining it wholly, and works in it according to what it asks from the body [Col. 0862A].

That the bladder, which receives and discharges drink, represents the courses of rivers spread throughout the earth; and that similarly the soul, victorious over flesh, ought to irrigate its body with the streams of God’s commandments, receiving good and discharging evil, with an appropriate verse of Psalm CXVIII adduced in testimony.

LXXXIV. But man’s bladder represents the flooding of rivers spread here and there throughout the earth. For as it receives and discharges the fluids of the belly, so rivers likewise now increase and now decrease, and water the whole earth. Therefore the soul, to which the nature of flesh and blood is opposed, teaches man to abstain from restless thoughts and not to despair of God’s grace on account of his sins, but to prostrate himself in true humility at the Lord’s feet for them, so that almighty God may deign mercifully to forgive him his sins in bitter repentance.

For when it has so overcome man in his humble nature that he consents to it in all things, it victoriously passes through heaven, saying: “I have desired thy salvation, O Lord, and thy law is my meditation” (Ps. CXVIII). This is understood thus: I, in my flesh, which of itself does not consent in good to thy commandments, desired and understood thee; and by the power of thy salvation I was so infused, as with swift water, that amid my powers and in the midst of my heart I might meditate upon thy commandments against the will of that flesh. And as a mill grinds grain for eating by water, so I, who am the torrent-course of water in the body, diligently observe all thy commandments by seeking them according to my nature.

For as man’s bladder receives and discharges the body’s watery moisture, and as rivers by growing and diminishing pour over the whole earth, so the victorious soul governs the whole body by receiving good and discharging evil through God’s commandments; its powers increase in good and decrease in evil [Col. 0862B].

That the bodily places through which the digestion of food and drink is discharged represent the hidden subterranean channels of rivers; and the lament of a soul polluted by muddy and stinking works, which breathes again toward God through hope of repentance and Christ’s Passion, with an appropriate verse of Psalm XLI adduced in testimony.

LXXXV. The places where the digestion of food and drink is discharged represent the hidden subterranean channels of the aforesaid rivers. For as digestion cannot remain in the human body but appears when expelled, so these channels also discharge rivers and bring them into open manifestation.

But when the soul is hidden from light in muddy sins, it cannot refrain from saying in a mournful voice: “Alas, alas! I am wretched, I who am so truly a living breath, entangled in such a stench of sins that I can behold heaven with no joy. Alas, whence have I come, or where am I going? And what good are all the good things which God created to me, when I shall be plunged into hell?” But afterward, returning to itself, it says again: “I trust in my God, that in true repentance I may be freed through His mercy from the infernal torments which I have deserved.”

And thus, comforted and strengthened through God’s grace, it says again: “Why art thou sad, my soul, and why dost thou trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Ps. XLI). This is understood thus: when a man, compelled by the nature of his soul, thinks of amending his sins, he says in the joy that has flowed into him from the streams of living water: “Why am I so greatly saddened and troubled in my soul, when through God’s grace I can blot out the wounds of my sins with sighs and tears—wounds from which I trust that I shall be delivered through the wounds of my Lord, who endured nails and a lance for my sins?”

Afterward he makes manifest all evil works in bitter repentance, just as the excretion of food and drink is discharged. And as lights are brought forth above the earth from subterranean waters, so an excellent report of these matters flies abroad over the earth: the person who had been extinguished in sins is revealed in good works [Col. 0862C].

That the back and sides of man signify the plain of the earth; the thighs and seat, however, signify its hills and the roughness of that lower part of the earth which is hard and impenetrable and holds fast the upper part, which is soft; and that likewise, through the powers of the soul, the softness of the flesh is restrained from vices, so that, adorned with the pearls of virtues, it kindles the holy angels both to wonder at it and to praise God.

LXXXVI. The back and sides of a human being represent the level surface of the earth; but the soul, which, while it works, is called spirit [Col. 0865B], works with the human being in holy deeds and bright virtues, through which God is praised by the angelic spirits. The soul itself is invisible to the body, which it wholly governs, just as God, who created the whole earth, is invisible to human beings. And as a person works powerfully with back and side, so the soul also accomplishes all its works with the body.

Moreover, in the thighs and in the seat are shown the hills and roughness of the aforesaid hard and impenetrable earth. For as the thighs adhere to the loins and belly and carry the person, and as the seat holds the person up, so this lower and impenetrable part of the earth is joined to its upper, tender and soft part, and, like steel, holds it by its strength lest it dissolve. [Col. 0865C] For just as a human being governs the whole earth by skills, turning it over with the plough now more deeply and now more lightly, so the soul traverses and overturns the body, according to the taste of the flesh, by its powers and virtues. By the strongest powers of this same soul a human being accomplishes grave and criminal sins; but lighter sins, which occur in thoughts without action, are accomplished only by other powers of the soul.

For the devil, because of the hatred he bears toward his Lord, suggests delight to a human being; from it, whenever a person is angry, smoke rises in that person’s body, because no one would ever be angry if deprived of fleshly delight. But the soul, which is immortal life, at whose departure the body dies, accomplishes every work according to the desires of the body, just as an airy wind makes the whole earth [Col. 0865D] germinate; and, working in the body, it never ceases, as a torrent of water never ceases in its flowing.

Indeed, all the angels marvel at that person who is clothed in holy works as in a most elegant garment, because he will also share their fellowship in praising God. And the soul supports all that person’s works, just as the thighs and seat support the entire human being. And as rough and sharp earth carries the soft part of the earth and the rivers, so the powers of the soul hold the whole person together, adhering to him in service, as the thighs adhere with the loins to the belly. The soul likewise, with its powers, supports a person’s works as the hind part supports the person himself; it compels him to rejoice in good and to grieve in evil, and surrounds him with good works [Col. 0866A] and diverse virtues as with berries and pearls. Therefore John also says:

Words of the holy apostle John in his Apocalypse, contemplating and describing the adornment of the bride of Christ—that is, the holy soul—and of David in the Psalm, proclaiming the excellence of the human being.

LXXXVII. “I saw Jerusalem descending from heaven, adorned as a bride for her husband” (Rev. 21). Its meaning is clear as follows: This bride signifies the holy and adorned soul, joined to Christ through the dowry of his blood, and looking to him as a bride looks to her bridegroom. For the Son of God himself descended from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, in which he built the new and holy city Jerusalem.

For the angels, who always behold the face of God, marvel at the works of the saints, which shine before God’s face with innumerable [Col. 0866B] adornments, continually build new tabernacles by ascending to the heavenly Jerusalem, and even gleam before them like golden writing. Therefore they resound with the music of psaltery, harp, and every voice of praise. God created the human being in order that he might perform shining works that would gleam in heaven, so that angels might marvel at the works of that human being as they marvel also at the face of God.

Thus it is also written: “Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels; thou hast crowned him with glory and honour, and hast set him over the works of thy hands” (Ps. 8). Its meaning is clear as follows: God is always present to the angels, who are his praise; therefore he is seen and known by them. But the human being, who is his work together with the soul, sees him in faith and not in [Col. 0866C] divinity. God glorifies, honours, and greatly adorns that person because he created him for obedience to his commandments and set him over all the works that he had made.

Likewise, concerning the comparison of hard and soft earth, earth uninhabitable through heat or cold, the causes of earthquakes, and the fact that this same earth, unless it were beneath as if iron and steel, would be broken apart by excessive heat at the sun’s rising and excessive cold at its setting; and concerning the manifold conflict of flesh and soul according to what has been stated above.

LXXXVIII. For to the tender part of the earth is joined another part, hard and as though iron, which persists in its hardness as though it were made of steel, so that no flood of waters running about it can either break it or soften it. [Col. 0866D] Likewise, when a person embraces the delight of the flesh, the soul says in its spiritual nature: “Alas for the softness of fleshly taste, which I afflict and by which I am afflicted!” Therefore the person immediately groans in sins, saying: “Alas for me, that I have been born into such great sins as I cannot overcome within myself!”

And as soon as the soul feels this grief, it draws the person to itself by punishing him more than before in his sins, and makes him sorrowful because of his sins, since the powers of the soul have dried up within him. Afterwards, by acting according to the nature of the soul, the person brings it forth in the mortification of fleshly desires, so that he may find it in heavenly desire.

Likewise, the soul overcomes the person in whom it does not find hardness of heart, [Col. 0867A] just as hard earth, as though iron, upholds soft earth under its power. And that soul strengthens him by the strength of faith as by steel, lest he fail through the surrounding evils of habitual sins. This part of hard and iron-like earth therefore has hills and rocks; and the rivers which flow in four divisions in the east cannot cleave it, though they sometimes move it without wounding it.

This motion comes from the excessive heat of the sun on that side of the firmament where the sun rises; and unless the earth beneath were iron or as though steel, it would all be torn apart by this excessive heat. On the other side of the firmament, where the sun sets, it would likewise be broken by excessive cold. For these regions of the earth are uninhabitable both because of immoderate heat of the sun and because of immoderate cold.

Accordingly, the soul, whose nature is humble, always fights against human pride and says to it: “Why do you rise to such a height, as though you had created yourself? For if you desire to exist or act through yourself, you will fall as the first angel fell.” The soul also knows and perceives God, from whom its spiritual essence was made, and understands that none is like him. Therefore it hates pride, which is joyless and desires to exist through itself and obey no one.

Thus it says also to the proud mind of its body: “Everything you seek is vain and deceptive, and what you call honour is blasphemy. When you think that you ascend without the help of God and human beings, [Col. 0867C] you will fall.” But the person often sighs from the soul’s grief; turning away from all works of pride, he ascends into the height of holy works of humility. Through this he is held and strengthened amid sins, as hard earth is held by hills and rocks.

Then the person performs good and holy works in a different manner, as though coming alive again with the elements, lest, condemned as though by mortal wounds, he be mocked before God and human beings; just as that earth is not broken apart in its strength by the four rivers. But the soul, which is windy, moves every creature in the person through heart and veins, while it works with him against sins that are burdensome and contrary to it. It often makes him weep after the joy of sins and turns the security he felt in them into great confusion.

A person also often falls into great weakness when, in carrying out the right path, all the inward organs [Col. 0867D] do not possess what he wishes. Thus the soul is like a tempest within the person, afflicting him through sins and also through penitence; and as much as it suffered in sins, so much does it make him suffer in penitence. In every fervour of sinning and repenting, the soul likewise supports the person as iron and steel earth supports soft earth, lest he fail; for it is the vital power of the body. It never permits the body joyfully to perform its sins, but afflicts it in sins so often that it scarcely hopes to rise from them.

Yet through this the soul rouses the person again and consoles him, so that he may trust that he will be delivered by God’s grace and not fall into the scattering of despair. This is also signified by the earth which is not broken by the excessive cold of the west. For earth made uninhabitable by excessive cold and heat signifies that a person, who after Adam’s expulsion inhabits a small place of habitable earth as an exile, can never have security amid the battles and wars of sins and penitence. In this tearful exile, one cannot see the full joy of the heavenly homeland, but only strives toward it from afar in the shadow of faith. Therefore, when the person sees that he has no security, he says:

Words of David in Psalm 101, lamenting the swiftness of his days and his decline.

LXXXIX. “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass.” Its meaning is clear as follows: Through original sin, a human being is blind regarding things past [Col. 0868B] and future. Therefore he has them in his knowledge as though they were a shadow. And because he has no security, he withers like grass, since all his works are uncertain to him. For all the days of a human being pass away into oblivion; but eternal life is steadfast and ever new, just as summer produces new fruits every year.

That the earth, though round over all its surface, is not level because it bears everywhere the swellings of hills and mountains; and that it signifies the uneven course of human life because of the diverse struggles of virtues and vices waged between soul and flesh.

XC. The earth bears mountains and hills, and is not flat within its roundness; nevertheless the air touches it everywhere, and it bears mountains and hills above and below, as a stag bears its antlers. The soul, which is breath from God, hates with gnashing distress avarice, which is the neck of luxury, because by these two vices a person can have neither peaceful nor gentle dispositions, either within himself or toward others.

The soul has also been sent into the body in order to fight with the person against the devil’s suggestion, to the devil’s confusion. For through that suggestion luxury rises up in the person as Leviathan, which desires to swallow the whole world; and through it Leviathan desires, as an avaricious person desires money, to defile souls and draw them to itself.

For the person who is proud and avaricious burdens himself through the possibility of sinning, just as earth is weighted with mountains and hills and is not level. Abandoning the fear of God, as though he were not to be judged by him, [Col. 0868D] he does whatever he wishes according to the desires of his heart. And just as the air does not fortify the earth but touches it according to the character of the weather, so that person acts unjustly, excusing works of iniquity according to the vanity of his heart.

But the soul, afflicting this person through its powers, makes him sigh to God for his sins. Casting down the mountain of pride within him, it compels him to perform holy and good works upon the earth in humility—he who formerly performed sins in pride, as though beneath the earth. The soul also acts in good and evil by the power of its knowledge; and because of the great affliction it suffers in the body through pride, it says: “Ah, ah! Whence have I come, and what am I now doing? I utter a weeping voice with sighs, I who mingle my knowledge with the rottenness of sins.”

And thus, by lamenting, it compels the person to worship the Lord with these words: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I have defiled my soul in sins; heal the wounds and scars of my injuries, because against thee alone have I sinned. O my God, teach me more and more to do holy and good things, by which my soul may be healed—a soul that I have grievously troubled.” Afterwards the person inclines his whole self to God, and, when the hunger of his soul has failed, he rejoices in the banquet of penitence.

That, just as the lower surface of the earth repels as though iron the waters beating upon and flowing around it, so the power of the soul, like steel which sharpens other tools, ought to master and repel the devil’s deceit and assaults.

[Col. 0869B] XCI. The earth’s surface beneath, as above, is round, and is like iron toward waters entering and flowing around it. Likewise, the soul, which lies hidden in the body and flies through all bodily senses in thinking, speaking, and acting, works with every creature in the person according to these things; whereas the other spirits are only the praise of God and do not work.

For the person at whose works angels marvel while praising God is heavenly and earthly. Hence he is gloriously praised in heaven and fills the whole earth by his working. Thus the power of his soul is likened to the earth’s roundness, since it moves about in the body and in all a person’s works, acting both according to the nature of the flesh and according to its own nature. [Col. 0869C] Therefore the power of the soul is like steel, by which all implements are sharpened and strengthened; for it overcomes in battle the fleshly desires that enter into its nature, lest the person perish and lest it itself be choked by the weight of sins. It is a warrior against every deception of the devil.

That the bendings, both equal and unequal, found in a human being from thigh through knee and ankle to the end of the greater joint of the foot, and from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, signify the curvatures and turnings of ocean and rivers in the world; and in a human being signify impulses and heats of lust, and the manifold interweavings of natures and oppositions of flesh and soul.

XCII. From the knees to the ankle there is the same measure as from the place of evacuation, or thigh, to the knee. And in the measure of this member—that is, from knee to ankle—is signified the ocean which surrounds the whole earth. For just as the legs curve back toward the hind parts, so these waters embrace the whole roundness of the earth and do not pass beyond their boundary.

These waters do not rush outside their course, because, flowing as though in a furrow and channels, they do not exceed those same limits; and in their depth they are equal to the waters above the firmament. So too the soul, which is established in all the members of a person, hastens through that person toward every desire of the flesh, as a bellows is compelled to blow. Therefore, lamenting, it says to that same person: “Ah, ah, ash-like rottenness, [Col. 0870A] why was I ever sent by my God into you? You have so entangled me in your desires that you compel me, by devilish persuasion, to accomplish criminal works with you!”

Then the person, although living in the wanton feast of sins, often says inwardly because of the soul’s complaint: “Alas for me! Why can I not restrain myself from sins? I know that my works are defiled before God and human beings; and why do I not fear my God, who, in judging, casts away every stain of sins as the malice of the devil?”

Afterward, in bitter penitence, the person turns away from sins by counting them one by one, and is brought into the same distress in which the soul was while he sinned, saying: “Ah, ah! I have forgotten my Creator, when I did not turn away from fleshly desire, through the knowledge of my rationality, for fear and love [Col. 0870B] of him!” And thus, casting himself down upon the ground in true penitence, he cries to God in prayer: “O my God, help me; through thy blood bring me out of the depth of my sins, in which I am submerged as though in hell; and by thy grace draw me to thee, that I may rise to salvation.” Thus, considering each of his sins in true penitence, he washes them away.

For the measure from the place of evacuation, or thigh, to the knee signifies that every impulse of lust is stirred in the loins of a man and in the navel of a woman through the devil’s first suggestion, when through the evil of that same deception they accomplish sins of luxury by desiring and acting with equal zeal. But afterward, through the soul, the person is brought into sorrow and distress over those sins; and this is also signified by the measure from the knees to the ankle.

The ankle indeed indicates the place of exile into which Adam was set: a person cannot forget it in any of his good and evil works. In evil works he remembers Adam’s expulsion; in good works he recalls how he was created by God. For God created for the rational soul a dwelling in such fullness that it might exercise all its powers in it, just as a person builds a house in order to do in it everything he wishes. So too winds were created by God in order that, now in pleasantness and at another time in danger, they might pass through all things by their breath.

And just as the ocean does not exceed the place in which it flows, so the soul does not abandon this mode: it rejoices in good works [Col. 0870D] and grieves in evil ones. For when a person sins according to fleshly desires, he is before God as a dark night; but when he works according to the soul’s nature, he shines before God and his angels like the light of day.

From the ankle to the end of the greater joint is the same measure as from the joint of the hand to the summit of the tip of the finger called the middle finger, as has been shown above. The feet also signify the other rivers which, dividing themselves through the whole earth, water it everywhere. And just as those feet adhere to the legs and the hands to the arms, so these rivers receive their powers from the ocean.

For God created the element of earth, which germinates through the powers of the other elements, just as a woman is made fruitful through the powers of a man. Therefore a human being is divine through the soul and earthly through earth, the complete work of God. Hence he knows earthly things and recognizes heavenly things in the mirror of faith.

And just as there is an equal measure from the ankle to the end of the greater joint, and from the joint of the hand to the summit of the middle finger’s tip, so the soul—through which the person understands that he possesses God—possesses the body in equal measure and without any deficiency; and the body supports it in equal measure, so that the soul has no deficiency in any of the works it performs with the body. And as the earth produces useful and useless things, so the feet carry the person to useful and useless works; and as all waters flow from the ocean, so all human works are carried out through body and soul.

[Col. 0871B] Likewise, that the bendings of shoulders and arms, hands, loins, knees, and feet—in which there are twelve greater flexures—indicate the breaths and stations of the four principal winds and their eight collateral winds, by which they differ from one another; and that these winds are mutually tempered by heat, cold, dryness, and moisture.

XCIII. In the knee of the right leg, where the human leg bends, the principal western wind is represented; but in the thigh and ankle of the same leg are indicated the breaths of its collateral winds. Likewise, in the knee of the left leg the principal northern wind is marked; but its collateral winds are shown in its thigh and ankle; and in the loins and foot of that leg the breaths of the collateral winds are manifested.

Therefore, as has been said, God marked the arrangement of the winds in the human being: namely, in the bendings of the arms, in the shoulders and hands, in the knees, likewise in the loins and feet, where there are twelve greater flexures, just as there are also twelve winds. The bendings of the arms, together with their attached members, signify the eastern and southern winds with their collateral winds, as stated above; but the knees, with their attached members, represent the western and northern winds with their collateral winds. And just as these members adhere to the whole body, so these winds, with their attendants, stand by the firmament.

One is tempered by another through heat, cold, dryness, and moisture, [Col. 0871D] and they fittingly perform their offices, just as a person performs with arms and hands everything that his knowledge directs. And as these members are separated from one another by equal measure, so the winds are separated by equal space.

Particularly concerning the dangerous harshness and harmful breath of the north wind, which in summer sometimes damages fruits with cold moisture and dries trees, obscures the sun, and alters the moon’s brightness through diverse heats.

XCIV. But among these, the north wind often displays its harshness and horror when it stretches its windy wing into the circle of the firmament and toward the east. There it often stirs up dreadful and harmful smoke and sends out cold moisture in summer, which damages the earth’s fruit and dries up trees. [Col. 0872A] When this occurs, that same horrible blast rises up with great fierceness and covers the cloud through which the sphere of the sun shines, so that the sun seems to human beings to have failed.

Likewise, this same blast causes confusion beneath the clouds, and darkness then comes upon the earth. But this cannot be seen by human beings except when great prodigies are foreshadowed, since they are moved through these elements, just as a hand can bend by means of an arm, make signs, and perform everything. And because of contrary human deeds, that same blast often plays with the moon so that she appears to them now black, now iron-coloured, and now marked with diverse colours. Therefore her appearance is then dreadful to human beings.

For the north wind is dangerous in every direction toward which it turns and harmful to everything on which it blows. By its coldness and harshness it disturbs the warm breath which flies gently from the sun with the moisture of dew and brings to fruition all greenery and the fruits of the fields upon the earth; it turns aside the prosperity of usefulness. Yet it supports the other winds, as a person leans against a wall, and thus serves them. And all the luminaries appear more adorned and beautiful in created things through the darkness of the north, because there is no light in it. In this same way the left arm supports and serves the right.

How all these matters concerning the measures and bendings of human limbs and winds, set forth in the two preceding chapters, together with the alternation of day, night, and hours, are to be referred to the soul; and how God equipped the soul with four powers which it has according to the body from the elements—namely fire, air, water, and earth—and likewise with four, as it were, wings according to itself, for governing itself and its body.

XCV. All these things concern the soul. While it remains in the body in the likeness of winds whose breath is not seen but heard, the soul, because it is airy, diffuses its breath, sighing, and thoughts like flying air. It is also likened to dew through the moisture of wisdom, by which it has good intentions toward God.

For as the sun’s brightness illumines the entire world and yet is not diminished in itself, so the soul is wholly present in the human being’s small stature; though by its thoughts it flies everywhere, ascending by holy works to the stars in praise of God [Col. 0872D] and descending by evil works of sins into darkness. This is also signified by the sun, which shines by its powers above the earth by day and beneath the earth by night.

The soul likewise ascends through good intention and descends by perversely acting through bad intention, just as legs with knees are moved above and below in different employments. The western wind, which is somewhat to be feared, signifies a person’s good intention, which should never be without fear. By it the person, while still in the stench of sins, is supported as though by the knee; its ankle and foot signify will and desire, through which good intention is brought to completion in works.

And as the collateral winds of the western wind stand by it in its office, so will and desire assist the work. The right collateral wind of the western wind signifies that a person, as though on the soul’s right side, conquers sins within himself by giving assent; the left signifies that, overcome by sins, the person lives as though on the left side in forgetfulness of God.

But the north wind, which dries up all the earth’s greenery by its breath, aided in this by its collateral winds, signifies the person who fulfils the flesh’s desires according to the will and delight of his heart, through which he is deprived of all happiness of heavenly honours. But when that person, like one on the left side, does not consent to the soul while doing evil, the power of rationality within him, as though on the right side, restrains him from it. Nevertheless, all good and evil works [Col. 0873B] are performed through the soul, just as all fruits of the earth are produced through summer.

God also created the soul wise for governing its vessel, namely the body, through the four powers it has from fire, air, water, and earth. With these powers it performs, working with the body itself, all the body’s offices. Before it is sent into the body, however, it has done nothing; and when it has put the body off, it will do nothing further.

For in the bendings of human limbs God marked the four winds with their collateral winds: in the shoulders, elbows, hands, and loins, in the knees and feet. One of these, namely the eastern wind, is joined to the strength of dawn, which possesses dew from the night’s coldness and sends it upon the earth. For in the morning dawn shines; in the first hour the sun illumines the day; it begins to burn upon the earth; and at the sixth hour it reaches the fullness of its heat.

This signifies that by good intention a person first sighs, then weeps; after tears, he begins good works, which he afterwards completes with great zeal of good intention. For a person who burns strongly in the holy course of good works is like the south wind: he first began to live holily through sighs and good intention, as though in the east; but afterward, as though in the west, the restless battles by which the soul subdued the body cease, just as the sun’s heat, which begins in the east and burns fully in the south, becomes mild in the west.

For as east and south are joined in the day’s heat, [Col. 0873D] so the soul joins virtue to virtue and accomplishes all good works as hands do with arms. But the sun descends in the west when the day is finished, just as people’s knees and feet run upon the earth. At evening the day’s pleasantness also turns to weariness; then one does not rejoice in daylight but experiences weariness in sleep.

This means that the person who acts according to the taste of the flesh, occupied in fleshly works and forgetful of heavenly goods, becomes nocturnal. But when, through the soul, he performs holy virtues in the fire of the Holy Spirit, he grows cool in Christ’s love from fleshly concupiscence.

For the rational soul brings forth words by multiplying them with sound, as a tree multiplies branches; and all a person’s powers proceed from it as branches from a tree. Its works, whatever they may be, which it performs with the person, are recognized as the fruits of a tree. [Col. 0874A] For it has four wings: sense, knowledge, will, and understanding. Through the wing of sense it feels itself wounded and turns away from what the flesh loves, because it is always a moving breath. Through the wing of knowledge the body has the desire to act, because it knows that it lives through the soul. Through the wing of will the soul desires to act with the body, because it sees that body to be made. But through the wing of understanding it knows the fruit of every work—whether useful or useless—because it remains in finite life.

Therefore, through these four wings, having eyes before and behind with knowledge of good and evil, it flies as a bird: through good knowledge, as though forward, in good works; but through evil knowledge, as though backward, in evil works.

Likewise, concerning the creation of the north wind, and how what has been said specifically concerning its harshness and the injuries it outwardly inflicts upon creatures should be understood of the suggestions of vices by which soul and body are inwardly provoked by the devil.

XCVI. For when the north wind has raised its blast horribly, the east wind resists it, and the west wind prevents it from blowing over it; but the south wind, which is stronger than those two, likewise opposes it together with them, so that it may not send forth its blast over it. Thus also all winds, from the sunrise to its setting, resist the north wind, which the sun’s light neither touches nor illuminates. For the north wind is worse than the other winds, because, at the fall of the devil, when God cast him into the lake of outer darkness, where he remains in darkness without any light, it was made dark. For since Adam fell, malignant spirits have sent forth their blast from the darkness in which they are, urging human beings throughout the whole world into error; and they do this in that same malice by which they contradicted the true light. But God does not permit them to appear to people who are beneath the sun in the horrible form which is theirs; rather, according to their purpose and habits, they appear to them in every form of creatures, deceiving them and turning them away from good works as far as they can.

For the north wind, which injures human beings and the fruits of the earth, and which with its wings emits, in the heat of summer, a contrary cold against east and west, by which it dries up the fruits of the earth, resembles the darkness and wickedness of aerial spirits. For those most evil spirits make cold within human beings the heat of the fire of the Holy Spirit through forgetfulness of God. Indeed, the soul which is so overcome by the conflict of the body that, consenting to it in the desires of the flesh, it coils itself like a worm into its dwelling-place, polluted by sins through the serpent’s foam, does not remember that it is a breath from God. Yet it does not remain long in these things; rather, it sighs and groans over the embrace of sins, for which it had greedily longed as though for great delights. It now possesses its sins not as delights, as before, but as affliction, and afterwards, as though contending against itself, applies itself to good works.

But when a human being has sold himself into evil knowledge and, through the heat of lust, has brought God into forgetfulness and looked to the serpent’s counsel, that same lust burns more fiercely in him through the blast of diabolical art, deceiving him thus:

> “How could you restrain yourself so that your flesh would not be shaken by pleasure, since you are human and can again be made clean by repenting?”

Thus that person, in the likeness of a wind that makes its terror beneath clouds, is clouded in his knowledge through the mockery of an erring mind, and sleeps in the darkness of forgetfulness of God together with grievous sins. And when, in such a manner, he sleeps in his sins by forgetting God, he is regarded, in the estimation of those people who see God by living justly, as like the most evil and horrible worms from which people flee. Therefore they say of him: “What kind of man is this, who, living in such great uncleanness, does not remember that he is a human being?” And so they flee him as a deadly sign, examining themselves and marking all their works with the fear of God because of the terror which they have recognized in that man, lest they become like him. They do this also in the likeness of those signs which prefigure miseries and useless things.

And just as the hand marks everything through the arm, and portents are prefigured in the movement of the elements, so a human being acts through the soul, considering within himself useful and useless things. The diversity of the north wind signifies the instability of the minds of those people who, foreseeing each thing according to their own will, judge what is suitable, trusting in themselves and not in God. Hence they are like a dense cloud through which the sun’s brightness is never perfectly seen, since, by choosing and establishing all things contrary to their Creator, they lay up such things as treasure. Thus they are troublesome to people in the blackness of malice.

For just as the moon appears distinguished by changing colour, so they, through forgetfulness of God, are so transformed into iron hardness through the duplicity of deceit that they sometimes show themselves gentle and useful to people, though without right faith; and, deceived by diabolical art, they are turned into shame before God and people through their hateful and malicious works. This north wind is dangerous in part and lacks every usefulness, because it has received from the judgment of the most just Judge that malicious one who contradicts God. It also signifies burning wrath, in which, through the devil’s suggestion, human blood is shed; and likewise the person who, in the hatred of his wrath and with his wickedness, kills, as far as lies in his power, the one whom the Holy Spirit has inspired, since he can never praise him in the sweet sound of love.

For such a person, in his malice, pours the water of dishonesty upon one whom he sees endowed with wisdom, and persecutes him everywhere by crushing him. He strips, as far as he can, a person possessed of charity of every honour through lying words; and he destroys peace everywhere, in all ways he can, with words of harshness and faithlessness. For the north wind, alienated from God, receives all human vices so that they may be tormented in it. For just as barley is sifted from wheat, so it, separated from every usefulness, blessedness, and holiness, sustains all the virtues which proceed through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and which through it become more adorned and luminous, just as a wall supports someone leaning against it. Through its darkness, moreover, all bright things that adhere to heavenly harmony, and that the Son of Man sowed in virginal nature, are made known. And just as the devil’s suggestion seduces people, so too the blast of the north wind is harmful to them.

Moreover, when a person who has performed iniquities and sins, as though on the left side, whispering with the devil, remembers them through repentance and conversion, as though on the right side, and through recollection of those sins becomes stronger and holier in good works, it is as the left hand serves the right.

### The reason why God, raising or setting Adam upright from the earth, first placed him so that he had the east before his face, the south at his right, and the north at his left; and how, in his short and small stature, He gathered together the immense structure of the whole world and subjected all creatures to his dominion and to the powers of his senses.

XCVII. God turned the face of the righteous shoot—that is, Adam—toward the east when He raised and set him upright; and He marked at Adam’s right the southern region of blessedness, and at his left the outer darknesses called the north wind. He also implanted in him the powers of the elements and of the other creatures, so that with them he might act against the north wind, which is the dwelling-place of the lost angels who separated themselves from God because, in the ownership of their own will, denying Him, they refused Him as God.

Therefore God also wills that a human being reject the north wind by his left side and cast it behind him, looking toward it in no imitation, just as he cannot possibly see his own back with his face; and that, with all the powers of creation, he fight against the serpent in Michael’s battle. He should hold the north wind wholly in the forgetfulness of the left side, just as darkness has been separated from light. Thus God strengthened the human being with the powers of all creatures and clothed him in them as in a complete armour: by sight he knows creatures; by hearing he understands; by smell he distinguishes; by taste he is nourished from them; and by touch he rules them.

Therefore he ought to know the true God, the Creator of all creatures, and should not seek to wage war against Him, even though he is often deceived through the counsel of the ancient serpent. For God did not fill him with the aforementioned powers in order that he might in any way attempt to raise his mind into the folly of the perverse angel. For God formed the human shape according to the constitution of the firmament and of certain other creatures, just as a caster has a model according to which he makes his vessels. And as God measured the great structure of the firmament by an equal measure, so He also measured the human being equally in his small and short stature, as was said above. He created him in such a way that, limb joined to limb, he does not exceed his proper measure or proper weight, unless this occurs by God’s judgment; and so that he bends himself in many parts of his body: namely, in the neck, shoulders, elbows, hands, thighs, knees, feet, and certain other limbs.

### Likewise, the manyfold reasons—sometimes accompanied by suitable Scriptural testimonies—why the seasons and months of the entire year, according to the distinctive properties of their qualities, the rising or setting of the sun, and the waxing or waning of the moon, are assigned to human qualities, both according to the distinctions or measures of bodily limbs and ages, or the properties of the bodily humours, and according to the various advances and failures of the affections of the mind.

XCVIII. But just as God marked creatures in the human being, so He also ordered the seasons of the year in him. For He displayed summer in the waking person and winter in the sleeper, because winter conceals within itself what summer brings forth in joy. So too the sleeper is strengthened through sleep, in order that, when awake, he may be made ready in his strength for any works.

He also distinguished the months in him when He differentiated their qualities and powers within him. For the first month, in which the sun rises upward, is cold and moist, full of great variation, and sweats out water turned to whiteness. Therefore its qualities are joined to the brain, since the brain, being cold and moist, cleanses itself by expelling base moisture through the eyes, ears, and nostrils. Likewise the soul in a person’s childhood, which has neither deceit nor carnal taste and is not shaken by acting contrary to its nature, works in joy. And in that same childhood, which according to its desire is simple and innocent, it is strong and powerful.

But later, deprived of the joy of childish innocence, it turns to great sadness, like an exile driven from his homeland, when bodily humours increase in the human being and he, made stained through the taste of the flesh, rejoices and is glad, embracing wantonness amid the feast of sins and forgetfulness of God. For just as the sun rises upward in the first month, so the soul in the first age is neither bound nor darkened by the taste and effect of sins, through which a human being, by diverse unstable habits, is changed into the hardness of filth and vanity, lacking the holiness of lawful works. But when that person has poured out the moisture of tears through the teaching and admonition of the Holy Spirit, he is cleansed from the foulness of sins into the sweetest fragrance of good repute, avoiding ignorance and weariness in good works.

The second month, however, is purgative in its quality and is represented in the eyes, because eyes that are watery, muddy, and diseased sometimes effect a cleansing in themselves. In this way the soul is in a person as sap is in a tree: as all the fruits of a tree grow through sap, so all human works are accomplished through the soul. When its veins and marrow have been filled, it begins to act according to fleshly desires; and when these have advanced, the soul, forced from its spiritual nature, very often groans. So too, having considered with the eye of knowledge how one began sins and how one completed them without repentance, when cleansed from every defilement one strives thereafter to avoid them.

By the third month, which is turbulent, bears storms, retains pestilences within itself, and moves all the earth’s shoots by diverse winds, the ears are understood. In them sounds every useful and useless sound, and through them the whole body is moved. Similarly, the soul has conflict in the body, which is moved and filled through it and bound together as though by veins, against the powers of its nature, when a person in the midst of youth resembles a tree that first puts forth unripe fruits and afterwards its fruits.

For a person has the storms of restless habits when he understands what he can do, because his marrow is now rich and his veins are full. Then the soul in him has a weeping and complaining voice, because its sorrow over his sins increases more and more, since it is that life which moves everything in the human being. But the person who is more eager for praise than is right, considering himself wise, becomes more foolish, when through his rashness and pride he is like a festering wound and is led into falsehood, since the reputation for honour and good report that he seeks never appears in him. Therefore the soul, into which all good and evil return, just as all useful and useless things sound in the ears, and through whose powers all things are accomplished, is saddened in mourning.

But when the swelling of the youthful mind has been restrained, and through God’s grace he turns to the better part by correcting his sins, the soul—which had previously been sad and which breathes through in him all useful and useless things—moves him to repentance because of evil and useless works, and makes him rejoice, as in a paradisal place, because of good and useful works.

But by the fourth month, which is green and fragrant and thunders, as it were, with fear, the nostrils are represented. In them the soul’s breath draws in and sends forth the odour of all things which a human being chooses for himself with fear.
