To this month is also likened the person who, through the breath of rationality, has wisely chosen in his knowledge the greenness of good works: all fruits flourish in him, and he is fragrant because the report of uprightness and usefulness is everywhere sent forth in the sweetest odour, to the praise of God.

Yet the tumult of hateful and evil people often rejects that person’s powers and good works and calls him unjust and evil, just as the Jews falsely said that the Lord Jesus Christ was unjust and defiled, although they knew Him to be holy and just in all His works. For just as this month resounds with danger and fear yet does not dry up the earth’s fruits, so the powers and virtues of the blessed person are not dried up by the aforesaid evils; rather, those who gnash their teeth against him fail. And just as, through the breath of rationality, a person draws toward himself through the nostrils whatever is sweetest and noblest, rejecting what is foul-smelling and muddy, so he earns eternal rewards and is honoured by people with praise; whereas his persecutor, lacking heavenly rewards, can never be praised in truth by people on earth. For one who fears and loves God guards his mind from everything evil, just as a person turns his nose away from a foul and unclean thing.

The fifth month is sweet, gentle, and glorious in all things of the earth, just as the taste of the mouth is sweet and delightful, because through it those things by which a person is refreshed with joy are recognized and known. Thus rationality is the pillar and marrow of the five senses, which are supported and directed to act by it, just as land, turned by the plough, becomes fruitful by germinating. For sight—the sense of the eyes, through which a person sees and knows all things—rightly holds primacy among the others, because, as it is higher in position than the rest, so it perceives more distant things than they do.

Thus the sight of the eyes is pleasant and glorious, because by knowing and choosing with it, a person distinguishes useful from useless things. Therefore, just as the fifth month, namely May, has the sweetest fragrance of flowers, in which human hearts rejoice because all the earth’s fruits by which a person is glad come forth in it, so too a person, naturally knowing through the sight of the eyes every use of natural things, distinguishes by the keenness of rationality what differs among the things he sees. The fruitfulness of this month resembles the taste of the mouth, through which a person knows things useful for his nourishment.

But the sixth month, dry with heat, rises together with that air which brings maturity to fruits in their growth, and at times pours out waters in excess. In it are signified the human shoulders, which, being dry with heat, bear every labour, complete all works, and sustain the whole body, though they sometimes seek rest from labour, just as a bird relaxes its wings from weariness and as a root holds its branches. In the same way, the second sense, hearing, is like a small wing of rationality for understanding the words it receives. Thus, when the ears receive the sound of any creature, one knows what that creature is, or where it is, and therefore the mind then applies itself more eagerly to investigating it.

For the power of the soul which senses through the ears, just as it does not grow weary through hearing, is not sated through weariness either; rather, it has a desire to know and notice many things. So too the sixth month, which is not moist, expands with manifold increase the fruits which it has produced with gentle heat and begins to impart maturity to them. And just as in this month floods of waters pour forth in fear with the dangerous sounds of thunder, so too among the things that hearing peacefully admits concerning human affairs are many which it receives with horror and sorrow.

Hearing is the beginning of the rational soul, because just as words that are written are first spoken, so through it whatever is spoken and composed is accomplished according to a person’s intention. Yet the soul is obliged to bear all these things—good and evil, useful and useless—which come through the beginning of hearing. In the sighs of tears, because it has not yet begun good works, it cannot fully rejoice. The shoulders also, which sustain the moisture of the entrails and the other human members just as they sustain the whole body, bear some likeness to hearing, which is the beginning of the soul, through which all works are accomplished, just as all burdens are carried through the shoulders.

For as the entrails adhere to one another, so a person’s works are joined together. Through good things by which evils are reproved, the soul has joy; through evils by which good things are recognized, it is sad. Thus, when it already remains in joy, it is immediately turned to sadness. Therefore it seeks rest, just as a person often desires the repose he cannot possess. Thus the same soul, which is wearied as long as it remains in the body, is received in the eternal tabernacles for good things, and for evil things is placed in punishments according to its merits.

The seventh month likewise has great power through the burning sun; it makes the fruits of the earth ripe and dry, and is torrential through storms of drought and rain. So too the bendings of the arms are strong through the shoulders and hands, by which a person gathers all necessities. Thus a person also tastes the nature of every thing by smell, distinguishing and knowing whether it is useful or useless; he chooses what belongs to the preservation of his nature and gathers it into his bosom, so that, harmful humours having been dried, he may grow in health. By these humours he is tempered, lest they be deprived of the strength of blood through corrupt fluid.

For the person, drawing all these things to himself in his knowledge, binds them under his power so that the pallor of the humours may be expelled and they themselves may remain in the strength of health. Thus he orders these things strongly with discernment, just as the bendings of the arms are strong through shoulders and hands. He also preserves in his mind what belongs to his health and so provides all that he needs, just as all fruits are now gathered ripe in this month.

But the soul, which is a breath from God, has a torrential course, just as Wisdom “went round the circuit of heaven by a torrential course.” Therefore, through it, with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and the five senses, a person begins and completes all his works, just as the seventh month brings all the earth’s fruits to maturity. These works are accomplished either for praise, as though on the right, or for shame, as though on the left, in a kind of ripeness and dryness of fruits.

For from the remembrance of sins tears are often poured forth in bitter repentance. Like a lion in its greatest strength, which surpasses other beasts, a person tramples down all vices and sins with earnest zeal of great purpose and, through the wisdom by which he knows God, mourns for the sinful works through which he had fled from God. For the soul, by its sighs through the admonition of the Holy Spirit, moves and supports a person with many powers, when it makes him gather in repentance all the greenness of virtues to wipe away the wounds of sins. Through this it rejoices, always desiring to reach the eternal tabernacles and remain in them without end.

The eighth month is like a great prince in his powers, possessing all things in his power through fullness. Therefore he displays joy within himself; and, burning through the sun’s heat, he also has dew from a certain coldness and is terrible in his storms, because the sun has now declined lower. Its qualities are accordingly displayed in human hands, which accomplish very many works and possess the power of the entire body. For they draw all things they can toward themselves and store them up, so that a person is often praised for the works of his hands.

Likewise, through the taste of the mouth, a person knows more perfectly than through the other senses the powers of those things by which he is nourished and holds them under the power of his knowledge, just as this month is great in its powers. He also possesses joy within himself, wisely distinguishing what things of cold and hot nature suit his health, just as this month contains the sun’s heat and the dew’s coldness. Turning away in his knowledge from dangerous and useless things, he gathers good and useful things, just as hands strongly accomplish praiseworthy works with integrity. And as a builder, under the power of his art, constructs all the buildings of his house, in which he wisely keeps all his substance, so does he act.

But the soul, being a combatant, penetrates by overcoming in its desires the illicit lusts of the human being; and, circling its circuit by a torrential course, it ascends in the beginning of its battle to the most high God. For it fights against the desires of the flesh with the shield of faith and the complete armour of virtues. When it has conquered them, it rejoices like a warrior who has overcome his enemies according to his will and purpose, because, burning in the heat of the true sun, it makes a person sigh so that, in the coldness of true repentance, which dries up all sins, he pours out tears.

For in repentance, in which very many oppositions confront him, a person descends in humility, accounting himself as mud, so that he scarcely hopes for his soul’s salvation. But the soul immediately sets before him the cross and all the sufferings of Jesus Christ, through which sins are washed away, raising him in hope. Through that repentance he ascends from virtue to virtue and flowers, so that for every sin perpetrated through it he may perform flowers of good works and holy virtues, of which he can never grow weary. Thus, progressing daily through repentance in great powers, he is raised up and stores good and holy works, over which the whole heavenly host rejoices in praising God.

The ninth month is of ripe season and does not show itself terrible through storms. It removes all unworthy juice from fruits that are good for eating, because it securely keeps all things as in a bag. Therefore in its qualities it is like the human belly, in which, through the heat of the liver and the other entrails, whatever is put into it is digested; and this, mixed with heat and cold, is properly expelled in its appointed manner. Yet this order is sometimes impaired by sicknesses, just as this month is sometimes disturbed in its regular course by passing seasons.

By the sense of touch, a person also knows and eats things ripe for eating, lest, with his humours disturbed by unripe things, he incur sickness, just as this month removes the unworthy juice of fruits. He also takes care that he may be nourished not immoderately but rightly and sufficiently, lest his humours be moved by worthless discharge; and he cautiously gathers useful things for himself, just as anyone carefully locks away the thing he loves so that it may not be taken from him. Thus a person is like the belly in his touch, which emits in due balance, constrained by heat and cold, those things it receives, just as in this month all things appear ripe, whose juice is afterwards dried out.

But the soul, troubled by many wars, labours, and tribulations arising from Adam’s fall and also by the battles of its flesh, ascends with joy to heavenly things through good works and descends through sorrow in evil works. For it puts on the strongest breastplate, carefully woven and interlinked—namely, patience—which no arrow can pierce. It advances the person in the ascent of good works, so that in the descent of true humility he may attribute whatever good he has done to Him who is the highest good and through whom he possesses it.

But when a person is in such sorrow for his sins that he scarcely hopes for his soul’s salvation, then his soul, again enduring patiently, sets before him that God assumed human form for humanity’s salvation and makes him rise from this doubt in hope, as it is written:

> “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm CXXXVIII).

This is understood thus: O God, every ascent of saints and of heavenly works among those whom You kindle with Your fire is Yours, for You instil into a person, in Your love, the dew of compunction of heart, through which the remaining virtues afterwards grow green and flourish. But when I descend, through forgetfulness of You, into the depth of sins, deserving infernal punishments, if I sigh out to You in true repentance, You anoint and save me with drops of Your blood; and thus You are present as my deliverer and saviour.

Patience with humility is in high places, overcoming pride; and it is also in the darkness of sins, warning a person not to despair of God’s mercy because of his sins. Thus it holds all works in right moderation, as though in ripeness: defending things done in holiness from vainglory, and saving from despair things performed in the rottenness of sins. For patience is on the straight path: it neither abandons heavenly things nor despises earthly things, but tramples down in the true light, which is God, every incitement of the deceiving devil’s vices. In all these things it neither rejoices excessively nor falls into sadness, although it is sometimes stirred by the devil’s deception, against which it resists strongly with the shield of faith.

The tenth month is like a seated person: it does not fly in the vigour of greenness nor generate heat, but strips the branches of trees and sweats out cold. So too, when a person sits, he draws himself together to escape the cold; in that month he draws clothing around himself, because then he receives warmth through clothing. By this example, when a person begins to grow cold through old age, he becomes wiser than before, finds childish habits tiresome, dries up the changes of wanton and foolish habits in this mature age, and avoids the company of fools lest they deceive him through ignorance. For the useless and varying tastes of his flesh now fail within him through the coldness of age, just as this month is not pleasant through greenness and its dryness with cold strips the branches.

The soul also, a living and prudent breath made by God, who is true wisdom, teaches the person to hold firmly what comes from God. Through God’s grace, with its powers, in the blessed person it subjects the body to itself as a mistress subjects a handmaid and gives it delight in good things. For if at any time that person’s flesh is stirred through the taste of pleasure, the soul indignantly marvels within him, extinguishes that poison in his veins and marrow, makes it cease, and, consoling him through the grace of the Holy Spirit together with the teaching of the Scriptures, gathers and carefully guards him from vices into virtues, lest he fall into sin.

But the eleventh month bends itself and builds up cold. It displays within itself not joy from summer but sadness from winter; cold falls from it upon the earth and causes it to foam with mud. A person imitates this when he bends his knees so that cold may not pass through him. Therefore, when he bends his knees in sadness, he intensifies thoughts of grief in his heart and accounts himself as mud. He has no gaze toward joy, because in sorrow he remembers that human knees were naturally bent at their beginning.

Likewise, when a person has reached old age, he is weakened by coldness; lacking the joy of youth, he is sad because of the failure of his dryness, in which he is afflicted by thinness and flows with unworthy humours. For every old person, warming himself by the fire because he fears the cold, draws his limbs together, since he is naturally cold. Thus this month, having all its days cold and lacking the pleasantness of summer, resembles human knees, which a person bends in sadness when he remembers his beginning: namely, when he sat in his mother’s womb as though captive, with his knees folded.

But when the soul has so overcome the person by its powers that through it he ceases somewhat from the sins he has committed, yet he cannot prevent it from desiring to sin, then it groans in its vessel, which is the flesh it inhabits. For it permeates and moves the whole body, like a wind blowing into a house, making its walls move and passing, while blowing, through its hollows or windows. But when a person wraps himself in the darkness of sins like a worm in a hole of mud, then the soul, situated in the veins and marrow together with all the joints of the limbs, fails in its powers because it is not warmed by the fire of the Holy Spirit. Since it cannot have joyful works through carnal nature, passing over the daylight of holiness, it always groans and forgets in its nature what it is and whence it came.

The soul’s groaning is full of pains when the taste of its spiritual nature has been alienated from it, because, not kindled by the grace of the Holy Spirit, it consents—even unwillingly—to perform the works which the body demands from it. Therefore, acting against its will, it has great sadness, just as the body sometimes has sadness when it is compelled to act according to the nature of the soul.

The twelfth month has cold with great power and hardens the earth by freezing; it covers the earth wholly with the foam of cold and makes it wearisome and laborious. Therefore human feet are signified in its quality: they tread down and scatter very many things and moderate the earth so that it cannot raise itself high, but they stand upon it.

Likewise, the soul of the person who, in his anger, has shed his neighbour’s blood or inflicted some other injury upon him through quarrelling, is gravely defiled. For just as the body remains cold after the soul’s departure, without any warmth, so it, hardened by anger without the warmth of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, forgets its nature and appears bloody before God, since, like Cain in his brother’s blood, it has been rejected by God. For blood overflows in a person’s anger. Thus, deprived of his right senses, he becomes like a madman; through irrational movements of anger and blasphemy, in heart and mouth he cuts off his brother from all blessedness through envy. As far as he can, in thought and speech, he scatters all his brother’s good things; and therefore through the evil of hatred he is a murderer before God in his soul.

For he gnashes his teeth against him, pouring upon him malicious words which he had dictated in his heart with hatred. Through the hardness of unjust paths, he can have no sweetness of holiness within himself or sow the seed of good works. Because of this hardness, in which he continually remains, he never sighs toward heavenly things. Therefore one who is such is blind to the good works of holy and pure knowledge and will never possess the joys of holiness which he scattered in anger, because he is like a camel burdened and polluted with foul loads of sins.

In this way the qualities and powers of the months are fitted to the human being. Therefore the Psalmist says by my inspiration:

### Words of David in Psalm CIII appropriate to these matters

XCIX. “He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting.” This is understood thus: God placed the moon as temporal, so that it might nourish all seasons as a mother nourishes her infant, first with milk and afterwards with food. For in its waning the moon is weak; therefore it nurses the seasons as though with milk. But in its waxing it nourishes them as though with solid food.

God also ordained that the sun should shine above the earth and hide itself beneath the earth. Therefore it shines above the earth in the day, just as a person is awake by day with open eyes; and it is beneath the earth at night, just as a person sleeps at night with closed eyes. Thus the earthly human being is in the flesh according to the lower regions, while the heavenly human being exists in the soul according to the height of heaven; and he knows the times of the seasons, because through all these things he moves as a living being.

That man, created in the image of God and sitting like another lord upon the throne of the earth, ruling over every creature made for his sake, is the complete work of God himself and greatly pleases him; and that the one sex was made for the help and consolation of the other, and that the man bears the figure of Christ’s divinity and the woman that of his humanity.

C. When God looked upon man, he was exceedingly well pleased with him, because he had created him according to the garment of his own image and according to his likeness, so that through the trumpet of his rational voice he might proclaim all God’s wonders. For man is the complete work of God, because through him God is known, and because God created all creatures for his sake and granted him, in the kiss of true love, through rationality, to proclaim and praise God himself. But he lacked a help corresponding to his own likeness. Therefore God made for him a helper, namely the contemplative form of woman, in whom the entire human race lay hidden, which was to be brought forth in the strength of God’s power, just as he had advanced the first man in the strength of his power.

Thus man and woman are so joined together that the work of one is through the other: for a man without a woman would not be called man, nor would a woman without a man be called woman. For woman is the work of man, and man is the sight of woman’s consolation; and neither of them could exist without the other. The man signifies the divinity, but the woman the humanity, of the Son of God.

Man therefore sits upon the throne of the earth and rules over every creature. That creature, existing under his discipline, is subject to him, and he stands over all creatures, as David speaks by my inspiration, saying:

Words of David in Psalm 109, and an exposition of those same words, showing how they are to be understood concerning Christ’s Incarnation and power, and the subjection of his enemies.

CI. “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.” Its meaning is clear as follows. Let man therefore say: He who is Lord and Father of all said to his incarnate Son—to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, so that he is my Lord, though I am a sinful man—“Rule, seated at my right hand”; that is, rule over man, who is my right hand, because I have subjected all creatures to him. Subject him to yourself through faith, so that he may abandon idols and turn to his Creator, that is, the true God.

And you shall do this until I make the rebellious, who are your enemies through unbelief, the footstool of your feet; for I shall subject them to you forever and make them worship the footsteps of your feet. For when they have turned from their unbelief, they will know you as the true God.

Thus God brought forth all creatures through his Word, and that same Word put on flesh in man, who is God’s right hand, because he is the grasp of his power. That same Word also, which is the Father’s Son, sits ruling over man until the number of his brethren is fulfilled, which will be on the last day. Then the devilish multitude with its followers shall be subjected to him like a footstool, even after the final age of the world; and then it will be seen and known who and what kind of Lord he is, since Satan himself will then be trampled down like a footstool and utterly scattered.

That man, marked with the signs of God’s omnipotence through the five senses, ought to know and venerate his Creator as one in Trinity and threefold in Unity; for this end he was both created and, after his fall, restored: that he might be lord of the world and constitute the tenth choir in heaven.

CII. For the Lord reigns mightily in heaven in his power, and beholds the stars that are kindled through him and the rest of creation. So too man sits upon the seat which is the earth and rules over the remaining creatures, because he is marked with the signs of God’s omnipotence. These signs are the five senses of man, through which, by God’s power, he understands and perceives that by right faith he ought to venerate in God the Trinity in Unity and Unity in Trinity. This veneration is the adornment of the nine orders of angels, from which the devilish multitude, cast out, fell.

But man is the tenth choir, which God restored in himself at the first establishment of the angels who were lost, because he willed to become man. In that humanity there is a tower in which those who are in the tenth choir walk. Therefore, as has been said above, God marked in man both the higher and the lower creatures. After man had been inspired with the breath of life, which is the soul, he rose up, knew all creatures, and embraced them in his mind with the strongest love.

That the nature of the soul is fiery and of manifold efficacy in its powers, by which it knows God, understands and governs itself, gives sensation to its body, and moves it to act.

CIII. The human soul is fiery, and it warms and gives life to the whole human body; and because it is fiery, man is blooded. It also has windy paths, drawing breath inward into man and sending it forth. When it draws this in, he is dried within; and this is very useful to him, because human flesh grows into health through this dryness. But when it sends it out, the fire within man is diminished and sends forth its heat.

Thus the entire body is built up together with sensation, so that man can live and govern all five senses of the body with their functions. And if this heat were not released, the fire of the soul would suffocate the body, like a house wholly consumed by fire. By the powers of the soul, moreover, man is clothed with flesh and blood and is made complete, just as all the fruits of the earth are completed through the blowing of winds.

But because the soul is fiery, man knows that he has God; and because it is a spiritual breath, he understands that he can work together with the body. Therefore he has a command from God to perform his works rightly and not to look toward the empty region of the north, where the first angel wished to reign and perished. For when arrogance has gathered to itself the property of its own will, pride at once takes flight and swiftly hastens northward whenever it accomplishes the property of its own will in whatever way it desires.

Arrogance and flying pride are like waters which a ship cannot cross, because they are burdensome to God and to human beings and leave all things destitute. Therefore their works flow away, nor does charity pass over them, since they can neither love nor be loved by the faithful. Rather, they wish to seize things they do not possess and establish them by their own ordering over things on which they have no authority; therefore they go to destruction.

The soul, then, is the mistress of the house of its body. In it God formed all the dwelling-places that it was to possess. No one can see it, just as it itself does not see God while it remains in the body, except insofar as it sees and knows him by faith. And with every creature that has proceeded from God it works in man: just as bees build a honeycomb in their vessel, so man completes his work as a honeycomb with the knowledge of the soul, which is like liquid.

And because it has been sent by God, it pours thoughts into the heart and gathers them in the breast; afterward these pass into the head and into all the members of man. It also penetrates the eyes, since they are its windows through which it knows creatures; for, being full of rationality, it distinguishes their powers in the word alone.

Hence man also completes all his work, according to the will of his thoughts, for each of his needs. For when the wind of the soul’s knowledge moves in the brain, it descends from the brain into the thoughts of the mind, and thus the work of the will is completed. In its knowledge the soul sows that the work of thoughts may be completed; this is cooked by the soul’s fire and turned into taste, by which it is tested knowingly.

The soul also conducts the refreshment of foods and drinks inward into man, so that his flesh may be restored. For through its powers it orders how man is to grow and subsist in all the natures of his flesh, and it fills his inward parts with its powers. For the soul is not itself flesh and blood, but it fills these, so as to make them live with it, because it has arisen rationally from God, who breathed life into the first formed creature. Thus soul and flesh are one work in two natures.

It also brings into the human body air by thinking, heat by gathering, fire by receiving, water by introducing, and greenness by sprouting—just as it was fashioned from the first constitution, above and below, around and within the body everywhere. And such is man.

[Col. 0888A] That God judges man according to his works, either for life or for punishment; and that the holy soul, stripped of the body, fully sees God—whom it cannot now see because of the hindrance of corruptible flesh—and longs expectantly for the day of judgment, when it will receive again its beloved garment, that is, its own body, in order to enjoy without end, in that body and with the angels, the contemplation and praises of God.

CIV. When man performs righteous works, the elements follow right courses; but when he accomplishes unjust works, he brings upon himself the elements with penal affliction. For the body works with the soul according to the will of its desire, and God judges man according to his works, either for life or for punishment.

The soul flows through the whole body by thinking, speaking, and sighing, just as a wind sends its blasts everywhere through a house. But so long as the body works together with the soul in man, he is localized and heavy and cannot lift himself from the earth. When, however, the body is renewed together with the living soul, namely after the last day, then it will be light and winged like a bird that has feathers.

While the soul is in the body, it perceives God because it comes from him; and so long as it is occupied in creatures, it does not see God. But after it has been brought out of the prison-house of the body and comes before the Lord’s presence, then it will know what it itself is and what adhered to it while it remained in the body. And because it will then know the glory of its great honor, it will demand back its dwelling-place, so that it may know its glory together with it.

Therefore it will eagerly await the last day, because it has been stripped of its beloved garment, namely its body. When it receives that body, it will fully behold with the angels the glorious face of God. Once this has happened, the angels will be kindled anew in praises, as on the first day they were kindled by the victory of their battle. For after the last day they will be perfected in God’s praises, when they praise the new wonder of God’s work, which is man, and strike from it the harp of glorious joy. They will not be wearied by this, fail, or come to an end. And just as they will desire always to gaze without failing upon the face of God, so they will never cease to marvel continually at God’s works in man.

Therefore, as has been said above, such is the form of man with body and soul: likewise God’s work, existing together with every creature, as John, inspired by my Spirit, wrote, saying:

Exposition of the first chapter of the Gospel according to John, from the words, “In the beginning was the Word,” up to “full of grace and truth.” This exposition treats of the eternity of the Word of God; of creatures, and how they existed in the Creator’s art, without being coeternal with him, before they existed in themselves; of the creation of angels and the vengeance of God’s zeal upon apostate spirits; of the plan to make man in God’s image; and of how the force of the Creator’s power and the light of his wisdom shine forth in the making of the human body. It also treats of God’s Incarnation, and of the words of teaching and examples of righteousness which he gave to the world; likewise of the restoration of fallen man and his blessedness after this life.

CV. “In the beginning was the Word.” Its meaning is clear as follows. I, who am without beginning, from whom all beginnings proceed, and who am the Ancient of Days, say: [Col. 0889A] I am, through myself, the day that never proceeded from the sun, but from which the sun was kindled. I am also reason, which did not sound forth from another, but from which all rationality breathes.

Therefore I made mirrors for the beholding of my face, in which I contemplate all the wonders of my antiquity, which never fail. I also prepared these mirrors to resound in praise, because I have a voice like thunder, by which I move the whole circuit of the earth with the living sounds of all creatures. These things I, the Ancient of Days, do, because through my Word, which always was and is in me without beginning, I commanded a certain great luminous being and with him innumerable sparks—that is, angels—to come forth. When they awoke in their light, they forgot me and wished to be as I am.

Therefore, in great thunder, the vengeance of my zeal cast them down for their presumption in opposing me, because there is only one God and another cannot exist. Hence I uttered within myself the small work that is man, and made it in my image and likeness, so that in some respect it might work according to me, because my Son was to be clothed in the garment of flesh in man. I also established this work rational from my rationality, and marked in it my capacity, just as human rationality in its art comprehends all things through names and number: for man distinguishes nothing except through names, nor knows the multiplicity of things except through number.

I am also the angel of strength, because I make myself known to angelic hosts through wonders, and because I show myself in faith to all creatures, where they know me to be their Creator; yet I can be perfectly declared by none of them. For man is that garment in which my Son, clothed about in royal power, shows himself to every creature as God and as the life of life. But no one but God can number the host of angels especially attendant upon that royal power; no one can bring to an end those who singularly confess him as God of every creature; and no tongue suffices to delimit those who especially cry aloud that he is the life of all life. Therefore blessed are those who dwell with him.

Moreover, God marked out his entire work in the form of man, as has been stated, as is also shown here through certain examples in man himself. In the circle of man’s brain he displays his dominion, because the brain holds and governs the whole body. In the hair of his head he marks his capacity, which is his ornament, just as hair adorns the head.

In the eyebrows over his eyes he reveals his strength, because the eyebrows are a protection for man’s eyes, turning away every harmful thing from them and displaying the beauty of the face. They are also like the feathers of winds, by which they are lifted and sustained, as a bird sometimes flies with its feathers and sometimes ceases from flight; for wind blows from God’s strength, and the gusts of wind are its feathers.

In man’s eyes God also declares his knowledge, by which he foresees and knows all things, because they display many things in themselves, being bright and watery, just as the image of other creatures appears in water. For by sight man knows and distinguishes everything, and if he lacked sight, he would be as dead in these respects.

In his hearing God likewise discloses all the sounds of the praises of hidden mysteries and angelic hosts, in which God himself is praised. For it would be unworthy if he were known only through himself, since one human being is known from another through hearing; there, too, man understands all things within himself, and would be as empty if he lacked hearing.

In the nostrils he shows wisdom, which is the fragrant ordering of all arts, so that through smell man knows what wisdom orders. For smell reaches out through everything, drawing things in so that it may know what they are and of what kind.

But through the human mouth God signifies his Word, through which he created all things; likewise, through the mouth all things are uttered with the sound of rationality. For man brings forth many things in sound, just as the Word of God did in creating through the embrace of charity, so that nothing necessary should be lacking to its work.

And just as cheeks and chin are set around the mouth, so, when that Word sounded, the beginning of every creature adhered to that same Word, when all things were created. Thus: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Its meaning is clear as follows. In the beginning of that beginning, when God’s will, which had been in him without beginning, had already opened itself to bring forth the making of creatures—before it had opened itself—the Word existed without the beginning of that beginning. “And the Word was with God,” as a word is in rationality, because rationality has word within itself and word is in rationality, and these are not divided from one another.

For without beginning, before the beginning of creatures, and also in their beginning, was the Word. And that same Word, before the beginning and in the very beginning of creatures, was with God and in no way divided from God, because God willed in his Word that his Word should create all things, as he had ordained before the ages.

And why is it called the Word? Because with a sounding voice it raised up all creatures and called them to itself. For what God uttered in the Word, the Word commanded by sounding; and what the Word commanded, God uttered in the Word. And so God was the Word. For the Word was in God, and God secretly uttered in it all his will; the Word sounded and brought forth all creatures, and thus the Word and God are one.

When God’s Word sounded, it called to itself every creature which had been preordained and disposed in God before time; and through its voice all things were raised to life. He also marked this in man, who secretly utters the Word in his heart before releasing it; when released, it remains with him, and thus the utterance of the word is in the word.

For when God’s Word sounded, that Word appeared in every creature, and that same sound was life in every creature. Hence human rationality also performs its works from that same Word, and brings forth its works by that same sound, sounding, crying out, and singing. By the keenness of his art man makes harps and drums among creatures resound, because man, according to God, is rational through a living soul. His soul, with its heat, draws flesh to itself, in which appears the first form of God’s finger that he fashioned in Adam, and which that same soul pervades by giving life and filling with its fullness in growth.

For flesh does not move itself without the rational soul, but the soul moves flesh and makes it live. Flesh is present to the rational soul, just as all creatures are present to the Word. Therefore God created man in the will of the Father. But just as man would not be man without the connections of veins, so he could not live without creatures. And because man is mortal, he does not give life to his work, since he himself, whose life had a beginning, is from God. But God gives life to his work, because he is life without a beginning of life.

“This was in the beginning with God,” namely in that beginning of which Moses, my servant, inspired through me, speaks, saying: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). For the Word that sounded “Let there be,” as is also written there, “And God said, Let there be light,” was in that beginning, when the creature received its beginning from the Creator, with God; that is, in the one equality of divinity. For this Word which is with God is equal to him in divinity, since the Word which is in God is inseparable from God and is consubstantial with him.

Thus all things were made through him, because all creatures were made through the Word of God as the Father willed; for there is no Creator except God alone. All useful things, formed and living realities, were made through him.

He also shows in the arms of man and in the joints adhering to them the strength of the firmament, with its signs, which support and govern that same firmament; just as the arms together with the joints of their limbs manifest the dominion and activity of the whole body. For the right hand is as the south, and the left as the north: they are the firmament, so that it may not proceed farther than has been established, as it is written. And in all these things between us and you there is a great chasm, a firmament—namely, lest darkness extinguish light and light drive out darkness.

“And without him was nothing made,” because without the Word of God no creature was made. For every creature, visible and invisible, was made through the Word of God, and subsists in that essence—that is, of living spirit, greenness, or power. And apart from him nothing was made, except evil, which is from the devil; and therefore it has been cast from God’s sight and brought to nothing, because there is only one God and no other.

Rational man also, in whom God placed the capacity to act, committed sin, which is brought to nothing because it was not created by God. For this nothingness God set unending darkness, because by fleeing it refused the light. But “what was made in him was life,” because all things that were created appeared in the reason of their Creator, since they were in his foreknowledge—yet not coeternal with him, but foreknown, foreseen, and preordained by him.

For God is the one life that did not receive the beginning of the life which has a beginning. Therefore everything “that was made in him was life,” because it was foreknown by him; and it lived for God, such that God never began to remember it, because he had never consigned it to forgetfulness, since it was in his foreknowledge, although it had not yet existed temporally in its own forms.

For just as there is no possibility that God should not exist, so there is no possibility that those works in creatures, foreknown and preordained in his wisdom, should not proceed through him. And just as that which was made in creation was life without extinction in God, because it was to be created, and in the creatures made nothing was lacking for them to have the fullness of their growth by increasing, so also the things which man does are life to him by aiding him toward life, because he subsists and is brought to completion in them.

And because God is full life without beginning and without end, therefore his work also is life in him, which in this respect is in no way deceived. God also marked this in the region of man’s breast, where by desiring, arranging, and elevating each thing, both good and evil, man gathers things in his thoughts, considering what pleases or displeases him. What pleases him he preserves with joy in order that it may retain life for him; what displeases him he casts away from himself in indignation, lest it harm his life.

Thus everything God made is life in him, because it is vital in its nature from God. Therefore, just as the Father’s Word gave human beings bodily life when he created them, so, when he put on his garment, he showed them spiritual life, so that, walking by another life and not according to the flesh, they might spread out among the multitudes of spiritual persons. Thus he holds both peoples in his hand, because he, the Son of God, is God and man. He embraces the spiritual people in love because he is the Son of God; but he holds the worldly people according to that justice by which it was said, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1), because he is the Son of Man.

“And the life was the light of men,” because the life which had raised creatures up, being the life of human life, since man lives through it, gave people light through reason and knowledge. In that light they might behold God by faith, acknowledging him as their Creator, and be suffused with that light just as daylight illuminates the world.

Man understands the wings of knowledge through heaven, which brings forth sun and moon, because day signifies good knowledge and night evil knowledge, just as the sun reveals day and the moon night. And just as man would be as blind in the service of his life among creatures without these lights, and as his body could not live without spirit, so man would not understand what he was without the wings of knowledge.

Therefore “the light shines in darkness,” just as daylight shines through the moon at night, so that man may know evil works in good works—works separated from light—because good knowledge, supported by reason, reproves evil and drives it from itself. “And the darkness did not comprehend it,” just as night cannot cloud the day, because evil neither wishes to know nor understand that which is good, but flees it.

God shows this in man’s heart, which is the life and firmament of the whole body and sustains the entire body, because in the heart man’s thought is ordered and his will fed. Thus the will is like the light of men, because, as light penetrates all things, so the will abounds in what it desires. Yet in that very desire, which it reckons as light for itself, it often walks into the darkness of evil works that it wishes to perform. But “the darkness” does not so “comprehend” that will as to be able to take from it the knowledge of good, so that it does not know the good, even though it does not do it.

“There was a man sent from God,” who had no taste of earth, because he had been sent by the heavenly Creator and not by man. For the heat of God’s Word had made green the dryness of the flesh of those who begot him, so that even his flesh in many works was, as it were, foreign to the customary condition of those born in sins. For those who begot him, touched by God’s grace, brought him forth; and thus he proceeded through God’s grace, sent as a witness of the Son of God. Hence the angel named him John.

“Whose name was John,” because the works he did accorded with his name, since the grace of God had strengthened him by going before and following after him. For the grace of the Word, which is God, sent John amid the changing motions of the dispositions of those human beings whom he cleansed in the changes belonging to persons born in sins. On that account he possessed a certain stability according to the uprightness of spirits, which neither have changing human dispositions nor desire to sin.

But God, who is wonderful, conforms to man’s belly the wonders he performed in John. For the belly calls for the powers of creatures which it receives and emits, in order that it may be nourished from their juice as God has ordained. Yet in all creatures—in animals, creeping things, birds, fish, herbs, and fruit-bearing trees—certain hidden mysteries of God lie concealed, which neither man nor any other creature knows or perceives except insofar as this has been given them by God.

John, however, was wonderfully sent to the elements and wonderfully nourished by them; and just as in some way he had been removed from the habit of sin, so through abstinence he lived wonderfully from the elements. This pure man was worthily and laudably the herald before the hidden Son of God, through whom the world was established with an innumerable multitude and all creatures were created.

This too is signified through the belly: just as the world contains all things, so the belly receives other creatures into itself in eating. And just as every creature proceeded from God, so Adam bore all human beings in his form; and to them the Son of God supplied true pastures when he bore man in his humanity.

“He came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him,” because John—made a man wonderfully amid the ordinary course of bodily birth, and being a wonderful man—came by divine dispensation as a witness to God’s mysteries, so that by the powers working in him he might bear witness to the light, namely God, from whom all lights are kindled, in order that all who are fiery through the Holy Spirit might believe God through his testimonies, which he uttered wondrously.

He came, therefore, bearing witness to divinity clothed in human form. And just as he himself was born, as regards his own dry nature, without greenness, so he said that my Son was born without sin from the Virgin Mary. “I willed this so that through this wonder which I worked in John, human beings might believe in the miracles of my Son.”

And just as this testimony appeared in John, so true testimony is also declared in man’s thighs, which are testimony to all who are born, and the offspring of his entire body, which sees, touches, thinks, and desires, and reckons in its knowledge all that it does. For man is God’s miracle, and it is therefore fitting that he bear witness to God’s wonders.

“He was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the light,” because John was not that light which is never divided or changed, namely God. But he came sent from God in order that he might bear witness to him who, being the true light, kindles all lights. For God exists in himself and through himself, without any lack of any necessity, because he was to make all things in all things. Therefore he is in every making of his work.

Thus John proclaimed the attested testimony concerning Christ, for as a fruit bears witness to the character of its root, so John arose amid God’s wonders. Therefore he bore witness to God’s wonders. But man is a work marked out by God and a light: he begins to live, will at some time fail in the flesh, and thereafter bears witness to God, because God is not so.

“There was the true light,” which has never been overshadowed by any shadow and to which no time of serving or ruling, diminishing or increasing, has ever been given. Rather, it is the ordering of every ordering, the light of every light, and shining from itself. For God never arose in any morning or dawn, but always existed before time.

“Which enlightens every man coming into this world,” because this light, together with the breath of life, suffuses every human being who has flesh and bones and comes by the beginning of birth into the present world of changing growth and decline, so that when the sun with its luminaries receives him, he may behold and know creatures.

For God raised up the first man, whom he formed from mud, through the living spark of the soul, so that through this same spark of the soul he became flesh and blood from mud. Hence in his descendants, when it has been milked with foam through human nature, flesh and blood are fully produced through the fiery spark of the soul. For if they were not raised up in this manner through the soul’s heat, flesh and blood would not be fully produced, just as the material of the first man would have remained mud if it had not been changed through the soul.

For as bread is made from flour through water and fire, so flesh and blood are made through the fire of the soul. Man is like the light of the other creatures dwelling on earth, which often run toward him and lick him with great love. Therefore man also desires the creature in whose love he burns, and frequently seeks it out diligently. But a creature which does not love man flees him, tramples down and scatters everything pertaining to him, and, terrified by fear of him, finds his existence burdensome. It therefore often attacks him in order to drive life out of him.

“He was in the world,” when he put on the royal garment from the Virgin’s flesh, where holy Divinity reclined in her womb. For he became man in an alien nature, and not like another human being, because his flesh was kindled through holy divinity.

Therefore, after the last day, when every human being has been transfigured, the souls of the elect will lift their bodies to heaven through faith—bodies which were formerly in the world. God will do this through himself in his power, which no creature can destroy. For then man, as has been said, will be clothed with flesh and his bones filled with marrow; but ‘ampli-’ [lacuna], if food, drink, and life do not fail, because then he will proceed in the powers of divinity without any alternation of change. For in goodness he is a member of Christ, who endured many sufferings and very many reproaches in the world, although he was the Son of God.

The devil, inventor of every deceit, could not know this. He, who had a beginning, hastened to deny him together with all his members who reject God; nevertheless, he could not prevent man from being raised into unfailing life.

“And the world was made through him,” so that the world arose from him, not he from the world; for creation proceeded through the Word of God—that is, everything among creatures, invisible as well as visible. For some things can neither be seen nor [Col. 0895D] touched, while others are both seen and touched. But the human being possesses both within himself, namely soul and body, because he was made in the image and likeness of God. Hence he commands by word and works with his hands. Thus God ordered the human being after his own pattern, because he willed that his Son should be incarnate from a human being. “And the world did not know him,” because the children of the world—that is, those who follow the world—through the blindness of their ignorance did not know him when he came, nor recognize him when he worked, just as an infant is ignorant of knowledge and action. Therefore here too God shows, in the thigh and knees of the human being, the ignorant infancy of unbelievers. For just as an infant cannot walk, because both its marrow and bones have not yet been strengthened, [Col. 0896A] since it is nourished by milk and soft food; and just as an adult cannot walk on thigh and knee without lower legs and feet, so unbelievers, whose knowledge and understanding were empty of the fire of the Holy Spirit, through whom they ought to have known God, will be unable to walk in the path of rectitude.

“He came unto his own,” because he had created the world and because he had clothed himself with human flesh. Therefore all creatures displayed him, as a coin displays its lord. For God created the world, which he willed to prepare as a dwelling-place for humankind; and because he willed to clothe himself with a human being, he therefore made him in his image and likeness. Thus all things were his own. “And his own did not receive him”: namely, those who were his own because he had created them, [Col. 0896B] because he had especially made them in his image. Yet they neglected him, in that they did not recognize him as their Maker and did not understand that they had been created by him alone. For unbelievers did not receive his humanity, nor, because of the blindness of their unbelief, did they recognize God in human form. Therefore his youth is signified in the human being’s legs: it is foolish and useless when it attends to greenery, flowers, and other created things, and when it judges itself wiser than others because its marrow and bones are then fully strengthened. Thus did the Jews and pagans, who, loving the vanity of the age, thought they knew what they did not know and were what they were not; and through faith they did not heed him who had given them flesh and spirit. For just as [Col. 0896C] youth delights in being deceived by created things, so the world then conducted itself in vanity. Therefore it was necessary that God should show himself to them and gather them to himself, just as he commanded the she-ass and her colt to be untied and brought to him, when he set himself over them together with the law of truth.

“But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God.” For to all people of both sexes who received him by believing him to be God and man—for God is first apprehended by faith, and then it is received that God became man—he gave, by his power, the capacity for this authority: that by their own free will they might become children of their Father [Col. 0896D] in the heavenly kingdom; that is, that, having become heirs of his inheritance, they might possess with him a share in his kingdom, with that authority by which a son is heir to his father. For because they recognized him as their God and Creator, embraced him in charity, kissed him in faith, and diligently and prudently sought all their things from him, the dew of the Holy Spirit fell upon them, so that the whole Church began to spring forth from them and bear the fruit of heavenly joys. Therefore it was granted them to be children of God through the strength of true faith. “To those who believe in his name”: to those who possess this faith by believing, so that they are saved through baptism in his name, participation in the heavenly kingdom is given. For they perform all their works in burning love, as though they saw God; they do not worship the name of God in [Col. 0897A] the shadow of faith without works, where they cast away alien gods, who cannot make themselves and do not exist of themselves, but are companions of human beings.

This name, in which true belief resides, is such that it has no beginning; through it all creatures arose; and it is life, through which every life breathes. Therefore it is worshipped by every creature. According to the three powers that are in this name, every creature that has a name subsists by three powers. But a dry and decayed creature lacks a name, because it is not alive. Yet a living creature’s name possesses three powers: one of them is seen, another is known, but the third is not seen. For the body of a living thing is seen, and that which begets is known; but whence it becomes alive is neither known [Col. 0897B] nor seen. Thus God also made great marvels manifest through the human being’s feet. For as feet support the whole body and carry it wherever it wishes, so faith strongly sustains and everywhere gloriously bears the name of God together with marvels that may be seen and not seen, known and not known. The human body and its works are seen; but far more exists within it which is neither seen nor known. But since such obscurity exists in the human being, how could he who created him be manifest? For no human being living in this age can know him as he is.

“Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.” For the Son of God said: “That which is born of [Col. 0897C] flesh is flesh; and that which is born of spirit is spirit” (John III), because flesh is born from flesh, conceived in sins. But because God is spirit, all spirits have arisen through him; neither is spirit turned into flesh nor flesh into spirit. Rather, through flesh and spirit the human being is made complete; otherwise he would neither exist nor be called a human being.

God indeed formed Adam so that he might live eternally unchangeable; but Adam transgressed through disobedience, listening to the serpent’s counsel. Therefore that same serpent thought that he would perish altogether. Yet God did not will this: he prepared for him the exile of the world, in which he conceived and begot his children in sins. Thus, having become mortal with all his race, [Col. 0897D] through the conceived foam of sin he is turned into decay, until the last day, when God will renew the human being, so that afterwards he may live with the unchangeable life in which Adam was created.

But this life could in no way exist in the children conceived and born in sins; rather, it arose in the humanity of the Son of God, through whom the heavenly Father remembered to free the human being who had perished. Those who become children of God through the power of good works do not have this authority to be children of God from the coagulation of their parents’ blood, in which they are blood-related; nor from the will of the weaker flesh, which sprouts toward childbirth; nor from the will of its stronger part, which is vigorous for begetting. Rather, through the reward of divine revelation in the washing of baptism and in [Col. 0898A] the fiery outpouring of the Holy Spirit, they receive that by which they are now born of God and become heirs of his kingdom.

For God foresaw all his works before they were formed; subsequently, when they were given form in creation, these formed things did not remain empty in themselves but became living. For flesh without life would not be flesh, because when life withdraws from it, it fails in decay. But the breath which God sent into Adam was fiery, rational, and life. Therefore, through its warmth, the red clay of the earth became blood. And just as all creation existed in God’s foreknowledge before time, so also all human beings yet to be born exist even now in his foreknowledge. But the human being is rational and sentient: rational, indeed, because he understands all things; sentient because [Col. 0898B] he feels those things which are present to him. For God fills all human flesh with life when he sends into it the breath of life. Therefore the human being chooses, through foreknowledge of good and evil, what pleases him and rejects what displeases him.

But God considers what a person sets before himself. If a person has set before himself things that are not from God, God withdraws himself from him; and immediately those who first began evil meet him—namely, those who wished to destroy heaven. This did not touch God, since it would be unfitting that God should destroy himself. But if a person longs for the name of his Father and calls upon him with good desire, angelic protections will be present to him, lest he be hindered by enemies. Through the delight of his desire for good works God first gently gives him, as it were, milk; then he pours into him the rain of his grace, by which he may ascend mightily from strength to strength. [Col. 0898C] In this way that person is always renewed in such virtues until his death.

But one who can accomplish only something small, and not something great, always proceeds with impetuosity, in order to accomplish what he can. One who can do many and great things, however, possesses moderation in them along with restraint. The devil wants only one thing: namely, to lead souls into death. He seeks nothing else, can do nothing else, and scarcely endures until he completes what he can do. But God, because he is powerful in all things and through all things, has moderation in all his works and acts with the restraint of discernment, so that the human being may become [Col. 0898D] stronger and more ready in steadfast goodness. For everyone who proceeds impetuously often brings himself to ruin.

But the human being is a signification of all God’s honor. For the good knowledge which is in him displays the angelic hosts who worthily serve God; but the evil knowledge which he possesses manifests God’s power, because God overcame it when he expelled the first human being from Paradise. Thus it happens in every human being: in the one who acts by good knowledge, choosing the good, God’s goodness is shown; in the one who seizes evil and accomplishes it, God’s power is declared, because God sometimes judges it and sometimes forgives it. Therefore, in the manner already stated, the human being is life, and all things that adhere to him are alive through him. For [Col. 0899A] God created the human being with all his appurtenances beneath the sun, so that he should not be alone on earth, just as God himself is not alone in heaven but is glorified amid all the heavenly harmonies. These things that are around the human being on earth endure with him on earth until the number which God has decreed shall be fulfilled. But after the future resurrection the blessed human being will not need to grow or to be fed by anyone, because he will then be in that brightness which will never pass away or change. In that brightness the blessed human being will then be clothed through the Holy Trinity, and he will behold him who has never had a boundary of beginning or end. Therefore he will never be afflicted by old age or weariness, because he will always sing psalms and play the harp in newness.

Thus, as stated above, [Col. 0899B] flesh lives through life, and without life flesh would not fully exist; so flesh with life and life with flesh are one. God considered this when, in Adam, he strengthened flesh and blood by the breath which he sent into him, because he then beheld that flesh with which he was to clothe himself and held it in burning love.

“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” For the Word, which was eternally with God before time and which was God, took flesh from the Virgin’s womb through the ardor of the Holy Spirit. He put it on as the veins are a structure of flesh: they carry blood, yet are not blood. For God [Col. 0899C] created the human being so that every creature might serve him. Therefore it was fitting that God should take the garment of flesh in a human being. Thus the Word clothed himself with flesh: that is, Word and flesh are one, not as though one had been transformed into the other, but as one in the unity of person.

The body also is the garment of the soul, and the soul has with the flesh the functions of acting. The body would be nothing without the soul, and the soul would not act without the body; hence they are one in the human being, and the human being exists. Thus the work of God—that is, the human being—was made in the image and likeness of God. When the human being’s breath is sent by God, that breath and flesh become one human being. But the Word of God took flesh from the untilled flesh of the Virgin, without any heat of burning, [Col. 0899D] so that the Word is Word and the flesh flesh, yet they are one, because the Word which was in the Father timelessly before times did not change himself but only clothed himself with flesh.

“And dwelt among us,” because, having become a human being [Col. 0900A] without sin, he dwells among us as a human being, not neglecting our humanity, wherein we too, with the breath of human life, are made in his image and likeness. Therefore we also dwell in him, because we are his work, and because he has always held us in his foreknowledge and has not forgotten us. “And we saw his glory,” because we who were with him especially saw him coming in a wondrous nature without any sin. “And glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father,” showing that the Only-Begotten, wonderfully born from the Father before the ages, coming wonderfully from the Father displayed his glory: the Virgin conceived him through the ardor of the Holy Spirit and had no need of a man’s act, whereas every other human being is begotten by a man—that is, from a father—with sin.

For God [Col. 0900B] formed the human being from clay and sent into him the breath of life. Therefore the Word of God assumed in the human being a royal garment together with a rational soul, drew all of it to himself, and remained in it. The breath, which in the human being is called soul, permeates the flesh and possesses it as a delightful garment and beautiful adornment. Therefore it loves the flesh and consents to it, though it cannot be seen within it. From the nature and desire of the soul, moreover, the human being seeks the garment of life; and because God created no creature empty of powers, the human being always performs wonders.

And that same Word is “full of grace and truth,” because in full grace he was wholly active in divinity in creating [Col. 0900C] and in humanity in redeeming; and he was full of truth, because no falsehood of wickedness and sin touched him, nor did he associate himself with it. For he is the Lord who conquered evils by his battle, evils which are nothing without him. That Word itself—the true Son of God—is full of grace, giving and forgiving according to his mercy. He did not empty himself of divinity but clothed himself with humanity; and his humanity is whole, because no wrinkle of the sin of human nature touched him. He is also full of truth, because he gives, forgives, and judges as is just—something the human being does not do, because he is conceived and born in the wrinkle of sins.

Thus God is round, like a wheel, creating all things, willing the good, and accomplishing the good. [Col. 0900D] For the will of God prepared all things which the Word of God created. Therefore every person who fears and loves God should disclose the devotion of his heart through these words, and should know that they have been uttered not by a human being but through me, both for the salvation of human bodies and souls.

## SECOND PART

[Col. 0901]

## FIFTH VISION

[Col. 0901A] A vision of great wonder, in which the globe divided into five parts, together with the dimensions and qualities of these same parts—filled both with light and loveliness and with the horror of punishments and darkness—is described with subtle precision; likewise two spheres, one surrounded by a sapphire-colored circle, the other shining with luminous rays, together with their surrounding features.

I. Then I saw the roundness of the earth divided into five parts: one part toward the east, another toward the west, a third toward the south, a fourth toward the north, and a fifth in the midst of these. The circumference of the eastern part and that of the western part were of equal measure, and each had the form of a drawn bow. The circumference of the southern part and that of the northern part, being of one measure, equaled the length and breadth of the first two parts, [Col. 0901B] except that at their inner boundaries, because of the curved inner boundaries of those same first two parts, they appeared, as it were, truncated; apart from those truncated inner boundaries, they resembled the form of a drawn bow.

For each of these two parts—the southern and the northern part—was divided into three sections. The two middle sections of these parts were of one form and one measure. The remaining four, which lay at the ends, also had a different form, yet a form and division equal to one another; and they were equal in length and breadth to the same two middle sections, except that at their inner boundaries they seemed narrower, and at their outer boundaries broader, than the other two, [Col. 0901C] according as the above-mentioned eastern and western parts, curving at both their boundaries as stated, granted these sections narrower space on one side and broader space on the other.

But the fifth part of the former parts, which was in the middle of all these, appeared in a square form; and in one place it was suffused with heat, in another with cold, and elsewhere with a temperate atmosphere. The aforesaid eastern part shone with much brightness; the western part, covered with a certain darkness, grew dark. But the southern part, which was divided into three sections, had its two end-sections filled with certain punishments. Its third section, which appeared in the middle, was shown dreadful not indeed with punishments but with certain other monstrous [Col. 0901D] terrors. The northern part likewise, having three divisions, was shown dreadful in its two extreme divisions, abounding in diverse punishments, and in its middle division with very many horrors or punishments.

But toward the east, [Col. 0902A] above the aforesaid roundness of the earth, at a certain height I saw a red sphere surrounded by a sapphire-colored circle. From its right and left side two wings proceeded on either side. One pair from those two sides of the circle extended upward into the height, so that both, bending back at their summit, faced one another. The other pair descended from the same sides down to the middle of the aforesaid roundness of the earth, so that, embracing that same middle roundness outside the firmament, the wings covered it.

From that same middle point a red circle, extending in the manner of a bow, [Col. 0902B] encompassed the whole outer part of the west and also certain divisions outside that roundness, bending around from the end of the aforesaid southern wing, around the west, as far as the end of the northern wing. From the roundness itself toward the east, between the aforesaid wings, there appeared something like a building ascending upward to the above-mentioned sphere; and from that sphere there extended upward, as it were, a roadway as far as the middle of the aforesaid wings, above which a white star shone.

Then, between the summits of the same wings, there appeared something like a fiery sphere emitting certain rays from itself, such that there were equal spaces from the summit of the aforesaid roundness of the earth to the aforesaid red sphere, from that sphere to the aforesaid white star, and from that star to the above-mentioned [Col. 0902C] fiery sphere. Between the first wings, on either side of the aforesaid roadway, from the mentioned sphere around the displayed star as far as the aforesaid fiery sphere, certain distinct rays of stars were visible, as it were.

But toward the west, outside the aforesaid roundness of the earth, darkness appeared. It extended in the manner of a bow from each side of that roundness to its middle point, to which the aforesaid wings likewise descended. Between the western corner and the northern corner there were other denser and sharper darknesses, having as it were the form of the horrible, devouring opening of a mouth, with certain other exceedingly dense, evil, and infinite darknesses attached to them beyond [Col. 0902D] these, as though they were their mouth and jaws. I knew these infinite darknesses, but did not see them. And again I heard a voice from heaven saying to me:

[Col. 0903A] Because the wisdom and power of God the artificer shine forth wonderfully in this: that, for a definite rational cause, he has suspended the element of earth, not angular but round and divided into neither more nor fewer than five parts, immovable in the midst of the other three elements; and that he has endowed the human being, corresponding to the earth’s fivefold division, with five senses in this life, and in the life to come will restore him whole from the dust of the grave.

II. God suspended the globe of the earth in the midst of the three elements so that it could neither slip nor dissolve; and in this he showed himself wondrous and powerful, since he does not reduce even the flesh and bones of the human being to dust in such a way that he will not restore them to their integrity on the last day. He also made one region of the earth bright, another dark, another terrible, [Col. 0903B] another punitive, another suited to humankind, and another unsuited to it; just as he joins certain souls to his kingdom and condemns others to hell by righteous judgment.

For you see the roundness of the earth divided into five parts: one part toward the east, another toward the west, a third toward the south, a fourth toward the north, and a fifth in the middle of these. This is because if the earth were angular and not round, its corners would bring upon it defect and an unequal distribution of weight. And if it were not divided into five parts, it would not be balanced in proper moderation, because the four outer parts weigh it toward rectitude, while the fifth, which is in the middle, makes it firm and stable in that rectitude. This also signifies that the human being, [Col. 0903C] whom the earth represents, is established by the five senses active within him for everything necessary to him and is directed toward the salvation of his soul.

### Again, concerning the five divisions of the earth: how their innate qualities temper one another, and how they correspond to the five human senses

III. Thus the part turned toward the east gives the middle part good sap and useful greenness, just as a human being’s sight, directed as it were toward the rising of brightness, supplies him—who is as it were in the middle of the elements—with the health of body and soul. The other part, facing west, supplies that same part with moisture, at times beneficial and at times harmful; just as hearing, shaking and penetrating the whole human body as though toward the west, now announces prosperity, now adversity, now the soul’s salvation, now despair. The third part, sloping southward, sends into that part warmth tempered by the cold blast of winds, just as smell, like vapor rising from heat, infuses into the human being an odor proceeding from hot and cold temperaments, and an odor coming from heavenly sighs.

But the fourth, extending toward the north, brings into the aforesaid middle part cold coming from the north and heat coming from the east, like taste, which receives cold things and distinguishes cold and hot, stirring the human being with diverse flavor and heavenly sweetness. The fifth, existing in the midst of these, is strengthened in solidity by them and tempered by their diverse influences, just as touch, vigorous as if in the midst [Col. 0904A] of the other senses, is strengthened by them when all give it powers and establish it for growth. This is also shown in the arrangement of the fingers, since through them works directed to eternal reward are accomplished.

And, as you see, the circumference of the eastern part and that of the western part are of equal measure, and each has the form of a drawn bow, because the sun in rising and setting occupies equal tracts of earth in the circuit of its course. This also shows that sight consists in this likeness through knowledge of good and evil: namely, that just as through knowledge of good sight rises upward toward what is good, so through knowledge of evil it descends downward toward what is evil—[Col. 0904B] by the former turning itself away from evil, but by the latter bending itself back from good.

The circumference of the southern part and that of the northern part, being of one measure, equal the length and breadth of the first two parts, except that at their inner boundaries they appear, as it were, truncated because of the curved inner boundaries of those same first two parts. Apart from these truncated inner boundaries, they resemble the form of a drawn bow, because the south occupies as much of the earth in heat as the north occupies in cold; in this too they imitate the length and breadth of east and west, except that their boundaries directed toward the fifth part are somewhat narrowed by the extension of the eastern [Col. 0904C] and western parts, though elsewhere they imitate the likeness of a circle.

Thus smell, through the fragrance of virtues, tends to the right; but taste, through the flavor of vices, tends to the left. In this regard they have a kind of equal, though contrary, striving; they resemble their origin, as the one adapts itself to good and the other to evil. Yet neither of them can possess the fullness of its endeavor at the beginning of its undertaking, because when a human being first begins either good or evil, he knowingly restrains himself in that deed, since he does not yet dare to commit his whole self to it.

### That, in the division of the two parts of the earth—the southern and northern—each subdivided into three, these things appear to the beholder; and how they are to be understood in relation to the human body, soul, and works

[Col. 0904D] IV.
