For both these parts—the southern and northern parts—are divided into three sections, which are uninhabitable to human beings: on this side because of heat, on that because of cold, and on another because of serpents. This also shows that smell, when it rises toward the fragrance of virtues, and taste, when it declines toward the flavor of vices, touch the human being’s body, soul, and works in different ways. In this they show him to be, as it were, uninhabitable if he does not understand what body, soul, and works are within him, and if he does not know how to discern in himself a right balance.

The two middle sections of these parts are of one form and one measure, because the southern and northern parts, existing in a proper measure, grant just moderations through their rectitude. [Col. 0905A] They also signify that the soul, existing as it were between the body and its works in the fragrance of virtues and the flavor of vices, is of one moderation and disposition when, fearing evils, it sighs toward God.

But the remaining four, which lie at the ends, have a different form but a form and division equal to one another. For on either side of the aforesaid middle sections, in both the southern and northern parts, they are expanded; at their inner boundaries, which face toward the aforesaid fifth part, they are somewhat narrowed; but at their outer boundaries they have some breadth. Thus they appear to have a form different from the above-mentioned middle sections, yet to be like one another both in their form and in their disposition. [Col. 0905B] This shows that the human body and its works, which as it were set a limit upon it when they feel deficiency in themselves, have a different function from the soul, though they agree with one another, since they fully bring to the human being the vital activity of body and senses. For when the body falls, its works are weakened; but when the soul raises the body up, the works of the body are lifted up.

And they are equal to the length and breadth of the same two middle sections, except that at their inner boundaries they appear narrower, and at their outer boundaries broader, than the other two, according as the above-mentioned eastern and western parts, curving at both their boundaries as stated, grant these sections narrower space on one side and broader space on the other. [Col. 0905C] This is because the parts on either side of the middle sections have the length of the same middle sections, but toward the aforesaid fifth part have less breadth than those middle sections; toward their outer boundary, however, they have greater breadth than them, and elsewhere equal breadth. For both boundaries—of the part directed toward the east and of the part extending toward the west—are drawn in according to the form of a bow beside the inner boundaries of the aforesaid four similar parts.

All these things also signify that the human body and its works extend within the human being for his support according as the soul within him is stirred up for strengthening. Therefore that body [Col. 0905D] and those works of the human being often make themselves narrower in security and broader in uncertainty than the soul’s longing desires, because the soul seeks the measure of rectitude, whereas the human body more often runs into excess in its works.

### That the fifth part of the earth, in the middle of all, also appearing square and divided threefold, is rendered uninhabitable here by heat and there by cold, but habitable elsewhere by temperateness; and what this signifies here in human conduct

V. But the fifth part of the former parts, which is in the midst of all these, appears in a square form, so that it may be equally contained and permeated by the others. It also signifies that touch possesses the perfection of works rather than the lightness of vices. And it is suffused in one place with heat, in another with cold, and elsewhere with a temperate [Col. 0906A] atmosphere, because the sun’s heat, scorching it here because of its proximity, and cold, constricting it there because of its remoteness, render it uninhabitable to human beings. But the tempering of heat and cold makes it habitable there, just as fingers, though different from one another, nevertheless strengthen the hand by holding it together with their strength; and just as the five human senses, although unlike one another, passing as it were through the trial of fire and water, furnish one another with the aids of help toward virtues.

These same habitable places also signify faithful people, who, always pondering the divine law and raising their whole selves toward heavenly life, make themselves habitable in good works. The uninhabitable places signify unbelievers, who strive to resist and oppose God’s words, deny faith, and tear apart and break through the truth and firmness of that faith. By these perversities they make themselves uninhabitable, because they do not grant the Holy Spirit a dwelling-place within themselves.

### Again, concerning the qualities of those four parts, and the places in which punishments are appointed for the purification of the penitent souls of human beings—light in some places, grave in others, and exceedingly severe elsewhere, differing according to the kinds of faults of those being examined—and why, at the middle boundaries of those same parts, there are not punishments but certain monstrous terrors
VI. And the aforesaid eastern region shines with great brightness, because in it is the place of pleasure and delight [Col. 0906C], containing within itself refreshment for blessed souls and admonishing the soul to fix its inward sight upon the vision of the true light. Against the vices of the many sinners by which human beings transgress justice, however, punitive and transitory places have been set at the four corners of the earth, in which the souls of those who are to be saved, stripped of their bodies, are examined according to the demands of their sins. Hence the western region grows dark, covered with a certain darkness, containing in that darkness punishments for slight and lesser sins—namely, those of people who sin through ignorance—and showing in them the hearing of human beings turned away from the cry of truth.

But the southern region, divided into three divisions, has two outer divisions filled with certain punishments [Col. 0906D], in which the grievous sins of those souls are punished that, while they were in their bodies, neglected the fragrance of virtues. For in the division at the corner between east and south are the most severe punishments of fiery and windy air, and other torments, in which the evil deeds of murderers, robbers, thieves, and certain other people are investigated; for God’s judgments are always prepared against impiety and unbelief, and against sins and horrible dispositions that strive to set themselves against God.

In the division at the corner between south and west, moreover, very evil punishments abound: there is cold there in summer and heat in winter, together with other punishments, through which the souls, stripped of their bodies, of those who have scarcely any repentance for their many and great sins, even at their end, are purified. Thus, lacking the fragrance of virtues, they will scarcely be saved. But the third division, which seems to lie between these, shows itself terrible not through punishments but through certain monstrous terrors. For if it too, like the other two, abounded in punishments, those same punishments, boiling over in their excess, would make human habitation on earth uninhabitable. As it is, because of the many terrors within it, it often sends pestilence upon human beings and animals and injury upon crops, since human beings do not bring the fragrance of virtues into their souls.

The northern region likewise has three divisions, and in its two outer divisions it displays an abundance of various punishments, in which [Col. 0907B] the souls of those are purified who, setting aside the taste of life, followed the desires of their flesh. In the division at the corner between east and north are the harshest punishments of cold and winds and other torments, in which the unbelief of certain incredulous people is examined. While they remained in the world, imitating unbelief, they neglected the taste of true faith; only at the hour of death, by repentance returning to the Catholic faith, did they at last receive the taste of uprightness.

And in the division at the corner between north and west, most foul punishments of muddy wetness, deadly stench and smoke, and other torments abound, in which the deeds of adulterers, gluttons, and drunkards [Col. 0907C] are investigated—those who regarded the taste of life as something alien. But the middle division is shown as terrible through very many horrors, without punishments, as has been said. For if it, containing many terrors, also abounded in punishments, the blasts from those punishments would infect the dwelling-place of human beings; whereas the horrors alone which are in it sometimes bring dangers upon people and other creatures, when human beings turn the savor of life into folly. And just as worms boil up from the stench of filth, so punishments rise from the stench of sinners in the aforesaid corners. Therefore smoke from these punishments often spreads into the land inhabited by human beings and causes great pestilence among people and animals.

[Col. 0907D] That God’s judgments which come upon the earth or upon human beings are poured forth from the penal places of these regions; that, lest the punishments or darkness of hell occupy the world, certain exceedingly high and hard mountains have been placed opposite them; and in what parts the souls are appointed to be examined according to the character of their deeds.

VII. These judgments which come upon the earth and upon human beings proceed from the aforesaid corners, so that very many evils are poured forth from them. Yet against the horrible darkness of infernal punishments there have been placed mountains exceedingly high and hard, which cannot be split by any storm. They resist the darkness and defend the earth, as walls hold up a house lest it collapse.

Because the human being, consisting in five senses, continually sins, he therefore undergoes purification in the aforesaid five regions of the earth. But slight punishments in the aforesaid darkness of the western region are borne by those for whom this present earth, while they were in their bodies, was like a prison because of their love for heavenly things. Those, however, who serve the pleasure of the flesh are purified in the other purgatorial punishments, which are in the southern and northern regions, as was said, because although they sinned, they did not reject God and the just faith.

Mortal man does not inhabit these aforesaid four angular extremities—the two principal regions of the earth’s roundness, east and west, and likewise south and north—for, because of the unchanging intensity of heat or cold, or because of their other inconveniences, he could not live in them [Col. 0908B]. Likewise, if a person exalts himself beyond measure, falls into despair, or, neglecting the right hand, turns toward the left, he does not receive the Holy Spirit as the inhabitant of his heart. Therefore God often exercises his judgments upon the four corners of the earth, as John, my chosen one, saw in the Apocalypse, as he says:

Words from the Apocalypse of John the Apostle corresponding to this subject, in which, through the four horses—white, red, black, and pale—the four periods and their qualities from the beginning to the end of the world are described with subtle meaning.

VIII. “And behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon [Col. 0908C] it had a bow, and a crown was given to him; and he went forth conquering, so that he might conquer” (Rev. 6).

This is to be understood thus: the first period, which began in Adam, was like a white horse, because the human being transgressed through ignorance. Upon it God set the wrath of his corrective judgment, which also contained vengeance; and God gave this vengeance the power of victory, to overcome enemies, so that it even fought in the battle of battles against the ancient dragon. He placed this vengeance in the failure of the law that he had given to Adam, just as at the end of the flood he made a bow in the clouds of heaven.

This period endured from Adam’s expulsion until the flood. In it God, in the wrath of his bow, drowned all people except those preserved in the ark, through the rushing waters that sounded like thunder [Col. 0908D]. And just as in the first period God displayed the bow of his wrath for vengeance, so after the flood he gave the bow in the clouds of heaven as a sign that thereafter he would not submerge the whole world through the thunderous sound of waters; and by this he prefigured that the faithful would be saved through baptism.

And again it follows: “And another red horse went forth; and to him who sat upon it was given power to take peace from the earth, so that they should kill one another; and a great sword was given to him” (ibid.).

This is to be understood thus: this horse is that period in which, after the flood, by God’s wrath and just judgment, peace was taken away from those who set themselves against God. For they did not seek peace from him, nor did they give it to human beings; and therefore God’s judgment also permitted them cruelly to kill one another [Col. 0909A], because they had departed from fidelity to him, just as the soul kills itself when it does not seek to cleave to God.

Then again it is written: “And behold, a black horse; and he who sat upon it had scales in his hand” (ibid.). And it follows: “Two pounds of wheat for one denarius, and three pounds of barley for one denarius; but do not harm the wine and the oil” (ibid.).

This is to be understood thus: the period in which, after the Passion of the Son of God, persecutors arose in the Church is this black horse—black, that is, through unbelief. There unbelievers, despising faith, drew upon themselves the blackness of infidelity. But the wrath of God, with a just measure, weighed the sufferings of the martyrs: fitting punishment for the torturers, but eternal glory for the martyrs.

For the victory of the martyrs was a rich root of all virtues [Col. 0909B], sending out its thick branches in them. By these they removed from themselves the feasts of self-will and of the law according to the flesh; and in them the failing of the will of the flesh became love of eternal life. This is the faith which every believer contains within himself; and these things also came about in blessed hunger, by which the faithful hunger and thirst for righteousness.

Thus the scales signify that a person is nourished, in spiritual abstinence, by the fruits of the earth, and that in virginity he loves the heavenly homeland beyond nature. Therefore this was the period of the martyrs, mingled with the blackness of the north, when martyrs were killed by the unjust, like lambs by wolves. Accordingly, scales were given to the judgment of this period, with which to weigh two pounds: namely, abstinence and love of the heavenly homeland, which belong to the martyrs, as stated above.

For the martyrs themselves afflict their bodies through abstinence and look toward heavenly desire, as an eagle fixes its eyes upon the sun. This is signified by two pounds of wheat, purchasing the one denarius of life. Those, however, who according to the precepts of the law restrain themselves from sins through abstinence, deny themselves the company of husband or wife, and, leaving their riches, make themselves poor—things all very hard and harsh—are bound through three pounds of these hardships in the love of the one denarius, which is the heavenly homeland. And wisdom does this, which has weighed all things equally through mercy, because God is merciful above all. In this way wine and oil are not harmed, when by repentance and mercy a person is redeemed from sins.

And again it follows: “And behold, a pale horse; and he who sat upon it, his name was Death, and Hell followed him. And power was given to him over four parts of the earth, to kill by sword, famine, death, and the beasts of the earth” (ibid.).

This is to be understood thus: this horse signifies the period in which all legal observances and the complete justice of God will be reckoned as nothing, as in pallor. Then people will say: “We do not know what we are doing; and those who commanded us to do these things did not know what to say.” Thus, without fear and trembling before God’s judgment, they will despise all these things, and will do so through diabolical persuasion as well. But God’s wrath will [the source reading is corrupt here] destroy these deeds, and they will perish in great battles, because he will judge them in his vengeance [Col. 0910A] and utterly trample them down. For he will bring death upon these unrepentant people and condemn them to Tartarean places. In that time, moreover, conflicts with swords will arise throughout all the regions of the earth; the fruits of the earth will be taken away; and people will perish by sudden death and the bites of beasts.

That the ancient enemy, envying human beings the heavenly glory which he lost, always rejoices in their punishments; and that for this reason he ardently strives to contaminate them with the horror of hatred, murder, the Sodomitic crime, and other vices.

IX. Therefore the ancient serpent rejoices in all the aforesaid punishments by which a human being is punished in soul or body, so that, because he himself lost heavenly glory, human beings may not attain it either. For when he perceived that the human being had consented to his counsel, he strove to make war against God, saying: “Now I shall fulfill my entire will in the human being.”

Then in his hatred he introduced hateful agreement among people, so that they might kill one another. And he said: “I shall make human beings die, and I shall destroy them more completely than I am destroyed; for when I exist, they do not.” In his breath, too, he brought it about that the succession of human children should perish, when men burned with desire for men, committing shameful acts. Therefore, rejoicing greatly, he cried: “It is the greatest blasphemy against him who formed the human being that the human being vanishes in his own form, having cast aside the natural use of women.”

Thus, in diabolical suggestion are the faithless and seducers; in hatred and murder, robbers and thieves; and in the contrary sin of men are most foul transgression and every vice. And when these sins have joined themselves together among peoples, then the ordering of God’s law will be divided, and the Church will be shaken like a widow. Princes, nobles, and rich people will be driven from their places by their inferiors and will flee from city to city; the nobility of their lineage will be reduced to nothing, and they will be brought from riches to poverty.

All this will happen when the ancient serpent hisses variety of manners and variety of clothing among the people. They will imitate him, casting off some things and drawing on others, as they continually renew and alter themselves in the aforesaid deeds [Col. 0910D]. But this same ancient enemy and the other most wicked spirits have indeed lost the beauty of their form, yet they have not lost the breath of rationality. Out of fear of their Creator, they do not show the form of their destruction as it is to any mortal creature; rather, through their suggestions they lie in wait for each person according to that person’s habits, whenever they find something resembling their malice in the rest of creation.

But God has established a great battle against their impiety, when human rationality resists and confounds their rationality. This battle will endure until the last day, when confusion will utterly defile them; and the human being who has overcome them will receive the reward of life.

[Col. 0911A] That, through the red globe and the wings surrounding it above and below on both sides in this vision, are shown the zeal of God, by which sins are punished with charity, and his defenses, by which those to be saved are protected.

X. But what you see toward the east, above the aforesaid roundness of the earth, at a certain height—a red globe surrounded by a circle of sapphire color—signifies this: in the quarter of the east, signifying the rising of righteousness, beyond human understanding and existing in the height of heavenly mysteries, the zeal of God is shown in his power together with the justice of charity. For although God has power to carry out his judgments, he nevertheless fulfills them through the equity of charity.

From its right and left sides two wings proceed. One of them extends upward from those same two sides to a height, so that both, bending back at their summit, face one another. This signifies that in prosperity and adversity alike—that is, in gentle inspiration and harsh correction—divine protection, showing itself for the safeguarding of human beings, preserves and encloses in the height of its majesty those things which through it strive upward. The other descends from these same two sides down to the middle of the aforesaid roundness of the earth, so that the wings, embracing that same middle roundness outside the firmament, cover it. For just as heavenly protection guards those things which are in heaven, so it protects those which exist below, while inclining toward the fullness of human good will [Col. 0911C] and placing it in the embrace of true love.

That, through the red circle extending in the manner of a bow around the outer western region, is signified the extension of God’s vengeance against those who are outside the integrity of true faith and the enclosure of good works.

XI. From that same middle point a red circle stretches out in the manner of a bow, encompassing the whole outer region of the west and also certain divisions lying outside its roundness. This means that, from that perfection by which God mercifully nourishes those who worship him, the fire of his zeal, through the vengeance of just extension, rightly judges those who walk outside the enclosure of good works and those outside the integrity of true faith, and condemns them to penal places. It curves back from the end of the aforesaid southern wing around the west to the end of the northern wing, casting guilty deeds down from the prosperity of the present life and sending them into the harshness of its scourges, because they have not held fast to the truth of justice.

And what appears from that roundness toward the east, between the aforesaid wings, like a building ascending upward as far as the aforesaid globe, signifies that the city constructed of living stones, turning away from earthly concerns through the rising of righteousness and standing between God’s protections, directs its gaze toward God’s judgment, glorifying him. For faithful souls continually praise God because he orders all things rightly.

[Col. 0912A] Concerning the building appearing above the earth’s roundness; the street and the star shining above it; another globe and rays of stars gleaming between the same wings; and the intervals by which all these were separated—how these refer to the city of God, which is the Church, and to Christ, the Holy Spirit and his gifts, and the angels by whose guardianship the saints are fortified.

XII. From the same globe a kind of street extends upward to the middle of the aforesaid wings, above which a white star shines. This signifies that from the judgments of God’s power a way leads to the perfection of his protections, above which virginity flourishes, where the incarnate Son of God, born of the Virgin, appears. A very great multitude, loving virginity and embracing perfection, follows him powerfully in devout commitment.

Then, between the summits of these wings, there appears something like a fiery globe emitting certain rays from itself, because in the height of heavenly defenses the Holy Spirit manifests himself by bestowing very many gifts upon his elect. The intervals from the summit of the aforesaid roundness of the earth to the aforesaid red globe, from that globe to the aforesaid white star, and from that star to the aforesaid fiery globe, are equal. For the judgments of God’s power, the works of virginity, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit do not disagree with one another, but accord through equal moderation: what the grace of the Holy Spirit breathes forth, works of holiness confirm, and divine judgments judge justly.

Moreover, between the upper wings on both sides of the aforesaid street, from the aforesaid globe around the indicated star to the aforesaid fiery globe, there appear distinct rays like rays of stars. They signify that, in that protection which is above in heaven, the paths of virginity are everywhere enclosed. For through invincible power that virginity which began in the Son of God, strengthened through the might of the Holy Spirit, is never without the guardianship of angelic spirits; since virginity, being the companion of angels, merits their fellowship. For my Son, through the gentleness of his humanity, gathers to himself those who imitate him in faithful devotion to chastity, and who, fearing God’s judgments, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit inflict the Passion of that same my Son upon their bodies [Col. 0912D] while resisting the desires of their flesh.

Concerning the outer darkness and punishments or torments of diverse kinds in which the souls of the damned are tortured with the devil and his followers; in what regions they are found; and that no one living in the body can comprehend the terrible torments of hell.

XIII. Toward the west, outside the aforesaid roundness of the earth, darkness appears. It extends in the form of a bow from both sides of that roundness to its middle, where the aforesaid wings also descend. In that region outside the world are the outer darknesses, stretching on one side as far as the middle of the southern quarter and on the other as far as the middle of the northern quarter. Thus they raise themselves, through the wickedness of rebellion, against the fullness of God’s protection. There the ancient warrior, who rules over souls given over to oblivion within them, delights to possess torments.

Between the western and northern corners are other darknesses, denser and harsher, having the appearance of a horrible, devouring gaping mouth. By their bitterness, existing in those regions outside the world as the mouth of the infernal pit, they devour the souls of the damned and torment them with dreadful afflictions, because those who perform works of damnation more than they love God follow the devil.

The aforesaid darknesses cling to certain other, most dense, evil, and infinite darknesses outside them, as though these were their mouth and jaws. These are the infernal places [Col. 0913B], in which every kind of punishment abounds without consolation, separate from other punishments because they are harsher than those and devour all whom God judges should be consigned to oblivion. By them the souls of those are tortured who, through the unbelief of faithlessness and through execrable deeds, consign their Creator to oblivion.

Therefore you know these infinite darknesses, but do not see them. For a human being can know through knowledge and understanding that hell and its dreadful torments exist; but while in the body, no mortal sight perfectly sees them, nor can anyone discern what torments, or how great, are in them—just as one does not know one’s own soul or its merits while living in the world.

That God, the one life subsisting in himself, received being from no one, but gave being to all; likewise concerning the creation of the angels, the fall of the proud, the confirmation of the blessed spirits, and the fact that the devil, though he continually labors to do so, cannot destroy the full number of those to be saved.

XIV. Therefore God, who made all the things aforesaid, is the one life from which every life breathes, just as a ray comes from the sun. He is the fire from which every fire directed toward blessedness is kindled, just as sparks proceed from fire. How could it be fitting that no living thing should adhere to this life, or that this fire should neither warm nor illumine anyone? And how would it be becoming that from the Godhead, which was life before time, no life and no brightness should proceed? What benefit would there be if light kindled by fire shone for no one, when neither fire conceals its light nor the sun its ray?

For God is that life by which the multitude of angels was kindled, as sparks proceed from fire. Hence it would be unfitting for this life not to shine. And this brightness is unfailing, because no death can be in it. How so? God alone exists through himself and in himself, and received being from no other; but every other creature began to be through him.

He created certain spirits of great honor and set a great prince over them, upon whom they all looked, as one looks upon a lamp in which a burning light shines, because in him all their adornments gleamed like precious stones. But he looked toward an empty place, where he desired to set his throne. Therefore he was cast with all his host like straw into the pit of hell [Col. 0914A], so that at his fall the outer darkness and the mouth of the infernal pit, together with the pit itself, were prepared. This pit is without measure, just as the number of lost angels has no number.

For against that likeness by which he desired to be like God, those outer darknesses were prepared; and because of the unlawful discord that he wished to create between God’s army and his own, the mouth of the infernal pit was made for him. Because of this envy, by which he in no way wished to confess God, the pit of hell was prepared for him. And God, in the strength of his majesty, surrounded the blessed spirits so that they would no longer be terrified by any astonishment caused by the ancient deceiver; and he so filled their faces with his brightness that they delight always to behold his face. In this way he extended his power over hell: the ancient deceiver can destroy the full number of those to be saved by neither war nor any art, just as he killed himself according to the ways of vipers.

That when God had made the human being in the power of divine light, but he had been deceived by the devil’s fraud, God created a garment from air and, clothing him, drove him from paradise into the exile of this world to pay for the guilt of disobedience; and that in this human being’s fall creation was darkened from its former beauty, and how the human being himself lives and works with the help of the elements.

XV. Then God made the human being in the light of his power and placed him in the inextinguishable light of paradise, which remains incorruptible with its fruits [Col. 0914C]. But the human being seized upon disobedience and thus knew himself to be naked. This greatly pleased the devil, who had stripped him naked, since he too had lost the beauty of his glory.

But God appeared in a pale cloud like a flame, as though alien to him—just as later he showed himself with covered face to Moses and his other beloved ones—and he did not wish him to be naked. For he willed that his own Son should one day be clothed in the garment of humanity. Therefore he gave him a garment from the air by which an animal lives, because Adam and Eve had obeyed the animal when they abandoned God’s command.

Thus, driven out into wretched exile, they became perishable along with the other fruits of the earth. At their fall and departure, all creation of the world was darkened, as when a ray of the sun shines through a dense cloud. Likewise the entrance to paradise was darkened to the ancient deceiver, so that thereafter he should not enter it.

Then the human being began to work with creation. For as fire kindles and brings all other things to completion, so the human being exists with the rest of creation; and creation lies hidden in fire, which pervades and tests all things. Water too is present to him, cleansing all things; and fire burns with such force that it would spare no one unless tempered by water. And as water comes to fire to spare it, so humanity is joined to divinity in order that it may spare; for it would not benefit the human being if it lay in darkness and gave no light.

For he is coagulated by fire and suffused with water, in order that he may have form; and for this reason he likewise completes every earthen form that he makes by fire and water. [Col. 0915A] God indeed is living light, from which all lights shine; therefore through him the human being remains a vital light, and God himself is also fire. Accordingly, God cooks the human being with fire and suffuses him with water; hence water, from excessive heat, reddens and flows in human flesh.

And how could it be fitting that the human being, who shines from light, should remain dark and not move when he lives from fire? If the human being were without work and had no dwelling-place, he would be empty. For God, who is fire and light, gives life to the human being through the soul and moves him through rationality. Thus God also created the whole world by the sound of his word; it is the human being’s dwelling-place. And the human being works with all these things, just as God made him complete in all respects.

[Col. 0915B] That no one could rescue the human being from perdition or defeat his deceiver, the devil, except God alone; and concerning the words of the book of the Apocalypse of John the Apostle, the sense in which they are to be understood, the dragon’s hatred and persecution of the woman and her seed, and how the woman was helped by the earth.

XVI. And who could raise up the lost human being, who had been deceived and forgotten his Creator, except him who, darkened by no shadow, took pity on that ignorance? But when the devil saw the clothed woman, in the envious knowledge by which he knew himself to have been cast down from heaven, he tore himself apart inwardly by asking why God had given her clothing, as it is written in the Apocalypse:

“And when the dragon saw that he had been cast down to the earth, he persecuted the woman who had borne the male child. And two wings of a great eagle were given to the woman, that she might fly into the wilderness, to her place, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, away from the face of the serpent” (Rev. 13).

This is to be understood thus: the ancient dragon, seeing that he had lost that place in which he wished to set his throne, because he had been cast into Tartarean places, sharpened his wrath against the woman, because he knew that she was the root of the whole human race through childbirth. Holding her in the greatest hatred, he said within himself that he would never cease persecuting her until he had, as it were, drowned her in the sea, because he had first deceived her.

But she, as though distressed in childbirth, finally seized the strongest aid of consolation. Supported by divine protection, she opposed herself to the devil in every way. For two defenses of blessedness were given to her: heavenly desire and the salvation of souls. Thus, as she reached in these toward the secret place of her heart and there received the nourishment of salvation, she endured through the time before the flood, the times after the flood, and half a time, which was in circumcision before the Incarnation of my Son and lasted until the full time of the Gospel. In this Gospel arose the entire fullness of true and just ordering against the ancient serpent.

Before the flood, after the flood, and also under circumcision, there were those who worshiped God and obtained the redemption of their souls through the shed blood of my Son. But when the time of the glowing dawn—that is, of complete justice—came through my Son, the ancient serpent was greatly terrified and astonished, because through the woman, namely the Virgin, he was wholly deceived.

Therefore in his fury he burned against her, as it is written in my will: “And the serpent sent water from his mouth after the woman like a river, so that he might cause her to be swept away by the river; and the earth helped the woman” (ibid.).

This is to be understood thus: from his most wicked voracity the ancient persecutor sent unbelief and faithlessness against the uprightness of the woman who had brought forth the man, into the peoples of the Jews and pagans. His purpose was to subjugate her when worn down by many persecutions, or wholly to drown her, as a ship is drowned by shipwreck, so that her name might be entirely erased from the earth, just as a thing is erased from the earth when it is cast into the depth of a river [Col. 0916B]. But the woman was rescued by the help of the earth, because my Son took from her the garment of his humanity; and in his body he endured very many reproaches and sufferings for the confusion of that serpent.

That, in establishing the world, God glorified himself by showing himself to the rational creature as creator of all things, and at the same time exalted the human being through the subjection of those things which are in the world; and how the beginning of the book of Genesis is to be understood according to the letter, from the words “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” to the words “and there was evening and morning, one day.”

XVII. Thus, as has been stated above, God adorned the world with heaven, established it with earth, and through it glorified himself; and through the things that are in the world he exalted man, when he subjected to him all earthly things. My servant, privy to my secrets, shows this when he says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood as follows: In the beginning—that is, in the inception of all things which were in God’s knowledge as to how they should be made—God created, that is, caused to proceed through himself, heaven and earth: namely, the matter of all heavenly and earthly creatures; heaven, that is, luminous matter, and earth, namely, turbulent matter. These two matters were created together and appeared in one circle; and that circle is the power of God in heaven and on earth. From that brightness which is eternity, the aforesaid luminous matter flashed like dense light; and that same light shone over the turbulent matter. Nor did he immediately illuminate either the firmament or the earth, just as a human being does not do so when preparing certain forms: for first he marks each one with his compass, and afterwards paints it in colours.

“But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep” (ibid.), because the earth was empty, that is, without form, and invisible, lacking light, since it was not yet illumined by the brilliance of light or the radiance of sun, moon, or stars; and it was uncultivated, since no creature ploughed it; and void, that is, unarranged, because it was not yet full, since it did not yet possess the greenness, shoots, or flowering of grasses or trees. [Col. 0917A] That it is not said that heaven was empty and void is because it was not destined to bear any fruits. But darkness, which had not yet vanished through the radiance of light, since no form was flashing forth, lay upon the face of the deep, namely upon the same undifferentiated confusion of earth. This is the face of the deep: it is seen, while the deep itself remains hidden, because the earth covers its deep as the body covers the soul, so that it may not be seen.

“And the Spirit of God was moving over the waters” (ibid.). For the Spirit of God is life, and this life moved the waters to flow, so that the earth might be established by them and not scattered like ashes by the wind. For as the Holy Spirit is poured into a human being, so waters have a rushing course and wash away all uncleanness, just as the Holy Spirit washes away the filth of sins. And God said: “Let there be light, and there was light” (ibid.). God, existing as an inextinguishable light obscured by no one, spoke through his Word as with a peal of thunder, saying: “Let there be light”; and there was light, because the unfailing night and the light invisible to human beings—which shall never be darkened—flashed forth. To it also the living spheres, namely the angels, clung; for God is life, and his Word does not sleep, but life appears. And what he brought forth God set to his own praise; this was not the light of the sun, because the sun did not yet exist, and because the sun’s radiance does not always appear upon the earth but is often clouded over.

“And God saw that the light was good, and he divided the light from [Col. 0917C] the darkness, and called the light day and the darkness night” (ibid.). For God saw that the light was good, because it reflected the splendour of his face; and therefore he separated it also from darkness, lest their functions be mingled with one another. Of these two, one is unfailing, while the other falls into deficiency. Day is from God, because through his Word God commanded the first light to come forth, and he called it day—not the day of the sun, but the unfailing day which in the heights is oppressed by no darkness. And he called night the darkness—not that which is driven away by the light of the sun, but that which possesses unfailing obscurity and is touched by no brightness of light; he also called night the darkness that lay upon the face of the deep and which he had not yet illuminated. For night without day is blind; and day, separated from night and from night’s blindness, is in brightness. Thus God separated light from nocturnal darkness.

“And there was evening and there was morning, one day” (ibid.). For the completion of this work and its beginning came to be, one brightness in perfection: since, when the Word of God commanded light to be made, its beginning was like morning, but its completion was like evening, when it appeared complete. And in another sense:

That, just as the Son of God, begotten timelessly from the Father, is the beginning in whom all things were created, so the same one, being born from a virgin mother, is the beginning of the creation or building up of the Church, and the author of full justification; for no righteousness of the fathers or sacraments of the Law sufficed for this, but it was restored in the preaching and reception of baptism and of the Gospel, and in faith in the Trinity.

XVIII. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood as follows: In the beginning of beginning time, when God created all things through his Word, he created heaven and earth—that is, the first matter, in which every heavenly and earthly creature that was to proceed through God’s Word lay hidden. God did likewise in creating the Church, before he built it. He began, beginning in the beginning—that is, in his Son—whom he sent into the world through the golden gate of the Virgin, within the enclosure of her chastity. Through him all things, namely heaven and earth, were created, as John the Evangelist, beloved of God, says; and in the same way all heavenly and earthly righteousness was made in him.

And how is he the beginning, who was begotten in the Father before the ages? Before the ages he was begotten in the Father spiritually, not carnally; but incarnate, he is the beginning of all righteousness, because whatever righteousness the ancient saints possessed before his birth did not live in salvation and did not restore humankind to it. But the righteousness which arose in him—namely baptism, the Gospel, and belief in one God in the name of the Holy Trinity—restores humankind to Paradise. Therefore he is the beginning of salvation in his work, as Adam was the beginning of perdition in his work. And just as he is that Word through which every creature was brought forth, because all things were made through him, so also in his humanity he is the beginning of all the building up of holy Church.

How? In the preaching of the prophets, who foretold that he would come, he was as it were a shadow; likewise, from Abel until the birth of the Son of God, every righteousness was a shadow of the Church, which arose from Christ’s side in his blood. Through the regeneration of Spirit and water—which had never previously existed except insofar as John the Baptist proclaimed it in the shadow of baptism—it then appeared fully in its own form. For Christ himself, who before his birth had been foretold by the prophets as it were in shadow, appeared as a human being in the flesh, as David the Psalmist says in my Spirit:

[Col. 0918D] Words of David the prophet in the first psalm, and how they are to be understood concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God and the fruitful fertility of his teaching throughout the whole world.

XIX. “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall give its fruit in its season.” This is to be understood as follows: The Son of God, who in all things followed the will of his Father, was the tree of salvation, conceived of the Holy Spirit, from whom living waters flow. He gave abundant fruit of holiness when he fully instructed his disciples in ecclesiastical teaching. For according to his divinity the Son of God was as a root in the Father’s heart and the power of divinity; and thus, descending into the Virgin’s womb, he brought forth full fruit through his humanity. For as the moisture of water is in the greenness of a tree, so the Son of God was always in the Father until the predestined time of his humanity, when he became the food of life for all spiritual persons. Heaven touched the Son of God when he appeared in heaven in the Father’s bosom; earth touched him when he lay in the manger; and water felt him when he walked upon the sea. Yet although peoples saw him bodily, they did not think him to be God.

That what is written, “But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep,” is to be understood allegorically of unbelievers empty of good works and darkened by unbelief; and that what follows, “The Spirit of the Lord was moving over the waters,” was fulfilled in the apostles and the believing people through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

XX. “But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep” (Gen. 1). Every people, namely Jewish and Gentile, dwelling upon the face of the deep—that is, the earth—was, through the stirring of its own spirit, empty of faith, blind and deaf in the knowledge of God, and void of good works, because it did not perform them according to the teaching of the Son of the Most High, until he ascended to the Father. Thus, upon the earth, which is the face of the deep, were the darknesses of unbelief, in which people lived as blind persons, not knowing God.

“And the Spirit of God was moving over the waters.” After the Lord’s ascension, the fiery Holy Spirit moved over the waters, that is, the apostles. This was brought about by the love of the Son in the will of the Father: for as waters arose before the other creatures in the creation of the world, so the apostles were the first teachers before the other teachers of the Church. And just as all waters flow forth from those waters that arose in the creation of the world, so all teachers of the Church have been propagated from the apostles, the first teachers, as David the Psalmist testifies, saying:

Further words of David the prophet in Psalm 28, concerning the apostles and teachers speaking with one voice, and how they are to be understood.

XXI. “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the voice of the Lord is upon many waters.” This is to be understood as follows: A voice first sounds and contains within itself the force of a word, so that whatever it announces may be understood knowingly. Thus the voice of him who rules all things came upon the waters, that is, upon the prophets, when he disclosed to them many mysteries, both heavenly and earthly. And the same Lord, being the God of majesty, because he is powerful over all things, made himself powerfully known when he sent his Son into the world. Then too this Lord of all peoples sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles and the other believers who had multiplied in the catholic faith, so that their teaching penetrated the whole world.

People beheld the Son of God in human form, but did not know how he had been conceived and born. A voice, moreover, is somewhat foreign and unintelligible, whereas a word is familiar and intelligible; through it a person knows in faith the God of majesty, who sent prophecy into humankind. Water likewise signifies prophecy; hence the Lord of the prophets is known in their voices.

How the words of God saying, “Let there be light,” and the rest as far as “There was evening and there was morning, one day,” were fulfilled in the rise of Christian faith, the preaching of the apostles, and the separation of believers from unbelievers according to the allegorical sense.

XXII. “And God said: Let there be light, and there was light.” God spoke through the Holy Spirit to the apostles, saying: “Be a burning light, teaching the truth in the name of the Holy Trinity.” Immediately kindled by the Holy Spirit, they opened the enclosure in which they had been shut up and became one light, shining into the world through their teachings.

“And God saw that the light was good, and divided the light from the darkness. And he called the light day, and the darkness night.” God saw that they would be a light useful to the world, and he divided the light—that is, the apostles—from the darkness, namely the unbelief of unbelievers. He called this light one day, which shines upon the world in their preaching through his Word, which is his Son, speaking to them in the flesh; and he called the darkness, namely the unbelief of the faithless, night.

“And there was evening and there was morning, one day.” As the unbelief of unbelievers began to decline as toward evening, this evening came to be with its passing away; and the morning of the first light—that is, the beginning of believers’ faith—became one day, namely the one faith through which one God is believed. For its first dawn was in Abel and it was brought to a good completion in Christ; and therefore evening perceived and touched the Son of God with the work of salvation. This one day endures to the end of the world, because Abel was as the morning and the Son of God as the evening of the day. And again, in another sense:

How these same things written in Genesis concerning the creation of heaven and earth, or the work of the first day, are to be understood morally in the conduct of a human being composed of the diverse natures of soul and body.

XXIII. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” This is to be understood as follows: When I, God, form a human being as though in the beginning of a certain creation in good morals, I create within that person a living knowledge of good and evil: namely, so that the person may avoid evil and imitate me, the Father, in goodness. I gave that person discernment of good and evil in my likeness, so that through this knowledge he might distinguish all creatures and, knowing them, possess authority over them after me. But that human being, through great vanity, abandoning me at the devil’s persuasion, falls into the tearful labours of sins, because, born in Adam’s frail nature, he abandons the joyful knowledge which would not injure him in any way.

Nevertheless, in his soul he possesses that by which he frequently pants in upright sighs for heavenly desires; this is as it were heaven. But in his flesh he has that which always seeks earthly desires; therefore, from the frailty that arose for him from Adam and from the counsel of the devil, the plotter, he can never be without the contagion of sin; this is as it were earth.

“But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep.” A human being who can never be stable in moral conduct is great emptiness, and is always flooded as though by the surging of the sea. Yet just as, in the creation of the world, creature after creature proceeded in order from the first matter, so a human being ought to ascend from virtue to virtue through good desires, as I established him in the first creation. But now, through the devil’s counsel, he overturns good desires into great vanity, as has been said, and in that very vanity of conduct willingly remains empty of good works. Therefore he is surrounded by dark deeds belonging to depraved conduct, which so rule over the body that whoever commits sin is the slave of sin.

The body is as the face of the deep, but the soul is like the deep: for the body is visible and tangible like the face of the deep, whereas the soul is invisible and intangible like the deep of the earth.

“And the Spirit of God was moving over the waters.” When a faithful person is entangled in sins, that person sometimes sighs to God. How? Through compunction which arises in him from the grace of the Holy Spirit, he sheds the moisture of tears, because sighs ought to precede every good work. And just as, in the first creation, waters were set before the other creatures through the breathing forth of God’s Spirit and were especially joined to the Holy Spirit in signification, so the Holy Spirit also brings forth from the human heart the moisture of tears before the beginning of good works.

And God said: “Let there be light, and there was light.” God says in the admonition of the Holy Spirit: “Now, after compunction of heart, let the building up of good works take place in this person, and let the greenness of fruit be brought forth in him, so that light may arise in his soul.” Then the person rises, with the sorrow of repentance, into the light of good works. How? Restoring himself from unlawful desires for the pleasures of the flesh, and removing evil from himself, he begins to work in that newness of light which he had not known before, while he slept in seductive desires of the flesh; and thus at the beginning his work is bright.

“And God saw that the light was good, and divided the light from the darkness. And he called the light day, and the darkness night.” When God sees that person beginning to do good and sees his house thus shining, knowing and observing the beginning of good in him, he looks upon him with love and embraces him. At that same beginning he separates those bright works from the contamination of dark deeds that belong to punishment. This is that division: God, seeing good in that person, removes evil from him. He calls bright works within himself the day of salvation, because through those good works he recalls souls to himself from the perdition that was in Adam; and he calls contrary works the night of perdition, which raised itself up in the devil, the father of murder.

“And there was evening and there was morning, one day.” Thus in that person the evening habit of evil work, together with the beginning of the commencement of good works, becomes as it were the morning of one virtue, one day; because, abandoning evil, he has joined himself to good, since compunction is the first virtue of light.

How the things read concerning the establishment of the firmament and the division of the waters are to be understood literally, and the words of David from Psalm 18 which pertain to the same subject.

XXIV. “And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood as follows: God, who is inextinguishable light, commanded through his burning Word that the firmament be made—namely this revolving expanse, so established by the signs above that it cannot slip—and placed it in the midst of the waters, thus separating waters from waters. He contained the waters that rose upward like a mountain, so that, just as a mountain does not descend from its height, neither might they incline anywhere except as he had placed them; gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin, which is the firmament, and placing the deeps in storehouses, which are the earth, because the earth is a storehouse of living things within itself. So too God prefigured this in Noah’s ark, which he supported in the midst of the waters while it held the creatures shut within.

In this manner God placed the firmament between the separated waters, in order that it might divide waters from waters. God made this division before he illuminated the firmament; and, not yet illuminated, it stood in its place without revolving, waiting until it should be illumined by its Creator. For every creature first exists as a root and afterwards multiplies by bearing fruit, just as winter possesses the root but summer the flowering of greenness. Thus God marked the creatures of earth with their circle, and afterwards gave them life according to their natures. Only humankind did he inspire with his own breath; the remaining creatures he gave life through an airy breath which passes with the cloud.

“And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from those which were above the firmament. And it was so” (ibid.). God placed the firmament to divide those waters which were below and above it, and thus the firmament appeared. And God called the firmament heaven, because every thing which supports another is rightly called that other’s firmament. He also called the firmament heaven because it surpasses all things and always declares his glory: when a human being looks upon it, he cannot fully know what it is, just as a human being does not perfectly know God, though he sees him in faith. But the heaven which is God’s dwelling a human being will not see unless first he becomes wholly spiritual, because it surpasses his sense and knowledge.

Therefore the Prophet says: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands” (Ps. 18). This is to be understood as follows: All the instruments of the firmament are rightly called heavens, because God alone established them through himself; nor did he require the knowledge of any creature, because there is no one who can define by his own understanding how he made them. Hence they proclaim the miracles of God, marked through him in the firmament as in a mirror: the sun shows the divinity of the Son of God; the moon, his humanity; and the stars display his other mysteries. In this manner so innumerable a multitude of believers clings to God, who is both God and human, that no one can number it, because he himself is innumerable in his glory.

The firmament also announces the human being, who is the work of God’s hands, in his bright office, because he was built according to it. Therefore it makes the human being manifest, since it openly bears his signs in itself. And there was evening and there was morning, the second day, because God completed his work in that firmament with the same purpose with which he began it, since he orders all his works in equity. Again, in another sense:

That allegorically the firmament is Christ, or faith in Christ; the division of the waters is the firm interposition of that faith by which believers are separated from unbelievers; and evening and morning are to be understood as the fall of vice and the rising of virtue.

XXV. “And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood as follows: God said: “Let there be the firmament of faith in the midst of unbelieving peoples, among those who understand the preaching of the apostles and who willingly receive their words with them; and let it divide waters—that is, believers—from waters, namely unbelieving Jews and pagans.” Thus my Son said to the Jews: “The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21). This is to be understood as follows: You who are unbelieving have lost your inheritance through unbelief. Therefore, by the just judgment of God, the kingdom in which you ought to have reigned with God shall be taken from you and given to those who, abandoning their sins, bring forth fruits by which the kingdom of God is glorified.

For there is great hardness in the hearts of unbelievers, who act not according to knowledge of the good but according to the unlawful desires of their hearts. Rationality is the material of knowledge of good and evil, and is like a craftsman, building and destroying. Whoever loves the day of faith builds his house in the heavenly Jerusalem; but whoever rejects it destroys his house, excluding it from the honour and blessedness of the heavenly inheritance. And because he performs everything he does in the harmful fruit according to his own desires, his works are dark, because they are done in darkness while fleeing the light. Thus the unbelievers rejected the true light, that is, the Son of God. They were unwilling either to see him or to do his works, and therefore they lost their inheritance. But those who received him in good faith and fulfilled his commandments obtained the heavenly kingdom as the dowry of his blood.

“And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from those which were above the firmament. And it was so” (Gen. 1). God made the firmament of faithful hearers through the preaching of the apostles, and divided the waters—that is, unbelieving peoples, who had been beneath the firmament among earthly things, idols, and the like—from those people who were above the firmament, that is, above Christ. And God called the firmament heaven, by which faith is understood, because faith itself is the firm and great city with heavenly works. How? It is the city of the whole ecclesiastical order and the most victorious contest against the unbelief of all unbelievers.

“And there was evening and there was morning, the second day” (ibid.). The ending of unbelieving hearts came to be together with the rising of the firmament of that day, namely right faith: the second day, which is as it were belief in Christ in the second light of faith.

That, as the second day was without the lights of heaven, so faith without bright works is worthy of no praise; and therefore in the work of that day, as in the works of the other days, the words “God saw that it was good” are not included.

XXVI. That it is not said here, “And God saw that it was good” (ibid.), means that this fiery work of faith and the other virtues had not yet arisen in action, but were shaped only in the hearing of the peoples, who had not yet tasted them in the experience of action. For just as a person does not know which food is good except by tasting it, so people had not yet tasted the works of faith by performing them, but only heard of them as in the shadow of hearing. Thus, as the firmament was still above the round of the earth without the splendour of sun, moon, and stars, so then, as it were in the second light of faith, faith itself remained without the bright work of rightly established ordinances; people received faith only as in a shadow. And again, in another sense:

That, according to the moral sense, the firmament is to be understood as the virtue of discernment, because every faithful person knows how in the active and contemplative life to distinguish bodily necessities from superfluities, and what benefits the soul from what harms it.

XXVII. “And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood as follows: God sometimes speaks to a person in the enlargement of the heart. How? In the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, because in that very person the place of his house shines. Then he makes the instruments of virtues for the protection of the work which he had begun in that person, so that no necessity of any virtue may be lacking to that person, just as he also did in heaven and earth, where no creatures necessary to human beings are lacking.

When God speaks, then, the firmament comes to be: this is discernment amid the diversity of spiritual and carnal persons. A person ought to possess heavenly desire and necessary care for the flesh, so that he may be held in things with discernment: lest through good works an exaltation leading to ruin be built up in him, and lest he be corrupted by another’s pressure of varied moral dispositions. Rather, at one time he should pray with sighs; at another, be occupied with good works; and at another provide what is necessary for the flesh, lest it fail. Whatever gifts of the Holy Spirit he possesses, he should repeatedly build them up through discernment; and he should apply himself always to the virtues that must be practised, according to their measure, so that through them he may pant toward heaven in burning sighs and serve the needs of the flesh only from necessity.

In these gifts of the Holy Spirit, vain glory—which God utterly rejects—must also be avoided; for a person who honours himself in place of God has it, and uproots one root of good after another. Thus, always unstable, he is unable in any way to stand in one place, and the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot rest upon such a person.

“And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from those which were above the firmament. And it was so” (ibid.). God likewise now makes all the instruments of virtues in a human being, along with the discernment which he established through the breathing of the Holy Spirit, so that the person himself may distinguish within himself all these instruments which God sees to be useful, lest any virtue which he begins be submerged through wandering of mind. Thus God divides earthly necessities from heavenly virtues, which the Holy Spirit waters and which always cling to heavenly things, so that the person may always pant with them toward the contemplative life.

Discernment contains these virtues as a maidservant retains her mistress by her service, because the mistress does not wish to be without her maidservant in earthly matters that concern the flesh and are subject to discernment. Thus discernment is the firmament, having earthly things—that is, the active life—beneath itself, and heavenly things—that is, the contemplative life—above itself. It is their ladder, by which human minds ascend to heaven through good works and descend to earth because of bodily necessity; just as Mary and Martha offered different services to God, yet both pleased him, because he is the founder of both lives.

Thus the firmament of virtue is between the two lives when a person exercises discernment for himself, so that he rightly possesses heavenly and earthly things in the measure established for them by God. “And God called the firmament heaven” (ibid.). Through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, God calls discernment in a human being heaven, and it is truly the most certain signification of heaven. For as the firmament holds within itself all the ornaments that illuminate, govern, and contain the world, so discernment holds all the instruments of virtues which proceed from God and by which body and soul are governed. Thus what lies hidden within does not fail, and what is outward is not darkened through ostentation.

“And there was evening and there was morning, the second day” (ibid.). This also occurs in that person who is evening-like in good habit, when he completes all his works in discernment. For at the beginning of all virtues God foresees their end, because he perceives that they touch him; and at their end he approves their beginning, because a good beginning is of no use unless a good end follows. Thus my Son speaks in the Gospel of the bridegroom, who said to the foolish virgins:

Testimony of the Gospel in which the Bridegroom says to the foolish virgins, “I do not know you,” and the purpose for which this is introduced here and the sense in which it is to be understood.

XXVIII. “Amen, amen, I say to you: I do not know you” (Matt. 25). This is to be understood as follows: I, who most certainly am, say to you: because, acting for the taste of the flesh according to your desires, you are utterly extinguished, “I do not know you,” because by knowing me you do not touch me in such a way as to perform the virtues of righteous works which I set before your good knowledge, nor do you ask them from me. You also restrain the sighs of your souls, compelling the soul to fulfil the will of the flesh and to seek no help from me.

For who can answer one whose voice and words are not heard? No one. For you direct no cry to me. And what gift shall be given to one who neither asks nor petitions, but flees from the gift with a mute voice? Truly, none. Therefore you ask nothing from me. For those who do not cry out to me with the sigh of the soul, and do not attend to me with heart and mind—as though they had forgotten me and as though I had not given them knowledge—I do not know; and above all because they provoke me by wicked works.

For through the idleness of their foolishness they do not look to me, and because of the embrace of the flesh they reject the discernment of virtuous minds kindled by the Holy Spirit. Therefore they are excluded from my sight. They choose one thing and reject another: they lay hold of earth with its greenness and neglect heaven because of their pleasures. They knock with voice alone and wish to enter without works; therefore its gate cannot be opened to them. For all virtues can be discerned through heavenly and earthly things, because a human being walks on earth and looks upon heaven; and in these two he must choose what he loves according to God and what he hates, so that in goodness he may tend toward heavenly things and turn himself away from evil.

Thus the beginning of each person whose end God does not approve is indeed said to be unknown to God. And just as at the end of the world—which is much more beneficial than its beginning—salvation arose in my Son, because at the beginning perdition proceeded but at the end salvation, so also a good end is much more beneficial than a good beginning. In this way discernment is the second light of good work, as the second day is.

Why, even according to the moral sense, the work of the second day, although good, lacks the praise of goodness.

XXIX. That it is not said here, “And God saw that it was good” (Gen. 1), means that discernment is the office of the other virtues, not by working but by ministering to the other virtues. Thus also the firmament, which is the support of the things by which it revolves, contains the other working creatures by serving them; these are called labouring creatures because, through it, they perform their individual works day and night for the service of humankind. And just as that same firmament, supporting each thing placed upon it, gives it a place, so discernment is not itself a worker through action, though the other virtues are called workers from their works; it is only the support of the other virtues.

How what is written, “Let the waters be gathered together,” as far as “There was evening and there was morning, the third day,” is to be understood appropriately according to the literal sense.

XXX. “And God said: ‘Let the waters which are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.’ And it was so (Gen. 1).” This is to be understood thus: by the word which is unquenchable, the waters that had remained beneath the firmament flowed together into one place, so that the earth might appear and not lie useless beneath their covering. And this was so done before the firmament was illuminated, so that, when it had been made bright with stars, it might shine over the expanses of water—that is, over the earth separated from the waters. And God called the dry land earth, which is the mother of all things that grow in the earth, because the first man also was made from it; and he called the gatherings of waters seas, from which waters flow, as though they were generated by them. “And God saw that it was good, and said: ‘Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.’ And it was so (ibid.).” God saw that everything he had made was rightly and well appointed for its function; and through his living Word he commanded the mother-earth to grow green for the bringing forth of flowering grass, also producing seed, so that it might be multiplied in its seed and be born again from it, since every shoot contains seed within itself lest it fail in its nature. He also commanded it to bring forth a fruit-bearing tree, producing fruit for food and containing within its nature seed in itself, by which it might sprout again when it fell upon the earth.

And so it was fulfilled, just as when a servant gladly carries out his lord’s commands, after the master of the household calls him, entrusts his business to him, and tells him what to do concerning each matter; for the earth too moved joyfully at the commands of its Lord, fulfilling them in all things. “And the earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree producing fruit, each having seed according to its species (ibid.),” because, as God commanded, the mother-earth produced the greenness of herbs containing their seed within themselves, and the greenness of trees yielding suitable fruit and renewed from their seed. For when the seeds of these fall into the earth, other things again rise up according to the species of their formation. “And God saw that it was good,” so that all these things necessary for the man whom he was about to make might precede him, lest they fail when human need followed. “And there was evening and morning, the third day (ibid.),” namely, an end and a beginning, by which the third work was completed, because God had brought forth the aforesaid three works within the circle of his knowledge, though they had not yet been illumined by the courses of the heavenly lights.

For as fire is silent before it is stirred by the breath of wind, but, stirred by that breath, burns brightly, so God’s work was silent in his foreknowledge before it came forth; but, aroused by the power of the living Word, it appeared in its form. Hence it is also written through my inspiration:

[Col. 0928A] The words of God speaking in the book of Isaiah the prophet, “I have kept silence, I have always been silent, I have been patient; like a woman in labour I shall speak”; and in the second psalm, speaking to the Son, “Today I have begotten you”; why these are placed here and how they should be understood.

XXXI. “I have kept silence, I have always been silent, I have been patient; like a woman in labour I shall speak” (Isa. 42). This is to be understood thus: I, prophecy imbued with the Holy Spirit of the prophets, kept silence in patience and was silent in gentleness; like a woman in labour, I shall speak after my pain. For before the incarnation of the Son of God, I kept silence as though dumb, holding his mysteries silently within myself and not bringing them forth openly, just as fire contains within itself a flame that does not move of itself but is moved by the wind. But now, after that pain which the same Son of God suffered in the flesh upon the cross, I shall speak like a woman in labour who has cast off her pain, openly and joyfully bringing forth those things which I had formerly concealed.

For the prophets silently restrained their voices, because they did not fully know what the knowledge contained in their utterance was. Therefore they said among themselves: “O, O, O! We do not fully see what we speak; yet we know that God will reveal it in his own times.” And so they waited patiently, entrusting those matters to God’s knowledge. But God afterward illumined them for the service of his work, which he had made in his image, just as a mother rejoices after childbirth when she sees the infant whom she has borne from herself, sighing toward him and saying: “This is my son.” So too the supreme Father speaks of his Son: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2).

[Col. 0928C] This “today” is that eternity in which, according to his divinity, he is always equal to the Father. After his incarnation, prophecy burned openly in the saints, who publicly spoke by expounding the prophecy of the prophets, just as God illumined the firmament with shining lights. In another sense: “And God said.”

Why that which God called dry land, and the gatherings of waters which he called seas, are allegorically understood, under differing aspects, of the Church—gathered from many peoples and founded upon the firmness of faith; called by David “the land of the living,” and by John the apostle in the Apocalypse “a sea of glass mingled with fire”—and in what sense these same testimonies should be understood.

XXXII. “Let the waters which are beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear. And it was so” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood thus: God gathered together the peoples of Christians, who were among pagans and were harassed in diverse places by many troubles and pains, and brought them into one Church; and thus they appeared as the land of the living, as the Prophet says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26).

This is to be understood thus: I who strive to follow God, when I perform what is good, believe and do not doubt that I shall see those good things which belong to the Lord of all, in that land where the blessed live, henceforth fearing no dangers of death. The Word of God also awakens the sleeping minds of human beings and enables them to see in the true vision of faith, so that those who had formerly been in unbelief, in untilled land, may afterward be overturned by the grace of the Holy Spirit with the plough of faith. He also prepares them as the land of the living, flourishing in every fruitful greenness and producing full fruit. Thus the prophets said that the Virgin would bear the Son of God, who raises the sleeping earth in his saints with the plough of true faith, so that they themselves may flow as running water from the living water of the Holy Spirit. And this was done by God’s command as God willed.

“And God called the dry land earth, and called the gatherings of waters seas” (Gen. 1). Thus God called the Church of Israel the promised land flowing with milk and honey, because it is both the sweetness and the brightness of the heavenly kingdom when it shines forth in the Christian people through faith and confession of God the Father, so that the same people might confess God in the true Trinity, which [Col. 0929B] the Jews refused to receive. This Church, gathered from the waters—that is, from the apostles—is also called a sea, because the hostilities of the devil’s warfare against souls, and the storms of evil Christians and pagans against bodies, flood into the Church amid great perils, seeking to overwhelm it, unless God delivers them. For he is always the sailor and rower of his own; since no Christian can enter the heavenly Jerusalem unless, with God’s help, he has passed through those storms.
