And the Church is also that very sea which John the Evangelist saw as a sea of glass mingled with fire, as he says in the Apocalypse: “And I saw something like a sea of glass mingled with fire, and those who had conquered the beast, and its image, and the number of its name, standing upon the sea of glass, having harps of God and singing the song of Moses, servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Rev. 15).

This is to be understood thus: I, to whom God’s mysteries were revealed, saw with inward eyes the Church which God called from the common people of Jews and pagans: pure in faith, yet shaken by many tribulations. There the faithful, kindled by the Holy Spirit, knew and contemplated the living God in true faith, because faith is like a shadow of the Divinity, which mortal man cannot see perfectly. And a shadow shows the form which is not seen, just as a compass marks out a form not yet formed; similarly the Son of God tells Philip, when he desires to see the Father, that whoever sees him sees his Father also (John 14).

For the holy Divinity lay hidden in humanity, and shone upon the world through the teaching by which it had illumined the whole world; just as water completely saturates the earth, which is like its body, and makes it fruitful for the refreshment of every creature. For as God is seen by heavenly spirits, so he also willed to be seen by creation in human nature. But I also beheld those who had overcome the ancient serpent, its members, and the number of its angelic host; for the place and number of those fallen spirits will be filled through the human being whom the devil, through envy, seduced from paradise. I beheld them, I say, standing upon the height of the Church, while they mortified their flesh with holy works and with signs through which they flew everywhere in praise of God.

[Col. 0930A] They also possessed that praise which is written by God’s command and which God established through creatures. For as the heavenly Jerusalem is founded in its first beginnings from unpolished stones lying upon the earth, so the old law, concealing spiritual things within itself, finally began to understand spiritual things by which the walls of that city were afterward built. They also sang the song of Moses, in the likeness of a singer who sings of things present and future which are nevertheless unknown and foreign to him, except that he only sighs toward them. So Moses, together with the old law, was like a voice in which the Word—that is, the humanity of the Saviour—lay hidden; and that Moses significantly wrote all the wonders of the incarnation of the same Son of God, as God taught him.

They also sang the song of the Lamb, which belongs to the order of virgins, who hold the Lamb of God in faith, setting aside the marriage of the flesh and looking upon him in love as though they had him present, whom they do not see in the flesh. Therefore it is very delightful to them that they are betrothed to the supreme King and sing to him with the rejoicing of praise, because they always pant for the life of another world with the longing of their soul, and commit all their care to God, praising him by voice and work.

How the womb of the Church, after the likeness of a certain earth, now brings forth green grass in the simplicity of little believers, and fruit-bearing trees in the strong activity of the perfect; how, according to the seed, the praise of faith is to be fruitful in the succession of believers until the end; and how this is on the third day, namely in the brightness of that faith.

XXXIII. “And God saw that it was good, and said: ‘Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.’ And it was so” (Gen. 1). The living earth is the Church, bearing the fruit of righteousness together with the teaching of the apostles, as they preached to their children in the beginning: that they might be like grass in the greenness of right faith, which they had received in the seed of God’s words; and that they might also become fruitful trees according to God’s law, so that fornications and adulteries might not be committed in their seed, but that they might bear children upon the earth in lawful generation.

“And it was so,” because the Church received faith at the sound of the apostles, and every ordering of peoples was subjected to the right law. “And the earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree producing fruit, each having seed according to its species.” The Church, which is the land of the living, brought forth the fruit of good works in the greenness of faith, bearing the seed of God’s Word and fruit, so that her children also—whether rich or poor, older or younger—might practice rightful marriage according to their respective conditions. “And God saw that it was good.” And this was good before God.

“And there was evening and morning, the third day.” Then the division and scattering of the Christian people, caused by the battles of unbelievers and by the sufferings inflicted upon them because of right faith, began as it were to turn away through evening toward the morning of that day: namely, toward stable faith, in which Christians received the established law by which they knew what they ought to do in that law of God. And this occurred as the third day, with the third light of right faith. And again, in another sense: “And God said.”

Likewise, how the things said to have been made on that same third day are found, according to tropology, in the moral conduct of the Church’s children; with an appropriate testimony from the Gospel appended, and the sense in which it should be understood.

XXXIV. “Let the waters which are beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear. And it was so” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood thus: in the compunction of the human heart, God says that all bodily necessities which are subject to discretion should be gathered into the calm place of a single use. How? So that a person may not be excessive in banquets, drunkenness, alluring adornment of clothing, or a crooked mind, seeking personal glory in all these things; but that bodily necessity alone may appear there. How? So that the body may be fed moderately, so that when it is properly refreshed the soul may have joy; and so that the soul may travel rightly with it, neither cast down into a precipice through excessive abstinence nor oppressed by the excess of the aforesaid immoderation. And thus all these things occur in a human being through the warning of the Holy Spirit, which that person receives in gladness of mind.

“And God called the dry land earth, and called the gatherings of waters seas.” And with that same warning God presses upon that person through holy humility, so that he may call himself wretched and dry earth because of the diverse needs of his body. Hence also, on account of worldly matters hidden in those necessities, he sighs, reckoning himself like the tossing of the sea; and for this reason he humbles himself, as though unworthy of spiritual joy.

“And God saw that it was good, and said: ‘Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.’ And it was so” (ibid.). When God sees in the embrace of sweet and profound humility that the person now despises himself because of earthly things, which, owing to his frailty, cannot exist without defilement, he says through the warning of the Holy Spirit: “Because the human being has received compunction of heart and discernment of good and evil, and, knowing himself to be earth, has cast himself down and subjected himself to holy humility, let him now diligently sprout in the greenness of virtues, so that he may not succumb in his thoughts and deeds to fleshly desires. For he has within his body a sap which continually entices him to begin sinning in his works.

And, having these good works as a habit, let him make seed: that is, correcting himself according to the words of teachers, let him draw himself away from the aforesaid desires and then ascend, according to the teaching of masters, to stronger virtues that bear fruit. How? A person ought to inquire from teachers what is good and what evil, and act according to their teaching, so that the instruments of those virtues which he has begun may contain within themselves this seed of God’s Word, and that it may be upon the earth—that is, upon the human being. Thus what he has ardently received from God’s warning will be fulfilled within him through love of God.”

“And the earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree producing fruit, each having seed according to its species” (ibid.). A person inwardly taught by the Holy Spirit then brings forth from his heart the greenness of abstinence, restraining fleshly pleasures, and the word of correction, when, according to the instruction by which he disciplines himself, he always pants toward God. For every virtue is dry unless it takes root within the human being through the word of correction, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: “Other seed fell upon the ground, and when it sprang up it withered away, because it had no moisture” (Luke 8).

This is to be understood thus: the seed of the Holy Spirit’s words of teaching is sown in the earth, so that the human being may be nourished in soul by it. But because these are the manifold gifts of the Holy Spirit, some seed falls upon the hard ground of unbelieving people, so that they sometimes receive it as though groaning, yet do not bring forth the fruit of piety, because they lack the moisture of gentleness; just as earth without moisture, being barren for fruits, yields no useful crop. For God created creatures for human understanding, so that people might choose what is useful in them and reject what is useless. Thus earth, where it is softened by poured-out moisture, bears fruit; but where it is hard and stony without moisture, it cannot produce fruit.

For the human being is denoted as good and tender earth in the knowledge of good; but in the knowledge of evil is understood as hard and stony earth. Thus the dew of the Holy Spirit is poured out in abundant fruit upon those who perform good works with the delight of spiritual life, while those who gather to themselves every sin of pleasure through the taste of the flesh remain unfruitful through hardness of heart, like stony ground, because the sap of good will has dried up within them. And how will virtue take root within a human being through the word of correction? By binding himself with the word of his own heart, by which he must fight against vices.

And so he will advance in the higher virtues by which he instructs himself through the teaching of elders; that is, he will understand how he ought to discipline himself with fear and withdraw from evil through abstinence. For the person who, while experiencing pleasure, abstains from wicked deeds possesses greater virtue than the one who avoids the works of his flesh because he feels no pleasure. Thus, wisely fulfilling all things through the words that have been spoken, a person will bring forth within himself fruit according to the example by which he has been taught, and will hold their words against himself together with the correction of his own words.

“And God saw that it was good” (Gen. 1). These aforesaid matters so touch God that, accepting them, he knows and sees that the person who restores himself has humbly risen from the instability that arose for him in Adam’s fall, and which he knows to be evil. And this is very good, because he comes alive to God when he desires to attain God. “And there was evening and morning, the third day” (ibid.). Thus this will become evening—that is, a good end—with the good beginning of the one who begins; the third day, as stated above, consists in this: that the person restrains himself from evil works, with humility made the third virtue of good work.

How what is written, “God said: ‘Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven,’” and the rest through “and there was evening and morning, the fourth day,” should be understood literally.

XXXV. “And God said: ‘Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night; and let them be for signs, and seasons, and days, and years; and let them shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth.’ And it was so” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood thus: by divine command, the illumination of the firmament displayed God’s work as beautiful and glorious, just as the soul will make the body beautiful and glorious. Although after the soul’s departure, because of its first conception, the body stinks in decay, it will nevertheless be changed, as the things above will be, when the human being himself rises again.

And God established and divided the functions of these lights into day and night, because upon these two divisions, namely day and night, depends the whole ordering of human necessity: so that the person, through reason, may know from the signs of those lights what each creature is, and how the seasons of days, nights, and years are named according to those signs; and so that the lights themselves, shining in the firmament, may be seen illuminating the earth and the things in it. And all these things were established as God commanded them to appear.

“And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine over the earth, rule day and night, and divide light from darkness” (ibid.). Through his Word God brightly illumined these two great lights: the greater in the day and the lesser in the night. One remains in its order and neither grows nor diminishes; the other grows and undergoes decline through the signs of the firmament. In these two lights God also foresaw how he would perfect his work, the human being, in two natures. Thus the human being is heavenly in good knowledge and earthly in evil knowledge.

For good knowledge comes from God and is heavenly; nor can anyone take it away from the rational soul, so that through good knowledge it surpasses the creeping things of earth which resemble evil knowledge—things that creep more boldly over the strengthened earth in the night and delight in filth. Evil knowledge, however, accompanied by the filth of sins, is subject to good knowledge and recognizes it as just, though it hates it. But good knowledge makes a most valiant warrior resist evil knowledge; and if he falls, it raises him through penitence and does not cease to strengthen him lest he return to the taste of sin. For good knowledge is like day, but evil knowledge like night.

[Col. 0934A] Therefore evil knowledge delights in evil and performs evil, when pleasure precedes sin; and through these two kinds of knowledge every person knows clean and unclean things. For day knows night and withdraws from it; night knows day and flees from it. In the same way good knowledge turns aside from evil, and evil separates itself from good, because each abhors the other. Thus the human being is both heavenly and earthly. For when heaven was moved in the first fall of the angel, God restored it with the lowly nature of earth; and in this way earth is the foundation of heaven, while heaven, with greater miracles than had existed in the first angel, was built upon earth, because the human being, made from earth, is God’s complete work.

The stars too blaze from the moon, as flame from fire, and are poured forth with shining light through the whole firmament, as though a flame shone through a sieve. Thus they illuminate the whole earth and, as they have been set, will remain until the last day. They also appear brighter during the moon’s waning than during its increase, because in its increase they cannot be perfectly seen owing to the strength of its brightness. They meet the sun, showing the day, and assist the moon, illuminating the night; and thus they divide light from darkness when they show day and night with their service.

And God saw that it was good: that is, he approved that, through the breathing sphere of light, his work was complete, ready for service, and beautiful, with darkness driven away. “And there was evening and morning, the fourth day,” because the four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—prepared and hidden by God’s grace, appeared in all things in which they were established. Again, in another sense:

Why, according to allegory, the firmament signifies the stability of Christian faith; the two great lights, the two powers—the spiritual power in priests and the secular power in kings; and the stars, lesser persons beneath them, namely prelates or judges. All are set in place to illuminate the earth, the Church, by instructing it through day and night with the light of spiritual teaching and examples, and by restraining the fleshly through the censure of justice.

XXXVI. “And God said: ‘Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, to divide day and night; and let them be for signs, seasons, days, and years; and let them shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth.’ And it was so” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood thus: God said through the Holy Spirit in the hearts of his disciples: “Let there be priests and teachers in my Son, who may illumine the Church built upon the firm rock, that is, Christ, from which stone the justice of true faith flowed forth.”

Let these priests also be sent throughout the whole Church, illuminating it so that by their words they may distinguish for the people the day—that is, the salvation of faith—and announce the happiness which they will obtain through that faith if they observe it. Let them also set before the people the night, namely eternal torments which pertain to infinity; and let these teachers prove this to them also by diverse signs, announcing the things which they must observe: namely, feasts which must be celebrated, seasons of fasting which are prescribed, and days in God’s law that are for remission, so that they may observe the year with its established commands. Let those commandments shine through faith in heaven—that is, in my Son—because they follow the praise of angels; and let them illumine the Church, the earth of the living, with God’s praise.”

And it was so. “Thus God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine over the earth, rule day and night, and divide light and darkness” (ibid.). God made two great lights necessary for the Church: the greater light to rule the day, namely the chief and spiritual teachers, who, set over the Church, are the light of the faithful’s eyes. Thus the other spiritual teachers—that is, the lesser persons—are subject and bound under their command as an ox under the yoke, lest, wandering without a shepherd, they be seized by the sharp bird, namely the devil.

He also made the lesser light, namely kings and other secular powers, to rule over earthly affairs and secular peoples as over the night. These are frequently darkened by the obscurity of many unlawful things, because the bodily pleasure which arose in Adam repeatedly rises within them. Therefore they calculate what they can do in themselves and conceal themselves, not rightly judging themselves by a just judgment. He also made the stars, namely those who are in lesser authority and subject to the greater rulers, that they might shine upon the living earth—that is, the Church—wherever it may stand upon the firmament of the rock, that is, Christ; so that they may rule over those who are bright, that is, living rightly, and those who are shadowed, that is, quarrelling in evil, judging the bright according to their works and the evil according to their wickedness.

“And God saw that it was good”: that is, in his good pleasure he ordered that, in the Church distinguished by diverse ranks, the simple should be illumined by the teaching of the wise and offenders corrected by the discipline of rulers. “And there was evening and morning, the fourth day” (ibid.). As God ordered the Church, that instability which existed in it when Christians had neither spiritual shepherds nor secular rulers began, as on the fourth day, to turn away from the darkness of that confusion toward the rising of a stable day. This shone in the same Church when it was strengthened by the light of true faith and the other virtues through zealous holy action. And again, in another sense:

Likewise, why, according to tropology, the firmament is understood as rational discernment; the two great lights as the two commandments of charity; and the stars as right thoughts. By these, every faithful person, illumined, should carefully discern what honour and grace are due to God, and what is owed, for the salvation of the soul and benefit of the body, to the necessities of oneself and one’s neighbours.

XXXVII. “And God said: ‘Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night; and let them be for signs, seasons, days, and years; and let them shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth.’ And it was so” (Gen. 1). This is to be understood thus: God said in the admonition of the Holy Spirit: “Let lights arise, from the gift of the Holy Spirit, in discernment, so that a person may love God and his neighbour as himself.” How shall he do this? Let him pant steadfastly toward God with all the greenness of his soul, so that in unbelief he may not seek a foreign god as though he himself were a stranger, but may look toward me with a manly mind.

Let him also love his neighbour as himself, carefully providing for that neighbour whatever necessities belong to his condition, because the neighbour is his likeness and his brother in humanity. Let him not regard him as unworthy, so as to treat him as a lowly creature subject to himself; but let him willingly receive him into fellowship, because God, who established the righteous person, also established that other person in the same form. Let him beware, too, lest by consenting to his neighbour’s sins he share in the death of that neighbour’s soul, and so kill that soul just as he must not kill his own.

Let these lights shine in the firmament of heaven—that is, in rational discernment—so that the person may rightly distinguish the day with discernment: namely, what honour he should render to me, almighty God, in the desire of his soul and how he should gladly sigh toward me in his groanings. Let him also illumine with that same discernment the night—that is, the darkness hidden in the body and belonging to earthly things, namely the needs of himself and his neighbour—so that he may not be diverted from hope in higher things for the sake of lower ones, but may sigh always even amid these things toward heavenly desires.

Let these lights also be inward signs for him, teaching how he ought to sigh, pray, and weep to God and invoke the Holy Spirit for help. Let them be seasons for him: that is, let them teach how he should conduct himself in the use of what belongs to himself and his neighbour. Let them be days of faith for him, so that all his works may shine in me in the building up of good work. Let them be years for him, so that he may observe the yearly season, beginning well in all these things through holy works with God and his neighbour and ending well in every law of God. Thus throughout the whole course of his life he will offer good examples to his neighbour in every established matter dependent upon the two commandments.

Let these lights shine in the aforesaid commandments in the firmament of heaven—that is, in the discernment of the mind—and let all the lights of this work illumine the earth, namely the human being, so that he may shine before God in mind and body. And this will occur in a person through the compunction of burning love for God and neighbour, so that he discerns all these things in God.

“And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine over the earth, rule day and night, and divide light and darkness” (ibid.). Through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit God brings it about in the human being that he may behold God lovingly with all his strength. Thus the greater light rules the day, that is, true faith which shines before God’s eyes; for the human being cannot see God with outward eyes, but inwardly touches him in the soul through faith.

And he makes the lesser light, namely love of neighbour, which is less than love of God: because a person beholds God within his soul with all desire, but sees his neighbour face to face by touch and sight with outward eyes. Therefore it rules the night, because the sight belonging to this world is nocturnal and cannot exist without the contamination of sin. He also makes the stars, namely right and good thoughts, which God places in the firmament—that is, in human discernment—so that in all things the person may perceive what is good and useful, lest ignorance darken his knowledge; so that he may remain watchful over bodily weakness by governing it; and so that he may foresee with his thoughts everything that must be done. These thoughts should also rule over the light of justice and bodily necessity, ordering them rightly and distinguishing the light of God’s justice from the dark necessity of the world and body by preferring the former to the latter.

“And God saw that it was good,” approving, that is, his house in the human being as rightly ordered according to his justice, and rejoicing that the person had fulfilled by works those commandments through which he was reconciled to him. “And there was evening and morning, the fourth day” (ibid.). God himself makes in the person a good end together with the beginning of the aforesaid law, because he provides a good end for all virtues. If the end is not good, the work begun is also cut short, just as a useless tree will perish: its branches grow green and begin to flower, yet it bears no fruit. And as that tree, if it continues so, will be cut down, so that person will be uprooted from God who begins to work well but does not bring what has been begun to its end; for God does not regard the beginning of good works without a good end.

And among believing peoples, who use the four elements, this fourth virtue will come to be as the fourth day: namely, love of God and neighbour, which spiritual and secular persons alike are bound to observe.

How what is written, “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature with a living soul, and winged creatures above the earth,” through “and there was evening and morning, the fifth day,” should be understood literally and applied to the human being.

### XXXVIII. “And God also said: ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping things with a living soul, and birds above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven’” (Gen. 1).

This is to be understood thus: through his living Word God commanded the waters to bring forth creeping things and birds possessing a living soul [Col. 0937D], like flowers that spring from the branches of trees. For God first created creatures and afterwards brought some forth from others, since he foresaw what would belong to each constitution in the firmament and beneath the firmament, which is touched by him; just as a form is first established and afterwards is set in motion toward each of its works.

And those things which swim in the waters and those which fly in the air came forth, lest the water be empty of fulfilling the work to be accomplished through it, and lest the air likewise lack bodily and living birds, which are filled and enlivened from the air. Hence fish are called able to swim from swimming, and birds able to fly from flight. But man can neither swim perfectly nor fly, but walks upon the earth with his feet, from which he was created [Col. 0938A].

Yet the generation of fish and birds is a cleaner generation than that of the other animals, because the Holy Spirit sanctified the waters above the other elements. And just as water surpasses all things clean and unclean, so the soul penetrates all things and excels the flesh. The human soul too was made in God’s image and works with all creatures in man. But God is in all creatures and surpasses all creatures, since neither beginning nor end is found in him.

“And God created the great sea-creatures, and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every bird according to its kind” (ibid.). God formed the kinds of fish in the waters and infused into them a living soul from the windy blaze. Therefore they too live as moving creatures [Col. 0938B], generated from the waters, and appeared first among all creeping things. And because living breath surpasses bodily forms, water first brought forth living things, since water is both sanctified and spiritual.

For the generation that occurs in waters is more wonderful than that generation which was deceived through the first fraud of the ancient serpent, because in the love of the flesh the taste of sin arises. But since the devil cannot destroy regeneration in waters, he hates the waters. God, however, washes away through the bath in his Son the scale of conceived sin, by which the devil cannot strip man bare, because he does not know whence the Virgin conceived that man who washes away every taste of sin through water. And because the Virgin’s childbirth is hidden from the devil—she knew that her womb remained not wounded [Col. 0938C] but intact—therefore he is unable to destroy this generation of Spirit and water.

By the fish, moreover, God signified that man is mobile through his living soul, just as fish are agile in the waters; but by the birds he showed that through rationality he flies everywhere, just as birds are borne through the air. Therefore spiritual persons who flee the common populace ought to be given spiritual foods suitable to their kind, just as fish and birds, separated from other animals, live in the waters and in the air.

“And God saw that it was good, and blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth’” (ibid.). God saw—that is, approved—that it was good for the aforesaid kinds of fish and birds to possess within themselves the air by which they live. Blessing them lest they fail, he commanded each kind to grow in formation and multiply in number, just as shoots and fruits of fields grow and flourish, so that fish might fill the waters, in which they move, and birds might rise into a multitude, since they remain on earth for pastures suited to them [Col. 0938D].

“And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day” (ibid.). This end and beginning of the work shows the same work which God assigned to man’s five senses, through which the soul ranges in man. For what the soul sees is spiritual, because from spiritual breath [Col. 0939A] it possesses sight of light, discerning what is visible and what invisible; for by rationality it understands that it has fellowship with angelic spirits. It too is invisible like an angel, and moves the form of its body, which is like its garment, through which it is covered so as not to be seen—although every creature understands it, because it is living motion.

In another sense:

### Because God sent his only Son into the world, through whose preaching the lofty precepts of heavenly conduct were given, by which spiritual persons were distinguished from carnal persons; and words of the Gospel concerning the abandonment of all things, with an elegant exposition pertaining to instruction in evangelical discipline.

### XXXIX. “God said: ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping things with a living soul, and birds above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven’” (Gen. 1).

This is to be understood thus: through the preaching of his disciples God said to the Church: “Now let us bring forth subtler precepts through abstinence: persons who, living faithfully in Christ with vigils, fasts, and prayers, do not cling to earthly things; and who beneath the firmament of heaven, which is Christ, may fly with the higher wings of virtues, like virgins and widows in the Church, and pursue heavenly things.”

“And God created the great sea-creatures, and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every bird according to its kind” (ibid.). That is, he revealed his only Son in the flesh, in whom [Col. 0939C] the Gospel arose, wherein it is said: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (Matt. 19).

This is to be understood thus: every faithful person who leaves house—that is, his own will—or brothers, namely carnal desires; or sisters, that is, the taste of sins; or father, namely delight of the flesh; or mother, that is, the embrace of vices; or wife, namely avarice; or children, namely robbery and theft; or fields, that is, pride, for the glory of my name—thus looking toward me, who am the Son of God and Savior of humankind—shall receive a hundredfold bodily in the tranquillity of his mind [Col. 0939D], because he has cast all worldly care away from himself and followed me. Therefore all these things will meet him in service.

For first the house must be abandoned, namely one’s own will, in which a person rests according to his pleasure, like one who remains at ease in his own house; then brothers, that is, carnal desires, which are joined to one’s own will; and afterwards sisters, namely the tastes of sins, which everywhere follow carnal desires. Then comes father, by whom delight of the flesh is signified, which takes great pleasure in carnal desires; and after this mother, that is, the embrace of vices, which in every way embraces fleshly delight. Then comes wife, namely avarice, which imitates the embrace of vices, so that one is not satiated by them [Col. 0940A], just as a man who has taken a wife falls into greedy gain. Thereafter come children, that is, robbery and theft, which follow avarice, just as a person strives to gather riches for his children; and finally fields, namely pride, which attempts to defend robbery and theft, because when someone has impunitously appropriated unjustly acquired things, he begins to be proud through boasting.

But when any faithful person has cast all these things away from himself, he receives better things in abundance, as has been said; he will also possess unending eternal life in blessedness, because for God’s sake he has neglected himself for a time and has longed for heavenly things. For the person who leaves himself, his family, and his children for God’s sake, as Abraham did, shall receive a hundredfold reward for each thing which he sees with his eyes and attends to with his heart. Thus it is also said of Mary: “Many sins have been forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 6), because she too, abandoning her whole self from the crown of her head to the sole of her foot, was rewarded for every individual thing [Col. 0940B].

Therefore this person too shall be adorned with all the aforesaid labors, just as a craftsman adorns his work with elegant beauty, and at last shall pass to heavenly joys. The old law did not know these things, because the humanity of the Savior had not yet touched it; but the new law faithfully gathered these things into itself. For the Son of God, begotten of his mother in the fire of the Holy Spirit, from whom human generation was wholly taken away and removed, taught the right generation of spiritual life: that a person might restrain and sanctify himself and, living thus, have angelic conduct. For that same Son of God, by his humanity, freed man and led him back to heavenly joys.

God also created every life of virtues, which abide in the living minds of persons who raise themselves from the earth, and who are also mobile in this: that they always turn themselves from evil to good and advance from virtue to virtue. Those waters over which the Holy Spirit came—that is, the apostles—brought forth these virtues when they went before the people in good examples and displayed heavenly conduct, which flies like a cloud, passing beyond all earthly things according to its capacity in the kind of virtues, as my Son says in the Gospel [Col. 0940D]:

### Likewise, words of the Gospel concerning the many dwelling places in the Father’s house, and concerning the twofold class of the Church’s children, namely spiritual and secular.

### XL. “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14).

This is to be understood thus: the Son of God, promising eternal life to his faithful, said: “In the heavenly dwelling, which belongs to my Father, there are very many resting-places according to human merits, so that each person may make for himself a dwelling there, just as in bodily life he seeks God by loving him.”

For in the person who denies himself, as though he were not a person, yet cannot wholly abandon the sensible taste of sins in his bodily vessel, God takes great delight in this victory over bodily desires, which he has in suffering for Christ’s love and in hope of true faith, because he consents more to the spirit than to the flesh [Col. 0941A]. His dwelling, moreover, is adorned with innumerable ornaments because of the zeal for victory by which he fights against himself; and he shall receive individual rewards for each such labor, in which he will also rejoice with living harps, because God forgets none of the splendor of their labors.

Therefore all harmony marvels in praising God that an earthly person, who is of the earth, looks in faith toward that height in which God is. The same praise, with every kind of music, resounds above the heavens because of the miracles God works in that person. For he is among those who have left the world, filling the whole world with good repute through the dew of the Holy Spirit, and drawing a multitude of people to themselves through the grace of the same Spirit, so that through their words and works very many are regenerated in God.

For such a person is pleasing to everyone; and just as water, necessary to human beings, sustains all their needs, so the rest of the people are sustained through him. But as the earth is fruitful in bringing forth shoots, so God also ordained that human beings be begotten one from another. And just as God in the first creation made the earth and brought forth water, so he foresaw that human beings should be separated into two parts: one, namely, to beget children; the other, to abstain from begetting in the garment of the Son of God [Col. 0941C].

But God elegantly adorns in heavenly joy, according to their merits, secular persons who for God’s sake heed their teachers, who guard them as angels guard human beings. Therefore spiritual peoples greatly rejoice over them, just as angels rejoice over them, because they are in their fellowship.

### That the blessing given by God to fish and birds for increase is fulfilled in the spiritual generation of the baptized and in the fruitfulness of each faithful person’s virtues; and why these matters are assigned to the fifth day.

### XLI. “And God saw that it was good, and blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth’” (Gen. 1).

God saw that it was good for righteous peoples to renounce themselves and their own wills; and he blessed this with the inward blessing of the heart in his Son, who also gave this example, saying: “Let these virtues grow in God, be multiplied in goodness, and fill the living and rushing waters—that is, the apostles—who lead the streams of God’s Scripture by their knowledge into the Church, which is the glassy and fiery sea, so that the remembrance of the Lord’s Incarnation may arise in human beings together with contempt for this world. And let the birds of spiritual peoples multiply above the earth of the Church, which is a figure of the heavenly Jerusalem; it will be filled together with the Church when the last day has passed.”

“And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day [Col. 0942A]” (ibid.). That hardship, when the Christian people possessed only the common life and lived only in secular works, began, as it were, through evening to decline toward the beginning of a strong day. In that day the solitary life sprang up in abstinence, fasting, and contempt for this world; confirmed by Christ in the fifth light of true faith, it is, with God’s blessing, the fifth day for the building up of the Church.

And again, in another sense:

### How the things belonging to the work of the fifth day and to God’s blessing bestowed upon that work should be referred to instruction concerning mortality, with the testimony of the prophet Isaiah saying: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?”—and how this too should be understood.

### XLII. “God also said: ‘Let the waters bring forth creeping things with a living soul, and birds above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven’” (Gen. 1).

This is to be understood thus: in the admonition of the Holy Spirit, God says that spiritual gifts should be built up in human minds; that, restraining themselves in the aforesaid matters, they should withdraw from secular concerns; and that these persons, who are waters, should bring forth every creeping thing of virtues—that is, souls living in the contemplative life—and also flying virtues surpassing the common precept of secular life. Thus, for love of God, they may rise in abundance above the established righteousness of their seed, like a good field which produces an abundant crop from the seed sown in it, as my servant Isaiah says: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves [Col. 0942C] to their windows?” (Isa. 60).

This is to be understood thus: Who are these who, rejecting earthly things, deny themselves, hasten in their minds toward heavenly things, consider themselves with dove-like simplicity, and thus look upon God? O how great is their reward with God, since they do not cast him behind their backs but worship him with every devotion!

For God foreknew his work before every creature, created heaven and earth, and between these two established the remaining creatures, as was necessary for that creation. For in water he signified spiritual things, and in earth bodily things; and everything unclean is cleansed in water. Likewise the body lives from the soul: a person touches bodily things, although unable to touch the soul; yet he knows that he lives from it, while nevertheless he does not know what it is or of what kind it is. In this his knowledge is weak. And the earth, with its greenness, subsists through water, which it also bears and by which it is watered.

God established certain creatures for the strength of his completed work, namely man, because man works with them. Therefore he also signified in creatures how great a capacity man has to accomplish the desires of the soul, which never fails and whose sighs fly to heaven through its own windiness [Col. 0942D]. For whoever ascends seeks the one to whom he may ascend. Thus the soul too knocks with its desires so that God may give it strength to act; and because God approves it in this, he grants it what it asks of him. But when it descends, it then performs the desires of the flesh according to what its taste desires.

Therefore it is afflicted in two ways: it suffers punishments in the flesh when it ascends to God, and it experiences much affliction through awareness of heavenly desire when it has fulfilled the flesh’s desire. Hence God distinguishes for man a twofold creation, one visible and the other invisible, just as the body is visible and the soul invisible, so that through this union he may choose what is good.

The body is nourished through creatures, and the soul moves the fleshly appetite to eat; through its sighs it strives that the body may not be so choked by an excess of foods that it cannot breathe [Col. 0943B]. In this mingled work the soul so acts that the body may be nourished by food in a proper manner through its breath. For if it is fed excessively, the powers of the soul are dissipated; but if suitable food is withheld from it by excessive abstinence, the proud devil so exalts the person as though he were about to ascend into heaven, in order to make him fall thus through pride.

Accordingly, God hates gluttony in this way and reproves irrational abstinence; therefore the faithful person should impose upon himself a just measure in both. All the aforesaid virtues ought to be under discernment, as under the firmament of heaven, so that discernment may govern them in such a way that, through favor or exaltation of mind, they do not rise higher than they can bear, nor, in returning to secular affairs, fall more deeply than the constitution they received from God allows [Col. 0943C].

“And God created the great sea-creatures, and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every bird according to its kind” (Gen. 1). Through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, God creates great virtues in human beings, namely bodily integrity and continence, withdrawing from them every display and pleasure of the flesh through desire for burning love of God, so that in carnal delight they trample themselves as if dead. He so confirms in them all the virtues of the living soul, which persist in an unstable life, that they are not defiled by the unions of human nature.

These are the living virtues which follow the Lamb, who was never stained by any stain of iniquity, and they are mobile toward better things when they refrain from the business of marriage, with its attendant secular care [Col. 0943D]. These illustrious virtues are produced among such peoples in varied diversity of kinds: one is chastity, another continence; the remaining virtues adhere to them and rise toward higher things like a palm tree in the multitude of their kind.

“And God saw that it was good, and blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth’” (ibid.). God saw these virtues to be very good, because he delights in them with great sweetness when the virtues touch that Word of God by imitating it. For since God created man to do good, but man, bearing good, did evil, God willed that his Word should become man, so that in his goodness he might more fully bring forth all the righteousness that Adam had abandoned. Therefore this people too brings forth, together with the Son of God, his examples, which holy divinity displayed in him; and these virtues are blessed because they rose in him.

Then God says to virtue: “Let these virtues, which began through me to imitate me, grow; let the offspring of good works multiply in them; and let them so fill human beings who fluctuate in the instability of the flesh that stronger virtues, deriving from the power of divinity, may appear in them than the frailty of human flesh. Thus let them, flying above the earth—that is, man—multiply [Col. 0944B], so that the weakness of the flesh may be subjected to their strength.”

“And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day” (ibid.). Thus, as has been said, in God there will be a good end together with the beginning of the fifth virtue, which is contempt for the world, as the fifth day.

### How the history written concerning the work of the sixth day—the bringing forth of cattle and creeping things from the earth and the formation of man—should be understood literally; and that man was made according to the body in the image of the humanity of the Son of God, which God foresaw from eternity that he would assume from the Virgin, and according to the soul in the likeness of divinity through knowledge or imitation of the good.

### XLIII. “God also said: ‘Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds’” (Gen. 1).

This is to be understood thus. In his inextinguishable Word, God commanded the earth to bring forth living animals according to their kind—that is, diverse kinds of animals in their forms: cattle, to serve man; creeping things, in which man might learn to have the fear of God; and beasts, which might display to him the honor of God—each animal possessing the form of its own kind [Col. 0944C].

And so it was fulfilled, in order that man might have in them every abundance, choosing what would serve his need and disregarding what was contrary to him; thus his honor would be complete. For cattle join themselves to man, creeping things shrink from him, beasts flee him, and he rules over all these.

“And God made the beasts according to their kinds, and the cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind” (ibid.): namely beasts which instill fear in man through their ferocity, cattle which serve him, and creeping things which hide themselves before him, as has been said.

“And God saw that it was good, and said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, the whole creation, and every creeping thing which moves upon the earth’” (ibid.). In the vision of his goodness God saw that it was good and useful for the whole world to possess the fullness of human honor, and he said—as though inviting man to a banquet—“Let us, who are one power of the one substance of divinity in three persons, make man in our image [Col. 0945A], that is, according to that garment which will grow in the Virgin’s womb. The person of the Son, clothing himself with it for the salvation of man, shall come forth from her womb while she herself remains intact. Divinity shall never depart from that garment; but the human soul, for the redemption of that same man, shall strip its body through death and, raising it by the power of divinity, shall take it up again.

“Let us also make him in our likeness, so that knowingly and wisely he may understand and discern the things he is to do through his five senses; so that by the rationality of his life, hidden within him and unable to be seen by any creature remaining in a body, he may know how to rule over fish swimming in the waters, birds suspended in the air, untamed beasts, the whole creation dwelling upon earth, and every creeping thing moving upon the earth—because human rationality will excel all these.”

“And God created man in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said: ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it; rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living thing which moves upon the earth’” (ibid.).

God created man according to the form of human flesh with which his Son was to be clothed without sin, just as a person makes his garment in his own likeness, according to that form which God foreknew before the ages [Col. 0945C]. He created man as male, of greater strength, and female, of gentler strength, making him in proper measure and ordering length and breadth in all his limbs, just as he set the height, depth, and breadth of the remaining creation in proper balance, lest any one of them improperly exceed another.

Thus God marked all creation in man and ordered within him the likeness of the angelic spirit, that is, the soul, which works in the human form and is not seen by any creature while it is in the body, just as divinity cannot be seen by any mortal creature. For the soul is from heaven and the body from earth; the soul is known through faith, but the body through sight.

God created male and female; but the male first, then the female taken from the man, and she gives birth, just as the male generates through the strength of powers hidden in him. For through winter and summer fruits grow and are produced, and without these none are brought to perfection. Likewise through the root of a tree, which contains greenness in itself, flowers and fruits are nourished and are from one source; thus through male and female many are begotten, though they proceed from one Creator. For if there were a male alone, or a female alone, no human being would be generated. Hence man and woman are one: for the man is as the soul, while the woman is like the body [Col. 0945D].

And he whom angels behold by knowing and praising him blessed them, and commanded them to grow in increase, advance in multitude, fill the earth by their rule, and subdue it, so that, when cultivated by man, it might burst forth into fruits. He also commanded that they rule over things swimming in the waters and flying in the air, because they would surpass them through the extension of the five senses, and over all living creatures possessing the motion of vital air upon the earth, because they would surpass them by the glory of rationality.

When man is perfected into the full number in which God established him, he will come to that land which is called the land of the living from earthly human beings; and afterwards he will have fellowship with the Lamb in heaven. O what great joy it is that God deigned to become man—divine among angels, human among human beings! Therefore he is truly to be believed God and man [Col. 0946B]. And therefore God placed man in relation to his garment and to the full number which never departs from man, as a father does for his son when he distributes to him an inheritance pertaining to himself, having subjected to him fish, birds, and all living things which move upon earth without rationality.

“And God said: ‘Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and all trees which have in themselves the seed of their own kind, that they may be food for you; and for all animals of the earth, every bird of heaven, and all things which move upon the earth and in which there is a living soul, that they may have food to eat.’ And it was so” (ibid.).

In his inextinguishable Word God said that he had given man seed-bearing grass and trees producing seed within themselves, that they might be food for him. This does not mean that man eats every herb and tree, but that he is nourished by those animals which eat herbs and the fruits of trees. He also granted him food in the animals inhabiting the earth, birds, and all things that move here and there in their motions upon the earth and contain vital air [Col. 0946C].

For everything living on earth is known to feed upon the greenness springing from the earth—not in the sense that every animal uses herbs or the fruits of trees, but because, when one animal presents itself as food to another, it is nourished by the use of the aforesaid herbs and green branches. And God’s command was fulfilled in this manner, because everything is subject to God’s will, and all God’s ordering in creatures was carried out for man’s sake.

For man, who is unfailing in soul, after the last day will see God, who never began and will receive no end. Yet as long as man grows and wanes like the moon—that is, while he is mortal—he shall not see God, except insofar as God himself shows himself to human beings in the shadow of prophecy as he pleases. When God made man’s beginning, he also foresaw his final time, and likewise this time in which, coming forth from his mother’s womb, he was to be regenerated anew through water in the Holy Spirit.

“And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good,” because he had created all creatures in complete perfection, without any defect; and it was good that they would have no defect [Col. 0947A]. “And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day” (ibid.). When that beginning which God made in the aforesaid creatures and in man—whom he predestined for the place of the lost angel—was completed, the sixth day shone forth with perfected man, and also foreshadowed that same man performing diverse works through the six ages of the world.

In another sense:

### How, according to allegory, through the Word of God speaking by the apostles, cattle, creeping things, beasts, and also man, who should rule over all things, were brought forth and formed from the earth of the Church in the Catholic faith, according to the differences of ages, understandings, or ranks of those living in the Church; and in what sense, or toward what end, they are understood to increase and multiply.

### XLIV. “God also said: ‘Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds.’ And it was so” (Gen. 1).

This is to be understood thus: Let the earth, namely my Church, bring forth all the living virtues which I established in every kind of virtue through the teaching of the apostles. Let married persons, who are under the yoke of the law, live rightly. Let those who creep in abstinence from carnal desires mortify their bodies with vigils, fasts, and prayers. But let those who offer all their substance to God also lay down their souls for him [Col. 0947C], abandoning every unlawful thing in their deeds so that they may please God the Savior by submission to the precepts appointed for them.

And just as the beasts of the earth do not pass beyond the nature established for them according to their kinds, so they too should observe the rule appointed to them according to their abilities. Thus abstinence from secular things will be perfected in these virtues.

“And God made the beasts according to their kinds, and the cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind” (ibid.). By God’s grace in the Holy Spirit, all those great virtues of spiritual institutions, all these ordinances of secular persons, and all these powers of those who practise abstinence were made in the Catholic faith.

“And God saw that it was good, and said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, the whole creation, and every creeping thing which moves upon the earth’” (ibid.). Likewise, God saw that all these virtues were good and said within himself: “Now let us make man in our image and likeness for the building up of the Church.”

How? Let us make him for the instruction of the Church, so that the Church herself may be raised up with man for all her building, and so that he may be formed, adorned in his form, in rationality—that is, in our image—and in knowledge and wisdom—that is, in our likeness. Thus, with divine work and human righteous works, he may build the Church; and let the law be given to him in my Son, who was born from my heart [Col. 0948A], which law is also kindled in the Holy Spirit.

And let man in the Church rule, through his knowledge, over earthly things, with observance of the Gospel which God gave, and with virtues flying toward the good. Let him also lay down for God his substance and soul, in submission to God’s precepts and together with all the other virtues of heaven; let him mortify his body in abstinence from carnal things, so that the man himself may perfect these virtues. Let the virtues themselves, through observance of all God’s precepts, perfect the man, so that, ascending from virtue to virtue, he may never be satiated by them, and may always be mobile in this: to depart from evil and do good.

[Col. 0948B] “And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said: Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living thing that moves upon the earth.”

God created the human being in the Church for the knowledge of his divinity, so that in the soul the person might be able to work the heavenly virtues with the soul’s sighings—the virtues with whose jewels the Church is adorned. He also created the person in the image of God, which is the Son, so that, surrounded by burning love, the person might accomplish every good thing in chastity through the more excellent virtues, and so that the Church of God might be perfected together with the works of God.

Thus God created the peoples so that they might possess the manly qualities—which belong to the male person—in heavenly virtues; and so that, also in the fear of God, amid the distress of the soul, they might overcome in worldly life under the care of children being born—which belongs to the female person—so that the Church too might be built up with it. In these aforesaid respects God blessed them with the full blessing of the holy Incarnation: namely, because the Son of God was clothed with humanity. Therefore every kind of virtue, both spiritual and worldly insofar as it advances for the love of God, ought strongly to pour itself forth, because God is God and man, and from him all greenness springs.

And, in the exhortation of the Holy Spirit, he said that peoples in the Church, growing in abundant righteous desires, should advance in every manner of life according to the fear of God, and should multiply in these things, [Col. 0948C] so that they might be fruitful in their endeavors and, continually renewing the virtues within themselves, might not wither. Thus they should fill that earth, namely the Church, subject it to Christ, and exercise dominion in it: that is, they should follow the Gospel and, with the flying and living virtues which withdraw themselves from earthly things and stand firm in goodness, raise themselves to heavenly things.

“And God said: Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and every tree that has within itself the seed of its own kind, that they may be food for you and for every animal of the earth, every bird of heaven, and everything moving upon the earth in which there is a living soul, that they may have food to eat. And it was so” (ibid.).

God said in every ordering of the Church: Behold, I have now given and sent you the right faith through my Son, whom you saw born upon the earth in the greenness of unploughed soil—that is, in the Virgin’s womb—as untouched earth brings forth flowers. But my Son brought the seed of God’s Word, so that it might be sown upon the promised land, namely the holy Church by which the heavenly Jerusalem is built. He also brought the law for married people, who have the propagation of their seed among the nations: how they ought to live according to the fear of my commandments. Thus my law, given to you, may be food for you, one thing in the building-up of the soul. As the body is nourished with foods, so be nourished, because my Son said: “My food is to do [Col. 0949A] the will of my Father” (John 4).

This must be understood thus: My food—I who am the Son of God—is that I should submit my body to the Passion, through which, having conquered the devil, I may restore humankind, according to my Father’s will, to the paradise from which it had been expelled; for my Father sent me into the world for this purpose, that I might save it. For I, sent by the Father, received flesh in my mother’s womb without male moisture. Therefore that food in which I am equal to my Father without age is better than the food by which I am nourished for an hour according to the flesh, when the heavenly Father willed that I should dwell for a time in this world and converse with human beings, so that through my words they might return to salvation, when I draw them upward with me to heavenly things. For this is my work: when I have redeemed humankind in my humanity, that it too may act according to me.

Therefore be nourished by my law, lest your souls fail; for I have appointed for you a season of food in God’s law, in which you will find pastures of life. In all these you will not fail if you keep them, but will live forever. Likewise, for those human beings who are subject through virtues to the commandments of the living God, who have become imitators of Christ in the heavenly militia, who withdraw themselves from earthly things, pant with all devotion for justice, and rise from virtue to virtue—being moved toward goodness—in the land of promise, there are to be distinctions of foods and seasons, appointed for them by their teachers. The people must also observe, by the institution of the law, those seasons [Col. 0949B] in which feasts are to be celebrated and fasts performed.

Concerning those foods, this distinction must be maintained: they are to be taken not to excess, but as the exigency of necessity requires; and they are to be carefully distributed to each person according to the measure in which that person has been strengthened and instructed in the Holy Spirit. Let the Christian person, who is the building of the Church, hear this, so as rightly to accord with his head. And so it came to pass, because the words of God and the virtues became the food of life in the Church among the Christian people.

“And God saw all that he had made”: that is, he approved all these purposes and commandments, and the appointed times of all the virtues mentioned above. “And they were very good,” because they were accomplished in the fullness of the desirable grace of almighty [Col. 0949C] God, so that nothing was lacking to them. Previously each virtue had been only one good in itself; but here all things were good together, when all appeared together, just as a banquet is complete when it is fulfilled in all its courses of righteousness.

“And there was evening and morning, the sixth day.” That changeability of instability, because firmness in the established commandments was not yet present in the Church, began to decline before the morning of the strong justice of the whole established law, just as day is strengthened by the sun’s powers while the sun stands in its order. Thus the sixth day came to be, so that, as it were in the sixth light of strong faith, the peoples might fulfill God’s commandments in the Church according to his will and according to the teaching of their teachers.

And again, in another sense:

[Col. 0950B] On the diversity of foods granted in Genesis to human beings and beasts: how this should now be understood spiritually in the Church according to the distribution or reception of spiritual nourishment, which is the Word of God; and how the added testimony of Christ saying, “My food is to do the will of my Father,” as also what is written, “And there was evening and morning, the sixth day,” should be understood.

XLV. “God also said: Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind—cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds. And it was so” (Gen. 1).

This must be understood thus: In the exhortation of the Holy Spirit, God speaks to human beings who subject themselves to all the aforesaid matters, namely, concerning how they should diligently join themselves to God in the desire of their souls. [Col. 0950C] Now let this earth—that is, the human being—bring forth the living virtues of the soul, so that the outer person, attending to the soul’s work, may always sigh toward God; so that soul and body may obey God in the kind of the strongest virtue, obedience, which in God secretly stripped death of its power. This is as beasts of burden are subject to human beings through submission; as a creeping thing is also subject to them in the service of lowliness; and as beasts of the earth serve them. So too a person subjects himself to another person by reason of humble submission, because obedience is the punishment of pride and utterly confounds it.

“And God made the beasts according to their kinds, the cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind.” From almighty God there rises in the human being, who had previously sinned freely through pride, [Col. 0950D] fear, so that the person begins to seek God—as the first human being received the commandment of obedience from God. Thus God brings it about in the human being that one prostrates oneself by one’s own will in subjection to other people for the love of God, just as beasts are taken in hand by people, who also feed and train them as they wish. Similarly, people are reckoned into that submission to teachers according to the character of holy humility: made slaves to obedience in the form of beasts of burden, and likewise in the lowliness of creeping nature, so that they are trampled in their own will according to the will of their teachers, just as the lowly nature of a creeping thing is trampled in its kind.

[Col. 0951A] A recapitulation of all that is written in Genesis concerning the work of the sixth day: how it ought to be understood or maintained morally; with the addition of two testimonies from the Psalm and the Gospel, and the sense in which these too should be understood.

XLVI. “And God saw that it was good, and said: Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts of the earth, all creation, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth” (Gen. 1).

God sees this to be good and takes great delight in it with the preceding sweetness: that the human being seeks him in the first justice which he himself established in the human being. And he says within himself: This human being, overcoming himself in his unlawful desires with every beginning of righteousness, touches me; and with the bright desire of my first ordinance—which I established at the first beginning, when the human being ought to obey me—he raises himself through good works. Now let us—the three Persons, the power of one substance, which in creating the first human being in its image and likeness touched that person—bring it about that great honor from holiness and knowledge of divine things be given to this human being. Let the person be regarded as a protector, possess toward the neighbor the love of the holy Incarnation in the image of God, and offer to divinity honor in the likeness of God through knowledge. Thus, by the instruction of the Gospel and by being set above temporal things through virtues, the person may offer even himself as a sacrifice to God: namely, by afflicting the body through abstinence and advancing from earthly to heavenly things, so that the person may work with the virtues [Col. 0951B] fulfilled in him, and the virtues with him; and in this preeminence may fear and love God.

“And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said: Increase and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living thing that moves upon the earth” (ibid.).

And now God creates the human being for honor to himself, so that he himself may be known in that person wholly in his divinity and humanity. How? The power of the Godhead, creating and governing all things, appears in the human being’s governance according to his image through the rational faculty, by which the person rules over other creatures. His mercy, by which he aids the world through humanity, is recognized in that human being’s compassion, by which he ought according to his ability to spare and pity his neighbor. And these are the good examples of the Word of God, as the Psalmist David says: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81 [82]).

This must be understood thus: I said to you human beings: in this you are gods, that the human being rules over every creature, subjecting it to every need as desired. For as the person has almighty God in faith, fear, and love, so creation looks upon and loves the human being as a god through the governance of fear, when it is fed by that person. And you human beings are called children of him who is high in the heights, because by the grace of the living [Col. 0951C] God you were created rational, as though born from him, and because you have from him every knowledge necessary to you. But an irrational animal knows nothing except what it apprehends by sense.

In the human being—that is, in the living knowledge of the person—he also creates the force and strength of manifest justice, so that the person may not perversely yield in any way to iniquity, either in oneself or in others; this is as it were masculine. He also creates in the person the capacity, by the gift of divine grace, to spare with mercy a human being wounded by sins, and to attend so closely to that person’s miseries as to pour in the wine of repentance and anoint the person with the oil of mercy—yet so that the person does not fall, because of excessive measure, into remiss repentance, nor become lukewarm and entangled in the vanity of evil works; this is as it were feminine.

And God blesses this because it touches the humanity of his Son, as the same Son of God says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12).

This must be understood thus: Every person supported by God’s grace who, with good intention, does the will of my Father—who is my Father dwelling in heaven by divinity—because I am the Son of the Virgin, so that, rejecting that in which he was born, the person wills to go to God with the inward person: such a one, in a nature other than that in which he was conceived, imitating God and always beholding him in the reverence of perfect fear, is my brother. One who faithfully and continually holds God in the embrace of love is my sister in this devotion, ascending to that same Father of mine in all works with the will of perfection. And one who bears him often in heart and body is my mother, because in this way that person gives birth to me, where, in complete zeal for holiness, I flourish in my Father through the fullness of blessed virtues.

Then God says within himself: Let this human being increase in the powers of the strongest virtues, and let the multiplication of these virtues be cultivated in that person, so that that earth—namely, other people—may be filled, by hearing and understanding that name, with the precious spices of good works, submit themselves to that person’s commandments, and so that the person himself, with superabundant blessedness, may rule over his desires. Let the person, in those same virtues, draw away from himself all the pomp of the world, which is as it were the sea; and let him run toward heavenly things in the virtues and in those things which, in their powers, are moved toward good by heavenly desire, so that these virtues may withdraw from that person unlawful desires, which are as it were the earth.

[Col. 0952D] “And God said: Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and every tree that has within itself the seed of its own kind, that they may be food for you and for every animal of the earth, every bird of heaven, and everything moving upon the earth in which there is a living soul, that they may have food to eat. And it was so” (Gen. 1).

And now he also says in the Holy Spirit: Behold, I have set all the shoots of virtues mentioned above, bearing the seed of my word upon the desires of this human being’s flesh, who thus restrains himself; and I have set all the stronger virtues, ascending to greater commandments, [Col. 0953A] so that, possessing within themselves in upright desire the good seed of their kind in my word, they may be food for the refreshment of that person’s soul. Thus all virtues, subject to God through humility, flying in the heavenly militia, removing the human being from earthly things to heavenly things, and having living powers from the planting of the Holy Spirit, may feed with that person in the soul; and that person too may be nourished with them in all these things.

And all these things thus occur in that human being who advances in God in this manner: “And God saw all that he had made, and they were very good” (ibid.). God now sees that all things which the Holy Spirit bestows are very good, because they are perfected in the fullness of all virtues. Previously each virtue had been only one good in itself; but here all things are good together because they are fulfilled by appearing together in the human being.

“And there was evening and morning, the sixth day” (ibid.). And now God brings it about in the human being that a good end, together with the good beginning of the sixth virtue, which is obedience, may shine forth like the sixth day.

On the perfection of heaven and earth, all their adornment, the completion of God’s works attributed to the seventh day, and the sanctification of that day; and how these are to be understood literally.

XLVII. “Thus the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were perfected” (Gen. 2).

This must be understood thus: The higher and lower elements, with all the powers adjacent to them, were brought to such fullness [Col. 0953B] and perfection that, with all want removed, they rejoice in an abundance of fitting usefulness.

“And God completed on the seventh day the work which he had made, and rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished” (ibid.). The completion of the six divisions of the aforesaid works was called the seventh day, when God brought to perfection everything he had preordained to create. Thus, ceasing to work on the seventh day, he rested, because he had completed all his work in its forms.

“And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created in order to make.” God blessed the seventh day with praise and sanctified it with the honor of solemn observance, because in it every creature which God had preordained to be made was fully created, and from it other generated things proceed. Hence the entire angelic host and all the hidden mysteries of divinity blessed God on account of the perfection of God’s work and praised him, because with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit he had completed all his work.

Again, in another sense:

How these things are fulfilled allegorically through the Incarnation of the Son of God, the preaching of the Gospel, and the operation of the Holy Spirit in the children of the Church and those subject to Christian faith.

XLVIII. “Thus the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were perfected” (Gen. 2).

This must be understood thus: All heavenly works which tend toward heaven in the passage beyond earthly things are perfected together with earthly matters required by the necessity of human children being born; [Col. 0953C] and thus all that perfect beauty of heavenly works has been established in the Church.

“And God completed on the seventh day the work which he had made, and rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished” (ibid.). This entire ordering was completed in all these things; namely, in this way: I, in my Son, on the seventh day—that is, in the fullness of every good—thus brought all my operation to its end, so that all the people of the Church, seeing, hearing, and searching through teaching, may know well what they ought to do in my commandments.
