The meaning of this statement must also be understood thus concerning future events: Those whose hearts are fixed upon earthly things will worship the beast of iniquity, bowed down in body and mind; their names are not engraved with the signs of holiness in the eternity of life of him in whose mouth no deceit was found. Therefore whoever worships this lost man by honoring his writings will be in perdition, as will whoever bears the writings of Satan in his heart—Satan who was expelled from God because he wished to be God by himself.

He is therefore called death because he fled life, in which no mortality is found, but which gives life to all things. All who cling to this son of perdition and perform his works will not be written in the book of life of the Lamb, because this Lamb is the Word of God, through whose word all created being came forth.

But the devil has continually had followers in both the Old and the New Testament: in the Old through Baal; in the New through the Sadducees, who are his sinews in schism. For they first violated the law of God, [Col. 1032A] which is the root of justice, in which the patriarchs and prophets lay hidden, with the filth of Baal. He also had those who afterward, in the New Testament, together with the Sadducees denied the resurrection amid the affliction of justice. For the Gospel is the branch of that aforesaid root, and the testimony of Christ is the fruit of the branches; it crushed powerfully both the idols of Baal and the Sadducees.

Yet heretics will afterward proceed from these, contradicting the condition of the first sprouting; and their error will be worse than the former, because they will utterly deny God in his creation and in living souls. But all these will worship the unhappy beast, namely the lost man, and, abandoning faith in almighty God, will say that it does them no harm if they neglect God’s commandments.

[Col. 1032B] On the signs or portents and storms which Antichrist will produce through magical arts; and on how, pretending to die and rise again, he will cause a certain writing, invented by the deceit of the devil, to be inscribed on the foreheads of his followers—a writing by which those deceived will thereafter be unable to be torn away and separated from him.

### XXXII.

And thus their unbelief descends to the aforesaid golden head of the leopard, appearing in the aforesaid chain of ornament, which signifies Antichrist. Calling himself God, as it were a golden head, he will by diabolical arts and by the stirring up of the elements perform dreadful prodigies and the greatest storms. God will permit this to happen so that the whole human race may know his downfall. For he too will pretend, as though for the redemption of his own people, to die by being slain [Col. 1032C] and to rise again by resurrection; and he will cause a certain writing to be inscribed upon the foreheads of those who follow him. Through it he will inflict every evil upon them, just as the ancient serpent, deceiving man and afterward holding him in his snare, inflamed him with lust. By means of this same writing, in opposition to baptism and to the Christian name, he will so imbue them by magical art that they will not wish to depart from him, and that all may be called after him, as Christians are called after Christ.

Lucifer long possessed this writing within himself and revealed it to no human being except this one alone, whom he will wholly possess in his mother’s womb. Therefore he is confident that through him he can accomplish [Col. 1032D] all his will. Yet this lost man will have his soul, and the fact that he lives, not from the devil but from God, although this most wretched investigator of the ancient deception, who hates all good things, himself received his life from God. For God alone is life; every breath, and everything that lives, moves through him, because he alone is beginning without beginning.

And as Lucifer fought against God in heaven, so through this lost man on earth he will attempt to contend against the humanity of the Son of God. And he will do this by means of this writing, through which he will deny God and the Creator of all things, being confident that he will bestow upon his followers a greater illumination of gifts than Christ, the Son of God, bestowed upon those who believe in him. This writing has never before been seen or devised in any language [Col. 1033A], because Lucifer first devised it within himself. He will bring it forth by that deceit through which he seduces human beings, so that they may not know their Creator; and by it he will thus mock the unbelievers, so that they will endeavor to worship nothing except what they see pleases him.

For this son of perdition will say that, just as a cut tree is laid aside until a painter fashions and adorns it so that it may be venerated by all, so also a human being born lacks honor until this writing is exalted, because there is greater salvation and power in it than there was in the creation of man. But God will destroy all the efforts of this writing together with its author. The writing which the Holy Spirit gave, however, will not pass away. And when, by these false signs, he begins to gather to himself persons from every race, the holy and the righteous will be shaken with great fear.

**The promise of God concerning the restoration of Enoch and Elijah; how they are dealt with meanwhile; how, when restored, they will conduct themselves among human beings amid adversities; how greatly they will shine through the power of preaching and miracles against Antichrist; and how, nevertheless, after being martyred by him, they will depart from the world with countless others, and the blessed number of martyrs will be brought to the fullness of its due perfection.**

### XXXIII.

But I, who am, shall remember how I first formed man; by what means I foresaw all the works through which Lucifer would fight against me through man; and how I marked out the holy virtues as they fought against him—just as I did in Enoch and Elijah, whom I chose from the offspring [Col. 1033C] of human beings who had clung to me with their whole desire. And near the last time I shall reveal them to humankind, so that people may confidently receive the testimony of those two witnesses.

For in my mystery I instruct them and make the deeds of human beings manifest to them, so that they know them as though they had seen them bodily; and they are wiser than the writings and sayings of the wise. For when they were bodily taken away from human beings, every fear and trembling was removed from them, so that they endure with equanimity everything around them; and I preserve them in secret places without any bodily injury.

And when the son of perdition vomits forth his perverse teaching, the same power through which they had formerly been removed from among human beings will bring them back as though in the wind. And as long as they remain with [Col. 1033D] human beings upon earth, they will always be refreshed after forty days, just as my Son also hungered after forty days had passed.

Now the head of the goat, shown in the aforesaid chain of the ornament of righteousness, signifies these strong and wise men. For just as the goat is strong and climbs on high, so they will be strong in my power, swiftly raised to the height of my miracles. For they will have such power in my miracles that they will perform greater signs in the firmament, in the elements, and in the other creatures than the son of perdition, so that his deceptive signs will be confounded by their true signs.

Therefore, because of the exceeding power of their miracles, people from all nations will run to them, believing their words and hastening with ardent faith toward the martyrdom which the son of perdition will inflict upon them as though to a banquet. Indeed, because of their excessive multitude, their killers will grow weary of counting the slain, for the abundance of their blood will be poured out like a stream of waters.

But at last, when the son of perdition cannot overcome these two men of true holiness either by flatteries or threats, nor obscure their signs and miracles, he will order them to be finished by a cruel martyrdom and their memory utterly erased from the earth, so that no person in all the world may thereafter dare to resist him. Then, as was said above, the golden number of blessed martyrs who were killed in the primitive Church for the true faith will, in these martyrs who are killed in the error of the last time, be brought [Col. 1034B] to the fullness of its perfection. For this time, trampling and devouring all things, signifies the wolf described in the book *Scivias*: just as a wolf devours whatever it can in its rapacity, so in that time the faithful who believe in the Son of God will be swallowed up.

Therefore the same Son of God again says to the Father, as was stated above:

**Again, the Son’s intercession to the Father: in showing his wounds he commends these very people to him, that he may spare them; and he exhorts them to bend their knees to the Father, that he may have mercy on them.**

### XXXIV.

“Now it wearies me that, by your ordinance, I am clothed with flesh: that my members—namely, those who had adhered to me through the sacrament of baptism—do not depart from me, and that they go into the mockery of diabolical [Col. 1034C] delusion when they hear and worship the son of perdition. Yet I gather back those who have fallen from among them, but cast away the rebellious and those who persist in evil.

“Father, since I am your Son, look upon those things with the charity by which you sent me into the world, and consider my wounds, through which at your command I redeemed man. I show them to you so that you too may have mercy on those whom I redeemed, and may not permit them to be erased from the book of life. Rather, through the blood of my wounds gather them back to yourself in repentance, lest he who mocks both my incarnation and my passion rule over them unto perdition.

“Therefore now, all you human beings who desire to forsake the ancient serpent and return to your Creator, heed that I, the Son of God and of man, show my wounds to my Father for [Col. 1034D] you. Therefore bend in purity of faith to your Father, who created you and gave you the breath of life, those knees which you have so often bent to the vanity of wicked perversity; confess your sins fully from the heart, so that he may stretch out to you, who are in affliction both of body and soul, his strong and invincible hand, and deliver you from the devil and from every evil.”

Thus the Son speaks to the Father, commends his members to him, and chastises them, so that they may adhere to their true head, lest the perdition of the first and last traitor swallow them up. For whenever the almighty Father is provoked by the wicked works of human beings, his Son shows him his wounds, namely so that, because of them, he may spare humankind; for he did not spare his own body [Col. 1035A], so that the sheep taken from him might be drawn back in his blood. Therefore those same wounds will remain open as long as man, remaining in the world, sins.

For this reason the same Son of God requires human beings to bend their knees to his almighty Father whenever they deserve his judgments, so that, because of his wounds which he suffered in the flesh and which his Father always beholds, he may free them from every evil.

**That when Enoch and Elijah, in the sight of all, are raised from death and taken up into the clouds, the resurrection of the dead will be confirmed in every respect; and the ancient serpent, through the son of perdition, will be stirred to the greatest fury against God and the saints.**

### XXXV.

After Enoch and Elijah undergo bodily death through the son of perdition, his followers [Col. 1035B] will rejoice greatly because they see that they have perished. But afterward, when the spirit of life raises them and bears them up into the clouds, their joy will be turned into fear, sorrow, and great astonishment.

For by the resurrection and exaltation of these men I, the Almighty, shall prove that the resurrection and life of the dead cannot be contradicted by any opposition of unbelievers: on that day, when the elements with which man had sinned are purified, man also will be raised from death and, through repentance pleasing to God, restored to a greater brightness than that in which he was first created. For just as the whole structure of man is moved by repentance, so by the mournful voice of repentance he moves heaven and wholly praises God with the cherubim.

Then, because of their resurrection, the ancient serpent will be aroused to the greatest wrath and will bring the lost man to that ambition of possessing the throne from which he himself was expelled, so that by this means the resurrection of the aforesaid men and the remembrance of the Son of God may be wholly erased among human beings. And he will speak within himself, saying: “In this my son I shall now wage a greater battle than I formerly waged in heaven, and through him I shall accomplish all my will. Neither God nor man will be able to resist this will of mine; and I know and recognize that I cannot be overcome. Therefore I shall be victorious in all things.”

Then the same son of perdition will summon a multitude of people so that it may plainly see his glory [Col. 1035D] when he attempts to go above the heavens, so that, if anything of the Catholic faith remains unshaken in the Church, it may altogether melt away through his ascent. But when, with the people standing by and listening, he commands the higher elements to receive him as he goes to heaven, the words of my faithful Paul, which he uttered when filled with the truthful Spirit, will be fulfilled:

**That, when this lawless one is revealed in his presumption and, with the multitude of people standing by and listening, commands the higher elements to receive him as he goes to heaven, he will be killed by the breath of the mouth of the Lord Jesus, according to the Apostle’s testimony; and those who see these things will abandon error and turn to the true faith, and thus all the devil’s exaltation will be overthrown.**

### XXXVI.

“But then that lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. [Col. 1036A] 2).

The meaning of this statement must be understood as follows. At that time the son of iniquity will be laid bare, and it will become evident to all people that he was a liar when he seizes upon the presumption of ascending to the heavens. For the condemner and savior of peoples, who is the Son of God, will kill him in that presumption; and he will do this through that power by which, as the Word of the Father, he will judge the whole world by righteous judgment.

For when this son of perdition raises himself on high by diabolical art, he will be cast down by divine power, and the stench of sulphur and pitch will receive him, so that even the people standing by will flee to the protection of the mountains. Such terror will seize those who see and hear these things that, renouncing the devil and his son, they will be converted to the true faith of baptism. [Col. 1036B] Therefore the ancient serpent, stunned and gnashing within himself, will say: “We too have been confounded. Henceforth we shall not be able to subjugate people to ourselves as we have done until now.”

**That after the fall of Antichrist the glory of the Son of God will be magnified; all who believe in him will praise it in a humble voice; and the testimony from the Apocalypse of John suited to these matters, together with the sense in which it should be understood.**

### XXXVII.

And all who faithfully believe in the Son of God will praise God in a mournful yet praiseworthy voice, as it is written through my beloved and truthful witness:

“Now salvation, and power, and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ have come, because [Col. 1036C] the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, he who accused them before the presence of our God day and night. And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony; and they did not love their lives even unto death” (Rev. 12).

The meaning of this statement must be understood as follows. Now that the devil has been conquered and his son Antichrist overthrown, there has come, through the heavenly dispensation, salvation fearing no diabolical dangers; power that utterly crushes; a kingdom ruling over all who are under the governance of our God; and the invincible authority of Christ, namely his Son, whom he established as the true Priest over the salvation of souls.

For the most obstinate accuser and most restless plotter of those who, being sons of God as we are, will possess the heavenly inheritance with us, has been cast into eternal condemnation. He accused, before the gaze of the highest Creator and Judge, those who consented to his various suggestions; and he did this at all times in every spiritual and worldly transgression, because man always sins.

God conquered the first battle of the lost angel, in which he fought against God, wishing to be God; and in that battle he also foresaw the last battle which he would wage with him, when he cast down his son and thus wholly confounded the devil himself through him. And those who truly confess God conquered him because they did not consent to him, through the blood of the Lamb by which they were redeemed, and through which, while enduring very many adversities in their bodies, they too proved victorious [Col. 1037A]; and because of the word—that is, the teaching—which he testified to in the Catholic faith, which likewise extends from that Word through which all creatures came forth.

Nor did they love their souls by retaining them in their bodies, but made them go before unto the death of their bodies, when they subjected their bodies to temporal death in very many sufferings, where they also rendered back those same souls to almighty God. For the martyrs ran unto death and subjected themselves to sufferings before they would deny the Son of God. Therefore Abel, the prophets, and the other martyrs who were killed for God unto the last day bear testimony to the Son of God: that he too, in obedience to the Father’s will, shed his blood for them.

Thus the war of the son of perdition has ended, and he will henceforth appear in no worship. Therefore rejoice, you who have a dwelling in heaven and on earth. After the fall of Antichrist, the glory of the Son of God will be magnified.

**Epilogue of the book itself, in which heavenly praise is rendered to God for his work—that is, the restoration of man—and this little work, together with its author, is earnestly commended to the same God and to his faithful.**

### XXXVIII.

And again I heard from heaven a voice teaching me these words:

“Now let there be praise to God in his work, namely man, for whose restoration he fought the greatest battles on earth, and whom he deigned to raise above the heavens, so that together with the angels he may praise his face [Col. 1037C] in that unity in which he is true God and man.

“But may almighty God deign to anoint with the oil of his mercy the poor feminine form through whom he brought forth this writing, because she lives without any security and does not possess even the learning that builds up through the Scriptures which the Holy Spirit set forth for the instruction of the Church and which are like the wall of a great city. For from the day of her birth she has been entangled as though in a net in the pains of infirmities, so that in all her veins, marrow, and flesh she is tormented by continual pains. Yet it has not pleased the Lord to dissolve her, because through the hollow of her rational soul she spiritually beholds certain mysteries of God.

“This vision has passed through the veins [Col. 1038A] of this same person in such a way that she is often shaken by great weariness because of it, suffering in the fatigue of infirmity—at one time more lightly, at another more heavily. Therefore she also has habits unlike the various habits of other people, like a child whose veins are not yet so full that it can discern the habits of people.

“For she is an instrument through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and has a constitution dependent upon the air. Therefore infirmity is so fixed in her from the air itself, from rain, wind, and every storm, that she cannot possess bodily security in herself; otherwise the inspiration of the Holy Spirit could not dwell in her. Yet the Spirit of God, by the great power of his mercy, sometimes raises her from this infirmity as though from death by the dew of a certain refreshment [Col. 1038B], so that she may live in the world as an instrument through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

“May almighty God, who truly knows every burden of the suffering of this person, deign so to perfect his grace in her that his mercy may be glorified in this, and that, when her soul departs from this world, she may rejoice to be mercifully received and crowned by him in eternal glory.”

But the book of life, which is the writing of the Word of God—through which every creature appeared, and which, according to the will of the eternal Father, had as it were preordained within itself the life of all things—has wonderfully breathed forth this writing, as it pleased, not through any teaching of human learning but through a simple and unlearned feminine form [Col. 1038C].

Therefore let no person be so bold as to add anything to the words of this writing by augmentation, or take anything away by diminution, unless this is done in copying out the letters or words simply uttered through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Whoever presumes otherwise sins against the Holy Spirit. Therefore it will not be forgiven that person either in this age or in the age to come.

Now again let there be praise to almighty God in all his works before the ages and unto the ages, because he is the first and the last. Let the faithful receive these words with the devoted affection of the heart, because they were brought forth for the benefit of believers through him who is first and last.

[Col. 1037]

# SOLUTIONS OF THIRTY-EIGHT QUESTIONS

Sent through Saint Hildegard to Wibert, monk of Gembloux, at his request.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition, vol. XXIII, p. 583.)

## WIBERT THE MONK TO HILDEGARD

[Col. 1037D]

To the most holy mother HILDEGARD, WIBERT.

The joy which I had believed had been divinely granted me through seeing and conversing with you—when, during the Lenten season, I was setting out toward you with our abbot—was, for a time, taken from me, as I think, through the envy of the devil. For when we had proceeded as far as Cologne, Satan hindered us three times and disturbed the abbot’s plan of proceeding to you through the wicked suggestions of his fleshly relatives; accordingly, we went no farther.

But I hope that divine grace will restore to me at a more favorable time, once all obstacles have been removed, what I grieve has been taken away. Meanwhile, however, I greatly desire to know what has been done concerning those questions which the brothers of Villers were sending to you through me to be resolved, and which, after I was recalled from the journey, I entrusted to my beloved Baldo to carry to you—namely, whether or not they reached you.

If they have reached you, we all beseech you—your friends in the Spirit on our side, prostrate at your feet—that, confidently entering upon the sea of their solutions, you may not fear to commit your sails to the breeze of the Holy Spirit. Trusting in such a guide, you will soon glide without difficulty into a calm harbor. [Col. 1039B] I also ask that you prefix their solutions to the aforesaid letters of the brethren of Villers and to our own, so that each may become more pleasing through the other and shine forth more clearly.

## HILDEGARD’S RESPONSE

Charity, which establishes faith together with abstinence from sins and builds chastity together with patience, is like a pillar supporting the four sides of a house. For charity itself had planted a most glorious garden with most precious spices and most noble flowers—roses and others—which breathed forth a most sweet fragrance, and in which the true Solomon was accustomed to feast his eyes.

This garden signifies the holy virtues which God, who is true charity, wrought in the rod of Jesse, namely Mary, who flourished in chastity and produced the noblest flower. Of that flower the voice of the turtledove was heard (Song 2), which called forth the virginal nature signified by the lily, which sends out white blossoms from its stalk with the fragrance of a most pleasant scent. So too virginity is honored in the world because of the most sweet fragrance of good intention.

Hermits likewise, or monks, who have renounced the world for Christ, ought to live without association with worldly pomp, as a virgin after her vow lives without remembrance of a man. For virgins and monks are one among the angelic orders, because, as angels desire to behold nothing but the face of God, so they too, casting away every worldly pomp, follow the Lamb of God—that is, Christ—bearing his cross. In them, because of true contempt for the world, the radiant flowers of the Lord’s passion are produced.

Now, O son of God, set in the valley of true humility, walk in peace without exaltation. Exaltation is like a precipitous mountain, offering those who lean upon it an arduous and almost impossible ascent or descent, and upon whose summit no building stands open. For the person who attempts to climb higher than he can reach possesses the name of holiness without security, because he glories merely in a name, without the structure of good works, and in a certain foolish delight of mind.

But behold the most glorious garden which charity planted, and gather to yourself every virtue in true humility and simplicity of heart. And although you are placed among the various dispositions of human beings [Col. 1040A], nevertheless learn that divine goodness bears us all with long-suffering and patience. Flee also the inconstancy of the lazy servant, who serves one master today and another tomorrow. Gird yourself manfully with the sword of the Word of God, after the example of the mightiest soldiers who guard the bed of the true Solomon as they stand about it (Song 3).

Again and again entrust the sincerity of your mind to almighty God with watchful eyes, lest you begin to sleep in doubt. Be the upright and beloved soldier of the true Solomon, whom he loves and crowns for victory in the daily battle. May the Holy Spirit set you ablaze with the fire of his love, so that you may persevere tirelessly in the love of his service and may one day merit to become a living stone of the heavenly Jerusalem.

## QUESTION I

[Col. 1040B] How should one understand what is read: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18), when God is said to have distributed his works over six days? (Gen. 1.)

## ANSWER

Almighty God, who is life without beginning and without end and who eternally possessed all things in his knowledge, created together the matter of all heavenly and earthly things: namely, heaven, which was luminous matter, and earth, which was turbulent matter.

This luminous matter flashed like dense light from the brightness which is eternity, and it also shone over the turbulent matter, to which it was joined. These two matters were created together so that they appeared as one circle. For at the first *Fiat*, the angels came forth from the aforesaid luminous matter together with their dwelling-place; and because God is God and man, he created the angels before the face of the Father, and formed man—of whom he was to be clothed in a tunic—in his own image and likeness.

Likewise, at the command of almighty God, when he said, “Let it be,” each creature appeared from the turbulent matter according to the species of its nature. For the six days are six works, because the beginning and completion of each individual work is called a day. After the creation of the first matter there was no delay; rather, immediately, as in the blink of an eye, the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters. Nor was there any delay afterward: God at once said, “Let light be” (Gen. 1).

## QUESTION II

[Col. 1040D] What is meant by the statement: “God divided the waters which were below the firmament from those which were above the firmament”? (Gen. 1.) Must it be believed that material waters are above the firmament?

## ANSWER

God divided the waters above the firmament from those beneath the firmament so that, just as the lower waters serve the lower earthly arrangements, so the upper waters might serve the higher arrangements. In the upper waters there is nothing that grows or diminishes as there is in these lower waters, in which everything that lives grows and diminishes as man does.

But those upper waters remain in their first state as God established them and flow in their circuit. They are material, yet not like the lower waters, since they are far subtler and wholly invisible to our sight. By their moisture and the heat of the fire existing there, the firmament is made firm from above, just as a body subsists through the soul, lest it be dissolved.

These lower waters beneath the firmament, being denser, are the mirror of the heavenly luminaries—the sun, moon, and stars—and contain innumerable animals of diverse kinds, which are born and subsist in them. Therefore the functions of the upper and lower waters are entirely unlike in all respects.

## QUESTION III

Before the first man sinned, did he see God with bodily eyes? Or shall we see him with bodily eyes when, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 15), we receive spiritual bodies in the resurrection?

## ANSWER

In the resurrection, when man receives a spiritual body and that same body is inseparably united to the soul, he will behold without end, with the angels, the radiant face of the holy Divinity.

Now Adam, who was formed by God so wise and perfect that he was filled with knowledge and wisdom beyond all human beings, never saw God in his divinity as he is. But when he saw with his outward eyes the brightness proceeding from God’s countenance, he truly knew that God was the true God. For before sin, while his soul still ruled his body, he beheld with his eyes—then spiritual through innocence—the aforesaid brightness. This he could not do afterward, because immediately after sin he lost this vision in paradise, when his eyes were opened through the carnal desire involved in transgressing God’s command which he had previously known.

## QUESTION IV

What manner of speech did God use, and in what form did he appear to the first man when he gave him the command? And in what form did he appear when he walked in paradise after the sin? (Gen. 2–3.)

## ANSWER

Almighty God spoke to Adam in angelic words, which he fully recognized and understood. For through the wisdom he had received from God and through the spirit of prophecy, he then possessed in his knowledge all languages afterward devised by human beings, and he knew completely the natures of all creatures.

The Lord also appeared to him in immeasurable brightness, in which there was the form of no creature; and again, after the sin, when walking in paradise, he appeared in a flame of fire.

## QUESTION V

What is this which God said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil”? (Gen. 3.)

## ANSWER

It means this: Adam had something in common with us through knowledge of good and evil; but he abandoned good in the knowledge of good, and chose evil in the knowledge of evil by tasting the forbidden tree.

And again, Adam was alienated from us because he despised, at the serpent’s counsel, the good which he had formerly known by experience, and, through the taste of pleasure, brought about the previously untried evil by consenting to it. And again he said: “See, lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live forever” (ibid.).

God said this because, in great mercy toward his work—namely, sinful man—he was moved lest man, thus changed from glory, should live miserably forever. In this way he mercifully drew him to himself, as a father draws to himself a son who wishes to leave him. For he greatly loved man, whom he had foreknown as the garment of his Word; indeed, he created every creature for man’s service and assigned man to the place from which that shining one fell into death like a corpse.

## QUESTION VI

[Col. 1042B] What eyes were opened to the first parents, since both saw before sin? For it says: “The woman saw the tree,” etc. (Gen. 3.)

## ANSWER

Before original sin the first parents had spiritual eyes, the soul ruling the body through innocence. But after sin, when they were deprived of the spiritual vision of those same eyes and made mortal through the condition of sin, carnal eyes were opened to them. Thus, through the knowledge of evil, by seeing and knowing sinful works, they acted according to the desires of the flesh at the devil’s persuasion.

They so consigned to forgetfulness all the glory which they had formerly possessed that they scarcely remembered any of it, like a person who sees something from afar and can scarcely make out what it is, or like a shadow seen in a mirror that passes away.

## QUESTION VII

What is meant by the Lord’s saying to Noah and his sons: “I will require the blood of your souls from the hand of every beast and from the hand of man”? And a little later: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed”? (Gen. 9.)

## ANSWER

After the last day, in the resurrection, God will require through man’s garment from the hand—that is, from the changeable nature—of every beast the blood of the souls of Noah and his sons and of the entire human race, which is the seat of the soul. For he does not wish the soul to be clothed with another body or blood than that which it warmed and which was its seat.

For in his mighty foreknowledge, by which he foresaw that man was to be formed from the mud of the earth with the breath of life, which is the soul, together with flesh and blood—as he afterward formed him—he will likewise require in that same foreknowledge that man should rise again.

He will also require the blood of souls from the hand of man: that is, the person who, by oppressing his neighbor, causes that neighbor’s soul to depart must continually cry to God his Creator, through the mortification of his own flesh and blood in repentance, with the sorrow of a weeping voice, because he compelled the soul which God had created to depart through the wounds of death.

But whoever sheds human blood, treating the matter as though it were worthless and without the toil of lost sweat, upon that person God’s judgment shall be executed—through the sword, poverty, or loss of possessions; or, if not upon the one made guilty of blood, then upon that person’s children and grandchildren.

## QUESTION VIII

What sort of bodies did the angels who appeared to Abraham have—the angels to whom he set fine flour, a calf, butter, and milk, and who ate? (Gen. 18.)

## ANSWER

The three angels who appeared to Abraham as he sat at the entrance of the tent appeared in human form, because otherwise they could in no way be seen by man. Changeable man cannot see the unchangeable Spirit. This arises from Adam’s disobedience: deprived of spiritual eyes in paradise, he transmitted his blindness to the whole human race.

Every creature—that is, man—has its shadow, which signifies that man is to be renewed unto unfailing life. And just as a person’s shadow displays that person’s image, so angels, naturally invisible, appear visibly in human form through bodies which they take from the air, to those to whom they are sent. They adapt themselves somewhat to the manners of those people; they speak to them not with angelic speech but with words they can understand; and they eat as human beings do, but their food vanishes like dew which continually falls upon grain and is dissolved in a moment by the sun’s heat.

Evil spirits, however, assume the appearance of whatever nature they use to deceive human beings, considering the nature of that creature which corresponds to the vice through which they may overcome the person they assail, just as the tempter also deceived through the serpent.

## QUESTION IX

Why did Abraham and Jacob—the former commanding his servant, the latter his son—order those who were to swear to place their hands beneath their thighs? (Gen. 24, 48.)

## ANSWER
Abraham, who at the Lord’s command left his country and kindred, went forth through the wound of his flesh—this being the seal of faith—as a glorious standard-bearer, to fight against vices. [Col. 1043D] For by the grace of the Holy Spirit he bore the banner of holiness before others, and through the completion of his works attained the prerogative of supreme holiness. Thus, by the oath taken under the thigh, he prefigured the holy humanity of Christ, who, by the ancient counsel of almighty God, would descend from his seed according to his humanity and, by setting humankind free, would destroy the design of the ancient serpent.

## QUESTION X.

Why did the holy patriarchs so earnestly desire to be buried in the double cave which Abraham bought from the sons of Heth? (Gen. XXIII.)

## ANSWER.

By the double cave, which Abraham purchased for himself as a burial-place, the Old and the New Law are figured. [Col. 1044A] For as the soul lay hidden in the body, so the New Law lay hidden in the Old; and in these two, death—which entered the world through a woman—was buried. The holy patriarchs desired to be buried in that same cave because, touched by the spirit of prophecy, they recognized the sacrament of the New Law in the Old. Thus also in Aaron’s rod, which blossomed (Num. XVII), the sacrament of the Son of God in the redemption of humankind lay hidden; for they knew the Creator in the creature. Likewise Christ, who was to suffer, was signified in the sacrifice of lambs and rams.

## QUESTION XI.

Was the fire which appeared to Moses in the bush and did not burn the bush (Exod. III), or that which shone on Mount Sinai (Exod. XIX), or that which fell upon the disciples on the day of Pentecost [Col. 1044B] in the form of tongues (Acts II), or that which appeared above Martin’s head while he was celebrating the sacraments, real fire?

## ANSWER.

The fire which Moses saw in the midst of the flaming yet unburned bush must be understood as the Holy Spirit; the sparks which leapt out were gifts of diverse powers. The varied appearance of this fire did not at all descend from the flashing of the higher elements, but from that fire which is life and which does not destroy what adheres to it by burning, but strengthens it by giving life.

## QUESTION XII.

What is meant by the statement in the Book of Kings concerning the Ark (III Kings VIII; II Chron. V), “There is nothing in the Ark except the tablets of the Testament”; whereas in the Epistle to [Col. 1044C] the Hebrews we read: “Beyond the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the Ark of the Testament covered on every side with gold, in which were a golden vessel containing manna, Aaron’s rod which had budded, and the tablets of the Testament”? (Num. XVII; Heb. IX.)

## ANSWER.

The one who said that nothing other than the tablets of the Testament was contained in the Ark—held in great veneration by the Israelite people—knew that there was no more in it, nor did he seek to know more from it. But Paul, who, through the profound knowledge of his spirit, was wiser than others by the revelation of divine grace, taught more fully what further secret things were kept in the Ark.

## QUESTION XIII.

[Col. 1044D]

Should Samuel truly be believed to have been summoned forth at the invocation of the pythoness? (I Kings XXVIII.)

## ANSWER.

Saul, who had been rejected and abandoned by God because of his sins, wished through the pythoness to learn the outcome of the coming battle. He therefore ordered Samuel to be called back to him from the dead, so that Samuel might tell him what he sought. But this could in no way have occurred, for it would be impossible for a holy and righteous man to speak falsehood after death, since no soul, faithful or unfaithful, once released from the body can speak falsehood. The souls of Samuel and Saul cannot have the same dwelling-place, because Samuel was God’s faithful friend, whereas Saul proved a rebellious [Col. 1045A] transgressor of His commandments. Nor can the devil deceive a human being through the soul of any person; rather, he deceives him through the form of some creature. Saul lost his kingdom together with his life because he had withdrawn from God; just as Adam, through transgression, was stripped of the glory of Paradise and made a son of death. Therefore he could not obtain from the Lord what he sought.

## QUESTION XIV.

What does Paul mean when he says, “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels”? (I Cor. XIII.) What are the tongues of angels?

## ANSWER.

Angels, who are spirits, do not speak words of rational discourse except on account of humankind, because [Col. 1045B] their tongues are sounding praise. A human being, who knows all sounding things through their sound, displays the joy of his heart in the sound of his voice, which he raises with the breath of his soul.

## QUESTION XV.

What are the length and breadth and height and depth which Paul desires the Ephesians (chapter III) to comprehend with all the saints?

## ANSWER.

By this length is understood the divine essence, which is without end and beginning, since it cannot be comprehended by any ascent of knowledge from its work, which has a beginning. By breadth, however, is signified the infinite power of God, which [Col. 1045C] began from no one, is not increased by advancement, and is not diminished by decline. By height must be understood the brightness of holy divinity, which never began to shine and whose radiance will never pass away. By depth is designated that God, in these three aforementioned powers, fights against the abyss of the north, which is under His power and cannot resist Him at all. In His brightness are comprehended all the saints who loved Him and persevered with Him in the good steadfastness of their ministry, with faith and works.

## QUESTION XVI.

What does the Apostle mean when he says, “In him we live and move and are”? (Acts XVII.)

## ANSWER.

[Col. 1045D] In Him we move with the elements, which we use in such a way that we seek from them all things belonging to our use. In Him too, illuminated and made alive through the breath of life, we live; through this we know that He is our God and Creator. In Him also we are, because we shall never have an end of life in the soul, whatever its merits may be; through it, with all our sense-faculties, we fly and move with the elements and in the elements, as the wind does.

## QUESTION XVII.

What does he mean in saying, “A night and a day I have been in the depth of the sea”? (I Cor. XI.)

## ANSWER.

Considering his labours, Paul uttered these words in [Col. 1046A] sorrow, thereby showing that by God’s permission he was in afflictions and labours as though he were amid the dangers of storms and waves of the sea, which never ceases to surge. God also willed that he should be wearied through the darkness of the devil’s deception, and that his weakness should be moderated in great quiet; yet, strengthened by God, he endured this faithfully and patiently.

## QUESTION XVIII.

Why does he say, “I am the least of the apostles,” when he laboured more than them all? (I Cor. XV.)

## ANSWER.

Paul calls himself the least because he was not, like the other disciples, with Christ, who appeared in human form without sin. And because he was compelled to faith—which he had never desired either to learn or to know—by the Son [Col. 1046B] of God in a spiritual vision, when his soul was neither wholly in the body nor wholly outside the body.

## QUESTION XIX.

What does he mean when he says: “Every sin whatsoever a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body”? (I Cor. VI.)

## ANSWER.

Every sin which a person, through sense-perception and his roaming knowledge, at the devil’s urging, commits against another person, is performed by the devil’s craft, which sows discord among people by inciting them to anger and hatred; and thus it is outside the body. But one who, in the heat of his flesh, stirred in veins and marrow by an incestuous [Col. 1046C] desire through fornication, continually excites and wounds himself until he is exhausted—such a one sins against his own body.

## QUESTION XX.

From the day of the resurrection until the day of the ascension, when the Lord was not among the disciples, where should He be believed to have been?

## ANSWER.

God, who by dwelling visibly among us in His humanity filled the whole earth with His miracles, after His resurrection, during those forty days, cleansed by that same humanity—which He assumed from the Virgin Mary, having been conceived of the Holy Spirit—all the elements that had contracted impurity through the transgression of the first human being. The souls of the saints and of those to be saved, whom He had redeemed as captives from hell, attended by a multitude of angels and bearing the victorious banner of His power, remained with Him in the air, where He sanctified all things.

## QUESTION XXI.

What is meant by what is written concerning the Lord, “And angels came and ministered to Him”? (Matt. IV.) In what did they minister, or what ministry did they render Him?

## ANSWER.

When the devil recognized that Christ was so separated from him that no suggestion could touch Him, [Col. 1047A] he then left Him and fled from Him as a person flees from an enemy by whom he fears being killed. Immediately the angels sounded forth in praises of the miracles of holy divinity, because the humanity which had been defeated in the first-created humans in Paradise had, in Christ the man, victoriously overcome all the devil’s temptations. Thus they ministered to Him alone, whom they knew to be both God and human.

## QUESTION XXII.

Since new souls, newly created from nothing, are believed by the Creator’s providence to be infused into the little bodies of children in their mothers’ wombs, on what grounds do they contract the stain of original sin, and by what justice are they punished?

## ANSWER.

[Col. 1047B] Just as a potter’s vessel which has been steeped in poison contaminates, with the danger of impurity, everything put into it, so all human flesh stands defiled and infected through the flesh of the first human being, unless it is cleansed in baptism and penitence through the pure flesh of the Son of God, which He put on from the Virgin Mary. For the soul contracts from the form which God fashions in the mother’s womb, in order that He may send into it the breath of life, the stain of sin for which it is punished, through the serpent’s counsel by which the first human being was deceived. This stain is washed away, by the ancient counsel of holy divinity, in the Son of God through faith and baptism. But whoever, together with faith and baptism, diligently fulfils carnal desires and does not repent for this, [Col. 1047C] will remain in perdition with those who have not been redeemed through Christ.

## QUESTION XXIII.

Since the Lord says of Himself in the Gospel, “I proceeded forth from God and came” (John VIII), and of the Holy Spirit it is said, “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John XV), what difference is there between the procession of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit, such that He is called Son, while the Holy Spirit ought not, and cannot rightly, be called Son? What distinction is there between the generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit, when both occur from the Father?

## ANSWER.

My Father is power. And I, His sounding Word, proceeded from Him when He created all creatures through [Col. 1047D] Me. And the Holy Spirit proceeded from Him—namely, from My Father—because I descended into the womb of the Virgin, whose flesh had not been wounded by the serpent’s deception, and put on humanity from her, conceived by that same Holy Spirit. For the fiery Holy Spirit, who is fiery life, true kindling, and equal life in eternity, and through whom all forms fashioned by the Son of God are invisibly moved, proceeded from the Father into the Virgin, who is a creature. With His fire He so kindled her womb that she, made pregnant through Him, gave birth without a carnal father to the Word of God, through whom all creatures were made. For just as the form of a human being is seen while his soul cannot be seen by bodily eyes, and yet the person is one in two natures, so [Col. 1048A] the Son of God, conceived in the Virgin’s womb by the Holy Spirit and made human, was seen by all flesh in His humanity but is invisible in His divinity; and likewise He is one God in the two natures, namely His humanity and divinity.

## QUESTION XXIV.

What does Paul mean when he says that he was caught up into Paradise and as far as the third heaven, not knowing whether this occurred in the body or outside the body: did he leave the body when his soul was caught up to these things, or, remaining in the body and giving it life, did he reach them? (I Cor. XIII.)

## ANSWER.

In ecstasy Paul flew by means of his rational soul, to the place to which Christ called it, as a sleeping person travels through many places in dreams; yet in the meantime that soul warmed the blood in his flesh so that it would not coagulate and dry out through cold, as the sun, standing on high, shines and burns from afar by its powers and brightness. He penetrated while beholding the miracles of the firmament as God established it; and he was caught up even to the third heaven—that is, to that brightness of his which flashes from the brightness that is holy divinity and in which blessed souls rest. There he received such strength from God that he could no longer doubt. But he did not come where holy divinity burns, where the angels are like the radiance of the sun, and where also are other angels who appear like the brightness of fire, who behold the unchangeable Divinity which is without beginning and [Col. 1048C] without end, because he could no more endure it than an eagle could endure the higher fire. He also came, in the brightness of those angels who perform their offices with human beings, into Paradise, where he fully knew all the secrets he saw through the soul; and he perceived them so in the body that he knew that they were unbearable for a human being, who is ashes. Thus he is wiser than all the prophets, whose prophecy, which they saw in shadow, was like bees’ honey, multiplied for many uses. For all that the soul saw, he sensed in the body. Hence he left it uncertain whether he saw these things in the body or outside the body; and therefore all his words are deep, sharp, and like steel. [Col. 1048D] But as soon as his soul returned and settled again in its body, God greatly humbled him, because he had fierce dispositions, lest he should learn in his own self-regard what did not belong to the height of a saint.

## QUESTION XXV.

What do the grace of God and free choice have in common, and what does each possess properly?

## ANSWER.

Free choice is in the soul, which is a breath from God, which God creates according to the form of His handiwork, and through which a person senses that he has God—whether faithful or unbelieving, whatever profession or opinion he may hold. When, by choosing evil in his knowledge, he inclines himself toward it, he does as Adam did: Adam knew God’s command and, through the serpent’s counsel, inclined toward evil (Gen. III). [Col. 1049A] The grace of God and free choice have this in common: in the knowledge of good and evil, a person can choose either good or evil to perform. Whatever he chooses by the property of free choice according to the taste and desire of the flesh—which he can never be compelled to relinquish—he accomplishes with the devil’s assistance; and whatever he chooses according to the will of the soul, he accomplishes with the assistance of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## QUESTION XXVI.

How should the saying be understood: “You have ordered all things by weight and measure and number”? (Wis. XI.)

## ANSWER.

[Col. 1049B] God has so established all the tabernacles of our bodies in proper measure that none of them exceeds those dwelling within them in weight or breadth. Likewise the sun, moon, fire, air, water, and earth are established in the firmament with equal weight, number, and measure. And the human being, who is every creature, stands in proper measure because all his limbs are so filled by the soul that, so long as the soul is in him, he can neither wither nor fail. But pride, which flies above all that God established and scorns the Lord, refusing either to know or worship Him, and which falls as an exile from all creatures, is death and has no right measure, because it scatters all that God has rightly ordered and established in [Col. 1049C] His providence and wisdom.

## QUESTION XXVII.

What and what sort is that harmony of the elements of which it is said: “While the elements are changed within themselves, as in an instrument the sound is altered according to its quality, and all things retain their own sound”? (Wis. XIX.) Does this relate to the Lord’s statement: “And who will cause the harmony of heaven to sleep?” (Job XXXVIII.)

## ANSWER.

From the torrent-like course of the higher ether through which the firmament revolves comes a pleasant and glorious sound of the elements; likewise the harmonious voice of the human spirit is sweet in its life. For each element has the sound assigned to it by God, and all sound together as the sound of strings and a lyre joined in one. But the harmony of heaven does not belong to the harmony of the elements which will be changed with humankind; just as the sun, set in the firmament, shines upon this world and not upon the highest heaven.

## QUESTION XXVIII.

How should this be understood: “A spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth”? (Gen. XXII.)

## ANSWER.

By God’s command a spring rose in the land of delight, watering it with all its fruits without alteration or change, as it was first established by the Creator. For it does not have the alternation [Col. 1050A] of summer, winter, and other seasons which are found in our earth and resemble the unstable dispositions of human beings. As the moon is veiled by the brightness of the sun, so sun, moon, and stars are obscured in the brilliance of the glory of this unchangeable land. In it there is nothing mortal, nor does it receive anything mortal; and if something mortal came into it, it would be suffocated to death by its powers as though by water. But the earth in which the heat of the sun is so great that it consumes drops of rain by its heat, as a great and strong fire consumes the drops of water poured into it, is watered by water flowing from the spring which rose in Paradise. This signifies the stable ascent of holy virtues kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1050B]

## QUESTION XXIX.

Since Enoch (Gen. V) and Elijah (IV Kings II) are believed to have been bodily translated into the earthly Paradise, should they be thought to require bodily food and clothing in a place of such happiness?

## ANSWER.

God had ordained in His providence concerning Enoch and Elijah that they should be in that place where they need neither food nor drink nor clothing. Thus everyone who has been caught up in God’s miracles does not use those things which belong to mortals as long as he remains in them.

## QUESTION XXX.

[Col. 1050C]

What is meant by the statement concerning Jonathan that, when he had eaten honey, his eyes were enlightened? (I Kings XIV.)

## ANSWER.

Jonathan was like rich and fruitful soil, easily turned by the plough and often producing useful herbs even in ploughed ground, because he was gentle in his dispositions and not harsh in judgments. He gladly affirmed what was true and just, without anger or hatred. Whoever has such dispositions has sound and excellent humours in his brain, veins, and marrow through all foods by which he is nourished, since in him anger and sadness do not arise through melancholy along with changes of diverse dispositions. For God’s gift is present in him and makes him sprout and flourish as dew does that upon which it falls. But the one weakened by melancholy is like hard ground, scarcely turned by the plough, because in his dispositions he has anger, sadness, and opposition to all justice, unless by the nature of his soul he constantly resists himself; nor can he have joy in his works. But one who has the dispositions mentioned above is well-disposed in all his works; through food his flesh and blood grow, and he is strengthened by them. Jonathan too, whose eyes had previously been clouded through bodily weakness, recovered sharp sight when he was strengthened by tasting honey which, through the air that had flown above it, possessed greater power than other honey.

## QUESTION XXXI.

[Col. 1051A]

Since evil thoughts frequently proceed from the human heart (Matt. XV), how can one know which arise from the corruption of our depravity and which are stirred by the suggestion of evil angels (Ps. LXXVII)?

## ANSWER.

Thoughts so implanted in human hearts by the first original sin that people are moved by them toward pleasure in their flesh, blood, and veins are human thoughts. But airy thoughts, by which people desire in their hearts to possess and seek to know things that are impossible because they cannot occur, are vain, for they fly uselessly everywhere like air. Of these [Col. 1051B] thoughts it is also written: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Ps. XCIII). What does this say? A human being who flies through rationality and knows those things which he recognizes by experience—seeing and touching—always investigates hidden matters belonging to the soul, which he cannot comprehend in advance of bodily sensation. But evil thoughts, sent into a person by the devil’s craft and proceeding from his heart and mouth, are the devil’s food, because through them he swallows souls as a person swallows food into his belly, when in his deception he makes them contradict God and His commandments through unbelief, and thus despoils them. Yet many, persevering with God through holy works and pure faith, strongly overcome him by God’s grace. [Col. 1051C]

## QUESTION XXXII.

Are bodily things seen with spiritual eyes, and conversely, are any spiritual things known with bodily eyes? (II Cor. IV.)

## ANSWER.

Spiritual eyes are the rational knowledge of the soul. They cannot see bodily things as they are, just as a blind person does not see with external eyes, but understands and knows through hearing alone what is seen. Bodily eyes also lack the power perfectly to behold spiritual things. But as the form of a person is seen in a mirror, though the person is not in it, so a person sees and knows spiritual things through hearing words in faith. [Col. 1051D] For no spirit can appear to a human being as it is in its own nature, because the human being is a living breath from God, which gives life and strength to its garment, namely the body, and does not cease to act with it. When it departs from the body, it will be either in the light of blessedness or in the darkness of punishments.

## QUESTION XXXIII.

Is the fire of Gehenna bodily or incorporeal? And if, as many faithful people believe, it is bodily, should it be thought to consist of the matter of the four elements?

## ANSWER.

By no means. For neither are those [punishments] made from these elements, nor is this fire from that one, and that fire is invisible. Bodily and spiritual punishments are not equal, just as the body is unlike [Col. 1052A] the soul and the soul is not equal to the body. For under bodily punishments the body withers and dies, while spirits and souls are tortured in the spiritual fire of Gehenna, yet do not die in it. The purgatorial fire too, in which souls to be saved live and are punished, is not kindled from the fire of Gehenna; rather, it arises by God’s judgment according to human sins. Many who have entered ecstasy have been greatly astonished by it.

## QUESTION XXXIV.

Do the saints in heaven and the wicked in hell know what is done on earth?

## ANSWER.

The saints who are in the heavenly homeland know everything done on earth, because all that is done on earth appears before God either in His judgment [Col. 1052B] or in the sounding praises of angels. The wicked also, who never ceased from their sins nor corrected them by penitence, know evil things through the mockery with which they deride their followers; and they understand good things through the howling with which they howl against the blessed, who do not follow them.

## QUESTION XXXV.

Did the parables variously narrated in the Gospels—such as that of the one who fell among robbers (Luke X), the king who made a wedding-feast for his son, the ten virgins (Matt. XXII, XXV), and others—occur according to the truth of actual events, or are they proposed merely as likenesses for showing something else?

## ANSWER.

[Col. 1052C]

Christ set forth His parables to human beings because of the spiritual vices by which they are often deceived, and also because of the virtues by which they fight victoriously against those vices, so that by them they might recognize that He would judge them for evil deeds and grant rewards for good ones.

## QUESTION XXXVI.

Since according to the soul Abraham and Lazarus are in refreshment, while the rich man is in hell, what are Abraham’s bosom, Lazarus’s finger, and the rich man’s tongue to be understood to be? (Luke XVI.)

## ANSWER.

[Col. 1052D] Abraham’s bosom signifies the obedience which he rendered to God through the offering of his son and through circumcision (Gen. XXII, XVII), because obedience preserves and supports every good, just as a bosom contains whatever is gathered together. Lazarus’s finger is understood as the ministry of obedience, which is the substance of God’s commandments, because it teaches all good things, just as a person points out what he wishes with his finger. The tongue signifies one’s own will, which brings forth the banquets of carnal desires; for as all foods are distinguished by the taste of the tongue, so the human will is recognized through it.

## QUESTION XXXVII.

What particular merit is signified by the fact that, as is found in the book of Gregory, bishop of Tours, [Col. 1053A] Saint Martin appeared so often in the form of fire?

## ANSWER.

Almighty God, who is love and strength, had suffused the soul of blessed Martin with a fiery outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, on account of the merits of humility, piety, and mercy, through which he always beheld the living God in a contrite heart, he appeared so often in fire.

## QUESTION XXXVIII.

In what body did blessed Nicholas appear to sailors who were awake and to Constantine and the prefect while they were asleep, since he did not do this in his own body? And Peter and Paul and the other saints, whose bodies are buried in the earth—when they become visible to sleepers or [Col. 1054A] to those awake, in what or what kind of body do they come?

## ANSWER.

If this spiritual vision did not appear to people, they would neither understand what it was nor believe it, since they themselves are body and spirit in two natures. The image of God, namely the human being, one part of whom is mutable and the other immutable, could never see the immutable spirit unless it appeared in a mutable form, because mutable form is given life only through spirit; just as a horn sounds by means of sound and not by itself. In the good intention which God had signified in these holy persons, He also answered the good intention of these people, just as people behold the signs of the firmament.

[Col. 1053]

# EXPLANATION OF THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT.

(Bibliotheca Patrum, Lyons edition, XXIII, 590.)

THE COMMUNITY OF HUNNIENSIS MONASTERY TO HILDEGARD. They request an interpretation of the Rule of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 1053B] To HILDEGARD, temple of the Holy Spirit and venerable, God-beloved bride of Christ, most desired mistress of the sisters of Saint Robert at Pingis; the whole harmonious community of Hunniensis monastery wishes eternal exaltation in glory, with the humility and earnestness of good works.

Sprinkled with the inestimable flower of your grace-revealing reputation, like a narcissus of Paradise, we are so delighted that we are compelled to say with the Apostle: “Thanks be to Him who always triumphs in us, in whom He manifests in every place the fragrance of His knowledge” (II Cor. II). For, contemplating the whole structure of the universal body of the Church, in which one Spirit distributes to each as He wills (I Cor. I), we rejoice that His abundance overflows in the excellence of your holiness. [Col. 1053C] Since, therefore, after the age of the apostles we behold you as a kind of mirror of divine mercy, we flee in this hour of need, as to the refuge of a most secure and impregnable stronghold, and beg you to assist us by your counsel and prayers. For our order, though in every respect we are unlike ourselves, is honoured and blessed through you. We have been told of your works: that you have bestowed, briefly and clearly, upon the children of the Church riches desirable to them. Since you do not lack even this gift, prostrate at the feet of your holiness, we all jointly entreat your gracious kindness to leave us some written memorial concerning the Rule of our blessed Father Benedict, a thing most necessary to us. [Col. 1054B] For we are called liars, perjurers, transgressors of the aforesaid Rule, and despisers of synodal decrees. This happens especially because each of our prelates, according to his own mental inclination, disregards both the institutions of the canons and the Rule; so that, while they are a law unto themselves, according to the testimony of the same Rule, whatever they wish they call holy and just, and whatever they do not wish they consider unlawful. Hence we are carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. IV) and are grievously burdened by human presumptions. Rejecting these, the blessed Father Augustine speaks thus: “They oppress our religion, which the mercy of God willed to be free through very few and very manifest sacramental observances, with such slavish burdens that the condition of the Jews is more tolerable.” [Col. 1054C] For although the Jews did not know the age of true freedom, they are nevertheless subject to royal sacraments, not to human presumptions. You would therefore offer us a work dearer than the riches of Croesus—indeed, than the treasures of the whole world—if you took pains to grant our petition in this matter, so greatly necessary to all cloisters. For even if you expounded the whole of Holy Scripture, you could offer us nothing so useful or so dear. Henceforth pray for us, that our community, gathered in the Holy Spirit, may never be disturbed by any contrivance of hostile deceit. May He who began a good work in us deign to make us persevere in works pleasing to Him. May your motherly love flourish.

# THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT EXPOUNDED ACCORDING TO SAINT HILDEGARD.

[Col. 1055]

[Col. 1055A] And I, a poor little woman in female form and untaught by human instruction, looked to the true Light and to the memory of blessed Benedict in accordance with your request, so that those matters in the teaching of his Rule which are more difficult and obscure to human understanding might be disclosed to me by the grace of God. And I heard a voice saying to me from the true Light:

“The most luminous and mystical breathings of the Holy Spirit worked in blessed Benedict, so that his mind glowed with the love of God and he carried out no persuasion of diabolical craft in his works. For he was so filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit that in none of his works—not even for the point of a moment or the blink of an eye—did he lack the power of the Holy Spirit. He was also a sealed fountain, pouring forth his teaching in God’s discernment. [Col. 1055B] He fixed the sharp nail of teaching neither too high nor too deep, but in the middle of the wheel, so that everyone, whether strong or weak, might suitably drink from it according to his ability.

“This wheel is the encompassing power of God, through which God worked in the ancient saints down to Moses, who gave the Law to the people of God, and through which He also worked in other most holy men, whose nail of labours was driven to such a lofty height that the common people could not grasp it. Blessed Benedict gently drew his teaching from the fear of God; in piety he taught God’s commandments; in charity he established the wall of holiness in his Rule; and in chastity he was a stranger to all the pomp and delights of the earthly age. Because he wrote his teaching in fear and piety, charity and chastity, nothing must be added to or taken from that teaching, for it lacks nothing, having been made and completed in the Holy Spirit.

“And because he was a son of the dove, he said, ‘Listen, my son, to the precepts of your father’; and for that reason also he was full of the holiness of the aforementioned virtues, like Moses, the meekest man above all people dwelling on the earth (Num. XII). [Col. 1055C] What this devout Father says, however, some monks dissipate by their diversity of conduct; and it is evident to those who consider the matter from what source they will be given recompense according to the merits of their works. For before the times of this blessed Father Benedict, monks, not established under any fixed rule, wandered here and there in diverse uncertainty and instability, lacking fixed instruction and a fixed dwelling-place. Therefore, describing the vices of their unstable conduct in order that their life might be avoided by faithful monks, he gives warning.”

But to those who truly follow his teaching, because of the seriousness of silence, permission to speak should be granted rarely—namely, when something must be done in consultation, in business, or in greater necessities; then permission should be given for them to speak with one another, not individually, and briefly and moderately about what is necessary. Then, when a signal has been given, let all keep silence according to the customary manner. [Col. 1056A] For Benedict himself did not prescribe this permission at a fixed hour every day, but retained it in his own power, as was fitting. He did not grant it unless compelled by some just necessity or pious usefulness. Yet, since it is inhuman for a person always to remain silent and never speak, this same Father leaves the matter to the authority and discernment of the abbot, as he entrusts many other things to him, so that he may provide his disciples with a suitable hour in which they may speak together of things honourable and necessary, and may not be afflicted by the weariness of indiscriminate silence. For after permission has been given for such mutual speech, they can more suitably and strictly be exhorted and constrained to the silence of quiet.

But when he says: “In winter time, that is, from the Kalends of November until Easter, they should rise at the eighth hour of the night, according to reasonable consideration, so that they may rest somewhat beyond midnight and rise having digested,” [Col. 1056B] this is because one who keeps vigil for a third part of the hours of the night in winter, or who sleeps for a third part of the hours of night and day in winter, is not weakened in brain or in the rest of the body either by these vigils or by this sleep. For a person who either keeps watch excessively or sleeps excessively incurs weakness of mind and body. Thus those who have slept rise having digested their food for the vigils, because, when food has been eaten and drink taken, during so many lingering hours they have already changed into something else; therefore a person ought to rise. These vigils also bring health to a person when he has shaken himself free from sluggish sleep and cleansed himself; for if one slept excessively, he would easily contract fevers and feel the stirring of his flesh through inward heat. But in order to defend himself from these things and faithfully serve God, let him fulfil with a good disposition the exhortation of the pious Father.

And it is added: “What remains after the night vigils should be devoted by those brethren who need some part of the psalter or of the lessons to meditation.” This warns them not afterwards to give themselves either to sleep or idleness, but carefully to the profit of the soul during this winter interval, so arranged according to what the season then permits, until the morning praise begins when daylight is already dawning. Here he appointed, after the night vigils—that is, after the night psalms had ended—an interval for meditation upon prayers or [Col. 1056D] readings. But he immediately speaks of the summer interval: “From Easter until the aforesaid Kalends of November, let the hour for performing the vigils be so moderated that, after a very short interval in which the brethren may go out for the necessities of nature, the Matins to be performed at the beginning of daylight may immediately follow.”

In these words it should therefore be observed that both in summer and in winter—namely, when three lessons are said and also when only one is said—the brethren did not return to bed to rest either after the nocturns or after Matins. Rather, in both seasons they so arranged the nocturnal vigils after midnight that, while already singing the praises, [Col. 1057A] they saw the day dawning. And, because of this rightly ordered moderation, they were not burdened but rejoiced: for when a person has rested for more than half the night and then shaken off sleep, he is not weakened in his strength by the subsequent vigils, as has been said.

When he subsequently says, “When these things have been said, after the verse has been said, let the abbot give the blessing,” he does not show that the Lord’s Prayer is to be said there beforehand. Nor does he do so where, concerning the first nocturn of Sunday, he writes thus: “After six psalms and a verse have been sung, as we have said above, let all sit in order on the benches, and let four lessons be read from the book, as we have said above.” Nor again does he mention it where he speaks of the second and third nocturns; for when the third nocturn has ended, he says: “After the verse has been said and the abbot has given the blessing, let [Col. 1057B] another four lessons be read,” making there no mention of the Lord’s Prayer, lest an interruption seem to occur there.

But after the six psalms of the second nocturn on an ordinary day have ended, he says: “After these, there follows a lesson from the Apostle, to be recited from memory; and after this, in place of the three lessons, let one from the Old Testament be read from memory.” And again: “Then, after one lesson from the Apostle has been recited from memory, let the following [psalm] be said.” By this he shows that, when brethren devote themselves to readings and meditations, they should commit to memory the things necessary from Holy Scripture, so that, when a suitable time arises and necessity presents itself, they may bring them forth among the community without a written text. Thus they will recite the aforesaid lessons by heart and from memory—that is, without a book—because they are brief, [Col. 1057C] lest their brevity prove an impediment if they do not have a manuscript ready for reading or light for seeing. But he is silent about this in the daytime hours of the divine office because he leaves it to their judgment whether they utter the capitula—that is, the aforesaid brief lessons—from memory or from a manuscript in the brightness of day; for then they will suffer less inconvenience because the day is light.

But by commanding that the Gospel be read after the nocturns on Sundays and other solemnities, he wishes it to be understood that at every time, both night and day, the message of God ought to be heard and fulfilled, and that God is to be served through it. He also intends that, after hearing [Col. 1057D] the Gospel, the monks should remember that Gospel: “Behold, we have left all things and followed thee” (Matt. 19). He also intends this: if, because priests are scarce or because of some hindering occupation, anyone cannot have Mass or attend Mass that day, the Gospel read and heard may suffice for him.

And when, after the Gospel has been read, he says, “When the blessing has been given”—that is, in the customary prayer—“let them begin Matins,” he does not indicate an interval for meditation on prayers or readings. Nor does he forbid the brethren on these days, when Matins have ended, to return to bed for rest; rather, he tacitly leaves it to their discretion that, if time permits and they have risen earlier, they may return to bed, since they have been wearied by the length of the nocturn and divine service. For those things which he refuses to have done he openly forbids, and those which he exhorts people to do he openly declares. But these matters concerning which he is silent in this way he leaves to the judgment and discretion of the abbot and brethren.

Hence, at the end of the nocturnal, morning, and daytime hours of divine service, after *Kyrie eleison*, he declares that the Lord’s Prayer is to be said, when he says: “In the other offices, however, let the last part of that prayer be said, so that all may answer: ‘But deliver us from evil’” (Matt. 6). [Col. 1058A] He does not show that a collect is to be said there, because, after “But deliver us from evil” has been said, he says: “And so let the night vigils end”; and again, “And it is completed”; and again, “They are dismissed”—with no collect specified. This is so that weariness may be removed from those praying, and so that the Lord’s Prayer, said beforehand, may not fall into neglect; for he finds no prayer more precious than the Lord’s Prayer, by which divine service should be concluded.

Then, concerning the end of Compline, he adds: “Let *Kyrie eleison*, the blessing, and the dismissal be made”—namely, that blessing which is in use at that time down to the present. And when he says, “Let us always remember what the Prophet says: ‘Serve the Lord in fear’” (Ps. 2); and again, “Sing wisely” (Ps. 46), he wishes this to be understood: he had abbreviated the divine service so that it might afterwards be performed diligently, joyfully, and without weariness, because it is known to be short. Where the division is long, breath must be sustained by those chanting; where it is short, one proceeds without needing to hold the breath. Chatter in the divine office is regarded before God as virtually worthless. For [Col. 1058C] it is fitting, as blessed Benedict declares, that one standing before a king should address him honourably.
