He then adds: “Nevertheless, in the assembly let the prayer be made quite brief.” For he had advised that prayer be said before each canonical hour; since in what follows he orders that the kiss of peace not be offered to a guest before prayer has first been said, much more must prayer be said beforehand, and briefly, when almighty God is to be greeted—lest those who afterwards begin the psalmody attend less to the psalmody itself because they have been wearied by a preceding and lengthy prayer.

That monks should receive bedding according to the manner of their life, under the ordering of their abbot, he makes clear when he speaks of the brethren’s clothing, [Col. 1058D] saying: “Let bedding suffice: a mat, a covering, a woollen blanket, and a pillow.” Let them sleep clothed—that is, in a simple single garment next to the skin, lest they lie naked. It was woollen, and they were not clothed in two garments, because they could not endure that; they were girded with belts or cords, lest the garment in which they slept slip off them and they thus appear naked.

He also says: “If any brother is contumacious, or disobedient, or proud,” and so forth. He immediately adds: “If he understands what the punishment is, let him be subject to excommunication”—not that pronounced by sacerdotal right under the stole, but the excommunication by which he is separated, merely by simple words, from the company of the brethren, whether in the refectory, in the choir during divine office, in the dormitory, or in similar places. For this punishment brings to those who understand a more grievous blush of shame [Col. 1059A] than bodily punishment; whereas bodily discipline must be imposed on those who do not understand. And it is added: “But if he is incorrigible, let him be subjected to bodily punishment”—that is, let him be chastised either with blows or other corporal punishments, because not words but the harsh bites of the flesh scarcely bring such a person to correction.

And concerning the cellarer of the monastery he says: “Let him offer to the brethren their appointed allowance without any *typus* or delay”—that is, without a pre-marked measure of a fixed arrangement. Here *typus* is also understood as *ti*, “to thee,” and *po*, “power”: namely, lest the cellarer say inwardly, “You have the power to give and withhold wherever you wish,” so that he gives more and better food to whomever he chooses, or provides fewer and worse foods to whomever he chooses, as secular men who distribute provisions in princes’ courts sometimes do. Nor should he take to himself this power, so that he does not provide a greater allowance to the one who needs it when he gives more to the needy person than to one who is not unworthy; nor should he make any delaying postponement in giving what ought to be given.

It is then added: “When the brother is about to leave his week of service, let him do the cleaning on Saturday,” wiping away dirt and dust with brooms where necessary. And again: “Both he who goes out and he who is about to enter shall wash the feet of all”—namely, at the foot-washing. Then: “An hour before the meal, let him receive the *mistum*, that is, the midday meal”: namely, bread and drink, bread dipped in drink, which are mouthfuls (*offae*), because the bread is mixed with the drink. Afterwards: “When leaving, let him receive the blessing”—namely, that of prayer; [Col. 1059C] and immediately follows: “And, having received the blessing, let him enter”—that is, into the appropriate prayer.

Then he says: “But let the eating of flesh be granted to the sick and utterly weak for restoration.” He intends meats both of quadrupeds and of birds, excluding none of the meats which people customarily eat. “But when they have improved, let all abstain from flesh as usual”: namely, from the flesh of quadrupeds, since healthy monks were not accustomed to eat it or its broth, but the sick were; healthy monks, however, may eat the flesh of birds, because it is clean and does not produce burning lust in those who eat it. He then adds: “Let them anticipate the canonical hours”—that is, in food; namely, the hours established in the Rule, [Col. 1059D] so that the old and children may receive their meal and more agreeable foods before the others and more frequently than the others.

And again he says: “And thus let them enter for the reading,” namely, with the blessing of prayer. Immediately follows: “Let no one presume there to ask any question concerning the reading itself or anything else, lest occasion be given—unless perhaps the prior wishes to say something briefly for edification.” For at that time the one set over the others there gave, in their presence, salutary admonitions concerning the same reading before they departed from one another. But there were then few; later, as their numbers increased, they avoided this, lest on this occasion they break out into idle words.

But let the brother who is weekly reader receive the *mistum*, as said above, before he begins to read, because of holy communion. [Col. 1060A] For in the time of blessed Benedict, the one who was to read at table served as though at God’s altar, because he had to utter holy words; on Sunday he received communion, but afterwards took his meal, lest, while fasting, he might perhaps feel a failing of heart while reading. In this also the aforesaid Father intended it to be understood that every faithful person, after receiving the Eucharist, should observe himself in all things more carefully and diligently than usual.

When he adds: “Let two cooked dishes suffice for all the brethren,” *pulmentaria* means those foods which, set upon the fire, are stirred here and there with a little stick lest they burn. And what follows, saying: “If there are fruits or fresh vegetables, let a third be added,” refers to beans, peas, and other such legumes, which are gathered fresh from the field as fruits are taken from trees. He orders these to be put before the brethren as a third dish, not cooked but stripped of their husks. [Col. 1060B] Fish, cheese, or eggs are likewise to be understood as the third dish, and are permitted. The pious Father did not name these because he foresaw that monks would not abstain from them; therefore he did not forbid them, since he did not name them either.

Later he writes again: “Let all abstain entirely from eating the flesh of quadrupeds, except those who are utterly weak and sick.” Here he is silent concerning birds, because he does not forbid their consumption to the healthy. For this same Father, because the monastic way of life in his time was still rough and almost unfamiliar, avoided forbidding them the eating of meat in every respect. Therefore he permitted them to use the flesh of birds.

Then he says: “Let him be seen by him or by all, until, when the work of God is completed, he penitently makes public satisfaction by lying prostrate and asking pardon.” And again: “Yet let the guilty person make satisfaction by this”—that is, by prostrating himself upon the ground. It is then added: “At the hour at which he had desired what he had previously refused, let him receive that or nothing else at all until suitable amendment.” For because of contempt, any necessary thing will be denied to an obstinate brother until, humbled through penitence, he shows amendment. And again: “Then at the feet of all the brethren, that they may pray for him,” namely to God, whom he offended by his grave sins. And immediately again: “Let them do this until he blesses them,” greeting publicly, [Col. 1060D] calling them to humility; and then, unless he has been humbled there before all by satisfaction—that is, by asking pardon upon the ground through the abasement of his body—he shall be subject to a greater punishment, namely before them in the affliction of his flesh.

But when he says, “If, however, the cause of the soul’s sin is hidden,” that is, if a brother has secretly transgressed in some matter or secretly permitted some sin, let him reveal it only to the abbot or spiritual elders, confessing the girdle of sin, and so obtain pardon. And he adds: “Nevertheless, let each one suggest to his abbot that which he offers, and let it be done with his blessing and will.” Therefore no brother ought wholly to avoid, without permission of his abbot, the regular or common food and drink regularly and commonly set before him in the community of his brethren; nor, while the brethren are engaged in common prayers or works, may he withdraw from them by his own will, unless this has been allowed him by his spiritual Father. Yet he may freely withhold from his body a portion of any regular and common food or drink regularly and commonly set before him in the community of his brethren—provided, certainly, that no clamour of complaint arises from it—following everywhere, regularly and humbly and without complaint, the common custom of the monastery. [Col. 1061A]

He then writes: “Let no one presume to eat outside, even if he is urgently invited by anyone at all, unless perhaps it is commanded him by the abbot.” If he acts otherwise, let him be excommunicated by the excommunication through which a contumacious and disobedient brother, as stated above, is separated from the communion and fellowship of his brethren until he makes satisfaction.

And he says: “When the work of God is completed, let all go out in the deepest silence, and reverence be shown to God.” That is, as they depart reverently, let them bow; and let them retain reverence in their other works as if they were in God’s service, taking up neither frivolity nor any excess.

He then adds: “When a guest has been announced, let the prior or brethren run to meet him with every office of charity, and first let them pray together”—that is, let all, whoever they may be, be led to the church to worship, so that the brethren may pray to God that they do not break their order because of the guests, while the guests may become better by seeing their manner of life. And again: “With head bowed or whole body prostrate [Col. 1061C] upon the ground, let Christ be adored in them, who is also received.” For when guests arrive, those who receive them then—or, when they depart, those who accompany and bless them—shall either bow before them out of reverence for Christ or ask pardon before them, as if Christ were present.

He immediately adds: “And after this let every kindness be shown him,” both in gracious and companionable conversation and in every necessary bodily need. Again: “Let the abbot give water into the hands of guests,” as an expression of humility, “and let both abbot and community wash the feet of all guests”—namely, those to whom the abbot assigns this work. For blessed Father Benedict, when the guests [Col. 1061D] whom he had received were about to eat, offered water to their hands; and when they had risen from table, he washed their feet. He did this after the example which the Son of God gave his disciples at supper, except in the case of women, whose feet he did not touch; rather, he showed them contempt for the world both in his habit and in his holy way of life. For at that time monks had not yet experienced the disturbance caused by the arrival of strangers; those who came to them sought Christ there and nothing else, and found him there also in holy works.

And he continues thus: “Let clothing be given to the brethren according to the conditions of the places in which they live or the temperature of the air.” Here he shows that clothing is to be given to brethren according to what they can endure, and so that they may be without [Col. 1062A] murmuring. For where a region is of such coldness that people cannot in necessity abstain from warm garments, since they will avoid excess in them, both the lamb’s-fleece fur garment and the lamb’s woollen thread of a tunic are pleasing to the heavenly Judge as the monks’ outer clothing.

He immediately follows: “Nevertheless, we believe that in temperate places there suffice for monks, for each one, a cowl and a tunic”: namely, a roomy cowl descending to the ankle, with short sleeves extending a little beyond the hand, and with two folds flowing down on either side from beneath the armpit, to which the hood above was attached. This is the distinctive sign of a monk, signifying that he should not look toward the world in this direction or that when he has it upon his head. The tunic, [Col. 1062B] however, was woollen and somewhat more closely fitting than the cowl, but somewhat roomier around the legs and reaching to the feet; its sleeves were neither very loose nor very tight, extending to the hands, and it had a fold descending on either side from beneath the armpit, while it lacked a hood above.

Then: “Let the abbot provide for the measure, so that they are not short, like those of certain laymen, but descend to the ankles,” because they did not use drawers in their cell. Therefore he adds: “Let those who are sent on a journey receive drawers from the wardrobe, and when they return, restore them there washed.” Here it may be understood that monks living under the direction of this Father used drawers only when leaving the cell. Since at that time the multitude of people did not wear drawers, this same Father did not permit his disciples to wear them while they remained in the cell, because of prevailing customs and as a sign of childlike simplicity and humility. Yet he allowed them to wear them when going out, whether on horseback or on foot, for an example of chastity and for masculine decency and regard for people. But now, since people’s customs are such, it does not displease God if monks use drawers because of the blasphemy of unchastity which they may experience in nakedness of flesh, lest, while naked flesh touches flesh, they remember carnal sins. [Col. 1062C]

And again: “Let bedding suffice: a mat, a covering”—namely, one made either of coarse linen or hemp, almost shaped like a sack and filled with some kind of bedding, placed upon the mat, which monks used as bed-covering—“and a woollen blanket,” namely of wool, which they spread over the bed by day for decency and under which they covered themselves at night when they wished. He immediately says: “Let all necessaries be supplied by the abbot”; and adds: “A belt”—that is, with which they girded themselves over the tunic lest it slip down, because they slept without drawers—“and a *brachiale*,” the garment next to the skin, from which tied hose hung. He immediately continues: “A cloth, like a linen handkerchief,” with which they wiped away sweat running from them while labouring at their work. [Col. 1062D]

Later he says: “And with the offering let them wrap the document of petition and the boy’s hand in the altar-cloth.” Here it should be understood that the parents’ petition concerning the boy was committed to writing as testimony and confirmation when they offered him to God, just as was that of the person who, as has been shown above, promised before God and his saints his stability, conversion of life, and obedience at his consecration.

Then: “If anyone of the priestly order asks to be received into the monastery, let consent not be given to him too quickly.” By “priest” is to be understood one who presided over a provostship, an archpresbyterate, or a parish, and who, because of such rank, can scarcely restrain his soul to subjection. It does not mean a bishop, because it would be improper for the leader of the people’s souls, who had also been the abbot’s teacher, to be subjected to an abbot. But if such a man wishes to convert, let him remain alone in penitence without subjection to monastic authority.

It is then added: “And if perhaps some matter of ordination or other business arises in the monastery”—that is, if something must be discussed there in consultation concerning obediences and offices of authority or external affairs—“let him consider the place at which he entered the monastery”: namely, the place, that is, the purpose of a life of humility and subjection, which gains for him a good and lofty rank. Let him keep before the eyes of his heart the rank to which he has come when he receives the monastic habit in the monastery, which signifies contempt of the world, not the rank granted him because of reverence for the priesthood. [Col. 1063B] That is, let him not consider that he formerly held the place of teacher—that he was formerly a doctor and master among the people or clergy—nor think or judge himself wiser, more learned, readier or more prudent in speech than his other brethren reared in the cloister, when he himself lived in the world, attached himself to secular people, and passed through all these things. Rather, because of his voluntary conversion, by which he has willingly subjected himself to the discipline of the Rule, and because of reverence for his priesthood, let him give with the others a good example of holiness, showing himself obedient and subject in every matter.

And the same Father then says: “But if afterwards he wishes to strengthen his stability, let such a will not be refused.” Then: “Not only, if he asks, should he be received to join the congregation, [Col. 1063D] but he should even be urged to remain, so that others may be instructed by his example; for in every place one Lord is served and one King is fought for.”

Thus the pious Father intended what he wrote above—“Let the novice who is to be received promise in the oratory before all concerning his stability”—and what he immediately added, “Concerning this promise let him make a petition in the name of the saints whose relics are there,” and what he says here, “Let such a will not be refused,” and afterwards, “He should even be urged to remain,” and again, “For in every place one Lord is served,” to be understood as follows. If any monk secretly or obstinately leaves his monastery, in which, as written above, he had promised his stability and made his petition, upon any pretext of his instability, and so comes to far-distant provinces, and if there sees a monastery suited to his way of life in which, led by penitence, he wishes to remain in stability and asks to be received by confirmation, then, if he is worthy, it is better that he be received even though, owing to the length of his journey, he has no letters of recommendation and cannot have them, than that entry be denied him. For if he were not received, perhaps, oppressed by weakness, illness, old age, or some other burden, or by the length of the journey back to the monastery from which he departed, he would be driven to despair, return to the world, remain in the world, and thus perish in soul and body. [Col. 1064A]

Nevertheless, it is far more useful for him, if he can possibly do so, to return to his own monastery, from which he went out without the permission of his spiritual Father, or to seek forgiveness, than stubbornly to remain in another—provided that he knows monastic religious discipline to exist there. The same Father confirms this in what follows: “But let the abbot beware of ever receiving for residence a monk from another known monastery without the consent of his abbot or letters of recommendation.” Here he does not wish monks bound by the aforesaid stability and petition to move from place to place freely and without permission, but to preserve their vow with firm constancy.

He continues: “Nor, on the pretext of priesthood, let him forget the obedience and discipline of the Rule, but let him progress more and more toward God. Let him always consider that place at which he entered the monastery, except in the office [Col. 1064C] of the altar.” This means: let a monk ordained priest in his own monastery not become proud of his priesthood, but with pious devotion let him keep before the eyes of his heart that place of humility and subjection in which, following Christ’s example, he received the monastic habit and embraced contempt of the world. At that hour he subjected himself to serve both God and human beings; moreover, let him humbly consider that he made himself God’s servant and minister when he subjected himself to the service of the altar. Therefore in all things he will show himself humbler and more subject.

For he should not merely consider that he received the monk’s habit humbly and devoutly, and therefore regard himself as lowly and obedient in all things without pretence; he should also consider that, because he subjected himself to God in the office of the altar, he must henceforth count himself humble, gentle, and last in his own estimation. And he adds: “Whenever brethren meet one another, let the younger ask the elder for a blessing,” namely as in greeting, because he will show in all humility that he is subject to his elder. [Col. 1064D]

He also says: “And always, at the final prayer of the work of God, let commemoration be made of all who are absent.” This prayer at the end of the work of God is understood to be the Lord’s Prayer, because above he says that divine office ends through that prayer, as he there shows: namely, “Let the litany and the Lord’s Prayer be said, and let the dismissal be made.” For when this Father’s disciples said in that prayer, “But deliver us from evil,” they added concerning the absent: “And [remember] thy servants, our absent brethren,” thereby commemorating them. At that time they did not yet fully possess collects of prayers; and therefore they frequently ended divine service with the Lord’s Prayer.

He then says: “But for children up to the fifteenth year of age, let the diligence of discipline and supervision be applied by all.” He says this because when a child is under fifteen, he is tender in body and tender in mind; meanwhile he has fear and can be bent toward every good thing, nor does he dare insolently resist those correcting him. But when he has reached his fifteenth year, he is already flourishing in youth, like a tree producing flowers, and marrow and blood are strengthened in him; [Col. 1066A] hence the powers of his mind also arise, so that he disdains to receive and endure childish corrections as he did before.

Finally, blessed Father confirms all these things thus: “For those who do these things the everlasting kingdoms will lie open.” For all the things described in this Rule are not excessively strict, but look to the right and the left; therefore they swiftly lead one who observes them to heavenly things. Thus I, a poor womanly form, have heard these words from Wisdom, which taught me the obscure words of the Rule of the aforesaid blessed Father Benedict, so that I might set them forth plainly. Therefore let the gentle, meek, and God-fearing hear these things, understand them with a pious heart, and receive them with humble devotion.

[Col. 1065]

## SAINT HILDEGARD’S EXPLANATION OF THE CREED OF SAINT ATHANASIUS TO THE COMMUNITY OF HER SISTERS

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition, XXIII, 594.)

[Col. 1065B] O daughters, who have followed the footsteps of Christ in the love of chastity, and who have chosen me, a poor woman, as your mother in the humility of subjection for the sake of heavenly exaltation: I speak to you through maternal bowels, not from myself but from divine revelation. I found this place—namely, the resting-place of the relics of blessed Robert the confessor, to whose protection you fled—in manifest miracles, by God’s will, as a sacrifice of praise; and with my teachers’ permission I came to it and, with divine help, freely drew it to myself and to all who follow me.

Later, however, at God’s admonition, I went to the mountain of Saint Disibod, from which I had departed with permission; and there, before all who lived in that place, I made this petition: namely, that our place and the landed possessions given in alms to our place should not be bound to them but free, while nevertheless seeking, where useful opportunity allowed, the salvation of our souls and the care of regular strictness. And according to what I received in a true vision, I said to the Father—that is, to the abbot of that place: “The Serene Light says: ‘Be thou the Father set over the salvation of the souls of the mystical planting of my daughters. Their alms belong neither to thee nor to thy brethren, but let your place be their refuge. But if you persist in your hostile words, gnashing against us, you will be like the Amalekites and Antiochus, of whom it is written that he despoiled the temple of the Lord’” (1 Macc. 1). [Col. 1065C]

[Col. 1066B] “And if any among you, in his unworthiness, says, ‘We wish to diminish their allodial lands,’ then I, who am, say that you are most wicked robbers. But if you attempt to take away from them the shepherd of spiritual healing, then again I say that you are like the sons of Belial, and in this you do not regard God’s justice; therefore God’s justice will destroy you.”

And when I, a poor womanly form, sought by these words from the aforesaid abbot and his brethren the stated freedom of the place and the allodial lands of my daughters, they all granted it to me with the authorization of a written document. All alike, both greater and lesser, seeing, hearing, and understanding these things, showed the greatest goodwill toward them, so that they were also confirmed in writing at God’s command. Therefore let the faithful learn, affirm, accomplish, [Col. 1066C] and defend these things, so that they may receive that blessing which God gave to Jacob and Israel.

But oh, what great lamentation these daughters of mine will have after the death of their mother, because the words of that same mother will no longer arise; and thus, in groaning and mourning for very many times, with tears: “Alas, alas, we would gladly suck at the breasts of our mother, if only we had her present with us now.” Therefore, O daughters of God, I admonish you to have charity among yourselves, as I, your mother, have admonished you from my girlhood, so that through your good will you may be a most beloved light with the angels, and most strong in your powers, as your father Benedict taught you. The Holy Spirit counsels gifts to you, because after my end you will henceforth no longer hear my voice.

[Col. 1067A] But let my voice, which has often sounded among you in charity, never be led into oblivion among you. My daughters now glow in their hearts, because of the sorrow which they have for their mother, panting and sighing toward heavenly things. Afterwards they will shine in most radiant and glowing light through the grace of God, and will become most valiant soldiers in his house. Therefore, if anyone in this company of my daughters should wish to bring about discord and the breaking-up of this dwelling and spiritual discipline, may the gift of the Holy Spirit turn this away from that person’s heart. But if, despising God, that person nevertheless does it, may the hand of the Lord kill that person before all the people, because that person deserves to be put to shame. Therefore, O daughters, inhabit with all devotion and steadfastness this place which you have chosen for fighting for God,

[Col. 1067B] so that in it you may obtain heavenly rewards. Hence Charity says in Wisdom: “I was ordained from ancient time, and I was present at the forming of the first man, when he was fashioned by God”; for God wisely created heaven, earth, and the remaining creatures for the sake of man, so that he might be sustained and fed by them. (Ecclus. 24.) Thus Wisdom may rightly be called an artificer, because she encompassed heaven and earth and weighed them with equal weight. But the flesh of man is wholly infused with soul in its veins and marrow, so that the flesh is always animated by the soul; and because man also knows creatures through the soul, he possesses them in pleasure and joy. Thus man in flesh and soul is lovable, as it were, through mercy and charity, just as Wisdom and

[Col. 1067C] Charity are one.

Through these two virtues, namely Wisdom and Charity, angels and human beings will obey God in humility, because humility frequently bends itself toward the honor of God and thus gathers all virtues to itself. In these virtues, therefore, God fashioned humanity lest it perish altogether; just as not all the angels perished, because many remained with God, while others fell with the ancient serpent. For God created humanity in wisdom, gave it life in charity, and governed it in humility and obedience, so that it might understand how it ought to live. But the first Angel was unwilling to understand these things—which could not be otherwise, since life is one from itself, from which all living things have life.

[Col. 1067D] Therefore he fell from life and withered, as also sometimes occurs among creatures—namely, trees, herbs, and other created things—when some of them fall and dry up because they have not tasted the sap. For an angel has life from God; but a human being is the complete work of God, because God is always at work in that person. A human being can understand this in himself, because as long as he lives in this life he does not cease to think and to do something, wherever he may be; but when he is finished in this life, he lives without end in another life. For when a human being does good, he becomes like the good angels; but when he does not recognize the great honor of how God formed him, and flees from right obedience, and does not act in humility

[Col. 1068A] but wishes to exist from himself, he becomes like the worst angels, falls from life like Satan, and withers. But you, O human being, wish to hold God guilty in these matters. Therefore this answer is given to you: “Did you create yourself?” No. Is it therefore more fitting that you should serve yourself rather than him who created you? And what reward can you prepare for yourself, since you did not make yourself? None, but the punishment of fire.

Thus angels, human beings, and the remaining creatures of God are divided into these two parts, as also happened to you when God marked humanity in circumcision. For the first deceiver deceitfully deceived the first human being, so that, made disobedient to God, he assented to that deceiver’s words and through disobedience did what he had advised. But that same matter was cut off in obedience through circumcision

[Col. 1068B] by the command of God, when Abraham willingly obeyed God, doing as he commanded him (Gen. 17). Then that same deceiver raged inwardly with guile, instilling this evil into certain people: that it would be impossible for them to confess as God one whom they could neither see, hear, nor touch. And so he reveled among the people marked by obedience, and remembered that he had deceived the first human being when he said, “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). He breathed into them a most evil inspiration, saying that they could by no means know God except through some fornication, because man too was a form; and, if God had created man, why would he hide himself so that man could neither see, hear, nor comprehend him?

[Col. 1068C] But the whole old law and the people truly marked could not crush this ancient deceiver and these erring people, nor will they yet be able to do so; but God will crush them before the last day and conquer before all the people. Thus the old law, together with all these—that is, with those who observed circumcision, and also with those who were in the aforesaid error—ran on until the birth of Christ, where he himself, the true Sun of righteousness, appeared in truth. And that same Sun gave great splendor through his teaching, being seen and heard in his humanity, because the prophets had gone before him, just as certain planets are above the sun—a thing God had foreseen

[Col. 1068D] when he established the firmament with all its adornments. But to the sun, together with the moon and stars, God joined water and set clouds with tempest, which lightning pierces and which are sometimes torn apart by the sound of thunder, so that they are moved. For just as God established this creation for the service of humanity, so he also prefigured through it his Son, whom the prophets foretold and whose humanity they touched through the service of prophecy, just as the planets support the sun by serving it.

For the prophecy which said, “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive” (Isa. 7), touched upon his humanity, because the virginity of the Virgin conceived from the heat of the Holy Spirit and not from the heat of flesh; just as the sun so penetrates a thing with its rays that from its heat it becomes wholly warm,

[Col. 1069A] yet is not consumed. For the Sun of righteousness came forth from the undefiled Virgin and illuminated the whole world, just as the sun illuminates the whole world through the firmament, which nevertheless remains whole. Thus the Virgin bore a son whose name is Emmanuel, because he came forth from her in integrity, as the sun flashes through the firmament without either being divided. Therefore God is with us, because in that same Incarnation, which arose from the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb, the holy divinity was wholly and entirely present, like the sun in the firmament; and the power of divinity transcends the heavens, the depths, and all creatures. Yet the Son of God was then with us through his holy humanity. And through the offering

[Col. 1069B] of his body and through his teaching, he is now with us and will be until we see him openly.

Water is likewise present to that same Sun of righteousness together with moon and stars: namely, that he might send his disciples throughout the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark 16). For what the prophets had foretold about him he fulfilled in himself, just as on the seventh day from the creation of the world God rested from all his work (Gen. 2). And just as God then subjected every creature to serve humanity, so now the Son of God, after his ascension, entrusted the works of his Incarnation to his disciples when, at his command, they preached the Gospel to every creature. For they showed people the right faith concerning the Son of God, as they had seen and known his miracles while remaining with him, just as the sun shines in the firmament.

[Col. 1069C] When an innumerable multitude of peoples received this faith, the Church was established, as the moon with the stars was set in the firmament. Those same peoples also established among themselves various teachers and prelates, inspired by the Holy Spirit, so that they might uphold the whole Church, just as the firmament was illuminated with sun, moon, and stars.

Then thunder and lightning were raised up through unbelieving people and cruel tyrants, who attacked the Lord’s faithful—burning in faith as the sun shines in its strength—like wolves, and shed their blood so that there was not even anyone to bury them. The thunder which sounded at Satan’s first fall, when

[Col. 1069D] he was plunged into hell, also rose through God’s enemies, who did not cease to sin in their sins; and lightning appeared in very many Christians who divided the faith by unbelief and burned many Catholics. This happened through Arius, whom Athanasius utterly trampled down, strengthened by John the Evangelist, who reclined upon Jesus’ breast and drew from it that which flew aloft when, in a mystical breathing, he set forth the Gospel concerning divinity.

Likewise Athanasius afterwards wrote concerning the unity of Divinity, strengthening the Church: namely, that every person who wishes to be saved should hold the faith whole and inviolate, believing perfectly in God, lest, plunged into Gehenna, that person become hellish. But the true faith is that one God in the Trinity of persons,

[Col. 1070A] and that same Trinity in one God, is to be gloriously honored without any confusion of division in the unity; because one God is inseparably one substance of divinity. For the Father is not one thing in substance, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; nor are they separated from one another in the substance of divinity. Rather, in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there is one divinity of one substance in the glory of majesty.

Nevertheless, the person of the Father is other than that of the Son or Holy Spirit; the person of the Son is other than that of the Father or Holy Spirit; and the person of the Holy Spirit is other than that of the Father or Son. Yet the divinity of these persons is inseparable, their honor equal and steadfast, their power coeternal and unconquerable. For as the Father is in divinity, but not in person,

[Col. 1070B] so is the Son in divinity, but not in person; and so also is the Holy Spirit in divinity, but not in person. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct in their persons; nevertheless, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not different in the substance of divinity.

And how are these persons to be understood? God is rational in his Word and lives. God created the world—namely humanity with all its glory—which God had always held in eternity as something that ought to exist. God alone did this, apart from whom there is no one. And who could make him who does not exist come into existence? No one at all. God made all things in his Word, as John, who reclined upon Christ’s breast, affirms (John 1).

[Col. 1070C] But God is fire; in this fire a flame lies hidden, and this flame is mobile in life. Yet in this fire there is no division, except the distinction of persons. Material and visible fire is golden in color, and in its fire a flame flashes, blazing in a strong wind. This fire would not flash unless it were fiery, and it would not be mobile except through wind; hence there are three terms in this fire. For the flame is from the fire, the fire flashes through the flame, and it is mobile only through a strong wind. Fire burns with flame, and this heat wholly pervades and inflames both fire and flame equally; and if heat were not in the fire, there would be no fire, nor would the flame have the sound of thunder.

The soul also is fire, and its fire pervades the whole body in which it is,

[Col. 1070D] namely the veins with their blood, the bones with their marrow, and the flesh with its bruise-colour; and it is inextinguishable. The soul’s fire possesses heat in rationality, by which it gives voice to speech. If the soul were not fiery, it would not burn away cold coagulation, nor would it build the body with blood-filled veins. Because the soul is airy in rationality, it rightly distributes its heat throughout all the parts of the body, lest it burn up the body. But when the soul has torn itself from the body, the body fails, just as logs do not burn when they lack the heat of fire.

For humanity is rational according to God, and human rationality sounds in wind with fire. Rationality is indeed a great power, fiery and undivided; and if it were not fiery, it would not be airy; and if it were not airy,

[Col. 1071A] it would not sound. Therefore God created all things, and apart from him alone no one has ever made anything living, although human beings fashion various things by their art; yet they do not make them live, because humanity has a beginning. And he who created all things was not created, because no beginning existed before him; rather, he is without beginning, and all things are in him, because through him all things were made (John 1).

Through those things which a human being flees from through fear lest they harm him, he has confidence in the Lord, crying that the Lord may help him and preserve him in the rest of peace. But through those things that exist for humanity, that exist within humanity, with which humanity works, and which are present to humanity gently and suitably, humanity learns to have charity toward God.

[Col. 1071B] For if a human being knew nothing except what was light and pleasant to him, he would not know what that thing itself was or what it was called. Thus from the weight and hardness of harmful things he has the highest knowledge, and knows what good and evil are, and knows how to name them, like Adam. For if he knew only one thing in things, God’s work in him would not be complete; he would not know the thing he saw, nor could he know what sort of thing that which he heard was. Therefore he would be empty and extinguished, like that which, burned by fire, is turned into charcoal.

Accordingly, as has been said, the Father is uncreated, the Son likewise uncreated, and so also the Holy Spirit uncreated; because these three persons are one God, and all creatures were created through the same God. But without him nothing was made

[Col. 1071C] (John 1). The beginning which was made at the beginning of creation wished to possess the likeness of him who is without beginning; but this could by no means come about, because it was nothing, since in God are life and truth, whereas in the fallen angel and in humanity is vanity, puffed up by pride, which passed by like wind. And what was made through God and in God has life in him; and God crushed the head of him who first seized upon the aforesaid evils and cast into hell him who is without life.

The Father is also immeasurable, unable to be contained by any capacity or limited by number, as can those things which were made in the beginning. For God held all things in his presence, yet did not create them all at once;

[Col. 1071D] hence there is also a certain interval among creatures, as in a human being who becomes infant, child, youth, old man, and decrepit person—something which can indeed be comprehended. And of the Son and Holy Spirit likewise it must be understood that they are immeasurable and cannot be comprehended either by capacity or number.

The Father is also eternal, in that eternity which never began and which resembles a revolving wheel in which neither beginning nor end is discerned. For God is spirit (John 4). Every spirit is incomprehensible and indivisible. Eternity, without any change in that which is called “was and is,” remains eternal, and no one in it is made like God. For eternity is one, and all his creatures were made through it.

[Col. 1072A] And the Son, coeternal with the Father in divinity, put on from a creature the garment which is humanity. Divinity revealed this garment just as the sun’s ray is fixed in it. The sun sends its light upon the earth, yet is neither increased nor diminished by doing so; nor was the Son of God, in coming into the world, increased or diminished in divinity, because he put on his garment just as God clothed Adam from fragile creation lest he appear naked. For humanity could by no means see eternity except in humanity, because divinity lay hidden in humanity; so the Son was known through the garment of humanity, just as a person clothed in armor is known although, concealed within it, he cannot be seen.

The Holy Spirit also is eternal, coeternal with Father and Son,

[Col. 1072B] present at the beginning of every creature and making it movable by inspiring it. There are not three eternities in God, however, but one eternity in him; it is not divided into three, as Arius made portions within it, just as a human being’s limbs are severed by amputation. Rather, eternity is one divinity, which human rationality cannot name by a single name because of its most powerful works. And because humanity has a beginning and turns into ashes, it cannot describe those things which are before the beginning and after the end; but holding one faith in its soul, it speaks of the substance of God, which is spiritual.

For the soul is a breath from God, and thus apprehends many invisible things and senses in right faith the unity of divinity:

[Col. 1072C] that there are not three uncreated gods nor three immeasurable ones, but one God—uncreated and immeasurable—not divided into three modes or three parts. The Father is also almighty, who created all things through his Word, his almighty Son; and the almighty Holy Spirit, who is life, so pervades all things as the heat of fire and flame burns. Yet there are not three almighties, but God in three persons is one almighty God.

And just as it would be incongruous for a human being—one human being with a rational soul—to be divided into three, since then there would not be whole life but a mortal corpse, how could the one life, in which there is no mortality of beginning or change, be divided? God is Father, who is powerful; God is Son,

[Col. 1072D] who is the power of the Father; God is Holy Spirit, who is life, through which every life proceeds. Yet they are not three gods, but, without any division, one divinity whose most powerful force is named by individual names. Thus in ruling, the Father is Lord; in working, the Son is Lord; in giving life, the Holy Spirit is Lord. These are the complete divinity of three names, just as God signified all his work in one power of divinity. Nor are they separately ruling lords, but in complete integrity one divinity exists in the three powers of the three persons: ruling, working, and giving life to all creatures, and moving them toward their function. Thus there is one Lord.

[Col. 1073A] This Lord made two works: namely, the angel and humanity with every creature. But the angel is spirit; humanity was made in the image and likeness of God in order to act through the five senses of its body. Through these it is not divided, but by them it is wise, knowing, and understanding in accomplishing its works. God marked these three powers in humanity through the fact that the human soul is rational: it moves the body to work, and in it the five senses of the human body are fully carried out.

For through sight a human being knows creatures; through hearing rationality tells him what that which he hears is; through smell he distinguishes what is suitable or unsuitable for his use; through taste he knows by what and what kinds of things he is nourished;

[Col. 1073B] and through touch he does good and evil, directing all his works through the aforesaid five senses. These five senses are so joined into one in a human being that none can lack another, and they are in one human being, who is nevertheless not divided into two or three human beings; rather, he performs all his works through these five senses and is one human being.

And through being wise, knowing, and understanding, humanity knows creatures. Again, through creatures and through God’s great works—which it scarcely comprehends even by its five senses—humanity knows God, whom it cannot see except in faith. Thus through its five senses humanity comprehends and knows all things in creatures: through sight it loves, through taste it savors, through hearing it discerns,

[Col. 1073C] through smell it chooses what is suitable for itself, and through touch it works what pleases it; and in this it images God, who created all creatures.

Likewise, through being wise humanity knows what is pleasing or harmful to itself; through being knowing, it binds a creature by command so that it may be subject in serving it, draws to itself what it wishes, and drives away what it does not wish; and through being understanding, it knows what function is suitable for each creature. With these three powers and their appendages humanity is rational in the soul, which is by no means divided; so that even if, through the devil’s persuasion, some limb of a human being is cut off, the rational soul is in no way divided on that account. But the body,

[Col. 1073D] the structure of the soul, works with it according to its capacity for sensation, just as a mill is turned by water.

Therefore let all peoples anointed with chrism confess that the three persons are in unity, and that the three persons are one true and steadfast divinity. And since there are not three souls in one rational soul, which possesses three powers, but one soul, why should there be a separable division in the unity of divinity, when all things have been created by God? Therefore it must by no means be said that there are three gods or three lords. Rather, one God is named, who created all things; and one Lord, whom all creatures invoke as Lord and whose own sheep they are. Therefore every singularity in the unity of divinity must be prohibited, because

[Col. 1074A] God is one.

The Father was made by no one, since no one appeared before him from whom he could be begotten or created; rather, he is eternal without beginning. The Son is from the Father alone without any separation: not made as something having a beginning, nor created in members, but begotten, as light is in the sun without any separation. He assumed flesh from the Virgin Mary; yet the brightness of divinity did not depart from him, because he was eternally with the Father in divinity, although in time he put on his garment, namely flesh, from the Virgin Mother.

But the Holy Spirit is life, which moves every breath in creatures. He was not made life through any breath, nor was he created by anyone or begotten by anyone else; rather, he exists coeternal and coequal with Father and Son in divinity.

[Col. 1074B] For he was present in the first creation of the world, because “the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1), illuminating the circuit of the whole world when the Word of God said, “Let it be.” Proceeding in the truth of prophecy from Father and Son, the Holy Spirit caused the prophets to prophesy. Yet they very often concealed the depth of prophecy even while writing its text, because they sometimes spoke by signification, as in shadow and a vision of the night.

Coming upon the apostles in fiery tongues, he filled them wholly and made them different people from what they had previously been, so that they saw those same tongues and felt the touch of the same Holy Spirit. Before Christ’s birth he appeared thus to no human being, nor will he appear afterwards, because Christ is the only-begotten of God.

[Col. 1074C] His appearance to them in fiery tongues occurred because the Virgin Mary conceived the Son of God in his fiery heat, and thus he also proceeds from Father and Son. And because the apostles saw him in fire, he spoke openly with wisdom and understanding. Since the Son of God was conceived in the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1), the Holy Spirit remained and remains in him, and is always with him; nor are they ever mutually separated. Therefore it is whole and pure faith that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, as has been said.

But when the Son said, “Who proceeds from the Father” (John 15), he said this for the Father’s honor, having regard to the fact that his Incarnation was in time, whereas time does not belong to the Father’s divinity.

[Col. 1074D] Therefore there is one Father, not three Fathers, but one Father; because if there were no Father, he would not have begotten the Son, and if the begotten Son had not existed, the world would not have been created. There is likewise one Son, not three Sons but one, through whom all things were made, consubstantial with the Father; and one Holy Spirit, not three Holy Spirits but one, giving life to and moving all things.

For every root contains greenness within itself, from which fruit proceeds. This is perceived unevenly, yet the three are in one. Why, then, should the Creator of all things not be in a Trinity of persons? The person of the Father is to be understood through the root, that of the Son through the fruit, and that of the Holy Spirit through the greenness; and they are not separated from one another,

[Col. 1075A] but are one God. In this unity of Trinity there is nothing earlier by preceding, nothing later by following, nothing greater in magnificence, nothing lesser in power. The persons of this whole Trinity join themselves together into one without any emptiness; in eternity and equality they are coeternal and coequal with one another. Thus in these persons there is nothing of which, according to divinity, one can say: “It is and was not,” “great and small.” For God, lacking beginning and end, receives neither increase nor diminution because he is unchangeable.

But God’s work in creation, formerly unformed, now appears formed; it passes through times, expanding itself into greater things and contracting itself into lesser. Therefore the three persons are in unity, and one God is to be worshipped in three persons,

[Col. 1075B] because he created all things and is life through which all living things proceed. Let every believer receive this without doubt. It is also necessary for the believer not to separate himself from the Catholic faith, but to believe that the Incarnation of the Son of God is true, and to consider himself: how he was created, and how, as a body working with a rational soul, he is one. For God foresaw before times the form of humanity in which he would assume flesh; and whoever doubts this denies himself, and does not believe that one human being is constituted in the two natures of soul and body through three modes. For if one of these three—soul, body, and rationality, of which humanity consists—were absent, there would be no human being.

For humanity

[Col. 1075C] is rational in the soul, which accomplishes everything in the body with the sound of words; because creatures attend humanity as branches attend a tree, since humanity was not created without the remaining creation, just as a tree was not created without branches.

Therefore the right faith is truly that Christ, the Son of God, born before times, is God and is also true human being through the garment of flesh. He is God from the substance of the Father, because he is coeternal and coequal with him without time, begotten before the ages, because all things were made through him (John 1). But through his humanity, which has time, he is human from the substance of his mother. For he is full God in the integrity of eternity, and full human being with a rational soul and pure flesh, without any male

[Col. 1075D] admixture of human nature. He is equal to the Father in the eternity of divinity, but lesser than him in the humanity which has time.

Being God and human, he was not divided into two, but is one Christ—not by a change of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of flesh, which divinity joined to itself and so pervaded with its brightness as a ray of sun shines in the sun. Yet by this no confusion occurred between the substance of divinity and the substance of flesh; rather, in the true unity of person, Christ is one, the true Son of God.

So too, in the rational soul there is no change caused by the human body, because it is itself rational breath from God, pervading the whole human body and moving every work of the acting human being. And

[Col. 1076A] just as soul and flesh are one human being, so also, without any doubt, the Son of God—born before the ages, wholly clothed, as has been said, in flesh assumed from the Virgin—is God and human and one Christ, called Christ, assuredly, through the anointing of God’s grace.

In his holy humanity he was wounded by the piercing of nails and spear (John 19; Isa. 53) on account of the one wound of the first human being, which that human being had inflicted upon his whole race, so that he might heal it with the bruise-colour of his blood, pervade it with the anointing oil of grace, and bind it through penitence when humanity grieves that it has sinned. Wounded, he descended spiritually into the pit of infernal depth, and there drew many to himself: namely, he took the first human being away from that hell, and all who had ever touched God in the customs of human honor,

[Col. 1076B] and placed them in the place of delights and joys which they had lost in the first parent.

But in rising on the third day from the death of his sleeping body, he signified the three persons of divinity. Ascending in that same body, he went to heaven and there sits ruling at the right hand of the Father. This is the salvation of the believing people, granting life to those whom he redeemed by his blood.

All these were foreknown before the times of all beginnings, because the Word of the Father, through whom all things were made (John 1), put on flesh in order to redeem the human being whom he had formed. The same Son of God will come at the end of the age as righteous judge to judge

[Col. 1076C] the living and the dead: the living, namely, those who worked the work of faith and were found in that good work; and the dead, those who worked deeds of death through unbelief. At the voice of the calling trumpet, human beings will lie subject to that same Son of God as a footstool for judgment, because then, on seeing him, each worthy person will recognize him.

For at the coming of this judge, through the aforesaid summons, the dead will rise with their bodies, just as every creature also came forth through the sound of God’s Word. All will answer to their judge concerning their own deeds performed in the perishing body. No one will be able to excuse himself, because then each person will openly see, recognizing them, those works which formerly he knew only that he had done; for they are upon him as if in a garment,

[Col. 1076D] and therefore they will follow him everywhere.

Those who have done just and right works will go into a brightness of life greater than the sun shines upon this world, their souls illuminated by grace. The angels praise God because these people performed such great works that they are gloriously surrounded by them, as a human being is clothed in a precious garment. The Son of Man will also raise to himself in his blood the innumerable multitude of those who, before their end or even at their end, perfectly performed penitence and confessed God amid their sins; and he will repay each one in life according to that person’s works.

But the wicked, having no excuse for their unjust works and not knowing what they can say—those who worshipped idols through the arts of the devil and performed evil works without end with

[Col. 1077A] the devilish host—will be clothed in the shame of their works and will descend with the devil into the pit of hell, which he occupied when he wished to be like God.

Therefore it must truly and confidently be believed that the one Godhead in three persons, and the three persons in one Godhead, are the one life of eternity; and whoever does not so believe shall be cut off from the day of salvation. But you, O masters and teachers of the people, why are you blind and dumb in the inward knowledge of the Scriptures, which God has set before you, just as he established the sun, moon, and stars so that rational man might know and distinguish the seasons of times by them? The knowledge of the Scriptures has been placed before you so that, as in a sunbeam, you may recognize every danger in it [Col. 1077B], and so that by your teaching you may shine like the moon in the darkness of night upon the unbelief of erring people—those who are like Sadducees and heretics, and many others who err in faith, who are enclosed among you and whom many even among you know to be like cattle and beasts, with faces bent downward. For they neither see nor wish to know that, through the breath of life, they are rational; nor do they lift their heads toward him who created them and governs them through the five senses which he gave them.

Why, then, is there in a rational human being the likeness of a downward-bent animal, which is stirred by a breath of air that it exhales again and thus comes to its end; which has no knowledge beyond what it feels and fears what strikes it; and which does nothing of itself [Col. 1077C] unless it is driven to do so? And how is it fitting that a human being should be in the company of cattle, which are subject to him for service, by which he is fed, and over which he commands and rules, because they are not rational? Hence the supreme Father speaks to the Son, as is written through the Holy Spirit: “You shall rule them with a rod of iron; like a potter’s vessel you shall break them” (Psalm 2). This means: Those who resist you, rule them with the iron rod, which chastises harshly; and like a potter’s vessel, made of clay, you shall break them, for they too are from the earth. They do not enter through the door of uprightness by faith, nor go forth through the renown of good works; for they are thieves and, through the self-will of their own desire, slaughter and destroy whatever they wish, because they are hypocrites, overturning the law to their own destruction [Col. 1077D].

But you who, in the teaching proper to masters, are as moon and stars to your hearers—yet who chew over Scripture more for the honor and riches of the world than for God—hear and understand that it would be far more necessary for you to cut through the nocturnal darkness of erring and unbelieving people, who do not know on what road they walk, so that you might draw them to us through faith. Therefore rule them now, showing them by true admonition that God in the beginning created heaven, earth, and the remaining creatures for humanity, and placed humanity in the delightful place of paradise, giving the commandment which humanity transgressed; for which reason humanity was expelled into the darkness of this exile. In that very transgression it was shown how great [Col. 1078A] an offense it was that humanity obeyed not the Creator but the one who seduced it (Genesis 3); for it is more just to obey the Lord than the deceitful servant who made himself like his master.

With these words, then, fill their hearts with the iron rod, so that they may know not to turn away from their Creator; or, if through unbelief they have turned aside from him, that they will fall into the grave of hell with the one whom they have imitated. For those who persist in unbelief shall be broken like a potter’s vessel which seems unworthy and unsuitable to the potter; and because they have not done works of faith, they will be unable to enter eternal life, just as a badly made potter’s vessel is not repaired but broken. Understand these things, you who rule the people; look to the invisible God, whom no one can overcome [Col. 1078B] or see with bodily eyes; and attend to how you govern the stewardship which you have received from him. For you have been glorified with great honor in his name; thus rule the people so that on the day of judgment you may not blush before him over your governance. Take care also that pleasure of the flesh and worldly delights do not so weary you that you can scarcely open even one eye to heavenly teaching.

But these things are hard for you, because whoever carefully attends to heavenly things wounds his whole body in what he governs, since he withdraws from himself the desires of the flesh. Therefore, for fear of God, who is life and truth, do not despise this human being, who writes these things in female form [Col. 1078C], unlearned in scholarly instruction, weak from childhood until the sixtieth year of her life, and one who neither saw nor heard this writing with the eyes and ears of the outward person, but saw and heard it only in the inward knowledge of her soul. Therefore do not exalt your minds on high by despising her, since God made an irrational animal speak as he wished (Numbers 22).

This vision, in which I, a little poor woman, saw this form, has not departed from my soul from my childhood until the aforesaid age. And I wrote the foregoing things in this place, which was destroyed by certain tyrants and remained desolate through very many courses of years; here rest the relics of Saint Robert, who was noble according to the rank of the present world [Col. 1078D], and whom God gloriously gathered to himself in the twentieth year of his life. This place, after those same years of desolation, has at last been restored by the grace of God in his wonders. For the Lord was mindful in this saint of those words which, speaking to his disciples, he said: “Even all the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matthew 10); nor did he wish to refrain from revealing him.

The merits of the saints ought to be written down, so that good and upright renown may sound in the ears of the faithful, just as creation also sounds praises to God because it was created by him. For God is eternal, and his work was made for the praise of his name; since if the soul were not in the human body, a human being would not live, nor would the soul work without flesh. Thus the angel [Col. 1079A] is praise in God, and the human being is work in God. Therefore let praise be to him in all his wonders and in the merits of the saints—he who is true eternity, creating all things and renewing heaven and earth on the last day; none has touched his height and depth, and none can comprehend the breadth of his knowledge.

Therefore this Scripture is to be heard and understood by the faithful: O how glorious is the Godhead, which, in creating and working, manifests itself through its creation, as it did in the three boys, whom it so infused that, without any sight of the Scriptures and without human instruction, they praised him in the furnace of fire (Daniel 3). For just as the blessed soul, stripped of flesh, desires to savor and know nothing but God, so these three blessed boys, still living in the flesh, by ardently desiring God imitated the nature of the soul.

God the Father also willed that, in Nebuchadnezzar's unbelief born of ignorance, his Son should be named, just as even evil spirits know him, though they do not confess him; and to all these God often displays his wonders. He also manifested his omnipotence in the mighty Samson, who overcame lions and fierce beasts by his strength (Judges 14), yet was deceived by his wife, as Adam was by Eve. Nevertheless, afterward recovering his strength, he conquered that woman and his other enemies (Judges 16), just as Christ, despoiling hell, laid waste the power of his enemies.

In David’s most severe battle against Goliath, he prefigured (1 Samuel 17) that through the humanity of his Son he would bind [Col. 1079C] the ancient serpent. He also sent such power into a woman’s tender feminine sensibility that a woman, killing Holofernes at night, delivered the Israelite people (Judith 13); and in this he prefigured the mother of his Son, through whom the faithful people were to be delivered. In the saints of old, through the prophecy of prophets and the burnt offerings of rams and bulls, he caused the covenantal pact to be foreshadowed, because he foretold that the Church would be joined to his Son in the union of betrothal.

For through the garment of the humanity of the Son of God, the Church clings to that same Son of God, who endowed her in his own blood as his inheritance, so that through baptism she regenerates unto life offspring whom Eve brought forth unto death [Col. 1079D]. For Christ betrothed the Church to himself in his blood, as was prefigured by the oath which Abraham’s servant swore under his master’s thigh (Genesis 24), namely, that the Church was to be betrothed to Christ.

But when Lucifer, with all who accompanied him, perceived that God the Father had publicly made wedding festivities for his Son, he raged within himself; and as Cain rose up against Abel’s blood (Genesis 4), so he invaded the hearts of unbelievers and tyrants, so that they might seize, wound, and kill the righteous, good, and chosen of God. Hence Christ spoke to his disciples the parable concerning a king who sent servants for those invited to the wedding; but when they would not come, he sent other servants to them that they might come, because his banquet was ready [Col. 1080A] (Matthew 22). When they disregarded this, they seized his servants, maltreated them, and killed them, because the Jews and other unbelieving people, often assembling in great rejoicing, wiped from the earth the ancient saints whom God had first sent and the apostles sent afterward.

But God remembered his covenant by the bow set in the clouds of heaven (Genesis 9), when he willed that his Son—whom that same bow signifies—should be born from the intact nature of a virgin. He overcame all his enemies by mightily conquering them, just as people were destroyed through the water of the flood (Genesis 7), though a new age of humankind was restored through the water of baptism, with Christ reigning in the Church, appearing as a bow in the clouds. For the Church is joined to the Son of God as circumcision is joined to the law: circumcision, serving as a sign, ran ahead of the Church. But the new age, gilded by the adornment of the Church, shall never be mocked in complete ruin. Just as the bow in heaven will not fail, but will be so compressed with fear that it can scarcely see with one eye, it will be restored again in the Son of God.

Moreover, in the various colors of the aforesaid bow are signified the powers of the virtues of the thousandfold number of saints: in the fiery color, chastity and continence; in purple, the martyrdoms of martyrs; in hyacinth, the teaching of the elders; and in green, the virtues of the saints’ good works, breathed forth through the Son of God and shining as rays proceed from the sun.

The aforesaid king, having sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned [Col. 1080C] their city. For when the sufferings—that is, the ancient ones—had passed on in their course, almighty God was angry with his enemies when the Roman rulers, by undermining Jerusalem, which had been drenched with the blood of the true Lamb and the blood of other saints, utterly overthrew it and, by killing and seeing them, destroyed all the lawful institutions of those who dwelt in it. Then the Church was rebuilt, just as the new holy city Jerusalem descended from heaven (Revelation 12), prepared by God like a bride adorned for her husband. For the Lamb of God gathered to himself people of nursing, childish, youthful, mature, and decrepit age; and he adorned the Church with them in the newness of good works and the humility of virtues descending from heaven [Col. 1080D], as each of them performed good and holy works, prepared by the Holy Spirit, just as a bride is adorned for her husband when she burns in his love.

And as the Church was joined to Christ, so God acted also in his chosen one, namely blessed Robert, whom he wholly suffused in childhood and led to a good end. Noble in birth and worldly riches, through the freedom bestowed by God’s blessing he became dear to God. For, as I see in a true vision, our blessed patron Robert, bereft of his father, living in this place with his widowed mother, laboring at good works, and serving God in chastity, humility, and holiness, purchased eternal rewards with things perishable and temporal. For as the living light showed and taught me in true vision, so I shall speak of him.

Wherever the reputation of true sanctity existed, there sanctity could stand and remain for a long time; wherever true sanctity was absent, there falsehood could not endure long. As the divine majesty openly showed, true sanctity existed in blessed Robert when it transported me and certain sisters with me to the place of his relics by the great miracle of great visions [Col. 1081A; 1082A], as is plain to all who see and wish to know. Therefore, the father of the mother of blessed Robert was of Lotharingian origin, etc. What follows is read at the beginning of the Life of Saint Robert, written by Hildegard herself.

[Col. 1081]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT RUPERT, DUKE OF BINGEN IN THE DIOCESE OF MAINZ, WRITTEN BY SAINT HILDEGARD, ABBESS

*(Acta Sanctorum Bollandiana, May, vol. III, 15 May, p. 503.)*

## [NOTICE]

Bingen, or Binga—formerly also called Pingia—is a German town on the Rhine, where that river receives the Nahe, four leagues below Mainz. For almost two hundred years it has been subject to the metropolitan chapter of that city. Its neighboring district, called Nachgouve, or the district of the Nahe, together with its dependent places, is extensively described by Marquard Freher in part II of his *Origines Palatinae*, chapter 11. Saint Rupert—called by some Robert or Ropert—was formerly duke of that territory after his parents. Of him Freher says: “The forename Rupert, as though of some ancestral saint, pleased the Palatines more than other names—for ten Ruperts are counted in this family.” Rupert, brother of the Count Palatine of the Rhine, is still alive.

Saint Hildegard, abbess, wrote this saint’s Life from a true vision “by which she had been instructed,” as she says in the prologue. As Trithemius writes in the *Chronicle of Sponheim* under the year 1148, while settled on Mount Saint Disibod, divinely admonished, she crossed to Bingen with eighteen holy virgins and built a monastery on the hill beyond the Nahe, beside the tomb of Saint Rupert, duke and confessor. As the same Trithemius adds in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1150, she “constructed a convent for sacred virgins in the place where Saint Rupert, duke, together with his mother Bertha, a holy woman, had a castle and dwelling in the time of Emperor Louis I.” In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Trithemius lists works written by Saint Hildegard, among them the *Life of Saint Rupert the Confessor*, beginning, “For, as I see in a true vision”; but he lacked the preceding three or four lines.

2. Johannes Busaeus of the Society of Jesus published this Life from a manuscript codex in the Mainz Jesuit library, together with the letters of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, and the Constitutions of Charlemagne, at Mainz in 1602. Nicolaus Serrarius reprinted the same Life in book II of his *Affairs of Mainz*, chapter 25. Here we give the same Life, elucidated in our customary manner. Saint Hildegard is commemorated on 27 September and is entered in the Roman Martyrology. We possess her Visions as we ourselves saw them, written in her own hand and divided into three books in her Bingen monastery; they were printed at Paris in 1513 and reprinted at Cologne in 1628. The prophecy once fabricated under her name against the mendicant Orders of Preachers and Friars Minor, and more recently applied with great calumny to our Society, is rightly absent from them. We discussed it in the notes to chapter 4 of the Life of Saint Thomas Aquinas, 7 March.

We found the Life of the same Saint Rupert, though abridged, in a Utrecht manuscript of the Church of Saint Saviour and in a manuscript of the abbey of Rood Klooster of Canons Regular near Brussels. Jacobus Kobelius, secretary of the town of Oppenheim, also translated it into German; he dedicated it to Adelheid, abbess of “the monastery on Saint Rupert’s Mount,” and published it at Oppenheim in 1524, adorned with splendid illustrations.

3. The sacred commemoration of Saint Rupert the confessor, Count Palatine, “on this 15th of May” is entered in these words in the manuscript *Florarium Sanctorum*. But Ropert is called “Duke Palatine of the Rhine and confessor” by Greven, the Carthusian of Cologne, in the supplement to Usuard, printed with the dates 1515 and 1521; by Canisius in the German Martyrology; and by Molanus in his Additions to Usuard, who adds: “At Bingen.” Ferrarius says in his general catalogue: “At Bingen in Upper Germany, Saint Robert, count.” Saussay likewise calls him Robert in the Gallican Martyrology, adding a lengthy encomium from the Life. Among other things Gelenius writes in the *Fasti Agrippinenses*:

> “In ancient Bingen . . . rests Saint Rupert, duke of Lotharingia and count palatine. From his relics, transferred to Cologne in 1632, a joint from his hand, in the chapel of Saint Margaret, bestows the benefits of restored health upon sufferers from fever.”

It appears that the relics of Saint Hildegard as well as of Saint Rupert were transferred to Cologne because of the Swedish wars. For in 1624 a solemn procession was held at Cologne on Pentecost to gain the Jubilee; along with the relics of Cologne’s churches, there were carried about Saint Hildegard’s heart, still whole, and tongue, likewise the head of Duke Saint Rupert, still almost entirely covered with flesh, as Franciscus vander Veken then wrote to Antwerp. In 1660 we were at Saint Hildegard’s very monastery and venerated among her relics her heart, still whole.

4. Serrarius, praised above, asserts in chapter 36 that Saint Rupert’s relics were still seen in the same monastery of virgins when he wrote in 1604, and adds: “Though the body has decomposed, it is still almost covered with skin, especially the feet; one of these is there contained in a silver shoe. Cardinal Albert is said to have taken the other foot from the remaining shoe and sent it elsewhere.” This was Albert, archbishop of Mainz from 1514 to 1545.

But formerly, when Saint Bernard came to that monastery, then, as Trithemius writes in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under 1148:

> Saint Hildegard gave to the man of God, who asked for it, a particle of the relics of Saint Rupert, Duke of Bingen and confessor; and he in turn later sent her several heads of saints. These things occurred on Mount Saint Rupert in the presence of Count Meginhard of Sponheim, under whose temporal jurisdiction the aforesaid convent was built. . . . Present there with that count were Cuno, abbot of Saint Disibod, and Bernhelm, first abbot of Sponheim, with many other clerics, monks, and laypeople. There the aforesaid Abbot Bernhelm, through the mediation of Saint Bernard, at the request of himself and Count Meginhard, obtained from Blessed Hildegard and her entire congregation of holy virgins the right leg of Duke Saint Rupert’s body, whole with skin and flesh, from below the knee down to but excluding the foot; and with great reverence and honor he brought it into his monastery at Sponheim, where we have it whole to this very day.

This is Trithemius, who relates the same matter somewhat more briefly in the *Chronicle of Sponheim*, but under the year 1150.

5. The ecclesiastical office of this saint is recited with double rite at Munich in the college of the Society of Jesus, on account of the sacred relics of that same saint preserved there: namely, a spine or a large part of one, eleven inches in length, and another bone of thirteen “inches.” Another reading there has: “Of the spine, a bone with flesh, eleven inches [long].” Thus Simon Mair, priest of the Society of Jesus and then prefect of the church at Munich, wrote to us on 5 June 1674. Later his successor, Maximus Ponzen, sent us an authentic certificate concerning various relics obtained from this saint, and others of Saint Hildegard, indeed also of Bertha his mother and Saint Satyria, virgin and martyr, which had been transferred to Bavaria. From these relics the above-mentioned relics were given to the Society at Munich. We give the full certificate after the Life itself.

In all this we acknowledge the singular kindness of the Very Reverend Father Christopher Scorrer, who, while Assistant for Germany and vicar general at Rome, treated us with every kindness and advanced our studies both there and in Bavaria and Upper Germany, which he governed as provincial and visitor, as he also several times governed the college at Munich.

6. Here the remembrance of Bertha, Saint Rupert’s mother, seems to be added. Below in the Life, just as Robert is called Blessed, so Bertha too is always called Blessed. She was laid in her son’s tomb, and likewise “the relics of herself and Blessed Rupert rest” there. In the instrument below, she is honored with the title Saint equally with her son; and “two bones of Saint Bertha the mother” were transferred along with the other relics. Trithemius calls her “a holy woman”; and in the German Life of her son, as early as 1524, she too, like him, is depicted with rays.
