Finally Arthur du Monstier, in the *Sacred Gynaeceum*, celebrates Saint Bertha on this same day with a fitting encomium.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 1083]

## CHAPTER ONE. Blessed Bertha’s marriage and widowhood. Saint Rupert’s devout childhood; his concern for the poor.

[Col. 1083A]

1. God wholly suffused blessed Robert with his grace in childhood and brought him to a good end. Though illustrious by birth and worldly wealth, through the liberality of God’s blessing he became dear to God. [Note: [Col. 1083C] Here Trithemius begins the Life.] For, as I see in a true vision, our blessed patron Robert, bereft of his father, living in this place with his mother, laboring at good works, and serving God in chastity, humility, and holiness, purchased eternal rewards with things perishable and temporal. For as the living light showed and taught me in true vision, so I shall speak of him.

Wherever the reputation of true holiness existed, there holiness could stand and remain long [Col. 1083B]; but wherever true holiness was absent, there falsehood could not long endure. True holiness, however, existed in blessed Robert, as the divine majesty openly showed when it transported me, together with certain sisters, to the place of his relics through the great miracle of great visions, as is evident to all who see and wish to know.

2. The father of blessed Robert’s mother, a native of [Note: [Col. 1083C] The name “Lotharingia” arose later; at first it was called the Kingdom of Lothair, commonly *Lother-rijck*. After the death of King Lothair, in 870, his kingdom was divided between his uncles Charles the Bald and King Louis; Bingen and the neighboring places then passed to the latter.] Lotharingia, was a prince there. Possessing a great extent of estates and wealth in the land of his birth, in other surrounding regions, and around the waters of the Rhine at Bingen, he was held great and renowned among the princes of the world. A true Catholic, he flourished in the time of Emperor Charlemagne [Col. 1083C]. He joined in marriage to himself a maiden—the mother, namely, of blessed Bertha—born in distant lands amid great wealth [Col. 1084A].

When he had had from her a daughter, the mother, namely, of blessed Robert, he solemnly united her, when she had grown up, in the glory of marriage to a certain pagan and tyrant, nevertheless noble and a duke according to worldly rank, named Robold. At that time pagans and Christians still lived together because the true faith was in its rudiments. He gave his daughter as dowry his estates around the Rhine at Bingen, so that, on account of the distinction of her birth and the extent of his estates, Robold might be compelled to embrace the Christian name; but this availed nothing. Although Robold lived commendably with her for some time, afterward, seeing her honorable character, he bore it heavily; and, joining himself to other women, he nonetheless did not abandon her in the manner of marriage. But maintaining the tyranny of an unbelieving mind, he did not love baptism.

Thus this blessed woman was greatly tormented in her heart. She vowed to God that, if she were freed from him, she would not be joined to another man’s marriage-bed. Therefore, offering God a sacrifice of praise with sighs, tears, prayers, and alms, she said: “O, O, when shall I be freed from the entanglement of this world, which is a bitter prison to my soul and body?” But let us speak rather of blessed Bertha’s benevolence than of her holiness, so that there may be glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will (Luke 2:14).

At length she conceived and bore a son; and, if it may be said, she wrapped him in swaddling-clothes, as blessed Mary, Mother of God, wrapped her son [Col. 1084C]. His father, abounding, as was said, in very great worldly glory, had a strongly fortified castle on the mountain called Lubun [Col. 1085A] and held the duchy throughout that whole province almost as far as the city of Mainz. When the blessed child Robert was three years old, his father, fighting in great battles against Christians, was killed and perished before God and men; and his wife, blessed Bertha, remained a widow.

3. Seeing herself freed from the bond of her husband and from worldly concern, she left the aforesaid castle and moved to another place, situated above the Nahe—where her relics and those of blessed Robert now rest—and there built a church. She cast aside the preciousness and splendor of clothing, no longer attending to the dignity of her birth or her wealth. Instead, clothed in cheap, coarse garments like sackcloth [Col. 1085B] and girded with a belt, she henceforth served God in the continence of widowhood, as she had long desired.

She also gathered many perfect and certain other good people to herself and remained in the aforesaid place. There, wearing herself down by vigils and fasts, daily serving God also with prayers and alms, she strengthened her son in holiness by good example. She feared that his relatives and friends might move him toward worldly pleasure; lest this happen, she commended him to God day and night. Yet very many tyrants, both worshippers of Christ and servants of idols, meanwhile assailed her. Attracted alike by the distinction of her birth and body, and coveting her wealth and estates, they desired to marry her [Col. 1085C]. But she repelled them all with one mind and one will, strove to please God alone, and labored to raise her son more for God’s glory than for worldly honor. When she saw good virtues rising in him with the good hope of heavenly life, and perceived that his mind leaned more upon eternal than transitory things, she rejoiced in the many gifts of the Holy Spirit which she saw in him.

4. For when blessed Robert was an infant at the breast, he did not display the malicious habits of infants—crying or anger. After he was weaned, in his childhood he was in his conduct like a person who, with the most diligent intention, yearned toward God. Therefore his father, hating him, had often declared while alive that he would become foolish [Col. 1085D] and stupid. But those who worshipped God with good and right faith, seeing this boy so benevolent in childhood, loved him greatly and, though through ignorance, yet spoke truly when they said that he would be blessed. For the Holy Spirit, who had suffused the patriarch Jacob in his mother’s womb with his grace, also inspired this infant, because God often performs his miracles even in those who, because of the tenderness of veins and marrow, do not yet possess full understanding [Col. 1086A]. [Note: [Col. 1085D] Here a long digression is inserted, omitted by Busaeus as less necessary and published in German by Kebelius.]

[lacuna]

For in the full blessing of fruitful soil—that is, benevolence—God loved Jacob before he was born, and in the same inspiration visited blessed Robert in his infancy. God foresaw that the receptive soil of this boy would desire to yearn for God; and because, while still at the breast, he began (to show) this in his conduct, all who saw him loved him greatly. For wherever benevolence is in a human being, people’s desires are kindled to love that person, just as dew falls upon grain for its greening.

Accordingly, when the boy Robert was seven years old, he wished to learn letters, and his mother had him instructed; yet she did not wish him to be a cleric, but intended him to become duke of his province in his father’s place [Col. 1086B] and defender of the churches. But through the grace of the Holy Spirit he was merciful toward the poor, which is the ministry and support of benevolence, just as the viscera, serving a human being, contain him. According to the ways of children, whenever he found poor little children, he brought them to his mother, saying: “Mother, behold your children.” She graciously received this action and replied: “My son, they are your brothers.”

Nourished suitably and honorably, advancing in age and wisdom before God and men, he reached youth, brought up in holy conduct and virtues. He was anointed with the oil of holiness, like David, with “the oil of gladness above his companions” (Psalm 45:8); and with all the effort of his mind he despised the glory of the whole world, though bodily he seemed to possess it before people [Col. 1086C]. For he lived holily in good conduct, frequented the church continually with devout prayers, and committed to faithful memory with pious zeal what was taught in the sacred books.

5. When he had reached the twelfth year of his age, his mother said to him: “My son, since we have very great resources and wealth [Note: [Col. 1086D] We have often noted that *oraculum* is used for an oratory.] let us make an oratory in honor of God and for the salvation of our souls.” He replied: “No, my mother; rather let us first attend to what the Gospel teaches [Note: [Col. 1086D] Thus the manuscripts; Busaeus and Serrarius incorrectly read, ‘For Christ says.’ The passage is Isaiah 58.]; and the prophet says: ‘Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and homeless into your house’ (Isaiah 58:7). And again: ‘When you see a naked person, cover him [Col. 1086D], and do not despise your own flesh’ (ibid.).”

When his mother heard this, she rejoiced exceedingly because her son had given her such sound counsel. For through the Holy Spirit good and holy desires sweated forth like balm in the mind of that youth. He silently considered with himself how what he had spoken might be done, and so fell asleep. Then, through the Holy Spirit’s admonition, he saw in a dream an old man with a beautiful face, washing certain little children in clear water. He then led them into an orchard most delightful with every kind of flower and tree and filled with the fragrance of all spices, and clothed them in a shining-white garment [Col. 1087A].

Attracted by the pleasantness of that place, blessed Robert said to the old man: “I wish to remain here.” The old man answered him: “You will not remain here now, because you will prepare for yourself a fruitful ladder into heaven, where you shall be a companion of angels. Therefore do not neglect to carry out what you have planned concerning the poor, so that through their food and clothing you may be fed with the food of life; and may be clothed with the garment of which Adam was stripped through disobedience. Become in mind a stranger to the world, and choose for yourself the better part.”

But after blessed Robert awoke, he told his mother what he had seen in the dream. Greatly rejoicing, she bent her knees to the Lord and prayed: “O Lord my God, you will fulfill my desire in my son.” Then both the mother and her son built certain dwelling-houses beside the bank of flowing waters and there sheltered poor and naked people. They supplied these with food and clothing through two faithful and holy men: one, called Wigbert, served them as priest; the other, one of their retainers, was unlearned. Blessed Robert himself also, forgetting his tender age and noble birth for Christ’s love, often washed the poor persons’ feet, set food and drink before them, and frequently made their beds. Thus he faithfully served God until the fifteenth year of his age [Col. 1087C].

## CHAPTER II. Pilgrimage to Rome. Deliberation concerning his state of life.

6. And since he was powerful in the pomp of the world through great wealth and a large household, by which he saw himself being drawn toward the world, he at length began to consider within himself how blessed Alexius had left father and mother, home and worldly riches, becoming a pilgrim; and he chose altogether to imitate him in this, so that he might serve God more freely in tranquillity. His mother, perceiving this in him from certain signs, although he concealed it from her, said to him with tears: “Son, remember the sorrow of a mother’s womb; heed the groans of your widowed mother; look upon your household, which relies upon you alone [Col. 1087D]; and take care not to bring unbearable misery upon us. For from our resources you may distribute to the poor and needy, and to all in want, as shall please you. And what is better or more advantageous for you than to serve God in this way?”

While his mother spoke thus with many tears and groans, this blessed young man was greatly troubled in his heart. At the same time certain nobles, both strangers and his own kinsmen, came to him, saying: “You who possess so great an honour of ducal rank and such riches of the world, why do you make yourself so contemptible?” With these and similar words [Col. 1088A] they harassed him daily, trying to see whether they could turn him away from his good purpose and good path. Seeing this, he said to his mother: “Behold, through the prompting of the devil, who envies my purpose and manner of life, I shall be ensnared and entangled in the world, and, though unwilling, I shall follow the ways of my father. For this was why I desired pilgrimage: that I might serve God alone more freely.”

On hearing this, his mother, who had placed all her hope in God, distressed and burdened by fear, feared that her son, enticed by the nobility of his birth, would become entangled in the world. Preferring to lack an heir rather than have her son, ensnared in worldly entanglements, serve the devil, she said to him, as far as grief allowed: “Son, since I see that you are disturbed by many counsels and improperly drawn [Col. 1088B] toward the world, do as you wish, and undertake the pilgrimage which you have long desired. And may he of whom it was said, ‘Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem?’ (Luke 24:18), be with you on your journey, and return you safely to me, to the glory of his name.”

Then, with his mother’s consent, he undertook the pilgrimage and set out with some of his men for the thresholds of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul. When the people of that region saw him, they marvelled at him and said among themselves: “Truly this man is noble; for his countenance, appearing bright, shone with graciousness, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured over him. Therefore all who looked upon him loved him in the embrace of charity.” [Col. 1088C] For just as a star shines and is bright when no cloud obscures it, so graciousness is visible in a man’s face, because that man lives in the good habit of the Holy Spirit. And while blessed Robert daily commended himself to God and to the merits of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, he remained there for some time.

7. While he delayed there, some religious men of that region asked him what manner of life or desire he had; and he disclosed to them everything in his heart. They advised him to heed the Gospel passage where it is written: “Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21), since pilgrimage would be good and useful for him, lest [Col. 1088D] the riches of nobility draw him to destruction. He submitted himself to their counsel and resolved in his mind to do so.

Finally returning to his mother, on his estate—which was very extensive—he caused villages and churches to be built in places where there were none, and distributed them among his people, so that, living there, they might serve his mother as long as she lived, and might assist all newcomers and those suffering need. But he himself intended to leave his dukedom, mother, household, possessions, and everything that he had, and to become a pilgrim for Christ’s name.

[Note: Freher published this entire passage, copied by himself, in *Origines Palatinae*, part II, chapter 11; but at [Col. 1088D], where we expected it, he did not indicate the sites themselves, especially those of the rivers.]

The extent of his landed possessions [Col. 1089A], which he held by hereditary right from both his father and mother and from his other forebears, stretched from the place where his relics were buried—namely, where the river Nahe flows into the Rhine—up the bank of the Rhine as far as the river Selsa; then it crossed two other rivers, of which the first is called Wiza and the second Apsa; and beyond the Nahe it extended up to a stream called Elra, which there is the middle one of three rivers bearing the same name; from there it went toward the river Simera, and thence curved back through the forest of Sane, where the stream called Heienbach empties into the Rhine.

[Note: Habelius, in the German Life, places the river Selsa at the town of Ingelheim, namely upstream on the Rhine; and not far from there are placed the little rivers Wiza and Apsa, commonly called Selss, Wijss, and Apffel.]

[Note: The town of Simera, famous through its ducal title, lies by [Col. 1090D] the river Simera, which flows into the Nahe; and from this point the boundaries of St Rupert’s dukedom seem to be assignable.]

8. At that time the dwelling-place both of blessed Robert and of his mother was, because of the pleasantness of the flowing [Col. 1089B] waters, in the very place where their relics are now buried. Their town, situated there and fortified with very strong buildings, extended across the whole adjoining plain to the foot of the nearby mountain and to the bank of the Rhine. But on the other side of the river Nahe was a village containing the dwellings of their servants and fishermen, their horse-stables, granaries in which their grain was stored, and presses in which their wine was pressed. In those places at that time there flourished greater splendour, greater abundance of riches, and every kind of worldly distinction than existed in other towns of that region, because the gathering and passage of many people from diverse provinces was continually frequent there.

[Col. 1089C] 9. Finally, when blessed Robert had reached young manhood, that is, when he was already nearly twenty years old, many of his relatives and retainers drew him, though resisting, toward worldly pleasure. Since he was wholly aflame with love for God, he repelled them from himself with devout and fitting words; for God, who knows all things future, past, and present, had foreseen something different for him. For, while that blessed man was like a tree full of fruit, of a nature so rich and refined that his mind might easily have been perverted, through nobility and worldly riches, into the opposite of good things and have withered in holiness—as often happens in certain men who have begun good works but later wither in them—God took him to himself [Col. 1089D].

[Note: Here another digression had been inserted.]

Finally, while the mother of this blessed young Robert, in the chastity of widowhood, devoutly served God by good and holy works, she saw in a divinely sent dream that a rib had fallen from her side. Greatly terrified by this, she endured frequent groans and repeated sighs from her heart, as became apparent not long afterward. For her son, blessed Robert, while intent upon fulfilling the devotion that he had vowed to God, began to be weakened by severe fevers.

[Col. 1090A] 10. During this illness the old man whom he had formerly seen in a dream appeared to him and said: “I am the Ancient of Days, who appeared to Daniel in a vision of the night; and now I reveal myself also to you and call you to the glory of infinite blessedness. For by the orchard which I once showed you in a vision I truly signified beforehand the good and holy works which you have now accomplished.”

When he awoke from sleep, terrified by sadness and fear because he would gladly have fulfilled what he had vowed to God in his desires, he told his mother what he had seen. But she was immediately struck by the deepest grief; how many groans and laments she uttered at this news may be understood by anyone who has suffered something similar. Therefore, after this blessed man had suffered for thirty days in the aforesaid illness, God took him from this life in his twentieth [Col. 1090B] year, in good confession and in the fear of God, lest, if he reached full age, he should walk in his father’s ways; for he who knows all things had foreknown that this was expedient for him. God anticipated him and removed him from this life while he shone in innocence.

He was buried with a very great gathering of people from the whole region in the oratory which he and his mother had built above the river Nahe on their aforementioned estate. Some wept over him because he had been removed from this present life prematurely; others rejoiced over him because, through the miracles God performed there through him, that whole region was illumined like the day by the sun. For during eight years God performed very many signs and miracles, through the merits of this beloved servant [Col. 1090C], in that place, among the sick, the lame, and captives, so that all who were oppressed by tribulations and came to his tomb were delivered through God’s grace.

11. After the blessed death of her son, blessed Bertha, the widowed chosen one of God, thereafter led a holy life in great contrition of heart. She offered at her son’s tomb everything that she possessed for God’s service, and from these goods fully supplied all necessities to the community of brothers who served God there in the divine offices. For after her son’s end she lived for almost twenty-five years in every good work of fasting, almsgiving, and prayer, piously and justly accomplishing many labours for God’s love. Then, seized by bodily sickness, she returned to God the spirit [Col. 1090D] which she had always fixed upon heavenly desires, and was honourably buried in peace in her son’s tomb on the aforesaid estate.

12. After her death, the aforementioned place remained in the honour of holiness and the peace of repose until the tyranny of the Normans. For some years after the happy departure of this blessed Bertha, the Norman people, leaving their own lands, devastated by divine judgment many towns around the waters of the Rhine. They also destroyed Trier; and thus [Col. 1091A], ravaging onward, they reached the town of Roboald, the father of blessed Robert, where the river Nahe joins the Rhine, of which we have spoken above, and reduced this also to nothing by ruin and fire.

[Note: The destruction of the city of Trier occurred in 882 and the following year.]

[Note: Bingen is here called the town of Roboald, father of St Rupert.]

After these wicked men had at last been repulsed, laid aside their savagery, and returned to their own lands, the inhabitants of the aforesaid place who had survived and had been scattered among various hiding-places returned. Seeing their town destroyed, they built other dwellings for themselves on the other side of the river Nahe, because of the protection afforded by the flowing rivers and adjacent mountains. Everything that they could carry away from the destroyed place—timber, stones, exposed foundations, and other implements—they transported to the other bank of the Nahe to live there. Thus the former place, once flourishing in populousness [Col. 1092A], height of buildings, and abundance of wealth, was desolated and in subsequent times reduced to still greater desolation.

Consequently all the estates which blessed Robert had possessed by hereditary right were divided among strangers and various people into scattered, opposed holdings, and nothing of them remained intact except the church in which that chosen one of God rested with his mother, as stated above. It has endured even to our own times: we ourselves saw it with our own eyes when, by God’s showing, we came to that same place. There also remained a few vineyards belonging to the same church, which we purchased for a price from Lord Hermann, bishop of Hildesheim, and his brother, the nobleman called Bernard.

[Note: Hermann governed the Church of Hildesheim from 1160 until 1174, when, returning from Palestine, he died in Italy. But St Hildegard lived until 1177.]

## AUTHENTIC TESTIMONY CONCERNING CERTAIN TRANSLATED RELICS

[Col. 1091]

[Col. 1091B] We, Johannes Suicardus of Cronberg, distinguished scholastic of the metropolitan church of Mainz and provost of St Alban’s, general vicar in spiritual matters of the most reverend and illustrious Father and Lord in Christ, Lord Wolfgang, archbishop of the holy see of Mainz, archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire in Germany, prince-elector, and commissioner specially appointed by him for the matters written below: to all and each to whom these our letters shall come, after our due and ready offices and services, make known and desire it to be known how the most reverend and most serene Lords and Princes, Lord Philip, by the grace of God bishop of Regensburg, and Ferdinand, provost of Strasbourg, Counts Palatine of the Rhine and Dukes of both Bavarias, after completing their residence in this our metropolitan city and church, according to its statutes and custom and not without a splendid example of virtues and religion, when they resolved to depart from us for the holy thresholds of the Apostles, requested, because of the ardent piety and devotion which they bear toward God and God’s saints—whose memory is in blessing—that before leaving our church and diocese they might, with the gracious consent of His Highness, visit holy places and religious monasteries in veneration, and carry and take away with them some portion of their sacred relics.

His Highness, wishing to oblige their praiseworthy zeal and piety, entrusted us by special mandate to fulfil their devout wishes and put their petition into effect as soon as possible. [Col. 1091D] In fulfilment of the duty of our obedience, we summoned the reverend man Vitus Miletus, doctor of sacred theology and provost in this place of St Maurice, and sent him, with letters and mandates in the name of our vicariate and commission, together [Col. 1092B] with the reverend and distinguished man and Lord Quirinus Leoninus, licentiate in the same sacred theology, canon of the cathedral church of Regensburg, theologian and tutor of the most serene princes, to the churches and surrounding holy places. We gave them full authority to seek out, open, and examine with due reverence the sacred relics in their archives and reliquaries, and to bring to us from them, in the fear of the Lord, as much as was fitting to discretion and religion.

Faithfully carrying out the charge committed to them, after diligent inspection and inquiry, they brought us from the abbey of virgins on the mountain of St Robert, commonly called Rupersberg, of the Order of St Benedict, near the town of Bingen, the following relics: two ribs of St Rupert, son formerly of Roboald, Count Palatine of the Rhine, and Bertha, duchess of Austrasia and Lorraine, still bearing flesh; likewise three other elongated bones of the same saint; likewise part of the backbone, still bearing flesh; likewise a tooth from his head, from the upper jaw beneath the right eye; likewise three bones of St Hildegard, formerly abbess there, a most noble and devout virgin, who, filled with the spirit of prophecy, wrote a most beautiful work of letters concerning her visions or revelations, in the time of Lord Bernard and Pope Eugenius III, whose books Eugenius IV approved and confirmed. Her feast is celebrated on 17 September. Likewise, one small rib and part of the spine of the same; likewise two bones of St Bertha, mother of St Rupert, duchess of Austrasia and Lorraine [Col. 1092D]; likewise the throat, with another portion, of St Satyra, virgin and martyr.

Having received and kissed these sacred relics with the reverence due to them, and having first received from the subcommissioners a solemn oath that they had in good faith found and ascertained them in their proper places, archives [Col. 1093A], and reliquaries to be true, certain, and undoubted sacred relics, reverently held and venerated everywhere and always from ancient times and beyond human memory by all truly Christian orthodox Catholics, and not infrequently in former times communicated and transmitted from them by archbishops of Mainz to supreme kings and princes, so that no truly Christian person could or ought to doubt their authenticity and truth: with fitting reverence and humility of spirit, in the name and on behalf of our most reverend and illustrious Lord, the archbishop and prince-elector of Mainz, we delivered them to the most serene princes during the very celebration of Holy Mass, together with many other relics not included in this instrument, in the presence of the notary and witnesses written below, specially summoned for this purpose, in the name of God and to the glory of him and all his saints.

We humbly and sincerely pray God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom all saints happily live and reign, that this poor service of ours may redound to their glory and honour, and, through their intercession, to the eternal salvation of their Serene Highnesses and of us all. Amen. In attestation of all and each of these matters, we have ordered these present letters to be made, subscribed with our own hand, and sealed with the seals of our vicariate and of the abbess and convent of the said monastery.

These acts were done in the metropolitan city of Mainz, in the chapel of the court of the most serene princes, in the year of Christ’s Nativity 1592 [Col. 1094A], on the tenth day of August, in the first year of the pontificate of our most holy Lord Pope Clement VIII, in the presence there of the reverend, noble, magnificent, and distinguished men and lords: Lord Adolf, called Wolffg. Metternich, canon of Speyer and provost of St Andrew’s at Worms, steward of the court of the said princes; Lord Aetherius Hoffmant, doctor of sacred theology, respectively dean and cantor of the collegiate churches of Our Lady ad Gradus and St Peter outside the walls at Mainz, and then rector of the venerable University of Mainz; Lord Balthasar Bafer of Holobus, chamberlain of the said princes; and Lord Johann Hager, a Bavarian, chaplain of the said princes, specially requested and summoned for the foregoing.

All and each of these things were, at the place and on the day already stated, about the seventh hour before noon [Col. 1094B], after the sacred office of Mass had first been devoutly celebrated with the relics placed upon the altar, truly and lawfully said, done, performed, and delivered by the aforesaid commissioners appointed by the most reverend archbishop of Mainz, who were then still present together there, having first touched the holy Gospels of God, according to the tenor of the letters granted. I, Georgius Molitoris, public notary and sworn secretary of the reverend lords of the chapter of the high holy church of Mainz, together with the witnesses named above, newly and specially called together with me for this purpose, attest this before all and each as the most evident testimony of truth, by the subscription of my own hand and the customary notarial seal affixed in the margin.

## PLACE FOR THE SEALS

[Col. 1093]

# LIFE OF SAINT DISIBOD, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR, AT DISIBODENBERG, IN THE TERRITORY OF MAINZ IN GERMANY, WRITTEN BY SAINT HILDEGARD

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, July, vol. II, 8 July, p. 581, from a manuscript of St Maximinus of Trier.)

## PREFATORY NOTICE

St Hildegard wrote the Life of St Disibod in 1170, by order of Helinger, fifth abbot of the mountain named after the saint. This Life of St Disibod is the sole and unique one which, having been published by Surius, is commonly cited, and which has been given such authority that it is regarded as “divinely revealed.” Hildegard herself certainly testifies to this in §1: “After setting forth the visions of the book *The Life of Merits* . . . from the wisdom of divine mercy, I heard a voice from heaven speaking thus.” And again in §52: “These things which have been set forth were made manifest by a true revelation through the Holy Spirit, for the glory of his name, the commemoration of the aforesaid patron, and the correction of the people who hear.”

This is indeed a remarkable assertion by Hildegard concerning a confused and intricate narrative, furnished with no genuine historical features, which Mabillon did not judge worthy of a place among the Acts of the Saints of his Order. “St Hildegard,” he says, “expanded Disibod’s deeds with passages that are almost commonplaces.”

I have repeatedly and attentively examined this fairly long work, both in our manuscript received through Rosweyde from St Maximinus at Trier and in Surius’s edition, more freely polished—or, as others say, corrupted. Yet nowhere did even slight indications appear to me by which the prerogative of revelation could be ascribed to such a writing, any more than to other saints’ legends of this sort—unless one calls revealed certain statements of sacred Scripture which the holy author expounded with an individual interpretation. The whole work is occupied with explaining moral teachings; if these are removed from the remainder, the history, such as it is, could be set out in very few words [Col. 1095], at least in the part that recounts the saint’s deeds.

I ask you to examine carefully this long and rather gloomy discourse; weigh each chapter, including the moral passages. I am mistaken if you find anywhere anything to which the name of revelation properly applies. For the facts which she herself could and ought to have known about the establishment of Mount St Disibod, where she had formerly lived, and about its various misfortunes and vicissitudes, did not need to be learned by revelation: all these things were sufficiently known and commonplace among the monks in St Hildegard’s own lifetime.

I should indeed have wished that, in this supposed vision, clearer dates had been presented to her for the individual persecutions and disasters, together with the birthplace, parents, episcopal see, and then an ordered sequence of St Disibod’s entire age and deeds. But she seems to have taken no concern for these matters, so that the entire revelation ultimately returns only to what she had formed in advance from things she had heard repeatedly, and what she “expanded with passages that are almost commonplaces.”

Not to labour a matter already handled, or revive controversies long discussed, let the reader consult what Papebroch formerly argued concerning visions and revelations of this kind in his *Responses to Article XX of the Presentation of Errors* wrongly imputed to him. Unless someone thinks the whole question may be settled more briefly, and reasonably doubts whether this mass of material, at least as it has come down to us, is Hildegard’s own and genuine work, rather than something later enlarged and expanded by an interpolator, then counted among that saint’s other revelations, known from elsewhere and approved to some degree. I do not wish here to investigate these matters more fully, nor does it seem worth the labour.

Besides this very widely circulated Life written by St Hildegard, I found another among our papers, which no one has hitherto ever mentioned. For, as the praised Mabillon observed, *Benedictine Century* III, part II, p. 498: “Apart from Hildegard . . . none of the ancients whom I have read mentions Disibod except Rabanus Maurus and Marianus Scotus.” And this second Life, transcribed by our Father Johannes Gamans from a parchment Passionary of the monastery of Böddeken, is not important enough to deserve much mention or praise. I call it a patchwork, perhaps embellished by some monk of Mount St Disibod; or rather, compiled tastelessly from the Acts of other Saints, with an opening almost taken from the Acts of St Kilian and other materials scraped together from elsewhere.

The most important part of the whole narrative clings to a description of King Dagobert’s hunt. Pursuing a hind marvellously with his companions for three whole days, he ascends “the mountain inhabited by the man of God,” finds him there hiding in his hut, and receives from him a frugal meal; meanwhile the beast, pressed and exhausted by the hunters, takes refuge with the Saint. It then tells how Disibod tamed the hind and gave her to the king as a gift; she followed him everywhere like a domestic dog.

Conversely, the king, amazed at the wonder and not ungrateful, is said to have granted the Saint, at his request, as much land “for his own and his successors’ benefit as he could ride around on a donkey from dawn until the evening hour arrived”; and the king supposedly confirmed all this “in writing by perpetual hand.” Indeed, the plagiarizing author wished to steal these things from other legends, which there is no need to enumerate here. I pass over the rest, equally childish, so childishly and wordily cobbled together that I do not judge it worth serious reading.

If my conjecture is correct, these materials were collected perhaps in the thirteenth or fourteenth century by someone ignorant of St Hildegard’s older Life, since he records matters wholly different and entirely alien to that author’s meaning. This may also be inferred from the few miracles appended by this later writer to his Legend. Since they were unknown to St Hildegard, who recounts others much more ancient, they must have been performed and written after her death; her death occurred in 1180. Hence, unless I am mistaken, it is evident that both the Legend and its miracles ought to be assigned to centuries nearer our own. We therefore judged that only the miracles now mentioned should be drawn from it, since the writer claims to be their witness while narrating them with long digressions and circumlocutions, though they could very conveniently have been reduced to a few lines.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 1095]

# CHAPTER ONE. The Saint’s lineage; his parents expelled by tyrants; his progress in learning; election as bishop; renunciation and departure from his homeland

[Col. 1095A]

In a mystical vision [Note: This legend, written from a “mystical vision,” or revelation, was discussed in the preceding prefatory notice. The author does not explain his meaning sufficiently clearly, but we have wished to alter nothing; Surius’s more polished edition may be consulted.], as God willed, at the request and command of my prelates—namely Abbot Hebiger [Helinger] and all the brothers serving God on the Mount of blessed Disibod—I beheld the life and merits of that blessed Father. After setting forth the visions of the book *The Life of Merits*, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1170, while Frederick was emperor of the Romans, under oppression of the Apostolic See, as I lay for nearly three years in a bed of sickness, I heard, while awake in body and mind, a voice from heaven, from the wisdom of divine mercy [Col. 1096A], speaking thus:

“God’s chosen one Disibod, inspired from his infancy by the Holy Spirit like blessed Nicholas, blessed Benedict, and those like them, thirsted with eager heart for every good thing that he saw and heard. Therefore it may be said of him: ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise because of your enemies, that you may destroy the enemy and the avenger’” (Ps. 8).

2. This is to be understood as follows [Note: We also said above, in the cited place, that several passages of sacred Scripture are expounded by St Hildegard through an individual interpretation; to scrutinize them too closely is not within our province. Whether interpretations of this kind belong to genuine revelations is for others to judge.]. In the good disposition of infants who do not yet possess speech, and of those who ought rather to suck milk than perform marvels, you, Lord of all, have brought your name to perfect praise when you have often worked your wonders in them. That is: when you have so inspired those who do not yet possess full marrow that they unknowingly uttered many things in speech and action; and when, contrary to the laws of the flesh, you strengthened others with such courage that, striving with their whole desire toward heavenly things, they did not sinfully perform the offices of the flesh.

But let no one entertain doubt in these matters, for serpentine deceit was unable to perform these good and holy things in those blessed persons. For you did these things because of your enemies, namely the fallen angels, so that to their confusion they might see your power in childish ignorance; and so that you might destroy the enemy, namely him who denies you in all good things; and the avenger, namely him who casts the stones and darts of his impiety against your words and miracles by condemning them.

3. These evils had no power at all in the blessed persons mentioned above [Col. 1097B], because they spoke what was right. For God worked in his gifts in blessed Disibod from his infancy to his decrepit old age, so that his childhood did not play in wickedness, his youth did not burn in wantonness, and the maturity of his old age did not look to the left. He so left behind with heart and body all the pomp of this world that some declared him thereby foolish, some vain, some wandering, and some remarkable in his works, saying: “What is this that this man is doing?”

4. The parents of blessed Disibod, flourishing in worldly freedom, derived their origin from an eminent Irish family; nevertheless they did not possess the pomp and glory [Col. 1097C] of the world in excess. Therefore certain tyrants, swelling with pride, after subjecting very many in that region to themselves by tyranny, also sought to oppress the parents of this blessed man, who was then a boy, and force them under their dominion. But they, mindful of their family’s freedom and refusing harsh and unjust subjection, withdrew from them to more remote places in the same region. With their son blessed Disibod and all their property, they took up residence in a certain town beside a river “which flows out from the sea,” and entrusted him to religious men to be educated in letters and the other liberal arts.

[Note: Everything said here about the saint’s birth, his parents’ flight, and so forth is obscure. But it is especially strange that they are said to have settled by a river “which flows out from the sea,” unless this indicates some inlet or river-mouth into which the tide of the sea periodically drove back its waves. The rest, to say it once for all, both here and in what follows, must be reduced to commonplaces.]

[Col. 1097D] 5. But through the grace of the Holy Spirit he committed to his capacious intellect and good memory the good things that he heard from his teachers. Thus he gave no small joy to his parents, who were labouring in the affliction of exile. Day by day this boy advanced, growing in body and holiness, and rising from one exercise of good works to another through prayer and almsgiving. Thus he hastened with his whole desire toward everything that he could hear or learn concerning [Col. 1098A] God; and so, by the steps of virtues and the growth of his age, having received each sacred order in turn, he attained the rank of priest when he was thirty years old.

Having received it in the fear of the Lord, he acted like a good grower of spices, who plants every kind of spice and aromatic plant in his garden, always taking care that his garden may be green and not dry.

6. In these pursuits the same saint remembered the words of Wisdom, where it says: “I have gathered my myrrh with my spices” (Song 5:1). This is to be understood as follows [Note: I shall add no more concerning these and all other moral interpretations of sacred Scripture.]: “I, who ought to labour diligently in righteous works, offer to God the mortification of my flesh with good intention, when for love of him I desire to become a stranger to vices, flee their common uncleanness [Col. 1098B], and have no fellowship with them. For amid the fragrances of virtues I hasten to love and venerate him, the true God; and, with the love of heavenly longing, this will not fail from my heart, with his help.”

In this upright and holy will, the saint was as though dead to the world, so that many who saw this acted as if they did not know him and shrank from remaining with him, because he compelled his whole self to serve the spirit and not the flesh.

7. While he thus served God praiseworthily in such virtues, and was therefore pleasing and blameless to those who loved God, it happened that a bishop in that region passed from the present life to the life to come. When the people, both lesser and greater, had assembled according to custom [Col. 1098C] to choose another as their bishop, some who knew the honourable conduct and holy life of blessed Disibod unanimously chose him as their bishop.

[Note: Some have conjectured that “the region” means Dublin, where St Disibod was supposedly bishop at that time; Wilson and Sirinus considered this view admissible. But we have rejected such anachronisms above.]

But certain others, whose life and conduct were blameworthy, opposed this, saying: “What advantage is there in making a silent and uncommunicative man, who does not know the people, their master?”

8. But God looked upon this blessed man, as it is written: “To justify the humble and the poor” (Psalm 81:3). This is to be understood thus: to sanctify in works the righteous person who humbles himself to the ground for God’s sake and confesses with his whole heart that he is needy and poor; for righteousness, with the open eye of mercy, looks upon him. For this humble man [Col. 1098D] always desired poverty and always looked toward God with the dove-like eye of simplicity, so that he might acquire eternal riches for himself; and therefore God loved him. He also regarded death as death, and counted all perishable things as nothing; he placed all his works in God, and therefore God chose him. The heavenly Judge had hidden this man from the common people, but had revealed him to those who loved Him; hence, although some were astonished, He willed that he should be both teacher and bishop.

9. And when this blessed man was compelled by the more prudent persons to undertake the aforesaid burden, protesting that he was unworthy of so great a dignity, he drew back his hands and feet with all the force he could; nevertheless, as those who feared God pressed and prevailed, even against his will, but by divine appointment, he was placed in the episcopal see. There the bishop himself happily began to proclaim and teach God’s righteousness. He exhorted all whom he could to be subject to God; and what he had been taught from his childhood by the Holy Spirit, he now made manifest by teaching, while with paternal affection he set before them in his own person good examples of holiness and virtue. Some [Col. 1099B], because of the merits of the virtues which they saw in him, loved him and eagerly desired his teaching with the attentive ear of the heart. Others, however, who had cast God behind their backs, cried out furiously against this holy man: “This man lives as though he were not human; and so he compels us also to live inhumanly. Who can listen to him?” And they subjected him to many injuries.

10. He, however, gathered to himself a few faithful men, who offered him consolation and assistance. Daily he afflicted his heart for God’s sake, saying: “O Lord God, I, Your servant, prostrate myself before Your mercy, doing what You have commanded. For You know that I desire You alone; therefore I trust that You will one day fulfill my desire, as it is written: ‘Delight yourself in [Col. 1099C] the Lord, and He shall give you the petitions of your heart’” (Psalm 36:4).

This is to be understood thus: O man, conceived and born in sins, delight, against the inclination of the flesh, in the commandments of Him who created you; and call to mind who it is that delivered you. When you have done this, He will give you what you ask, because you do not ask for the things that ought to be asked for, but, showing Him the affliction of your heart with humbled spirit, and crying aloud and grieving, you will constrain yourself like a beast to labor at the things that are right. Therefore those who have endeavored to repent and in this manner amend their evils are wiser than the children of light, because these neither wished nor did this. For it pleases God that a person should wage a hard war against himself and against the dragon [Col. 1099D]; and when one has done this, God swiftly fulfills both his prayers and desires, as He also did in blessed Disibod, who endured hard conflicts as long as he lived in the body, yet happily brought them to completion with a good end.

11. Meanwhile, while this holy man presided over his people in the faith, by words and examples, in the aforesaid dignity, [Col. 1100A] great mockery and great schism erupted throughout that whole region. Some resisted the Old and New Testaments and denied Christ; others embraced the heresies of heretics; others adopted the sect of the Jews; others loved the sect of the pagans.

[Note: [Col. 1099D] What is one to understand here amid such confusion of matters? Sirinus took from this an occasion to investigate whether the Pelagian heresy had revived in Ireland at that time; but if the author had wished to indicate that, he would have spoken somewhat more distinctly.]

Others burned with a shameful zeal to live not humanly but in the disorder of beasts; while others indeed maintained discipline for the sake of humanity, yet made no effort to do any good. Opposing himself manfully and fearlessly to these very great errors and confusions, blessed Disibod patiently endured many reproaches and many injuries, preferring to lose the present life rather than consent to evils so great and so improper.

[Col. 1100B] 12. And after he had endured these things for some years, without the uprooting of those evils and even at peril to his own body, he was at last overcome by weariness and said to God in his prayers, with great weeping: “O God, and O Judge of all holy men, what profit is there for me in laboring with this people, who pierce Your righteousness with rabid bites?”

Finally, the supporters of the aforesaid errors, together with the people entangled in the same errors, saw that this blessed man did not consent to their errors and perversity, but everywhere steadfastly rebuked them without fear of death. They laid many snares for him and, at last, having assembled a host of unbelievers, drove him from his see with many insults. He [Col. 1100C], however, preferring to serve God in peace rather than linger longer without the fruit of usefulness, gathered to himself a few religious men and left, for Christ’s name, the seat of his dignity—which he had governed vigorously and religiously for ten years—his homeland, and all that he possessed, saying that it benefited neither himself nor others for him to remain there. Since such great unbelief, together with the hardness of iniquity, had increased there, he gladly embraced the pilgrimage which he had long desired, for the sake of eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 1099D] You see that this entire chapter, expanded with so many words, can be reduced to these few historical facts: Saint Disibod, born of noble family in Ireland, piously reared and educated in letters, was consecrated priest in the thirtieth year of his age [Col. 1100D]; afterwards he was raised to some unspecified bishopric, and, after enduring many snares and persecutions from wicked men, was finally expelled by them.]

## CHAPTER II. Journey into Germany; instruction of the people by the Rhine; solitary and austere life on the mountain; beginnings of the monastery and miracles.

13. After leaving Ireland and traveling through many regions—

[Note: [Col. 1100D] Here is another decade spent “traveling through regions”; yet the author of the *Life* nowhere states to what lands he proceeded or where he made any stay.]

—and carefully examining many places, [Col. 1100D] he finally came to Alamannia, seeking rest for his soul. There he found a harsh and savage people; and, weary, he set his steps there for a time. While he offered that people words of salvation and examples of holiness, many who heard him loved him, but many others cared neither to hear nor to love him.

While he stayed in that province, deliberating with himself where he might turn, he heard a good and pleasing report concerning the religious life of blessed Benedict, who had only recently departed this life—

[Note: [Col. 1101] If the saint had traveled through so many regions, there is no doubt that he might have heard elsewhere also of “Saint Benedict’s renown.”]

—and had left very many lovers of his religious observance. Thus, through the admonition of the Holy Spirit, he recognized that his desire, long cherished but not yet fulfilled, was this: to associate with the people once entrusted to him some men of true and perfect religious life. For this reason he again proceeded from place to place, yet found neither in places nor in the customs of peoples anything that pleased his soul.

14. Then he began to weep and pray, saying: “Incline Your ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am needy and poor” (Psalm 85:1). This is to be understood thus: Condescending to my tribulations, incline, [Col. 1101B] O Lord, You who are the ruler of all, the ear of mercy and hear the words of my prayer; for I am needy in soul through the faint-heartedness of my mind, and poor in body through the contrition of afflictions—I who ought to have followed You and loved You above all things. Remember, therefore, that from my childhood I endeavored to serve You and that, for love of You, I always loved poverty and contempt of the world.

Then God, because of the freshness of his good desire, received these prayers and sent sweet consolation of rest into his mind, as dew falls upon grass. Even in a vision of the night He made known to him by a certain manifestation that a place suited to his desire would someday be found by him. For God seemed to be present to this blessed man, as He did to His other beloved ones who desired Him with their whole love, appearing, speaking, and hearing with them [Col. 1101C] because of the great and good intention by which they confidently directed themselves toward Him with all their heart.

15. The Holy Spirit also removed from him every fabulous reputation of vain glory, which is found in many people who pray and fast hypocritically according to their own will when they unjustly seek something from God; and if something should happen to them as they wish, they regard it as though granted by God for display. If any such persons exist, they shall be scattered like straw by the wind. But when a person mortifies himself to vanities, he takes, as it were, sleep among them; then pride, vain glory, the acquisition of honors from the people, and the other vices are restrained by God’s power, lest that person should in any way be turned away from the love [Col. 1101D] of the Creator’s nature by their suggestions.

16. Blessed Disibod, rejoicing in hope of his good desire because he knew that it would one day be fulfilled through God’s help, heard a favorable report about a people living in the regions of Gaul on this side of the Rhine: namely, that the people were indeed harsh, yet nevertheless devoutly maintained the ecclesiastical religion in their way of life. Weary of the mockery of the scoffing people, and scarcely able to wait, he swiftly directed his journey toward the end of the Rhine. Turning aside from there and proceeding through every kind of trackless place, he reached the river Glan. Having crossed it, [Col. 1102A] he saw a high, wooded mountain, which he ascended after ten years of his pilgrimage. There, weary, he sat down and rested; and, touched by the Holy Spirit, he said to his companions—three men, who had come with him from Ireland, the first an elder named Gillilald, the second Clement, and the third Salustus—“This shall be my resting-place.”

17. Then, after traveling all around the same mountain and carefully considering each of its slopes, its pleasantness pleased his soul more and more as a place to dwell. Its height made access difficult for arrivals, while streams flowing on either side would supply bodily refreshment to those living there. He prayed, saying: “Lord, who dwell above the heavens and rule the abyss [Col. 1102B], I pray that the pleasantness of this place may be transformed into the pleasantness of souls, because it is fitting that in this place You should be faithfully served by a faithful people.”

Having said this, he marked out for himself a dwelling on the eastern descent of the mountain, for easier access to water; and, vigorously beginning the mode of life he had long desired, he led a harsh and austere solitary life in prayer, vigils, and fasting.

18. His companions who were with him built their dwellings separately and at a greater distance from him, lest they have any mutual enjoyment. It should be known that for a while they sustained themselves there on roots of herbs, having no other food. That mountain, together with the woods adjoining it and places both passable and impassable, was at that time more than one mile in circumference; it belonged not to one man [Col. 1102C], but to fellow inhabitants of the province, both lesser and greater. It therefore happened that when people occasionally entered the same forest, whether to catch wild animals, fish in the neighboring rivers, cut wood, or meet other needs, they often saw this blessed man digging up roots or gathering around him other necessities; and thus, after some time, he became known.

19. A report went out among the people that a certain holy man, with several others, had come to that place sent by God. Many, marveling at this, came to him with good desire and shared with him whatever useful things they had; and he in return gave them words of salvation and life. For from the time of his exile until that time he had labored especially to learn the language of those people; thus, according to his ability, he both understood and spoke it. It came about that those to whom he gave words of life and counsels of unfailing life often brought bodily necessities to him and to those living with him. The servant of God, together with the men associated with him, gathered poor and needy persons to himself; and whatever remained to him beyond his daily sustenance, he used to feed them.

For he always remembered that Adam perished through food [Col. 1103A]. Therefore he frequently kept Anthony and Macarius, and men like them, in his heart, since they had lived on herbs and harsh food, so that by their example he might restrain his body from soft and delicate foods, lest he be deceived by the ancient serpent. And the more this blessed man afflicted his flesh, the more abundantly God multiplied His grace with him. Thus very many sick and infirm persons were brought to him, whom the Holy Spirit suddenly healed through his merits. Yet he himself, humbly fearing this, fled the praise of men as far as he could.

20. When the fame of his holiness spread throughout this province by the report of the people, certain God-fearing persons came to him and built for him a small oratory on the eastern descent of the aforesaid mountain, [Col. 1103B] in which he might celebrate the divine offices with his companions, so that both they and others who came for God’s sake might there receive from him the words and pasture of life. Others, toward the west, cut down brambles and thickets on the flat ground at the foot of the same mountain, and there prepared gardens, pastures, and small huts for the blessed man. Thus the place was first called *Studenheim*, from the thickets cut down there, which in common speech are called *studim*.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Germans know *Stauden* as the word for thickets; hence *Staudernheim* ought to have been formed. Perhaps Trithemius expressed the place-name better when he writes *Sobernheim* [Col. 1104D]; yet in the appendix of miracles *Studernheim* is again read.]

Many also came to this blessed man from distant regions and commended their souls to him in good faith and hope. The people dwelling in the same province, moved by divine inspiration, were troubled by this and said that they had been negligent in this matter, since God [Col. 1103C] had visited for the glory and honor of His name that place through His saint, though they, living near it, had neglected to visit it and honor it more often from their resources.

21. It therefore came about that the princes and other nobles and wealthy persons, together with the rest of the people inhabiting those lands, offered to this blessed man and to his successors the mountain itself with all its boundaries, extending beyond the rivers that flowed past it—namely the Nam [variant: Nahe] and the Glan—and stretching lengthwise and breadthwise as aforesaid. They did so because they saw God’s wonders in him, in order that, once good men had gathered there in holy observance, the necessities of the present life might be sufficiently supplied without want. With one voice and cry they said: “Praise to You, Lord God, because [Col. 1103D] You have deigned to send us this Your holy man.”

Having received this offering, the blessed man was afraid, remembering that he had previously endured many adversities from peoples while bearing the episcopal burden. Bending his knees to God, he prayed that the same offering might, by the Spirit’s gift, grow into fruitfulness and the flourishing of souls.

22. Then, day and night, fervently pondering in his heart, he considered how and where he might gather men of religious and austere life, as he had cherished in the desire of his mind for many years past. For he understood in the spirit that it befitted God that a spiritual congregation should serve its Creator in that place [Col. 1104A]. Inspired by the Holy Spirit, he directed all the devotion of his heart toward the religious practices and teaching of blessed Benedict, who had already passed to God and had left alive and surviving at that time certain blessed men, faithful ministers of his holy institution. With humble petition he sent messengers to distant regions where that same religious and holy way of life flourished, seeking men who would plant the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts according to the teaching of the aforesaid Father, who, taught by the Holy Spirit, had established from the whole life of the saints a rule suited to a spiritual people.

23. In this way he drew to himself very many religious men of the same way of life. He ordered suitable an oratory and dwellings to be built for them on the brow of the same mountain, [Col. 1104B] toward the east, because access was difficult: namely, so that they might no longer be harassed by the people, and so that perhaps their strictness and religious observance might not be turned into softness and sloth through the daily visits of newcomers.

He himself, however, in order to be ready for all occasions and to satisfy all arrivals in his answers according to their circumstances, remained alone on the eastern descent of the mountain, in the dwelling and oratory which he had prepared for himself, as stated above. The congregation of those brothers increased both before God and before men; and whatever they were to do or possess was done by the command or permission of this holy man [Col. 1104C]. They practiced the common life according to the institution of blessed Benedict.

24. For the devout Father Disibod strove to ensure that his congregation, ordered and made firm by the custom of the rule established for it, should be such that the devil could not prepare in it a pit of vices, nor pierce it through its gates and separate it one from another; and that, terrifying through the restraint of vices and like an army set in array, it might appear in the harmony of virtues before the devil and men. Wisely, he taught it to fight in humility against the hostile troops of aerial spirits, to avoid the vanity of pride and the arrogance of mind amid the pleasure of this world, and he diligently set before it the praise and glory of the victor who had fought lawfully and afterward carefully preserved himself in the vigilance of right circumspection [Col. 1104D].

He also surrounded and fortified it with the rampart of the strictness and severity of all spiritual discipline, lest the devil secretly and suddenly rush upon it. He knew that the devil strives most earnestly to attack a spiritual people, and rejoices much more if he has overcome a spiritual person according to the will of his perversity than if he had conquered many secular persons; for he sees that he has made that person like himself when he falls away from heavenly desire, just as he himself fell from heaven through pride.

25. In this manner the holy man began to gather [Col. 1105A] and strengthen his children. When secular people saw this, they flocked from the whole province; and whatever he began to work and do for his needs, they themselves willingly and diligently completed. Thus it came about that over twelve years that blessed congregation increased to the number of fifty perfected brothers. At that time few persons of this way of life were to be found, and no one entered upon this path unless he had been tested. But the Holy Spirit, who had planted this congregation, also watered it. As dew falls upon a rich field, so whoever was found in it under discipline ascended from virtue to virtue and met with no hindrance from the ancient plotter. For where the Holy Spirit is in His miracles, there the same ancient enemy is afraid [Col. 1105B] and will not dare to enter; but if he has secretly sown anything there, the Holy Spirit again tramples it down to his confusion.

The signs and miracles of God followed the merits and holiness of blessed Disibod; they were repeatedly renewed without weariness, because God always makes new things.

26. A certain man, whose tongue had become so weakened through excessive bodily infirmity that he could not utter human words, came to him from distant parts. By gestures and signs of his hands, as best he could, he tearfully begged him to assist him before God in this affliction. But the devout Father, having prayed over him and sensing God’s grace to be present, remembered the Lord’s example when He made the mute [Col. 1105C] speak. He breathed into this man’s mouth and said: “In the name of Him who said to the mute man, ‘Ephphatha,’ and he began to speak, I command you, bond of infirmity, which has weakened this man’s tongue: be loosed and depart from here; nor henceforth hinder his tongue from speaking.”

Immediately the bond on his tongue was loosened, and he uttered human words properly, giving thanks to God and to this holy man.

27. After this, a certain dropsical man, swollen by a remarkable distension, was brought to the same saint in the hands of his friends. With many tears shed, he sought from him health of body. But when he hesitated somewhat and declared himself unworthy of such a deed, at last overcome by the prayer of the supplicants, he prayed to the almighty Lord for the man. Touching him [Col. 1105D] with his hands, he blessed him, and thus the disease gradually disappeared from him through God’s grace.

28. A leper also, disfigured with dreadful skin, came to him. After first pouring out prayers for his infirmity, he even threatened in words that he would never leave him until he had been restored to health. At last the blessed man, moved by the man’s importunity, led him into his dwelling and kept him with himself for some time. Pouring out prayers for him repeatedly, he sent him back to his own home with the flesh of his body whole and beautiful. Truth itself, which then saw and did these things, has here brought them forth openly through itself for those who did not know them.

## CHAPTER III. The subjects’ reverence toward the saint; growth of the monastery; prophecy of its coming destruction; death; fragrant odor; burial; and various cures after it.

29. Many other signs and miracles were performed through him among blind, lame, and infirm people, among persons possessed by the devil, and also among those who had lost their senses because of the storm of evil humors. They were brought to him from distant and neighboring parts, and all were healed through him, because God’s power was in him.

For the same servant of God lived among his own people as a hermit—a life which is the root of the life of monks [Col. 1106B], because men of that way of life, wholly withdrawn from the world, live in solitude amid the praise of angels. Their life is so laborious that very many people, through frailty of both body and mind, could not endure it if they undertook it rashly and suddenly.

Living in this strict discipline, the blessed Father strengthened his subjects by teaching and example for every good work, just as one who makes a burning fire burn intensely does so. And they neither sought nor wished for another master while he lived, especially because they had among themselves, by his command, men who directed them in the uprightness of their way of life without offense or murmuring.

30. He had not assumed the monastic habit used by [Col. 1106C] his congregation.

[Note: [Col. 1105D] From this it is clear that Saint Disibod was neither a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict nor an abbot, as we have also pointed out above more than once.]

For he had granted his subjects a gentler observance according to the Rule of blessed Benedict than that which he himself maintained. He did this lest, if he were like them in habit while refusing to lay aside the harshness of his own rigor in vigils, fasts, and other mortifications of his flesh, he might appear to disparage their religious profession and destroy their common life.

But he frequently used, as long as he lived, the most wretched food, by which he barely sustained his body, and rough, harsh clothing, just as when he had gone forth from his homeland in pilgrimage. He imitated blessed Paul, the first hermit, and men like him, who preferred to be in forests rather than in villages. From the time when he was expelled from his see until [Col. 1106D] the end of his life, he also celebrated the divine rites at the altar not according to the order of bishops but according to the custom of poor priests.

[Note: [Col. 1106D] Hence it should not seem surprising if Rabanus did not know that he had been a bishop.]

In this he experienced no oppression of mind, but joy of heart, imitating Christ’s Passion.

31. He also frequently endeavored, as was right, to appoint a spiritual Father and protector over his congregation; but all those under him refused this, because they wished to have no father and teacher except him. They said that they did indeed have overseers of their way of life among themselves, [Col. 1107A] but that they would never replace him, so long as he lived, because he shone more sublimely for them in the Lord.

Therefore they became widely known through many provinces because of the good resolve which they held in their hearts. Many came to them seeking counsel and aid concerning their souls. Moreover, very many living in this province and in the vicinity of the aforesaid mountain, whose circuit was long and broad, offered without any reservation to the holy and blessed Disibod whatever they could possess or hope to have left over from their estates and resources; and they built small villages here and there in the aforesaid forest for the brethren’s use.

32. But when the saint of God had already labored there for a long time and his bodily strength had nearly failed from excessive exertions, he foretold tremblingly to his sons in the spirit that the prosperity and security which they had attained for a time without offense could not last forever. They would suffer many great oppressions and tribulations, because the devil—whom they had often put to great confusion by living well—would strive with the utmost zeal to trouble both them and their successors through the great derision which he strove to cause among the people. Yet he comforted them kindly and abundantly, saying: “Until now I have labored with sighs, sorrow of heart, and great desire, lest I should see your tribulation while I live in this world; and I trust in the Lord that this will indeed be so. [Col. 1107C] But know that after my death, which will come soon, since the strength of my body is now failing, and after the tribulations which you shall suffer, your latter times will be better and more prosperous than the former, so that then you and your descendants will abound more than while I was living in everything necessary for soul and body.”

33. When they heard these words, they mourned with tears in great grief, because they understood that his end was near. This report went out among the people and stirred many to come see him. They heard him and commended themselves to his prayers and holiness. Giving them counsels of salvation and words of blessing, he also commended to them his sons and the place [Col. 1107D] given to him, and, so that they might impress these matters more attentively upon their hearts, he did not conceal from them that his end also was near.

When they heard that the end of his life was at hand, they gave many groans in mournful voice and visited him more frequently than usual as long as he lived. He revealed to no one the source from which he knew his end, except a few religious men who knew nearly all his secrets. To them he had also said that it had been made known to him by an angelic manifestation. He concealed this from the others, since he hid all his works as far as he could, lest they perish through praise.

[Col. 1108A] 34. After he had faithfully served God on the aforesaid mountain for thirty years and had fully supplied his brothers with all the necessities of the present life, now worn out more by labor than by old age, he began to fall ill because his bodily strength had wholly failed. Soon he summoned all the brothers and named for them a Father; while still living, and then for the first time at their request, he placed this man over them and entrusted to him everything belonging to that place. For in times past he had refused to appoint a Father over them, because they had always followed that same saint in all things as their Father.

He also showed them the place of his burial and begged them with groans [Col. 1108B] and tears to bury him not in an exalted place but in the lowly shelter of his oratory, in which he had served God alone.

[Note: [Col. 1107D] The already mentioned engraved copper tablet rendered the sense of these words thus: “Bury me in the lowly place of the oratory where I served God alone.”]

Weeping in great sorrow, they promised that they would fulfill this request. In grief they also recounted one by one all his good works and teaching, and, weeping bitterly, cried: “Alas, alas! What will become of us when we lose you, the defender and comforter of our bodies and souls?”

[Note: [Col. 1107D] These words, however, have been rendered thus: “O Father, what will become of us when we lose you, our shepherd?”]

And as the thirsty stag desires springs of water, so they desired to keep him longer with them—something they had previously been unable to impress upon their hearts because of the joy they frequently had with him.

35. Finally, as his pain grew heavier, he summoned the brothers again and, as best he could, informed them that his end was at hand. After many labors and many tribulations, in the eighty-first year of his age, [Col. 1108C] on the eighth day before the Ides of July, he reached the end of his present life. In their presence he rendered his spirit to the Lord whom he had faithfully served.

At his departure there immediately followed a most sweet fragrance of balsam, like the scent of myrrh, incense, and every aromatic substance; and very many signs occurred there. News swiftly flew through the whole province that blessed Disibod had departed this life. A very great multitude of people hurried to his funeral, desiring both to be present at his burial and to see the signs which God performed there.

The most sweet odor that had appeared at his departure remained about his tomb until the thirtieth day after his death. During these days seven persons possessed by evil spirits, thirty lame persons, many blind and deaf persons [Col. 1108D], and very many others afflicted with various illnesses were truly healed through God’s grace when they touched his tomb.

36. Since these individual occurrences were many, and since the people of that time customarily regarded signs as matters to be imprinted more unusually upon their hearts—

[Note: [Col. 1108D] I think he means that the miracles were so frequent that people exulted over them with excessive novelty and gradually came to think little of them, as can sufficiently be inferred from what follows.]

—that people, seeing them, said: “God shows us greater signs and more miracles after the death of this blessed man than while he was alive; therefore we also trust that through his merits we shall be rescued from all [Col. 1109A] our dangers.” But because many rejoiced in these signs which were then performed there, and in all those afterward performed there through God’s grace, more and more carelessly than they ought, God withdrew them as a correction.

For the Holy Spirit does not wish a person to glory in miracles that come from Him, but that glory should be attributed with awe-filled praise to Him alone who has the power to perform them. God distinguishes the works of His saints just as He established the creatures: that is, He grants good works and holiness to some without signs; to others He attributes good works and great miracles also; and to still others He grants by His grace that many may be converted to Him through their good examples—just as He distinguishes the sun [Col. 1109B] for the day, and the moon and stars for the night, in their seasons.

37. He also filled the whole circuit of the world with birds, creeping things, and the other living animals, so that it is nowhere empty in any need. Thus each creature prompts him concerning its functions in that monastery which pertains to man. For every creature multiplies in its own kind, as God commanded it in the first creation; but the irrational creature comes to man’s aid by serving him, because the master of the household, who is man, cannot govern his house without help and service.

But God made man alone to live by a rational and living soul; therefore [Col. 1109C] his breath does not fail, just as the branches of a tree do not fail, because God infused knowledge into him, so that by thinking he dictates what he wishes, and what he has in his mind he afterward multiplies by a crying voice and rational speech, just as leaves multiply upon a tree.

38. An irrational creature has no knowledge of rationality, and therefore is windy and passes away. But the human being, being rational, recognizes usefulness through knowledge, loves it, and draws it to himself; and in that same knowledge he sees what is evil and what is harmful, fears and flees it, and guards himself against it. By these two things—namely fear and love, which he possesses in the knowledge of good and evil—he governs himself everywhere, just as a bird flies with two wings. [Col. 1109D] For he alone was formed in the image and likeness of God, because God created him to act according to that image and likeness. Hence, wherever his conscience raises itself toward good, there the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit comes to meet him. For, as has been said, God placed all creatures within this distinction; and because He made the human being in His own image and likeness, He gave him complete knowledge beyond every mortal creature.
