39. And because his flesh has an end and a failing, his soul can possess the accomplishment of good only from Him who is without end. But those who persevere in good unto the end ascend to God in heaven; and there the cherub counts all their good works before the throne of God, [Col. 1110A] and then the face of God looks upon them as most pure gold and as most precious and noble stones. Therefore all heavenly harmony sings a new song over them, and thus the Holy Spirit always makes new things in the works of the saints. But those who persevere in evil imitate the lost angels, who fell from the glory of heaven because of their wickedness; and thus, through foul vanities, they lose the reward of eternal life.

40. For God bestowed upon the human being complete knowledge of rationality, as has been said, because He foresaw that through it the human being could overcome the devil: for by good knowledge a person knows evil, and by evil knowledge knows good. Therefore he fights a most victorious battle against that ancient enemy, in order to conquer him and possess the place which he lost. This he could by no means do unless he possessed complete knowledge, since a person can scarcely keep himself from occasionally turning by choice toward that which he knows by knowing. But if dark shadows rise into the human heart, so that a person perceives in his flesh that he can sin, and if he then chooses sin and perseveres in it without repentance, he will be made like him who withdrew from the brightness of light in order to fulfil the desires of his dark nature; and for this reason the punishments of Gehenna arose.

41. But the blessed person desires to do what he does not perceive in his flesh, [Col. 1110C] and asks help from the Holy Spirit, that he may look into the mirror of holiness. And just as a person considers his face in a mirror—though he is not in that mirror—and, whatever he sees there to be unseemly, corrects as far as he can, so the blessed person desires by faith to perform good works, in this manner and to the devil’s confusion, against his own flesh; he performs what the flesh does not prescribe to him. Thus, overcoming himself and his desires through exceedingly harsh and powerful battles, he will possess the charity which the lost angels had possessed.

For God established creatures in such a way that the human being completes his works together with them. Thus He also endows certain persons so that they build holy structures and gather others to serve God; yet God Himself often permits them many and varied reversals, according to His will. He endures all these things, yet does not at once inflict His vengeance upon them. But where the Holy Spirit builds in buildings and in persons, even if they have lived carelessly in sins, should anyone there bring destruction through the obstinacy of his perversity, the fire of the Holy Spirit swiftly consumes him in its zeal and judgment. [Note: [Col. 1109] I doubt whether anyone can clearly discern where this long excursus is tending, or how it came to be introduced here.]

## CHAPTER IV. The monks’ dispersal and return; the translation of the sacred body by St Boniface; the ruin of the monastery and its fortunes and vicissitudes.

42. In this manner the Holy Spirit also worked in the aforesaid place, where blessed Disibod had served God in good works, [Col. 1111A] and where, departing from this life, he had rendered his blessed spirit to the Lord. For, some years after his passing, a great pressure of wars seized the whole aforesaid province, so that certain men, arriving in tyrannical fury, devastated that province together with the districts and lands adjoining the Rhine on every side. The inhabitants of these places, terrified by this dread and fear, fled wherever they could.

But the princes of the aforesaid province, together with the rest of the people, knowing the aforesaid mountain to be high and impregnable, fled hastily onto it before it could be occupied by the enemy, against the wishes of the brothers serving God there. They fortified it with strong walls and made dwellings upon it, trusting [Col. 1111B] that, both through the merits of blessed Disibod and through the fortifications of that mountain, they would be rescued from the aforesaid cruel tyranny.

43. But because of the multitude and disturbance of those people who had occupied the mountain, the congregation of brothers serving God there could neither remain in peace nor serve God rightly. Therefore, by the counsel and request of those same princes and people, the brothers dispersed into distant regions, because they promised that, after these tribulations and labours, they would bring them back with honour. A few devout and perfect men excepted, they withdrew to the tomb of the blessed man, that is, of their patron, in order to preserve it in honour. [Col. 1111C] These men were so perfect that they cared nothing even for their own lives.

That aforesaid affliction, however, [Note: [Col. 1111D] Concerning this first migration of the monks from their mountain, here described confusedly, and likewise concerning the other events which followed, enough has been said in the first paragraph of the Commentary. Likewise concerning the elevation of the sacred body by St Boniface and the other translations, [Col. 1112D] so that it would be pointless here to pile up further notes.] did not last for many years; rather, this province was freed, with God’s help, from the tyranny of the hostile invaders. When this had happened, those who had occupied the mountain, remembering their promise and having regard for the fear of God, sought out the brothers of the aforesaid congregation wherever they could and brought them back with great honour. They granted them all that they had gathered and built there, together with greater resources and more extensive freehold estates than they had formerly possessed.

44. Thus it came about, according to the words of blessed Disibod which he had foretold while alive, that their latter times [Col. 1111D] after his death and after their tribulations became better and more prosperous than their earlier times had been. Indeed, very many people, spiritual and secular alike, came there even from distant regions and sought and received from them counsel and assistance for both souls and bodies.

But God purified these blessed men as often as they sinned, on account of their negligences. So He did then, when they rejoiced piously but more carelessly than they should have done in the signs and miracles wrought through the merits of the aforesaid holy Father; therefore, from then onward they did not appear in such abundance as they had formerly appeared. But where the works of the Holy Spirit are seen and recognized, and are nevertheless displayed for show, there that same Holy Spirit investigates such an offence by judicial punishment down to the last farthing.

45. When signs and miracles ceased to occur at the tomb of this blessed Father, although his descendants had reverently observed his passage to God for many years, at length they groaned inwardly with sighs. By divine prompting they remembered that, because their sins demanded it, God had withdrawn His hand from the prodigies of miracles there, and that He showed them only [Col. 1112B] occasionally, for the remembrance of that saint. Accusing themselves, they said to one another:

“What are we doing, languishing in negligence, that we do not venerate this saint of God, when through his merits God has performed for us very many miracles and good things?”

Accordingly, they approached the elders and all the wise persons of that province and, taking counsel from them, set a time and day, with the consent and authority of Boniface, bishop of the see of Mainz, on which they would elevate the bones of blessed Disibod. They announced this day throughout all the people of that land. When the appointed day arrived and a multitude of people had assembled, they approached the holy man’s tomb in the presence of the aforesaid bishop and, with great veneration, raised his bones and ashes. [Col. 1112C] With hymns of praise and the loud voices of the people, many years after his passage to the Lord, they translated them from the shelter of the oratory in which they had been buried to a monastery built on the same mountain, almost toward its western side, and honourably deposited them in a place prepared for this purpose.

46. But God, who knows hidden things, again made the merits of His saint manifest there. On that same day, while these things were being done, a dropsical man and other sick persons burdened with various infirmities were cured. More remarkably, the most sweet fragrance which had appeared at his passing appeared again throughout that day with wonderful sweetness. Thus the people of that province thereafter regularly observed, with great veneration of prayers and offerings, both the annual day on which these things took place [Col. 1112D] and the day of his passage to the Lord, coming to his tomb. [Note: [Col. 1112D] St Hildegard expressly notes here a double feast; yet, remarkably, she does not even indicate the day on which this first elevation took place and its commemoration was celebrated.]

The brothers of the aforesaid congregation therefore lived in peace for many years and served God and blessed Disibod quietly and without offence. The people greatly loved and blessed them, supported them everywhere with their help and goods, and consequently they became wealthy and rich in many resources.

[Col. 1113A] 47. Finally, after the passage of very many courses of years and kings, the greatest conflicts again arose with the inhabitants of the province concerning the aforesaid religious house. Therefore the elders, together with the princes of that land, approached the emperor—namely Charlemagne, who at that time held the Roman Empire—and said that it was not fitting for those who ought to serve the spirit rather than the flesh, God rather than the world, to possess in excess the riches and splendours of the age, as those on the mountain of St Disibod did, while they themselves were oppressed by wars and hardships and had no wealth or resources by which they could serve the kingdom and assist themselves.

The emperor received their words wisely and wisely disregarded them, saying that he would on no account take away from those brothers either the freehold estates [Col. 1113B] or other resources which the faithful had granted them. Having received this answer, they refrained from their intended course.

48. After this emperor had died, and after very many other times and successors, tyranny of cruel wars again arose. It grew so powerful in cruelty that certain cities adjoining the Rhine were destroyed by these oppressions. Therefore the nobles of the aforesaid province, who were descended from the aforesaid princes, likewise approached the emperor who then held the Empire, together with the bishop of the see of Mainz allied with them. They pressed the aforesaid complaint more vehemently, saying that they had no abundance of resources [Col. 1113C] by which they could serve the Empire and defend their lives, because those who lived on the mountain of St Disibod possessed their own freehold estates and those of their ancestors; and they said that they did not know how this could be.

Having heard them, the emperor gave his assent. Summoning the other princes and judges, he wished, as if under judicial inquiry, to investigate by what grant and confirmation such widespread and extensive freehold possessions had been bestowed upon the brothers.

49. But, understanding the emperor’s disposition and blinded by envy and malice, they brought forward many false and unjustly contrived testimonies. They said that the aforesaid brothers possessed unjustly and without imperial judgment or grant those estates which they had held for very many ages without complaint. Therefore, [Col. 1113D] by the judgment of unjust judges, an imperial sentence having been issued and permission having been received from that emperor, the proclaimers of the aforesaid complaint, together with the aforesaid bishop, who was the chief author of this invasion, disturbed through a most cruel invasion and seizure the possessions and freehold estates belonging to the mountain of blessed Disibod, as well as the boundaries of that mountain—divine vengeance permitting it.

Troubled and dismayed by this persecution and injury, wholly stripped of possessions and terrified by the dread of impending wars, the brothers living there left that mountain with loud lamentation and crying, and went wherever they could to foreign places.

50. After they had departed, lest they retain hope of returning, the aforesaid invaders also razed their dwellings to the ground, [Col. 1114A] except for the consecrated place in which the bones of the aforesaid saint had been interred after his translation. Yet, lest that place be left utterly desolate of the divine office, those who had been the authors of this destruction appointed there a priest to govern the people living nearby. From the benefices belonging to that place they assigned him barely sufficient food and clothing. Thus this place remained for a long time in such desolation.

Finally, after many courses of years, a certain leading and noble man, a count of the aforesaid province named Liuthard, devoted to the secular world and surrounded by great wealth, saw the aforesaid mountain, high, beautiful, and desolate. Moved by divine grace, he sighed and, for the glory of the Holy Trinity and in memory of St Disibod, resolved to establish three priests there to serve God. [Col. 1114B] From his own resources he provided them with sufficient necessities for the present life.

51. Later, after some years had passed, an archbishop of the see of Mainz—pious, humble, and contrite in heart—ascended that same mountain and devoutly bent his knees at the tomb of blessed Disibod. He deeply grieved that he had become great and wealthy from possessions unjustly taken from that saint. Making a vow to God, he arranged for canons, in the number of the twelve Apostles, to serve God and the aforesaid patron there day and night. He also caused as much as he could of the freehold estates belonging to that place [Col. 1114C] to be restored to them.

Thus divine correction gradually somewhat withdrew its scourges; yet it had not fully completed this work. Accordingly, when it afterwards pleased the Holy Spirit in His hidden counsel, He inspired a certain man prudent in worldly matters, who also presided over the see of Mainz, and made him desire that the often-mentioned place might recover the splendour which it had received at its first foundation.

For he acted as a prudent householder who divided his substance among his children with charity: he kindly placed the canons remaining on the aforesaid mountain in other places suitable for them, and restored there religious men who lived in great discipline according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, and among whom every good thing was brought to fulfilment by holy living. [Col. 1114D]

52. When this was done, he regarded them with the embrace of his heart; and, as a blessed man generous in giving, he ministered to them, as far as he could, alms from the substance and resources that he possessed.

The congregation then and afterwards suffered many scourges there by divine permission, just as those who had formerly been there had often suffered; as indeed now often happens there under the scourges of God, and as will happen thereafter when those dwelling there have deserved it. But many foolish tales concerning all the aforesaid matters circulate and are related among the people through the variety of many vicissitudes; these the Holy Spirit does not gather, and therefore they are scattered like straw. But the things set forth here [Col. 1115A] have been made manifest by a truthful revelation through the Holy Spirit, for the glory of His name, the remembrance of the aforesaid patron, and the correction of the people who hear them. Therefore nothing from earlier opinions should be added to them, lest the words of Him who Is be turned into mockery.

53. It must therefore also be considered what God has worked among human beings from the first human being until now. When Adam first fell, he went into exile from Paradise; and because he fell through a lowly creature, God also wished creatures to be offered to Him [or perhaps: not to be offered], just as an infant is first nourished with milk. But after the Son of God put on humanity, He offered Himself as a sacrifice to the Father and opened the human mouth to the food of righteousness, [Col. 1115B] just as a child is fed.

But when that same Son ascended into heaven, He filled human beings with the fire of the Holy Spirit, and taught them to fight against vices and desires and thus make themselves a sacrifice to God. Thus they chose to live according to heavenly harmony, as spiritual people do, who have left themselves and the world for the love of God; and as other good people also strive to do, who in ardent desire undertake strong self-restraint according to the gift of the Holy Spirit—just as [Col. 1116A] a person at mature age takes food by himself.

54. Thus God acted here also, because He removed wavering opinion and commanded truth to come forth walking confidently. The same God has often purified those who dwelt and dwell in the aforesaid place, as has been said, just as He has often chastised very many others; yet He did not abandon them altogether, just as He dealt with Israel, who, although they had begun well, suffered many persecutions because of the many vanities which they later committed. They will also be sought out in an evil time, and thus they will not utterly perish.

Now let there be praise to God, who always wages war against the ancient serpent, so that He has cleansed every wrinkle of sin [Col. 1116B] until the consummation of the age, when the whole constitution of His faithful will appear in fullness—into which He first ordained it. Then the ancient enemy will be utterly confounded, because he will be able neither to benefit himself nor others nor give glory to anyone.

These words were spoken by true Wisdom:

“But I, a poor little woman, lying in the bed of my illness, saw and heard all these things, and began and completed writing them; but God has power to raise me from my bed, if it please Him. Amen.”

[Col. 1117]

# Nine Books of St Hildegard, Abbess, on the Subtleties of the Diverse Natures of Created Things

Now first transcribed from an ancient manuscript codex of the Imperial Library of Paris, under the care of Dr C. Daremberg, Prefect of the Mazarine Library, etc.; with Prolegomena and Notes by Dr F. A. Reuss, Professor at Würzburg.

## Prolegomena and Notes

Medicine, the gracious gift of the divine power [Note: [Col. 1117] Ecclesiasticus 38:1; Scribonius Largus, *Medical Compositions*, I.1.], was cultivated in temples and by priests in the most ancient times in Egypt and Greece, as though it were an invention of the gods [Note: [Col. 1117] Pliny, *Natural History*, XXV.1; XXIX.1; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I.521.]. So too, after the Christian religion had penetrated various regions of the West and had begun to render milder the wild manners of their inhabitants through the cultivation of sciences and arts, while enriching their long-deserted fields with diverse kinds of newly introduced crops, medicine was customarily practised throughout the whole Middle Ages in monasteries and by monks with the greatest diligence.

Whatever sacred antiquity had transmitted concerning the wholesome powers of natural things and the healing art which cures by the hand, we owe to the studies of earlier cenobites, who diligently investigated nature and carefully preserved and cultivated it. Relying on the authority of the Church, these same men venerated certain saints as, so to speak, tutelary protectors of medicine as a whole—Cosmas, Damian, and Pantaleon, [Note: [Col. 1118] Procopius, *On Buildings*, I.6–7.] men exceedingly renowned in the healing art while alive. They were also accustomed to invoke many heavenly beings in their prayers as present powers in particular kinds of illness and patrons of the sick: Christopher, namely, the averting saint of sudden death, whose image is seen painted here and there in ancient buildings, with the inscription:

> Whenever you see Christopher’s face in daylight,  
> On that day you shall not die an evil death.

Or:

> Holy Christopher, so great are your powers  
> That whoever sees you in the morning laughs in the night-time.

Patrick was invoked against the bites of rabid dogs and vipers; Liborius against stones of the bladder; Roch against plague; Urban in gout; Blaise in disorders of the throat; Apollonia in toothache; Minum in syphilis; and also Crescentia, believed able to cure every infirmity except leprosy. Not to mention very many others, there were countless cures of diseases [Col. 1119] occurring everywhere on earth at altars and the tombs of heavenly saints. [Note: [Col. 1118] St Vitus’s dance and St Anthony’s fire also seem to belong here. See Haeser, *History of Medicine*, §256.]

Monks also dedicated to saints, as their guardians, various kinds of herbs which they cultivated either after transferring them from the fields into monastic gardens or after receiving them from foreign lands. In kind remembrance of their grace, they made these plants better known by the saints’ bynames. Such names include:

- Eye of Christ = *Myosotis scorpioides* L.
- St Mary’s rose = *Paeonia officinalis* L.
- St Mary’s flower = *Bellis perennis* L.
- St Mary’s thistle = *Carduus Marianus* L.
- St Mary’s little shoe = *Cypripedium Calceolus* L.
- St Mary’s seal = *Polypodium vulgare* L.
- St Mary’s straw = *Galium mollugo* and *G. verum* L.
- St Barbara’s herb = *Erysimum Barbarea* L.
- St Catherine’s herb = *Antirrhinum linaria* L.
- St Margaret’s herb = *Anemone silvestris* L.
- St Cunegund’s herb = *Eupatorium cannabinum* L.
- St Clare’s herb = *Valeriana officinalis* L.
- St Paul’s herb = *Primula veris* L.
- St James’s herb = *Senecio Jacobaeus* L.
- St Quirinus’s herb = *Tussilago Farfara* L.
- St Gerard’s herb = *Aegopodium Podagraria* L.
- St Rupert’s herb = *Geranium Robertianum* L.
- St John’s herb = *Hypericum perforatum* L.
- St Anthony’s herb = *Plumbago vulgaris* L.
- St Zacharias’s herb = *Centaurea Cyanus* L.
- Herb of the Holy Cross = *Nicotiana Tabacum* L.
- St Ignatius’s bean = *Strychnos nux vomica* L.
- Root of the Holy Spirit = *Angelica Archangelica* L. [Note: [Col. 1119] Is it so called in honour of that archangel in Tobit 12:15?]
- Lance of Christ = *Ophioglossum vulgatum* L.
- Herb of good Henry = *Chenopodium bonus Henricus* L.
- Seal of Solomon = *Convallaria polygonatum* L.

According to tradition, *Carlina acaulis* L. was shown by an angel to Charlemagne as a most excellent remedy during plague. [Note: [Col. 1119] Caesalpinus, *On Plants*, XIII.38. Compare Johann Bacchini, chapter “On Plants Taking Their Names from the Blessed and Saints,” in C. Gesner’s *Letters*.]

Conversely, people believed that the devil, the ancient enemy of humankind, had discovered how to destroy the powers of health-giving plants so that they might be unable to bring help to the sick. This belief was reflected in the herb commonly called *Praemorsa* (“pre-bitten”) or “Devil’s Bite,” *Scabiosa succisa* L., according to Brunfels, *Herbal*, II.50:

> “It is called the Devil’s Bite because it bears a root bitten off below; they say in a fable that the evil demon snatches it away as soon as it begins to grow or be dug up, lest it come into use for human life.”

The same devil, when he infests houses, was believed to be driven far away by perforated herb, or St John’s wort, hence called “Flight of Demons,” *Hypericum perforatum* L. It held great authority in ancient magical practice, as though it were a “plant above images” (*phytòn hypèr eikónas*, φυτὸν ὑπὲρ εἰκόνας), Dioscorides III.146. [Note: [Col. 1120] *Hypericum*, together with *Eryngium campestre* L. and *Stachys recta* L., was used in love-potions. Compare G. a Reiss, *Pleasant Questions, Elysian Fields*, XXIX and XCVII; Simon Maioli, *Dialogues*, II.215.]

Many plants also received names from their special nature and power, including:

- Grace of God = *Geranium Robertianum* L.
- Gracious herb = *Gratiola officinalis* L.
- Hundred-illness herb = *Lysimachia nummularia* L.
- Blood-stauncher = *Poterium Sanguisorba* L.
- Eye-herb = *Euphrasia officinalis* L.
- Urinary herb = *Ononis spinosa* L.
- Rheumatic herb = *Geranium pratense* L.
- Ulcer-healing herb = *Ballota nigra* L.
- Hernia herb = *Herniaria glabra* L.
- Cross herb = *Gentiana cruciata* L. (*Fuchs, On Plants*, 158: because its root is divided in the form of a cross.)
- Eagle fern = *Pteris aquilina* L.
- Paralysis herb = *Primula veris* L.

And many others.

The flower of the dandelion was called the Monk’s Head or Crown. *Dianthus Carthusianorum* L. drew its name from the Carthusian order. Monks were accustomed to celebrate the powers of such herbs in leonine mnemonic verses, for example:

> Borage says: “I always bring joys.”  
> Spurge gives milk; toadflax grows without milk.  
> Amaranth stinks; its like, chamomile, is fragrant.  
> Elder is *Actis*, but dwarf elder is *Chamaeactis*.  
> Pimpernel bears hairs; saxifrage bears none.  
> Iris bears a purple flower; *Ireos* a white one;  
> Gladiolus a saffron-coloured flower; but foul-smelling spathula none.  
> There is no herb in the world more excellent than tobacco.

And similar verses.

How greatly monastic medicine flourished in the Carolingian age is attested by the most charming poem of Walahfrid Strabo, entitled *The Little Garden* (*Hortulus*), which seems to breathe the tranquil life and studies of the cenobites. From the same order of St Benedict came the illustrious Constantine the African [Note: [Col. 1121]

Some verses on the powers of scabious (*Scabiosa arvensis* and *S. columbaria* L.), composed under the name of Pope St Urban II [d. 1099], survive. They first occur in a parchment manuscript of the *Regimen of Salerno*, written in the fourteenth century and preserved in the Palatine Library at Vienna:

> Urban, in seeing it, knows not the worth of scabious:  
> It strengthens the breast which sick old age weighs down;  
> It soothes the lung and removes pain in the sides;  
> Drunk internally, it thereby evacuates the bowels;  
> Applied outwardly as a plaster, it kills anthrax within three hours;  
> It removes the sickness of cattle and destroys poison;  
> By proven power it gently breaks an abscess.

The same verses, with slight alterations, appear in print in Matthaeus Silvaticus, *Medical Pandects*, Lyons, 1478, folio, chapter 631; in the Mainz herbal of 1484, quarto, p. 139; and the Paduan herbal of 1485, p. 139; in Musa Brasavola, *Examination of Medical Simples*, Lyons, 1537, octavo; and in René Moreau’s edition of the School of Salerno, Paris, 1625, octavo.

It is said that Pope St Urban, at the request of a sister who was short of breath, sent her the following verses concerning the powers of this herb, since he himself used it continually:

> Urban, for himself, knows not the worth of scabious:  
> For it cleanses the breast which sick old age constricts;  
> It soothes the lung and cleanses the region of the sides;  
> It breaks an abscess, if, when drunk, it touches the place;  
> Applied outwardly, it relieves anthrax within three hours.

] a monk at Monte Cassino, d. 1087; Aegidius of Corbeil, a most expert author on uroscopy; Bartholomew the Englishman; and many others. Marbod, bishop of the Church of Rennes, and Bishop Theobald belonged to the secular clergy. That celebrated Albert the Great, a polymath equal to Aristotle and Pliny, professed the Rule of St Dominic.

Yet St Hildegard surpasses all who practised medicine in the Middle Ages and adorned it with their writings. [Note: [Col. 1122] The oldest mention of St Hildegard occurs in a German poem in von der Hagen’s *Collection*, III.468, by Marner, 118:

> Lady Hildegard of Bingen—it is written in the books  
> That I have thoroughly examined all her words in truth;  
> The names of kings are in them; may that book grant you this.

] According to the testimony of the monk Theodoric, so powerful a grace of healing shone forth in her that scarcely any sick person came to her without immediately recovering health.

Among the surviving books of the prophetic virgin is a work partly physical and partly medical, *On the Nature of Man, the Elements, and Diverse Creatures*. [Note: [Col. 1122] Compare Reuss, *Historical-Medical Commentary on the Physical Books of St Hildegard*.] In it, as the same Theodoric explains more fully, she disclosed the secrets of nature by the prophetic spirit. This work, in which the holy virgin, wholly initiated into the sacred mysteries of nature, expounds—under divine admonition—whatever she had investigated by the keenest contemplation and a deeper knowledge of things, as though hidden in obscurity and recesses, will always deserve an eminent place in the history of medicine and natural science. [Note: [Col. 1122] Choulant, *Handbook of Bibliography for Older Medicine*, 2nd ed., 302.]

It is clear that St Hildegard already knew very many things unknown to other medieval writers, which only the acute investigators of more recent times discovered and advertised as new. Yet these matters can finally be understood more clearly only through much and constant study and through a grasp of the character of all St Hildegard’s works. In them, using a distinctive manner and form of expression unusual among other authors [Note: [Col. 1122] Hildegard briefly mentions the sources from which she drew at I.51; VII.5; and II.58.], she habitually investigates the entire system of the whole world, especially in her book *On the Divine Works of a Simple Man*, [Note: [Col. 1122] Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin*, III.264; Haupt, *Journal*, VI.321.] which contains many curious matters concerning the organism of the whole world, human nature, diseases, and the influence of air and stars.

These books, entitled *On the Nature of Man, the Elements, and Diverse Creatures*, or *Simple and Compound Medicine*, were written between 1150 and 1160. That they are a genuine work of St Hildegard, although different persons at different times have dared to deny it, [Col. 1123] is attested by a passage in her book *The Merits of Life*, in the unpublished Wiesbaden manuscript, in these words: “The same vision had shown me, for explanation, the subtleties of the diverse natures of creatures.” Parallel or common passages, consonant thoughts, and similar words occur very frequently in these medical books as well as in the letters and other works published under St Hildegard’s name, and show that all have one and the same author.

This medical work of St Hildegard, whose manuscripts Bruno, canon of Strasbourg, saw in the monastery of St Rupert, and Alberic, a monk, saw at Strasbourg, was very well known to and highly esteemed by the famous Johann Trithemius, abbot of St James of the Scots at Würzburg. He had a copy made for himself from the archetype preserved on Mount St Rupert. [Note: [Col. 1124] Trithemius, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, p. 138: “In the medical books she refers many wonderful things and secrets of nature, by subtle exposition, to a mystical meaning, such that a woman could know such matters only from the Holy Spirit.” Trithemius, *Chronicle of Hirsau*, p. 175.]

The Strasbourg manuscript was first printed through the agency of the bookseller Johann Schott at Strasbourg, 14 January 1533, in folio, under the title:

> *The Physica of St Hildegard: transmitting to posterity, in four books and with wonderful experience, the natures and operations of the elements; certain rivers of Germany; metals; legumes, fruits, and herbs; trees and shrubs; and finally fishes, birds, and land animals.*
This edition appends Latin translations of short medical works by Oribasius, Theodorus, and Aesculapius. The *Physica*, which immediately precedes them, is arranged in four books: the first, divided into 22 chapters, contains the natures and operations of the elements, several rivers of Germany, and metals; the second, in 179 chapters, treats vegetables, fruits, and herbs; the third, in 53 chapters, the natures and effects of trees and shrubs. Finally, the fourth, divided into three parts, pursues the natural history and medicinal powers respectively of fishes (the first part, with 25 chapters), birds (the second, with 53 chapters), and terrestrial animals (the third, with 44 chapters). In 1544 this entire edition was reprinted in G. Kraut’s *Experimentarium*; in it a copyist seems to have copied incorrectly from an autograph manuscript very many words that were more difficult to read. We deeply regret that we do not know where this autograph went, or where it now lies hidden. Both editions of the *Physica* are now counted among the rarer books.

> [Note: Col. 1124. Compare Meiners, *Progr. de S. Hildegardis vita, script. et meritis*; Dahl, *Die heil. Hildegard*; Remling, *Geschichte d. Abteien und Kloster in Rheinbayern*, I, 159; Tiraquellus, *De nobilitate*, I, 31; Paschal Galli, *Bibliotheca medica*, 281; *Spicilegium Dacherianum*, III, IV, 15; *Chronicon Senonense*.]

The text of our edition has principally been prepared according to the standard of an old fifteenth-century paper manuscript, consisting of 75 leaves, preserved in the Imperial Library at Paris under no. 6952 and already cited by the distinguished Haller in *Bibliotheca botanica*, I, 218. Dr. C. Daremberg—an outstanding physician and philologist, and librarian of the Mazarine Library—most generously shared with me a copy transcribed for this purpose **with the greatest accuracy** (*πλείστῃ σὺν ἀκριβείᾳ*). We must therefore thank him, since this most important genuine and complete work of St Hildegard can now for the first time appear in print in this volume. I judged that the manuscript’s archaic spellings should generally be retained, with very few exceptions—for example, *comedere, comestus* for *commedere, commestus*; *his* for *hiis*—or where there were obvious scribal errors, such as *hyeme, amentia* for *hieme, amendia*, etc.

> [Note: Col. 1123. Furthermore, I carefully compared the edition with the copy; extracted the most valuable variety of readings; enclosed in brackets additions taken from the edition; transcribed at the foot of the pages those chapters in the edition which differ wholly from chapters of the same subject in the copy; examined the printed text, as far as the short time allowed me permitted; and finally reread the German words in the manuscript. But alas! Such monstrous errors had escaped the eyes of the compositors that one must fear many inaccuracies may still lurk there. Certainly, so far as depended on me, nothing more or better could have been done.]

CAR. DAR.

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF THE BLESSED HILDEGARD ON THE SUBTLETIES OF THE DIVERSE NATURES OF CREATED THINGS, AND THUS ON VERY MANY OTHER GOOD THINGS

[Col. 1125]

# BOOK ONE: ON PLANTS. PREFACE

[Col. 1125A] In the creation of the human being, another earth was taken from the earth, and that is the human being. All the elements served him, because they perceived that he lived; they worked with him in all his dealings, and he with them. The earth gave forth its greenness according to the kind, nature, character, and whole condition of the human being. For the earth, through useful herbs, displays the course of a person’s spiritual dispositions, distinguishing them; but through useless herbs it reveals that person’s useless and devilish dispositions.

For there are certain herbs that are cooked with certain foods. These make a person quick for nourishment and are light, because they do not make a person very heavy; and they are likened to human flesh. The juice of fruit-bearing trees, when uncooked, is harmful, but when cooked it is light; it is compared to human blood. Fruitless woody plants which do not bear produce are woods, not trees, and have only leaves, useless for human food. If anyone eats them, they are of little benefit, although they do not harm him greatly; they are compared to human wasting disease (*tabes*). That in trees and woody plants from which ropes are made is likened to human veins. The stones of the earth are also compared to human bones, and the moisture of stones to the marrow of the bones, because a stone which possesses moisture also possesses heat. But stones used for roofing are likened to the fingernails and toenails.

And certain airy herbs grow [Col. 1126A]; these too are light for human digestion and of a cheerful nature, so that they make cheerful the person who eats them. They are likened to human hair, because they are always light and airy. But certain other herbs are windy: they grow from wind, are dry, and are heavy for human digestion and of a sad nature, so that they make sad the person who eats them. They are compared or likened to human sweat. The juice, however, of useless herbs that cannot be eaten is poisonous, because they are deadly as human food; it is compared to human excrement.

> [Note: Col. 1125B. Genesis 1:27; Ecclesiasticus 17:1; Hildegard, letter to the abbess of Ebrach (letter 30); the same author’s letter to the prelates of Mainz (letter 47); the same author’s *Scivias*, III.2. Compare chapter 56 below, “On Mandrake.”]

> [Note: Col. 1126B. Genesis 1:2; Hildegard, letter to Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg (letter 14).]

The earth has sweat, moisture, and sap. Its sweat produces useless herbs; its moisture, useful herbs that may be eaten and are of value for other human uses; and its sap produces vines and budding trees.

Herbs that are sown through human labour and rise and grow little by little—like domestic animals which a person carefully raises in the home—lose, through the labour by which they are ploughed and sown by human beings, the sharpness and bitterness of their juices. Thus the moisture of those juices somewhat partakes of the quality of human juice and is, in a certain way, good and useful in foods and drinks. But herbs that grow, when their seed falls, without human labour, and rise suddenly and hastily like untamed beasts, are contrary to human beings as food. For a human being is nourished gradually, through suckling, eating, and growing, in a temperate time; this does not occur in the herbs mentioned above. Yet some of them restrain harmful and diseased humours in people medicinally.

> [Note: Col. 1126B. Compare the preface to Book VII, “On Animals.”]

Every herb is either hot or cold, and grows accordingly; for the heat of herbs signifies soul, and their coldness body. In these, according to their kind, they flourish, as they abound either in heat or in cold. If all herbs were hot and none cold, they would create an imbalance for those who use them. If all were cold and none hot, they would likewise produce an inequality in human beings, because hot herbs withstand a person’s coldness and cold herbs that person’s heat.

Certain herbs contain in themselves the power of the strongest spices and the harshness of the most bitter spices. Hence they restrain very many evils, because evil spirits produce these evils and hold those herbs in aversion. There are also certain herbs that possess, as it were, the foam of the elements; through them people, deceived, try to seek their fortunes. The devil loves these and mingles himself with them.

> [Note: Col. 1129. Chapters 170–202 occur in the text below after chapter 188.]

# Here Begins Book One

[Col. 1129]

## Chapter I—On Wheat

> [Note: Col. 1129C. *Triticum vulgare* [common wheat]. In the edition, II.1.]

[Col. 1129A] Wheat is hot and is complete fruit, so that it has no defect in it. When proper flour is made from wheat, bread made from that flour is good for healthy and sick people, and produces sound flesh and sound blood in a person.

But whoever sifts from that flour the pith—that is, the fine meal, *griesz*—and makes bread from this *donft* [fine flour?], that bread is weaker and more feeble than if it had been made from the proper flour itself. For the *donft* [the same pith, ed.] loses some of its powers and produces more *slim* [“lividity,” ed.; and so below] in a person than proper wheat flour itself.

Whoever cooks wheat without its whole grains, and not ground in a mill, and thus eats it as though it were another food, produces in himself neither sound blood nor sound flesh, but much *slim*, so that it is scarcely digested. Thus it is of no use at all to a sick person, although a healthy person may be able to overcome this food. Nevertheless, if someone has an empty brain and is thereby so afflicted with madness that he is as if frenzied, take whole grains of wheat and cook them in water. Then, after removing the grains from the water, place them all, while hot, around his head and tie a cloth over them. Thus his brain will be replenished by that juice and will recover its powers and health. Do this until he returns to his right mind.

And whoever suffers pain in the back and loins should cook wheat grains in water and place them, while hot, upon the painful spot; the heat of the wheat will drive away the force of that affliction.

> [Note: Col. 1129C. “Because this fruit is full of richness,” added in the edition.]

> [Addition in the edition, Cols. 1129C–1130A.] If a dog bites a person with its teeth, let that person take a paste prepared from fine wheat flour and egg white, and apply it over the dog-bite for three days and the same number of nights, so that it draws out that poisonous bite. The bite is more poisonous from its breath than that of another animal. Then remove the paste; crush yarrow with egg white and apply it over the same bite for two or three days, then remove it. Afterwards heal it with ointments, as another wound is usually healed.

## Chapter II—On Rye

> [Note: Col. 1130C. *Secale cereale* [cereal rye]. II.2.]

Rye is hot, though colder than wheat, and possesses many powers. Bread made from it is good for healthy people and makes them strong. It is good for those who have fat flesh, because it reduces their flesh while nevertheless making them strong. But it is contrary to those with cold stomachs who are greatly weakened by this condition, because their weakness cannot overcome it in digestion. It therefore produces much disturbance in them, because they can scarcely digest it.

> [Addition in the edition, Col. 1130B.] Whoever has swellings or glands in the body, of whatever kind, should heat rye bread at the fire, or bring it hot from the oven, break it, and lay it upon the swellings. The heat of its power consumes them and makes them disappear. Do this until they disappear. If anyone has scabies on the head, reduce the crust of rye bread to powder and put the powder there, because it removes this evil. After three days, anoint the same place with olive oil, because it is warm and heals. Do this until healing occurs. If cancers—that is, very slender worms—are eating a person’s flesh, place a hot crumb of bread upon them. Do this often; they will perish from its heat.

## Chapter III—On Oats

> [Note: Col. 1130C. *Avena sativa* [cultivated oats]. II.3.]

[Col. 1130C] Oats are hot, sharp in taste, and of strong vapour.

> [Note: Col. 1130C. The words “sharp … vapour” are absent from the edition.]

They are cheerful and wholesome food for healthy people; they produce in them a cheerful mind, a pure and clear understanding, good colour, and sound flesh. They are also good as food, both in bread and flour, for those who are slightly and moderately ill, and do them no harm. But they are unsuitable as food for those who are very ill and cold, because oats always seek heat. If such a person eats oat bread or flour, it coagulates in the belly and produces *slim* [“lividity,” ed.] in him, giving him no strength because he is cold.

But whoever is afflicted with *virgichtiget* [the edition: “afflicted by paralysis”] and thereby has a divided mind and vain thoughts, becoming somewhat mad, should in a dry bath pour upon heated stones oats cooked in water. Let him do this often; he will come to himself and recover health.

## Chapter IV—On Barley

> [Note: Col. 1131D. *Hordeum vulgare* [common barley]. II.4.]

[Col. 1131B] Barley is cold, colder and weaker than the grains mentioned above. If eaten in bread or flour, it harms both healthy and sick people, because it does not possess as much strength as the other kinds of grain. But a sick person whose whole body is already failing should boil barley thoroughly in water, pour that water into a tub, and bathe in it. Let him do this often until he is healed; he will regain the flesh of his body and recover health.

Likewise, a person so ill that he cannot eat bread should take equal weights of barley and oats, add a little fennel, and cook them together in water. When they have cooked, strain the juice through a cloth and drink it as broth in place of bread. Do this until recovery. But one who has hard, rough facial skin, which readily becomes *schebet* [is drawn into roughness, ed.] by wind, should cook barley in water. Then let him gently wash his face with that water, strained through a cloth and moderately warm: his skin will become smooth and soft, and he will have a beautiful complexion. If a person’s head is sick, wash it often with this water, and it will be healthy.

## Chapter V—On Spelt

> [Note: Col. 1131D. *Triticum spelta* [spelt wheat]. II.5.]

Spelt is the best grain. It is hot, rich, powerful, and sweeter than other grains. It produces sound flesh in the person eating it, prepares sound blood, and makes a cheerful mind and joy in the human mind. However it is eaten—whether in bread or in other foods—it is good and pleasant. If anyone is so sick that he cannot eat because of his illness, take whole spelt grains and cook them in water, adding fat or egg yolk so that, because of the better flavour, it may be eaten willingly. Give this to the sick person to eat; like a good and healthy ointment, it heals him inwardly.

## Chapter VI—On Peas

> [Note: Col. 1131D. *Pisum sativum* [garden pea]. II.6.]

Peas are cold and somewhat phlegmatic. [Col. 1132A] They somewhat weaken the lungs. Nevertheless, they are good food for a person of hot constitution and make him fierce. But they are of no use to a person of cold constitution, especially when ill, because in eating they produce *mulslim* in him.

> [Addition in the edition.] Peas are also harmful in every illness and have no power in themselves to drive illnesses away. Yet if someone suffers in the forehead from excessive phlegm, he should chew white peas with his teeth, mix them with the purest honey, apply this to his temples, and bind it tight. Do so until he improves. Likewise, one whose internal organs are weak should often sip hot pea broth, and will improve.

## Chapter VII—On Beans

> [Note: Col. 1132D. *Vicia faba* [broad bean]. Compare the charming little poem of Walther von der Vogelweide: “*Waz eren hat fro bone*” [“What honour Lady Bean possesses”]. II.7.]

[Col. 1132B] The bean is hot, and good food for healthy and strong people; it is better than the pea. For if sick people eat beans, they are not harmed greatly, because beans do not produce in them as much lividity and *slim* as peas do. Bean flour is good and useful for both sick and healthy people, because it is light and can easily be digested. But a person with internal pain should cook beans in water with a little fat or oil; after the beans have been removed, let him sip the hot *soff* [broth, ed.] often. It heals him inwardly.

> [Addition in the edition, Cols. 1132B–C.] Whoever has burning pain, scabies, or ulcers of any kind in the flesh should take bean flour, add a little powder of fennel seed, and mix these with a very little wheat flour in water, so that it can hold together. Thus make small cakes at the fire or in the sun and apply them frequently over the affected place. It will draw out the pain and he will be healed.

## Chapter VIII—On Lentils

> [Note: Col. 1132D. *Ervum lens* [lentil]. II.8–9.]

The lentil is cold. Eaten, it increases neither a person’s marrow, blood, nor flesh, nor gives strength; it merely fills the belly and fills it with emptiness, stirring diseased humours into a storm in people.

> [Addition in the edition, Col. 1132D.] If patches of scabies and unclean hairs which contain the root of ulcers grow on a person’s head, let him gently reduce lentils to powder over a heated stone. Reduce a tortoise-shell with the *livor* [dark fluid] contained in it to powder, add an equal weight to the lentil powder, and apply it to the patches. It will wipe away the *livor* of that pain, and healing will result.
>
> **Chapter IX—On Vichbona.** *Vichbona* is cold. Whoever has internal pain as though swelling within should reduce *vichbona* to flour; add a little powdered bread and a little fennel seed, or juice of lovage; cook it with water like food and eat it somewhat warm. Do this often: it heals weak internal organs.

## Chapter IX—On *Hirs* [Millet]

> [Note: Col. 1133D. *Panicum miliaceum* [millet]. Compare below chapter 193, “On *mitio*.” II.13.]

[Col. 1133A] *Hirs* is cold and a little hot, because it neither increases blood or flesh in a person nor gives strength, but merely fills the belly and reduces hunger only insofar as it has no taste of restoration. It also makes the human brain watery, renders the stomach tepid and sluggish, throws the humours in a person into storm, and is nearly like a weed (*unkrut*), not wholesome food for human beings.

## Chapter X—On *Venich*

> [Note: Col. 1133D. *Panicum Italicum* [Italian millet]. II.14.]

*Venich* is cold and has a little heat. It has little value, because it gives little restoration and little strength to the person eating it. Yet it does not harm him as much as millet commonly does, nor does it stir up bad humours and diseases in a person as strongly as millet does.

> [Addition in the editions, Col. 1133B.] Whoever has burning fevers should cook *venich* in wine and drink that wine hot often; he will be cured.

## Chapter XI—On Hemp

> [Note: Col. 1134D. *Cannabis sativa* [cultivated hemp]. II.16.]

Hemp is hot. It grows when the air is neither very hot nor very cold, and its nature is likewise. Its seed possesses health and is wholesome food for healthy people. In their stomach it is light and useful: it somewhat removes *slim* from the stomach, is easily digested, diminishes bad humours, and makes good humours strong. But if a person is sick in the head or has an empty brain, eating hemp easily gives him some pain in the head. It does not harm one whose head is healthy and whose brain is full. Yet it also gives a very sick person some stomach pain; it does not harm one who is moderately ill when eaten.

> [Addition in the edition.] Whoever has a cold stomach should cook hemp in water, squeeze out the water, wrap it in a little cloth, and apply it hot to the stomach frequently. It strengthens the stomach and restores it to its place. Likewise, hemp gives some headache to one with an empty brain if he eats it, but does not harm a healthy head and full brain. Cloth made from hemp is also useful for binding ulcers and wounds, because it has a temperate heat.

## Chapter XII—On *Ratde*

> [Note: Col. 1134D. *Nigella sativa* [black cumin]. II.64.]

[Col. 1133D] *Ratde* [the edition: *Zizania*] is hot and dry and is of no use as food for any person, because it would cause pain. It neither benefits nor greatly harms livestock. But if someone has ulcers on the head, provided they are not scabies, pound *ratden*, mix lard with the crushed material, and often anoint the head ulcers with it. It will eat away his ulcers, and he will be healed. Pound *ratden* also and mix it with honey. Where there are many flies, smear it on a wall—that is, make *striche* [streaks]—and the flies that taste it will become sick, fall, and die.

## Chapter XIII—On Galangal

> [Note: Col. 1134D. *Alpinia galanga*. II.17.]

[Col. 1134A] Galangal is wholly hot, contains no coldness, and is powerful. A person with burning fever should powder galangal and drink the powder in spring water; it will extinguish the burning fever. Whoever has pain in the back or side from bad humours should boil galangal in wine and drink it hot frequently; the pain will cease. Whoever has heart pain, or weakness in the heart (*unmecht*), should at once eat a sufficient amount of galangal and will improve.

A person suffering from foul breath which reaches the lungs, so that he sometimes also has a hoarse voice, should take equal weights of galangal and fennel, twice as much nutmeg and pellitory as each of those two ingredients, powder and mix them. Every day while fasting, he should eat, with a small piece of bread, powder to the weight of two coins; then drink a little hot wine. He should also frequently eat other noble herbs with a good scent, both after meals and while fasting, so that their good smell restrains the foul breath.

Whoever suffers pain in the lungs in any way should avoid fatty meats and food suffused with much blood, and abstain from uncooked food, because these produce wasting around the lungs. Let him also avoid peas, lentils, raw fruit, raw vegetables, nuts, and oil, since they bring *livor* to the lungs. If he wishes to eat meat, let him eat lean meat. If cheese, let him eat neither cooked nor fresh cheese, but dry cheese, since its harmful *livores* are calmed. If he wishes to eat oil, let him eat it sparingly, lest he acquire *livores* in the lungs from it. He should not drink water, because it produces *livor* around the lungs. Nor should he drink new must which has not yet expelled its impurities in fermenting, because it is not yet purified. Beer does not harm him much, because it has been cooked. But let him drink wine, because its good heat aids the lungs. Let him protect himself from damp and misty air, because its moisture harms the lungs.

If bad humours have become excessive in a person’s viscera and spleen, and through melancholy have brought many sufferings upon the heart, let him take equal weights of galangal and pellitory, and white pepper equal to a fourth part of either of them; or, if he has no white pepper, let him take *pfeffertruch*, four times the quantity of white pepper, and reduce these to powder. Then take bean flour, add the aforesaid powder, and mix everything with fenugreek juice, without water, wine, or other liquid. Make small cakes from all these ingredients and dry them in the sun’s heat. Therefore make them in summer, while the sun is available, so that they may be kept for winter. Eat these cakes both after meals and while fasting. Then take liquorice, five times as much fennel and sugar, measured by the weight of the liquorice, and a little honey; make a drink from these and drink it against heart pain both after meals and while fasting.

A person whose phlegm produces vapour in the head and confuses the hearing should take galangal; aloe equal to one third of its amount; oregano equal to twice the amount of galangal; and peach leaves of the same weight as the oregano. Make a powder from them and use it daily, both after meals and while fasting.

Whoever suffers pain in the chest, heart, or spleen, and has a stomach chilled by phlegm, should take galangal, twice as much oregano, celery seed equal in weight to the oregano, and a little white pepper. Reduce these to powder, add a little boiled honey, and make an electuary from it, so that it is cooked gently without sudden boiling. Let him eat this electuary often and use pure, mild, good wine frequently.

Whoever is afflicted by paralysis should take galangal; nutmeg equal to half its amount; spike equal to half the nutmeg; *githerut* and lovage in equal weights, though each separately greater than the spike; and add saxifrage and polypody in equal weights. The latter two together should equal the quantity of the preceding five. Reduce them all to powder. If the person is healthy, let him eat this powder in bread; if sick, make an electuary from it and let him eat it.

> [Addition in the edition.]

## Chapter XIV—On Zedoary

> [Note: Col. 1135D. *Amomum zedoaria* [zedoary]. II.18.]

Zedoary is moderately hot and has great power in itself. A person who trembles in the limbs—that is, “*bibet*” [uncertain reading]—and whose strength is failing, should cut zedoary into wine, add slightly less galangal, and boil this with a little honey in wine. Then drink it hot—that is, *melch*—and the trembling will leave him and he will recover strength.

Whoever has much saliva and much foam should powder zedoary, bind the powder in a small cloth, place it in a little vessel after pouring in water, so that the water takes on its flavour, and leave it in the water overnight. Let him drink it often fasting in the morning, and the saliva and foam will cease. But whoever has severe head pain should moisten the forehead and temples with the same powder, bound in cloth and soaked in water, and will improve.

Whoever has a stomach filled and greatly burdened by bad foods should powder zedoary, make a small cake from the powder, a little fine flour, and water, bake it in the sun or in an oven almost cooled, then reduce the cake to powder. Let him frequently lick this powder in his hand while fasting—that is, *lecke*—and also when he goes to sleep at night; his stomach will be relieved.

> [Note: Cols. 1135D–1136D. The edition correctly reads: “Let him frequently lick this powder in his hand while fasting, and also when he goes to sleep at night; it removes the heaviness of the stomach.”]

## Chapter XV—On Ginger

> [Note: Col. 1136D. *Amomum zingiber* [ginger]. II.19.]

Ginger [the edition: *zinziber*] is very hot and diffuse—that is, *zufloszlich*. Eaten, it harms a healthy and fat person, because it makes him ignorant, unknowing, tepid, and lustful. But one who is dry in body and nearly failing should powder ginger and take a little of the powder fasting in *suffen* [soup/broth], and sometimes eat a little with bread; he will improve. But as soon as he has improved, he should eat it no longer, lest it harm him.

Whoever is ulcerous—that is, *suerecht*—and has cloudy eyes should powder ginger, bind the powder in a cloth, and place it in wine until the wine becomes dark—that is, *zanger*. At night, when going to bed, smear this wine around the eyelids and eyes. If a little enters the eyes, it will not harm them; thus it removes *eyther* [ulcerous poison, ed.] and cloudiness from the eyes.

> [Addition in the edition, Cols. 1136A–C.] While a person still has the sight of his eyes, he can aid them in this way; but after he has lost his sight, they cannot be helped by this method. Whoever has dim eyes should take equal measures of rue juice and hyssop juice, add three times as much of the aforementioned wine, and pour this into a bronze vessel so that it retains its power. At night, when going to bed, anoint the exterior of the eyes and eyelids all around with it. If it touches the eyes slightly within, it will not harm them. Do this often: it will drive away dimness of the eyes.
>
> Whoever suffers obstruction in stomach and belly should powder ginger and mix the powder with a little juice of alkanet (*ancusa*). From this powder and bean flour make small cakes, bake them in an oven whose fiery heat has already abated, and eat these cakes often both after meals and while fasting. It diminishes the foulness of the stomach and strengthens the person.
>
> Likewise, a person suffering any pain in the stomach should powder ginger, twice as much galangal, and zedoary equal to half the quantity [of ginger, apparently]; after food put this powder into wine and drink it, including at night when going to bed. Do this often, and he will improve in the stomach.

If anyone has *citerdrose* in the body, put the aforesaid powder, bound in a cloth, into vinegar, adding a little wine if available, so that it does not become excessively sharp—that is, *zanger*. With that cloth and powder, anoint the skin at the place where the *citerdrosae* are, and he will be healed.

[But a person troubled by *vich* should take a little ginger and much cinnamon [Col. 1136D] and pulverize them. Then let him take less sage than ginger, more fennel than sage, and more tansy than sage; grind these in a mortar into a juice, and strain it through a cloth. Then boil a little honey in wine, adding a little white pepper—or, if he does not have that, a little *nimmolo*—and add the aforesaid powder and juice. Afterwards take *merlinsen*, twice as much tormentil, and field mustard in an amount equal to the tormentil but less than the *merlinsen*; grind these in a mortar into a juice, put them into a little bag [Col. 1137A], pour over them the aforesaid honeyed and spiced wine, and make from these a clear drink. The person suffering from the aforesaid pain should drink, while fasting, as much of this beverage as he can swallow in one breath, and likewise at night when he goes to bed; and he should do this until he is healed.

But a person wishing to prepare and take medicinal draughts should pulverize and strain ginger, half as much licorice, and one third as much *zituar* as ginger. Then weigh the powder together; afterwards take as much sugar as this powder weighs. Weigh all these together to a total weight of thirty *nummi*. Then take as much of the finest flour of semolina as half a walnut shell holds, and as much milk of *citocatia* as a scribe’s cut quill can hold in its slit [Col. 1137B]; and with the aforesaid powder, the flour, and the milk of *citocatia*, make a very thin dough or little cake. Divide this dough into four parts, and dry it in the sun in March or April, since in these months the sun’s ray is so temperate that it is neither too hot nor too cold, and therefore especially brings health. But if in those months he cannot obtain milk from the aforesaid *citocatia*, and must defer the matter until May, then, after making the aforesaid little cake in May, dry it likewise in the sun of May and keep it until an appropriate time.

When someone then wishes to take the draught, let him take one fourth of the aforesaid dough while fasting. But if his stomach is so strong and thick that it does not feel the effect of this draught [Col. 1137C], let him take again half of a third part of the aforesaid little cake, moisten the whole of it anew with milk of *citocatia*, dry it again in the sun, and take it fasting. Before anyone takes this draught, if it is cold, he should warm himself and then take it. After taking it, he should rest a little in bed without sleeping; then, rising, he should walk about a little here and there, provided that he does not suffer cold. After the evacuation, he should eat wheaten bread—not dry, but dipped in a little broth—young chickens, pork, and other delicate meats. He should avoid coarse bread, beef, fish, other coarse foods, and roasted foods, except roasted pears; and he should abstain from cheese, raw vegetables, and fruit. He should drink wine, though moderately [Col. 1137D], and leave water aside. He should also avoid the brightness of the sun, and observe these rules for three days. Added in the edition.]

## CHAPTER XVI.—ON PEPPER  
[Note: [Col. 1137D] Long and black pepper.] [III, 4].

Pepper is very hot and dry and has a certain precipitous quality in it. Eaten in large quantities, it harms a person, causes pleurisy in him, exhausts his humors [Col. 1138A], and produces bad humors in him. If someone has an ailment of the spleen and has such a distaste for food that he does not wish to eat, he should eat a little pepper with bread in some food; he will fare better in his spleen, and his aversion to eating will cease.

[Note: [Col. 1137D] The edition: “On the pepper tree. The tree on which pepper grows is very hot; pepper likewise is very hot and dry. Eaten in large quantities, it harms a person, causes pleurisy in him, and exhausts his good humors. But a person who has eaten apples or pears and suffers from them should immediately eat pepper, and he will fare better. And one who has an ailment of the spleen and an aversion to eating [Col. 1138D] should eat a little pepper with bread in some food, and he will fare better in his spleen.”]

## CHAPTER XVII.—ON *KUMEL*  
[Note: [Col. 1138D] Cumin, *cyminum*.] [II, 20].

*Kumel* [cumin, ed.] is of moderate heat and dry. For a person who *danphet*, it is good, useful, and wholesome to eat, however it is eaten; but it harms one who suffers in the heart if he eats it [because it does not warm the heart perfectly, though the heart should always be warm, added in the edition]. Yet it is good for a healthy person to eat, because it gives him good understanding and brings moderation to one who is excessively hot. But it harms every infirm person who eats it, because [Col. 1138B] it stirs up pestilence in him—except one who suffers in the lung.

[A person wishing to eat cooked or roasted cheese should put cumin on it, so that he may not suffer from it, and eat it thus. One who suffers nausea should take cumin, one third as much pepper, and *bibinella*, about one fourth as much as the cumin; pulverize these, take fine clean semolina flour, and put this powder into the flour. Then make little cakes with egg yolk and a little water, either in a warm oven or beneath hot ashes, and eat these little cakes. He should also eat the aforesaid powder spread over bread; it restrains the hot and cold humors in the viscera which cause nausea in a person. Added in the edition.]

## CHAPTER XVIII.—ON *BERTRAM*  
[Note: [Col. 1138D] *Anthenis pyrethrum*.] [II, 21].

[Col. 1138C]

*Bertram* [pyrethrum, ed.] is of moderate warmth and somewhat dry; this moderation is pure, and it possesses a good greenness. For it is good for a healthy person to eat, because it lessens wasting in him, increases good blood in him, and gives a person clear understanding. It also restores strength to an infirm person whose body has almost failed, leaves nothing undigested in him, and gives him good digestion. A person who has much phlegm in his head will, if he eats it frequently, have less phlegm in his head. Frequently eaten, it also drives pleurisy away from a person, produces pure humors in him, and clears his eyes. However it is eaten—whether [Col. 1138D] dry or in food—it is useful and good for an infirm as well as a healthy person. For if a person eats it often, it drives illness away from him and prevents him from falling ill. Its causing moisture and saliva to flow in the mouth when eaten is due to its drawing out bad humors and restoring health.

## CHAPTER XIX.—ON LICORICE  
[Note: [Col. 1138D] *Glycyrrhiza glabra*. It occurs very frequently under the name *Henigwurz*. Its cultivation in the Bamberg district was instituted by the holy Empress Cunegund; cf. Walafrid Strabo, *Hortulus*, ed. Reuss, p. 56.] [II, 22].

Licorice is of moderate warmth, and however it is eaten it gives a person a clear [Col. 1139A] voice, makes his mind pleasant, clears his eyes, and softens his stomach for digestion. It is also very beneficial to one suffering frenzy if he eats it often, because it extinguishes the madness in his brain.

[Note: [Col. 1139C] The words “because—it extinguishes” are absent from the edition.]

## CHAPTER XX.—ON CINNAMON  
[Note: [Col. 1139C] *Laurus Cinnamomum*.] [III, 3].

Cinnamon too is very hot and possesses strong powers; it also contains a little moisture, but its heat is so strong that it suppresses that moisture. One who eats it often lessens bad humors in himself and produces good humors.

[Note: [Col. 1139C] Edition: “On the cinnamon tree. The tree whose bark is cinnamon is very hot. Therefore a person troubled by paralytic gout, and one who has quotidian, tertian, or quartan fevers, should take a vessel made of steel, pour good wine into it, add wood and leaves [Col. 1139D] of the aforesaid tree while they still contain juice, bring it to a boil over the fire, and drink it hot often; he will be healed. And a person whose head is heavy and dull, so that he has difficulty breathing out and drawing breath in through his nostrils, should pulverize cinnamon and often eat this powder with a morsel of bread, or lick it from his hand; it dissolves the harmful humors by which the head is made dull.”]

## CHAPTER XXI.—ON NUTMEG  
[Note: [Col. 1139D] *Myristica moschata*.] [III, 2].

Nutmeg has great heat and a good balance in its powers. If a person eats nutmeg [Col. 1139B], it opens his heart, purifies his senses, and gives him good understanding. Take nutmeg in any amount, an equal weight of cinnamon, and a little clove—that is, *nelchin*—and pulverize these. Then make little cakes with this powder, semolina flour, and a little water, and eat them often. They calm all bitterness of your heart and mind, open your heart and dull senses, make your mind glad, purify your senses, lessen all harmful humors in you, give good juice to your blood, and make you strong.

[Note: [Col. 1139D] Edition: “On the nutmeg tree. The tree on which nutmeg grows is hot. Its wood and leaves, however, are not especially suitable for medicinal use. Nutmeg likewise has great heat and a good balance in its powers. If anyone eats nutmeg, it opens his heart, purifies his senses, and by its good heat and pleasant power gives him good understanding. A person should also pulverize nutmeg, an equal weight of cinnamon, and a little clove; with this powder, semolina [Col. 1140C] flour, and a little water, he should make little cakes and eat them often. They calm all bitterness of his heart and mind, open his dull senses, make his mind glad, and lessen all harmful humors in him. Further, one troubled by paralysis in the brain should pulverize nutmeg and twice as much galangal, and pound in a small quantity of equal weights of the root of *gladiola* and plantain, with salt added. From all these he should make a little broth [thus] and consume it; and he should do this once or twice a day until he is healed.”]

## CHAPTER XXII.—ON THE ROSE  
[Note: [Col. 1140D] Hundred-leaved rose.] [II, 76].

The rose is cold, and that coldness contains a useful balance. In the morning, or once daylight has come, take a rose leaf and place it over your eyes: it draws out their moisture [Col. 1139C], that is, their *trieffen*, and clears them. A person who has small ulcers on his body should put rose leaves upon them; they draw out their discoloration.

[Note: [Col. 1140D] After “draws out,” the edition adds: “One who is rash in anger should take rose and less sage, grind them to powder, and when anger rises in him at that moment, apply it to his nostrils; for sage comforts and the rose gladdens. Take rose and half as much sage, adding fresh infused lard; boil these together in water so that an ointment is made. Where a person is troubled by cramp or paralysis, let him anoint that place with this ointment, and he will fare better.” The edition omits what follows: “but the rose,” etc.]

The rose is also effective when added to draughts, ointments, and every kind of medicine. These are made all the better if some rose, however little, is added to them, by reason of its good powers, as stated above.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—ON THE LILY  
[Note: [Col. 1140D] White lily. Hildegard, letter to Wibert; *Scivias*, III, 8.] [II, 77].

[Col. 1140A]

The lily is more cold than hot. Take the head of a lily root, pound it thoroughly with old lard, melt it in a little pan, and put it into a small vessel. Then let one who has white leprosy, namely *quedick*, anoint himself frequently with it, after first warming the ointment, and he will be healed. Red leprosy can be treated in the same way.

A person who has *uzslecht* should often drink goat’s milk, and the *uzslecht* will entirely leave him. Then let him take the stem and leaves of lilies, pound them, press out their juice, knead that juice together with flour, and continually anoint wherever his body hurts from *uzslecht*. Yet before anointing himself with this ointment, he should always drink goat’s milk. The fragrance even of the first emergence—that is, *blut*—of lilies, and likewise the scent of their flowers, gladdens a person’s heart and gives him upright thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 1140D] The words “The fragrance—gives him” are absent from the edition.]

## CHAPTER XXIV.—ON PSYLLIUM  
[Note: [Col. 1140D] *Plantago psillium*.] [II, 78].

Psyllium is cold in nature, and in that coldness has a sweet balance. A person who boils it in wine and drinks the wine hot thus restrains strong fevers—that is, *fiber*. By its sweet balance it gladdens a person’s oppressed mind, and by both its coldness and its moderation aids and strengthens his brain toward health. A person who has fevers in his stomach should boil psyllium in wine; after pouring off the wine, put the psyllium into a cloth, bind it hot over his stomach, and he will drive the fevers [Col. 1140C] out of his stomach.

## CHAPTER XXV.—ON SPIKE  
[Note: [Col. 1140D] Spike lavender.] [II, 79].

Spike is hot and dry, and its heat is wholesome. Whoever boils spike with wine—or, if he has no wine, with honey and water—and drinks it lukewarm often will ease pain of the liver and lung and *dumphedinem* in his chest, and it produces clear knowledge and clear understanding.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—ON CUBEBS  
[Note: [Col. 1141D] *Piper cubeba*.] [II, 23].

[Col. 1141A]

Cubeb is hot, and that heat contains moderation; it is also dry. If anyone eats cubeb, the unworthy ardor within him is moderated; it also makes his mind glad and makes his understanding and knowledge clear.

[Added in the edition: “For its useful and moderate heat extinguishes the unworthy fires of lust, in which foul and muddy discolorations lie hidden, and, by kindling, makes clear a person’s mind and understanding.”]

## CHAPTER XXVII.—ON CLOVES  
[Note: [Col. 1141D] *Eugenia caryophyllata*.] [II, 24].

Cloves, *nelchin*, are very hot and also have a certain moisture by which they spread pleasantly, like the pleasant moisture of honey. If someone has pain in the head, so that his head is swollen and he is, as it were, deaf [Col. 1141B], he should eat cloves often; they lessen the swelling in his head. When a person’s weak viscera sometimes swell, this swelling of the viscera very often brings on the growth of dropsy in him. Therefore, when dropsy begins to grow in someone, he should eat cloves often, and they will restrain that diseased defect, because their power enters the person’s viscera, lessens their swelling, and thus drives away dropsy, permitting it to grow no further.

[Note: [Col. 1141D] The words “because—the further” are absent from the edition.]

The heat of a person’s marrow also often sweats out and produces gout in him. When this begins to grow in someone, if he then eats cloves often, their power enters that person’s marrow and prevents the gout from growing or proceeding further in him, while it is still at its beginning [Col. 1141C].

[Note: [Col. 1141D] The words “and from proceeding further—it is at its beginning” are absent from the edition.]

[One who suffers hiccups should eat clove frequently. He should also eat *zituar* frequently after meals, and continue this for a month. Added in the edition.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—ON *CRISTIANA*  
[Note: [Col. 1141D] Black hellebore.] [II, 25].

*Cristiana* contains both fiery heat and coldness. A person in whom very bad and deadly humors rise up, so that they boil in some limb—what they call *freischlich* (*freislichaz*, ed.)—should continually eat *cristiana*, and he will improve. One who has quartan fevers should eat it at the very onset of their attack, and he will fare better. One greatly troubled by *gicht* should eat it during the attack, and he will improve. One who has burning fevers in the stomach should cut it into wine, warm the wine, and drink it hot; he will be cured.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—ON *LUNCKWURCZ*  
[Note: [Col. 1141D] *Pulmonaria officinalis*.] [II, 80].

*Lunckwurcz* is cold and somewhat dry, and is of little use to humans. Yet a person whose lung is swollen, so that he coughs and can scarcely draw breath, should boil *lunckwurtz* in wine and drink it often while fasting; he will be healed. If sheep frequently eat it [Col. 1142A], they become healthy and fat, and it does not harm their milk. When the lung is swollen, if a person often drinks *lunckwurtz* cooked in wine, as we have said, his lung returns to health, because the lung has much the nature of a sheep.

## CHAPTER XXX.—ON *HIRTZUNGE*  
[Note: [Col. 1141D] *Asplenium scolopendrium*.] [II, 81].

*Hirtzunge* (*Scolopendria*, ed.) is hot and is beneficial for the liver, lung, and painful viscera. Take *hirtzunge* and boil it thoroughly in wine; then add pure honey and bring it to a boil once more. Next pulverize long pepper and twice as much cinnamon, boil these once more with the aforesaid wine, strain through a cloth, and thus make *luterdranck*.

[Note: [Col. 1141D] *Luterdranck*: claret, a beverage prepared from wine, honey, and aromatic spices [Col. 1142D]. See Bartholomew the Englishman, *On the Properties of Things*, I, 19, 56.]

Drink it often both after meals and while fasting: it benefits the liver, cleanses the lung, heals painful viscera [Col. 1142B], and removes inner putrefactions and *slim*.

[Note: [Col. 1142D] The words “and removes—*slim*” are absent from the edition.]

Again, gently dry *hirtzunga* in blazing sun or upon a hot brick, pulverize it, and frequently lick this powder from your hand both fasting and after meals—that is, *lecke*. It restrains pain of the head and chest and eases other pains in your body.

[Note: [Col. 1142D] The words “and eases—your body” are absent from the edition.]

Further, a person who suddenly becomes very weak from some pain should immediately drink some of this powder in hot wine, and he will fare better.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—ON GENTIAN  
[Note: [Col. 1142D] *Gentiana lutea*.] [II, 80 bis].

Gentian is fairly hot. A person suffering heart pain as though its chords could scarcely hold together [“as though his heart could scarcely remain standing,” ed.] should pulverize gentian and eat that powder in a broth; it strengthens his heart [Col. 1142C]. One who has *fiber* in the stomach should often drink some of the same powder in hot wine, warmed with glowing-hot steel, and his stomach will be cleansed of fever.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—ON *QUENULA*  
[Note: [Col. 1142D] Wild thyme.] [II, 81 bis].

*Quenula* (wild thyme, ed.) is hot and temperate. A person whose bodily flesh is infirm, so that it breaks out like scabies, should often eat *quenula* cooked either with meat or in *muse*; the flesh of his body will be healed and cleansed inwardly. But one who has fine scabies, that is, *cleynengriut*, should pound *quenula* with fresh lard, make an ointment from it, and anoint himself with it; he will have health. When the brain [Col. 1142D] is weak and, as it were, empty, pulverize *quenula*, mix the powder with semolina flour in water, make little cakes, and eat them often; his brain will fare better.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—ON *ANDRON*  
[Note: [Col. 1142D] Should one read *Andorn*? *Marrubium vulgare*.] [II, 82].

*Andron* [horehound, ed.] is hot, contains a good deal of juice, and is effective against various ailments.
