One who has deaf ears should boil *andron* in water [Col. 1143A], remove it from the water, allow its hot *donft* [steam, ed.] to enter his ears, and also place it thus hot around his ears and over his whole head; he will hear better. One who is ill in the throat should boil *andron* in water, strain the boiled water through a cloth, add twice as much wine, bring it to a boil again in a pan with enough fat added, and drink it often; he will be healed in the throat. A person with cough should take equal weights of fennel and dill, add one third as much *andron*, boil these with wine, strain them through a cloth, and drink it; the cough will cease. One who has weak and injured viscera should boil *andron* with wine and a sufficient quantity of honey, leave the preparation in a pot, drink it often once cooled, and his viscera will be healed.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—ON *HIRTZSWAM*  
[Note: [Col. 1143D] Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1143B]

*Hirtzswam* is cold and hard and is harmful for a human being to eat, and also for livestock not afflicted by any illness, because it has such powers that, when it finds no disease, it ulcerates within a healthy person and healthy livestock. But where such dangerous humors erupt in a person that he is so afflicted in his limbs by *gicht* that his limbs seem to be breaking, if he then eats *hirtzswam*, it drives away the danger of those humors and makes them break out and expels them. For its nature is such that it is accustomed always to break apart whatever it encounters, and thus, wherever it finds what is foul, it breaks it up. It also makes a pregnant woman miscarry, at danger to her body, if [Col. 1143C] she eats it.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—ON LAVENDER  
[Note: [Col. 1143D] *Lavendula vera*.] [II, 83].

Lavender is hot and dry, since it has little juice, and is of no use for a person to eat; yet it has a strong fragrance. A person who has many lice, if he smells lavender frequently, will have the lice in him die. Its scent also clears the eyes.

[Added in the edition: “Because it possesses a certain power of the strongest and also the benefit of the bitterest aromatics, it therefore constricts many bad things; and for this reason evil spirits are frightened away.”]

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—ON FENUGREEK  
[Note: [Col. 1143D] *Trigonella foenum-graecum*.] [II, 84].

Fenugreek is more cold than hot. A person who has quotidian fevers, which often bring sweat out from him [Col. 1143D], and whom food troubles—that is, harms—should take fenugreek herb in summer, warm its seed in wine, and drink it hot often while fasting; he will fare better. One who has quartan fevers should boil fenugreek in water; after pressing out the water, he should often bind it hot around the shins of both legs at night, fastening a cloth over it, and should often drink fenugreek warmed in wine, as stated above; he will be healed.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—ON *SYSEMERA*  
[Note: [Col. 1144D] Cf. Book III, chapter 59. Absent from the edition.]

*Sysemera* is hot. A person who has eaten or drunk poison [Col. 1144A] should take equal weights of *sysemera*, rue, and *bathema*, pound them in a mortar, squeeze out their juice, then take twice as much juice of *springwurtz* as there is of any one of these, add it to the aforesaid juice, mix all together, strain it through a cloth, and drink it fasting. When he drinks it, he should sit in a warm place, lest he become cold; for if he were cold then, it would be dangerous for him. After drinking it, he should drink *huneckwurtz*, and the poison will foam out through nausea or pass out through his lower parts, and thus he will be freed. A person with many lice should pound *sysemera* with lard, mix them together, and anoint himself with it around his neck and beneath his armpits; the lice will die, and he will not be harmed by it. But [Col. 1144B] a person in whom leprosy appears to be growing should boil *sysemera* in water, add fat, make *mus* from it, eat it often, and it will drive leprosy away from him.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—ON *PEFFERKRUT*  
[II, 26].

*Pefferkrut* is hot and moist, and that moisture contains moderation. It is good and useful to eat for the healthy and infirm alike. What is *sur*—that is, bitter—in it does not bite a person inwardly but heals him. A person with a weak heart and feeble stomach should eat it raw, and it strengthens him. It also makes glad a person who has a sad mind; when eaten, it heals and clears a person’s eyes.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—ON *SCHERLING*  
[Note: [Col. 1144D] Poison hemlock? *Conium maculatum*?] [II, 85].

[Col. 1144C]

*Scherling* is hot and contains danger, so that if a person ate it, it would destroy everything well and rightly ordered in his blood and humors and produce evil inundations in him—such as create disturbances in water after the manner of a storm. Once this storm had ceased, it would leave the worst discolorations and illnesses in the person. But one who has been severely beaten with poles or clubs, or has fallen from a height so that his flesh and limbs are bruised, should boil *scherling* in water, place the pressed-out water upon the limbs that hurt, and bind a cloth over them. It will thus disperse the humors gathered there [Col. 1144D], because *scherling* too is accustomed to disperse. Likewise, a person swollen between skin and flesh from a *stosze*, a blow, or a projectile should warm *scherling* in water, bind it over the swelling, and it will drive the swelling away. But it is of no use for expelling a swelling in some limb that arises from a disease within the person: if it were put upon it, it would dangerously force back inside the person those humors which, through diseased ulcers, ought to proceed outward and leave the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1144D] The words “if it were put upon it—force back” are absent from the edition.]

## CHAPTER XL.—ON CAMPHOR  
[Note: [Col. 1145D] *Dryobalanops camphora*.] [III, 9].

[Col. 1145A]

Camphor, that is, gum, contains pure coldness; but the tree from which camphor exudes has a sharp and clean quality. If anyone ate simple camphor, not tempered with these herbs, the fire in him would be impeded by its coldness. The cold also in him would rush forth through its power, so that he would become like wood that is *olemechte*: neither cold nor hot in his body. Therefore no one should eat it by itself. Take equal weights of aloes and myrrh, and a little less camphor than either of these; melt them together in a little pan—that is, *zulasze*—add a little wild lettuce, and make little cakes from these with semolina flour. Dry them either on a stone heated by fire [Col. 1145B] or in the sun; when dried, grind them to powder. Take a little of this powder often while fasting in hot *hunigwurtz*. If you are healthy and strong, you will become remarkably healthier and stronger, and your powers will be established in this manner. If you are infirm, it will lift up and strengthen you wonderfully, as the sun lights a cloudy day.

## CHAPTER XLI.—ON *AMPHORA*  
[Note: [Col. 1145D] *Rumer acetosus*.] [II, 27].

*Amphora* is neither hot nor cold in the proper measure; therefore it is of no use as food for a person whose constitution is opposed to its nature. If a person ate it, it would make him sad and diffuse his nature through his viscera in an improper measure. Yet it is useful as fodder for livestock and cattle [Col. 1145C].

[Added in the edition: “For what is weak in it for human strength is useful for the strength of livestock.”]

## CHAPTER XLII.—ON *HUSZWURTZ*  
[Note: [Col. 1145D] Houseleek. Cf. below, chapter 203.] [II, 86].

*Huszwurtz* is cold and is not useful for a person to eat, because it is of a rich nature. If a person sound in his sexual constitution ate it, he would burn wholly with lust, so that he would become as if mad. If a man were dry in his seed, so that his semen failed before old age, he should put *huszwurtz* into goat’s milk until it is entirely steeped in that milk; then cook it in the same milk, adding some eggs so that it can be food. Let him eat it for three or five days, and his semen will regain its power of generation [Col. 1145D] and flourish for offspring. But food prepared in this way is of no use against a woman’s sterility; if a woman ate it, it would provoke her to lust but would not remove her sterility. A person deaf in the ears, so that he cannot hear, should take the milk of a woman who bore a boy ten or twelve weeks previously, add juice of *huszwurtz*, gently instill three or four drops into his ear, and do this often; he will recover hearing.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—ON *STICHWURTZ*  
[Note: [Col. 1146D] Cf. below, chapter 204.] [II, 87].

[Col. 1146A]

*Stichwurtz* [bryony, ed.] is hot and useless for human use, like *unkrut*, a useless weed. Its heat is dangerous except where poison is prepared. For if it is burned in fire, so that both its heat and odor touch that poison, it weakens the poison’s power, just as wine loses its power when it is left overnight in a cup. If it is thrown into a fire, roasted like turnips, removed hot from the fire, and cut into pieces, it emits a smell. If that smell touches a serpent or toad, it harms them so severely that the serpent foams and the toad suffers so much that it flees its place. If its smell touches a person, it causes pain, unless he has first eaten rue, because it contains humors so unworthy and grievous [Col. 1146B] that it kills both humans and harmful worms. But if a person’s feet have been wounded by ulcers—that is, *uszgebrochen*—boil *stichwurtz* in water; after pouring off the water, put the *stichwurtz*, while hot, over the places on his feet where they are broken, and foment them with it. It removes their putrefaction, and he will be healed.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—ON *WUNTWURTZ*  
[II, 89].

*Wuntwurtz* [*Frasica*, ed.] is more cold than hot, and its juice is more dangerous than that of certain other herbs, just as one worm is worse and more bitter than others. But where a person has large, raised ulcers in himself—that is, *uszgedroszenser*—he should boil *wuntwurtz* in water, place it hot over those ulcers [Col. 1146C], and foment them often in this fashion; he will be healed. But if a person has been wounded by iron and then puts *wuntwurtz* on the wound, it is dangerous for him, because it suddenly heals the skin outwardly at the surface and leaves corruption within.

[Added in the edition: “For it rapidly closes formed ulcers outwardly and thus harms inwardly unless they have first been treated inwardly with other good aromatics and ointments.”]

But if spots and pustules—that is, *blatern*—break out between a person’s skin and flesh, that is, *uszbrechent*, then *wuntwurtz* should be boiled in water and applied hot; he will be healed. The same should be done for livestock if they have ulcers of this kind.

## CHAPTER XLV.—ON SANICLE  
[Note: [Col. 1146D] *Sanicula europaea*.] [II, 90].

[Col. 1146D]

Sanicle is hot, contains much cleansing power, and has sweet, wholesome juice—that is, *heylsam*—and is very good for a weak stomach and weak viscera. In summer, when it is green, pull it up by the roots and boil it in water. Then strain this water through a cloth, add honey and a little licorice, and make *honigwurtz* from it; drink it often after meals, and it removes *slim* from your stomach and heals weak viscera. Dry sanicle slowly in the sun so that its powers are not diminished; for the sun does not take away the powers of herbs when they are dried in it [Col. 1147A], but fire does.

[Note: [Col. 1147D] The words “for the sun—dried in it” are omitted in the edition.]

Then pulverize the dried herb moderately, so that it is not entirely crushed, and keep this powder for winter. In winter, boil wine with a little honey and licorice—that is, make it *welle*—put this powder into the water, and drink it often after meals; it purges *slim* from the stomach and restores painful viscera to health. A person wounded by iron should press out sanicle juice, pour it into water, and drink it after meals; or, if it is winter, put its powder into water and drink it often after meals. It cleanses wounds inwardly and heals them slowly and well.

[Note: [Col. 1147D] From “or, if it is winter” through “heals” is absent from the edition.]

## CHAPTER XLVI.—ON *HEYLHEUBT*  
[II, 91].

*Heylheubt* [hermodactyl, ed.] is cold and dry; it contains neither soundness nor health and is of no use for anyone to eat. For if a person ate it, it would produce in him a failure of good works and dryness [Col. 1147B].

[Note: [Col. 1147D] The words “for if—dryness” are omitted in the edition.]

If someone eats it, then for a little and brief time his flesh indeed [“grows outwardly, because its power fails inwardly, which raises the flesh a little as if it were growing, and which also,” supplied from the edition] often dies, because it is more poison than health. But if livestock eat *heylheubt*, they will not die from it, though they will become sluggish and ill-conditioned.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—ON FERN  
[Note: [Col. 1147D] Male and female shield fern.] [II, 92].

Fern (Filix in the edition) is very hot and dry, and has little juice in it; but it possesses great power—namely, such power that the devil flees from it. [It also has certain virtues resembling the power of the sun: for as the sun illumines darkness [Col. 1147C], so it drives away phantasms; and therefore evil spirits disdain it, addition in the edition.] In the place where it grows, the devil rarely practices his delusions; and it avoids and abhors a house or place in which the devil is; lightning, thunder, and hail rarely fall there, and hail rarely falls in a field where it grows. Magical practices, demonic incantations, diabolical words, and other phantasms likewise avoid a person who carries it with him.

And if an image is prepared by someone to injure or kill a person, it cannot harm him if he then has this fern with him. For a person is sometimes cursed through an image, so that he is injured by it and becomes deranged. For when the devil drew humankind to himself in Paradise, [Col. 1147D] a certain memorial sign was made in the devil which will remain in him until the Last Day. And then, when he is sometimes summoned by a person through certain words which have at some time been made through his deceits, the sign remaining in him is touched; and thus, provoked and chosen, he often either injures the person through those words or fulfills the will directed toward the person over whom they are spoken.

Sometimes, too, a person is blessed through a made image, so that it benefits him in prosperity and health. But evil is prepared through hatred and envy, and evil is joined to evil. Diabolical suggestion observes a person's bodily composition and joins itself to it; thus it always lies in wait for the person, and so evil is joined to evil. And as a person has good and bad knowledge, so good and bad herbs have also been created for humankind.

But the juice of fern is appointed for wisdom, and in the nobility of its nature it signifies goodness and holiness; therefore all such evils and magical practices flee and avoid it. For in any house in which it is present, poison—that is, *virgilnisse*—and phantasms cannot be brought fully about. Hence, when a woman gives birth, fern should be placed about her, and also around the infant in its cradle; and the devil lies so much the less in wait, because when the devil [Col. 1148B] first looks upon an infant's face, he hates it greatly and plots against it. [Note: “Because he plots against it” is omitted in the edition.]

It is also useful for these remedies. Whoever has *virgichtiget* [gout-affliction/paralysis] should take fern while it is green, boil it in water, and bathe often in that water: the *gicht* will cease. [Note: From “For whoever” to “will cease” is lacking in the edition.] Also, in summer, while it is green, often place its leaves upon your eyes and sleep; it cleanses your eyes and removes their dimness. But one who is deaf, so that he cannot hear, should tie fern-seed in a little cloth and put it often into the ear, taking care that it does not enter the head through the ear: he will recover his hearing. And one who has *virgichtiget* in the tongue, so that he cannot speak, should place its seed upon his tongue, and the *gicht* in the tongue will cease. [Note: Here the chapter ends in the edition.] And he will speak. Moreover, if anyone is forgetful and uncomprehending, holding fern-seed in his hand restores him to memory [Col. 1148C] of himself and gives him understanding: he who is *unverstentlich* [without understanding] will become intelligent.

### Chapter XLVIII.—On Haselwurtz [II, 95]

[Note: *Asarum Europaeum*—European asarabacca.]

Haselwurtz is very hot and possesses a dangerous power; it is to be feared, is very dark, and therefore has an unstable nature, like a storm, because its heat and danger run toward harm. Thus it damages a person's nature more than it benefits health. For if it were given as food to someone who had *sucht ad vidden* [an uncertain ailment] or was *vergichtiget*, it would cause him greater pain. If a pregnant woman ate it, she would either die or miscarry her child, at danger to her own body; or, if she ate it when she did not have her menses, [Col. 1148D] she would suffer more severely. [Note: From “Or, if” to “more severely” is omitted in the edition.]

### Chapter XLIX.—On the Herb Aaron [II, 96]

[Note: *Aaron piaculatum*—spotted arum.]

The herb Aaron is neither lukewarm nor excessively strong, but has an even and temperate warmth, like the gentle warmth held by the sun after dawn; it is also like the pleasant dew before daybreak in summer. Therefore it can be turned to every use, like a gentle man who can endure danger and rightly bear prosperity.

When wasting in a person turns into a black pustule, in which lies the person's death, [Col. 1149A] called *seltega*, then either the leaves or the root of this herb should be given to him to eat. It moderates the excessive heat and excessive cold which are in that pustule, so that it gently disappears. And if a person is so *vergichtiget* that all his limbs collapse in failure and his tongue fails in speaking, let the leaves of the herb Aaron at once be given to him with a little salt to eat, and the *gicht* will cease. Or, if it has not yet ceased, let its root be dipped in cooked honey and immediately given to him to eat, and he will improve.

Likewise, let a person who has *slimecht fiber* [slimy fever] in the stomach, from which diverse *riddo* arises, boil the root of the herb Aaron in pure wine. Then let him allow it to cool; afterward put red-hot steel into the wine, so that it is heated again, and drink it hot. [Col. 1149B] It removes from him the slimy fever in his stomach, as fire makes snow melt away. And a person in whom melancholy rages has an acute disposition and is always sad; let him often drink wine cooked with Aaron-root, and it diminishes in him melancholy—that is, *virswindet* [causes it to vanish]—and fever.

### Chapter L.—On Humela [II, 94]

Humela contains a lukewarm coldness and a certain torpor of heat that excites lust in a person, so that it makes him foolish. For it produces lust in a person who has eaten it or taken it in drink, as strong wine does if he drinks it; it also makes him like a fool. It produces more wasting than blood in a person and is therefore useful for almost nothing—[because it has neither much strength [Col. 1149C] nor health in itself, unless it is added to other herbs or spices, addition in the edition.]

### Chapter LI.—On Wulffesmilch [II, 98]

[Note: *Euphorbia esula*—leafy spurge.]

Wulffesmilch (*Cardus niger* in the edition) is called poison and has a sudden heat which burns human flesh. It also has an unwholesome moisture, because it ruins human flesh. It has no other use except that physicians have found that it is sometimes added to certain drinks against a hardened stomach, so that useful medicines may sometimes be tempered by it and so that an evil in the human body may be driven out by this evil.

### Chapter LII.—On Dolone [II, 97]

Dolo (*Stignus* in the edition) contains coldness; but this coldness nevertheless bears weariness and torpor. In the earth and place where it grows, diabolical suggestion has some share and participation in its art. It is dangerous for a person to eat or drink, because it shakes his spirit as though he were dead.

Yet if anyone is pierced in his skin and flesh by great and very acute ulcers—that is, *durchsoden*—let him take a little *gensesmalcz* [goose fat; *arvina anseris* in the edition], as much deer and goat tallow as he can obtain, and add to these only a little—about one drop applied with a feather—of the juice of *dolo*. Mix them together and make an ointment in this way. With it let him moderately, and not often, anoint [Col. 1150A] his great ulcers, lest he be injured by it. Only a little *dolone* should be added to this ointment, because if he adds much and anoints himself with it often, it eats and perforates his flesh.

### Chapter LIII.—On Dauwurtz [II, 99]

Dauwurtz is hot and dry, has strong powers, and is pure in nature. If anyone frequently eats it as another herb, it cleanses his stomach and removes the dimness of his eyes.

### Chapter LIV.—On Brachwurtz [II, 100]

Brachwurz (*Esula* in the edition) is hot and dry and useful for many things. Whoever has a moist *gicht* in his body, as though it were consuming his limbs, and whoever has impatient *gicht*—that is, *vugedultig*—within [Col. 1150B] his body, so that he has diverse and many thoughts and his understanding seems to vanish, should boil brachwurtzel with wine and honey, strain it through a cloth, and drink it lukewarm often after meals and at night. Let him also put the same brachwurtz, boiled in wine, hot upon his chest and bind a cloth over it. Let him do this often, and he will improve.

Pulverize licorice and *beoniam* [briony] in equal weight. Take as much brachwurtz powder as the combined quantity of those two, mix them together, adding a little bright salt or roasted salt, and often eat this powder, prepared in this way, both fasting and after meals. It makes your voice clear, heals your chest, makes it bright like clear air, and so suppresses [Col. 1150C] and diminishes *gicht* that your limbs are not broken by it and you do not lose your mind's understanding because of it.

### Chapter LV.—On Funffblat [II, 101]

[Note: *Potentilla* species.]

Funffblat (*Quinquefolium* in the edition) is very hot, and its juice has a moderate moisture. It is useful against severe fevers. Take funffblat and crush it thoroughly; mix fine wheat flour with water, as if you intended to make a little cake. Then melt a little *baumoleo* [tree oil], or, if you do not have that, a little poppy oil, so that it becomes soft. Moisten with it a hempen cloth—that is, *striche* [spread or smear it]—and, after warming the cloth, wrap the entire abdomen of a person with severe fevers in it. [Col. 1150D] After half a day or half a night has passed, remove the same cloth, warm it again at the fire, and lay it upon that person's abdomen. Do this often, and the fevers will flee; it also makes him belch.

If anyone suffers dimness in the eyes, let him take funffblat, put it into pure wine, crush it in the wine, strain it through a cloth, and preserve that wine in a bronze vessel. When he goes to sleep, let him anoint the area around his eyes with it, so that a little enters the eyes as well. Let him do this often, and it removes the dimness of the eyes.

Likewise, one who has *gelsucht* [jaundice; *regius morbus*, “royal disease,” in the edition] should make little cakes from funffblat, fine wheat flour, and water, and for [Col. 1151A] nine days eat these while fasting; he will be cured. This herb is useful to a person for remedies, unless God forbids it. [Note: From “This herb” to “forbids it” is omitted in the edition.]

### Chapter LVI.—On Mandrake [II, 102]

[Note: *Atropa Mandragora*—mandrake.]

Mandrake is hot and somewhat watery, and it sprang from that earth of which Adam was made; it somewhat resembles a human being. Yet, because of the herb's human likeness, [Note: Hildegard, letter to Glodesindis (letter 42); her letter to the bishop of Jerusalem (letter 22); and to St Bernard (letter 29). A woodcut image of each sex appears in the work entitled *Hortus sanitatis*.] diabolical suggestion is more present in and lies more in wait for it than for other herbs. Therefore a person is aroused through it according to his desires, whether good or evil, just as he once was through idols. [Note: From “Therefore” to “idols” is lacking in the edition.]

When it is dug from the earth, it should immediately be placed in a spring—that is, a *queckbornen*—for one day and one night; thus all evil and contrary humors within it are expelled—that is, *uszgebiszen* [driven out]—so that it is no longer efficacious for magic and phantasmagoria. But when it is uprooted, if it is then laid aside with earth adhering to it and is not cleansed in the *queckborn* as stated, then it is harmful for many useless magical practices and phantasmagorias, [Col. 1151B] just as many evils were once wrought with idols. [Note: From “But when it is uprooted” to “with idols” is lacking in the edition.]

If any man is incontinent, whether through magic or through the ardor of his body, let him take the female form of this herb after it has been cleansed in the spring mentioned above, and bind that part of the herb which is between its breasts and its navel upon himself for three days and three nights. Then divide the same fruit into two parts and bind one part over each *lanckun* [hip; *ilium* in the edition] for three days and three nights. Also pulverize the left [right in the edition] hand of that image, add a little camphor to the powder, eat it, and he will be cured. [Note: From “Also pulverize” to “will be cured” is lacking in the edition.]

If a woman suffers the same ardor in her body, let her take the male form of the same image between her breasts and navel and do likewise, as stated above. Pulverize its right hand, add a little camphor, and eat this powder as aforesaid; that ardor will be extinguished in her.

But anyone who suffers in his head from any infirmity should eat of the head of the same herb, however he wishes. If he suffers in his neck, let him eat of its neck; if in his back, of its back; if in his arm, of its arm; [Col. 1151D] if in his hand, of its hand; if in his knee, of its knee; if in his foot, of its foot. [Note: From “If in his arm” to “of its foot” is omitted in the edition.] Or, whatever member pains him, let him eat of the corresponding member of the same image, and he will improve. The male form of this image is more useful for remedies than the female form, because a man is stronger than a woman.

[Col. 1152A] If anyone is by nature so afflicted that he is always sad and always in misery, so that he continually has weakness and pain in his heart, let him take mandrake when it has just been uprooted and place it in a *queckborn*, as stated above, for one day and one night. Then let him take it from the spring and lay it beside himself in his bed, so that the herb may be warmed by his sweat, and say: [Note: Prayers of this kind occur in this work at II, 14; III, 20, 25; IV, 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 13, 18; VII, 3, 9.]

> “God, who made man from the clay of the earth without pain, I now place beside me this earth which has never transgressed, so that my earth also may feel that peace in which you created it.”

If you do not have mandrake, take the *inicium*, that is, the first shoot from a beech tree [“the first thick shoots emerging from a beech,” in the edition], for they happily possess the same nature for this purpose. [Col. 1152B] Break them from their small branches in such a way that you do not break them, but remove them whole from the tree. Place them beside you in your bed, so that they are warmed by you and receive sweat from your body. Say over them the words stated above, and you will receive joy and feel healing in your heart. You may do the same with cedar and aspen, and it will help you.

### Chapter LVII.—On Winda [II, 103]

[Note: *Convolvulus arvensis* and *C. sepium*—field and hedge bindweed.]

Winda is cold, has no strong powers, and is not very useful. If anyone eats it, it neither hurts nor benefits him. But if a person's nails are beginning to become *grindig* [scabby; “beginning to have scabies,” in the edition], and this is at its beginning, let him take winda and crush it—that is, *stampe*—add a little *quecksilber* [quicksilver; “living silver,” in the edition], mix these together, then place the mixture upon the nails and bind it with a cloth; they will become beautiful.

### Chapter LVIII.—On Boberella

[Note: Absent from the edition.]

Boberella. Whoever has dim eyes should take a red silk cloth and spread boberella upon it as an ointment. When going to sleep, let him place the silk cloth over his eyes. Let him do this often, and it will drive away dimness of the eyes.

Likewise, whoever has *dyszent* in the ears, so that he is thereby almost deaf, should take boberella, spread it upon felt, place the felt over the entire neck and the *nack* [nape] as far as the ears, and bind it. Let him do this often when going to sleep, and the *dizo* [ringing/noise] in the ears will cease. Dry boberella a little in smoke and eat it: it somewhat checks *dumphen* [shortness of breath], although only slightly. But whoever suffers inwardly from ulcers of the viscera should take wheat bran, warm it in a pan with boberella, put it upon a cloth, and lay it, hot, all around his abdomen and navel often; he will be cured.

### Chapter LIX.—On Binsuga [II, 104]

[Note: *Lamium album*—white dead-nettle.]

[Col. 1153A]

Binsuga (*Apiago* in the edition) is hot, and a person who eats it readily laughs, because its heat touches the spleen and the heart is thereby made joyful. But if *wisza* [a white opacity; *albugo* in the edition] grows in someone's eye, let him uproot it from the earth and place it, once uprooted, in the water of a living spring overnight. Then take it from the water, steam it in a pan, and place it hot upon that eye. Do this for three nights, and the *wisza* in his eye will be healed and disappear.

### Chapter LX.—On Sunnewirbel [II, 105]

[Note: *Cichoreum Intybus*; *Solsequium* in the edition.]

Sunnewirbel is hot and moist; in its nature it tends toward beauty and is earth-born. Yet the person who carries it with him [“just as one who desires to be above others,” addition in the edition] is hated by other people. [Col. 1153B]

Whoever suffers around the chest so that his voice is hoarse should take sunnewirbel and an equal weight of greater *cletta* [uncertain], boil them in pure wine, strain them through a cloth, and drink this often after meals and at night; he will improve in chest and voice. Whoever cannot have proper digestion should take equal weights of sunnewirbel and greater *cletta*, dry them in the sun or upon a heated brick, reduce them to powder, add to this powder one third as much bright or roasted salt as either of these ingredients, and then make from it with honey a *honigwurtz* [honey drink; *potum*, “drink,” in the edition]. Let him drink it often after meals and at night, and he will have digestion at its proper time. In this way the herb is useful for remedies, unless God forbids it. [Note: From “In this way” to “forbids it” is lacking in the edition.]

### Chapter LXI.—On Hoppho [II, 74]

[Note: *Humulus Lupulus*—hop.]

[Col. 1153C]

Hoppho (*Humulus* in the edition) is hot and dry and has little moisture. It is not very useful for human benefit, because it makes melancholy increase in a person, makes the mind sad, and weighs down the viscera. Yet its bitterness prevents certain putrefactions in beverages to which it is added, enabling them to last longer.

### Chapter LXII.—On Lilim [II, 106]

Lilim is very hot. A person who is *demphig* because of the spleen, stomach, or weak viscera [“has difficulty breathing in or out,” in the edition], as though he were *virdumet* [bruised; “broken,” in the edition] around his chest, provided that he does not have pain in the lung, should take lilim [Col. 1153D] and boil it with a little beer and a little honey. Strain it through a cloth, then drink it often fasting, after meals, and when going to sleep. It gives him relief and good belching, so that he will improve from the aforementioned infirmities.

Whoever has weak humors within him, so that phlegm arises in him from them, should boil lilim in pure wine. Then crush pennyroyal in a little vinegar and make it boil with the aforementioned lilim and the wine in which it was boiled. Strain it through a cloth and cover it in some vessel—that is, *demphe*—while it cools. [Col. 1154A] Drink it often after meals and at night; it makes the primary moisture in him vanish, purges his humors, and diminishes phlegm, as a wound is cleansed.

### Chapter LXIII.—On Selba [II, 28]

[Note: *Salvia officinalis*—common sage.]

Selba (*Salvia* in the edition) is hot and dry in nature. It grows more from the heat of the sun than from the moisture of the earth and is useful against weak humors because it is dry. Raw and cooked, it is good to eat for one afflicted by harmful humors, because it restrains them. Take sage, pulverize it, and eat this powder with bread: it diminishes the excess of bad humors in you. [“And whoever suffers a foul odor from any unclean thing should put sage into his nostrils, and it will help him,” addition in the edition.]

If [Col. 1154B] anyone abounds in excess phlegm or has foul breath, let him boil sage in wine, strain it through a cloth, and drink it often; the bad humors and phlegm in him will be diminished. If the person with these infirmities is somewhat *virgicht* [afflicted with paralysis; “wearied by paralysis,” in the edition], let him boil sage in water and drink it, and the humors and phlegm in him will diminish.

[If the person suffering these infirmities is somewhat afflicted by paralysis, let him boil sage in water, as stated above, drink it, and its heat, tempered with water, will restrain paralysis in the person. For if it were given to him with wine, the wine would cause the paralytic humors in him to exceed their proper measure. Whoever has an aversion to eating should take sage, [Col. 1154C] a smaller amount of chervil, and a little garlic; crush these together in vinegar and make a sauce. Let him dip into it the foods he wishes to eat, and he will have an appetite for food. When food possessing a watery juice causes a person headache, let him take equal weights of sage, oregano, and fennel, with more horehound than all of these; add sufficient freshly churned butter to the crushed juice—or, if he does not have it, add fat—and make an ointment from these. Anoint the head, and he will improve. If a bad vapor rises from the stomach to a person's flanks and causes pain there, take sage, five times as much *seuwurtz* as sage, and ten times as much rue [Col. 1154D] as sage. Boil these herbs with water in a new pot until the first boiling; then squeeze out the water and place the same boiled, hot herbs upon the painful place, binding a cloth over them. If anyone cannot retain urine because of the coldness of his stomach, boil sage in water, strain it through a cloth, and drink it hot often; he will be cured. If bad, congealed, and poisonous humors have become excessive in a person and cause him for a time to spit and discharge blood, he should meanwhile apply no medicine to himself, lest the blood, stirred up by medicine, ulcerate him inwardly [Col. 1155A] and flow out more than usual. But after the blood has diminished somewhat, boil sage in mild, pleasant wine mixed with a little water; add a little olive oil or butter, strain it through a cloth after boiling, and drink it in moderation—not fasting, but after a meal. It strengthens him and heals him inwardly, addition in the edition.]

### Chapter LXIV.—On Rue [II, 29]

[Note: *Ruta graveolens*—common rue.]

Rue grows more from the strong and full—that is, *queckin*—greenness of the earth than from heat, and it has a temperate warmth, though more warmth than cold. It is strong in its moist powers and good against the dry bitterness that grows in a person whose proper humors fail. It is also better and more useful when eaten raw than when pulverized. [Col. 1155B] When eaten, it restrains the unruly boiling of blood in a person. For the heat of rue attenuates the undue heat of melancholy and moderates its undue coldness. Thus a melancholy person improves when he eats it after other food. If anyone eats another food from which he suffers pain, let him afterward eat rue, and he will suffer less.

[A person whose eyes are watering should take rue, twice as much sage, and twice as much chervil as sage. Crush these herbs slightly in a mortar so that they yield some juice; dip the crushed herbs in egg white and, at night when going to sleep, lay them upon the forehead extending to both temples: they draw out the bad humors. Or let someone suck juice from an apple. [Col. 1155C] Whoever has black or clouded eyes, as the sky sometimes is, and experiences some dimness in them, should take rue juice, mix with it twice as much clear liquid honey and a little good clear wine, place a crumb of wheaten bread in the mixture, and bind it over the eyes at night with a cloth. If a person sometimes suffers pain in the kidneys and loins, this often arises from weakness of the stomach. Then let him take equal weights of rue and wormwood, add more bear fat than both of these, crush them together, and vigorously anoint himself with them beside the fire around his aching kidneys and loins. If someone is so aroused by desire that semen reaches the point of emission, but is somehow retained within the body [Col. 1155D] and he begins to become ill from this, let him take rue and a somewhat smaller quantity of wormwood, press out their juice, and add sugar to it, more honey, and as much wine as there is of these juices. Heat it five times with red-hot steel in a new pot or pan, and, after eating a little, drink it hot. If it is winter and he cannot obtain the herbs just mentioned, let him pulverize laurel berries and twice as much dittany, and, after a little food, drink them in hot wine heated with red-hot steel. Thus the harmful bruising remaining in him is expelled with urine [Col. 1156A] and digestion. If anyone eats something from which he immediately suffers pain, let him at once eat rue mixed with salt and twice as much sage, and he will improve, addition in the edition.]

### Chapter LXV.—On Hyssop [II, 30]

[Note: *Hyssopus officinalis*—common hyssop.]

Hyssop is dry in nature and moderately hot, and of such great power that even stone cannot prevent it from growing where it has been sown. When frequently eaten, it purges weak and foul foams of humors—that is, *reyniget* [cleanses]—as heat makes a pot *wellet* [boil; “cast out foams,” in the edition]. It is useful with every food. Cooked and pulverized, it is more useful than raw. When eaten, it makes the liver *querck* [vigorous] and cleanses the lung somewhat.

Whoever coughs [*hus*; “coughs,” in the edition], suffers from the liver, or is *dumphet* [short of breath] from a diseased lung, [Col. 1156B] should eat hyssop with meat or fat, and will improve; for anyone who eats hyssop with wine alone or water alone is harmed by it more than helped.

Whoever suffers in the liver or lung should take licorice, more cinnamon than licorice, more hyssop than those two, and more fennel than those three. Boil these in a new pot, adding enough honey that no bitterness remains in them, and boil them very strongly. Then keep this pot with the same herbs for nine days and the same number of nights; afterward strain it through a cloth and drink it. If pain in the liver or lung is severe, drink it every day for nine days. Before drinking it in the morning, eat a little and then drink it. But [Col. 1156C] eat sufficiently at night and, when going to sleep, drink enough of it. If pain in the lung is slight and there is pain in the liver, drink it in the same way after three days have passed; do this often, and he will be cured, unless God does not will it.

[But if the liver is weakened by a person's sadness, before the infirmity becomes excessive in it, boil young hens with hyssop and eat both the hyssop and these hens often. Also frequently eat raw hyssop steeped in wine and drink the same wine, because hyssop is more useful to him for this infirmity than to one who suffers in the lung, addition in the edition.]

### Chapter LXVI.—On Fennel [II, 31]

[Note: *Anethum Feniculum*—fennel.]

Fennel has a pleasant warmth and is neither dry nor [Col. 1156D] cold in nature. Eaten raw, it does not harm a person. However it is eaten, it makes a person cheerful, gives him pleasant warmth and good perspiration, and produces good digestion. Its seed too is hot in nature and useful for human health if it is added with other herbs to medicines. Whoever eats fennel or its seed fasting every day diminishes bad phlegm and putrefactions in himself, restrains the foulness of his breath, and makes his eyes see clearly through its good warmth and good powers.

[Whoever cannot sleep because he is disturbed by some contrary condition should, if it is summer, cook fennel and twice as much yarrow slightly; after squeezing out the water, place the herbs, hot, around the temples, forehead, and head, and bind a cloth over them. He should also take green sage, sprinkle it lightly with wine, and place it above his heart and around his neck; sleep will relieve him. If it is winter, boil fennel seed and yarrow root in water, apply them around the head as stated above, and place pulverized sage, slightly moistened with wine, upon the heart and neck; he will improve. When a person with gray eyes experiences dimness and pain in them while the pain is still recent, let him crush fennel or its seed, take its juice and the dew found upon sound grass, [Col. 1157B] add a little fine wheat flour, mix this into a little cake, place it around his eyes at night, and bind it with a cloth; he will improve. If someone has eyes like a cloudy sky—neither wholly fiery nor wholly turbid, but somewhat gray-green—and suffers dimness and pain in them, let him crush fennel in summer; or, in winter, place its crushed seed upon well-clarified egg white. When he lies down to sleep, let him put it upon his eyes; it diminishes their dimness. If excessive pain has arisen from much discharge in a person's nostrils, take fennel and four times as much dill, lay them upon a stone roofing-tile or a thin brick heated by fire, and turn the fennel and dill this way and that so that they smoke. Draw this smoke [Col. 1157C] and its odor inward through the nostrils and mouth; then eat the herbs thus heated with bread. Do this for four or five days, so that the flowing humors may separate more gently. A person who has harmful bruising in his weak stomach should take fennel, a little more nettle, and twice as much lovage as both of these, make food from them with a little flour or bread, and eat it often: it removes the bruising from the weak stomach. A person troubled by melancholy should crush fennel for its juice and often anoint his forehead, temples, chest, and stomach; the melancholy in him will cease. Whoever eats roasted meat, roasted fish, [Col. 1157D] or anything else roasted and suffers from it should immediately eat fennel or its seed, and will suffer less.

If at times a swelling of the worst tumor arises from bad humors in a man's genitals and causes pain there, let him take fennel, three times as much fenugreek, and a little cow's butter; crush them together and apply them above, and they will draw out the bad humors. Then let the same man take the little cakes from which beer is made, moisten them slightly with hot water, warm them, and place them upon the aforesaid swelling. If a pregnant woman labors severely in childbirth, then, with caution and great moderation, boil gentle herbs, such as fennel and asarabacca, in water. After squeezing out the water, place them hot around her thighs and back, bind a cloth over them, and keep them gently in place, so that her pain and constrictions may be relieved more gently and easily. [Col. 1158A]

Let a person take fennel seed, half as much galangal, the same half-quantity of dittany, and half as much mouse-ear as of dittany. Pulverize these together, strain them through a cloth, and, a short time after a meal, put this powder into hot but not boiling wine and drink it. This powder keeps a healthy person healthy, strengthens the sick, promotes digestion, gives strength, supplies a good and beautiful complexion, and benefits every person, healthy or sick, when taken after food. [Col. 1158B] If sheep begin to fall ill, take fennel and more dill, put them into water so that the water takes their flavor, and give it to the sick sheep to drink, addition in the edition.]

### Chapter LXVII.—On Dill [II, 32]

[Note: *Anethum graveolens*—dill.]

Dill (*Anetum* in the edition) is dry, hot, and temperate in nature. However it is eaten, it makes a person sad. It is not good to eat raw, because it contains more of the earth's moisture than fennel and draws to itself a certain fatness from the earth. Thus it is harmful to a person when eaten raw; yet, when cooked and eaten, it restrains *gicht* and is therefore useful as food.

[Col. 1158C] Therefore, whoever has much blood flowing from the nostrils should take dill and twice as much yarrow, and apply these fresh herbs around his forehead, temples, and chest. These herbs must be fresh, since their power flourishes especially in their greenness. But if it is winter, let him reduce these herbs to powder, sprinkle the powder with a little wine, put it in a small bag, and apply it to the forehead, temples, and chest as stated above.

Thus, in order that a person may extinguish within himself the delight and lust of the flesh, let him take in summer dill, twice as much *bachminza*, a little more *brochvurtz*, and the root of Illyrian iris; cut all these into vinegar, make a seasoning from them, and eat it often with all his foods. [Col. 1158D] In winter, however, reduce these to powder and likewise eat the powder with food, since at that time he cannot have the herbs themselves fresh. In damp and mild weather, when oxen then readily begin to fall ill, mix dill and a smaller quantity of Illyrian iris-root into their fodder; it consumes their bad humours. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—ON PARSLEY

[Note: [Col. 1158D] *Apium Petroselinum*] [II, 33].

Parsley is of a robust nature and contains more heat than cold; it grows from wind and moisture. Eaten raw, it is better and more useful for a person than when cooked. When eaten, it lessens fevers which shake a person but affect him mildly; [Col. 1159A] nevertheless, it produces heaviness in the mind.

But one who has pain in the heart, spleen, or side should cook parsley in wine, adding a little vinegar and sufficient honey; then strain it through a cloth and drink it often. It heals him.

[Also, one who has a weak stomach should take parsley, twice as much fennel, and as much *lanaria* as parsley; make a pottage from these, adding butter or beef fat and roasted salt, and eat it cooked in this way often. Also, one who has eaten garlic and suffers from it should immediately eat parsley and will suffer less. Addition of the edition.]

And one who suffers from stone should take parsley, add to it one third part of *steinbrechent* [saxifrage, edition], cook these in wine, strain it through a cloth, and drink it in a dry bath. [Col. 1159B] Again, cook parsley with one third part of saxifrage in water; pour the same water over the heated stones of the dry bath, and do this often. He will improve.

[Likewise, one who is tormented by paralysis should take equal quantities of parsley and fennel, and a somewhat smaller quantity of sage; lightly crush these herbs together in a mortar, add rose-scented olive oil, apply it to the afflicted place, and bind a cloth over it. One who has soft flesh and suffers in some limb from gout caused by excessive drinking should take parsley and four times as much rue, fry them in a pan with olive oil, or, if he does not have that oil, have them fried with goat’s fat; [Col. 1159C] apply the warm herbs to the painful place, bind a cloth over them, and he will improve. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXIX.—ON CELERY

[Note: [Col. 1159D] *Apium graveolens*] [II, 34].

Celery is hot, and of a nature more green than dry; it contains much juice. Raw, it is not good for a person to eat, because it produces bad humours in him. Cooked, however, it does not harm a person when eaten, but produces healthy humours.

Whatever way it is eaten, it induces a wandering mind in a person. [For its greenness sometimes harms him and sometimes makes him sad through instability. A person whose eyes are watery, so that tears overflow in drops from excessive humours, should take celery and [Col. 1159D] a little more fennel, crush them into juice, dip them in the white of an egg without its yolk, and, when going to sleep at night, bind them with a cloth over the watery eye. Do this often, and he will be cured. Addition of the edition.]

But one so afflicted by *gicht* that his mouth is distorted by contraction, his limbs tremble, and he is likewise contracted in other limbs, should reduce celery seed to powder; add one third part rue, nutmeg in a quantity less than the powder of rue, cloves in a quantity less than the nutmeg, and *steinbrechen* [Col. 1160A] in a quantity less than the cloves. Reduce all these to powder, and eat this powder both fasting and after meals. The *gicht* will cease, for it is an excellent remedy against *gicht*. Indeed, if one suffering from *gicht* frequently eats this powder, it drives the *gicht* away so that he is not harmed.

## CHAPTER LXX.—ON CHERVIL

[Note: [Col. 1159D] *Scandix Cerefolium*] [II, 35].

Chervil [*Cerifolium*, edition] is of a dry nature. It grows neither from strong air nor from strong moisture of the earth, but in weak weather, before the fruitful heat of summer has arisen. Yet it is more hot than cold, and that heat is wholesome. It somewhat resembles useless herbs because, if eaten raw, it produces much vapour in a person’s head. For neither cooked nor raw is it beneficial to the human body as food, [Col. 1160B] except that it is useful as a medicine and heals ruptured internal wounds.

Crush chervil—that is, *stamphe*—squeeze out its juice into wine, and give it to drink to one who has ruptured internal wounds. Do this often, and he will be cured.

[When a person at times eats uncooked food, the bad humours of that food, because they have not been moderated by any seasoning, rise to the spleen and make it painful. Therefore let that person take chervil and a smaller amount of dill, prepare a seasoning with wheaten bread in vinegar, like morsels, and eat it frequently. Then take linseed and cook it in a frying-pan; pour off [Col. 1160C] the water into a small bag and apply it, as hot as can be endured, in the bag to the region of the spleen.

A person who suffers from various ulcers and scabies should take chervil, three times as much polypody, and elecampane in a quantity five times that of the chervil, and cook them in water. Then, after squeezing out and straining the water through a cloth, pour it into a frying-pan; add a little fresh frankincense and sulphur, and fresh pork fat in an amount greater than all the other things named. Let it thicken together somewhat over the fire in the frying-pan, like an ointment. Let the sufferer anoint himself around the ulcers with this ointment for five days. By this treatment his skin and flesh will be renewed; afterward let him wash himself in a bath, so that these bruised discolorations and the foul smell may be removed from him. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXXI.—ON PUNGO

[Note: [Col. 1160D] *Veronica Beccabunga*] [II, 37].

[Col. 1160D]

Pungo is of a hot nature. Whoever cooks a mash from it [“makes food from it alone,” edition], adding fat or oil, and eats it, has his bowels loosened as by a certain drink. Eaten also, it checks *gicht*.

## CHAPTER LXXII.—ON CRASSO

[Note: [Col. 1160D] *Levidium Sativum*] [II, 38].

Crasso [cress, edition] is more hot than cold, and is also moist; it grows more from the greenness of the earth than from the sun. Eaten, it increases bad humours in a person and harms the spleen, [because the latter is soft and easily injured. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXXIII.—ON WATERCRESS

[Note: [Col. 1161D] *Nasturtium aquaticum*] [II, 39].

[Col. 1161A]

Watercress is of a hot nature. Eaten, it neither greatly benefits nor greatly harms a person. But one who has *gelsucht* [the royal disease, edition] or fever should sweat this watercress in a pan and eat it warm often; it will cure him. One who can scarcely digest food that he has eaten should likewise sweat watercress in a pan, since its strength comes from water, and eat it thus; it will help him.

## CHAPTER LXXIV.—ON PURSLANE

[Note: [Col. 1161D] *Portulaca Sativa*] [II, 40].

Purslane [*Portulaca*, edition] is cold; eaten, it produces bruised discoloration and mucus (*slim*) in a person, and is of no benefit as food.

## CHAPTER LXXV.—ON WATER-MINT

[Note: [Col. 1161D] *Mentha aquatica*] [II, 41].

*Bachmyntza* is hot, but also somewhat [Col. 1161B] cold. It may be eaten moderately; eaten, it neither benefits a person nor harms him much. When one’s stomach is burdened by many foods and drinks and thereby suffers from *dumphet*, let him eat *bachmyntza*, raw or cooked with meat, or cooked in soups or mash, often; the *dumpho* will cease, because it somewhat cools the fatty, hot internal organs and their fatness, and thus the *dumpho* will lessen.

But one who suffers from *dumphet* through a weak lung coughs up phlegm and coughs only with difficulty in moving himself. One who suffers from *dumphet* through fatness and many foods and drinks merely draws breath with difficulty and does not cough up phlegm. Thus these conditions are distinguished; and he should use this *bachmyntza* as stated above.

## CHAPTER LXXVI.—ON THE LARGER MINT

[Note: [Col. 1161D] Wild mint] [II, 42].

The other mint [*Mentha*, edition], which is large, is more hot [Col. 1161C] than cold. It should be crushed and bound over the place where *suern* [*sotim*, edition; uncertain] or *snebelcza* injure a person by biting; they will die.

## CHAPTER LXXVII.—ON THE SMALLER MINT

[Note: [Col. 1161D] Field mint] [II, 43].

The mint called the smaller mint is more hot than cold. Crush it and apply it to eyes suffering from *augswer* [“which suffer painfully from bruised discoloration,” edition], binding it with a cloth; thus it draws out the *augswer*.

Also, one who has a cold stomach and cannot digest food should eat this smaller mint, either raw, cooked with meat, or cooked with fish. It warms his stomach and prepares digestion.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII.—ON ROSSEMYNTZA

[Note: [Col. 1161D] Perhaps *Romischemynoza*?—curled mint] [II, 14].

[Col. 1161D] *Rossemyntza* [Roman mint, edition] has moderate, sharp heat, though it is also somewhat temperate. Whoever is harmed by *gicht* should crush it, strain its juice through a cloth, add a little wine, and drink it in this way morning, evening, and at night; the *gicht* will cease.

And just as salt, moderately added, seasons every food—because it is harmful if too much or too little is added to foods—so Roman mint, moderately added to [Col. 1162A] meat, fish, dishes, or mash, gives that food a good taste and good seasoning. Eaten thus, it also warms the stomach and promotes good digestion.

## CHAPTER LXXIX.—ON GARLIC

[Note: [Col. 1161D] *Allium sativum*] [II, 46].

Garlic has proper heat and grows from the strength of dew. It is *queck* [vigorous; “it grows,” edition] from the first sleep of night until it is almost beginning to grow light and morning has come. When ripe, it is more wholesome for healthy and sick persons to eat than leek. [Note: [Col. 1162D] “And when it is ripe, for healthy and sick persons, etc.,” edition.]

It should be eaten raw, for if it were cooked it would become like spoiled wine—that is, *seiger*—because its juice is temperate and it has proper heat. It does not harm the eyes; nevertheless, because of its heat, blood rises very strongly around a person’s eyes, [Col. 1162B] but afterward they become clear. Yet it should be eaten moderately, lest the blood in a person become overheated beyond measure.

When garlic is old, its healthy and proper efficacy disappears; but if it is then tempered with other foods, it recovers its powers.

## CHAPTER LXXX.—ON ALSLAUCH

[Note: [Col. 1162D] Shallot] [II, 47].

*Alslauch* [shallot, edition] is cold and poisonous, and is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat. Nevertheless, whoever wishes to eat it should first put it in wine and *beysze* it [temper it, edition]; then both healthy and sick persons may eat it. Yet for a sick person it is better eaten raw in a moderate amount than cooked, because if he ate it cooked, [Note: [Col. 1162D] Addition from the edition: “it would cause certain gripings in his belly.”] Therefore, when he wishes to eat it raw, let him first *beysze* it in wine, as [Col. 1162C] stated above.

## CHAPTER LXXXI.—ON LEEK

[Note: [Col. 1162D] *Allium porrum*] [II, 47].

The leek called *Lauch* [Note: [Col. 1162D] “Which is called—Lauch” omitted in the edition] has swift and useless heat within it, like worthless wood—namely, *spachin* [brushwood of hedges, edition]—which quickly catches fire and quickly falls away. It produces disturbances in a person’s sexual desire.

Eaten raw, it is as bad and contrary to a person as a poisonous and useless herb, because it perverts his blood, wasting, and humours into their opposite—that is, *wal*—so that blood does not properly increase in him through it, wasting is not diminished in him by it, and bad humours are not cleansed in him through it.

But one wishing to eat leek [raw] should first *beysze* it in wine with salt added, or in vinegar, so that it lies in the wine or salt [Col. 1162D] until it is so tempered in them that it loses its bad powers there: from morning until midday, or from the ninth hour until evening. Tempered in this way, it is good for healthy persons to eat. Prepared raw in this manner, it is better for healthy persons than cooked.

But it is good for sick people neither raw nor cooked, because their blood does not have proper heat, their wasting is turbid, and [Col. 1163A] their humours are foamy—that is, *feymechte*. Therefore, if a sick person continually ate it, it would pervert all these things in him. [Note: [Col. 1163D] “Because their blood—would pervert” omitted in the edition.]

Nevertheless, if certain sick persons have a great desire to eat leek, let them eat a moderate amount of it raw and tempered as stated above, because raw so prepared is better than cooked. [And it is not very suitable for medicines because it grows in unstable weather, namely when the heat of the air contains moisture and the moisture contains heat. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXXXII.—ON LAUCH

[Note: [Col. 1163D] Welsh onion] [II, 50].

Every *Lauch* [leek, edition] that is hollow, such as *hol*, *surige*, *prieslauch*, *planza*, and similar kinds, is not excessively hot but temperate, and has a somewhat wine-like juice. They grow from wind and the moisture of [Col. 1163B] the earth. Yet among leeks, *Lauch* is especially less harmful: it does not produce storms in a person’s humours and can be digested quickly. Eaten raw, it does not harm healthy persons; for sick persons it should be cooked, lest its moisture join their moisture, since sick people have diverse humours within them. [Note: [Col. 1163D] “Lest its moisture—they have” omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII.—ON UNLAUCH

[Note: [Col. 1163D] Onion] [II, 49].

*Unlauch* [onion, edition] does not have proper heat but sharp moisture, and is *queck* [vigorous; “it grows,” edition] from that dew which occurs about daybreak, when the powers of the dew are already fading. Raw, it is as harmful and poisonous to eat as the juice of useless herbs; cooked, it is wholesome food, [Col. 1163C] [because fire lessens the harmful properties in it, addition of the edition]. It is good when cooked for those who have *vidden*, fever, or *gicht*. But for those who are *magensich* [who have a weak and feeble stomach, edition], both raw and cooked, it causes pain because it is moist. [Note: [Col. 1163D] “Because it is moist” omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXXXIV.—ON CABBAGE

[Note: [Col. 1163D] *Brassica oleracea*] [II, 51].

*Kole*, *Weydenkole*, and *Kochkole* [cabbage, *Wendolkoel*, and red cabbage, edition] are of a moist nature; and *kappus* is somewhat more cold than hot and of a somewhat dry nature. They grow from the bruised darkness of dew and air. Accordingly, they have, as it were, strength and internal organs; yet their juice is somewhat harmful, ailments are generated in people by them, and weak internal organs are injured.

But healthy persons [Col. 1163D] who have strong veins and are not very fat can overcome them by their strength if they eat them. They are harmful to fat people, however, because their flesh abounds in juice; eaten, they harm them almost as much as they harm the sick. Cooked in mash or with meat, they are harmful and increase bad humours rather than diminish them. [Note: [Col. 1163D] “And cooked in mash—diminish them” omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXXXV.—ON WISZGRAS

[II, 52].

[Col. 1164A]

*Wiszgras* [*Weggrasz*, *Suregrasz*, and *Roemesgrasz*, edition] is of a temperate nature and moderately dry. For healthy and sick persons alike, it is, as food, like *melda* and *latichen* [“as though a remedy,” edition]; it does not generate harmful humours and is easily digested healthfully.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI.—ON STUTGRAS

[Note: [Col. 1164D] It appears again below, with a few changes. See chapter 196.] [II, 53].

The smaller varieties of *stutgras* produce weak and unhealthy humours in weak persons and increase melancholy in them. They are hard to digest and are therefore as contrary to people as weeds [because their greenness is bad. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.—ON GOURDS

[Note: [Col. 1164D] Bottle gourd] [II, 55].

Gourds [*Cucurbita*, edition] are dry and cold, and [Col. 1164B] grow from the air; they are good for both sick and healthy persons to eat. [Note: [Col. 1164D] Here the edition places the chapter “On melons”: “Melons are moist and cold, and grow from moisture … are of no use.”] They grow from the moisture of the earth, stir up the bitterness of humours in people, and are not good for the sick to eat.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—ON TURNIP

[Note: [Col. 1164D] *Brassica rapa*] [II, 57].

Turnip [*Rapa*, edition] is more hot than cold and is heavy in a person’s stomach, yet it can be easily digested. Whoever wishes to eat it raw should remove all the outer skin, since it is thick, for its greenness harms a person; once the skin has been removed, let him eat what is inside. But cooked it is better than raw and does not produce bad humours.

If at any time humour rises up in ulcers, let him eat turnip and the ulcer will be checked. But if anyone suffers from *dumphet* in [Col. 1164C] the lungs, eating cooked or raw turnip will trouble him somewhat in the lungs [because it does not have strength enough to resist great infirmities. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.—ON RADISH

[Note: [Col. 1164D] *Raphanus sativus*] [II, 58].

Radish [*Radix*, edition] is more hot than cold. After it has been dug up, it should be buried in the earth in a moist place for two or three days, so that its greenness may be tempered and it become all the better for eating. Eaten, it cleanses the brain and lessens harmful humours of the internal organs. For if a strong, fleshy person eats radish, it heals and purges him internally; but it harms one who is sick and dry of body.

[Col. 1164D] But if a sick person wishes to eat it, let him first dry it upon a heated stone, reduce it to powder, add bright or roasted salt and fennel seed to this powder, and eat it with bread. It purges his inward foulness and strengthens him [*crefftiget*, edition]. But one who has an abundance of phlegm should powder radish in this manner, cook honey with wine, add this powder, and drink it slightly cooled [Col. 1165A] both after meals and fasting. This powder purges phlegm from him [Note: [Col. 1165D] The remainder is lacking in the edition], and the honey prevents him from becoming dry.

What is perceived to be its effect when eaten is that it expels bad humours and foul odours from a person. One who eats radish should afterward eat galangal; it checks the foulness of the breath, and thus radish does not harm the person.

## CHAPTER XC.—ON LETTUCE

[Note: [Col. 1165D] *Lactuca sativa*] [II, 60].

Domestic lettuces that may be eaten are very cold. Eaten without seasoning, by their useless juice they make a person’s brain empty and fill the stomach with weakness. Therefore, one wishing to eat them should first *beysze* them with dill, vinegar, or garlic [season and temper them, edition], so that they are steeped in these for a short time before being eaten. [Col. 1165B] If eaten tempered in this manner, they strengthen the brain and promote good digestion.

[If anyone suffers pain or swelling in the gums, let him take lettuces; or, if he does not have them, let him take the first leaves sprouting from an oak, add a little more chervil, lightly crush these, add wine, apply it to his mouth, and keep it in the mouth for some time. They expel the unhealthy humours of the gums. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER XCI.—ON WILD LETTUCE

[Note: [Col. 1165D] Poisonous lettuce. Compare below, chapter 198.] [II, 61].

Wild lettuces have almost the same nature. But whoever eats, raw or cooked, those useless lettuces called *vukrut* would become insane—that is, *unsinnig*—and empty in the marrow. For they are neither hot nor cold, [Col. 1165C] but are merely an unprofitable wind which dries up the fruits of the earth—that is, *derret*—and bears no fruit. Those lettuces grow from the foam of the earth’s sweat and are therefore useless.

[But if an ass has pain in its belly, cut wild lettuce into bran moderately warmed in water, mix it in, and do this often; it will be cured. If anyone has scrofulous swellings, before they burst let him take the larger lettuce, which is white outside and green within; break off a piece beside it according to the breadth of the swellings, throw away the rest, spread honey on the part retained, and lay it on the swellings for three days and nights. When it dries up, apply another in the same way; they will begin to diminish.]

## CHAPTER XCII.—ON WILDE LATICH

[II, 63].

[Col. 1165D]

Wild lettuce [wild lettuces, edition] is cold and extinguishes sexual desire in a person. A man who is excessive in the loins should cook wild lettuce in water, bathe himself in that water in a dry bath, and put the same cooked, hot wild lettuce around his loins in the bath. Do this often and it will extinguish his sexual desire without harming his bodily health.

If a woman has a swollen womb through sexual desire, so that she is incontinent, she too should make a dry bath with wild lettuce. While sitting in the bath, she should pour the water in which it was cooked over heated stones [Col. 1166A] and lay the same cooked, hot lettuce over her navel. Do this often, and it will drive sexual desire from her, while not diminishing her bodily health.

Also, whether man or woman, one who is incontinent in sexual desire should dry wild lettuce in the sun, reduce it to powder in the hand, drink this powder often in warm wine, and it will extinguish sexual desire without harm to the body.

## CHAPTER XCIII.—ON THE HERB SENFF

[Note: [Col. 1166D] Field mustard] [II, 64].

*Senff* [mustard, edition], the herb which grows in fields and vineyards and is eaten, is hot, but of unstable heat; it is also moist and in that moisture has an unworthy coldness [torpor, edition], because it grows from varying whirlwinds and diverse weather. It is not [Col. 1166B] useful for eating—although poor people eat this herb, it is nevertheless useless, addition of the edition—because it is poisonous, produces unhealthy humours in a person, and burdens the stomach. Yet it can be digested quickly.

It does not harm healthy and lean persons, but harms the sick and the fat: it burdens the sick in the stomach, while in the fat it produces *demphet* [causes difficult breathing, edition].

## CHAPTER XCIV.—ON MUSTARD

[Note: [Col. 1166D] White and black mustard] [II, 65].

Mustard is of a very hot and somewhat dry nature. It grows in moderate heat and cold—that is, temperate weather—and has the powers of trees or herbs, since it grows from the wind which brings forth fruit and also from the greenness of the earth; thus it has some juice.

Its herb is harmful to eat, [Col. 1166C] because its power is weak and unstable: it would tear up internally a person who ate it. But its seed gives *gesmach* [flavour] to other foods. It is not good for a sick, weak, and cold stomach, because it burdens rather than purges it; but a strong stomach overcomes it.

Eaten, it clears the eyes, but produces vapour in the brain and a certain sharpness in the head, so that it draws some moisture from the head. Yet it introduces a greater and more harmful evil into the head. It does not promote sound and proper digestion, but causes digestion with pain and produces something like vapour in a person.

Nevertheless, everyone should eat it moderately, because it harms the sick, who [Col. 1166D] do not have the strength to avoid it; but it cannot harm the healthy very much, because their strength restores them. One who likes to eat mustard should warm wine, pour it over the mustard, and work it about—*zutribe*—when he is about to eat it, and then eat it. Eaten in this way, it does not harm sick persons, because its harmfulness is removed by the heat of the wine. If he has no wine, let him pour cold vinegar over it; eaten thus it does not harm. [Note: [Col. 1166D] What follows is omitted in the edition.] Unless it is tempered with wine or vinegar in this way, it is not good for a person to eat; for it does not benefit the sick, even if it harms the healthy.

## CHAPTER XCV.—ON ELECAMPANE

[Note: [Col. 1167D] *Inula Helenium*] [II, 67].

[Col. 1167A]

Elecampane [*Enula*, edition] is of a hot and dry nature and possesses useful powers. Throughout the year, whether dry or green, it should be put into pure wine. But after it has shrunk in the wine, its powers fail; then it should be thrown away and fresh elecampane put in.

One who has pain in the lungs should drink it thus daily in moderation before and after food. It removes poison—that is, *eyther*—from his lungs, checks migraine, and clears the eyes. But if anyone drank it frequently in this way, it would harm him by its strength.

If you have no wine in which to put it, make a pure drink of honey and water, *honigwurtz* [a drink, edition], put in elecampane, and drink it as stated above. Also take figs [*vigim*, “fruit of the fig,” edition] and twice as much elecampane, add galangal, [Col. 1167B] make from these a *luterdrang* [pure drink, edition], and drink it if you have pain in the lungs and no other ailments; it is good for an ailment of the lungs. But if, together with the lung ailment, you have other ailments, do not drink it in this way, for it would be too strong for you to drink and would harm you.

## CHAPTER XCVI.—ON POPPY

[Note: [Col. 1167D] Opium poppy.]

Poppy is cold and moderately moist. Its grains, eaten, bring sleep and prevent itching; they check proliferating lice and nits, and may be eaten in water, *gerrellet* [uncertain preparation]. Yet raw they are better and more useful for eating than cooked. The oil pressed from them neither nourishes nor restores a person, nor fully brings either health or illness; this oil is cold, but the grains [Col. 1167C] are hot.

## CHAPTER XCVII.—ON BABELA

[II, 107].

*Babela* [mallow, edition] has moderate coldness in it, like dew, though it is more cold. But no one should eat it raw, because raw it would be like a poison: it is slimy (*slimecht*) and has thick, poisonous humours, which it produces in a person.

For those with a weak stomach, it is good when eaten cooked and new—that is, when it has only just begun to grow—prepared as a mash with fat added, and eaten; it somewhat promotes digestion. A person weak in the stomach should eat it for this necessity, but moderately, lest he be harmed by it. A healthy person, however, should wholly avoid it.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] In the edition this chapter reads as follows: “Mallow has moderate coldness in it, like dew and like the air when it is temperate in the morning. If melancholy drawn by various fevers makes a person’s brain ache, let him crush mallow and twice as much sage in a mortar, sprinkle them with a little olive oil, apply this from his forehead over the crown of his head to the nape, and bind it with a cloth. Do this for three days, and during these three days, about nightfall, renew it with either olive oil or vinegar; continue thus until he improves.

“To make the sight of the eyes clear, let a person seek dew upon mallow, or upon bindweed, or upon the leaves of pear, oak, or beech [Col. 1168D] (for these are pleasant); with the dew found at night or in the morning, when the night is clear, pure, and pleasant, anoint the eyelids and the surrounding parts of the eyes, and afterward sleep a little.

“But no one should eat mallow raw, because it would be like a poison to him, since it is livid. For one with a weak stomach, however, it is good when it has just begun to grow, cooked with fat added, because it somewhat promotes digestion. Let the sick person eat mallow for this need, but moderately; a healthy person should wholly avoid it.”]

## CHAPTER XCVIII.—ON CLETTA

[Note: [Col. 1168D] Greater burdock] [II, 109].

The herb called *Cletta* [burdock, edition] has a somewhat [Col. 1168A] contrary heat, grows from the juice and sweat of the earth, and is both useful and useless. Its root is of no use whatever; its leaves, whether raw or cooked, are dangerous for a person to eat, except for one in whose body a stone is forming. Such a person should cook the leaves of this herb in excellent wine, strain the wine through a cloth, and drink it warm both after meals and fasting; by its strength the stone in him is broken up.

Also reduce its flowers to powder, and likewise a shell, with the tortoise removed; mix these powders so that there is more shell-powder. If anyone has scurf (*grint*) on the head, sprinkle this powder on those ulcers for nine or fifteen days, and on the fourth and fifth days wash his head with lye made from beech—that is, [Col. 1168B] *buchen*—and he will be healed.

## CHAPTER XCIX.—ON THISTLE

[Note: [Col. 1168D] Blessed thistle and *Eryngium campestre*] [II, 108].

Thistle, both smooth and *stechelechter* [thistle both smooth and bristly, edition], has swift heat which quickly grows numb, because it sweats from the earth. This sweat of the earth, from which the herb grows, is *stechelecht* and produces twisted herbs. [Note: [Col. 1168D] The remainder of this chapter is lacking in the edition.]

Just as sweat comes from a person when he is distressed, so the sweat of the earth sends forth twisted herbs which tear people. One thistle is indeed smooth—that is, *ane stechel*, “without prickles”—and it too is useless to a person when eaten raw. For if anyone ate it raw, it would thin his blood, produce wasting in him, and cause his humours to *zuflossen* [flow together or run together], just as the strength is taken from good wine when water is poured into it. [Col. 1168C] Consequently, a person would become empty of understanding and deprived of blood and humours.

But if that thistle is cooked and eaten cooked, it neither greatly harms nor benefits healthy people, because it adds no richness to the blood, although it takes away hunger. It harms sick people both cooked and raw, because it arouses ailments in them.

But *vehedistel* has coldness in it and is very useful. Whoever suffers from *stechen*—a stabbing pain—in the heart, another location, or any limb should take *vehedistel*, somewhat less *orechten salben* [uncertain plant-name], reduce them to juice in a little water, and drink it immediately at the hour when he is afflicted by *stechen*; he will improve.

## CHAPTER C.—ON NETTLE

[Note: [Col. 1168D] Stinging and burning nettle] [II, 111].

[Col. 1168D] Nettle is very hot in its kind. It is in no way good to eat raw because of its roughness. But when it first emerges from the earth [addition of the edition, Col. 1169A], it is useful cooked as food for people, because it cleanses the stomach and removes mucus (*slim*) from it. Every kind of nettle does this.

[If worms have developed in someone from harmful and bad humours which are poisonous in a person, let him take equal quantities of the juice of burning nettle and the juice of *blandonia*, together with as much of walnut leaves or the bark of the same tree as of those two substances; add a little vinegar and much honey. Boil it in a new pot, remove the froth from the top, and, after it has boiled, take it off the fire. For fifteen days let him drink this moderately while fasting, but sufficiently after food; the worms in him will die.

A person who is involuntarily forgetful should crush burning nettle to juice, add a little olive oil, and, [Col. 1169B] when going to sleep, thoroughly anoint his chest and temples with it. Do this often, and his forgetfulness will lessen.

If the heat of rheum runs from a horse’s nostrils so that it coughs from it, cook burning nettle and a larger quantity of lovage in water. With the bridle put on, allow this warm steam to pass into its nostrils and mouth, and it will be healed. But if a horse has pain in its belly, mix burning nettle and a larger quantity of lovage often into its fodder, so that it eats them together, and it will be healed. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER CI.—ON PLANTAIN

[Note: [Col. 1169C] Greater, hoary, and ribwort plantain] [II, 112].

Wegerich [plantain, ed.] is hot and dry. Take therefore plantain, press out its juice, strain it through a cloth, mix it with either wine or honey, and give it to drink to one afflicted by gout; and the gout will cease. [Col. 1169C] Moreover, let one who has glands in his body roast its root over the fire and lay it, while hot, upon the glands—that is, *druge*—and bind a cloth over it; and he will be better. But do not lay it upon *orfime* [“but let him not apply too much,” ed.], for he would be harmed thereby. And one afflicted by *stechen* should boil its leaves in water and apply that expressed water, hot, to the painful place; and the *stechen* will cease. And if a spider or any other worm touches or stings a person, immediately anoint the puncture with plantain juice, and he will be better. And if likewise a man or woman has eaten or drunk a love-charm (*zauber*; *maleficium*, ed.), let the juice of *wegerich* be given to drink, either without water or with water; afterwards let the person take some strong draught and be purged internally, and afterwards will be better.
