[But if a bone is accidentally broken in some part of a person, cut up plantain roots in honey and eat them daily while fasting; also eat the fresh leaves of mallow. Boil in a new pot, with water, five times as much of plantain leaves or roots, moderately; and apply them hot and frequently to the painful place. The broken bone will be healed. Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CII.—ON MENNA [II, 113].

*Menna* is hot and dry, and its leaf, laid upon a broken ulcer, draws out poison and heals. But boiled in *muse* and eaten thus, it heals painful and ulcerated internal organs.

## CHAPTER CIII.—ON THE VIOLET [Note: [Col. 1169D] *Viola odorata*.] [II, 113].

The violet stands between hot and cold. Yet it is [Col. 1170B] cold and grows from the air—namely, when, after winter, the air first begins to grow warm. It is effective against dimness of the eyes. Take therefore good oil and make it boil, either in the sun or over a fire, in a new pot; and when it boils, put violets into it so that it may be thickened by them. Then put it into a glass vessel and preserve it. At night anoint around your eyelids and eyes with that oil, taking care that it does not touch the insides of the eyes; and it will drive away dimness of the eyes.

And if anyone is oppressed in mind through melancholy, with distress, and thus injures the lung, let him boil violets in pure wine, strain them through a cloth, add galangal and as much licorice as he wishes to this wine, make a *luterdranck*, and drink it. It restrains melancholy, makes him cheerful, and heals his lung. [Col. 1170C]

[Note: [Col. 1169D] In the edition this chapter reads as follows: “The violet is between hot and moist, but is especially of a temperate quality; and it grows from the sweetness and mildness of the air. Let a person make olive oil boil in the sun or over a fire in a new pot, and while it boils put violets into it, so that it may be thickened by them; then put it into a glass vessel and keep it. At night let him anoint the eyes and eyelids all around with it, taking care that it does not touch the insides of the eyes, and it will drive away their dimness.

“And a person whose eyes are inflamed, dim, and painful should take violet juice, twice as much rose juice, and fennel juice amounting to a third part of the rose juice; add a little wine, and, when going to sleep, anoint this eye-salve around the eyes, taking care not to touch the insides of the eyes.

“Moreover, a person who has heaviness in the head or kidneys, or is afflicted anywhere by paralysis, should press out violet juice through a cloth; add sufficient goat fat and old lard equal to half the amount of the fat; melt these together in a pan [Col. 1170C–D], and make an ointment. Let him anoint his head and other painful places with it, and he will be better.

“And if anyone has pain in the head, or whose flesh is being eaten by cancer, or has any ulcers in his body, let him take violet juice, olive oil amounting to a third part of this juice, and goat fat equal to the quantity of violet juice. Let him make these boil together in a new pot and prepare an ointment. One who has pain in the head should anoint the forehead crosswise with this ointment, and he will be better. Wherever cancer or other worms are eating a person, let him anoint it from above, and they will die when they taste it.

“And one who suffers from tertian fevers should take violet, plantain amounting to a third of it, and *pefferkraut* twice as much as the plantain, and often eat these herbs with vinegar or roasted salt. And if anyone,” etc.]

## CHAPTER CIV.—ON MELDA [Note: [Col. 1170D] *Atriplex hortensis*.] [II, 115].

*Melda* [orache, ed.] is colder than hot, though somewhat temperate; eaten, it produces good digestion. If poisonous glands—that is, *orfimae*—begin to grow in anyone, let him often prepare and eat *muse* with *melda*, with less *prieselauch* than *melda*, and less hyssop than *prieslauch*; and the *orfimae* will dry up. Let *melda* also be boiled in water, and let its expressed water be applied hot to the same *orfimae*; and that person will be better.

[Note: [Col. 1170D] “But—will be better” ends in the edition.]

## CHAPTER CV.—ON GUNDEREBE [Note: [Col. 1171C] *Glechoma hederaceum*.—Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1171A]

*Gunderebe* is more hot than cold, and dry; it possesses certain medicinal qualities, because its greenness is beneficial. Thus, a person who languishes and whose reason fails should bathe in heated water and often eat it cooked in *muse* or in *suffen*, or with meat or with *cucheln*; it will help him. And if anyone frequently washes his head with it in lye, he drives many infirmities from his head and prevents sickness.

But for one whose head is afflicted by evil humours like *doum*, so that even his ears ring (*diczent*), let *gunderebe* be made to boil in hot water and let the expressed water, hot, be laid all around his head. It lessens the *doum* in his head and opens his hearing. And one who suffers in the chest and around the chest, as though he had ulcers within, should apply it, boiled in a bath and hot, around his chest; and he will be better. [Col. 1171B]

## CHAPTER CVI.—ON STAGWURTZ [Note: [Col. 1171C] *Artemisia Abrotanum*.] [II, 117].

*Stagwurtz* [southernwood, ed.] is hot and dry. Its odor, even if someone anoints himself with it and thus gives off its scent, arouses melancholy and anger in a person and afflicts his head. But where *grint* begins to form on a person’s head, pour its juice into those ulcers, and it will be cured. Where *buln* rise up on a person’s body, or where one of his limbs contracts, pound *stagwurtz* and apply it around the place; also anoint the place with its juice, and he will be better.

[But when scabies and contraction of the limbs persist, remove southernwood at once [Col. 1171C], because it then harms more than it benefits. Addition, ed.]

And if anyone is afflicted by gout in his limbs, let him take plenty of *stagwurtz*, plenty of old lard, and a little tree-oil; sweat these together in a frying pan, then put them hot upon the limb in which the gout rages, bind them on with a cloth, and do this often. The gout there will cease.

[Note: [Col. 1171C] “And if anyone—will cease” omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER CVII.—ON BIBOZ [Note: [Col. 1171C] *Artemisia vulgaris*.] [II, 71].

*Biboz* [mugwort, ed.] is very hot, and its juice [Col. 1172A] is very useful. If it is boiled and eaten in *muse*, it heals weak internal organs and warms a cold stomach. If someone has eaten or drunk something from which he suffers, let him cook and eat *biboz* with meat, with fat, in *muse*, or in some other preparation and seasoning; it removes and drives away the putrefaction which he has acquired through the earlier foods or drinks.

[But if *troffo* and evil humours, gathered in some place of the human body, flow out through broken skin without a poisonous ulcer, let that person take mugwort and press it, add honey to the juice so that the mugwort juice exceeds the honey, and anoint the painful place. Then immediately smear over it egg-white clarified from the white of an egg, and bind a cloth over it. Do this until [Col. 1172B] it is healed. Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CVIII.—ON CLE [Note: [Col. 1171C] *Trifolium pratense*.] [II, 118].

*Cle* [*Cithysus*, ed.] is both hot and cold, and is also dry; it is useful as pasture for livestock. But it has little medicinal value, except against dimness of the eyes. Put its flowers into tree-oil and rub them in it without boiling; immediately anoint around the dim eyes and eyelids. These flowers should be put into the tree-oil only at the hour when the eyes are to be anointed, and, once the eyes have been anointed, should immediately be thrown away, because they lack the power to lie and keep in oil for a long time. If this is done often in this manner, it will drive away dimness of the eyes.

## CHAPTER CIX.—ON WERMUDA [Note: [Col. 1171D] *Artemisia Absinthium*.] [II, 119].

*Wermuda* [wormwood, ed.] is very hot and [Col. 1172C] very powerful, and is the chief mistress for all ailments. Pour a sufficient quantity of its juice into hot wine, and, when a person’s head pains him, wet his whole head with it, as far as the eyes, ears, and neck. Do this at night, when you go to sleep; cover his whole head with a woolen cap until morning, and it relieves the pain of the swollen head. It also drives away the pain which stirs in the head from gout, and internal headache.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] From this point to the end of the chapter the edition does not agree, but continues as follows: “For if *huorlen* enter a person’s ears, or other worms grow in them, let him take wormwood, rue equal to half its quantity, and hyssop equal to half the quantity of rue. Boil these herbs in water; once they are cooked, bend his head and permit the vapor issuing from these hot herbs to enter, through a reed, the ear that does not hurt, so that the same vapor may reach the other ear, in which the worms are, and they may flee.

“But first let him anoint the ear in which the worms are with a little honey and place a little old lard in it as well, so that, when they perceive the aforesaid vapor, they may turn toward the sweetness of these things. Also set fire to an ear of barley, with or without grains, so that its smoke may pass through a reed [Col. 1172C] into the ear, as stated above. Let the person do this often during the day, and he will be freed—unless God does not will to free him.

“If the worms come out of the ear, make olive oil boil over the fire in a new vessel, and allow its vapor to pass into the ear in which the worms were, so that the ulcerated ear may be anointed. Then, after the same oil has cooled, anoint the inside circumference of that ear with it; and if a little enters the ear, it will not harm. Also boil *mettra* in water; allow the vapor to enter the sound ear, and press that same ear closed with the hand so that the vapor cannot escape. Do this often, and it will be healed.

“A person whose teeth ache from putrid blood and a discharge from the brain should boil wormwood and vervain in equal weights in good wine in a new pot; strain this wine through a cloth and drink it with a little sugar added. When going to sleep, apply the same herbs hot around his jaw and bind a cloth over them. Do this until he is healed.

“Pour wormwood juice into olive oil, so that the oil exceeds the juice twofold; warm it in a glass vessel in the sun, and preserve it thus for a year. Whenever a person has pain around the chest and coughs as a result, let him anoint himself with it; if he has pain in the side [Col. 1173D], let him anoint it there. This anointing heals him within and without.

“Pound wormwood in a mortar to make juice, and add deer fat to deer marrow, so that there is twice as much juice as fat, and twice as much fat as deer marrow. Prepare an ointment from this. One suffering from the most severe paralysis, which threatens to break his limbs, should anoint himself with it by the fire where he hurts, and will be healed.

“When wormwood is fresh, let a person press out the juice, boil wine with honey a little [Col. 1174D], and pour that juice into the wine, so that the juice exceeds the wine and honey in taste. From May until October, not every day, but every third day while fasting, let him drink it cold. It restrains pain in the kidneys and melancholy, clears the eyes, strengthens the heart, does not allow the lung to become infirm, warms the stomach, purges the internal organs, and produces good digestion.”]

Pour some of its juice into tree-oil, so that the oil exceeds that juice twofold; warm it in a glass vessel in the sun, and preserve it thus for a year. Whenever a person has pain in the chest and around the chest, so that he coughs as a result, anoint his chest with it. One who has pain in the side should anoint it there; it heals him inside and outside.

Pound *wermuda* in a mortar to make juice, add *unslecht*, deer fat, and deer marrow, so that there is twice as much wormwood juice as fat and twice as much fat as deer marrow; make an ointment. A person afflicted with the severest gout, such that his limbs threaten to break, should immediately anoint the painful place with it by the fire, and he will be healed.

When *wermunda* is fresh, pound it and press out its juice through a cloth. Then boil wine with honey a little and pour this juice into that wine, so that the juice exceeds the wine and honey in flavor. From May until October, every third day—namely, while fasting—drink it; it restrains kidney pain (*lauksucht*) and melancholy in you, clears your eyes, strengthens the heart, does not permit the lung to become infirm, warms the stomach, purges the internal organs, and produces good digestion. [Col. 1173A–B]

## CHAPTER CX.—ON BILSA [Note: [Col. 1174D] *Hyoscyamus niger*.] [II, 120].

*Bilsa* is cold, soft, and without strength; if anyone ate it, or oil made from its seeds, it would produce deadly poison in him. But where *surm* are on a person, so that they ulcerate his flesh, grind it with juice upon that place, and the *suren* [Col. 1173C] will die. Oil made from its seed is not very useful; but where excessive heat arises in some part of a person’s limbs, anoint that place with this oil, and it cools it without any other medicine. The virtue of this oil is not useful for other ailments.

[To make a drunk person recover himself, put henbane in cold water and wet his forehead, temples, and throat; he will be better. Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CXI.—ON REYNFAN [Note: [Col. 1174D] *Tanacetum vulgare*.] [II, 70].

*Reynfan* [tansy, ed.] is hot and a little moist, and is effective against all excessive and flowing humours. One who has *nasenboz* [catarrh, ed.] and coughs because of it should eat *reynfan*, in *suffen* [a little soup, ed.], in *cuchen* [little cakes, ed.], with meat, or in any preparation whatsoever. It restrains the humours so that they do not increase in him, and thus they fail.

One who has a harsh cough should make *suffen* with semolina flour and *reynfan*, eat it often, and thus the dryness and internal ulcers of his cough are loosened, so that he expels the foul matter by spitting and will be better. [Col. 1173D–1174A]

One who has heaviness and weight in the stomach because of various bad foods should take broth [*jus*, ed.] cooked without vegetables or other herbs, put *reynfan* into it, boil it again, and eat it cooked often. It softens his stomach, makes it light, and produces pleasant digestion. Whoever cannot pass urine because he is constricted by a stone [“provided that . . . he is not constricted,” ed.], should pound *reynfan*, strain its juice through a cloth, add a little wine, and drink it often; he will be freed from the urinary constriction and pass urine.

[A woman who suffers from obstructed menses and pain as a result should take tansy and febrifuge in equal weights, and *vullena* in a quantity somewhat greater than either of those; boil them in an open, flowing stream tempered by both sun and air. She should then take bricks, put them in the fire, and make a steam-bath with the aforesaid water and herbs. When she has entered this bath, let her put the hot herbs upon a stool and sit above them. If they become cold again, let her warm them again in the aforesaid water. Let her do this for as long as she sits in that bath, so that through the humours of these herbs her skin and flesh may be softened externally and her womb internally, and so that her closed veins may be opened.

“Then let her take *rifelbire*, yarrow amounting to a third part of it, rue amounting nearly to a third part of the yarrow [Col. 1174C], an amount of birthwort (*aristologia longa*) equal to the *rifelbire* and yarrow together, and a large quantity of dittany. Pound these in a mortar and boil them with good pure wine in a pot; pour them, cooked with that wine, into a little bag. Pound together as many cloves as she can obtain and less white pepper than cloves; add plenty of new, fresh honey free of impurity; make it boil in the best wine; pour it into the little bag with the aforesaid herbs; and prepare a *claretum* from these things. Each day, both fasting and after eating, let her drink it—but not while in the aforesaid bath, because the bath constricts a person somewhat—and continue until she is well.

“Meanwhile, while she suffers the aforesaid constriction of blood [Col. 1174D], let her avoid beef and other coarse, heavy foods, eat mild foods, and drink wine. If she drinks water in the meantime, let her drink well-water and avoid water from a leaping or flowing spring, since such waters are somewhat harsher.” Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CXII.—ON DOST [Note: [Col. 1175D] *Origanum vulgare*.] [II, 111].

[Col. 1175A]

*Dost* [oregano, ed.] is hot and dry, though neither quality is strongly active in it. If a person ate or drank it, or in any way took it into his body, it would bring him leprosy and swell his lung; it makes his liver fail—that is, *swinden*.

But one who has red leprosy, whether recent or longstanding, should take the juice of *dost*, a little less *adron* juice, more henbane oil than the quantities of those two, and a little wine. Let him mix these together and, in a steam-bath when he is about to leave, anoint himself with this liquid preparation. After he comes out of the bath, he sweats heavily (*swiczet*); therefore immediately and often anoint him over it with goat fat melted in a pan over the fire, and put him to bed until he dries out.

After he has dried, take *dost* again and pound it; add bran to the bark, mix these in a hot pan, and after the anointing has dried apply it hot to the ulcers of leprosy and bind it over with a bandage. Leave it thus for some hours, until it becomes warm from his body. If he does this often, he will undoubtedly be healed, unless it is his death.

[Or unless the Lord does not will him to be healed. And one suffering from a quotidian fever should pulverize oregano, a little camphor, and more *dornella* than both those together; put this powder into hot wine at the very onset of the fever, drink it, go to bed, and will be healed. Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CXIII.—ON GARWA [Note: [Col. 1175D] *Achillea Millefolium*.] [II, 122].

[Col. 1175C]

*Garwa* [yarrow, ed.] is somewhat hot and dry, and has discriminating and subtle powers for wounds.

[Note: [Col. 1175D] Edition: “Yarrow is hot and dry. A person whose eyes are dim through the flow of tears should pound yarrow moderately, apply it to the eyes at night, taking care not to touch the insides of the eyes, and leave it there nearly until midnight [Col. 1176D]; then remove it. Having done this, immediately moisten the eyelashes lightly all around with the best and purest wine, and the eyes are healed. Yarrow also has discriminating,” etc.]

For if a person is wounded by a blow, after the wound has been washed with wine, let *garwa* be boiled moderately in water and the water pressed out moderately; hot, let it be lightly bound over the cloth lying on the wound. It removes from the wound putrefaction and *swern*, that is, ulceration, and heals the wound. Do this often, as long as necessary. But after the wound begins somewhat to contract and heal, discard the cloth and apply *garwa* to the wound without it; it will be healed more soundly and completely.

One who has received a wound within the body, so that he has been internally broken by a spear [“by accident,” ed.] or constricted, should pulverize this *garwa* and take the powder in hot water. When he is better, let him then take the same powder in hot wine until he is healed. [Col. 1175D]

[And one whom tertian fever afflicts should boil yarrow and twice as much polypody in sweet, good wine; strain it through a cloth and drink this wine at the onset of the fever. Let him drink these herbs in wine for three days; if necessary, renew them with like fresh herbs, and it will mitigate this fever, and he will be healed. Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CXIV.—ON AGRIMONY [Note: [Col. 1176D] *Agrimonia Eupatoria*.] [II, 123].

[Col. 1176A]

Agrimony is hot. In a person whose knowledge and senses have been emptied, cut the hair of his head, because the hair causes him the shuddering and shaking of trembling. Boil agrimony in water and wash his head with that hot water. Bind this same herb, hot, upon his heart with a cloth, when he first feels the failure of his mind; then lay it hot upon his forehead and temples. It clears his knowledge and senses and removes madness from him.

But one who coughs up and expels *livor* and much phlegm from weak internal organs also has a cold stomach. Let him drink agrimony steeped in wine continually, both after eating and while fasting; it lessens and clears the *livor* of expectoration and warms the stomach.

[Col. 1176B] [Likewise, for a person to be purged of saliva, expectoration, and nasal discharge, let him take agrimony juice and twice as much fennel juice; add *storkenschnabel* juice in the quantity of an obol. Then take as much galangal as all these three together, storax weighing six coins, and polypody to the weight of two coins. Pulverize these, compress the powder with the aforesaid juice, and make from it pills the size of beans. Afterwards take greater celandine juice in a quantity weighing a fourth part of a coin; dip the pills in it and set them in the sun to dry. If he does not have the sun’s heat, put them in a gentle wind and mild air, so that they dry gently. [Col. 1176C]

“When the person wishes to take these pills, bind his stomach and belly with lambskins or other skins, so that he may grow warm, because their warmth is healthful. Let him not go too near the fire, but use the warmth of clothing; let him take them before sunrise, because the dawn at that time is mild and gentle. Let him take either five or nine pills, dip each one separately a little in *molle*, swallow it, and, after taking them, walk a little in a shady place and not in the sun’s heat until he feels the purge. At about midday, after he feels the purge within himself—or, if his hardened stomach cannot yet produce it—let him first sip a little soup of semolina flour, so that the internal organs may be healed by the mildness of the soup [Col. 1176D], or so that the hardened stomach may thereby be softened.

“If a person becomes leprous through lust or incontinence, boil agrimony, hyssop amounting to a third of it, and twice as much *aseri* as both those together in a cauldron. Make a bath of these and mix into it as much menstrual blood as can be obtained; let him put himself in the bath. Also take goose fat, twice as much hen fat, and a little chicken dung, make an ointment from them, and, after he comes out of the aforesaid bath [Col. 1177A], anoint himself with the same ointment and return to bed. Do this often until he is healed.” Addition, ed.]

Pound agrimony in a mortar and lay it, thus crushed, upon the eyes at night of one whose eyes are dim; bind a cloth over it, taking care that it does not enter the eyes. It relieves dimness of the eyes and clears them.

## CHAPTER CXV.—ON DITTANY [Note: [Col. 1177D] *Dictamnus albus*.] [II, 124].

Dittany is hot and dry, and has in itself the powers of fire and of stone; for as a stone is hard in its powers and possesses heat in the fire that proceeds from it, so dittany is powerful against the ailments over which it prevails. For a stone—that is, *steyn*—grows in a person from an oily nature. When it begins to grow, let him pulverize dittany [Col. 1177B] and often eat this powder with wheaten bread; it prevents the *steyn* from growing. A person in whom the *steyn* has grown should put dittany powder into vinegar mixed with honey and drink it often while fasting; the *steyn* in him will break.

One who has pain in the heart should eat powder made from dittany, and the pain of the heart will cease.

[Also, if anyone begins to limp in some part of his limbs, boil dittany thoroughly in water, discard what is in the middle like a heart, and, while it boils, add twice as much *husmuosz* and twice as much stinging nettle as *huszmoszes*. Mix these together. When they are cooked, press out a little of the water and apply it hot to the joint of that limb and to the veins in which lameness begins. Do this often [Col. 1177C], and he will be cured. Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CXVI.—ON METRA [II, 125].

*Metra* [febrifuge, ed.] is hot and has a pleasant juice; for painful internal organs it is like a soothing ointment. One who has pain in the internal organs should cook *metra* with water and fat or oil, add semolina flour, prepare *suffen* thus, and eat it; it heals the internal organs. When women menstruate, let them drink and eat the same *suffen*, as stated above; it gently and mildly brings about the purging of *livores* and foul internal matter, and brings forth the menses.

[A person suffering from *stechedim* should mix febrifuge juice and cow’s butter, anoint himself where he hurts, and will be healed. Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CXVII.—ON MUSORE [Note: [Col. 1177D] *Hierarium Pilosella*.] [II, 126].

[Col. 1177D]

*Musore* [mouse-ear hawkweed, ed.] is cold. Eaten, it strengthens the heart and lessens evil humours gathered together in one place in a person. But one who eats it should not eat it alone or plain, because it is too harsh; add a little dittany, galangal, or *zitwar*, and eat it as stated above.

[“And it disperses cold humours.” Addition, ed.]

## CHAPTER CXVIII.—ON SWERTULA [Note: [Col. 1178D] *Gladiolus communis*.] [I, 127].

*Swertula* [gladiolus, ed.] is hot and dry; all its power is in its root, and its greenness rises into the leaves. In May take the juice of these leaves, melt lard in a pan, add this juice, and prepare an ointment so that it appears green. Anoint frequently with it one who has slight scabies, and he will be cured.

One who has facial skin hard as bark, or whose face is *bulecht*, or has a bad complexion, should press out the juice of the same leaves, pour it into a vessel with water from great rivers, as has already been said, and warm them together moderately. Let him wash his face with this water and juice, moderately warmed, and do this often; it gives the face soft skin and a good, handsome color.

Boil the root and leaves of *swerteln* in water. With the expressed water, hot, surround the head of a madman, one who is *hirnwudig* [“brain-mad”], binding a cloth over it, so that he sleeps thus; do this often. Then cut the root of the same *swertela* internally into round pieces, season them with honey, and give them frequently to that madman—that is, the *hirnwutigen*—to eat; he will be cured. [Col. 1178B]

Pound its root with good wine in a mortar, warm this wine after straining it through a cloth, and give it hot to drink to one who has a *steyn*. One who is constricted by difficulty of urination will be relieved: the stone in him softens, and the urinary passages that were constricted are opened.

Against recent leprosy, pound the root of the same *swerteln* and put it in ass’s milk so that they curdle together. Immediately pour pork fat into a pan, add the pounded root with the ass’s milk to the fat in the pan, and cook them vigorously while mixing together. When this is done, strain it through a cloth and collect the liquid in a vessel, so that you have an ointment from it. Then make lye from alder ashes. One beginning to be leprous—namely, while the leprosy is still recent—should first wash the part of his body where he feels the leprosy with this lye; then anoint himself there with the aforesaid ointment. Do this often, and he will be healed. [Col. 1178C]

## CHAPTER CXIX.—ON MERRICH [II, 59].

*Merrich* [radish, ed.] is hot [“cold,” ed.]. When all herbs grow green in March, *merrich* likewise becomes tender, but only for a short time; then, eaten, it is good for healthy and robust persons, because it strengthens in them the greenness of good humours. But once it has become hard and strong in its rind, it is dangerous to eat, because it has no greenness; it then makes a person dry, as though he were eating wood. Therefore one should not eat it, but may suck it if it has juice and spit out the rest.

A lean and dry person who wishes to eat *Merredich* should eat only a little, so that he may gain some strength from it; if he eats much of it, he will suffer from it, because it has only slight powers in itself.

[Note: [Col. 1178D] “But a lean person—itself” omitted in the edition.]

When *merrich* is green, dry it in the sun and add to it an equal weight of galangal powder. One who has pain in the heart should eat this powder with bread, both after eating and while fasting, and will be better. One who has pain in the lung should drink the same powder, either in hot wine or hot water, both fasting and after eating, and will be healed. [Col. 1179A]

## CHAPTER CXX.—ON HATICH [Note: [Col. 1179D] *Sambucus Ebulus*.] [II, 128].

*Hatich* [dwarf elder, ed.] is cold and moist, and contrary to human nature, such that if a person ate it, it would be dangerous to him. But if a person’s head drips like a torrent of water from evil humours, apply it cold around his head, and he will be better. If anyone has *grint* [scabby nails, ed.] on his fingers or feet, bind *bere atich* over those nails often, so that they are either cleansed or fall off; then other, handsome nails will grow again.

## CHAPTER CXXI.—ON NACHTSCHADE [Note: [Col. 1179D] *Solanum nigrum*.] [II, 129].

[Col. 1179B]

*Nachtschade* [nightshade, ed.] is hot and dry. One who has pain in the heart, or is faint at heart (*unmechtigz*), should boil *nachtschade* moderately in water and lay it, with its expressed water and hot, upon his heart; he will improve. One who has toothache should warm it in water, and, when going to sleep at night, apply it hot to the cheek and jaw where the pain is; the pain will cease. When the feet swell, apply it to the feet, moderately warmed in water, and they will cease to swell. One who has pain in the marrow of the legs should boil *nachtschaden* in water, apply it warm around the legs, bind it round with a cloth, and will be better.

## CHAPTER CXXII.—ON RINGULA [Note: [Col. 1179D] *Calendula officinalis*.] [II, 130].

[Col. 1179C] *Ringula* [*Ringella*, ed.] is cold and moist, possesses strong greenness, and is effective against poison. One who has eaten poison, or to whom poison has been administered (*virgeben*), should boil *ringula* in water and lay it hot upon his stomach with the expressed water; it softens the poison and it is expectorated by him. That person should immediately warm good wine, add plenty of *ringula*, warm the same wine again with it, and drink the wine lukewarm because he has taken poison. He will expel the poison either through his nose by foaming, or cast it out from himself as foam—that is, *schum*.

If oxen or sheep have eaten something harmful, from which they suddenly swell—that is, *erblewent*—pound *ringula*, press out its juice, and pour the juice, with a little water, into their mouths so that they taste it; they will be cured. If an ox or sheep coughs, pour *ringula* juice without water into its nostrils; immediately they will cough up harmful humours and improve. [Col. 1179D]

A person whose head is scaly (*vellecht*) should cut off the soft part of bacon, cut off also the rind (*swarten*) of that bacon, discard it, take the hard part in the bacon next to the same rind, pound it with *ringula* in a mortar [Col. 1180A], and often anoint his head with it. The scales (*vellen*) will fall off, and his head will be handsome.

One who has *grint* on his head should take the flowers and leaves of *ringeln*, press out their juice, make dough (*deyck*) from this juice, a little water, and semolina flour or rye flour, and leave all his head covered with it, bound by a cloth and cap, until it grows warm and the dough splits—that is, *schrinde*. Then remove it, prepare dough again in the same manner, and lay it around his head. Do this for nine days; every time he removes the dough from his head, let him have lye prepared from *ringeln* juice and wash his head with it each time. He will be healed.

## CHAPTER CXXIII.—ON WULLENA [Note: [Col. 1179D] *Verbascum thapsus*.] [II, 131].

[Col. 1180B] **Wullena** [*Blandonia* in the edition] is hot and dry, and somewhat cold; and whoever has a weak and sorrowful heart should cook Wullena either with meat, or with fish, or in cakes (*Kucheln*) without other herbs, and eat it often: it strengthens and gladdens his heart. Likewise, whoever is hoarse in voice and throat, and whoever has pain in the chest, should cook Wullena and fennel in equal weight in good wine, strain it through a cloth, and drink it often; he will recover his voice, and it heals the chest.

### CHAPTER CXXIV.—ON GAMANDREA  
[Note: [Col. 1179D] *Teucrium chamaedrys*.] [II, 132]

Gamandrea [*Alentidium* in the edition] is hot and rich; and, eaten or drunk, it benefits neither people nor livestock, because it drives off and wards off bruising and scab, enters the blood, and makes it less abundant and thinner. [Note: [Col. 1179D] “Because it drives off—thinner” omitted in the edition.]

For it diminishes the blood and [Col. 1180C] increases wasting without removing it. If someone takes it in some purgative preparation in order to lessen the bruising and wasting remaining in him, illness sometimes follows, because his blood has been diminished while the wasting remains, and therefore his flesh will be weakened. Yet whoever suffers from a slight scab that lies between skin and flesh should pound gamandrea with old fat and anoint himself with it, and his flesh will be healed. But once it has already begun to heal somewhat, he should no longer anoint himself with it, because it harms his blood if he keeps anointing that place for long.

It is of no use against the skin, because the *grint* is deep in the flesh; and if one is anointed with it, it diminishes the blood and would leave the wasting within. [Note: [Col. 1179D] “It is of no use against the skin—within” ends in the edition, which [Col. 1180D] adds: “But if blood in a person, stirred by bad humours, begins to flow out through his lower parts with the evacuation of food, he should not restrain it, because it brings him purification. But if it passes through him excessively, let him add *alentidium* to vegetables and other good herbs, make food from them, and they will restore him.”]

### CHAPTER CXXV.—ON CENTAUREA  
[Note: [Col. 1180D] *Centaurea cyanus*. Compare Pliny, *Natural History* XXV, 6.] [II, 133]

[Col. 1180D]

Centaurea is hot and dry. Whoever has a bone or leg (*beyn*) broken somewhere in his body should often drink centaurea, or its root, mixed with wine or water, and the broken bone is joined together—*wellet*, “knits.” He should also warm centaurea in water and, after pressing out the water, apply it hot and often to the place where the bone is broken; thus he should bathe (*bewe*) that place with it, and he will be healed.

For whoever is so gout-afflicted (*virgichtig*) [Col. 1181A] that his tongue fails him in speaking, and that some limb likewise fails him, should mix the root and leaves of centaurea with fresh deer fat, make cakes—that is, *kucheln*—with flour, and eat them often; then the gout (*gicht*) that oppresses and afflicts him is subdued. Likewise, one who is gout-afflicted should often drink centaurea prepared in this wine, and the gout in him will cease.

### CHAPTER CXXVI.—ON POLEYA  
[Note: [Col. 1181D] *Mentha pulegium*.] [II, 68]

Poleya has a gentle warmth, yet is moist. [“And it possesses in itself some virtue of these fifteen herbs: namely, zedoary, clove, galangal, ginger, basil, greater comfrey, lungwort, aristolochia, yarrow, southernwood, polypody, agrimony, *stur*, cranesbill (*storckenschnabel*), and water-mint (*bachminza*). And [Col. 1181B] all these herbs are opposed to fevers,” added by the edition.]

Whoever has pain in the brain, so that he is feverish or disordered (*virseret*), should put poleya in wine and boil it, apply it hot about his entire head, and bind a cloth over it, so that the brain is warm; the madness in it is thereby subdued. Whoever has dim eyes should press out its juice and anoint the area around the eyes and eyelids with it, taking care not to touch the eyes [within]; it will drive away their dimness. [“But if it touches the eyes within, by its power it will ulcerate their flesh,” added by the edition.]

Take also gall of a rooster and twice as much poleya juice, add a little pure wine, and make an eye-salve from them; put it in a small vessel. Anoint around the eyes and eyelids [Col. 1181C] of a young person whose eyes are dim from illness, or even of an elderly person of moderate age, so that a little also enters the eyes. Do this for twelve nights, when he goes to sleep, and it removes dimness from the eyes.

Powder poleya, put this powder into equal weights of vinegar and honey, and drink it often while fasting—that is, sip it (*suffe*); it purges your stomach and clarifies your eyes. Likewise, whoever often eats raw poleya leaves with salt, added alone to meat, warms a cold stomach; and if his stomach is full of poison—that is, *eyter*, “pus/poison”—it purges and heals it.

### CHAPTER CXXVII.—ON BEONIA  
[Note: [Col. 1181D] *Paeonia officinalis*.] [II, 134]

Beonia [*Dactylosa* in the edition] is fiery and possesses good power, and is effective against tertian and quartan fevers. [Col. 1181D] Pound its root a little, put it into wine, and drink it often; it drives tertian and quartan fever away from you. Again, powder beonia, put the powder into flour, and add fat or poppy oil. Make it like *habim* [uncertain preparation], and eat it often; again, tertian and quartan fever will leave you.

If a person loses his mind, as though he knew nothing and lay in ecstasy, dip beonia seed in honey and put it upon his tongue. Thus the powers of beonia rise to his brain and rouse it, so that he quickly returns to his senses and recovers understanding.

Likewise, whoever has much [Col. 1182A] phlegm in his head and about his chest, and therefore spits out much foul matter and has foul breath, should cut beonia root into small slices, add some of its seed, let it boil in wine, and drink it often, moderately hot. It purges his head and chest and makes his breath sweet-smelling. After he has drunk this wine, he may heat other wine with the same beonia up to a third time.

Likewise, take beonia seed, dip it in leech’s blood, and immediately roll it thickly in fine wheat flour. When a person falls in the falling sickness—that is, *wallendsucht*—put it into his mouth while he lies thus; do this whenever he falls from this illness, and eventually he will be healed.

If moths—that is, *milwe*—damage [Col. 1182B] a person’s hair, make a lye with beonia root and seed and wash his head often; the moths will die. Put its root and leaves also among garments, and moths flee and do not damage them.

### CHAPTER CXXVIII.—ON BATHENIA  
[II, 135]

Bathenia [*Pandonia* in the edition] is hot, and displays in itself signs of human knowledge more than other herbs, just as tame and clean animals have more dealings with human beings than wild animals. [Note: [Col. 1181D] “Just as—wild animals” ends in the edition.] Therefore the Devil’s deception sometimes lays its shadows upon it, and also upon certain other herbs, because he is aerial; hence he also knows all the powers that are in herbs. [Note: [Col. 1182D] “And also—knows” ends in the edition.]

Whoever is stupid or foolish, so that knowledge fails in him, should pound bathenia nearly to a juice, put it over his entire chest at night, and bind it with a cloth until morning. Let him do this often, and he will return to understanding. Whoever is accustomed to be troubled by false dreams should keep bathenia with him when he goes to sleep at night and while he sleeps; he will see and experience fewer false dreams. [“A woman who suffers many irregular menstrual flows at an improper time should put pandonia into wine so that the wine takes its flavour, drink it often, and be healed,” added by the edition.]

But if any man has been deceived by a woman, or any woman by a man, through some magical art; or has been touched by some trick of that kind; or has been bewitched by any fantastic and devilish incantations, so that a man crazed by such an enchantment raves in love for a woman, [Col. 1182D] or a woman in love for a man, then let him seek bathenia through which some remedy or fantasy has previously been made. For if anything of that sort has previously been done through it, it is thereafter of no value for medicinal healing, because it has first been entangled by fantasies. [Note: [Col. 1182D] “Because—it has been entangled” ends in the edition.]

When he has found it, let him take leaves from it: put one leaf into each nostril, one leaf under his tongue, hold one leaf in each hand, and put one leaf beneath each foot. Let him also gaze intently at bathenia with his eyes, and do this until the same leaves grow warm upon [Col. 1183A] his body. Let him repeat it often, until he improves; thus he will be freed from the madness of that love—provided, however, that he has not tasted or introduced into his body any stimulant of love by eating or drinking.

Likewise, whoever, man or woman, has been ensnared in love for another by magic words should always keep bethania with him or her, and will improve. If it is winter, so that its leaves cannot be obtained for the remedy described, take its root and do as stated above. No one should eat bethania in any way, for if he eats it, it harms his reason and understanding and makes him nearly mad.

### CHAPTER CXXIX.—ON BLACK SICHTERWURTZ  
[Note: [Col. 1183D] *Rumex acutus*, as in the following chapter.] [II, 136]

[Col. 1183B] Sichterwurtz, which is called black, is hot and cold, and in its heat is hard and rough. If anyone, afflicted by some illness and sickness in the head, loses his reason and understanding so that he becomes insane, take Sichterwurtz, add to it a smaller quantity of *Quenula*, pound them together, and simmer (*sweysze*) them in a pan with old fat. Apply it hot over his whole head and around all his neck, bind a cloth over it, and do this for five days, warming it once in the morning and once at night each day.

After the fifth day, make a lye with beech ashes, wash his head with it, and he will be healed. If he has not yet recovered his mind, apply the same ointment again about his head and neck for another five days, as was stated [Col. 1183C] above; after the fifth day wash his head again with the aforesaid lye. However severe the plague of his madness may be, it will flee from him, and he will recover his reason and understanding.

### CHAPTER CXXX.—ON SICHTERWURTZ  
[II, 137]

White Sichterwurtz has the same nature described above for black Sichterwurtz, except that the black is harsher than the white. White Sichterwurtz mixed with Quenula, fennel, and fat, as stated above, likewise drives madness from a person, as was said, and is also very useful when added to other spices and ointments. [Note: [Col. 1183D] “And white—added” ends in the edition.]

A young woman whose menstrual periods are absent at the proper time should take oil infused with roses, and half of a third part of white Sichterwurtz [Col. 1183D] in proportion to the same roses, infuse this likewise in the oil, and anoint herself strongly and often with that oil near the groin, around the navel, and over the flank (*lankim*). Her menstrual members [read: menstrual flow] will move and be released. But if, entangled by some impediment, she has not had her menstrual flow in this manner, the aforesaid anointing will nevertheless cause the flow in her to pour out and diminish it—that is, *zusluszet*, “makes it flow out”—so that she will suffer less if it does not occur at the proper time.

[“Likewise, a person who suffers pain in the heart and in the *vobin* [sic; perhaps throat], should pound white *cittervurtz*, southernwood in a third of its amount, and a smaller amount of *menua* than of southernwood, all together. Add cow’s butter prepared in May; this is an excellent ointment. When there is pain in the heart, anoint that place; if there is pain in the *vobim*, anoint about the throat. Do this often, and he will improve,” added by the edition. [Col. 1184A]]

### CHAPTER CXXXI.—ON BIBENZLLA  
[Note: [Col. 1183D] *Pimpinella saxifraga*.] [II, 139]

Bibenella is more cold than hot and is not of much use for human purposes, because its juice is sharp. [Note: [Col. 1183D] “Because—sharp” ends in the edition.] Nevertheless, always wear it suspended from your neck, and meanwhile you will not be deceived by invocations of demons, magic words, or *zauber*—sorcery—which you have neither eaten nor drunk.

### CHAPTER CXXXII.—ON AGLEYA  
[Note: [Col. 1183D] *Aquilegia vulgaris*.] [II, 140]

[Col. 1184B]

Agleya [*Acoleia* in the edition] is cold. A person in whom *freischlich*, called *selega*, begins to arise should eat raw Agleya, and the *freischlich* will disappear. In one in whom *orfimae* [scrofulous swellings in the edition] begin to grow, let him often eat raw Agleya, and the *orfimae* will diminish. Whoever brings up much phlegm should season Agleya in honey (*beysze*; *condiat* in the edition), eat it often, and it lessens the phlegm and thus purges him. Whoever has fever should pound Agleya, strain its juice through a cloth, add wine to that juice, and drink it often; he will improve.

### CHAPTER CXXXIII.—ON SPRINGWURTZ  
[Note: [Col. 1183D] *Euphorbia lathyris*.] [II, 141]

Springwurtz [*Citocatia* in the edition] is cold and contains a small amount of sharp juice; by itself it is not very [Col. 1184C] useful to a person. [Note: [Col. 1184D] “And a small amount—person” omitted in the edition.] For any person who ate it alone and unprepared would be internally loosened or torn apart (*indrede*) by it, so that it would pass through him dangerously and unhealthily (*ungesuntliche*). [Note: [Col. 1184D] “That is—unhealthily” omitted in the edition.]

But whoever wishes to take a small and mild purge should take equal weights of cinnamon and liquorice, powder them, and roll this powder with a little fine wheat flour in Springwurtz juice into pills the size of beans. Dry them in the sun or by an oven. Then take in the morning as much as weighs five, nine, or fifteen pennies, and it will purge him gently. Afterwards he should observe the proper regimen of food and drink. [Note: [Col. 1184D] “Afterwards—proper” omitted in the edition.]

### CHAPTER CXXXIV.—ON FRIDELES  
[Note: [Col. 1184D] *Myosotis scorpioides*.—Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1184D] Fridelesauga has neither proper heat nor proper cold, nor does it possess any powers useful to humankind; it is a weed (*unkrut*) and has no medicinal value. Hence, if someone ate it, it would harm him more than benefit him.

### CHAPTER CXXXV.—ON BERURTZ  
[Note: [Col. 1184D] *Athamanta Meum*.] [II, 142]

Berwurtz is hot and contains a dry greenness. [Note: [Col. 1184D] “And a dry—greenness” omitted in the edition.] A person who has strong and burning fevers should powder berwurtz and eat this powder [Col. 1185A] with bread, fasting and after a meal; he will improve. Whoever has gout (*gegicht*) should often eat the same powder, and the gout in him will cease. Whoever has jaundice (*gelsucht*) should pound fresh berlwurtz root in vinegar and eat it thus. He should then prepare some soup (*suffen*) with the same vinegar and eat it often, and he will be healed. [Note: [Col. 1185D] “While it is green” omitted in the edition. “And then—eat it” ends in the edition.]

### CHAPTER CXXXVI.—ON STEMBRECHA  
[Note: [Col. 1185D] *Asplenium ruta-muraria*.] [II, 143]

Stembrecha [*Saxifrica* in the edition] is cold and contains strong powers. It is not suitable as food for a person with a tender body, because it would be too strong for his body. But when *slim*—coagulated mucus—forms somewhere in the stomach or bladder or elsewhere in a person’s body and hardens like a little stone, he should pound Stembrecha seed in water and drink it often after a meal, [Col. 1185B] not fasting. This drink breaks what is hard and harmful in the person like a little stone, and he will be healed.

Whoever has jaundice should grind the same seed in wine, allow it to lie in that wine for a short time, then drink it often after a meal, and jaundice will be extinguished in him; for it sometimes also arises from excess bile and very often produces in a person a certain hardness like a stone. [Note: [Col. 1185D] “And he will be healed,” in the edition, which ends the chapter here.]

### CHAPTER CXXXVII.—ON UGERA  
[II, 144]

Ugera is very hot and has a certain sharpness in it, and this sharpness is very strong; therefore it breaks up large and severe ulcers—that is, *swern*. [Note: [Col. 1185D] The edition, more briefly: “It is hot and breaks up a large and severe [Col. 1186D] ulcer.”] Pound Ugera in a mortar, add a little tree-oil (*baumoleum*), and apply it [cold, in the edition] to the ulcer.

If you do not have tree-oil, add a little raven fat and simmer it (*sweysze*; “heat it,” in the edition) in a pan; allow it to cool, then apply it cold to the ulcer. Its strength softens and draws out the poison and heals it. If large red and specifically *gedoszen* ulcers are on a person, pound the same ugera, add either tree-oil or deer fat as stated above, and apply it to those ulcers; it draws out the poison—that is, *eyther*. But when those ulcers have begun to redden, discard the ugera. Then make a dressing (*beneduch*) of hemp with tree-oil or deer fat and apply it to those ulcers; they will be healed, because the poison has then been drawn out. [Note: [Col. 1186D] “Because—drawn out” omitted in the edition.]

Likewise, season (*beisze*) ugera root in vinegar and lay it overnight upon the place where warts (*warczen*) have newly begun to grow on your body. Bind a cloth over it; do this often, and the warts disappear.

### CHAPTER CXXXVIII.—ON GRINTWURTZ  
[II, 145]

Grintwurtz [*Chelidonia* in the edition] is very hot and contains poisonous—that is, *slimech*, slimy—juice. For it has in itself poison so black and bitter that it can offer no healing to a person, because if it gave health in one respect, it would internally cause him a greater illness in another. If anyone eats or drinks it, it ulcerates and harms him internally; thus it sometimes produces evacuation and digestion in a person with pain and not with health.

But one who has eaten, drunk, or touched something unclean and thereby becomes ulcerated in the body should take old fat, add enough Grintwurtz juice, pound it together, melt it together in a pan, and anoint himself with the fat; he will be healed.

### CHAPTER CXXXIX.—ON LUBESTUCKEL  
[Note: [Col. 1186D] *Ligusticum levisticum*.] [II, 36]

Lubestuckel [*Levisticum* in the edition] is of moderate warmth. If eaten raw, it makes a person lax in his bodily nature (*zufloszlich*; “loosens,” in the edition), and thus enfeebles his constitution. If anyone eats it cooked by itself without other seasonings, [Col. 1186B] it makes him heavy and joyless (*unlustig*; “weary,” in the edition) in mind and body. But when it is cooked and eaten with other seasonings, it does not greatly harm the eater.

If someone suffers from swellings (*druse*; “glands” in the edition) in the neck, so that the veins of his neck are swollen, he should take Lubestuckel and a somewhat larger amount of Gunderebe, boil them together in water, pour off the water, and apply them hot around the neck. For the veins of his neck are overstretched, and he will be healed.

[“If someone coughs in the chest and it first begins to hurt there, let him take lovage and sage in equal amounts, and twice as much fennel as of those two; leave them together in good wine until the wine takes their flavour. Then discard the herbs, heat the wine, [Col. 1186C] and drink it hot after food until he is healed. But if the cough is slight, let him drink the aforesaid draught unheated, because the pain is mild. If the pain is severe, let him drink the wine heated, so that it may be relieved more gently.

“If rheum flows from a horse’s nostrils, so that it coughs from it, the person wishing to cure it should take lovage and a somewhat smaller quantity of stinging nettle, boil them in water, remove them from the water, and let their hot vapour pass into its nostrils and mouth, with a bridle in place; it will be healed. If a horse suffers in its belly as though from bites, take lovage and a somewhat smaller quantity of stinging nettle, mix them often with its fodder so that it eats them together, [Col. 1186D] and it will be healed,” added by the edition.]

### CHAPTER CXL.—ON EBICH  
[Note: [Col. 1186D] *Hedera helix*.] [II, 146]

Ebich is more cold than hot and, like a weed (*unkrut*), is unsuitable for a person to eat. But a person who has jaundice should simmer ebich in a pan with deer fat or old fat (*svveysze*; “heat it,” in the edition), apply it hot above his stomach, and the jaundice passes into that herb—that is, *uszflecht*, “flows out”—so that yellow colouring (*gelware*) appears outwardly also in that person’s skin.

After he has applied these herbs above his stomach as stated, [Col. 1187A] immediately pound *bruncrasse* in cold water, strain it through a cloth, and give it to him cold to drink; the jaundice is expelled and he will be healed.

[“Likewise, a woman who suffers many irregular menstrual flows at an improper time should boil ebich in water and apply it hot to her thighs and navel; its coldness resists the contrary flow.

“If, in any person, the inner membrane in which the intestines are enclosed is torn by some accident, he should boil ebich and twice as much greater comfrey in good wine. After boiling the herbs, separate them from the wine, add a little powder made from zedoary, as much sugar as there was ebich, and sufficient cooked honey; let it boil again a little, [Col. 1187B] then make it into a clear drink by straining it through a small bag. Drink it after food and at night, and do this often. Tie the herbs boiled in the aforesaid wine, hot, over the place where the inner membrane has ruptured; they unite its tears. Cut greater comfrey root into small pieces and put it into wine so that the wine takes its flavour; drink this wine continually until healed,” added by the edition.]

### CHAPTER CXLI.—ON YBISCHA  
[Note: [Col. 1187D] *Althaea officinalis*.] [II, 147]

Ybischa is hot and dry and is effective against fevers. A person with fevers, of whatever kind, should pound ybischen in vinegar and drink it thus fasting in the morning and at night; the fever, whatever its nature, will cease. Whoever has pain in the head should take Ybischa, [Col. 1187C] add a somewhat smaller amount of sage, pound them together, mix in a little tree-oil, warm it only in his hand beside the fire, apply it only to his forehead, bind it with a cloth, and sleep thus; he will improve.

### CHAPTER CXLII.—ON DENEMARCHA  
[Note: [Col. 1187D] *Valeriana officinalis*.] [II, 147]

Denemarcha is hot and moist. Whoever suffers from pleurisy, or from gout, should powder Denemarcha and add to this powder a somewhat smaller quantity of nebetta powder. [Note: [Col. 1187D] “And add to this powder—a smaller quantity” omitted in the edition.] Then make little cakes with flour and water, or cakes (*kucheln*) in a pan with fat, mix in the aforesaid powders, and eat them often; pleurisy [Col. 1187D] and gout will cease in him, so that he will improve.

### CHAPTER CXLIII.—ON NEBETTA  
[Note: [Col. 1187D] *Nepeta cataria*.] [II, 149]

Nebetta [*Calamentum* in the edition] is hot. A person with *orfime* [“scrofulae” in the edition] in the neck, before they rupture, should powder Nebetta and eat the powder often with bread, in *muse*, or in cakes (*kucheln*); the *orfimae* will disappear. But if the *orfimae* rupture, lay its raw and fresh leaves upon them, and they will dry up.

### CHAPTER CXLIV.—ON CRANCHSNABEL  
[Note: [Col. 1187D] *Erodium cicutarium*.] [II, 150]

[Col. 1188A]

Cranchsnabel is very hot, has a little moisture, and possesses nearly the powers of spices. Take therefore cranchsnabel, a smaller quantity of bertram [“pyrethrum” in the edition] than of cranchsnabel, and nutmeg in a smaller quantity than bertram. Reduce these to powder and mix them together.

Whoever has pain in the heart should eat this powder either with bread or without bread, licking it from his hand, [Note: [Col. 1188D] “Licking it from his hand” omitted in the edition, as also below.] and will improve, because it is an excellent powder for the health of the heart. Whoever has *nazeboz* should apply the same powder to his nostrils and draw its scent inward; the *nazeboz* will dissolve more lightly and pleasantly and quickly disappear without danger to that person.

Whoever has cough (*husten*) and constriction (*gebrech*) [Col. 1188B] in the chest should make cakes (*kuchelu*; “tortellos” in the edition) in a pan with flour and this powder, adding fat or butter, and eat them often fasting and after a meal. It gently and pleasantly loosens and brings to an end the cough and ulcer of the chest, and thus he will improve. Whoever has pain in the chest so that the chest oppresses him (*demphet*), or pain in the throat so that the voice is lost, should drink the same powder in hot wine; he will improve in chest and throat. Whoever has pain in the head should add bright salt or roasted salt to this powder and either eat it in bread or lick it from his hand; he will improve.

### CHAPTER CXLV.—ON CONSOLIDA  
[Note: [Col. 1188D] *Symphytum officinale*.] [II, 151]

Consolida is cold. If a person eats it without [Col. 1188C] proper reason, it displaces all humours that are rightly established in him. [Note: [Col. 1188D] “And if—displaces” absent from the edition.] But if a limb in a person is displaced, ulcerated, or wounded, and he then eats it, it immediately follows the bruising that issues there, and heals that bruising and the ulcers above in the skin, but not within the flesh.

It may be compared to when stones are thrown into a great ditch to prevent water from flowing out, as in some *vacht* [uncertain]; since the water cannot flow out, it settles in the depth of the place. [Note: [Col. 1188D] “It may be compared—settles” omitted in the edition.] In this way worms and every harmful thing remain within when prevented from flowing out. Thus consolida, eaten improperly and not in the right manner, heals ulcers outwardly and leaves every putrid thing [Col. 1188D] within.

### CHAPTER CXLVI.—ON BYVERWURTZ  
[II, 152]

Byverwurtz [“rustica” in the edition] is hot and somewhat cold. Powder the root and leaves of biverwurtz; add bertram powder in an amount weighing half as much as it, and cinnamon powder in an amount equal to the bertram powder, and mix them. Drink this mixed powder daily either with bread, with hot wine, or eat it in soup (*suffen*), and you will have no great or prolonged illness until [Col. 1189A] your death.

No one should avoid this powder when prepared in this way; for if a healthy person eats this powder every day, he will not lie sick in bed for a long time; and if a sick person eats it, he will become well. You may preserve the powder sound in a cloth: put it in a new dry earthenware vessel made of clay, bury it beneath the earth, and cover it closed; thus it will retain its powers.

[Note: [Col. 1189D] “We present the text of this chapter, defective and corrupt in the manuscript, from the edition: ‘Rustica is hot in a good balance. A person who wishes to remain healthy should powder the root and leaves of rustica; add pyrethrum powder in an amount weighing half as much as it, and mix cinnamon powder in an amount equal to half the pyrethrum powder. Let him daily take this powder with bread, or in broth, or drink it in hot wine, and he will have no great or prolonged sickness until his death. Let no one avoid this powder, because if a healthy person eats it daily, he will not lie ill in bed for a long time; if a sick person eats it, he will be well. But in order that this powder may be preserved sound for a year, it should be put in a new earthenware [Col. 1190D] vessel and, closed, covered with earth; thus it will retain its powers.’”]

### CHAPTER CXLVII.—ON GRENSING

Grensing is a weed (*unkrut*) and has no value for any human healing. Thus, if someone ate it, it would neither benefit nor harm him.

### CHAPTER CXLVIII.—ON MORKRUT  
[Note: [Col. 1190D] *Parnassia palustris*.—This chapter is repeated below in chapter 200, but under the heading “On parsnip,” as in the edition.] [II, 66]

Morkrut is nourishment for a person. It neither benefits nor harms him for health, [Col. 1189B] but when eaten fills the belly.

### CHAPTER CXLIX.—ON GENSEKRUT  
[Note: [Col. 1190D] *Potentilla anserina*.—This chapter is absent from the edition.]

Gensekrut is cold and is a weed (*unkrut*). If eaten, it does not benefit a person’s health, but harms him more.

### CHAPTER CL.—ON LINSAMO  
[Note: [Col. 1190D] *Linum usitatissimum*.] [II, 15]

Linsamo is hot, etc., as below in chapter 194, “On flaxseed,” where many matters are read that are absent here.

### CHAPTER CLI.—ON HUNSDARM  
[Note: [Col. 1190D] *Alsine medica*.] [II, 173]

Hunsdarm is hot and is a weed (*unkrut*). But if a person falls by accident, or is struck by a pole, so that his skin is thereby *weydden* [“has various spots,” in the edition], boil Hunsdarm in water. After pressing out the water, apply it hot and often upon [Col. 1189C] the place of the fall or blow, bind a cloth over it, and it drives away the bruises collected there.

### CHAPTER CLII.—ON NYESEWURTZ  
[Note: [Col. 1190D] *Helleborus niger*.] [II, 153]

Nyesewurtz [*Gelisia* in the edition] is hot and dry, and a little moist, but it has a useful greenness. [Note: [Col. 1190D] “And a little—useful” omitted in the edition.] Whoever is afflicted with gout, and likewise whoever has jaundice, should pound Nyesewurtz, strain its juice through a cloth, and add that juice to wine. If he has gout, he should often drink it thus fasting; if he has jaundice [“the royal disease” in the edition], he should often drink it after a meal; he will be healed.

Likewise, boil Nyesewurtz in wine with honey added, strain it through a cloth, and drink it after a meal and at night when going to sleep. Do this often; it will heal him, make him pleasantly light in the chest, purge his stomach, and lessen whatever is foul and fetid within his body. [Col. 1189D]

### CHAPTER CLIII.—ON THE HERB GICHT  
[II, 154]

[Col. 1190A]

The herb called *gicht* is very hot and has a certain greenness in it. Whoever has pain in the stomach should pound a little of this herb and its seed, boil it in wine and a little honey, strain it through a cloth, and drink it hot. But whoever wishes to guard against becoming ill in the stomach should often drink the same draught cold, and will preserve health in the stomach.

Whoever is often afflicted by gout should pound the same herb with its seed, add bear fat, and tree-oil, in the proportion of about a third part tree-oil to bear fat. Boil this in water and make an ointment; let him anoint himself where he hurts. It immediately passes through that person’s skin, so that the storm or force of the affliction of gout will cease from him. [Col. 1190B]

### CHAPTER CLIV.—ON YSENA  
[Note: [Col. 1190D] *Verbena officinalis*.] [II, 155]

Ysena [“verbena” in the edition] is more cold than hot. Where a person has putrid flesh from ulcers or worms, boil Ysena in water. Then lay a linen cloth over the putrid wounds or places affected by worms; press out a little water from that Ysena, place it moderately hot upon the linen cloth which you laid over this putrid flesh, and, after it dries, apply another boiled preparation in the same way. Do this until the putrefaction is removed.

Likewise, if anyone has swelling in the throat, warm Ysena a little in water, apply it moderately hot to his throat, [Col. 1190C] bind it with a cloth, and continue until the swelling disappears.

### CHAPTER CLV.—ON SATEREIA  
[Note: [Col. 1190D] *Satureia hortensis*.] [II, 156]

Satereia is more hot than cold. A person afflicted by gout, so that his limbs are always moving, should powder Satereia. To this powder add less cumin powder than sage powder, mix these powders together in *honigwurtz* [honey-wort], and drink it often after a meal; he will improve.

### CHAPTER CLVI.—ON WOLFESGELEGENA  
[Note: [Col. 1190D] *Arnica montana*.—Absent from the edition.]

Wolfesgelegena is very hot and contains poisonous heat. When a male or female burns with lust, if someone touches him or her on the bare skin with green Wolfesgelegena, that person will burn in love for [Col. 1190D] him or her. Afterwards, when the herb has dried, the male or female touched with that herb [Col. 1191A] becomes nearly mad from the love with which he or she was inflamed, so that he or she will thereafter be foolish.

### CHAPTER CLVII.—ON SYME  
[Note: [Col. 1191D] *Stellaria media*.] [II, 170]

Symes is cold. If maggots (*maden*) or worms are eating a person, powder Symes by the fire, put the powder on the ulcerated place, and the worms and maggots will die.

### CHAPTER CLVIII.—ON RUSH  
[Note: [Col. 1191D] Absent from the edition.]

Rush is neither properly hot nor properly cold, but lukewarm; therefore it has no medicinal value.

### CHAPTER CLIX.—ON MEYGILANA  
[II, 157]

Meygelana is cold and has the coldness possessed by earth when it brings forth flowers into fruit. [Note: [Col. 1191D] “And has the coldness—brings forth” omitted in the edition.] If *orfimae*, *freyslich*, or any ulcer containing poison grows in any person, let him often eat Meygelana fasting, and they will disappear.

Likewise, whoever has *vallendsucht* [“the royal disease” in the edition] should often eat Meygelana; when he falls to the ground from this illness, put the same herb under his tongue, and he will rise more quickly and suffer less.

### CHAPTER CLX.—ON DORNELLA  
[Note: [Col. 1191D] *Potentilla tormentilla*.] [II, 158]

Dornella is cold, and that coldness is good and wholesome. [Note: [Col. 1191D] “And that coldness—is wholesome” omitted in the edition.] It is effective against fevers arising from harmful foods. Take Dornella, boil it in wine with a little honey added, strain it through a cloth, and drink it often fasting at night; you will be healed of the fever.

### Chapter 161.—On Scharley[a]  
[Note: [Col. 1191D] *Salvia sclarea* (clary sage).] [II, 159]

Scharleya [Cicula, ed.] is hot and is effective against poison. [Note: [Col. 1191D] “And is effective against poison” omitted in the edition.] For if anyone has taken poison, let him take Scharleya, add a little honey and a little rue; after it has been cooked, add a little stramonium, strain it through a cloth, and drink it three times after food. The poison will pass from him either by vomiting or through the bowels, unless it is poison of such a kind as will cause his death.

And if someone has a stomach so weak that he easily becomes *Eyterech* from food, let him take Scharleya, one third as much pennyroyal, and fennel—one fourth [the text is uncertain: “a third part of pennyroyal” follows]—and cook these together in good wine, adding a little honey. Strain it through a cloth, and drink it frequently after food and at night. His stomach will be gently cured, or purged, and he will have an appetite for eating.

Likewise, whoever has pain in the head should cook Scharleya in water and, after the water has been expressed, apply it hot around his head; let him cover his head with a cloth and sleep thus, and he will be better.

### Chapter 162.—On Storcksnabel  
[Note: [Col. 1191D] *Geranium pratense* (meadow cranesbill).] [II, 160]

Storcksnabel is more cold than hot, and is effective against stone. [Note: [Col. 1192D] “And is effective against stone” omitted in the edition.] Whoever has *Steyn* [“a stone,” ed.] in his body should take Storcksnabel and a lesser quantity of Steinbrecha, cook them in water, strain them through a cloth, and prepare a steam-bath [“and enter it,” added by the edition]. Let him cook oats in water and pour the water in which the oats were cooked over heated stones. After he has sweated in this way, let him drink hot, in that bath itself, the aforesaid water in which Storcksnabel and Steinbrecka were cooked; and the stone in him will be gently broken up.

And whoever has pain in the heart and is always sad should take Storcksnabel, a lesser amount of pennyroyal, and less rue than pennyroyal; let him powder these and often eat this powder with his bread. His heart will be strengthened, and he will be cheerful.

### Chapter 163.—On Benedicta  
[Note: [Col. 1192D] *Geum urbanum* (wood avens).] [II, 162]

Benedicta is hot; and if anyone takes it in a drink, it kindles the desire of lust. But if a person is failing throughout his whole body in bodily strength, let him cook benedicta in water and drink that water hot frequently; he will recover bodily strength. Once his body is better, however, he should avoid it. [Note: [Col. 1192D] “Once his body is better … avoid it” omitted in the edition.]

### Chapter 164.—On Risza  
[II, 163]

Risza [Rubea, ed.] is cold and is effective against fever. Whoever has fever and loathing for food should cook Risza lightly in water, leave the herb itself in that water, drink the same water hot in the morning and at night, and lay the herb cooked in the water, hot, upon his stomach for a short time. Let him do this for three days, and the fevers in him will cease.

—[But whoever suffers from quartan fevers should cook equal amounts of madder and bramble-herb, and *brachvurtz*, three times as much as the other two together, in wine. Then add clear, excellent wine and put in heated steel; do this ten times with the same wine and steel. Afterwards take the wine cooked with the aforesaid herbs, pour into it the wine into which he placed the steel, bring them to the boil together once, and drink it during the fever-attack until he is healed. Added by the edition.]

### Chapter 165.—On Musetha  
[Note: [Col. 1192D] Absent from the edition.]

Musetha is more hot than cold, and, when added to any ointments, makes them altogether better and stronger; but by itself it has little value as a remedy.

### Chapter 166.—On Birckwurtz  
[II, 167]

Birckwurtz is more cold than hot. A person who has superfluous and poisonous humours in himself—that is, *eytherecht*—should take Birckwurtz, which is *blutwurtz* [bloodwort], pound it for its juice with twice as much Brachwurtz, place it in an earthenware vessel, pour good clear wine over it, and drink it after food and when going to sleep for fifteen days. It will benefit him for a year, inasmuch as this drink diminishes the superfluous and poisonous humours in him. [Note: [Col. 1192D] “Inasmuch as … diminishes” ends here in the edition.]

### Chapter 167.—On Astrencia  
[Note: [Col. 1192D] *Astrantia ostruthium*.] [II, 161]

Astrencia is hot and is effective against fevers. [Note: [Col. 1192D] “And is effective against fevers” omitted by the edition.] Whoever has fevers, of whatever kind, should take Astrencia, bruise it lightly, pour over this crushed or ground Astrencia half a *piccarium*, filled to the brim, and let it stand with the wine overnight. In the morning add wine to it again; drink it fasting, and do this for three or five days, and he will be cured.

—[Whoever cannot digest food which he has eaten should take juice of long aristolochia, to the weight of two coins; juice of *bibinella*, to the weight of one coin; juice of *citocatia*, to the weight of one obol; and ginger of the same weight. Mix fine flour with these juices and make little cakes the breadth of a coin but somewhat thick. Bake them in the sun, or in an oven which has already become nearly cool.

If the person who is ill in the aforesaid manner is inwardly hot, so that food is burnt up in him, let him take one of these little cakes fasting in the morning. Or, if he is inwardly cold, so that food in him is congealed and compressed by cold, let him take two or three little cakes fasting in the morning. The first food he then eats should be broth or a little soup; afterwards let him eat other good and pleasant foods. Let him continue thus until he feels himself relieved in the stomach. Added by the edition.]

### Chapter 168.—On Ertpeffer  
[Note: [Col. 1193D] *Polygonum hydropiper* (water-pepper).] [II, 168]

Ertpeffer is cold and grows from bright air. [Note: [Col. 1193D] “And grows from bright air” omitted in the edition.] A person with fever should take sufficient ertpeffer, steep it in good wine for one night, discard the ertpeffer, warm the wine with heated steel, and drink it fasting in the morning and at night when going to sleep. Let him do this until he feels health in himself.

### Chapter 169.—On Brema  
[Note: [Col. 1193D] *Rubus caesius* and *Rubus fruticosus* (dewberry and blackberry).] [II, 177]

Brema, on which *bramber* grow, is more hot than cold.

[If anyone has pain in the tongue, so that it is either swollen or ulcerated, let him have his tongue lightly incised with brema, or with a small phlebotome, so that the dark blood may escape. Whoever has toothache should do the same to his gums, and he will be better. Added by the edition.]

If worms are eating a person, powder that same brema and place the powder upon the spot where worms are eating the flesh of a person or an animal; they will die, and the person will be healed.

If anyone has pain in the lung and coughs in the chest, let him take bertram, a lesser quantity of the same brema than bertram, less hyssop than this brema, and less dost than these; add honey and cook strongly in good wine. Then strain it through a cloth. After he has eaten a little food, let him drink it; after a full meal, let him drink a sufficient quantity of it. Do this often: the lung will recover health, and *slim* will be removed from the chest.

The fruit of the bramble—namely, that which grows on brema—harms neither a healthy nor a sick person and is easily digested; but no medicinal virtue is found in it. [Note: [Col. 1193D] “But no medicinal virtue is found in it” is absent from the edition.]

### Chapter 170.—On Erperis  
[Note: [Col. 1194D] *Fragaria vesca* (wild strawberry). Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1194A]

The plant on which erpere grow is more hot than cold. It produces *slim* in the person who eats it and has no medicinal value. The fruit of erpere likewise produces something like *slim* in the person who eats it. It is of no value for food to either a healthy or a sick person, because it grows close to the ground and also grows in corrupt air.

### Chapter 171.—On Walt Beris  
[Note: [Col. 1194D] *Vaccinium myrtillus* (bilberry).] [II, 179]

The plant on which *walt bere* grow, also called *heydel bere*, namely the black ones, contains the greatest coldness: that is, when cold has already yielded somewhat to heat, so that the moisture of cold coming out of the earth and stones does more harm than good. It has no value for remedies; its fruit harms the eater, in that it excites *gicht* in him.

### Chapter 172.—On Fungi  
[Note: [Col. 1194D] Absent from the edition.]

Mushrooms which grow above the ground, of whatever kind, are like foam and like the sweat of the earth, and harm a person who eats them somewhat, because they produce *slim* and *schum* [foam] in him.

Yet mushrooms which grow in dry air and dry earth are more cold than hot, and are somewhat better than those which grow in moist air and moist earth; but little medicinal virtue is found in them. Mushrooms growing in moist air and moist earth are neither fully hot nor cold, but tepid; and if a person eats them, they excite a bad humour in him, and they possess little medicinal virtue.

Mushrooms which grow upon certain trees, whether standing or fallen, are somewhat good as human food, like some garden herbs; they harm the eater less and are sometimes also useful as remedies. The mushroom which grows on a walnut has neither proper heat nor proper cold, but torpor; it is not suitable for eating, because it excites … [lacuna].

But if a worm develops in someone, before that worm is alive, take the *swam* which grows on a walnut, while it is new—that is, freshly taken from the tree—and hold it over boiling water so that it becomes hot and moist. Apply it, hot and moist, often to the swelling; that swelling, where worms are beginning to grow, will disappear. But if the worm has grown so that it is alive, dry the same *swam* in a hot oven without coals, reduce it to powder, and apply that powder frequently to the ulcer; those worms will die.

The mushroom which grows on a beech is hot and is good to eat for both the sick and the healthy. A person whose stomach is chilled or full of *slim* should take a fresh beech mushroom, cook it in water with good herbs and a little fat, and, after dining, eat a little of it sufficiently and often. It warms his stomach and removes *slim* from it.

Likewise, if a pregnant woman is exhausted, so that she is sluggish, heavy, and oppressed in body by the burden of childbirth, she should take a beech mushroom and cook it in water so thoroughly that it entirely breaks down. Then strain it through a cloth; with the resulting juice, adding sufficient fat, make *suffen* [a broth or soup]. Let her eat this once or twice daily after dining, and she will be more gently delivered from the pain of her labour.

The mushroom which grows on *holder* [elder] is cold and is not fit for a person to eat, so that anyone who eats it is weakened. Nor is it very useful medicinally.

The mushroom which grows on willow is hot and good to eat. Whoever has pain in the lung and from it *demphet* in the chest should cook the mushroom in wine, add a little cumin and a little fat, sip that broth, and also eat the mushroom itself. This mushroom, eaten in this way, also alleviates pain of the heart and pain of the spleen, because the heart sometimes hurts because the stomach, lung, and spleen affect it with bad humours.

But if you wish to take a purgative drink, take a fresh willow mushroom, dry it either in the sun or in a hot oven, and powder it. Then, when you wish to take the drink, take stramonium, add powder of this mushroom to the weight of a coin, and milk of *springwurtz* to the weight of an obol; mix them together and take this drink fasting, as one takes other customary potions, and it will purge you. For the powder of this mushroom tempers the stramonium and springwurtz and searches out bad humours in a person like good spices.

If anyone has *wisza* in the eye, let him dry a willow mushroom in the sun. Then, whenever he wishes to treat the *wisza* of the eyes, let him put it in water for a short time, shake out the water which it absorbs, and then, with a feather, apply the juice which it contains to the eyelids in strokes, so that it touches the inside of the eyes a little. Let him do this for three or five nights when going to sleep, and he will be cured.

The mushroom which grows on a pear-tree is cold and moist, and neither harms nor benefits a person as food. But a person whose head is *grindig* should take a fresh pear-tree mushroom, press its juice into *baumoleum* [tree-oil], discard the mushroom, and frequently anoint his head with that tree-oil; he will be cured.
