Whoever has scabrous nails should take from the pear mushroom a piece as broad as his nail where there is *grinte*, dip it in the gall of an ox—not of a cow—and, when the part soaked in this gall which he has placed upon his nail has dried within, dip it again in the same gall; the nail will grow beautiful there.

The mushroom which grows on aspen is hot and slimy, is unfit for human food, and has no medicinal use.

### Chapter 173.—On Wichwurtz  
[Note: [Col. 1195D] Absent from the edition.]

Wichwurtz is more cold and moist than hot. A person who has burning fevers, that is, *brinnende fiber*, should take Wichwurtz and twice as much basilica, cook them in pure wine, allow it to cool, and drink this fasting each morning and at night when going to sleep. Let him continue until he is cured.

### Chapter 174.—On Aloe  
[Note: [Col. 1195D] Compare below, chapter 224.] [III, 6]

[Col. 1196B]

Aloe. The juice of this plant is hot and possesses great power. If anyone has severe daily fevers in the stomach, let him make a *beneduch* with aloe in hemp and place it upon the stomach and above the navel; the fever will cease. For its smell strengthens the body inwardly, but [perhaps “not”] the head; rather, it purges the exhaustion which is in a person’s head.

Whoever has a cough, that is, *husten*, should place this same prepared *beneduch* with aloe upon his chest, so that he also receives its smell through his nostrils, and the cough will cease.

Likewise, whoever has *ridden* should take juice of horehound; or, if it is winter, take its powder and more aloe; also more liquorice than *lorber* [laurel], cook these in wine, strain through a cloth, and add *honigwurtz* [honeywort]. When he is troubled by *ridden*, he will quickly be cured, whatever kind of *ridde* it may be, except quartan fever.

Whoever has *gelsucht* should put aloe in cold water and drink it in the morning and when going to sleep. Let him do this three or four times, and he will be cured.

[Note: [Col. 1195D] In the edition this chapter is presented very briefly as follows: “The aloe-tree is hot. A person who has fevers in his stomach, and who suffers from daily, tertian, or quartan fevers, should put some of this wood into his drink, and they will improve.”]

### Chapter 175.—On Frankincense  
[III, 8]

Frankincense is more hot than cold, and its scent rises without fire [“is useful,” ed.], because it clears the eyes and purges the brain. Take frankincense, powder it, add to it a little fine flour and also egg-white [Note: [Col. 1196D] “And also egg-white” omitted in the edition], make little cakes, and dry them in the sun or by a hot brick. [Note: [Col. 1196D] “Or by a hot brick” omitted in the edition.] Afterwards apply them often to your nostrils. Their scent strengthens you, clears your eyes, and fills your brain.

Whoever has pain in the head, so that he thinks his head is splitting, should place a little cake prepared as described above upon each temple and bind it moderately with a cloth when going to sleep; the headache will cease.

Whoever has daily fevers should take frankincense and *Romischmyntza*, pound them together, apply them often above his navel, and bind them with a cloth so that they grow warm; he will be cured. [“Because fevers afflict the stomach and liver,” added by the edition.]

### Chapter 176.—On Myrrh  
[III, 7]

[Col. 1197A]

Myrrh is hot and dry. If you wish to carry myrrh with you, first warm it in the sun or over a brick heated by fire, so that it melts slightly [Note: [Col. 1197D] “Or over a brick … melts slightly” omitted in the edition], that is, *zufliesze* [flows or melts]; then keep it beside you, so that it warms from your flesh and sweat. It drives away from you phantoms, magical arts, invocations of demons, evil words, and the harmful operations of herbs, so that they can injure you less—provided that you have neither eaten nor drunk magic.

Whoever burns with lust should rub his chest and belly with it, and it drives from him the excess of lust. The smell of myrrh also drives lust from a person, but does not make his mind cheerful; rather, it oppresses, burdens, and makes it sad. Therefore, whoever keeps myrrh with him should also carry *gebrant* [burnt] gold, because this makes a person’s mind cheerful.

When severe fevers attack a person, if myrrh is then given to him to drink in hot wine, the fever ceases. Likewise, if lust attacks someone and he eats myrrh, it extinguishes lust in him; but it makes him very dry. Therefore it is neither proper nor useful for anyone to eat it except in great necessity.

### Chapter 177.—On Balsam  
[III, 5]

Balsam is of royal nature and is very hot and moist. It must be used medicinally with such moderation and great caution that its strength does not harm a person [Note: [Col. 1197D] “That its strength … harm a person” omitted in the edition], just as noble persons ought to be honoured and feared lest they be provoked to anger.

Whoever has severe fevers in the stomach should take a little balsam, add a sufficient amount of *baumoleum* [tree-oil], and more deer marrow than that oil; make an ointment from them and anoint himself with it around the stomach, and it will remove the fevers from him.

If anyone is frantic, take the same ointment and anoint his temples and *nack* [the back of the neck; “occiput,” ed.], without touching either the crown of his head or his brain, lest they be harmed by its strength. [Note: [Col. 1197D] “Lest they be harmed …” omitted in the edition.] He will return to reason and health.

Whoever is *virgichtiget* should add a little balsam to *paulum* [“paulinum,” ed.] or to other good electuaries and eat it; the *gicht* in him will cease. [Note: [Col. 1197D] The remainder is omitted in the edition.]

Dead bodies are preserved for a rather long time in balsam so that they do not rot. Likewise balsam is a strong and formidable liquid for all constitutions, and they must be properly tempered with it; otherwise they are easily thrown into disorder by it.

### Chapter 178.—On Honey  
[Note: [Col. 1197D] Absent from the edition.]

Honey. If a person is fat and has thick flesh, frequent consumption of honey produces wasting in him. But if he is lean and dry, cooked honey harms him. If anyone eats honeycomb with wax, it excites melancholy in him, harms him thus, produces heaviness in him, and causes melancholy to grow within him.

### Chapter 179.—On Sugar  
[Note: [Col. 1198D] Absent from the edition.]

Sugar, while still raw, that is, before it has been prepared for any human use, should be dried in the sun in summer or over a heated stone in winter. When it is dry, if someone afterwards eats or drinks it, it refreshes him. If someone has pain in the brain or chest and is so obstructed that he cannot purge himself or bring anything up by spitting, eating or drinking it clears his brain and opens his chest for purgation.

### Chapter 180.—On Milk  
[Note: [Col. 1198D] Milk and butter are discussed in the edition in the chapter “On the Cow.” See below, chapter 14 of Book VII, *On Animals*.]

Milk of cows, goats, and sheep—and all milk—is more wholesome in winter than in summer, because then it does not draw into itself the variety of humours as it does in summer. Healthy persons who consume milk in summer are somewhat harmed by it; but if they are sick and weak, let them eat a little milk.

If healthy persons wish to consume milk in winter, let them take the root of *eyter neszeln* [nettle], dry it thoroughly, put it in the milk, and consume it, because the bad humours in the milk are restrained by the nettle. But if sick and weak persons desire milk in winter, let them boil it and add dried nettle. In summer, however, nettle should not be put into milk, because at that time it itself contains humours, juices, and greenness; if it were then put into milk in this way, the milk would be harmed by its fresh juice.

### Chapter 181.—On Butter

Cow’s butter is better and more wholesome than butter of sheep or goats. A person who is *dunphig*, who coughs, or whose body is dry should eat butter: it heals and refreshes him inwardly—that is, it gives sustenance (*labet*) to one who is sick and dry.

For a healthy person, or one whose body has moderate flesh, butter is good and wholesome to eat. But if he has fat flesh, let him eat it moderately, lest his weak flesh grow more swollen.

### Chapter 182.—On Salt  
[Note: [Col. 1198D] Compare below, chapter 2 of Book II.] [I, 3]

Salt is very hot and somewhat moist, and is useful for many human purposes. If someone eats food without salt, it makes him inwardly tepid; but if he eats it suitably seasoned with salt, it strengthens and heals him. Whoever eats excessively salty food is made inwardly dry and harmed; then salt falls upon the lung like sand and dries it, because the lung seeks moisture, harms the lung, and *demphet* [oppresses; “oppresses,” ed.] it. If it then also falls upon the liver, it somewhat harms that too, although the liver is strong and although salt prevails.

Therefore all food ought to be salted so that the food has more taste than the salt is perceptible within it. Salt roasted over fire is more wholesome than raw salt because the moisture which was in it has been dried out; if one eats it moderately in bread or with any food, it is good and wholesome for him.

[“Salt is like blood and like the flower of waters; therefore it gives strength to one who uses it moderately, but to one who uses it immoderately it is like a flood and a storm.” Added by the edition.]

Bright salt has greater heat than other salt, and also some moisture. It is [useful] for human use and for all remedies: if a little is added to them, they are so much the better; it is also more precious than other salt, just as spices surpass other herbs.

If a person eats a little of this salt with food or bread, and not without other seasoning, it strengthens and heals him and helps his lung. But if he eats it immoderately and without moderation, it causes his lung to *welhet* within him and [weakens, ed.] and harms it.

[For it sweats from the most powerful force of the moisture of waters and earth; therefore it gives strength through its good heat and good powers to one who uses it moderately, but overwhelms one who uses it immoderately like a sudden wave. Added by the edition.]

The reason why a person suffers great thirst when he has eaten much salt is that salt dries his lung and dries up the good humours in it. Then the lung and humours seek moisture, and so the person thirsts. If he then drinks much wine to quench his thirst, he brings madness upon himself when he drinks wine excessively [“as Lot did,” added by the edition]. Therefore it is healthier and more wholesome for a person to drink water after thirst than wine, in order to quench it.

### Chapter 183.—On Vinegar  
[Note: [Col. 1199D] Absent from the edition.]

Vinegar is made from wine and is suitable for all foods, provided that it is added to foods in such a way that their flavour is not taken away but only a slight taste of vinegar is discernible in them. Vinegar thus taken with a little food purges foulness in a person, diminishes humours in him, and makes a straight passage for food within him.

But if so much vinegar is added to food that the flavour of vinegar overcomes the flavour of the food, so that the food tastes more of vinegar than of its own flavour, it harms the person eating it. For its heat cooks the food a second time in the person and makes it so hard that it can scarcely be digested.

If anyone has broken *orfime* in his body, let him take *eszigkalp*, which lies in vinegar, press out the vinegar as cheese is pressed, allow it to dry, reduce it to powder, and put this powder upon the broken *orfime*; they will dry up and heal. But if the *orfime* have not burst, then apply the same *kalp* with its juice over them, put it also upon them, bind a cloth over it, and it will disappear (*virswindet*).

Vinegar made from beer is not as good as that made from wine; it is also tepid and weak, readily causes fever in a person, readily hardens his stomach, and is therefore of little value to the eater.

### Chapter 184.—On Meranda  
[Note: [Col. 1199D] Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1200A]

Whoever wishes to make *meranden* should cut thin bread into pieces in wine, beer, or water, allowing the liquid to pass sufficiently through the bread; then let him eat it, because bread softened in this way is more pleasant and can be digested more easily.

For if someone merely dips bread and eats it immediately, before it has been permeated by the moisture of these liquids, it weighs upon and constricts him inwardly and cannot easily be digested. But wine-meranda is strong, makes a person somewhat dry within, and does not greatly benefit him, even though it does not greatly harm him.

Beer-meranda is more wholesome than wine-meranda because the juice of bread is joined with the nearly related juice of beer and does not make a person dry within; nevertheless, it does not benefit him greatly. Water-meranda is more wholesome than beer-meranda, because it is pleasant and light in the stomach and can be digested pleasantly and lightly, like soft food which passes easily and harmlessly through a person.

Frequent meranda does not benefit one who has a hot and strong stomach, because it chills and dries the heat of his stomach. Nor does it greatly benefit one with a cold stomach, because his stomach is chilled all the more by it and becomes somewhat hardened. It also does not greatly benefit those with weak and delicate stomachs, because it somewhat burdens them; yet it removes and diminishes *slim* from them.

### Chapter 185.—On Eggs  
[Note: [Col. 1200D] Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1200C]

All eggs are more cold than hot and can produce powerful injury. They are harmful to eat because they are sticky and slimy—that is, *slimechte*—and almost like poison. A person should not eat them, because if he did, *orfime* and the bad worm which eats a person would readily grow in him.

The eggs of domestic hens may be eaten, but moderately, because they harm a person’s weak internal organs as untempered and uncooked flour does: they cause *seick* that clings to them, *sliri*, and putrefaction in his stomach. A person with healthy internal organs can indeed overcome them if he eats them, but should eat them moderately, because he will readily become ill from them.

For a healthy person soft eggs are better than hard ones, which make his stomach hurt; for a sick person neither soft nor hard eggs are fit to eat. But if a sick person wishes to eat eggs, let him pour a little wine into water, boil it in a pan, break the eggs into that water, throw away the shells, cook them thus, and eat them cooked. They will not harm him, because the poison and putrefaction in them are cooked away by fire.

An egg roasted with its shell over fire is better and more wholesome to eat than an egg boiled in water with its shell, because the fire draws the putrefaction in it out through the shell, whereas water does not remove its putrefaction because the shell is on the outside.

The yolk of an egg is healthier to eat than its white, and a moderately hard yolk is better food than one that is wholly soft. If anyone eats a raw egg, it harms him greatly because it generates putrefaction in him.

Goose eggs by themselves are harmful to eat unless they are cooked with some other food. Duck eggs are likewise bad to eat and harm a person, but they are more wholesome and better than duck flesh, because all the foulness in a duck remains in its flesh and does not pass wholly into its eggs.

### Chapter 186.—On Pitch  
[Note: [Col. 1201D] Absent from the edition.]

Pitch is very hot and is wholesome in vessels containing drink. If maggots are eating a person, put pitch on the place of the ulcer; it draws those worms to itself so that they may be pulled out and scraped away. Once they have been removed, put pitch over it again, and do this until they have all been removed. After the flesh has been cleansed of worms, anoint that spot with *baumoleum* and other good ointments, and it will heal.

### Chapter 187.—On Hartz  
[Note: [Col. 1201D] Absent from the edition.]

Hartz is tepid; and a vessel in which it is placed is not wholesome, because it afflicts the head and produces *dum* in the head.

### Chapter 188.—On Sulphur  
[Note: [Col. 1201D] Absent from the edition.]

Sulphur is hot and, in burning as in cooking, attracts bad humours to itself. It has no medicinal value unless *virgibnisse* or *zauber* [magic] are prepared for someone, or unless someone has phantoms: if sulphur is burned there, its smoke is so strong that it weakens all these things for that person, so that they inflict injuries upon people all the less—just as, where there are two wicked companions, one overcomes the other by despising him.

### Chapter 189.—On Vigbona  
[Note: [Col. 1201D] *Lupinus albus* (white lupin). Absent from the edition.]

Vigbona is cold. Whoever has pain in the internal organs, so that they seem almost swollen, should grind vigbona into flour, add a little powdered bread and a little fennel seed, or a little lovage juice, and cook it with water as a food. Let him eat a little and do this often; it heals weak internal organs.

### Chapter 190.—On Kicher  
[Note: [Col. 1201D] *Cicer arietinum* (chickpea).] [II, 10]

[Col. 1201D]

Kicher is hot and pleasant, light and pleasant to eat, and does not increase bad humours in the eater. Whoever has fevers should roast kicher on live coals and eat it; he will be cured.

### Chapter 191.—On Wisela  
[Note: [Col. 1202D] *Ervum ervilia* (bitter vetch).] [II, 11]

Wisela is cold and also dry; when eaten it excites fevers, chills the stomach, and is of little use for medicine.

### Chapter 192.—On Wichim  
[Note: [Col. 1202D] *Vicia sativa* (common vetch).] [I, 12]

Wichim is cold and is not fit for human food, though it does not greatly harm livestock. If a person’s flesh boils up between skin and flesh, so that an eruption like *impetigo* [“wart,” ed.] develops there, take wichim, cook it in water, and apply it hot to that place. The rising eruption, which began to coagulate there from corrupt humours, will disappear.

### Chapter 193.—On Millet  
[Note: [Col. 1202D] *Panicum miliaceum* (millet).] [II, 13]

Millet is cold and not useful as food, because it neither increases blood or flesh in a person nor gives him strength. Instead, it fills his swollen belly and lessens hunger because it has no taste of nourishment. It also makes a person’s brain watery, makes his stomach tepid [“and sluggish,” added by the edition], stirs up a storm among the humours in him, and is nearly like a useless field-herb, not wholesome for human consumption.

Whoever has pain in the lung should heat millet on a heated stone, powder it, add twice as much powdered scolopendria, and eat it often with a morsel of bread, both fasting and after dining; he will be cured.

### Chapter 194.—On Linseed  
[II, 15]

Linseed is hot and not suitable for eating. Whoever has pain in the side should cook linseed in water, dip a linen cloth into that hot water, and, without the seed itself, place the cloth often upon his side. The pain, however severe, is somewhat eased and relieved.

Likewise, whoever has pain in the side should take linseed and a slightly smaller quantity of gum from the peach-tree, so that the linseed exceeds the gum by one fourth. Cook them in a pan with common *glut* [“glue,” ed.]. Then pound pear-tree mistletoe in a mortar for its juice, so that there is more of this juice than of the aforesaid gum. Put this juice and deer marrow, in a greater quantity than the aforesaid gum or pear juice, into the pan with the linseed and gum, and bring it to the boil again.

If he does not have deer marrow, let him add the fat of a young bull in the same proportion in which the deer marrow should have been used. When this is done, strain it through a cloth pierced everywhere with pinholes, pour it into a new waxed earthenware vessel, and frequently anoint the painful side with it by the fire.

Whoever has been burned anywhere on his body by fire should cook linseed thoroughly in water, dip a linen cloth into the water, lay it hot upon the burned place, and it draws out the burn.

### Chapter 195.—On Balsamita  
[Note: [Col. 1202D] *Tanacetum balsamita* (costmary).] [II, 45]

Balsamita is more warm than cold. But if a person’s knowledge and understanding are emptied by many and varied thoughts, so that he is driven into madness, let him take balsamita and three times as much fennel, boil them together in water, discard the herbs, and drink that same cooled water frequently. He should avoid dry foods, but eat good and delicate ones that supply him with juice for blood [good blood, ed.]. He should also eat gruels made with fine flour, butter, or fat, but not oil, because oil, by filling the brain, would draw phlegm to it. He should not drink wine, because it would further disperse the dispersed humours within him; nor should he drink plain water, because it would lead his understanding into still greater emptiness. For three days [the aforesaid period, ed.], however, he should drink a beverage and beer, and cover his head with a cap or felt [filter, ed.] made of pure wool, so that the brain may be warmed gently and gradually.

And a person who has eaten or drunk poison should immediately take equal weights of balsamita, rue, and pandonia; crush them in a mortar, express their juice, then take no less than twice as much of the purgative juice as of these, add it to the aforesaid juice, mix them together, strain it through a cloth, and drink it fasting. When he drinks it, he should sit in a warm place, lest he become chilled; for if he is cold at that time, it will be dangerous for him. After drinking it, he should immediately drink a beverage prepared from honey; and he will either vomit up the poison he has taken through nausea, or it will pass out through his bowels, and he will be freed.

Whoever has many lice should crush balsamita with lard, mix them together, and anoint himself with it about his neck and armpits; the lice will die. As balsamita resists poison, so it is also hostile to lice.

Further, if leprosy begins to grow in a person, let him boil balsamita in water, add sufficient fat, prepare food thus, and eat it frequently; it drives leprosy from him. But a person suffering from a tertian fever should take balsamita and greater *hufflatichen* in equal weight, and three times as much radish as the combined amount of these two; boil these in wine and strain them through a cloth. Let him take twice as much clove (*garlofel*) and one third as much ginger (*zinzebri*) as the combined amount of the two herbs; reduce these to powder, and from them, together with the aforesaid strained wine, prepare a pure drink. Let him use it during the attack itself and for the following nine days, so that he may be helped more fully.

## Chapter 196.—On *Stutgras* [II, 53]

The smaller kinds of *stutgras* are cold and weak in their nature; they produce weak humours in weak persons, increase melancholy, are difficult to digest, and are unsuitable for human food, because their greenness is bad.

## Chapter 197.—On *Stur* [II, 54]

*Stur* is more cold than warm; it neither greatly benefits nor greatly harms one who eats it. Of itself it has no powers; and because it is so useless, when added to any other herbs it sometimes helps to expel certain useless humours.

## Chapter 198.—On Wild Lettuce

(See below, chapter 91, col. 1165, where the same material appears with a few changes and also occupies a more suitable place among the various kinds of lettuce. We supply from chapter 198 certain things lacking in chapter 91.)

## Chapter 199.—On *Gerla*  
[Note: [Col. 1203D] *Sium sisarum*.] [II, 62]

*Gerla* is warm and dry. Eaten moderately, it neither greatly helps nor harms; but if someone ate much of it, its warmth and dryness would bring on fevers in him and injure his internal organs. Whoever has delicate facial skin, so that it cracks easily, should take *gerla*, crush it in a mortar, and add oil to it after it has been crushed. Then, at night when he goes to bed, he should anoint his face with it, and continue until he is healed.

## Chapter 200.—On Parsnip  
[Note: [Col. 1204D] *Pastinaca sativa*.] [II, 66]

Parsnip is cold and serves as nourishment for a person. It neither greatly benefits health nor harms it; but when eaten it merely fills the person’s stomach.

## Chapter 201.—On *Borith* [II, 72]

*Borith* is warm and moist. A person whose sight is dim should take a red silk cloth, crush *borith*, spread it over the cloth, and place it thus smeared upon his eyes at night. Let him do this often, and it will drive away the dimness of his eyes. If someone touches the inside of his eyes with the same ointment, it will not harm them. But if there is a white or green colour in that same silk, let him take the juice of *borith* in it, smear it upon felt [filter, ed.], place it about his whole neck, over the back of his head, and up to his ears—but not over the ears—and bind it there. Let him do this often, and the ringing of his ears will cease. If someone is oppressed in the chest, let him steep *borith* a little in wine, though only moderately, because it drives away the harmful humours that injure the lungs. [And one who suffers internally in the body from ulcers of the internal organs, supplied from the edition,] should take wheat bran, heat it in a pan with *borith*, put it upon a cloth, and lay it, while hot, all around his belly and navel; and he will be cured.

## Chapter 202.—On Spike

(See chapter 25, col. 1140, where this is repeated verbatim.)

## Chapter 203.—On Houseleek [II, 86]

Houseleek is cold and is not useful for human food, because it is of a fatty nature. If someone is deaf in the ears, so that he lacks hearing, let him take the milk of a woman who has borne a male child, when ten or twelve weeks have passed since she bore her son; add a little houseleek juice to this milk; and have three or four drops of it put gently into his ear. Let this be done regularly, and he will recover his hearing.

## Chapter 204.—On Bryony

(This is the same as chapter 43, col. 1146, under the heading “On *Stichwurtz*.”)

## Chapter 205.—On Polypody  
[Note: [Col. 1205D] *Polypodium vulgare*.] [II, 93]

Polypody is warm and dry. If a person suffers pain in the internal organs, is thin, and is not seriously ill, let him take polypody, add sage amounting to one third of it, reduce it to powder, and eat this powder; it diminishes harmful humours. But if the same person is seriously ill, let him boil wine with honey over the fire, allow it to cool after straining it through a cloth, add the aforesaid powder, and drink it. But a person whose internal organs are healthy and who has fleshy bodily fat should neither eat this powder nor drink the beverage, lest the healthy humours in him be weakened.

## Chapter 206.—On *Vehedistel* [II, 110]

*Vehedistel* contains in itself the coldness that comes from dew and is very useful. If someone suffers a stabbing pain (*stechen*; *stechedo*, ed.) in the heart or in any other limb, let him take *vehedistel* and a slightly smaller amount of *orechter salben*, make them into juice with a little water, and drink it immediately at the hour when he is afflicted by the stabbing pain; he will fare better.

## Chapter 207.—On Lesser Celandine  
[Note: [Col. 1205D] *Ficaria verna*.] [II, 164]

Lesser celandine is cold and moist. A person suffering burning fevers should boil lesser celandine and twice as much basilisk herb (*basilisca*) in pure wine, allow it to cool, drink the wine fasting every day, and do the same at night when he goes to bed, until he is healed.

## Chapter 208.—On *Weyt* [II, 165]

*Weyt* is cold, and this coldness is very sharp. A person afflicted in his body by paralysis of whatever severity should boil *weyt* strongly in water and strain it through a cloth, discarding the herb. Then let him put vulture fat and half as much deer tallow into the aforesaid water, boil them together, make an ointment from them, and anoint himself with it frequently; the paralysis will cease.

## Chapter 209.—On *Hymelsloszel*  
[Note: [Col. 1205D] *Primula officinalis*.] [II, 166]

*Hymelsloszel* is warm and has all its greenness from the sharp force of the sun. Some herbs are especially strengthened by the sun, others by the moon, and still others by both sun and moon together; but this herb receives its powers particularly from the sun’s strength. Hence it restrains melancholy in a person. For when melancholy arises in a person, it makes him sad and troubled in his disposition, and causes him to utter words against God. When aerial spirits see this, they run to him and often drive him into madness by their persuasions. Therefore, let that person put this herb upon his flesh and near his heart, so that he may be warmed by it. The aerial spirits that afflict him, disdaining the power which this herb receives from the sun, will cease to trouble him.

Moreover, if someone is so oppressed by bad humours in the head that he is sometimes deprived of his understanding, let him take this herb, shave the hair from his crown, lay it there, bind it on, and likewise lay it upon his breast. Let him not remove it for three days, and he will be restored to his senses. Whoever is afflicted by paralysis throughout his body should put this herb in his drink, so that it imparts flavour, and drink it frequently; he will be cured.

## Chapter 210.—On Greater *Hufflatta*  
[Note: [Col. 1206D] *Tussilago Petasites*.] [II, 169]

Greater *hufflatta* is cold and moist, and for this reason grows vigorously. By its very sharpness and coldness, when placed upon ulcers, it draws out harmful humours. If someone has scrofulous swellings on his body, before they break open, let him pluck this herb near its stem, to the width of the swellings, discard the rest, spread honey upon the part he has retained, and lay it thus on the swellings for three days and nights. After it has dried out, let him apply a fresh one in the same way, and the swellings will begin to diminish. On the fourth day, let him temper and mix wheat flour with honey, make a preparation to the width of the same swellings, first apply *ackeleia* to them, then place on top the honeyed mass of flour. Let him do this daily for nine days and longer, until they disappear.

## Chapter 211.—On Lesser *Hufflatta*  
[Note: [Col. 1206D] *Tussilago Farfara*.] [II, 170]

Lesser *hufflatta* is warm. If someone has eaten immoderately of different foods and his liver is injured and hardened, let him cut this herb, together with twice as much plantain root and an amount of *mus* found about mistletoe on a pear tree equal to the lesser *hufflatta*, into small pieces. [Let him pierce these pieces with an awl or another small instrument; insert into these holes the aforesaid *muesz*; and put them in pure wine. But let him take, in the weight of a coin, the swelling that grows on either a leaf or a small branch of walnut, like a bean or pea, and put this into the aforesaid wine. Let him drink it both after eating and fasting—not boiled, but merely steeped in wine—and his liver will be cured. Addition in the edition.]

## Chapter 212.—On Asarabacca [II, 1167]

Asarabacca is warm and dry and possesses certain powers of spices, because its greenness is pleasant and useful. Thus, if someone who has long been ill and whose flesh wastes away drinks water warmed with it [bathes in water warmed with it, ed.], and frequently eats it cooked in broth, with meat, or with little cakes, it will greatly benefit him, because its good juice heals a person inwardly.  
[Note: [Col. 1206D] “Because—heals” is lacking in the edition.]

If someone makes lye with it and washes his head frequently with it, it drives illnesses from his head by its good powers and prevents him from becoming ill. Further, if bad humours afflict a person’s head like smoke, so that his ears ring as with the sound of waters, let him boil asarabacca in hot water and, after expressing the water, apply it hot around his head. By its good powers the herb diminishes the smoke in his head and opens his hearing in the ears.

Likewise, a person who suffers pain in the chest and around it, or has internal ulcers, should lay cooked, hot asarabacca around his chest in a bath; he will fare better through its gentle power, tempered with the gentleness of the water.  
[Note: [Col. 1207D] “And—tempered” is lacking in the edition.]

If a person suffers from any pain in the lung—that is, as soon as pain begins in the lung—such that this pain also brings every pain to the throat and removes the clearness of the voice, let him take asarabacca, a little more basil (*basilia*), and more *humeln* than basil. Let the herbs exceed the pot by one third, boil them, and strain them through a cloth. Then let him take nutmeg in whatever quantity he can obtain, galangal (*galgan*) amounting to one third of the nutmeg, and twice as much pear-tree mistletoe as nutmeg; reduce these to powder. Let him boil this powder with the best wine in a new pot, so that the wine exceeds the powder in the pot by one third. Having done this, let him again bring the same powder and wine to the boil in the pot, adding a little honey; add to this wine the herb cooked with the aforesaid herbs, so that there is twice as much of this wine as of that water. Let him drink this moderately before food; after food, let him drink as much with wine added as he wishes [as much as he can drink in one breath, ed.]. First warm it with heated steel and drink it.  
[Note: [Col. 1207D] The remainder is lacking in the edition.]

For the warmth of asarabacca removes the decay of the lung; the coldness of basil fattens the lung and makes it sad; and the coldness of *humeln* cleanses the lung. These are tempered in warmed water, as stated above. The warmth of nutmeg and of galangal is also tempered by the coldness of pear-tree mistletoe; and, strengthened by the modified warmth of wine and the modified warmth of heated steel, they preserve the lung, so that it falls neither into wasting nor into fatness, but retains a proper balance in itself, when all these things are tempered together as stated above.

## Chapter 213.—On *Hirceswurtz*  
[Note: [Col. 1207D] Lacking in the edition.]

*Hirceswurtz* has sharp warmth and is also moist. Therefore, by its sharpness, coldness, and moisture, it restrains the evils which arise in paralysis from excessive warmth, coldness, and moisture.

## Chapter 214.—On *Scampina* [II, 172]

*Scampina* [*Scamphonia*, ed.] possesses sharp, harsh, and useless coldness; it tends toward every kind of destruction and has the nature of useless herbs.  
[Note: [Col. 1207D] “And has the nature—herbs” is lacking in the edition.]

When physicians wish to hasten and make more rapid the potions they customarily give, they add *scampina* to them; by its useless coldness and its nature it expels from a person both healthy and unhealthy humours. But if someone gives it to a person uncombined and untempered, whether as food or drink, it tears him apart inwardly in the internal organs, draws out from him both vital and mortal humours, and sends him into bodily destruction.  
[Note: [Col. 1207D] “And both vital—destruction” is lacking in the edition.]

## Chapter 215.—On *Nimphia*  
[Note: [Col. 1207D] Lacking in the edition, as are also nos. 216–222 which follow.]

*Nimphia* is cold, uncultivated, and like a useless herb; it will neither greatly benefit nor greatly harm.

## Chapter 216.—On *Catzenzagel*  
[Note: [Col. 1208D] *Hippuris vulgaris*.]

*Catzenzagel* has neither complete warmth nor complete coldness; it is lukewarm in both respects, arises from the harmful humours of the earth, and gives no power to a person who eats it. Yet if someone prepares it in such a way that flies taste it, it kills them through both torpor and its harmful humours.

## Chapter 217.—On *Zugelnich*

*Zugelnich* is warm and arouses sexual desire in a person. Its powers would be somewhat effective against both leprosy and paralysis, were it not that the warmth of this little herb, which produces sexual desire in a person, suppresses those very powers, so that it is not of much value against these conditions.

## Chapter 218.—On *Psaffo*

*Psaffo* has moderate coldness, is useful, and grows in its weak warmth. If its juice is added to ointments or potions, it makes them more useful.

## Chapter 219.—On the Herb upon Which *Rifelbere* Grow

The herb on which *rifelbere* grow has neither strong warmth nor strong coldness and is not very suitable for the body. Its fruit is cold, yet it possesses a certain kinship with blood, because it grows from that air which nourishes blood; hence it provokes menstruation. To a person who eats this fruit it neither greatly benefits nor greatly harms.

## Chapter 220.—On *Merlinsen*  
[Note: [Col. 1208D] A species of *Lemna*.]

*Merlinsen* is cold and has no strong powers by itself, unless it is added to other potent substances; when it is added to them, it diminishes useless humours in a person.

## Chapter 221.—On *Dudelkolbe*  
[Note: [Col. 1208D] A species of *Typha*.]

The herb in which *dudelkolbe* grows is more cold than warm and is not suitable for human medicine, because its juice is fatty and muddy.

## Chapter 222.—On *Hartenauwe*

*Hartenauwe* is cold and is useful to grazing livestock; but it is not very suitable for medicine, because it is an uncultivated and neglected little herb.

## Chapter 223.—On Thyme  
[Note: [Col. 1208D] *Thymus vulgaris*.] [II, 181]

Thyme is warm and dry.  
[Note: [Col. 1208D] Something appears to be missing. The edition omits what follows down to the words “diminishes the decay of that leprosy.” In the remainder also it varies considerably.]

And if someone adds good herbs and spices, it removes the decay of that same pain by its warmth and strength. For if it were not seasoned with other herbs and spices, it would pierce the same ulcers by its strength and would not heal them if applied on top. Moreover, whoever has leprosy should season this herb with other good herbs and spices, then anoint the leprosy with it; by its warmth and strength it diminishes the decay of that leprosy, whatever kind the leprosy may be.

Let him take thyme together with the earth at its roots, bring it to the boil over fire, and prepare a steam-bath from it. He should also boil thyme with the earth clinging to it in a cauldron of water and make himself a bath in this manner. Let him use this often; the warmth and dryness of the herb, together with the dry earth heated as stated above, diminish harmful humours—or it will not please God.

But if someone is afflicted with paralysis, with *stechedo*, and with that plague which afflicts human limbs as though they were gnawed and eaten away, let him take sage, twice as much spurge (*esula*), and three times as much thyme as spurge, boil them in water, then add goat tallow and twice as much old lard, and make an ointment. Let him anoint himself with it by the fire wherever he suffers pain. The warmth of sage, spurge, and thyme, tempered by the gentleness of warmed water and joined with the warmth of goat tallow and old lard, diminishes the pains of the aforesaid humours, whether excessively warm or excessively cold. This same ointment also kills lice in a person when he is anointed with it.  
[Note: [Col. 1209D] The remainder is lacking in the edition.]

If blood and water in a person’s eyes are excessively thinned, either by old age or by some illness, let him go to green grass and look upon it until his eyes become moist as if with tears; for the greenness of that grass removes what is clouded in his eyes and makes them clear and bright.

## Chapter 224.—On Aloe  
[Note: [Col. 1209D] See also chapter 174 above.] [III, 6]

The herb aloe is warm. A person who has severe ulcers—that is, scabies—on his body should take this herb, make some incisions in it and pierce them with an awl or another small instrument, insert the aforesaid *mus* into these holes, and put it into pure wine. Let him also take, in the weight of a coin, that swelling which grows either on a walnut leaf or on a small walnut branch, like a bean or pea, and put this into the aforesaid branch. Let him drink it both after eating and fasting—not boiled, but steeped in wine—and his liver will be cured.  
[Note: [Col. 1209D] These things do not agree with the beginning of the chapter. [Col. 1210D] See above, chapter 211, “On Lesser *Hufflatta*.”]

## Chapter 225.—On *Plionia* [II, 171]

*Plionia* is cold. A person frequently afflicted or shaken by paralytic gout should crush the root of *plionia* moderately, steep it in wine so that it imparts flavour, and drink it at night when he goes to bed; he will fare better.

## Chapter 226.—On *Rasela* [II, 174]

*Rasela* has sudden warmth. If worms are eating the flesh of a person or animal, let him add salt to the juice of *rasela* and apply it to the place where the worms injure the flesh; it kills them completely.

## Chapter 227.—On *Dorth* [II, 175]

*Dorth* is warm. If someone has deep and harmful scabies on the head, let him reduce *dorth* to powder, mix it with old lard, and anoint the scabies frequently; it diminishes its decay.

## Chapter 228.—On Thistle [II, 176]

Thistle is warm. If a person has eaten or drunk poison, let him powder the head, root, and leaves of the thistle and take this powder in food or drink; it expels the poison from him. If someone has *uzslecht* in his body, let him mix the same powder with fresh lard, anoint himself with it, and he will be healed.

## Chapter 229.—On Dwarf Elder  
[Note: [Col. 1210D] In edition II, 128. Lacking in the manuscript.]

Dwarf elder is cold and moist and opposed to human nature, so that it would be dangerous if someone ate it. But if a person’s head makes a sound like rushing water, let it be applied cold around his head, and he will fare better. If someone has scabby nails on his fingers or feet, let him frequently apply and bind on the fruits that grow on dwarf elder; the nails will either be cleansed or pulled out by the roots, and others will then grow again.

## Chapter 230.—On *Basilisca*  
[Note: [Col. 1210D] Edition II, 128. Lacking in the manuscript.]

*Basilisca* is cold. A person whose tongue has paralysis, so that he cannot speak, should put *basilisca* under his tongue, and he will regain speech. Also, one who has severe fevers—tertian or quartan—should boil *basilisca* in wine with honey, strain it, and drink it often fasting, after eating, and at night; the fevers in him will cease.

# Second Book: On the Elements

## Chapter 1.—On Air [I, 7]

Air is the breath that sweats into the dew of things germinating, so that all things become green; that brings forth flowers through its blowing; and that confirms all things in ripeness through its warmth. The air nearest to the arrangement of the moon and stars moistens the stars, just as earthly air vivifies and moves the earth and rational [irrational, ed.] and sentient animals according to their natures; and therefore they diminish within it. But when those animals die, that same air returns to its former state: it is neither increased from them nor increased in itself, but remains as it was before. The earthly air that moistens the earth makes trees and herbs grow green and move. Nor does it diminish in itself when it is in them, nor, when they are cut off or uprooted and it departs from them, does it increase in itself; but it remains in its condition as it was before.  
[Note: [Col. 1211D] The edition continues: “With *vre*,” chapter 59, Book III, in the manuscript.]

## Chapter 2.—On Water [I, 2]

Water is from the living fountain,  
[Note: [Col. 1211D] Numbers 20:6; Revelation 21:6.]  
and waters springing up are also from it; they wash away every impurity. If blood and water in a person’s eye are excessively thinned, whether through old age or another illness, let him go to a river, or pour fresh water into some vessel, bend over it, and receive the moisture of that water with his eyes. Thus that moisture stirs up the water of his eyes which is drying up in them and makes them bright.

Let him also take a linen cloth, dip it in pure cold water, bind it about his temples and eyes, taking care that it does not touch the eyes lest they be ulcerated by the water. Because linen cloth is gentle, the cold water will moisten the eyes so that the water of the eyes may be restored to sight by this water. For the eyes are fiery, the membrane of the eyes is thickened by fire, and when, as stated above, that membrane is touched by water, it is thinned by the coldness and moisture of the water.

Whoever wishes to have healthy and sound teeth should, in the morning when he rises from bed, take pure cold water into his mouth and hold it there briefly, so that the discoloration about his teeth may soften and the water which he holds in his mouth may wash his teeth. Let him do this often and the discoloration will no longer grow about his teeth, but they will remain sound. For discoloration clings to the teeth during sleep; when a person rises from sleep, let him cleanse it with cold water. Cold water cleanses the teeth more than hot water, because hot water makes them more brittle.

Moreover, a woman who suffers an excessive and disordered menstrual flow at an improper time should dip a linen cloth in water and frequently wrap it around her thighs, so that she may become cool inwardly and the improper flow of blood may be restrained by the coldness of the linen cloth and cold water. Then she should frequently move her veins—those in her legs, belly, chest, and arms—by gently pressing them upward with her hands, so that they may be restrained from making an improper course for the blood. She should take care neither to labour excessively nor to tire herself much by walking, lest the blood be stirred. She should also take care not to eat hard and bitter foods, lest they cause improper digestion; instead, meanwhile let her take soft and pleasant foods, so that they may heal her inwardly. Let her drink wine and beer, so that she may be strengthened by them and thus able to retain the blood.  
[Note: [Col. 1211D] The manuscript continues without division: “Just as blood and [Col. 1212D] just as the flower of waters,” etc., which belong to chapter 182, “On Salt,” above, Book I, “On Plants,” in the edition chapter 2 of Book II, “On the Elements.”]

## Chapter 3.—On the Sea [I, 4]

The sea sends forth rivers, by which the earth is irrigated, just as the human body is irrigated by the blood of its veins. Some rivers issue from the sea in violence, some in gentleness, in storms [some in storms, ed.]. Along the course of every river the earth contains some kind of ore, except where it is excessively rich, excessively dry, or rough [watered, ed.], so that ores cannot be made from it. But ores [crops, ed.] are produced from earth that is moderate in these respects.

## Chapter 4.—On *Seh* [I, 5]

[*Seh*] arises from the violence of the sea, and its bottom and sand become foul like a marsh, because it sometimes rises with storms and sometimes falls with them. Its water, whether drunk raw or used cooked in food, is not healthful for digestion or other forms of health, because it arises from sea foam. But one who makes a bath from it and washes his face prepares white and healthy skin outwardly, because it is salty; yet it harms him inwardly. Various kinds of fish from the sea occur in this same *seh*; they become healthy and fat from the saltness of its sandy bottom.

## Chapter 5.—On the Rhine [I, 6]

The Rhine is sent forth violently from the sea.  
[Note: [Col. 1212D] The edition omits “from the sea,” here and below.]  
It is therefore clear and runs through sandy land, whose sand is light and well-balanced; hence ore is also found in it. Because it issues violently from the sea, it is somewhat harsh like lye; when drunk raw, it consumes harmful and discoloured humours in a person [“consumes; but if [Col. 1212C] harmful and discoloured humours in a person,” ed.]. But if it does not find harmful and discoloured humours in a person, its water, drunk raw, more greatly ulcerates the healthy person, because it finds in him nothing to cleanse. Therefore, when food is cooked with it, it consumes the discolourations of that food and thus makes the food somewhat healthful.

Yet if this water is used in foods or drinks, or if a person’s flesh is soaked in it in a bath or by washing the face, it swells and makes it puffy, distorted, or black; it also makes meat cooked with it black and swollen, because it is harsh and quickly passes through human flesh. Fish of this river, when newly caught, are healthful to eat; but when old they quickly decay, because they are worn down by this same harshness.

## Chapter 6.—On the Main [I, 7]

The Main is driven rather mildly from the source of the sea; because it is slow, it is easily obstructed and comes to a halt. Therefore its water is also rich and its sand muddy. Its water, used in food and drink, and human flesh washed in a bath or the face washed with it, makes skin and flesh bright and smooth; it does not alter a person or make him ill. It also makes meats cooked with it white and swollen, because it is not harsh but gentle in its course. Its fish, newly caught, are healthful and can last a long time, because they are not worn down or afflicted by the gentleness [lightness, ed.] of this water; therefore their flesh lasts.

## Chapter 7.—On the Danube [I, 8]

The Danube [*Dunowa*, ed.] arises from the violence of the sea. Therefore its water is bright and harsh, and its sand is healthy and fine. Yet this water is not healthful for food or drink, because by its harshness it injures the internal organs. Through its harshness it makes human skin excessively black, though it does not make it unhealthy, because it is bright and harsh. Its fish are healthy and can keep, because the water is harsh.

## Chapter 8.—On the Moselle [I, 9]

The Moselle arises from waters flowing from the sea and is therefore light and bright. Its turbidity sinks to the bottom, whence its sand is muddy. Therefore its fish are not healthy and cannot keep for long, because they feed on filth.

## Chapter 9.—On the Na [I, 10]

The Na arises from foul waters flowing out of the sea, from which some clear streams sometimes flow. Therefore it is wholly unstable in its course, so that at one time it flows violently and at another sluggishly. Because it sometimes runs swiftly, it is quickly obstructed and quickly stops; it does not deeply cut out much sand or shore. It makes human skin white and thick, though wrinkled, and does not cause pain in the internal organs, because the violence and sluggishness of its course, though unstable, are not harmful. Its fish are fat and healthy and do not quickly decay. Its water is unstable, running now swiftly and now mildly, and does not dig into the sand; therefore its fish too are more stable, because much fodder is found in it.

## Chapter 10.—On the Glan [I, 11]

The Glan rises from other rivers; therefore its water is somewhat harsh and healthful, and is useful for foods, drinks, baths, and washing the face. Its fish are likewise healthy, but cannot keep long because of the harshness of the water. Its sand also is fine and healthful.

“*Sara* is, and the river *via* [perhaps *Seh* and the river *Na*, etc.] is at Busendorf [a town, Bossonville, on the Nied], as is the Rhine.”  
[Note: [Col. 1213D] Perhaps “*Seh* and the river *Na*, etc.” These words seem to have intruded into the text from the margin. [Col. 1214D] “*Sara*—Rhine” is lacking in the edition.]

## Chapter 11.—On Earth [I, 12]

Earth is naturally cold and has very many powers within itself. In summer it is cold beneath and warm above from the heat of the sun, because the sun then generates warmth by the power of its rays. In winter, however, it is warm within [“is warm,” supplied], since otherwise it would split from cold dryness, and it is cold above because the sun then withdraws its powers from the earth. Thus earth displays greenness in warmth and dryness in coldness. For in winter the sun is sterile over the earth and fixes its warmth upon the earth, so that the earth may preserve diverse plants; thus, through warmth and coldness, it produces every kind of plant.

Earth is white—that is, pale—black, red, and greenish. Earth which is white, that is pale and sandy, is somewhat dry and has thick moisture and large drops of rain. From this thick moisture it produces wine, fruit-bearing trees, and a little grain. For earth which retains fine moisture, like small drops, produces from that fine moisture grain, a little wine, and few fruit-bearing trees. Black earth has cold moisture in proper balance, neither too much nor too little but moderate. From this moisture it does not produce every fruit, but whatever fruit it produces, it bears fully; yet when its moisture is sometimes shaken by storms, it suffers failure in its fruit. Red earth has a proper balance of moisture and dryness; it therefore produces very many fruits, which cannot attain complete perfection because of their abundance. Because it has proper balance, it is not easily harmed by storms.

## Chapter 12.—On Calamine [I, 13]

Earth called calamine is neither moderately warm nor moderately cold, but lukewarm. It does not produce fruits to perfection, yet produces certain fruits which do not come to perfection because it is lukewarm. If added to other spices, it diminishes the discolourations of certain decays [“diminishes the discolourations of certain things after three days,” ed.].

## Chapter 13.—On *Crida* [I, 14]

Earth called *crida* [chalk, ed.] is cold and dry and produces little fruit because it is cold and dry. But when placed upon fleeces, it prevents them from rotting; it is not suitable for medicine.

## Chapter 14.—On Greenish Earth  
[Note: [Col. 1214D] Lacking in the edition.]

The earth that has neither a white, black, nor red colour, but is greenish and as if stony, is cold and dry; and therefore it does not productively yield either wine or grain or other fruits, because it lacks a proper balance in dryness. But if it produces any, they quickly fail. If anyone is weakened by numbness, as though he had *halczer* [a paralysis?], another person should take a little earth from the right and left sides [Col. 1214D] of the place where that person’s head lies in bed, and likewise earth from the right and left of his feet; and, as he removes it by digging, let him say: “You, earth, sleep in this person N. . . .” Let him place beneath that person’s head the earth removed from both sides of his head, so that it may grow warm there; and likewise let him place the earth beneath his feet, so that it may receive warmth from them. And when this same earth is put beneath his head and beneath his feet, let the person placing it say: “You, earth, grow and prosper in this person N. . . , so that he may recover greenness [vitality], in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, who is almighty and living God”; and let this be done for three days.

# THIRD BOOK: ON TREES. PREFACE

[Col. 1215]

[Col. 1215A] All trees contain either warmth or cold, just as herbs do. Yet some trees are warmer than others, and some colder, because some trees contain greater heat than other warm trees, while others retain more cold than other cold trees. For fertile trees, which bear proper fruits, such as wild trees, are colder than they are warm. [Col. 1216A] But wild trees which produce larger and more abundant fruits than others do are warmer than other wild trees. Those that produce small and few fruits are colder than other wild trees.

# HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 1215]

## CHAPTER I.—ON THE APPLE TREE [Note: [Col. 1215D] *Pirus malus* (apple tree).] [III, 19]

[Col. 1215C]

The apple tree [*Malus*, ed.] is warm and moist—of so much moisture, indeed, that it would even run off if it were not held together by warmth. [Note: [Col. 1215D] “And of so much … held together” omitted in the edition.] And whether a person is old or young, if he suffers dimness in his eyes in any [Col. 1215D] way, he should take, in springtime, leaves from that tree before it bears the fruit of that year, when they are at the first emergence of spring, because they are then sweet and wholesome, like young [Col. 1216C] girls before they bear offspring. [Note: [Col. 1216D] “When they are at the first … bear offspring” omitted in the edition.] He should pound these leaves and press out their juice; add to it an equal measure of drops flowing from the vine; put them together into a small vessel; and at night, when he goes to sleep, lightly anoint his eyelids and eyes with it, using a dipped feather, [Col. 1216D] as dew falls upon grass [Note: [Col. 1216D] “As dew … grass” omitted in the edition.], taking care that it does not enter the eyes. Then he should sprinkle the aforesaid leaves, lightly crushed, with the aforementioned drops flowing from the vine, place them over his eyes, bind them [Col. 1217A] with a cloth, and sleep thus. If he does this often, it will drive away the dimness of his eyes, and he will see more clearly.

But in spring, when the first shoots arise on the apple tree—that is, the *ceppini* [shoots]—break off one small branch without an iron cutting-tool, and draw a deer-hide strap through the shoot of the tree and branch, this way and that, so that it becomes wet with its sap. When you no longer perceive any more wetness there, make slight cuts in that shoot with a knife, that is, *hacke*, so that more moisture may flow out; and, drawing that strap at the same place and on the same branch, soak it as much as you can in that sap. Then put it in a damp place, so that it may absorb into itself still more of the sap that it received from the tree and branch. [Note: [Col. 1217D] All this is explained more briefly in the edition; much is also missing.]

If anyone is afflicted by *gicht* in the kidneys or in the *dincken* [possibly the thighs], let him bind that same [Col. 1217B] strap there against the bare flesh, so that the sap which it drew from the aforesaid apple tree may pass into his flesh; and he will be better.

And whoever suffers from a disease of the liver or spleen, from bad humours of the belly or stomach, or from migraine in the head, should take the first shoots—that is, *ceppini*—of the apple tree, put them into tree-oil, warm them in a vessel in the sun, drink it at night when going to sleep, and do this often; he will be better in the head.

And in spring, when the flowers have already appeared, take the earth around the root of the aforesaid tree and warm it at the fire. If anyone suffers in the shoulders, loins, or belly, place it thus warm upon the painful spot, and he will be better. But after the fruits of that tree have grown [Col. 1217C] and begun to enlarge, that earth is no longer effective against these illnesses, because the moisture of the earth and the sap of the tree have then ascended into those fruits; and thus they are much weaker in that earth and in the branches.

The fruit of that tree is light and can easily be digested. Eaten raw, it does not harm healthy people, because apples grow—that is, *queckent*—from the dew when the dew is in its strength, namely from the first sleep of the night, when its power extends until almost daybreak. Therefore raw apples are good for healthy people to eat, because they are produced from strong dew. But raw apples harm sick people somewhat, because they themselves are weak. Cooked or roasted, however, they are good for both sick and healthy people. But when they have grown old and contracted a skin, as in [Col. 1217D] winter, then they are good for sick and healthy people to eat raw.

## CHAPTER II.—ON THE PEAR TREE [Note: [Col. 1217D] *Pirus communis* (common pear tree).] [III, 20]

The pear tree [*Pirus*, ed.] is colder than it is warm, and is as heavy and firm in likeness to the apple tree as the liver and lung are. For just as the liver is stronger, more useful, and also more harmful than the apple tree. Its roots, leaves, and sap, however, are of no use for medicines because of its hardness; but its mistletoe is of some use medicinally. [Note: [Col. 1217D] “For just as the liver … some use” omitted in the edition.]

[Col. 1218A] Therefore, if anyone suffers in the chest and lungs—that is, has *dumphet*—let him take mistletoe from the pear tree [pear mistletoe, ed.], reduce it to powder, add to this powder another powder of licorice, and consume it often both fasting and after eating; he will be better in his chest or lung.

But one who suffers from *gicht* [paralysis, ed.] should steep sliced pear mistletoe having a pleasant taste in olive oil for three days and nights. Afterwards, let him melt at the fire twice as much deer tallow as oil, place well-pounded and crushed spike nard in that tallow for two days and nights, then pound the oil strongly with the mistletoe that was steeped in it, and press out the juice through a cloth. He should also lightly melt the deer tallow with the spike nard again over the fire. [And wherever paralysis rages in a person, let him anoint him with it, [Col. 1218B] and it will be driven away, unless the foundation of death is there. Added in the edition.]

The fruit of the pear is heavy, weighty, and harsh. If anyone eats it raw to excess, it produces migraine in his head and makes *dumpfen* [“fumes,” ed.] in his chest. [Note: [Col. 1218D] What follows as far as “Therefore, whoever wishes to eat pears,” etc., is omitted in the edition.] For the liver and lungs draw from its sap and take some of it into themselves, so that that sap hardens around the liver and lungs like lead dross or *winsten*; consequently, serious illnesses very often arise in the liver and lung. And just as a person is sometimes filled by the smell of wine, so too his breath is mingled with pear sap and takes on its harshness. Therefore, after he has eaten a raw pear, he draws breath with difficulty, [Col. 1218C] and many illnesses sometimes arise in his chest from this. For when the powers of dew decline around sunrise, pears then grow—that is, *queckent*—from that dew; therefore they produce harmful humours in a person, because they grow in diminishing dew, unless they are cooked.

Thus whoever wishes to eat pears should put them in water or roast them at the fire. Yet cooked pears are better than roasted ones, because hot water gradually cooks out the harmful sap in them; fire is too swift and does not draw out all their moisture by roasting. Cooked pears somewhat burden the person who eats them, because they reduce and break down putrefaction in him by seeking it out; nevertheless, they produce good digestion in him, because they carry out putrefaction with themselves. [Col. 1218D] [Note: [Col. 1218D] The remainder is omitted in the edition.] Apples, however, are easily digested and do not carry putrefaction away with them.

Take pears, cut them, discard their cores, and cook them thoroughly in water. Mash them into a substance like *brimus* [a mash or pulp]. Then take *berwurcz*, less galangal than *berwurcz*, less licorice than galangal, and less *peferkrut* than licorice; or, if you have no *berwurcz*, take fennel roots. Reduce these to powder, mix the powders together, put them into gently warmed honey, add the aforesaid pears, and mix them vigorously together, that is, *zutribe*. [Col. 1219A] Put this into a jar. Each day eat, while fasting, as much as one small spoon holds; after eating, as much as two spoonfuls; and at night in bed, as much as three spoonfuls. This is an excellent electuary, more precious than gold and more useful than purest gold, for it removes migraine, lessens the *dumphed* which raw pears produce in a person’s chest, consumes all bad humours in a person, and purges him as a vessel is cleansed of sediment.

## CHAPTER III.—ON THE WALNUT TREE [Note: [Col. 1219D] *Juglans regia* (royal walnut).] [III, 21]

The walnut tree [Walnut, ed.] is warm [Note: [Col. 1219D] What follows until “where worms eat a person” is omitted in the edition.], and it has bitterness. Before it bears fruit, there is bitterness and warmth in its trunk and leaves; this bitterness sends forth warmth and produces nuts. When [Col. 1219B] the kernel begins to grow, the bitterness diminishes and sweetness arises. But when sweetness has grown in the kernel, that sweetness has sharpness; thus the sweetness and sharpness mingle and produce the kernel, while bitterness and warmth remain in the trunk and make the nut grow externally.

After the enlargement and ripening of the fruits of all fruit-bearing trees, their leaves are no longer useful for medicine, because their sap passes into the fruits. Therefore, from the first emergence of the walnut tree’s leaves until its fruit grows—while the nuts are still unripe and cannot be eaten—take the tree’s leaves while they are fresh and press out their juice into the place where worms eat a person, or where maggots [*maden*] or [Col. 1219C] other worms grow in him. Do this often, and they will die.

And if worms arise in your stomach, take walnut leaves and peach leaves in equal weight, before fruit ripens on them, powder them on a hot glowing stone, and often eat this powder in an egg, in a *suffen* [broth; “sorbicio,” ed.], or in a little cooked flour; the worms in your stomach will die.

Let one in whom leprosy is beginning to grow press out the juice of these leaves, add old fat to it, and make an ointment. Then, while the leprosy is still new in him, [Note: [Col. 1219D] “Then, while … new in him” omitted in the edition.] let him anoint himself by the fire. If he does this often, he will undoubtedly be healed, unless God does not will it.

And one afflicted by *virgichtiget* [troubled by paralysis, ed.] [Col. 1219D] should take earth around the roots of that tree before its fruit ripens, heat it in the fire until it glows like stones, and make a dry bath with it. While sitting in that bath, let him pour water over the same heated earth, so that he receives warmth and sweat from it; let him bathe himself thus. Then the *gicht* which has sought to contract and break his limbs will be driven away, and his injured limbs will be healed, provided that he does this often when the *gicht* first begins to rage in him.

And one who has much phlegm in himself should take that which sweats from the walnut tree when its branches are cut—whether it is sap from the trunk or sweat—[Col. 1220A] cook it lightly in wine with fennel and a little *peferkrut*, strain it through a cloth, and drink it warm often. It expels phlegm, and he will be cleansed.

And one who has *grint* [a grievous scab, ed.] on his head should take the outer skin of the nut, namely the shell, and press its juice over the sores, that is, over the *grint* on his head. When the bitterness of the juice makes it swell, he should immediately anoint it with tree-oil, so that the bitterness may be checked. If he does this often, the *grint* will be healed.

But fever is readily aroused in a person who eats many nuts, whether fresh or old. Healthy people can overcome them, but sick people are harmed by them. The oil pressed from them is warm, makes the flesh of those eating it fat, and makes a person’s mind cheerful; but it increases phlegm, [Note: [Col. 1220D] Here the chapter ends in the edition.] so that it fills a person’s chest with *livor*, that is, *slim* [phlegm]. Nevertheless, both sick and healthy people can overcome and tolerate it when eaten; but it causes some *dumphet* in a weak chest.

## CHAPTER IV.—ON THE QUINCE TREE [Note: [Col. 1220D] *Pyrus Cydonia* (quince tree).] [III, 22]

The quince tree [*Quotanus*, ed.] is rather cold, and resembles cunning, which is sometimes useless and sometimes useful. Its wood and leaves, however, are not very useful for human use. [Note: [Col. 1220D] “And resembles cunning … human use” omitted in the edition.] Its fruit is warm and dry and has a good balance in itself. When ripe, eaten raw it harms neither sick nor healthy people; but cooked or roasted it is very beneficial for both sick and healthy people [Col. 1220C] to eat.

For one afflicted by *virgichtiget* should often eat that fruit cooked and roasted: it restrains the *gicht* in him so that it neither dulls his senses nor breaks or disables his limbs. One who emits much saliva should often eat this fruit cooked or roasted, and it dries him internally, so that the saliva is reduced. But where a person has sores or foulness, let him cook or roast that fruit and place it upon those sores with other seasonings, and he will be healed.

## CHAPTER V.—ON THE PEACH TREE [Note: [Col. 1220D] *Amygdalus Persica* (peach almond).] [III, 23]

The peach tree [*Persicus*, ed.] is warmer than it is cold, yet it has another quality in itself and bears the likeness of envy. Its juice is more useful for medicines [Col. 1220D] than its fruit. For one who has various spots in his body from various illnesses, such as *ung* [an eruption?], should take the inner bark of that tree before its fruit ripens, crush the bark, press out its juice, add a little vinegar and as much cooked honey as the combined quantity of the other two ingredients, and place it in a new earthen vessel. Wherever he has bad spots or *roseln* on his body, let him anoint himself frequently until they diminish.

And one whose breath smells badly should take peaches before their fruit is ripe, [Col. 1221A] crush them, then take a handful of licorice, a little pepper, and enough honey; cook these in pure wine and make *luterdranck* [a clarified drink]. Let him drink it often after eating and at night: it makes his breath fragrant and removes putrefaction from his body and chest.

But one in whose stomach and belly little worms grow should powder the root and leaves of *bathemen*, add twice as much powder of peach leaves gathered when the tree has begun to put forth flowers, cook this in a new pot with good, pure wine, and drink it often while fasting and at night; the worms in him will die. The fruit of that tree, however, is good for neither a healthy nor a sick person to eat, because it causes good humours to fail in a person and produces *slim* in his stomach.

Yet one who wishes to eat that [Col. 1221B] fruit should discard its outer skin and remove its kernel; put what remains into wine with salt and a little pepper. Prepared thus, it does not harm him greatly, but it does not have a good taste.

Take also the fresh inner kernels of that fruit; after discarding the shell, crush them in milk and press them through a cloth to the measure of five spoonfuls. Take galangal to the weight of three coins, licorice to that of two coins, and euphorbium to that of one halfpenny; powder them. Add *springwurtz* to the aforesaid milk of those kernels, prepare a small cake from fine wheat flour, and dry it gradually and gently either in the sun or in a warmed oven. Then mix into the aforesaid milk some of this cake to the weight of one halfpenny. Before sunrise, warm it first a little at the fire and take from it, with a spoon, the weight of five coins; [Col. 1221C] lie down in bed for a short while. It restrains *gicht* in you, removes the *dumph* from your chest, and removes *slim* [Col. 1222A] from your stomach; it also purges you gently to some extent, like a pleasant drink. If necessary, take it twice a month. On the day when you take it, abstain from heavy food, from *saligenius* bread, peas, and lentils; eat soft foods and drink wine.

Moreover, one who suffers in the chest, so that his throat is somewhat constricted, or because something bad is growing there, or because a certain harmful vapour—that is, *damph*—is present there without ulcer or swelling, should take a wheat *deick* [dough] and let *flius* from the peach flow over it. Place it warm over his throat for a short time, and do this often; he will be better. But if he suffers in the throat from an ulcer or swelling, he should not put it on, because it would cause pain.

And if a person suffers in the *halsedruszen* [neck glands], so that they are either excessively contracted or distended, he should often place upon them the same *deick* prepared as stated above, if there is an ulcer or swelling there, and he will be healed; for if his *halsadern* [neck veins] were ulcerated or swollen, and he then placed this *deick* upon them, he would be worse. But one who suffers in the head should take wheat *deick*, let *flius* from the peach flow over it as said above, and apply it warm to his crown, that is, his *schedeln* [skull], for some time; he will be better.

And one whose eyes are watery should press gum from the peach or from the shell of a nut, warm it slightly upon a glowing stone, and put it around the eyes until they are warmed by it. Let him do this every fourth day, once a day, lest, by doing it excessively, he harm them. For gum from the peach contains within itself the first power [Col. 1222C] of its wood, and draws natural moisture into itself.

[Note: [Col. 1221C]

Edition: “The peach tree is warm. A person whose eyes are frequently watery should press gum from the peach, or from the shell of a nut-tree plum, and, after warming it slightly on a glowing brick, put it around his eyes until they are warmed by it. He should do this every fourth day, and once a day, lest he harm them by doing it excessively.

“And one whose breath smells badly should crush peach leaves before its fruit ripens, take a handful of licorice, a little pepper, and sufficient honey, cook these in pure wine, and drink it often after food and at night; it makes his breath fragrant.

“But one in whose stomach and belly little worms grow should powder the root and leaves of *bachenia*, add twice as much powder of peach leaves (and let this be done when the tree puts forth flowers), cook it in a new pot with good, pure wine, and drink it often while fasting and at night; the worms in him will die.

“Likewise, against pain in either side, however it may hurt there, and against pain in the chest and paralysis, a person should lightly cook peach leaves, *balsamita* equal to their weight, basil equal to a third part of the *balsamita*, and plantain equal to a third part of the basil in water; then strain it through a cloth by squeezing it strongly. Afterwards he should warm slightly in a pan, with the aforesaid water, laurel oil, twice as much deer or goat tallow, and old fat equal to a third part of that tallow. Thus let an ointment be made; then let him anoint the painful side with it, and do this often, and he will be better.

“The fruit of the peach tree is almost tepid and is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat. But one wishing to eat that [Col. 1222C] fruit should remove the skin and kernel, put what remains in wine with salt and a little pepper added; prepared in this way, it does not harm greatly.

“Likewise, a person who wishes to be healthy should crush fresh inner peach kernels in milk and press them through a cloth to the measure of five spoonfuls. He should also powder galangal to the weight of three coins, licorice to that of two coins, and euphorbium to the weight of one halfpenny; add them to the milk of the kernels, together with juice of *citocatia*, and make a small cake of fine wheat flour. Let him dry it gradually in the sun or at an oven, and mix into it some of this cake to the weight of one halfpenny. [Col. 1222D] Before sunrise, after first warming it slightly at the fire, let him take with a spoon an amount weighing five coins and lie down in bed for a brief time; like a pleasant drink, it purges him somewhat. If the same person needs it, let him take it twice a month. On the day he takes it, let him eat soft foods and drink wine.

“But one who suffers in the throat, so that it is somewhat constricted, or because a certain harmful vapour is present there without ulcer or swelling, should take wheat paste, dissolve over it the gum flowing from the peach, place it warm on his throat for a short time, and do this often; he will be better. And if anyone suffers in the *halsadrin* [neck veins], so that they are excessively constricted or distended, let him often apply the aforesaid paste to them; if there is neither ulcer nor swelling there, he will be healed.”]

.

## CHAPTER VI.—ON THE CHERRY TREE [Note: [Col. 1222D] *Prunus cerasus et avium* (sour and sweet cherry).] [III, 24]

The cherry tree is warmer than it is cold and fully [Col. 1223A] has the likeness of a joke, which displays merriment but is also harmful. Its juice and leaves are not very useful medicinally, because they contain weakness. Its fruit, however, is moderately warm and neither very useful nor very harmful. [Note: [Col. 1223D] “And, completely … harmful” omitted in the edition.] It does not harm a healthy person when eaten, but it causes some pain to a sick person or one who has bad humours in himself if he eats much of it.

Take the fresh inner kernels of this fruit, pound them well, dissolve bear fat in a pan, and mix them together, that is, *kneyt*. Make an ointment thus, and frequently anoint by the fire with it one who has sores in his body so bad that they nearly resemble leprosy, though they are not leprosy; [Note: [Col. 1223D] “Though they are not leprosy” omitted in the edition.] [Col. 1223B] he will be healed.

One who has *biszende* [colic pains, ed.] in his belly, not caused by worms, should often eat these kernels raw, and he will be better. But one who has worms in his belly should put these kernels in vinegar and eat them often while fasting; the worms in him will die.

One who has pain in his eyes, so that they are red from pain and ulcerated, that is, *maczerech*, should take warm crumbs of rye bread and put *flius* [gum, ed.] from the cherry upon them, so that the *flius* is placed against the skin of the eyes. Let him bind it on and do this often; it draws *droppen* [drops or discharge] from his eyes, and he will be healed.

And one into whose ears some pestilence and bad humours fall, so that he becomes as if deaf and [Col. 1223C] his ears *diezent* [ring or make noise], should take the aforesaid *flius*, dissolve it over the fire in a pan, spread it warm upon rye crumbs, and at night put this *flius* with the rye crumbs into the openings of his ears. He should also surround both entire ears and his temples with the said crumbs smeared with the aforesaid gum, bind it over with a linen cloth, and do this often. The pestilence, bad humours, and *dizedo* [ringing] will be driven from his ears, and he will be healed.

## CHAPTER VII.—ON THE PLUM TREE [Note: [Col. 1223D] *Prunus domestica et insititia* (domestic and damson plum).] [III, 25]

The plum tree [*Prunus*, ed.] is warmer than it is cold, and also dry; it is *stechelecht* [prickly] like a thorn and signifies anger. [Note: [Col. 1223D] “And also … signifies anger” omitted in the edition. Of what follows, [Col. 1224D] some things are absent from the edition; most, however, may be found scattered throughout it, but arranged in another order.]

If worms eat a person’s flesh, [Col. 1223D] let him take the outer bark of that tree down to the sap, dry it and its leaves in the sun or at the fire beside a pot, or in a pot warmed by the fire, and reduce them to powder. Let him put this powder into the place where the worms eat the person.
