When the worms begin to stir because of it, so that the person feels this, let him take vinegar and a little honey, mix them together, and pour them into that place of the worms; they will die. When they have fallen dead from the wounds, dip a linen cloth in wine and place it over the sores: it draws out the putrefaction, [Col. 1224A] and the person will be healed.

Make ashes from the bark and leaves of that tree, make lye from those ashes, and if your head is *stuphete* or *wellcht* [perhaps dull or withered], wash it often with this lye. Your head will be healed and beautiful, and it will produce much beautiful hair.

And if anyone is made mad by magic or cursed words, take earth around the roots of that tree and heat it strongly at the fire until it glows somewhat. When it has been heated by the fire, immediately put a sufficient amount of rue and slightly less pennyroyal upon it, so that it receives their sap and odour; or, if you do not have pennyroyal, place green fenugreek upon it. Or, if it is winter, place the seeds of these herbs upon the same moderately warm earth. After he has eaten, surround the head, bare belly, and bare sides of that person with the same herbs, bind it over with a cloth, lay him in bed, and cover him with clothing, so that he may sweat somewhat with that earth. Do this for three or five days, [Col. 1224B] and he will be better. For when the ancient serpent hears magic [Note: [Col. 1224D] Revelation 12:9; 20:2.] and cursed words, he receives them and lays snares for the person against whom they are spoken, unless God prevents him.

Take the *flius* of that tree. If the lips of any person’s mouth swell or become inflated, that is, *erbulsent*, or if *gicht* returns to him by leaping attacks, then at night, when he goes to sleep, bind the same *flius*, slightly warmed, over the painful lips with a cloth. Do this often, and the pain will cease. [Col. 1224C] And one whose fingers and hands continually move with trembling from *gicht* should often bind this same *flius*, warm in a cloth, over the whole hand, and that swelling will cease.

The fruit of this tree is harmful and dangerous to both healthy and sick people when eaten, because it arouses melancholy in a person, increases bitter humours in him, and makes every pestilence within him boil up. Therefore it is as dangerous for a person to eat as *unkrut* [weed or noxious herb]. Thus whoever wishes to eat it should eat only a little. A healthy person can indeed overcome it when eaten, but it harms the sick.

Yet one who has a dry cough should take the inner kernels of this fruit, discard the shell, put them in wine, and let them be soaked by the wine until they swell somewhat. Let him eat them often; then prepare these also as a *suffen* [broth] in good wine, take it by sipping, and he will quickly be healed. Every kind of plum tree—whether *roszprumen*, garden sloes, *kriechen*, or the wild kind—has the aforesaid powers in its bark and leaves and the same nature in its fruit, as stated above, except that trees bearing larger fruits of this kind have stronger powers of this kind within themselves.

## CHAPTER VIII.—ON THE SERVICE TREE [Note: [Col. 1225D] *Sorbus domestica* (service tree).] [III, 26]

[Col. 1225A]

The service tree [*Esculus*, ed.] is warm and dry, but its warmth is not very useful, and in its splendour it signifies dissimulation. Its bark, leaves, and sap are not very useful medicinally. Yet throw earth that lies under this tree and around its root into gardens, and scatter it where *rupen* and *zwyfeldern* eat and devastate vegetables; because of its unpleasantness they will depart and cannot thrive there. The fruit of this tree burdens a person as if by a certain swelling weight and stirs his humours, but it is corrected [*dirigitur*, as printed] and does not produce *slim* in a person. Thus, eaten, it neither greatly benefits nor harms a healthy person, but it is of no use to sick people. [Note: [Col. 1225D] Edition: “The service tree is warm and dry. Let a person scatter in his gardens earth that is beneath this tree around its roots; little worms which gnaw vegetables depart because of its unpleasantness and cannot thrive there. Its fruit, when eaten, neither greatly benefits nor harms a healthy person, but it is of no use to a sick person.”]

## CHAPTER IX.—ON THE MULBERRY TREE [Note: [Col. 1225D] *Morus nigra* (black mulberry).] [III, 27]

[Col. 1225B]

The mulberry tree [*Mulberboum*, ed.] is cold in a good way, but “the same is,” that is, *queck?* [uncertain]. One who has scabies should cook the leaves of this tree in water and bathe in that water, or wash himself vigorously in a dry bath with that water; if he does this often, his skin will be healed.

And one who has taken poison by eating or drinking should crush these leaves and press out their juice, add slightly less *helsum* [juice of wormwood, ed.] and twice as much good, pure wine, [Note: [Col. 1225D] “And twice as much … pure wine” omitted in the edition.] boil these together, and, when it has cooled, let him drink a moderate amount after eating. He will expel the poison either by vomiting or it will pass from him through evacuation. [Col. 1225C] Its fruit is abundant, and it harms neither healthy nor sick people; rather, it benefits a person more than it harms him. [Note: [Col. 1225D] “Rather, it benefits … harms him” omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER X.—ON THE ALMOND TREE [Note: [Col. 1225D] *Amygdalus communis* (common almond).] [III, 28]

The almond tree is very warm and has a little moisture in itself. Its bark, leaves, and sap are not very useful for medicines, because all its power is in its fruit. [Note: [Col. 1226D] “And has a little … in its fruit” omitted in the edition.]

One whose brain is empty [“foolish,” *fatuum*, in the text; “empty,” *vacuum*, ed.] and whose face has a bad colour, and who consequently has pain in the head, should often eat the inner kernels of this fruit: they fill the brain and give him a proper complexion. [“Let him eat them, and he will be better,” ed.] And one who is ill in the lung and has impairment in the liver should often eat the same kernels, whether raw or cooked. They give and bring strength to the lung, because they do not in any way cause *demphent* [oppression or fumes] in a person, nor make him dry, but render him strong. [Note: [Col. 1226D] Edition: “Let him eat them often, and he will be better,” omitting the remainder.]

Hazel tree [hazel, *Corylus*, ed.] is more cold than hot, and is of little value for medicine, and signifies lustfulness [Col. 1226A] [Note: [Col. 1226D] “And is of little value for medicine—signifies lustfulness” omitted in the edition.]. Nevertheless, take its catkins—that is, the places where the flowers ought first to burst forth—dry them in the sun, reduce them to powder, and put this powder wherever there are *orfimae* in a person, and he will be cured. [Moreover, a man who has an excessive discharge of his semen, so that he does not beget offspring, should take these same large hazelnuts, and one third as much *erdpeffer* [“earth-pepper”], and as much *uvinda* as is one fourth part of the *erdpeffer*, with a little ordinary pepper; cook these with the liver of a young he-goat already mature for breeding, adding also some raw fatty pork. After discarding these herbs, let the same man eat this meat, and also dip bread in the water in which such meat was cooked and eat it; and if he does this often [Col. 1226B], he will flourish for offspring, unless the just judgment of God prevents this from happening. Added by the edition.] Its fruit, however—that is, the nuts—does not greatly harm or benefit a healthy person who eats it; but it harms an invalid, because it oppresses him in the chest.

## CHAPTER XII.—ON THE CHESTNUT TREE [Note: [Col. 1226D] *Castanea sativa*.] [III, 13]

The chestnut tree [chestnut, ed.] is very hot, but it nevertheless possesses a great power mingled with that heat, and signifies discernment. Both what is in it and its fruit are useful against every infirmity present in a human being [Note: [Col. 1226D] “But it nevertheless—present in a human being” omitted in the edition.]. But a person afflicted with *virgichtiget* [whom paralysis troubles, ed.] and thereby made irascible—for *gicht* is always accompanied by anger [Note: [Col. 1226D] “And thereby—accompanied by anger” omitted by the edition.]—should boil its leaves, husks [bark, ed.], and [Col. 1226C] fruit in water, make a bath with that water, and do this often; the *gicht* will cease in him, and he will have a gentle disposition [Note: [Col. 1226D] “And he will have a gentle disposition” ends here in the edition.].

If *schelmo* [pestilence, ed.] kills livestock [Note: [Col. 1226D] Mattioli, *Epistles* III.1, says nearly the same things about the fruits of horse chestnut.], crush its bark and put it in water so that the water acquires a flavour from it; let asses, horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, and all other livestock drink this often, and the *schelmo* will cease from them and they will be cured [“let them drink it, and the pestilence will cease from them,” ed.]. But if a horse, ox, ass, or any other animal is *verfangen* [has brought pain upon itself through excessive drinking or eating, ed.], give it the leaves to eat in its fodder if it can; or, if it refuses to eat, pulverize the leaves, throw that powder into water, and give it to drink often [Note: [Col. 1226D] “Or, if it refuses—to drink” ends here in the edition.], and it will be cured.

[Col. 1226D] But a person who makes a staff from its wood and carries it in his hand, so that the hand is warmed by it, has his veins and all the powers of his body strengthened by that warming. Frequently inhale the scent of this wood: it imparts health to your head. [Col. 1227A] And a person whose brain is empty through dryness, and who consequently suffers in the head, should boil the inner kernels of the fruit of this tree in water, add nothing else, pour off the water, and eat them frequently, fasting and after meals; his brain will grow and be filled, his sinews will become strong, and the pain in his head will thereby cease. A person who suffers in the heart, so that his heart does not advance in strength and he consequently becomes sad, should often eat these same kernels raw; they will pour into his heart a juice like *smalh* (*smalx*?), and he will advance in strength and regain gladness. A person suffering in the liver should often crush the same kernels, put them in honey, and often eat them with that honey; his liver will be healed. One suffering pain in the spleen should roast these kernels moderately by the fire [Col. 1227B], then eat them frequently while moderately warm; his spleen will become warm and tend toward complete health [Note: [Col. 1227D] “And a person whose brain—tend toward complete health” omitted in the edition.]. A person suffering in the stomach should boil the same kernels vigorously in water, break them up when cooked in that water, namely into *drab* [dregs or mash], then mix a little fine wheat flour with water in a bowl—that is, *cloppe*—add powdered liquorice and a somewhat smaller quantity of powder from the root of *stemfarn* [polypody, ed.] to the flour, boil it again with the aforesaid kernels, prepare it as a *mus* [porridge; “a dish,” ed.], and then eat it. It will cleanse his stomach [Note: [Col. 1227D] “And—will cleanse it” omitted in the edition.], make it warm, and strengthen it.

## CHAPTER XIII.—ON THE MEDLAR TREE [Note: [Col. 1227D] *Mespilus germanica*.] [III, 14]

The medlar tree is very hot and signifies pleasantness [Col. 1227C] [Note: [Col. 1227D] “And signifies pleasantness” omitted in the edition.]. Its bark and leaves, however, are of little value for medicines, because all their power is in its fruit [Note: [Col. 1227D] “Because—all their power is in its fruit” omitted in the edition.]. Nevertheless, a person who suffers from *ridden* [daily, tertian, or quartan fevers, ed.] should pulverize its root and drink this powder in warm wine, fasting, after meals, and at night, and also during the attack of that infirmity [Note: [Col. 1227D] “And also—of that infirmity” omitted in the edition.]; let him do this often, and he will be cured. The fruit of this tree is useful and good for healthy and sick persons, however much they eat of it, because it makes their flesh increase and purifies their blood [Note: [Col. 1227D] “Because—it purifies their blood” omitted in the edition.].

## CHAPTER XIV.—ON THE FIG TREE [Note: [Col. 1227D] *Ficus carica*.] [III, 15]

The fig tree is more hot than cold, will always possess heat, and cold has no power in it; it signifies fear [Note: [Col. 1227D] “And will always—signifies fear” omitted in the edition.]. Take its leaves and bark [Col. 1227D], crush them moderately, and boil them vigorously in water; then add bear fat and a somewhat smaller quantity of *augssmere*? [butter, ed.], and make an ointment. If you have pain in your head, anoint your head with it; or if your eyes are *swerent* [sore or aching], anoint your temples and the area round your eyes with it, but do not allow it to touch the inside of the eye. [Col. 1228A] Or if you have pain in the chest, anoint the chest; or if in the *lenden* [kidneys, ed.], anoint them with it, and you will improve.

But if its wood is kindled in a fire and someone is touched by its smoke, it harms him somewhat, so that he becomes *unmechtet* [enfeebled]. Or if someone carries a staff of this wood in his hand, it likewise weakens him in his powers, namely by *unmechte* [weakness] [Note: [Col. 1228D] “But if its wood—by weakness” omitted in the edition.]. Moreover, the fruit of this tree is unsuitable as food for a person healthy in body, because it makes him have pleasure and a swollen mind [changeable habits, ed.], and become *zychern* and *glusclich* [probably “arrogant” and “covetous”], so that he seeks honours, gives attention to greed, and develops changeable habits, not persisting in one settled state of mind. It is also unsuitable as food for a person’s body, because it produces *zufloszlich* flesh [excessively flowing or loose flesh] [Col. 1228B] and opposes all a person’s humours, provoking them to evil as though it were their enemy [Note: [Col. 1228D] “And become—were their enemy” ends in the edition.].

For an invalid who is failing in body it is good to eat, because he is failing in mind and body; he should eat it until he improves, and avoid it afterwards. If a healthy person wishes to eat it, he should first *beysze* it in wine or vinegar [Note: [Col. 1228D] “Season it,” ed., omitting the rest.], so that its harmful quality may be tempered; then he may eat it, though only moderately. But an invalid need not temper it in this way, that is, *beysze* it.

## CHAPTER XV.—ON THE LAUREL [Note: [Col. 1228D] *Laurus nobilis*.] [III, 16]

Laurel is hot, has a little dryness, and signifies constancy [Note: [Col. 1228D] “And has a little dryness—signifies constancy” omitted in the edition.]. Take the bark and leaves of laurel, crush them, press out their juice, and with this juice and wheat flour make *kucheln* [little cakes; “tortelli,” ed.] [Col. 1228C]. Dry these and reduce them to powder. Then make *honigwurcz* [a honey-spiced drink] with honey and water, put a little of this powder into it and drink it; or take it in another powder-drink which you drink with wine. Do this whenever you wish, and it will cleanse your stomach of every impurity without injuring it much.

Also boil the root, bark, and leaves of the same tree in water, and make an ointment from that decoction and goat’s suet. If you have pain in your head, chest, side, back, or *lenden* [kidneys, ed.], anoint the affected place with it and you will improve. The fruit of this tree is very hot and somewhat dry, and is useful for medicines [Note: [Col. 1228D] “And the fruit—is useful for medicines” omitted in the edition.]. For if anyone frequently eats it raw, it checks every fever in him. [Note: [Col. 1228D] In what follows, the edition reproduces most passages here and there, but in a changed order.] But one troubled by *gicht* and fevers should reduce these same *bachas* [berries] to powder, add half as much powder of the fruit which grows on *pinapeles* [pineapple?], or, if he has no *pinapel*, mix in powdered fenugreek to half its quantity [Note: [Col. 1228D] “And add half as much—mix in powdered fenugreek” ends in the edition.], warm this in wine—that is, *welle* [bring it to the boil]—and drink it hot. The *gicht* and fever will cease.

[Col. 1229A] Also press oil from the same berries, and anoint with it wherever *gicht* troubles your body; you will improve. If you add to this oil one third part of juice of *sibenbaum* [savin], or one third part of box-tree juice, this oil will be so much stronger and will penetrate your skin so much more swiftly in order to heal you; thus the *gicht* will cease. If you have pain in your head, crush the same berries in a mortar with a little wine poured in; with that wine anoint the crown, forehead, temples, and entire head—*bestriche* [smear]—then cover your head so that it grows warm and lie down in bed. However severely you suffer, that pain will cease.

If you suffer in the lungs, so that they are even putrefying, pulverize the same berries and frequently eat the powder with bread [Col. 1229B], and you will be cured. If you have pain in the stomach, boil the berries in wine and drink the wine hot; it removes *slim* [phlegm or mucus] from your stomach, cleanses it, and also drives fever from it. While the berries are still raw, press oil from them and touch the inner parts of your eyes with it; it removes dimness from them. Or if you have pain in the heart, anoint that place with it; if you languish in the side or back, anoint the affected place and you will improve. If you have a foul stomach and also spit unclean saliva, make little cakes with this oil and a little flour and eat them; they will cleanse the stomach, overcome foul humours, and produce sound and good humours in you.

## CHAPTER XVI.—ON THE OLIVE TREE [Note: [Col. 1229D] *Olea europaea*.] [III, 17]

[Col. 1229C]

The olive tree is more hot than cold and signifies mercy [Note: [Col. 1229D] “And signifies mercy” omitted in the edition.]. Boil the outer bark and leaves of this tree in water, then make an ointment with the water and old fat. If anyone has pain from *gicht* in the heart, back, side, or *lenden*, anoint him there with this ointment; it penetrates his skin as *smaltz* [fat] penetrates a new pot when it is set upon the fire, and he will improve [Note: [Col. 1229D] “Make an ointment, and wherever he has pain from paralysis, let him anoint himself and he will improve,” ed.].

For a person whose stomach has grown cold, boil the bark and leaves of this tree in water, strain the water through a cloth, then melt in a pan over the fire a smaller quantity of *hartz* [resin] and a still smaller quantity of myrrh—that is, *zulasze* [melt]—and add them to the aforesaid juice. Make a plaster, dip a cloth of hemp into it [Col. 1229D], lay it on his stomach, and his stomach will grow warm and produce good digestion for him.

The oil from the fruit of this tree is not very suitable for eating [Col. 1230A], because, if eaten, it causes nausea and makes other food troublesome when eaten [Note: [Col. 1229D] “And makes other food troublesome when eaten” omitted in the edition.]. But it is useful for very many medicines. When its oil is first prepared, let it be boiled over a fire; then put roses and violets into it. Thus it is useful against various fevers; and because it has been boiled over fire, it need not afterwards be set in the sun [Note: [Col. 1229D] “And because—it need not afterwards be set in the sun” omitted in the edition.—We stop here the more extensive ending of this chapter in the edition: “If anyone has pain in the head, let him make olive oil and a smaller quantity of rose-water boil in a frying-pan; let there be less fruit of nightshade than oil, and more stinging nettle than fruit of nightshade; let him grind these, strain them through a cloth, pour this juice into the frying-pan with the oil, and make it boil again. When he has done this, let him strain it once more and pour it into a new earthenware vessel. Then, whenever he has pain in his head, let him anoint the crown, forehead [Col. 1230D], and temples with the ointment and bind them round with a waxed cloth. If an ulcer or pustule causes a person acute pain, before it bursts let it be smeared with olive oil. If anyone suffers from paralysis, let him put roses into olive oil, anoint himself, and he will improve. If cramp hurts a person anywhere in his body, let him anoint himself vigorously with olive oil, and he will improve.”].

If anyone is troubled by *gicht*, let him put roses into this same oil and anoint himself wherever the *gicht* attacks his body; he will improve. But if anyone has pain in the head or *lenden*, or if a swelling arises of itself somewhere in his body without fall or blow, let him put violets into the aforesaid oil and anoint the painful place; if there is a swelling, let him anoint beside the swelling, not upon it.

## CHAPTER XVII.—ON THE DATE PALM [Note: [Col. 1230D] *Phoenix dactylifera*.—Absent from the edition.] [III, 17]

[Col. 1230B]

The date palm is hot, contains moisture, and has the same tenacity as a bruise; it signifies blessedness. A person with pleurisy should boil in water bark, wood, leaf-stalks, or leaves of this tree; after pressing out the water, place the wood and leaves, still hot, around his head, and do this often. He will recover his senses. While the leaves are green, dry them in the sun, crush them, reduce them to powder, add a little bright salt to this powder, and frequently eat the powder with your bread. It will prevent inward putrefaction and prevent evil or excessive phlegm from growing in you. But if someone cooks and eats the fruit of this tree, it imparts almost as much strength to his body [Col. 1230C] as bread does; nevertheless, if he eats too much of it, it easily oppresses and burdens him.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—ON THE CITRON TREE [Note: [Col. 1230D] *Citrus medica*.] [III, 18]

The *bontziderbaum*, that is, the tree on which the large *Bonczider* grows, is more hot than cold and signifies chastity [Note: [Col. 1230D] “And signifies chastity” omitted in the edition.]. A person with daily fevers should boil the leaves of this tree in wine, strain the wine through a cloth, and drink it often; he will be cured. The apples or fruits of this tree, when eaten, also check fever in a person.

## CHAPTER XIX.—ON THE CEDAR [Note: [Col. 1230D] *Juniperus phoenicea* and *Oxycedrus*.] [III, 10]

Cedar is hot and somewhat dry, and signifies strengthening [Note: [Col. 1230D] “And signifies strengthening” omitted in the edition.]. A person suffering from the spleen should crush branches and wood from this tree while they are green and still full of sap, grind them to powder, make an electuary from it with [Col. 1231A] boiled honey [Note: [Col. 1231D] “With boiled honey” omitted in the edition.], and eat a little after meals. His spleen will return to health. Once he is well, he should eat no more of this electuary.

A person inwardly infirm and inwardly putrefying should put this same green wood into pure wine overnight, so that the wine takes on its flavour, and drink a little of that wine after meals. The infirmity and putrefaction within his body will be cleansed [Note: [Col. 1231D] “And the infirmity—will be cleansed” omitted in the edition.] and he will be healed. Once he feels inward health, he should drink no more of that wine. For if a healthy person ate this electuary or drank this wine, he would become inwardly hard and rigid as wood, and become a *baumechte* (?) [perhaps “tree-like”] man, and would thus perish, because the power of this tree is so great that it would injure a person inwardly [Note: [Col. 1231D] “For if a healthy person—would injure a person inwardly” omitted in the edition.]. One troubled by *gicht* should eat green fruits of cedar [Col. 1231B], and the *gicht* will cease and disappear [Note: [Col. 1231D] The remainder is omitted in the edition.]. Or if he cannot preserve that fruit throughout the year, let him pulverize it, put some of the powder in water, and drink it often while fasting; the *gicht* will cease.

## CHAPTER XX.—ON THE CYPRESS [Note: [Col. 1231D] *Cupressus sempervirens*.] [III, 11]

The cypress is very hot and signifies God’s secret [Note: [Col. 1231D] “And signifies God’s secret” omitted in the edition.]. A person with pain in the stomach should take its wood, whether green or dry, cut it moderately into wine and boil it; let him drink this often while fasting, and he will improve. A person who is infirm, or even failing throughout his whole body, should boil branches with leaves in water, bathe frequently in that water, and will be healed and recover his strength.

[Col. 1231C] Take wood from the middle of the tree, which is the heartwood, and carry it always with you. The devil will avoid you all the more, because this tree, on account of its strong nature, possesses among other tree-woods a certain prosperity; the devil flees in disdain from everything endowed with power, because he himself has no power [Note: [Col. 1231D] “Because this tree—has no power” omitted in the edition.].

If a person has been ensnared by the devil or by magic, take wood from the middle of this tree, bore through it with a *nebegor* [auger, ed.], take water from a living spring in an earthen vessel, pour it through that hole, and catch it in the earthen vessel. As you pour it, say: “I pour you, water, through this hole, and in that efficacious [Col. 1231D] power which is God, so that, with the strength which belongs to you in your nature, you may flow into this person who is ensnared in his mind; and that you may destroy in him all the contrary things which are in him and restore him to that rectitude in which God placed him: to sound understanding and sound knowledge.” Then give this water to him fasting, for nine days, to drink, because he has been troubled or ensnared by the devil, phantoms, or [Col. 1232A] magic [Note: [Col. 1231D] “Because he has been troubled or ensnared” omitted in the edition.], and he will improve. For nine days it should likewise be blessed in the same manner.

## CHAPTER XXI.—ON THE SAVIN TREE [Note: [Col. 1232D] *Juniperus sabina*.] [III, 30]

The *sybenbaum* [savin, ed.] is more hot than cold, and this heat is so strong that it preserves its greenness through the year. It signifies harshness [Note: [Col. 1232D] “And this heat—is so strong—signifies harshness” omitted in the edition.]. If worms consume anyone, crush savin and press out its juice; add a little vinegar to the juice, and pour it into whatever sores the worms are consuming in a person’s body. The worms will die and cannot live. A person suffering in the lungs, whose lungs are poisonous and putrefying [Note: [Col. 1232D] “Whose lungs are poisonous and putrefying” omitted in the edition.], should take juice of this savin, add to it powdered liquorice equal in weight to half [Col. 1232B] the juice, boil it in wine with a little fat added, and drink it often. After drinking it, because it is bitter, he should immediately drink *honigwurtz* [a honey-spiced drink] over it; it removes poison and putrefaction from the lungs [Note: [Col. 1232D] “After drinking it—removes poison and putrefaction” omitted in the edition.] and he will be cured.

## CHAPTER XXII.—ON THE BOX TREE [Note: [Col. 1232D] *Buxus sempervirens*.] [III, 31]

Box is hot and so strong that it keeps its greenness throughout the year; its heat exceeds that of savin. It is also dry, and its dryness exceeds its moisture. It signifies abundance [Note: [Col. 1232D] “So strong—is dry—signifies abundance” omitted in the edition.]. A person who has *uzslecht* or *urslecht* in his body should crush its bark and leaves, press out their juice, add a somewhat smaller quantity of liquorice, warm it in pure wine [Col. 1232C], and drink it hot often. It drives the pain and poison of *uzslecht* out of the body, so that it does not enter it. Immediately afterwards he should mix a little more tree-oil with the aforesaid juice of the same tree, dip a feather in it, and gently anoint himself with it around the *uzslecht* and around its *ruse* [eruption or scab]. Let him do this often and he will be cured.

Before anointing himself in this manner, however, he must always first drink the same juice with liquorice added and warmed in wine as stated above, so that this anointing does not drive the outer foulness into the body, but rather so that this drink expels the inner foulness. Thus the man will be cured; for the juice of this tree is healthful and strong, and therefore its wood too is healthful and firm [Note: [Col. 1232D] “Before anointing himself—healthful and firm” omitted in the edition.]. A person who makes a cup or drinking-vessel from this wood, pours wine into it so that the wine takes on a flavour from the wood, and drinks it frequently: it removes fever from his stomach and makes his eyes clear. A person who often touches his eyes with this wood will have his flesh, head, and eyes thereby become so much healthier. [A person who also makes a staff from it, often carries it in his hand, frequently holds it to his nostrils [Col. 1233A] or inhales its scent, and touches his eyes with it, will have his flesh, head, and eyes become so much healthier. Added by the edition.]

## CHAPTER XXIII.—ON THE FIR [Note: [Col. 1233D] *Pinus abies*.] [III, 32]

Fir is more hot than cold and has many powers in itself. It signifies strength [Note: [Col. 1233D] “And signifies strength” omitted in the edition.]. Wherever fir wood is present, aerial spirits hate and avoid it more than other places; *zauber* [sorcery; “evil spells,” ed.] and magic are less effective and have less power there than elsewhere. Take bark and leaves of this tree, and cut very small pieces also from its wood while the tree is green and has not yet lost its sap, as it is in March and May; add sage equal in weight to half of these ingredients [Col. 1233B], boil all of this vigorously in water until it becomes thick, add butter made from cows in May, strain it through a cloth, and make an ointment.

If someone has pain in the head because he is *virgichtiget*, *hirnwudig* [mad in the brain], or frenzied, and through this loses strength in his heart, first anoint his heart with this ointment; then, after shaving his hair, anoint his head with it. Repeat this on either the second or third day, and his head will recover health and he will return to his senses. If anyone suffers pain in the stomach or spleen, first anoint his heart with the same ointment because of the weakness of the heart, then anoint above the stomach if he has pain in the stomach, or above the spleen if he has pain there [Col. 1233C]. Its power will penetrate the whole skin, and he will quickly be cured.

One oppressed in the chest and coughing [“coughing,” ed.], and also suffering in the lungs so that they are swollen and have already begun to putrefy, should burn fresh fir wood, still containing its sap, into ashes, without adding any other ash. To these ashes add twice as much *bibenella* [burnet?], as much fennel as *bibenella*, and liquorice equal to half the *bibenella*; boil all this in good wine with a little honey added, strain it through a little bag, make a *luterdrang* [clear drink; “pure beverage,” ed.], and drink it often. It will cleanse the chest, restore the lungs to health, and cure him.

When cancers consume a person, let him reduce to powder upon a heated brick the seed of the fir which grows at its top [Col. 1233D], and sprinkle this powder upon the wound where the cancers consume him [Note: [Col. 1233D] “Where the cancers consume him” omitted in the edition.]; the cancers will die. Then heat the same brick on which that seed was pulverized again intensely with another heated stone, lay it, hot, upon the wound where the cancers consume him, and they will die [Note: [Col. 1233D] “Then heat—will die” omitted in the edition.].

If your mouth [Col. 1234A] and lips are swollen and inflamed by some infirmity, put fir seed or fruit upon a brick heated at the fire so that it becomes hot, but do not reduce it to powder [Note: [Col. 1233D] “But do not reduce it to powder” omitted in the edition.]; apply it hot to your mouth often, and the swelling and inflammation will cease. [Note: [Col. 1233D] “But fir—are stirred up” omitted in the edition, in place of which it has: “If rheum flows excessively from the nostrils, receive smoke from fir wood, and that discharge [Col. 1234D] will dissolve more gently and cease. Make ashes from fir wood, prepare lye with them, and wash the head; it heals the head and clears the eyes.”] But fir has strong heat, and its scent dries out the humours within a person so that they pass into a kind of flooding. A person should not inhale the smell of fir unless certain spices and other aromatic herbs of whatever kind are added to it, lest the humours within him be disturbed beyond their proper measure, and so be held and strengthened as though roused into the storm of a flood.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—ON THE LINDEN [Note: [Col. 1234D] *Tilia europaea*.] [III, 34]

[Col. 1234B] The linden has great heat; all that heat is in its root, and rises from there into its branches and leaves. It signifies frailty [Note: [Col. 1234D] “And all that heat—signifies frailty” omitted in the edition.]. A person suffering in the heart should take the inner root and that which is in the middle of the linden root, reduce it to powder, and frequently eat the powder with bread; he will improve in the heart.

From the trunk (?) of this tree, not its branches, remove the bark down to the white wood while it is green in summer; cut a *spechen* [a splinter], place it in a pierced gold ring, and place green glass—not another stone—upon the *span* [splinter, ed.]. Put a spider’s web or *baumwulle* [cotton; “bouvel,” ed.] between the splinter and the glass, lest the power of the splinter pass through the glass. Always wear the ring upon your finger, so that the warmth of your finger rises to the splinter [Col. 1234C] and the force of that splinter touches your finger and its veins. This is a most powerful protection against every most dangerous human pestilence, and prevents them from reaching a person, just as some *vach* [uncertain term] prevents an incoming flood of waters from taking an unjust course, even if these pestilences flow moderately into a person [Note: [Col. 1234D] “Just as some *vach*—flow moderately into a person” omitted in the edition.].

In summer, when you go to sleep, lay fresh linden leaves over your eyes and cover your whole face with them; they clear and purify your eyes. A person afflicted with *virgichtiget* should take earth lying around the root of that linden, put it into the fire, pour water over it when heated in a hot bath [Col. 1234D], bathe thus, and do this for nine days; he will be cured.

## CHAPTER XXV.—ON THE OAK [Note: [Col. 1234D] *Quercus pedunculata*.] [III, 35]

Oak is cold, hard, and bitter, but whatever little [power] it has is fully efficacious. It signifies wickedness. It is hard and bitter, and no softness can exist in it. Its fruit is not suitable for a person to eat, and even worms [Col. 1235A] do not readily eat its wood. But if they do eat it, they soon cease and fail [Note: [Col. 1235D] “But yet, little—cease and fail” omitted in the edition.]. Yet certain twisting [virtuous, ed.] animals feed on its fruit and grow fat, as pigs do. Neither its wood nor its fruit is useful for medicine.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—ON THE BEECH [Note: [Col. 1235D] *Fagus sylvestris*.] [III, 36]

[Note: [Col. 1235D] The edition, very briefly: “Beech has a proper balance of heat and cold. If anyone prepares and eats a dish from beech leaves while they are fresh, and also eats its fruit, it does not harm him, but he becomes fat from it. But if an ass has pain in its head, let a person place hot ashes of beech, from which lye has been made, before it, and allow the smoke rising from them [Col. 1236D] to enter the ass’s mouth and nostrils.”]

Beech has an even and proper balance of heat and cold, and both are good in it. It signifies discipline. When beech leaves are beginning to emerge but have not yet fully appeared, go to the tree, take hold of a branch with your left hand, hold a bowl in your right, and say: “I cut off your greenness so that you may correct all the humours of a person which turn toward a foreign path [Col. 1235B] and the unjust yellow of bile, through the living Word which made humanity without its ruin.” Hold the branch in your left hand while you speak all these words; then cut it with iron that is *calibs* [steel], preserve that branch for the circuit of the year, and do this every year.

If anyone has *gelsucht* [jaundice] during that year, cut small pieces from this branch, put them in a little vessel, pour a little wine over them three times, and each time as you pour the wine over the pieces say these words: “By the holy *scincturam* [reading uncertain: perhaps ‘cutting’ or ‘girding’] of the holy Incarnation, by which God became man, draw from this person N. the pain of *gelsucht*.” Then heat the wine with the little sticks you have cut in a pan or crucible, and give it hot to him while fasting to drink for three days; he will be cured, unless God does not will it.

If anyone has *ridden* [fever], take beech fruit when it first appears and mix it in pure water, namely water from a *springbornen* [spring]. Say these words: “By the holy *scincturam* of the holy Incarnation by which God became man, you, *riddo*, and you, fevers, fail and perish in your coldness and heat in this person N.” Then give him that water to drink. Prepare it for five days; if he has either a daily or quartan fever, he will quickly be freed from them, unless God does not will to free him.

Take the beech root where it appears above ground, remove the outer bark of that root, cut from it as much as you can take in one cut, and say: “By the first manifestation [Col. 1235D] in which God saw a human being at the root of Mamre [Note: [Col. 1236D] Genesis 18:1.], break the waves of this person’s poison without his death.” Cut off again as much as you can take in a second cut and say the same words; make a third cut in the same root in the same manner. Thus cut three times from the same root, so that it does not fail you during the year; preserve these pieces for the circuit of the year [Col. 1236A], and do likewise every year.

When anyone has in that year *freyszchlich*, which is *selega*, in his body, cut a little from one of these cut sticks, put it in a little vessel, pour a little pure *springbornes* water over it three times, and each time say these words: “By the first manifestation in which God was baptized in the Jordan [Note: [Col. 1236D] Mark 1:1.], through this poison, remove from this person N., without his death, every delusion of this pestilence, just as Jesus was pure life.” Give him this water while fasting for three days. On each day that he drinks it, prepare it in the same manner as stated above; he will be freed from *freischlich*, unless God prevents it.

If anyone prepares a *mus* [porridge] from fresh, new beech leaves and eats it, it does not harm him; likewise, if anyone eats its fruit, he is not harmed by it but becomes fat from it [Col. 1236B].

## CHAPTER XXVII.—ON THE ASH [Note: [Col. 1236D] *Fraxinus excelsior*.] [III, 37]

Ash [*Fraxinus*, ed.] is more hot than cold and signifies counsel [Note: [Col. 1236D] “And signifies counsel” omitted in the edition.]. If anyone is troubled by *gicht* in his side or another limb, as though all his limbs were broken and *zustoszen* [bruised or crushed], boil ash leaves in water, strip the sick person naked, lay him in a linen sheet, and, after pouring off that water, wrap him in the boiled and hot leaves, especially around the place that hurts. Do this often, and he will improve [Note: [Col. 1236D] “And he will improve” omitted in the edition.].

If you wish to make ale from oats without *hoppen* [hops], boil it only with *grusz* [grout or grain] and many ash leaves; this ale cleanses the drinker’s stomach and makes his chest [Col. 1236C] light and pleasant. [If goats become ill in any way, give them ash leaves often to eat, and they will be cured. Added by the edition.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—ON THE ASPEN [Note: [Col. 1236D] *Populus tremula*.] [III, 38]

Aspen [*Tremulus* in the edition] is warm, and signifies excess. [Note: [Col. 1236D] “And signifies excess” is omitted in the edition.] When an infant lying in a cradle is repeatedly suffused with blood and wounded between skin and flesh, so that he suffers greatly from it, take fresh, newly gathered aspen leaves, lay them upon a plain linen cloth, wrap the infant in these leaves and this cloth, put him to sleep, and cover him with garments so that he may sweat; the power of these leaves will draw it out, and he will be healed. But if anyone suffers from gout, or has a cold stomach, let him take the bark of the same tree while it is green, and its wood from the outer part down to its inner heartwood—but not that which is called the heart of the tree—cut it into small pieces, boil it in water, then pour that water, with the pieces of wood themselves, into a tub and bathe in it. Let him do this often: the gout will leave him, and his cold stomach will become warm; thus each condition will improve. [Note: [Col. 1237D] “And his cold stomach … improve” is omitted in the edition.] In May also take the bark of this tree and its outer wood down to the heartwood, cut these into small pieces, pound them in a mortar, press out their juice, and add that juice to other ointments which you prepare. They are thereby much more effective against every affliction that troubles a person in the head, back, loins, stomach, and other members, and they restrain bad humours all the more. [Note: [Col. 1237D] The chapter ends here in the edition.]

## CHAPTER XXIX.—ON ARLA

[Note: [Col. 1237D] *Alnus glutinosa*—black alder.] [III, 39.]

Arla [*Alnus* in the edition] is colder than warm. It signifies uselessness and is of little benefit for medicines. [Note: [Col. 1237D] “It signifies uselessness … medicines” is omitted in the edition.] But if anyone has slight ulcers on his skin, let him lay fresh, newly gathered leaves of this tree upon the ulcers, and meanwhile he will fare more easily.

## CHAPTER XXX.—ON AHORN

[Note: [Col. 1237D] *Acer pseudoplatanus*—sycamore maple.] [III, 40.]

[Col. 1237B]

Ahorn [*Platanus* in the edition] is cold and also dry, and signifies every sort of terror. [Note: [Col. 1237D] “And also dry … signifies” is absent from the edition.] Whoever has daily and prolonged fevers should boil the branches of this tree with their leaves in water and bathe frequently in that water. Immediately after leaving the bath, he should crush its inner bark, press out the juice, pour it into pure wine, and drink it cold after the aforesaid bath. Let him do this often, and the prolonged fevers will cease in him; their foulness and violent attacks will also disappear. [Note: [Col. 1237D] “And their foulness … disappear” is omitted in the edition.]

And if anyone suffers from gout in any of his limbs, let him take wood from that tree and heat it thoroughly at the fire; then place it hot upon the painful spot, and the gout will be driven away. Or, if he cannot bear the whole piece of wood there, let him shave off pieces from the heated wood, put them upon the painful place, bind them on tightly, and he will improve. If someone’s nostrils are swollen from some ailment—that is, *erblasent* (“blown up, swollen”)—let him heat thoroughly the earth around the roots of this tree, apply it to his nostrils overnight, fasten it there with a bandage, and lie so for a short while. Let him do this often: the swelling will disappear, and he will improve.

[Note: [Col. 1237D] The remainder of this chapter does not agree with the edition, which reads as follows: “After an acute fever has attacked a person, let him make this remedy, and he will fare somewhat more easily and come more gently to sweating. Therefore scrape a little into cold water from the wood of the plane tree, and twice as much from dry willow; add an equal quantity of agrimony, let him drink it frequently, and he will suffer less. But if he postpones this remedy until the fifth or sixth day, it will afterwards do him no good. And if anyone suffers from paralysis in any place, let him heat its wood thoroughly and put it hot upon the painful place, and he will improve. If anyone’s nostrils swell, let him heat thoroughly the earth around the roots of the plane tree, put it upon his nostrils at night, lie thus for a short while, and he will improve.”]

## CHAPTER XXXI.—ON YBENBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1238D] *Taxus baccata*—yew.] [III, 41.]

Ybenbaum [*Taxus* in the edition] is more cold than warm, and is also dry. It signifies joy. [Note: [Col. 1238D] “It signifies joy” is omitted in the edition.] When its wood is burned in the fire, neither the *damph* [“vapour”; *humor* in the edition] nor the smoke issuing from it harms anyone. For if a person has an ailment (*gebreche*) in his nostrils and chest from bad humours, let him receive the smoke of this wood into his nostrils and mouth. Those bad humours will then be gently and pleasantly dissolved and will disappear without danger to his body. [Note: [Col. 1238D] “And will disappear without danger …” is omitted in the edition.] Moreover, if someone makes a staff from this wood and carries it in his hands, it is good and useful to him for the well-being and health of his body.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—ON BIRCKA

[Note: [Col. 1238D] *Betula alba*—birch.] [III, 42.]

Bircka [*Vibex* in the edition] is warmer than cold, and signifies good fortune. [Note: [Col. 1238D] “And signifies good fortune” is omitted in the edition.] But if someone’s skin begins to become red and *bulechte* [to develop swellings; “or to have swollen pustules” in the edition], so that a swelling arises there or worms threaten to boil forth, [Note: [Col. 1238D] “So that … threaten to boil forth” is omitted in the edition.] let him take the *coppini*, that is, *uszproszen* (“shoots”), of this tree, warm them in the sun or at a fire, lay them hot upon the painful spot, and bind them with a cloth. Let him do this often, and the swelling will cease.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—ON FORNHAFF

[Note: [Col. 1238D] Absent from the edition.]

Fornhaff is warmer than cold and moist; it likewise signifies grief and has no good fortune in its nature. But its juice is very useful in ointments and eye-salves, so that if someone makes ointments, let him add to them juice from its twigs: they become stronger and better. Or, if someone makes eye-salves, let him add a little of this same juice; it causes the eyes to burn in the light and see more clearly. By itself and on its own, however, it is useful for no remedy, since its juice alone would be too strong unless it were tempered with other ingredients. Yet if pestilence—that is, *schelmo*—afflicts and kills livestock, place fresh branches of this tree before the animals, so that they take in their scent. Have the animals led to the places where these trees grow, and let the scent pass through their nostrils. Then they will begin to cough and discharge the corrupt matter in their nostrils and heads, and the plague afflicting them will disappear. Nevertheless, care must be taken that the animals taste nothing from these trees, lest they be injured and suffer from it.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—ON SPYNELBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1238D] *Euonymus europaeus*—spindle tree.] [III, 43.]

Spinelbaum is colder than warm, signifies generosity, and has a certain good fortune in its nature. [Note: [Col. 1238D] “It signifies generosity … nature” is omitted in the edition.] A person who has dropsy should strip bark from this tree, burn its inner wood in the fire, make ashes from it without adding any other ashes, tie these ashes in a cloth, and place them in pure, good wine—from morning until midday. Let him frequently drink this while fasting, and it will consume (*swaendet*; *consumit* in the edition) the disease in him. But a person suffering in the spleen should boil in pure wine the fruit that grows on this tree, strain it through a cloth, and drink it often after eating; his spleen will be healed. Whoever is eaten by worms in his belly and suffers *stechen* (“stabbing pains”) in the belly should frequently drink the same potion, and will improve.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—ON HAGENBUCHA

[Note: [Col. 1239D] *Ulmus campestris*—field elm.] [III, 44.]

Hagenbucha is colder than warm and displays a certain prosperity in its nature. [Note: [Col. 1239D] “And displays a certain prosperity …” is omitted in the edition.] Take its twigs with their leaves while green and boil them in cows’ or sheep’s milk, but not goats’ milk. Then discard the twigs and leaves, prepare the milk with flour or eggs so that it can be eaten, and let women whose pregnancies are apt to miscarry—though they are not sterile but fertile—often eat the milk prepared in this way. It greatly helps them toward fertility and toward retaining conception.

Also boil the twigs of this tree with their leaves in water, make a bath from it, and put into it a person who is mad, that is, *hirnwutig* (“brain-mad”). Shave his head, dip a linen cloth into the bath, and continually warm his head in the bath with the wet, hot cloth. After he has left the bath, lay him in bed; then boil the fruit of this tree in water, pour away the water, place the boiled, hot fruit upon his head, bind it on with a cloth so that he falls asleep, and do this often. He will improve and recover his senses. If anyone has bad spots on his body, cut from beneath its bark a piece of its wood, namely a *span* [“splint”; *hastulam* in the edition], warm it at the fire, lay it hot upon the spots—that is, *flecken*—and they will disappear. [Note: [Col. 1239D] The chapter ends here in the edition.]

It is also good and useful for a person always to keep some wood of this tree with him. For hagenbucha and other woods in which, as stated above, certain prosperities are displayed, when they burn in a house fire, cause aerial spirits and demonic illusions to withdraw and flee away in disdain, since they perceive some prosperity there. If someone is benighted in the forest or wishes to rest at midday, let him lie and sleep beneath a hagenbucha and in its shade; evil spirits will be so much less able to prepare their illusions and terrors around him. A person may likewise lie and rest beneath other trees whose nature is shown to possess some prosperity, in order to avoid demonic terrors, but especially beneath the hagenbucha.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—ON WIDA

[Note: [Col. 1239D] A species of willow. Absent from the edition, as are the following nos. 37–39.]

Wida is cold and signifies vices, because it seems beautiful. It is of little use to people, except that it serves them in certain external matters; [Col. 1240A] but it is useful for no medicines. Its fruit and juice are bitter and unsuitable for human use, because if someone ate it, it would arouse and increase melancholy in him, make him inwardly bitter, and diminish his health and joy.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—ON SALEWIDA

[Note: [Col. 1239D] *Salix caprea*—goat willow.]

Salewida has the same nature as wida, and is useful for everything in the same way as wida.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—ON FOLBAUM

Folbaum has neither proper warmth nor proper coldness. It is useful for no medicine or any other purpose, nor is its fruit; rather, it is like a certain useless weed (*unkrut*).

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—ON FELBAUM

Felbaum is colder than warm and is useful neither for medicines nor for human purposes. If a person eats its fruit, it harms him and diminishes his health, because it increases bad humours and coldness in him, on account of the uselessness inherent in it.

## CHAPTER XL.—ON ERLIZBAUM

[III, 85.]

Erlizbaum [*Cornus* in the edition] is warm; its warmth is pleasant, and it possesses a sweet moisture. [Note: [Col. 1240D] “And its warmth … possesses” is omitted in the edition.] Therefore take its bark, wood, and leaves, boil them in water, make a bath with them, and let anyone suffering from gout—whether infant, youth, or old person—bathe in it often and apply these baths about himself. Let this be done in summer, when the tree is green. It will help an infant and a youth exceptionally well toward health; it will benefit an old person sufficiently, though not as much as an infant or youth. Thus they will improve. [Note: [Col. 1240D] “It will help an infant … improve” is omitted in the edition.] The fruit of this tree, when eaten, does not harm a person, but cleanses and strengthens a weak as well as a sound stomach, and benefits a person’s health. [Note: [Col. 1240D] “And benefits a person’s health” is omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER XLI.—ON MASCEL

[Note: [Col. 1240D] Absent from the edition.]

Mascel possesses an unhelpful and harmful warmth, and the coldness it has is likewise useless. Its wood, juice, and leaves are useless for every human use, harmful to health, and dangerous to sexual desire, because they would arouse lust in a person. If a person ate its fruit, he would become ill from it. Neither its fire nor its smoke is beneficial to human health.

## CHAPTER XLII.—ON MIRTELBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1240D] *Myrtus communis*—common myrtle.] [III, 46.]

[Col. 1240D]

Mirtelbaum is warmer than cold. If *orfimae* arise on a person before they burst, boil its leaves in water and apply them hot repeatedly; they will disappear. But if the *orfimae* are about to burst, heat wood from this tree at the fire and apply it hot in the form of a cross repeatedly to them; they will disappear. If the *orfimae* have burst, powder its twigs and leaves, apply the powder to them repeatedly, and they will dry up. [Note: [Col. 1240D] “But if … dry up” is absent from the edition.] If anyone wishes to brew beer, let him boil the leaves and fruit of this tree with the beer; it will be wholesome and will not harm the drinker.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—ON WACHOLDERBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1241D] *Juniperus communis*—common juniper.] [III, 48.]

Wacholderbaum is warmer than cold and signifies excess. Take its fruit and boil it in water; strain the water through a cloth, then add honey, a little vinegar, and liquorice to the water, with less *zengebern* (“ginger”) than liquorice. Boil it again, put it in a pouch, make a *luterdrang* [a strained medicinal drink], and drink it often, both after eating and while fasting. It relieves and lessens pain of the chest, lungs, and liver. Also take its green twigs, boil them in water, make a steam bath (*assum balneum*) with that water, and bathe in it often; it lessens the various harmful fevers in you.

[Note: [Col. 1241D] The edition does not agree: “Juniper is warm. Let a person boil its green twigs in water, make a steam bath with it, and bathe often therein; they lessen various fevers in him. But a person whose head is so sound and strong that bad humours cannot injure his brain, yet nevertheless infect his lungs with filth and wasting, should boil juniper berries, twice as much *lanaria*, and *piretrum* in an amount twice that of the *lanaria*, in pure good wine. Let him leave it in the pot and add raw elecampane, cut into small pieces, and drink this wine both fasting and after eating, until he is healed.”]

## CHAPTER XLIV.—ON HOLDERBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1242D] *Sambucus nigra*—black elder.] [III, 48.]

[Col. 1241B]

Holderbaum is warmer than cold and is of little use for human purposes; so too is its fruit, except that it merely serves people. [Note: [Col. 1242D] “And is of little use … serves people” is omitted in the edition.] Yet a person who has *gelsucht* (“jaundice”) should enter a steam bath, put leaves of this tree upon hot stones, pour water over them, and also put its *zechen* [probably twigs; uncertain] into pure wine so that the wine takes on their flavour. Let him drink moderately in that bath, then, after leaving it, go to bed in order to sweat. Let him do this often, and he will be healed.

## CHAPTER XLV.—ON MELTZBOUM

[III, 49.]

Gelbaum [*Meltzboum* in the edition] is colder than warm and has much greenness. It signifies struggle and is contrary to human nature, so that if a person tasted any of its juice or fruit in any way, it would cause many adverse effects in him, even overturning the warmth of his stomach, so that because of the coldness of this juice he would vomit up his food through nausea. It is useful neither to human beings nor livestock, and is of little medical use, except as fuel for a fire. [Note: [Col. 1242D] “And has much greenness … fire” is omitted in the edition.]

But a person who has *orfimae* on his body should take the *coppim*, that is, the first fruit emerging from the gelbaum, pound them in a little wine, add one third as much powdered mole, mix all these things together, boil them in a pan, make an ointment, and frequently anoint the *orfimae* with it before they burst; they will disappear. If the *orfimae* have burst, powder the *coppim* of gelbaum, put the powder into the burst *orfimae*, and they will dry up.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—ON HARTBROGELBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1242D] Absent from the edition.]

Hartbrogelbaum is colder than warm, signifies a limited art, and is of little use to human beings, because a person neither grows, is strengthened, nor is nourished from it. It is also of no use in medicines.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—ON IFFA

[III, 50.]

Iffa has a summer warmth, for it is neither very warm nor very cold, but temperate. [Note: [Col. 1242D] “For it is neither … temperate” is omitted in the edition.] Whoever suffers from gout should kindle a fire from its wood alone and immediately warm himself by that fire; the gout will cease for that time. A person suffering from gout such that his tongue fails in speaking should put its fresh, newly gathered leaves in cold water and drink it; the gout in his tongue will cease, and he will recover speech. A person who has *freischlich* in his body—that is, *selega*—should often drink the same water prepared with the same leaves, and the *freyschlich* will disappear. But one who kindles a fire from its wood alone, heats water over it, and bathes in that water will have malignity and evil will—that is, *ubelwillekeit*—taken away from him; it will bestow goodwill upon him [Note: [Col. 1242D] “Will have malignity … goodwill” is omitted in the edition.] and make his mind joyful. [Note: [Col. 1242D] The remainder is omitted in the edition.] Moreover, the tree itself possesses a certain prosperity in its nature, so that aerial spirits will not be able through it to accomplish their phantasms, injuries, and illusions in anger and in many conflicts.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—ON HARBAUM

[III, 51.]

Harbaum has a temperate summer warmth within it and signifies boldness. [Note: [Col. 1242D] “Temperate … boldness” is omitted in the edition.] A person with slight or severe scabies should pound its leaves with fresh pork fat, melt them together in a pan (*smeltze*; *dissolvat* in the edition), and anoint himself with it often. The scabies will diminish and he will be healed. If anyone boils its twigs with leaves in water, adds rue, more sage than rue, and more fennel than sage, strains it through a cloth, and drinks it, it repeatedly purges fevers and the corrupt disorders caused by impurities from him, and makes him well.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—ON SCHULBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1242D] Absent from the edition.]

Schulbaum is cold and is like a weed (*unkrut*), useful for no medicines. Its juice and fruit are useless for human use. If a person ate its seed or fruit, it would be like poison to him.

## CHAPTER L.—ON PRUMA

[III, 52.]

Pruma [*Mirica* in the edition] is very warm. A person with leprosy should rub Pruma in his hands, press out the juice, and frequently anoint the affected places with that juice; it alleviates leprosy and makes it milder, that is, *seuffut*. Boil its flowers in cows’ butter, make an ointment, and anoint yourself with it often; the leprosy will diminish. A person whose eyes grow dim and weak should gaze for a long time upon the flowers of *Prymen* [sic], until his eyes become moist—that is, *weszern*—and then place the flowers themselves upon his eyes and fall asleep thus. Let him do this often: it clarifies the eyes. If they are sound, it is good and healthful; if they are diseased, it is good and useful, and they will become sound. [Note: [Col. 1243D] “If they are sound … become sound” is omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER LI.—ON AGENBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1243D] Absent from the edition.]

Agenbaum has neither proper warmth nor proper coldness and is like a weed (*unkrut*), so that neither its juice nor its fruit is useful for medicines or any other human purpose.

## CHAPTER LII.—ON HYFFA

[Note: [Col. 1243D] Absent from the edition.]

Hyffa is very warm and signifies affection. A person who has pain in the lung should pound hyffen with its leaves, add uncooked honey, boil them together, frequently take *sumac*—that is, *seyme*—then strain it through a cloth, make a *luterdrang* from it, and drink it often. It removes corruption from his lung, cleanses it, and heals it. One who kindles a fire from its wood alone, makes ashes from it, prepares lye from those ashes, and washes his head frequently with it, will have a sound and strong head from the good warmth of its juice.

If a person is sound in body but has only a weak stomach, let him boil the fruit of tribulus, namely *hanelpeffe*, and eat it often; it cleanses the stomach and removes *slim* (“phlegm”) from it. But it is not suitable cooked for someone sick throughout the body, because it would injure his stomach, since his stomach is as though *welk* (“withered, weak”). If he wishes to eat it often, however, let him eat it raw and *deyck* [“soft, tender”; uncertain] in moderation; this is better for him than eating it cooked, or hard and raw. But a person sound throughout the body is harmed by it neither raw nor cooked when eating it.

## CHAPTER LIII.—ON THORNS

[Note: [Col. 1243D] *Prunus spinosa*—blackthorn.] [III, 54.]

Thorns are warmer than cold and are also dry, and are likened to *frebelkeit* (“weakness, frailty”). [Note: [Col. 1243D] “And are also dry … likened” is omitted in the edition.] A person suffering from gout so that his senses fail and he becomes mad, or because of it begins to limp in his limbs (*lamet*; *claudicare incipit* in the edition), should take green or old thorns, burn them alone in the fire, then add to their ashes powdered clove—that is, *nelchin*—and twice as much cinnamon as the clove powder, together with boiled, pure honey. Mix it with wine so that the ashes exceed the clove powder by one third, and likewise the cinnamon powder; prepare a *luterdranck* in this way. Let him drink a moderate amount while fasting and take a sufficient quantity after eating. Let him do this often: the gout will cease, so that he will recover his senses and regain the health of his limbs, because this drink is better than gold. [Note: [Col. 1243D] “So that … better than gold” is omitted in the edition.]

Temper its fruit, namely *slehen* (“sloes”), with honey (*sulcze*; *temperet* in the edition), and eat it often; the gout will cease in you. A person suffering in the stomach should roast sloes in the flame of a fire—that is, *brulwe*—or boil them in water and eat them often; this removes filth and *slim* (“phlegm”) from his stomach. If he eats their kernels, they will not harm him. [Note: [Col. 1243D] The edition is shorter: “But let a person temper the fruit of thorns with honey; it removes paralysis, filth, and lividity from his stomach.”] If crabs—and no other worms—eat a person in his body, let him take the inner kernels of thorns, dry them at the fire in an earthen vessel, reduce them to powder, and put that powder where the crabs are eating him; [Note: [Col. 1243D] “And they will die”; the rest is omitted in the edition.] then pour a few drops of wine over it, and the crabs will die.

## CHAPTER LIV.—ON THE VINE

[Note: [Col. 1243D] *Vitis vinifera*—wine grape.] [III, 55.]

The vine has fiery warmth and moisture, but that fire is so strong that it changes its juice into a different kind of taste from that possessed by other trees or herbs. Thus this great fire also makes its wood so dry that it is almost unlike other woods. The vine is a wood forced out of the earth and is more like trees. Because the earth before the Flood was fragile or *melmechte* (“crumbly”), it did not produce wine; but when it had been soaked and strengthened by the Flood, it produced wine. For the earth now stands in relation to the earth before the Flood as sandstone (*grieszstein*) to the earth that now exists.

But if someone’s flesh around the teeth is rotting and his teeth are weak, let him put hot vine ashes into wine as though making lye, and then wash his teeth and the flesh around them with that wine. Let him do this often: the flesh will heal and the teeth will become firm. Even if his teeth are sound, this washing benefits them and makes them handsome. If anyone has ulcers on his body or has been struck by a wound, and on the second or third day the ulcer or wound shows corruption or blackness, add one third part of *baumolei* (“tree oil”) to pure, good wine. If the ulcer or wound is large, warm the aforesaid oiled wine slightly, dip a linen cloth into it, and with the soaked cloth foment (*bewe*) the ulcer or wound until the corruption diminishes. If the ulcer or wound is small, dip a feather into the aforesaid oiled wine cold, not warmed, and lightly cleanse the ulcer or wound with that feather until the corruption diminishes.

[Note: [Col. 1243D] The printed text of this chapter differs greatly: “The vine has fiery warmth. If someone’s eyes are dim, let him anoint his eyelids with the drops that flow from the vine when a shoot is cut, allowing them to enter the eyes slightly. Let him do this often, and it will undoubtedly make the eyes clear. For when a shoot is first cut from the vine, the drops that flow from the cut from morning until midday are good and useful for the clarity of the eyes. Therefore let a person catch them in a little vessel, add olive oil, and, if he has pain in his ears or head, anoint himself with it; he will improve. A person who coughs and has pain in the chest and stomach should cut off the tip of a vine-shoot with its leaves, when its flowers first begin to emerge, boil it strongly in water, strain it through a cloth, and drink it often while fasting and after eating; he will improve. To bring a drunken person back to himself, if it is autumn, wrap a shoot from a green vine with fresh leaves about his forehead, temples, and throat; he will cool down. If someone’s flesh around the teeth is rotting and his teeth are weak, let him put hot vine ashes into wine and wash his teeth and the flesh around them with it; let him do this often, and he will be healed.

“The wine produced from the vine, if pure, makes good, sound blood in the drinker; if cloudy, it makes bad blood, as though sprinkled with ashes. Strong Franconian wine produces something like storms in the blood; therefore, a person who wishes to drink it should temper it with water. There is no need to mix Hunnish wine with water, because it is naturally watery. When a person goes to bed, let him moisten his eyelids with pure Franconian wine, taking care not to touch the eyes themselves; it removes the corruption which clings to sleepers’ eyes and makes them dim. When someone is moved to anger or sadness, let him immediately warm wine at the fire, mix it with cold water, and he will fare more easily. If someone cannot retain urine because of coldness of the stomach, let him often drink wine warmed by fire, mix all his foods with vinegar, and drink vinegar often in whatever way he can.”]

## CHAPTER LV.—ON GICHTBAUM

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1245A]

Gichtbaum is very warm. Its greenness and juice are not useful by themselves unless they are added to other herbs or ingredients; for when added to other herbs or ingredients, those herbs or ingredients are more useful and effective for medicines. Trees grow green from their pith, just as a person does from his pith; if a tree’s pith is injured, the tree will feel the loss of itself.

## CHAPTER LVI.—ON SMOKE

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Absent from the edition.]

Smoke is the moisture of woods, because when woods are burned in the fire, the moisture in them emerges through smoke. The smoke of certain woods is harmful and injures a person; it makes his eyes ulcerated in their flesh, but nevertheless brings much dimness upon them. Smoke rising from oak *demphet* (“damps, oppresses”) a person’s chest and makes him inwardly dry. Smoke from beech does not harm a person as much as oak smoke, though it is harmful. Smoke from aspen tightens the flesh around a person’s eyes and causes headache.

## CHAPTER LVII.—ON MOSS

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Absent from the edition.]

When trees grow old, so that they begin to lose their inner greenness, or when they are young but are nevertheless inwardly weakened by some accidental occurrence, they release to their outer bark the greenness and health which they ought to possess inwardly; thus mosses (*mose*) grow upon the bark because they lack inward greenness. Moss growing upon certain trees possesses medicinal power, but the kind that grows on rotten wood has almost no medicinal efficacy, because the corruption present in the foul moistures of roofs, rotten woods, and stones breaks forth and grows into moss; therefore it is almost without usefulness.

If someone suffers from gout in any limb, let him take moss that grows on a pear tree, *affaldra* [apple tree? uncertain], or beech; add to it one third as much [material unspecified in the source], boil them together lightly in water, press out the water, apply it hot to the limb afflicted by gout, and do this often. The gout will cease. But when someone suffers a burning from *ridden*, if he puts upon himself moss from roofs or rotten woods, he will indeed feel that burning for a short time, but he will not thereby be cured of that fever, namely *ridden*.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—ON THE OINTMENT OF HILARH

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Absent from the edition.]

The ointment which Hilarius [Note: [Col. 1246D] “Should one read Hilarion, whose Life St Jerome narrates in *Works*, vol. IV?”] the Egyptian showed against pain in either side, wherever it occurs, against pain in the chest, and against gout. Take peach leaves and, in an equal weight, *sysemera*; take basil in an amount one third of the sysemera; take plantain in a weight equal to the basil. Boil this lightly in water, then strain the herbs with the water through a cloth, squeezing strongly. Afterwards take bay oil, twice as much deer tallow, and old lard in an amount one third of the deer tallow. Sweat (*sweysze*: simmer gently) all these things with the aforesaid water a little in a pan, then allow them to cool. Make an ointment, and with it frequently anoint a person suffering in either side, around the painful chest, or wherever gout occurs in a person; he will improve.

## CHAPTER LIX.—ON SYSEMERA

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Compare above, I, 37. It is the second part of the chapter “On Air” in the edition.]

Concerning that which is called *sysemera*. When the sun rises from spring toward summer and when it inclines toward winter, the air is *seyger* [meaning uncertain], like wine and gives off a certain white deposit. Collect as much as possible of this sysemera. If a *wisza* or *herbrado* has already grown in someone’s eye, bind it often upon that eye, and it will be cured. Where worms are eating or beginning to eat human flesh, lay some of this white deposit of the air upon the place; the worms will go no further but will die.

## CHAPTER LX.—AGAINST SCROFULOUS SWELLINGS

Against *orfimae* not yet burst: take a little dry, hard excrement passed by a healthy, strong person, whether male or female; spread it upon a linen cloth and place it upon the *orfimae*. Then tie over that linen cloth a bandage anointed with goat fat, and keep it tightly bound for three days, or for two days and the same number of nights. Renew it with human excrement, and do this often: the *orfimae* will disappear. Also frequently lay dried blood of a swallow or dried liver of a vulture upon the *orfimae*, and they will disappear.

## CHAPTER LXI.—ON THE PALM

[Note: [Col. 1247B] Edition III, 12. Absent from the manuscript, as are the following chapters “On Spruce” and “On Tribulus.”]

[Col. 1247A]

The palm is warm and moist. A person who has pleurisy should pound its bark, wood, and leaves, press out the juice, drink it often in warm wine, and will be cured. Let him also eat the fruit of this tree often; it restrains pleurisy in him.

A person who is frenzied should boil its wood and leaves in water, apply them hot around his head, and do this often; he will recover his senses.

If someone boils and eats the fruit of this tree, it supplies his body with almost as much strength as bread, but it easily weighs him down in the chest.

## CHAPTER LXII.—ON SPRUCE

[Note: [Col. 1248B] Edition III, 33.]

[Col. 1247B]

Spruce is warm and moist. If pestilence afflicts and kills livestock, fresh branches should be set before them so that they take in their scent; or the animals should be led beneath these trees. They will begin to cough and discharge corrupt matter. Care must nevertheless be taken that they taste nothing from this tree, lest they be harmed.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—ON TRIBULUS

[Note: [Col. 1248B] Edition III, 33.]

Tribulus is very warm. Whoever makes lye from the ashes of its wood alone and washes his head with it, if his head is sound, will make it sounder and stronger. A person sound in body but weak only in the stomach should boil the fruit of tribulus and eat it often; it will cleanse his stomach. But for someone sick throughout the body, this fruit is unsuitable as food.

[Col. 1247] **Here ends Book III, On Trees.**

**Here begins the Third (Fourth) Book: On Stones. Preface.** [Note: [Col. 1247D] Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1247C] Every stone contains fire and moisture within itself. But the devil abhors, hates, and despises precious stones, because he remembers that their beauty appeared in him before he fell from the glory given him by God; and also because certain precious stones are generated from fire, in which he suffers his punishments. For by God’s will he was overcome through fire and fell into fire [Note: [Col. 1247D] Matt. III, 2.], just as he is also overcome through the fire of the Holy Spirit when people are snatched from his jaws by the first inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

In the eastern region, and in those regions where the sun’s heat is excessive, precious stones and gems arise. For the mountains in those lands are intensely hot from the sun’s heat, like fire; and the rivers flowing in those same regions continually boil from the sun’s excessive heat. Thus, when at times the flood of those rivers bursts forth and rises in swelling toward those burning mountains, and the mountains themselves, burning from the sun’s heat, are touched by those rivers, then in certain places where water touches fire they emit a sort of foam, that is, they *singelent* [singe], as red-hot iron or a heated stone does when water is poured over it. In that place the same foam adheres like *glitten* [glue], and in three or four days hardens into stone.

But when the flooding of those waters ceases, so that the waters return again to their channel, the foams which have adhered in various places to those mountains are dried by the sun’s heat according to the different hours of the day and the temperate quality of those hours. Accordingly, according to the temper of those daytime hours, they receive their colours and powers; and, hardened from dryness into precious stones, they break away from their places in great numbers [Note: [Col. 1248D] “Perhaps *pluvis*?”] like scales and fall into the sand. When thereafter the flooding of those rivers increases again, the rivers carry up many of these stones and take them to other regions, where they are later found by people. The aforesaid mountains, endowed in this way with so many and such great gems, shine there like a kind of daylight. Thus precious stones are produced from fire and water; hence they contain fire and moisture in themselves, and also possess many powers and produce many effects, so that very many operations can be performed with them—yet only works that are good, honourable, and useful to human beings, not works of seduction, fornication, adultery, enmity, murder, and the like, which tend toward vices and are contrary to humankind. For the nature of these precious stones seeks whatever is honourable and useful and rejects human perversity and evil, just as virtues cast out vices; and vices cannot work together with virtues.

There are, however, other stones which are not generated from those same mountains or from the aforesaid nature, but arise from certain other and useless things; and through them both good and evil may be done by their nature, with God’s permission. For God had adorned the first angel as if with precious stones. Seeing these shine in the mirror of the Godhead, Lucifer received knowledge from them, and recognized in them that God intended to do many wonders. Then his mind was lifted up, because the beauty of the stones [Col. 1250A] [Note: [Col. 1249] Isa. XIV, 12.] which was in him shone in God; he thought that he could do things equal to, and greater than, God, and therefore his splendour was extinguished. But just as God restored Adam to the better part, so God did not allow either the beauty or the power of these precious stones to perish; rather, he willed that they should be on earth in honour and blessing, and for healing.
