## Here begins the Fourth Book

[Col. 1249]

### Chapter I.—On the Emerald

[Col. 1249B]

The emerald grows in the morning of the day and at sunrise, when the sun is powerfully set in its course [Note: [Col. 1249] Similar accounts are related by Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVII, 5, and Marbod, *On Stones* 134.] to complete its journey. Then the earth’s greenness and the grasses are at their strongest, because the air is still cold while the sun is already hot. The herbs then draw in greenness as strongly as a lamb sucks milk, so that the day’s heat scarcely suffices to warm and nourish that day’s greenness enough for it to become fertile in producing fruit.

Therefore the emerald is powerful against every weakness and infirmity of the human being, because the sun prepares it and all its substance comes from the greenness of the air. Hence, whoever suffers pain in the heart, stomach, or side should keep an emerald with him, so that the flesh of his body may be warmed by it, and he will fare better. But if those afflictions so flood him that they cannot be restrained by their storm, let him immediately put the emerald in his mouth, so that it becomes wet with his saliva; then let him repeatedly draw into himself and breathe out the saliva warmed by the stone, and the sudden inundations of those diseases will without doubt cease.

If anyone falls while afflicted by the falling sickness, then, as he lies prostrate, put an emerald in his mouth and his spirit will revive. After he rises and removes the stone from his mouth, let him look attentively at it and say: “As the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, so may he fill the house of my body with his grace, that it may never be shaken.” Let him do this likewise for the following nine days in the morning, and he will be cured. He should always keep the same stone with him and look upon it every day in the morning; while looking at it, he should say the aforementioned words, and he will be healed.

Whoever suffers severe pain in the head should hold it to his mouth and warm it with his breath, until it is moistened by that breath; then let him anoint his temples and forehead with it while wet. Afterwards let him put it in his mouth and keep it there for a short while, and he will fare better.

Whoever has excessive phlegm and saliva should heat good wine, place a linen cloth over some vessel, and put the emerald upon that cloth. Let him pour the hot wine over the stone so that the wine passes through the cloth; let him do this again and again, as one preparing lye. Then let him make a preparation with that wine and bean flour and eat it often; let him also drink the wine so prepared often. It cleanses his brain and diminishes the phlegm and saliva in him.

If worms are eating someone, let him put a linen cloth upon the ulcer, place the emerald above it, and bind other small cloths over it, as one dresses a boil. Let him do this in order that the stone may grow warm there. Do this for three days, and the worms will die.

### Chapter II.—On the Hyacinth

The hyacinth arises from fire in the first hour of the day, when the air has mild warmth. It is more airy than fiery, and therefore responds to the air and sometimes derives its heat from the air; nevertheless it is also fiery, because it is generated from fire.

A person who suffers dimness in the eyes, whose eyes are clouded or *swerent* [uncertain eye ailment], should hold the hyacinth toward the sun. It immediately remembers that it was generated from fire, quickly grows warm, and should then be slightly moistened in saliva and very quickly applied to the eyes, so that they are warmed by it. Let him do this often, and the eyes will become clear and sound.

If anyone has been *bezaubert*—bewitched—by phantoms or magical words, so that he becomes deranged, take warm rye bread and cut the upper crust in the form of a cross, without breaking it completely through. Draw this stone downward through the cut and say: “God, who cast away from the devil all the preciousness of stones when he transgressed your command, may cast away from you, N., all phantoms and all magical words, and free you from the pain of this madness.” Then draw the same stone crosswise through the warm bread and say: “As the splendour which the devil possessed was taken from him because of his transgression, so may this madness, which afflicts N. through various phantasies and various magical practices, be taken from you and fail in you.” Give the sufferer the bread to eat around the cut through which you drew the hyacinth.

If, because of bodily weakness, he cannot eat rye bread, then bless warm unleavened bread—that is, *der brot*—with the hyacinth and the aforesaid words, as described above, and give it to him to eat. Moreover, draw it in the form of a cross through all the warm foods that he is to eat—namely, through meat, *warmuse* [a warm vegetable dish], and his other foods—and, as you make crosses in them, bless them with the aforesaid words. Do this often, and he will be cured.

Whoever suffers pain in the heart should make the sign of the cross over his heart with the hyacinth, say the aforesaid words, and fare better.

### Chapter III.—On Onychinus

Onychinus is warm and grows about the third hour of the day in a thick cloud, when the sun burns fiercely but various clouds rise over it, so that the sun cannot appear through them because of the flooding of waters. It does not possess the great heat of fire, but retains the warmth of air; it arises from the sun’s root and is joined together from diverse clouds. Therefore it has great power against illnesses that arise from the air.

Whoever’s eyes grow dim, or are otherwise afflicted—for example by *augswern* [eye sores]—should put pure, good wine in a bronze, copper, or iron vessel; put the onychinus into that wine and let it remain there for fifteen or thirty days, *beysze* [“until”; reading uncertain]. Then remove the stone but leave the wine in the vessel. Every night touch the eyes lightly with that wine, and they will become clear and sound.

Whoever suffers pain in the heart or side should warm the onychinus in his hands or against the skin of his body. He should again heat wine in a vessel over the fire, remove the vessel from the fire, and hold the onychinus over the steaming wine so that the sweat issuing from it mixes with the wine. Then put the stone into that hot wine and drink it at once; the heat in the heart and side will cease.

Whoever suffers pain in the stomach should prepare wine with onychinus as aforesaid, then make *suffen* [a soup] with that wine, hens’ eggs, and fine meal. Let him do and eat this often: it will cleanse and heal his stomach. Whoever suffers pain in the spleen should cook goat’s meat or young sheep’s meat, dip the cooked meat in wine prepared with onychinus as described above—as food is customarily dipped in vinegar—and eat it often. The spleen will be healed and will swell further.

Whoever has severe *fiber* [fever] should put onychinus in vinegar for five days. After removing it, let him season and flavour all his food with that vinegar and eat it so; the fever will cease and pass away gently, because the good warmth of the onychinus, mingled with the warmth of vinegar, drives away the harmful humours from which fevers arise.

If you are oppressed by sadness, look attentively at it and immediately put it in your mouth, and the oppression of your mind will cease. If *schelmo* [an uncertain cattle disease] attacks and kills oxen, heat water in a vessel over the fire. Once removed from the fire, hold the onychinus over the steaming water so that the sweat issuing from it mingles with the water. Put it in that water for three days; then remove it. Give the same water often to the oxen to drink, sprinkle their fodder with it, mix bran with the same water, and offer it to them to eat. Do this often, and they will fare better.

### Chapter IV.—On Beryl

Beryl is warm and grows each day between the third hour and noon from the foam of water, when the sun strongly kindles it. Its power is more from air and water than from fire, though it is somewhat fiery.

If anyone has already eaten or drunk poison, immediately scrape a little from beryl into *queckbronen* [a spring; literally “living spring”] or another water, and drink it at once. Let him do this for five days, drinking once a day while fasting, and he will either foam up the poison through nausea or pass it out through his bowels.

Whoever always keeps it with him, often holds it in his hand, and often looks at it, does not readily quarrel with other people or become *stridig* [contentious], but remains peaceful.

### Chapter V.—On Sardonyx

Sardonyx is warm and grows each day when the sixth hour has passed and one division of the ninth hour of the day has gone by. Then it is warmed by the pure sun, when the sun shines in its purity, because the air then begins to cool. Thus it is more of fire than of air or water, has strong powers by its nature, and imparts some power to the five human senses. It is a remedy for them because it is produced in the purity of the sun, when no foulness appears in the sun’s brightness.

When a person places it against his bare skin and often puts it to his mouth, so that his breath touches it, he breathes it outward and then draws it into himself. By this means his understanding, knowledge, and all the senses of his body are strengthened; great anger, foolishness, and lack of discipline are removed from him. The devil hates and flees because of this purity.

If a man or woman burns intensely by nature in carnal desire, let the man place sardonyx upon his loins, and the woman above her navel; they will find a remedy for that lust. Whenever anyone has a sharp *sucht* [acute illness], after he has sweated from it and begins to fare better, let him immediately place the stone in a ring on his finger, and he will not fall into that *sucht* again.

### Chapter VI.—On Sapphire

[Col. 1253B]

Sapphire is warm. It grows at the noonday season [Note: [Col. 1253D] Marbod, *On Stones* 126.], when the sun burns so intensely that the air is somewhat blocked by its heat. Then, because of the excessive heat it possesses, the sun’s brightness pierces the air so that the brightness does not appear as fully as it does when the air is somewhat tempered. Therefore sapphire is turbid and more fiery than airy or watery, and signifies the fullness of the love of wisdom.

Whoever has a *vell* [film] in the eye should hold sapphire in his hand and warm it either there or in fire; let him touch the film in his eye with the moistened stone. Do this morning and night for three days, and the film will lessen and disappear. If someone’s eyes are red and *seregent* [uncertain ailment] because of pain, or grow dim, let him put sapphire into his mouth while fasting, so that it is moistened with the saliva of his mouth. Then let him take upon his finger some of the same saliva with which the stone was moistened and anoint around his eyes, also touching the eyes inwardly. They will be healed and clear.

A person who is entirely *virgichtiget*—afflicted with gout or rheumatism—so that through excessive oppression he cannot endure the suffering in his head and the rest of his body, should put the same stone in his mouth, and the *gicht* will cease in him.

A person desiring good understanding and sound learning should, every morning when he rises from bed, put sapphire in his mouth while fasting. Let him keep it there for a short time, until he has sufficiently taken in the saliva with which it is moistened; then remove it from his mouth. Let him warm a little wine over the fire in a vessel and hold the stone in the vapour of that wine, so that it is moistened by sweating; then let him touch his tongue with its moisture, and let the saliva with which the stone was warmed, together with the wine, pass into that person’s stomach. Thus he will have pure understanding and pure knowledge, and his stomach will also be healthy from this.

Whoever is foolish, so that all learning fails in him, yet wishes to be wise and cannot be wise—provided that he does not look toward malice or extend himself toward it—should often anoint his tongue with sapphire while fasting. For its warmth and power, together with the warm moisture of saliva, drive away the harmful humours that oppress human understanding; thus the person acquires good understanding. Whoever is greatly stirred by anger should immediately put sapphire in his mouth, and it will be extinguished and cease in him.

If this stone is set in a ring of the purest, namely *gebrant golt* [refined gold], without *blech mal* [base-metal alloy; uncertain], and if there is nothing beneath the stone but gold, then a person may put in his mouth as medicine the gold setting, without the *blechmal*, in which the stone is placed, and it will not harm him. But if there is anything else there besides gold, it is of no use, and he should not put it in his mouth, because there is an admixture in the ring.

If someone is possessed by an evil spirit, let another person cause sapphire to be placed in earth, put that earth in a leather pouch, suspend it thus from the possessed person’s neck, and say: “O most foul spirit, depart quickly from this person, just as, at your first fall, the glory of your splendour fell most swiftly from you.” The evil spirit will be greatly tormented and depart from that person, unless it is a most fierce and wicked spirit; and the person will fare better.

If the devil has incited a man to love a woman so that, without magic and without invocation of demons, he begins to rage in love for her, and if this is burdensome to the woman, she should pour a little wine three times over sapphire and say each time: “I pour this wine upon you in burning powers, as God withdrew your splendour when the angel transgressed, so that you may withdraw from me the love of this man’s burning lust.” If the woman does not wish to do this, another person troubled by that love may do it for her and give it to the man to drink, fasting or fed, knowingly or unknowingly, for three days or more. If a woman burns in love for a man and this is burdensome to the man, he should do the same to that woman with wine and sapphire as described above; that inflamed love will cease.

### Chapter VII.—On Sard

Sard grows after noon amid the flooding of rains, when the leaves of *laubrorum* trees are destroyed in autumn—namely, while the sun is very hot and the air cold, and the sun warms it in its redness. Therefore it is pure from air and water, well tempered in a good balance of heat, and by its power turns away the adversities of pestilence.

If someone suffers in the head from many diseases and infirmities, so that he becomes as if deranged, bind sard over the crown of his head in a cap, cloth, or leather, and say: “As God cast the first angel down into the abyss, so may he cut this madness away from you, N., and restore sound understanding to me.” He will be cured.

If someone’s hearing has been dulled by an infirmity, dip the stone in pure wine, lay it when wet upon a slender linen cloth, place it in the deaf ear, and put very fine *werck* [tow or fibre] outside upon that cloth, so that its warmth enters the ear. Do this often, and he will recover his hearing.

Whoever has *gelsucht* [jaundice] should do likewise at night with urine and sard, as described above, say the aforementioned words, and do this for three nights; he will be cured. If a pregnant woman is overcome by pain and cannot give birth, stroke sard around both her loins and say: “As you, stone, shone in the first angel by God’s command, so you, child, come forth, a shining human being, and abide in God.” Immediately hold the same stone at the child’s exit, that is, at the female organ, and say: “Open yourselves, ways and gate, in that manifestation in which Christ, God and man, appeared and opened the bars of hell; so may you, child, come out through this gate without your death and without the death of your mother.” Then bind the same stone into a belt, gird her about with that belt and stone, and she will be relieved.

### Chapter VIII.—On Topaz

Topaz grows around the ninth hour of the day, in the sun’s heat, when it is nearly before the ninth hour; for the sun is then exceedingly pure and warm from the day’s heat and the varying air. It contains little air and water and is clear; that clearness resembles water. Its colour is more like gold than *gelo* [yellow], and it resists heat and poison—that is, *virgibuisse* and *seichmisse* [uncertain ailments]—and does not tolerate them, just as the sea cannot tolerate any foulness within itself.

For if poison is in bread, meat, fish, any food, water, wine, or other drink, and topaz is near and present, it immediately *swadet* [sweats], as the sea *schumet* [foams] when foulness is in it. Therefore, when a person eats or drinks, he should wear topaz upon a finger beside the food and drink and look at it often; if poison is in his food or drink, it immediately sweats.

Whoever has dim eyes should put topaz in pure wine for three days and nights. At night, when he goes to sleep, let him *bestriche* [anoint] his eyes with the topaz so moistened, so that the liquid also touches the eyes slightly within. Once the stone is removed, the wine may be kept for five days. Whenever he subsequently wishes to anoint his eyes at night, let him dip the same stone in the aforesaid wine and anoint around his eyes with it while wet, as stated above. Let him do this often, renewing the wine with topaz every five days; it clears the eyes like the finest eye-salve.

If anyone has fever, that is, *fiber*, let him make three small hollows in soft bread with topaz and pour pure wine into them. If that wine disappears, pour in fresh wine again. Let him look at his face in the wine poured into those hollows as in a mirror and say: “I behold myself, as in that mirror the cherubim and seraphim behold God, so that he may cast these fevers away from me.” Let him do this often, and he will be healed.

Whoever has leprosy should heat a brick intensely and put straw—that is, *spru* of oats—over it so that it steams, that is, *demphe*. Hold topaz over that steam, that is, *damph*, so that it sweats, and *striche* [rub] that sweat over the leprous place. After doing this, take *baumoleum* [tree oil], mix into it one-third part violet juice, and anoint with this oil the leprous place that has been moistened with the sweat of topaz. Do this often, and the leprosy will break open and the person will fare better, unless death is his lot.

Whoever suffers pain in the spleen, or has decay within, as though his body were rotting inwardly, should put topaz in genuine *morach* [possibly “moret,” mulberry wine; uncertain] for five days. Then remove the topaz and make the wine boil so that it steams. Hold the topaz over that steam so that it sweats and its sweat mingles with the wine. Put the stone also into the same heated wine for a short while, then remove it. Make either *suffen* [soup] or *jussal* [broth] with that wine, without fat, and do this often and sip it. His spleen will be healed and his inward decay diminished.

Every morning place topaz over your heart and say: “May God, who is magnified above all and in all, not cast me away from his honour, but preserve, strengthen, and establish me in his blessing.” So long as you do this, evil will abhor you. For topaz, a most powerful stone from God, has this power because it grows at the sun’s decline: it causes insults to decline away from a person.

### Chapter IX.—On Chrysolite

[Note: [Col. 1255D] Marbod, *On Stones* 195.]

Chrysolite grows from the sun’s heat and the moisture of the air after noon, toward the ninth hour of the day. It has almost a life-giving power in itself, so that if it lay beside the young of a bird or beast when it is being born, the offspring would be so strengthened by its power that it would begin to depart before its time.

Whoever has fever should heat wine, hold chrysolite over the steam of that wine so that its sweat mingles with the wine, drink that wine hot, and put the same stone in his mouth for a short time. Let him do this often, and he will fare better. Whoever suffers pain in the heart should dip the stone in *baumoleum* [tree oil] and rub it, dipped in the oil, over the painful place; he will fare better.

The same stone strengthens knowledge in a person who keeps it with him. Thus, one who has sound knowledge and a good art should put it over his heart, and as long as it lies there, his knowledge and good skill will not fail. For chrysolite has certain powers from the seven hours of the day, as also in those hours. Aerial spirits somewhat abhor this stone.

### Chapter X.—On Jasper

[Note: [Col. 1256D] Marbod, *On Stones* 101.]

Jasper grows when, after the ninth hour of the day, the sun inclines toward setting and is warmed by the sun’s fire. Yet it derives more from air than from water or fire, and therefore has varied heat, because when the sun inclines to setting after the ninth hour, the sun’s heat often appears varied by cloud.

A person deaf in the ear should hold jasper to his mouth and breathe out his warm breath into it, so that it becomes warm and moist. He should immediately put it into the ear, place fine *werck* [tow or fibre] over the stone, and close the ear thus, so that the stone’s heat may pass into it. Since this stone grows from green air, it also dissolves various humoral infirmities, and the person will recover his hearing.

Whoever has severe *nasebosz* [an uncertain nasal complaint] should put jasper to his mouth, breathe his warm breath into it until it becomes warm and moist, insert it into the nostrils, and press the nostrils with his hand so that its warmth enters the head. Then the humours of the head are dissolved more swiftly and gently, and he will fare better.

If humoral storms, that is, *gicht*, arise in the heart, loins, or any other member of a person, let him put jasper upon that place and press it until it grows warm there. The *gicht* will cease, because its good warmth and good power heal and calm those improperly hot and cold humours.

When lightning and thunder appear in dreams, it is good for a person to have jasper with him, for phantasies and *gedrognuze* [deceptive dream-visions] will then flee and leave him. When a woman gives birth, from the hour when she has borne the child and throughout all the days of the same *knicbeke kindbette* [lying-in period; phrase uncertain], let her hold jasper in her hand. Then evil aerial spirits will be less able to harm her or the child during that time, because the tongue of the ancient serpent stretches itself toward the sweat of the child coming forth from the mother’s womb; therefore it lies in wait for both child and mother at that time.

If a serpent emits its breath in any place, put jasper there. Its breath will be so weakened that it is less harmful, and the serpent will cease to breathe there.

### Chapter XI.—On Prasius

Prasius grows when the sun withdraws its rays from the upper regions of the earth toward evening and the dew is already approaching; as the sun gradually falls upon the stone of the aforesaid mountain and strongly kindles it, prasius is produced there from the sun’s heat, the moisture of air and water, and the greenness of dew.

Whoever has burning fever should wrap prasius in a small rye loaf, *deicht* [tightly; uncertain], bind it thus wrapped in a cloth, and keep it bound over his navel for three days and nights. The fever will cease.

Whoever has been bruised anywhere in the body by a fall or blow should take old fat and mix with it equal weights of sage and *reynefan* [tansy], press prasius into these ingredients, and warm them in this way in the sun or over a fire. Then place all these things, mixed with the stone and still hot, upon the painful place, and he will fare better.

### Chapter XII.—On Chalcedony

Chalcedony grows when the sun has almost withdrawn after evening, while the air is still somewhat warm. Therefore it draws more heat from air than from the sun and has good powers.

If anyone carries this stone, let him keep it so that it touches his skin and rests over some vein of his body. That vein and the blood which receive its warmth and power convey these powers to the other veins and to the rest of the blood. Thus the stone drives infirmities away from a person and gives him a most steadfast mind against anger, so that he will be so gentle in disposition that scarcely anyone will be able justly to find a reason, provoked by anger, to harm him through injustice.

Whoever wishes to have a steady manner of speaking and to utter wisely what he says should hold chalcedony in his hand, warm it with his breath so that it becomes moist from it, and then lick it with his tongue. He will be able to speak more steadily to people.

### Chapter XIII.—On Chrysoprase

Chrysopassus (sic) grows at the hour when the sun wholly withdraws itself; then air and water have a more turbid and *grunfar* [greenish] colour. Therefore this stone has nocturnal power, when the moon is strongest from the sun—namely, when it is half full and not yet full. It also possesses great powers in a moderate and even warmth: it is not excessively hot but temperate.

In whatever limb *gicht* afflicts a person, let him place chrysopassus upon his bare skin, and the *gicht* will cease. If anyone becomes very angry, let the same stone be placed at his throat until it becomes warm; he will be unable to utter words of anger until his anger subsides.

But wherever this stone is, if deadly poison is present, it loses its powers, becoming powerless and weak like water—that is, *unkrefftig*—and directs its warmth into weakness, so that it becomes less harmful. A person suffering from the falling sickness should always keep chrysopassus with him, and the nocturnal disease, namely the falling sickness, will harm him less. For aerial spirits will not be able meanwhile to prepare this mockery around him, causing the sufferer to cast foam from his mouth.

If anyone is possessed by the devil, pour a little water over the stone and say: “O water, I pour you upon this stone in that power by which God made the sun together with the moving moon.” Give this water to the possessed person to drink in whatever way you can, for he drinks it unwillingly. Throughout that day the devil in him will be tormented and weakened, and will not show his powers in him as before. Do this for five days. On the fifth day prepare with the same water a small *tortellum*, like *der broit* [bread], and give it to him to eat in whatever way you can. If the demon is not fierce, it will depart from that person.

This is how one must recognize whether a demon is aerial and mild, or bitter. If the person laughs readily, views people kindly—that is, *holtselich*—and sometimes gnashes his teeth, that is, *griszgramet*, a mild aerial spirit is present. But if the person speaks unwillingly, gladly falls silent, does not readily laugh, strongly *krymet* [clenches or cramps] with his hands, and casts foam from his mouth, it is a bitter and fierce demon. This stone is not greatly effective in expelling that bitter demon, because the demon is bitter and fierce; nevertheless, it torments the demon within that person and renders it weak. It must be expelled in another way, when God wills.

### Chapter XIV.—On the Carbuncle
Carbuncle grows during an eclipse of the moon. For when the moon is now in distress, as though it wished to fail—for at times it shows itself failing, when by divine command it portends that famine, pestilence, or changes of kingdoms are to occur—then the sun plunges all its powers into the firmament, cherishes the moon with its heat, kindles and raises it with its fire, and makes it shine again [Col. 1259B], as one who puts her tongue into another’s mouth in order to raise from death one already dead. And then, at that hour, the carbuncle is born. Therefore, from the sun’s fire at the moon’s increase it has brightness, so that it shines more by night than by day; and it grows until the sun’s heat drives it forth.

Since an eclipse of the moon is rare, this stone too is rare, and its power is rare and to be feared, so that it must be employed with much fear and care. For if *sucht*, or *riddo*—which is fever—or *gicht* [gout], or any other illness, has attacked a person through an alteration of the humors, place the carbuncle upon the sufferer’s navel about midnight, because its power is then especially strong. But do not leave it there longer than until the person feels himself somewhat warmed by it [Col. 1259C]; remove it immediately, for its power will then have penetrated that person and all his internal organs more than any medicinal ointment could do. As soon as the person feels even a slight movement in his body, remove the carbuncle; for if you allow it to lie longer upon his navel, its power will pass through his whole body so that he will dry up. Thus this stone drives away and checks every kind of pestilence in a person.

If anyone has pain in the head, let him place the carbuncle upon the crown of his head for a short time, namely until his flesh there is warmed by it, and remove it at once. For the power of the stone will have penetrated his head more swiftly and more thoroughly [Col. 1259D] than the costliest ointment or balsam could do, and thus his head will be better. If you put this stone among clothes or any other objects, they can endure for a long time and decay only with difficulty. Wherever a carbuncle is, aerial spirits cannot fully accomplish their phantasms there, for they flee and turn away from it.

## CHAPTER XV.—ON AMETHYST

[Note: [Col. 1259] Marbod, *On Stones*, 253; and his mystical application, p. 141.]

Amethyst grows when the sun displays its circle as though it were crowned; and it does this when it foretells that some change is to take place in the Lord’s garment, that is, in the Church. And it grows as [the] *flius* [uncertain reading], and therefore they are numerous. It is hot and fiery, and somewhat aerial, because at the time when the sun displays its circle, as has been said, the air is somewhat mild.

A person who has blemishes on his face should moisten an amethyst with his saliva and rub the blemishes with it while wet. He should also heat water over a fire, hold the same stone over the water so that the sweat issuing from it mingles with the water, then put it into that water as well; let him wash his face with the same water, and do this often. He will have smooth skin and a beautiful complexion. But if someone has newly swollen anywhere on his body, let him moisten the same stone with saliva and touch every part of the swelling with it while wet; the swelling will diminish and disappear. [Col. 1260B] Wherever a spider has bitten a person’s body, rub the bite with the stone, and he will be cured. A serpent and a viper—that is, a *nater* [adder]—flee the same stone and avoid a place where they know it to be.

## CHAPTER XVI.—ON AGATE

Agate is born from a certain sand of water; it stretches from east to south, and is hot and fiery. Yet it has more force from air and water than from fire. When the water diminishes so that the sand appears without water, a certain part of that sand is suffused by the sun’s heat and the air’s purity, so that it shines forth as stone. But when afterwards the waters rise in flood, they lift the stone from the sand and carry it to other lands.

If a spider or another worm has poured its poison upon a person [Col. 1260C], provided it has not entered the body, heat an agate strongly in the sun or upon a heated brick, and lay it, while hot, upon the painful spot: the stone removes that poison. Then heat it again in the same way, hold it over the steam of hot water so that its sweat mingles with the water, place it in that water for a short time, and then dip a linen cloth in the water. Rub with that cloth the place on the body where the spider’s bite is, or where another poison has been poured over it, and it will be cured.

If anyone carries this stone with him, let him put it against his bare skin so that it becomes warm; its nature makes that person fit, sensible, and prudent in speech, because it is born of fire, air, and water. For just as some harmful herb laid on a person’s skin sometimes causes a pustule or ulcer to arise, so too certain precious stones, laid upon the skin, make a person healthy and sensible by their power.

A person who has the falling sickness [epilepsy] or is a lunatic should always keep an agate laid against his skin, and afterwards he will be better. For people are often born with these infirmities, and also bring them upon themselves from an excess of harmful humors and pestilences. A person with the falling sickness should put an agate [Col. 1261A] in water for three days when the moon is already full; on the fourth day remove it, cook the water slightly so that it does not boil, and preserve it. Let him cook in it all the food he eats while the moon wholly wanes. Whatever he drinks in the meantime, whether wine or water, let him put the agate into it and drink in this way. Let him do so for ten months, and he will be cured, unless God does not will it.

Likewise, a lunatic, three days before he knows the time of his madness is approaching, should put the same stone in water for three days and remove it on the fourth. Then warm that water slightly, cook in it all the food he eats while he is in madness, put the stone into every drink he has in the meantime, and drink from it. Let him do this for five [Col. 1261B] months, and he will recover his reason and health, unless God forbids it. For when [the patient is] roused by water slightly warmed through the power of the same stone—

[Note: [Col. 1261D] The passage is corrupt.]

—so that he is not made ill by its boiling, the food of that person should be seasoned with that water, and his drink in the same manner, as was said above; thus, through the power of these temperaments and by God’s power, the humors that bring madness upon him are calmed.

Every night, before a person places himself in bed, let him carry an agate openly along the length of his house and then across its breadth, in the form of a cross. Thieves will then be less able to pursue and succeed in their designs, and will gain less by stealing.

## CHAPTER XVII.—ON DIAMOND

[Note: [Col. 1261D] Pliny, *Natural History* XXXVII.4; Marbod, *On Stones*, 28.]

[Col. 1261C]

The diamond is hot. It is born from certain mountains in the southern region that are like *legechte* [perhaps *leymechte*, “clayey”] and, like a kind of crystal, *glasechte* [“glassy”]; and from this same *leym* [clay] there sometimes arises a certain *gedosze*, as it were a heart, of great strength. Since it is strong and hard, before it becomes large the clay of the mountain lying around it splits, and it thus falls, as though into water, in the form and size of a *krisolo* [uncertain term]. Afterwards, however, the clay at that spot is weaker than before. When a flood of rivers subsequently rises, it carries the stone away to other regions.

Some people are by nature and through diabolical influence malicious; for that reason they are inclined to silence. But when they speak, they have a sharp gaze, and at times almost lose their minds, as though carried into madness, yet quickly return to themselves. Such persons should often, or always, put a diamond in their mouths. Its power is such and so strong that it extinguishes the malice and evil present in them. A person who is frenzied, deceitful, or irascible should likewise always keep the stone in his mouth; by its force these evils are turned away from him. Whoever cannot fast should put the same stone in his mouth; it diminishes his hunger, so that he can fast much longer.

A person afflicted with *virgichtiget* [a form of gout or paralysis], or with apoplexy—that is, the illness which seizes one half of the body [Col. 1262A] so that one cannot move—should put a diamond in wine or water for one whole day and drink from it. His gout will cease, even if it is so severe that it threatens to tear apart his limbs; apoplexy too will diminish. A person with *gelsucht* [jaundice] should put the stone in wine or water and drink from it; he will be cured.

The diamond is of such hardness that no hardness can overcome it; therefore it attacks and pierces iron. Since neither iron nor steel can cut its hardness, it strengthens steel so that it neither yields nor breaks before it cuts it. The devil is hostile to this little stone because he resists strength; thus the devil disdains it by night as well as by day.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—ON MAGNET

[Col. 1262B]

The magnet is hot and is born from the foam of certain poisonous worms that live in a certain sand and water, though more in the sand than in the water. For there is a poisonous worm, like a *snecko* [snail], near a certain water and living in it, which sometimes ejects its foam upon a place of earth from which iron is usually smelted. When another poisonous worm sees this—one which likewise lives around and in that water, and feeds upon the earth from which iron is produced—it runs eagerly to the foam and pours out its poison, namely black poison, upon it. This poison penetrates the foam by its strength so that it hardens into stone. Therefore the magnet has an iron-rust colour and naturally draws iron after it, because it is coagulated from the poison nourished from the earth from which iron is produced.

The water beside which this stone lies, frequently flooding over it, thins and diminishes the great poison that is in it. If a person is mad, or has in some manner been *virgogelecht* [afflicted by fantasy or madness], rub a magnet with saliva; rub the mad person’s crown with the stone thus moistened, and rub his forehead crosswise, saying: “You, mad evil, depart through that power by which God changed the power of the devil falling from heaven into the goodness of man.” Then he will recover his senses.

For this stone has useful and useless fire: the fire it has from iron-bearing earth is useful, while the fire it has from the poison of worms is harmful. When it is aroused by the healthful, warm moisture of human saliva, [the defective text then refers to] harmful humors that overthrow human understanding.

[Note: [Col. 1262D] Something is missing.]

## CHAPTER XIX.—ON LIGURIUS

[Note: [Col. 1262D] Compare below VII.27; Marbod, *On Stones*, 358.]

Ligurius is hot. It is born from a certain urine—and not from every urine—of the lynx. For the lynx is neither a wanton nor lustful nor unclean animal, but is moderate in one respect. Its power is so strong that it even penetrates stones; hence it has sharp sight and its eyes are not easily dimmed.

This stone is not always born from its urine, but when the sun burns fiercely and the breeze is light, gentle, and well tempered. Then this animal sometimes rejoices because of the sun’s heat and purity and the sweetness of the lovely breeze. When it wishes to urinate, it digs the ground with its foot and discharges its urine into that hollow; thus ligurius coagulates and grows through the sun’s heat. For it is warm from the sun’s purity, the gentle breeze that shines upon the animal by touching it, its gladness of heart, and the great force possessed by its urine; when it is discharged in this way, it coagulates into this stone. Thus the coagulation of a beautiful stone occurs in the earth, a stone softer than other stones.

A person with severe pain in the stomach should put ligurius into wine, beer, or [Col. 1263B] water for a short time, then remove it. The liquid is then suffused with the powers of the stone and receives strength from it. Let him do this for fifteen days, and give it to him in a small quantity to drink after he has eaten a little, not while fasting. No fever or pestilence in his stomach, however strong, short of imminent death, will prevent his stomach from being cleansed, purified, and saved.

No other person should drink this preparation for any cause except stomach pain: he could not live, for its strength is so great that it would *virseriget* [uncertain term] his heart and split his head apart. But a person suffering from difficulty in urination, so that he cannot urinate, should put ligurius into cows’ or sheep’s milk—not goats’ milk—for one day; remove it on the second day; warm the milk, that is, *welle* [make it hot], and drink it in sips. Let him do this for five days, and it relieves his urine retention.

## CHAPTER XX.—ON CRYSTAL

Crystal is born from certain cold waters, which are of a somewhat blackish colour—

[Note: [Col. 1263D] Something is missing.]

—when air coming upon the water touches it, the water in some place coagulates through cold like a certain mass, and, as it were, the heart of the water coagulates into strength. When afterwards the heat of air or sun touches it, it removes by its heat the dense whiteness which that mass then has, so that it becomes somewhat clear; yet it cannot be dissolved by that heat. But then cold returning makes that same mass coagulate ever more, and more purely [Col. 1263D]. It becomes so strong that it cannot be dissolved by heat, although all the surrounding ice melts; and thus crystal arises and is crystal.

A person whose eyes grow dim should heat crystal in the sun and frequently lay it, while warm, upon his eyes. Since it is of the nature of water, it draws bad humors from the eyes, and he will see better. If *drusae* or *orfimae* arise in a person’s neck, heat the same stone in the sun, bind it while warm over the *drusae* or *orfimae* by day or night, and do this often: they will disappear. If a *hubo* grows or swells in a person’s throat, heat crystal in the sun, pour wine over it while hot, and drink of it often [Col. 1264A]. Also lay the crystal, heated in the sun, frequently and warmly upon the *hubin* in the throat; it will diminish.

A person with pain in the heart, stomach, or belly should heat crystal in the sun, pour water over it while warm, place the same crystal into the water for a short time, then remove it, and drink that water often. He will be better in heart, stomach, or belly. A person troubled by *nesseden* should heat the same stone in the sun and lay it warm upon the painful place; the *nessia* will be driven away.

## CHAPTER XXI.—ON PEARLS

There are certain salty waters of rivers from which pearls are born. For the rich substance of these rivers, together with their saltness, falls to the sand [Col. 1264B], so that the upper water is purified; this rich substance, together with its saltness, coagulates into pearls, and these pearls are clean.

Take these pearls and put them into water. All the *livor* and *slim* [slime] in that water gathers around the pearls, and the upper water is purified and cleansed. A person with fever should often drink that upper water, and he will be better. A person with pain in the head should heat pearls in the sun, place them warm around his temples, bind a cloth over them, and he will be cured.

## CHAPTER XXII.—ON BERLIN

Berlin are born from certain shellfish—namely, creatures that lie in shells and live in the sea and in certain large rivers. Some of these shelled creatures move about near the bottom of such rivers, seeking their food there. They are somewhat poisonous; from the filth they draw into themselves from that bottom, and from their poison when they spit it out, certain *berlir* coagulate and are born. These are sometimes cloudy because the animals themselves move about the bottom of those waters, and they have almost no usefulness.

Some of the same shelled creatures are accustomed to move about in the middle of those rivers, where the waters are pure. There they draw less filth into themselves and therefore have little poison in them. Consequently the *berlin* born from the waters taken into themselves by these animals [Col. 1264D], and from the poison they spit out, become clear there, since there is a certain purity of water in the middle of the rivers. Yet they have almost no medicinal use, except that some are clearer and contain less poison than others.

Other shelled creatures move about at the surface of those rivers, where foam and much floating filth of those waters flow. From this foam and upper filth, together with the poison of the animals, certain *berlin* coagulate. These too are somewhat cloudy, because they are born from foam and accumulations of filth; they have no medicinal usefulness, since they bring people more illness than health [Col. 1265A]. If anyone put them in his mouth, he would almost bring upon himself such an illness that he would become sick as though he had taken poison. If he laid them on his skin until his flesh was warmed by them, he would draw their poison into himself and thus become ill and suffer pain.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—ON CORNELIAN

Cornelian has more of warm air than of cold, and is found in sand. If blood flows from anyone’s nostrils, heat wine, put cornelian into the heated wine, and give it to him to drink. The blood will cease to flow.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—ON ALABASTER

Alabaster has neither true heat nor true cold in itself, but is as it were temperate in both; thus scarcely any medicinal power is found in it.

## CHAPTER XXV.—ON LIME

Lime is hot; chalk is made from it when it has been burned, and chalk is therefore hot. When lime is reduced to powder by fire, it is strengthened and binds earth and sand together by its fire. But if a person or an animal eats lime, the force of its heat destroys and makes the eater ill.

A person whose flesh has been eaten in some place by a worm should take chalk and twice as much *criden* [uncertain substance], make of them with vinegar or wine a thin plaster-like cement, and apply it with a feather to the place where he suffers from the worm. Let him do this every day through the fifth day. Afterwards he should take aloe and one third as much myrrh, grind them together, prepare from them with fresh wax an *eyn plaster* [a plaster], lay it upon a hempen cloth, and bind it over the painful place for twelve days. For chalk is hot and *crida* is cold; thus the heat of the chalk, moderated by the coldness of *crida* and by the heat and sharpness of wine, kills the worms. The heat of aloe increases that of myrrh, draws out the corruptions of these ulcers, and heals the place.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—ON OTHER STONES

Other stones, which arise in different soils and regions and acquire from the soils in which they are born different natures and colours, are of little use in medicines: marble, *grieszstein* [gritstone], *calckstein* [limestone], *ducksteyn*, *wacken*, and the like. For they possess either excessive moisture that is not tempered by proper dryness, or excessive dryness that is not moistened by proper moisture.

[Col. 1265] Here ends the third (fourth) book, on stones.

The fourth (fifth) book begins: On fishes. Preface.

[Col. 1265B]

There are certain fish which by nature move about near the bottom of sea and rivers, seek their food there, and furrow the bottom as pigs furrow the earth. There they eat certain roots in certain plants, by which they live long; and they continually seek there whatever else suits their nourishment.

[Note: [Col. 1265D] “And they continually seek whatever else…” omitted in the edition.]

They also sometimes rise almost to the middle of the waters, and sometimes descend to the bottom; but they dwell chiefly there. Their flesh is somewhat soft and weak, and they are not wholesome to eat, because they always move about near the bottoms of waters. Some of them love the day and the brightness of the sun more than the night or the brightness of the moon. Others love night and the brightness of the moon more than day and the brightness of the sun.

Some of these fish discharge all their *rogim* [roe] in succession—that is, they *leychent* [spawn]—without pausing from this discharge, so that after they have discharged their *geleyche* [spawn], and thus emptied themselves wholly of roe and *milche* [milt], they are weakened somewhat because they hasten in this discharge. Others make intervals in the discharge and wait [Col. 1266B] until they are strengthened further; then they spawn again, so that at least from March until autumn they discharge their roe.

Other fish move chiefly in the middle and purity of sea and other rivers, and seek their food there. They also find there certain very healthful herbs on projecting rocks, on which they feed—herbs of such healthfulness that, if a person could obtain them, he would drive every illness away from himself by them. These fish are wholesome to eat, and their flesh is somewhat firm because they live chiefly in the purity of the waters. Yet they sometimes descend to the bottom and sometimes rise, but are chiefly in the middle of those rivers.

[Note: [Col. 1266D] “Because they live in the purity … those rivers” omitted in the edition.]

They are also smaller than the fish which willingly move near the bottom. Some love day and sun more than night or moon; others moon and night more than day or sun. Some of them likewise discharge all their roe before ceasing, and are thereby somewhat weakened. Others make intervals in this discharge, in order to regain strength for the task, as was said of the former fish.

[Note: [Col. 1267D] “And some … as was said above” omitted in the edition.]

Other fish are accustomed to move about near the surface of sea and other rivers. There they seek food in foam and in much upper filth; they are more steeped in the sun’s heat than others. They sometimes hide in little hollows containing foul water that cannot flow out. Therefore their flesh is weak and soft, and they are not wholesome to eat. They also sometimes descend a little way into the water and are accustomed to move near the shore. Some love day and sun more than night and moon; others, night and moon more. Some, when they spawn, discharge all their roe before resting from the discharge, and are thereby somewhat weakened; others make intervals in this work and occasionally regain their strength, as has been said of the rest.

[Note: [Col. 1267D] “They also sometimes … said of the rest” omitted in the edition.]

All fish, according to their kind, eat herbs suitable to them in winter and also sometimes in summer. Hence *milche* [milt; “milk,” ed.] and *rogim* [roe; “seed-granules,” ed.] grow in them, and they feed delightfully upon these things. If a human being, namely an infertile woman, ate them, she would become fertile and conceive. They do not join one another in any other intercourse for conception; *rogim* or *milcher* is born in them—

[Addition in the edition: “just as other animals are accustomed to join with one another”]

—but they have as great a desire solely for their discharge, that is, for *leychens* [spawning], as other animals have for sexual intercourse. Each seeks a mate suited and fitting to itself. When the time of their discharge approaches, they seek a place near the shore where neither winds nor storms can harm them, but where there is good rest and a quiet, temperate condition of the waters—

[Note: [Col. 1267D] “But where … waters” omitted in the edition.]

—and where little herbs have grown around for them to feed upon in the meantime. Then the fish that is female proceeds straight ahead, that is, in the manner of a line, until according to her nature she stops this discharge. Where she ends the discharge, she waits for another fish, namely the male, to arrive. At once the male, namely the *milcher* [milt-bearing male], follows and pours out his milt in order and measure over the roe [Col. 1267D] where the female fish has gone before. When he reaches her, he ceases pouring out his milt. Exhausted and wearied, they become somewhat weak and seek rest near that same place until they recover their strength, feeding meanwhile on the surrounding little herbs.

[Note: [Col. 1267D] From this point the edited text varies in many respects, too many to record. It reads as follows: “From the time when they discharge together, they recognize one another and move about together; after they have grown, they discharge their seed together. If some of them are caught, those that remain seek out again others like themselves in age. And just as a human being abandons his own nature by coupling with beasts, so beasts too are sometimes led into mixture outside their own kind; likewise fish sometimes depart from their own kind into another kind in the discharge of their seed, and produce another kind foreign to their own, as may be observed in the eel and in certain other fish. [Col. 1268D] But God has given certain fish a kind of knowledge according to their nature and kind: they recognize certain herbs and roots in the waters, which they sometimes eat when they have no other food. Their strength and nature are such that, once they have tasted them, they require no food for half a year or for four months. That fish do not have clamorous voices, as other animals do, is understandable; and in place of the cry of a voice, which they do not have in their belly, the water in which they move makes a sound in its course. Creeping creatures, and those which are sometimes in water and sometimes upon earth, have some kinship with animals and therefore have tongues for hissing and vocal sounds.”]

From the time when they discharge their seed until the little fish begin to live, many varied and sudden conditions and disturbances of the air sometimes arise. But these discharges of fish, that is, *geleyche*, are often broken up before the young fish begin to live by floods of rains, storms, and passing vessels; thus they perish and do not come to fruition. If anyone ate this discharge of fish, that is, *geleyche*, it would be almost like poison to him. Therefore nets must be washed with great care, lest it cling to them [Col. 1268B] and thus be drawn out in the capture of fish.

After fish have discharged their seed, that is, *geleyche*, they become weak because, as was said above, they are greatly wearied; then they do not have flesh as wholesome for human food as at another time. The little fish which are discharged together—that is, which *geleichet werden* [are spawned] and move about together—after they have grown likewise discharge their seed. If some of them are caught, those that remain again seek others similar to themselves in age.

Some fish, as has been said, delight in the brightness of day and the sun’s radiance and seek food in it; others delight in night and the brightness of moon and stars, and seek their food then, because at times they have a better tempering in the water at night than by day [Col. 1268C]. Just as a person forsakes his nature by coupling with cattle, so cattle too sometimes join in mixture with another kind. Likewise fish sometimes turn from their kind to another kind in the discharge of their seed, and produce a kind alien to their own, as may be observed in the eel and certain other fish.

God has given certain fish a kind of knowledge according to their nature and kind, so that they recognize certain herbs and roots in the waters. They sometimes eat these when they have no other food; their strength and nature are such that, once the fish have recognized or tasted them, they need no food either for half a year or for four months [Col. 1268D], and yet their flesh does not thereby fail or diminish. When they afterwards are hungry and have no other food, they are sustained again for a long time by the same herbs and roots, once they have recognized them.

If a person likewise knew and recognized these herbs and roots, could obtain them, and ate them at times, then after having tasted them once he could go without other food for four or five months. But his flesh would become hard and twisted, and would not be as smooth as it now is. Adam, when he was expelled from Paradise [Col. 1270A], knew them, sought them in the waters, and sometimes ate them when he had no other food. But after he was able to have other food, he avoided them. These herbs neither grow nor perish easily; therefore, when fish or beasts taste even a little of them, they lie undigested in their stomachs for a long time because they are difficult to digest. Thus animals which eat them do not suffer hunger for a long time; instead, they are digested along with the other foods that they eat later.
