## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1269]

## CHAPTER I.—ON THE WHALE

[Note: [Col. 1269] *Balaena mysticetus* [the bowhead whale].] [IV, 2].

[Col. 1269B]

The Whale has fiery heat and watery air within itself, and the nature of fishes, and also a certain kinship with the nature of beasts—namely, of the lion and the bear. [Note: [Col. 1269] What follows as far as “and the flesh of this fish” is omitted in the edition.] By its fish-nature it moves about in the waters, and by its beast-nature it grows to a great size. Nor does it flee from man; for if beasts could live in the waters, they would grow beyond measure in size, so that man could not dwell in the waters for fear of them. It seeks both day and night, and the bottom as well as the surface of the sea. It feeds on the food of fishes and on the food of beasts, and it also eats fishes; for if fishes were not diminished in the sea by being eaten and devoured, the sea would not be passable because of their multitude. And when it has swallowed much, it becomes fat and corpulent, so that it can scarcely move itself from place to place. Then it raises itself somewhat upward, emits foam from its mouth, and spits out some of what it has swallowed; in this way it relieves itself. But when it feels that it can then move, it gradually moves from place to place, and thus loses some of its thickness and fat and becomes lighter. Then it rejoices that it can move, and in its ferocity ranges here and there, destroying or devouring in fury whatever meets it. Yet men very often capture it by traps at that time.

When it has been relieved in this manner, as stated above, it seeks those herbs and roots by which it can endure for some time without other food. And when the sun rises high, so that the days grow longer, then these fishes—the male and female—seek out earth which has sap from that soil and is stronger than other earth; and dew from the air then falls upon the herbs which grow in that same soil. Both fishes raise themselves upon that earth and are moistened with the said dew; and their spawn (*geleyche*) begins to grow within them from those herbs. They then leave that place; but when afterward they discharge their *geleich*, they seek earth moistened by the sap previously mentioned. The female, where the elevation of that earth is, emits grains—that is, she spawns—and lays them upon that earth with her fins; the male follows and pours his milk over them. Meanwhile they rest there until they receive vital air; and they do this once each year. From those grains comes one fish, and such is the power of that earth that it quickly begins to live; once they have begun to live, the parents depart.

Their flesh has such strength that, when eaten, it resists every evil and weak humour. For God made certain forms among all created animals in which He displays His strength, as He does also in this fish; and therefore this fish sometimes perceives the wickedness of the devil, and for that reason emits its blasts against him. The flesh of this fish is wholesome, and good for healthy and sick persons to eat; and aerial spirits flee in disdain from its strength, because whenever it senses anything diabolical nearby, it contracts its skin, makes itself terrible in appearance, and emits dreadful blasts against that phantom. [Note: [Col. 1271D] “And aerial—blasts” ends in the edition.]

But a person who is frenzied and *unsinnig* (“out of his senses”) should often eat sufficiently of its flesh, with bread alone added, and will recover his senses. And one who is gout-afflicted (*virgichtiget*) should often eat this flesh, and the gout (*gicht*) will cease in him. Its brain, however, is not fit to eat, nor is the brain of any fish, animal, or bird; for the brain of an animal makes weak—that is, *unmechtiget*—and afflicts the person who eats it. But cook the brain of this fish vigorously in a new pot with water, and stir it vigorously with a spoon—that is, *zutribe*—then pour it into another vessel and pound it vigorously. Add the herb called *gicht* and enough tree-oil, and cook it again in the first new pot; stir it vigorously again, and thus make an ointment. Whoever is troubled by severe *gicht*, or has *ridden* or other ulcers, should anoint himself with it and will be cured.

And whoever suddenly feels *unmechtet* in his heart [“feels a failing,” [Col. 1271C] ed.] should reduce its heart to powder and drink it in water, and he will fare better. Likewise, whoever suffers from gout (*vicht*) should frequently drink this same powder in wine and water, and the *vicht* will cease in him. And if anyone eats of its liver, it cleanses his stomach inwardly and removes all its foulness from the interior, like an excellent draught. But in whatever house or place aerial spirits are accustomed to prepare their mockeries, burn the liver of this fish there upon live coals: they will depart and, because of the strength of the smell, will be unable to remain there. Whoever has nocturnal, prolonged, or shifting fevers—which change according to the condition of the air—should cook its lung in water and eat it often, and the fevers will cease in him. But because the lung cannot be kept for a year, reduce the same lung moderately to powder, and often drink this powder in water or wine; whatever the fevers may be, even if they are *riddo*, they will cease in him. [Note: [Col. 1271D] “But whoever suffers from *wicht*—will cease” is omitted in the edition.]

Whoever has eaten or drunk poison should reduce its lung and liver to powder in equal weight, add as much *andron* [horehound, ed.] as there is of this powder, add a little honey, cook it with pure good wine, and drink it warm—that is, *welch*—while fasting, two or three times in the morning before daybreak; the poison he has taken will either foam out through nausea or pass through him by evacuation. [Note: [Col. 1271D] The edition omits much of what follows and arranges other matters differently: “Further, whoever has a white opacity, a film, or a little stone in his eye, or suffers from dimness of the eyes, should apply the raw gall of the whale to his eyes and also anoint his eyelids with a feather, so that it touches the eyes slightly within; and he will have clear eyes for seeing. Likewise, let the bladder of the whale be kept for a year, so that if an ulcer or *flier* grows in any person’s body, the bladder itself may be softened in water [Col. 1272D] and laid upon it, and he will be cured. Let him also place the same bladder upon scrofulous swellings, and they will disappear. Let a man hold in his hand the handle of a knife made from the bone of this fish, so that it grows warm, and there is scarcely any pain in him that does not cease from its violence. Let a man also make a belt from the whale’s skin and gird himself with it against his bare skin, and it will drive all illnesses away from him; and let him have shoes from its skin, and he will have healthy feet and healthy legs.”]

And whoever keeps its bladder for a year—if [lacuna] an ulcer or *slyer* is ruptured—will be cured; but after the ulcer has burst, remove the bladder. And if you have *orfime* in your body, soften it again in water and lay it upon them, and they will disappear.

If anyone also has *druszewaczent* in his body, soften the same bladder with your saliva and lay it over them, and they will disappear. Whoever suffers in the liver or is ill in the lungs should cook the lesser entrails of this fish with hyssop in water, make *sulczen* from them, and eat them often; the pain in his liver will cease and his lungs will recover health. Whoever is troubled by *gicht* should steep this fish’s eyelids in wine for a night or a day, then heat that wine at the fire and drink it often; the *gicht* will cease. Further, if someone is *virgichtiget* in his tongue so that he cannot speak, scrape these same eyelids into water and give it to him to drink; he will speak at once, and his tongue will regain its strength. The tongue is often hindered from speaking by paralysis caused by cold humours, but is cured by the fiery heat of the eyelids. Make also a knife-handle from the bone of this fish and hold that handle in your hand so that it grows warm there; then there is no pain in your hand or arm which will not cease. And if oxen, sheep, and pigs are dying of pestilence, reduce this fish’s bones to powder, cast the powder into water, and frequently give it to them to drink; *schelmo* will cease among them. Make shoes from its skin and wear them, and you will have healthy feet and healthy legs. Make also a belt from its skin and gird yourself with it against your bare skin; it will drive various diseases away from you and make you strong.

## CHAPTER II.—ON THE HUSO

[Note: [Col. 1272D] *Acipenser Huso*.] [IV, 4].

The Huso [*Echinus*, ed.] is more of warm than cold air. [Note: [Col. 1272D] What follows is omitted in the edition as far as “But a person.”] It loves the nocturnal brightness of the moon and stars, and night more than day; it rests during the day, prospers in swiftly running, vigorous waters, loves them, and labours so much in swimming in them that its flesh becomes soft from that labour. It swims in mid-water and seldom seeks the bottom; it feeds on clean pasture, and therefore its flesh is good for healthy persons to eat, though it harms the sick somewhat. It spawns as other fishes do.

But a person in whom dropsy has begun to grow should put this fish’s bladder into water so that the water takes flavour from it, and drink it frequently; the dropsy in him will improve and disappear. [Note: [Col. 1273D] The edition extends to this point.] For this fish’s bladder is watery, rough, and somewhat bitter; and therefore, when tempered by the sweetness of water, it diminishes the disease.

## CHAPTER III.—ON THE MERSWIN

[Note: [Col. 1273D] A species of seal.] [IV, 3].

The Merswin is more of warm than cold air, [Note: [Col. 1273D] “And it has the nature of fishes,” etc., is omitted in the edition. It continues: “But a person”; it ends: “and the *gicht* will cease in him.”] and has the nature of fishes and almost that of pigs. It loves night more than day, gladly remains in caverns of the waters, and sometimes rises above the waters. It sometimes feeds on unclean food and on human flesh—when people are drowned in the waters—and on unclean foam floating upon the water. Therefore its flesh is not wholesome for human food. Both male and female eat certain herbs from which they become *swanger* (“pregnant”).

And when the time is at hand for them to discharge their *geleych*, the male and female join their necks together and rub them together (*strichet*); thus both grow warm. Then the female emits her seed, and the male, seeing it, devours it. The female is angered by this and emits other seed; she lies over it and *ruwet* (“rests”). Soon the male comes and emits from his mouth his *milch* (“milk”) over it, together with that which he had devoured. Thus both moisten the same *geleyche*, and remain there until it has begun to live; one fish will thus result. Once it has received vital air, they proceed again and do the same, because they discharge all their *geleyche* at one time.

But a person who is *virgichtiget* should reduce its liver and lung to powder in equal weight, put the powder in water, and drink it often; the *gicht* will cease in him. The rest of its parts are of little value for medicines.

## CHAPTER IV.—ON THE STORO

[Note: [Col. 1273D] *Acipenser Sturio*.] [IV, 4].

The Storo [*Rombus*, ed.] is more cold than warm. [Note: [Col. 1273D] The edition, omitting the intervening material: “A person whom *vich* afflicts should eat sufficiently and often of this fish’s liver, and the *vich* will cease in him. And if the flesh around a person’s eyes swells out, or his eyes grow dim, he should mix the gall of this fish with rue-juice and a smaller quantity [Col. 1274D] of *caliminum*, put it in a copper vessel, and often anoint his eyes above with it; and he will see clearly. But if a bone is broken in any part of a person’s body by any accident, reduce the bone of an ostrich to powder, put this powder into pure unsalted water drawn from a well, and drink it fasting. Let him do this, though moderately, until he is cured.”] It moves about more by day than by night; it also seeks at the bottom of the waters those roots and herbs by which it can live long without other food, and gladly moves about here and there in the waters. Its flesh is wholesome and does not harm healthy persons when eaten, though it causes some discomfort to the sick because it is too strong for them.

When *geleyche* is to grow in it, it raises itself above the waters, dew from the air falls upon it, and then both male and female eat certain herbs resembling *cle*, and receive fertility. But when the time comes to spawn, it seeks some black earth and emits certain grains there, over which the male pours nothing; thus those grains become one fish. Again they rest beside that seed until it receives vital air. Once it has lived, they proceed again and spawn with other grains, in sequence, until they have discharged all their *geleyche*.

A person troubled by *vicht* should eat enough of this fish’s liver frequently, and the *vicht* will cease in him. If flesh rises around someone’s eyes—that is, *uszwelczet*—or his eyes are dim, let him take its gall, an equal weight of rue-juice, and a smaller quantity of chamomile (*camillen*), mix them together, place them in a copper vessel, and often anoint the outside of his eyes with this around nightfall, so that it touches the inside of the eyes slightly. He will be cured in his eyes and see clearly when the dimness has been driven away. Moreover, if its bones are burned in a house, aerial spirits avoid it meanwhile and do not perform their illusions there; just as a human being flees a foul smell, so evil spirits then flee it, because they do not love a clean animal.

## CHAPTER V.—ON THE SALMON

[Note: [Col. 1274D] *Salmo Salar*.] [IV, 5].

The Salmon is more of cold than warm air and moves about more at night than by day; it loves the moon more than the sun. When the moon appears, it swims most vigorously in its brightness, as in the brightness of the sun; therefore its flesh somewhat resembles the moon, and is soft and weak. It is good for no one to eat, because it stirs up all the bad humours in a person. It seeks the bottom of the waters, and sometimes eats those roots and little herbs by which it can be sustained for a long time without other pasture. It also eats the grass which grows from grain that falls into waters, and receives fertility from it. When it spawns, it seeks *leymecht* earth and emits its roe (*rogim*) there; the male pours his *milch* over it, and one little fish comes from the grains. They then proceed again until they are emptied of their *geleyche*, pouring it out in diverse places at one time; there they rest until they receive life from the air.

[Note: [Col. 1274D] Here the edited text begins, omitting what precedes.]

A person whose teeth are decaying, whose teeth are weak and brittle, should reduce this fish’s bones to powder, add a little burnt salt, and often apply this powder round his teeth at night. Let him allow the saliva—that is, the gums—to flow out; it cleanses and heals the flesh around his teeth. Its remaining parts are of no value for other medicines.

## CHAPTER VI.—ON THE WELCA

[Note: [Col. 1275D] *Silurus Glanis*.] [IV, 6].

The Welca is more of warm than cold air, loves day more than night, and feeds upon grain which falls into the waters and upon other good herbs. [Note: [Col. 1275D] “And it loves day more—feeds” is omitted in the edition.] It has wholesome flesh, good for both sick and healthy persons to eat, and it spawns as other fishes do. [Note: [Col. 1275D] “And it—fishes” is omitted in the edition.]

A person whose eyes are dim should take its gall, add fennel juice and a few drops of wine, and with this mixture gently anoint around his eyelids and eyes; but he must take care that it does not touch the inside of the eyes. It will drive away dimness of the eyes. If anyone eats its cooked liver, it gathers and draws to itself all the *livor*—that is, *slim*—and all the poison—that is, *eyther*—in his stomach, and casts it out with itself through evacuation; thus his stomach will be healthy. Its heart is fit neither for food nor for medicines, and harms the person who eats it. Its other parts are of no value for medicines. [Note: [Col. 1275D] “And if anyone—are of no value” is omitted in the edition, which has instead: “If a person, whether male or female, has dimness in the eyes from an excess of sexual desire, let him dry in the sun the little skin of this fish’s gall after the gall has been poured out, steep it in the purest and best wine, and at night when going to bed bind it with a cloth over his eyes. Let him remove it about midnight, lest it pierce the eyes. Let him do the same on the third night, [Col. 1276D] the fifth, and the seventh, but not on the second, fourth, or sixth. If a person experiences dimness from another affliction, this remedy will not help him.”]

## CHAPTER VII.—ON THE LASZ

[IV, 8].

The Lasz [*Esox*, ed.] is more of warm than cold air, loves day, and does not seek the bottom of the waters. Rather, it seeks its pasture in mid-water and in certain *leym* where little herbs grow, and eats them. [Note: [Col. 1276D] “And it loves day—eats them” is omitted in the edition.] Its flesh is healthier than salmon flesh and is good for healthy persons to eat, though it burdens the sick somewhat. Since this fish belongs to warm air, its flesh is good for healthy persons who are warm, but does not benefit sick persons who are cold; and it spawns as other fishes do. [Note: [Col. 1276D] “Since this fish—fishes” is omitted in the edition.] But its liver is soft and harms a person. Its other parts are of little use. [Note: [Col. 1276D] “And its other parts—use” is omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER VIII.—ON THE COPPREA

[Note: [Col. 1276D] Absent from the edition.]

The Copprea is more of cold than warm air. It loves day, always moves about in fresh cold waters and near the bottom, sometimes delights in pure waters and spends the night in them, and seeks wholesome food. Its flesh, when eaten, does not harm healthy persons. Sick persons should eat it moderately, because it belongs to cold air. No one should eat its liver unless it is made into *gesultze* with dill or fennel and eaten thus; but its *rogim* and *milch* may be eaten. The little herbs from which it receives fertility resemble *catzenzagel* somewhat. When its time comes, it seeks *leym* and emits grains there, from which one fish will come; the male pours his milk over them, and they remain beside them until they receive life from the air. Then they proceed and spawn in the same way, as stated above, until both are wholly emptied.

If anyone is *virdroszkeyt*, that is, has a sorrowful spirit, let him set the eye of this fish in a gold or silver ring, so that the eye touches the skin of the finger and the skin is warmed by that eye; let him also put it frequently to his mouth, and his understanding will awaken—that is, he will become *wacker* (“alert”). If this eye cannot remain long in the ring in this manner, put a fresh eye of the same fish in it again.

## CHAPTER IX.—ON THE HECHT

[Note: [Col. 1276D] *Esox Lucius*.] [IV, 9].

The Hecht [*Lucius*, ed.] is more of warm than cold air. [Note: [Col. 1276D] Edition: “The pike is of warm air. And if anyone eats its liver,” etc., as below.] It gladly moves about in pure water and in mid-water; it loves day and is sharp and *grim*, like some beast in a forest. Wherever it remains, it consumes fishes and empties those waters of other fish. It seeks clean pasture and has firm, wholesome flesh, good for sick and healthy persons to eat. It has a moderate, well-tempered heat, and therefore its flesh is wholesome. The male and female eat certain little herbs, from which *geleyche* grows in them, and discharge it like other fishes.

If anyone often eats its liver, it produces good and pleasant digestion. If a worm eats a person or a beast, reduce this fish’s bones to powder and lay the powder upon those places, and the worms die.

## CHAPTER X.—ON THE BARBO

[IV, 10].

The Barbo [*Silurus*, ed.] is more of warm than cold air, loves day and warmth, and whenever it feels cold enters little hollows in order to have warmth in them. It gladly remains in the sun and is very wakeful (*vachet*) there; therefore its flesh is soft and *zufloszlich*. It moves about in mid-water and seeks clean pasture. Like other fishes, it lays out its seed, which it spawns from certain little herbs, and labours most diligently at this work, so that it even strives at spawning. It spawns in very many places at one time before it stops.

But if a healthy person eats it frequently, it produces in him neither healthy flesh nor healthy blood. If anyone frequently eats its head, it produces and excites pain in his head and causes other fevers in him. No one should eat its *grumum*, for if he eats it he will suffer from it. Since the head of this fish lacks aerial greenness, it draws muddy poison inwardly, by which its brain and throat are infected; thus it harms when eaten. Its *rogum* is like poison, since its grains can scarcely be separated from one another and are more *gebrechen* (“a defect, infirmity”) than food of health. [Note: [Col. 1277D] The edition very briefly: “The catfish is of warm air. But if anyone frequently eats its head, it excites pain in his head and causes other fevers in him. Let no one eat its brain, its throat, its milk, or the little grains in it, because they are like poison to him.”]

## CHAPTER XI.—ON THE CARP

[Note: [Col. 1277D] *Cyprinus carpio*.] [IV, 11].

[Note: [Col. 1277D] Edition: “The carp is warm, and its flesh, milk, and grains do not kill a healthy person when eaten; they harm a sick person somewhat. But a person,” etc., as below, omitting the intervening material.]

The Carp is more warm than cold, loves day more than night, has the heat of marshes within itself, and from marshes has soft and weak flesh. It seeks pasture in them and gladly remains in the foam of waters. Its flesh does not harm a healthy person when eaten, though it harms the sick somewhat. A healthy person may eat its *milich* and *rogum*, but a sick person should not eat them. This fish sometimes swims into pure water and bathes itself there; then it feeds there on clean pasture, draws there from the sap of a certain earth, and eats certain little herbs from which it receives fertility. When the time comes for them to spawn, they seek *gallendesteyn*, spawn there at one time, the male following, and rest there until they receive vital air, unless they are driven away, as other fishes do.

A person who has fever (*fiber*), so that he is weary of eating and food disgusts him, should cook this fish, remove its head, divide it in the middle, roast it on a spit at the fire, and then steep it in wine. Add a third part of vinegar and pour a little honey into these things; eat it prepared thus often, and the *fiber* will cease in him and he will put away his disgust for food. Its other parts are of little value for medicines.

## CHAPTER XII.—ON THE BRESMA

[Note: [Col. 1278D] *Sparus pagrus*.] [IV, 12].

[Note: [Col. 1278D] Edition: “The Bresma is warm and is not very suitable for either healthy or sick persons to eat. Whoever suffers in the stomach should cook this fish in water and eat it with cumin and vinegar added; it cleanses the stomach of *livor* and fever.”]

The Bresma is more warm than cold, has the sap of earth within it, gladly moves about near the bottom of the waters, and sometimes eats earth. It loves night and bathes itself in the moon’s brightness; therefore it is of little benefit for healthy or sick persons to eat, although they can nevertheless digest it. Near the earth it seeks certain herb-leaves resembling *bremium*, eats them, and is made fertile by them. When its time comes, it spawns into a certain soil, and at the proper time the male pours his milk over it; they guard it thus until it receives life from the air.

A person who is *magensiech* (“stomach-sick”) should cook this fish in water, season it in vinegar with cumin added, make it into *sulze*, and eat it; his stomach will be cleansed of *slim* and fever.

## CHAPTER XIII.—ON THE ELSUA

[IV, 13].

The Elsua [*Elna*, ed.] belongs to cold air. [Note: [Col. 1278D] Edition: “It is of cold air—and if anyone often eats its liver—are of no value,” omitting the rest.] It loves night and, at the bottom of the waters and in dungy earth, eats certain little herbs, from which it grows fat; yet it also seeks clean pasture. After it has wearied of filth, it rises to the purity of water and washes itself in it. When eaten, it does not greatly harm either healthy or sick persons. Near the shore it eats red and *stechelecht* herbs, from which it becomes *swanger* (“pregnant”).

When it wishes to spawn, it seeks little caverns and spawns in them; it spawns from a cavern into the water, draws itself along, enters another little cavern, and spawns in that one too. It thus passes from cavern to cavern until it has discharged all its *geleych*, and the male pours over it; so their seeds receive vital air. That this fish sometimes dies in the waters is because, in the great heat of summer, it is greatly frightened and distressed by storms, great winds, and great floods of water which then arise. It has soft flesh, so that when it hears thunder it wedges itself so tightly into little caverns that it cannot draw itself out; and in this manner it often dies.

But if anyone often eats its liver, he will be strengthened in his heart and healthy in his stomach. Its other parts are of no value for medicines.

## CHAPTER XIV.—ON THE KOLBO

[IV, 15].

The Kolbo [*Scollus*, ed.] is warm. [Note: [Col. 1278D] Edition: “It is of no great value for healthy or sick persons to eat. But as for,” etc., as in the manuscript.] It loves night, moves about near the bottom of the waters, feeds on certain unclean pasture, and is of little value for healthy or sick persons to eat, because its sap is weak. When it spawns, it emits its grains, and again into another little pouch, until it has discharged all its *geleyche*. Immediately the male is present and emits foam from his mouth over them; this adheres to the grains until vital air moves them. Because these fishes are coagulated by the male’s foam, as stated above, they have weak flesh and do not sufficiently restore the person who eats them.

That they have almost no flesh on one side of their body, only skin stretched over the spine, is because if they had flesh there, that flesh would be poisonous to eat and would harm like poison. They also bear poison in the head; therefore whoever ate it would be harmed. This fish is of little value for medicine.

## CHAPTER XV.—ON THE FORNHA

[Note: [Col. 1278D] *Salmo trutta*.] [IV, 16].

The Fornha is more of warm than cold air, loves night, and moves about near the bottom in *bruchwaszern* (“marsh waters”); nevertheless, it does not feed very uncleanly. [Note: [Col. 1279D] “And it loves night—feeds” is omitted in the edition, as are the words below, “and is of little value for medicine.”] It is of little value for sick persons to eat, though it does not harm the healthy; it is also of little value for medicines.

## CHAPTER XVI.—ON THE MONUWA

[IV, 17].

The Monuwa is more of cold than warm air. [Note: [Col. 1279D] The edition: “It is, and its flesh is useful,” omitting the rest.] It loves day, gladly remains in little caverns and in the foam of waters, and sometimes feeds on unclean worms. Therefore its flesh is not wholesome and does not greatly benefit either healthy or sick persons as food, although it does not greatly harm them. It receives its seed from little herbs and discharges it at the proper time. But it contains no medicines.

## CHAPTER XVII.—ON THE BERSICH

[Note: [Col. 1279D] A species of perch.—Absent from the edition.]

The Bersich is more of warm than cold air, loves day, gladly remains in the sunshine, and also gladly moves about in pure water, where it seeks clean pasture. It sometimes enters crags, stones, and little caverns; there it seeks certain good and health-giving herbs on which it feeds. Therefore its flesh is wholesome and good for both sick and healthy persons to eat. It spawns as other fishes do.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—ON THE MEYSISCH

[IV, 14].

The Meysisch belongs to cold air and is more moist. When eaten, it does not greatly harm either healthy or sick persons, but when eaten frequently it produces some *livor* in a person’s stomach.

## CHAPTER XIX.—ON THE FISH WHICH HAS SHELLS

[IV, last].

There is a kind of fish which has shells upon it. It is not fit for healthy or sick persons to eat. [“For if oxen are sick either from harmful blood or from severe labour, let a person reduce these shells to powder, put them into water with betony, and give it to the oxen; they will be cured,” added by the edition.] It loves night, moves about near the bottom of the waters, and feeds on certain unclean pasture.

## CHAPTER XX.—ON THE ASCHA

[Note: [Col. 1279D] *Salmo Thymallus*.—Absent from the edition. Compare above, chapter 1.]

The Ascha is more of cold than warm air, loves day, gladly moves about in mid-water, and gladly rests upon stones and *leym*. It feeds on grass and little herbs; therefore its flesh too is wholesome and good for both sick and healthy persons. It spawns as other fishes do. A person who has *wisza* in his eye should take its gall, add a drop of pure wine, anoint with it so that it touches the inside of the eye slightly, and do this often; he will be cured. Its other parts are of no value for medicines.

## CHAPTER XXI.—ON THE ROTEGA

[Note: [Col. 1279D] Absent from the edition.]

The Rotega is more of warm than cold air, loves day, and moves about above in the foam of the waters. Sometimes it washes itself in mid-water; it eats *mos* growing on crags, little herbs growing there, and also feeds on things flowing in the foam of the waters. It is good for healthy and sick persons to eat and spawns like other fishes which are neither too large nor too small.

## CHAPTER XXII.—ON THE ALLEC

[Note: [Col. 1279D] *Clupea Harengus*.] [IV, 20].

The Allec belongs to cold air, but has an unstable and cold nature. It loves day and moves about at the bottom and surface of the waters, seeking clean pasture. [Note: [Col. 1279D] “But it has an unstable—seeking” is omitted in the edition.] When it is caught fresh, it is not suitable for a person to eat, because it easily makes him swell and causes *yderecht* within his body. Therefore, while fresh, it is harmful to healthy and sick alike as food. But when it is afterward covered with much salt, the foulness—that is, *eyther*—in it is diminished by the salt, so that it harms the eater correspondingly less. A healthy person can digest it when prepared this way; but if a sick person eats much of it, it will harm him. [Note: [Col. 1280D] “Because it easily makes him swell—will harm him” is omitted in the edition.]

For sick or healthy persons, roasted allec is better and more wholesome to eat than boiled allec; its *milch* and *rogim*, as stated above, may be eaten. But if the allec is fresh, cook it; while it is still hot from cooking, pour wine mixed with vinegar over it and let it steep (*beysze*) for a short time, and it will harm the eater correspondingly less.

A person who has *grint* on his head, a fine scab on his body, or leprosy, should take allec which has long been covered with salt, cleanse it in water, then wash his head, scab, or leprous place in that same water. After a short time let him wash himself there in other warm water. On the second day make *calbaz* [harsh lye, ed.] from beech ashes and wash again with it either the head, the scab, or the leprosy. On the third day anoint those same places with goat’s fat. Do this repeatedly in order, as stated above, and he will fare better from *grint*, fine scab, or leprosy.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—ON THE CRASSO

[IV, 21].

The Crasso is more of warm than cold air, loves day, gladly remains where there are springs of water, and often moves about in small streams. It eats what is clean and is good for healthy and sick persons to eat. It spawns as other little fishes do. [Note: [Col. 1280D] Edition: “The Crassus is of warm air and is good for healthy and sick persons to eat. But a person who has raging paralysis should cook these little fishes moderately in a pan, then reduce them to powder upon a heated stone, add a little powder of *gith*, like pennyroyal, and a little burnt salt, and eat this frequently while fasting and after a meal; he will be cured.”]

## CHAPTER XXIV.—ON THE HASELA

[Note: [Col. 1280D] Absent from the edition, as are the following numbers 25–29.]

The Hasela is more of warm than cold air, loves day and warmth, moves about at the surface of the waters, seeks clean pasture, and is good for healthy and sick persons to eat. It spawns as other fishes do.

## CHAPTER XXV.—ON THE BLICKA.

Blicka is more of warm air than of cold; it loves daylight and warmth, willingly frequents foam and the surface of the waters, eats clean fodder, and is good for healthy people to eat. But those who are ill should eat little of it, because its flesh is soft. It spawns like other little fish.

## Chapter XXVI.—On Pafenduno

Pafenduno is more of warm than of cold air; it loves daylight and warmth, and frequents the shore amid the foam of the waters. It eats little worms and herbs [Col. 1281B], and is good for healthy people to eat, but is of little benefit to the sick. It spawns like other fish, but has no medicinal virtue.

## Chapter XXVII.—On Slya

Slya belongs to the warmth of marshes, loves the night, and frequents the bottom and the shore. It feeds more upon unclean than clean fodder and is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat. When it spawns, male and female draw *mos*, which grows on rocks, to the opening of a small cavity; there, in that same cavity, each of them emits foam from its mouth upon the aforesaid *mos*. They remain beside it and direct their mouth and breath toward it, until it receives congealed vital air; then they depart, and in this way slyae are born. It is unsuitable for medicines [Col. 1281C].

## Chapter XXVIII.—On Gerundula

Grundula is more of moist air than dry; it loves the night, frequents both the bottom and the surface of the waters, and willingly remains in cavities among rocks. It feeds on certain herbs and other fodder. But its flesh is not wholesome to eat: healthy persons may indeed overcome its effects if they eat it, but it greatly harms the sick, and especially those suffering from gout (*gichtige*), and readily stirs up every illness in a person. This little fish is more of the female than the male sex.

They press themselves against rocks and sand; from this *rogim* swells, and it receives him, and thus becomes pregnant. And when it spawns in the foam of the water and is congealed from *slim* without the male’s milk, it does this in particular places; then it brings together, now in one place and now in another, the grains from which one little fish comes to be, separately gathering the grains for each and likewise for others, until the water or the coagulated matter receives vital air. But after this little fish has divided these same grains of its own into very many scattered portions, as stated above, it does not rest beside them, but departs before they live. It is of little use in medicines [Col. 1281D].

## Chapter XXIX.—On Stechela

[Col. 1282A]

Stechela is more of warm air than cold; it loves daylight, feeds upon certain herbs, has wholesome flesh, and when eaten harms neither sick nor healthy people. It is of the nature of *hechtes* and *birsches*.

For when *bersich* at times emits its *rogum*, the male *hecht*, seeing this, drives away the male *porche*, which ought to pour its *fac* over those grains, and itself pours its *milch* over them; and, once this has been poured out, they then receive vital air as other little fish do. But when that *birsich* sees that they are alive and are not of its own kind, it departs from them.

## Chapter XXX.—On Steynbisza [IV, 22]

Steynbisza is more of cold air [Col. 1282B] and moisture than of warmth; it frequents the bottom of rivers, loves the night, eats unclean things, and is not wholesome for a person to eat. Rather, it is almost like a maggot and is born from fish. For diverse fish lie together in one place in a cluster, and there produce certain foams and excretions; this matter clings together and congeals, finally receives vital air—just as little worms are born from horse or cow dung—and thus steynbisza comes into being. It is of no use for a person to eat.

> **Note [Col. 1281D].** The edition reads differently: “Steinbiza is of cold air and is not wholesome for a person to eat, but is almost like a worm. But if anyone is incontinent in lust, let him pulverize steinbiza and *brunecrassim* in equal weight, add to this a third part of camphor, and drink a little of it in cold water for fifteen or more days; and he will have continence.”

## Chapter XXXI.—On Rulheubt

> **Note [Col. 1282D].** Absent from the edition.

Rulheubt is more of cold than warm air; it loves daylight and frequents the middle and surface of the waters. It feeds on both clean and unclean fodder, and whatever is unclean in its food [Col. 1282C] rises into its head and grows in its brain. Therefore its head, together with its stomach, is harmful and unclean; the rest of its body grows from clean food and may be eaten.

When it spawns, it enters a little cavity and emits *rogim* here and there; the male pours over it a certain moisture, not milk, and that moisture is so strong that the grains are congealed by it. After they have discharged their seed, they depart immediately.

## Chapter XXXII.—On the Crab

> **Note [Col. 1282D].** Freshwater crayfish.

[IV, 23]

The crab is more hot than cold, and has more warmth from the earth than from the air. It loves day and night, because it walks forward in accordance with the sun [Col. 1282D] and backward in accordance with the moon.

> **Note [Col. 1282D].** “And it has warmth … walks” is omitted in the edition.

It has wholesome flesh, and both sick and healthy people may eat it, except one whose stomach is cold and *bestoppet*—that is, obstructed—so that he can scarcely digest food which he has eaten. For such a person the crab is too strong as food and is digested only with difficulty; thus it is not good for him to eat.

There is in its head a certain green substance called *crebeszmar* [*crebezes malz* in the edition]. Take this and add butter of greater weight; knead them together. Whoever has *quedelechte* [very tiny pustules, ed.] on the face and about the nostrils, as though pain and ulcers wished to boil up there, should anoint himself therewith frequently at night; and when he rises from bed in the morning, he should wash this ointment from his face with wine. He will have fair skin, and ulcers will not arise there.

## Chapter XXXIII.—On the Eel

> **Note [Col. 1283D].** *Muraena Anguilla.*

[II, 24]

How is the eel made? In the later time, as it is now, the eel is made in a certain other manner. For when winter arrives, the water-serpent, which is female, separates herself from the male, rubs herself either on stones or on sand, and thus loses her skin; so she rests in a pit throughout the winter.

But when the time of summer comes, she seeks a certain stone and emits her breath from her mouth upon it [Col. 1283B]. Then she spits out upon that same stone certain grains from her mouth, namely grains the size of beans. She has great desire and zeal for this work, because she is then clean, having already cast off her old skin in which there had been poison.

And the eel, which is male, seeing this, hastens there; the female serpent flees him and withdraws from the grains which she spat out. Immediately the eel emits from its mouth, as it were, milk upon those grains—that is, *kuwet*—covers them with its tail, and, stretching itself over them, twists about. When the aforesaid water-serpent sees this, she is indignant; but approaching beneath the eel’s tail, she emits many breaths meanwhile. Thus both lie there: the eel covering the grains with its tail, and the serpent beneath its tail blowing upon them [Col. 1283C], until they receive vital air.

But after they begin to live and the eel perceives this, both it and that serpent immediately flee in horror, because they have exceeded their nature. Thus eels are made, and many will arise from the one aforesaid grain. Therefore, once they have begun to germinate, their multitude quickly rises.

The eel is more of warm air than cold; it loves the night and has the nature of certain worms which willingly dwell in cavities and are not unclean. It also has the nature of fish and does not seek very unclean food. Nevertheless, its flesh is somewhat unclean and is not good for a healthy person to eat, like the flesh of pigs; yet it does not greatly harm healthy people. But in every fever and harmful humour, and in all their infirmities, it violently disturbs sick people; and it makes those who eat it bitter in mind, crafty, and *argehse* [uncertain term].

Its gall is fat. Whoever anointed his eyes with it against dimness of sight would become clear-sighted for a little while, but afterward would become all the more ill from it.

> **Note [Col. 1283D].** We print the text of the edition, which differs in many respects: “The eel is of warm air, and its flesh is somewhat unclean and not wholesome for a person to eat, like pork; yet it does not greatly harm healthy people, but it violently disturbs the sick in all harmful humours and their infirmities, and makes those who eat it bitter in mind, crafty, and suspicious. But its gall is fat, and whoever anointed his eyes with it against dimness would become clear-sighted for a little while, but afterward would become all the more ill.
>
> “But if lice harm any person internally and do not come out, let him boil eel gall, three times less of very sharp vinegar, and as much soft [ingredient: reading uncertain] as these two amount to, vigorously in a pan. Then add ginger, twice as much long pepper, and an equal quantity of basil; further, ivory to a third part of the basil, and vulture’s beak to a third part [Col. 1284D] of the ivory. Let him put this powder into the aforesaid vinegar and make it boil together again. When he has done this, let him put it into a little bag and pour in wine, so that it passes through it like a clear drink, and receive it in a new earthen vessel. A person internally harmed by lice should drink this draught every day while fasting; by night the lice will fail and die, and fat will be renewed in him.”

## Chapter XXXIV.—On Alroppa

> **Note [Col. 1284D].** *Gadus Lota.* Absent from the edition.

How Alroppa is made. At times the female eel emits from her mouth a certain coagulated matter upon a stone, not grains as other fish do. Another eel, namely the male, sees this, drives the female away, coils itself over the matter [Col. 1284B], and cherishes it with its tail until it receives vital air; thus alroppae are born.

Alroppa is more of cold than warm air; it loves daylight and frequents the middle of the waters, but seeks unclean food more than clean. It is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat, except for its liver, which both sick and healthy people may take as food; it is useful and good.

> **Note [Col. 1284D].** The edition reads: “Alropa is of cold air and is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat, except for its liver, which is useful and good for healthy and sick alike. If scrofulous sores burst in a person, pulverize the head of an alropa and lay it upon the ulcers; they will dry up.”

## Chapter XXXV.—On Punbelen

> **Note [Col. 1284D].** Absent from the edition.

How are punbelen made? Alroppae, both male and female, each emit together from their mouths a certain coagulated matter, like filth; once they have emitted it, they go away. They do not remain, but the matter itself receives vital air like a maggot, and punbelim are born [Col. 1284C]—namely those creatures which are accustomed to have a nature like little *kulheuvtchen* in marshes and dust. It is unsuitable for medicine.

## Chapter XXXVI.—On Lampreda

> **Note [Col. 1284D].** *Peiromyzon* species. Absent from the edition.

How lampreda is made. A certain serpent, when it sees the eggs of a water-serpent, immediately drives that serpent away, coils itself over the eggs, and cherishes them; thus moray eels are born from those eggs.

Lampreda is more of warm air than cold; it has the nature of *invederslage* fish and also retains the nature of serpents because it is venomous, and has some poison in its tail. It has only two eyes, because the openings that appear like eyes in it are not eyes but merely blind openings [Col. 1285A]. It loves the night and willingly remains in cavities and watery marshes, and uses unclean food. It is bad for both healthy and sick people to eat, produces bad digestion [Col. 1286A] in a person’s stomach, and stirs up storms in all the veins. It has no medicinal usefulness whatsoever.

[Col. 1285] **Here ends the fourth (fifth) book on fishes.**

# Here begins the fifth (sixth) book: On birds

## Preface

> **Note [Col. 1285C].** The edition reads: “Chapter 1.—The nature and variety of flying creatures. Flying creatures are colder than animals which live upon the earth, because they are not generated with such heat of lust; and they have cleaner flesh than land animals, because they do not proceed naked from their mother but covered by a shell. Some also live by fiery air and therefore tend upward like fire. But those which seek height in their flight have more fiery air in themselves than those which remain near the earth. Those, however, which dwell in waters, on land, and in the air do not seek the upright height of the air, but go as far as the air of earth and the air of water extend. Those also which abound in many feathers are warmer than those which suffer a scarcity of feathers. And because flying creatures live from the air, they sometimes naturally perceive a movement in some occurrence by which the air is affected; and because they are aerial, they frequently feel in themselves a change in the air and, in accordance with it, very often utter their calls—as the cock distinguishes the hours of day and night with its calls, and as it sometimes begins to sing when the breeze seems to alter itself into another condition.
>
> “Flying creatures likewise signify that power by which a person directs matters in thought and considers many things beforehand within himself before proceeding to a shining work. And as flying creatures are lifted into the air by their wings and range everywhere in the air, so too the soul, while it is in a human body, is raised by its thoughts and extends itself everywhere.”

[Col. 1285]

Since the soul in a human body is aerial, as long as it remains in the body it is lifted and sustained by air; otherwise it would be suffocated in the body. In the human body it operates with sentient understanding and steadfastness; and for this purpose flying creatures were created and set in place, together with which it must perceive and know what it ought to know. For birds are lifted by their wings into the air and range everywhere in it; so likewise the soul, while it is in the body, is raised by its thoughts [Col. 1286B] and extends itself everywhere.

And in the moisture of the earth that perfection is shown: that a human being is perfect in his formation. In corporeality it is discerned that a human being recognizes himself to be bodily in trees. By these two things—namely, moisture and corporeality—he ought to understand that he cannot grow while the soul is in him.
