# Sixth Book

[Col. 1287]

## Chapter I.—On the Griffin

[IV, II, 2]

[Col. 1287A]

The griffin is very hot and has something of the nature of birds and something of the nature of beasts. By its bird-nature it is so swift that a weight upon its body would not burden it; but by its beast-nature it eats human beings. When it flies in the air, it does not fly into burning heat, though it approaches it somewhat.

> **Note [Col. 1287D].** “And it has something … approaches it” is omitted in the edition.

Its flesh is not fit for human food, for if a person ate its flesh he would be greatly harmed by it.

> **Note [Col. 1287D].** “He would be harmed; and neither its flesh, nor its eggs, nor the other things in it are suitable for medicine,” the edition reads, omitting the rest.

For in this respect it possesses fully the nature of beasts. Yet it is deficient in both natures. When the time comes to lay its eggs, it seeks a cave, spacious within but so sharp and narrow at the mouth of the opening that it can scarcely enter [Col. 1287B]. There it diligently guards its eggs because of its fear of the lion. The lion smells them from afar, and, if it can reach them, tramples and breaks them, because the griffin always lies in wait for it and does not allow it to remain near, disdaining its strength. Yet it permits the bear to remain near because the bear is weaker than the lion.

It lays its eggs in such a way that neither the brightness of the sun nor the breath of the wind can touch them. Neither its flesh, its eggs, nor the other things in it are of much use for medicines, because in its two natures it has more deficiency than perfection.

## Chapter II.—On the Ostrich

> **Note [Col. 1287D].** Job 39:16; *Struthio Camelus.*

[IV, II, 3]

[Col. 1287C]

The ostrich [*struthio* in the edition] is very hot and has in itself the nature of beasts. It has birds’ feathers but does not fly with them, because it runs swiftly like a beast and ranges about the earth, feeding on fodder. It is of such great heat that its eggs would be burnt and would not produce young if it incubated them itself; therefore it hides them in sand, where they are warmed by moisture, heat, and the sand itself. But after the chicks have emerged from the eggs, they run after and with their mother, as other chicks do.

> **Note [Col. 1288D].** “For it has birds’ feathers … as other chicks do” is omitted in the edition.

A person who has *vallentsucht* [the falling sickness, ed.] should often eat ostrich flesh; it gives him strength and removes from him the madness of the falling sickness. Its flesh is also wholesome for stout and strong people to eat, because it reduces their superfluous flesh [Col. 1287D] and makes them strong. But it is not good for thin and sick people, because it would be too strong for them as food.

> **Note [Col. 1288D].** “Because … as food” is omitted in the edition.

Whoever is melancholic, so that he has heaviness and torpor of mind, should often eat its liver; it lessens melancholy in him and, by lightening his mind, makes it gentle and clean [Col. 1288A].

> **Addition in the edition.** “Its eggs are not fit to eat because they are poisonous. But if anyone is dropsical, let him pulverize the shells of those eggs from which chicks emerge, put them in water, and drink it often both after eating and while fasting; he will be cured.”

The ostrich’s heart, lungs, and other parts are of no use for medicines, because it possesses neither the power of birds nor that of beasts perfectly.

## Chapter III.—On the Peacock

> **Note [Col. 1288D].** *Pavo cristatus.*

[IV, II, 4]

The peacock is hot and moist and has in itself the nature of [birds and] beasts. Its voice is mingled and sounds according to birds and beasts.

> **Note [Col. 1288D].** What follows, down to “But peacock flesh is fit to eat,” etc., is omitted in the edition.

For before there was a peacock, certain little beasts, following their desire, coupled with certain birds [Col. 1288B]; from this peacocks were born. The peacock is keen and crafty and does not greatly seek the heights of the air in flight.

The male peacock has twisted and incestuous habits and sometimes couples with small animals and little beasts. When they produce young, the young take their form from the mother and not the father; yet some of them are sometimes coloured after the colour of the father’s feathers and in their crests. When the peacock sees those little beasts running, it recognizes and loves them as born from itself.

But the female peacock, when she lays her eggs, hides them lest her male see them, as though ashamed to have borne eggs rather than produced a chick in naked flesh, covered instead by an eggshell. Therefore the male hates the eggs and breaks them [Col. 1288C] if he finds them. Thus the female hides her eggs from the male until the chicks emerge. She continues to conceal the chicks until they have grown more and can run. Once they are so strengthened that they can go about, she brings them with her to her male. Seeing them walk, he understands them to be his chicks; he beats his wings for them and shows that he is joyful. Nevertheless, the female still keeps the chicks apart from him and moves them away until they are stronger, because she fears he may trample them with his feet.

The male also seeks a certain height where he understands that the air blows by which his feathers will quickly grow in number and length. When he sees this, he rejoices in them [Col. 1288D], as beasts rejoice in their leaping. But afterward another air blowing upon the same feathers softens and draws them out; they are sad until they grow again. The female, however, does not seek that air for the growth of her feathers, but stays as though constrained near the lower regions.

[Col. 1289A]

> **Note [Col. 1289D].** The edition continues thus, adding much: “Its flesh is fit for neither healthy nor sick people to eat, because it stirs and excites every harmful humour in a person. But a person suffering from dropsy should boil a peacock—namely a male—in well water, not in water from a running spring, with hyssop, and eat the flesh. Then pulverize its heart, the bone which moves in its knee, and its claws, so that the powder from the knee-bone is twice as much as the powder from the claws, and the powder from its heart exceeds the powder from the bones and knees by three parts. Then boil *pandoniam*, three times as much lovage, and a little eel’s blood in wine; strain it through a cloth, add the aforesaid powder to the wine, and drink it. Do this for eighteen days.
>
> “Let a person dry and preserve the peacock’s bladder. If an ulcer or *slier* boils up in anyone, bind it over the spot; it will break gently. After it breaks, put it over the place again: it draws out corrupt matter, and the person will heal much more quickly [Col. 1290D]. If a person has a suppurating wound, sew the bladder over its covering; it will smell less, draw out filth alone, and not sound flesh. Let him also make a small ball from its tiniest feathers and apply it to his suppurating wound: they draw out what is harmful and make it smell less. Its eggs are not fit to eat.”

But peacock flesh is fit for neither healthy nor sick people to eat. A healthy person may nevertheless overcome its effects. It stirs and excites every harmful humour in a sick person. Dry the peacock’s bladder and preserve it; if an ulcer or *slyr* boils up in anyone, bind it over the spot, and it will break gently. Once it has broken, place it over the spot again; it draws out the corrupt matter, and he will heal much more quickly.

## Chapter IV.—On the Crane

> **Note [Col. 1290D].** *Ardea Grus.*

[IV, II, 5]

The crane is hot, has a clean nature, and possesses the capacity both to fly and to walk upon land. It willingly flies in a flock and escapes snares more easily thereby. It has great strength in its neck; it is simple and provident, has a watchful sense [Col. 1289B], and possesses this skill: it takes precautions so that neither bird nor beast can readily harm it.

> **Note [Col. 1290D].** “And possesses the capacity … harm it” is omitted in the edition.

Its flesh is good for both sick and healthy people to eat, but its eggs are not fit to eat. A person tormented by *gicht* should often eat its flesh, and the gout will cease in him. Whoever has *vicht* should often eat its liver.

If *schelmo* afflicts and kills pigs, pulverize the crane’s beak and give them the powder in the *muz* which they eat or in the water which they drink. They will improve, and *schelmo* will cease in them.

Dry and preserve crane’s blood, and dry and preserve its right foot. If any woman is then suffering difficulty in childbirth, crumble some of this blood in a little water [Col. 1289C] and anoint with it the upper part over the mouth of the vulva. Make the woman look at herself, as in a mirror, in the same water mixed with this blood; bind the crane’s right foot over her navel. Such power resides in these things that closed viscera and closed *lenden* [“closed viscera,” ed.] are opened for childbirth all the more quickly. Its other parts are of no use for medicines.

## Chapter V.—On the Swan

> **Note [Col. 1290D].** *Anas olor.*

[IV, II, 6]

The swan (*cyngnus*, thus written) is cold and moist and has something of the nature of the goose and of the duck. It willingly bathes in water, loves water and land more than flight, and sometimes roots about in certain unclean things in the water.

> **Note [Col. 1290D].** “And has something … roots about” is omitted in the edition.

Its flesh is good for healthy people to eat but is of no use to the sick [Col. 1289D]. A person who has *dumphet* should boil and often eat its liver; it removes decay from his lung, and he will be cured. Whoever has pain in the spleen should boil and often eat swan’s lung, and his spleen will be healed.

Whoever has *urslecht* in his body should fatten a swan; after killing it, take its fat and first melt it in a pan—that is, *zulasz*. Then add *biboz*, *sepo* [superscript: ashes], and oak bark in equal weights, so that there is twice as much fat; boil all together again in a pan and make an ointment from it. Let him frequently anoint himself with it. The skin where he first anoints himself becomes *bulechte* [pustular, ed.], but afterward it will quickly heal. Its remaining parts are of little use for medicines.

> **Note [Col. 1290D].** “And its remaining parts … medicines” is omitted in the edition.

## Chapter VI.—On the Heron

> **Note [Col. 1290D].** Species of *Ardea*.

[IV, II, 7]

[Col. 1290B]

The heron [*Ardea*, ed.] is hot and dry and descends only *dus donne* [reading uncertain] of the waters. Therefore it also sometimes frequents waters.

> **Note [Col. 1290D].** “And descends only … frequents waters” is omitted in the edition.

Its flesh is good for both sick and healthy people to eat because it does not produce *slim* in the stomach. Whoever has a sad mind should often eat its heart; it makes his mind joyful.

For one whose eyes are dim or [whose condition is designated] *sergent* [reading uncertain], boil a heron’s head in water. After it is boiled, take out its eyes and dry them in the sun. Then put them in cold water for a short while so that they soften in it; dry them in the sun again. Do this three times. Afterward grind the eyes to powder. Whenever his eyes grow dim [Col. 1290C] or hurt, put this powder in pure, good wine, dip a feather in it, and with it anoint round the eyelids and lashes of his eyes; if it touches the eyes a little inside, it will do no harm. Do this frequently at night when he goes to sleep; it removes dimness and pain from the eyes.

Whoever has a hardened stomach, so that he has *getwang*, should often eat its liver, and it softens his stomach. Whoever has pain in the spleen should scrape a sufficient quantity from its bones into water and drink it often while fasting and at night; he will improve.

## Chapter VII.—On the Vulture

> **Note [Col. 1290D].** A species of falcon.

[IV, II, 17]

The vulture is of a cold nature and knows the arts of birds [Col. 1290D] and beasts. Among other birds it is like a prophet [Col. 1291A]. It flies at the same height to which the moisture of the earth rises—that is, up to the warmth of the air. It harms no bird and takes care that it is not harmed by others. It feeds on carcasses and sometimes roots in earth soaked with animals’ blood, namely where animals are killed.

> **Note [Col. 1291D].** “And it flies at the same height … animals are killed” is omitted in the edition.

Its flesh ought not to be eaten, because the coldness which is in it would be deadly to a person as food.

> **Note [Col. 1291D].** “Because the coldness … is in it” is omitted in the edition.

But while the vulture lives, its brain has this nature: if a person could possess it uncorrupted, he would drive every illness except death away from himself. Yet a person cannot possess it uncorrupted, because whenever death attacks that bird in any way, so that vital air leaves it, the membrane of the brain breaks as it dies [Col. 1291B], and the brain immediately disperses and loses its power.

But when you kill a vulture, while it is still warm remove its feathers and cut up its body. Throw away only the entrails containing excrement; boil all the rest of the body—namely, with its head intact and with heart, liver, and lung—

> **Note [Col. 1291D].** “Namely, with its head intact … lung” is omitted in the edition.

—vigorously in water in a new pot. Then add *smaltz*, a little olive oil, and less henbane oil than olive oil, and make an ointment. Anoint with it all over the head of one who is *unsinnig* [frenetic, ed.]; and anoint everywhere on the body one who is *virgichtigit* and is tormented by gout. Also anoint with it whoever has an illness in the back, loins, or body, and he will be cured—unless God does not wish to cure him [Col. 1291C]—because this ointment is more precious than the most precious ointment: it swiftly passes through the skin of a sick person and heals him.

> **Note [Col. 1291D].** The remainder is absent from the edition.

If the vulture’s head is boiled with the aforesaid *smalcz* as stated above, juice from its brain can be obtained, and not otherwise. Divide its heart in two so that it may dry better; dry it gently by the fire, so that it is not roasted, and then dry it in the sun. Sew it into a deerskin belt and gird yourself with it. If anyone wishes to kill you by poison, while you are girded with that belt containing the heart, you will immediately tremble and sweat throughout your body; thus you will be able to understand that poison is near you and avoid it.

For since poison harms the vulture [Col. 1291D], every harm also flees from it. The vulture naturally knows the seasons of breezes and the breezes of seasons, and it also avoids one intending to kill it. Therefore, when its heart is placed by the fire so that whatever blackened matter is in it may be dried out, and also in the sun so that its firmness may be strengthened by the sun’s warmth, then placed in a deerskin belt because the deer is swifter and more sensitive than other animals, and girded about a person as stated above, it causes him to avoid dangers of poison as his body is warmed by it.

For the air around a person repels, through the power of the same heart and deerskin belt—for that air also operates around them—the harmful approaching air and air sent forth through snares [Col. 1292A]. When that same air perceives poison to be present, through the power of the aforesaid heart and belt it stirs the person to trembling, just as by good works places and people are led into holiness and prosperity, and by evil works are likewise turned into scandals and harm.

When the vulture is boiled, set its eye in a ring; if you wear it on your finger, it restrains paralysis and gout in you. Its lungs and feathers are of no use for medicines.

## Chapter VIII.—On the Eagle

> **Note [Col. 1291D].** *Falco Aquila.* Compare Job 39:30.

[IV, II, 18]

[Col. 1292B]

The eagle is very hot, as though it were fiery [Note: [Col. 1291D] “As though—it were fiery” omitted in the edition], and its eyes are more fiery than watery; therefore it looks intently at the sun. And because it is almost fiery, it can endure both heat and cold, and it flies high because it bears heat well [Note: [Col. 1292D] “And therefore also—bears” omitted in the edition]. But its flesh would be deadly for a human being to eat [Note: [Col. 1292D] Ed.: “is deadly.” But eagles, although they bear different names, nevertheless all have the same nature, except that one is fiercer and another gentler, and that one flies more swiftly and another more slowly; with these words the chapter concludes, omitting the rest.] if he ate it, because it would be too strong for him on account of the excessive heat in it. And because it is steeped in the sun’s heat, and also looks at it intently, it is therefore *grim* [fierce], and consequently has great sensitivity in its heart. It carries off and transports very many things, which it throws away and does not eat; it eats only things that are wholesome and warm.

When it lays eggs, it seeks a place very hot either from the sun or from the air, so that they may be strongly imbued and strengthened by that heat [Col. 1292C]. If it should happen by chance that one of them is left void, so that it cannot be suffused with heat, the chick which emerges from it will be weak and feeble, and not strong enough to live. Its heart has such a wonderful nature—and so it would have it within itself [Note: [Col. 1292D] Corrupt passage.]—and such knowledge would shine forth in it beyond all measure, that a human heart could not bear it. For at the very hour when an eagle is killed or dies of itself, all its force is in its heart, so that that heart becomes as though *unmechtig* [powerless], and is even weaker than the hearts of other birds or animals. Therefore no human being can possess that heart as strong as it is while the eagle lives.

So too the *scotbaro*, *gensaro*, and *hasenaro* have the same nature as this bird of which we speak, except that one is fiercer, another milder, and that one flies more swiftly, another more slowly—just as human beings differ in their dispositions, although they possess one nature of humanity. They are useful for the same operations as were also mentioned above.

## CHAPTER IX.—ON THE ODEBERO [IV, II, 19]

The *odebero* [stork, *Ciconia*, ed.] is hot and has the nature of foolish animals. It flies in the middle region of the air [Col. 1293A], because birds which move about in the middle part of the air perceive the earth and understand the seasons more than those which fly in the heights and in the high air [Note: [Col. 1293D] Cf. below, chapter 32.]. For those which are high up move amid heat and are often deceived by that burning heat, so that winter and certain other seasons often come upon them before they perceive them [Note: [Col. 1293D] “And has the nature—perceive them” omitted in the edition]. Its flesh is not suitable for human food, since it would harm a person.

Take, therefore, an *odebero*; discard its head and entrails, remove all its feathers, and burn the remaining carcass over the fire, without water, in a new pot perforated with a small hole. Place another new pot beneath this pot and collect the dripping *smaltz* [fat; *sagimen*, ed.]. Then add to it bear fat equal to one-third of it, and as much butter as one-third of the bear fat [Col. 1293B]. Pound in equal weights the herb called *gicht* and *kranchsnabel*, boil them with these things in a new pot, and then strain through a cloth, making an ointment. Let one who is frenzied, afflicted with paralysis, or troubled by *gicht* in any limb of his body anoint himself with this ointment; he will improve. The remaining parts of it are of little value for medicines [Note: [Col. 1293D] “The remaining parts—value” omitted in the edition].

## CHAPTER X.—ON THE GOOSE [Note: [Col. 1293D] Duck; goose.] [IV, II, 8]

The goose, namely *gans*, is hot; it also derives from that air by which beasts live, and from the watery air which produces its feathers. But it cannot fly high, because it has the air of beasts; yet because of its watery air it willingly lives in water and feeds on both clean and unclean food. On account of this double nature [Col. 1293C], its flesh is not fit for the sick to eat, because it often produces in a person malignant humours and sores, such as scabies and sores resembling those of leprosy, since it sometimes eats unclean things [Note: [Col. 1293D] “But it cannot fly high—eats” omitted in the edition]. Healthy people, however, can in some way overcome its flesh when eaten.

If anyone wishes to eat goose, let him allow it to go very hungry for either three or two days, so that the bad humours in it may disappear [Note: [Col. 1293D] “So that the bad—disappear” omitted in the edition], and then let it be fed with grain. Afterwards, when it has been killed, roast it over the fire; while it is roasting, put *selba* and other good little herbs upon it, so that their juice may pass through it. Continually sprinkle it with wine and vinegar by means of a fan, so that its blood may flow out. For its fat must not be eaten, because it makes a person ill, being fattened from bad humours [Col. 1293D; Note: [Col. 1293D] “For its fat—fattened” omitted in the edition]. A healthy person may eat a moderate amount of it roasted in this manner.

But when boiled in water it is bad for human food, because the bad humours in it are not removed by water as they are when it is roasted over the fire [Note: [Col. 1294D] “Because the bad—roasted” omitted in the edition]. Its eggs, prepared in whatever way, are bad for human food, [because they produce scrofula and many other illnesses in a person, addition of the edition].

## CHAPTER XI.—ON THE *HALEGANS* [IV, II, 9]

[Col. 1294A]

The *halegans* [jackdaw, *Grandula*, ed.] is very hot, swift in flight, and labours in flying [Note: [Col. 1294D] “And swift—flying” omitted in the edition]. It is therefore good for both sick and healthy persons to eat. It flies in the heat of the air, since it would perish in cold. It flies in a flock, so that it may be the less harmed by anyone. It is unafraid by day and therefore somewhat wakeful by night. Yet it is afraid at night and feeds on unclean food [Note: [Col. 1294D] “And it flies in the heat of the air—feeds” omitted in the edition. The remainder is present, but arranged differently.].

Let a person whose eyes are dim or *serigent* take its gall, add twice as much pure wine, put it in a copper vessel, and at night apply it from that vessel around the eyes with a feather, so that it also touches the eyes within. Let him do this often; his eyes will become clear and healthy, and neither *wisza*, nor film, nor abscess will readily grow in them. Let one who suffers from *vicht* [Col. 1294B] boil and often eat its liver; he will improve. Let one who has *husten* [a cough] often eat its boiled lung, and the cough will cease.

Further, let one who suffers in the stomach take a *hagelgans*, discard its head and entrails, boil the remaining body thoroughly in water, remove it from the water, separate every bone from the flesh, pound the flesh in a mortar, and press out through a cloth the juice within it. Make a *suffen* [soup] with that juice and a little flour, and let him drink it fasting. It will gently remove *slim* [phlegm] and bad humours from his stomach without his knowing it. The other parts of it are of no medicinal value.

## CHAPTER XII.—ON THE DOMESTIC DUCK [Note: [Col. 1294D] Domestic duck.] [IV, II, 10]

[Col. 1294C]

The domestic *aneta* [duck] has a heavy heat and something of the air of beasts, but naturally has more of watery air. It feeds on unclean things, but the impurities which it devours are cleansed in it and pass through it by means of the water in which it often swims [Note: [Col. 1294D] “And something of the air—pass through” omitted in the edition]. Healthy persons can overcome its flesh when eaten, but it is not suitable for the sick. All its other parts are useless. [But whoever wishes to eat duck should not eat it boiled in water, but should roast it over the fire, as was said above concerning the goose. Its eggs are poison to a person, like the sting of a spider. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER XIII.—ON THE WILD DUCK [Note: [Col. 1294D] Mallard.] [IV, II, 11]

[Col. 1294D] The wild duck has the same nature as the domestic duck; but the wild one is healthier for human food than the domestic, because it is always occupied with waters. Burn a wild duck to ashes in a new pot, after discarding its head, entrails, and feathers; frequently put this powder into broken *orfimas* [ulcers], and they will be healed. Duck feathers are somewhat more useful for beds and pillows [Col. 1295A] than hen feathers [Note: [Col. 1295D] “Duck feathers—hen feathers” omitted in the edition].

## CHAPTER XIV.—ON THE COCK AND HEN [Note: [Col. 1295D] Pheasant; cock.] [IV, II, 12]

Both cock and hen have a cold and dry nature and do not fly high, because they derive chiefly from the air of terrestrial animals [Note: [Col. 1295D] “And do not fly high—animals” omitted in the edition]. Their flesh is good for healthy people, but when eaten does not make them fat; it somewhat restores the sick. But if anyone is very ill and eats this flesh frequently, it produces *slim* in his stomach and makes that stomach so weak that it can scarcely digest food eaten, because this flesh is cold [Note: [Col. 1295D] “But if anyone—cold” omitted in the edition].

If a person who is very ill wishes to eat hen flesh, let him have it cooked with any other meats, so that it may be tempered by their juice [Col. 1295B], because it is dry; let him eat it thus, but avoid it roasted, since he will scarcely be able to digest it. A hen is better food for the sick than a cock, because hen flesh is more tender than cock flesh [Note: [Col. 1295D] “Because—cock flesh” omitted in the edition]. A person healthy in body may eat both.

A capon is good for a healthy person to eat, but of little use to the sick, because a capon does not labour enough but is always at rest; consequently its flesh is so much stronger [Note: [Col. 1295D] “A capon is good—stronger” omitted in the edition]. The liver of both hen and cock, eaten often, is useful against illnesses which injure a person internally. The liver of cock and hen is neither hard nor weak. Hen feathers are bad for pillows, since they excite *gicht* in the person who lies upon them. The other parts of these birds [Col. 1295C] are of no medicinal value.

[The eggs of every kind of bird are more cold than hot in nature and are harmful to eat; but domestic hen eggs may be eaten, though moderately. If a sick person wishes to eat eggs, let him mix water and wine, bring them to a boil in a pan, and cook the eggs in this way after removing the shell; they will not harm him.

A person suffering from dysentery should beat egg yolks by rubbing them in a bowl, add cumin and a little pepper, put them back into eggshells, roast them over the fire, and give them to the sufferer to eat after he has eaten a little. Whatever this sick person eats meanwhile should be warm and soft: namely, young chickens and other tender meats, and fish. But let him avoid herring, salmon, beef, cheese, raw and coarse vegetables, leeks, rye and barley bread, and everything roasted, except roasted pear; and let him drink wine.

If anyone has a flow of blood, let him blend two egg yolks, add juice of *metridati* in an amount equal to half of one yolk, vinegar in an amount held by two [Col. 1296A] eggshells, a little cinnamon powder, and less powder of *zituaris*. Let him make from this a somewhat thick drink and sip it moderately warm, whether fasting or after eating; he will improve. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER XV.—ON THE *URHUN* [Note: [Col. 1296D] Capercaillie.] [IV, II, 13]

The *urhun* is hot and somewhat moist, and therefore good to eat for both sick and healthy persons. If *maden* [maggots; *tarmus*, ed.] or other worms consume a person, pulverize the bladder of the *urhun*, place this powder on the site of those sores, and, when they taste this powder, they die.

## CHAPTER XVI.—ON THE *REPHUN* [Note: [Col. 1296D] Grouse; partridge.] [IV, II, 14]

The *rephun* [partridge, ed.] is cold, but the domestic hen is colder than the partridge [Note: [Col. 1296D] “But the domestic hen” omitted in the edition]. It has imperfection [Col. 1296B] in itself, and the partridge is also less stable than the domestic hen. Its flesh is not weak but fragile, because it is not wholly of the earth; when eaten it does not greatly harm healthy people, but is unsuitable for the sick because it produces *slim* in their stomachs.

Take its gall and mix it with old fat. Let one in whose skin lice grow externally from the sweat of the flesh often anoint himself with it. It penetrates his skin and purifies the sweat, so that lice no longer grow. [But if they grow inwardly from its fat, this ointment will not help. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER XVII.—ON THE *BIRCKUN* [Note: [Col. 1296D] Black grouse.] [IV, II, 15]

The *birckhun* has almost the same nature as the *rephun*, except that *birckhun* flesh is better and healthier to eat for both sick [Col. 1296C] and healthy people than *rephun* flesh. If cancer consumes a person, dry its bladder in the sun or over a fire, then moisten it slightly with a little wine, lay it over the place of the sores, press it down from above, and let it remain there a long time; the cancers will die.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—ON THE FALCON [Note: [Col. 1296D] Species of falcon, as chapters 19–22.] [IV, II, 20]

The falcon [heron, *Herodius*, ed.] is hot and somewhat dry, has great force of heart, and is swift in flight; it flies high upward, low downward, and in the middle region of the air [Note: [Col. 1296D] “And swift in flight—flies” omitted in the edition]. Its flesh is not eaten. If *orfimas* occur in a person, whether whole or broken, anoint them with its *smaltz* [fat] [Col. 1296D], and they will dry up. But the falcon has such bitterness in itself that it is not useful in medicines [Note: [Col. 1296D] “But the falcon—useful” omitted in the edition]. Other falcons, from whatever land they come, have the same nature as this one and are useful for the same medicine, except that, according to the regions in which they are raised, one is sometimes stronger and swifter than another.

## CHAPTER XIX.—ON THE *HABICH* [IV, II, 21]

The *habich* [hawk, *Accipiter*, ed.] is hot and moist [Col. 1297A] [and its flesh is not eaten because of its fierceness, addition of the edition]. It knows other birds and perceives their nature; according to what it knows of them, it lies in wait for and seizes them. It flies high and moves about in the middle air [Note: [Col. 1297D] “It knows other birds—moves about” omitted in the edition].

Let a person who has pain in the liver or right side boil the lung of a *habich* in water; add *scherling* [hemlock; *cicuta*, ed.], more comfrey than *scherling*, and cow butter prepared in May in a quantity greater than that of these three ingredients. Boil them together, strain through a cloth, make an ointment, and anoint the region of his liver and his right side with it; he will improve.

Let one who is leprous take its gall and add twice as much wine; where the leprosy is on his body, let him anoint himself there, and immediately anoint the same place with the *smaltz* of the hawk [Col. 1297B]. Let him do this often, and the leprosy will be healed [Note: [Col. 1297D] The edition ends here]. Its feathers are of use neither for beds nor for cushions, because a person lying upon them would sleep heavily and with difficulty.

## CHAPTER XX.—ON THE *SPERWERE* [IV, II, 22]

The *sperwere* [sparrowhawk, *Nisus*, ed.] is hot, cheerful, and swift in flight; it flies high, among the stars, and in the middle air [Note: [Col. 1297D] “And high—flies” omitted in the edition]. If a man or woman burns with sexual desire, let them take a *sperwere*, kill it, remove the feathers, discard its head and entrails, and burn the remaining body over a fire without water in a new pot perforated with a small hole. Put another new pot under it and collect the dripping *smalcz*.

Then pound *calandria*—“investigate what it is” (is it sufficient?) [Col. 1297C]—and less *gamphora* [camphor], mix them with the said *smalcz*, warm it slightly over the fire again, and make an ointment. Let the man anoint his genitals and *gelancken* [loins/flanks] with it for five days; the ardour of sexual desire will cease in him for one month, without danger to his body. Let the woman anoint herself around the navel and in the opening of the navel with it; that ardour will cease in her for a month. When the month is finished, let both man and woman anoint themselves again, and thus they will have a remedy for sexual desire.

If they cannot obtain *calandria* and *gamphora*, let them take the smallest feather of a sparrowhawk and place a sufficient quantity thereof in *baumeolum* [tree-oil] for five days, so that it warms in the sun and thus boils in it; let both man and woman anoint the aforesaid parts of their bodies [Col. 1297D] with it, and the ardour of sexual desire will disappear in them. The remaining parts of it are of no value either for food or for medicines [Note: [Col. 1297D] “If they cannot obtain *calandria*—no value” omitted in the edition].

## CHAPTER XXI.—ON THE KITE [IV, II, 23]

The kite is hot, loves heat, and when the sun shines it willingly flies in warmth and willingly remains even in warm shade. But it avoids the burning heat of the air and its height, flying rather in the middle and lower regions, and it willingly seizes small birds [Col. 1298A]. Yet it is not very fierce [Note: [Col. 1297D] “It loves heat—not very fierce” omitted in the edition]. Its flesh is unsuitable for food, because every bird which *kryment* [preys with its claws; “birds of prey,” ed.] is unsuitable for human consumption.

Let a person who has *orfimes* in his body take a kite, kill it, remove its feathers, discard the entrails which contain excrement, and burn everything else—including head and claws—over a fire without water in a new pot perforated with a small hole [Note: [Col. 1297D] “Without water” omitted in the edition]. Place another pot above this pot [Note: [Col. 1298D] “Place another pot above it” omitted in the edition] and collect its *smalcz*. When this has been done, burn to ashes in that pot the flesh remaining in it. If the *orfime* are whole, anoint them often with the said *smalcz*, and they will disappear. If they are broken, put some of this powder into the same ulcers, and they will dry up.

## CHAPTER XXII.—ON THE *WEHO* [Note: [Col. 1298D] Absent from the edition]

[Col. 1298B]

The *weho* is cold, has furtive habits, does not fly high, and feeds on unclean food, sometimes even on poisonous things. It is therefore of no medicinal use, but would rather harm a person.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—ON THE RAVEN [Note: [Col. 1298D] Common raven, *Corvus corax*. Absent from the edition]

The raven is more hot than cold and flies, as it were, in the middle air. It is cunning, bold, and fearless; it neither avoids nor fears humans much, so that it could even readily converse with a person and would almost have the knowledge to do so, were it not an irrational animal. Since it recognizes people, it often carries off things that a person has with him [Col. 1298C]. Its flesh is unsuitable for human food because it has the nature of robbers and thieves. Its other parts are of no medicinal value.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—ON THE *KREWA* AND *KRAHA* [Note: [Col. 1298D] Absent from the edition]

The *krewa* and *kraha* are cold in nature and fly in a certain middle region of the air. They imitate human voices and belong to the race of the raven. For at first, before the crow and jackdaw existed, the magpie saw raven eggs, stole them, sat upon them, and brooded them. Thus crows and jackdaws first came forth. But afterwards they laid eggs among themselves as they do now: the crow with the crow and the jackdaw with the jackdaw; and so they are now multiplied.

They have no medicinal use, because a bird or other animal which is associated with a human being through cunning is of little benefit to him for healing; rather, he would use it as an evil and wicked person employs his own habits, and thereby become *arg* [wicked].

## CHAPTER XXV.—ON THE *NEBELKRAHA* [Note: [Col. 1298D] Absent from the edition]

The *nebelkraha* is hot and has boastful habits. It knows the air and the seasons; it can scarcely wait for changing events, and wherever it knows future sorrow will be, it hastens there. It uses both clean and unclean things. But [Col. 1299A] its flesh is of little use in medicines.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—ON THE *MUSAR* [Note: [Col. 1299D] Raven; crow.] [IV, II, 24]

The *musar* [gull, *Larus*, ed.] comes from the sun’s warm air. When it is young, it is hot and strong and eats stronger food; but as it advances in age, it becomes cold and weak and then seeks weak food. When it reaches old age, it returns to its first heat and first strength and, as before, seeks stronger food [Note: [Col. 1299D] “When it is young—seeks stronger food” omitted in the edition]. Its flesh is good for healthy and sick people to eat.

Let a person who has in any way taken *virgibnisse* [poison; *venenum*, ed.] boil its heart, liver, lung, and cleansed entrails in water. Then prepare them with wine, white pepper, and a somewhat smaller amount of *komel sultzen*. Or, if he does not have white pepper, let him add a little aloe, namely less than the *komel* [Col. 1299B], and place that flesh in these ingredients so that it may be steeped in them. Let him often eat it fasting. If the poison that he ate or drank has hardened even in his stomach, this will remove and purge it, and the person will be healed.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—ON THE *ORDUMEL* [Note: [Col. 1299D] Absent from the edition, as are the following chapters, nos. 28 and 29]

The *ordumel* has a perverse heat within it and is unsuitable for food, because everything in it is contrary to a person. Nor is it useful for medicines.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—ON THE *ALKREYA*

The *alkreya* is more cold than hot. It feeds on clean food and certain poisonous foods, and sometimes also eats sick fish. Its flesh is suitable for neither healthy [Col. 1299C] nor sick people to eat: healthy people can overcome it, but it harms the sick. There is no medicine in it.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—ON THE *MEWA* [Note: [Col. 1299D] Beautiful dove]

The *mewa* is hot and is in a proper balance of air and water, and is moderately moist. It does not fly high and is good for both healthy and sick people to eat.

## CHAPTER XXX.—ON THE DOVE [IV, II, 16]

The dove is more cold than hot. It loves the morning of the day—that is, its first rising, which is moderately cool—more than heat. It is simple and timid, and therefore flies in a flock so that it may be the less harmed by other birds. Because it is cold, it readily becomes hungry, and food does not warm within it as it does in another bird; therefore it soon becomes hungry and eats more than another bird of its size [Col. 1299D; Note: [Col. 1299D] “And it loves the morning—eats” omitted in the edition].

Its flesh is not firm but somewhat dry and provides little juice to a person [Note: [Col. 1299D] “But somewhat dry—provides” omitted in the edition]. It is of little benefit to a healthy person as food, even if it does not harm him. When eaten, it harms a sick person failing in body. The *holtzduba* [wood pigeon] and *ringelduba* [ring dove] have the same nature, except that they dwell in forests, are therefore somewhat [Col. 1300A] fiercer and larger than these, and feed on forest fare. Neither these nor those are useful in medicines [Note: [Col. 1299D] “And feed on forest fare—useful” omitted in the edition].

## CHAPTER XXXI.—ON THE TURTLEDOVE [Note: [Col. 1299D] Turtledove, *Columba turtur*. Absent from the edition]

The turtledove is hot and dry, possesses manly strength, is not timid, and always has, as it were, a servant. Since it has no moisture and does not direct its life toward diverse things, gall cannot grow in it. So too in a person who has good will, gall cannot grow, but diminishes; when he has a wicked mind, gall increases in him. Turtledove flesh is unsuitable for food, because it excites *gicht* in a person. Its other parts are useless.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—ON THE PARROT [Note: [Col. 1300D] Species of parrot]

[Col. 1300B] The parrot is very hot and also moist. It has something of the flight of the griffin and something of the strength of the lion; but it ventures nothing either in flight or in strength that it could accomplish [reading uncertain]. It knows the seasons and accommodates itself to their occurrences, gives voice to its songs accordingly, and has certain colours in its feathers according to the fire of gall [sic]. But it is of no medicinal use, because it possesses no power fully in itself, but only imperfectly, since its nature is diverse.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—ON THE MAGPIE [Note: [Col. 1300D] Magpie, *Corvus pica*] [IV, II, 25]

The magpie has a heavy heat within it, is *arg* [wicked], possesses diverse feathers from air and earth, and naturally follows, as it were, boastfulness, so that when it sees strangers approaching [Col. 1300C], it raises its voice at their arrival. It seeks poisonous and harmful food, whether little herbs or carrion [Note: [Col. 1300D] “And *arg*—carrion” omitted in the edition]; therefore its flesh is as poison, unsuitable for human food. It is accustomed to move about a person like a devil [Note: [Col. 1300D] “It is accustomed to move about—a devil” omitted in the edition].

If anyone has *grintslecken* [deep scabies, ed.] on his head, let him take its *smalcz* and anoint his head with it; he will be healed. The other parts of it are of no medicinal value [Note: [Col. 1300D] “The other parts—value” omitted in the edition].

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—ON THE *HERA* [Note: [Col. 1300D] Nutcracker, *Corvus caryocatactes*] [IV, II, 26]

The *hera* is hot and somewhat dry and can fly well in changing winds and storms. But it does not fly high, has dog-like habits, is itself unclean, eats food harmful to people [Col. 1300D], imitates to the best of its power whatever it sees done, and greets by voice every person whom it sees clearly [perhaps *clare* for printed *care*; Note: [Col. 1300D] “And can fly in changing winds—greets in voice” omitted in the edition]. Its flesh would be like poison to anyone who ate it, because it is steeped in storms and has a diverse nature of habits.

Take a *hera*, discard its head and entrails, remove its feathers, cut up the remaining body, and put the pieces into a new pot [Col. 1301A]. Add fenugreek and less *babellum*; then add *hirczmarck* [deer marrow], less hen fat, and cow butter prepared in May, in an amount equal to that of those two ingredients. Boil all together in water and make an ointment from the *raum* [fatty scum] which floats on top. This is excellent against pain of the head, shoulders, loins [*lenden*; kidneys, ed.], or flanks [*glancken*; ilia, ed.], if you often anoint yourself therewith. *Gicht* will cease there, however severe it may be, and the person will improve. [If oxen, pigs, or sheep become ill in any way, let this bird be boiled in water and given to them to eat, and they will be healed of whatever plague afflicts them. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER XXXV.—ON THE OWL [Note: [Col. 1301D] Species of screech-owl] [IV, II, 27]

[Col. 1301B] The owl is hot and has the habits of a thief, for it knows the day but flees it and loves the night; it hates other birds because it does not love their nature. It knows a human being’s death. Where grief and lamentation are to come, it perceives that odour through the air as [it does] the carcass of a bird, immediately hastens there, and flees away before the lamentation begins. It feeds on things contrary to human nature [Note: [Col. 1301D] “It has the habits of a thief—contrary to human nature” omitted in the edition, as is immediately following “because of—the nature it has.”]. If someone ate its flesh, it would be like poison to him, on account of the evil nature it has in itself.

Discard its head and entrails, remove its feathers, roast the remaining body over the fire, and collect its *smalcz*. Then boil *bisch* [hibiscus, ed.] and twice as much *reynfano* [tansy, ed.] in water. When you have boiled them, add and pour in the owl’s fat, put it again to the fire [Col. 1301C], add tree-oil in an amount equal to a quarter of that fat, press all these things through a cloth, and make an ointment. Let a person who has paralysis or is afflicted by *virgichtigit* often anoint himself with it, and he will be cured.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—ON THE *HUWONE* [IV, II, 28]

The *huwo* [*Rubo*, ed.] is hot and has almost the same nature as the owl, except that it is stronger and more robust in wickedness than the owl. It has the habits of a thief, knows the day but flees it, loves the night, and hates other birds which fly by day [Note: [Col. 1301D] “It has almost the same nature—fly by day” omitted in the edition]. Its flesh is harmful to human sight.

Take its *smalcz* and melt it in a pan. Let one who has *orfimas*, whether whole or broken, anoint himself with it, and they will dry up [Col. 1301D]. The other parts of it are of no medicinal value.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—ON THE *SISEGONINO* [Note: [Col. 1301D] Absent from the edition]

The *sisegonino* is hot and loves the night and the moon’s brightness more than the day or the sun’s brightness, though it loves the day more than the owl does. It is therefore active at night, because it abhors other birds and does not much wish to be seen. It has somewhat the habits of a mad creature, as though it were sometimes *wudich* [raging], like one who does not care [Col. 1302A] what he does.

When it first sees its young emerge from the eggs, it thinks they belong to another and kills them. When it sees them not moving, it is grieved and tears itself, so that they are revived by its blood. Then it loves them greatly, because it knows that they have been revived by it. It also perceives and understands a person’s happy and sad times: if they are happy, it rejoices with him in song; if sad, it shows itself sad by silence. Sometimes it hangs in the air with its back turned toward the earth, and looks and considers in the air when times of joy and gladness or times of sorrow will come. If it foresees that people will die there, it reveals this in a few cries and falls silent.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—ON THE CUCKOO [Note: [Col. 1301D] Common cuckoo, *Cuculus canorus*] [IV, II, 30]

The cuckoo is hot and has within itself the habits of birds and beasts [Col. 1302B]. It greets people who hear it with its voice and moves about in a *blind aura* [uncertain phrase]. It can endure neither great heat nor great cold. When there is great heat in summer, it seeks the shadows of forests, and the great heat of summer stirs its feathers so that they fall in winter. When it senses that its feathers will die, it gathers its food into its nest and strives to leave its little feathers in that nest; it lies in them through winter, so as to receive warmth from them. Its feathers are reborn again about the beginning of summer; it then cleans its nest of those feathers and goes forth [Note: [Col. 1301D] “It has within itself the habits of birds—goes forth” absent from the edition].

Its flesh is not fit for human food because it has scabies and because it would be like poison to one who ate it [Note: [Col. 1302D] “Because it has scabies—ate it” omitted in the edition]. If a person has *urslechte* [perhaps *uzslechte*] in his body [Col. 1302C], so that even his skin splits, and if some *gicht* afflicts his limbs, let him discard the cuckoo’s head, entrails, and feathers. To the remaining body add equal weights of *biboz* and sage, a little more dittany, and a little bear fat. Boil all this in water in a new pot, take the *raum* which floats on top, make an ointment of it, and let him often anoint himself with it. The *urslechte* will be healed, and the *gicht* that afflicts his limbs will cease.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—ON THE *SNEPHA* [Note: [Col. 1302D] Species of woodcock] [IV, II, 31]

The *snepha* is hot and derives from the high air; its flesh is good for both healthy and sick people to eat [Note: [Col. 1302D] “And derives from the high air—good to eat” omitted in the edition]. Let one whose eyes are dim take its gall and add a little wine, namely less than the gall itself [Note: [Col. 1302D] “Namely—gall itself” omitted in the edition], put or pour it into a copper vessel [Col. 1302D], and at night, when he goes to bed, apply it around his eyes. If it touches the eyes slightly within, it will not harm him. Let him do this often; it diminishes the dimness of the eyes. Its other parts are of little medicinal value [Note: [Col. 1302D] “Its other parts—value” omitted in the edition].

## CHAPTER XL.—ON THE WOODPECKER [Note: [Col. 1302D] Species of woodpecker] [IV, II, 32]

The woodpecker (*Specht*) is warm and of pure air, and flies in a certain middle region of the air. It is swift, loves warmth and summer, and its food is not poisonous. But the specht that has a green colour is better and stronger than any other. The other is quite vigorous, but not as much as the green one. [Note: “[And] of pure air—green” omitted in the edition.]

A person with leprosy should roast a green specht over the fire and eat it often; it consumes the leprosy—that is, makes it disappear (*swendet*). Take also a green specht; discard its head and entrails, pluck off its feathers, roast the remaining body over the fire, remove and preserve the upper *ronst*—the coating on its skin produced by the fire—and then pound the other roasted body a little in a mortar and boil it vigorously in water, until it is reduced throughout by one third (*addreb*). After boiling it, remove it from the water; separate the bones from the flesh and discard them. Put the flesh on a heated stone and reduce it to powder; add this powder, together with its upper roasted skin, a sufficient amount of rue, to the water in which you first boiled the specht; add also a sufficient amount of vulture fat and a little goat suet. Boil all these together vigorously; from the *raum* floating on top make an ointment, discarding the rest. Anoint a person’s leprosy frequently with that ointment; however severe the leprosy is, he will be healed—unless God’s judgment does not permit it, or unless his death lies in the leprosy. [Note: “Unless—leprosy” omitted in the edition.]

Dry its heart and have it worked in gold or silver, as in a ring (*virwircke*). So long as you wear it with you, *gicht* will cease from you. For the nature of this bird is clean, and its heart is simple and has no evil craft; therefore the power of its heart, through pure air, calms the diversity of humours which produces the drops of paralysis. [Note: “For the nature—calms” omitted in the edition.] Its remaining parts are unsuitable for medicine.

## CHAPTER XLI.—ON THE SPARROW

[Note: Domestic finch. Absent from the edition.]

The sparrow is rather cold and has many changes in its habits because of its cunning and guile. It gladly flies in a flock, lest it be harmed by larger birds. It spends much of its time in dense air, and therefore has weak flesh, which is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat. Nor is it useful in medicines.

## CHAPTER XLII.—ON THE *MEYSA*

[Note: A species of titmouse. Absent from the edition.]

The *meysa* is warm, dry, and tame, and gladly flies in pure air. It has wholesome flesh and is good for healthy and sick people to eat. A person suffering from *virgichtigit* should boil a *meysa* in water, make a broth (*Jussal*) from it with butter, and eat this often; he will be cured.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—ON THE *AMSLA*

[Note: Blackbird (*Turdus merula*).]

The *amsla* is warm, dry, and tame, gladly flies in pure air, and also grows from pure air. It is good for healthy people to eat, but harms sick people because it is dry. [Note: “And tame—dry” omitted by the edition.] Dry its liver, have it worked into whatever object you wish, and always carry it with you; then the devil will not trouble you with terror (*grusale*) or deception (*getrugnisze*), because he hates it for its purity. [Note: “Because he hates it—for its purity” omitted by the edition.]

## CHAPTER XLIV.—ON THE *DROSELA*

The *drosela* is warm and tame in its habits. If a person has any inward pain in the throat, or is hoarse of voice, boil it in water; soak a linen cloth in that water, and gently bind the whole throat with the wet cloth up to the *orclatum (?) belbe* [the edition reads: “gently bind it up to the ears”]. Make a soup (*suffen*) from what remains of the same water and eat it. Do this often, and the person will improve in throat and voice. [Note: “Thus far the edition.”] Whoever has pain in the liver or lungs should take a *drosela*, eat it often after it has been boiled in water, and will be healed.

## CHAPTER XLV.—ON THE *LERCHA*

[Note: A species of lark. Compare Hugh of Trimberg, *Der Renner*, verse 19527.]

[Col. 1304B]

The *lercha* [“laudula,” the lark, in the edition] is very warm and of a dry nature. It loves summer, gladly flies in the brilliance of the sun, and flourishes in warmth, but readily dies in cold. It is pleasant (*wunsam*), clever, and seeks clean food; it is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat. [Note: “And of a dry nature—good” omitted in the edition.]

But if someone’s throat is swollen—that is, *swillet*—take a lark, discard its head, entrails, and feathers, and dry the remaining body gradually upon a hot brick, without burning it. Add powdered *milwa* [lime-tree/linden, *tilia*, in the edition] to the weight of three coins; tie it in a cloth and bind it, within the cloth, upon that person’s throat. The swelling will be driven away. If you have a large *swern* [ulcer, in the edition] anywhere on your body, bind the same powder over it; because of its same nature and power, as stated above, the ulcer will become soft and burst. If you have *drusze* [glands, in the edition], first moisten them with your saliva, then bind the aforesaid powder over them in a cloth, and they will disappear. If a dog is rabid, cut off the head of a lark and give that head to the raging dog to eat; it will abandon its madness and become tame.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—ON THE *ISENBRADO*

[Note: Common kingfisher, *Alcedo hispida*.]

The *isenbrado* is warm, temperate in that warmth, and somewhat moist; it always seeks purity of air. It has prosperity in it, and sometimes seeks waters that are clean and clear of filth. If a person could dwell and remain in the air or by the water where it nests, no sickness would befall him there, because it always seeks air in which there is no filth and feeds on clean things. [Note: “And temperate in that warmth—feeds” omitted in the edition.]

Discard its head, entrails, and feathers; wrap the remaining body in oak leaves and place it on coals, until those leaves are consumed by the fire. Do the same a third time, until the bird itself is burned. [Note: “And a third time—burned” omitted in the edition.] Then put the bird in a new pot over the fire without water, burn it moderately so that it can be powdered, and gradually reduce it to powder. Give a person who has apoplexy—that is, who can no longer move anywhere on one side—this powder daily while fasting, in a little water, in an amount slightly less than a nutmeg; it will cure that illness if the person is young, unless the illness has then become inveterate in him through a long time. If someone is so afflicted by *virgichtigit* that he seeks to tear himself wholly apart, let him drink some of the same powder in water during the attack; he will improve because of the good power of the things mentioned above. [Note: “But if any person—above” omitted in the edition, which adds: “A person who cannot sleep should place the bones of this bird beneath his head; he will sleep, and terrors will not harm him meanwhile.”]

## CHAPTER XLVII.—ON THE *VEDEHOPPO*

[Note: Hoopoe, *Upupa epops*.]

[Col. 1305B]

The *wedehoppo* [“upupa,” hoopoe, in the edition] is warm and moist [and unsuitable as human food, added in the edition]. It flies about a certain middle region of the air, loves daylight, and has an unclean nature. Therefore it is always occupied in filth and around filth, thrives in it, seeks very foul filth, and makes its dwelling there. [Note: “And flies about a certain middle region—makes its dwelling” omitted in the edition.]

Discard its head and entrails, pluck off its feathers, and reduce the rest of the body to powder in a new pot. If *orfimae* in a person are ruptured, or if worms consume someone, put this powder into the wounds: if they are *orfimae*, they will dry up; if they are worms, they will die.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—ON THE *WACHTELA*

[Note: Quail, *Tetrao coturnix*.]

The *wachtela* is warm and moist, seeks clean food, and is good for healthy people to eat. It is unsuitable for sick people who are flooded by bad humours, because it stirs up their humours, since it possesses sluggish moisture.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—ON THE NIGHTINGALE

[Note: Nightingale, *Motacilla luscinia*.]

The nightingale [“luscinia” in the edition] is warm and somewhat dry, derives its life from nocturnal air, and is clean. Since it comes from nocturnal air, it rejoices and sings more by night than by day, because the sun gives it too much brightness in the daytime, which it abhors. [Note: “And derives its life from nocturnal air—abhors it” omitted in the edition.]

If someone’s eyes are dim, let him catch a nightingale before daybreak, take its gall, pour it out, and add one drop of dew found upon clean grass. When he goes to sleep, let him often anoint his eyelids and eyelashes around his eyes with this; even if it touches the inner eye a little, it does no harm. It wonderfully removes dimness from the eyes, just as foam—that is, *schum*—is purified and cast off by the heat of fire in summer. [Note: “Just as—cast off” omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER L.—ON THE STARLING

[Note: Common starling, *Sturnus vulgaris*.]

The starling is warm and timid, and therefore flies in a flock. It has affection for its own kind, does not hate other birds, and flies moderately high. Remove its head, entrails, and feathers; reduce the rest of its body to powder by burning it in a new pot. Put this powder into ruptured *orfimae*, and they will dry up.

Take a whole dead starling and hold it over what you suspect to be poison. If it is poison, its feathers separate, disentangle themselves from one another, and move, yet fall away; for if it were alive, it would suffer from this and flee. If it is not poison, its feathers neither separate nor move.

## CHAPTER LI.—ON THE *VYNCO*

[Note: Chaffinch, *Fringilla coelebs*.]

The *vynco* [“frigellus” in the edition] is warm and seeks its food in the green growth of earth and herbs. It does not greatly harm healthy people when eaten, but it harms the sick. It is of a dry nature and does not seek high places in the air. [Note: “And seeks food in the green growth—does not seek” omitted in the edition.]

Take a *vincken*, discard its head, entrails, and feathers, place it on live coals, and roast it slightly so that it merely becomes warm. Where an infant has broken out in the skin (*uszgeslagen*) and become ulcerous, lay it on while warm; heat it again and lay it on another place. Do this often over the infant’s whole body: it draws unclean and bad humours from the skin. Then anoint the area with goat suet, and the ulcers will be healed. Its other parts are of little use. [Note: “Then anoint—of little use” omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER LII.—ON THE GOLDFINCH

[Note: Goldfinch, *Fringilla carduelis*.]

The goldfinch is warm and comes also from that air which first brings forth bursting flowers; therefore it has a beautiful colour. A person with an internal *brustswern* [a breast ulcer], or pain in the stomach or loins, or sickness in the body, should take a goldfinch, clean it after discarding its head and feathers, roast its flesh lightly with liver and lungs, and, after roasting it, pull apart the flesh—that is, *zuzeyse*—and crush its bones. Then take fine wheat flour, add a little fat, put in the aforesaid flesh, and cook it again in a pan. Make a broth in this way and eat it often. If the person is young, it heals him inwardly; if old, it lessens these pains in him, because it is like an excellent ointment that heals a person inwardly.

## CHAPTER LIII.—ON THE *AMERA*

[Note: A species of bunting, *Emberiza*.]

The *amera* is warm and gladly flies in pure air. It is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat, because its food is clean and unclean and bitter.

## CHAPTER LIV.—ON THE *GRASEMUCKA*

[Note: A species of wagtail, *Motacilla*.]

The *grasemucka* is cold and comes from the air of foaming waters; its food is clean and unclean. It is of little value for medicines.

## CHAPTER LV.—ON THE *WARGKRENGEL*

[Note: Absent from the edition, as are below chapters 56 and 60.]

The *wargkrengel* is cold and belongs also to that air where the noonday demons are. [Note: Psalm XC, 6.] It has no joy until it sees sadness in other animals. It sometimes breaks its own eggs and is more hostile and harsh toward its young than other birds are. Yet it has no such powers in itself that either good or evil can be accomplished by it in medicines.

## CHAPTER LVI.—ON THE *MERLA*

The *merla* is cold, and its food is unclean and harmful. It is good for neither healthy nor sick people to eat, nor does it contain any medicinal property.

## CHAPTER LVII.—ON THE *WASZERSCELTZA*

[Note: White wagtail, *Motacilla alba*.]

The *waszerstelsa* [perhaps *waszersteltza*] has moderate warmth and also comes from whirlwinds; therefore it constantly moves its tail, can endure whirlwinds and storms because it belongs to them, gladly remains near water because it belongs to whirlwinds, and chiefly seeks food in the water. It has tender flesh and is good for healthy and sick people to eat, because it restores the sick.

Dry and preserve its throat. When someone has pain in the heart, or is troubled by *gicht*, put that throat in water for a short time, then remove it, pour the water into the throat, and give it to the person to drink. He will improve in the heart, and *gicht* will cease from him. Dry its heart also and always keep it with you. When *gicht* troubles you, put the heart in water for a short time and drink the water; the *gicht* in you will cease. Keep its dried bladder with you; if *freischlich* arises in a person, moisten it slightly with your saliva and place it beside—not upon—the *freischlich*, and it disperses it, that is, makes it disappear (*swendet*). Place the same bladder, slightly moistened with saliva, upon *ziterdrusze*, and they will disappear.

[Note: The edition reads: “The pelican is warm. A person who is frantic or mentally forgetful should dry the pelican’s heart in the sun and bind it upon his crown, so that his flesh is warmed by it; he will return to intellectual understanding. If anyone has pain in the head, which even seems to burn, let him powder pelican liver, add a little more fennel seed and a little less fenugreek seed, put it on a cloth, and bind it upon his forehead and temples; he will improve. Let the bladder of the same bird also be dried. Where *slier*, or another swelling, arises anywhere in a person’s body, moisten the bladder with human saliva or a little water and place it upon the swelling; the swelling will gently burst. If a person’s bone is broken, or a limb slips from its place, dry the cleansed intestine of this bird in the sun. After the broken bone has been set, lightly anoint the intestine with olive oil and bind it over the fracture; it joins the bone together.”]

## CHAPTER LVIII.—ON THE *BEYNSTERCZA*

[Note: Yellow wagtail, *Motacilla flava*.]

The *beynstercza* is warm and moist, and comes from whirlwinds; therefore it moves its tail and seeks somewhat poisonous and harmful food. If someone eats its flesh, it excites *gicht* in him.

## CHAPTER LIX.—ON THE SWALLOW

[Note: A species of swallow.]

The swallow is warm, seeks warmth and gentle air, and has warmth where it nests. It is somewhat sharp—that is, fierce (*grim*)—and therefore flies swiftly; it feeds much upon unclean food. [Note: “And seeks warmth and gentle air—feeds” omitted in the edition.] It is harmful for a person to eat.

Wherever a person has *orfimae*, whether ruptured or unruptured, anoint them with swallow fat (*smalcz*), and they will heal. If a person suffers from *morklacdrim*, burn whole swallow eggs with their shells and reduce them to powder; add to this powder a little more cock-fat (*hanensmalcz*), mix them together, and anoint the *orclackdrim*; you will improve.

[Added by the edition: “If someone becomes leprous through gluttony and drunkenness, let him make a powder of swallow dung and four times as much of the herb called burdock, which has red flowers. Let him also fry stork fat and a little more vulture fat in a pan; mix the aforesaid powder and a little sulphur into this fat; make an ointment; and have himself anointed in a dry bath. Then let him lie down in bed. Do this until the fifth day, or for more days.”]

## CHAPTER LX.—ON THE *CUNGELM*

The *cungelm* is warm and comes from the air of the sun’s brightness. Its flesh does not harm the person who eats it. By itself it is not especially effective as a medicine, because it is small. But when ointments are being prepared in May, remove its head, discard its entrails, reduce the remaining body to powder in a new pot, and add this powder to other good herbs from which ointments are made. No herb there is more precious against illnesses.

## CHAPTER LXI.—ON THE BAT

The bat is more warm than cold. It abhors warmth and daylight and flies at the time when aerial spirits especially range about because of human repose—that is, when a person rests and experiences various changes within himself. [Note: “And it abhors warmth and daylight—within himself” omitted in the edition.]

If anyone has *gelsucht* [jaundice], strike the bat lightly so that it does not die, bind it upon his *glaucken* [uncertain bodily term], with the bat’s back turned toward the person’s back. Remove it after a little while, then bind it upon his stomach and leave it there until it dies.

## CHAPTER LXII.—ON THE *WIDDERWALONE*

[Note: Pliny, *Natural History*, XXX.28.]

The *widdervalo* is warm and unstable and has a sad nature. A person with *gelsucht* should bind this dead bird, with its feathers, upon his stomach; the jaundice will pass into it and he will be cured. Or a person with *gelsucht* should reduce the same bird to powder, moisten this powder slightly with olive oil (*baumoleo*), bind it upon his stomach for two or three days, and be cured. Whoever is deaf in an ear should put its heart into that ear, so that the ear is warmed inwardly by the heart, and he will recover hearing. Whoever has *nazeboz* [a nasal ailment] should powder its liver, apply the powder to his nostrils, draw its scent inward through them, and the bad humours of his head will dissolve more gently and flow out more easily; he will be cured all the sooner.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—ON THE BEE

[Note: Honeybee, *Apis mellifica*.]

The bee comes from the sun’s heat, loves summer, and has swift heat, so that it cannot endure cold. If someone develops *uberbeyn*, if a limb has moved from its place, or if limbs are bruised, take bees that have died in their vessel—not living bees—put a sufficient quantity in a linen cloth and sew them within it. Soak this cloth, with the bees sewn inside, in olive oil (*baumoleo*), lay it upon the painful limb, and do this often; he will improve. If a worm consumes someone’s flesh, take bees dead in their vessel, make them into powder, and frequently put this powder into the ulcerated place; the worm will die.

[Added by the edition: “The honey made by bees is very warm. If a fat person eats honey often, it produces bruising and wasting in him; but if a dry and lean person eats cooked honey, he will not be greatly harmed by it. Cooked honey, thoroughly skimmed, will not greatly harm fat or lean, healthy or sick people. But if someone eats the honeycomb with wax, it excites melancholy in him.”]

## CHAPTER LXIV.—ON THE FLY

[Note: Housefly, *Musca domestica*.]

The fly is cold. In summer, if someone is stung or injured by a small worm [such as a spider, added in the edition], bind a crushed fly upon it; the heat that the fly then possesses in summer weakens the poison somewhat. [Note: “The heat—the fly possesses” omitted in the edition.] But in winter the fly is wholly poisonous and dangerous to a person, unless God protects him. If someone eats or drinks a fly, immediately crush *scharleya*, put some of its juice into good wine so that the wine exceeds the juice, warm it over the fire, and drink it, so that any poison from the fly remaining in him may be expelled through nausea.

[Added by the edition: “If the pustule called *freislichaz* swells up in a person, crush flies after removing their heads and make a circle around the swelling with them; this resists the poison so that it does not spread further. Then grind a red snail without a shell and make, with it, a circle around the circle made with the fly. Afterwards anoint with lily juice the skin around the circle made with the snail. Place a leaf of *vehendistel* upon the pustule. Then make a small cake from pure fine wheat flour and bind it with a cloth over the leaf and over the entire swelling, so that it may soften and burst by itself. If it does not burst by itself, open it with a dry wooden thorn or another dry splinter, but not with any heated or cold iron or needle. While the person suffers from this pustule, he should protect himself from fire, cold, wind, and damp air; abstain from all hot roasted and rich food and from wine; and avoid raw vegetables and raw fruit.”]

## CHAPTER LXV.—ON THE CICADA

[Note: A species of cricket.]

The cicada is more cold than warm, and harms a person more than it benefits him, whether alive or dead, because it contains a bad *livor* [corrupt humour/bruise]. If a person touches it, he suffers pain from it. [Note: “And harms a person more—suffers pain” omitted in the edition.] But if a cicada has died naturally, let a person troubled by ruptured *orfimae* take it dead, reduce it to powder upon a heated stone, and frequently apply the powder to the place where the *orfimae* are; they will dry up.

## CHAPTER LXVI.—ON THE LOCUST

[Note: Absent from the edition.]

The locust is cold as dew; it is neither very useful nor very dangerous. But in regions where air and ground are cold, locust flesh is somewhat poisonous and dangerous to eat. Where air and ground are warm, it is less dangerous; there it may almost be eaten like a crab. For it gathers poison from the coldness of the earth, but in warm ground, because of its good heat, it lacks poison. It has no medicinal value.

## CHAPTER LXVII.—ON THE GNAT

The gnat is warm. Whoever has deep scabies on the head should collect gnats in a little vessel, burn them from above with straw, and place them in a cleansed spot upon live coals, so that they become ashes along with the coals. Then make lye from these ashes, wash the head—or wherever scabies or bad spots are on the body—with it, and do this often; he will be healed.

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—ON THE BUMBLEBEE

[Note: Ground-bee, *Apis terrestris*.]

Bumblebees are cold. A person with dim eyes should remove the little bladder between the bumblebee’s head and belly and put a little of the liquid in it into his eyes when he lies down to sleep. But immediately afterwards he should anoint his eyelids and eyelashes with olive oil; do this once or twice a month, and he will see more clearly. Whoever has dirty nails should anoint them with the liquid in the bumblebee’s bladder and bind them with a bandage, doing this until they become beautiful. Whoever has deep scabies on the head should often anoint his head with the aforesaid liquid, and he will be healed.

## CHAPTER LXIX.—ON THE WASP

The wasp is warm and clean. Powder *berwurcz*, add twice as much powdered wasp, and hold these powders over warm smoke so that they become warm gradually and gently. Hold them warm over the food which you wish to eat; the poison will thereby be weakened so that it cannot harm you.

## CHAPTER LXX.—ON THE *GLIMO*

[Note: Glowworm, *Lampyris noctiluca*.]

The *glimo* is more cold than warm. If someone suffers from the falling sickness, when he begins to fall bind as many living *glimen* as can be obtained in a cloth and place them over his navel; he will immediately recover his strength.

## CHAPTER LXXI.—ON THE *MEYGELANA*

[Note: Compare above, I.159.]

The *meygelana* is cold. If a person has scrofulous swellings, he should take this little worm, squeeze out the poison in it, add a smaller amount of powdered *meygelana*, and drink it in a little wine or water. Immediately it attacks the putrefaction of the scrofulae like an arrow and consumes them.

## CHAPTER LXXII.—ON THE *PARICE*

[Note: Edition, IV.II.34. Absent from the manuscript.]

The *parix* is warm, and its flesh is good for healthy and sick people to eat. A person troubled by paralysis should boil this bird in water, add fat, vinegar, and a little wine, eat this often, and will be cured. Whoever has the royal disease should bind the same bird whole, with its feathers removed, upon his stomach; the *gelsuocht* will pass into the bird, so that it becomes yellow-coloured (*gelfarb*).

[Col. 1311] HERE ENDS THE SIXTH BOOK, ON BIRDS.

THE SEVENTH BOOK BEGINS: ON ANIMALS. PREFACE.

[Note: The edition: Chapter 1, “Comparison of terrestrial animals with man.”]

[Col. 1311]

[Col. 1311B] Birds that move through the air signify the power by which a person, through thought, directs many things and assigns them to himself in advance through inward deliberation, before they proceed into a shining work. [Note: “Birds—proceed” omitted in the edition.] But animals that run over the earth and live on the earth signify the thoughts and deliberations that a person brings to completion in action. As works follow thoughts, so too, when good will, upright desires, and devout sighs go forth, the Maker of the world accomplishes them in heaven; nor are they accomplished there unless they have first gone before here, in pure thoughts and spiritual desire.

The lion and animals like it signify the human will that already wishes to bring forth works; the panther and animals like it signify ardent desire already present in the work as it begins. Other wild beasts signify the abundance of outflow, and show that a person has within his power to perform useful and useless works. But tame animals walking upon the earth show the gentleness a person possesses through right paths. Thus human rationality discovers what it says to each person: “You are this or that animal,” because certain animals have within themselves natures resembling that of a human being.

Animals that devour other animals, feed on bad food, and multiply offspring by breeding—such as the wolf, dog, and pig—are contrary to human nature, like herbs that are useless for eating, because humans do not act in this way. But livestock nourished by clean food, such as hay and similar fodder, and not multiplying offspring by breeding, are good for people to eat, like good and useful herbs. In both sorts certain medicines are found.
