# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1313]

## CHAPTER I.—ON THE ELEPHANT

[Note: The great elephant.]

[Col. 1313A]

The elephant has the heat of the sun, not of flesh, and possesses much sweat. This sweat is so strong that it bakes its bones as fire bakes food; hence those bones are beautiful. [Note: What follows is omitted by the edition down to “But whoever has pain in the lungs.”] Its sweat beneath the skin is very thick and holds its outer skin firm in its strength. It has more bone than flesh, lest it pass into diversity of dispositions, because flesh is always changed into various dispositions. It has strong veins because it lacks much flesh.

Its navel is as it were the head of its entrails, and its entrails are very warm. It is for the honour of humankind, as a ruler acts for the honour of his city. It is neither deceitful nor evil in its uprightness. It is sometimes fierce; it goes and seeks earth having sap from Paradise, digs that earth with its foot until it smells through its nostrils the sap of the earth of Paradise, and through the smell of it seeks union in mating. After the female has conceived, she carries the young she bears for a long time; it cannot grow quickly, because it is more of bone than flesh. After she gives birth, she seeks no further union until she sees that her young is as strong as she herself is.

[Note: Something is missing here, which we supply from the edition: “A person whose brain has been chilled and emptied should prepare the hollow bone in the elephant’s forehead, like a hollowed cap, and warm it in the sun; he will improve. Whoever has *nasebor* and much phlegm in his head should warm in the sun the bone in the elephant’s nostrils and lay it often upon his nostrils until he is warmed by it; he will be healed. A person who has pain in the breast, heart, spleen, or stomach, or who has the royal disease, should powder equal amounts of nutmeg and liquorice; scrape elephant bone, mix into the aforesaid powder twice as much of this scraping, add a sufficient amount of honey, and make an electuary. Let him eat this frequently while fasting and after meals, and he will improve. But whoever has pain in the lungs,” etc.]

But whoever has pain in the lungs, so that he is short of breath (*dumphet*) and coughs (*hustet*), should warm the same bone in the sun, scrape powder from it, put it in wine, cook it in a pan, then strain it through a cloth; he should add this powder and drink that wine often, and he will be healed. The elephant’s heart, liver, lungs, and other parts are of no medicinal use.

## CHAPTER II.—ON THE CAMEL

[Note: A species of camel.]

[Col. 1313C]

The camel has precipitous heat in itself, yet somewhat tepid; hence it is warm and also subject to the vicissitude of unstable dispositions. In its humps it has the strength of lion, panther, and horse, while in the rest of its body it has the nature of the ass. For the hump near its neck possesses strength from the lion-panther; the hump nearest it, strength from the panther; and the hump after that, strength from the horse. From these natures it grows in bulk and height, and from them it has such strength that, were it not tame, it would surpass the lion and other beasts in power. [Note: “For the hump near its neck—surpass” omitted in the edition.]

Whoever suffers from pain in the heart should scrape (*schabe*) into water bone from the hump that possesses the strength of the lion, and drink it often; the pain in his heart will cease. Whoever suffers in the spleen should scrape into water bone from the hump that possesses the strength of the panther, and drink it often; his spleen will be healed. Whoever has scabies and various fevers (*fiber*), and readily emits bad sweat, should scrape into water bone from the hump that possesses the strength of the horse, drink it often, and will be healed.

Dry its hoof and *gesvvel peds* [uncertain term], and keep them in a house or any place you wish. There aerial spirits will neither play their tricks nor stir up many conflicts, because the devil flees these things on account of the camel’s power and strength. Its other parts are of little value for medicines. [Note: “Because the devil flees—of little value” omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER III.—ON THE LION

[Note: Lion, *Felis leo*.]

Leo is exceedingly hot. If [he has within himself both human strength and the nature of beasts, and is of such great strength that, if him, etc.; added by the edition] his bestial nature did not restrain him, he could penetrate stones. [Note: [Col. 1314D] The edition omits what follows down to: “But if any man is deaf.”] He recognizes a human being; and if, in his rage, he has injured one, he grieves after inflicting the injury. When the lion mates with the lioness, he forgets his strength and bestial nature, so that he mates with her properly. But when the lioness does not feel her cubs alive within her, she becomes sorrowful and hostile to the lion, because she does not know that she has conceived; and after she has borne the cubs and sees them dead, she withdraws from them. But the lion, seeing her then, [Col. 1315A] understands that she has borne cubs; he immediately smells them and runs roaring toward them, recovers the strength he lost in coupling with the lioness, and utters roars so powerful that the cubs are revived by them. After these cubs have been revived, they utter roars so loud that the lioness hears them; she at once runs up joyfully, drives the lion away from them, cherishes them and makes them rise, and permits the lion to come near them no more until they have grown.

Adam and Eve did not cry aloud in lamentation before any human being had been born; but after the first infant was born, he immediately lamented aloud up to the height of many elements [the reading is uncertain: *planxit?*, “lamented”]. Hearing this voice as something unknown, Adam ran up; and, on hearing the same voice of lamentation, [Col. 1315B] he too then for the first time cried aloud in like manner, and Eve together with him—just as the lion, lioness, and cub roar together when the cub is revived.

Strip the lion’s skin from its neck over its head and crown, and keep it. Then, if a man has become *vironsinnigt*—out of his mind—from some disorder in the head, warm this little skin from that hide upon his head, and he will recover his senses. Whoever suffers from any other ailment in the head should place this same piece of lion’s head-skin upon his head until his head is warmed by it, and then remove it at once. He must not allow it to remain longer upon him, lest he be harmed by it, because it is strong; and he will be better.

But of the rest of its hide make neither a belt nor gloves nor shoes, and do not wear it upon yourself, because its strength would harm [Col. 1315C] more than help.

But if any man is deaf, cut off the lion’s right ear, and let another person place it in the deaf man’s ear until that ear is warmed inwardly by the lion’s ear, but no longer; and say: “Hear, *adimacus*, by the living God and by the sharp power of the lion’s hearing.” Do this often [Note: [Col. 1315D] “And say … do this often” is omitted in the edition.], and he will recover his hearing.

And he who is foolish—that is, *wanwiczig*—should place the dried heart of a lion upon his breast for a short time, namely until the place is merely warmed by it. For if he lets it lie there longer, he will become, through its strength, as if *unsinning* (“out of his mind”); and thus for a long while he will be prudent. A woman who is in difficulty in childbirth [Col. 1315D] and cannot give birth should place the lion’s heart above her navel for a short, not a long, time; the child will loosen within her and quickly come forth.

Dry and keep its liver. If anyone cannot digest food he has eaten, place this liver in water for a short time, and not long, lest that water become too strong from the power of the liver; then give that water to the person who cannot digest, for him to drink, and he will immediately digest the food he has eaten. Bury a lion’s heart in your house, or in any place where you wish; as long as it lies buried there, lightning and fires will do no harm there, nor will thunder strike there. [Col. 1316A] For when the lion hears thunder, it is accustomed immediately to roar.

[But let its liver also be dried; and if anyone cannot digest food he has eaten, let him put that liver in water for a short time and drink it; he will immediately digest the food he has eaten. Let a man also dry the tip of a lion’s tail and always keep it with him; meanwhile he cannot easily be harmed by the whistlings of aerial spirits or by magical arts. When he eats or drinks, let him keep this tip beside his food and drink; if poison is present in them, they move in the vessel in which they are contained, and the vessel containing the poison also sweats, and thus it may be detected. But if a man has eaten or drunk poison, let him put the same tip of the lion’s tail in hot wine for a short time, [Col. 1316B] drink the warmed wine, and the poison he has taken will immediately pass through him with his digestion. Let a man dip steel in a lion’s blood, and he will be strong against iron and against every other thing in knowledge. Added by the edition.]

The other things found in it are not suitable for medicine. [Note: [Col. 1315D] “For the lion … not suitable” is omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER IV.—ON THE BEAR

[Note: [Col. 1315D] Bear, *arctos*.] [IV, III, 6].

The bear has heat almost like a human being’s, so that it is sometimes cold. [Note: [Col. 1315D] The edition lacks what follows down to “And bear’s flesh is fit for eating” at [Col. 1316D].] Even when it is hot, it has a loud voice and is gentle. But when it is cold, it keeps its voice subdued and is irascible; for in sexual desire it has gentle manners and is not easily angered, whereas those who are continent from sexual desire are irascible.

For when God created man, He made him [Col. 1316C] in his joints and divisions, in the course of his veins, and in all the pathways which the soul possesses in the body. But He had first created birds, fishes, and animals; all these did nothing before man acted, but waited to see what work man would begin first. After man ate the apple and sweated in distress, his blood was changed into the nature man now has, and all the other animals were changed into their respective natures. Therefore the bear has an affection for sexual desire joined with affection. [Note: [Col. 1316D] Something is missing.]

When a human being is in sexual desire or wantonness, as he ought not to be, a bear can smell him from almost half a mile away and would run toward him if it could—the male bear toward a woman and the she-bear toward a man [Col. 1316D]—and they would mate with them. But if the human being then inclines to reason and does not act according to irrational cattle, the bear or she-bear would tear that person to pieces.

When the she-bear conceives, she is so impatient to give birth that through impatience she even miscarries before the cubs within her reach maturity. Yet they receive vital air in their mother, though they do not move within her. When she gives birth [Note: [Col. 1316D] Compare Pliny, *Natural History* VIII.54.], what she brings forth is like flesh and does not move, although it has vital air in itself; nevertheless, it has all the outlines of its form. Seeing this, the mother grieves over it and [Col. 1317A] licks it; with her tongue she forms all those outlines, until all the limbs are separated from one another. She stretches herself over it and cherishes it; and within five or six days it grows so large from her warmth that it can rise. Nor does she then leave them, even if she is pursued by hunters: she carries it in her claws and runs on three feet before setting it down, while they are still immature.

Bear’s flesh is not good for a human being to eat, because if it is eaten it inflames a person toward sexual desire, just as water, conversely, extinguishes a person’s thirst. Pork and the flesh of certain other animals do this likewise, though not so much as bear’s flesh; they make a human being roll toward sexual desire like a wheel, but render him unclean in another manner. [Col. 1317B] Yet animals that chew the cud do not quickly rest in sexual desire. [Note: [Col. 1317D] “And make a human being roll toward sexual desire … do not quickly rest” is omitted in the edition.]

[When a young man’s hair first begins to fall out, let him mix bear’s fat with a little ash made from wheat or rye straw. With this he should anoint his whole head, especially where the hair has begun to fall. Afterwards let him refrain for a long time from washing his head of this ointment. Let him do this often, and the hair which has not yet fallen will be so moistened and strengthened by the ointment that it will not fall for a long time. Added by the edition.]

But if any person is timid, fearful, trembling, and anxious, so that he is always in fear, let him take the little skin between a bear’s ears [Col. 1317C] and prepare it slightly (*gerwe*); then let him place it over his breast and heart until he is warmed by it, and he will at once become *balch* (“bold”), and fear, trembling, and anxiety will depart from him. [Note: [Col. 1317D] The edition ends here.]

This little skin should be prepared like another skin so that its sweat is removed. For if a person is warmed by the bear’s hide—which is not flesh—so that the sweat in it does not touch the person’s bare flesh, then it will not harm him by sexual desire. Bear’s fat is added to certain ointments and medicines, and those medicines will be more valuable for it. By itself it is of no use in medicines, because the bear has unstable manners.

## CHAPTER V.—ON THE UNICORN

[Note: [Col. 1317D] The unicorn.] [IV, III, 7].

[Col. 1317D] The unicorn is more hot than cold. [Note: [Col. 1317D] The edition omits what follows down to “Powder the unicorn’s liver,” etc., at [Col. 1318D].] Yet its strength is greater than its heat. It eats clean herbs and moves almost by leaps; it flees from human beings like other animals, except those of its own species, and therefore cannot be captured. It fears a man greatly and turns aside from him. Just as the serpent, in the first Fall, turned aside from the man and looked at the woman, so this animal turns aside from a man and follows a woman.

There was a certain philosopher who had investigated the natures of animals. He could capture this animal by no art, and therefore wondered greatly. [Col. 1318A] One day he went hunting as he had been accustomed to do, accompanied by men, women, and girls. The girls went apart from the others and meanwhile played with flowers. When the unicorn saw the girls, it shortened its leaps and moved slowly; then, at a distance, it sat upright on its hind legs and looked intently at them. Seeing this, the philosopher considered it with all diligence, understood that the unicorn could be caught by means of girls, approached it from behind, and captured it through those very girls.

For when the unicorn sees a girl from afar, it wonders that she has no beard yet bears a human form. If two or three girls are together, it wonders all the more and is captured more readily when it fixes its eyes on them. These girls by whom it is captured [Col. 1318B] must be noble rather than rustic, neither fully grown nor very small, but in moderate adolescence. It loves them because it knows them to be gentle and sweet.

Every year it goes once to the land that has the sap of Paradise. There it seeks the best herbs, digs them up with its foot, and eats them; it gains much strength from them and thus also flees other animals. Beneath its horn it has bronze [perhaps *os*, “bone”] as transparent as glass, so that a person can look at his face in it as in a mirror; nevertheless it is not very precious.

Powder the unicorn’s liver and put this powder into prepared yolk-fat—that is, *smalcz*, fat prepared from egg-yolks—and make an ointment. No leprosy, of whatever kind, will fail to be cured if it is often anointed with that [Col. 1318C] ointment, unless the person who has it is to die or God does not wish to cure it. The liver of this animal has good warmth and purity, and yolk-fat is the most precious substance in an egg and is like an ointment. But leprosy most often arises from black bile and from an excess of black blood. [Note: [Col. 1318D] “For the liver of this animal … black blood” is omitted in the edition.]

Therefore make a belt from its hide and gird your skin with it; no severe plague or fever will harm you inwardly. Make shoes from its skin too and wear them, and you will always have sound feet, healthy legs, and healthy *gelancken* (“joints”) within; nor will plague meanwhile harm you in them.

[A man who fears being killed by poison should place a unicorn’s hoof beneath the dish containing food or the cup [Col. 1318D] containing drink. If they are hot and poison is in them, it makes them boil in the vessel; if cold, it makes them smoke, and thus he can know that poison has been added. Added by the edition.]

The other things found in it are not suitable for medicine.

## CHAPTER VI.—ON THE TIGER

[Note: [Col. 1318D] Cat, tiger.] [IV, III, 8].

The tiger is hot; it runs in mountains and valleys, and has something of the nature of the *Steinbock* [ibex in the edition]. Through its much running, pustules flow from it like a liquid; it wipes them from itself, [Col. 1319A] and they have a pleasant smell and are useful in medicines. [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Through its much running … useful” is omitted in the edition.]

But its flesh is *slimechte* [“bruised/discolored”; *livosa*, “livid,” in the edition], and because of its strength and swiftness [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Because of … swiftness” is omitted in the edition.] it is not fit for human food. If anyone has recent rather than chronic leprosy, let him take the tiger’s heart as it has just been killed and place it fresh and warm upon the leprous spot; the leprosy will pass into that heart and he will be healed. But if the leprosy is chronic, it will not help to place the heart upon it. For if a heart, whether fresh and hot or old and cold, is placed upon leprosy, whether recent or chronic, the leprosy does not pass into that heart, but into the person’s flesh, and injures him so that the same person’s heart might readily burst. [Note: [Col. 1319D] The edition omits “But if the leprosy … burst,” but has instead: “If a man cannot digest food he has eaten, when the tiger is killed let him place its warm liver upon his stomach for a short time, namely until it loses warmth; his stomach will immediately loosen and digest. And if there is an ulcer, or *slier*, in a human body, provided it is not what is called *freislichaz*, let the pustules found on the tiger be placed upon those ulcers; they will burst and he will be healed.”]

## CHAPTER VII.—ON THE PANTHER

[Note: [Col. 1319D] Cat, leopard.] [IV, III, 5].

[Col. 1319B]

The panther is exceedingly hot in its nature. It seeks, as it were, vain glory, so that it would gladly imitate all the other animals in its acts. It does not love the other animals out of affection for them, but because it gladly performs their deeds in accordance with its own nature. Nor does it feed entirely on clean pastures, and thus its breath is not clean but somewhat poisonous, although it sometimes seems to smell good. The things found in it are not of much use in medicines. [Note: [Col. 1319D] Edition: “On the leopard: ‘The leopard is hot, cheerful, swift, and strong. A person weak in the chest and stomach, who often feels failing in the heart, should dry a leopard’s heart in the sun and powder it; whenever he feels such failure, let him apply this powder to the place where he suffers, and he will be better. [Col. 1320D] Let a person also keep its claw together with the skin of its foot, and wherever magical operations may be, they cannot be fully carried out there.’”]

## CHAPTER VIII.—ON THE HORSE

[Note: [Col. 1320D] Horse, steed. Job 39:22.] [IV, III, 10].

The horse is more hot than cold, has a good nature, and possesses such great strength [Col. 1319C] that it does not know it possesses it. It always desires to advance and eats clean food. Its flesh is tough, hard to digest, and harmful for human consumption, so that it can scarcely be digested because of its strength. For the flesh of ruminating animals is tempered as though placed in a press; that is, it can more easily be eaten and digested. But the flesh of non-ruminating animals is heavier and is not digested as readily. [Note: [Col. 1320D] “So that it can scarcely … digested” is omitted in the edition.]

A person with scabies, however severe, should take goat fat—that is, *unslet*—draw blood from a horse’s ear, mix the blood with this fat, and often anoint himself with it by a fire; he will be healed.

[If a person contracts leprosy from anger, let him go where a small quantity of horses’ blood runs onto the ground when blood is let from their vein, and where clean animals are slaughtered. Let him take that blood together with the stained earth, boil it in a cauldron with water, taking care not to use so much water that it deprives the blood of its strength. Then let him sit in this bath up to his throat and put a little of the same blood and earth into a small bag, which he should place on his face if it hurts there. When he comes out of the bath, he should recline upon a bed and put the little bag containing blood and earth upon his heart, lest he become weak. Let him do this four or five times, or more. Added by the edition.]

The other things found in it are not useful in medicine.

## CHAPTER IX.—ON THE ASS

[Note: [Col. 1320D] Horse, ass.] [IV, III, 11].

[Col. 1320B] The ass is more hot than cold, foolish, and nearly blind from the excess of nature which it has in sexual desire. It has neither *grimheit* (“fierceness”) nor submissiveness. It does not flee from a person, but gladly remains with one, because in some part of its nature it touches human nature. [Note: [Col. 1320D] “And it does not flee … human nature” is omitted in the edition.]

Its flesh is not fit for human food, because it is foul from the foolishness it has in itself. If anyone suffers from paralysis and has those changing afflictions which increase and diminish in him according to the moon, as in lunatics, observe a place where an ass is slaughtered or dies of itself, or where it rolls itself on the ground—that is, *walgert*. Immediately let the person lie there, either on grass or on earth, with a cloth spread over it; if he is very ill, use thin cowhide. Let him lie [Col. 1320C] there for a short time and sleep if he can; afterwards take his right hand and say: “Lazarus slept [Note: [Col. 1320D] John 11:43.], and rested, and rose; and as Christ raised him from stinking foulness, so rise from this dangerous plague and from the changing courses of fevers, in that union by which Christ Himself, sitting above this kind of thing, united it to Himself, foreshadowing that He would redeem man from his sins and raise him up.” Then, after a short time, do this three times in the same place on one day; on the second or third day do the same three times in the same place, and again three times on the second and third day, and he will be healed. [Note: [Col. 1320D] The edition omits “And if anyone suffers from paralysis … he will be healed,” replacing it with: “Milk from an ass benefits a leprous person if he drinks it often. If a person has scrofulous swellings in his body, frequent drinking of that milk prevents their increasing, because what is unclean expels what is unclean. If a worm eats a person’s flesh, powder an ass’s bones and place the powder on that spot, and the worm will die.”]

## CHAPTER X.—ON THE STAG

[Note: [Col. 1320D] Stag, *elaphus*.] [IV, III, 12].

The stag has sudden heat in itself and becomes cold less readily; it is more hot than cold, gentle, and eats clean fodder. Its flesh is good for healthy and sick people to eat. [Note: [Col. 1321D] The edition omits what follows down to “if anyone eats the somewhat warm, not boiling, flesh of the stag,” but inserts: “If a person suffers from paralysis in any limb, let him melt deer fat in a pan, add half as much goat fat and a little powdered myrrh, dip a hempen cloth in it, and bind it warm upon the limb affected by paralysis. Let him do this often, and the paralysis will cease.”]

When it senses that the branches of its antlers no longer grow, it knows that it is beginning to wither and become slow. It enters a certain river, draws into itself the *damph* (“vapour”) rising from the river, and upon coming out of the river eats herbs suitable for it on the bank. Then it seeks a place where it can find an *unck* (“serpent”). When it finds one, it bellows loudly, so that the serpent is greatly provoked and even emits its breath against the stag. But the stag raises its voice more and more, bellows, and gapes with its mouth; at last the serpent, as if angry through weariness, twists itself into the stag’s mouth and enters its belly. [Col. 1321B] Feeling this, the stag immediately hastens to a *queckbronnen* (“living spring”), known by it to have the property of removing every corruption and poison. It drinks from it exceedingly deeply, so that the serpent itself is drowned in that water within it—that is, *erdrincket*. Having done this, it seeks herbs which purge and eats them, and thus expels the serpent through its hind parts, as if with a drink; for unless the serpent passed out through it, it would die from its poison.

Then it begins to be ill; afterwards it seeks a valley where the best healing herbs grow, eats them there, and lies there resting for almost a month. Its antlers and hair also fall from it there, and then it begins to recover somewhat. Afterwards it again goes to the aforesaid *queckbronnen*, [Col. 1321C] drinks a little from it, so that anything foul left in it may again be gently purged; then it eats the aforementioned herbs again, begins to be healed, its antlers grow, and its hair comes forth again. Thereafter its flesh and everything in it are healthier than they had been before.

If anyone eats the somewhat warm, but not boiling, flesh of a stag, it purges his stomach and makes it light. Scrape some of its antler, add frankincense to what you have scraped, and burn them together by the fire. Its odor, through the strength which the antlers possess, drives away aerial spirits, restrains magical practices, and banishes *zauber* (“sorcery”) and harmful worms. Whoever eats its liver checks *gicht* (“gout”) in himself, purges his stomach, and makes it light.

## CHAPTER XI.—ON THE ROE DEER

[Note: [Col. 1321D] Stag, roe deer.] [IV, III, 13].

The roe deer (*Rech*) is temperate [“cold” in the edition], gentle, and has a clean nature. It gladly climbs mountains, seeks air neither too hot nor too cold but temperate, and on those mountains [Col. 1322A] seeks herbs which grow from that same air and eats them. [Note: [Col. 1322D] “And seeks air … eats them” is omitted in the edition.] Thus it has good and wholesome grazing. Its flesh is good for healthy and sick people.

A person afflicted by *wicht* should often eat of its liver, and it checks *wicht* in him. If anyone often eats its flesh, it purges *slim* (“slime/phlegm”) and foulness from him. Whoever suffers from *gicht* (“gout”) between the shoulder-blades should dry and keep its heart; when he has pain between the shoulder-blades, he should dip the heart in *baumoleo* (“tree oil”) and bind it upon the painful place, and he will be better.

If anyone has pain in the stomach, so that the stomach is *vireytergit* (“disordered/obstructed”), cold, or hardened, and cannot digest food eaten, let him take its *unslet* (“fat”), add one-third part oil from the fruit of *hagenbucha* (hornbeam) or beech, [Col. 1322B] mix these together, spread them on a hempen cloth, place this cloth upon his stomach, and wear it. However severe the stomach pain, he will be better. If he cannot obtain either oil, let him put the roe deer’s fat upon the aforesaid cloth as stated and bind it around his stomach. But for making this *eynplaster* (“plaster”), hornbeam oil is better than oil of *rutha* (“rue”). [Note: [Col. 1322D] The edition omits “If he cannot obtain either … oil of rue,” adding at the chapter’s end: “Let a person make from its hide a belt, gloves, and even a shirt, and wear the latter next to the skin like a linen shirt; no severe plague will harm him meanwhile.”]

## CHAPTER XII.—ON THE IBEX

[Note: [Col. 1322D] Goat, ibex.] [IV, III, 14].

The ibex (*Steynbock*) is more cold than hot, crooked in its manners, and gladly dwells in mountains, mist, *doffte*, and *dauwe* (“dew”). Its strength is so sudden that it often suffers from it. [Note: [Col. 1322D] “And gladly dwells in mountains … suffers from it” is omitted in the edition.] Its flesh is *slimechte* [“bruised/discolored”; *livosa*, “livid,” in the edition] [Col. 1322C] and weak; it is fit for neither healthy nor sick people to eat. Nevertheless, a healthy person can overcome it when eaten.

Make a belt and shoes from its skin, wear them, and they preserve health for your body. Dry its tail together with its skin and the flesh of the tail, carry it in your hand, and meanwhile you will not be led away by *zauber* (“sorcery”; *magica* in the edition) against your will. If you have taken poison in food or drink, immediately put the same tail in wine or any other drink for one hour, then drink it; the poison will pass through you either by vomiting or evacuation, and you will be healed. Make a knife-handle from its horn and keep it always either [Col. 1322D] in your hand or otherwise with you, and it confers health upon you. The other things found in it are of no use in medicine. [Note: [Col. 1322D] “The other things … medicine” is omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER XIII.—ON THE WISENT

[IV, III, 15].

The wisent is hot and has nearly the character of a stag, but is swifter and somewhat healthier than a stag. Its flesh is wholesome and good for people to eat. If [Col. 1323A] *schelmo* [“pestilence” in the edition] afflicts horses or asses, cattle and sheep, goats and pigs, or any other animals, scrape wisent horn into water and give it to them to drink for nine days; the *schelmo* will cease from them. The other things found in it are not wholly suitable for medicines. [Note: [Col. 1323B] “The other things … suitable” is omitted in the edition.]

## CHAPTER XIV.—ON THE OX

[Note: [Col. 1323B] Ox, bull.] [IV, III, 16].

The ox is cold and dry in complexion. Yet it is not hostile to a person in the matter of aerial spirits, nor can they perform many illusions in a place where an ox is, because the ox is clean; and for this reason it was often offered to God in sacrifice in former times. [Note: [Col. 1323B] “Yet it is not hostile … former times” is omitted in the edition.]

Because of the coldness it possesses, its flesh is not suitable for a cold person to eat; but for a hot person, hot by nature, it is good food because of the coldness in the flesh. If someone has a *schenden* affliction in his limbs and joints, and also suffers in his stomach, let him cook the feet—that is, the *geswil* and the fat of an ox’s feet—and eat enough of them; this checks the stabbing affliction in the joints and the stomach pain. Whoever often eats ox liver is strengthened by it because of its good nature; but the heart and lungs [Col. 1324A] are not very useful as food. You will find the same nature in a cow. The other things found in it are not of much use in medicines.

[Note: [Col. 1323B]

The edition differs in many respects:

“The ox is cold and dry in complexion; its flesh is not suitable for a cold person [Col. 1323C] to eat, but does not harm much one who is hot by nature. If anyone suffers from a fresh film on the eyes, let him apply fresh ox-gall to his eyes at night and bind it on so that it does not slip; do this for three days, but moderately. After three days, put fenugreek into rose oil and apply it to the eyes.

“If anyone has a stone within him, dry fresh gall of a young bull together with twice as much of its blood; add as much powdered saxifrage as there is gall, tie all together in a fine cloth, and put it in strong, good, pure wine. Let him drink from it fasting and after eating, but not during a meal.

“If anyone has a stabbing affliction in his limbs, let him cook the hardened soles of oxen’s feet and eat sufficiently and often from them; he will be healed. The same nature is found in a cow. If anyone has scrofulous swellings in his body, dry on a heated stone the uterus of a young cow which has not yet borne and which a bull has not yet approached in mating, then powder it and add powdered mole’s liver. Let him take this powder in a spoonful prepared from wheat flour for nine days or more, and the scrofulous swellings will disappear.

“Milk from cows [Col. 1323] [Concerning milk and butter, the manuscript codex treats separately above, in chapters 180 and 181 of Book I.] and other animals—namely sheep and goats—and all milk is more healthful in winter than in summer. Those who consume milk in summer, if they are not healthy, are somewhat harmed by it; but if they are sick and weak, let them consume a little. Butter pressed from milk has gentle warmth; cows’ butter, however, is better and more healthful than sheep’s or goat’s butter. A person who is consumptive and dry in body should eat any butter, and it heals and refreshes him inwardly. Butter is also good and healthful food for a healthy person whose flesh is moderate; but if he has fat flesh, let him eat it moderately, lest he become still fatter.

“Thus the sick and healthy, cold and hot alike, may eat moderately milk, butter, and cheeses made from cows’ milk. Cheese made from any milk has in itself a different nature according to the nature of the animals from whose milk it is made, and so adheres to the person eating it. A hard and dry cheese, when eaten, does not much harm a person [Col. 1324C] whose bodily flesh is sound, firm, and dry. Soft and fresh cheese does not harm one whose flesh is soft, fat, and moist.

“When you see oxen become ill either from harmful blood or severe labor, take shells lying on the sandy shore, reduce them to powder, mix this powder with *bathemia*, and give it to them to drink. For since oxen are somewhat aquatic, the shell of the sands, which comes from watery air and is also dry and hot, together with *bathemia*, which is hot and has manifold powers, is tempered in the mildness of water and diminishes the oxen’s illness. The powder of shells diminishes their bad humors; *bathemia* consumes them altogether. Meanwhile give them dry hay to eat, lest bad humors in them increase from green grass.”]

## CHAPTER XV.—ON THE SHEEP

[Note: [Col. 1324D] Goat, sheep.] [IV, III, 17].

The sheep, whether ram or ewe, is cold, though warmer than an ox; it is also moist and simple and has neither bitterness nor sharpness. Its flesh is good for healthy and sick people to eat. But one whose whole body is failing and whose veins are *virwolket* [“weakened and lukewarm” in the edition] should, if he wishes, often sip the juice of sheep’s flesh and the *suffe* [broth in the edition] in which it is cooked, and eat a little of the flesh. When he has recovered strength, he may eat enough of it if he wishes.

This flesh is good food in summer, [Col. 1324B] because the heat warms it; in winter, however, because it is cold, it is not suitable for food, since winter too is cold. [Note: [Col. 1324D] The edition omits “This flesh … is cold,” adding: “Let a person often and sufficiently eat its liver, and it diminishes phlegm in him and purges foulness from his stomach. One who coughs in the chest and has difficulty drawing and expelling breath without pain in the lungs should often eat of its lung, and he will be better in the chest. A woman whose uterus is cold and thin within, so as to be unable to conceive offspring, should cook the uterus of a ewe or cow—while they are still clean, not having been burdened and not being burdened with any fetus—with bacon and other rich meats, when she ought to be joined with her husband, and frequently consume such meats. If God wills, she will conceive so much more easily, because by God’s judgment it often happens that the power of generation is taken away from people.”]

The skins of sheep are good for human clothing, because they bring neither pride nor sexual desire nor plague upon a person, as the skins of certain other animals do. Hence God gave Adam a garment of sheepskins. [Note: [Col. 1324D] Genesis 3:21.]

If anyone suffers from quotidian, tertian, or quartan fevers, whatever their kind, [Col. 1325A] take a ram’s *scheper* [“fleece” in the edition], without the skin and shorn only from the ram. On the side which had been next to the ram’s skin, lightly sprinkle the fleece with sheep’s fat warmed by the fire, and warm them together again by the fire. When the *riddo* [perhaps a chill] is afflicting the person in coldness, immediately place the fleece upon his stomach and chest and around his shoulder-blades, so that he may be warmed and sleep thus. Do this whenever the *vicho* [perhaps “attack”] afflicts him, and he will soon be healed.

## CHAPTER XVI.—ON THE HE-GOAT

[Note: [Col. 1325C] Goat, he-goat.] [IV, III, 18].

The he-goat has a very sudden heat and unstable habits, and its flesh is good for healthy and sick people to eat; if eaten frequently, it heals broken and bruised internal organs, and heals and strengthens the eater’s stomach. A she-goat, if strong, may be eaten until August, whereas a he-goat is good to eat in August. But kids, whether male or female, are wholesome for a person to eat until autumn. A person with stomach pain should roast a he-goat’s liver and eat it frequently until the middle of August; it cleanses and heals his stomach like a good drink. [Moreover, a he-goat’s fat is good and healthful and is suited to many medicines. The she-goat has the same nature as the he-goat, except that the he-goat is stronger than the she-goat. If anyone has pain in the lung, let him drink goat’s milk frequently, and he will be cured. Addition of the edition.] The other things found in them are of no use for medicines.

## CHAPTER XVII.—ON THE PIG

[Note: [Col. 1325C] Sow and wild boar.] [IV, III, 19]

[Col. 1325C]

The pig is hot and has an ardent nature within it; it is muddy [*livosus*, “livid,” edition], since no cold purges it. It is also somewhat suppurating (*eyterecht*), and is always greedy for food; therefore it does not care what it eats, and at times eats unclean things. In its greed it has wolfish habits, since it tears other animals apart; and it has canine habits in that, like a dog, it gladly stays with people. But it is an unclean animal [Col. 1326A] [Note: [Col. 1325C] “And it is somewhat *eyterecht*—animal” omitted by the edition]. Therefore its flesh is not wholesome but twisted, and is good for neither healthy nor sick persons to eat, because it neither diminishes phlegm nor other illnesses in a person, but increases them, since its heat joins itself to human heat and arouses storms in a person’s character and actions that are evil [Note: [Col. 1325C] “For its heat—arouses” omitted by the edition].

But someone who is very ill, so that he is failing physically and is dried out, should, while ill, eat a little of young piglets in order to acquire heat from their heat. After he has recovered, he should eat no more of them, since they would again increase his illnesses [Note: [Col. 1325C] The edition adds much:

“But one who is leprous should avoid pork, [Col. 1325D] because it increases leprosy in him. And a person afflicted by paralytic gout should place lard in wine day and night so that it becomes soft, and grind it in the wine so that it yields its liquid. Then grind *aserum* [reading uncertain], and add its liquid to the lard’s juice, so that the liquid of *aserum* is one-sixth that of the lard’s. Add a little ash made from oat straw to the aforesaid liquid and make it all boil together. Then strain it through a cloth and make an ointment. Whenever he has pain from the aforesaid affliction, let him anoint himself with it, and he will fare better.

“But a person leprous with any kind of leprosy should boil fatty pork, already slaughtered and of moderate age, in water alone, without any other seasoning, so vigorously that the whole water is saturated with fat, though the meat should still be cooked so that it can afterwards be eaten. When it has been cooked, remove it from the water, and immediately put into the same water a sufficient quantity of hen dung; add also crow fat, twice as much raven fat, [Col. 1326C] and three times as much deer fat. Boil all these things in the aforesaid water. When this is done, reserve the fat floating on top. A leprous person, whatever form of leprosy afflicts him, should wash the site of the leprosy vigorously with the aforesaid water, and then anoint it with this ointment [Col. 1326D]. Continue this, without throwing away the water and using the same ointment, until he is cured. Mild leprosy will quickly be driven away in this manner; severe leprosy lasts for some time, but it will nevertheless be cleansed—unless God does not will this to happen, or death overtakes him.

“Again, if someone is leprous, let the dry skin of a pig, on the side where the flesh had been, be placed over the leprosy, so that it grows warm and sweats and the leprosy passes into this skin. After the sweating, remove the skin and immediately anoint the sick person with goat fat. Then wrap the same leprous person in another pigskin in the same manner, anoint him with goat fat, and do this a third time—and even further, until he is cured. And the wild pig,” etc., as in the manuscript codex.]

Further, a person whose body is almost failing should often eat cooked pig’s liver; it restores him—that is, revives and strengthens him. The wild pig [Col. 1326B] has the same nature, except that it is cleaner than the domestic pig. The other things found in it are not of much use for medicines.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—ON THE HARE

[Note: [Col. 1326D] Timid hare.] [IV, III, 20]

The hare is more hot than cold and has the gentleness and leaps of the roe deer (*Rech*). Its seeming at times to change sex means this: the male sometimes draws its genitals inward, so that it is then, as it were, female; at other times it does not. The female, near its navel, puts forth something like a bone, as though a *darm*, so that on this account it is thought to be male; yet it is in no way male. For neither will a male become female nor a female male: thus the male does not give birth, and the female will not possess male seed [Note: [Col. 1326D] “And it has its gentleness—will not possess” omitted by the edition].

Pour hare’s gall over a person’s leprosy, and anoint it frequently with this as well; the scabs of that leprosy will fall off and the person will be healed, because hare’s gall is very beneficial for this. The other things found in it are not of much medical use [Note: [Col. 1326D] “The other things—use” omitted by the edition].

## CHAPTER XIX.—ON THE WOLF

[Note: [Col. 1326D] Wolf (*Canis lupus*).] [IV, III, 21]

The wolf is very hot and has somewhat of the habits of aerial spirits and of the lion. Aerial spirits often delight in its nature and accompany it, and the wolf constantly lies in wait for a person; it would gladly tear him to pieces if it could, even if it were not suffering hunger. But, according to the lion’s nature, it recognizes and understands a person, and smells him from far away. When the wolf sees a person first, the aerial spirits accompanying it weaken the person in his powers, because the person does not then know that the wolf sees him. But when the person sees the wolf first, he holds God in his heart and, by that intention, drives away both the aerial spirits and the wolf with them [Note: [Col. 1327D] “It has the lion’s habits—drives away” omitted by the edition].

A person severely afflicted by gout (*gicht*) should take equal weights of leaves of the *gichtbaum* and *scalwurcz*, grind them in a mortar, add rather more wolf fat [*sanguine*, “blood,” edition], mix them together, and make an ointment. Let him anoint with it the place that hurts; then, on the second or third day, let him enter a steam bath [Col. 1327B]. The gout will sweat out of him with the ointment; he should wash himself vigorously in the same bath. He must not leave this ointment on his skin without washing it away, because it is so strong that gout can in no way remain in the place anointed.

And if someone is delirious and frenzied because of an illness in the head, shave the hair from his head and boil a wolf in water, discarding its skin and entrails. Wash the mad person’s head in the broth of that water, binding his eyes, ears, and mouth with a cloth, lest any of it enter his eyes, ears, or mouth; for if some of that broth entered his body, he would rage more violently, because it would be like poison to him. Do this for three days, and however severe the frenzy may be, he will recover his senses. If he will not permit you to bind his eyes, ears, and nostrils with a cloth [Col. 1327C], then dip a linen cloth in the same broth and moisten his head with that cloth while it is hot; leave it lying on his head for a short time [Note: [Col. 1327D] “But if he will not permit—leave it” omitted by the edition]. Do this for three days, and he will return to his senses. When he has improved, wash his head with warm wine, so that the grease is washed and removed from it.

In any house where there is a wolf’s skin, hair, or bones, people readily quarrel and fight, and aerial spirits readily roam there because of its extremely evil nature [Note: [Col. 1327D] “And fight—roam” omitted by the edition].

## CHAPTER XX.—ON THE DOG

[Note: [Col. 1327D] Domestic dog.] [IV, III, 22]

The dog is very hot and has something shared and natural with human character; therefore it senses and understands a person [Col. 1327D], loves him, gladly remains with him, and is faithful. Therefore the devil hates and abhors the dog because of the fidelity it has toward a person [Note: [Col. 1327D] “Therefore it senses a person—has” omitted by the edition].

The dog recognizes hatred, anger, and treachery in a person and often growls at him. If it knows that hatred and anger are in the house, it mutters and grinds its teeth quietly, both in the house and in itself—that is, it *grimet*. If a person also harbors treachery [*consilia perfidiae*, “treacherous designs,” edition], the dog grinds its teeth at him, *zanckelt*, even if that person loves the same dog [Col. 1328A], because it senses and understands this in the person. Likewise, if there is a thief in a house, or someone who has the intention of stealing, it mutters and *grimet* at him; it acts differently towards him than towards another person, follows him, tests his smell with its nostrils, and *stancket* after him. Thus a thief can be detected.

It also sometimes foreknows, according to its understanding, the events and outcomes of joy or sadness that are about to happen to a person or are already imminent, and gives voice and shows them accordingly. When good things are to come . . . it happily wags its tail; but if sadness is to come, it howls mournfully [Note: [Col. 1328D] “It also events—howls” omitted by the edition].

The warmth in its tongue brings healing to wounds and ulcers if it touches them with the warmth of its tongue [Col. 1328B] [Note: [Col. 1328D] The edition ends here]. But if shoes are made from its skin, they make the feet of sick people hurt because of the uncleanness it contains, since it has often been steeped in the unclean sweat of its flesh. Its flesh is of no use to a person; its liver and entrails are almost poisonous, and therefore its breath is harmful.

If a dog bites any bread or other food, or drinks from any drink, a person should neither eat nor drink what remains of these, because the dog may at some time have tasted food or drink that releases poison into those remnants. Therefore, if a person afterwards eats or drinks from them, he takes poison into himself. A dog has a soft and weak brain, which is sometimes affected by evil mists. The dog also at times smells a watery, foul vapor of the air [Col. 1328C], in which aerial spirits carry out their mockeries and certain evil whistles; as a result, it sometimes goes mad. The other things found in it are not of much use for medicine.

## CHAPTER XXI.—ON THE FOX

[Note: [Col. 1328D] Fox (*Canis vulpes*).] [IV, III, 23]

The fox is very hot and has something of the habits of the panther and something of the lion’s knowledge: it knows much by the nature of the lion’s knowledge, has diversity of habits by the nature of the panther, and knows a person to some extent. It sometimes feeds on unclean pasture. Because of the diversity within it [Note: [Col. 1328D] “It has something of the panther’s habits—it has” omitted by the edition], its flesh is unfit for human food. But its skin is wholesome, and the warmth of its skin is good for clothing.

A person [Col. 1328D] who has *orfimas* in his body should take fox fat and add to it a smaller amount of the fat of egg yolks. Let him often anoint the *orfimas* with these; then put *metra* into the same fats and heat them together in a small pan—that is, *sweysze* them. Bind this *metra* over the *orfime* with a cloth; when it has dried, *sweysze* another in the same manner and lay it over it. Do this with the *metra* for three days and three nights. Thereafter, discard the *metra* and anoint the same *orfimas* with the aforesaid fats mixed together [Col. 1329A], and they will disappear.

## CHAPTER XXII.—ON THE BEAVER

[Note: [Col. 1329D] *Castor fiber*.] [IV, III, 24]

The beaver is very hot and also has the air of water within it; it has a nature from earth and water, so that it could not always live on land without water, nor can it remain always in water without land. Since, when it dries out in its body, it runs to the water, takes liquid from it, and is strengthened; from the water its hair grows, and its skin is thick [Note: [Col. 1329D] “It also has the air of water—thick” omitted by the edition].

Its flesh is good for healthy and sick people to eat. A person who has pain in the spleen should often eat a cooked beaver’s tongue and will be healed in the spleen; or reduce the tongue to powder, put some of this powder in honey [Col. 1329B], and eat it with the honey, and he will fare better in the spleen [Note: [Col. 1329D] “Or reduce the tongue—fare better” omitted by the edition]. And anyone who has a fever should dry its liver and reduce it to powder, put a little of it in warm wine, and drink it often; he will fare better. [Moreover, its testicles, drunk in warm wine in the same way, restrain fever in a person. Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER XXIII.—ON THE OTTER

[Note: [Col. 1329D] A species of otter.—Absent from the edition.]

The otter is hot and has a clean nature, though it uses both clean and unclean pasture. Its head, tail, and flesh would be like poison to anyone who ate them. But the warmth of its skin is wholesome for a person. The other things found in it are of no medical use.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—ON THE MONKEY

[Note: [Col. 1329D] A species of monkey.—Absent from the edition.]

The monkey is hot; and because it somewhat resembles a human being, it always watches people in order to do what they do. It also has the habits of beasts, but fails in both its natures, so that it cannot act perfectly either according to human beings or according to beasts; therefore it is unstable. When it sometimes sees a bird flying, it raises itself, leaps, and attempts to fly; when it cannot accomplish what it wishes, it immediately becomes angry. Since it somewhat resembles a human being, it also has monthly periods according to the moon; and because it is unstable and weak in both natures, it is of no medical use.

## CHAPTER XXV.—ON THE *MERKACZA*

[Note: [Col. 1329D] A species of monkey.—Absent from the edition.]

The *merkacza* is more cold than hot, and is of air and water, so that it can sometimes move about in water. It also has something of the nature of the wolf and of the cat. But it does not lick earth or snakes. The *merkacza* has a certain poison within itself, from which it becomes ill; it also then spits it out and, disdaining it, hides it beneath the earth [Col. 1330A], because it knows that it is evil. Likewise, it hides the excrement which comes from it, since, if a person touched what the *merkacza* spits out in this way, it would be poison; indeed certain snakes and certain harmful worms are very often born from it.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—ON THE CAT

[Note: [Col. 1329D] Cat (*Felis catus*).—Absent from the edition.]

The cat is more cold than hot, draws bad humors to itself, does not abhor aerial spirits, nor do they abhor it, and has some natural affinity with the toad and snake. For in the strong and summer months, when the heat is greatest, the cat is dry and cold; it then thirsts so that it licks either toads (*creden*) or snakes, in order to strengthen its own moisture with their liquid, so that it may thereby have *labezocht* [reading uncertain] [Col. 1330B]. Otherwise it could not live but would perish—just as a person gladly tastes salt in order thereby to have a good flavor.

The liquid it receives from these is almost like poison within it, so that its brain and all its flesh are poisonous. It does not gladly remain with people except with the person who feeds it. At the time when it licks toads and a snake, its heat is harmful and poisonous to a person. When it carries kittens in itself, its heat stirs a person to lust; at another time its heat does not harm a healthy person.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—ON THE LYNX

[Note: [Col. 1329D] Cat; lynx. Compare above, IV, 19.] [IV, III, 25]

The lynx is hot and follows its own will, doing what it wishes. It rejoices in beautiful, bright summer air and sunlight, and also in fair weather and snow in winter [Col. 1330C]. But it has almost no constancy, except that it behaves according to the tempering of the weather. Since it follows its own will, its eyes shine like stars at night.

If pestilence (*schelmo*) devastates and kills horses, asses, oxen, and pigs, mix lynx blood with water and give it to them to drink once daily for three days if you see that they are sick; they will immediately recover. But if the aforesaid animals are not sick, this blood, mixed as stated, must not be given them to drink, lest they be harmed by it when the pestilence finds no subjects in which to display its force. Do not give it to sheep and goats to drink even if they are sick, because it would be too strong for them because of their weakness, since they are weak livestock. The other things found in it, apart from *ligurium*, are not of much medical use [Note: [Col. 1329D] Edition: “The lynx is hot; it desires to appear glorious, follows its own will, and has a strong nature. Therefore its eyes shine like the star that illuminates the night. If pestilence devastates and kills horses, asses, oxen, and pigs, lynx blood should be mixed with water and given them to drink once daily for three days, and they will immediately recover. It should also be given to sheep and goats to drink if they are ill. But *ligurium* is produced from this animal’s urine.”]

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—ON THE BADGER

[Note: [Col. 1330D] Badger (*Ursus meles*).] [IV, III, 26]

The badger is hot and has quiet habits, but it is nevertheless *arg* and not *frevele* [uncertain German terms]. It has strengths almost as powerful as a lion’s [Col. 1331A], but considers the power it has as nothing, except that it sometimes suddenly displays it and quickly ceases again. If it always displayed it, it would almost equal the strength of a lion. Yet it tires of displaying its powers, unless it sometimes does so from delight and exultation.

Take its heart and boil it very vigorously in water until it becomes *trab* [reading uncertain]. Then add fat from the same beast, and also *gichtbaum*, with less *stalwurtz* than *gichtbaum*. Boil these together in the aforesaid water, and make an ointment which is excellent against gout, against loosened limbs at the joints, and against limbs crushed by gout. A person who suffers these things should anoint with it the places in his limbs that hurt, and he will be healed.

Further, a person with pain in the head [Col. 1331B] should anoint his neck, the nape of his neck, temples, and forehead with the same ointment. Or someone with pain in the side or back should anoint himself there with it, and will fare better through the aforesaid power. Likewise, someone who has weak, black, spotted flesh on his body should anoint himself there with the same ointment, and his flesh will become clean, because it restrains every illness in a person.

There is also great power in its skin: make a belt from it and gird yourself with it against your bare skin, and every affliction in you will cease, just as a great storm is checked by good weather and calm air; meanwhile, dangerous disease will not seize you. Make shoes and leggings from the same skin and wear them, and you will be healthy in your feet and legs [Note: [Col. 1331D] Edition: “The *helus* is hot and has a quiet nature, but is nevertheless somewhat wicked. Let a person boil its liver in water so vigorously that it is entirely broken down; then add fat from the same animal, also *githboum*, and a smaller quantity of southernwood; boil them together in the aforesaid water and make an ointment. This is excellent against paralysis and loosened limbs at the joints. Anyone with weak, black, spotted flesh should anoint himself with this ointment, and his flesh will become clean. Let a person also make leggings from badger skin and wear them, [Col. 1332D] and it is healthful for him.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX.—ON THE *ILLEDISO*

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Polecat (*Mustela putorius*).—Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1331C]

The *illediso* is cold and foul-smelling, has the habits of a thief and the nature of a wolf, and often eats unclean things. Its skin is not wholesome for human clothing, because it brings cold to a person. The other things found in it are also unsuitable for medicines.

## CHAPTER XXX.—ON THE HEDGEHOG

[Note: [Col. 1332D] European hedgehog.] [IV, III, 27, 28]

The hedgehog, namely *swinegel*, is cold and of an unclean nature; it eats wild fruits and *hecbere* [Note: [Col. 1332D] “Wild fruits—it eats” omitted by the edition]. It somewhat resembles a pig, but the uncleanness which ought to be in its flesh rises into its spines; therefore it is cleaner than a pig [Note: [Col. 1332D] What follows until “the hedgehog that imitates the dog” is omitted by the edition]. For, just as spines injure a human hand, so pig flesh diminishes human [Col. 1331D] cleanliness and health.

But someone healthy in body who wishes to eat hedgehog should boil it in water like a hare, powder equal weights of cinnamon, *bertram*, and *bibenella*, warm these powders together in wine, and, after the cooked hedgehog has been removed from the pot, pour this wine with its powders over it, as pepper is usually poured over meat. Let him eat it thus: it will not harm him, but will make him strong and maintain his health.

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Here the edition begins another chapter under the heading: “On the dog-hedgehog.”]

The hedgehog, namely that which imitates a dog, this *egel* is cold and has something of the dog’s nature. It sometimes eats earth, and both the clean and unclean things in it rise into its spines. Its flesh is unfit for human food, just as dog flesh is. If *orfimas* have burst in someone, let him discard this hedgehog’s entrails and reduce all the remaining flesh to powder. Let him frequently put this powder into the burst *orfimas*, and they will dry up. The other things found in it are of no medical use [Col. 1332B].

## CHAPTER XXXI.—ON THE SQUIRREL

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Common squirrel.] [IV, III, 29]

The squirrel [*spiriolus*, edition] is hot and has in itself the nature of beasts and birds; from birds it is windy [Note: [Col. 1332D] “It has the nature of beasts and birds—it is windy” omitted by the edition]. Its skin is good for human clothing.

If terrible gout lies in the joints of a person’s limbs, so that the limbs seem to be contracting and dislocating, take a squirrel, discard its head and entrails, remove its skin, and roast the remaining body over a fire. While it is roasting, anoint it lightly on top with bear fat, so that fat runs from it. After it has been roasted, take the fat that has run from it, put it in a cloth, squeeze through that cloth all the liquid and fat in it, add some of the aforesaid fat [Col. 1332C], and often anoint with it the limbs in which you suffer from gout; you will be healed.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—ON THE HAMSTER

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Marmot-hamster (*Marmota Cricetus*).] [IV, III, 30]

The hamster is cold and sharp, somewhat resembles a bear, is somewhat of a clean nature, and its skin is good for clothing [Note: [Col. 1332D] “It is sharp—it is good” omitted by the edition].

A person who has *orfime* and *druse* in his body should powder a hamster’s liver and either eat this powder with bread or drink it in broth; the *orfime* and *druse* will disappear from this more effectively than from mole flesh. If someone suffers from gout between his shoulder blades, dry out a hamster’s right shoulder together with its right foot, bind these between his shoulder blades, and he will fare better.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—ON THE MARTEN

[Note: [Col. 1332D] Pine marten (*Mustela martes*).] [IV, III, 31]

[Col. 1332D]

The wild marten [*martarus*, edition] is hot and has gentle habits; therefore many live together, as though they shared a common life. But it has an evil sweat in its flesh [Col. 1333A], which makes its flesh unsuitable for human food. This sweat remains in the flesh and does not pass through its skin [Note: [Col. 1333D] “Therefore many live together—does not pass through” omitted by the edition]. Therefore its skin is good and wholesome for human clothing.

If a person has *orfime* in his body, skin a wild marten and melt the fat in it in a small pan. Discard its head and entrails; boil the remaining body in a little water and add the fat which can then be obtained from it to the former fat. Add also, in a smaller amount, fat from egg yolks; mix them and make an ointment. Anoint *orfime* with it before they rupture and they will disappear; or, if they have ruptured, anoint around them and they will be healed [Note: [Col. 1333D] “Or, if they have ruptured—they will be healed” omitted by the edition].

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—ON THE WATER MARTEN

[IV, III, 32]

[Col. 1333B]

The water marten is cold, lives in little hollows beside waters, and is sharper than the wild marten; but the wild marten’s skin is better than this one’s [Note: [Col. 1333D] “It lives beside waters—this one’s” omitted by the edition]. Make an ointment from its fat and egg-yolk fat, as was said above for the wild marten. If someone suffers from gout, anoint him with it; it restrains the gout, because it is of a cold nature.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—ON THE SABLE

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Sable (*Mustela zibellina*).—Absent from the edition.]

The sable is hot and somewhat resembles the squirrel’s nature, but is cleaner and gentler than the squirrel. Yet its skin is not good for human clothing, because, when it grows warm on a person, it causes evil sweat. The things found in it are of no medical use [Col. 1333C], because it is weak.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—ON THE ERMINE

[Note: [Col. 1333D] Ermine (*Mustela erminea*).—Absent from the edition.]

The ermine is cold and somewhat resembles the cat’s nature. It does not have clean flesh, because it is foamy and livid, like poison. When it emits foam, it often also emits short hairs. Its skin is not good for human clothing, because it is cold. The things found in it are not much suited to medicines, because its flesh is somewhat poisonous.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—ON THE MOLE

[Note: [Col. 1333D] European mole.] [IV, III, 33]

The mole is cold and likes to dwell in rich, muddy earth; it avoids lean soil and throws out earth that is bad, perverse, and useless [Note: [Col. 1334D] “It dwells in rich earth—throws out” omitted by the edition]. [Col. 1333D] It remains in soil that is good and wholesome; it does not see because it does not move about in the air, but it has great inward knowledge, smells and understands where it ought to go, and eats earth. Its flesh is unfit for human food, since it is nourished on moisture; no one should eat it as a medicine [Note: [Col. 1334D] “It does not see—eat it” omitted by the edition].

For a person who is rotting inwardly in his body, or has *orfime* in his body, should boil a mole in water and eat it, or powder it and eat this powder in whatever manner he can; he will be sound internally, and his *orfime*, if they have not yet burst—[the source syntax is defective]—because just as the mole casts out bad earth, so it expels the inward corruption that is in a person’s body. He should also eat the mole’s liver with the rest of its body, because it removes corruption from his body; but he should not eat its heart or lungs.

[One afflicted by falling sickness should powder mole’s blood, the bill of a female duck, and the claws of a female goose, so that the duck-bill powder is twice as much as the goose-claw powder, and the mole’s blood is twice as much as the duck-bill powder. Bind these things together in a cloth and place them for three days where a mole has freshly thrown up earth. Afterwards, remove them and place them where there is ice, so that they freeze. [Col. 1334B] Remove them again and dry them in the sun. Then take as much liver as can be obtained from every edible animal and bird, make little cakes from these with a little fine wheat flour, add a smaller quantity of the aforesaid powder and a little cumin, and eat them.

“The person suffering from the aforesaid illness should eat the little cakes for five days; if he has not yet recovered, use them for another five days; if they still do no good, repeat this seven times, each time for five days. Meanwhile he should eat bread and kid meat cooked with celery and parsley; he may also eat lamb. But during this time he should avoid pork, beef, eel, cheese, eggs, raw fruit, and raw vegetables. Let him drink sweet wine mixed with water, and beer.” Addition of the edition.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—ON THE WEASEL

[Note: [Col. 1334D] Common weasel. Compare Pliny, *Natural History* VIII, 40.] [IV, III, 34]

The weasel [*mustela*, edition] is hot [Note: [Col. 1334D] What follows, as far as “and likewise dry its heart,” is omitted by the edition]. In its swiftness it has something of the strength of the griffin when it raises its feathers; it has corruption in an insensible nature, so that it knows a certain little herb in which there is life-giving health. Thus, if it sees that its young or another weasel is sick, it quickly seeks this herb, which is small and slender, digs for it in the earth, and when it has found it, breathes upon it and urinates over it. It thus mingles its own power with the herb’s power, waits a short time until the little herb is thoroughly and fully drenched in its urine, then seizes it in its mouth [Col. 1334D] and puts it into the mouth of the weasel that is dying, whose vital breath is already in its throat. That weasel will be healed, rise, and go away.

This little herb is unknown to people and other animals, because, if people or animals knew it, their breath and urine would not avail to drench it; for the herb does not by itself possess life-giving healing power, unless it receives such powers from the weasel’s breath and urine. The weasel also always eats such good and powerful [Col. 1335A] herbs that scarcely any sickness can come upon it. Its flesh is unfit for human food, because it would be weak in the stomach.

Strip off the weasel’s skin and dry it. Then hold it over balsam, but do not let it become wet with the balsam; let it take in its smell. Or, if you do not have balsam, place it beside musk so that it takes in its smell. Then frequently place this skin against your eyes and nostrils, and it will preserve health in them.

Likewise dry its heart, work it into thin wax, and, when you have pain in the head, place that wax with the heart in your ear for a short time, so that its warmth may enter your head and you will fare better in the head. Or, if you are becoming deaf in either ear [Col. 1335B], put the same wax with the same heart into that ear so that its warmth touches the ear inside, and you will recover hearing.

Cut off its head and dry the rest of its body, divided into two pieces, either in the sun or by the fire. Then sew the pieces separately into a belt made from any hide, so that one piece is placed at your navel and one piece at each of your sides. Always gird yourself with this belt against your bare skin; it will strengthen you and make you sound and robust, so that gout will not trouble you in the meantime.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—ON THE MOUSE

[Note: [Col. 1335D] A species of mouse.] [IV, III, 35]

The mouse is hot and has lurking habits [“and devilish arts,” addition of the edition], because it always flees. Therefore [Col. 1335C] its flesh too is harmful to a person, though it is not of much use for medicines [Note: [Col. 1335D] “Because it always flees—is of use” omitted by the edition].

Nevertheless, if someone has falling sickness and falls to the ground, after he rises put a mouse in a small vessel and give the water itself to the person to drink; wash his forehead and feet with that water. Do this as often as he falls, and he will be cured. For, because the mouse flees everything, it also drives away falling sickness itself.

When a mouse is about to give birth, it is distressed and has difficulty delivering. In pain it goes to a bank of water and looks there for very small pebbles. It swallows as many as it can hold in its throat, runs to its hole, spits them out there, breathes on them, lies upon them, and warms them; it then gives birth immediately. After it has given birth, it hates them and throws them away with its feet [Col. 1335D]—that is, *uszschirrit*—then lies upon its young and warms them.

If someone could find these little stones within the same month after the mouse had thrown them away, and bind them over the navel of a pregnant woman who is already in labour and cannot give birth, she would give birth immediately; after she had delivered, they should be removed at once.

Further, if someone has *ridden*, take a mouse and strike it slightly so that it cannot escape. Before it dies [Col. 1336A], bind the back of that mouse between the shoulder blades of the person when the *riddo* is already troubling him, and let it die there between his shoulder blades. That person will be cured and it will no longer attack him.

## CHAPTER XL.—ON THE *LIRA*

[Note: [Col. 1335D] Absent from the edition.]

The *lira* is also hot and has the same nature as another mouse, except that it is wilder and stronger than mice. It is useful against the same dangers as the other mouse, as stated above.

## CHAPTER XLI.—ON THE *SPICZMO*

[Note: [Col. 1335D] *Sorex araneus*.—Absent from the edition.]

Spiczmus has almost the same nature as the mole, except that the spiczmus can remain more beneath the earth and more in the air than the mole, and therefore does not remain wholly beneath the earth. Its medicinal properties are of no use.

### CHAPTER XLII.—ON THE FLEA  
[Note: [Col. 1335D] *Pulex irritans*] [IV, III, 37].

[Col. 1336B]

The flea is warm and grows from the dust of the earth. In winter, when the earth is moist and warm within, fleas lie in the earth and hide themselves in it. But when in summer the surface of the earth is dried by heat, they come forth from the earth, attack people, and trouble them. Therefore take earth, and not dust of earth [Note: [Col. 1335D] “And in winter—earth” is omitted in the edition. The remainder is explained thus at [Col. 1336D]: “Let a person heat a potter’s shard very thoroughly and scatter it in his bed; and when the fleas sense its dryness, they flee.”], and heat it thoroughly in a potter’s vessel so that it is dried out and no moisture remains in it. Scatter that earth in your bed; when the fleas sense its dryness, they cannot endure it, but flee and perish. Thus a person may have relief from them.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—ON THE ANT  
[Note: [Col. 1336D] Species of ant.] [IV, III, 36].

The ant is warm and grows from that moisture which brings forth aromatic plants; it also produces, as it were, eggs like those of birds within its nature. [Note: [Col. 1336D] “And grows from that moisture—within its nature” is omitted in the edition.] A person who has much phlegm in his head, chest, and stomach should take a heap—that is, a *huffen*, or mound—of ants, together with the ants themselves, boil it in water, pour that water over a heated stone, and draw its steam into his nostrils and mouth ten or five times. The phlegm in him will be diminished.

Likewise, one who has an excess of bad humours—that is, *gicht*—should take a mound of ants with the ants themselves, boil them in water, and prepare a bath from it. He should enter the bath and keep his whole body in it, leaving only his head exposed, covered with a little cloth soaked in the same water. For if his head touched the bath [Col. 1336D] and received the strength of that water, it would easily hurt. Let him do this often, and the *gicht* will cease.

And whoever has leprosy, of whatever sort, should take the earth where an ant-hill is, taking care to observe how much that earth has been moistened by the ants themselves. He should put it among burning beech ashes, so that it may be kindled by the ashes, with the earth exceeding the ashes in quantity. Let hot water pass nine times through this hot earth as through lye. Then mix into it goat’s fat, and a little more old pig’s lard; put these together in the aforementioned lye-water, and after they have congealed in it, remove them from the water. Then add to this fat powder of *habichswamp* [the edition: *habersuam*], and less powder of *meter* than of violet; make an ointment, and anoint the leprous place with this ointment for nine months, or longer, beside a fire. He will be cured, unless that leprosy is his death, or unless God does not will him to be cured.

When he is anointed with this ointment, he must take care not to approach another person or any pig, lest the strong vapour of leprosy issuing from him infect them; for they would then easily contract leprosy from him. [Note: [Col. 1337D] “When he is anointed with this ointment—contract leprosy from him” is omitted in the edition.]

[Col. 1337B] A person who has swellings and *orfimas* should spread ants’ eggs upon a green oak leaf and spread hen-dung upon the same leaf over the eggs. He should then apply it warm, often, to the swellings or to the aforementioned scrofulous *orfime*, and they will disappear.

Likewise, if someone is angry, oppressed in mind, or sad, he should take young ants, while their eggs are still attached to them, with a little *bache* [*buthe*?; the edition reads “with their little nests”]—that is, with the little lump [Col. 1338A] in which they lie—and bind these in a linen cloth. Afterwards, whenever he feels burdened in mind, let him unbind the cloth containing these ants and place them upon his heart until he sweats from them. He will have a pleasant disposition, be cheerful, and gain good understanding in the matters with which he is then occupied.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—ON HELIM  
[Note: [Col. 1337D] Edition IV, III, 9. Absent from the manuscript, as is the following chapter, “On Dromeda.”]

Helim is warm, very strong, and bold; because of its strength, its flesh is unfit for human food. Let its liver be pulverized and mixed with bear’s lard or cow’s butter. A person who is frenzied, or whose head is afflicted by paralysis, should be anointed with it often, and will fare better.

### CHAPTER XLV.—ON DROMEDA  
[Note: [Col. 1337D] Edition IV, III, 9, repeated.]

[Col. 1338B]

Dromeda possesses the heat of fire, the moderation of water, the strength of a lion, and the swiftness of flight of strong and great birds. If a person or another animal ate its flesh, the strength of fire and the strength of swiftness within it would destroy all the powers of the eater. But if anyone possesses some of its skin or the nails of its feet, magic and phantoms flee from him.

[Col. 1337] HERE ENDS THE SIXTH (SEVENTH) BOOK.

THE SEVENTH (EIGHTH) BOOK BEGINS. PREFACE.  
[Note: [Col. 1338D] Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1337]

[Col. 1337C] From the beginning God created every creature good. [Note: [Col. 1338D] Mark 10:6.] But after the devil deceived man through the serpent, so that he was cast out of Paradise, creatures, insofar as they heed the divine will, were changed for the worse together with man, for the sake of vengeance. Thus the broods of cruel and poisonous worms arose for this vengeance, both to show by their deadly cruelty that infernal punishments exist and, by instilling in man fear of hell, to kill him with their poison by divine permission—although before man’s fall they had possessed nothing deadly, but only pleasant sap within themselves.

Moreover, when the earth was defiled by the shedding of Abel’s blood, [Note: [Col. 1338D] Genesis 4:2.] immediately a new fire, by which homicide might be punished, blazed up in hell. Immediately too, by the divine will, [Col. 1337D] a certain mist, boiling up from hell, spread over the earth and infused the earth with a most evil moisture, so that certain very evil, poisonous, and deadly worms, being born from the earth, often boiled forth, in order that human flesh might be punished by them because man had killed human flesh.

And later, when people were destroyed by divine vengeance in the flood [Note: [Col. 1338D] Luke 17:27.] of waters, those same worms, which could not live in water, were drowned in it. But when their bodies had been scattered over the whole earth by the flooding waters, and afterwards, when the flood had ceased, [Note: [Col. 1338D] Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 416.] the corpses of those worms, full of poison, had decayed, other worms of the same kind arose from that very decay and were thus scattered over the whole earth.

Some worms kill both people and animals with their poisons; others kill people only. For worms that in their nature somewhat resemble diabolical arts [Col. 1338D] kill both other animals and people with their poisons. But those which do not imitate diabolical arts, and therefore have somewhat weaker poisons within them, sometimes inflict upon people many illnesses and dangers, even death, by their poisons, [Col. 1339A] but cannot kill other animals. [Col. 1340A]
