## EIGHTH BOOK

[Col. 1339]

### CHAPTER I.—ON THE DRAGON  
[IV, III, 38].

[Col. 1339B]

The dragon [Note: [Col. 1339D] On medieval dragons see Jules de Saint-Genois, in *Messager belge*, 1840, p. 58.] has in itself a certain dry and alien heat and a certain fiery excess, though its flesh is not fiery within. But its breath is so strong and sharp that when it emits it, it immediately kindles, like fire struck from a stone. It hates mankind intensely and has in itself, as it were, a certain nature and diabolical arts. Hence, when it sometimes emits its breath, aerial spirits are sometimes stirred by the issuing of that breath and agitate the air.

Everything in its flesh and bones is contrary to human remedies, except its fat. For when the dragon emits its breath, its blood dries up and is not fluid; but when it holds its breath inwardly, its blood is moist [Col. 1339C] and flows. Therefore no medicine is found even in its blood. [Note: [Col. 1339D] “And a certain fiery excess—no medicine is found in its blood” is omitted in the edition, which adds: “For a person whose eyes are dim should put dragon’s blood into water for a short time, and, after removing the blood, lightly anoint the eyelids and eyelashes with that water at night, taking care not to touch the inner eye. Let him do this only three times in a month, and it will drive away their dimness.”]

A person who has a stone should take dragon’s blood and put it in a moist place so that it becomes slightly damp. He should then put that blood in a small quantity of pure water for a short time, namely until the water takes some heat from it. Having removed the blood, he should drink a little of that water fasting, and immediately eat some food. Let him use the blood and water moderately in this way for nine days; by the strength of that blood, the stone in him will be broken, and he will be freed.

No person should eat or drink its pure, unmixed blood, for if anyone did so, he would immediately die. [Note: [Col. 1340D] “No person—would immediately die” is omitted in the edition.]

### CHAPTER II.—ON A CERTAIN SERPENT  
[Note: [Col. 1340D] Absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1339D]

There is a kind of serpent which is very warm and can dwell both in earth and in water, and which also possesses diabolical arts in its ambushes against humankind. This kind of serpent is hostile to man, emits its breaths against him, and is full of deadly poison. Indeed, because of the poison within it, its skin thickens and contracts into wrinkles; and its outer skin is also split by the heat of the sun. When it feels this, as if burdened by sores, it seeks a narrow hole in a rock and rubs itself against it until it casts off those foams. It then becomes somewhat less harsh than it had been when it was oppressed by those foams.

When it has cast off the foams, its skin becomes fine and shining, as though new. The serpent rejoices greatly in this, and then is somewhat less harsh also in its poison and its ambushes. A person who finds it at that time [Col. 1340C] should kill it, carefully remove its heart, dry it in the sun, and seal it for preservation in some thin metal. Whenever he is afterwards oppressed by great sadness or distress, he should hold it in his right hand and will become cheerful. As long as he holds it in his hand, he cannot be harmed inwardly by any poison, for if in the meantime he eats or drinks poison, it will pass from him through sweat, vomiting, or excretion.

But its liver, and the other things in that serpent, are deadly and suit no human remedy.

There is another kind of serpent, also warm, which dwells only in the earth, not in water. Its poison harms a person somewhat less if he touches or tastes it, because it is somewhat weak. This kind of serpent sometimes lives with people, in human houses or dry places, and lays fewer ambushes for them. But when it sees that a person wishes to strike it, it puts out its tongue and moves him to plead, because it is of the kind that deceived Adam; therefore it often seeks human dwellings. [Col. 1340D] [Col. 1341A]

### CHAPTER III.—ON BLINTSLEICH  
[Note: [Col. 1341D] Slow-worm, *Anguis fragilis*.—Absent from the edition.]

Blintsleich is cold. While alive, it does not harm people, but is of no use either for utility or medicine. After it is dead, however, people are harmed by its poison if they touch or taste it.

### CHAPTER IV.—ON CREDDA  
[Note: [Col. 1341D] Toad, *Rana bufo*.] [IV, III, 39].

Credda [the edition: *Rubeta*, “toad”] has in part great heat and in part great harshness, like a dangerous storm when lightning, thunder, and hail come forth. In its greenness it possesses something like a diabolical art, seeks its abode in the earth and beneath [Col. 1341B] the earth, and therefore keeps some company with humankind, sometimes being with people to their danger. [Note: [Col. 1341D] “Like a dangerous storm—being with people” is omitted in the edition.]

A person who has *orfimas* should take a toad’s liver [the edition: “the liver of a *Rubeta*”], wrap it in moist earth, and bury it with that moist earth in any other earth for nine days. On the tenth day, he should throw away the liver, take the moist earth in which it was wrapped, heat it in a potter’s vessel, and apply it to unbroken *orfime* for three days. They will undoubtedly disappear, unless it is that person’s death or God does not will it. [Note: [Col. 1341D] “Unless it is—does not will it” is omitted in the edition.]

If the *orfime* have burst, he should heat the same earth mentioned above at the fire and put it into an old linen cloth which has at some time received human sweat. But first he should place a spider’s web on the ulcers, then lay over it the same cloth with the hot earth sewn into it. When it loses its heat, he should heat it again and lay it on; let him do this twice or three times a day for three nights, and the *orfime* will dry up. [Note: [Col. 1341D] The edition ends here.]

That same earth should indeed be placed in a linen cloth because of the cleanliness of linen: linen draws bruising to itself, whereas *lina* [so written] does not do so. It should be put in an old cloth because that cloth ought to be more thoroughly imbued with human sweat than a new one. Human sweat must be in it so that decaying sores may flee that sweat, which is itself foul-smelling; for what is evil often drives away evil.

### CHAPTER V.—ON FROSCH  
[Note: [Col. 1341D] Edible frog, *Rana esculenta*.—Absent from the editions, as are the following nos. VI–VIII.]

[Col. 1341D] Frosch is cold and somewhat watery, and therefore does not have powers as harmful as those of the toad. If someone is afflicted by *gicht* in any part of his body except the head, let him take a frosch and suffocate it upon a little plant or under some other herb. Immediately lay a warm cloth upon the limb in [Col. 1342A] which the *gicht* rages, and place the frosch, now dying, upon the same cloth for a short while. The *gicht* in that place will cease for a year or half a year.

### CHAPTER VI.—ON LAUBFROSCH  
[Note: [Col. 1341D] Tree frog, *Rana arborea*.]

Laubfrosch is more warm than cold and grows from that air through which trees bring forth their greenery and flowers. When they bring forth their greenery and flowers, aerial spirits lie in wait for people more at that time than at another, because then human minds rise more readily to the vanity of playing and laughing, just as the greenery of trees grows then. At that time people also perform idolatry and many vanities with this worm through diabolical arts.

But if anyone wishes to ensnare it, so that diabolical arts may not be performed through it, [Col. 1342B] he should throw it into a *queckbronen* so that it becomes wet; thereafter no one will be able to accomplish anything diabolical with it. It is of no use for remedies.

### CHAPTER VII.—ON HARUMNA

Harumna is cold, and the heats it has in itself are bruising and poison. But that poison is not so strong that a person is much harmed by it. There is no medicine in it.

### CHAPTER VIII.—ON MOLL  
[Note: [Col. 1341D] *Molc*, *Molch*? A kind of lizard.]

Moll is more warm than cold, but its heat quickly becomes cold, and its poison is deadly. Yet the moll itself, while it lives, does not greatly harm people by itself; rather, people are killed by its poison if they taste it. The other things in it [Col. 1342C] are of no use for remedies.

### CHAPTER IX.—ON THE LIZARD  
[Note: [Col. 1341D] A kind of lizard.] [IV, III, 40].

The lizard is warm and dry, but its poison is somewhat weak and not very harmful to people. Yet the lizard is harsh and sharp in its nature. The things in it are of no use for remedies. [Note: [Col. 1341D] Edition: “The lizard is warm and dry. But a person who has foul scab on his head should burn a lizard to powder, put this powder in pure, good wine, dip old bacon in this wine, and anoint the scab of the head with it; he will be cured.”]

### CHAPTER X.—ON THE SPIDER  
[IV, III, 41].

The spider is more warm than cold and is almost as dangerous in its poison as the scorpion, except that the scorpion has a large, fat heart, while the spider has a small, weak heart. [Note: [Col. 1342D] “Except—heart” is omitted in the edition, which continues: “While it lies in its little cave, it is fierce in its ambushes against both people and other animals. The spider’s web itself is not of much use, except that it is found to be, as it were, soothing upon certain human ulcers.”] If the spider’s poison touches human flesh outwardly, it is dangerous to the person. If someone eats or drinks its poison, he will die or scarcely escape death.

### CHAPTER XI.—ON THE VIPER

[Col. 1342D]

The viper is hot like fire, and everything in it is deadly. It allows nothing near it to live which it can overcome. It is of such great malice [Col. 1343A] that a viper even flees from another viper until the time when its nature requires it to conceive.

In a region where a viper lives, if a person finds a dead viper—for he cannot have it alive—let him kindle a great fire of strong wood in a secluded place where no people are, and throw the dead viper into that fire. [Note: [Col. 1343D] Acts 28:5.] Then let him leave that place quickly, lest its poison or evil vapour touch him. After it has been reduced to ashes, he should leave behind whatever remains of it; but take its ashes and the ashes of the coals by which it was burned, and preserve them in a linen cloth.

Then, if any person has a swelling in his body, lay that same cloth with its ashes upon the swelling, and the swelling will immediately subside.

### CHAPTER XII.—ON THE BASILISK

[Col. 1343B]

The basilisk is born from certain worms which have something of diabolical arts in themselves, namely the toad. For when a toad is at times gravid and impregnated so as to bring forth its young, if it then sees an egg of a serpent or a hen, it loves it, spreads itself over it, and broods it until it gives birth to the young it had naturally conceived. Once it has produced them, they immediately die. Seeing them dead, it lays itself again upon that egg and broods it until offspring begin to live in that egg.

Immediately a certain force from the diabolical art of the ancient serpent [Note: [Col. 1343D] Revelation 12:9.] touches it—a force which also rests in Antichrist—[Col. 1343C] so that, just as Antichrist resists all heavenly beings, so this animal opposes all mortals by killing them. But when the toad perceives that it is alive in the egg, it is immediately astonished by its unlawful habit and flees. The creature breaks the shell of its egg and comes out, emitting by its nature an exceedingly strong breath, containing in itself a most sharp and mighty fire, such as may exist even without Tartarean torments, resembling lightning and thunder.

When it comes out of its egg, it immediately causes the earth to split by the strength of its breath almost to a depth of five cubits. There it lies in moist earth until it has grown to maturity. Then it rises to the surface of the earth and kills by its breath everything that it finds alive, for it neither wishes nor can endure anything living. When it sees something alive, it immediately sends forth cold in anger, and then its breath; thus it kills the creature upon which it breathes, so that it immediately falls as though struck by lightning and thunder.

If a basilisk dies in any field or vineyard and its corpse decays there, that place becomes unproductive and barren. Or if it dies and decays in any tower or house, people dwelling there are always sick, and the animals there are often attacked by pestilence—that is, *schelmo*—so that they frequently die from it. [Col. 1343D]

### CHAPTER XIII.—ON THE SCORPION  
[Note: [Col. 1344D] Absent from the edition, as are the following Chapters XIV–XVI.]

[Col. 1344A]

The scorpion has burning heat and ardour in itself, as well as a certain harshness of infernal punishments. Whatever is in it is wholly deadly poison, bringing death to people and sometimes to animals. Thus, if someone wished to prepare poisonous substances with it, and the preparer gave them to anyone to taste or touch, that person would be subject to death. It has no remedies in it, only certain death.

### CHAPTER XIV.—ON DARANT

Darant is very warm and poisonous, and puts all its poison into its tail, so that its tail is always full of poison, as the udders of animals are full of milk. By the poison of its tail it brings death to people and animals. There is no usefulness or remedy in it. [Col. 1344B]

### CHAPTER XV.—ON TYRIACA

Tyriaca is a very warm worm and by nature seeks dry air. It also has sound moisture, because it is neither excessively warm nor excessively cold, but healthy; at the same time it purges itself of all its harmful humours. Otherwise it would be very dangerous to people.

Whenever unhealthy air or weather arises, it seeks little sandy hollows and hides itself in them for the time being. There it eats certain little herbs conducive to health, and through these remains healthy. It does not, however, contain many precious ointments; rather, when tasted in some fashion by a person, it produces a kind of alarm and brings out sweat, but does not greatly drive out a person’s inner illnesses. [Col. 1344C]

### CHAPTER XVI.—ON SCHERZBEDRA

Scherczbedra (?) is warm and also has moisture in itself. But a person who has eaten or drunk poison should reduce an entire scherczbedern to powder and add a little fine wheat flour, so that the powder exceeds the flour fivefold. He should mix in water and make little cakes. Bake them in the sun or in a warm oven somewhat cooled down; then reduce the cakes again to powder. Let him take this powder in an egg, and the poison will be purged from him by vomiting or excretion. [Col. 1344D]

### CHAPTER XVII.—ON ULWURM  
[Note: [Col. 1344D] Earthworm.] [IV, III, 42].

Ulwurm is very warm and grows in that greenness in which grasses begin to sprout, and in the stirring of that same greenness. Because of its clean nature, it has no bones, and, like other useful things, such as cinnamon, it is good and useful.

For the earth has a certain moisture in itself by which, as by veins, it is held together so that it does not flow apart. When rain is about to descend from the air, that moisture of the earth senses the coming rain, by which the veins of the earth will be filled; understanding this by their nature, ulwurms come forth because the veins of the earth are being filled. [Col. 1345A] [Note: [Col. 1345B] “It grows in the greenness of the earth—the veins of the earth” is omitted in the edition.]

A person who has *orfimas* should, at the hour when ulwurms come forth at the approach of rain, take a sufficient quantity of them and put them in a potter’s vessel or pot. Let him lightly smoke them with barley straw so that they die; then add wheat flour to them and mix them vigorously together with oak wood. Then add a little wine and vinegar in equal measure and mix again; then add a little wine and vinegar in equal measure once more and mix again, making a paste—that is, *deick*. From this *deick* he should apply a dressing to unbroken *orfimas* for three days, and the cleanliness of these clean worms diminishes the uncleanness of that flesh, which can no longer remain there. [Col. 1345B]

If the scrofulae and *orfimae* have burst, dip the aforesaid paste, or *deick*, prepared as described above, in an abundant quantity of sharp lye [the edition: “in the superabundance of sharp lye”], and apply it to the broken *orfimae*. It removes their corruption and heals them.

A person who has stomach pain should heat the same dung of ulwurms in an earthen vessel, as previously stated, upon a *broscleffel*, and lay it upon his stomach. Let him do this often, and his stomach will be cleansed and become light. [Col. 1346A]

If you cannot have ulwurms at the time when you would gladly have them, and it does not rain so that they do not come out of the earth, then dig the earth in a moist place and look for them there, and make the aforementioned remedies with them. Nevertheless, for the remedies stated above, they are much more useful when they come forth of themselves at the descent of rain. [Note: [Col. 1345B] “If you cannot have ulwurms—at the descent of rain” is omitted in the edition.]

### CHAPTER XVIII.—ON THE TESTUDO  
[Note: [Col. 1345B] Snail and slug, *Helix* and *Limax*.] [IV, III, 43, 44].

The testudo which is in a shell moves upon the earth and is of a cold nature. But the testudo which is not in a shell is of little use in medicine. Nevertheless, if worms are eating a person, let him take the shell of this testudo, reduce it to powder, and scatter that powder upon the place where the worms are eating him. The worms will die and the person [Col. 1346B] will be healed.

The testudo without a shell, being cold, is of use for nearly the same remedies if you prepare it as was said of ulwurm—except that the remedy made from ulwurm is much better and stronger than that made from this testudo. Therefore, when you cannot obtain ulwurm, prepare with this shell-less testudo the remedies previously described from it, though they are weaker than those prepared from ulwurm. Thus the person who uses them as stated above will be healed. [Note: [Col. 1345B] Edition: “The testudo without a shell is of use for the same remedies if a person prepares it as was stated above concerning ulwurm, except that the remedy from ulwurm is much better and stronger.”]

## NINTH BOOK. PREFACE. ON THE KINDS OF METALS

[Col. 1345]

[Col. 1345C] On the kinds of metals. When in the beginning the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters, [Note: [Col. 1345B] Genesis 1:2.] and when water flooded the world, and spirits remained without the agitation of the flood, by their breathing He caused the waters to flow; and those waters then permeated the earth and made it firm, lest it should fall apart.

Where the fiery force flowing in the water passed through the earth, there the fire of that water transformed the earth into the substance of gold. But where the purity of the flood-water passed through the earth, there that purity of the flood, poured out of itself together with the earth, became the substance of silver. Where, however, the motion of water stirred by winds passed through the earth, there that motion became, together with the earth which it permeated, the substance of steel and iron. Therefore steel and iron are stronger than the other metals, just as the movement of waters stirred by winds is stronger than the stillness of gentle breezes. And as the Spirit of the Lord first caused the waters to flood, so He also gives life to humankind and gave greenness to herbs, trees, and stones. [Col. 1346C]

### CHAPTERS

[Col. 1345]

| Metal | Chapter |
|---|---:|
| Gold | I |
| Silver | II |
| Lead | III |
| Tin | IV |
| Copper | V |
| Brass | VI |
| Iron | VII |
| Steel | VIII |

## NINTH BOOK. ON METALS

[Col. 1347]

### CHAPTER I.—ON GOLD  
[I, 15].

[Col. 1347A]

Gold is warm, has a nature like the sun, and is, as it were, of the air. A person who has *virgichtiget* should take gold and cook it so that no impurity remains in it and nothing is taken away from it. He should reduce it to powder—that is, *male*—then take a little fine wheat flour, in the quantity of half a palm, and knead it with water. To this *deick* add gold powder weighing one obol, and eat it fasting in the morning.

On the following day, he should again make a little cake in the same way with flour and the same weight of gold, and eat it fasting that day. A little cake prepared and eaten in this way checks *gicht* in him for a year. [Col. 1347B] This gold remains in his stomach for two months and neither irritates nor ulcerates the stomach. But if it is cold and *slimechte*, it warms and purges it without danger to the person. If a healthy person does this, it will preserve his health; and if he is sick, he will become well.

Again, take pure gold, heat it in a pot or potter’s vessel, *ghiwe* (*gluwe*?), and put it, glowing, into pure wine so that the wine is warmed by it. Drink it warm, and do this often; *gicht* will leave you. Likewise, whoever has *fiber* in the stomach should warm pure wine in this way with glowing gold and drink it; the *fiber* will leave him.

If a swelling rises anywhere in your body, warm gold in the sun and rub it around the *geswolst*—the swelling—of that tumour, and the swelling will disappear. A person with deaf ears should prepare a *deick* with *gemalem* gold and fine wheat flour in the manner stated above, place a little of it in his ears so that its heat may pass into the ear, and do this often; he will recover his hearing. [Col. 1347C] [Note: [Col. 1347D] Edition: “Gold is warm, has a nature like the sun, is, as it were, of the air, has redness from fire, and is also from moist air. But whoever has fever in the stomach should warm pure, good wine with glowing gold and drink it; the fever will leave him, because the good power of this gold, with its heat altered by the force of fire as stated above, removes the bad humours of the stomach. It should be put into wine, not water, because wine consumes bruising in the human stomach more than water does. If a swelling rises anywhere in a person’s body, let him warm gold in the sun and move it around the swelling of that tumour as though anointing it; the swelling will disappear. For when the good power of gold is stimulated by the fire of the sun, the gold, which is from fire, is as though revived by the sun’s heat and drives away rising humours by its strength.”]

### CHAPTER II.—ON SILVER  
[I, 16].

Silver is cold [the edition adds: “because it has that cold wind which also makes the earth cold”]. A person who has an excess of humours and often expels them [the edition adds: “by expectoration”] should heat very pure silver in fire, *gluwe*, and put it hot into good wine. Let him do this three or four times so that the wine is warmed by it; then let him drink it often, fasting and at night, and it will diminish his excessive [Col. 1347D] humours—that is, *swendet*.

[The edition adds: “For the strong nature of silver’s coldness, by its sharpness together with the heat of fire and the warmth of the altered wine, diminishes hot, cold, and moist humours, as stated above. But if a person takes food or drink in a silver vessel, it neither greatly benefits nor harms him in respect of bodily health.”] [Col. 1348A]

If, however, anyone ate silver reduced to powder, it would be excessively cold and excessively heavy in his stomach, and he would afterwards be harmed by it, even if it then helped him against some illness.

### CHAPTER III.—ON LEAD  
[I, 17].

Lead is cold and would harm a person if he introduced it into his body in any fashion, [the edition adds: “and it would do this because of the coldness it possesses, and because it is also at times crude and like the scum and dross of other metals”]. But if a dead person swells and lead is placed beneath him, it somewhat restrains that swelling [the edition adds: “because he has no vital breath”].

If, however, it were placed upon a living person who was swelling, he would be torn apart and could not live [the edition adds: “because its coldness passes through him and would tear him apart, since it is like the scum of other metals. Neither food nor drink in a lead vessel is beneficial, because of the coldness that it contains.”]. [Col. 1348B]

### CHAPTER IV.—ON TIN  
[I, 20].

Tin is more cold than warm. If someone places tin upon his skin so that his skin and flesh are warmed by it, it removes bodily illness by its coldness. But if anyone eats or drinks from a tin vessel, he contracts illness from it, so that it is almost like poison to him.

But a person whose flesh around the eyes *uszwilezet* should reduce tin to ashes and put them into pure wine. At night, when going to sleep, he should anoint with this wine the *augleder*—the eyelids—which *uszwelczent*, or swell around the eyes; the eyelids will become healthy and beautiful. For the coldness of tin, tempered by the warmth of wine, heals and restores the flesh which hot humours shake and force outward. But it does not drive away dimness of the eyes. [Col. 1348C]

### CHAPTER V.—ON COPPER  
[I, 18].

Copper is hot, and quickly cools; and it is [Col. 1348D] like the ashes of gold—that is, like the ashes which fall from burning coals. And whoever has any fevers, [Col. 1349A] including those fevers that arise in the stomach—not quotidian, tertian, or quartan fevers—but *riddo*, that is, one who yawns, is sluggish, and has an aversion to food, should take five coins’ weight of pure copper and put it into as much Franconian wine as a small cup holds; then boil that wine vigorously, namely until it begins to diminish. Remove it from the fire, and afterwards drink a little of it while fasting for nine days, and those fevers will cease.  

And if anyone has *virgichtiget* [possibly “afflicted with gout/paralysis”], so that he contracts his whole body—this is called *crymphet*—take pure copper and cast it into the fire until it glows; then cast it again into the fire so that it grows hot once more; remove it again from the fire and let it cool again; cast it into the fire a third time, and when it then glows, put it while glowing into good wine [Col. 1349B] and cover the vessel on top, lest its heat or vapour escape. Then give this, moderately warm, to drink to the person who has *virgichtiget*, and the *gicht* [gout/paralytic illness] in him will cease.  

And if horses, asses, oxen, goats, sheep, pigs, or any other animals have *strengel* or *heuptsichtum* [throat-constriction or head-ailment], put a large piece of copper into a cauldron, pot, or pan, pour water over it, and heat that water over the fire together with the copper until it boils. Then sprinkle the fodder of those beasts—whether oats or hay—with this hot water once or twice, so that they may eat it thus sprinkled; and the disease will cease from them.

[Note: [Col. 1349C]

The edition varies in many places:

“Copper is hot, and quickly cools; and it is like the ashes of gold—that is, like the ashes which fall from burning coals. But a person who has any fevers, including those fevers which arise in the stomach, provided nevertheless that they are neither quotidian, tertian, nor quartan; but that the person yawns, frequently stretches out his arms and whole body, is sluggish, and has an aversion to food—should take five coins’ weight of pure copper and put it [Col. 1349D] into as much pure, good Franconian wine as a small cup holds. He should then boil that wine vigorously, namely until it begins to diminish; remove it from the fire; and afterwards, while fasting, drink a little of that wine for nine days, and the fevers in him will cease. For copper possesses heat from a sudden and raging fire, a heat which is a certain burning derived from direct fire. It should be put into wine and boiled vigorously, so that the power of the copper may be fully mingled with the power of the wine, and may thus destroy the harmful humours and their coagulation.

“And if anyone is weakened by paralytic gout, so that he contracts his whole body, he should take pure copper and cast it into the fire until it glows. Then he should take it out, so that it cools; cast it again into the fire, so that it grows hot once more; take it again from the fire, so that it cools again; and put it into the fire a third time. When it then glows, he should put it while glowing into good wine and cover the vessel containing that wine on top, lest its heat or vapour escape. He should then drink that wine moderately warm, [Col. 1350C] and the paralysis in him will cease. This copper is put into the fire a third time so that whatever foulness and corruption there may be in it may be tested by the fire; and so that, when the wine heated by it is drunk, through its good heat and power together with the good heat of the wine, it may drive away the harmful humours from which paralysis arises.

“And if anyone has eaten or drunk poison, let him take good wine and add vinegar amounting to one third of it; then mix in rue juice equal to, as it were, half of these two together; and then put about a quarter-measure of pure copper into the fire. When it is glowing, put it into that wine [Col. 1350D] so that it becomes warm. Then, while fasting, drink it hot for three days, and the poison will depart from him either through nausea or through evacuation.

“And if horses, asses, oxen, sheep, goats, pigs, or any other animals have constriction of the throat or pain in the head, a person should put a large piece of copper into a cauldron, pot, or pan and pour water over it. He should then make the water boil over the fire together with that copper, and sprinkle the fodder of those animals, whether oats or hay, once or twice with the same hot water, so that they may eat it thus sprinkled; and the aforesaid disease will cease from them. For when the aforesaid heat and power of copper is stirred up in water by the fire, and is thus given in fodder or drink to sick livestock, it diminishes the harmful humours that injure them and that have gathered in their heads from corrupt air.”]

.

## CHAPTER VI.—ON BRASS [I, 19]

[Col. 1349C]

Brass [*auricalcum*, “gold-copper,” in the edition] is hot, and is made from another thing, as lime is made from stone. And because brass is not brass by its own nature but is made from another metal [Note: [Col. 1350D] “As … made” is absent from the edition], it is like a knight who is not a knight by birth, but [Col. 1350A] has been made a knight. Therefore it is of no use in medicines, but harms a person more than it benefits him. Thus, if a person wears a ring of it upon his finger, or if another part of his body is made warm by it, he draws more sickness than health to himself [because that metal has no power in itself, addition in the edition].

## CHAPTER VII.—ON IRON [I, 21]

Iron is exceedingly hot in its nature, and is therefore strong. Its strength is useful for very many things. And if anyone has iron near him, so that his flesh becomes warm from it, he is harmed less by it than by tin [because iron is hot and of a proper temperament; when its heat is stirred up by fire and it is laid upon a person’s stomach, it drives away the cold humours from which the stomach [Col. 1350B] suffers pain, as was stated above, addition in the edition].

But a person whose stomach has become chilled so that it hurts from this should take a thin *blech* [plate; “lamina” in the edition] of iron, heat it at the fire, lay it hot upon his stomach, and remove it again. He should heat it anew and lay it hot once more upon his stomach, and do this often; and he will fare better. [For this iron contains heat within itself, and because it is a proper metal, addition in the edition.]

## CHAPTER VIII.—ON STEEL [I, 22]

Steel is very hot and is the strongest part of the metal of iron. It almost signifies the divinity of God; hence the devil flees and avoids it. And [Col. 1350C] if you suspect that there is poison either in food or drink, or if the food is moist, such as *warmume* or *suffen* [possibly dishes of vegetables or soup], secretly place glowing steel in it; and, if poison is in it, it weakens and thins it. Or if the food is dry, such as meat, fish, or eggs, put glowing [Col. 1351A] steel into wine, pour that wine over the food in question, and if poison is in it, apply the dry food to wine heated by glowing steel; and if poison has been in it, it is suppressed within it, so that it harms the person eating it less.

Likewise, put glowing steel into drink, whether wine, beer, water, or any other beverage; and, if poison is in it, it is immediately weakened. For if steel heated to glowing in the fire is put into food or drink in this manner, or if wine heated with glowing steel is poured over food—whether bread, meat, fish, or other foods of this kind [Col. 1352A]—then, if poison is in it, the strength of that poison is restrained and weakened. Steel has such force that in this manner it makes the poison dry, so that it can harm the eater and drinker less. Thus, if anyone tastes poison so treated, it can by no means bring him to death; even if he swells up or remains ill for some time, he can nevertheless escape death, if that poison has been weakened with glowing steel, as stated above.

[Note: [Col. 1351A] Edition:

“Chapter XII.—On steel. Steel is very hot, and is the strongest element in the metal of iron; and by its strength it signifies the divinity of God. Therefore the devil flees and avoids it. But if a person suspects that poison is in food or drink, then, if the food is moist, such as a little soup or food made from vegetables, let him put glowing steel into it; and, if poison is in it, it weakens and thins it. Or if the food is dry, such as meat, fish, or eggs, let him put glowing steel into wine and pour that wine over the food in question; and, if poison is in it, it weakens it. Or if it is bread, let him apply the bread itself, or similar dry food, to wine heated by glowing steel; and, if poison has been in it, it is suppressed within it, so that it harms the person eating it less.

“For the strength of steel is the strongest strength, beyond which no greater strength of metals can proceed; it is the foundation of all cutting implements [Col. 1352A] and has such strength in itself that, when its heat is stirred up by fire, it weakens poisons and reduces them to nothing by its good heat and strength, both without the heat of wine and with the heat of wine. For if steel heated to glowing in the fire is put into food or drink in this manner, or if wine heated with glowing steel is poured over food—whether bread, meat, fish, or other foods of this kind—and poison is in them, then its strength is restrained and weakened. For the greatest force of steel is that it makes poison dry in this way, so that it can harm the eater or drinker less. Even if that person swells up or is ill for some time, he will nevertheless certainly escape death; so that even if anyone tastes that poison, it can by no means bring him to death, if the poison has been weakened with glowing steel, as stated above.”]

[Col. 1351] Here ends the book of the blessed Hildegard, *On the Subtleties of Diverse Natures*.

## ORDER OF THE MATERIAL CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## SAINT HILDEGARD, ABBESS

## THE BIRTH, DEEDS, AND WRITINGS OF SAINT HILDEGARD  
*(from the Bollandists)*

§ I.—The already published Acts of St Hildegard and their authors; certain other materials to be published from a manuscript; the Life to be supplemented in this commentary chiefly from the Saint’s writings. 9

§ II.—Birth, childhood, monastic life on Mount St Disibod; illuminated by visions from childhood and at last compelled to write them down; how she wrote her works. 12

§ III.—As the number of nuns increased, St Hildegard founds a convent on Mount St Rupert; she did not see St Bernard there, nor did she embrace the Cistercian rule; the Saint’s writings approved by Eugenius III; completion of the work *Scivias*. 20

§ IV.—The Saint’s fame shines forth greatly; St Bernard, Conrad, King of the Romans, and many bishops write to her, to whom she replies with complete frankness. 28

§ V.—Anastasius IV and Adrian IV, Roman pontiffs, Emperor Frederick, bishops, and many others write to the Saint, and she replies to them. 31

§ VI.—The Saint is consulted by many persons about hidden and secret matters which she could not have known without divine revelation. 35

§ VII.—The Saint is consulted by many communities about matters that might be corrected, and also about other secrets; she is invited to set down admonitions in writing. 43

§ VIII.—The Saint is also consulted about theological, scriptural, and other questions pertaining to faith or morals. 48

§ IX.—Many write to the Saint in order to obtain prayers, consolation, admonitions, and other such things; she writes back to them. 50

§ X.—Certain letters of St Hildegard to Philip, Abbot of Park, and his letters to her, from a manuscript; her dealings with St Gerlach; other letters later sent to the Saint, with her replies. 58

§ XI.—The Saint frees her monastery from every burden; a possessed woman is delivered there; because of the burial of someone formerly excommunicated, the Saint’s church is placed under interdict. 61

§ XII.—Various journeys of St Hildegard, and places where she appeared publicly. She founds the convent of Eibingen. 67

§ XIII.—The writings of St Hildegard celebrated by the praises of many; catalogue of her writings; some works ascribed to her. 73

§ XIV.—The Saint’s death established as occurring in the year 1179; burial; relics transferred to Eibingen after the destruction of the convent of St Rupert; miracles; an attempted but uncompleted canonization; her name entered in martyrologies, and her cult. 84

## THE LIFE OF SAINT HILDEGARD, BY THE MONKS GODFREY AND THEODORIC

Theodoric’s preface to the whole Life. 91

## BOOK ONE—ON THE SAINT’S DEEDS

Chapter I.—The Saint’s birth; childhood illuminated by visions; monastic life under her teacher Jutta. 91

Chapter II.—She founds a convent on Mount St Rupert near Bingen and lives there with her sisters; she continues to be illuminated by unceasing visions. 95

## BOOK TWO—ON THE SAINT’S VISIONS

Prologue. 99

Chapter I.—Although ignorant of the Latin language, the Saint nevertheless writes books in Latin; she enjoys visions from childhood and is compelled to write them; she assists many by counsel and admonitions, and rightly guides her own affairs. 101

Chapter II.—In a vision the Saint learns the site for founding a monastery, and on that account suffers many things; nevertheless, in all things she has God as helper and comforter. 105

Chapter III.—The Saint’s remarkable illnesses; instruction of the nuns; [Col. 1353] conversion of a philosopher who had entertained wrongful suspicions; various visions. 110

## BOOK THREE—ON THE MIRACLES AND DEATH OF THE BLESSED WOMAN

Prologue. 117

Chapter I.—The Saint heals various sick people by her patronage, including some absent persons; explains letters divinely produced; visits many places for the salvation of the people. 117

Chapter II.—The prolonged illness of St Hildegard; a noblewoman possessed by a demon, who had been taken in vain to various places, is delivered in her monastery. 122

Chapter III.—The grave illness of the Saint, who is healed in a vision; benefits bestowed upon various persons; death and burial honoured by miracles. 127

Proceedings of the inquiry into the virtues and miracles of Saint Hildegard. Notice concerning the life and writings of St Hildegard. 139

## LETTERS OF ST HILDEGARD
EPISTLE I.—Pope Eugenius to Hildegard.—By apostolic authority he grants her permission to set forth and write whatever she has learned through the Holy Spirit, and encourages her to commit to writing without fear the things revealed to her. 145

Hildegard’s reply.—She admonishes the pontiff concerning the secrets he held in his heart, and indicates the divine will and good pleasure concerning these matters. 145

EPISTLE II.—Pope Anastasius to Hildegard.—He approves her writings. He asks her to offer prayers to God for him. 150

Hildegard’s reply.—In God’s name, she exhorts the pontiff to root out evils courageously. Then she foretells various prophetic matters and adds something concerning her visions. Again she urges Anastasius to correct those subject to him. 151

EPISTLE III.—Pope Adrian to Hildegard.—He exhorts her to perseverance. 153

Hildegard’s reply.—She foretells grave struggles for the pontiff and exhorts him to steadfastness. 154

EPISTLE IV.—Hildegard to Pope Alexander.—That the abbot of Saint Disibod opposes the privileges of the convent on Mount Saint Rupert. 154

Pope Alexander’s reply to Provost Wezelin.—Concerning the appointment of a provost over the convent on Mount Saint Rupert, notwithstanding the opposition of the abbot of Saint Disibod. 155

EPISTLE V.—Archbishop Henry of Mainz to Hildegard.—That she should permit a certain nun, elected abbess, to depart with those who had come to take her away. 156

Hildegard’s reply.—By the example of Nebuchadnezzar she foretells that Henry will be deprived of his rank and will not live much longer, as in fact occurred. 156

EPISTLE VI.—Archbishop Arnold of Mainz to Hildegard.—He requests the holy woman’s prayers. 157

Hildegard’s reply.—She sternly rebukes Arnold and foretells his death. 157

EPISTLE VII.—Archbishop Christian of Mainz to Hildegard.—He commends himself to her prayers. 158

Hildegard’s reply.—She admirably exhorts him to pastoral care. 158

EPISTLE VIII.—Hildegard to Christian, Archbishop of Mainz.—Because a certain young man, once excommunicated but long since absolved, had been buried in the cemetery on Mount Saint Rupert, and she had received an order from the prelates of Mainz either to command the body to be exhumed or to refrain from celebrating the divine offices in her church, she implores the pontiff’s aid. 159

EPISTLE IX.—Archbishop Christian of Mainz to Hildegard.—He sympathizes with her affliction and states that he has notified the Church of Mainz “that, if the absolution of the aforesaid deceased is demonstrated to her by the truthful testimony of good men, the divine offices are to be celebrated by the sisters of Mount Saint Rupert.” 160

EPISTLE X.—Archbishop Hartwig of Bremen to Hildegard.—He announces the death of his sister, Abbess Richardis. 161

Hildegard’s reply.—She praises Hartwig and Richardis and offers excellent counsels. 162

EPISTLE XI.—Archbishop Arnold of Cologne to Hildegard.—He asks for her book. 163

Hildegard’s reply.—She speaks mystically and somewhat obscurely, but then adds clearer remarks about her book. 164

EPISTLE XII.—Archbishop Eberhard of Salzburg to Hildegard.—He commends himself to the holy woman’s prayers and requests her letter. 164

Hildegard’s reply.—She praises Eberhard in various ways. She beautifully teaches that outward labours undertaken from charity and obedience do not at all harm a man who loves God. 165

EPISTLE XIII.—Archbishop Hillin of Trier to Hildegard.—He asks that she deign to let a few drops from the king’s wine-cellar trickle down to him in writing. 166

[Col. 1354] Hildegard’s reply.—She writes prophetically and exhortatively. 167

EPISTLE XIV.—Bishop Eberhard of Bamberg to Hildegard.—He puts forward a very subtle question: “In the Father abides eternity, in the Son equality, in the Holy Spirit the bond of eternity and equality.” 167

Hildegard’s reply.—After a brief exhortation in which she urges Eberhard carefully to feed his flock, she proceeds to the question. 168

EPISTLE XV.—The Bishop of Speyer to Hildegard. 171

Hildegard’s reply.—In many ways she exhorts Gunther to amend his life. 172

EPISTLE XVI.—The Bishop of Worms to Hildegard.—He adorns the holy woman with praises and requests an answer. 173

Hildegard’s reply.—She praises and exhorts him. 173

EPISTLE XVII.—The Bishop of Constance to Hildegard.—He requests the holy woman’s prayers and letter. 173

Hildegard’s reply.—She reproves in him empty glory. 174

EPISTLE XVIII.—The Bishop of Verdun to Hildegard.—He exhorts the holy woman to humility and requests her prayers and letter. 174

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to pastoral care. 174

EPISTLE XIX.—The Bishop of Liège to Hildegard.—He says that he is placed amid the greatest turmoil of mind and body because, as he confesses, he has offended God by innumerable evils. He requests the prayers and reply of Saint Hildegard. 175

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to a good life and to the care of souls. 175

EPISTLE XX.—The Bishop of Utrecht to Hildegard.—He declares his affection for the holy woman. 176

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to perseverance in what is good. 176

EPISTLE XXI.—The Bishop of Prague to Hildegard.—He asks her to aid him with her prayers and offer good counsel. 177

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to greater constancy in virtue, both in prosperity and adversity. 177

EPISTLE XXII.—The Bishop of Jerusalem to Hildegard.—He commends himself to the prayers of her and her sisters. He launches into praise of the holy woman. 178

Hildegard’s reply.—She consoles the patriarch. 179

EPISTLE XXIII.—The Bishop of Beauvais to Hildegard.—He urgently requests her prayers and letter. 180

Hildegard’s reply.—She employs a beautiful parable by which she exhorts him to true wisdom and charity. 180

EPISTLE XXIV.—The Bishop of Trier to Hildegard.—He graciously declares his affection for Saint Hildegard and testifies that he was elevated to the episcopate against his will. 181

Hildegard’s reply.—After salutary instruction, she seriously warns him to beware of pride and vanity and to embrace virtues suited to his rank. 182

EPISTLE XXV.—The Bishop of Cologne to Hildegard.—He praises the holy woman and asks her to seek from God’s hidden counsel and send him admonitory words, as God may grant. 183

Hildegard’s reply.—She makes known what she heard and saw in a vision, then adds a splendid exhortation. 183

EPISTLE XXVI.—Emperor Conrad to Hildegard.—He pledges his favour and commends his son to the holy woman’s prayers. 185

Hildegard’s reply.—She quite plainly foretells the schisms and other evils of the Church that arose under Frederick I, Conrad’s successor. She adds much else, in the same prophetic spirit, concerning various times and vicissitudes of the Church. 185

EPISTLE XXVII.—Emperor Frederick to Hildegard.—He reports that certain things foretold by the holy woman in conversation at Ingelheim have been fulfilled. He requests her prayers. In a controversy between certain persons and Saint Hildegard, to be settled in his court, he promises to judge solely with regard to equity. 186

Hildegard’s reply.—She condemns Frederick’s various schemes. She foretells that his reign will be quite long but turbulent. 186

EPISTLE XXVIII.—Count Philip of Flanders to Hildegard.—He requests Saint Hildegard’s prayers and asks for counsel whether he should remain in the Holy Land or, after undertaking his expedition, return to his own people. 187

Hildegard’s reply.—She sends instruction in which she especially exhorts him to justice. 188

EPISTLE XXIX.—Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux to Hildegard.—He extols her merits and holiness. 189

Hildegard’s reply.—She adorns him with great praise. 189

EPISTLE XXX.—Abbot Adam of Ebra to Hildegard.—He commends himself to the holy woman’s prayers and requests her reply concerning his doubt, apparently whether he ought to retain or lay aside the office of abbot, as may be inferred from Saint Hildegard’s answer. 190

Hildegard’s reply.—Urging him not to lay down his office, she introduces various virtues, especially charity and humility. 191

EPISTLE XXXI.—The Abbot of Eberbach to Hildegard.—He requests the holy woman’s prayers and offers her his services. 194

Hildegard’s reply.—She returns excellent counsels and at the end foretells the best things. 195

EPISTLE XXXII.—The Abbot of Saint Anastasius to Hildegard.—Whether he ought to retain or relinquish the office of abbot in order to devote himself to contemplation. 196

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should adhere to his office. 196

EPISTLE XXXIII.—The Abbot of Kaisheim to Hildegard.—He presents the holy woman with a similar doubt. 197

Hildegard’s reply.—She does not conceal the crimes of his subjects, nor does she seem to excuse Conrad himself, but exhorts him to repentance. Yet she adds a qualification in obscure words, suggesting that he should relinquish his office where he could accomplish no good among his own people. 197

EPISTLE XXXIV.—The Abbot of Hirsau to Hildegard.—He adorns the holy woman with great praises. 199

Hildegard’s reply.—She foretells various matters. 199

EPISTLE XXXV.—The administrator of Saint Emmeram to Hildegard.—Concerning a certain man despairing of his salvation. 199

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts the abbot in grave words to care for his flock. 200

EPISTLE XXXVI.—The Abbot of Nuenburg to Hildegard.—He says that fear of war prevented him from coming to her. He earnestly requests her prayers. 200

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to courage in pastoral care: in time of war the soldier must not cast away his weapons because difficulties have arisen. 201

EPISTLE XXXVII.—The Abbot of Saint Mary to Hildegard.—After much praise of the holy woman, he asks whether he ought to retain or resign his office. 201

Hildegard’s reply.—She says that he is excessively anxious; rather than thinking of resigning his office, he ought to think of correcting himself and his subjects. 202

EPISTLE XXXVIII.—The Abbot of Saint Disibod to Hildegard.—He asks her to disclose to him anything God may have revealed to the holy woman concerning Saint Disibod. He earnestly commends himself to her prayers. 203

Hildegard’s reply.—After some general remarks on Saint Disibod, she freely reproves Cuno for excessive severity toward his subjects and foretells his approaching death. 203

EPISTLE XXXIX.—Abbot Helenger of Saint Disibod to Hildegard.—He accuses himself and complains that monastic discipline has been badly observed in his monastery. 204

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to amendment of life. 205

EPISTLE XL.—The Abbot of Kempten to Hildegard.—He commends himself to her prayers. 206

Hildegard’s reply.—She sends a splendid exhortation. 206

EPISTLE XLI.—The Abbot of Saint Martin at Cologne to Hildegard.—He commends himself to her prayers. 207

Hildegard’s reply.—She offers beautiful instruction and great consolation together with perpetual exhortation. 208

EPISTLE XLII.—The Abbess of Saint Glodesindis to Hildegard.—She sets out her anxieties and doubts while compelled to govern the souls of many. 210

Hildegard’s reply.—She gives various counsels for right government and quite clearly suggests that the office of superior should not be relinquished. 210

EPISTLE XLIII.—A certain priest to Hildegard.—He asks to be instructed concerning the body and blood of Christ. 212

Hildegard’s reply.—Concerning the body and blood of Christ. 212

EPISTLE XLIV.—The Abbess at Elostat to Hildegard.—That she is greatly troubled in the government of an abbey. 214

Hildegard’s reply.—She kindly exhorts the abbess to continue labouring for her own people. Yet prudence is necessary in God’s service. 214

EPISTLE XLV.—Mistress Elisabeth at Schönau to Hildegard.—She requests prayers and words of consolation. 214

Hildegard’s reply.—She discusses the human being and God’s inspiration, by which He deigns to illumine certain persons more than others. 216

EPISTLE XLVI.—The Provost at Frankfurt to Hildegard.—He commends himself to her prayers. 218

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to reform his conduct. 218

EPISTLE XLVII.—To the prelates of Mainz.—Because of the divine services prohibited by them. 218

EPISTLE XLVIII.—Dean Philip and the clergy of Cologne to Hildegard.—They request her prayers. They ask her to commit to writing and send them what she had previously told them orally. 243

[Col. 1356] Hildegard’s reply.—In most grave words and in God’s name, she rebukes the clergy’s negligence in the care of souls and other vices; she gives many counsels and mingles with them many predictions. 244

EPISTLE XLIX.—The Provost of Saint Peter and all the clergy of Trier to Hildegard.—They ask her to commit to writing and send what she had recently foretold to them on the days of Pentecost. 253

Hildegard’s reply.—After repeatedly rebuking the negligence of pastors and prelates, she proceeds to predictions of future good and evil. 254

EPISTLE L.—The dean of the Holy Apostles at Cologne, chief master of the schools, to Hildegard.—Concerning a demon-possessed woman freed by Hildegard. 258

Hildegard’s reply.—She replies most humbly, attributing the casting out of the demon to the good works of many together. God directs the diverse good works of diverse persons toward one end. 258

EPISTLE LI.—Prior Meffrid at Eberbach to Hildegard.—They request the holy woman’s prayers and the letter which they had heard she had written concerning persons converted from secular to spiritual life, whom “we call conversi.” 259

Hildegard’s reply.—She praises the Cistercian Order, but reproves those whom they call conversi, since very many of them do not turn to God in their conduct; she adds further instruction. 260

EPISTLE LII.—Werner of Kirchheim, with the other brethren of his community, to Hildegard.—They earnestly request the holy woman’s prayers and wish to possess her words committed to writing. 268

Hildegard’s reply.—She introduces the image of the Church pouring out most grievous complaints against the sins of priests. She foretells many things which were wholly fulfilled in the sixteenth century. 269

EPISTLE LIII.—The brethren of Hagenheim to Hildegard.—They pray that she will not fail to calm and eradicate the discord that has arisen among them. 271

Hildegard’s reply.—She sends splendid instruction and admonition concerning many vices and virtues, and an exhortation to the pursuit of virtues. 272

EPISTLE LIV.—The monk Guibert of Gembloux to Hildegard.—He requests solutions to thirty-eight questions. 275

EPISTLE LV.—The sisters of the convent at Hunni to Hildegard.—They ask her to explain the Rule of Benedict to them. 275

EPISTLE LVI.—Hildegard to Abbot Philip of Park.—She sends him a certain penitent woman who had not confessed rightly and whose sin, as will be clear from Philip’s reply, she had directed to be disclosed. 275

EPISTLE LVII.—Abbot Philip of Park to Hildegard.—He replies to the preceding letter. 276

EPISTLE LVIII.—Hildegard to Abbot Philip of Park.—She offers splendid counsels. 277

EPISTLE LIX.—The same to the same.—A reply to Philip’s inquiry: he was fearful because of a sign that had happened to him during the celebration of the divine offices and about which he was greatly troubled. Hildegard relieves his fear. 278

EPISTLE LX.—Abbot G. and the brethren of Brauweiler to Hildegard.—Concerning a demon-possessed woman. 278

Hildegard’s reply.—She gives counsel concerning the woman’s deliverance. 279

EPISTLE LXI.—Abbot G. and the brethren of Brauweiler to Hildegard.—That the same woman is again tormented by a demon. 280

NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTERS. 281

EPISTLE LXII.—Abbot A. of Eberbach to Hildegard.—He asks her to consult the divine oracle concerning his enemies and write back what he should expect from God’s mercy. 281

Hildegard’s reply.—She consoles the afflicted man, exhorts the sluggish, and rouses him to fight manfully. 282

EPISTLE LXIII.—Abbot H. of Maulbronn to Hildegard.—Anxious concerning the governance of souls, he requests the support of her prayers. 283

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to good works and to restrain within himself worldly cares. 283

EPISTLE LXIV.—Abbot B. of Saint Michael at Bamberg to Hildegard.—He asks her to implore divine mercy, that it may moderate the scourge by which he is afflicted; and, being soon to depart from this world, he commends his soul to her. 284

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should vigilantly keep watch and honourably bear the Father’s rod, which will profit him. 284

EPISTLE LXV.—Abbot Berthold of Zwiefalten to Hildegard.—Suffering persecutions, he seeks from her some aid of consolation. 284

Hildegard’s reply.—She declares that the son of inheritance has been wounded by the rod because of the restless disorder of his mind and conduct. 285

EPISTLE LXVI.—Abbot G. of Salem to Hildegard.—The abbot of Röttinhaslach, elected abbot of Salem, wishes to resign both offices and asks her to seek out God’s will. 285

Hildegard’s reply.—A man who has undertaken the governance of a flock for the sake of faith ought not abandon pastoral care; but he who leaves one flock in order to take up another is a transgressor. 286

EPISTLE LXVII.—Abbot B. of Saint Eucharius to Hildegard.—He praises God’s gifts in her and commends himself to her prayers. 286

Hildegard’s reply.—She gives him devout counsels, especially that he should exercise gentleness toward his subjects. 287

EPISTLE LXVIII.—Abbot L. of Saint Eucharius to Hildegard.—He testifies to his reverence for her and asks that she reply concerning a matter entrusted to him. 287

Hildegard’s reply.—She teaches how he ought to conduct himself toward his subjects. 288

EPISTLE LXIX.—Abbot W. of Bosen’s Villa to Hildegard.—Having suffered persecution and calumnies, he asks her for prayers and consoling letters. 289

Hildegard’s reply.—She teaches that his monastery is sustained by God’s help and warns him to flee certain things that must be avoided. 289

EPISTLE LXX.—Abbot R. of Zwettl to Hildegard.—He asks whether he ought to relinquish pastoral care. 290

Hildegard’s reply.—She gives him devout and salutary counsels for governing his own community. 290

EPISTLE LXXI.—Abbot Nicholas of Halesbrunn to Hildegard.—He requests consoling letters from her. 291

Hildegard’s reply.—She praises his good intention toward God and exhorts him to labour. 291

EPISTLE LXXII.—The abbots of Belleval, G. of Cherlieu, A. of Clairfontaine, R. of Charity, and G. of Bethany, to Hildegard.—They praise the divine gifts in her and send her a noble barren woman, that through the assistance of Hildegard’s merits and prayers to God she may be able to bear a child. 292

Hildegard’s reply.—After giving them various devout counsels, she says that it lies in God’s will whether to make the woman fruitful or not; meanwhile, she promises to pray for her. 293

EPISTLE LXXIII.—Abbot N. of Eberbach to Hildegard.—He gives immense thanks to God for the gifts bestowed on Hildegard and asks her for the aid of prayer. 295

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to teach his flock diligently and to turn his eyes upon himself. 295

EPISTLE LXXIV.—Abbot Richard of Springiersbach to Hildegard.—Wearied by pastoral care, he consults Hildegard whether he ought to retain or reject it. 296

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him courageously to bear the burden laid upon him by God. 296

EPISTLE LXXV.—A certain abbot to Hildegard.—He gives thanks to God for the gifts bestowed on Hildegard, of which he himself has been a witness, and asks for consoling words in his uncertainty. 297

Hildegard’s reply.—Under certain figures, she exhorts him to act well. 297

EPISTLE LXXVI.—Provost H. of Flonheim to Hildegard.—He commends himself to her prayers. 298

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should correct his flock and behold God in the most pure fountain. 298

EPISTLE LXXVII.—Abbot W. of Heggenheim to Hildegard.—He discloses to her the failings of his soul and his bodily weakness, and asks her prayers to heal both. 298

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should avoid holding office if he is useless to his own people. 299

EPISTLE LXXVIII.—The Abbot of Vessra to Hildegard.—Doubting whether he ought to retain his office, he seeks help and counsel as to whether he should abandon the care of souls. 300

Hildegard’s reply.—She raises him from his uncertainty and assures him of God’s grace. 300

EPISTLE LXXIX.—Abbot N. at Elvestat to Hildegard.—He complains that she has not answered him despite his frequent letters and asks her to deign to relieve him, surrounded as he is by troubles. 301

Hildegard’s reply.—She seems to exhort him to celebrate more frequently. 301

EPISTLE LXXX.—Abbot H. at Selboth to Hildegard.—That she should not disdain to pray to God for his calamities and miseries. 301

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts the wavering man to humility. 302

EPISTLE LXXXI.—Provost H. at Herde to Hildegard.—He gives thanks that, though weak, she has visited his monastery, and commends himself to her prayers. 302

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to remain in his place and avoid wandering. 303

EPISTLE LXXXII.—Administrator B. of the monastery of Hameln to Hildegard.—Pressed by grave illness, he desires to learn whether the end of his labours is near. 303

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to have recourse to God. 304

EPISTLE LXXXIII.—Abbot H. at Wadego to Hildegard.—He asks that, if she cannot visit him in body, she may at least visit him by letter. 304

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should beware of enemies and repent. 305

EPISTLE LXXXIV.—Provost N. at Underestlorf to Hildegard.—That she should provide him with the aid of consolation. 305

Hildegard’s reply.—Under a figure, she exhorts him to fear and courage. 305

EPISTLE LXXXV.—Provost Frederick of Vallis Dei to Hildegard.—He commends himself to her prayers. 306

Hildegard’s reply.—Under a figure, she warns him not to abandon his people, but rather to help them and do penance. 306

EPISTLE LXXXVI.—Abbot N. at Rappenberh to Hildegard.—He asks her counsel concerning the present condition of the Church. 307

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him not to fear torments but to receive sheep fleeing to him. 307

EPISTLE LXXXVII.—Provost G. of Saint Victor to Hildegard.—Enmeshed in many sins, he asks whether any hope of salvation remains to him. 308

Hildegard’s reply.—She encourages him to rise, exhorting him to turn from evil and do good. 309

EPISTLE LXXXVIII.—Provost S. at Koblenz to Hildegard.—Since everything Saint Hildegard had predicted concerning him has been fulfilled, he asks consolation concerning the things that oppressed him outwardly and inwardly. 309

Hildegard’s reply.—God’s judgments are hidden; He also punishes parents’ sins in the fourth generation. Nevertheless, he should hope in the Lord. 309

EPISTLE LXXXIX.—Provost A. of Saint Andrew at Cologne to Hildegard.—Tempted inwardly and outwardly, he has recourse to her in order to learn what he ought to do. 310

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to perform good works. 310

EPISTLE XC.—Provost A. of Erfurt to Hildegard.—He commends to her the bearer of this letter. 311

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should keep the eye of his heart pure and turn from sins. 311

EPISTLE XCI.—Provost H. of the Dom at Mainz to Hildegard.—He desires to learn from her what displeases God in him and what must be corrected. 311

Hildegard’s reply.—That through good works he should make himself worthy of God’s protection. 312

EPISTLE XCII.—Provost Helderic of Saint Simeon at Trier to Hildegard.—He praises God’s wonderful gifts in her and commends himself to her prayers. 312

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should forestall death with good works. 313

EPISTLE XCIII.—Provost H. at Knethstehtde to Hildegard.—He asks how he may appease God for his sins. 313

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should sigh to God and have recourse to Him with confidence. 314

EPISTLE XCIV.—Provost H. at Bonn to Hildegard.—Since he prays for her without ceasing, he in turn requests her prayers. 315

Hildegard’s reply.—She rebukes him because he loves the world and exhorts him to purify his desires in good work through the fear of God. 315

EPISTLE XCV.—Abbot H. to Hildegard.—While the Church suffers from schism, he asks what he should do. 316

Hildegard’s reply.—One must obey teachers so long as they do not oppose the Catholic faith, and have recourse to God, who will not abandon His Church. 316

EPISTLE XCVI.—Abbess Hadelheid of Gandersheim to Hildegard.—Raised by Hildegard, she requests the help of her and her sisters, and mutual fellowship between the sisters of their respective convents. 317

Hildegard’s reply.—That in the day of her prosperity she should perform good works with pure faith and give to God what is His. 318

EPISTLE XCVII.—Abbess N. to Hildegard.—She requests her prayers for herself and her congregation. 318

Hildegard’s reply.—That she should not be unstable or investigate vain matters. 319

EPISTLE XCVIII.—Abbess M. at Wetherswinkel to Hildegard.—That she may be willing to receive her and her own among the number of her daughters and aid them with prayers. 319

Hildegard’s reply.—That discretion must be observed in abstinence. 319

EPISTLE XCIX.—Abbess H. of Althena to Hildegard.—She rejoices in God’s gifts and desires to see her. 320

Hildegard’s reply.—Under figures, she exhorts her to fight for God. 321

EPISTLE C.—Abbess S. at Alturich to Hildegard.—Desiring to renounce the burden of government and shut herself up in a solitary cell, she asks that God’s good pleasure be made known through Hildegard. 321

Hildegard’s reply.—That it is not beneficial for her to cast away the burden of government. 322

EPISTLE CI.—Abbess Sophia at Kisingun to Hildegard.—She asks whether she ought to abandon the burden she bears. 322

Hildegard’s reply.—That the burden she bears, since it is acceptable to God, is not to be abandoned. 323

EPISTLE CII.—Abbess R. of Saint Mary at Regensburg to Hildegard.—She commends herself to Hildegard’s prayers, by which, she declares, she has been rescued from the jaws of death. 323

Hildegard’s reply.—That she should correct herself in certain corrupt customs and look to God. 324

EPISTLE CIII.—Abbess N. at Kaufungen to Hildegard.—She exhorts her to stir up the princes of the Church. 324

Hildegard’s reply.—That few days remain to her and that she should forestall death with good works. 324

EPISTLE CIV.—Abbess N. at Gerbstedt to Hildegard.—She asks to be helped by Hildegard’s prayers and promises her own in return. 325

Hildegard’s reply.—Concerning the fall of the first parents and their raising up through Christ. 325

EPISTLE CV.—Abbess N. of Mount Saint Cyriacus to Hildegard.—She commends herself and those entrusted to her to Hildegard’s prayers. 326

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts her not to be troubled in mind and not to exceed moderation in abstinence. 327

EPISTLE CVI.—Abbess N. at Lubboldesberge to Hildegard.—She requests consoling letters from her. 327

Hildegard’s reply.—That she is greatly loved by God. 328

EPISTLE CVII.—Abbess N. to Hildegard.—Assailed by temptations, she requests her counsel and the aid of her prayers. 328

Hildegard’s reply.—That one’s own will and fleshly desires must be abandoned in order to obey God. 328

EPISTLE CVIII.—Abbess N. at Widergoldesdorf to Saint Hildegard.—Desiring to renounce her rank, she asks what she ought to do. 329

Hildegard’s reply.—That she should steadfastly bear the burden imposed upon her and trust in God. 329

EPISTLE CIX.—Abbess H. of Crouchdal to Hildegard.—That she should indicate what in her is worthy of correction. 329

Hildegard’s reply.—That she judges others in matters in which she would not wish to be judged. 330

EPISTLE CX.—Abbess L. at Bamberg to Hildegard.—She requests from her and her convent a mutual fellowship of sisterhood. 330

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts her to labour and to hold her daughters under discipline. 331

EPISTLE CXI.—Abbess N. of the Old Monastery at Mainz to Hildegard.—That she should endeavour to appease God for her sins. 331

Hildegard’s reply.—That she should bear her burden most devoutly and persevere in God’s service. 331

EPISTLE CXII.—Abbess E. of the Upper Monastery at Regensburg to Hildegard.—Whether she may relinquish the charge entrusted to her, and whether she should fear anything concerning matters she had already investigated. 332

Hildegard’s reply.—That things God wishes to remain unknown must not be investigated, nor should she relinquish the charge imposed upon her. 333

EPISTLE CXIII.—Abbess N. of Nussim Monastery to Hildegard.—She requests the aid of her prayers concerning the unsettled condition of her monastery. 333

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts her to repentance and the performance of good works. 333

EPISTLE CXIV.—Abbess N. of Cologne to Hildegard.—Desiring to have her as a mother, she asks for consoling letters. 334

Hildegard’s reply.—That she should bear her burden firmly and restrain her sheep. 334

EPISTLE CXV.—Abbess N. of Didenkirkim to Hildegard.—She asks her for admonitory words that may build up her soul. 334

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts her to cultivate the soil of her heart, so that she may be useful to her own people. 335

EPISTLE CXVI.—Abbess T. of Andernach to Hildegard.—She wishes to be assured concerning certain customs of her monastery, especially whether she should admit only noble virgins. 336

Hildegard’s reply.—Women ought not seek adornment; white garments befit virgins; noble women must be distinguished from those of low birth, lest they hate one another. 337

EPISTLE CXVII.—Abbess A. of Crouchdal to Hildegard.—That she should pray to God, so that she may make satisfaction for offences committed in her office. 338

Hildegard’s reply.—She commends to her charity, obedience, and the renunciation of her own will. 339

EPISTLE CXVIII.—The nun G. to Hildegard.—How grievously she feels Hildegard’s absence. 341

Hildegard’s reply.—She congratulates her that she has embraced the narrow way. 342

EPISTLE CXIX.—The priest B. to Hildegard.—He is distressed that his purpose of leaving the world is delayed; he requests her prayers and her book for copying. 343

Hildegard’s reply.—She encourages him to pursue his purpose. 343

EPISTLE CXX.—V. to Hildegard.—He excuses himself for having visited her neither in person nor by writing. 344

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to contempt of the world. 344

EPISTLE CXXI.—The monk T. of Saint Benedict to Hildegard.—He desires to enjoy her presence, or at least to be strengthened in God by her letters. 344

Hildegard’s reply.—That his desires are good, and that he should be strong in battle. 345

EPISTLE CXXII.—B. to Hildegard.—Burdened with sins, he requests her prayers. 346

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to repentance, setting out its various stages. 346

EPISTLE CXXIII.—Master H. of Utrecht to Hildegard.—Refined in the furnace of tribulation, he desires to be refreshed by her writings and to know whether he is among those to be saved. 346

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should turn from evil and do good. 347

EPISTLE CXXIV.—The priests C. and B. at Rüthlingen to Hildegard.—They commend themselves to her prayers. 348

Hildegard’s reply.—That they should run to God and fight courageously for His sake. 348

EPISTLE CXXV.—The priest B. of Trier to Hildegard.—That she should write him consoling words, and instruct him how he may preside over those whom he must govern under the rule of priesthood. 349

Hildegard’s reply.—She teaches how he ought to conduct himself toward sinners. 350

EPISTLE CXXVI.—Brother S. to Hildegard.—Burdened with sins, he commends himself to her prayers. 350

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should sigh to God through repentance. 351

EPISTLE CXXVII.—Master V., theologian of Paris, to Hildegard.—He asks Saint Hildegard whether it may be said that fatherhood and divinity are not God. 351

Hildegard’s reply.—She answers that it has been shown to her in a vision that fatherhood and divinity are God. 352

EPISTLE CXXVIII.—Brother O. to Hildegard.—He laments the Church’s division by schism and asks her to intercede with prayers for it, and also for himself, since he was tormented by demons. 353

Hildegard’s reply.—Concerning the various kinds of demons and how they may be overcome. 354

EPISTLE CXXIX.—Dean N. of Saint Martin at Mainz to Hildegard.—He desires to see her and commends himself to her prayers. 355

Hildegard’s reply.—She exhorts him to repentance. 356

EPISTLE CXXX.—N. to Hildegard.—He commends to her faith his soul, body, and entire congregation. 356

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should understand what is beneficial and what is harmful. 357

EPISTLE CXXXI.—The monk H. of Maulbronn to Hildegard.—That she should send him something by way of heavenly admonition. 357

Hildegard’s reply.—Under a parable, she teaches that one must labour in this world. 358

EPISTLE CXXXII.—The monk N. of Ebra, of the Cistercian Order, to Hildegard.—He commends himself to her prayers and requests consoling words from her. 359

Hildegard’s reply.—She promises him future consolations, since he is pleasing to God. 360

EPISTLE CXXXIII.—V. of Vessonne to Hildegard.—Oppressed by sins, he asks whether he should still hope for pardon from God. 360

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should restore his mind to good things and hunger for righteousness. 361

EPISTLE CXXXIV.—Canoness H. of Utrecht to Hildegard.—That she should reveal to her the secrets of divine revelation concerning her condition. 361

Hildegard’s reply.—That she should rise quickly and flee from the devil. 362

[Col. 1361] EPISTLE CXXXV.—The monk and priest M. to Hildegard.—He requests the prayers of her and her sisters, promising his own to them in return. 362

Hildegard’s reply.—Under a certain parable, she exhorts him to charity, flight from the world, and love of true wisdom. 363

EPISTLE CXXXVI.—The priest N., master of the poor at Lutherum, to Hildegard.—He earnestly desires to hear salutary instruction from her, being ready to obey it. 363

Hildegard’s reply.—That he should imitate Christ’s example: as the true Samaritan, Christ healed the man who fell among robbers through Himself and the innkeepers, that is, the apostles. 364

EPISTLE CXXXVII.—The monks of Sigeberg to Hildegard.—They complain that she does not reply to them and ask that she disclose something concerning the condition
…may disclose something concerning the monastery of Sigeberg and send words of admonition. 366  
Hildegard’s reply.—That some of them shine like stars, while others languish in the darkness of weariness; and concerning the fall of the first angel through pride. 366  

EPISTLE CXXXVIII.—Of the monks of Hirsau.—They complain of their abbot, who, though they had done him no injury, did not cease, on the occasion of a disagreement between himself and the prior, to burden them with reproaches and slanders. 367  
Hildegard’s reply.—That God has not forgotten them, provided only that they trample down vices and do penance. 368  

EPISTLE CXXXIX.—Of the monks of Eberbach to Hildegard.—That she not conceal what in them requires correction. 369  
Hildegard’s reply.—That they beware lest they cast away the felicity which seems to be present in them through God’s predestination. 369  

EPISTLE CXL.—Of N., prior of Zwiefalten, to Hildegard.—How he may restore the discipline that has collapsed in his monastery. 370  
Hildegard’s reply.—She rebukes their negligence and urges them to come to their senses. 370  

EPISTLE CXLI.—Of the nuns of Zwiefalten to Hildegard.—That she show how they ought to return from the path of negligence to the path of correction. 371  
Hildegard’s reply.—That they avoid pride; that they not be dancers, nor go outside the monastery; and that they return to their first espousal. 371  

EPISTLE CXLII.—Of A., prior, and the convent of Mount Saint Disibod, to Hildegard.—They complain that, although she was brought up among them, she does not write to them or send admonitory words. 373  
Hildegard’s reply.—That they return to God. 374  

EPISTLE CXLIII.—Of the monks of Saint Eucharius at Trier to Hildegard.—They desire to be stirred up by the goads of her admonition. 376  
Hildegard’s reply.—She praises their holy manner of life. 376  

EPISTLE CXLIV.—Of N., prior, and the monks of Cîteaux, to Hildegard.—They desire to learn from her what in their order is displeasing to God. 380  
Hildegard’s reply. 380  

EPISTLE CXLV.—Of Abbot Henry and the convent of Mount Saint Disibod to Hildegard.—They desire her to write back to them concerning what in themselves displeases God, and ask that she commit the life of Saint Disibod to writing. 381  
Hildegard’s reply. 382

# *Book of Divine Works of a Simple Person*

Notice to the Reader. 739  

## Part One

# First Vision

I.—Presentation of the wondrous vision upon which the following work depends; and, within it, a detailed description of a certain divine image appearing in human form, together with its clothing and surroundings. 741  

II.—The words of that same image, through which Love is understood: it calls itself the fiery life of God’s substance and recounts the manifold effects of its power in the various natures or qualities of creation. 743  

III.—That God marked every creature in the human being made in His image and likeness; that, after the Fall, He restored that human being through His Incarnation solely out of the love of His goodness, and placed him in the blessedness which the fallen angel had lost; and that this is shown by the mystical meaning of the vision set forth above. 744  

IV.—That devout faith embraces the excellence of divine love, and that through this faith God is recognized as one in Trinity; and that, by the merit of this faith, God Himself protects human beings and brings them back to heavenly things. 745  

V.—That love of God and of neighbour, strengthened by the power of faith, cannot be separated. 745  

VI.—That everyone who submits to God in humble devotion, set aflame with the help of the Holy Spirit, overcomes both himself insofar as he is sinful and the devil; and that the angels, rejoicing in the good deeds of the righteous, praise the omnipotence of God. 745  

VII.—That from eternity all things existed without spatial location in God, and that, through His act of creation, they came forth distinguished by number, order, place, and time. 746  

VIII.—That the devil and the angels who deserted righteousness, although formerly endowed with great power, were reduced through their ingratitude or pride to being unable to do anything in any creature except insofar as they are permitted by heavenly command. 746  

IX.—That a human being who directs himself in imitation of his Creator, as though drawn away from a certain beastly irrationality, begins to shine with the radiance of rational nature. 747  

X.—That in the word of God saying, “Let there be light,” rational light—that is, the angels—was created; and that, after certain of them fell from blessedness, the Lord made another rational life, clothed in flesh—that is, the human being—to obtain the place and glory of the fallen. 747  

XI.—That God, gathering to Himself in the strength of His love those whom He has predestined, instructs them in every necessary matter by the infusion of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. 747  

XII.—That the Son of God, assuming human nature without the stain of sin and appearing in the flesh, called tax collectors and sinners to repentance and justified them through faith in Himself. 748  

XIII.—That the imitation of the love of the Son of God, who crushed the devil by His cross, still tramples down in His faithful people discord and the other vices, as well as that ancient deceiver of humankind himself, and reduces them to nothing. 748  

XIV.—That Adam and Eve, consenting to the persuasion of the devil, who envied them, lost the glory of their heavenly garment—that is, immortality. 749
