XV.—That God, taking pity on them, drove them from paradise into this exile in order to punish the fault of their transgression; and that whoever violates the fidelity of marriage established by God between them must, unless he repents, be punished by severe vengeance. 749  

XVI.—That, in the preaching of the incarnate Son of God, with the rise of the spiritual people, God’s promise to Abraham was fulfilled: that his offspring would be multiplied according to the number of the stars of heaven. 750  

XVII.—That God chose the Virgin Mary from the lineage of Abraham, who believed and obeyed Him, so that Christ, founder and ruler of the new—that is, spiritual—generation, might be born from her bodily. 750  

# Second Vision

I.—Description of the sphere of the whole world, with its circles, planets, and winds, appearing like a wheel in the breast of the image described in the first vision. 751  

II.—That the Godhead, like a complete wheel, having neither beginning nor end and bounded neither by place nor time, comprehends all things within itself. 755  

III.—Why the sphere of the world was shown or described in the book *Scivias* in the shape of an egg, but in this work in the likeness of a wheel. 755  

IV.—Concerning the two circles of bright and black fire: why one is placed beneath the other, how they cooperate with one another, and what they signify. 756  

V.—Concerning the circle of pure ether, which is third: what it accomplishes by its constitution, what it signifies, and why it is as dense as the two higher circles. [Col. 1363] 756  

VI.—Concerning the fourth circle, which appears in the form of watery air: how dense it is and what it signifies. 757  

VII.—Concerning the circle of strong, white, and bright air: with what usefulness it occupies the fifth place, how dense it is, what it signifies, and why it is joined to the circle above it so as to be, as it were, one with it. 757  

VIII.—Concerning the sixth circle, which seems to proceed from the higher regions in the likeness of thin air: what it accomplishes in its place and what is figured through it in mystical interpretation. 758  

IX.—Why these six circles are joined to one another without intervals, and what is indicated by this connection. 758  

X.—That the first circle kindles the others with its fire, the fourth moderates them with its light, and that this is shown figuratively in us. 759  

XI.—Concerning the line appearing to be stretched across the aforesaid wheel, as though from the sun’s first rising to its final setting, and what this likewise effects mystically. 759  

XII.—A testimony from the Apocalypse, and how it ought to be understood in order to express the same matter. 759  

XIII.—That the mass of the earth, like a globe, is set beneath the aforesaid six circles, at an equal distance from the five higher ones, fixed immovably in the middle of the sixth—that is, the thin-air circle—and what meaning is to be inferred from this. 759  

XIV.—Words of Paul appropriate to the same meaning, and how they are to be understood. 760  

XV.—Concerning the image in human form appearing in the middle of the aforesaid wheel, with its head, feet, and hands outstretched and touching the circle of strong, white, and bright air; and what both the image itself and this posture signify. 761  

XVI.—Concerning the four heads of beasts appearing in the four regions of the same wheel, and what they signify both in the world and in the human being. 761  

XVII.—Why the principal eastern wind is seen in the form of a leopard’s head above the head of the human image, in the circle of pure ether; and why its two accompanying winds are shown, one in the appearance of a crab’s head and the other in the likeness of a stag’s head. 762  

XVIII.—Why these heads in the wheel breathe toward the human image, and a moral description of their meaning. 763  

XIX.—A testimony from the Song of Songs appropriate to the same matters, and how it is to be understood. 764  

XX.—Why the principal western wind appears in the likeness of a wolf’s head beneath the feet of the aforesaid image, in the circle of watery air; and why its two accompanying winds are shown, one in the form of a stag and the other in the form of a crab’s head. 765  

XXI.—Why these heads too, like those above, direct their breath toward the human image, and their moral meaning. 766  

XXII.—Words of Isaiah pertaining to the same matter, and how they should be understood. 767  

XXIII.—Why the principal southern wind is shown on the right side of the same image as a lion’s head, in the circle of bright fire; and why its two accompanying winds are seen, one in the form of a serpent and the other in the figure of a lamb’s head. 768  

XXIV.—Why these, like the preceding heads, emit their movements into the wheel and toward that same image. 769  

XXV.—That a human being must diligently investigate how all these things relate to the salvation of his soul and to the judgments of God, who leaves nothing unexamined in carrying them out. 770  

XXVI.—That no order of virtues, distinct either from itself or within itself, should be neglected by anyone, because the effect of virtue brings a human being to the righteousness or rectitude of heavenly things. 770  

XXVII.—A testimony from Psalm 117 agreeing with this, and how it is to be understood. 771  

XXVIII.—Why the principal northern wind appears on the left side of that human image as though a bear’s head, in the circle of black fire; and why its two accompanying winds are seen, one in the form of a lamb and the other in the form of a serpent’s head. 772  

XXIX.—Why these likewise, as the heads above do, direct the force of their movements into the wheel and toward that same image. 773  

XXX.—Words of David in the same Psalm 117, relevant to these matters, and their explanation. 774  

XXXI.—Concerning the seven planets appearing at distinct intervals in different circles of the wheel of the aforesaid image. 775  

XXXII.—How these planets were arranged in the firmament by God, the maker of the world, and concerning their various effects. 775  

XXXIII.—What is signified by the appearance of three of these planets in the circle of bright fire, one in the region of black fire, and likewise three in the circuit of pure ether. 780  

XXXIV.—Toward what the rays of the first three planets, which are seen issuing from them in this vision, are directed; and [Col. 1364] what is signified both by the planets themselves and by their rays. 780  

XXXV.—Why the sun, situated in their midst, appears to emit more rays than the others; and what both it and its rays signify. 781  

XXXVI.—Toward what the three lowest planets direct their rays, and what is figured both by them and by their rays. 782  

XXXVII.—That every faithful person, although eminent in virtues, is nonetheless at times beneficially deprived, as it were, of them and assailed by temptations, lest, deceived by presumptuous pride, he perish. 783  

XXXVIII.—A testimony from the book of Isaiah introduced to indicate these matters, and how it is to be understood. 784  

XXXIX.—Concerning the sixteen principal stars, set at equal intervals in the circle of bright fire around the firmament, in order to strengthen the firmament and moderate the winds. 784  

XL.—That the distinct multitude of other stars, placed in the two circles—namely, those of pure ether and of white, bright air—warms the firmament and restrains the clouds from passing their bounds. 785  

XLI.—Concerning the four states, appearing on the right and left of the image in the form of tongues because of their movement, and what usefulness they possess. 786  

XLII.—A mystical and clear explanation of the number, order, and position of the sixteen principal stars. 786  

XLIII.—Likewise, a mystical explanation of the distinct multiplicity and arrangement of the other common stars. 787  

XLIV.—Likewise, a mystical explanation of the usefulness of the four states moving like tongues on the right or left side of the image. 787  

XLV.—That every faithful person who devoutly follows the footsteps of the Son of God is strengthened amid temptations by the defense of virtues and reaches heavenly joys; and words of Isaiah, suitably explained in confirmation of this. 788  

XLVI.—Concerning the exceedingly bright light proceeding in the likeness of children from the mouth of the image bearing the wheel in its breast; with these children it appears to measure the signs of that image, wheel, and the circles shown beforehand; and the mystical explanation of these matters. 789  

# Third Vision

I.—A brief collection of certain visions touching on natural philosophy: concerning winds whirling about the firmament above and below; concerning the upper circle, which sends forth a wind to turn back the planets from west to east and regulate them in their course; concerning the humours of the human being, which receive the qualities of air and mutually colliding winds; and concerning the veins and intestines of the whole human body—how they adhere to and cooperate with one another in their different functions, and for what causes they sometimes depart from their balance or proper tempering. 789  

II.—That all creatures serve usefulness no less in the soul than in the body; and what is signified by the eastern and southern winds, with their accompanying winds, being seen to revolve around the firmament from east to west. 794  

III.—What is signified by the southern and northern winds likewise, at the different solstices of the year: the former gradually rising from south to north, the latter gradually descending from north to south. 795  

IV.—What the circle appearing in the upper fire signifies, both as encircling the whole firmament and as sending forth a wind that blows through the upper regions and moderates the planets’ course by turning it back. 795  

V.—Words of the prophet Habakkuk introduced to make the same meaning clear, and their exposition. 796  

VI.—What is signified by the changing of the human humours when, according to the differing qualities of mutually colliding winds and air, they are stirred and altered. 796  

VII.—A testimony from the Proverbs of Solomon inserted to elucidate this meaning, and how it is to be understood. 798  

VIII.—That, through the manifold interdependence of winds and air, the differing course of sun and moon, or the additional judgment of God, the human being also undergoes change and sometimes experiences variations of health and illness; and what is figured thereby in the spiritual life. 798  

IX.—That the humours in the human being move now more sharply, now more mildly, according to the type of temperament found in certain animals or beasts; and that, in accordance with the changes or impulses of these humours, affections and thoughts in the human being vary through frequent alternation. 799  

X.—That a human being is readier for work on the right side because the liver, in which is the source of heat, lies on the right; but is better suited on the left for bearing burdens because the heart or lung, positioned toward the left and possessing the pulse of respiration, is there; and what these things spiritually signify in that person. 800 [Col. 1365]  

XI.—Words of the prophet Isaiah appropriate for establishing the meaning of these matters, and the sense in which they should be understood. 801  

XII.—What is signified in the human being by the humours within him: sprinkling the navel, which is considered the head of the viscera, and the loins, in which wantonness resides; sometimes touching the veins of the kidneys and those regions; and through these ascending even to the veins of the spleen, lungs, and heart. 801  

XIII.—That the veins of the brain, heart, and liver strengthen the kidneys; that the veins of the kidneys strengthen the calves by their downward course; and that, returning upward with the veins of the calves and joined to one another in suitable places, they confer upon both sexes the powers of generation. Also, that the muscles, arms, and legs are full of veins and humours, with a brief illustration of these matters. 802  

XIV.—That excessive stretching of the nerves and veins throughout the body brings weariness to a person who runs; which combination or impulse of veins excites that momentary pleasure; and a moral and useful explanation of these matters in the human being. 802  

XV.—For what reasons, when phlegm and humours in the human being are at times corrupted, that person suffers in the body either epilepsy or other illnesses; and by what evils, according to their meanings, the soul is generally afflicted. 803  

XVI.—Words of the prophet Hosea applicable to these matters, and the sense in which they should be understood. 804  

XVII.—That the veins of a person’s kidneys, sometimes affected by humours stirred unjustly, shake other veins and even dry out the marrow of the bones; and what affliction, signified by these things, seizes the person inwardly. 804  

XVIII.—What, in a person’s spiritual life, is signified by humours excessively abounding in the chest, agitating the liver and the veins of the ears or kidneys, and ascending from the navel to the brain. 805  

XIX.—What advance in the inward life of thoughts is signified by the same humours in the human body when they are balanced and properly tempered; and a testimony from the Song of Songs agreeing with this, together with its exposition. 806  

# Fourth Vision
I.—Various visions briefly gathered under one chapter: concerning the firmament—how dense it is together with all that adheres to it; concerning the harmful effects of certain circles, how these are repelled or moderated by the opposition of others; and concerning the milky zone, which appears like a bent bow. 807

II.—That God, Creator of all things, confirms the lower by the higher, and by them also purifies sinners through punishment; and what the firmament’s equal density on every side of the earth signifies in the human being. 807

III.—Likewise, concerning the firmament suitably arranged by the Creator, for its several functions, with fire, ether, waters, stars, and winds; whence scales are produced, falling like sparks from the bright fire of the upper circle and harming both the earth and its inhabitants; and what inner vengeance is shown by this. 808

IV.—That black fire enclosed in the second circle, whether stirred by God’s judgment or by the collision of winds, sends forth a cloud that dries up the earth’s greenery, becoming dangerous now through heat, now through a flooding of the limbs; and what this signifies. 808

V.—That the circle of pure ether moderates upper and lower things by its pleasantness, resists the scales of the first and the cloud of the second circle lest they harm the lands excessively; and what usefulness or signification belongs to the smoke proceeding from the upper waters made hot by heavenly fire. 809

VI.—Concerning the pestilential cloud extending toward the earth from the circle of strong, white air: whence it arises; how the density of watery air resists it lest it become excessively harmful; that no plagues are ever brought upon human beings except by God’s judgment; and what all these things signify. 809

VII.—Concerning the moisture issuing from thin air, of what use it is; that drops of rain are turned into snow by the upper cold; and that this same thin air protects and fertilizes the earth from above. 810

VIII.—How clouds in this upper air, modified by fire or cold, appear now bright and now shadowy; how they pour out rain, as though pressed from certain breasts, not suddenly but gradually; and what they signify within us. 810

IX.—Concerning the cloud called milky: that by its extension or curvature it strengthens the air enclosed by it; and what this signifies. 811

X.—Words of Job consonant with this subject, and the sense in which they should be understood. 811

XI.—That, strengthened in God as a kind of firmament, the human being ought always diligently to consider Him and His works, since God made the human being, among all creatures, especially rational, in order to know and glorify Him. [Col. 1366] 811

XII.—That God marked the beauty of His works in the first angel; that, in order to show in which region of the world hell lies, He illuminated three parts by the presence of sun and moon, but left the fourth part, namely the north, devoid of light; that darkness is exposed by the brilliance of light; and that light is more pleasing by contrast with darkness. 812

XIII.—Concerning the pride or swelling of the first angel and his followers against God; their casting down into the place of darkness; and the cry of the blessed angels who abhor them. 812

XIV.—That God, holding from eternity in the secret of His counsel that humanity itself should come into being—a humanity always to oppose the devil, who could not discover this mystery, and to take his place—made the human being in His image and likeness; and that in this human being, formed of soul, bones, and flesh, He recapitulated all the creatures of the greater world. 813

XV.—How a human being’s external bearing or form is assigned to the soul in accordance with its inward progress or decline. 814

XVI.—That in their constitution the firmament and the human being received much likeness from God their maker; and what this shows in the human soul. 814

XVII.—That in a human head, through three equal divisions of measurement, namely from the crown to the throat, the three upper circles of the firmament, together with the two circles inserted between them, are to be assigned; how the density of those circles is allotted in an equal division around the head; and how these correspond symbolically to the powers of the soul. 815

XVIII.—A description of certain measurements found in the lips, ears, shoulders, and throat of the human being; how, in accordance with them, the inward person ought to conduct himself in God’s work or in penitence; and that the wicked and unrepentant are often greatly confounded because they cannot take penitence away from humankind. 816

XIX.—Concerning the two powers of the soul: one is assisted in matters pertaining to God; the other performs its office in animating or governing its body. 817

XX.—Words of David, and the sense in which they should be understood, pertaining to the diverse exercises of soul and body. 818

XXI.—That, as the earth’s functions are fulfilled through the firmament and the differing qualities of its circles, so the whole body is governed through the head and the senses especially active in it; and that in accordance with these a ruling faculty—namely reason, by which it calls upon heavenly things—and other powers by which the soul administers the body have been bestowed upon the soul. 818

XXII.—Concerning the intervals and reciprocal cooperation of the seven planets; how, from the summit of the human brain to the bottom of the forehead, these planets are to be marked off in seven places of equal measure; and how, in accordance with this, the soul, existing through five senses, ought to exercise itself and its body in good dispositions and works according to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. 819

XXIII.—That the human brain, divided into three chambers and supplying sensation to the whole body, occupies the place of the sun, which, shining upon three regions of the world, strengthens all things on earth by moderating or nurturing them and also kindles the moon with its fire. 820

XXIV.—That in the same way the soul, governing its body by its powers and worshipping God as one in Trinity, seems, as it were by imitating that planet, to make alternately a kind of day or night: provided that, strengthened and elevated by the spirit of fortitude signified by the sun, it shines with the light of holy works; but at another time it acts while yielding to the desires of the flesh. 821

XXV.—That, just as all the veins of the body supply heat to the brain when it draws moisture from the internal organs, so the upper circles stand by the sun with their fires when it at times spreads dew and rain, lest it fail through heat; and that corresponding harmonies or discordances are found between soul and flesh. 822

XXVI.—That, as brain and intestines need purging when they overflow with humors, so air and earth in autumn appear to be purged—the former by long coagulated threads, the latter in certain places by filthy foam; and that in the same way lustful flesh is shown to be dried out by exudation, while the soul is cleansed by the labor of penitence. 823

XXVII.—That the vessel of the brain holds the place of the upper fire approaching the sun; that the moisture of watery air moderates that sun and heat, setting a limit to its course lest it burn up what lies beneath; and how, in accordance with this, the soul, placed under God’s power and judgment and endowed with reason, ought discreetly to govern both itself and its body in all things. 824

XXVIII.—That, as the blackness of the brain, coagulated by heat and moisture, diffuses phlegm or bruising through the human body, so the black fire in the second circle brings storms and lightning upon the world; and that in this manner too, the soul corrupted by pride and the flesh by desires have diverse conflicts, each resisting the other. [Col. 1367] 825

XXIX.—That, as the human body is strengthened by the brain, so upper and lower things are strengthened by the sun, which stands in the middle of the planets; concerning the fact that, when three parts of the world are illuminated by the sun, God left the fourth dark and cold; and the mystical meaning of this with respect to the inward person. 826

XXX.—What the sun’s rising or setting signifies in human actions; and what it signifies when it does not appear, now hidden by clouds or the severity of storms, and when, these having been wiped away, it restores its light to the lands. 827

XXXI.—That the forehead, situated between brain and eyes, receives diseases arising from brain and stomach just as the moon receives what descends from above and rises from below; that the eyes, by their whiteness and pupils within their moisture, indicate pure ether, stars, and vapor rising from the waters below; and the manifold consideration of these things in relation to dispositions of the soul. 828

XXXII.—For what reasons both tears, collected from the humors of the body, flow from the eyes, and rains, drawn upward from the lower waters, flow down from the clouds; and a careful exposition of these matters in relation to the affections of the soul. 829

XXXIII.—That, just as no visible form exists without a name, neither does it exist without measure; and what the equal outward measure of the eyes signifies in the inward person. 831

XXXIV.—That the judgment of the rational soul ought to assign reward to good and punishment to evil; that no penitence would suffice in comparison with eternal recompense, even if it exceeded all the sand and drops of the sea. 831

XXXV.—That, as the human being is fitted together by eyes and the other senses, and heaven is illuminated by sun, moon, and stars supplying one another with alternating light, so the soul is illuminated by the true works of penitence and quickly washed from sins by sighs or tears. 831

XXXVI.—That, as the chin supports the head and upper parts through the clouds, as bones in the human being are hardened by fire and marrows coagulated by cold, and as the earth is cultivated through summer and winter to bear fruit, so the minds of the faithful are strengthened for every good thing by the fire of the Holy Spirit and the dew of compunction, while they are weakened by the sluggish numbness of torpor and negligence. 832

XXXVII.—Likewise, concerning the usefulness of the senses in the human being and the stars in the world; that the devil’s deceit, by which he deceived Eve and through her transmitted original sin to all posterity, is like a mist which, rising from harmful air, covers the earth and damages its fruits, hindering sight so that the brightness of day cannot be seen. 833

XXXVIII.—That the eyebrows, given as a defense to the eyes, signify the courses of the moon, subject to monthly increases and decreases; and that accordingly constancy and confidence in the fear of God must be maintained by souls amid prosperity and adversity. 833

XXXIX.—Concerning the nose, mouth, and ears: how much they avail in the human being; what their diverse effects signify in the elements of the external world and in the inward realities of the soul; and that in all things the examples of the saints must be followed. 834

XL.—That the flooding of waters is shown in the human tongue; and what is figured inwardly by that outward inundation of waves. 835

XLI.—What power or strength is expressed in us by the teeth, which are hollow and have no marrow. 836

XLII.—Why an infant, although it has bones, is born without teeth; why people often lose these same teeth as they decline into old age; and what is shown by these things. 836

XLIII.—How and whence teeth are formed in children, why they are meanwhile afflicted by severe pain, and the meaning of this in us. 837

XLIV.—That the teeth, which break down and carry about the foods by which the human being is nourished, resemble a mill; and how the soul imitates these things within itself. 837

XLV.—That through chin, throat, and neck, which have diverse offices in the body, are indicated the various effects of clouds in the world and the manifold effects of virtues in the soul. 838

XLVI.—That by the hair, which outwardly adorns the head fittingly, are shown drops of dew or rain, by which the earth, made fruitful, is clothed in the beauty of grasses or fruits; and inwardly, the cultivation of innocence, chastity, and humility by which the soul shines before God. 839 [Col. 1368]

XLVII.—Whence it comes that the hair on some people’s heads, retaining its strength, is not uprooted, while on others’ heads, weakened by baldness, it falls away; and that accordingly both fertility and barrenness are denoted—outwardly, that of the earth and its fruits; inwardly, that of virtues in the soul. 839

XLVIII.—That the position of a human being, having east before the face, west behind, south to the right, and north to the left, signifies diverse effects in the soul. 840

XLIX.—That, as shoulders and arms with hands adhere to the neck, so the four principal winds with their collateral winds adhere to the firmament; how four powers in human beings—thought, speech, intention, and groaning—are likened to these same four winds; and what is signified by the greater strength of the right side than the left. 840

L.—That the soul, sent into the body through God’s Spirit, permeates the whole of it with its powers, just as the dispositions of the winds traverse the entire world. 842

LI.—That, as a human being is governed and supported by arms and legs, so certain winds assist others in strengthening the firmament; and what either these things, or the gentle breathing or turbulent course of those same winds, figure in the soul. 842

LII.—How the turnings of the winds are to be assigned in the bends of the arms and the joints of shoulders or hands; that, as right and left, firmament and earth are compared with one another in certain respects, so the human being performs all works, though contrary, through knowledge of good and evil. 843

LIII.—Concerning the threefold dimension of the human body and the thickness of the sphere of the world; and how human life, according to childhood, adolescence, and old age, corresponds to the same dimension. 843

LIV.—That the upper part of the earth is tender, soft, and penetrable, whereas its lower part is tenacious, hard, and impenetrable; and what is found in the human soul in accordance with these things. 844

LV.—What the measure of shoulders, elbows, hands, and feet, down to the tip of the great toe, resembling the winds in a certain proportion, shows in the qualities of the inward person. 844

LVI.—What the breadthwise measure of the thighs toward the front, and the lengthwise measure from the navel to the places of digestion, proportionally corresponding to the breadth or thickness of the earth, show in diverse dispositions of the soul. 845

LVII.—That the space from the end of the throat to the navel signifies air; that the soul, which vivifies the whole body and moves it to action, is compared to this air, which penetrates all empty spaces and tempers the earth in different ways for bearing fruit. 845

LVIII.—That birds are borne through the air for flight, and that certain fishes are nourished in the waters in such a way that they live for some time without food; and that in this manner the human being, following not the desires of the flesh but those of the soul, should fly through contemplation and be fed by the sweetness of the Scriptures. 847

LIX.—That sea and rivers are moved through the air, the body through veins infused with blood, and the soul through virtues, through which it may, like earth watered with rivulets, bring forth the shoots of good works. 847

LX.—That, as earth dissolved into mud by summer heat and winter cold is made pregnant for every kind of germination, so the human being, soul and flesh contending with one another, brings forth now the fruit of virtue, now that of vices. 848

LXI.—That, as a human breast contains heart, liver, and lung, so air contains in reality the heat, dryness, and moisture of the breezes; and that in this manner memory contains thoughts and works, arranging them for the soul. 848

LXII.—That, as the heart is sustained by liver, lung, and the other intestines connected with it, and as the seasons of day and night and the air vary by alternating calm and storms, so human life is now shaken by the whirlwind of vices amid conflicts between flesh and soul, now rejoices in the brightness of virtues. 849

LXIII.—That, as the belly encloses and retains within itself, for the usefulness of the whole body, the organs and foods crushed by the teeth’s grinding, so the soul ought to store in the secret place of memory thoughts for its correction and ponder them with careful discernment. 849

LXIV.—That the swellings of flesh which project on the breast and are called breasts signify, outwardly, the fertility of the air and, inwardly, human desires attached to the heart; and that, as woman is soft and weak in comparison with man, so the pleasure of the flesh has no strength compared with the powers of the soul. 850

LXV.—That woman, in view of her weakness, looking to the man’s provision, ought always to be subject to him and ready to serve; and what their outward common manner of life signifies inwardly. [Col. 1369] 851

LXVI.—That whoever has wiped away sins through penitence should no longer be ashamed of them; and that one who afflicts oneself through fasts and prayers adorns one’s soul as with a purple garment. 852

LXVII.—That, as air brings the fruits of the earth to ripeness through heat and moisture, so heart, liver, and lung warm the belly for preparing and digesting food; and that God consumes the perverse habits of sinners with the fire of His zeal. 852

LXVIII.—Words of David pertaining to the same subject, and the sense in which they should be understood. 852

LXIX.—That the softness of the belly, enclosed by ribs and bones, signifies the softness of fruitful earth interspersed with stones; what is also expressed through these things in the differing condition of human life; with a verse of Psalm XVI adduced as supporting testimony. 853

LXX.—That, as flowers are cast off when fruit succeeds them, so hunger is driven away when satiety comes; and that in the same manner the soul, having completed penitence for the sins in which it was wasting away as if from hunger, is satisfied by God’s justice in the performance of holy works. 854

LXXI.—By what correspondences stomach, world, and soul mutually strengthen one another; that God never wishes the human being to be without the law of a commandment; and what the greenery of summer, the dryness of winter, and the world’s own vast capacity signify in that person. 854

LXXII.—That, in likeness to air assisting earth in fruitfulness, the soul too moves the body through its powers to carry out every work; and that if these works are upright, it, adorned for eternity, perfectly beholds God, angels, and blessed souls, but if they are perverse, it is driven, as unclean, from this vision. 855

LXXIII.—That, as earth, if it became green and bore fruit everywhere twice yearly, would dry out and turn to dust, so the soul would fail in its work if it served all its desires and pleasures of the flesh without moderation; and that, like earth bearing fruit unevenly, because of its own mutability and its conflict with flesh, now in progress and now in decline, it can attain perfectly in this life neither the faith commended in the Gospel nor the vision of God lost in paradise. 856

LXXIV.—That, as the veins of heart, liver, and lung assist the stomach in receiving or expelling foods, while continual or excessive fullness or emptiness would harm that stomach, so the soul is indeed present to the body in all its works, but it would weary of it if it allowed that body always to follow the desires of the flesh. 857

LXXV.—That, as human flesh is harmed if it receives food-nourishment either excessively or less than necessary, so the soul is harmed if it adheres more or less than is just to strictness or relaxation; and that the stomach, receiving clean foods but rejecting foul-smelling ones, signifies the person who delights in sins but is afterward cleansed through penitence. 857

LXXVI.—That, as the navel is the strength of all the inward parts attached to it and the circumference of the earth is the container of the other creatures, so all things done through body and soul, whether good or evil, refer to the soul itself; and that there is a great difference between those who sin through pride and those who sin through negligence. 858

LXXVII.—That the navel is also compared to the earth which sends forth muddy and watery impurities in marshes, because heat, cold, and moisture force food and drink digested beneath it downward to be expelled; and that likewise the soul, overcome by pleasures of the flesh and entangled in filthy works, must be cast down to lower places of punishment unless it is cleansed by penitential sighs. 859

LXXVIII.—That, as earth flourishes and blooms through summer and the human being through youth, and likewise earth through winter and the human being through old age become dry and wither, so the soul, remaining in the body and compelling it to serve itself, grows green by ascending from virtue to virtue through good works and the examples of the Son of God; and afterward, drawn from the body as though adorned with precious stones, it rests before God while eagerly awaiting the recovery of the body in which it had labored. 860

LXXIX.—What the strength or wantonness of the kidneys, and the richness of earth—which, moderated, produces abundant fruits but, unmoderated, barren ones—signify in the diverse dispositions of the soul. 860

LXXX.—That earth is set in the midst of the air, fortified against storms by mountains and hills, partly warm or cold and partly tempered by heat and frost, like a city secured with towers and bulwarks; and that in this way the soul is adorned and defended, in its manifold conflict against the desires of the flesh, by the protection of holy works. [Col. 1370] 861

LXXXI.—That, as earth is so situated as to be tempered on every side by the sun, so the soul subject to God ought to be permeated and illuminated by the light of wisdom through the power of discernment. 862

LXXXII.—That a human being, made in the likeness of earth, has bones without marrow in the place of stones and bones with marrow in the place of trees; and that, according to the quality of one’s conduct, one receives symbolically either the hardness of stones or the pleasantness of a flowering garden or fruitful orchard. 862

LXXXIII.—Likewise, that as air supports and holds earth, set in its midst at an equal distance on every side, so body and soul, joined by God, though greatly different in nature, ought patiently to support and instruct one another in jointly carrying out the commands of their Creator. 863

LXXXIV.—That the bladder, which receives and expels drink, shows the courses of rivers flowing through the earth; and that in this manner the soul, victorious over the flesh, ought to irrigate its body with the streams of God’s commandments, receiving what is good and casting out what is evil, with a verse of Psalm CXVIII adduced as supporting testimony. 863

LXXXV.—That the parts of the body through which food and drink are digested signify the hidden subterranean channels of rivers; and the complaint of a soul defiled by muddy and foul-smelling works, yet breathing toward God through hope of penitence and Christ’s passion, with a verse of Psalm XLI adduced as pertinent testimony. 864

LXXXVI.—That the back and sides of the human being indicate the plains of earth, while the thighs and buttocks indicate its hills and ruggedness—earth below hard and impenetrable, constricting its upper part, which is soft; and that likewise, by the powers of the soul, the softness of flesh is restrained from vices, so that, adorned with the pearls of virtues, it may stir the holy angels to wonder at it and to praise God. 865

LXXXVII.—Words of Saint John the Apostle in his Apocalypse, contemplating and describing the beauty of Christ’s bride, that is, the holy soul; and of David in the Psalm proclaiming the excellence of the human being. 866

LXXXVIII.—Likewise, concerning the comparison of hard and soft earth, uninhabitable through heat or cold; whence earthquakes occur; that if the same earth were not, as it were, iron and steel beneath, it would be rent by the excessive heat at the sun’s rising and the excessive cold at its setting; and concerning the manifold contest of flesh and soul according to the foregoing. 866

LXXXIX.—Words of David in Psalm CI, lamenting the swiftness of his days and his failing strength. 868

XC.—That earth, though round over all its surface, is not flat because of the swellings of hills and mountains which it bears on every side; and that this signifies the uneven course of human conduct because of the various conflicts of virtues and vices occurring between soul and flesh. 868

XCI.—That, as the lower surface of the earth repels like iron the waters striking and flowing about it, so the power of the soul, like steel which sharpens other tools, ought to tame and repel from itself the devil’s deceit and assaults. 869

XCII.—That the bendings, alike and unlike, found in the human being from thigh through knee and ankle to the end of the great joint of the foot, and from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, signify in the world the curvatures and turnings of oceans and rivers; and in the human being signify impulses, the heat of lusts, and the manifold interlockings of natures and oppositions of flesh and soul. 869

XCIII.—Likewise, that the bends of shoulders and arms, hands, loins, knees, and feet, in which there are twelve greater flexions, indicate the currents and spaces of the four principal winds and their eight collateral winds, by which they differ from one another; and that these same winds are mutually moderated by heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. 871

XCIV.—Specifically, concerning the dangerous harshness and harmful blast of the north wind, which sometimes in summer harms fruits with cold moisture and dries trees, obscures the sun, and changes the moon’s brightness by various heats. 871

XCV.—How all these matters concerning the measures or bends of human limbs or winds, treated in the two preceding chapters, as well as the alternation of day, night, and hours, are to be referred to the soul; and that God equipped the soul with four powers, which according to the body it possesses from the elements—fire, air, water, and earth—and likewise, according to itself, with four powers as with certain wings, for governing both itself and its body. 872

XCVI.—Likewise, concerning the creation of the north wind, and how what has been said specifically concerning its harshness and the injuries it outwardly causes among creatures should be understood of the suggestions of vices by which soul and body are inwardly provoked by the devil. [Col. 1371] 874

XCVII.—The reason why God, raising or setting Adam upright from the earth, first arranged him so that he had east before his face, south on his right, and north on his left; that in his short and small stature He gathered the immense structure of the whole world; and that He subjected all creatures to Adam’s dominion and to the powers of his senses. 876

XCVIII.—Likewise, manifold explanations, sometimes with fitting scriptural testimonies added, of how the seasons and months of the whole year, according to the properties of their qualities, the sun’s ascent or descent, and the moon’s increase or decrease, are assigned to human qualities: both according to the divisions or measurements of limbs and ages, or the properties of bodily humors, and according to the diverse progress and decline of dispositions of the mind. 877

XCIX.—Words of David in Psalm CIII relevant to these matters. 884

C.—That the human being, created in God’s image and sitting like another lord upon the throne of earth, ruling every creature made for his sake, is God’s complete work and greatly pleases Him; that the one sex was made to help and console the other; and that man bears the form of Christ’s divinity, woman that of His humanity. 885

CI.—Words of David in Psalm CIV, and an exposition of them: how they should be understood concerning Christ’s incarnation and power, and the subjection of His enemies. 885

CII.—That the human being, marked by signs of God’s omnipotence through the five senses, ought to know and worship the Creator as one in Trinity and three in unity; for this purpose the human being was both created and restored after the Fall, that he might be lord of the world and make up the tenth choir in heaven. 886

CIII.—That the nature of the soul is fiery and of manifold efficacy in its powers, through which it knows God, understands and governs itself, gives sensation to its body, and moves it to action. 886

CIV.—That God judges the human being according to works, whether for life or for punishment; that the holy soul, stripped of the body, fully sees God, whom it cannot now see because of the hindering corruption of the flesh; and that it longingly awaits the Day of Judgment in order to receive its beloved garment, that is, its own body, so that in it it may enjoy without end, with the angels, contemplation of and praise for God. 888

CV.—An exposition of the first chapter of the Gospel according to John, from the passage where it is written, “In the beginning was the Word,” to “full of grace and truth.” This exposition treats of the eternity of the Word of God; of creatures, and how they existed in the Creator’s art before they existed in themselves, without being coeternal with Him; of the creation of angels and God’s zealous punishment of apostate spirits; of the counsel to make the human being in God’s image; and of how the power of the Creator’s might and the light of His wisdom shine forth in the construction of the human body. It also treats of God’s incarnation, the words of teaching and examples of righteousness which He set forth to the world, the restoration of fallen humankind, and its blessedness after this life. 888

## Part Two

## Fifth Vision
I.—Vision of great wonder, in which the globe is distinguished into five parts, and the dimensions and qualities of those parts, filled alike with light and pleasantness, and with the horror of punishments and darknesses, are related; likewise two spheres, one encircled by a sapphire colour and the other shining with luminous rays, together with their surroundings, are described with subtle precision. 901

II.—That the wisdom and power of God the Artificer shine forth wondrously in this: that He has suspended the element of earth, not angular but round, divided neither into more nor fewer than five parts for a determinate rational cause, motionless amid the other three elements; and that He has endowed man, after the pattern of the earth’s fivefold division, with five senses in this life, and will restore him whole from the dust of the grave in the life to come. 903

III.—Likewise, concerning the five divisions of the earth: how they are mutually tempered by their natural qualities, and how they correspond to the five senses in human beings. 903

IV.—That, to one contemplating the division of the earth’s two parts—the southern and the northern—each distinguished into three subdivisions, these things appear; and how they are to be understood in relation to the body, soul, and works of man. 904

V.—That the fifth, central part of the whole earth, appearing square and itself divided into three distinctions, [Col. 1372] is rendered uninhabitable here by heat, there by cold, and habitable elsewhere by temperateness; and what is signified here by these things in human conduct. 905

VI.—Likewise concerning the qualities of those four parts, and the places in which punishments are assigned for the purification of the penitent souls of human beings: mild in one place, grave in another, and most severe elsewhere, differing according to the kinds of faults of those who are examined; and why, in the middle regions of those same parts, there are not punishments but certain monstrous horrors. 906

VII.—That the judgments of God which come upon the earth or upon human beings are poured out from the punitive places of those same parts; that certain very high and very hard mountains are set in opposition to the punishments and darknesses of hell, lest they occupy the world; and in which places of the parts souls are appointed to be examined according to the character of their deeds. 907

VIII.—Words from the Apocalypse of John the Apostle corresponding to this subject, in which, through the four horses—white, red, black, and pale—the four periods and their qualities, from the beginning to the end of the world, are subtly described. 908

IX.—That the ancient enemy, envying man the heavenly glory which he lost, continually rejoices in man’s punishments, and therefore eagerly strives to defile him with the horror of hatred, murder, the Sodomitic crime, and other vices. 910

X.—That the red sphere and the wings surrounding it on both sides, above and below, displayed in this vision, signify the zeal of God by which sins are punished with charity, and His protections by which those to be saved are defended. 911

XI.—That the red circle, extending in the form of an arc around the outer western region, signifies the extension of God’s vengeance against those outside the integrity of the true faith and the compass of good works. 911

XII.—Concerning the structure appearing above the roundness of the earth; the pavement and the star shining above it; the other sphere and the rays of stars glittering between the same wings; and the intervals by which all these were separated: how they refer to the City of God, which is the Church, to Christ, to the Holy Spirit and His gifts, and to the angels, by whose guardianship the saints are protected. 912

XIII.—Concerning the outer darkness and punishments or torments of diverse kinds in which the souls of the damned are tortured with the devil and his followers; in which parts these are found; and that no one living in the body can comprehend the dreadful torments of hell. 912

XIV.—That God, the one life subsisting in Himself, received being from no one but gave being to all; likewise concerning the creation of the angels, the fall of the proud, and the confirmation of the blessed spirits; and that the devil, although he always labours at this, cannot destroy the number of those to be saved. 913

XV.—That when man, made in the power of the divine light, was deceived by the devil’s fraud, God created a garment from the air and expelled him, clothed, from paradise into the exile of this world, to pay the penalty of disobedience; that in the fall of that same man creation was darkened from its former beauty; and how man himself, helped by the elements, lives and acts. 914

XVI.—That no one could rescue man from destruction, nor overcome again the devil who deceived him, except God alone; and the words of the book of the Apocalypse of John the Apostle, and the sense in which they are to be understood: concerning the dragon’s hatred and persecution of the woman and her seed, and how she was aided by the earth. 915

XVII.—That in establishing the world God also glorified Himself, by showing rational creation that He is the Creator of all things, and at the same time exalted man through the subjection to him of the things in the world; and how, according to the letter, the beginning of the book of Genesis is to be understood from the words, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” to the words, “and there was evening and morning, one day.” 916

XVIII.—That, just as the Son of God, begotten timelessly from the Father, is the beginning in whom all things were created, so that same One, born from the Virgin Mother, is the beginning of the creation or building-up of the Church and the author of complete justification, for which neither the justice of the patriarchs nor the sacraments of the Law sufficed, but which was restored through preaching, the receiving of baptism and the Gospel, and faith in the Trinity. 917

XIX.—Words of David the prophet in the first Psalm, and how they are to be understood concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God and the fruitfulness of His teaching throughout the whole world. 918

XX.—That the words written, “But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep,” are to be understood allegorically of unbelievers, empty of good work and darkened by unbelief; and that what follows, [Col. 1373] “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” was fulfilled in the apostles and the believing people through the grace of the Holy Spirit. 919

XXI.—Likewise, words of David the prophet in Psalm XXVIII, consonant with the voice of the apostles and doctors, and how they are to be understood. 919

XXII.—How the words of God saying, “Let there be light,” and the rest down to “and there was evening and morning, one day,” were fulfilled, in an allegorical sense, in the dawning of Christian faith, the preaching of the apostles, and the separation of believers from unbelievers. 920

XXIII.—How these same things written in Genesis concerning the creation of heaven and earth, or the work of the first day, are to be understood morally in the conduct of man, who consists of the diverse natures of soul and body. 920

XXIV.—How the passages concerning the establishment of the firmament and the division of the waters are to be understood according to the letter, together with words of David from Psalm XVIII bearing on the same matter. 922

XXV.—That, according to allegory, the firmament is Christ or faith in Christ; the division of the waters is the firm interposition of that faith, by which believers are separated from unbelievers; and evening and morning are to be understood as the fall of vice and the rising of virtue. 923

XXVI.—That, just as the second day was without the lights of heaven, so faith without shining works deserves no praise; and therefore in the work of that day, unlike the works of the others, it is not said, “God saw that it was good.” 924

XXVII.—That, in the moral sense, the firmament is to be understood as the virtue of discernment, since every faithful person knows how, in the active and contemplative life, to distinguish what is necessary for the body from what is superfluous, and what is wholesome for the soul from what is harmful. 924

XXVIII.—The Gospel testimony in which the Bridegroom says to the foolish virgins, “I do not know you”: why it is introduced here and in what sense it is to be understood. 925

XXIX.—Why, even according to the moral sense, the work of the second day, although good, lacks the praise of goodness. 926

XXX.—How the words, “Let the waters be gathered together,” down to “and there was evening and morning, the third day,” are fittingly to be understood according to the letter. 926

XXXI.—Words of God in the book of the prophet Isaiah, saying, “I have kept silence; I have always been silent; I have been patient; like a woman in labour I shall speak”; and in the second Psalm, speaking to the Son, “This day I have begotten thee”: why they are placed here and how they are to be understood. 928

XXXII.—That what God called the dry land, and the gatherings of the waters He called seas, is to be understood allegorically of the Church under different aspects. Gathered from many peoples and founded upon the firmness of faith, it is called by David “the land of the living,” and by John the Apostle in the Apocalypse “a sea of glass mingled with fire”; and in what sense these same testimonies are to be understood. 928

XXXIII.—That the womb of the Church, after the likeness of a certain earth, now brings forth green grass in the simplicity of little faithful ones, and fruit-bearing trees in the robust activity of the perfect; that, according to the seed, the praise of faith is fruitful in the succession of believers unto the end; and that this occurs on the third day, namely in the brightness of that faith. 930

XXXIV.—Likewise, how the things said to have been made on that same third day are found historically in the conduct of the children of the Church according to the tropological sense, with an appropriate Gospel testimony added, and in what sense it is to be understood. 931

XXXV.—How the words, “God said: Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven,” and the rest down to “and there was evening and morning, the fourth day,” are to be understood according to the letter. 933

XXXVI.—What, according to allegory, is signified by the firmament as the firmness of Christian faith; by the two great lights as the two powers, spiritual in priests and secular in kings; and by the lesser stars under them as prelates or judges. All are set to illumine the earth, that is, to instruct the Church by day and night: the spiritual by the light of teaching and examples, and the carnal by the restraint of the censure of justice. 934

XXXVII.—Likewise, that, according to the tropological sense, the firmament is discernment of reason, the two great lights are the two commandments of charity, and the stars are right thoughts; so that each faithful person, enlightened by these, may carefully discern what he owes to God in honour and grace, and what he owes, according to the salvation of the soul and the benefit of the body, to the needs both of himself and of his neighbours. 935

XXXVIII.—How the words, “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing with living soul, and fowl above the earth,” [Col. 1374] down to “and there was evening and morning, the fifth day,” are to be understood according to the letter and applied to man. 937

XXXIX.—That God sent His only Son into the world, by whose preaching the sublime precepts of heavenly conduct were given, by which the spiritual might be distinguished from the carnal; and words of the Gospel concerning the forsaking of all things, with an elegant exposition relevant to instruction in evangelical discipline. 939

XL.—Likewise, words of the Gospel concerning the many dwelling-places in the Father’s house, and concerning the twofold class of the Church’s children, namely spiritual and secular. 940

XLI.—That the blessing given by God to fishes and birds for increase is fulfilled in the spiritual generation of the baptized and in the fruitfulness of the virtues of every faithful person; and why these matters are assigned to the fifth day. 941

XLII.—How the things belonging to the work of the fifth day and to God’s blessing bestowed upon that work should be referred to instruction concerning mortality, with the testimony of the prophet Isaiah saying, “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?”; and how this also is to be understood. 942

XLIII.—How the history written concerning the work of the sixth day—the bringing forth of beasts of burden and creeping things of the earth, and the formation of man—is to be understood according to the letter; and that man, in body, was made in the image of the humanity of the Son of God, which God foreknew from eternity that He would assume from the Virgin, and, in soul, in the likeness of divinity through knowledge or imitation of the good. 944

XLIV.—How, according to allegory, through the Word of God speaking by the apostles, beasts of burden, creeping things, and wild beasts were brought forth from the earth of the Church in the Catholic faith; and how man also, who ought to preside over all, was formed according to the distinctions of ages, understandings, or ranks of those living in the Church; and in what respect or toward what end they are understood to increase and multiply. 947

XLV.—Concerning the diversity of foods granted in Genesis to man and to beasts: how it is now to be maintained spiritually in the Church according to the distribution or reception of spiritual nourishment, which is the word of God; and how the testimony of Christ added here—“My food is to do the will of my Father”—as well as the words, “and there was evening and morning, the sixth day,” are to be understood. 950

XLVI.—A recapitulation of all that is written in Genesis concerning the work of the sixth day: how it ought to be understood and observed according to the moral sense; with the addition of two testimonies from the Psalm and the Gospel, and the sense in which these too are to be understood. 951

XLVII.—Concerning the perfection of heaven and earth and all their adornment; the completion of God’s works, which is assigned to the seventh day; the sanctification of that same day; and how God’s rest is to be understood according to the letter. 953

XLVIII.—How these things are fulfilled allegorically in the children of the Church and in those subject to Christian faith through the Incarnation of the Son of God, the preaching of the Gospel, and the operation of the Holy Spirit. 953

XLIX.—Likewise, how these same things are brought to completion tropologically in the advancement and perfection of every faithful person. 954

## PART THREE

## SIXTH VISION

I.—A mystical vision concerning a structure shown in the form of a city; likewise concerning a mountain and a mirror shining upon it; a cloud white above and black beneath; and the other things appearing in the same vision. 955

II.—Concerning the foreknowledge, predestination, and ordination of God, who knows all things beforehand from eternity, creates all things in time, and examines the works of rational creatures by strict judgment. 956

III.—That the knowledge of God, containing within itself many unknown and secret things, brings forth the manifestation of His wonders according to His pleasure; and what is signified by the threefold order of angels appearing in this vision. 957

IV.—Concerning the Spirit of God, stirring up His zeal through the blessed angels to repel and restrain the presumption of the reprobate angels; and concerning the tireless harmony of the good angels, who praise God beyond human understanding with inestimable and ever-new wonder. 958

V.—That some part of the blessed spirits, remaining in the secret places of heaven and ever standing before the face of their Creator, is rarely sent forth to exterior things; while another part, called by the name of angels, continually goes out on diverse ministries and, when necessary, appears to human beings; and that every rational creature ought always to seek not its own glory, but that of its Creator. 959

VI.—Words of the Psalmist from Psalm XCII bearing on the same subject, [Col. 1375] and the sense in which they are to be understood. 960

## SEVENTH VISION

I.—A mystical vision concerning a marble stone, like a mountain, standing in the eastern part of the structure of the city previously shown; likewise concerning an innumerable multitude of people appearing both in the eastern and in the southern region of that same structure; and concerning the wondrous form and apparel of two figures placed near the eastern corner. 961

II.—That God Almighty, without any change in Himself, condemned the proud angels by just judgment; and, in merciful compassion, came to the aid of deceived man, having first sent many marvellous heralds of his future salvation in the Old Testament, and finally accomplished his deliverance through very many miracles in the New Testament; and that prophecy, divinely given for instruction and correction, has never been and never will be lacking to any age of the world. 962

III.—Words of David from the first verse of Psalm XLIV, that is, “My heart has uttered a good word,” relating to the same matter and to Christ’s two generations, and how they are to be understood. 963

IV.—That the first of the two figures standing at the eastern end of the structure shown, appearing almost wholly in beast-like garb, signifies the time before the flood, in which people lived without law and without knowledge of the true God, according to a cruel way more beastly than human. 964

V.—Concerning the strength, cruelty, and impure morals of people before the flood, and how, through the devil’s art, all but a few departed from the worship of God. 964

VI.—That God, unable to endure the iniquities and crimes of the people of that age, destroyed the whole human race and all living things by the waters of the flood, except those which He had enclosed in the ark; concerning the alteration of the sun, moon, stars, and earth from the qualities which they had before the flood; and that, at the end of the world, fire will consume the earth to the same depth to which it was penetrated by the pouring in of waters. 965

VII.—That through the alteration of the elements human powers too were diminished after the flood; concerning their correction for a time, terrified by the dread of that judgment; and concerning the rainbow, then first set as a covenant or sign between God and human beings. 966

VIII.—That the other figure signifies the period after the flood which was under the Law; and that the variations in its diverse attire signify the distinctions of the periods from the flood itself to the coming of the Lord, or to the end of the age, and the moral qualities of the people who are or will be in them. 967

IX.—Concerning the meanings of sacrifices, circumcision, and the Law, which, through prophecy in the patriarchs, preceded the Son of God who was to be incarnate; concerning the preaching of the prophets; that man could not be saved unless the Word became flesh; and concerning the devil’s suggestions, by which he deceives people through deception, and the means of assistance by which God always resists him. 968

X.—Concerning the innumerable multitude of faithful people who, in diverse ways in this life, both in spiritual exercises and in mortifying vices, struggle bravely for the honour of God and their own salvation, and receive diverse rewards according to their merits by God’s gift. 971

XI.—Words of David from Psalm LXII bearing on the same matter, and the sense in which they are to be understood. 972

XII.—That all things were created through the Word arising from the Father without beginning, and that man was redeemed through that same Word made flesh in the Virgin. 973

XIII.—Words of David from Psalm CIII bearing on this very subject, and how they are to be understood. 974

XIV.—That in the things which the Son of God did or suffered in the flesh, He fulfilled everything signified concerning Him before the Law and in the Law by typical deeds or foretold by mystical words; and that after His Ascension, like the twelve winds or the twelve signs of heaven, He strengthened the twelve apostles by sending the Spirit, illumined the world through their preaching, and changed all things for the better. 975

XV.—Words of Christ in the Gospel concerning the power given Him by the Father, and how they are to be understood. 977

XVI.—That the words of the prophets before the Incarnation of the Lord could not be understood, being obscure and unknown; but that Christ, living in the world according to them and fulfilling them, rendered them intelligible; and that through the water of baptism both original and actual sins are washed away in faith in the Trinity. 977

XVII.—Words of David from Psalm CIII; concerning those who do not receive remission of sins in baptism through faithfulness, and those who are cleansed in it through faith. 978

## EIGHTH VISION

I.—A brief vision concerning three figures, a description of their condition or apparel, and the orders of saints appearing before them. 979 [Col. 1376]

II.—Words of the first figure, namely the virtue of charity, recounting the magnificence of its works in angels and human beings, and in the teaching of prophets and apostles, and extolling with highest praise the excellence of the virtues of wisdom and humility. 979

III.—That whatever God has wrought, He has completed in charity, humility, and peace; and an exposition of the foregoing vision shown under the figures of these three virtues. 981

IV.—Words of David from Psalm XLIV commending the Church adorned with the varied cultivation of virtues. 983

## NINTH VISION

I.—A vision concerning two figures shining with marvellous brightness, and a description of their apparel; concerning darkness occupying the whole western region of the structure; and concerning fire with sulphur and other darknesses bending as far as the middle of the northern region. 983

II.—That the first of the two figures represents wisdom, and that the manifold beauty of its apparel signifies every kind of creature which God created in diverse natures and species of things. 984

III.—That the other figure signifies Almighty God; and what the brightness in the place of its head, the human head appearing in the middle of its belly, and its feet bearing the likeness of a lion’s feet express. 985

IV.—How that same figure appeared clothed about with six wings, and what those wings signify. 986

V.—What is signified by the fact that this same figure seems veiled over its whole body with the little fins of fishes, and not with the feathers of birds; that the Son of God entered the world through flesh without the devil’s knowledge; and why the Father willed Him to endure such great sufferings. 987

VI.—Concerning the five mirrors appearing in diverse places of the two middle wings of the same figure: what they signify and how the writing displayed in them is to be understood. 989

VII.—Words of God in Exodus speaking to Moses: “I shall show thee every good thing,” and how they are to be understood concerning the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation. 990

VIII.—Likewise, words of David from Psalm XCII, where he says, “Wonderful are the liftings up of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high,” and how they are to be understood. 991

IX.—Likewise, words of the same Psalm, where he says, “For He has established the world, which shall not be moved.” 992

X.—That the fact that the aforementioned figure had turned its back toward the north signifies that God concealed from the devil and all evil spirits His plan for the Incarnation of His Son and the redemption of humankind. 992

XI.—Words of David from Psalm CI, where it is written, “The Lord has prepared His throne in heaven,” and the sense in which they are to be understood; with a brief recapitulation concerning the Incarnation. 994

XII.—Likewise, words of the same author from Psalm LXXI, where it is read, “He descended like rain upon the fleece,” and that this too must be referred to the Lord’s Incarnation. 994

XIII.—That the darkness seen in the western region, and likewise the fire with sulphur and other denser darknesses shown in the northern part of the aforesaid structure, indicate where, in the outer world, the penal places are in which the souls of sinners are tormented; and also signify the inner blindness of those same sinners, by which they are darkened through unbelief. 995

XIV.—That God made all things through wisdom in order to confute the devil’s malice, and so that, although invisible to man, He might be understood through faith and known through His work; and that He held within Himself, before time, the ordering of His whole work which He created in time, establishing man in this respect also after His own likeness, so that man might first arrange in thought within himself whatever he would afterwards carry out in action. 996

## TENTH VISION

I.—The final vision, in which a wheel of great magnitude is shown and carefully described as to its nature; and the figure of charity is again beheld under another form. 997

II.—That God could not truly be called one if He had one like Himself by nature; that the quality of the wheel previously shown displays God Himself, lacking beginning and end and ready for every good; and how the entire description of that wheel refers to the eternity or power of God and to the salvation of souls. 998

III.—Why the virtue of charity is seen adorned in this vision with an apparel different from that in the preceding vision. 1000

IV.—Concerning the board, transparent like crystal, appearing before the figure of charity; what is signified by the movement of the line of its seat as that figure looks upon the board; and a brief recapitulation concerning the creation of heaven, earth, angels, and man. 1001 [Col. 1377]

V.—Concerning God’s punishment of transgressors of the natural law through the waters of the flood, and the diverse condition of the ages from the beginning down to the Incarnation of the Lord. 1002

VI.—Words of Paul concerning the fullness of time, in which God sent His Son, made of a woman; who, at His coming, completed the mystical sayings and deeds of the ancients by fulfilling them, and, by His teaching and the preaching of the apostles and teachers of the Church, illumined the world and changed all things for the better. 1003

VII.—That these times decline from the former manly strength of apostolic discipline into a kind of womanly weakness, and that all things deteriorate, both in the disturbance of the elements and in the corruption of morals. 1005

VIII.—Certain secret words of the Son addressing the Father on account of the affliction which He endures in His body, which is the Church, from certain of its members abandoning justice; and on account of the completion of the number of the elect ordained from eternity; and how these same words are to be understood according to the diverse conditions of the periods from the beginning of the world to the present. 1005

IX.—A mystical description of how the apostles adorned, with the manifold clothing of glory, the justice which they had received from the Lord to preach throughout the world, according both to the diversity of their natural dispositions and to the distribution of the graces poured into them from heaven; concerning the excellence of the teaching of Paul the Apostle; and why he who was raised by the sublimity of revelations was brought low by the weight of infirmity. 1007

X.—A brief recapitulation of the foregoing: how, in these days that lack manly strength, all ecclesiastical institutions decline for the worse; and the testimony of the Psalmist where he says, “Thou art just, O Lord,” why it is added and how it is to be understood. 1012

XI.—The complaint or cry of justice to God the Judge against the wicked and impious, defiled by diverse crimes, who reject the ancient institutions of the Fathers and despoil justice, stripping it of the ornaments of its glory. 1013

XII.—That God, beholding these injuries done to justice in the unfailing light of His brightness, does not consign them to oblivion, although He overlooks human sins for the sake of repentance; and His own words concerning this same matter. 1014

XIII.—A testimony from the Apocalypse of John the Apostle appropriate to these matters, and the sense in which it is to be understood. 1015

XIV.—Likewise, the Son’s complaint to the Father concerning the tribulation He suffers in His body from those who, through wickedness, kick against Him; and concerning little ones who fall away from the good by embracing vanity; and that angels, although they shine with immeasurable brightness, behold the works of holy human beings as a mirror, approving their praise. 1016

XV.—That justice, upright morals, and the dignity of virtues, strengthened by the prophets from the days of the flood until the coming of the Lord, and then shining for a long time through apostles and doctors in the Church, but now corrupted after these days that languish in injustice, will again be restored among humankind before the end, after many tribulations. 1016

XVI.—That the heavenly Judge, meanwhile heeding justice’s complaint, will bring His vengeance, through many judgments of afflictions, upon transgressors against equity—and especially upon wicked prelates of the Church—until, purified by due examination, they come to their senses through repentance; and thus every order, restored in uprightness, will return to the honour of its dignity. 1017

XVII.—That, once God’s punishment has been quieted through the correction of transgressors, the ordering of justice and the tranquillity of peace will shine forth before the end of the age, as also before the Lord’s first coming; with some part of the Jews converted and rejoicing, confessing that He has come whom they now deny. 1019

XVIII.—Words of the prophet Isaiah testifying to the Lord’s first coming, which will be fulfilled especially in the age through the enlightenment of the Jews, who, blinded by the scandal of Christ, had withered in His Passion from the greenness of faith and good works. 1021

XIX.—Words of the same Lord Christ, which, while He was being led to death, He spoke in answer to those lamenting Him, concerning the green and dry wood; and how they are to be understood. 1021

XX.—How greatly, with diverse joys in the Church, people will enjoy for some time in the next-to-last days the restored condition of justice, an abundance of temporal things, and plenty of spiritual goods; while that part of the Jews and heretics who persist in evil exults in destructive presumption at the near coming of Antichrist. 1022

XXI.—That this same quiet of peace and abundance of fruits will again be followed, for people who ascribe them to themselves and not to God and begin once more to grow sluggish in religion, by tribulations [Col. 1378] so great as have never before raged in the world. 1023

XXII.—Words of David from Psalm XXI, in the person of Christ and the Church, foretelling the persecutions of the wicked, and how they are to be understood. 1024

XXIII.—Likewise, the Son’s intercession to the Father for the deliverance of His body, which is the Church. 1024

XXIV.—That at that time, when the Christian people have been brought to repentance and worn down by many afflictions for their sins, divine grace will assist them through many miracles, as it did His ancient people; and, once their enemies are subdued, will add a very great multitude of pagans to His faith. 1025

XXV.—That in those days, as the Roman emperors fall away from their former strength, the empire will gradually diminish and fail in their hands; and that even the island of apostolic honour will be divided, with different masters or archbishops set over different places. 1026

XXVI.—That then, when wickedness is again repressed and justice prevails, the discipline of honourableness and the laws of ancient customs will spring up anew and be observed; that there will be many prophets; that the hidden things of the Scriptures will be opened to the wise; while meanwhile very many heresies will bubble up everywhere, announcing the near coming of Antichrist. 1027

XXVII.—Concerning the character of the judgments of divine power to be manifested near the end of the world; and that at that time the greater part of humankind, abandoning the sincerity of the Catholic faith, will turn to the son of perdition. 1027

XXVIII.—Concerning the conception and birth of Antichrist: that, filled from the beginning with a diabolical spirit, hidden and nourished in secluded places, he will be instructed in every magical art until manhood; and how great will be the disturbance and uncertainty in those days in the world and in the Church, whether of events or of times. 1028

XXIX.—Testimonies from Paul’s Epistle to the Thessalonians foretelling the end of the world and the coming, works, and judgment of Antichrist, and how they are to be understood. 1029

XXX.—That the ancient enemy, who conquered the first man by deceiving him and was conquered again through the man Christ, thinking that he can conquer again through another man, Antichrist, will by God’s just permission pour out all his malice, striving to attack the Catholic faith and destroy the teaching of Christ. 1030

XXXI.—Why Antichrist is called by the Apostle “the man of sin” and “the son of perdition”; a suitable testimony from the Apocalypse of John and how it is to be understood; and that the devil has had followers both in the Old and in the New Testament, deceiving some through idols and others through heretics. 1031

XXXII.—Concerning the signs, portents, and storms which he will produce by magical arts; and how, pretending to die and rise again, he will cause a certain writing, devised by the deceit of the devil, to be inscribed on the foreheads of those who follow him, so that those deceived by him can thereafter no longer be torn away and separated from him. 1032

XXXIII.—God’s promise concerning the restoration of Enoch and Elijah; how matters proceed with them meanwhile; how, once restored, they will conduct themselves amid adversity among humankind; with how great a power of preaching and miracles they will shine against Antichrist; and that, nevertheless, martyred by him, they will depart from the world together with innumerable others, and the blessed number of martyrs will be brought to the fullness of its due perfection. 1033

XXXIV.—Likewise, the Son’s intercession to the Father, displaying His wounds and commending those very people to Him so that He may spare them, and exhorting the same people to bend their knees to the Father that He may have mercy on them. 1034

XXXV.—That when Enoch and Elijah are raised from death before the eyes of all and taken up to the clouds, the resurrection of the dead will be confirmed in every way; and that the ancient serpent will be roused to the greatest fury against God and the saints through the son of perdition. 1035

XXXVI.—That, when that wicked one, revealed in his presumption, commands the higher elements, while a multitude of people stands by and hears, to behold him going into heaven, he will be slain by the spirit of the mouth of the Lord Jesus, according to the Apostle’s testimony; that those who see these things will abandon error and turn to the true faith; and that thus all the devil’s exaltation will be overthrown. 1035

XXXVII.—That after the fall of Antichrist the glory of the Son of God will be magnified, and all who believe in Him will praise it in humble voice; with a testimony from the Apocalypse of John suitable to these matters and the sense in which it is to be understood. 1036

XXXVIII.—Epilogue of the book itself, in which heavenly voices render praise to God for His work, namely the restoration of man; and this little work, together with its author, is earnestly commended to that same God and to His faithful. 1037

**SOLUTIONS TO THIRTY-EIGHT QUESTIONS**, sent by Saint Hildegard to Wibert, monk of Gembloux, at his request. [Col. 1379] 1037

## EXPLANATION OF THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT
The community of Hildegard’s monastery at Hünningen requests an interpretation of the Rule of St Benedict. 1053. Rule of St Benedict explained according to St Hildegard. 1055. **EXPLANATION OF THE CREED OF ST ATHANASIUS** according to St Hildegard, addressed to the congregation of her sisters. 1065. **LIFE OF ST RUPERT.** 1081. Notice. The Life begins. CHAPTER I.—The marriage and widowhood of Blessed Bertha. The pious childhood of St Rupert; his affection for the poor. 1083. CHAPTER II.—Pilgrimage to Rome. Deliberation concerning his state of life. 1087. Authentic testimony concerning certain translated relics. 1091.

# LIFE OF ST DISIBOD

Notice. 1093. The Life begins. CHAPTER I.—The saint’s lineage; his parents expelled by tyrants; his progress in learning; his election as bishop; his abdication and withdrawal from his native country. 1095. CHAPTER II.—Journey into Germany; instruction of the people on the Rhine; solitary and austere life on a mountain; beginnings of the monastery and miracles. 1100. CHAPTER III.—The subjects’ veneration for the saint; growth of the monastery; prophecy of its coming destruction; death, fragrant odour, burial, and various cures after it. 1106. CHAPTER IV.—The monks’ dispersal and return; translation of the sacred body by St Boniface; the monastery’s ruin, disasters, and vicissitudes. 1110.

# PHYSICA, OR NINE BOOKS ON THE SUBTLETIES OF THE DIVERSE NATURES OF CREATED THINGS

Introduction and notes by Dr F. A. Reuss. 1117.

# BOOK ONE—On Plants
